en: Preface to the Propagation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra-vyākhyāna* (The Explication of the Lotus Sutra) Composed by the Śramaṇa Daoxuan of Zhongnan Mountain during the Tang Dynasty.
Tiantai Teaching and Contemplation: Lecture Record by Master Yisong.
Compiled and edited by the Eastern Ou Buddhist Xiaorou and Guanghe.
△ Explanation of the Preface, divided into two parts. First, the explanation of the title.
To explain this sutra, one must first explain its preface. The preface consists of two distinct parts: the title of the preface and the text of the preface.

The eight characters beginning with "Miaofa" (The Wonderful Dharma) constitute the title of the preface; the nine characters beginning with "Tang Zhong" (Tang Dynasty, Zhongnan) constitute the colophon identifying the person [who compiled it].

Within the title of the preface, the five characters beginning with "Miao" (Wonderful) are the title of the entire sutra, while the three characters beginning with "Hong" (to propagate) are specifically the heading for this particular preface. If...
It merely mentions the "Preface to the Propagation" (*Hongchuan xu*) without mentioning the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Thus, one does not know for which sūtra this preface serves as a preface, nor what it intends to propagate. Therefore, [it refers to] the title of the entire sūtra itself.
It was used as the title for the preface. Thus, it is generally inscribed: "Preface to the Propagation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
From this, one knows that this preface is certainly the preface to the present sutra. Now, first I shall clarify the title of the sutra, and next I shall set forth the headings of the preface.

Within the title of the sutra, the two characters "Miaofa" (Wondrous Dharma) constitute the essence of the dharma; the two characters "Lianhua" (Lotus Flower) constitute the metaphor. This is because the wondrous dharma...

It is difficult to understand. Therefore, it is elucidated through the use of metaphors; thus, the analogy of the lotus flower is employed to illustrate the essential nature (*dharmatā*) of the wondrous Dharma.
That which is called "wondrous" refers to that which is inconceivable. Since it cannot be grasped by the mind nor discussed in words, it is termed "wondrous.
That which is called "Dharma" refers to that which possesses the nature of being a standard for guidance and upholding.
That is to say, it sustains its own nature and gives rise to understanding in sentient beings; therefore, it is called "Dharma.
Since this Dharma is inconceivable, those who do not possess superior faculties and sharp wisdom will be unable to understand it. Thus, it is compared to a lotus flower.
If one does not understand the wondrous Dharma, one should contemplate the lotus flowers seen by the eyes in the world; yet, if one does understand it...
By means of the lotus flower, one comes to know the wondrous Dharma. For the lotus flower represents the simultaneity of blossom and fruit, remaining ever pure while dwelling amidst defilement.
The wondrous Dharma likewise signifies the identity of sage and ordinary person, and the common source of sentient beings and Buddhas.

Therefore, if one does not understand that sentient beings and Buddhas share a common source within the wondrous Dharma, one should contemplate the simultaneity of blossom and fruit in the lotus flower. If one understands that the lotus remains ever pure while dwelling amidst defilement...

Through this purification, one knows that the wondrous Dharma and the Buddha are of one essence. The title *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* combines both the metaphor and the reality, collectively termed the "Lotus Sutra of the Wondrous Dharma.
Ultimately, by what kind of dharma is it designated as "wondrous"? Generally, there are three kinds of dharma:

the dharma of teaching (*deśanā-dharma*), the dharma of principle (*tattva-dharma*), and the dharma of practice (*pratipatti-dharma*). Since the teaching elucidates the principle, and practice arises based on the principle, these three exist.
Regarding these three kinds of teachings: although these same three kinds of teachings were also spoken forty years ago, they could not be called "wondrous.
It is only the three kinds of teachings now spoken in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* that are truly called "wondrous.

This is because the teachings spoken forty years ago were those of precepts and goodness taught for the sake of humans and devas, and the teachings on the Truths and Conditions taught for the sake of the Two Vehicles.
Regarding the teachings: for Bodhisattvas, there are taught the partial and gradual teachings. As for the nature of these teachings as Dharma, they are coarse rather than subtle.
The principles elucidated by the former [teachings]—namely, the teachings on precepts and goodness—elucidate the principle of conventional existence.

The principles elucidated by the teachings on the Truths and Conditions (the Four Noble Truths and Dependent Origination) elucidate the principle of partial emptiness. Such is the nature of the partial and gradual teachings.
"Exposition" refers to the principle of "only-middle" (but-madhyama). As for this principle as a dharma, it is likewise coarse and not subtle.
The practices initiated in the past were based on the principle of conventional existence, whereby one initiates tainted (sāsrava) practice;
based on the principle of partial emptiness, one initiates untainted (anāsrava) practice; and based on the principle of "only-middle," one initiates that which is both tainted and [untainted]..."
The untainted practice (*anāsrava-caryā*)—this practice is indeed a Dharma, yet it is coarse and not subtle.

This refers to what was taught during the forty years prior [to the turning of the wheel of the Dharma]; whether in terms of teaching, principle, or practice, all were coarse dharmas and could not be called subtle dharmas.
If the teachings expounded in this present sutra constitute the perfect and sudden One Vehicle—as the sutra states:

"Directly abandoning expedient means, he speaks only of the Unsurpassed Way"—then they are not the coarse, partial, and gradual methods of the past, such as the precepts, good roots, truths, and conditions.
This teaching as a dharma is subtle rather than coarse. The principle elucidated in this sutra is the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
As the sutra says: "These dharmas abide in their own positions; the characteristics of the world are eternally constant.
Thus, it is not the coarse dharma of the past, which was a biased emptiness within conventional existence. This principle as a dharma is likewise subtle.
It is not coarse. The practice initiated by this present sutra is, in fact, ultimate and unsurpassed. As the sutra says: "The path you all are practicing is the bodhisattva path.
This is not the coarse path of the past—whether it be with outflows (*sāsrava*), without outflows (*anāsrava*), or both with and without outflows.
Such is the nature of this practice; it is sublime and not coarse. Therefore, in today’s *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*...

The High Assembly explains that whether it be the teaching (*śāsana*), the principle (*nyāya*), or the practice (*pratipatti*), none of these are coarse phenomena; they are merely designated as "sublime" (*praṇīta*).
This is the sublime according to relative discourse (*sāpekṣa-vāda*). If one speaks of the sublime according to absolute discourse (*anapekṣa-vāda*), there is the function of transcending the coarse.

As for the teaching, it opens up those precepts, virtues, truths, conditions, partial, and gradual [teachings], so that they all become the One Vehicle of the Perfect and Sudden, like a jar, a plate, or a hairpin [all being gold].
The vessel of the bracelets, if cast into a great furnace, becomes one single entity. As the Sūtra says: "The definitive teaching of the Śrāvaka Dharma is the king of all sūtras.
Thus, it is not only the teaching of this present sūtra that is sublime; rather, there is no teaching from the past that is not likewise sublime.
In principle, this opens up those conventional views of biased emptiness and the limited Middle Way, such that they all become the various [aspects of the ultimate truth].
The true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is like the waters of the Yangtze, Huai, Yellow, and Han rivers; when they converge in the great ocean, they share the same salty taste.
As the Sūtra says: "All worldly things, including secular discourse and the activities for sustaining life, are all non-contradictory with the true nature.
Thus, it is not only the principles of this present sūtra that are sublime, but also the principles of those from days of old.

There is nothing that is not wondrous. When practiced, it opens up for others both the outflowing (*sāsrava*) and the non-outflowing (*anāsrava*), as well as that which is both outflowing and non-outflowing, such that all become ultimately unsurpassed.
It is like the four directions—east, west, south, and north—if one reaches a great city, they all share the same perception of joy.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Even those who merely raise one hand, or slightly lower their heads, have all already attained the path to Buddhahood.
Thus, it is not only the practice of walking meditation in this present sūtra that is sublime; rather, there is nothing among the practices of the past that is not likewise sublime.
What has been discussed above—whether in terms of dependence or transcendence—cannot be conceived by the mind nor deliberated upon through speech.

Thus, a sutra says: "My Dharma is subtle and difficult to conceive; it cannot be proclaimed in words. It further states: "This Dharma cannot be understood through calculation or conceptual discrimination.
Therefore, based on this, the name is established as "Sublime Dharma" (Miaofa). Yet, since this Sublime Dharma is difficult [to realize]...
Explanation: If one does not employ a metaphor, by what means can it be clarified? Therefore, it is illustrated by means of the lotus flower.
Now, the flowers of the world’s aquatic and terrestrial plants and trees are exceedingly numerous, yet none of these are used as metaphors; why, then, is the lotus alone chosen as the metaphor?
It is because other flowers may have blossoms but lack fruit, such as the peony and others; this [lotus] serves merely as a metaphor for that.
They practice asceticism in vain and achieve nothing. Among the non-Buddhists who practice asceticism, there are those who have fruit but no flowers, such as the ginkgo tree;
these can only be compared to those who calculate that results arise spontaneously and thus do not engage in cultivation.

Among the non-Buddhists who believe in spontaneity, there are those who have many flowers but only one fruit, such as the peach and plum trees; these can only be compared to those who cultivate separately [from the natural].
Various practices may yield only the initial fruit of *nirvāṇa*, or like sesame seeds, produce many fruits from a single flower;

this can only be used as a metaphor for ordinary persons who, through loyalty to their sovereign and filial piety toward their parents, are reborn in the Brahma heavens to experience various pleasures.
Or, like persimmons, there may be one fruit from one flower; this can only be used as a metaphor for those who cultivate a single [practice].
The Pratyekabuddha who attains nirvana through practice far removed [from society] may have the fruit first and the flower later, like a melon or eggplant;
this can only be used as a metaphor for the subsequent fruit that follows after repeatedly contemplating the Truth once one has already entered the Path of Seeing.

Alternatively, it may have the flower first and the fruit later, like rice or wheat; this can only be used as a metaphor for the subsequent fruit that arises after having previously relied upon conditions for cultivation.
The gradual Bodhisattvas of partial cultivation are like these coarse flowers; they cannot serve as metaphors for the wondrous Dharma.
Only the lotus flower is suitable, for it is both flower and fruit simultaneously, remaining eternally pure even while amidst defilement, such that defilement and purity coexist in one place.
This is truly the wondrous flower that can metaphorically represent the wondrous Dharma: that the Buddha and sentient beings share the same source, and the sage and the ordinary person are one.
This is consistent. It is known that this is not something that can be illustrated by the *saddharma*;

it is not worthy of being compared to a lotus flower, nor is the lotus flower capable of illustrating it, for it cannot serve as a metaphor to clarify the *saddharma*. Now, both the dharma and the metaphor are sublime;

as both subject and object are designated together, it should be called the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. As for the term "sūtra" (*jing*), it means "to proceed. It proceeds from the golden mouth [of the Buddha].
Because it is what has been proclaimed, it is called a "sūtra. Furthermore, "sūtra" is glossed as "dharma" and "permanence. As for "dharma," it means that which all ten realms equally follow;

as for "permanence," it means that which does not change throughout the three periods of time. Now, this sūtra reveals and clarifies that all sentient beings can attain the opening, showing, awakening to, and entering into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Since there is nothing that is not revealed and clarified—ranging from the hell realm below to [the highest realm above]—it is called a sūtra.
Among the realms of all Buddhas, how could there be a single realm that does not follow this? Therefore, this sutra is the fundamental essence through which all Buddhas descend as spirits.
It is not only our Śākyamuni who acts thus; rather, it is so for all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.

There is nothing that is not thus. Since this is true for all Buddhas, then among the past worlds that preceded and the future worlds that follow, how could there be even a single world that might be altered? Because they are equally followed, it is explained as "Dharma" (Law);
because it is unalterable, it is explained as "Constant. Although these two meanings differ, they are collectively termed "Sūtra. Next—

Regarding the term "propagation" (*hongchuan*): "propagation" (*hong*) carries the meaning of vastness; "transmission" (*chuan*) refers to successive passing down. As for "preface" (*xu*), it has the sense of a wall-arrangement.
This is because when the Tathāgata preached this sutra, he did not intend its benefit to be restricted to a single moment;

rather, his fundamental desire was for it to circulate through the heavens and the human realm, across other regions and this land, until the end of the future limit, throughout oceans of lands as numerous as motes of dust. Regarding the Vinaya...
The Master composed this preface to the sutra, taking the mind of the Tathāgata as his own mind.

Desiring that future generations understand the purpose of the preface, he sought to ensure the transmission of this sutra would be propagated and expanded ever further, thus passing it on without ceasing.
Therefore, it is titled "Preface to the Wide Propagation.
Next is the title of the person [who wrote it]: "Tang" is the name of the era; "Zhongnan Mountain" is the name of the mountain, as detailed in the commentary.
The phrase "the superior Way propagated by the inferior" refers to the name of the Vinaya Master. Indeed, the Vinaya Master was able to take the Way of the Tathāgata and...

He practiced it himself and further proclaimed this Way to others, thereby enabling them to transform themselves through it; his fame was manifested through his virtue, hence it is called "proclaiming the Way.
Although the preface was composed by the Vinaya Master himself, its meaning actually derives from the present sutra; therefore, he did not say he "wrote" it.
This is merely a restatement. The above constitutes the title of the initial preface. Although the two subsequent titles differ, they together constitute the title of the single preface.
As for their ultimate source, they all derive from our Buddha, the World-Honored One, at the Great Assembly on Mount Lingjiu.
He preached this one section of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in order to fulfill his original intention for transcending the world;
that is to say, to cause all sentient beings to universally attain the opening, showing, awakening to, and entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Subsequently, after the World-Honored One entered parinirvāṇa, Ānanda compiled it in that region, and it eventually reached this land, where some translated it so that it might circulate.
As for those who have transmitted it—whether there were those who recited and upheld it, or those who transcribed it and explained it to others—it is impossible to know their number.
Only our Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai was born during the Chen and Sui dynasties;
on Mount Dasu, he recited this sutra while entering into contemplation according to the text, reaching as far as the "Chapter on the Medicine King. This is the true [transmission].
Diligence—this is called the true offering of the Dharma. It is as if one personally beholds the single assembly on Vulture Peak, solemnly and without dispersal.
Thereupon, he arose from samādhi and expounded the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) to explain the titles of the sutras; he expounded the *Wenju* (Textual Phrases) to analyze the scriptural passages;
and he expounded the *Mohe Zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation) to elucidate the various samādhis. Reaching the Tang dynasty, there was the Vinaya Master Nanshan.
I have therefore composed this preface. By means of this preface, I shall clarify the origins of this sūtra.
If one examines the preface, one will know in which era this sūtra was transmitted, at what time it was translated, such as the purport of the sūtra’s text, and such as the benefits of upholding it.
This is why the preface could not but be written. The brief explanation of the title of the preface is concluded.
△ The text is divided into three parts. First, the title is presented:
*The Lotus Sutra of the Wondrous Dharma*. "Unifying" (*tǒng*) means to encompass; "original intent" (*běnzhì*) refers to the fundamental aspiration.
Regarding the phrase "The Lotus Sutra of the Wondrous Dharma," "unifying" signifies the act of comprehensive inclusion, while "original intent" refers to the core purpose.

It is the ultimate goal. This means that this single sutra encompasses and unifies the fundamental intent and ultimate aim of all Buddhas throughout the ten directions and three periods of time, as well as my own, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, regarding his descent into birth. How, after all, can this be known?
Only this sutra can unify the fundamental purpose of all Buddhas, whereas other sutras cannot. It is like the initial *Huayan*...

Vairocana manifested a body one thousand *zhang* in height and preached the Perfect Sūtras for the forty-one stages of Dharma-body Bodhisattvas, as well as for the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings whose roots of virtue had matured in previous lives.
He elucidated the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) of phenomena and principle, which is infinitely layered and unimpeded;
he also taught that mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three—are without distinction; and he further taught...
How marvelous, how marvelous! All sentient beings possess the wisdom and virtuous nature of the Tathāgata;
thus, this may be called the Perfect and Sudden [Teaching]. However, it reaches only those of great capacity; as for those of small capacity present here, though they have ears, they do not hear.
There are those with eyes who do not see. The great is separated from the small; the capacity [of the teaching] does not reach everywhere.

Since the capacity does not reach everywhere, then although it is said that the Tathāgata’s fundamental intention for appearing in the world has already been fully expressed, in reality it has not yet been fully expressed.

It is clear, therefore, that the *Avataṃsaka* cannot encompass the essential purpose of the Tathāgata’s descent of his spirit. Even though sentient beings may be like the deaf or the mute, how could the Tathāgata...
They may be abandoned but cannot be transformed. Therefore, within the Deer Park, he preached the Four Āgamas. What the Āgamas clarify does not exceed the teaching for the sake of the śrāvakas:
he spoke of the Four Noble Truths of arising and ceasing, causing them to know suffering, sever the origin [of suffering], aspire toward cessation, and cultivate the path.
For the sake of the pratyekabuddhas, he spoke of the twelve links of dependent origination, causing them to contemplate the process of its sequential arising.

Observing the process of cessation through reversal, for the sake of bodhisattvas, he taught the six perfections of phenomenal characteristics, merely requiring them to subdue their afflictions over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* and cultivate causes for a hundred eons.

Since what is elucidated therein is exclusively the Tripiṭaka—the "half-word" teaching of the Lesser Vehicle—it is also clear that the Āgamas cannot encompass the fundamental intent of the Tathāgata’s descent into the world. As for the Vaipulya [sūtras], however—

Facing the half-bright [teaching], it is full; facing the partial-bright [teaching], it is perfect. Thus, while Prajñāpāramitā encompasses both the general and the specific, it faces and carries over toward the Perfect Teaching.

Since it faces and carries over [toward the higher], its capacity (*indriya*) is not yet pure. Furthermore, it is even clearer that the two "milks" (Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles) cannot encompass the fundamental intent of the Tathāgata’s descent of his spirit.
Even when the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* is preached, although it shares the single flavor of *amṛta* (clarified butter), it cannot avoid...
There are those who subsequently expound the four teachings, yet their schools are a mixture of provisional and Hinayana elements;
thus, it becomes even clearer that their *Nirvāṇa* cannot encompass the fundamental purpose for which all Buddhas descend as spirits.

Since they cannot encompass the fundamental purpose of Śākyamuni, it is evident that they likewise cannot encompass the descent of the spirits of all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time. Nevertheless, beginning with the *Avataṃsaka* and culminating in...
None of these [teachings] can fully encompass the fundamental purpose for which all Buddhas manifest their spiritual power. There is no other reason than this:
when the Tathāgata appears in the world, he seeks only to clarify that all sentient beings possess the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and that the long-lasting lifespan of all Buddhas.
From the beginning with the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* until its conclusion in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, there has never been such a teaching as this.
This is because they were unable to provide a comprehensive synthesis. As for the two gates of the Trace and the Origin in the present sutra, both are revealed and elucidated.
Regarding the Trace, it clarifies that all sentient beings may attain the opening, showing, awakening to, and entering into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;

it opens the provisional [teachings] of the three vehicles and nine realms, and reveals the reality of the One Vehicle of the Buddha-realm. For those of the three capacities, there is none who does not sever their attachment to the provisional.
Doubt was dispelled and true faith arose; they received the prediction of their future enlightenment (*bodhi-vyākaraṇa*).

This fundamentally revealed that Śākyamuni Tathāgata had already attained Buddhahood countless aeons (*kalpa*) ago, thereby unveiling the traces of his recent sojourn at the nearby city of Gayā and manifesting the basis of his vast and eternal lifespan.
All those in the assembly abandoned their doubts regarding the near and gave rise to faith in the far-reaching, attaining the realization of the *dharmakāya*.
Commentary. Thus, the causes and conditions of the six matters have been clarified; the original intent for appearing in the world has been fully expressed;
the long and distant lifespan has been made manifest; and the realization attained over eons has been revealed. The fundamental purpose of descending as a spirit is exhausted herein.
Therefore, it is only this sutra that can encompass the fundamental purpose of all Buddhas descending as spirits. △ Second, the Exegesis. Above.
Although this work clearly sets forth the fundamental intent of all Buddhas, it remains unknown for how long this sutra was compiled in that land,
for how long it has circulated in this realm, how many translators there have been, what its original source should be,
what the purport of the scriptural text is, and furthermore, what the causes and conditions for its upholding are. Therefore, [I shall now] address each of these one by one.
An exposition is provided for this, divided into three parts: first, an account of the source and transmission of the translation; second, an account of the purport of the sūtra text;
and third, an account of the reasons for receiving and upholding it. The first part has two sections, the first of which concerns its transmission.
They were preserved and compiled in Mahācīna for a thousand years before being transmitted eastward to Zhendan (China) over three hundred years ago.
To clarify this transmission, one must first understand the period prior to its transmission. "Preserved" (*yun*) means stored away; "compiled" (*jie*) means collected together.

"Mahācīna" is an honorific title for the Western land, referring to where the sublime scriptures on the fundamental intent of all Buddhas were kept. During the time when the Buddha was in the world, the golden...

It was expounded orally. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Ānanda performed the compilation (*saṃgīti*). Since the Buddha’s teachings were entirely composed of speech, he took that speech and established it as written text.
Although Ānanda had already completed the compilation, it remained stored within those [western] lands and had not yet been transmitted to this land;
thus it is said, "The compendium was compiled in the Great Xia. It remained there in such a state for more than a thousand years because...
This is because the Buddha-dharma had not yet reached this land. Regarding the phrase "transmitted to the East" and so forth, it precisely clarifies the process of its dissemination.
Now that the Buddha-dharma has reached this land, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* has been transmitted from the West to the East for more than three hundred years.

Thus we know that the two lines concerning the "aggregation" (*skandha*) and "knotting" (*granthi*) have not been transmitted. Although the two lines transmitted to the East have been transmitted, they have likewise not circulated widely.

△ Second, the translation, which has two parts: first, the formal explanation; second, the incidental reference. The first part also has two sections: first, the presentation of three translations side by side.
During the Yongkang era of Emperor Hui of the Western Jin, the Dharma-protector from Dunhuang, Zhu Fahu, first translated this sutra, titling it the *Zhengfahua* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka).
During the Long’an era of Emperor An of the Eastern Jin, in the Hongshi era of Later Qin...
The Kuchean śramaṇa Kumārajīva subsequently translated this sūtra, naming it the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Later, during the Renshou era of the Sui dynasty,
at Daxingshan Monastery, the śramaṇa from North India Jñānagupta produced a translation that was given the same title, *Saddharma*.
This means that although this sutra had already been transmitted to the East, it had not yet been translated.
By the time of the Western Jin dynasty and continuing until the Sui dynasty took control of the realm, there were three translations in total; hence the reference to "the Western Jin and so forth.

Within these three texts, the time periods, locations, surnames [of the translators], and titles of the sutras are all clearly visible. Regarding the first translation, titled *Zhengfahua* (The Lotus of the True Dharma), it is as follows:
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa said: "We are all people of false views; we know that those prior to the distinct stages have already returned [to error], and none possess right view.
Because it is now neither three, five, seven, nor nine [stages], it is called the True Dharma (Saddharma).
Regarding the 'three cycles' at the Great Xingshan Temple and other locations, 'succession' is the intended meaning. One who succeeds the lamp of the Dharma shall dwell therein. If, by reason..."
When the Buddha-dharma first arrived, it was respectfully treated as a great furnace; it was given the name "temple" (*si*), for it was essentially one and the same Dharma.

Just as in the Western Regions there were also temples such as Zhulin (Bamboo Grove) and Zhaoti, we can know by this analogy that it is clear temples already existed in this land even before the Buddha-dharma had arrived.
II. The Qin Version is Merely Partially Correct.
The three sutras overlap one another, with their texts and purports presented alternately; those currently esteemed and followed all propagate the Qin edition.
△ Second, the incidental references:
as for the remaining auxiliary chapters and individual verses, there are indeed such currents, as fully detailed in the preface; therefore, they are not recounted here.

"Those who possess a detailed account as in the preface" refers to such works as the verses of the "Universal Gateway Chapter" (*Pumen pin*) and the "Chapter on the Attainment of the Way" (*Dadata pin*), which each have their own periods of translation and specific causes and conditions. These are fully contained within their respective original prefaces;

they are not cited here in full, as they are not essential to the present purpose. II. An Exposition of the Text’s Essential Meaning, divided into three parts. First, clarifying the meaning by means of the sutra.
Second, pointing out the meaning according to the text; third, manifesting the Buddha’s compassion. The first [section] also has three parts. First, clarifying the response and stimulus.

Now, as for the descent of spiritual power upon the sacred mountain, it could not have been brought about without a Great Sage to transform and guide. Furthermore, regarding the reach of this transformation, there would be no way to lead the mind [of beings] without the conditions of their past lives.
Regarding these four phrases, ancient commentators explained them by correlating the capacity [of the audience] with the response [of the Buddha].

The first two phrases clarify the response in terms of the capacity, while the latter two phrases clarify the capacity in terms of the response. For now, I shall explain the response using the first two phrases concerning the Sacred Peak (Vulture Peak).
To speak of the Tathāgata: because he is a Great Sage (*mahāmuni*), he is able to manifest in response to sentient beings.
Regarding the term "Great Sage," there are many kinds of sages: there are mundane sages and supramundane sages; there are sages of shallow rank and sages of profound rank;
there are minor sages and great sages. The Master [Confucius] and Lord Lao are mundane sages; the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are... [supramundane sages].
Those who have transcended the world are noble ones (*ārya*). Those dwelling in the stages of *śrāvaka*—the stages of abiding, practice, and penetration—are noble ones of shallow rank.
Those who have ascended to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) are noble ones of profound rank. Bodhisattvas are minor noble ones.

Now, the Tathāgata not only transcends the noble ones of the mundane world, but also transcends the noble ones who have transcended the world; he not only transcends the noble ones of shallow and minor rank, but also transcends [those of profound rank].
Because they are sages of the profound stage, they are called "Great Sages. The subsequent two phrases concerning "adapting to transformation" clarify the capacity [of the disciples].
Speaking from the perspective of the disciples, it is because they possess past understanding that they are capable of serving as the responsive stimulus.

Nevertheless, there has never been a capacity apart from the response, nor has there ever been a response apart from the capacity; this is what is meant by the mutual accord between teacher and disciple, and the convergence of the path of resonance and response.
Therefore, it is said that "the numinous peak descended its spirit," and so forth. △ Second, the distinction between the beginning and the end:

Thus, when the Immortal Garden (Lumbinī) was completed, the capacities [of beings] were divided into the categories of Small and Great; when the Golden River (the Nirvana) witnessed the final testament, the teachings were distinguished by the curricula of the Half and the Full.

Regarding the phrase "the completion of the Immortal Garden" (*sen'en kōjō*), some do not permit the Immortal Garden to be the site for attaining the Way, asserting that it can only be the place where the Wheel of Dharma is turned.
However, according to the doctrine elucidated by our own school, this represents the dual manifestation of the two aspects; the two beginnings are simultaneous.

For there is no distinction of great or small in the Buddha; greatness and smallness arise from the capacity of the sentient beings. Thus, those with great capacity perceive the ten-thousand-foot Śākyamuni preaching the Dharma.

In the *Avataṃsaka*, there is the limited vision of Śākyamuni as a sixteen-foot [tall] figure; in the *Āgamas*, it is not contradictory to have the vast vision of Vairocana attaining enlightenment at the site of tranquility (the Bodhimaṇḍa).
There is the limited vision of Śākyamuni completing his work at the Garden of the Seers (Lumbinī). The Vinaya Master has deeply grasped this meaning;

how could it be that [the Buddha] merely belongs to the category of preaching the Dharma? Once he had attained enlightenment, he necessarily preached the Dharma; and the Dharma he preached was necessarily...
They are adapted to the capacities [of beings], and these capacities are distinguished by being either great or small.
Thus, within the Āgamas, Cunda alone attaining the first fruit is "small," while the eighty thousand devas awakening to the non-arising of dharmas is "great.

If one discusses this in terms of the *Avataṃsaka* and the Deer Park, the distinction between great and small is even more evident; therefore, it is said that "capacities are divided into great and small."
"Small. To cite the beginning, it is as follows. The "bequeathed charge at the Golden River" is explained as in the *Śāstra-ṭīkā*.

Regarding the distinction between the "half" and the "full" paths and so forth: if the four teachings are contrasted with one another, the Tripitaka is the half, while the Shared, Distinct, and Perfect are the full.
This is because the principle elucidated by the Tripitaka is only the True and not the Central, and the wisdom manifested is only the Provisional and not...
This is not the reality. The delusions to be destroyed are merely those of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi* and *kleśa*), rather than ignorance (*avidyā*).
That which emerges from birth and death is merely the segmented (*paricchinna*) type, rather than the transformative (*pariṇāma*) type. Since each obtains only one half, they are called "half.

The Separate and Perfect [teachings] do not merely express the Truth (*satya*), but also express the Middle (*madhyama*); furthermore, they do not merely transcend the segmented, but also transcend the transformative.

It is easy [to understand]. Therefore, it is called "full" (*pūrṇa*). If one takes the preceding *āgama* teachings as the "half," then by extending [the application] to the subsequent *vaipulya* and *pariniṣpanna* [teachings], they may be termed "full.
Now, as this is the initial gateway to the Mahāyāna, it is likewise "full. At the assembly of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, there was a retrospective exposition of the four teachings;
thus it is said that "the paths differ as half and full. To cite the latter as an example, it is as follows. First, it speaks of the "capacity" (*indriya*).
The subsequent mention of "the Way" (dào) is likely due to the sequential order of the transformative teachings, which are differentiated according to the capacities of sentient beings.

Thus, at the beginning, only "capacity" (jī) was mentioned, whereas later all [beings] are known to possess the eternal (cháng); therefore, it is called "the Way. △ Third, the direct correspondence and manifestation.
Is it not the case that when the teaching is applied according to the capacity of the vehicle (*yāna*), there is no means to fully scrutinize its sublime convergence?

"When the teaching is applied according to the capacity of the vehicle" means that when the Tathāgata expounds the teaching, he does so by tailoring it to each respective capacity at their particular time.

For instance, when he was riding upon the *Avataṃsaka* [Sūtra], he expounded the distinct and perfect teachings (*bhedavibhāga-pūrṇa-dharma*), applying them exclusively to those of great capacity. When riding upon the *Āgama*...
At that time, the teachings of the Tripiṭaka were expounded, which exclusively benefited those of small capacity.

When the time came for the Vaipulya Prajñāpāramitā, he taught the Perfect (Pūrṇa) in contrast to the Half (Ardha), and by teaching the Perfect while retaining the Two [vehicles], he simultaneously benefited both those of great and small capacity.
Even until the Nirvāṇa Sūtra, he taught the subsequent sublation of the four teachings, and likewise simultaneously benefited both those of great and small capacity. Although each...

Taking advantage of that opportunity, however, within those various schools, some combined [teachings], some were exclusive, some were contrastive, some were inclusive, and some mixed provisional and Hinayana doctrines;
none of these were sufficient for the critical examination of the present sutra. Therefore, it is said: "There is nothing sufficient to examine its sublime assembly.
Here, "examine" (*he*) carries the sense of comparison. The word "its" (*qi*) refers specifically to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Yet, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is also...
The teaching that adapts to the timing and responds to the capacities of beings is such that the doctrine it proclaims is singularly pure, perfect, and complete.

It differs from the preceding periods, which were characterized by the combined, the partial, and the accommodated; nor does it resemble the subsequent period, which was interspersed with provisional and Hinayana elements.
Therefore, the Lotus Sūtra alone is transcendentally superior; the four preceding periods and the subsequent Nirvāṇa Sūtra are all insufficient to compare with its excellence. (5)

At this time, [the author] merely cites the beginning of the Āgamas and the aftermath of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* to clarify that there are Great and Small, and Half and Full [teachings], thereby manifesting the *Avataṃsaka*, as well as the two *Prajñāpāramitā* (Sūtras), all of which possess both Great and Small aspects.

Indeed, the inclusiveness of the *Avataṃsaka*, the counteraction of the Vaipulya, and the accompaniment of the *Prajñāpāramitā* make the distinction between the Great and Small clearly visible; however, the Āgamas alone...

These are the Three Baskets (Tripitaka). The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the present sutra share the same flavor, yet the distinction between the Great and Small Vehicles appears difficult to manifest clearly;

therefore, this [distinction] is specifically raised for clarification. Thus, they are contrasted and revealed. Regarding the four periods and the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, none of them examine the sublime assembly of the *Lotus Sūtra*.
II. Pointing out the meaning according to the text, divided into two parts: first, indicating the Trace Gate; second...
This illustrates the Original Gate. The first section also has two parts. First, an example is cited:

it is known that the five thousand who withdrew from their seats did so to advance those of arrogant disposition, while the five hundred who received predictions of enlightenment were all manifestations of the profound transformative influence.

These two characters, "is" (是) and "know" (知), follow closely upon the preceding text. They mean that since the assembly of the Lotus Sūtra is so exalted and supreme, the reason its influence reaches all capacities without exception is known through this.
Thus we understand that although five thousand people withdrew from their seats, their withdrawal was actually an advancement;
it was not a severance of their spiritual potential. Furthermore, the bestowal of predictions upon the five hundred disciples reveals the principle of the inner secret and the outer manifestation.

This is fundamentally "high. However, regarding these four phrases, there are those who offer alternative interpretations. They claim that the five thousand [monks] withdrawing from their seats did not actually withdraw;

it was merely a skillful means (*upāya*) to urge on those in the assembly who were conceited. Thus, they were shown as withdrawing as a provisional demonstration, but in reality, there was no withdrawal.
The five hundred receiving predictions of enlightenment did not actually receive them; it was merely intended to honor those of inferior capacity in secret.
This is the trace of his transformation; thus he provisionally manifested the bestowal of a prediction, yet there was no actual bestowal of a prediction.

If one interprets it in this way, there are two faults for each [position]. Regarding the first two faults: first, it contradicts the root sūtra; second, it contradicts the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. As for contradicting the root sūtra:
the sūtra says, "For such people of overweening pride, it would be better even if they were to regress. Now, within this assembly...

There are no longer branches or leaves; there is only pure, solid substance. In the sutra, it is clearly indicated that five thousand people left their seats, yet it is said that they did not actually leave their seats.
In the sutra, it is clearly indicated that those remaining in the assembly are the solid substance, yet it is said this was intended to urge on those with overweening pride.
Is this not in contradiction with the original sutra? As for contradicting the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, the Tathāgata...
Finally, because he wished to bring those who were not yet mature to full ripeness, he preached the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra to gather them in.
If those who withdrew from their seats were merely a provisional demonstration, then who would be the "unripe" people?
If so, there would be no one for whom the taught Nirvāṇa was intended; would this not mean that [the Buddha] lacks a connection to Nirvāṇa?
This is not so. Regarding the next two faults: first, it would reveal that the *Lotus Sūtra* lacks the merit of bestowing predictions upon śrāvakas of true practice;
second, it would prevent those of inferior capacity from accomplishing the task of purifying buddha-fields.

This is because, although they are those who keep their realization secret within, since they now manifest outwardly, the provisional leads to the real, making them identical to those of true practice. Provisional...

Since the practice has already been recorded, the realization may likewise be recorded. This is why the merit of this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* surpasses that of all other teachings throughout the dispensation.
If one were to say that there is no such record, it would reveal the lack of merit in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; is this not an error?

It is precisely because of the bestowal of the prediction of Buddhahood (*vyākaraṇa*) that one cultivates various practices and thereby attains the adornment of kalpas and lands. If one were to say that from the beginning there was no such prediction...
If there were no records, then there would likewise be no matter of purifying Buddha-lands. Would this not be an error?

Furthermore, you say that it is precisely because there are records that the traces of his secret transformation are honored; it is only through these records that the loftiness of those traces is revealed.
If there were originally no records, one would not know of the traces of his secret transformation—by what means, then, could they be honored? Now, regarding the five...

Fifth, those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*). Having heard the brief exposition that reveals the provisional to manifest the ultimate, the seeds of the perfect One Vehicle have already been deposited within the field of the eight consciousnesses.
Although they depart from their seats, this still serves as a causal condition for their future liberation.
Thus, even though they withdraw, they are in fact advancing; hence, it is called the fifth.

A thousand people withdrew from their seats. This was for the sake of those whose pride had increased; if the benefit of those who withdrew from their seats was already such as this, then the benefit of those remaining in the assembly can be known.

These five hundred disciples were of inferior capacity; since the nature of those of inferior capacity has been revealed, the capacities of those of middling and superior faculties may likewise be understood.
Furthermore, provisional practice is fundamentally intended to lead toward the ultimate reality; since provisional practice is thus...

Since they have received their predictions, it can also be known that those who practice according to reality likewise do so. Thus, whether of sharp or dull faculties, or practicing through provisional or real means, all receive their predictions.
This is why the *Lotus Sūtra* alone is preeminent and supreme, while the other sections lack anything sufficient to rival its sublime assembly. △ Second, the analysis of the text.

Therefore, he emitted light and manifested auspicious omens to open up the source of the teachings that inspire and request [the Dharma]. Emerging from meditative concentration, he extolled his virtues to fully unfold the grand strategy of the Buddha’s wisdom.
He compared the decaying house to the textual path for entering the Great Vehicle; the city of transformation was used to ensure that past karmic conditions do not fall into ruin;
the tied pearl illustrates that the fundamental nature is ever-present; and the digging of the well demonstrates the manifold methods of awakening.

The two characters "therefore" (是以) also follow from the preceding text. This means that since this sutra is now established as sublime and supreme, its three divisions are likewise distinct from other sutras:
thus, the six auspicious omens constitute the introductory section (序分) of this sutra; the three assemblies (三周) constitute the main body of the teaching (正宗) of this sutra;
and the practice of the bodhisattva path constitutes the dissemination section (流通) of this sutra. Therefore, at the beginning...
The "Emission of Light" (Raśmipramokṣa) in a single phrase constitutes the introductory section of the "Section on the Manifestation of the Trace.

The emission of light is the final of the six auspicious omens in this land and the general summary of the six auspicious omens in other lands; therefore, by citing this single instance of the emission of light, all six auspicious omens of both lands are fully encompassed.

Next are the four phrases beginning with "Emerging from Samādhi. These constitute the main body (*śarīra*) of the introductory section. The first phrase, "Emerging from Samādhi," introduces the conclusion of the Dharma-exposition (*dharmadeśanā*).

The second phrase, "The Decayed House," introduces the conclusion of the Parable-exposition (*aupamyadeśanā*). The third phrase, "The City of Transformation," introduces the conclusion of the Exposition on Causes and Conditions (*nidānadeśanā*).
Regarding "Emerging from Samādhi" and so forth: because the Tathāgata arises from samādhi, it is called "emerging from samādhi. This is an expression of praise.
The Buddhas possess two kinds of wisdom; therefore, it is said that they "exalt virtue. "Makyo" (宏) means vast and great, while "ryaku" (略) means skillful strategy;
these refer to the gate of wisdom. Phrases such as "profoundly deep and immeasurable," as well as "only a Buddha and a Buddha can fully exhaust [its depths]," refer to this very point.

"Uniformity of script and tracks" refers to the citation of external (non-Buddhist) classics. These classics state: "When the world is in great order, the scripts shall be unified and the carriage tracks shall be uniform.
Now, this Sūtra opens up the nine realms and three vehicles to reveal the single vehicle of the Buddha-realm; it is like the great order of a unified empire.
Therefore, there is a single, identical script of the Perfect and Sudden, and a single track of the Great Vehicle. [This was] due to past conditions...

"Not falling" specifically refers to the time of the Great Penetration (*mahā-abhisambodhi*), which is when the karmic connection is established. Regarding "tying the jewel," some say that tying the jewel illustrates the constant presence of past seeds;

one should not, however, speak of the constant presence of the principle-nature (*dharmatā*). This is because tying the jewel is a metaphor for the *pariniṣpanna-hetu* (the perfecting cause), whereas the principle-nature is the *prakṛti-hetu* (the causal nature).
It appears they do not understand that the perfecting cause is that which performs the tying, while the causal nature is that which is tied.
This is that which is bound. If there is no revealing cause (*vijñapti-hetu*), the true cause (*samyag-hetu*) does not arise; if there is no true cause, the revealing cause does not manifest.
Although there are two names, their essence is in fact one. This is explained in terms of the object to clarify the subject; hence it is called "the principle of nature" (*li-xing*).

This Vinaya Master had a profound insight into this meaning; it was not merely superficial. The single phrase "digging a well" is from the section on the traces (*śeṣa-mukha*) of the introductory chapter.
This is the section on the Dissemination. △ Second, the indication of the Root Gate.
The words and meanings are as they were; the metaphors presented are simply far-reaching.

Regarding the fact that the Root Gate merely mentions "words and meanings" and so forth: since the three divisions of the Trace Gate have already been detailed above, [the text] now intends to indicate the Root Gate.
The [Entrance] Gate should likewise have three parts. Since the Trace Gate has already been fully demonstrated, the Original Gate can be understood by analogy;
therefore, it is presented here in brief. Thus, both the words that express and the meanings they convey in these three sections are clearly visible;
hence it is said that "the words and meanings are manifest," as in the case of the words and meanings concerning those who "emerge from the earth" and so forth in the Original Gate.

The sequence of the introductory section (*nidāna*) is perfectly manifest; the terminology and meaning of the long lifespan and so forth are perfectly manifest as the main teaching (*saddharma*) of the Essential Gate;
and the terminology and meaning of the fourfold faith and five grades of practice are perfectly manifest as the dissemination (*pariṇāmanā*) of the Essential Gate.
To further illustrate its main teaching, as in the "Life Span" chapter (*Ayuḥpramāṇa-parivarta*), the metaphor of the speck of dust illustrates my [own]...
The Buddha’s long-standing fundamental origin and the analogy of the physician clarify that the three periods of time are neither arising nor ceasing, yet they manifest as arising and ceasing;

thus it is said that the presentation of the analogies is "only remote. One should know that a single phrase concerning words and meaning generally indicates the distinct clarity of the three divisions [of the sūtra], while a single phrase presenting the analogies specifically indicates the words and meaning of the main teaching. Therefore, one should know how to rely upon the text.
Pointing it out: whether regarding the traces or the source, each has its own sequential and correct circulation; there is not one that does not have a preface provided for it.
△ Third, manifesting the Buddha’s compassion.

Were it not for Great Compassion that universally rescues and uproots those submerged in the flowing current of stagnation, and a singularly ultimate heart of pity that saves those who have lost their nature through delusion and confusion—"stagnation and submersion" refers to being stuck in emptiness and drowning in existence;
"submerged in the flowing current" refers to the two extremes; and "delusion and confusion" refers to losing the Middle Way.

This truly benefits the principle of reality (*dharmatā*). Were it not for the Tathāgata’s unconditioned great compassion (*nirupadhiśeṣa-mahākaruṇā*), by what means could they be rescued and uplifted?
Therefore, it says, "Were it not for the Great Pity," and so forth. "One extreme" refers to the ultimate limit.

Furthermore, this section concludes the preceding and introduces the following to manifest the Buddha’s compassion; that is to say, were it not for the Great Pity of the Tathāgata, how could he have taught [this]?
Regarding this wondrous sutra: were it not for the Great Compassion of the Tathāgata, even though he had preached this sutra, how could it have been transmitted and translated into this land?

Were it not for the Great Compassion of the Tathāgata, even though it had been transmitted to this land, how could it alone have enjoyed such flourishing reception and preservation over more than six hundred years and in over four thousand fascicles? If it were not for the Tathāgata...
"Great Compassion" is the mind that universally rescues; it uproots those who are mired in the loss of their true nature.

How could it be otherwise? Therefore, it is said: "Were it not for... (and so forth). This concludes the preceding section on the lineage of the transmission and translation, thereby manifesting the Buddha’s compassion.

It then introduces the subsequent passage concerning the causes and conditions for receiving and upholding [the teaching]; thus, the two characters "zi fei" (were it not for) have their meaning extended throughout the following text.

[End of section on] Hearing. △ Third, the account of the causes and conditions for receiving and upholding [the text]. This also has two parts. First, clarifying that the practice of receiving and upholding it alone flourishes:

From the Han to the Tang dynasties, over six hundred years have passed; one surveys the various scriptures in total, numbering more than four thousand fascicles. Among these, that which flourishes in terms of being received and upheld is [this text].

It has been more than six hundred years since this sutra appeared; this speaks of the extreme length of its era. It comprises over four thousand fascicles; this speaks of the extreme abundance of its scriptures.
Within such a long period and such a vast number of sutras, those who receive and uphold [the teachings] do so solely through this sutra.
This is the flourishing [of the Dharma]. △ Second, clarifying the joy and gratitude one should feel upon being born [into this teaching]:

Is it not that the faculties and the teaching have struck one another in resonance? We are both the lingering dust of the wisdom of the Victorious One (Ji-sheng); having heard [this], we should hold it in deep reverence. We are both the remaining achievements of King Wei; [we should rejoice].
"Leaving behind only a trace of dust" is a metaphor for "few. In the past, while acting as a prince, he taught and transformed six hundred trillion *yè* (a vast number) of sentient beings.
As for those encountered and matured during the intervening period, there were none whose faculties and his teaching did not strike one another with resonance.
To clarify this through analogy, they are as numerous as the great masses of earth. Today in the royal city, and even throughout future ages, those who reach maturity [are likewise vast].

"Those who have attained liberation" refers to the mutual resonance between the capacity of the recipient and the teaching; this is clarified through analogy as being like a small amount of residual dust.
Thus, it is called "residual dust. "Remaining achievements" likewise refers to residual merit.

As for the terms "both" and "together," they mean that those who heard this sutra during the assembly on Vulture Peak were all equally the residual dust of Buddha Jñānavijaya and the remaining influence of King Bhīṣmagarjitasvara.
Even if one were to hear this sutra today, or even five hundred years hence, it would be none other than the lingering dust of Jñānavijaya and the remaining merit of King Bimbisāra.
Thus, it is said that they are both "lingering dust" and "remaining merit.
Since these are both the lingering dust of Jñānavijaya and the remaining merit of King Bimbisāra, what further need is there to speak of the great fortune of being born [in such a time]?
"How so! The above concludes the second section of the exegesis. △ Third, the conclusion, which is divided into two parts. First, the formal conclusion:
I have thus briefly introduced and synthesized [the contents] at the beginning of this scripture."
△ Second, the Vow:
May I soon purify the six sense faculties to behold the sublime assembly of the Compassionate Honored One; may I swiftly accomplish the four virtues to follow the profound path to the Land of Bliss.
My praise shall be inexhaustible, and these words are offered to be perpetuated for all future generations.
May the six sense faculties be purified. May the four virtues be perfected. Furthermore, may this sutra be perpetually transmitted to future generations.

Regarding the purification of the six sense faculties, it is as described in the "Chapter on the Merits of a Dharma Master. As for the "Gathering of Maitreya’s Compassion," some say it refers to the three assemblies under the Dragon-Flower Tree;
the four virtues are permanence, bliss, self, and purity; and the "Land of Bliss" refers to the Pure Land of the West. Now, I shall comment upon this.

Since it is said that one has already purified the six sense organs early on, and further that one will swiftly accomplish the four virtues, how could this refer to the time of Maitreya’s descent, or to rebirth after the end of one’s life?

If one can follow the text into contemplation as did the Great Master Zhiyi, then one will naturally behold the assembly on Vulture Peak as if it were still present, solemnly undispersed. Thus the Sutra says: "Then one shall see the Buddha constantly residing at the Jeta Grove."
Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain. Thus, the Tathāgata is taken as the Honored One of Compassion, and Vulture Peak as the auspicious assembly.

If one can accomplish the four dharmas of the "Universal Worthy Chapter," then this defiled land of common dwelling can be manifested as the true realm of *śāntaprabhāsvara* (the Land of Tranquil Light).
Consequently, these four dharmas are taken as the four virtues (*catvāri guṇāni*), and the Land of Tranquil Light is taken as the Land of Bliss. Therefore, the six...
Regarding the "roots," it is said they are "early-purified"; regarding the "four virtues," it is said they are "swiftly accomplished. Furthermore, this single phrase serves as a summary title.
In the preceding section, I have briefly introduced and synthesized [the content] at the beginning of the scripture;
this is the "one word" that concludes the introduction. The term "briefly" (輒) means "arbitrarily" (擅); it refers to the source and transmission of all that is contained within this scripture.
The essential purport of this text and the causes and conditions for its upholding are summarized and introduced at the beginning of this single sutra;

this is the modest expression of the Vinaya Master. Thus, there is no other reason for the frequent inclusion of prefaces to the sutras than the wish that [practitioners] may quickly purify the six sense faculties and swiftly accomplish the four virtues.
That not a single phrase of the propagation can be exhausted is the conclusion of the section on propagation.
The characters [mean]: "Hong" (弘) signifies vast expansion; "zan" (贊) signifies praise and accomplishment, which is also equivalent to extolling and recounting.

This refers to the vast expansion and the accomplishment of this sutra, such that there is no further limit. The phrase "to be perpetually bequeathed to all future generations" (永貽諸後) is the concluding word for the transmission.

Because its expansion and praise are inexhaustible, it is said "to be perpetually bequeathed to all future generations. It is precisely because its expansion and praise are inexhaustible that it is perpetually bequeathed.

Because it follows all the preceding sections, this introduction is called the "Preface for the Propagation. Thus far, the three divisions—introduction, explanation, and conclusion—have been completed;
the explanation of the Preface for the Propagation is finished.

△ To explain this sutra, it is first divided into two parts. First, the explanation of the title and the division of the text.
Within the title, there are both the title of the sutra and the title of the author. Now, first, I shall explain the title of the sutra.

The five characters beginning with "Wondrous Dharma" (Miaofa) constitute the general title of this entire scripture, while the three characters beginning with "Scroll" (Juan) constitute its specific sub-title. Within this general title:
There are specific titles and general titles. Regarding the specific: every single sūtra has its own particular designation;
for example, the *Avataṃsaka* is not the same as the *Śūraṅgama*, and the *Śūraṅgama* is not the same as the *Laṅkāvatāra*. Since each sūtra differs from the others, they are called "specific.
Regarding the general: although the designations of each individual sūtra differ from one another, with the exception of the Vinaya and the Śāstras, [the term "Sūtra" applies to them all].
Because they share the same name, it is called "common" (*sāmānya*). Now, the four characters *Miaofa Lianhua* (The Lotus of the Wondrous Dharma) differ from other sutras;
this is the specific title (*viśeṣa-nāman*) of the present sutra. The single character *jing* (sutra) is the same as in all other scriptures; this is the common title of the present sutra.

Furthermore, the seven characters from *Miaofa* down to *Yanyi* (Expounding the Meaning) also possess both common and specific titles. [The term] *Yanyi*... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.)

The characters [of the specific title] differ from those of other sections, as noted in the *Wenju ji* (Record of the Textual Phrases); each has its own distinct name, which constitutes the "specific title" (*bié-tí*).

The five characters beginning with "Sublime" (*miào*) are the same as those in other sections; as it is also the case in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), they do not depart from these five characters and thus share the same name, which constitutes the "general title" (*tōng-tí*).
Because both the general and the specific are raised together, it is named the *Miaofa lianhua jing yanyi* (Exegesis on the Lotus Sutra of the Sublime Dharma).
The distinction between the general and the specific is thus established. If one wishes to explain their meaning: "Wondrous" (*miao*) refers to that which is inconceivable;

"Dharma" (*fa*) is a designation for that which is capable of serving as a norm or standard. Because it cannot be conceived by the mind and cannot be deliberated upon through speech, it is called "wondrous.
Because it can maintain its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and can further serve as a norm to give rise to phenomena, it is called "Dharma."
It is understood; therefore, it is called "Dharma. This is a general explanation of the term.

If one were to discuss its specific origin, that which is called the "Sublime Dharma" is none other than the provisional [means] revealed and the reality manifested in the "Trace Gate" (Jikimon) of this sutra, as well as the traces revealed and the fundamental [reality] manifested in the "Origin Gate" (Honmon). Such are the dharmas of provisional and real, and of origin and trace.
For forty years, this was avoided and not spoken of; only until today has it been able to be explained openly.

This is what was rare in the past, and is therefore marvelous. Indeed, for those forty years, the three vehicles, the five teachings, and the seven kinds of expedient means that were taught were the Tathāgata’s provisional [teachings], yet they were never declared to be provisional. IV.
Ten years ago, that which was spoken as the One Vehicle of Perfect and Sudden was the reality of the Tathāgata, yet he had never previously declared it to be reality.
Only upon approaching the city of Gayā and sitting at the site of enlightenment did he manifest this as the trace of the Tathāgata;
yet forty years prior, he had never declared it to be a trace. Long before even a speck of dust in kalpas, it had already been accomplished.
The Samyaksaṃbuddha. This is the fundamental essence of the Tathāgata; yet for forty years prior, he had never declared this to be the fundamental essence.

Today, at this great assembly of the Lotus Sūtra, he declares that the three vehicles and five teachings are definitively provisional, while the teaching of the One Vehicle, perfect and sudden, is definitively real.
He declares that his enlightenment at the city of Gayā was definitively a trace, while his realization of the distant past is the reality.

It is attained. Concentration is the foundation of concentration. This is the teaching of both the provisional and the real, and of the trace and the source—a teaching never before expounded, which is now being expounded;
this is why it is wondrous. Moreover, it is not merely that its exposition constitutes the provisional and the real.
To speak of this in terms of "trace" and "source," it is simply designated as "wondrous.

Furthermore, it can open the provisional gateways of all phenomena to reveal the true aspect (*dharmatā*) of the One Vehicle; it can open the near trace at Gayā to reveal the far-reaching, eternal source.
This is what is meant by opening and resolving the provisional to manifest the real, and opening and resolving the trace to manifest the source. This is...

Thus, the provisional means (*upāya*) that existed in the past did not exist apart from the reality; rather, they were the provisional means bestowed by reality. Provisional means are originally reality.
The reality that exists today does not exist apart from the provisional means; rather, it is the reality revealed by the opening of the provisional means.
Reality is originally provisional means. The traces at the nearby city of Gayā did not exist apart from the fundamental.

There is something distinct. It is the trace originally manifested from the fundamental; the trace originates in the fundamental. The basis of the long and distant lifespan does not exist apart from the trace as something separate;
rather, it is the fundamental revealed by opening up the trace. The fundamental originates in the trace. Thus, the provisional and the real are one body;
the fundamental and the trace are non-dual. This is the wondrous provisional and the wondrous real; the wondrous trace and the wondrous fundamental. Provisional...
Although the names "Reality" (shitsu) and "Original-Trace" (honjaku) differ, their inconceivability is one; this is why it is called the "Wondrous Dharma" (Myōhō).

Although it is said that the Wondrous Dharma is itself the provisional and the real, as well as the original and the trace, yet one does not know what kind of ontological essence (ri-tai) it truly is.
Upon thorough investigation, it is found to be nothing other than the "suchlike marks" (nyoze-sō) and "suchlike nature" (nyoze-shō) elucidated within the sutra. Thus...
Reaching thus to the ten suchnesses (*daśatathatā*), from their beginning to their ultimate end; these ten suchnesses are discussed in relation to the ten realms (*daśadhātu*).
Within each single realm, all ten suchnesses are fully present; thus, across the ten realms, there are one hundred suchnesses. Within a single realm...
Furthermore, each of these ten realms possesses ten further realms, such that the ten realms constitute one hundred realms; and these one hundred realms possess one thousand suchnesses (*tathatā*).

When categorized according to the five aggregates (*skandha*) as substantial dharmas, the nominally designated sentient beings, and the land of dependent retribution, they form the three thousand [realms].
These three thousand natures and characteristics—the hundred realms and one thousand suchnesses—do not transcend the present, infinitesimal moment of thought.
This mind—this very thought-moment manifesting before one—is the entirety of the three thousand natures and aspects and the ten realms with their thousand suchnesses.
Furthermore, these very three thousand natures and aspects, the ten realms with their thousand suchnesses, serve as the provisional means that are opened up and the reality that is revealed;
yet within the provisional and the real, there is no distinction between the provisional and the real. It is thus.
These three thousand natures and characteristics, the hundred realms and thousand suchnesses, constitute the traces that are revealed and the fundamental reality that is manifested.
Yet, these fundamental and phenomenal aspects (honji-suijaku) do not exist as something distinct from one another.

Thus, although there is a distinction between the provisional and the real, or the fundamental and the phenomenal, it is simply the three thousand in a single thought-moment; and these three thousand are fully present within this single thought-moment. If [one contemplates] the three thousand...
When all is contained within a single thought-moment (*ekacitta*), then the three thousand realms are not many.
If a single thought-moment fully possesses the three thousand realms, then that single thought-moment is not few.
Such a Dharma—how could it be grasped by the intellect or discussed in words? If this Dharma were not wondrous, what other Dharma could be considered wondrous?

Indeed, for those of sharp faculties, upon hearing what was taught once, they immediately understand that this Dharma’s provisional and ultimate aspects share the same essence, and its traces and origin are of one suchness.
Desiring to enable those of middling and inferior capacities to understand as well, he further employs the skillful metaphor of the lotus.
In the world, there is only the lotus such that when it is in full bloom, the fruit is already present within the flower. And yet, the flower...
Because the fruit is simultaneous [with the flower], the wondrous Dharma is compared to it.
If one does not understand that the provisional and the real of the wondrous Dharma share the same essence, and that the fundamental and the trace are identical, I ask you to examine the lotus.

If you know that when the lotus is about to bloom, the flower and the fruit are simultaneous, then you will know that the wondrous Dharma is such that the provisional is itself the real, and the trace is itself the fundamental.

The provisional and the real are of one essence; the original and the manifested are identical. Thus, the "wondrous Dharma" (myōhō) is the essence of the Dharma, while the "lotus flower" (renge) is a metaphorical comparison.
First the essence of the Dharma is indicated, and subsequently the metaphor is presented; hence it is called the *Myōhō Renge*. Regarding the general title "Sūtra":
the Sanskrit term is *sūtra*, which here means "scripture that accords with the truth. Whenever the Buddha preaches the Dharma, he necessarily accords with principle.

It accords with the fundamental principle: this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* above accords with the principle of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena as expounded by all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time;
below, it accords with all sentient beings of the nine realms and the six paths of existence.

Because it is intended for those of the capacity for the complete and sudden One Vehicle, it is called a *sūtra*. Regarding "Volume One": in the Qin translation of this scripture there are seven volumes;
as this is now the very first, it is called the "First. The meaning of the title is manifold, and I cannot explain it all here;

as was explained in the "Preface to the Wide Propagation" regarding the title, and as will be seen at the beginning of the "Introductory Chapter" (*Nidāna-parivarta*) and the beginning of the "Chapter on Expedient Means" (*Upāya-kauśalya-parivarta*).

The beginning of the second fascicle: the Parable Chapter; the beginning of the Faith and Understanding Chapter. The third fascicle: the beginning of the Parable of the Medicinal Herbs Chapter. The fourth fascicle:
the beginning of the Chapter on the Prediction for the Five Hundred Disciples. Together with the current general title, there are eight sections in total.
As for each respective chapter, they are not explained all at once because they serve as the basis for their emergence, their arising, and the understanding of the chapters themselves.

Regarding the title of the person [who translated], the meaning of "Yao Qin" and so forth is fully detailed in the commentary to the treatise. As for the phrase "one who translates by imperial decree," "decree" (詔) refers to an official edict.

Since ancient times, all instances of speaking from a superior to an inferior have been termed "edicts" (zhào). It was only since the Han dynasty that the Son of Heaven was permitted to use this title.
This concludes the explanation of the title.
The Text in Two Parts: This sutra consists of seven fascicles and twenty-eight chapters. If divided into two major sections, they are as follows:

first, the Trace Gate (*jimen*), which reveals the One by opening up the Three, revealing the Real by opening up the Provisional; second, the Source Gate (*benmen*), which reveals the Remote by opening up the Proximate, and reveals the Source by opening up the Trace.
The first four and a half fascicles comprise fourteen chapters, beginning with the "Introductory Chapter" (*Xǔpǐn*) of the first fascicle.
Finally, the first half of the fifth fascicle is the "Chapter on Peaceful Practices" (*Anle-xing pin*), which is termed the "Trace Gate" (*ji-men*).

The subsequent two and a half fascicles, comprising fourteen chapters beginning from the "Chapter on the Earth-Sprouting Bodhisattvas" (*Cong-di-yong-chu pin*) in the middle of the fifth fascicle and ending with the "Chapter on Samantabhadra’s Exhortation" (*Pu-xian-quan-fa pin*) at the end of the seventh fascicle, are termed the "Root Gate" (*ben-men*).
As for what is called the "Trace," it refers to the manifestation of transformation after the attainment of the fruit. Indeed...
The Tathāgata has long ago attained equal and right enlightenment and has thoroughly exhausted the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Desiring to cause all sentient beings to likewise realize the true nature of all phenomena, he seeks to enable each of them to open, show, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Therefore, from the fundamental [state], he manifests traces; he repeatedly appears in birth and repeatedly manifests extinction.

Such manifestations of birth and extinction constitute the transformative activity performed after attaining the fruit; thus they are called "traces. As for what is called the "fundamental," it refers to the long-distant realization, as clarified in the *Ayuṣpramāṇa-parivarta*:
all those in the world—gods, humans, and asuras—all believe that [the Buddha] emerged from the Śākya clan.
The Palace. Not far from the city of Gayā, he sat at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
However, in truth, it has been immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *nayuta* kalpas since I truly attained Buddhahood.

Having realized this through such a vast duration, it was the Tathāgata’s initial and ultimate realization of the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*), whereby he attained unsurpassed *bodhi*. Therefore, it is called [the Palace].
Fundamentally, the two gates of the Trace and the Origin each consist of three parts: the Introduction, the Main Body, and the Circulation.
The six items at the beginning of the sutra, such as "Thus have I heard," constitute the General Introduction to the Gate of the Trace.

Next, the fourfold assembly surrounds [the Buddha], the Tathāgata preaches the sutra and enters meditative absorption, the heavens rain down four kinds of flowers, the earth shakes in six ways, and he emits light from the tuft of white hair between his eyebrows, illuminating the East.
In the ten thousand and eight thousand lands, Maitreya consequently harbored doubts and posed questions, while Mañjuśrī, based upon this, reflected on the past and provided answers;
this constitutes the specific preface to the Trace Gate (*jijimon*).

Once the origins of both the general and the specific have been clarified, the True Teaching (*shōsō*) may then arise. Thereupon, the Tathāgata emerged from samādhi and extensively praised all Buddhas.

Regarding the realm of wisdom concerning the provisional and the real, [the Buddha] briefly opened up three [vehicles] to reveal the One. Upon hearing this, those of the Two Vehicles all shook their fixed attachments and gave rise to doubt.
Only after Śāriputra had requested three times did the Tathāgata finally provide a broad and detailed revelation.

He established parables for the sake of the Dharma and again clarified the causal conditions of past lives. Thus, throughout these three cycles of teaching, there was nothing that did not open up the nine realms.
The provisional teaching of the Three Vehicles reveals the reality of the One Vehicle of the Buddha-realm.

Thus, those of the three capacities—superior, middling, and inferior—all sever their doubts regarding the provisional and give rise to faith in the real, thereby receiving the prediction of their future Buddhahood.
In this way, the Tathāgata’s original intent is fulfilled, and the great causal purpose is clarified; this is the orthodox core of the "Trace Gate."

Furthermore, the intent behind the Tathāgata’s preaching of this sutra was not merely to benefit those of a single time; he truly wished to provide a thorough nourishment for the future. It is therefore natural that one should circulate it.
However, since the propagation of the Way depends on people, it must rely upon Dharma-preachers. Thus, there is the "Dharma-preacher Chapter.
First, it extensively praises the excellence of the Dharma and the sublimity of the person [who preaches it] in order to encourage its circulation. Next, it provides a detailed exposition.
