The three—robes, seats, and dwellings—are established as the standard model. Furthermore, the Stūpa of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna is cited to testify to the supremacy of the Dharma, and Devadatta is cited to testify to the supremacy of the person.

Since both the supremacy of the Dharma and the supremacy of the person are thus attested, whether they be bodhisattvas or śrāvakas, each shall make vows and take oaths, either desiring to propagate [the teaching] in this land, or...
On the other hand, there is the propagation [of the Dharma] abroad. However, enduring hardships while widely disseminating the sutra is the fundamental resolve of a bodhisattva;

yet, if there were no hardships to endure, that would likewise be the original intention of the Tathāgata. Therefore, Mañjuśrī is again entrusted with posing questions, so that the four modes of peaceful and happy practice may be further detailed as the model for those of initial resolve who propagate the sutra. All of these belong to the category of the "Trace Gate" (jimon).

This concludes the introductory section. The section on the Trace has now been completed; it is appropriate that the section on the Origin be elucidated. Since the section on the Origin does not stand at the beginning of the sutra, it lacks a general introduction (*sādhāraṇa-nidāna*).
Within this section, immeasurable bodhisattvas emerge from the earth, and the disciples of the two lands give rise to doubts and pose questions.
This is the introductory section (*nidāna*) that initiates the Fundamental Gate (*mūla-mukha*). Next, regarding the brief opening concerning the near:
it says, "In the city of Gayā, I attained perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*)," thereby teaching and causing them to first give rise to the mind of the Way (*bodhicitta*).
Regarding the brief manifestation concerning the distant: it says, "I now speak words of truth; you all should believe with a single mind. From long ago, I have taught..."

Having transformed these multitudes, when Maitreya and the other bodhisattvas heard this teaching, there were none who did not give rise to a sense of intimacy toward the Tathāgata and shake off their distant doubts regarding the bodhisattva path.
They remarked, "The attainment of the Way is exceedingly near, and those transformed are exceedingly many;
it is like a father in the world being young while his son is old—a thing difficult for people to believe. Thereupon, the Tathāgata, for their sake...

To extensively clarify what is near, it is said that all worlds refer to the present Śākyamuni, who departed from the palace of the Śākyas and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. To extensively manifest what is far, [it is shown that] he [attained it] long ago.
And so it is, good son. Truly, since I attained Buddhahood, an extremely long time has passed.
Suppose there were hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeyas of three-thousandfold world systems, which were ground into fine dust.
Then, passing beyond five hundred thousand millions of billions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeyas of worlds to the east, one particle of dust were dropped. Just as...

This is traveling eastward until all these atoms are exhausted. Taking all the lands that have been thus covered by dust, as well as those not yet covered, and reducing them further to atoms—let one atom represent one kalpa.
Since I attained Buddhahood, more time has passed than this. Furthermore, within the three periods of time, I have manifested birth again and again;
yet in reality, there is no birth. I have manifested extinction again and again; yet in reality, there is no extinction.
It is not cessation. In sum, it is for the sake of delivering sentient beings; thus, all is real and not false.

It is like a skilled physician who comes and goes among humans, yet in reality there is no coming or going; in sum, it is for the purpose of treating wayward children, and from the beginning there is no falsehood.
Thus, he extensively reveals his immediate traces and extensively manifests his remote origin, whereby all bodhisattvas then sever...
Doubt arises from the proximity [to the truth], while faith arises from the distance [from it]. Some may ascend to the ten abodes (bhūmi) and ten practices (caryā);

some may attain the ten transferences (pariṇāmanā) and ten stages (bhūmi), and receive the prediction (vyākaraṇa) of the Dharma-body; or even those within the stage of the ten faiths (daśa-śraddhā) that resembles [the true path].
Regarding those who have resolved to attain Bodhicitta, Maitreya Bodhisattva has here provided a comprehensive explanation for each of them;
this constitutes the orthodox teaching of the Root Section. Since there is an orthodox teaching, it must be disseminated; therefore, he elucidates it.
In the present age, there are four levels of faith; after my extinction, there will be five grades. To clarify the causal merit of the first grade, there is the "Chapter on the Merit of Rejoicing.
To clarify the resultant merit of the first grade, there is the "Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma Master.
Furthermore, to provide additional testimony regarding the transgressions of disparagement and the blessings of faith, there is the "Chapter on Never-Disparaging. All of these...
This is the exhortation and praise for its circulation. Having already offered this exhortation and praise, it must now be entrusted.
Therefore, the Tathāgata, accepting the request of the Bodhisattva, manifested ten kinds of supernatural powers and established five layers of essential principles.
He placed his hand upon the crown of the Bodhisattva’s head and spoke these words: "Throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of asaṃkhyeya kalpas..."
The practice of this Dharma for attaining Bodhi is difficult to master; I now entrust it to you.
You should disseminate it with a single-minded resolve so that all sentient beings may hear and know it. You should study and follow the teachings of the Tathāgata accordingly.

Do not give rise to stinginess. Consider, for example, the ascetic practice of burning the body by King Bhaiṣajyarāja, the supernatural power of Samantaghoṣa in transmitting the sutra, and the universal manifestation of Avalokiteśvara; all these are what is meant by following and learning from the Tathāgata.

However, in propagating the sutra in the world, there will inevitably be many obstacles and afflictions; it must rely upon external protection to ensure its circulation everywhere. Therefore, the *Dhāraṇī*...

The Chapter on the Bhikṣuṇīs. They serve as external protectors for the propagation of the sutra. If one propagates the sutra by means of the *Sarvarūpasaṃdarśana-samādhi* (Samādhi of Universally Manifesting Physical Forms), it should be like the fundamental narrative of King Wonderful Adornment (*Su-prabhūta-rāja*), causing all who are not in the right way to return to the correct path, ultimately leading to Samantabhadra Bodhisattva exhorting and inspiring them.
Whether this constitutes exhortation and praise or formal entrustment, it belongs to the Fundamental Gate.
...and the dissemination [of the teaching]. The preceding major divisions of the text are thus concluded.

△ Second, the explanation of the meaning of the text concerning clothing. This is divided into two parts: first, the Trace Gate; second, the Origin Gate. The first [the Trace Gate] has three sections:
first, the Introduction; second, the Main Body; third, the Dissemination. The first [the Introduction] further has two parts: first, the title of the chapter.

In the first chapter, the "Introduction" (*Nidāna-parivarta*), of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the initial five characters—"Wondrous Dharma Lotus Flower"—constitute the general title of this sutra.

The subsequent four characters—"Introduction"—are the specific title of this particular chapter. If one were to speak only of the "Introduction Chapter" without mentioning "Wondrous," [the full significance would not be conveyed].
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* does not manifest this "Introductory Chapter" (Nidāna-parivarta); rather, it is the introductory chapter of the present scripture.
Therefore, the title of the entire sūtra is first indicated, followed by the title of the specific chapter. Thus, it is said: "The Introductory Chapter, First, of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
There are versions lacking the sūtra title, such as those abbreviated by the Junior Master (Shaoshi). However, regarding...

As for its summary: it is also the title of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Since there is the title of this single sūtra, there must consequently exist the fundamental principle of this single sūtra, the essential tenet of this single sūtra, the functional efficacy of this single sūtra, and the pedagogical characteristics of this single sūtra.
Therefore, when the Great Master Zhìzhèi explained this title, he did so by means of five [aspects].
The Meaning of the Profound Mystery (*Chongxuan Yi*). Regarding the five stages: first is the explanation of its title; second is the discernment of its fundamental essence (*li-ti*);
third is the elucidation of its essential tenet (*zong-yao*); fourth is the discussion of its functional power (*li-yong*); and fifth is the judgment of its doctrinal characteristics (*jiao-xiang*).
As for the explanation of the title, it employs both dharma and metaphor to constitute the name of this present sutra. As for the discernment of the essence...

Taking the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena as the essence of this present sutra; clarifying its central tenet (*mūla*), it takes the cause and effect of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) as the tenet of this present sutra;
discussing its function (*prayojana*), it takes the severing of doubt and the engendering of faith as the function of this present sutra;
and determining its doctrinal classification (*śāsana-lakṣaṇa*), it takes the unsurpassed *amṛta* (the finest cream) as the doctrinal classification of this present sutra. This is because...
The fivefold profound meaning (*pañca-gambhīrārtha*) is that which is elucidated by this entire sutra.
The Great Master, wishing for people to grasp the purport of the present sutra through its single title, has therefore revealed it within the opening title itself.
However, as the entire sutra is vast and extensive, I cannot cite from it at length; rather, I shall cite and clarify it from within the present chapter, as follows:
The *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-gāthā* states: "I saw the Buddha Dīpaṃkara; his original radiance was such as this.

By this I know that the present Buddha intends to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. This serves as proof that the name of this sūtra consists of both a dharma-name and a metaphorical name. It further states:

"Now, the present signs are as they were originally auspicious; these are the skillful means of all Buddhas. Now the Buddha emits light to assist in the revelation of the meaning of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
This proves that this sutra takes the true mark of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as its essence.

Furthermore, it says: "All you people, you should now know: with palms joined and single-mindedness, wait! The Buddha shall rain down the Dharma-rain to satisfy those who seek the Way. This proves [the same].
The Sūtra takes the cause and fruit of the One Vehicle as its primary tenet. Furthermore, it states:

"If there are those seeking the three vehicles who harbor doubts or regrets, the Buddha shall eliminate and sever them for them, so that they are exhausted without remainder. This serves as proof that the function of this Sūtra is to sever doubt and engender faith.
As for its doctrinal characteristics (*śāstramukha*), it consists merely of the differentiation of the four aforementioned levels; these are termed the "Dharma."
Regarding the designation of metaphors: the names established in the various sūtras consist of only seven types, namely the three single [terms], the three compound [terms], and the complete [term].
As for the three single [terms], these are the single person, the single dharma, and the single metaphor. As for the three compound [terms]...

"Person" refers to the person, "Dharma" to the Dharma, and "Parable" to both the person and the Dharma. To be "complete" in these three means that the person, the Dharma, and the parable are all fully present.

The present sutra is neither the former type of single triad nor the latter type of complete triad; among the intermediate types of triads, it is neither based on the person and the Dharma, nor on the person and the parable.
It is correctly titled according to the "Dharma" and the "Parable. This is because the "Wondrous Dharma" constitutes the Dharma, and the "Lotus Flower" [constitutes the parable].

This is a metaphor; therefore, it is named after both the teaching (*dharma*) and the analogy. As for the statement that "the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) is its essence," the name serves as the signifier (*vācaka*), while the essence is that which is signified (*vācya*). Since there is a signifying name, there must necessarily be a signified essence.
In the Hīnayāna, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self constitute its essence; in the Mahāyāna, it is the single true mark.
and constitutes its essence. Now, this sutra does not take the three [vehicles] of the Hīnayāna as its essence; it takes the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as its essence.

Therefore, the sutra says: "Only Buddhas and Buddhas can exhaustively fathom the true mark of all dharmas," which refers to all dharmas having such a mark, such a nature, and so forth, up to such ultimate identity from beginning to end. Regarding the Chapter on the Origin, it says:
It is neither identical nor different; it does not conform to the three realms, yet it perceives the three realms. Therefore, it takes the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as its essence.
As for saying that cause and effect constitute its central tenet (*siddhānta*): based upon this essence, one gives rise to practice, which necessarily possesses a core tenet.
All immeasurable wholesome deeds are subsumed under "cause," and all immeasurable realizations are subsumed under "effect. Thus, cause and effect are taken as the essential tenet. However...
Regarding the cause of the Mahāyāna, there is no separate cause; it takes the true reality (*dharmatā*) itself as its cause.
Regarding the fruit of the Mahāyāna, there is no separate fruit; it likewise takes the true reality itself as its fruit.

Since this present sutra is the perfect and sudden Mahāyāna, it is neither the cause and fruit for transforming others, nor is it the cause and fruit for both self and others. Therefore, it pertains solely to one's own practice.
It takes the cause and effect of the vehicle as its primary tenet (*śāstra*). Regarding the statement that "severing doubt and engendering faith" constitutes its function:

by relying on the tenet to manifest the essence, one is able to give rise to its dynamic power and function. In this sutra, the Trace Gate (*jibon*) severs doubts concerning the provisional and engenders faith in the real, thereby constituting its power and function;
the Source Gate (*honmon*) severs doubts concerning the near and engenders faith in the distant, thereby constituting its power and function. This is because...
Forty years ago, I knew only that there were the three vehicles and five teachings, and the provisional skillful means of the seven kinds;
I did not know that these very provisional means are entirely the reality of the One Vehicle’s sudden and perfect teaching.

Now, with the opening and revelation of the Trace Gate of the *Lotus Sūtra*, it is shown that all provisional means are entirely reality, and there is no provisional means apart from reality. All doubts regarding the provisional have, from this point on, [been resolved].

All true faith arises from this. Furthermore, throughout all the worlds, people have known only that the World-Honored One left the palace of the Śākyas and proceeded to the city of Gayā, where he first sat at the site of enlightenment;

they did not know that he had already attained equal and perfect awakening countless kalpas ago. Now, with the opening of the "Original Gate" chapter in the *Lotus Sūtra*, this truth is revealed for the first time.
When [the ultimate] is revealed, the provisional traces are entirely the fundamental reality; there are no traces apart from the fundamental.
All proximate doubts are severed thereby, and all remote faith arises thereby. Therefore, the function [of this teaching] consists in severing doubt and generating faith.
As for saying that the *amṛta* (ghee) represents the characteristic of the teaching, it is as clarified in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: "The Tathāgata first preached the *Avataṃsaka*. Just as...
When a cow produces milk, the *Avataṃsaka* takes the flavor of milk as its teaching characteristic. Following the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Āgama* is taught;
this is like producing curd from milk, so the *Āgama* takes the flavor of curd as its teaching characteristic. Following the *Āgama*, the *Vaipulya* is taught;
this is like producing fresh butter from curd, so the *Vaipulya* takes the flavor of fresh butter [as its teaching characteristic].
Thus, it constitutes the characteristic of the teaching. Following the Vaipulya period, the Prajñāpāramitā was taught;

just as one extracts clarified butter from cream, the Prajñāpāramitā takes the flavor of clarified butter as its characteristic of the teaching. Following the Prajñāpāramitā, this present sutra was taught.
It causes all sentient beings to attain the opening, revealing, awakening to, and entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
The nine realms thus return to the Buddha-realm, and the three vehicles all converge in the One Vehicle. This is like extracting *ghṛta* (clarified butter) from matured *sarpis* (butter);

therefore, *ghṛta* is taken as the doctrinal characteristic (*śāsana-lakṣaṇa*) of this present sutra. Such is the entire sutra when considered through its single title. If, however, [one considers it] merely...

Regarding its title: "wondrous dharma" (*saddharma*) refers to the Dharma itself, while "lotus" (*padma*) is a metaphor. Since both the Dharma and the metaphor are presented together, it is called the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

As for the term "sūtra": *sūtra* means "to proceed. This name, consisting of both the Dharma and the metaphor, proceeds from what was proclaimed by the Golden Mouth [of the Buddha], and is therefore called a "sūtra.
Furthermore, "sūtra" is the Sanskrit term *sūtra*, which here is translated as "scripture of concordance" (*yijing*). This means:
This is the essence of the true reality (*dharmatā*). Above, it accords with the principle of cause and effect realized by all Buddhas;
below, it accords with the various capacities—great and small—of all sentient beings. Therefore, it is called a *sūtra*. Furthermore, "sūtra" is glossed as "Dharma" and "constant.
Thus, its function of severing doubts regarding provisional teachings and engendering faith in the ultimate truth is that which is universally followed by the ten realms of existence.
Because it is that which cannot be altered throughout the three periods of time, it is called a *sūtra*. Furthermore, "sūtra" means a path (*kṣetra*).
If one can practice in accordance with such a teaching of the essence of clarified butter (*sarpirmaṇḍa*), one may reach the abode of true reality (*bhūtārtha-lakṣaṇa*).
It is just as when one follows a worldly road and reaches home; therefore, it is called a *sūtra*. [The Prologue Chapter]
These two characters are explained in detail in the commentary (*śāstra*). This sutra consists of twenty-eight chapters; as this is now the very first, it is called "the first.
Part Two: The Main Text, which is divided into two sections: First, the General Introduction (*sādhāraṇa-nidāna*); Second, the Specific Introduction (*asādhāraṇa-nidāna*).

The General Introduction serves as the certification of faith for the entire sutra, while the Specific Introduction serves as the catalyst for the entire sutra. Although there is a distinction between the general and the specific, they together constitute [the introduction].
This is the introductory section (*nidāna*) of a single sūtra. The first part consists of five sections. First is the essence of the Dharma as it was heard.
Regarding the term "Thus" (*evam*): "Thus" is a word that points to the Dharma; it is also a designation for faith and compliance. As for pointing to the Dharma, [it refers to] what precedes...
The former refers to the general title of a single topic; the latter refers to the specific details of a single scripture.
This means that such a scriptural title and such a scriptural text are both the essential nature (*dharmatā*) of what is explained.
Regarding "faithful compliance": it is like worldly affairs; if a person faithfully complies, they say, "This matter is thus"; if they do not faithfully comply, then they say this...
The matter is not as [you] think. Now, the essence of the Dharma of this sutra is that which is believed and followed by the ten realms;
therefore, it is called "Thus" (evam). This is a superficial explanation based on a preliminary understanding. If one wishes to clarify its meaning deeply:

what is called "not different" is named "Thus" (tathā), and being "without exception" is called "Is" (satya). Now, this sutra reveals and clarifies that which was previously taught for forty years—the three vehicles and the five [vehicles].
The seven kinds of expedient means (*upāya*) taught are not different from the ultimate One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), the perfect and sudden true reality (*dharmatā*).
It is like taking raw iron and transforming it entirely into pure gold; therefore, it is called "suchness" (*tathatā*).

Once those expedients are opened up and fully realized as the truth, there is only the single true reality, and no further error remains regarding the three vehicles, the five teachings, or the seven kinds of expedient means. Therefore...
This is what is meant by "thus" (evam). Only when it is like this can it be the "thus" of the present sutra, and not the same as that of other sutras.
△ Second, the person who is able to hear.
I have heard.
△ Third, the time when the sutra was preached:
At one time.
△ Fourth, the location where the sutra was preached:
The Buddha was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha.
All that precedes this is to be understood as usual; it is not recorded here in full. △ Fifth, the companions who heard the teaching together.
Regarding the listing of the assembly herein: if arranged from the shallow to the profound, one should first list the miscellaneous assembly, next the śrāvakas, and finally the bodhisattvas;
if arranged from the profound to the shallow, one should first list the bodhisattvas, next the śrāvakas.

The miscellaneous assembly is listed last. Since this is neither arranged from shallow to deep nor from deep to shallow, but rather lists the śrāvakas first, followed by the bodhisattvas, and finally the miscellaneous assembly, there are two interpretations:
one based on phenomena (*dharma*) and one based on principle (*tattva*). Regarding the phenomenal interpretation:

first, they have shaved their hair and donned dyed robes, and they constantly remain near the Buddha; therefore, they are listed first. As for the miscellaneous assembly, they wear [secular] clothing...
Their forms differ and they deviate from the Buddha; thus, they are listed last. The forms of the Bodhisattvas are not restricted by fixed categories, and their attire is also indeterminate.
Sometimes they are distant from the Buddha, and sometimes they are near to the Buddha; as they stand between these two types, they are listed in the middle.
From the perspective of principle, Śrāvakas delight in Nirvāṇa and are attached to the Truth in every thought-moment; therefore, they are listed first. The Bodhisattvas...
The Bodhisattvas do not cling to the two extremes and constantly cultivate the Middle Way; therefore, they are listed first.

The assembly of Śrāvakas delights in birth and death and clings to the mundane at every thought-moment; therefore, they are listed later. The text is divided into four parts: first, the assembly of Śrāvakas;

second, the assembly of Bodhisattvas; third, the miscellaneous assembly; and fourth, the conclusion on the gathering of the assembly. Of the first two, the first concerns the Bhikṣus, and the second concerns the Bhikṣuṇīs. The first [section on the Bhikṣus] is further divided into two.
First, a general explanation; second, a specific enumeration. Regarding the first [section], there are five parts. First, clarifying the category:
"with a great assembly of bhikṣus.
Second, stating the number.
Together with twelve thousand people.
△ Third, the discussion of their stages: they are all arhats.
All that above is as stated in the text. △ Fourth, the praise of his virtues: All outflows are exhausted;
he is no longer subject to afflictions. He has attained his own benefit and severed all fetters of existence. His mind has attained mastery and sovereignty.
The first two phrases praise the "slayer of thieves. The next phrase praises the "worthy of offerings" (*arhat*). The final two phrases praise "non-arising. Regarding "all outflows" (*āsrava*):
"outflow" (*āsrava*) means leaking away or seeping through; "affliction" (*kleśa*) means mental turbidity and vexation; and "disturbance" (*upāyāsa*) means agitation and confusion.
The reason why ordinary beings possess afflictions is that they are unable to exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*).

Thus, when the eye sees forms, it immediately gives rise to greedy attachment and falls into the outflow of form; when the ear hears sounds, it immediately gives rise to greedy clinging and falls into the outflow of sound;
and so on, until when the mind conditions mental phenomena (*dharma*), it immediately gives rise to discrimination and falls into the outflow of phenomena. Therefore...
These six internal sense-faculties, in relation to the six external sense-objects, give rise in between to the six consciousnesses, which then fall into the defilements of delusion and affliction.
Now, these twelve thousand arhats have already been able to exhaust all outflows; thus, they are no longer troubled by delusion and affliction.
As clarified in the *Vajracchedikā*, those who have attained the first fruit do not enter into form or sound.

Regarding fragrances and flavors: if even those who have attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) are thus, how much more so those who have attained the four fruits? Therefore it is said, "All outflows (*āsrava*) are exhausted, and there are no further afflictions (*kleśa*).
This refers to the ability to slay the thieves of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). Next, the praise of being "Worthy of Offerings" (*arhat*) may be understood accordingly.

Third, within the praise of "Non-arising" (*anutpāda*), "existence" (*bhava*) refers to the fruit, while "bondage" (*saṃyojana*) refers to the cause. Because cause and fruit do not perish, it is called "existence. As for the statement:
Regarding "all existences" (*sarvabhava*): briefly stated, there are three existences; extensively stated, there are twenty-five existences;
stated from a middle perspective, there are nine existences. Thus, it is called "all existences. As for "exhausting the fetters of all existences":

this refers to severing only the fetters of the cause (*hetu-bandhana*), while the fetters of the fruit (*phala-bandhana*) still remain; therefore, it is said that "the mind attains mastery. If the fetters of the fruit were also...
Once these are severed, not only will the mind attain mastery, but the body will likewise attain mastery.

It is precisely because ordinary beings cannot sever the fetters of existence that they do not escape the cycle of birth and death. Now, these twelve thousand arhats have already been able to sever the fetters of existence;
therefore, they shall no longer undergo rebirth. Thus, one knows that this is a praise of non-arising.
This is the virtue. △ Fifth, listing the names, in two parts. First, the individual listing of twenty-one persons.
Their names are: Ājñātakauṇḍinya; Mahākāśyapa; Uruvilvākāśyapa; Gayākāśyapa; Nadīkāśyapa; Śāriputra; Mahāmaudgalyāyana; Mahākātyāyana; Aniruddha.
Lokānanda, Kapphiṇa, Gavāmpati, Revata, Piṇḍola-bhāradvāja, Bakula, Mahākauṣṭhila, Nanda, Sundarananda, and Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra.

Subhūti, Ānanda, Rāhula: at the beginning of the sūtra, it says, "Thus have I heard. Here, "I" refers to Ānanda himself addressing his own name; now that he is listed among those who heard the teaching together with others, why is he mentioned again as "Ānanda"?
Is there another Ānanda apart from this one who heard [the teaching]? One must understand that the "those who heard together" mentioned herein are originally...

This is explained within the section concerning Ānanda. If it concerns the Buddha being in a certain place together with a certain person, then the Ānanda listed therein is mentioned from the perspective of the Buddha’s own section.
One must not restrict the interpretation solely to the two characters "hearing together" (tóngwén).
Furthermore, there are instances where Ānanda hears together with such-and-such persons, and such-and-such persons hear together with Ānanda.

[They] are fellow-hearers. Therefore, there is no inconsistency in listing Ānanda here as a fellow-hearer. This scripture’s description of the śrāvakas differs from that in the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra*.
If [the *Śūraṅgama*] were to praise their smallness, the intent of "concealing within and manifesting without" would not be revealed.
Now, if it praises their greatness, how could the merit of "opening up the provisional to reveal the real" be made manifest? Thus, the *Wenju ji* states:

Volume Seven, Fascicle Twenty-one and Twenty-two. Question: Since the various śrāvakas have already had their provisional [teachings] opened to reveal the real, and their original and trace [identities] manifested, through the three cycles of preaching, why does the scribe still list the names of the śrāvakas at the beginning of the sutra? Answer:

They have been listed from antiquity so that the interpreter must first follow the sequence of the sutra; thus, one first praises their "smallness" (inferiority) and only then applies the doctrinal analysis.
Regarding the "original and trace" (honjaku) and so forth, these are merely interpretations derived from the underlying meaning within the main text.
This is why the two sutras differ in their descriptions of the assembly of śrāvakas. △ Second, a general reference to the twelve thousand people.
Thus were the great arhats and others well-known to the multitude.
△ Second, the specific enumeration:
Furthermore, there were two thousand persons, both those still in training and those beyond training.
△ Second, the assembly of nuns:
The bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī was present together with her retinue of six thousand;
the bhikṣuṇī Yaśodharā, mother of Rāhula, was also present together with her retinue.
△ Second, the assembly of bodhisattvas has five parts. First, clarifying their category:
"bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Second, stating their number.
Eighty thousand people.
△ Third, the manifestation of their status:
they have all attained non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Regarding those who are non-retrogressive: these bodhisattvas have all been able to shatter ignorance, manifest the three virtues, and realize the Middle Way;
they have personally attained the non-retrogression of mindfulness. △ Fourth, the praise of their virtues, which has two parts. First, the general praise.
All have attained *dhāraṇī*.

Regarding the title "General Praise," this means that these eighty thousand bodhisattvas—whether they be at the stages of the ten abodes or the ten practices, up to the ten grounds and the stage of Equal Enlightenment—none lack these virtues of self-cultivation and the transformation of others; thus, in every rank, they are all [endowed with them].
Therefore, it is called "total. In Sanskrit, it is *dhāraṇī*; here it is translated as "obstructing and upholding" (*zhachi*).
It is so named because it obstructs all evil and upholds all goodness. What kind of evil does it obstruct, and what kind of goodness does it uphold?

It means obstructing the three kinds of evil—namely, the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), the dust-like [afflictions], and ignorance (*avidyā*)—and upholding the three kinds of goodness: the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and liberation (*vimukti*).
Thus, there is no evil that is not warded off and no good that is not upheld; all this is due to having attained this dhāraṇī.
This praises the virtue of one's own practice.
"Turning the irreversible wheel of Dharma with the eloquence of joyful exposition.
These two phrases praise the virtue of transforming others. Regarding "the eloquence of joyful exposition," this is one of the four types of unimpeded eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*).
By citing the last one, the preceding three are implied; therefore, it is simply called "joyful exposition. This...
All bodhisattvas, by means of unimpeded eloquence (*pratibhāna*), can turn the non-retrogressive Dharma they have personally realized and cause it to enter the minds of all sentient beings,
enabling those beings likewise to realize non-retrogression; therefore, it is said that they possess the eloquence of joyful speech and turn the non-retrogressive wheel of Dharma.

To make offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddhas is what constitutes the cultivation of merit. However, this making of offerings to the Buddhas does not require the passage of a long period of time.
In a single thought-moment and at a single instant, one is thus able to make offerings to immeasurable Buddhas.

This is because all Bodhisattvas thoroughly realize that both the mind capable of making offerings and the Buddhas who are the objects of those offerings are nothing other than the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

Therefore, they give rise to an offering from their own mind, which is the Dharma-realm itself, and offer it back to the Buddhas of their own mind, which are the Dharma-realm itself. Thus, in a single thought-moment—
To have one's body pervade the worlds of the ten directions is true offering. This is as clarified in the *Amitābha Sūtra*:
when one holds flowers to offer in the early morning, the meaning of this can be understood.

To plant the roots of all virtues in the presence of the Buddhas is that which constitutes the cultivation of wisdom. For wisdom is the source of all myriad good deeds and the foundation of all virtues;
since this bodhisattva is able to serve and make offerings to the Buddhas, the Buddhas will surely expound the wondrous Dharma for them. And...
Having heard the essentials of the Dharma, one cultivates wisdom through this very hearing;
this is the planting of the roots of all virtues, and one is constantly praised by all Buddhas.
This is a summary praising the merit and wisdom of both self and others mentioned above.

That which makes the Buddhas "Buddhas" is their ability to benefit themselves and others by cultivating merit and wisdom, thereby fulfilling both self and others and becoming complete in both merit and wisdom.
Now, these Bodhisattvas are already able to practice for themselves and [strive] toward Bodhi...
They retreat no more; furthermore, they are able to transform others and turn the wheel of Dharma. Being able to cultivate merit, they make offerings to the Buddhas;
being further able to cultivate wisdom, they plant the roots of virtue. Thus, they accord with the Buddha’s mind and are therefore constantly praised by all the Buddhas.
△ Second, the specific praise.
Cultivating the body through loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Regarding the specific praise: among these eighty thousand people, some are at the stage of the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*) and possess the virtues of the Ten Abodes;

others have reached Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) and possess the virtues of Equal Enlightenment. Because each stage possesses its own distinct qualities, it is called "specific. This is the praise.
Regarding the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*): upon first ascending to the First Abode, one destroys one grade of ignorance and realizes one portion of the three virtues (*triguṇa*).

Thereby, one is able to manifest as a Buddha within a hundred realms, manifesting divided bodies to transform and guide beings. In the Second Abode, one manifests as a Buddha within a thousand realms. In the Third Abode, one manifests as a Buddha within ten thousand realms.
Continuing in this manner up to the Tenth Abode, one manifests as a Buddha within immeasurable worlds to lead and benefit sentient beings. All of these...
It is precisely because they are able to permeate their inconceivable bodies with objectless great compassion that they are capable of such [attainments].
To "skillfully enter the Buddha-wisdom" means nothing other than being able to accord with the principle of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). And as for the ten...
Practicing as a bodhisattva, one is able to cultivate the subtle, wondrous, and inconceivable practices of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
In accord with the inconceivable principle of the dharma-realm, one enters the wisdom of the Buddha. This is precisely the Buddha-wisdom;

from it, one gives rise to the practices of the dharma-realm, and by means of these practices of the dharma-realm, one again enters the Buddha-wisdom. Thus, it is the Buddha-wisdom returning to enter the Buddha-wisdom. By means of this—

The Dharma-realm returns to the Dharma-realm; fundamentally, there is neither one who enters nor that which is entered. Therefore, the ten practices are praised as "skillful entry," for they constitute the thorough penetration of great wisdom.

The "Great Wisdom" is precisely the *sarvākārajñatā* (all-aspect omniscience). Yet the essence of this wisdom is fundamentally vast, pervading the entire *dharmadhātu*, and is originally without obstruction.
It is solely due to the deluded attachments of all sentient beings that the vast becomes narrow and the pervasive becomes obstructed.
From this, both principle and phenomena, cause and effect, self and other—[are all...]

[Otherwise], there would be a separation between phenomena and reality. However, for a Bodhisattva at the stage of the Ten Dedications (*daśamī-bhūmi*), the three types of wisdom shine forth perfectly and the three truths are fully manifested.
Being able to turn phenomena toward principle, turn causes toward the fruit, and turn the self toward others, then phenomena and principle are no longer separated.

Self and other are non-dual; cause and effect are identical as one. Thus, regarding the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), there is nothing it does not pervade in its vastness, and nothing it does not reach in its omnipresence.
Reaching the other shore:

birth and death constitute this shore, while nirvāṇa constitutes the other shore. Although a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage has already shattered forty grades of ignorance and is thus able to shoulder all things and give rise to all things, they can yet bear the ocean of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge).
Entering the stream of destiny, one may reach the other shore of nirvana as if pointing it out.
His fame shall be heard throughout immeasurable worlds, and he will be able to deliver hundreds of thousands of sentient beings who have not yet received instruction.

This praises Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*). "Name" (*nāman*) refers to that which expresses the essence and manifests its virtues; "appellation" (*yaśas*) refers to the beautiful resonance that is manifested externally.
This is because one who has attained Equal Enlightenment has ascended to the dignity of the Stage of Rebirth (*upapatti-bhūmi*);

the virtues he manifests are about to be fulfilled, the wisdom he realizes is about to be perfected, the stages he traverses are about to reach their limit, and the afflictions he has severed are about to be exhausted. Therefore, his existing name and appellation are able to—

This shall be heard throughout immeasurable worlds. Having already attained the state of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksaṃbodhi), one must necessarily further pass through the gates of profound mystery to sever the subtle ignorance of the final mark of birth.
Thereafter, one will again take what was previously cultivated and what was previously delivered [to others].
Once again, he personally experienced this process. At this point, those transformed were ever more numerous and those reached were ever more far-reaching;
thus it is said that he was able to deliver countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings. △ Fifth, the listing of names, which has two parts. First, the individual listing.
Their names were: Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva,
Nityodyukta Bodhisattva, Anikṣiptadhura Bodhisattva, Ratnapāṇi Bodhisattva, Bhaiṣajyarāja Bodhisattva, Sūradatta Bodhisattva, Ratnacandra Bodhisattva,
Candraprabha Bodhisattva, Pūrṇacandra Bodhisattva, Mahābala Bodhisattva, and Trailokyavikrama Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattvas—Bhadrapāla Bodhisattva, Maitreya Bodhisattva, Ratnakūṭa Bodhisattva, and Nāyaka Bodhisattva—are all characterized by constant diligence without rest;
their names differ, but their meaning is the same, differing only in that some employ negation (paryudāsa) while others employ affirmation (vidhi).
Regarding "transcending the three realms," there are two kinds of three realms: those within the realm and those outside the realm. II. Summary.
Thus, there were eighty thousand such Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas present together.
△ Third, the miscellaneous assemblies, sevenfold: first, the assembly of devas; second, the assembly of nāga kings; third, the assembly of kinnaras.
Fourth, the assembly of gandharvas; fifth, the assembly of asuras; sixth, the assembly of garuḍas; seventh, the assembly of human kings.
Regarding the first [of these], there are again two [subdivisions]: first, the desire realm.
At that time, Śakra Devānām-indra was present together with his retinue of twenty thousand devaputras.
There were also the devaputra Candraprabha, the devaputra Samantagandha, and the devaputra Ratnaprabha.

The Four Great Kings were also there together with their retinues of ten thousand devaputras, as well as the devaputra Īśvara and the devaputra Maheśvara, together with their retinues of thirty thousand devaputras.
△ Second, those of the Form Realm (rūpadhātu):
Śikhin Mahābrahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World, Mahābrahmā Prabhāsa, and others,
together with their retinue of twelve thousand devaputras.
△ Second, the assembly of nāga kings.
There are eight nāga kings: Nanda the nāga king, Upananda the nāga king, Sāgara the nāga king, Vāsuki the nāga king, Takṣaka the nāga king, Anavatapta the nāga king, and Mucilinda the nāga king.
The Utpala Dragon King and others, each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.
△ Third, the Kiṃnaras:
there were four Kiṃnara kings—Dharma Kiṃnara King, Sudharma Kiṃnara King, and Mahādharma [Kiṃnara King].
King Nara and King Dharmadhara Kinnara, each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.
△ Fourth, the Gandharvas:
there are four Gandharva kings—King Rati, King Rutasvara Gandharva, and King Manojña Gandharva.
The Asura King Vemacitra and the Gandharva King Manojña, each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.
△ Fifth, the Asuras: there were four Asura kings—Vemacitra Asura King, Khara-karṇa Asura King, [Bali Asura King, and Rāhu Asura King].
The Asura King Vemacitrin and the Asura King Rāhu each came accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues. 6. The Garuḍas.

There were four garuḍa kings: the garuḍa king Mahātejas, the garuḍa king Mahākāya, the garuḍa king Mahāpūrṇa, and the garuḍa king Manojña; each was accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.
Among the eight classes [of beings], the two classes of yakṣas and mahoragas are absent; this is merely an omission, for they were not excluded from the assembly.

Thus, in the section on the auspicious omens of the joy of the multitudes below, they are both present. Initially, among the celestial hosts, there are only those of the desire realm and the form realm, but none of the formless realm.
Dragons and birds belong to the category of animals; the rest are all subsumed under the category of ghosts (preta). However, there are simply no [beings of the] earth [realm].
As for those in the hells and the gods of the formless realm who do not participate in this assembly, it is as clarified by the four propositions in the Great Sūtra:

first, those who are urgent in their vehicle but lax in their precepts; second, those who are urgent in their precepts but lax in their vehicle; third, those who are urgent in both vehicle and precepts; and fourth, those who are lax in both vehicle and precepts.
That ghosts and animals are now permitted to join the assembly indicates that they are those who are urgent in their vehicle but lax in their precepts. Regarding the precepts...
Because their practice was lax, they fell into the realms of ghosts and animals; because their practice was urgent, they were able to hear the sound of the Dharma.

As for the gods of the formless realm who did not join the assembly, it was because their adherence to the precepts was urgent while their practice was lax. Because their adherence to the precepts was urgent, they were able to be reborn as gods.

If one’s practice of the vehicle (*yāna*) is lax, one will not be able to hear the Dharma. Those among the devas of the desire and form realms, as well as the human multitudes, who are permitted to attend the assembly, are those for whom both the vehicle and the precepts are urgent.
Because their precepts are urgent, they are born among humans and devas; because their practice of the vehicle is urgent, they further obtain the opportunity to hear the Dharma.
Those in the hells who are not permitted to attend the assembly are those for whom both the vehicle and the precepts are lax. As for the precepts...
Laxity is the reason for falling into hell; negligence is the reason for not hearing the Dharma. △ Section Seven: The Assembly of Kings.
King Ajātaśatru, the son of Vaidehī, together with several hundreds of thousands of attendants.
Although there are three different categories above, they all constitute the fifth section on the assembly of fellow listeners. The listing of the multitude is now complete.
△ Fourth, the conclusion of the assembly:
each paid homage at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit on one side.
This is the general conclusion. △ Second, the specific introduction (*pratyaya-nidāna*). "Specific" is said in contrast to "general. The "general" applies universally to all scriptures;

the "specific" pertains exclusively to the present sutra. The five matters—such as the essence of the Dharma (*dharma-tattva*)—that establish faith are common to all scriptures, and thus they are called "general.
The five chapters—such as the assembly of the congregation—that initiate the teaching are distinct from other scriptures, and thus they are called "specific. This concludes the specific introduction.

Regarding the "Introduction": Since the Tathāgata desired to preach this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, if there were no introduction to serve as its causal basis, by what means could the "Correct Main Body" be preached?

Therefore, at the time when the fourfold assembly had gathered like clouds, he immediately preached the *Anantaparyāya-sūtra* and entered the *Anantaparyāya-samādhi*; thus did the heavens rain down [flowers].
The earth shook in such a manner. Maitreya arose from this to express his doubts and pose questions, while Mañjuśrī contemplated the past to provide answers.
Once this sequence of inquiry and response had been established, the Tathāgata arose from samādhi and was able to preach this sutra.
Therefore, there is the first chapter of text, "The Prologue," which serves as the introduction to the present sutra.
The *Zhengzong* (Orthodox Lineage) serves as the preface. Yet, how can it be seen that this preface alone is capable of initiating this sutra?
It is because it reveals the great purport of the entire scripture. What is this great purport? It is that the person, principle, practice, and teaching—these four—are all wondrous.
Therefore, there are five chapters in the preface and four sections in the main body; if these two were not interrelated, [the work would be incomplete].
Thus, what constitutes the sequence of the "Preface" (xu) and the "Main Body" (zheng)? It is such that by reading one chapter, the purport of the "Four-in-One" (sì-yī) becomes manifest before one;
and upon investigating the "Four-in-One," the meaning of the five chapters resonates with it.

Only then is it the sequence of the Preface being the Preface, and the Main Body being the Main Body. The preceding four periods correspond to this; how could the present *Myōhō-kyō* (Lotus Sūtra) ever transcend this?
Therefore, these five chapters are initiated; each of the four [sections] is wondrous. How is it that we know this person is a wondrous person? As the sutra says:
"If there are those who hear the Dharma, there is not one who does not become a Buddha. Since there is none who does not become a Buddha, then this person is indeed a wondrous person.
How is it that we know this principle is a wondrous principle? As the sutra says: "This Dharma abides..."
The Dharma-position: the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding. Since the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding, then the principle is the wondrous principle.
How is it known that practice is wondrous practice? As the sutra says:
"Even raising a single hand, or slightly bowing the head, all have already attained the Buddha-way. Since all have attained Buddhahood, then practice is wondrous practice. Why?
One sees that this teaching is the wondrous teaching (*miaojiao*). As a sutra says: "Within the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the One Vehicle Dharma;
there is neither a second nor a third. Since there is neither a second nor a third, the teaching is indeed the wondrous teaching.

Thus, what is elucidated throughout this single sutra does not exceed these four types, all of which are wondrous. Furthermore, within this preface, there is the assembly of the multitude and the manifestation of auspicious omens.
The fourfold sequence of raising doubts and providing answers is able to give rise to the four excellences of this sutra. What are they?
Because the fourfold assembly surrounds [the Buddha], they are able to perform offerings through the three karmas, thereby becoming inconceivable persons;
thus, the "Preface on the Gathering of the Assembly" can give rise to the excellence of the person who delivers the formal teaching. This follows next.
The light of the white tuft between the eyebrows fully represents the wondrous wisdom of the Middle Way;

that which it illuminates—the eighteen thousand lands—fully represents the wondrous realms of the three thousandfold world-system. That these eighteen thousand lands are illuminated by a single ray of light signifies that the entire realm is identical to wisdom.
That a single ray from the white tuft illuminates the eighteen thousand lands signifies that the entirety of wisdom is identical to the realm. This is thus...
If wisdom and its object are entirely non-dual, then the manifestation of auspicious omens in the introduction can serve to initiate the subtle principle of the formal exposition.
If there were no doubt, one would not pose questions, and furthermore, one would be unable to give rise to practice from understanding.
Now, the great assembly of Maitreya each gave rise to doubts in their minds; where there is doubt, there must be inquiry; where there is inquiry, there must be an answer.
Through the answer they hear, and through hearing they attain understanding. Once they have attained understanding, they will naturally give rise to practice based on that understanding.
Therefore, the Introductory Chapter on Doubt serves as the means to initiate the excellence of the practice of the True Teaching.
As for the questioner who asks and the respondent who answers: by citing the ancient Buddha Dīpaṃkara, they corroborate the present Śākyamuni;

since the ancient Buddha emitted light and preached the Sublime Dharma, the present Buddha’s manifestation of auspicious signs likewise indicates that he shall preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Thus, the Introductory Chapter on Question and Answer may proceed.
This refers to the initiation of the sublime teaching of the correct exposition. As it is with this present sutra, so it is with other sutras as well;
some are expounded with an introductory occasion (*nidāna*). For example, the *Vimalakīrti* uses the offering of the canopy to express praise as its introduction;
the *Prajñāpāramitā* uses the donning of robes and holding of the alms bowl as its introduction; and the *Śūraṅgama* uses the accidental entry into a brothel as its introduction.
Now, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* initiates its discourse by means of the assembly gathering, the manifestation of auspicious signs, the posing of questions, and the providing of answers.
The text is divided into five parts; the first is the "Preface of the Assembly Gathering."
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by the fourfold assembly, who made offerings to him with reverence and praised his supreme majesty.
"At that time" refers to the period immediately after the fourfold assembly had gathered, but before he had yet preached the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*.
The World-Honored One (Bhagavat) is none other than our Buddha, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, the sovereign of this single transformation in the Sahā world.

Because the Tathāgata has perfected the three types of awakening and fulfilled the ten bodies—awakening like one from a great dream and blossoming like a lotus flower—he is revered and gazed upon by all the worlds;
thus, he is called the World-Honored One. Regarding the "fourfold assembly" (catur-parṣad), some say it refers to...
It is not improper for these bhikṣus to serve as the fourfold assembly; however, while the name is narrow, its meaning is not comprehensive.

To explain this in detail: first, those who act as echoes and shadows (*prati-bimba*); second, those who initiate [the teaching]; third, those who are the appropriate recipients (*yathā-bhavya*); and fourth, those with whom a karmic connection is established (*saṃbandha*). Regarding "echoes and shadows":

Just as a form has a shadow, and a sound has an echo, when the Tathāgata preaches a sūtra, there must be ancient Buddhas and sages who descend while concealing their forms to assist in the transformation of the Dharma;
these are called "shadows and echoes. Those in the present sūtras such as Avalokiteśvara and others are examples of this.
As for "initiating," it means to lead forth and give rise to [the teaching]. If the Tathāgata intends to preach a sūtra, he must first manifest [this].
This serves as the introduction; only then can the formal exposition begin, which is why it is called "initiation. In this sutra, Maitreya and others are such individuals.

As for those who are "responsive to the occasion," they are those capable of eliciting the Buddha’s coming to respond to them. When the Tathāgata preaches a sutra, there must necessarily be a responsive capacity to whom it is addressed.
These are people whose faculties have matured and whose conditions have been activated. If they do not hear the teaching, that is the end of it; yet, as soon as they listen even once—

Upon hearing it, they will certainly be able to awaken, enter, and attain liberation; therefore, they are called "those who meet the occasion. Those in the present sutra, such as Śāriputra and others, are examples of this.
As for those with whom one forms a karmic connection, they possess none of these three supreme capacities; their roots and faculties from previous lives are extremely shallow.
Thus, although they hear what is taught, they are not only unable to practice, realize, or enter into it, but they are also unable to believe or accept it.
This is understood. It is called "forming a karmic connection" (*kyōen*) because it serves as the causal condition for attaining liberation in the future;

those who withdrew from their seats during the present sutra are examples of this. As for "surrounding," when the Tathāgata first attained perfect enlightenment, devas and humans wished to pay him homage but did not know the proper method.
Thereupon, a deva from the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven manifested in human form and came [to lead the way].

They went to where the Buddha was, prostrated before him, and circumambulated him; having circumambulated him, they prostrated again. They did this three times—three prostrations and three circumambulations.

Because all people took this as their model, it is called "circumambulation. Now, it is said that when the Tathāgata wished to preach this sutra, there were first those śrāvakas listed above who, having heard the Buddha’s voice-teaching, realized the principle of the Four Noble Truths. They contemplated the process of arising in forward order and... in reverse order.

One contemplates the Pratyekabuddhas who follow the path of cessation and extinction, the Bodhisattvas who transform themselves and others, and the eight classes of beings who protect and uphold the Buddha-dharma;
whether as those who have been inspired by the Buddha’s influence or as those with whom he has established a karmic connection through the teaching, they all surround the Buddha.

Therefore, it is said: "At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by the fourfold assembly. Regarding "making offerings, revering, honoring, and praising," this does not consist merely of surrounding him;
they were further able to perform acts of offering, specifically within the sphere of bodily action (*kāyakarman*).

Thus, they reach the utmost in humility, reverence, and respect, without any negligence or laxity. Within their mental karma (*manas-karman*), they reach the utmost in focused attention and veneration, without any distraction.
Within their verbal karma (*vāk-karman*), they are able to offer praise through various forms of speech;
hence it is said that they "make offerings" and so forth. △ Second, the sequence of manifested auspicious omens. This...
This is called the "Preface of Manifesting Auspicious Omens. For instance, when Maitreya poses a question, he asks: "By what causes and conditions do these auspicious omens appear?
When Mañjuśrī provides the answer, he says: "In the past, I have seen such omens under various Buddhas.
Desiring to cause all sentient beings to hear and know this Dharma that is difficult for the world to believe, I manifest these omens."
Based on this, we know that this is the introductory section manifesting auspicious omens (*prātihārya*). How, then, can this be known? These six [sections] are all called "omens.
This is because forty years ago, when other sutras were being taught, he also first spoke of the Dharma to serve as an introduction to the main body of the teaching.
However, the Dharma he then taught only spoke of two dharmas, three paths, and four fruits; it did not speak of the two dharmas [of the present].
The three paths and four fruits emerge from a single dharma. Now, it is taught that the immeasurable emerges from this one;
this is the definitive teaching of retribution, which gathers the immeasurable back into the one. Therefore, the preaching of the Dharma is an auspicious omen.
In the past, he would likewise enter samādhi, but necessarily before preaching the Dharma; now, however, he enters samādhi after preaching the Dharma.
Therefore, entering into meditative concentration is an auspicious omen. In the past, flowers also rained down; however, they could not fall as four distinct types simultaneously.
That which was manifested and reported was nothing more than the gradual causes of the two vehicles—the partial and the small. Now, however, the four flowers rain down together.
This fully manifests the retribution of the forty stages of the perfect cause; thus, the raining of flowers is an auspicious omen.
In the past, there was also an earthquake, yet it could not pervade the entire Buddha-world with its sixfold trembling.

What such [past] manifestations signified was merely the breaking of view-delusions and thought-delusions, or the breaking of delusions as numerous as motes of dust, or at most the gradual breaking of ignorance. Now, however—
Throughout all Buddha-worlds, the earth shook in six ways; this fully signifies the retribution for the complete shattering of the six stages of ignorance—shattering the one, one shatters all;
severing the one, one severs all. Therefore, the trembling of the earth is an auspicious omen. In the past, there was likewise universal joy.
However, they were not able to do as the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings did—rejoicing all together and contemplating the Buddha with single-minded focus.

What was manifested and reported was nothing more than the distinction between the great and the small, or the small and the great, or perhaps the arousal of faculties that were a mixture of the great and the small.
Now, however, the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings all rejoice together and contemplate the Buddha with single-minded focus.
This is because the movement of those whose karmic conditions are fully matured and perfectly complete has been stirred; thus, the multitude rejoices in this auspicious omen.

In the past, he also once emitted light from the white tuft between his eyebrows, yet [beings] were unable to fully perceive the tenfold dharma-realm or witness the perfect illumination of the Dharma-transformation across the five periods.
Now, from the Avīci Hell below to the vision of the Buddhas above, the ten realms are fully manifested.

From the initial vision of the sūtras and dharmas being preached to the final vision of those entering parinirvāṇa, the five periods are perfectly illuminated. Thus, the emission of light is an auspicious omen.
Since each of these six is individually an auspicious omen, they constitute the "Preface of Manifesting Auspicious Omens. This is divided into two parts: first, the auspicious signs within this land;
second, the auspicious signs in other lands. The first part has six sections; the first is the preaching of the Dharma.
For the sake of the bodhisattvas, he preached a Mahāyāna sūtra titled *The Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*, a teaching for bodhisattvas, which is protected by the mindfulness of the Buddhas.

It was the Tathāgata’s original intention to preach this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* for the sake of the śrāvakas, in order to reveal that the path you have been practicing is actually the bodhisattva path; therefore, he first preached it for the bodhisattvas as a preliminary indication of this. As for "Mahāyāna":

"Vehicle" (yāna) has the meaning of "transportation. If one speaks of the vehicles of humans and devas, they can only transport one out of the three miserable realms, but cannot transport one out of the triple world (*tridhātu*).
The vehicle of the śrāvakas and the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas can only transport one out of the triple world, but cannot transport one out of the three emptinesses (*trishūnyatā*).
The partial and gradual vehicle of the bodhisattvas can only transport one out of the three emptinesses, but cannot transport one back to the three virtues (*triguṇa*).

The secret treasury (guhyakośa) is not, in all cases, designated as the Mahāyāna. That which is now taught for the sake of Bodhisattvas does not merely transport one out of the three miserable realms (tridurgati);
it can also transport one out of the triple world (traidhātuka). It does not merely exit the triple world; it can now lead one out of the three emptinesses (trishūnya).

Not only can it lead one out of the three emptinesses, but it can also transport one back to the secret treasury of the three virtues (triguṇa). Therefore, it is called the Mahāyāna. This is its name.
The "Infinite Meanings" refers to the realization of the single true reality (*ekasatyalakṣaṇa*), which gives rise to the infinity of the two dharmas, the three paths, and the four fruits.
That is to say, whether it be the teachings, the principles, or the practices, all are infinite. However, since even the principle itself is not merely one, how could it not be infinite?
This is because the names of the gates are applied to the principle; the principle follows the gates. Since the gates are manifold, the principle is likewise manifold.

It is immeasurable. Regarding the "Dharma for teaching Bodhisattvas": this Dharma does not teach those in the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātu*), nor does it teach the two vehicles (*dvi-yāna*); it teaches only Bodhisattvas.

Regarding the "Dharma protected by the Buddha's mindfulness": if one says that [the Buddha] long remained silent regarding this essential point and did not strive to preach it quickly, it is therefore called "protected by the Buddha's mindfulness.
This refers to the Immeasurable Meaning (*apramāṇārtha*), which is an alternative name for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

This is the explanation. If one were to provide an introduction to and explain the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* by way of the *Anantārthika-sūtra*, it would mean that this very *Anantārthika-sūtra* is that which is protected and remembered by all Buddhas.

Specifically, for forty years prior, [the Buddha] had only spoken of the "innumerability" (*ananta*) of two dharmas, three paths, and four fruits; he had never yet spoken of these [other] kinds of innumerability arising from a single dharma.
It emerges. Now, in the *Anantārthika-sūtra*, it is precisely taught that the infinite arises from a single dharma;
therefore, the *Anantārthika-sūtra* is that which is protected and remembered by all Buddhas. Since the infinite emerges from this one dharma, [it is so].
Thus, one may gather the immeasurable and return it to the One; for this reason, I have composed this preface for the present sutra. Question:

Regarding the assembly that heard the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*, namely those previously listed—śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and so forth—within a single period of teaching, the bodhisattvas were already able to enter [the truth] everywhere.
Therefore, the *Āgamas* teach only half [of the path], and even the *Prajñāpāramitā* [teaches only the other half].
The general and specific expositions of the Perfect Teaching are all intended for those śrāvakas of dull faculties. Today’s *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* specifically intends for those śrāvakas.
Why is this? Because the *Anantamukhasamādhi-sūtra* (the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*) was preached as a prologue to this present sūtra.
It merely states that [the Buddha] "expounded Mahāyāna sūtras for the sake of all bodhisattvas" and "taught the Dharma for bodhisattvas.
Yet, was it not the case at that time that he did not [teach] for the śrāvakas, nor did he teach the śrāvakas? Answer: There are three points to this. First, it explains the infinite meanings.

I have therefore composed this preface for the present sutra. Since this sutra seeks to bring all back to the stage of the śrāvaka and clarify that what they practice is the bodhisattva path, it is intended solely as a token of gratitude for the various bodhisattvas and the teachings for bodhisattvas.
Second, it is not for the sake of the śrāvakas, but is correctly intended for the bodhisattvas; the śrāvakas are merely peripheral.
Now, we follow only that which is primary. Third, while the śrāvakas follow after Prajñāpāramitā, they secretly obtain distinct benefits.
Since these distinct benefits pertain exclusively to the dharma of the bodhisattvas, at this time the śrāvakas are also, in fact, bodhisattvas. △ Second, entering meditative concentration.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, he sat cross-legged and entered the Samādhi of the Station of Immeasurable Meaning.
His body and mind were unmoving. As for his body and mind being unmoving, it was because at the time he entered samādhi, his entire being became one with that samādhi.
In this state of profound stillness, the entire samādhi consists of body and mind. One does not perceive a subject who enters nor an object entered.
Thus, observing the body externally, the body has no self; one sees it as being like a vajra, immovable. Observing the mind internally—
Thus, the mind has no mind; one perceives only that it is as tranquil as empty space. Therefore, it is said that body and mind are unmoving.
△ Third, the raining of flowers.
At that time, the heavens rained down māndārava flowers, mahāmāndārava flowers, mañjūṣaka flowers,
and mahāmañjūṣaka flowers, scattering them over the Buddha and the great assembly.
"At that time" refers to the period immediately following when the Tathāgata had finished preaching the sutra and entered meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
*Mandārava* flowers—translated here as "pleasing flowers"—are first called "small pleasing flowers" and subsequently "great pleasing flowers";
they are also termed "small white flowers" and "great white flowers. *Mañjūṣaka* flowers—translated here as "soft flowers"—are first called "small soft [flowers]."
Soft. Next is the Great Softness (*mahāmṛduka*), also called the Small Red Flower (*kṣudra-rakta-puṣpa*) and the Great Red Flower (*mahā-rakta-puṣpa*).

Now, flowers signify the cause (*hetu*); these four flowers that rain down from the heavens signify that which issues forth from the Heaven of Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-deva*) as the subtle and wondrous perfect cause of the forty stages. Thus, Tiantai said: "The *māndārava*..."
The Ten Abodes (daśabhūmi) open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; the Mahāmandara corresponds to the Ten Practices (daśacaryā), which demonstrate the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;

the Mañjuṣa corresponds to the Ten Transferences (daśapariṇāmanā), which awaken to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; and the Mahāmañjuṣa corresponds to the Ten Grounds (daśabhūmi), which enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Although there are these differences among the forty stages, they are all collectively the single Heaven of the Ultimate Meaning (paramārtha). It is merely...
The one ultimate celestial nature manifests through the differences of the forty stages;
thus, the four flowers fall from the heavens as a symbolic response. That they are scattered upon the Buddha and the great assembly signifies this.
This inconceivable perfect cause is precisely what is realized by all Buddhas and what is inherently possessed by all sentient beings.
Yet, when the Buddhas realize it, there is nothing realized; they fully realize that which is possessed by sentient beings. When sentient beings possess it, there is nothing possessed;
they fully possess that which is realized by the Buddhas. Thus, the Buddha and sentient beings are equal, and cause and effect are one.
They originate from the same source. Therefore, after scattering them over the Buddha, they again scatter them over the great assembly to manifest this meaning. △ Fourth, the shaking of the earth:
throughout the entire buddha-world, it quakes in six ways.

Regarding the six kinds of earthquakes: the earth represents ignorance. Now, as we wish to preach this wondrous *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, we cause all sentient beings to fully attain the Buddha’s knowledge and vision—its opening, revealing, awakening, and entering—and to reach the ultimate fulfillment of the fruit of wondrous enlightenment.
Thus, they will certainly be able to overturn and shatter ignorance; it is for this reason that the six kinds of earthquakes are used to symbolize the shattering of ignorance.
△ The Five Assemblies Rejoice.
At that time, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, devas, nāgas,
yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and all others within the assembly rejoiced.

The minor kings, the wheel-turning sage-kings, and this great assembly attained what they had never before experienced. With joy, they joined their palms and gazed upon the Buddha with single-minded devotion.
Regarding "attaining what they had never before experienced": forty years ago, they had also heard him preach the Dharma, yet they had never before heard [it in such a manner].
It has been taught that from one arises many; it has also been seen that [the Buddha] enters meditative absorption, yet never before has he entered absorption after preaching the Dharma.
The heavens have also rained flowers, yet not as they rain today;
the earth has also trembled, yet not as it shakes today. Such auspicious omens as these, which are witnessed today, are indeed...
To see what has never been seen before; that which is heard today is indeed hearing what has never been heard before. Therefore, it is said that one has attained what was never before attained.

Regarding "single-mindedly contemplating the Buddha," there are two meanings. First, the multitude perceives an extraordinary omen and realizes that the Buddha must surely preach an extraordinary Dharma;
they wait expectantly to hear this wondrous teaching and sever all other thoughts, and thus single-mindedly contemplate the Buddha. Second, [the second meaning follows...]
The minds of the assembly do not turn toward the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*), nor do they accord with the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).

Furthermore, they do not turn toward the partial, gradual, provisional, or inferior [teachings], but turn solely toward the One Buddha’s Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*); therefore, they contemplate the Buddha with a single mind. △ Six: Gathering the Light.
At that time, the Buddha emitted a ray of light from the white tuft between his eyebrows, which illuminated eighteen thousand worlds in the eastern direction, pervading them all without exception;
it reached downward as far as the Avīci Hell and upward as far as the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
This statement regarding "illuminating the eastern direction" refers to horizontal illumination; illuminating above and below refers to vertical illumination.

Akaniṣṭha—translated here as "obstructive matter"—is the Heaven of Ultimate Form (Rūpa-kṛtsnāyatana). Now, if this emission of light is explained according to the characteristics of the phenomena that serve as its indicators, then those illuminated include the six realms of existence and the four types of noble ones; thus, it encompasses both ordinary beings and sages, as well as the causes for their respective states.
The fruition results in the differences between the delusion and enlightenment of Buddhas and sentient beings.
Furthermore, regarding a single ray of light and the eighteen thousand lands, there are variations in their quantity and magnitude, as well as in their distance and spatial orientation.
Now, within a single ray of light, it is able to illuminate the eighteen thousand lands and perceive the ten kinds of dharma-realms; thus, their quantity and magnitude are unified.
Thus, distance and proximity, as well as self and other, are non-dual; ordinary beings and sages, as well as cause and effect, share the same essence;

and living beings and Buddhas, as well as delusion and enlightenment, are without distinction. Therefore, this is able to manifest the subtlety of the principle. If one explains it by way of the essential nature of the principle that is manifested:
Thus, the single light between the eyebrows is entirely the mind that is capable of contemplation in a single momentary thought;
the eighteen thousand lands are entirely the objects of contemplation, consisting of the three thousand natures and appearances. This single light fully illuminates all eighteen thousand lands.

The eighteen thousand lands are all simultaneously illuminated by a single light; this is because within a single, infinitesimal thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*), the three thousand realms (*tri-sahasra-lokadhātu*) are fully and perfectly present.
These three thousand realms are fundamentally co-existent within that single thought-moment.

The single thought-moment does not precede them, nor do the three thousand realms follow after it. The single thought-moment is not diminished, and the three thousand realms are not increased. Therefore, between the eyebrows...
The light from the mark of the white tuft of hair illuminates eighteen thousand lands.

I [personally] maintain that the phrase "illuminating the eighteen thousand lands of the eastern direction, reaching everywhere without exception" precisely clarifies the object of illumination in order to manifest this auspicious omen;
it is the complete inclusion of what is seen in those other lands, as stated below regarding the omens in those lands: "All see the multitudes of the six realms of existence in those lands."
They are born. Furthermore, they see the Buddhas currently residing in those lands, and so on, until it says:

"They further see the Buddhas after their parinirvāṇa, where stupas made of the seven treasures are erected for their relics. Thus, within a single ray of light, the ten kinds of dharma-realms and the flavors of the teachings of the five periods are all fully perceived.
Therefore, one knows that the four characters "nothing is not encompassed" (靡不周徧) exhaustively include everything.
"Other lands" refers precisely to what is seen here; this is the auspicious omen of the emission of light.
That it extends "down to Avīci and up to Nirmāṇarati" means that it illuminates the six realms of existence within this land. As for the six realms of other lands, it is stated below:
"I see all the sentient beings in the six realms of those lands. Thus, if one is preaching the Dharma in the presence of this land, it is as follows:
The Buddha and those who hear the Dharma are the Three Vehicles; they see for themselves without waiting for the light to illuminate them.
Furthermore, from the Avīci Hell below to the Nirmāṇarati Heaven above, the entire assembly on Vulture Peak is fully contained within the white tuft of light.
Thus, while this land speaks only of the six realms of existence, the ten realms are likewise complete therein. This, then, is the auspicious omen of light in this land.
The text originally concludes with "upward as far as the Akaniṣṭha Heaven. From this point downward, it concerns the auspicious signs of other lands.

If one were to take the passage beginning with "downward as far as the Avīci Hell" and apply it to the illumination of the eastern direction, then the single description of emitting light would entirely resemble the auspicious signs of the earth and would not pertain to this land.
△ Second, the auspicious signs of other lands. Formerly this was also divided into six parts; now they are combined into two.
First, seeing ten kinds of dharma-realms:
within this world, one sees the entirety of those lands and the sentient beings of the six destinies therein; furthermore, one sees the Buddhas currently residing in those lands.
The first two lines refer back to the preceding section concerning the gathering of light.
