It is likewise so. Thus we know that when the Buddha of the present preaches the Great Dharma, after he has entered meditative concentration, the heavens rain down four kinds of flowers.
This is intended to moisten and cause growth; therefore, it is said that "he rains the great rain of Dharma. Next is the phrase, "blows the great conch of Dharma."

This is the auspicious sign that answers the joy of the assembly. Furthermore, he reflected that when the Buddhas of the past, after the fourfold assembly had rejoiced and following one round of manifestation and response, transformed the three vehicles into the one vehicle and redirected the nine realms back to the Buddha-realm—just as it was with the Buddhas of the past, so it shall be for the Buddha of the present.
Following the joy of the fourfold assembly of the present Buddha, he should likewise proceed to blow the great Dharma conch, causing...
The fourfold assembly transforms the nine realms and the three vehicles, thereby returning to the Buddha-realm and the One Vehicle. Thus it is said, "Blowing the great Dharma conch.
The subsequent phrase, "Beating the great Dharma drum," answers the auspicious sign of the earth quaking.

I reckon that after the six kinds of earth-quakings experienced by the Buddhas of the past as a manifestation of their realization, there were Bodhisattvas who overturned and shattered the ignorance of the six stages.

Now the Buddha likewise causes the earth to quake in six ways; this must be because he intends to beat the great Dharma drum to cause all sentient beings to overturn and shatter the ignorance of the six stages.
Therefore, it is said that he beats the great Dharma drum. Next, the single phrase "expounding the great meaning of the Dharma" answers the auspicious omen of the emission of light.
I surmise that when the Buddha of old emitted light from between his eyebrows, it illuminated eighteen thousand [worlds].
After first manifesting these signs, [the Buddha] causes all sentient beings to hear the unsurpassed Great Dharma so that they may achieve ultimate perfection.
Now, the Buddha emits light from between his eyebrows, illuminating eighteen thousand lands;
this must be because he intends to expound the great meaning of the Dharma, so that all sentient beings may together attain ultimate perfection. Therefore, it is said: "To expound."
Regarding the Great Dharma Teaching, these five phrases answer the preceding manifestation of omens.

Although the entry into meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is not explicitly mentioned, since the four omens—such as the raining of flowers and so forth—all appear by virtue of entering concentration, citing those four inherently includes the entry into concentration.
If one explains these five phrases according to the subsequent main body of the teaching, the first phrase, "desiring to expound the Great Dharma," is a general clarification of its accomplishment.
The forty stages constitute the perfect cause (*pariniṣpanna-hetu*). My intention is this:

as I reflect upon the Buddhas of the past, immediately after manifesting auspicious signs, they would preach the Great Dharma, thereby enabling sentient beings to open, show, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, thus accomplishing the perfect cause of the forty stages of abiding, practice, direction, and ground (*vihāra-caryā-pratipatti-bhūmi*). Now, the World-Honored One has likewise manifested these auspicious responses.

Furthermore, he wishes to expound the Great Dharma of the One Vehicle’s perfect reality, so that all may attain the opening, revealing, awakening, and entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, thereby accomplishing the perfect cause consisting of the forty stages.

Next, the four lines beginning with "raining down the great [Dharma]" specifically clarify the accomplishment of the perfect cause of the forty stages. "Raining down the great Dharma rain" clarifies...

The Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*) open up the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. "Rain" carries the meaning of moistening and growth; if one hears the wondrous Dharma, one can naturally open up the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
From the first abode to the tenth abode, the entire life-force of wisdom is progressively moistened and nourished.
Since all *dharmakāyas* increase part by part, it is said that "the great rain of Dharma is showered.

Blowing the "great conch of Dharma" clarifies the ten practices (*daśacaryā*) and demonstrates the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. This is because the conch has the significance of transforming and proclaiming commands;
if one preaches the Great Dharma, it can cause sentient beings to demonstrate the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, thereby transforming the designation of the ten abodes (*daśavihāra*). And...
This constitutes the Ten Practices; hence it is said that he "blows the great Dharma conch.
Striking the great Dharma drum clarifies the Ten Transferences, which is the awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. For a drum carries the meaning of admonition and exhortation:

if one preaches the Great Dharma, it can cause sentient beings to awaken to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, providing the alertness and encouragement to progress from the Ten Practices to the Ten Transferences; therefore, it is said:
This is the striking of the great Dharma drum. It expounds the great principles of the Dharma. This clarifies the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and leads one into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

Generally, "expounding" implies making clear the underlying meaning. If one preaches the Great Dharma, it can cause sentient beings to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and achieve the ten stages;
that is, it destroys the forty grades of ignorance and manifests the forty divisions of the three virtues.
Compared to the previous stages of abiding, progressing, and heading toward [enlightenment], this is profound; therefore, it is said that "the great Dharma and its principles are expounded.

Nevertheless, by considering a single passage and applying it both to what precedes and what follows, these two interpretations exhaustively clarify the meaning and fully capture the essential intent.
△ Second, the verification. This is divided into two parts. First, the general verification:
"O sons of good family, in the past, I have seen this omen among the Buddhas of the past. After emitting such light, they immediately preached the Great Dharma.
Therefore, you should know that the present Buddha’s manifestation of light is likewise so; he desires that all sentient beings may attain [it]."
It is because [the Buddha] has heard and known that this is a teaching difficult for all the world to believe that he manifests this auspicious sign.
Regarding the phrase "in the past, etc.," it means: "How could my previous answer lack a definitive basis?
It is an auspicious sign that I have previously witnessed in the presence of the Buddhas of the past," thus speaking these words. Now, he cites the past to provide empirical proof; first—

This is a general clarification; hence it says, "I [attain enlightenment] under all Buddhas" (and so forth). Regarding the phrase "desiring to cause sentient beings [to attain awakening]," one might ask:

since the present Buddha is just like the Buddhas of the past, and he wishes to preach the Great Dharma, why does he not simply expound it directly, rather than first manifesting various auspicious omens before speaking?
One should know that regarding the Dharma to be preached, it can only be heard by means of this [manifestation] to reach that [understanding].

They have not heard it; they have heard this, yet they have not heard that. Now, you wish to cause all sentient beings—whether those or these—to hear and know this Dharma that is difficult to believe and difficult to understand. To do so, you must first verify their ordinary dispositions and give rise in them a desire for joy;
therefore, you have first manifested these various auspicious omens. Yet, by what Dharma is it considered difficult to believe?

If one were to say that the three vehicles are the three vehicles, the one vehicle is the one vehicle, the nine realms are the nine realms, and the Buddha-realm is the Buddha-realm, this would be a teaching easy to believe. However, the present sutra synthesizes the three vehicles into the one vehicle.
Thus, the three are entirely one; outside of the one, there are no three. When the nine realms are opened to become the Buddha-realm, then all sentient beings are entirely Buddhas;
outside of the Buddha, there are no sentient beings. This mutual fusion of the three and the one—the Dharma of the equality of sentient beings and Buddhas—is that which is most difficult to believe.
As for the statement that "all have heard and known it," this is because for forty years prior, he had never failed to speak of it.
There has never been a time when I have not heard it, nor a time when I have not known it; yet I am unable to cause all those in the world to hear and know it entirely.

Just as in the *Avataṃsaka* there is the non-differentiation of the three [natures], in the *Āgama* there is the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), in the *Vaipulya* there is the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), and in the *Prajñāpāramitā* there is the true emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
All these are teachings difficult to believe. While I have never failed to speak of them, they are for the person of perfect capacity in the *Avataṃsaka*.

[The Buddha] was heard and known [by them], whereas other individuals did not hear or know it. Regarding the *Āgamas*, they were heard and known from the perspective of the secret aspect, but not from the perspective of the manifest aspect.
As for the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā, these too were heard and known only by those of the Perfect Teaching; the people of the three preceding teachings did not hear or know them.
Thus, although during the forty years prior [to this teaching] he had preached dharmas that are difficult to believe, difficult to hear, and difficult to know—therefore...

It cannot be said that all have heard and known it. Now, I wish to expound the perfect and wondrous Great Dharma, which opens the nine realms to be one Buddha-realm and unites the three vehicles into one Buddha-vehicle.

Whether they be ordinary beings, followers of the two vehicles, or those of partial or gradual teachings, I desire that all may hear and know this dharma that is difficult to believe and difficult to understand, so that all may receive its revelation.
To awaken to and enter into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is no small matter. It is necessary to verify this through ordinary experience and increase one's yearning for it;
this is why these various auspicious omens are manifested. Thus, we know that the manifestation of these omens is none other than for the sake of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

Therefore, in the preceding passage where the assembly gathers, the "wondrous person" is indicated by the report, while the "wondrous principle" is indicated by the manifestation of the omens. This is the point of doubt.
The "Recollection" (Nien) section expresses the marvelous practice; the "Question and Answer" (Wenda) section expresses the marvelous teaching.

That which initiates [the discourse] is entirely through the "Correct Exposition" (Zhengshuo), and the "Correct Exposition" is itself entirely the initiation. This is the great purport of the sequence between the introduction and the main body.
That which one must know. △ Second, the specific verification, divided into three parts: first, clarifying the very first Buddha;
second, clarifying the middle twenty thousand Buddhas; third, clarifying the final Buddha. The first part [of the first section] further has three sub-sections. First, citing the time period.
"O sons of good family, in the past, immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago— [this is] the second [section],
which sets forth the names of the Buddhas. At that time,
there was a Buddha named Candrasūryapradīpa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata..."
The Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One—this Buddha was named Candrasūryapradīpa (Moon-Sun-Lamp Radiance).
Just as the sun illuminates the day, it serves as a metaphor for that Buddha’s knowledge of the paths and their fruits (*mārgajñatā*).
The moon’s ability to illuminate the night is used as a metaphor for that Buddha’s omniscience (*sarvajñā*), which is able to know existence.

The lamp is that which can illuminate what the sun and moon cannot reach; this is used as a metaphor for that Buddha’s knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), which is able to know the intermediate state.
Because that Tathāgata is fully endowed with these three types of wisdom, he observes and realizes them perfectly; it is in accordance with these virtues that [he is so described].
He manifested his name; thus he was titled "Sun, Moon, and Lamp Brightness," which is his specific epithet. "Tathāgata" is the general title.

"Arhat" (Worthy of Offerings) means that he is fully endowed with the two virtues of wisdom (*jñāna*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*); therefore, he is worthy of receiving offerings from all sentient beings.

"Samyaksaṃbuddha" (Perfectly and Fully Awakened One) means that if one only knows existence and does not know emptiness, or knows emptiness but does not know the Middle Way, or knows the Middle Way... [and so forth].

Not knowing both emptiness and existence is not universal knowledge (*parijñā*). If one knows only existence and does not know emptiness, then the existence known is not "wondrous existence" (*miaoyou*);
it cannot be that by means of one existence all existences are known.

Furthermore, if one knows only the Middle Way and does not know emptiness and existence, then the Middle Way known is not the "perfect Middle Way" (*yuanzhong*); it cannot be that by means of one Middle Way all Middle Ways are known. Thus...
This is because it cannot be called "correct knowledge. That Tathāgata not only knows existence, but also knows emptiness;

not only knows the middle way, but also knows both emptiness and existence. Therefore, he is called the "Omniscient One" (sarvajña). Since these three types of knowledge are perfectly realized, that which is known as existence—
This is indeed wondrous existence (*sadbhāva*). Within this single existence, all existences are contained; even among all objects of knowledge, this is the perfect middle.

Within this single middle, all middles are contained; therefore, it is called "right knowledge. Regarding the term "one whose conduct is perfected by clarity" (*vidyācaraṇasampanna*): "clarity" (*vidyā*) is precisely wisdom (*prajñā*).
Conduct is itself merit. If one possesses wisdom but lacks merit, that wisdom becomes madness. If one possesses merit but lacks wisdom, affairs do not accord with principle.
That Tathāgata is fully endowed with both merit and wisdom; therefore, he is called "One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct" (*vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna*).
"The Well-Gone One, Knower of the World" (*sugato lokavidū*) is another title, because he is able to transcend birth and death and reach nirvāṇa.

Therefore, he is called the Sugata. Although he has attained nirvāṇa, he does not cling to nirvāṇa; he returns to the realm of birth and death to deliver sentient beings, and is thus called the World-Honored One (Lokanātha).
Although he remains in the world, he is not defiled by the world, and is therefore called the Liberated One (Mukta).
As for the Unsurpassed Being (Anuttarapuruṣa), the unsurpassed path is realized solely by the Buddha alone, transcending both the mundane and the supramundane.
He is called the Unsurpassed One (*anuttara-puruṣa*). As for "Tamer of Men" (*puruṣa-damya-sārathi*):
because the Tathāgata can preach the Dharma of the Truths and Conditions, he tames ordinary beings who are attached to existence and leads them to Emptiness;

because he can preach the Dharma of the Six Perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), he tames those of the Two Vehicles who are attached to Emptiness and leads them to Existence; and because he can preach the Perfect and Sudden One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

He is the Dharma that tames those sentient beings who are bodhisattvas yet remain biased or gradual, leading them back to the Middle Way; therefore, he is called the "Tamer of Men" (Puruṣadamyasārathi).

He is the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Great Master of the three realms and the Compassionate Father of the four modes of birth. In the Sanskrit language he is called Buddha, which in the Chinese language means "Awakened.
He has awakened himself and awakened others; his awakening and practice are perfected. The three types of awakening are complete and the myriad virtues are fully possessed.

Therefore, he is called "Buddha. Possessing the nine titles mentioned above, he is the most honored among those of both the mundane and supramundane realms; therefore, he is called "World-Honored One" (Lokanātha).
△ Third, the explanation of the teaching of the Dharma, which also has three parts. First, the explanation of the Sudden Teaching is the same [as before].

He expounds the True Dharma, which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; its meaning is profound and far-reaching, its phrasing is exquisite, it is pure and unadulterated, and it is fully endowed with the characteristics of the pure and holy life of Brahma-faring.
Within the exposition of the Dharma, the five periods are fully elucidated. That which expounds the True Dharma (*saddharma*) is the Great, Ultimate, and Perfectly Correct Dharma.
If there were distinctions among mind, Buddha, and sentient beings, it could not be called "Correct. The *Avataṃsaka* clarifies that mind, Buddha, and sentient beings are non-distinct;
therefore, it is named the True Dharma. Regarding "good in the beginning," this refers to the *Avataṃsaka*'s means of expression (*vyañjana*).
The excellence of the teaching refers to the perfection of the *sūtras*.
The excellence of the middle refers to the principle elucidated by the *Avataṃsaka*, which is the Great Universal Characteristic Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

The excellence of the end refers to the practice initiated by the *Avataṃsaka*, which is the inconceivable conduct of Samantabhadra. Since the teaching is the means of expression, it is called "the beginning," while the practice is [the end].
Because it arises based on principle (*yukti*), it is called "subsequent" (*paścima*). Principle is that which is expressed (*vācya*) and is also the basis (*āśraya*);

as it stands between the two pillars of teaching (*deśanā*) and practice (*pratipatti*), it is therefore called "middle" (*madhya*). Since the expressive teaching is already complete, the expressed principle is the *dharmadhātu*, and the practice that arises from it is that of Samantabhadra;
thus, all are virtuous (*kuśala*). Some claim that these three virtues constitute the three vehicles (*triyāna*), but they do not understand [this].
That sutra consists only of the Separate and Perfect [Teachings]; how could there be three vehicles? Its meaning will be established in the following explanation.

Regarding "the meaning is profound and far-reaching": this refers to the excellence within the establishment of the meaning. It means that the principle being expounded is good; therefore, its meaning is profound and far-reaching.
Vertically, it penetrates the Three Truths, such that no one can fathom its depths; hence it is called "profound. Horizontally, it exhausts...

Within the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), there is no one who can exhaust its boundaries; therefore, it is called "distant. Furthermore, the principle elucidated by the *Avataṃsaka* possesses two aspects of teaching:
in its specific meaning, it is "profound" because it follows a sequential order; in its perfect meaning, it is "distant" because it is characterized by perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*).
Its phrasing is skillful and subtle; this explains the fulfillment of the "goodness in the beginning," meaning that the teaching which serves as the means of expression is itself good.
Its language is skillful and subtle. Regarding "skillful and subtle": although the *Avataṃsaka* incorporates the Separate (Bia) teaching, its primary intent lies in the Perfect (Yuan).
However, because the Purely Perfect alone is difficult to believe and understand, it employs the Separate as an auxiliary means for manifestation.
Because the Separate serves as an aid, it is called "skillful"; because it succeeds in manifesting the Perfect, it is called "subtle. The phrase "Purely One, etc. is an explanatory elaboration.
"Subsequent goodness" means that because the conduct that has been aroused is wholesome, it is "pure, singular, and unadulterated," and so forth.

Because it is solely the inconceivable, wondrous conduct of Samantabhadra, it is called "pure and singular. Because there is no conduct of the outflowing or non-outflowing, nor of ordinary or Hinayana practitioners, it is called "unadulterated.
That which can destroy delusions is termed "clear"; that which can manifest virtues is termed "white. [To destroy delusions...]

Thus, there are no delusions that are not destroyed—whether they be those of views and thoughts, those as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, or the ignorance of the ultimate; all are utterly destroyed.
As for the manifestation of virtues, there are no virtues that are not manifested—whether it be the Dharma-body, Prajñā, or Liberation; all are fully revealed.
Therefore, it is said that they are "complete and pure. Furthermore, the practice of the Separate Teaching (biejiao) belongs exclusively to the Bodhisattva Dharma;
hence, it is called "purely singular" (*chunyī*). The practice of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao), however, is nothing other than the cause for Buddhahood; hence, it is called "unmixed" (*wúzá*).

In the Separate Teaching, one must destroy afflictions to realize Bodhi and sever birth-and-death to manifest Nirvana; hence, it is called "clear" (*qīng*). In the Perfect Teaching, however, it is not so...
It must be overturned and shattered. Afflictions and birth-and-death are from the beginning entirely Bodhi and Nirvana; therefore, it is called "white.
△ Second, the teaching of the gradual dharma is the same.
For those seeking the state of a śrāvaka, he teaches the Dharma corresponding to the Four Noble Truths, so that they may transcend birth, old age, sickness, and death, and ultimately attain nirvāṇa.
For those seeking the state of a pratyekabuddha, he teaches the Dharma corresponding to the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination.
This refers to the teaching of the Tripiṭaka of the Āgamas, which correctly transforms those of the two vehicles; it is identical to the initial gradual teachings now spoken by the Buddha.
For the sake of the bodhisattvas, he teaches that they should practice the six pāramitās.
In this Vaipulya Prajñāpāramitā, during these two periods, there are bodhisattvas belonging to all four teachings; therefore, it says "all.
The six pāramitās likewise differ according to the four teachings. In the Tripitaka Teaching, they are the six pāramitās with signs (sanimitta). In the Shared Teaching...
These are the six *pāramitās* of signlessness; this is the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*). These are the six *pāramitās* that are both with signs and without signs;
this is the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). These are the six *pāramitās* that are neither with signs nor without signs;
this is identical to what the Buddha has now taught as the "gradual within the gradual" at its final stage. △ Third, reconciling the Perfect Teaching.
To cause them to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and achieve the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*)—this is the preaching of the Lotus Sūtra.
It is said that whether they be followers of the two vehicles or bodhisattvas, upon reaching this, the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are all revealed to them.
They attain unsurpassed bodhi and achieve all-encompassing wisdom (sarvākārajñatā); therefore it is said, "causing them to attain... and so forth.

The Āgamas represent the beginning of the gradual [teaching], while the Vaipulya Prajñāpāramitā represents the middle and end of the gradual, culminating in the convergence of the gradual toward the sudden.
These are merely the texts of the Three Vehicles. Now, classifying according to the texts: those for the śrāvakas and others belong to the Āgamas, while those for the bodhisattvas...

The passage beginning with "Sakyamuni and others" belongs to the two *sūtras*. To cause [beings] to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and so forth is where they ultimately converge. This single phrase alone fully encompasses all four flavors.
This is the skillful teaching of Mañjuśrī, the skillful compilation of the scribe, and the skillful interpretation of Tiantai.
△ Second, clarifying the twenty thousand Buddhas of the intermediate period.
Next there was another Buddha, also named Candrasūryapradīpa. Next there was another Buddha, also named Candrasūryapradīpa.
In this way, twenty thousand Buddhas all shared the same name, Candrasūryapradīpa. Furthermore, they shared the same clan; their clan was Bharadvāja.
Maitreya, you should know that from the first Buddha to the last Buddha, they all shared the same name, Candrasūryapradīpa. (10)
The title is "Complete. Regarding the Dharma that is preached, it is good in the beginning, middle, and end.
As for the phrase "the Dharma that is preached," this means that among all dharmas that can be expressed, there are none that are not good.

When considering the essence of the Dharma, it is fundamentally inexpressible; yet, because of causes and conditions, it can also be expressed. Such expression accords with the capacities of sentient beings.

Therefore, it is said that the Dharma which can be taught is identical to the *Avataṃsaka* of the One Buddha. Regarding the three aspects of teaching, practice, and principle (*śāsana*, *caryā*, *tattva*), there is nothing that is not good;
hence, it is called "good in the beginning, middle, and end. If one considers the two phrases "that which can be" [taught], they may also fully clarify the three periods [of time].

As for the causes and conditions of those with the capacities for the Separate (Vaipulya) and Perfect (Ekayāna) teachings, the sudden Dharma can be taught; thus, it is taught in accordance with their specific capacities.
The *Avataṃsaka* constitutes the "goodness at the beginning. If there are the causal conditions of those with the capacities for the four teachings, then the gradual Dharma may be preached;
thus, in accordance with their capacities, one preaches the *Āgama*, the *Vaipulya*, and the *Prajñāpāramitā*. This constitutes the "goodness in the middle.

If there are the causal conditions of those with the capacity for the pure and perfect [teaching], then a Dharma that is neither sudden nor gradual may be preached; thus, in accordance with their capacities, one...
The preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* constitutes "goodness at the end. The *Avataṃsaka* belongs to the earliest period of the teaching and thus is called "the beginning";

the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* represents the ultimate culmination of the proclamation and thus is called "the end. The three flavors (*trivyañjana*) occupy the intermediate space between the "milk" and the "clarified butter" (ghee), and are therefore termed "the middle.
Whether beginning, middle, or end, each accords with the capacities of sentient beings; hence they are called "good. △ Third, the clarification.
Regarding the last Buddha, there are again three points. The first two have already been explained as being the same [as the previous Buddhas].
As for that last Buddha, before he had left the household life, he had eight princes. The first was named Yǒuyì (Possessing Intent).
Some say: "In the past, the Buddha had eight sons; now the Buddha has but one son. How can they be the same?
Now it is said that although their numbers are unequal, they are the same in being sons. One name is "That Which Possesses Intention" (*yǒuyì*);

"possessing" (*yǒu*) refers to wondrous existence (*mìoyǒu*), namely the three thousand natures and characteristics and the ten suchnesses of the hundred realms. By means of this prince, one is able to thoroughly comprehend and manifest [reality].
Within a preceding momentary thought of consciousness, the wondrous existence of the three thousand natures and characteristics is fully and perfectly present.
Taking this as the basis for circular contemplation and circular illumination, one designates it with a name based on its inherent qualities; thus, it is called "possessing meaning."
The second is named "Good Intention" (*Sādhumati*).

"Good" refers to the myriad practices of the six perfections and all manner of virtues. Because of this prince, even his infinitesimal mental consciousness is able to enter universally into the gates of the myriad practices and all virtues; therefore, he is named "Good Intention."
The third is Immeasurable Intention (*Amitābha*).
The essence of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) pervades the entire dharma-realm; this is what is meant by "immeasurable.
Because this prince is able to know that within even a single, infinitesimal thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*), this dharma-nature is fully present, he is called "Immeasurable Intention."
The fourth is named Ratnamati.
All the merit and the wealth of the Dharma possessed by the Buddhas are called "jewels.
Because this prince is able to accumulate all the merit and the wealth of the Dharma of the Buddhas within a single moment of causal thought, he is named Ratnamati.
Furthermore, the fifth is called "Increasing Intention" (*vṛddhyāśaya*).
Because the three virtues become partially manifest, it is termed "increasing. By means of this, the prince is able, in the present moment, for even a mere instant—

The mind of mindfulness takes this as the subject of contemplation; it is precisely this very mind that becomes the object of contemplation. The three virtues thus attained are clearly manifested through partial realization.
To designate them by names based on what is thus revealed is precisely what is meant by "increasing the meaning" (zēngyì).
The sixth is named "Dispelling Doubt.
As for "dispelling doubt": "dispel" means to eliminate and sever; "doubt" refers to uncertainty.
Because this prince was able to completely sever the three delusions within a single moment of mental consciousness, it is called "Dispelling Doubt."
The seventh is named Resonant Mind.
Just as sound has its resonance, this prince is able, within a single moment of mental consciousness, to internally harmonize with principle and externally observe the capacities of beings;
from this, he responds to their capacities by preaching the teaching, employing the teaching to meet their needs.
It is like an echo responding to a valley; therefore, it is called the "echo-intention" (*pratiśrutkā-manas*).
Eighth is the "dharma-intention.

Dharma refers to the eighty-four thousand treasuries of the Dharma (*dharmapiṭaka*). By means of this, the prince is able, within a single moment of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), [to comprehend them].
Within this [assembly], they were all able to receive and uphold the Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas;
therefore, he was named Dharmamati. These eight princes possessed sovereign majesty and virtue, each governing four continents.

When these princes heard that their father had left the household life and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they all renounced their royal thrones and likewise followed him into the homeless life, vowing...

The intention of the Mahāyāna is that they constantly cultivate the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) and all serve as Dharma-preachers. They have already planted various roots of goodness under ten million Buddhas.
Some say these are the names of the eight princes; these are all secular appellations, so how could they be used for the Dharma?
Regarding the explanation of the "gate": one must realize that the Eight Princes had long since planted the roots of all manner of wholesome virtues;

therefore, upon leaving the household life, they were immediately able to give rise to the Mahāyāna aspiration and become Dharma-preachers. If this is so, how could it be that they did not already know the Dharma-gate?
Yet why is it designated by a conventional name? Therefore, all [explanations] are provided by way of the *dharmaparyāya*.
To speak of "generating the mind of the Mahāyāna" refers precisely to generating the four great vows (*caturmahāpraṇidhāna*) of seeking enlightenment above and transforming beings below.

The four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa-citta*)—compassion (*maitrī*), pity (*karuṇā*), joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*)—are called the "Brahma-conduct" (*brahmacarya*). One practices them at every thought-moment, at all times, and in every place; hence it is said:

This refers to constant cultivation. △ Second, clarifying that the present [assembly] is identical [to the past] in two ways. First, the manifestation of auspicious omens is identical; second, the arising of doubt is identical. Regarding the first, there are again two parts.
First, the six auspicious omens in this land are identical to those of the present Buddha.
At that time, the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa preached a Mahāyāna sūtra titled *Ananta-artha*, a teaching for bodhisattvas, which is protected by the Buddhas.
Having finished preaching this sūtra, he sat cross-legged in the midst of the great assembly and entered the *Ananta-artha-vyūha-samādhi*.
His body and mind remained unmoving. At that moment, the heavens rained down *māndārava* flowers and *mahāmāndārava* flowers.
Rohita flowers, Mañjūṣaka flowers, and Mahāmañjūṣaka flowers were scattered over the Buddha and the great assembly.
The entire Buddha-world shook in six ways. At that time, within the assembly, there were bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, [and upāsikās].

The upāsikās, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans and non-humans, as well as the minor kings and the wheel-turning sage-kings—this great assembly attained what they had never experienced before.
With joy, they joined their palms and gazed upon the Buddha with single-minded devotion. At that time, the Tathāgata emitted a ray of light from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows.
The light of the marks shines upon eighteen thousand Buddha-lands in the eastern direction, pervading them all without exception.
The meaning of these six auspicious omens is as explained previously; here we shall simply read the text and conclude by stating that this is the omen of the preaching of the Dharma.
...up to the sixth cloud, which says: "This is an auspicious sign of the emission of light. △ Second, the six auspicious signs in other lands are the same as those of the present Buddha;
they are just like the various Buddha-lands seen here now.

"Those who are as they are now" refers to the fact that as this Buddha’s single ray of light shines eastward, the ten kinds of dharma-realms and the five periods of dharma-transformation within eighteen thousand lands are all made manifest; therefore it says, "as is seen now," and so forth.
△ Second, the identity of their doubts.
Maitreya, you should know that at that time, within the assembly, there were twenty billion bodhisattvas who desired to hear the Dharma.

When these bodhisattvas saw this radiance universally illuminating the Buddha-field, they experienced what they had never known before and wished to understand the causes and conditions for which this light appeared.
Since doubts have already arisen, there should likewise be questions and answers; they are merely abbreviated here. △ Third, the clarification that [the two cases] are identical.

This also has three parts: first, showing their identity; second, resolving doubts; third, synthesizing the connection. The first part has seven sections. First, identity in terms of the causes and conditions.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Wondrous Light (Prabhāsa) who had eight hundred disciples.
As for this bodhisattva Wondrous Light, he was so named because he was able to perfectly illuminate the three truths with the three wisdoms;
wisdom is entirely identical to the object, and the object is entirely identical to wisdom. The perfect fusion of object and wisdom is inconceivable; therefore, he is called Wondrous Light.
Furthermore, the phrase "there were eight hundred disciples" constitutes a refutation of an objection; it serves merely as a foundational basis for the subsequent section that resolves doubts.
△ Second, the identity of the teaching.
At that time, the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa arose from his samādhi and, through the Bodhisattva Prabhāketu, preached a Mahāyāna sūtra titled the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*,
the Dharma taught for the sake of bodhisattvas and protected by the Buddhas.
Regarding the phrase "because of Wondrous Light and others," these are the ones for whom the teaching is intended (the *pratipakṣa*).
However, while that Buddha [Dīpaṃkara] had bodhisattvas as his intended audience, the present Buddha has śrāvakas as his intended audience. How, then, are they the same?

One should understand that in that case, Wondrous Light’s work of transformation was already accomplished; therefore, he was called a bodhisattva. Now, however, Śāriputra’s work of transformation is not yet complete; therefore, he is called a śrāvaka.
One should know that before the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, Wondrous Light (Prabhāketu) was never anything other than a śrāvaka.
After the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, Śāriputra likewise ought to have attained the status of a bodhisattva. Regarding "the teaching for bodhisattvas":

if those of the two vehicles hear this sutra and their Mahāyāna faculties are stirred, they too are indeed bodhisattvas. Regarding "those whom the Buddha protects and keeps in mind": because [they have practiced] for a long time...
This is the essential point: do not strive for rapid speech. △ Third, the duration is the same:
for sixty minor kalpas he did not rise from his seat, and those in the assembly who were listening likewise remained seated in one place for sixty minor kalpas.
With body and mind unmoving, they listened to what the Buddha taught for what seemed like the duration of a meal;
at that time, not a single person among the assembly felt weariness or fatigue, whether in body or mind.

Regarding the statement that "sixty minor kalpas are like the duration of a meal": this is generally because one’s mind is so intensely focused on the Dharma that one perceives a long duration as short.
Conversely, if the mind is distressed or weary, even a short time is perceived as long. Someone has asked:
"If those Buddhas' sixty minor kalpas are like the duration of a meal, why are the present Buddha's fifty minor kalpas said to be like half a day?"
How can it be that ten kalpas, which previously seemed as brief as the time it takes to eat a meal, now seem as long as half a day when reduced by those same ten kalpas?
One fails to realize that the shortening of what was long is entirely due to the supernatural power of the Tathāgata.
If he were to further shorten them, even sixty kalpas would be like the time it takes to eat a meal; if he were to shorten them slightly less, even fifty kalpas would likewise be so.
Just as with half a day, there is no one who can shorten fifty kalpas to half a day, yet there is no one who cannot shorten sixty kalpas to the duration of a meal.
△ Fourth, the same applies to the proclamation of extinction.
After the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa had preached this sutra for sixty intermediate kalpas, he addressed these words to the assembly of Brahmās,
Māras, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, humans, and asuras: "This very day, at midnight,
the Tathāgata shall enter parinirvāṇa without remainder."
Regarding those who enter *nirvāṇa* at midnight: the Tathāgata must necessarily have been born during the day and pass away at midnight;

this is surely intended as a symbolic representation. Since the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have exhausted the five abodes and forever extinguished the two deaths, how could there be birth or extinction?
That they now manifest birth and extinction is solely because they wish to transform and deliver sentient beings.
It appears to undergo arising and ceasing, yet in reality it neither arises nor ceases; that is to say, its arising has never truly arisen, and its ceasing has never truly ceased.
Now, it is said that it arises at midday and ceases at midnight. Although midday is the height of yang, its latter portion belongs to yin;
thus the Tathāgata is born from this, signifying that his arising has never truly arisen. Although midnight is the height of yin, its latter portion belongs to [yang].
In the realm of Yang, the Tathāgata passes away through this; yet this manifestation of passing away is never truly a passing away. Since he has arisen, he has never truly arisen;
since he has passed away, he has never truly passed away. Although he repeatedly manifests birth and repeatedly manifests passing away, it is solely for the sake of transforming sentient beings.
In truth, there is no arising or ceasing. △ Fifth, the Bestowal of Prophecy is the same.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Guṇākara. The Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa immediately bestowed upon him a prophecy, addressing the bhikṣus:
"This Bodhisattva Guṇākara shall next become a Buddha, titled Viśuddhakāya, a Tathāgata, an Arhat..."
"Raha Samyaksaṃbuddha. After the Buddha had bestowed this prediction, he entered *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder) during the middle watch of the night.
As for the Bodhisattva named Guṇakaraṇḍa, his name was established because he is able to contain within himself all the merit and the wealth of the Dharma belonging to all Buddhas.
Furthermore, he is himself able to enter the secret treasury of the three virtues (*triguṇa-guhya-kośa*), and is likewise able to transform others so that they may enter it together with him.

For these reasons, he is named Guṇasaṃcaya (Storehouse of Virtue). Now, when the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa arose from his meditative absorption, it was because of the preaching of the Lotus Sūtra by Prabhāpāla that Guṇasaṃcaya received his prediction.
One should know that Prabhāpāla is equivalent to Śāriputra; thus, he had already received his prediction during the preaching of the Dharma.
As for Guṇasaṃcaya now, he received his prediction after the proclamation of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, and this is merely a partial [prediction].

Regarding the "Successor" (the Bodhisattva in his final birth), one should know that this refers merely to the commonality of receiving the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), and is not discussed solely in reference to the specific individual for whom the teaching was intended.
As for the name of the Buddha, "Pure Body" (*Viśuddhakāya*): "Pure" means being able to destroy all delusions; "Body" means being able to accumulate all virtues.
This is because when the Bodhisattva Guṇagañja was in the causal stage, there were no delusions he did not eliminate and no virtues he did not cultivate.
Because it is an accumulation, the designation for the fruit is "the pure body" (*śuddhakāya*). △ Sixth, "sameness after extinction.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, this section on "after extinction" is combined with the following section on the *Sūtra* by the commentary; according to the sub-commentary, they form a single section. Here, they are divided into two.
The following verses concern the distribution of the *śarīra* relics, the construction of stupas, and various texts concerning the pursuit of the Way;
these are clearly distinguished from the sections on Miaoguang (Prabhāketu) upholding and expounding the sutra. Therefore, they are divided. △ Seven: Common to the Sutra.
The Bodhisattva Wonderful Light upheld the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and expounded it for others for a full eighty minor kalpas.
△ Second, resolving doubts, in two parts: first, resolving the doubt concerning Mañjuśrī and Śākyamuni.
The eight sons of the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa were all disciples of Prabhāsa. Prabhāsa taught and transformed them, causing them to become firm in their resolve for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
After these princes had made offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas, they all attained the Way of the Buddha.
The last among them to attain Buddhahood was named Dīpaṃkara.
The doubt is as follows: although Mañjuśrī is said to possess great wisdom, he still resides in the causal stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi) and is a disciple;
whereas Śākyamuni has attained Wondrous Enlightenment (prabhāsvara-bodhi) and is his teacher. How then can a disciple of Equal Enlightenment know his teacher of Wondrous Enlightenment?
Therefore, the text explains: "The eight sons of the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa were all disciples of Prabhāketu," and so forth.
The one who finally attained Buddhahood was named Dīpaṃkara. Since Subhāṣita (Wondrous Light) served as the teacher for the eight sons, they successively transmitted the prophecy of enlightenment;
the last of these was named Dīpaṃkara, who became the teacher of Śākyamuni.
Tracing back from this, Śākyamuni looks upon Subhāṣita as his ninth-generation ancestor. Although Mañjuśrī today serves as the teacher of Śākyamuni...
Disciple: If one traces this back to the past, he was originally the ancestor of Śākyamuni. Since he was his ancestor, what doubt could there be regarding his knowledge and understanding?
As for the statement that "Miao Guang (Prabhāsa) taught and transformed others," it refers to the time when the eight princes previously followed their father to leave the household life.
To "give rise to the Mahāyāna intention" is precisely to have already generated the bodhicitta. Subhūti feared that he might regress from the Great Vehicle and take up the Small Vehicle;
therefore, he instructed him regarding the mind he had generated so as to prevent his retrogression. Thus it is said, "to cause it to be firm.
△ Second, resolving the doubts of Maitreya and Mañjuśrī.
Among his eight hundred disciples, there was one named *Yashaskāma* (Seeker of Fame). He was greedily attached to gain and offerings;
although he recited many sutras, he did not master them and forgot much of what he had learned, which was why he was called "Seeker of Fame.
Because this man had also planted various roots of goodness, he encountered immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas, whom he served, honored, and revered.
He praised them again.
A doubt arises: since both Mañjuśrī and Maitreya are equally *samyaksambuddhas*, why does he question Maitreya specifically, rather than Mañjuśrī?
Why does he answer specifically for Mañjuśrī, rather than Maitreya? To resolve this, the commentary states: "Among the eight hundred disciples, there was..."
There was one person named *Yāśas* (Seeker of Fame). In this way, Maitreya was indeed a disciple of Mañjuśrī; as a disciple, he ought to have questioned him.
Mañjuśrī was indeed the original teacher (*mūla-ācārya*) of Maitreya; as the original teacher, he ought to have answered. Why, then, is there any doubt?
As for the mention of "Seeker of Fame" and the like, it does not refer to an ordinary person who craves fame and seeks profit; rather, it refers to—

Their greed for fame and profit arises because they do not realize that the *parikalpita* (imagined) nature is fundamentally empty, the *paratantra* (dependent) nature is illusory existence, and there is only the *pariniṣpanna* (perfected) nature.
Therefore, it is said that they are greedy for gain and offerings, and even fail to penetrate the profound meaning. △ Third, the conclusion and synthesis.
Maitreya, you should know this: at that time, was the Bodhisattva Wonderful Light anyone else? It was my very self.
As for the Bodhisattva Seeking Fame, he was you yourself.
△ Section Five: Mañjuśrī’s Response and the Judgment of the Text.

Now, seeing this auspicious omen, it is no different from that of old. Therefore, I reflect: today the Tathāgata shall preach a Mahāyāna sūtra entitled the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the Dharma taught for the sake of bodhisattvas, which is protected by the mindfulness of the Buddhas.
This is Mañjuśrī’s response. As for the necessity of citing the Buddha as a witness: if one were to speak of this directly on one's own authority, there would be no means of verification;
who then would be willing to believe it? It is said that empty words are not as good as evidence from actual facts; therefore, he cites the past as his answer.
Furthermore, as for the necessity of extensively citing twenty thousand Buddhas: if he were to cite only one or two Buddhas, [the proof would remain incomplete].

Regarding the three, four, or five Buddhas, their realization is the same; yet people still do not place great faith in this, thinking, "Even if those Buddhas were thus, how could the present Buddha be so?
Therefore, [the text] extensively cites twenty thousand Buddhas, none of whom are otherwise, so that people may come to believe and accept it.
Furthermore, in Maitreya’s question, he refers to the eighteen thousand [Buddhas] seen in the light in the eastern direction.
The question regarding the thousand lands reveals the horizontal [dimension], which is identical to the present Buddha’s establishment of transformation.

Mañjuśrī’s answer, however, responds by citing the Buddhas seen throughout incalculable kalpas of the past, thereby revealing the vertical [dimension], which is likewise identical to the present Buddha’s establishment of transformation.
In sum, whether taking up the horizontal or the vertical, there is nothing that is not identical, thereby manifesting that the present Buddha has emerged from samādhi.
He rises and must surely preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. There is nothing that differs from what has been preached by all the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time;
thus, through this single question and answer, the introduction to the main teaching is established.

△ Second, the verse summary. Above, there were three sections in the long prose; now, it is merely a brief reflection thereof. In the preceding section on "Verification," the divisions were made into general and specific.
Second: Now, only the specific [verses] are recited. Above, there were three distinctions: the first, the middle, and the last. Here, only the first and the last are recited;
the middle is not recited. The text is divided into two parts: first, the verses on the proof and verification; second, the verses on the concluding judgment.
The first part is further divided into two: first, the verses on the very first Buddha.
At that time, Mañjuśrī, wishing to reiterate this meaning within the great assembly, spoke these verses:
"I recall a past age, immeasurable and incalculable kalpas ago, when there was a Buddha, the Honored One among Men, named Candrasūryapradīpa."
The World-Honored One expounds the Dharma, delivering immeasurable sentient beings and countless billions of bodhisattvas, causing them to enter the Buddha’s wisdom.
The first two lines praise the time; the next two lines praise the Buddha’s name; the single line “World-Honored One” praises the *Avataṃsaka*.
This refers to the passage beginning with "expounding the True Dharma, which is good in the beginning," and so forth. The line "delivering immeasurable [beings]" praises the aforementioned [purpose].
Regarding the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, the teaching of the Four Noble Truths and Dependent Origination is the Āgama.

A single phrase of immeasurable meaning, composed in verse for the sake of the Bodhisattvas, teaches the application of the six pāramitās; this is the Vaipulya Prajñāpāramitā. These are the two periods.
To cause them to enter into a single phrase is to cause them to immediately attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and achieve the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Whether they be humans or devas, followers of the two vehicles, or bodhisattvas, all shall be enabled to open, show, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
This preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* possesses five periods. II. Verse on the Final Buddha (three parts): 1. The first verse is identical to what has already been stated.
Before the Buddha had left the household life, his eight royal sons, seeing the Great Sage renounce the world, also followed him in practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
The term "Great Sage" refers to the Buddha Dīpaṃkara. The meaning of "Great Sage" is as explained in the Preface to the *Hongchuan* (Extensive Propagation).
There are three meanings of leaving the household life: first, the shaving of hair and beard; regardless of whether one’s appearance or dharma are identical, it is equally [a form of] leaving.

First is the characteristic of the household; this refers to leaving the secular home. Second, having already left the home, one practices according to the Dharma, breaks through the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāva-kleśa*), and departs from the birth-and-death of segmented existence (*paricchinna-jarāmaraṇa*); this refers to leaving the home of the triple world (*tridhātu*).

Third, relying on the Mahāyāna teachings, one practices further, breaks through the affliction of ignorance (*avidyā-kleśa*), and further departs from the birth-and-death of transformation (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*), proceeding until—
Upon attaining equal enlightenment, one becomes entirely free from even a single grade of ignorance and a single portion of transformation;
this is what it means to depart from the house of ignorance. That Buddha does not merely depart from the mundane house of the triple world, but rather departs from the house of ignorance itself.
As for the Eight Princes, although they departed from a secular household, according to the prose section of the text, they gave rise to the Mahāyāna aspiration;

thus, they may also be said to have departed from the house of ignorance. △ Second, the verse on the present commonality in two parts. First, the verse on the commonality of manifesting auspicious omens.
The two verses regarding the shared doubt are as follows; the first section also has two parts. First, the verse on the auspicious omens in this land:
At that time, the Buddha was preaching the Mahāyāna sūtra titled *Anantārtha*; amidst the great assembly, he made extensive distinctions and explanations.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, he sat cross-legged upon the Dharma-seat in a samādhi called the "Station of Immeasurable Meanings.
Heavenly *māndārava* flowers rained down, and celestial drums resounded spontaneously. The devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits made offerings to the Honored One among Men.
All Buddha-lands immediately shook with a great trembling; the Buddha emitted light from between his eyebrows, manifesting various rare and wondrous events.
As for what is called "discrimination," it refers to the differentiation of two dharmas, three paths, four fruits, and so forth, from within a single dharma.
Because there are immeasurable dharmas, it is called "vast. △ Second, the verse on the auspicious omens in other lands has two parts: first, the verse on seeing the ten kinds of dharma-realms;
second, the verse on seeing the dharma-transformations of the five periods. Regarding the first of these two, there is first the verse on the ordinary beings of the six destinies.
This light shines upon eighteen thousand Buddha-lands in the eastern direction, revealing to all sentient beings the places where they undergo birth, death, and karmic retribution.
Some see these Buddha-lands adorned with various jewels, possessing the colors of lapis lazuli and crystal; this is due to the illumination of the Buddha’s light.
Furthermore, one sees the various devas and humans, the hosts of nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and kiṃnaras, each making offerings to their respective Buddhas.
Regarding "each making offerings": among the eight classes of beings, including devas and humans, there are none who do not offer; thus it says "each.
Moreover, because there are as many as eighteen thousand lands, it says "each. △ Second, the verse on the Buddha’s teaching of the three vehicles.

Furthermore, I see all the Tathāgatas spontaneously attaining the path of Buddhahood; their physical forms are like mountains of gold, majestic and exceedingly subtle, like the image of pure gold appearing within clear lapis lazuli.

Regarding the term "Tathāgata": since the principal subject is thus raised, the accompanying elements are naturally included. This Dharma-body is equal for both ordinary beings and sages; it is one and the same in both sentient beings and Buddhas.
Sentient beings, however, remain entirely immersed in delusion and are therefore unable to manifest it. The Buddhas, on the other hand, are able to realize what is inherently present;
hence it is said that they "spontaneously accomplish the Buddha-way. As for the two lines concerning the body and its color:

This clarifies the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body) of the Tathāgata. There are two types of reward bodies: first, the *svasaṃbhogakāya* (self-enjoyment reward body), which takes the Dharma-gates as its body and possesses no visible form or appearance.

What is now described as a body and color like a mountain of gold refers to the *parasaṃbhogakāya* (other-enjoyment reward body), specifically the sublime and distinguished *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) for those of the tenth stage. This is because it is majestic, dignified, and endowed with the [major] marks.

"Excellently adorned. Therefore, it is said that he is "dignified and exceedingly subtle. The two lines beginning with "like pure lapis lazuli" clarify the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) of the Tathāgata.
Arising from the *dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya*, this response body manifests through spontaneous transformation, appearing in manifold ways without fixed location.
To illustrate this by means of a metaphor, it is like a golden image appearing within lapis lazuli; it is transparent and radiant both inside and out.
And there is no obstruction whatsoever. Yet, it is simply that the Dharma-body and Reward-body manifest as the Response-body. II. Verses on Seeing the Dharma-Transformation of the Five Periods:
The World-Honored One, amidst the great assembly, expounds the profound meaning of the Dharma. In each and every Buddha-land, the multitude of śrāvakas is incalculable.
Illumined by the Buddha’s light, I saw that entire great assembly. There were some bhikṣus dwelling amidst mountain forests, diligently upholding the pure precepts as if guarding a bright pearl.
I also saw various bodhisattvas practicing generosity, patience, and the other perfections.
Their number is like the sands of the Ganges, all due to the illumination of the Buddha’s light. Again, one sees various bodhisattvas deeply entering various meditative concentrations;
their bodies and minds are tranquil and unmoving as they seek the unsurpassed path. Furthermore, one sees various bodhisattvas who know the mark of the quiescence of all phenomena.
In each of their respective lands, they preach the Dharma and seek the Buddha-way.

The first two lines refer to the time when the *Avataṃsaka* was preached; it is "good in the beginning, middle, and end," and so forth, up to being "endowed with the characteristics of pure and white Brahma-conduct.
Next, one by one, line by line, there are innumerable śrāvakas; this refers to the *Āgamas*. Three.

Alternatively, the single line beginning with "Or there may be" (*vā punaḥ*) praises the Vaipulya (*vaipulya*). Furthermore, the two lines beginning with "Again, one sees" (*punar api paśyati*) praise the Prajñāpāramitā (*prajñā*).
Moreover, the three lines beginning with "Each and every one" (*ekaikaṃ vā*) praise the Āgamas (*āgama*), because they contain all three vehicles (*triyāna*).

Again, the two lines beginning with "Furthermore, one sees" (*punar api paśyati*) praise the two *Sūtras* (the *Prajñā* and *Dharmapada*), because they contain all the bodhisattvas (*bodhisattva*). One who knows the mark of the quiescence of phenomena (*dharmāṇāṃ śāntalakṣaṇam*) refers to... [text ends]... by means of...
The wondrous wisdom of *prajñā* contemplates all phenomena as neither arising nor ceasing, neither departing nor arriving, neither identical nor different, and neither discontinuous nor permanent.
Thus, arising and ceasing are of one essence; departure and arrival are equal; and identity, difference, discontinuity, and permanence are all unapprehendable.
This is what is meant by the fact that all phenomena are, from the very beginning, characterized by quiescence; they do not undergo further cessation.
...and so forth. △ Second, the verse on the shared doubt:
At that time, the fourfold assembly, seeing the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa manifest such great supernormal powers, their hearts were all filled with joy.
"Each asks one another: 'What are the causes and conditions for this matter?
As for "each asking one another," this does not mean that the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings speak words to question one another;

rather, they each give rise to doubts and engage in conjecture, which constitutes their mutual questioning. If it were a matter of speaking words to ask, it would have to be initiated by the assembly as a whole; [such a formal inquiry] occurs only in specific cases.
One person is none other than Maitreya within this present assembly. △ Third, the verses on the identity [of the two] consist of three parts:

first, verses clarifying their identity; second, verses resolving doubts; third, verses concluding the identification. The first part has seven sections; the first is the verse on the identity of the causal conditions.
The Honored One, revered by devas and humans, has just arisen from samādhi. He praises the Bodhisattva Wonderful Light: "You are the eye of the world; all turn to you for refuge and faith.
You are able to uphold the treasury of the Dharma. Just as I have taught the Dharma, only you can verify and know it."
The World-Honored One, having offered this praise, caused Subhūti to rejoice.

The statement that he had "just arisen from samādhi" refers to the precise moment—neither before nor after—when, following the previous manifestation of auspicious signs, the fourfold assembly had all given rise to doubt and reflection; thus, the great capacity for awakening had already been stirred.
It is thus. The Tathāgata spoke in accordance with their capacities and movements; therefore, it was merely appropriate to them.
You, who are the Eye of the World, if you did not know the wondrous principle of the true mark (*dharmatā*), would be like a blind person without eyes.
Now, as soon as the Bodhisattva Wonderful Light heard what the Tathāgata had said, he was able to understand for himself the true mark of all phenomena, just like a person with eyes. Furthermore—
Being able to guide others and perceive the sublime principle of the true reality—would this not make one the eye of the world?
Only you are capable of realizing this through direct knowledge (*pratyātmajñāna*). If others hear what the Buddha has spoken, they merely know the names and recognize the characters;
this is called intellectual understanding, not realization. Now, when the Bodhisattva Wonderful Light hears the Dharma taught by the Buddha, he does not merely...
It is known that he was literate and, moreover, was able to practice according to what he had heard and enter realization based upon it; thus, it is said that he "realized through knowledge.
As for causing Wonderful Light to rejoice: his joy did not arise merely because of the Buddha’s praise.

Previously, having seen the Buddha manifest various extraordinary omens, a sense of doubt had arisen in his mind which he had not yet resolved. Now, as the Buddha emerged from meditative concentration...
He arose and spoke of the Dharma of impermanence, saying: "The Dharma I have taught, you are able to realize and know.
This is because the Buddha’s words are not false; I am certain that I can understand what the Buddha has spoken, and thus I give rise to joy. △ Second, the verse on the identity of the teaching.
He preached this Lotus Sūtra.
△ Third, the verse on the identical duration of time:
For sixty full intermediate kalpas, he did not rise from this seat. This sublime and wondrous Dharma that was preached was [the teaching of] the Dharma Master Varaprabha.
They are all able to receive and uphold it.
△ Fourth, the verse on the simultaneous entry into extinction:
After the Buddha had preached this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and caused the assembly to rejoice, he immediately, on that very day, addressed the assembly of devas and humans.
I have already explained for you the meaning of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena. This very night at midnight, I shall enter *parinirvāṇa*.

If the meaning of the true reality of all phenomena had not been explained, my original intention for appearing in the world would remain unfulfilled and the great causal purpose would not have been clarified.
Now that it has been explained, the work of transformation is complete; there is nothing further to be done.
This is what must be done; therefore, you should enter into parinirvāṇa.
With single-minded diligence, you should abandon all heedlessness. Buddhas are extremely difficult to encounter; they appear but once in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Regarding the phrase "single-minded diligence": it is not dual regarding duality, nor triple regarding triplicity; it is simply a single mind—refined and unmixed, advancing without retreating.
Since one has already heard the wondrous principle of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), one should naturally practice in accordance with it and naturally propagate it;
therefore, he exhorts them to be diligent. As for "being free from negligence": [it means]...
Just as the six sense organs encounter the six sense objects, the six consciousnesses arise; to pursue these six objects is called heedlessness (*pramāda*).
Now, one must depart from this heedlessness. The two phrases "The Buddhas are difficult to encounter" explain the entrustment (*parindanā*);
that is to say, they cause you to be diligent and further to abandon heedlessness because the Buddhas are difficult to encounter and difficult to meet. Difficult to encounter...
Now that we have encountered this, and having met what is so difficult to meet, how could we not exert ourselves with diligence and remain free from negligence?
O sons of the World-Honored One, hearing that the Buddha has entered nirvana, each harbors grief and distress: "How swift was the Buddha’s passing!"
The Holy Lord, King of Dharma, comforts immeasurable multitudes. When I enter parinirvāṇa, you should not grieve or fear.
The Holy Lord, the Dharma-King, because he wishes to preach the wondrous Dharma, immediately preaches the wondrous Dharma;
because he wishes to manifest nirvāṇa, he immediately manifests nirvāṇa. Because he has attained great mastery over all dharmas, he is called "King. (Verse 5)
The prophecy is the same:
this Bodhisattva Guṇagañja has already attained penetration into the outflow-free true mark (*anāsrava-lakṣaṇa*).
He shall next become a Buddha named Viśuddhakāya, and he too shall deliver immeasurable multitudes.

Regarding the so-called "uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) true reality" (*dharmatā*): as the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states, "The meaning of the true reality of all phenomena is attained by those of the Three Vehicles, yet they are not called Buddhas.
One should know that the true reality attained by those of the Three Vehicles is indeed contaminated;
this is because they perceive only its emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and do not perceive its non-emptiness (*aśūnyatā*). Now, the uncontaminated true reality is such that both extremes and deviance are...
"Centrality and Rectitude" means not falling into either of the two extremes. Having attained the untainted true reality (*anāsrava-dharmatā*), the mind has already reached full penetration;
thus, the so-called "three virtues" are manifested and the "three wisdoms" are perfected. Therefore, it is said: "Next, he shall become a Buddha. △ Sixth, the verse on being equal after extinction.
That night the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, like a fire extinguished when its fuel is exhausted. His relics were distributed and immeasurable stūpas were erected.
Bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, redoubled their diligence in seeking the unsurpassed path.
The phrase "like fire being extinguished when the fuel is exhausted" is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s entry into *nirvāṇa*. This is because [the Buddha's] capacity to respond is exhausted.

Just as worldly fire exists by means of fuel, if the fuel is entirely consumed, the fire is accordingly extinguished. The faculties of sentient beings are like the fuel, and the Tathāgata’s responsive manifestation is like the fire.
When the fuel of their faculties is exhausted, the fire of his response should likewise be extinguished; therefore, it is said to be "like fuel."
When the fire is extinguished, those who redouble their diligence do so because at the time the Tathāgata announced his extinction, he charged them with single-minded diligence.
Now that the Tathāgata has entered extinction, they recall what was entrusted to them and give rise to a heart of longing and devotion;
thus, regarding the sublime Dharma he taught, they will surely attain thorough realization—namely, that which is to be attained through parinirvāṇa.
As for "delivering," it means to bring about extinction (nirvāṇa). △ Seventh, the verse on the general correspondence with the sutra:
This Dharma Master Miaoguang upheld the treasury of the Buddha’s Dharma; throughout eighty intermediate kalpas, he widely proclaimed the Lotus Sutra.
△ Second, the two verses that resolve doubts. First, the verse that resolves the doubt concerning Mañjuśrī and Śākyamuni:
"These eight princes, transformed by Prabhāsa, have become firm in the unsurpassed path; they shall behold countless Buddhas."
Having made offerings to all the Buddhas, they followed and practiced the Great Way, succeeding one another in attaining Buddhahood and receiving successive predictions of enlightenment.
Finally, there was a God among Gods named Dīpaṃkara Buddha, a guide for all sages, who delivered and liberated immeasurable multitudes.
Regarding the term "God among Gods" (*devātideva*): "God" (*deva*) refers to that which is natural and spontaneous, in the sense of excellence in bliss and excellence in body.
However, there are four different types of gods: namely, worldly gods (*laukika-deva*), born gods (*upapatti-deva*), pure gods (*śuddha-deva*), and the god of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-deva*).
Worldly gods are kings, because all their enjoyments are obtained spontaneously; therefore, they are called "worldly."

The "Heavenly Beings" (*deva*) refers to the various devas of the three realms. Because they are able to be born there through the cultivation of the ten wholesome paths of action as well as meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and because they experience spontaneous bliss, they are called "Heavenly Beings. The "Pure Beings" (*śuddhadeva*) refers to the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*.

Because they are able to cultivate the Dharma that takes the Truths as its object, they destroy the afflictions of views and thoughts, transcend the birth and death of the triple world, and attain the six supernormal powers to travel without obstruction; for these reasons, they are called Pure Heavens (*śuddhāvāsa-deva*).

As for the Ultimate Truth Heavens (*paramārtha-deva*), these are the Dharma-body Bodhisattvas from the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*) onward, because they rely upon the Middle Way of the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*) to give rise to [their realization].
Regarding the inconceivable wisdom of the Middle Way, it in turn illuminates the inconceivable realm of the Middle Way.
Upon ascending to the first stage (Prathamā-bhūmi), one is able to partially manifest the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) and evoke the land of true retribution adorned with non-obstruction;
therefore, it is named the "Ultimate Heaven" (Paramārtha-deva). Now, the Tathāgata not only transcends the heavens of the mundane world, but even transcends...
He is the Heaven of the Ultimate Truth; therefore, he is called the "God among Gods" (*devātideva*). Regarding the phrase "the guide of all sages":

"sage" (*ṛṣi*) carries the meaning of "transmigration" or "transformation," and there are many kinds. If a person of the world can cultivate the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), attain various spiritual faculties, and exercise mastery over transmigration, they are called a "worldly sage. Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas can contemplate the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and sever the three [fetters].
Those born within the realms who have attained mastery over the mind are called the *ṛṣis* of the Two Vehicles.
The great Bodhisattvas, who have shattered ignorance and sport with supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), manifesting their bodies throughout hundreds of realms, are called the *ṛṣis* of the Bodhisattvas.

If one is a Tathāgata, then the five stages of dwelling are fully exhausted and the two types of death are forever extinguished; having attained great mastery among all phenomena, one is called the *ṛṣi* of the Tathāgata. If [it concerns] the world...
The immortals of the mundane realm have not yet severed all afflictions; the immortals of the Two Vehicles have severed only the afflictions of views and thought;
and the immortals who are Bodhisattvas have not yet exhausted ignorance. None of these are called True Immortals (bhūta-ṛṣi). Only the Tathāgata is entitled to be called a True Immortal.
Furthermore, he is able to guide the various immortals of the world so as to become ultimate True Immortals; therefore, he is called the Teacher of All Immortals.
...Furthermore: △ Second, the verse explaining the doubts of Maitreya and Mañjuśrī:
"At that time, the Dharma Master Wonderful Light had a disciple whose mind was constantly steeped in indolence and who was greedily attached to fame and profit."
Seeking fame and profit without satiety, he frequented the households of the noble clans. He abandoned what he had studied and recited; his memory failed him and he could no longer master the texts.
For these reasons, he was called "One Who Seeks Fame. Yet, he also performed many wholesome deeds and succeeded in seeing countless Buddhas.
Having made offerings to all Buddhas and practicing in accordance with the Great Path, he was endowed with the six *pāramitās*. Now he beholds the Lion of the Śākyas;
hereafter he shall become a Buddha named Maitreya, who will extensively deliver sentient beings in numbers beyond measure.

"Practicing in accordance with the Great Way" means being able to follow and trust the teachings of Subhūti (Wondrous Light), thereby practicing the Mahāyāna path of a bodhisattva. △ Third, the concluding summary in verse.
After that Buddha passed into extinction, you were the one who was indolent; the Dharma Master Wonderful Light is now my own self.
△ Second, the verse summary and conclusion has four parts. First, answering the names and titles.
I saw that the Buddha Dīpaṃkara’s original radiance and auspicious signs were just like this; by this I know that the present Buddha intends to preach the Lotus Sūtra.
Regarding the phrase "the original radiance and auspicious signs were just like this," "original" (ben) refers to the past;

it means that which was manifested and reported by the auspicious signs, such as the emission of light, during the past. After the Buddha Dīpaṃkara of the past preached the Dharma and entered samādhi, he once again manifested these auspicious signs.
Thus, it is said that within the Great Dharma, the immeasurable is gathered to return to the One.

Furthermore, in the past, when the Buddha rained down the four flowers from heaven, after each manifestation of such an auspicious sign, he rained down the great rain of the Dharma, causing all sentient beings to attain the forty stages.

This completes the cause. Furthermore, in the past, after the fourfold assembly of the Buddha rejoiced and a single manifestation of auspicious signs occurred, he blew the great Dharma conch, transforming the nine realms and the three vehicles so that they all return to the single vehicle of the Buddha-realm.
Moreover, in the past, after the six earths shook and a single manifestation of auspicious signs occurred, he struck the great Dharma drum, causing all sentient beings to turn [toward enlightenment].

This destroys the ignorance of the six stages. Furthermore, in the past, after the Buddha emitted light from between his eyebrows and manifested auspicious signs once, he then expounded the great Dharma teachings so that all sentient beings might fully achieve ultimate Bodhi.
Regarding the manifestation of auspicious signs by the Buddha in the past, it was certain that he would preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. How could it be otherwise for the Buddha now? For...
From this it is known that the Buddha is now also preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. "Dharma" refers to the essence of the Dharma, while "Puṇḍarīka" (Lotus) is a metaphor.
Thus, it can be understood that the title of the present sutra is established by combining the Dharma with its metaphor. 2. Second, answering regarding the principle-essence (*li-ti*).

The present signs are identical to those of former auspicious omens; these are the skillful means (*upāya*) of all Buddhas. "Now the Buddha emits radiance to assist in the manifestation of the meaning of the True Aspect" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Regarding the statement that these are the skillful means of all Buddhas, it means that the manifestation of omens in the past was precisely a skillful means for revealing the True Aspect.
How is this known? It is because the Buddha emits this radiant omen to assist in the manifestation of the meaning of the True Aspect.
The wondrous meaning of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is made manifest by this; is it not, therefore, a skillful means (*upāya*) for the true mark?
Regarding the term "aiding and eliciting" (*sahakārin*): "aiding" is spoken of in contrast to the "correct.

If one uses the wisdom that contemplates to illumine the objective realm of the principle of the true mark, and in turn uses the objective realm of the principle of the true mark to elicit the wisdom that contemplates—thus using wisdom to illumine the realm, and using the realm...

To "bring forth" (prabhāvita) means that when the object and the wisdom are in profound accord, the true nature (dharmatā) is revealed; this is "bringing forth" in the primary sense, not an auxiliary bringing forth.

Now, [this text] merely manifests various auspicious signs to give rise to the wondrous meaning of the true nature; therefore, it is called "auxiliary bringing forth. Furthermore, regarding "auxiliary bringing forth":
