Those seeking the state of a Pratyekabuddha—monks and nuns, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas alike—looked at one another with hesitation and gazed up at the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings, wondering: "What is the meaning of this? We pray that the Buddha will explain it for us."

Among all the śrāvakas, the Buddha declared me to be foremost; yet now, regarding my own wisdom, I am beset by doubt and unable to discern whether this is the ultimate Dharma or the path that must be traversed.
The first [verse] concerns the three lower practices of the untainted (*anāsrava*). The verse summarizes that the fourfold assembly all harbored doubts;

above, the fourfold assembly was mentioned briefly, whereas now the three vehicles and the eight classes of beings are explained in detail. Since they now have doubts, it asks, "Why did the Buddha speak this?
This precisely reveals that [the teaching] had never been heard before. In the middle of the second lower practice, the verse summarizes: "From my own past until now, I have never..."
"I have heard such a teaching from the Buddha, yet since I did not hear it before, I am currently without understanding regarding this wisdom.
This clearly demonstrates that he now harbors doubt. When the Buddha declared me "foremost," it was because I was foremost in wisdom among those of the *Hīnayāna*.
The two lines beginning with "Is this the ultimate Dharma? precisely clarify his lack of understanding; that is to say, [he wonders] regarding the Tathāgata’s past...
Please speak for our sake of the ultimate Dharma of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, which we have already attained and entered.
Speak of the path practiced through precepts, concentration, and wisdom, which we have already cultivated.
Now the Tathāgata, without being asked, speaks of his own accord, further praising the Buddhas' foremost skillful means and their profound, subtle, and wondrous Dharma. As for me...
This cannot be resolved; it is unknown from where one should enter through practice. Therefore, it is said that "doubt and confusion prevent full understanding," and so forth.
△ Third, the verse requesting the teaching of the Dharma.
The sons born from the Buddha’s own mouth stand with palms joined, gazing up in expectation; we pray that you will emit a subtle and wondrous sound and, for our sake, speak according to reality.
The devas, nāgas, and spirits are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and the bodhisattvas who seek the Buddha number eighty thousand in total.
Furthermore, when the wheel-turning sage-kings from billions of lands arrive, they join their palms with a reverent heart, desiring to hear the complete path.
When the two vehicles request the teaching, a single line issues from the Buddha’s mouth; when the devas request it, two lines issue.
As for what is called "the son born," having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, he attains growth in the Dharma-body and nourishes his life of wisdom. He is able to...
One who succeeds to the family business of the Tathāgata is said to be "born from the Buddha’s own mouth. There are differences between the great and the small [vehicles].

Now, having severed the views and afflictions (*kleśa*) and having emerged from the realm of birth and death by分段 (*bhavāgra-pratibaddha*), one is a son of the Buddha of the Small Vehicle. At such a time, one is called a speaker of reality as it is.
This refers to what the Tathāgata stated above: "The Buddha, by the power of skillful means, has manifested the teachings of the three vehicles.
From this, one knows that what was previously taught was provisional and not ultimate. Furthermore, he said: "After a long time, the Buddhas must speak the truth."
Thus, one knows that whatever is spoken today must be true and not false. Yet, forty-odd years have already passed;
it may be called a long time. Now is the time for this. Therefore, I pray that the World-Honored One will respond to this time and deliver a teaching according to reality.
That which is not different is called "suchness" (tathatā), and that which is not false is called "reality" (bhūta). It is in accordance with that true mark (dharmatā) that...

Thus it is called "speaking according to reality. Next, the two lines beginning with "Then all the devas descended" conclude the request for the teaching made by the Bodhisattvas, the eight classes of beings, and the fourfold assembly.
Regarding the phrase "the complete path": the contemplations practiced by the followers of the Two Vehicles in the past were merely partial emptiness;
the principle revealed by them was merely the *satyā* (Ultimate Truth); and the afflictions they eliminated were merely those of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*).
If that which is severed—the cycle of birth and death—were merely the segmented [birth and death], then it could not be called the complete path.
If the three contemplations are cultivated in their perfection, the three truths are manifested simultaneously, the five abodes are all shattered, and both forms of death are transcended;
only then is it called the complete path. △ Second, the Tathāgata’s cessation.
At that time, the Buddha said to Śāriputra: "Stop, stop! There is no need to speak further.
If this matter were to be spoken, all the worlds—including gods and humans—would be filled with alarm and doubt."
At that time, when the Tathāgata spoke "Stop, stop," he meant that since the matter cannot be understood through words, he had previously refrained from speaking.
Yet, because the fourfold assembly has doubts and requests [an explanation], my intention is that it would be more excellent to simply refrain and not speak.
Therefore, he said, "Stop, stop; there is no need to speak further. Next, regarding the passage "If one were to speak," the underlying meaning is as follows: Why?
It is not said to be wonderful. That is to say, if my speaking it would be of benefit to humans and devas, I would naturally speak of it myself;
for now, since I do not speak it, let it be. If I were to speak of it once, all humans and devas would be startled and give rise to doubt.
Once they doubt, they cannot have faith; if they do not have faith, they will give rise to slander; if they slander, they will fall into suffering. This, then—
It would not only be of no benefit to humans and devas; on the contrary, it would actually cause harm to them. This is why [the Buddha] said, "Stop, stop, do not speak.
△ Second, the request according to the faculties and lineages, in two parts: first, the prose; second, the verse. The first part has two sections: first, the formal request.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha again, saying, "World-Honored One, I only pray that you will speak; I only pray that you will speak.

To say "I only pray" twice means that because I have requested on behalf of the fourfold assembly who harbor doubts, the Buddha might surely refrain from speaking due to the presence of doubts among humans and devas.
From my own perspective, I further wish for the Tathāgata to explain it; therefore, I say, "I only pray."
(As stated above). △ Second, the explanation of the underlying intent.
Why is this so? Because the assembly consists of countless hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeya sentient beings who have seen various Buddhas in the past;
their faculties are sharp and keen, and their wisdom is clear and lucid. Upon hearing what the Buddha has taught, they are able to respond with reverent faith.
My intention in requesting the Buddha to speak again was this: had everyone in the assembly been filled with alarm, doubt, and disbelief, it would have been acceptable for the Tathāgata not to speak.
However, as I observe the assembly, there are countless hundreds of thousands of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* sentient beings;
regarding their past, they have previously seen various Buddhas, and regarding their present, their faculties are sharp and vigorous.
[They possess] sharp faculties and clear wisdom. If they have previously seen various Buddhas, then their past seeds are superior;

if [their faculties] are fierce, sharp, and clear, then their present causes are powerful. It would be better not to hear the teaching at all, but if they hear the Buddha’s discourse, they will not only fail to give rise to alarm or doubt, but will also be able to generate reverent faith. Therefore, they request the Tathāgata to speak. △ Second.
There are two verses. The first verse is the formal request.
At that time, Śāriputra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"O Dharma King, Supreme Honored One, please speak; pray do not hesitate."
Regarding the term "Dharma King": it refers to one who has attained great mastery over all dharmas.

This means that for forty years prior to today, when the Tathāgata wished to employ expedient means, he employed them; when he wished to conceal the ultimate truth, he concealed it. Now, at this Great Assembly on Mount Lingjiu...
When he wishes to reveal the provisional (upāya), he reveals the provisional; when he wishes to manifest the ultimate (bhūta-artha), he manifests the ultimate.

Within these teachings of the provisional and the ultimate, whether concealing, revealing, hiding, or manifesting, there is nothing in which he is not sovereign; therefore, he is called the Dharma King. △ Second, the verse stating the intention.
In this assembly there are immeasurable multitudes; among them are those capable of respectful faith.

△ Third, regarding the request for transformation, there are two parts: first, indicating the intent for the cessation [of the teaching]; second, properly explaining the acceptance of those to be transformed. The first part has two sub-sections.
In the initial prose section:
The Buddha again stopped Śāriputra, saying, "If this matter were to be spoken, all the worlds—including devas, humans, and asuras—would be filled with alarm and doubt;
those bhikṣus of overweening pride would be on the verge of falling into a great abyss."
Regarding the phrase "if one were to speak," etc., it means: I previously desisted because gods and humans were struck with alarm and doubt;

you, however, have requested again based on your perception that my faculties are sharp. Nevertheless, as I observe it, if this matter were to be spoken, not only would gods and humans be struck with alarm and doubt.
Among the bhikṣus, there are those with overweening pride who, upon hearing this, will not believe it and will surely give rise to slander, thereby falling into a great abyss.
This is why I have again desisted from speaking. The word "about to" (jiāng) refers to what has not yet occurred. It would be better not to speak at all;
for if I were to speak, they would slander it upon hearing it, and having slandered it, they would subsequently fall into suffering.
Therefore, it is said: "I shall merely indicate. △ Second, the verse summary:
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Cease, cease! There is no need to speak; my Dharma is subtle and difficult to conceive. Those with overweening pride, upon hearing it, will certainly not show respect or faith."

Regarding "my Dharma is inconceivable": if the teachings I have previously spoken—wherein the provisional is provisional, the real is real, the three are three, and the one is one—were still conceivable, then the Dharma now being taught would not be so.
This present teaching is such that the provisional is itself the real, and the three are themselves the one;

the three and the one are perfectly interfused, and the provisional and the real are non-dual. Thus, it is inconceivable. Since it is difficult even for thought to conceive, it is called inconceivable.
How could it be easy to speak? Thus it is said, "Stop, stop," and so forth. If I were to continue speaking, those who are arrogant would certainly be unable to believe it;
therefore, I have again ceased and will not speak. The previous statement spoke of falling into a great pit; this statement says that upon hearing it, they will surely not believe.
Falling arises from lack of belief, and lacking belief inevitably leads to falling. This prose passage describes the fruit of their lack of belief.
Verse: This cites the cause for falling into the pit; the text likewise clarifies this through mutual implication. △ Second, the actual explanation of receiving transformation, which has two parts:
first, the prose; second, the verse. The first of these [the prose] has two parts: first, the formal request.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha again, saying: "World-Honored One, I pray you, speak of this! I pray you, speak of this!

Although the Tathāgata has ceased [teaching] because monks with overweening pride heard it and did not respect or believe it, yet as I observe those in this assembly, how could there be only countless sentient beings who have seen various Buddhas in the past? Indeed, even in their present lives, they have followed our Buddha."

As for those who have been transformed by the teaching and are thus naturally able to revere and believe, we pray only that the World-Honored One will preach for the sake of this assembly. II. Statement of Intent:
Within this assembly now, there are hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis like ourselves, who in life after life have already received transformation from the Buddha.
People such as these will certainly be able to develop reverent faith; they will enjoy peace and security for a long night and receive great benefit.
The intention is that since they have received transformation through the Buddha in life after life, they will not merely have seen various Buddhas, and thus they will certainly be able to believe.
Question: Regarding "receiving transformation through the Buddha in life after life" and "having previously seen various Buddhas," if it is as stated in the following text...
Only after this exposition has been completed will one understand that the Buddha constantly taught and transformed [beings] in the presence of twenty trillion Buddhas in the past.
Now, why does Śāriputra say that he has seen various Buddhas and received their transformation life after life? The answer is as follows:
This is not otherwise. It follows generally from what was previously stated in the introductory section, where Mañjuśrī said:
"In the past, when the Buddha Dīpaṃkara preached the Lotus Sūtra, I was Varaprabha and Maitreya was Yaśaskāma.
Śāriputra, by inferring from this, one knows that at the time that Buddha preached the sūtra, it was not only Varaprabha and Yaśaskāma [who were present]. Now...

At present, countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings will also certainly participate in this assembly. Since they have already been in the assembly of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, they must also have been in the assemblies of other Buddhas;
therefore, it was said above that they "have seen various Buddhas. Since they have been in the assemblies of those Buddhas, they must also have been in the assembly of Śākyamuni;
thus, it is now said that "in life after life, they have already received transformation from the Buddha. This refers to the long duration [of their practice].
"Peaceful at night" means that when the Tathāgata preaches the true Great Dharma, such persons as these will certainly be able to revere and believe it.
Even if they cannot rely upon it for practice to destroy ignorance, they have already received the seed within their hearts.
One should know that one will certainly attain Buddhahood; even while dwelling in the long night of ignorance, one remains secure and at ease.
If one can practice in reliance upon this, one will surely attain the opening, revealing, awakening to, and entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Its abundant benefits are many; thus it is said that "it brings great benefit. △ Second, the verses in praise, which have two parts. First, the verses on the formal request.
At that time, Śāriputra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"O Unsurpassed Honored One among Two-legged Beings, I pray you, speak of the foremost Dharma.
As for the 'foremost Dharma,' it refers to what the Tathāgata previously briefly revealed regarding the provisional means, saying: 'The Buddha, by the power of skillful means, manifests...'"
Regarding the teaching of the three vehicles: we know that the three vehicles previously taught were merely skillful means and are therefore not the supreme dharma.
Furthermore, the reality was briefly revealed, saying: "After a long time, the World-Honored One must surely speak the truth.
Thus we know that what is to be spoken today is the truth, and being the truth, it is the supreme dharma. Therefore, I pray that the World-Honored One [will explain it].
And thus he spoke. △ Second, the verse expressing the intent:
"I am the eldest son of the Buddha; please deign to explain this in detail. The immeasurable multitude in this assembly is able to revere and believe in this Dharma."

The Buddha has already, throughout successive lifetimes, taught and transformed those such as these; they all stand with palms joined in single-minded devotion, desiring to hear and receive the Buddha’s words.
We twelve hundred, along with the others who seek Buddhahood, pray that for the sake of this assembly, you will deign to explain it in detail.
When these individuals hear this Dharma, they give rise to great joy, thinking:
"Since I am the eldest son of the Buddha, I can personally believe what the Buddha has taught. Therefore it is said: "I am... (and so forth).

Furthermore, there are immeasurable multitudes who are likewise able to believe what the Buddha has taught; this is not due to anything else, but rather because the Buddha has taught and transformed them throughout successive lifetimes.
Therefore it is said, "This assembly... (and so forth). While those of overweening pride naturally lack faith, these bhikṣus will certainly be able to revere and believe;
for this reason, I pray that you will speak of it. Moreover, it is for the sake of the Buddha [that they do so].

As for the "eldest son," the Dharma he has been taught is said to be the foremost; it is nothing other than the desire to cause sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*).
This knowledge and vision of the Buddha is none other than the Tathāgata’s wisdom (*jñāna*). Now, Śāriputra is foremost in wisdom among those of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*);
if this [wisdom] were once revealed, then that very wisdom of the Lesser Vehicle would be the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
Because he has come forth with wisdom, he has become the eldest son of the Buddha. Thus, one knows that the previous sons of the Buddha still belonged to the Hīnayāna;
whereas the meaning of the present eldest son lies in the Mahāyāna. As for his giving rise to great joy:
since the Dharma he has heard is both true and real, it is not a minor teaching. Since it is a Great Dharma, the joy produced is likewise great, and not otherwise.
This concludes the brief exposition above. △ Second, the extensive opening of the provisional and manifestation of the real. This has three parts.
First, from here onwards, there is one cycle of the Dharma taught for those of superior faculties. Second, from the second fascicle, the Parable Chapter, where it says:
"At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying: 'World-Honored One, I now have no further doubt or regret,' and so forth; this is for those of middling faculties."
One cycle [of teaching] was delivered. Three cycles follow from the "Parable of the City of Illusion" (Tathāgataguṇaparikīrtana-parivarta) in the third fascicle onward;
these were taught for those of inferior faculties as a cause and condition. The first cycle of the Dharma-exposition consists of five parts: first, the Tathāgata’s direct exposition;

second, from the beginning of the second fascicle, "At that time, Śāriputra," downward, the response and realization of the appropriate recipient; third, from the second fascicle, "At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra," downward...
1. Śāriputra’s descent; the Tathāgata’s confirmation. 2. From the second fascicle, "Śāriputra, you [are prophesied] by the Tathāgata in this world" onwards:
the superior faculties receive the prediction. 3. From the second fascicle, "At that time, the fourfold assembly... onwards: the four assemblies rejoice.

Regarding the first [of these], there are two parts: first, the prose; second, the verse. Regarding the first [of the prose], there are three parts: first, the granting of permission to speak; second, receiving the mandate; third...
The formal exposition begins with the first three sections. First is the compliant acceptance:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra, "Since you have already made your earnest request three times, how could I not speak?"
"At that time" refers to the moment when Śāriputra had for the third time requested instruction on the transformation of beings, and the verses were just concluding.
△ Second, the admonition and permission:
"Now listen attentively and reflect well upon it; I shall analyze and explain it for you."
This first admonishes that one must give rise to the three types of wisdom before being permitted to speak. That is to say, "if you listen, your words will be truthful;
if you contemplate, your words will be good. This is because all that has been taught in the past and present has been proclaimed from the golden mouth of the Tathāgata.
The past was provisional; the present is real. If you do not listen attentively and reflect well upon it, how can you distinguish between them?
Furthermore, the provisional of the past is entirely the reality of the present, and the reality of the present is likewise the provisionality of the past.
Only when the mind is single-mindedly focused can one fully comprehend this. Therefore, regarding the instruction to listen, one must be attentive; regarding reflection, one must be...

"Excellent. Regarding the detailed explanation: although all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time, as well as I, Śākyamuni, appear in the world with differences of distance, proximity, and individuality, there is none who does not first employ the provisional to manifest the real, next open up the provisional to reveal the real, and finally discard the provisional to establish the real. △ Third, the formal granting [of permission], in two parts. First:
The Sūtra author records their withdrawal. Second, the Tathāgata’s selection and permission. The first [section] has two parts.

First, the introductory statement: When these words were spoken, there were five thousand bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās in the assembly who immediately rose from their seats, prostrated to the Buddha, and withdrew.

"When these words were spoken" refers to the time when the two permissions for the gradual instruction had just been concluded. Regarding "five thousand [monks] withdrawing," there are both exoteric and esoteric meanings.
Exoterically, it means that although their inner hearts were already lacking faith due to the Tathāgata’s brief exposition above, they heard the Buddha further instructing Śāriputra to stop;
thus, those bhikṣus with overweening pride (*adhimāna*) were on the verge of falling away.
Regarding the words "the great pit," his mind again gave rise to a thought; therefore, when the Buddha permitted him to explain in detail, he naturally withdrew from his seat.
As for "secretly," as the verse below states: "He departed due to the Buddha’s majestic virtue.
This refers to the power of the Tathāgata’s majestic virtue, which caused him to depart secretly; thus, he paid homage to the Buddha and withdrew. △ Second, the explanation of the underlying intent.

Why is this? It is because these people have deeply rooted and heavy karmic offenses, as well as overweening pride; they claim to have attained what they have not attained, and claim to have realized what they have not realized.
Since they possess such faults, they do not abide [in the teaching]. The World-Honored One remained silent and did not restrain them.
It is said that five thousand [disciples] withdrew. What was their intention? It was because their offenses were grave and they possessed overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
Having committed offenses, they were unable to hear this Great Dharma; possessing overweening pride, even if they heard it, they could not believe it.
Furthermore, because the World-Honored One remained silent and did not restrain them, they withdrew. This was due to the roots of their offenses and their overweening pride.

This reveals the meaning of "retrogression" (*parihāṇi*). To remain silent and fail to restrain [the offense] is the secret meaning of retrogression. Regarding the statement that "the root of the transgression is deep and heavy":
from the seeds (*bīja*), manifest activity (*samudācāra*) arises; conversely, by means of manifest activity, the seeds are perfumed (*vāsita*).
This is the mutual reinforcement of seeds and manifest activity, revolving without end; therefore, the root of the transgression is not only deep but also heavy. The Buddha...

Regarding the failure to restrain them: some may harbor doubts, saying, "The Tathāgata preached this wondrous sutra desiring that all sentient beings should fully attain the opening, showing, awakening to, and entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Now that five thousand have withdrawn and he does not restrain them, thereby causing them not to hear the Great Dharma, could it be that the Tathāgata’s great compassion is still lacking?"

However, that the Buddha alone does not prohibit [this teaching] is precisely the Great Compassion of the Tathāgata. Since they are characterized by overweening pride (*adhimāna*), they would certainly not believe upon hearing it;
lacking faith, they would inevitably give rise to slander; and giving rise to slander, they would inevitably fall into suffering. Fearing that they might fall into suffering, he does not prohibit it.
Furthermore, having already heard this brief revelation, they may still serve as a condition for future ripening and liberation. Thus, it is set aside.
Thus, it is beneficial; whereas remaining [in that state] would be detrimental. Therefore, he does not prohibit it. Is this not the Great Compassion of the Tathāgata?
△ Second, the Tathāgata’s selection and permission. First, the formal selection.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra: "In this assembly of mine now, there are no longer any branches or leaves; it consists purely of the solid core.
Śāriputra, it is well that such people of overweening pride have departed."
The selection involves two meanings. First, the selection of the assembly. To say "no longer having branches or leaves" means that branches are the surplus of the trunk;

to become a great vessel, it cannot be accomplished by branches or twigs, much less by leaves. Those people of overweening pride, whose karmic conditions were not yet mature, could not become supreme vessels of the Dharma.
Now that they have withdrawn from their seats, there are no longer [such persons] within the assembly.

Though there may be branches and leaves, they shall be purely of firm substance. Next, he distinguishes those who must withdraw from their seats, saying that such persons of overweening pride should depart.
It is truly excellent for the assembly to remain, and it is likewise excellent for them to leave.

For they have already previously heard the brief exposition on "opening the three to reveal the one," which they have taken to heart like seeds; in days to come, they will ultimately realize the fruit of the Perfect Teaching. As for those present now...
Furthermore, one avoids the suffering of falling into the pit of slander; thus, although this is a retreat, it is in fact progress.
Therefore, it is said that "retreating is also excellent. This is not for the sake of those who remain, but precisely for the sake of those who retreat.
Nanshan said, "The five thousand who withdrew from their seats were a group of those with superior pride (*adhimāna*). The meaning is likewise so. △ Second, further permission.
Listen well now; I shall explain it for you.
△ Second, receiving the command.
Śāriputra said: "Yes, indeed, World-Honored One; I wish and desire to hear it."

The word "although" (*sui*) is a term used in Confucian instruction to indicate that one should act with speed and without doubt; here, it simply means that one should act with speed, for as long as there is doubt, one has not yet attained freedom from it.
This is because Zengzi had already heard the teaching on the "single thread," and thus he was able to be without doubt; now, however, Śāriputra—

This is because they have merely heard permission to speak, but have not yet heard the actual teaching. △ Third, the actual teaching is divided into three parts. First, praising the excellence of the Dharma:
The Buddha addressed Śāriputra: "Such a wondrous Dharma as this is spoken by the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, only from time to time, like the udumbara flower."
The "lotus in the bowl" appears but once in a long while;
such a phrase refers to the Dharma. The former refers to the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, while the latter refers to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
The true reality of all phenomena is the non-duality of the provisional and the ultimate; as for the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, it is...
Sentient beings and Buddhas are of one essence; therefore, all are termed "wondrous. As for the timing of this teaching:

the Dharma is fundamentally timeless, yet it appears according to the capacities of beings. Forty years ago, the great capacity [of beings] was not yet matured; thus, it was not the time, and so it was not taught.
Now, at this sublime assembly of the Lotus Sutra, the great capacity is fully matured; this is the time, and so it is taught. Furthermore, regarding the bestowal of the three [vehicles]...
It was only at a later time that this wondrous Dharma was preached; hence it is said, "it was preached at the [right] time.
This is illustrated by the metaphor of the *udumbara* flower and so forth. In Sanskrit, *udumbara-puṣpa*; in Chinese, it is called "spiritual omen" (*ling-shui*) or "responsive omen" (*ying-shui*).
It blooms once every three thousand years. When the flower blooms, a Golden Wheel-turning King appears; therefore, it is named "Auspicious Omen" and "Responsive Omen.
Now, after forty years have passed, as soon as the wondrous Dharma is preached, all sentient beings shall attain Buddhahood.
The Buddha is the Dharma King; the Golden Wheel-turning King is the Human King. Although the human and the Dharma differ, the principle of kingship is the same;
therefore, he draws this analogy. △ Second, the admonition that it is not in vain.
Śāriputra, you all should believe what the Buddha has spoken; his words are not false.

That they are not false means that what was spoken forty years ago and what is spoken today, though both issue from the golden mouth in a single voice, were provisional in the past and are real now. Whether provisional or real, neither is false.
The Buddha, through the power of skillful means (*upāya*), manifests the teachings of the three vehicles; thus, his provisional [teachings] are not false.
After a long time, the Buddhas must speak the truth; thus, his reality is not false.

The reason for admonishing them to believe that it is not false is to cause them to sever doubts regarding the provisional and give rise to faith in the real. As the "Original Chapter" says: "You all should believe and understand as..."
These words of sincere truth are also intended to admonish for faith and ensure they are not in vain, so as to cause them to sever immediate doubts and give rise to distant conviction.
Thus one knows that whenever the Great Dharma is preached, it must necessarily exhort one to believe; hence, in the subsequent section on Śāriputra’s realization and understanding:

There are those who claim that it was not Māra who manifested as a Buddha and so forth. △ Third, the actual revelation and manifestation has three parts: first, a general clarification of all Buddhas;

second, a specific clarification of the three periods of time; third, a further clarification of Śākyamuni. The first part [the general clarification] has two sub-sections: first, the actual clarification of all Buddhas; second, the concluding revelation of the ten directions.

The first of these [the actual clarification] has three parts: first, clarifying the opening of the provisional to reveal the real; second, clarifying the establishment of the provisional for the sake of the real.
The Threefold Clarification sets aside the provisional to establish the real. [Section] One, Part Six. First, the formal designation:
"Śāriputra, the Buddhas preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate; their underlying intent is difficult to understand. Why is this?
By means of countless skillful means, various causes and conditions, parables, and modes of expression, I have expounded all dharmas."
First, to clarify how the Buddhas reveal the provisional (*upāya*), the text cites the expedient means of Śākyamuni as an illustration.

From the phrase "innumerable expedient means" up to "expounding all dharmas," this refers to the teaching of the provisional dharma. Since the entirety of the provisional dharma is itself the real (*tattva*), that which the Buddhas teach according to what is appropriate is likewise entirely real.
However, because its underlying intent (*abhiprāya*) is difficult to understand, [the text] uses the example of Śākyamuni.
"Expedient means" (upāya) refers simply to the provisional skillful methods of all Buddhas. What the Buddhas teach according to what is appropriate means:
teaching precepts and wholesome deeds for those suited to the realms of humans and devas; teaching the Truths and the Causal Links for those suited to the Two Vehicles;
and teaching the Six Perfections for those suited to Bodhisattvas. All such teachings given according to what is appropriate are provisional. If they are revealed and made manifest...

The whole body is the reality itself; thus one knows that what has been taught—though it concerns the precepts, wholesome deeds, the truths, conditions, and the six perfections—its underlying intent (*abhiprāya*) lies solely in the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
Therefore, it is said that this intent is difficult to understand. Such is the manner in which the Buddhas teach through skillful means (*upāya*);
the following section provides the explanation for this. That is to say, how can we know that what the Buddhas have taught is difficult to understand? Take me, Śākyamuni, for example: by...
Through immeasurable and innumerable expedient means, they expound all dharmas, yet their intent does not reside in those dharmas; it rests entirely upon the One Reality.
Therefore, the meaning behind what the Buddhas teach according to what is appropriate is likewise difficult to understand.

If one knows that what I, Śākyamuni, have taught through my innumerable expedient means is entirely the Reality itself, then although the teachings of all Buddhas are said to be difficult to understand, [they will be understood].

This can also be understood. Therefore it is said: "I [use such expressions]... (and so forth). That which expounds all dharmas is precisely that which unfolds from the single true reality (*ekadharmatā*) to become the teachings for the two vehicles, the five teachings, the seven kinds of expedient means, and so on. △ Second, the explanation and clarification.
This Dharma cannot be understood through thought or discrimination; only the Buddhas can know it.
This clarifies that Śākyamuni reveals the ultimate reality, explaining it by citing the fundamental intention of all Buddhas.

Thus, this section and the preceding one—concerning the Buddhas and Śākyamuni—mutually clarify and complete one another, demonstrating that their realization of the Way is identical. Therefore, the two characters "this Dharma" (shì fǎ) [are] from above...
The text concerning skillful means has arrived; therefore, this is the true path. It consists of only two phrases, which constitute the fundamental intention of all Buddhas:
namely, that although all phenomena are provisional, the provisional is itself the real. Thus, it cannot be understood through discursive thought and the like.

Why can it not be understood through discursive thought and the like? When the Tathāgata speaks of existence, his intention does not lie in existence; yet sentient beings understand it in terms of existence.
Even when speaking of the "Middle," the intention does not reside in the Middle; yet sentient beings understand it through the Middle.

They do not realize that this is the wondrous existence (*miao-you*), wherein one existence is all existences, and even the Middle is the perfect Middle (*yuan-zhong*), wherein one Middle is all Middles.
How could such a meaning be understood through discursive thought or calculation? It is as the saying goes: "The mouth wishes to speak, but words fail."
The mind desires to contemplate, yet deliberation vanishes; therefore it is said, "This Dharma... (and so forth).
Since it cannot be understood through the conceptualization and such of sentient beings, who ultimately could possibly understand it? Thus it is said: "Only the Buddhas are able to know it."
There is nothing else; it is because they have attained full realization. Only through realization can one know it;
therefore, it cannot be understood through the conceptual deliberations of sentient beings. △ Third, the formal explanation.
Why is this? It is because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world solely for the sake of the one great causal matter.
This means that it cannot be understood through the deliberation or discrimination of sentient beings; only a Buddha knows it.
Therefore, the commentary states: "The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones... (and so forth). This is indeed my skillful means; the underlying intent is that the provisional is itself the real.
The original aspiration for the appearance of all Buddhas in the world is solely for the sake of the one great causal matter. Thus, it is the fundamental intention of all Buddhas.
One must surely obtain the skillful means of Śākyamuni to be able to reveal and manifest it.

That which is the "one great causal condition" is, in its upper sense, the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, and in its lower sense, the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. As for true reality, it is the non-duality of the provisional and the real.
Through knowledge and vision, the Buddha and sentient beings are realized as one and the same. Thus, once the Great Matter is clarified, one’s original aspiration is also fulfilled.
If explained by analyzing the individual characters, it is as clarified in the Commentary and the Sub-commentary. △ Fourth, the counter-interrogation.
Śāriputra, for what reason do the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world solely for the sake of the one great cause and condition?
△ Fifth: The Explanatory Turn.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world because they desire to cause sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, so that it may become pure;

they appear in the world because they desire to show sentient beings the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; they appear in the world because they desire to cause sentient beings to awaken to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
they appear in the world because they desire to cause sentient beings to enter the path of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

Regarding this single passage, there are three sections. First, the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (jñāna-darśana) is explained individually. Second, the terms "opening," "showing," "awakening," and "entering" are interpreted collectively.
Third, the terms "purity" and "path" are analyzed in detail. First, as for "knowledge and vision," this is an abbreviated expression; [it is] complete...
The feet should be understood as seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing. When these reside in the mind, they are called "knowing"; when they reside in the eyes, they are called "seeing.
To know through the three types of wisdom within a single moment of mind is called the Buddha’s knowing; to see through the five eyes within a single eye is called the Buddha’s seeing.

Yet this knowing and seeing are, from the beginning, identical for both ordinary beings and sages, and equal for both those born as deluded beings and Buddhas. It is only because of the entire body of sentient beings in the nine realms...
In their delusion, they cause the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to be renamed as the "knowledge and vision of sentient beings.
This is because sentient beings may know only existence, or know only emptiness, or know only the Middle Way; thus, they cannot possess the perfect knowledge of the three wisdoms.
Therefore, it cannot be called the "Buddha-knowledge," but is merely termed the "knowledge of sentient beings. The Tathāgata, however, not only knows existence, but also knows...
Emptiness. Not only does he know emptiness, he also knows the Middle Way; not only does he know the Middle Way, he also knows both emptiness and existence.
Because he is able, within a single mind, to perfectly illumine the three types of wisdom and perfectly manifest the three truths, it is called the Buddha’s knowledge.
Furthermore, that which sentient beings perceive is either obstructed rather than penetrating, or penetrating rather than obstructed; or they observe only the conventional, or...
Knowing only emptiness, this too cannot be the complete observation of the five eyes; therefore, it cannot be called the Buddha’s vision, but is merely the vision of ordinary beings.
The Tathāgata, however, can possess the function of all five eyes within a single eye.
This is unlike the fleshly eye of ordinary people, which is obstructed and not penetrating, and even unlike that of bodhisattvas, who are able to observe only the conventional. One.

To see all seeing is therefore called the Buddha’s seeing. Taken together, the perfect knowledge of the three wisdoms and the perfect vision of the five eyes constitute what is termed the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

The combined explanation of "opening, showing, awakening, and entering" is further analyzed in four aspects: first, in terms of the Dharma; second, in terms of analogy; third, in terms of contemplation; and fourth, in terms of stages.
If the Dharma is not clearly understood, one must rely on analogies; through analogies the Dharma is clarified, and based upon them, contemplation is established.
When the practice of contemplation is perfected, one will certainly be able to enter into realization; therefore, it is necessary to explain it by means of these four aspects.
First, regarding the Dharma: the wisdom and vision of the Buddhas consist in the equality of sentient beings and Buddhas.
However, while sentient beings remain entirely immersed in delusion, the Buddhas have attained ultimate realization.
Now, because the Buddhas desire to cause all sentient beings to share in what they themselves have realized, they appear in the world and teach them, saying: "All you sentient beings..."
All knowledge and vision presently manifest are, in their entirety, the knowledge and vision of the Buddha.
Upon hearing this, sentient beings immediately realize that their own knowledge and vision is itself the knowledge and vision of the Buddha.

If they have not yet realized this, the Buddha’s knowledge and vision remains unopened; now that they have realized it, this is precisely the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. From this realization...
"Knowing subsequently" means being further able to discern and reveal; this is precisely the demonstration of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*).
Following this revelation, one is able to realize and know: that such is the knowledge and vision of sentient beings, and such is the knowledge and vision of the Tathāgata.
Thus, the knowledge and vision of sentient beings is itself the knowledge and vision of the Tathāgata; this constitutes awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

It is seeing. Once one has awakened to this knowledge, one is able to realize and enter it; this is precisely entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana*). Yet, there is nothing opened in that which is opened:
it is the knowledge and vision of sentient beings that is opened, thereby becoming the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Likewise, there is nothing entered in that which is entered:
it is the knowledge and vision of sentient beings that is entered, thereby becoming the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Therefore, it is said: "All..."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, appeared in the world desiring to cause sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; even as it says:
"He appeared in the world because he enters the path of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision."
Second, regarding the analogy: it is like a poor man who has a treasure trove within his house, yet the poor man himself does not know of it.
A wise neighbor, knowing that there is a treasure trove in his house, informs him of it. Having heard this, the poor man realizes there is a treasure trove;
he then clears away the sand and gravel and weeds out the thickets of grass until he sees the treasure. Once he has seen it, furthermore—
Upon further digging and stripping away the earth, a treasure trove immediately appears before him.
Once it has appeared, he recognizes that "this is gold" and "this is silver," understanding each one clearly. Having understood them, he takes them and puts them to practical use.
The poor man represents all sentient beings; the treasure trove represents the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
The "wise person" is a metaphor for the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas. "Weeding out the sand and grass" is a metaphor for opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

"The manifestation of the treasure store" is a metaphor for showing the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. "Awakening to each of these one by one" is a metaphor for awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Taking this as its function is a metaphor for entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Third, regarding the practitioner: taking the supreme *śānta-prabhāsvara* (tranquil light) as the object of contemplation; since it is by means of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision...
Taking it as the object of contemplation, one further takes the Buddha’s knowledge and vision as the subjective wisdom that contemplates it.

This is to illuminate the object with wisdom and to give rise to wisdom through the object; when object and wisdom mutually stimulate one another, this is precisely the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
When the object and the contemplation are distinct and clear, and the subject and object are perfectly defined, they manifest vividly before one, revealing [the truth].
Obscurity is precisely the Buddha’s knowledge and vision being revealed. When the object is penetrated, it is the contemplation; when the contemplation is fully realized, it is the object.
When object and contemplation are fused together, the subject and object are mutually identical—this is the awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

By means of the object engaging with the contemplation, and by means of the contemplation entering the object, the subject and object interpenetrate, and the object and wisdom become one in profound stillness—this is the entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

Furthermore, regarding the fourth point, the classification by stages (*bhūmi*), there are two further sections: first, a general application to the six stages of identity; second, a specific application to the forty stages.
As for the general application to the six stages: the Buddha’s knowledge and vision neither increases in the sages nor decreases in ordinary beings. Therefore...
Although all sentient beings are entirely immersed in delusion and remain utterly unaware, they are fully endowed with this;

this is the "Buddha’s knowledge and vision as the principle" (*li-ji*). If one perceives this Buddha’s knowledge and vision from within a scripture, or hears of it from a spiritual teacher, this is the "Buddha’s knowledge and vision as name-only" (*ming-zi-ji*). If one can, as follows...
That which one hears and then cultivates is the "contemplative practice" (guanxing), which is the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana*).

If the merit of contemplative practice is perfected, the coarse defilements fall away first, and one accords with the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; this is the "semblance" (xiangsi) stage of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Once one has ascended to the first *bhūmi* and beyond, one gradually shatters ignorance and gradually manifests [the Buddha's knowledge and vision].
From the Middle Way up to the attainment of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), there remains only the unbroken portion of the *avidyā* (ignorance) of the "characteristic of arising.

This is the knowledge and vision of a Buddha attained through partial realization (*pradeśa-prativedha*). If this *avidyā* of the characteristic of arising is destroyed, one ultimately ascends to the summit of the mountain of Nirvāṇa;
the three knowledges are perfectly luminous and the five eyes see perfectly. This is the ultimate state of Buddhahood.

Regarding this knowledge and vision: secondly, as for the specific enumeration of forty stages, although the Buddha’s knowledge and vision pervade all six levels of realization, the intention behind the Buddhas’ appearance in the world is not merely to cause sentient beings to attain the stages of name, semblance, or contemplative practice;

rather, it is solely to cause them to ascend from the stage of "entry" (*ju*) onwards, up to the tenth ground (*bhūmi*), so that they may spontaneously flow into [the ultimate state] by their own power.

From Equal Enlightenment (*sambodhi*), one advances to Wondrous Enlightenment (*prabhāsvara-bodhi*). For this reason, it is explained by separately delineating the forty stages of the ten abidings (*vihāra*), ten practices (*caryā*), ten transferences (*pratipatti*), and ten grounds (*bhūmi*).
The phrase "opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision" refers specifically to the stage of the ten abidings.

By ascending to the first abiding, one is able to shatter one grade of ignorance and manifest one portion of the Middle Way; continuing thus up to the tenth abiding, one has already shattered ten grades of ignorance.

This is clear. Reaching this point, one attains the three wisdoms in their entirety and realizes them perfectly; the five eyes behold all things in their perfection, and the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (jñāna-darśana) are thereby opened and developed.

Thus, the Ten Abidings (daśa-vihāra) are called such because they "open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. As for "showing the Buddha’s knowledge and vision," this refers to the stage of the Ten Practices (daśa-caryā).
Within the Ten Abidings, since one is already able to open and develop the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, it is made manifest.

This is indeed the wondrous principle of the inconceivable. Now, advancing into the stage of the Ten Practices (*daśabhūmi-pratipatti*), one again takes that manifested inconceivable wondrous principle as the basis for giving rise to the wondrous practices of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

This is the process of fully utilizing nature to initiate cultivation, and fully utilizing cultivation to return to nature; thereby, the merits of the sands of the Ganges inherent in nature naturally become entirely manifest. And...
The Buddha’s knowledge and vision become even more manifest; therefore, it is called the Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*). This is to demonstrate the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

Those who awaken to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are at the stage of the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*). Within the preceding Ten Practices, one has already initiated the wondrous practices of the *dharmadhātu*.
Now, advancing this within the stage of the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pratipatti*), one is further able to turn phenomena toward principle, turn oneself toward others, and turn causes toward the fruit.
Thus, one causes phenomena and principle to be mutually fused, self and other to be equal, and cause and fruit to be as one;
consequently, the Buddha’s knowledge and vision become even more clearly realized. Therefore, it is named the "Ten Dedications," signifying the awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Furthermore, "entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision" refers to the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
Although within the preceding thirty stages one destroys delusions and manifests principle, that which is destroyed is not yet exhausted, and that which is manifested is not yet ultimate.
Now, by advancing into the ten stages, one has already destroyed forty grades of ignorance and manifested forty aspects of the three virtues (*triguṇa*); that which is to be destroyed is nearly...
When that which is manifested is nearly exhausted, one will then spontaneously flow into the ocean of the fruit of wondrous enlightenment.
Thus, before long, one will ultimately realize and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; for this reason, the tenth stage is called the "Entry into the Buddha’s Knowledge and Vision."
Regarding the "triple elimination and purification" and the "path": in the text, following the phrase "opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision," it says that one "attains purification";

following the phrase "entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision," it speaks of the "path. This is because for those who have not yet shattered ignorance, the Buddha’s knowledge and vision remain unopened and are entirely defiled;
now, from the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) onward, since the knowledge and vision have been opened and ignorance has been shattered.
Therefore, it is called "purity. Up to the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), the severance of delusions is about to be exhausted and the realization of wisdom is about to be fulfilled;

before long, one will universally attain the fruit of *sarvajñā* (omniscience). Therefore, it is called the "Path" (*mārga*). However, this is merely an abbreviated expression by the compiler of the sutra.
To speak fully, the terms "purity" and "path" should follow every single phrase. This is because ignorance is eliminated part by part.

[This] refutes [the objection]. One realizes the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) step by step. That is to say, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world because they desire to cause sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (buddhajñānadarśana) and to attain the pure path;

and so on, up to their appearance in the world because they desire to cause sentient beings to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and to attain the pure path. The two phrases in the middle refer to "showing" (darśana) and "awakening" (avabodha).

It is also thus. Only by comparing the subsequent with the preceding can one know that the preceding also possesses the Path; by comparing the preceding with the subsequent, one knows that the subsequent also possesses purity;
and by comparing the middle with both the preceding and the subsequent, one knows that the middle also possesses both purity and the Path.
This is the skillful teaching of the Tathāgata; it is the skillful wisdom of the compiler of the sutra. △ Sixth, the conclusion of the title:
"Śāriputra, this is why all Buddhas appear in the world for the sake of one great causal matter."
△ Second, explaining the establishment of provisional means for the sake of the ultimate truth.
The Buddha addressed Śāriputra: "All Buddhas, Tathāgatas, teach and transform only bodhisattvas. All that they do is always for a single purpose:
solely to use the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to reveal and awaken sentient beings."
All that has been enacted is the provisional; that which is always for the sake of the One Matter is the real.

What was taught during the forty years prior—the three vehicles, the five teachings, and so forth—was merely for the purpose of various enactments. △ Third, the clarification of the abolition of the provisional and the establishment of the real.
Śāriputra, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma for sentient beings solely by means of the Single Buddha Vehicle (ekabuddhayāna).
There is no other vehicle, whether a second or a third.

By means of the Buddha Vehicle alone, he establishes the reality; there is no other vehicle, as any such would be discarded according to their capacity. If one were to speak of it from a general perspective, the others...
"Vehicles" (*yāna*) refers to the Two Vehicles and the Three Vehicles. The Two Vehicles refer to the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas;

the Three Vehicles refer to the Bodhisattvas. If one discusses them according to their actual substance: "the others" refers to the distinct [teachings] encompassed by the *Avataṃsaka* and the "Small" of the *Āgamas*;
"two" refers to the two [vehicles] associated with the *Prajñāpāramitā*; and "three" refers to the three [vehicles] addressed in the *Vaipulya*. Thus, it is one...
This was spoken in accordance with the capacities of those present, merely to establish the reality of the teaching. II. Conclusion revealing the ten directions:
"Śāriputra, the Dharma of all Buddhas in the ten directions is likewise."
"The Dharma is also like this" means that although the Buddhas of the ten directions are numerous and the teachings they proclaim are not identical,
they all first employ the provisional based on the real, next reveal the real by opening up the provisional, and finally discard the provisional to establish the real.
Question: The commentaries explain this passage by clarifying the "Four Kinds of One. Why, then, do you now interpret it through the three categories of "Bestowing, Opening, and Abolishing"?
Will this not contradict the Great Master’s intention? Answer: The name "Four Kinds of One" originated with Guangzhai.

Because Guangzhai’s established doctrines were incorrect, the Great Master refuted his positions and established his own. Therefore, he [the commentator] follows the Master’s teaching, practice, and principle.

Fourth: The full elucidation of non-utility; all [other views] are without standing. Now, the three—bestowal (*śāstra*), opening (*kai*), and abandonment (*fei*)—are what the Great Master himself established.
They are the essential framework of a single sutra, the fundamental tenet of the Shanjia school, and the functional application of the *Lotus Sūtra*.

It is by relying on these three meanings that the *Xuanyan* (Profound Meaning) commentary explains the three meanings of the Trace Gate of the Lotus. These meanings truly emerge from this; how much more so...

The present text of the "Revelation" (Kaien) is precisely the core essence of the "Trace Gate" (Jikimon). Thus, it should be understood that by now employing the three stages of bestowing, revealing, and abolishing, we are once again explaining this very text;

this perfectly accords with the Master’s intent and truly follows the Master’s meaning. How could there be any contradiction? II. Specifically Clarifying the Three Periods. This has two parts: first, the specific clarification itself; second, the conclusion of its significance. First: *The Lotus Sutra in Chinese and Japanese* provides the original text for reference. However, as per your instructions, I have provided a direct translation of the provided Chinese segment. If you require a translation of a different portion of the *Lotus Sutra*, please provide the specific text. I am ready to assist.
Furthermore, there are three. First, regarding the past:

Śāriputra, the Buddhas of the past, by means of immeasurable and innumerable skillful means, various causes and conditions, parables, and modes of expression, expounded all dharmas for the sake of sentient beings. All these dharmas were for the purpose of the Single Buddha Vehicle. These...
Sentient beings, having heard the Dharma from the Buddhas, will ultimately all attain the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Such things as the "innumerable skillful means" are the provisional (*upāya*); these teachings are all equal, which constitutes the real (*bhūta*). These sentient beings are equal;
this is the disclosure of the provisional to reveal the real. Since the Buddhas first provisionally bestow the three [vehicles] and subsequently must necessarily reveal the one, now...
When sentient beings hear from the Buddha, they immediately hear that there is no provisional [truth] apart from the real; the provisional is itself the Dharma of the real.
Therefore, this is the opening of the provisional to reveal the real. Third, that all ultimately attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) is the establishment of the real.
If the Real (the ultimate) is established, the Expedient (the provisional) naturally ceases. Thus, this is the cessation of the expedient and the establishment of the real.

"The Knowledge of All Modes" (*sarvākārajñatā*) is simply another name for the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Regarding the three types of knowledge, the term "Knowledge of All Modes" alone is used because it cites the last to encompass the preceding ones.
Furthermore, in each of the subsequent passages concerning the future and the present, there are instances of bestowing, opening, and abolishing.
The three meanings can be understood by analogy with this. △ Second, the future:

Śāriputra, all Buddhas of the future who shall appear in the world will likewise, through immeasurable and innumerable skillful means, various causes and conditions, parables, and modes of expression, expound all dharmas for the sake of sentient beings; these dharmas are all for the sake of the One [Vehicle].
Because of the Buddha Vehicle, all these sentient beings, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, will ultimately attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
The meaning is as explained previously (etc.). △ Third, the present.

Śāriputra, in the present, throughout the immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddha-fields in the ten directions, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, bring great benefit and peace to sentient beings.

These Buddhas also, by means of immeasurable and innumerable skillful expedients, various causes and conditions, parables, and modes of expression, expound all dharmas for the sake of sentient beings; these dharmas are all for the sake of the One [Vehicle].
Because of the Buddha-vehicle, all these sentient beings, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, ultimately attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
The meaning is as explained previously (etc.). △ Second, concluding its significance.
Śāriputra, these Buddhas teach and transform bodhisattvas solely because they desire to reveal the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to sentient beings,
because they desire to awaken sentient beings through the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and because they desire to cause sentient beings to enter into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
This means that the intent of all Buddhas of the three periods of time in appearing in the world is identical in its significance:

there is none who does not first employ provisional means and subsequently reveal the ultimate reality, thereby causing all sentient beings to open, show, awaken to, and enter into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, so that they ultimately all attain the wisdom of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
Now, "opening," "showing," and so forth, pertain to the Buddhas as the agents who open; sentient beings are the objects who are opened.
However, it is truly the sentient beings themselves who open [the Dharma] for themselves and reveal it;
it does not depend upon the Buddhas. *The Explication of the Lotus Sutra*, Fascicle One, Part Three.
