△ A third time Śākyamuni is elucidated. Since he was already elucidated in the preceding general explanation, the term "repeated" (chóng) is used.
The text is divided into four sections; the first opens up the provisional to reveal the real.

Śāriputra, I am now likewise thus. Knowing that all sentient beings have various desires and deep-seated attachments, I preach the Dharma for them through various causes, conditions, parables, and expressions, employing the power of skillful means according to their fundamental natures.
Śāriputra, all this is for the sake of enabling them to attain the Single Buddha Vehicle and the knowledge of all modes.

The text contains three intended meanings. From "I now" [onward], there is the revelation of the provisional to manifest the real (*kai-gen-jitsu*). This single phrase represents the application of the provisional for the sake of the real (*se-ji-kon*).

Every single phrase represents the abolition of the provisional to establish the real (*he-kon-ryū-jitsu*). Regarding "I now," etc., it means that these three—application, revelation, and abolition—are identical to those of all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods;
therefore, it says, "I now am likewise. From "Knowing the... [onward], there is the observation of capacities (*kan-ki*).
This refers to preaching the Dharma according to their inclinations. "Inclination" (*chanda*) means desire;
because these sentient beings may desire existence, or desire emptiness, or desire the Middle Way—each being different—it is called "various."
This desire for pleasure is indeed a present cause. However, because this present cause arises from seeds planted in the past, it is said that "the deep mind is attached.
"Attachment" here refers to craving. This means that the reason there are these various desires for pleasure in the present is due to various cravings existing in past seeds.
Because one was attached to existence (*bhava*) in the past, one now delights in existence, and so forth, even unto the past.

They are attached to the middle; therefore, one now delights in the middle. The Tathāgata, by means of his inconceivable skillful wisdom for transforming others, perceives that sentient beings currently possess various desires for pleasure due to their present causes, and possess various attachments due to their past seeds.
Having thus observed their capacities, he establishes teachings according to those capacities and adapts those teachings to suit those capacities. Therefore...
He then accords with their fundamental natures and preaches the Dharma for them through various skillful means. "Nature" here refers to the nature of habitual practice;
what is called "fundamental nature" means the nature formed by past habits. Since they were previously attached to existence, they now again delight in existence.

Thus, their nature is habituated to existence and cannot be changed; even when they have long been established within the state of "the middle," and now again take pleasure in it, their nature is habituated to the middle and likewise cannot be changed.
Since the desires, attachments, and habitual natures of sentient beings are manifold, the Tathāgata, when teaching the Dharma, employs various causes and conditions accordingly.
He teaches them by means of various parables, various modes of expression, and various powers of skillful means (*upāya*).
As for the fact that these skillful means are likewise manifold, this may be understood from the preceding passage praising Śākyamuni’s provisional wisdom (*prajñā*).

Since that [passage] concerns the provisional wisdom of Śākyamuni, and this [present case] also concerns the provisional wisdom of Śākyamuni, they should naturally be identical. The meanings of the causes and conditions (*nidāna*) and so forth are as in that [preceding] text.

Furthermore, it can be known that for sentient beings who habituate to existence, he teaches the Dharma of existence by employing the causes and conditions, parables, and verbal skillful means of existence;

likewise, for sentient beings who habituate to the middle, he teaches the Dharma of the middle by employing the causes and conditions, parables, and verbal skillful means of the middle. However, regarding this...

It is said that all [previous teachings] were expedient means (*upāya*). Previously, expedient means were not mentioned; now, since it is stated that they are expedient means, this opens up their provisional nature.
Once the provisional has been opened, the real (*bhūta*) is spontaneously revealed. Therefore, by opening the provisional, the text simultaneously reveals the real.
"All for the sake of attaining the One Buddha Vehicle" means that the provisional is established for the sake of the real. These two characters refer to the provisional teachings opened up above;
they were originally the provisional means employed, yet these provisional means were originally intended for the reality of the Buddha Vehicle.

Therefore, it is said, "all for the sake of attaining the One Buddha Vehicle. As for the term "all-encompassing wisdom" (sarvajñā), it refers to the sublation of the provisional and the establishment of the real.
This is indeed so. This single phrase, "all have attained," should be read in conjunction with the three characters "all have" from the preceding line.

For the meaning of those three characters fundamentally extends through this phrase; it means that all have attained the One Buddha Vehicle, and all have attained the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
Since this knowledge and vision of the sole Buddha Vehicle is the knowledge of all modes, there is no such thing as a second [vehicle].

If [the teaching] were for the three vehicles as well as other vehicles, then the provisional would be established while the real would be discarded. Therefore, this is the discarding of the provisional and the establishing of the real.
△ Second, clarifying the skillful means, in three parts: first, stating the intention.
Śāriputra, in the worlds of the ten directions, there are not even two vehicles, let alone three.
This refers to the fact that both the skillful means taught forty years ago and the reality taught today were proclaimed from the golden mouth [of the Buddha];
why then would they not both be preserved? Therefore, the commentary states: "In the worlds of the ten directions, there are not even..."
As for the two vehicles, how much less could there be three? Since neither two nor three exist, there is only the one reality.
This is why the provisional is set aside to establish the real. △ Second, showing the characteristics has three parts; first, the heading.
Śāriputra, the Buddhas appear in the world of the five turbidities and evil ages.
Regarding the statement that "the Buddhas are equal," it means that since there is only the reality of the single Buddha-vehicle, with no second or third, why not teach the One Vehicle directly?
Therefore, the explanation says: the Buddhas originally intended to teach the single vehicle of ultimate reality, but because conditions [were] in the five...

In this world of turbid evil, the capacities of sentient beings do not accord [with the ultimate truth]. Therefore, one first preaches the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles to bring them to maturity;
thereafter, one preaches the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of the One Vehicle to deliver them, leading them from the provisional back to the real.
Thus it is said: "The Buddhas... (etc.). △ Second, the enumeration.

These are what are called the *kalpa-kāṣāya* (degeneration of the eon), the *kleśa-kāṣāya* (degeneration of afflictions), the *sattva-kāṣāya* (degeneration of sentient beings), the *dṛṣṭi-kāṣāya* (degeneration of views), and the *āyuṣka-kāṣāya* (degeneration of lifespan).
Regarding the *kalpa-kāṣāya*: in Sanskrit it is *kalpa*, which here means "time-period. Time itself is originally not turbid;

however, because the four [other] turbidities—afflictions and so forth—congregate within a single period, it too becomes turbid. This refers to the simultaneous manifestation of the great and small three calamities. That is to say: [The text continues with the description of the three calamities.]

The four [defilements], beginning with afflictions (*kleśa*), constitute their essence; they themselves have no inherent substance. As for the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*), it consists of greed, hatred, delusion, and pride;

its essence is the delusions of thought (*vitarka-vicāra*). Because these four—greed and the others—are all states of confusion and vexation that can disturb the mental faculties of the practitioner, they are called the turbidity of afflictions.
As for the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*), it is merely a conventional designation (*prajñapti-mātra*). Furthermore...
They lack intrinsic nature. Because they arise from the three turbidities of views, life-span, and afflictions, they also constitute turbidity.

Since this body, which is the fruit of retribution, is brought about by the causes of accumulation, one encounters ill-repute and foul names; therefore, it is called the *sattva-kāṣāya* (the turbidity of sentient beings).
Regarding the *dṛṣṭi-kāṣāya* (turbidity of views): "view" has the meaning of discrimination. Its essence consists of the five sharp fetters (*pañca-tīkṣṇa-kleśa*), as these five fetters—
All of these are able to turbid and disturb both body and mind; therefore, they are called the *dṛṣṭi-kāṣāya* (corruption of views). As for the *āyuḥ-kāṣāya* (corruption of lifespan):

the continuous maintenance of the physical form and mind throughout a single lifetime constitutes "lifespan. Because this [corruption] destroys the years and diminishes the longevity—such that one dies in the evening and is born in the morning—it is likewise a corruption.
This takes the two corruptions of views and afflictions as its essence, and brings about the *āyuḥ-kāṣāya*. △ Third, the explanation.

Thus it is, Śāriputra. In times of turmoil during the *kalpa*-dregs, sentient beings are heavily defiled; because they are stingy, greedy, and envious, they bring to fruition all roots of unwholesomeness.

These two characters [“dregs” and “turmoil”] collectively summarize the aforementioned five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*). They are also the very essence of the five turbidities. The "turmoil" of the *kalpa*-dregs—
"Time and so forth" refers to the emergence of the four turbidities (*kaṣāya*) occurring simultaneously, which constitutes the characteristic of the *kalpa-kaṣāya*.
This means that since sentient beings are impelled by [wrong] views and afflictions (*kleśa*), their minds are neither pure nor clear; their faculties are not light and sharp, but heavy.
Regarding their own possessions, they are mind after mind unwilling to give them away to others, which is termed stinginess (*mātsarya*). Regarding others...
Regarding things, the constant desire to possess them for oneself is greed (*lobha*); furthermore, one feels envy toward those who are capable and jealousy toward those who are virtuous.
Through these various unwholesome roots, all are fully accomplished. Because these four turbidities (*kaṣāya*) converge at one time, the *kalpa-kaṣāya* (the turbidity of the eon) is formed.
This is an explanation of how the *kalpa-kaṣāya* is established based on the four turbidities. If [one were to explain] separately...

Regarding the explanation in terms of the five corruptions (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*): "the period of turmoil during the *kalpa*-corruption" explains the aforementioned corruption of the eon; "the heavy defilements of sentient beings" explains the aforementioned corruption of sentient beings;
the two characters "miserliness and greed" explain the aforementioned corruption of afflictions; the two characters "jealousy and envy" explain the aforementioned corruption of views;
and "accomplishing all roots of unwholesomeness" explains the aforementioned corruption of life. △ Third, the summary and clarification.
"The Buddhas, by the power of skillful means (*upāya*), distinguish and teach three vehicles within the single Buddha-vehicle (*ekayāna*).

This clarifies that the Buddhas' revelation of provisional teachings is precisely intended to manifest the ultimate reality. That is to say, when the Buddhas appear in the world, they originally intend to teach the Single Vehicle directly;
however, because the capacities and dispositions of sentient beings in this defiled age do not accord with it, they employ skillful means.
Power. Within the single Buddha-vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*), it is distinguished and taught as three; hence it is said, "The Buddhas... and so forth.

Regarding the two lines beginning with "Within the single Buddha-vehicle," if one were to explain them according to the conventional interpretation, it would mean that from the single Buddha-vehicle, they are divided and taught as three—this is the provisional (*upāya*).
Then, having withdrawn the three vehicles, one returns to the single Buddha-vehicle—this is the ultimate reality (*tattva*). However, in the final analysis, what...
Thus, the single Buddha-vehicle is taught as three; yet these three vehicles can likewise be gathered back into the one.
This is truly because the single Buddha-vehicle takes the entirety of the ten dharma-realms as its essence; although they differ in their relative heights and depths, [they are fundamentally one].

Yet, in total, these are all contained within the single Buddha-vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*). As for śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas, they are merely a small portion of the ten dharma-realms (*daśadhātus*).

Because sentient beings do not find resonance with hearing the single Buddha-vehicle, it is explained as three vehicles (*triyāna*) from within that which is possessed by the single Buddha-vehicle. For instance, if one wishes to accommodate the capacity of a śrāvaka, then one says:
The Śrāvaka vehicle contained within the One Buddha Vehicle, up to and including the Bodhisattva vehicle taught to suit the capacities of bodhisattvas—
since all three vehicles are fully expounded as being subsumed within the One Buddha Vehicle,
they can likewise be gathered back into the One Buddha Vehicle. △ Third, urging and exhorting them to...
II. Faith. First, the exclusion of those who are not disciples:
Śāriputra, if there are my disciples who claim for themselves to be arhats or pratyekabuddhas, they have neither heard nor known [this].
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, concern themselves solely with the task of teaching and transforming bodhisattvas. This person is not a disciple of the Buddha, nor an arhat, nor a pratyekabuddha;
he merely claims to be equal [to them]. He is not one of those with overweening pride who claim realization without having attained it; rather, he is a truly realized arhat.
[They are] Pratyekabuddhas. Although they have realized the truth, when the Buddhas appear in the world, they transform only Bodhisattvas and there are no followers of the two vehicles (dvayayāna).
Therefore, those of the two vehicles consider themselves to be of the two vehicles; it is not that the Buddha taught the existence of two vehicles.
Hence it is said: "They consider themselves... and so forth. Because they consider themselves to be of the two vehicles, the Tathāgata transforms only Bodhisattvas.
They have neither heard of nor known the matters concerning the great causal conditions; therefore it is said, "they have not heard" (and so forth).
If they had heard and known that the Tathāgata transforms only bodhisattvas, these people could then be called disciples of the Buddha.
Since they have neither heard nor known this, they are not disciples of the Buddha; therefore it is said, "these are not disciples of the Buddha. As they are not disciples of the Buddha...
"Son, even those who have attained the state of an Arhat or a Pratyekabuddha are likewise not [the ultimate]. Therefore it is said: 'Not an Arhat' (and so forth).
△ Second, the censure of them as being conceited, in four parts. First, the direct censure."
Furthermore, Śāriputra, these bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, claiming for themselves that they have already attained arhatship—
that this is their final body and that they have reached ultimate nirvāṇa— no longer aspire to seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
You should know that these people are all those of overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
These individuals—referring to those mentioned above who claim for themselves the status of Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas, as well as those who are not disciples of the Buddha—are all such persons.
However, they are not merely non-disciples of the Buddha; they are also people of overweening pride (*adhimāna*). Therefore, it says, "These various [people]...
(and so forth). That they no longer aspire to seek *bodhi* is because they do not know that the Tathāgata transforms only bodhisattvas.
△ Second, the explanation and clarification.
Why is this? If there were a bhikṣu who had truly attained arhatship and yet did not believe in this Dharma, such a thing is impossible.
That he would not believe in this Dharma is because the dharmas of the arhats and others are merely the skillful means taught by the Tathāgata; they are but one.

The Buddha Vehicle is the Tathāgata’s discourse on ultimate reality. Since you previously believed in the Tathāgata’s skillful means and have already attained the state of an Arhat, how could you now fail to believe in the Tathāgata’s discourse on ultimate reality—the Dharma of the One Vehicle? Therefore it is said:
"If there were one who had truly attained Arhatship and yet did not believe in this Dharma, such a thing is impossible. Thus we know that one who has truly attained Arhatship...
The Han [monk] must certainly be able to believe this. If he does not believe, it is because he calls himself an Arhat while in reality he is not;
this is merely overweening pride (*adhimāna*). △ Third, the temporary indulgence.
Except after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when no Buddha is present before one. Why is this?
Because after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those who receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain the meaning of such sūtras as these are difficult to find.
Regarding the phrase "except for those such as the Buddhas," the intended meaning is that to lack faith in this Dharma constitutes *adhimāna* (arrogance). One might then ask:

"Does this mean that from the time of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* until now, all those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) are considered to have *adhimāna*? Therefore, for the sake of argument, it is provisionally stated:

excepting the period after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa when no Buddha is present before one, it is permitted that their lack of faith in this Dharma does not constitute *adhimāna*. Hence, it says "except."
The Buddha said (as above). This means: why is this so? Those who do not believe in this after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa do not constitute those of overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
Because such sutras as these will be difficult for others to believe and accept after the Buddha has passed into extinction, they do not believe;
therefore, it is granted that they do not constitute those of overweening pride. Thus it is said: "After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa" (as above). △ Fourth, the resolution of doubts.
If one encounters another Buddha, one will then attain definitive understanding within this Dharma.
Alternatively, one might doubt, saying: "Since this was not believed after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, does this not constitute the fault of overweening pride?

Would such a person ultimately remain a follower of the Hīnayāna and fail to receive the revelation? Therefore, it is explained: "If one encounters another Buddha, one will then attain definitive understanding."

It opens up the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; hence it says, "If one encounters [the Buddha]... (and so forth). Since they have attained definitive understanding that there is only the Single Buddha Vehicle, they are still able to realize and enter it—how much more so, then, for those who simply believe!
This passage follows from the previous section concerning "if my disciples" and extends here.

This is called "urging them toward faith. There is no other [meaning]. First, it distinguishes those who have not heard or known that the Tathāgata transforms only bodhisattvas, stating that they are neither Buddhas nor sons of the Buddha.
Second, it states that those who do not believe in this Dharma constitute those of overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
Third, even if one grants that they do not constitute those of overweening pride, they nonetheless exist after the parinirvāṇa of the Buddha. Fourth, [it concerns] those who do not...

Only after their cessation will they no longer give rise to overweening pride; ultimately, within the *upāya-śeṣa* (convenient remaining) lands, they encounter a Buddha and attain definitive understanding.

Because those of the two vehicles are born outside the realms [of ordinary beings], the Bodhisattvas who serve as the four reliances (*catur-apāśraya*) are also called "remaining Buddhas" (*śeṣa-buddha*).
Since they propagate the wondrous sutras and are likewise able to bring definitive understanding to those of the two vehicles, this is a profound and repeated encouragement.
He presses them to ensure they will certainly believe; thus it is said that he "exhorts and presses them to believe.

In this way, there is nothing among the teachings of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* that the two vehicles do not have revealed and clarified. For this reason, the delusions regarding Consciousness-Only must necessarily be shattered. △ Fourth, the admonition against falsehood.
"Śāriputra, you all should with single-minded resolve believe and understand this; receive and uphold the words of the Buddha. The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, speak no falsehoods.
There is no other vehicle; there is only the Single Buddha Vehicle."

This means: why must one have faith and understanding in the Buddha’s words? It is because the Buddha’s words are without falsehood; thus it is said, "The Buddhas... and so forth. Regarding "without falsehood":

whether they are definitive (real) or provisional (expedient), they are all without falsehood. Since they are without falsehood, one should with single-mindedness believe, understand, receive, and uphold them.
The two phrases concerning "there being no other vehicle" mean that the provisional and the real are mutually identical. Since the real...
There is no falsehood; even expedient means (*upāya*) is without falsehood. II. Verse Recitation (in four parts). First, the verse on withdrawing from one's seat.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
There were five thousand members of these four assemblies— monks and nuns who harbored overweening pride, laymen with arrogance,
and laywomen lacking faith— who failed to recognize their own faults and possessed deficiencies in their precepts.
They conceal their own flaws; these are those of small wisdom who have already departed. They are the dregs among the assembly; it is by the Buddha’s majestic power that they have gone.
Such people possess meager merit and are incapable of receiving this Dharma.

This was not previously stated in verse as a formal admission; rather, it was stated in verse regarding those who had withdrawn from their seats. By means of the three "cessations," it was originally intended for the fourfold assembly that had not yet withdrawn.

Now, since they have already withdrawn and [the Buddha] has granted permission to speak, then according to the text, those who withdrew from their seats should have been mentioned first in verse. As for the phrase "those who harbored [doubts] at the outset":
"harboring" refers to a private, self-centered sense of meaning. Regarding the upāsakas’ arrogance: although their bodies were close to the Buddha, [their minds were distant].
This is because their minds were still stained by worldly attachments. As for those *upāsikās* who did not believe, it does not mean they lacked faith in the Triple Gem;
rather, they did not believe that a female body could immediately become a Buddha.

As for those who departed due to the Buddha’s majestic power (*vibhūti*), these five thousand individuals and more were all made to leave through the majestic power of the Tathāgata’s great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and the virtue of his great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*).

This pertains to the two gates of *samgraha* (gathering) and *nigraha* (subduing). Had these five thousand people not been removed while hearing the extensive exposition, they would certainly have lacked faith;
they would have given rise to slander and fallen into suffering. Thus, by the power of his great compassion, the Tathāgata caused them to depart;

this is the gate of subduing (*nigraha*). These five thousand had already heard the brief opening and manifestation [of the truth], whereby the seeds of the One Vehicle’s perfection were already received within them.
[The Buddha] harbored this thought: "This may serve as a cause and condition for their future liberation.

However, if they hear this extensive teaching without regressing [in faith], they might still fail to avoid slander, thereby falling into suffering and losing the opportunity for liberation. Thus, by virtue of his great compassion, the Tathāgata...

Furthermore, he commands them to depart; this is the gateway through which the Tathāgata gathers [the assembly]. The rest may be understood by inspection. △ Second, the verse on those present in the assembly:
"This assembly has no branches or leaves; it consists only of those who are truly real."
△ Three verses on the promise to speak:
“Śāriputra, listen well.
△ Four verses on the actual exposition, which are threefold. First, from here onwards, the verses generally clarify all Buddhas. Second, from the past...

"Countless kalpas" and below: this verse separately clarifies the three periods of time. "Thirdly, I am also like this" and below: this verse again clarifies Śākyamuni. This section also has four parts.

First, the verse on opening the provisional to reveal the real. Second, one line and three phrases from "In the Buddha-lands of the ten directions," which verse clarifies the establishment of the provisional based on the real.
Third, three lines and three phrases from "The Buddhas appear in the world," which verse clarifies the [abandonment of]... (the provisional).
Provisionally establishing the reality. Fourth, if a person believes and takes refuge in the sixteen aspects of the lower [teachings], the verse encourages that this faith is not in vain.

This section also has two parts: first, clarifying how the various Buddhas open up the provisional; second, from "I have established these skillful means" onwards, clarifying how Śākyamuni reveals the real.
The first part is divided into two sections. The first explains the provisional [teachings]:
"The Dharma attained by all Buddhas, through immeasurable powers of skillful means, is preached for the sake of sentient beings, according to what is in the minds of those beings."
The various paths they travel, their diverse dispositions and desires, and their past deeds of both good and evil—the Buddha knows all these.
Through the power of skillful means, using various causes, analogies, and modes of expression, he brings joy to all; at times he speaks the sūtras.
Gāthās and Itivṛttakas, Jātakas and Adbhutadharmas, as well as the exposition of Nidānas,
Avadānas together with Geyas, and Upadeśa-sūtras.

The Dharma attained by all Buddhas is precisely the attainment of true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*); their immeasurable power of skillful means (*upāya*) is precisely the attainment of provisional wisdom (*prajñā*).
Having thus attained these provisional and true wisdoms, they descend to preach them for the sake of sentient beings; yet first, they examine the capacities of those beings.

The Buddha has fully descended. Having clearly discerned the capacities [of sentient beings], he establishes the teaching according to those capacities. Previously, he did not speak of this as being a provisional means (*upāya*);
now that he speaks of it as a provisional means, he is revealing the hidden authority (*kaiquan*). △ Second, the exposition of the underlying intent.

Those of dull faculties who delight in inferior teachings and are greedily attached to birth and death, failing to practice the profound and wondrous path under the countless Buddhas and being distressed by manifold sufferings— for their sake, I preach nirvana.
Regarding those of dull faculties and so forth: it means that the Buddhas first establish skillful means because sentient beings delight in inferior teachings;

thus they are called "those of dull faculties" (and so on). It is said that they not only delight in inferior teachings, but furthermore, because they are greedily attached to the pleasures of the five worldly desires, there is birth and death. Moreover, because they delight in inferior teachings, regarding all [phenomena]...
They are unable to practice the profound, subtle, and mysterious Way of the Buddha; hence it is said, "Regarding all [dharmas]... (and so forth).
This profound and subtle Way is precisely the knowledge and vision of the Buddha. Because they are attached to birth and death, they are afflicted and disturbed by manifold sufferings;
thus, they are unable to practice the profound and subtle Way and are beset by these manifold afflictions and disturbances.
Therefore, he first explains the *nirvāṇa* of the Hīnayāna to guide them; thus it is said, "For their sake, he speaks of *nirvāṇa*.
However, the intention of all Buddhas fundamentally lies in the Mahāyāna. Because those with dull faculties delight in the small vehicle, he establishes skillful means (*upāya*).
As for the essence of the power of expediency (*upāya*), it is entirely identical to reality (*tattva*); thus, the intention behind the revelation of the provisional is made clear.
△ Second, clarifying Śākyamuni’s manifestation of the real. This also has two parts. First, stating the intent.
I have established these skillful means to enable you to enter the Buddha’s wisdom. I have never said to you, "You shall attain the path of Buddhahood.
The reason I have not said so is that the time for such a teaching had not yet arrived. Now is precisely that time; I shall definitively proclaim the Mahāyāna.
"These ninefold teachings of mine are spoken in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings; they take entry into the Mahāyāna as their foundation, and for this reason I preach this sutra.

This passage explains the intent of revealing the ultimate reality. Since the purpose of the skillful means employed was fundamentally to lead sentient beings into the Buddha's knowledge and vision, that which was not previously spoken of was because the time had not yet arrived; now that the time has come, it is therefore preached. Thus...

He said: "As for my exposition [and so forth], those who definitively proclaim the Mahāyāna state that the ninefold provisional teachings previously expounded were merely in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings;
they were never the original intent of the Tathāgata. The original intent of the Tathāgata lies solely in the One Reality."
Therefore it is said, "I [now]... (and so forth). Having already bestowed the provisional teachings of the Hīnayāna, the Buddha-way of the One Vehicle may now be proclaimed.
This is why this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is taught: to open up the former provisional [teachings] and to reveal the present reality. Thus it is said, "For this reason, I preach this sūtra.
The intent behind revealing the reality is as described above. △ Second, the actual revelation has three parts. First, regarding the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavasthāna-śāsana*).

[The Buddha] manifested: "There are sons of the Buddha whose minds are pure, who are gentle and of sharp faculties; having served immeasurable Buddhas, they have practiced the profound and wondrous Way.
For these sons of the Buddha, I preach this Mahāyāna sūtra. I grant this prediction to such people: in a future age, they shall attain the path of Buddhahood."
Regarding the phrase "the purity of mind," etc.: in the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), there are no two vehicles; it is exclusively the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas.

Because the Bodhisattvas succeed to the family enterprise of the Tathāgata’s Mahāyāna, they are called "Sons of the Buddha. However, at their initial stage, they contemplate only pure *tathatā* (suchness).
Furthermore, they cannot immediately regard afflictions and birth-and-death as being *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*. It is therefore necessary to pass through these nine realms in order to realize Buddhahood.

The One Vehicle is precisely this: severing the nine [grades of afflictions] by means of the principle. This is why it is called "purity of mind. In the Perfect Teaching, when one practices, everything is practiced;
when one severs, everything is severed. Therefore, it is not merely gentle. Specifically, one must first practice emptiness to sever the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*);
next, one practices the provisional to sever the dust-like afflictions (*rajas-kleśa*); and only afterwards does one practice the Middle. By...
They sever ignorance. Because they cannot sever all that is to be severed through cultivation by means of a single cultivation, they are called "pliant" (*mṛdu*).
In the two teachings of the *Tathāgatagarbha* and the *Āgamas*, one is dull rather than sharp; in the Perfect Teaching (*Vimalakīrti*), one is sharp rather than dull.

Now, the Distinct Teaching (*Pratyekabuddha*) is called sharp in comparison to the former, yet it is also called dull in comparison to the latter; therefore, it is said to be "also of sharp faculties. As for those who practice the profound and wondrous path, regarding—
Throughout immeasurable kalpas, he has served immeasurable Buddhas and practiced as many dharma-gates as there are sands in the Ganges.
Because these can be approached both horizontally and vertically, they are profound and subtle; yet they are truly not the profound subtlety of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

This clarifies that the capacity for the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*) is such as this. Following this, it clarifies how the provisional is opened for those of separate capacity, and how this Mahāyāna Subtlety is preached.
This scripture reveals the ultimate reality. △ Second, the revelation according to the Shared Teaching (Pāryāptika-yāna):
"Because they deeply mindfully recollect the Buddha and cultivate and maintain the pure precepts, upon hearing that such as these shall attain Buddhahood, great joy suffuses their entire bodies."
The Buddha, knowing their mental activities, therefore expounded the Mahāyāna for them.

As for the "profound mind," it refers to those who, through the Shared Teaching, are able to realize that both the Buddha who is the object of mindfulness and the mind that performs the mindfulness are [empty].
All things are immediately empty. The *zàng* (Treasury) [stage] can only perceive emptiness and does not perceive non-emptiness;
the *tōng* (Penetration) [stage] can simultaneously perceive non-emptiness, and is thus deeper than the *zàng*. Because one recollects the Buddha by means of this, it is called the "deep mind.

The phrase "practicing and upholding the pure precepts" clarifies the external body. Above, the recollection of the Buddha was briefly mentioned; here, the practice of the precepts is briefly mentioned. Since—

When one recollects the Buddha, one must necessarily recollect the Dharma and the Sangha; thus, the Three Jewels are recollected together. Once one has cultivated the precepts, one must necessarily cultivate concentration and wisdom;

thus, the three trainings are cultivated together. In each of these cases, the first is mentioned to encompass the subsequent ones. This clarifies that the capacity of those for whom this Shared Teaching is intended is as described above.
Below this, it clarifies how the provisional is opened for the sake of those with shared capacities, by preaching this wondrous Mahāyāna sūtra and revealing—
Indeed. Upon hearing these two phrases concerning the Buddha, they realize that he is not merely a Buddha who has attained the wisdom of a single thought-moment and severed residual habits;
if they can hear that he is a Buddha whose seat is space, they will experience nothing less than joy.
He then rejoices greatly. Not only does his mind rejoice, but his body also rejoices. Therefore it is said: "These [people]... (and so forth).
The phrase "The Buddha knows their mental activities" concludes the preceding section. "Knowing their minds" concludes the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha with a profound mind;
"knowing their activities" concludes the cultivation and maintenance of the pure precepts. △ Third, the manifestation according to the Tripiṭaka teachings.
Whether they be śrāvakas or bodhisattvas, upon hearing the Dharma I have taught—even if only a single verse—they will all undoubtedly attain Buddhahood.

The first phrase identifies those who are the recipients of the Tripitaka teachings; since the primary transformation of the Tripitaka is for the sake of the two vehicles, it first mentions the śrāvaka.

Because he transforms others as a bodhisattva, he is next called a "bodhisattva. The passage beginning with "Hearing me" clarifies that for those of hidden capacity (*gūḍha-āśaya*), the sublime Mahāyāna sūtras are preached to reveal their true nature.

While the preceding general and specific [explanations] were all based on the speaker, and thus used expressions such as "for this person" and "therefore for him," the present section concerns the recipient of the teaching;
hence it says, "hearing us," and so forth. He hears the Dharma that is being preached.
This refers to hearing the wondrous Dharma of the non-duality of the provisional and the real in this present sutra.
Whether one hears the entire work, a single fascicle, a single chapter, or even a single four-line verse, it is therefore said, "even down to...
(and so forth). Although there are differences in the amount heard, there is no doubt that all shall attain Buddhahood. This...
Among them, someone raises an objection, saying: "If one can all attain Buddhahood upon hearing a single verse, why is it that those present here who hear the sutra do not yet become Buddhas?
This person fails to realize that the statement regarding the certainty of attaining Buddhahood is a statement of revelation.
For those of the three vehicles did not themselves know they could become perfect Buddhas; now, through the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, this is revealed.
This is to cause them also to know the Perfect Buddha. Once they have known this, they will naturally act in accordance with the Buddha and subsequently achieve realization.

How could one become a Buddha at the very moment of hearing this, without awaiting the process of cultivation? If one were to become a Buddha immediately upon hearing it, then one would merely be a "Buddha by name.
As for those who are currently present and hearing the sutra—if they immediately act in accordance with their understanding and give rise to practice...

If one practices, one will soon attain realization for oneself. Even if one cannot immediately practice and realize it, having already planted the seeds within one's heart, what doubt can there be regarding future Buddhahood?
Therefore, the subsequent text states: "Those who hear even a single phrase or a single verse and rejoice for a single moment shall all become Buddhas.
2. Verse on Bestowing the Ultimate and Establishing the Expedient.
Within the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the One Vehicle Dharma; there is neither a second nor a third, except for the Buddha’s skillful means of teaching.
He employs only provisional names to guide sentient beings, speaking thus in order to reveal the wisdom of the Buddhas.
Using provisional names to guide [beings] is the employment of skillful means (*upāya*). To speak of the Buddha’s wisdom is the ultimate reality (*tattva*).

Because one wishes to explain the reality of the Buddha’s wisdom, one first employs the provisional means of the three vehicles (*triyāna*). This is the common ritual for the Buddhas’ establishment of transformation.
△ Third, the verse on abolishing the provisional and establishing the real.
When the Buddhas appear in the world, this alone is the one true reality; the other two are not real. They never, by means of the Lesser Vehicle, deliver sentient beings.
The Buddha himself abides in the Great Vehicle, according to the Dharma he has realized, adorned with the power of concentration and wisdom.
By means of this, I deliver sentient beings and personally realize the unsurpassed path.
Regarding the equal Dharma of the Mahāyāna, if I were to transform even a single person by means of the Hīnayāna, I would fall into stinginess and greed; such a thing is not permissible.
The first two lines establish the reality; the following three lines discard the provisional. Both are evident. Below this, the Buddha himself provides the intent behind establishing the reality:

namely, that since the Tathāgata himself abides in the Mahāyāna and has attained the Mahāyāna, he uses that which he abides in and that which he has attained to deliver sentient beings, causing them likewise to abide in what the Buddha abides in and to attain what the Buddha attains.
The adornment of meditative concentration and wisdom is that which the Buddha alone dwells in and attains; hence it is said, "The Buddha himself... (and so forth).

The following one and a half lines, beginning with "Self-realization" (*svasaṃvedya*), express the intention of setting aside provisional means. This means that while the Buddha has personally realized the Mahāyāna, if he were to deliver sentient beings by means of the Hīnayāna, he would not avoid falling into stinginess.
However, when the Buddha delivers sentient beings, he first destroys their stinginess; yet, if he himself were not free from stinginess, [he could not do so].

"How could one be able to deliver sentient beings? Therefore, it is not possible. Thus, the fact that he ultimately does not use the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) to save sentient beings makes clear his intention to set aside provisional means. △ Fourth, the verse on exhorting faith in its non-falsity, in three parts: First, the direct exhortation to believe; Second, "If I... and below, citing the five turbidities; Third, "I have... and below, concluding that it is not false. Raising his mind and exhorting those of form:
"If a person has faith and takes refuge in the Buddha, the Tathāgata does not deceive or mislead them, nor does he harbor thoughts of greed or envy.
Having severed all evils within the dharmas, the Buddha alone among the ten directions is free from fear. I adorn my body with the marks; my radiance illuminates the world."
Honored by immeasurable multitudes, he proclaims the Seal of the True Reality (*tathatā-mudrā*).
The first line exhorts by means of the mind; the subsequent line exhorts by means of form.
Whether mind or form, both are entirely sublime, manifesting that the Dharma he teaches is not false. With faith they accept it; with devotion they take refuge in the Tathāgata.
Since you are neither deceptive nor possess greed or envy, why did you previously fail to declare that the Single Buddha Vehicle is fundamentally real?
For forty years prior, you never stated it was real, which seems like a deception. Furthermore, why did you previously fail to state that the Three Vehicles are fundamentally provisional?
For forty years prior, you never stated they were provisional, which seems like a fraud.
Furthermore, forty years ago, when I did not preach the Great [Vehicle] for the sake of those of the Two Vehicles, it appeared as though I were attached to the Great Dharma;
yet, when I preached only the Small Dharma, it appeared as though I were jealous of the Two Vehicles.

Not realizing why this was so, one must understand that it was entirely because the time had not yet arrived and the faculties of beings were not yet matured. Now, at this assembly of the Lotus Sūtra, [the time has come].

When the time has arrived and the capacity [of beings] has matured, it does not hinder one from clearly stating that the three vehicles previously taught were provisional, while the single vehicle taught today is the reality.
Thus, one knows that although the Tathāgata may seem to have deceived, he is in truth not deceptive.
Furthermore, since the former small [vehicle] is opened up and is entirely identical to the great [vehicle] of today, one knows that although the Tathāgata may seem to...
Regarding greed and envy: in reality, there is no greed or envy. This is why sentient beings ought to place their faith and take refuge in the Buddha.
Yet, the Tathāgata does not merely do so; he is able to sever all evils whatsoever that exist within all phenomena.

Because the Tathāgata has reached the ultimate consummation of the five stages of dwelling and the two types of death have forever perished, it is said that he has severed all evils among all phenomena.
Thus, his inner mind is pure; throughout the worlds of the ten directions, he is naturally free from timidity and possesses a majestic presence that inspires awe.
When it is said, "I adorn my body with marks," this refers to the thirty-two marks, each of which is boundless. By means of these...

It is adorned. As for "radiance," it does not consist merely of the adornment of physical marks; furthermore, each mark possesses immeasurable light, and each ray of light possesses immeasurable brilliance.

By means of this radiance of adorned marks, he illuminates and presides over the world, such that there is nothing in all the worlds that is not revered. Therefore, it is said: "Honored by immeasurable multitudes. Since he is thus—
He who is honored by immeasurable multitudes returns to preach the Seal of the True Mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇamudrā*) for immeasurable multitudes.
As for the "Seal of the True Mark," "seal" (*mudrā*) signifies that which is fixed and unalterable, just like a seal of authentication in the world.
Indeed, the True Mark is the same path shared by all Buddhas; it cannot be altered by any devas, humans, māras, or followers of external paths. Therefore, it is called a "seal."
If one speaks only of existence, it is subverted by emptiness; if one speaks only of emptiness, it is subverted by existence;
if one speaks only of the Middle Way, it is subverted by the two extremes. In none of these cases can one speak of it as a "seal.

However, the true reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is neither empty, nor provisional, nor the Middle; it is precisely emptiness and the provisional, and therefore it is not the Middle, which is precisely the provisional.
Because it is within the Middle, it is not empty; because it is within emptiness, it is not provisional. Thus, while it is not empty, it returns to being precisely emptiness:
when one thing is empty, all things are simultaneously empty. Likewise, while it is not the Middle, it returns to being precisely the Middle:
when one thing is the Middle, all things are simultaneously the Middle. This is that which is upheld by all Buddhas, and which even Māra and his minions cannot alter. Therefore, it is said:
This is the Seal of the True Mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇamudrā*). Thus far, the internal mind has been presented; with the internal mind purified, one is fearless throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
Now, external forms are presented; with external forms adorned with light, one is honored by those of the three periods of time.
What is further explained here is precisely the Seal of the True Mark. Since it cannot be altered, how could there be any falsehood? For this reason, it is used as a basis for exhorting faith.
△ Second, the exhortation by means of citing his original vow:
"Śāriputra, you should know that I originally established this vow: 'I desire to cause all sentient beings to be no different from myself.'"
"As I have previously vowed, it is now fulfilled. I shall transform all sentient beings and cause them all to enter the Buddha-way.
By "original vow," he refers to the vow established at the very first moment of generating the aspiration for enlightenment in the past.
That which is initiated by the mind is called a "vow" (*praṇidhāna*); that which is aimed at by a vow is called a "pledge" (*samaya*).
This refers to the desire to deliver boundless sentient beings, up to and including the desire to achieve the unsurpassed path of Buddhahood; these constitute a "vow-pledge.
"All sentient beings" refers to the beings of the nine realms. "No different from me" means desiring to cause the beings of the nine realms to also become like [me].
"I have made a vow to sever all afflictions until the attainment of unsurpassed Buddha-way.
Those who are 'like us' refer to those who, in the past, desired to deliver sentient beings and have already delivered them;
and who, in the past, desired to attain the Buddha-way and have already attained it. Therefore, it is said, 'those like me' (and so forth). By this, one knows that today..."
What has been taught was spoken in accordance with his original vows; how could there be anything false or untrustworthy?
Therefore, it concludes by saying, "To transform all beings" (and so forth). However, the purpose of encouraging faith is to desire that they believe what the Buddhas have taught:
that there is only the Single Buddha Vehicle (*ekayāna*) and no other vehicles. For this reason, he first raises up form and mind to offer encouragement.
The conclusion states: "For them, the Seal of the True Reality (bhūtatathatā-mudrā) is taught. Since the seal is the true reality, then every mark is truly real.
How could there be any other vehicle outside of the One Vehicle that is empty and thus unreliable? Next, the exhortation through vows is raised, concluding: "Causing all to enter the Buddha-way.
Since all who enter are the Buddha-way, then every dharma is equally real. How could there be [anything] outside of the One Vehicle?
Furthermore, could there be other vehicles that are empty and thus untrustworthy? It is for this reason that these two exhortations to believe are given;
what doubt would not be severed thereby? △ Second, citing the five turbidities, in three parts: First, stating the intent.
"If I encounter sentient beings, I teach them all the Buddha-way. Yet those lacking wisdom become confused and deluded, failing to accept the teaching.

[The interlocutor] says: "Since there is only the One Vehicle, and you wish to cause all sentient beings to enter the Buddha-way, why do you not directly preach the One Vehicle, but instead first preach the Three Vehicles?
To this, the intention is expressed: "If we [encounter sentient beings]... and so forth. "I encounter sentient beings... [and so on].
Birth is like people in the world: one comes from the south and another goes from the north; they will never meet.
But if one comes from the south while the other comes from the north, they will certainly meet. Now, the Buddhas are the ultimate sages, whereas sentient beings are lowly ordinary folk;
how could they possibly meet? It is entirely due to the Buddhas who, through their unconditional great compassion (*anālambana-mahākaruṇā*), universally take all beings as their object.
All sentient beings within the *dharmadhātu* are the objects of the great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) of all Buddhas;
it is as natural as a magnet attracting iron. Therefore, it is said that they "encounter" [it]. This refers to the meeting of compassion and suffering.
However, not all these sentient beings are capable of this. If one were to speak directly of the Great [Vehicle] to those who possess wisdom...
The wise are certainly able to believe and accept [this teaching], whereas those without wisdom will inevitably become confused and deluded.

Once they are confused and deluded, how can they receive the instruction? Thus, the reason for not speaking directly of the Great [Vehicle] is clearly understood as the intention to first preach the Small [Vehicle] within the world of the five turbidities. To be "confused" means to regard the Small [Vehicle] as the ultimate. Not...
To believe in only the Single Buddha Vehicle is for the small and the great to become confused with one another. One is deluded by the small and bewildered by the great;
being deluded by the small, one cannot relinquish it, and being bewildered by the great, one cannot accept it. This is why they do not receive the teaching. △ Second, showing the signs.
I know these sentient beings who have never cultivated the roots of goodness; they are stubbornly attached to the five desires, and through deluded craving, they give rise to affliction.
Due to the causes and conditions of various desires, they fall into the three evil realms and transmigrate within the six destinies, undergoing all manner of bitter suffering.
The subtle form at conception grows ever more so from lifetime to lifetime. Those of meager virtue and little merit are oppressed by manifold sufferings;
they enter the dense forest of false views—views such as "existence" or "non-existence"—and relying upon these various perspectives, they become fully possessed of the sixty-two [wrong views].
Deeply attached to false and illusory dharmas, they cling to them firmly and cannot let go. Arrogant and self-conceited, their minds are crooked and insincere.
For thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, such people will not hear the name of the Buddha, nor will they hear the True Dharma; they are difficult to deliver.

The first line demonstrates the characteristics of the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*). "I know" refers to the illumination and clear realization through the skillful wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) used for transforming others.
"Roots of goodness" refers to the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*). To lack clear understanding regarding the objects of the five desires is called delusion (*moha*);
to give rise to various defiled attachments toward the objects of the five desires is called craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Due to this delusion and craving, confusion and affliction arise.

Because it causes affliction and disturbance, it is called "giving rise to affliction. Second, the line beginning with "By means of all" (*zhī yǐ zhū xià*) indicates the characteristics of the *sattva-kaṣāya* (the turbidity of sentient beings).

"All desires" refers to the five desires (*pañca-kāma*). With the five desires as the cause and the three poisons (*tri-viṣa*) as the condition, one [becomes attached] to the five desires that accord with one's emotions.
Thus, greed arises toward agreeable fivefold sensual desires; hatred arises toward disagreeable fivefold sensual desires;
and delusion arises toward neutral fivefold sensual desires. By these causes and conditions, one invites bitter fruits and falls into the evil realms.
Due to greed, one falls into hell; due to hatred, one falls among the hungry ghosts; and due to delusion, one falls into [the animal realm].
Animals. Therefore it is said, "By means of these... and so forth. When the retributions for offenses in the three miserable realms are exhausted, one attains birth among humans or devas;
yet when humans and devas commit offenses, they fall back into the three miserable realms. Within the three realms and six paths, they emerge and submerge like the wheel of a cart, never ceasing;
they revolve like a ring, without end. Hence it is called "saṃsāra" (revolving). As for the "six destinies":
If one is in the realm of hell, there are mountains of knives and trees of swords, cauldrons of boiling water, and furnaces of burning coals;
even within a single day and night, one undergoes eighty-four thousand cycles of birth and death. In the realm of hungry ghosts, their throats are as narrow as the eye of a needle.
Their bellies are as vast as the great ocean, yet their throats are so narrow;

since the belly is thus immense while the throat is so slender, even if they were to drink and eat at every moment, they still could not satisfy their hunger and thirst—how much less so after passing through hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas without hearing the names of water or grain?
In the realm of animals, they are covered in fur and bear horns, burdened by debts and harboring grievances. To speak of them all in brief: if...

Among the species of birds, the species of fur-bearing animals, and the species of scaly and armored creatures, some lose their bodies upon the blade and the chopping block, while others perish in boiling water and fire.
How great indeed are the bitter retributions of these three paths! As for the asuras, they suffer the pain of being defeated in battle with the devas;
among humans, there are the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death; and in the heavens, there are likewise five [sufferings].
The manifestation of the signs of decay and so forth constitute suffering; hence it is said that "one fully experiences all manner of bitter poisons.

Third, the single line beginning with "entering the womb" demonstrates the characteristics of the *kalpa* of life (*āyuṣkaṣāya*). Regarding "entering the womb": this refers to the convergence of the three conditions—the father, the mother, and oneself—to receive the womb.
"Subtle form" refers to that which maintains the continuity of matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) as the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), namely the *kalala*. From lifetime to lifetime...
"Increase" refers to the five stages within the womb. "Those of meager virtue and little merit" means they lack the adornment of merit;

they are "of meager virtue. They lack the wealth of supramundane dharmas, meaning they have "little merit. "Oppressed by manifold sufferings" refers to the destruction of years and the reduction of lifespan, such as being born in the morning and dying in the evening.
Entering the two lower paths of the heterodox indicates the characteristics of the *kaṣāya* of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*). Five.
One line at the end of the thousand [stanzas] reveals the characteristics of the *kalpa*-defilement (*kalpa-kaṣāya*).
△ Third, the conclusion and manifestation: "Therefore, Śāriputra, I have established skillful means and taught the various paths for the exhaustion of suffering, demonstrating them as *nirvāṇa*."
Although I speak of nirvāṇa, it is not a true extinction. All phenomena, from their very origin, have always been characterized by quiescence.
Once the sons of the Buddha have practiced the Way, they shall become Buddhas in a future age.

Thus, these two characters [“is” and “therefore”] refer back to the characteristics of the five turbidities mentioned above. In the prose section, the two characters “thus” (rúshì) are used with the same intent;
that is to say, what all Buddhas have taught is fundamentally but the One Vehicle, yet because of sentient beings in the age of the five turbidities...

Because their capacities were not yet in accord with the ultimate truth, he first bestowed the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles; thus it is said, "I have established skillful means," and so forth.
Although he first established the nirvana of the Lesser Vehicle, this was not true extinction, being rather like the quiescence of all phenomena.
This is true extinction. Therefore it is said: "Although I... (and so forth). To say that it is not true extinction refers to the *nirvāṇa* of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).

This is because the delusions it eliminates are merely those of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*), and the birth-and-death it transcends is merely the *paricchinna-bhava* (segmented existence);
thus, it is not ultimate, true extinction. How, then, is there true extinction? Therefore, it is immediately stated: "All phenomena, from the very beginning..."
It is eternally characterized by quiescence and extinction. As for all phenomena (*dharmas*), there are mundane phenomena and supramundane phenomena;

there are the phenomena of ordinary beings and the phenomena of noble ones. If one views these various phenomena through the lens of emotional perception, one regards mundane phenomena as subject to change, supramundane phenomena as immovable, the phenomena of ordinary beings as transmigratory, and the phenomena of noble ones as... [quiescent].
If one were to regard them as eternally abiding, none could be called the mark of quiescence (*śānta-lakṣaṇa*).

However, if one examines their essential nature (*dharmatā*) through rigorous analysis, it is not only supramundane phenomena (*lokottara-dharma*) that are immovable; even mundane phenomena (*laukika-dharma*) are, in their entirety, immovable.

It is not only the phenomena of the sages (*ārya-dharma*) that are eternally abiding; even the phenomena of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana-dharma*) are, in their entirety, eternally abiding. Therefore, it is said that all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*)...
From the very beginning, it has always been characterized by quiescence. This characteristic of quiescence is precisely the wondrous principle (*li*).
If one gives rise to wondrous practice of quiescence based upon this wondrous principle of quiescence, then one can accomplish the wondrous fruit of quiescence.
Therefore, it is said: "When the Son of the Buddha has practiced the Way, he shall become a Buddha in a future life. If one becomes a Buddha, then...
When the five abodes are completely exhausted and the two deaths are forever extinguished, this is true cessation.

Thus one knows that if there were those capable of hearing the single vehicle (*ekayāna*) of the quiescent nature of all phenomena, it would certainly have been unnecessary to first preach the three vehicles.

However, because the faculties and dispositions of sentient beings in the five turbidities do not accord [with such a teaching], it could not be avoided to preach them. Nevertheless, although the three were preached, the intent was always the single vehicle. Regarding this:
Throughout the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the Single Vehicle Dharma; there is neither a second nor a third. △ Third, the conclusion that this is not in vain:
"I possess the power of skillful means to reveal and teach the teachings of the Three Vehicles, yet all the World-Honored Ones preach the path of the Single Vehicle."
Now, this great assembly should all eliminate their doubts and delusions; the words of all Buddhas do not differ, for there is only the Single Vehicle, without a second.
The first two lines clarify that Śākyamuni reveals the provisional, while the subsequent two lines clarify that all Buddhas manifest the real.

This is merely a matter of mutual clarification within the text: because Śākyamuni reveals the provisional, he manifests the real; likewise, because all Buddhas manifest the real, they must also reveal the provisional.
"All speak of the phrase of the One Vehicle," which means that it is ultimate. The subsequent line correctly clarifies that this is not in vain:
"Now these great assemblies" refers to all those present in the gathering.

The intent is that since I have previously used skillful means to open up the Three Vehicles, and since all Buddhas must likewise first open up the Three, one can know that the teaching of the provisional is not empty.
Since all Buddhas have taught the path of the One Vehicle, it can be known that my own teaching of the path of the One Vehicle must likewise be true and not false.
Thus, by means of Śākyamuni’s non-falsity, the non-falsity of all Buddhas can be understood; and by means of the non-falsity of all Buddhas, the non-falsity of Śākyamuni can be understood.
Therefore, one should eliminate doubt. By means of the non-falsity of all Buddhas, one should understand Śākyamuni.
That this is not in vain can be further understood. One should also eliminate doubts; therefore, he addressed the great assembly, saying:
"All should eliminate their doubts. Now, that which must ultimately be eliminated is nothing other than this: since the words of all Buddhas are entirely without difference.
Thus, outside of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), there are no other two vehicles; what the Buddhas have taught is therefore true and not false.
This is why such doubts must be eliminated. △ Second, the verses separately clarify the three periods of time, divided into three parts.
The first twenty-seven and a half lines praise the past; the second six and a half lines praise the future;
the third four and a half lines praise the present. Of these three sections, the first two briefly reveal the exposition.
In the past, throughout incalculable kalpas, there were immeasurable Buddhas who have entered parinirvāṇa—hundreds, thousands, tens of millions, and billions in number, beyond all measure.
These World-Honored Ones, by means of various causes and conditions, parables, and countless powers of skillful means, have expounded the characteristics of all dharmas.
All these World-Honored Ones preach the Single Vehicle Dharma, transforming immeasurable sentient beings and causing them to enter the Buddha-way.

The first two lines reveal the provisional means (*upāya*). As for the mention of "hundreds of thousands of billions" and so forth, this refers to the Buddhas who have entered parinirvāṇa in the past.
Since they are immeasurable, there are immeasurable hundreds of thousands of names and titles, as well as immeasurable hundreds of thousands of lands and so forth.
Such varieties of numbers are inherently impossible to fathom; therefore, it says "hundreds of thousands" (and so on).
The final line of verse clearly reveals the reality, which may be understood. △ Second, the verse extensively elucidates [the meaning] in two parts.
First, the general introduction:
Furthermore, all the great and holy lords, knowing the deep-seated desires of the various classes of beings among gods and humans in all worlds,
employ further diverse skillful means to assist in manifesting the ultimate truth.

Regarding the word "furthermore" (*yòu*): what has been stated above was a brief verse summarizing one cycle of the Buddhas' revelation; now it is recited again in detail, hence the word "furthermore.
"To know" refers to the expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) for transforming others; it is immediate illumination.

The phrase "gods and humans" specifically designates the two vehicles (*dvi-yāna*), while "the various classes of sentient beings" collectively encompasses the three vehicles (*tri-yāna*). "Profound mind" (*gambhīra-citta*).

"What is desired" refers to the desire for the Dharma of the five vehicles. Regarding the phrase "further by other skillful means," the word "further" (更) is used in contrast to the preceding brief verse.
The preceding statement, "expounding the characteristics of all phenomena," refers to the teaching as the expressive medium (*vyañjana*).

These words serve to further clarify the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*); this refers specifically to the principle being expounded. To employ "different skillful means" (*upāya*) is precisely to open up the provisional;
to reveal the ultimate truth is precisely to manifest the real. Some have said that "different skillful means" is spoken in contrast to the "correct.
The three vehicles that were previously taught constitute the correct skillful means, while further teaching the [paths of] humans and devas constitutes the different [skillful means].

This is a matter of skillful means (*upāya*). Now, when we speak of the five vehicles (*pañca-yāna*), they are equally provisional teachings revealed [by the Buddha]. Why, then, distinguish between them as being "correct" or "different"?
Generally speaking, there are two senses in which they are considered different: first, the difference of distinctness; second, the difference of separation.

Regarding "distinctive" (*bīeyì*): the five vehicles are each distinct and different, yet all belong to the realm of skillful means; therefore, they are called "different skillful means. Regarding "separated" (*géyì*):
if [the truth] has not yet been revealed, then the five vehicles and the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) are separated and distinct;
they are merely skillful means for the true reality and cannot be fully identical with it; therefore, they are called "different skillful means. It is said:

Regarding "aiding manifestation": if one relies on the primary truth (paramārtha), by means of the principle of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa), one gives rise to the sublime contemplation of the true mark to illuminate the principle of the primary truth.
When such object and contemplation mutually investigate one another, the primary truth is thereby manifested;
this is "correct manifestation. Now, however, it is not manifested through the mutual investigation of object and contemplation, but rather, by simply opening up the five vehicles, it is manifested.

Because it reveals the true mark (*dharmatā*), it is said to "assist in its manifestation. △ Second, the specific demonstration has two parts. First, twenty-two lines clarify the opening and manifestation by way of the *pratyaya-hetu* (conditioning cause).
Second, one line concerning "all past [Buddhas]" clarifies the opening and manifestation by way of the *jñāna-hetu* (understanding cause). The first part further has three sections;
the first concerns the Bodhisattvas.
If there are any classes of sentient beings who encountered the various Buddhas of the past, and whether they heard the Dharma and practiced giving, or observed the precepts, practiced patience,
diligence, meditation, and wisdom— cultivating all manner of merit and insight— all such people have already attained the path to Buddhahood.
Regarding those who cultivate merit and wisdom, these are divided by means of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*): the first five constitute merit, while the last one constitutes wisdom.

However, there are differences among the three teachings: some cultivate merit and wisdom with signs (*sanimitta*), some cultivate merit and wisdom without signs (*animitta*), and some cultivate merit and wisdom both with and without signs.
Thus, it is said they are "various. This is the disclosure of the provisional; all have already attained the Buddha-way.

This refers to the manifestation of reality. If the various practices cultivated as described above were not revealed and manifested, then those who cultivate with signs would merely achieve the path of the *piṭaka* (Tripitaka) bodhisattvas;
those who cultivate signlessness would merely achieve the path of the bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*);
and those who cultivate both signs and signlessness would merely achieve the path of the bodhisattvas of the Distinct Teaching (*libie*).

None were able to achieve the unsurpassed Buddha-way. It was because the Buddhas of the past revealed and manifested [the truth] once and for all that they were enabled to all achieve the unsurpassed Buddha-way. △ Second, regarding the two vehicles.

After the parinirvāṇa of the Buddhas, those people who possess a virtuous and gentle mind—all such individuals have already attained the path to Buddhahood. Regarding those with a "virtuous and gentle mind":

compared to those of the Two Vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha), who are able to contemplate the truths and conditions and thereby give rise to true outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava*), they are superior to humans and devas;

yet, because they only sever the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhava-kleśa*) but cannot sever ignorance (*avidyā*), they are inferior when compared to bodhisattvas. Thus, [the Two Vehicles] are "gentle."

Thus, the latter two lines correctly clarify the revelation and manifestation (*kaixian*). Because [the truth] had not yet been revealed, contemplating the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination would only result in the Two Vehicles of the *Zang* (Tripitaka) and *Tong* (Shared) teachings. It was through that single act of revelation by those Buddhas [that this changed].

That which is observed—the arising and ceasing, the non-arising, the Four Noble Truths, and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination—is itself the inconceivable and unconditioned Four Noble Truths and Twelve Links of Dependent Origination. It requires no alteration or transformation to become entirely the perfect cause;
therefore, it is said that "all shall attain the Buddha-way. As the text below states: "We who are now truly Śrāvakas [shall do so] by means of the sound of the Buddha-way."
To cause all to hear this. △ Third, regarding humans and devas, there are three parts. First, explaining the erection of stupas:
After the various Buddhas have entered parinirvāṇa, those who make offerings to their relics erect billions of kinds of stupas made of gold, silver, and crystal.
With conch shells and agates, rose-colored gems and lapis lazuli beads—pure and extensively arrayed—they adorned the various stupas.
Some constructed stone shrines using sandalwood, aloeswood, *kālānusārī*, and other timbers, as well as bricks, tiles, clay, and earth.
If, in the midst of a wilderness, one piles up earth to form a temple for the Buddha, or even as children at play gather sand to make a stupa for the Buddha—
all such people have already attained the path to Buddhahood.
The meaning of this passage is as follows: the first three and a half lines clarify the celestial beings (*devas*), while the final two lines clarify humans.
Thus, these last two lines, according to the intent of revelation, clarify that all shall attain the Buddha-way. The term *śarīra* is a Sanskrit word;
in the language of China (*Hua-yen*), it means "sacred bone" or "relic," and is also called "firm and solid. As for ordinary worldlings, in every thought-moment...
They give rise solely to greed, hatred, and delusion, and their entire bodies are permeated and congealed by these three poisons;
consequently, all their bones eventually decay and rot, failing to attain solidity.
In contrast, the Buddhas and noble sages cultivate precept, concentration, and wisdom in every thought-moment, so that their entire being is permeated and congealed by these three trainings.
Because they have been bound [by merit], the bones they possess are most spiritually luminous and moreover firm; for this reason, they are called *śarīra*.
As for the expression "pure and adorned," it need not be explained solely in terms of having realized that the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*) are empty in essence.

Regarding the labor and materials for silver coins, if there is not even the slightest element of negligence, this is itself purity. Furthermore, it is also appropriate to explain this through the profound principle that the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*) are empty in essence.

Within the context of "opening and revealing" (*kaixian*), the phrase "all have already attained Buddhahood" means that if one does not open and reveal [the true nature], then building stupas and temples with a respectful mind merely becomes a cause for the celestial vehicle (*devayāna*);
building stupas and temples with a distracted mind merely becomes a cause for the human [vehicle].
The causes for the vehicles—if revealed as one—are both the vehicles of humans and devas and the Buddha-vehicle;

therefore, both a respectful mind and a distracted mind are causes for attaining Buddhahood. This is because the vehicle of humans and devas and the Buddha-vehicle are fundamentally the same single reality (dharmatā).
Yet, if they are not so revealed, ordinary beings do not know that the very cause of the human and celestial realms is entirely [the Buddha-vehicle].
Regarding the true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*): if it is revealed and made manifest, one realizes that humans and devas are entirely identical to the true aspect;
thus, one is able to take the causes of humans and devas to accomplish the Buddha-way. △ Second, explaining the creation of images.
If people, for the sake of the Buddha, establish various images, carving and sculpting them into manifold forms, they have all already attained the path of Buddhahood.
Whether made of the seven treasures, or of brass, bronze, red or white copper, white tin, lead, or pewter; whether of iron, wood, or clay—
Or those who used glue, lacquer, and cloth to solemnly adorn and fashion images of the Buddha—all such people have already attained the path to Buddhahood.
Those who painted images of the Buddha with its marks adorned by a hundred blessings, whether doing so themselves or employing others, have all already attained the path to Buddhahood.
Even those who, as children at play, used grass, wood, pens, or their fingernails to draw images of the Buddha—
all such people gradually accumulate merit, fulfill the mind of great compassion, and have all already attained the path of Buddhahood.
It merely transforms all bodhisattvas and delivers immeasurable multitudes.
The first four lines clarify the karmic activities of the celestial realm; there are various types of images—sculpted, jeweled, and painted—which can be understood through their exposition.
Next, down to the first line below, the "human karma" is clarified. Thus, these one and a half lines, regarding the manifestation [of the teaching], state that he only transforms bodhisattvas;
this means that having himself already attained Buddhahood, he further transforms others.
△ Third, the three types of offerings. First, the mental karma.
If a person, at a stupa or temple, or before a precious image or a painted image, makes offerings with flowers, incense, banners, and canopies out of a reverent heart;
or if they cause others to perform music—beating drums, blowing horns and conchs, or playing flutes, pipes, lutes, *kōhō*, *pipa*, gongs, and cymbals.
In this way, with all such wondrous sounds, they made offerings; or with a heart of joy, they sang hymns in praise of the Buddha’s virtues.
Even those who produced but a single small sound have all already attained the path to Buddhahood. If a person, even with a distracted mind, offers but a single flower—
By making offerings to painted images, one gradually beholds countless Buddhas.
Within these three types of action (karman) mentioned below, there are both states of reverent mind and distracted mind. The first line clarifies the object of form (*rūpa-viṣaya*);

the subsequent one and a half lines clarify the object of sound (*śabda-viṣaya*). Regarding the objects of form, as for the flowers, incense, banners, and canopies: the flower serves to symbolize the cause; the cause...

"One will surely achieve the fruit. Offering flowers represents that the practitioner manifests the cultivation of causes in the present, which shall result in the achievement of the fruit of the Tathāgata.
Offering incense—since incense is pure, far-reaching, and subtly pervasive—represents that the practitioner subtly penetrates the merit of the fruit.
Offering banners—since banners possess the significance of movement and transformation—represents the transformation of birth-and-death into [nirvana].
Nirvana is the transformation of afflictions into bodhi. As for the offering of the parasol: "parasol" carries the meaning of protection;
it symbolizes that the Tathāgata, through his unconditioned great compassion, protects me and all sentient beings.
