Yet, as for this single flower or single incense, even down to a single raising of the hand or a single invocation of the name—all these lead to the realization of the Buddha-way—this is because a single flower or incense is, in its entirety, the wondrous practice of the true reality (dharmatā) of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). Thus, it may be that one does not offer them;
however, if one can indeed offer them, then although they are small, such as a single flower or a bit of incense, they are not small in the Dharma.
The great reality of the dhātu is not "great" because each phenomenon is true and every characteristic is real;

there is nothing that does not possess inherent virtue (*dharmatā-guṇa*). Since practice arises entirely from nature, and nature is identical with practice, whether one is in a state of reverence or distraction, or whether it be the karma of devas or humans, all are causes for attaining Buddhahood. However, this is a broad discussion regarding the past...
To clarify and reveal this, there is nothing else required: rather than relying on empty words, it is better to verify it through actual facts;
therefore, I speak in terms of what has already been accomplished in the past. As for the present and the future, they have not yet become manifest.
Thus, by analogy with this, it can be seen. Even if one who is able to perform such various offerings has not yet become prominent, they may nevertheless be known.
△ Second, the physical action (kāyakarman).
If there are those who prostrate, or even merely join their palms, or even raise a single hand, or even slightly bow their heads, and thereby make offerings to this image,
they will gradually behold immeasurable Buddhas, personally attain the unsurpassed path, and extensively deliver countless multitudes.
They enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, like a fire extinguished when the fuel is exhausted.
△ Third, regarding verbal karma:
If a person with a distracted mind enters a stupa or temple and utters "Namo Buddha" even once, they have all already attained the path of Buddhahood.
△ Second, the clarification through the revealing cause (*vijñapti-hetu*):
"Regarding all the Buddhas of the past, whether they were in the world or had passed into extinction—if there were those who heard this Dharma, they have all already attained the path of Buddhahood."
Regarding those who hear this Dharma: some hear the Dharma of marks (*sanimitta*), some hear the Dharma of marklessness (*animitta*), and some hear the Dharma of both marks and marklessness.
Once it is revealed through this single teaching, all are the Perfect Teaching (*paripūrṇa-yāna*) by which one attains the Buddha-way.
Thus, we know that hearing the Dharma is the seed of the *vidyā-hetu* (the cause of enlightenment). Therefore, the topical outline designates this as the "cause of enlightenment."
Furthermore, this "Dharma" refers specifically to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. As the preceding text states:

"Whether śrāvakas or bodhisattvas, upon hearing the Dharma I preach, even so much as a single verse, they shall all undoubtedly attain Buddhahood. This indicates that hearing the preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* constitutes its revelation and clarification;
it also means that hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* serves as the seed for the cause of realization (*pariniṣpanna-hetu*). The meaning of this is even more evident. △ Second.

The verses concerning the future [teachings] consist of three parts: the first verse reveals the provisional to manifest the ultimate; the second verse establishes the provisional for the sake of the ultimate; and the third verse discards the provisional to establish the ultimate.
Regarding the first two [verses], the first provides the formal explanation.
The future World-Honored Ones shall be immeasurable in number; all these Tathāgatas likewise teach the Dharma through skillful means.
All Tathāgatas, by means of infinite expedients, deliver and liberate all sentient beings, causing them to enter the untainted wisdom of the Buddha.
"If there are those who hear the Dharma, not one shall fail to become a Buddha.
The first line and a half reveals the provisional (upāya); the next line reveals the ultimate reality (bhūtārtha).

Next, regarding "untainted wisdom" (anāsrava-jñāna), this is precisely the "knowledge of all modes" (sarvākārajñatā), because it does not leak into either of the two extremes, nor does it leak into the middle.

Therefore, it is called "outflow-free wisdom" (*anāsrava-jñāna*). Regarding the phrase "if there are those," etc., this means that whether they be humans or devas, followers of the two vehicles, or bodhisattvas, once they hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and its meaning is revealed, there are none who do not achieve the Buddha-way.
△ Second, the statement of the underlying intention.
"The original vows of all Buddhas are: 'The Buddha-way that I have practiced, I desire that all sentient beings may likewise attain this same way.
This means that although the Buddhas speak of provisional means, their ultimate purpose is to reveal the truth by opening up those provisional means;
there is no other reason for this than that it stems entirely from the vows of the Buddhas, who, having themselves attained Buddhahood, still desire that all others likewise attain the Buddha-way."
These are indeed sentient beings who are only fit to first hear the provisional teaching. Therefore it is said: "The Buddhas... (and so forth).
△ Second, the verse on establishing the provisional based on the real, in two parts. First, the explicit explanation.
Although the Buddhas of future ages may preach hundreds of thousands of billions of countless Dharma-gates, their reality is but the One Vehicle.
Countless phrases are the provisional application (*upāya*), while the phrase of reality is the truth (*satya*). △ Second, the explanation of the underlying intent.

The Buddhas, the Honored Ones among two-legged beings, know that all phenomena are eternally without intrinsic nature. Since the lineage of the Buddhas arises from conditions, they therefore teach the One Vehicle.

"Knowing that all phenomena are eternally without intrinsic nature" means that the Buddhas, by means of their wondrous wisdom in which the provisional and the ultimate are non-dual, fully realize that all phenomena—both mundane and supramundane—are eternally empty and quiescent, being originally devoid of intrinsic nature. They have no...
What is this nature? It is that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, lack extrinsic nature, lack a nature common to both self and other, and lack a nature apart from both self and other.
Not only do they lack these four natures, but even the absence of nature itself is likewise non-existent.
Why is this? Because all phenomena have been empty of intrinsic nature and characteristics from the very beginning.
For example, as soon as a single, infinitesimal thought-moment arises before one, it is already fully endowed with the three thousand modes of being and the ten suchnesses of the hundred realms;
yet these three thousand do not arise from an intrinsic nature, nor do they arise from an extrinsic nature, a common nature, or a nature devoid of others. Therefore...
The Tathāgata has attained ultimate and thorough knowledge of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Thus he knows that all phenomena are eternally without intrinsic nature.
Yet this dharma of the absence of intrinsic nature is the Buddha-nature (*buddhagotra*) of all sentient beings.
This Buddha-nature must depend upon causes and conditions to arise, just as a worldly grain seed must depend upon the conditions of earth and water before it can sprout. Such is the Buddha-nature.
It is likewise so. One must rely upon the causes and conditions of teaching and practice in order to be able to give rise [to awakening].

Because the Buddha-seed arises from conditions, for this reason the Buddhas, for the sake of all sentient beings, preach the teaching of the One Vehicle, causing them to give rise to practice in accordance with that teaching, whereby they may give rise to the various [aspects of enlightenment].
Thus one knows that the original intent of the Buddhas appearing in the world was fundamentally to...
To initiate the Buddha-seed and to cause the Buddha-seed to arise, one must necessarily take the teaching of the One Vehicle as its condition.

Therefore, all provisional means employed are for the sake of the single reality; thus it is said, "the Buddha-seed," and so forth. △ Third, the verse on the abolition of the provisional and the establishment of the real.
This Dharma abides in its fixed position; the characteristics of the world are eternally constant. Having realized this at the site of enlightenment, the Teacher taught it through skillful means.
Regarding the phrase "this Dharma," it refers back to the term "Dharma" in the expression "knowing that the Dharma is eternally without nature.
This means there are mundane dharmas and supramundane dharmas, dharmas of the sages and dharmas of ordinary beings, pure dharmas and defiled dharmas. There are...

Defiled phenomena (*āsrava-dharma*) and undefiled phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*): although these various phenomena differ in a thousand ways and are manifoldly distinct, they are all, in their very substance, entirely identical to the true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
There is not one that does not abide within the locus of the *tathatā* (suchness).
This is what is called the "sole *tathatā*, the true aspect"; therefore, it is said that "these phenomena abide in the locus of phenomena. The characteristics of the world are eternal.
Regarding "abiding": the characteristics of the world consist of the characteristic of arising, the characteristic of abiding, the characteristic of change, and the characteristic of cessation.
Regarding "eternal abiding": eternity means neither arising nor ceasing; abiding means neither going nor coming.
If all phenomena did not abide in the station of reality (*dharmatā*), then neither worldly characteristics would be permanent, nor would supramundane characteristics be permanent.
Now, since all things abide in the station of *tathatā*, both supramundane characteristics are permanent, and mundane characteristics are likewise permanent. Why? Because of all phenomena.
If one observes with the perspective of emotional perception (*qingjian*), there appear the characteristics of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing.

If one discusses them from the standpoint of the true suchness (*tathatā*) and the dharma-position (*dharmapada*), then all are the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*); there is not a single dharma that is not true, nor a single characteristic that is not real.
Therefore, while it is the characteristic of arising, it is in reality non-arising; and so on, up to the characteristic of ceasing, which is in reality non-ceasing.
This is truly because the dharma-position is eternally abiding; therefore, all dharmas abide in the dharma-position and likewise abide eternally.
Thus, the marks of the world are eternally abiding. In summary, this "dharmas abiding in the dharma-position" is nothing other than the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all dharmas.
That "the marks of the world are eternally abiding" is likewise nothing other than the true reality of all dharmas.
This dharma-position is eternally abiding. It is here that all Buddhas attain the site of the Way; having already realized and known it themselves, they must then guide others.

Yet, because their capacities do not yet accord with the truth, they teach through skillful means (*upāya*). Since these are called "skillful means," then expedient means (*prajñapti*) is itself reality;
thus, reality is established. Since expedient means is itself reality, there is no expedient means apart from reality; thus, expedient means...

They are set aside. Therefore, this is called "abolishing the provisional and establishing the real. △ Third, the verses on the present Buddhas, in three parts. First, the verse on opening the provisional to reveal the real:
"The Buddhas of the ten directions in the present, Honored by devas and humans, Are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; They appear within the world."
For the sake of bringing peace and security to sentient beings, he likewise preaches such a Dharma.
This "such Dharma" refers precisely to the provisional (upāya) Dharma. Because sentient beings delight in the Small Vehicle, he first bestows the provisional Dharma to bring them peace and security.

The character "likewise" (yi) is used in contrast to the preceding [discussion of] the past and future; it signifies that the Buddhas who bestow the provisional Dharma are all identical in this regard.

[This is] the ear. This is an explanation based on the provisional (*upāya*). If explained according to both the provisional and the real (*tattva*), such a dharma is precisely the dharma of the provisional and the real.
Sentient beings delight in the small [vehicle]; thus, he bestows the three provisional dharmas to bring them peace and security. When the faculties (*indriya*) of sentient beings have matured...

He preaches the one true Dharma and brings beings to peace and security. The first phrase refers to that which is brought to peace and security; the second phrase refers to that which is able to bring about peace and security.

By means of these provisional and ultimate teachings, he brings peace and security to sentient beings of both great and small capacities; this is the case throughout the three periods of time. Therefore, it is said, "He also preaches.
△ Second, the verse on establishing the provisional based upon the real.
They know the foremost tranquility. By the power of skillful means, although they manifest various paths, in reality these are for the Buddha-vehicle.
"Knowing the foremost tranquility" means that the Buddhas, through the true wisdom of their own practice, realize that all phenomena are entirely the true mark (*dharmatā*);
because this is not the three vehicles, the nine realms, or the seven kinds of skillful means, it is called "foremost. Of all phenomena—

The essence is fundamentally quiescent from the beginning; it is not made quiescent anew. It is fundamentally extinguished from the beginning; it is not extinguished anew. Therefore, it is called "quiescent extinction" (*śānta-nirvāṇa*).
The rest may be understood accordingly. △ Third, the verse on the abolition of the provisional and the establishment of the real.

Knowing the various conducts of sentient beings, their deep-seated thoughts, the karma practiced in the past, their desires, natures, and powers of diligence, as well as the sharpness or dullness of their faculties,
he teaches through various causes and conditions, parables, and modes of speech, employing skillful means according to what is appropriate.

The single word "knowledge" (jñāna) refers to the provisional wisdom for transforming others, serving as the illumination that brings things to light. "All activities" (saṃskāra) are those performed by the external body;
"mental thoughts" (citta-vitarka) are those conceived within the internal mind. The three phrases beginning with "the past" explain and clarify the aforementioned activities and mental thoughts.
This constitutes the discernment of capacities. From the phrase "by means of various [expedients]" onwards, the text correctly elucidates the preaching of the Dharma.

Furthermore, since it is said that this is taught through skillful means (*upāya*), then the provisional (*prajñapti*) is naturally set aside. If the provisional is set aside, the real (*bhūta*) establishes itself.
△ Third, the verse reiterates and clarifies the two aspects of Śākyamuni. First, the verse briefly reveals the manifestation.
Now I am likewise; for the sake of bringing peace and security to sentient beings, I proclaim the Buddha-way through various Dharma-gates.
By the power of my wisdom, I know the dispositions and desires of sentient beings, and through skillful means I teach all dharmas so that they may all attain joy.

The verse reiterates that there are two [aspects] regarding Śākyamuni; this first part is a brief verse on the revelation, while the section beginning with "Then, Śāriputra" is an extensive verse on the revelation.
There is a specific intention behind providing these two versions, the extensive and the brief.

It is because the Tathāgata foresaw that when the Dharma was taught through direct explanation (*dharmadeśanā*), only those of superior faculties would attain awakening, whereas those of middling and inferior faculties would remain deluded and thus still require teaching by means of parables (*avadāna*). Now, as for the parables...
The Dharma is established through metaphors; the Dharma must be clarified by means of metaphors so that the Dharma and its metaphor may mutually support one another without any inconsistency.
If one does not understand the Dharma, one attains understanding through the metaphor; once one has attained understanding of the metaphor, one knows the Dharma for oneself.

Therefore, the brief verses herein serve as the basis for the general analogies within the subsequent detailed exposition. The extensive verses that follow serve as the basis for the specific analogies within that same detailed exposition.
The initial brief section consists of two parts: the first line reveals the reality (*tattva*), and the second line opens up the provisional means (*upāya*).
Regarding the first part, "the various [vehicles]" refers to the provisional means; "the Buddha-way" refers to...
This is indeed so. Since it is said that various dharmas manifest the Buddha-way, the reality thus manifested is precisely the provisional as reality.
Furthermore, "wisdom" refers to reality, while "all dharmas" refers to the provisional.
Since it is said that one speaks of all dharmas through the power of wisdom, the provisional thus revealed is precisely reality.
And as for "skillful means," the phrase "causing all to rejoice" indicates that the ultimate reality is revealed through expedient means.
When ignorance is shattered, the Middle Way is manifested, and one immediately attains the first stage of the Joyful Ground (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). Therefore, it is said that "all are caused to rejoice.
Thus, one should know that this phrase is an alternative name for "opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision," for by opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision—
This is because it corresponds to the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). Such is the general purport of the original text.
If we speak in terms of the basis for the subsequent parables, within these two lines, the single word "I" serves as the basis for the parable of the elder that follows;

"peace and security" (*kṣema*) serves as the basis for the parable of the burning house that follows, as it corresponds to "lack of peace and security. "Sentient beings" serves as the basis for the parable of the five hundred people that follows.

The "Fundamental" [section] serves as the basis for the analogy of the single gate below; "knowing the dispositions and desires of sentient beings" serves as the basis for the analogies of the thirty sons below.
△ Second, the verse provides a detailed exposition in four parts: first, from "Śāriputra...

up to "...great compassionate mind," the verse clarifies and explains the skillful means (*upāya*); second, from "Since I began... up to "...shall also become Buddhas," the verse reveals the provisional [teachings].

[The section] "Revealing Reality" (Xian shi) has three parts: from "As in the three periods of time" (*yathā triṣv adhvatsu*) down to "the udumbara flower," which is a verse praising the rarity of the Dharma;

fourth, from "You all" (*yūyam*) down to the end of the fascicle, which is a verse exhorting [the audience] that [this teaching] is not in vain. The first of these [three] also has two parts: first, showing the signs (*lakṣaṇa*).
Śāriputra, you should know that with my Buddha-eye I observe the sentient beings of the six realms. They are impoverished, lacking in merit and wisdom;
they enter the perilous paths of birth and death, where suffering continues without interruption. They are deeply attached to the five desires, like a yak that loves its tail.
Shrouded by their own craving and blinded by ignorance, they see nothing; they seek neither the Buddha of Great Power nor the Dharma that severs suffering.
Deeply entrenched in various false views, they seek to abandon suffering through further suffering.

The first line shows the characteristics of the turbidity of sentient beings. "I observe with the Buddha-eye" refers to Śākyamuni Tathāgata observing sentient beings from within the stage of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) by means of unconditioned great compassion (*nirālamba-mahākaruṇā*).

If this were an observation of the sentient beings of the six realms, it would be the Dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*); why then is it called the Buddha-eye? There are two reasons for this: first, to cite the superior [to represent the inferior];...
The Buddha-eye is superior and subsumes the inferior; because the Dharma-eye is inferior, it is not mentioned, and the Buddha-eye is spoken of instead.
Second, among the Tathāgata’s five eyes, they are all observed through a single eye, as the four eyes enter into the Buddha-eye and are thus given the same name, "Buddha-eye.
Therefore, the Dharma-eye is not mentioned, and the Buddha-eye is spoken of instead. As for those who are poor and lack merit and wisdom, it is not that they do not [possess them].
The merit of enjoying worldly clothing and food, as well as the wisdom of worldly erudition and eloquence, constitute poverty due to the absence of supramundane Dharma-wealth;
they constitute destitution due to the absence of the adornment of merit. Because they are thus poor and destitute, they lack the great merit and great wisdom possessed by the Tathāgata.
Next, the two phrases beginning with "entering birth and death" demonstrate the life-span.

The characteristic of turbidity (*āvilakṣaṇa*). Because the physical form and mind are continuously maintained without interruption, it resembles the crushing of years and the diminishing of lifespan;

born in the morning and dying by evening, revolving without end, the various characteristics of suffering continue in succession without cessation. This concludes the first line following "deep attachment" (*gādhābhiniveśa*).
This demonstrates the characteristics of the turbidity of afflictions. As for the simile of the yak:

sentient beings greedily crave the five desires, which causes them to lose their Dharma-body and forfeit their life of wisdom, just as the yak loses its body and life because of its attachment to its tail.

The four lines beginning with "not seeking" (*bùqiú*) demonstrate the characteristics of the *kalpa-kaṣāya* (the age of corruption). The Buddha is able to sever what sentient beings find difficult to sever and shatter what sentient beings find difficult to shatter;
because he possesses such great power, he is called Mahāsthāmaprāpta. If one does not seek the Buddha, one does not see the Buddha; if one does not seek the Dharma, one does not hear the Dharma.
Since there is neither Buddha nor Dharma, there is only the confluence of the four corruptions (*catur-kaṣāya*). These are gathered together in one place.
At that time, one kalpa of turbidity is formed. The last two lines of the fifth [section], "deeply entering," demonstrate the characteristics of the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kāṣāya*).
Wrong view is the cause of suffering, yet this cause of suffering inevitably summons its fruit. Calculating this cause of suffering—wrong view—one still desires to abandon its fruit;
therefore, it is said: "one seeks to abandon suffering by means of suffering. △ Second, the explanation of the underlying intent.
It is for the sake of these sentient beings that the Great Compassionate Mind is aroused.
Thus, the original intention of the Tathāgata was to speak directly of the One Vehicle;

however, because the capacities and inclinations of these beings in the five turbidities were not in accord with it, the Tathāgata, out of his Great Compassionate Mind, first spoke of expedient means. Therefore it is said: "For the sake of..."

[This is] as [stated above]. △ Second, the verse on opening the provisional to reveal the real has two parts. First, from "I began... onwards, there are seventeen and a half lines on opening the provisional.
Next, from "Śāriputra, you should know... onwards, there are six lines on revealing the real. The first part [of the section on revealing the real] further has two sub-sections.

First, six and a half lines on concealing the real. Second, eleven lines on bestowing the provisional. The first of these [two sub-sections] further has two parts. First, four and a half lines: the Great Vehicle is presented as a model.

It is appropriate. The next two lines concern the cessation of transformation due to a lack of receptive capacity. The first [section] also has two parts. The first three lines concern the seven days of contemplation:
"When I first sat at the site of enlightenment, I gazed at the tree and also walked in meditation; during those seven days of three weeks, I contemplated these matters."
The wisdom I have attained is subtle, wondrous, and supreme. Yet sentient beings have dull faculties;
they are attached to pleasure and blinded by ignorance. How can such as these be delivered?
Regarding the phrase "I began," etc.: if one discusses the Tathāgata, that which was realized long ago is the root of all roots; how could there be a beginning?
This is because the Tathāgata, having already realized this for a long time, out of great compassion remembers sentient beings and desires to cause them to realize what the Tathāgata has realized.
Therefore, he manifests the traces within the root, as well as [the traces] within the traces.
Regarding the traces (*liǎo*): it is not contradictory to speak of a "beginning" within that which is beginningless.

When one speaks of my "beginning," this refers to the time when Śākyamuni of the present day first sat at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) to manifest his transformative teachings throughout his single lifetime. However, there are two distinct periods, the Great and the Small, which differ from one another.
The Tathāgata is fundamentally one; it is only because of differences in the capacities of sentient beings that there appear the Great and Small [Vehicles].

If one sees the thousand-fathom Śākyamuni body seated upon a throne of the seven treasures preaching the sūtras, this is the beginning of the Great [Vehicle]. If one sees the sixteen-foot inferior response-body, [this is the beginning of the Small Vehicle].
On a seat of living grass, he preached the Four Āgamas; this was the "Small Beginning. What is now called the "Beginning" is, in fact, the "Great Beginning.

Having sat at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and contemplated the tree while practicing walking meditation, once he has sat at the site of enlightenment, he must then preach the Dharma to deliver sentient beings.
If he wishes to preach the Dharma, he must first discern their capacities (*indriya*); therefore, he reflects and deliberates within his mind.
He contemplates the tree while walking in meditation (*caṅkrama*). Since he attained the Way while sitting beneath the tree, he contemplates the sentient beings and returns to contemplate that tree.
Since he attained the Way by relying upon that ground, he contemplates the sentient beings and returns to walk in meditation upon that ground.

This is for no other reason than what the ancients called "repaying the debt of gratitude to the tree and the ground. That which is obtained as wisdom is precisely the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana*). Not...

It can be contemplated through the mind and discussed through speech; therefore, it is subtle and wondrous. It is "the foremost" because it is not within the reach of the nine realms or the three vehicles.
As for the phrase "how can they be saved," this precisely refers to contemplation; it is not a word of abandonment.
It means that while one truly desires to save them, one simply cannot help but hesitate, meaning one does not know by what method one might be able to do so.
Sentient beings of dull faculties obtain benefit; even those who are ignorant and blind obtain clarity, thereby attaining the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
△ Second, the request by the devas to turn the wheel of Dharma.
At that time, the Brahma kings, the various Śakras, lords of the gods, the four world-protecting kings, and Maheśvara,
together with the rest of the celestial hosts and their hundreds of thousands of myriads of attendants, joined their palms in reverence and paid homage, entreating me to turn the wheel of Dharma.

Regarding "the various devas requesting [him] to turn [the wheel]": having known that the Tathāgata was contemplating the capacities of sentient beings and would certainly preach the Dharma, they requested the Tathāgata to turn the Great Wheel of Dharma for the sake of their benefit and salvation. △ Second, the cessation of transformation due to a lack of receptive capacity.
I then reflected to myself: "If I were to preach only the Buddha-vehicle, sentient beings submerged in suffering would be unable to believe this Dharma.
Because they would reject the Dharma and lack faith, they would fall into the three evil realms. It would be better for me not to preach the Dharma at all, but to quickly enter nirvana."

This refers to sentient beings who do not accord with the Great Transformation. To say they are "sunk in suffering" means that these are beings of dull faculties who are attached to the pleasures of the five desires and are blinded by ignorance; therefore, it is said they are submerged in suffering.

Such beings will certainly be unable to believe in the Single Buddha Vehicle Dharma. If they do not believe, they will inevitably slander it; if they slander it, they will inevitably fall [into the evil realms].
"Suffering. As for the statement, "I would rather not preach the Dharma," it means that the Tathāgata’s original intent in preaching the Dharma was for sentient beings to attain happiness;

yet now, instead of attaining happiness, they have fallen into suffering. It would have been better had he not preached it at all. Therefore, he says, "I would rather not preach the Dharma," and so forth.

△ Second, the application of expedient means (upāya), which has two parts: first, the thought to be equal to all Buddhas; second, the compliance with [the capacities of beings] by bestowing the Lesser Vehicle.
The first two [verses]: First, Śākyamuni’s right mindfulness:
"Recalling the skillful means practiced by the Buddhas of the past, I shall now also preach the Three Vehicles regarding the Path I have attained."

Regarding "seeking and recollecting" (*xúnniàn*): "seeking" (*xún*) means to follow. This refers to the time when one seeks to accord with the great transformation; that is, one immediately recollects being equal to all Buddhas.

Furthermore, one should first bestow [benefits] upon those of lesser capacity. Therefore, it is said: "seeking and recollecting" (and so forth). △ Second, the consolation and encouragement of all Buddhas, in two parts.
At first, the praise was identical.
While I was engaged in this reflection, the Buddhas of the ten directions all appeared before me, consoling me with Brahma-sounds: "Excellent, Śākyamuni!
You, the supreme guide, have attained this unsurpassed Dharma; following the example of all Buddhas, you employ the power of skillful means."
We, too, have all attained the most wondrous and supreme Dharma. For the sake of the various classes of sentient beings, we distinguish and explain the three vehicles (*triyāna*).
Regarding the words "Excellent! and so forth: if one were to speak directly of only the single vehicle (*ekayāna*), it could not be called "excellent";

if one were to speak only of the three vehicles, it would not be called "supreme. Now, first the three vehicles are taught, followed by the single vehicle; thus, one returns to the three vehicles through the single vehicle.
They enter together into the One Vehicle; therefore, it is said: "Excellent! Śākyamuni, the foremost guide. △ Second, the explanation of the underlying intent:
Those of small wisdom delight in small teachings and do not believe they can become Buddhas themselves. For this reason, by means of skillful expedients, he distinguishes and teaches various fruits.
Although the three vehicles are taught, it is solely for the purpose of instructing bodhisattvas.
2. Conforming to the Bestowal of the Lesser [Vehicle]. Part One: Conforming.
Śāriputra, you should know: I heard the holy lion’s deep, pure, subtle, and wondrous voice proclaim, "Namo to all Buddhas."
Again, he formed this thought: "I have emerged from a turbid and evil world. Just as all Buddhas have taught, I shall likewise practice in accordance with them.
Regarding the phrase "Noble Lion": the Buddhas of the ten directions are the most noble among the noble; they are the lions among men. Regarding the phrase "Profound, Pure, and Subtle":
the Buddhas of the ten directions take the three virtues (*triguṇa*) as their profundity and the severance of the five abodes (*pañca-vāsa*) as their purity; they do not belong to the nine realms.
That which is known is subtle; that which does not contradict the true nature of reality is wondrous. This is why he was able to console Śākyamuni:

first establishing the provisional means (*upāya*), and subsequently revealing the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Now, I wish to praise the person who is capable of speaking, rather than praising the sounds of what is spoken.
*Namo* means "taking refuge in life" (*prāṇa-namaskāra*). It is also translated as "save me" and "reverently following.
In this context, it carries only the sense of reverently following. △ Second, bestowing the Lesser Vehicle.
Having reflected on this matter, he proceeded at once to Vārāṇasī. The mark of the quiescence of all dharmas cannot be expressed in words;
yet, by the power of skillful means, he preached it for the sake of the five bhikṣus. This is called the turning of the wheel of Dharma, and from it there arose the sound of nirvāṇa.
And as for the Arhats, these are the distinct names for the Dharma and the Saṅgha.
Regarding the phrase "the cessation of all phenomena" and so forth: this Dharma has already ceased and does not cease again; it has already been extinguished and is not extinguished again.
This is the characteristic of true emptiness. It cannot even be conceived by the mind, much less be grasped through words and discursive reasoning.
Therefore it is said: "All dharmas... (and so forth). Nevertheless, there are causes and conditions by which it may also be explained.
Thus, employing skillful means, he preached the *nirvāṇa* of the Small Vehicle for the sake of the five bhikṣus. Therefore it is said: "By means of skillful means... (and so forth).
As for the statement that there was the sound of *nirvāṇa*, this refers to when the Tathāgata had finished teaching the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths and asked Cunda: "You..."
"Do you understand? Chenru replied, "I already know. "Do you comprehend? "I have already comprehended. Therefore, it is said that there is the sound of Nirvana.
Even if one attains only the first fruit [of the path], this is partial realization of Nirvana. △ Third, resolving doubts.
Since kalpas long ago, I have praised and revealed the Dharma of Nirvana, wherein the suffering of birth and death is forever extinguished; this is what I have always taught.

Any doubts regarding this may be resolved according to the explanations of the text. As for the term "kalpas long ago," it refers to the time when the sixteen princes of former days preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* again after having established karmic connections, only to subsequently regress from the Great Vehicle and adopt the Small Vehicle; it refers to how, upon meeting one another in the interim, each was individually exhorted and reconciled.
As for today, the royal city has been opened and revealed; upon hearing it but once, one attains awakening. This can be seen by examining the facts;
if it were not so, why would you speak of "long ago"? Part Two: Revealing the Reality, in two sections. First: Clarifying the Awakening of the Mahayana Capacity.

Śāriputra, you should know: I see my sons among the Buddha’s followers who are resolutely seeking the Buddha-way—countless thousands of myriads of koṭis—all of whom, with hearts full of reverence, have come to where the Buddha is. They have all heard from various Buddhas the Dharma taught through skillful means.
Regarding the phrase "Buddha-sons" (*buddhaputra*) and so forth: this does not refer to bodhisattvas as Buddha-sons, but rather to those of the two vehicles (*dvayayānika*).
Once a single sūtra is revealed and clarified, they are immediately able to inherit and succeed to the Mahāyāna family estate of the Tathāgata; therefore, they are called "Buddha-sons.
△ Second, clarifying the Tathāgata’s discourse has four parts. First, forming a thought.
I then had this thought: "The reason the Tathāgata has appeared is to preach the Buddha-wisdom; now is precisely that time.
Regarding the single character *chū* (appears/comes forth) in the phrase "the Tathāgata appears," there are two meanings: first, it is the appearance of the Tathāgata in the world;
second, it is the emergence from meditative concentration, the coming forth from *samādhi*. Thus, the Tathāgata appears.
The World-Honored One emerges from samādhi. This is precisely because he intends to expound the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and now is the very time when it may be properly taught;
hence it is said, "The reason why the Tathāgata emerges. "The reason why he emerges" refers to the purpose for his emergence. △ Second, distinguishing the capacities of the audience.
Śāriputra, you should know that those of dull faculties and small wisdom, who are attached to signs and arrogant, cannot believe in this Dharma.
Regarding "those of dull faculties and so forth": because their faculties are dull, their wisdom is small; because they are attached to signs, they are arrogant.

People such as these—how could they possibly believe and accept it? This refers precisely to the five thousand who withdrew from their seats. Therefore, it was previously stated that they possess "small wisdom."
[He] emerged. It would also be well if those with overweening pride were to retreat. △ Third, the actual teaching:
"Now I rejoice in fearlessness; among all bodhisattvas, I shall directly abandon expedient means and teach only the unsurpassed path."
Regarding "joyful and fearless": "joyful" means rejoicing that those in this assembly are no longer mere branches and leaves, but consist only of the true and substantial core.
"Fearless" means that if those of small wisdom were seated here, they would surely not believe upon hearing [this teaching];

their lack of faith would give rise to slander, and through such slander they would fall into suffering—this would cause me fear. Now that they have departed, I am therefore fearless. "Abandoning expedient means" refers to...
This is the relinquishing of provisional means. △ Fourth, the conclusion on the benefits:
When the Bodhisattvas hear this Dharma, their net of doubts is entirely removed; the twelve hundred Arhats shall all likewise become Buddhas.

"Removing the net of doubt" means that when the Tathāgata enters meditative concentration and emits light, manifesting various auspicious omens, the Bodhisattvas likewise all harbor doubts, not knowing what the causes and conditions are; they are as if fallen into a net from which they cannot escape.
Now, by opening up the teaching of "three to reveal one," their doubts are resolved, just as one removes a net. Therefore, it is said that "the net of doubt is removed. Bodhi...
Since Śāriputra’s doubts have been removed, he too shall become a Buddha; since the Arhat has become a Buddha, he too has removed the net of doubt.
These statements are mutually illustrative. Furthermore, when it is said that the Bodhisattva has removed the net of doubt, this highlights his ability to sever provisional doubts;
when it is said that the Arhat shall become a Buddha, this highlights his ability to give rise to true faith. △ Third, the verse of praise.
There are two rare things regarding the Dharma. The first verse states that such a Dharma is sublime:
"Just as the Buddhas of the three periods of time have the ritual for teaching the Dharma, so do I now likewise teach the non-conceptual Dharma."
Regarding "as in the three periods [of time] and so forth": first, the provisional is established for the sake of the real; next, the provisional is opened up to reveal the real;

finally, the provisional is discarded and the real is established. This is the ritual procedure and formal method by which all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods establish their transformations.
Therefore it is said, "as in the three periods" (and so forth). Regarding "the dharma without discrimination": this is because the essence of the dharma is wondrous.
It cannot be understood through discursive thought or conceptual discrimination; therefore, it is called the "non-discriminative dharma.
△ Second, the verse on the time of its teaching, in three parts. First, the Dharma.
The appearance of Buddhas in the world is rare and difficult to encounter; though they may appear in the world, it is further difficult for them to preach this Dharma.
To hear this Dharma throughout immeasurable and incalculable kalpas is likewise difficult; and those who are able to listen to this Dharma—such persons are also difficult to find.
This passage generally clarifies four difficulties. The first two phrases clarify the difficulty of a Buddha appearing in the world, as well as the difficulty of encountering such a Buddha.
That is to say, when the Buddhas appear in the world, I am submerged in debate; and when I appear in the world, the Buddhas have entered parinirvāṇa. Therefore, encountering a Buddha is difficult.
Next, the following two phrases beginning with "Even if" clarify the difficulty of preaching the wondrous Dharma. For instance, although Śākyamuni has now appeared...
World-honored One, for over forty years, whether combined or alone, in pairs or as adjuncts, we have lingered for more than four decades until this very day;
yet even now, there are three requests and three refusals. To have just begun to explain it—how difficult this is!

Next, the two lines concerning "immeasurable" clarify the difficulty of hearing the sublime Dharma. When the sound of the Dharma passes through the ears, regardless of whether one is deluded or awakened, it is collectively termed "hearing the Dharma.
For example, when five thousand people were about to receive the Tathāgata’s formal permission to preach, they instead prostrated to the Buddha and withdrew;
thus, hearing this sublime Dharma is likewise difficult. Next, the two lines concerning "those who can listen" clarify the [difficulty of] listening to the sublime [Dharma].
The Dharma is difficult to encounter. To hear it, believe and understand it, and be able to receive and uphold it—this is called "listening.

Just as the World-Honored One has now extensively explained through prose and verse, with each point revealed by the five Buddhas, those who can merely attain faith and understanding with superior faculties are rare;
yet those of middling and inferior capacities remain deluded. Therefore, those who are able to listen to this Dharma are likewise rare. Although it is said that both hearing and listening are...
Difficult. Hearing does not reach the level of listening; listening is deeper than hearing. △ Second, the analogy:
It is like the udumbara flower, which all love and delight in; it is rare among gods and humans, appearing only once in a great while.
"Only at that time does it emerge" means that it is precisely when the time is right that it emerges in accordance with the occasion; hence it is said, "only once in a long while does it emerge.
The meaning of this single line of verse serves as a general metaphor for the four difficulties mentioned above (and so forth). △ Third, the synthesis.
To hear the Dharma with joy and praise it, even uttering but a single word, is to have already made offerings to all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Such a person is exceedingly rare, surpassing even the udumbara flower.
In summary, this sutra is the fundamental intention for the appearance in the world of all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
Therefore, upon hearing it, to speak words of praise is to make an offering of the Dharma to all Buddhas.
Regarding the statement that it is rarer than the udumbara flower: the udumbara appears only once every three thousand years; thus, its appearance is strictly limited by time.
As for those who, upon hearing the Dharma, are able to praise it, their timing is not fixed; yet because they must necessarily exist, it is said that such people are rare.

Furthermore, "hearing the Dharma" corresponds to the third difficulty mentioned above regarding the rarity of hearing the Dharma, while "rejoicing and praising" corresponds to the fourth difficulty mentioned above regarding the rarity of listening to the Dharma.
The difficulty of hearing and listening to the Dharma exceeds that of the *udumbara* flower; even more difficult than that is encountering a Buddha preaching the Dharma.
It is likewise. By citing the latter, the former is subsumed; therefore, only the latter two difficulties are mentioned. △ Fourth, the verse on exhorting faith that it is not in vain, in three parts.
First, the verse on the formal exhortation.
Do not harbor any doubts; I am the King of all Dharmas. I announce to the great assembly: I teach and transform all bodhisattvas solely through the path of the One Vehicle.
I have no śrāvaka disciples. You, Śāriputra—whether you are a śrāvaka or a bodhisattva—[should understand this].
One should know that this is the sublime Dharma, the secret essence of all Buddhas.
This verse consists of two parts: the first clarifies that the person who can preach it is the Dharma King, and what is preached by the Dharma King [is the Dharma].
One should naturally believe this. Next, it is clarified that the Dharma being taught is a secret and essential matter.
This secret and essential Dharma should also be believed. Regarding what is called "secret and essential": for forty years, it has never been revealed or preached; therefore, it is called "secret.
It is the sole primary intention of all Buddhas appearing in the world; therefore, it is called "essential. △ Second, the verse on earnest exhortation.
In this world of the five turbidities, sentient beings such as these take pleasure only in attachment to various desires and ultimately do not seek the Buddha-way.
In future ages, wicked people, upon hearing the Buddha preach the One Vehicle, will be deluded and fail to believe or accept it; they will destroy the Dharma and fall into evil realms.
For those who possess a sense of shame and remorse and are pure, and who aspire to seek the Buddha-way, one should extensively praise the path of the One Vehicle for such as these.
This verse consists of three sections. The first line clarifies that one should not preach it to those currently attached to desire.
The second line clarifies that one should likewise not preach it to wicked people of the future. The third line...

Whether manifest or not yet manifest, for those who possess a sense of shame and remorse, this shall be explained in detail. These three successive exhortations press one repeatedly to engender faith;
thus one knows that [the teaching] is not spoken to those attached to desire or to evil persons. Since it is now being spoken, how could one not give rise to faith?
This is precisely the profound intention of the Tathāgata—how could one fail to believe it? If one does not believe, how would such a person differ from one who is attached [to worldly things]?
"To desire [to associate with] evil persons" is intended as a means of admonition and earnest exhortation. Regarding "those who possess shame and are pure":

if one is a person of overweening pride who claims to have attained what they have not attained, or claims to have realized what they have not realized, this constitutes a lack of shame and is unclean.
Conversely, if one is not such a person of overweening pride, they are said to possess shame and be pure. △ Third, the concluding verse.
Manifestly, Śāriputra, you should know that the dharmas of all Buddhas are thus: by means of ten thousand koṭis of skillful means, they preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate.
Those who have not practiced and studied cannot understand this. Since you all already know that the Buddhas are the Teachers of the World...
Regarding these matters of skillful means as appropriate, they no longer harbor any doubts; their hearts give rise to great joy, for they know for themselves that they shall become Buddhas.
The first one and a half lines conclude the opening of the provisional (upāya); the second one and a half lines conclude the manifestation of the real (bhūta).

The phrase "The Dharma of all Buddhas is thus" refers to the natural principle (*dharmatā*) by which the provisional was first bestowed. The two phrases beginning with "Those who have not practiced" refer to those who are unable [to realize it].

Having understood the provisional, one then bestows it as the real. This is because those who deeply realize that the provisional and the real are mutually identical do so for the sake of practice and study.
Next, from "You all" onwards, the text concludes by manifesting the real; that is to say, since you all already know that the Buddhas have spoken according to what was appropriate for each occasion.
Since all are of one reality, there is no longer any doubt that the three vehicles are provisional and not yet identical with the reality of the One Vehicle.
If one were to doubt that the three are not identical with the one, then those of the two vehicles would never know that they themselves shall become Buddhas.
Now, having realized that the three are entirely identical with the one, they will know for themselves that they shall become Buddhas and should give rise to great joy. Thus it is explained.
The Section on "Convenience" concludes.

The Third Chapter, "The Parable," of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
Regarding what is called the "Sublime Dharma" (*saddharma*), if one discusses its origin, it is as found within this chapter: the three chariots and the single chariot.
This serves as an analogy for the teachings of the Three Vehicles and the One Vehicle.

However, during the forty years prior [to this teaching], he spoke of the provisional expedient of the Three Vehicles without ever declaring it to be provisional; he spoke of the reality of the One Vehicle without ever declaring it to be real.

Thus, the three and the one were separated, and the provisional and the real were distinct. Now, arriving at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, they are discussed in relation to one another; thus, by means of the former...
What was previously taught as the provisional three vehicles is coarse; what is taught today as the true one vehicle is subtle and wondrous.
If discussed from the perspective of absolute transcendence, then the opening up of the former three provisional teachings is itself the single reality.

Thus, the three and the one are non-dual, and the provisional and the real are mutually identical; this cannot be conceived or expressed by the mind or in words. Therefore, it is called the "Sublime Dharma" (Saddharma).
Furthermore, if one does not understand the wondrous Dharma, one should contemplate the lotus flower.

This is because the provisional and the real of the wondrous Dharma are of the same essence, just as the flower and fruit of a lotus appear simultaneously. Therefore, by contemplating the lotus flower, the wondrous Dharma can be known.
The term "sūtra" (經) is explained as meaning "constant," because it remains unchanged throughout the three periods of past, present, and future.

Next, regarding the explanation of the chapter title, one must clarify the intent behind its establishment. Since this section still consists of passages concerning the Dharma-exposition, the summary of understanding, and the confirmation of realization, why is it specifically titled the "Parable Chapter"?
It is because, upon examining its underlying purpose, there is no other reason than that which arises from the sūtra.
The *Jiayù tiáojīng* (The Scripture on Adjusting the Text) states that one should ensure the thickness of the scrolls is uniform;

therefore, although this passage belongs to the "Expedient Means" chapter of the *Dharmaparyāya*, it is divided here as the opening text of the second scroll’s parables. Regarding the term "parable" (*píyù*):

to compare by means of analogy is called a "parable" (*pí*); to entrust words for the purpose of instruction and enlightenment is called a "parable" (*yù*). That is, to use the shallow to illustrate the profound.
The moon hidden behind heavy mountains is illustrated by the raising of a fan; the wind ceasing in the great void is taught through the movement of trees.

These are precisely what are called "parables. Although the Tathāgata has extensively clarified and revealed above that the three vehicles are identical to the one vehicle, only those of superior faculties have attained realization, while those of middling and inferior capacities still harbor delusion. Therefore, he once again reiterates what was previously granted.
The three carts are used as a metaphor for the three vehicles (triyāna) previously taught; the subsequent bestowing of the great cart is a metaphor for the one vehicle (ekayāna) now taught.
This causes them to understand that the entirety of the three is in fact the one—that there is only the one and no three.

That is to say, by means of this shallow analogy of the three carts and the single cart, it illustrates the profound dharma of the three vehicles and the one vehicle. Therefore, it is called the "Parable Chapter" (Upamā-parivarta).
This is the Tathāgata’s correct teaching, which includes the parable of the three carts and the one cart; the understanding [of this teaching] is illustrated by the parable of the impoverished son;
the confirmation [of that understanding] is illustrated by the parable of the medicinal herbs; and the request for a prediction [of enlightenment] is illustrated by the parable of the royal feast.
Therefore, from this point onward, there is one complete cycle of parables. II. The Audience Members Express Their Understanding. A. Prose Exposition.
There are two verses. The first section also has two parts. First, the narrator describes the scene:
At that time, Śāriputra was leaping for joy and filled with delight; he immediately rose, joined his palms, gazed up at the Honored One’s countenance, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"At this time" refers to the moment when the Tathāgata, having spoken in prose, completed the detailed elucidation of the five Buddhas by means of verses.
"Leaping for joy" (tadyathāpi nāma... prahṛṣṭaḥ) is interpreted by some as "leaping" referring to outward form and "joy" referring to the inner mind;
however, the present term "leaping" also pertains solely to the inner mind, as in the expression "the heart harbors leaping [joy]."
As for this realization, Śāriputra: previously, it was said that the three vehicles and the one vehicle were two things mutually opposed and separated.
Now, having heard the opening of the three to reveal the one, he has realized that even a śrāvaka can destroy ignorance and enter the first stage, the Dwelling of Joy.
Thereupon, his thoughts surged forth uncontrollably; thus, he leaped for joy.
Regarding "joining the palms": previously, it was said that the provisional and the real are two, like two palms not joined together.

Now, understanding that the provisional and the real are one, like two palms joined together, one joins the palms to symbolize the realization that the provisional and the real are non-dual. Regarding "gazing up at the Honored Countenance":
having already attained realization and understanding, one initiates practice based on that understanding; since the cause must yield its fruit, one gazes upon the Buddha’s countenance.

This is the "Manifestation" (Table of Contents). First, "leaping for joy" describes his mental karma (*manas-karman*); next, "joining palms and gazing up" describes his physical karma (*kāya-karman*);
and "addressing the Buddha" describes his verbal karma (*vāk-karman*). This precisely refers to the presentation of his three types of karma.
II. Śāriputra’s Statement in Three Parts: 1. First, the heading indicating what has been received.
Now, having heard this Dharma-sound from the World-Honored One, my heart leaps with joy at having attained what I have never experienced before.

To say that one "hears this Dharma-sound" means to hear the Dharma-sound of all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time, as well as myself, Śākyamuni, each opening up the three and manifesting the one. Having heard it, I have understood and realized it; therefore, my heart harbors [this joy].
With joyful exuberance, having understood, they give rise to practice; having practiced, they are able to realize. Thus, they attain what has never been attained before.
Furthermore, that which did not exist before now exists; that which was not previously obtained is now obtained. Therefore, it is said that "they have attained what has never been attained before.

II. Explaining and Clarifying What Was Understood. This section has two parts: first, the direct explanation; second, the further interpretation. The first part has two sub-sections: first, the direct narration of past delusion.
Why is this? In the past, I heard such a teaching from the Buddha: that various bodhisattvas received the prediction of attaining buddhahood, while we ourselves were not included in this matter.
This caused us profound personal grief, as we had lost the immeasurable knowledge and vision of the Tathāgata.
"Why is this so?"—this single phrase serves as an inquiry and explanation for the reason why [the assembly] attained what they had never experienced before.
The statement "having heard such a Dharma" refers to the words spoken after Śāriputra’s realization;

for it was during the two periods of the Vaipulya and Prajñā teachings that Śāriputra heard from the Tathāgata the teaching that clarifies the Perfect (Pūrṇa) in contrast to the Half (Ardha), and which brings the Two Vehicles to clarity while manifesting the One Vehicle in its fullness.

If one does not yet know even the provisional teachings of the "half" and the "partial," how can one know the fulfillment and the perfect reality? Furthermore, how can one know that the half is itself the full, and that the partial is itself the perfect?
How, then, can one know that the provisional is itself the real? This is why it is necessary to have heard the revelation of the opening and the manifestation.
Thus, it is not only that we know the provisional and the real as clarified in the past are identical to those of today;
we also understand that the partial and provisional teachings expounded in the past are no different from those of today. Therefore, it is said that "we have heard such a Dharma.
As for the statement, "We were not involved in this matter," it refers to how the Tathāgata, within the Vaipulya sūtras, rebuked and rejected those of the two vehicles. Just as...
Like a scorched sprout, it will never again produce a sprout; like a rotten seed, it will never again function as a seed;
like a broken jar, it will never again function as a jar. Although they have thus been rebuked and dismissed, they still remain in their thatched huts, dwelling on their own poverty.
Even though they understand all things within the Prajñāpāramitā, they do not harbor a single thought of wishing to take them up; therefore, they cannot participate.

This concerns the matter of receiving the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). "Deeply moved by self-pity" means being moved that the Bodhisattvas have received their predictions, while feeling sorrow that one has not been included.
It is not merely a matter of being moved; it is a matter of being deeply moved.

"To lose the Tathāgata’s immeasurable knowledge and vision" means that when the Bodhisattvas receive their predictions, they have already attained the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, whereas we have not been included.
This means they have already lost the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision. The Tathāgata possesses the three knowledges within a single mind and the five eyes within a single eye;
therefore, it is called immeasurable knowledge and vision. △ Second, a further analysis according to location.
“World-Honored One, when I dwell alone in mountain forests or beneath trees, whether sitting or walking, I constantly reflect:
‘We have all entered the same Dharma-nature; why then does the Tathāgata deliver us by means of the Hīnayāna? This is our own fault.’”
"It is not the World-Honored One [who speaks thus].

He says: 'Since the Vaipulya [sūtras], whenever I have been in mountain forests, whether sitting or walking, I have contemplated that the Bodhisattvas receive their predictions of enlightenment, yet I myself have no matter for receiving a prediction. Therefore he says, 'World-Honored One' (and so forth). 'We, etc.'—this concludes the citation."

This refers to the mental orientation within the mountain forests. To say that they "enter the same dharma-nature" means that those of the three vehicles enter emptiness through the same path beyond words.
Although they enter it together, their faculties differ: those of dull faculties perceive only emptiness, while those of sharp faculties additionally perceive non-emptiness.
Those who perceive non-emptiness should naturally receive their prediction of enlightenment; as for those who perceive emptiness—
Regarding this, one should not provide a prediction oneself; that is to say, the names are identical but the meanings differ.
Śāriputra did not know the reason for this, and therefore he merely said they had entered together. When he asked, "In what way are we equal? his intention was:

"Since the entry is the same, why does the Tathāgata not grant us a prediction, but instead only delivers us by means of the Hīnayāna dharma? Such were his thoughts, thinking, "This is because of us..."
[The disciples] said below: "We have now realized that what we previously thought was the case—that the path we entered was the same as theirs—is not so.

Why is it that the Tathāgata delivers bodhisattvas by means of the Mahāyāna, granting them predictions of enlightenment, yet delivers us by means of the Hīnayāna, not allowing us to receive such predictions?
We harbored doubts that the Tathāgata was partial. Today, hearing what the Buddha has taught, we know [the truth]."
The Tathāgata has never had a dual mind regarding this matter; therefore it is said, "This is mine," and so forth. △ Second, the further explanation.
Why is this? If we were to wait for the explanation of the causes by which one achieves *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*...

"Enlightenment is necessarily attained through the Mahāyāna and thereby one achieves liberation. However, we did not understand the skillful means by which the Buddha taught according to what was appropriate for each occasion;
upon first hearing the Buddha's Dharma, we accepted it immediately as we encountered it, contemplating it and seeking realization therein."
The meaning is this: how do we know that the fault lies with us and not with the World-Honored One? Therefore, it is asked, "For what reason?
If it is said, "We wait for the teaching," the term "wait" (*dai*) carries two meanings: relative waiting and stationary waiting. There are likewise two reasons for this:
first, the *Avataṃsaka*, and second, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. First, regarding the *Avataṃsaka*, it speaks of the perfect *sūtra*.
The "Ruo" (羅) is the basis for the teaching (*śāsana*), which clarifies the four kinds of *dharmadhātu*. This is the basis for the principle (*yukti*).
Furthermore, today’s *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* states: "Directly abandoning expedient means, he speaks only of the unsurpassed path.

This is likewise the basis for the teaching, and the clarification of the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena is likewise the basis for the principle. The Tathāgata uses the basis of the *Avataṃsaka* as a point of contrast.
Regarding myself: I could have attained the Mahāyāna, yet I lost it previously.
The Tathāgata, by means of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, waited for me so that I might attain the Mahāyāna, yet I lost it again afterwards. Therefore, it is said: "If I... (and so forth).
However, in the passage beginning with "Yet I," it is not understood that the Tathāgata preached the Lesser Vehicle; rather, the meaning is that since we [previously]...
We lost the *Avataṃsaka*, and later we also lost the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Therefore, the Tathāgata, by the power of skillful means, preached the Lesser Vehicle according to what was appropriate.
We, failing to understand this, hastily sought realization [of that lesser path]. Thus it is said: "But I... (and so forth).
From this we know that the Tathāgata has never failed to deliver us by means of the Mahāyāna; it is only we who have ourselves taken the Lesser Vehicle.
Therefore, as I said previously: "This is our own fault, not that of the World-Honored One. △ Third, the general conclusion and dedication:

"World-Honored One, from the past until now, throughout the day and night, I have constantly reproached myself. But today, following the Buddha, I have heard the Dharma never before heard, the unprecedented teaching.
All doubts and regrets are severed; my body and mind are at ease, having attained swift peace and security. Today..."
Thus one comes to know that these are truly the sons of the Buddha, born from the Buddha’s mouth and transformed by birth from the Dharma, having obtained a portion of the Buddha-dharma.
The meaning is that while formerly they were deluded, now they have awakened in this way; in the past there was nothing but sorrowful lamentation, hence it is said, "I [have come]...
(and so forth). Now, however, they have already attained peace and security, hence it is said, "But now... (and so forth). This refers to the present *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

This refers to what was taught forty years ago. That is to say, what was taught forty years ago—where the three vehicles were indeed the three vehicles and the one vehicle was indeed the one vehicle—was that which had already been heard and possessed.

What is heard now, namely that the three are the one, is that which was previously unheard and unpossessed; because it is heard for the first time, it is called "hearing what has never been heard before."
(As stated above). The three phrases regarding "severing all doubts and regrets" represent a detailed exposition; they are spoken in contrast to the brief exposition.
This means that when one first hears the Tathāgata briefly open up the three and manifest the one, one cannot help but give rise to doubt and regret.

Consequently, both the external body and the internal mind become茫然 (máng'rán—bewildered) and lack peace. Now, hearing the detailed opening of the three and manifestation of the one, [one's doubts are severed].
Knowing that these three are one, doubt and regret are severed; body and mind become expansive and tranquil, attaining swift peace and security. Therefore it is said, "Severing all...

(and so forth). Regarding the phrase "Today I finally know," this means that at the assembly of the *Āgama*, the Tathāgata declared that we were able to transcend the triple world and destroy [the afflictions of] views and thought, naming us his children. Today, I finally know that in the past...
These were like sons; now we are true sons. Therefore it is said, "On this day... and so forth. The Tathāgata has spoken this wondrous Dharma from his golden mouth.
We have grown and developed our Dharma-body through this milk of the Dharma; hence it is said that we are "born from the Buddha’s mouth.
The Tathāgata has proclaimed the transformation of the Dharma, and we have attained awakening and entry through it; hence it is said that we are "transformed by the Dharma."

Śāriputra said: "Formerly, I believed that the Three Vehicles were not identical to the One Vehicle, and I thought myself utterly devoid of a share in the Buddha-dharma. Now I know that the Three are indeed the One;
I have already obtained my share of the precious treasury of the Buddha-dharma. Therefore, it is said that I have obtained a share of the Buddha-dharma."
△ Second, the three verses in praise. First, a verse that sets forth what was received.
At that time, Śāriputra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
Having heard this sound of the Dharma, I have attained what I never had before; my heart harbors great joy, and the net of doubt has been entirely removed.
From of old, I have received the Buddha’s teaching and have not lost the Mahāyāna. The Buddha’s voice is most rare and extraordinary; it can eliminate the afflictions of sentient beings.
"I have attained the exhaustion of outflows; hearing this also removes my grief and affliction.
As for "great joy," it is because the Dharma heard is great that the joy is likewise great.

"The net of doubt has been entirely removed" is explained as before. Regarding the two phrases concerning the past, they refer to the former [distinction between] the three vehicles and the one vehicle.
"Separated. Therefore, we thought to ourselves: 'We have lost the Mahāyāna of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision.
Now that we hear that the three are one, we know that in the past, although we received the Buddha's teaching on the Four Noble Truths of the Hīnayāna, we did not lose the Mahāyāna in its entirety.
That the Buddha’s voice is rare means that the Dharma he teaches is rare; therefore, he is able to teach it."

The sound of the Dharma is likewise rare and marvelous. As for the statement that it "can remove" [afflictions]: because the nine realms all return to the Buddha-realm, the sorrow and distress of sentient beings are removed.

When I say, "I have already attained the exhaustion of outflows," this does not mean anything more than having shattered view-delusions and thought-delusions so as not to fall back into the three realms.
Now, hearing that the three vehicles are entirely identical to the one vehicle, this removal of my distress is, in fact, the removal of ignorance.
It is vexation. Therefore it says, "I have already... (and so forth). △ Second, the verse-explanation clarifying what has been understood.

First, from "I was situated below" up to "all doubts and regrets are entirely removed," there are fourteen lines of verse. These discuss delusion and awakening by comparing the [teachings] of forty years ago with the present *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
Next, from "When first hearing" up to "claiming it was the work of Māra," there are six and a half lines.

To briefly elucidate this, one discusses delusion and awakening in contrast to the extensive elucidation. Furthermore, within both the brief and the extensive sections, each is divided into two parts:
first, eight lines clarify delusion within delusion; second, six lines clarify awakening within delusion; third, one line clarifies delusion within awakening;
and fourth, five and a half lines clarify awakening within awakening. Dividing the text into four sections, the first clarifies delusion.
Deluded in the midst, I dwell in mountain valleys or beneath forest trees; whether sitting or walking in meditation, I constantly contemplate this matter:
"Alas! How deeply I reproach myself—how have I deceived myself? We too are sons of the Buddha, having equally entered the outflow-free Dharma."
They will be unable, in the future, to expound the unsurpassed path—the golden hue, the thirty-two marks, the ten powers, and the various liberations—within this single Dharma;
they shall not attain these things, nor the eighty minor marks of excellence, nor the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Such virtues as these, I have lost them all. While I was walking alone in meditation, I saw the Buddha amidst the great assembly;
his fame filled the ten directions, and he brought vast benefit to sentient beings. Reflecting that I had lost this advantage, I realized I had deceived myself.
Day and night, I have constantly contemplated this matter, wishing to ask the World-Honored One whether I have lost it or not.
I have often seen the World-Honored One praise the various bodhisattvas; for this reason, day and night, I have deliberated upon such matters.

Regarding the phrase "I dwell in mountain valleys and the like": whenever a practitioner wishes to cultivate *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, if they remain amidst markets or within city walls, they cannot avoid much distraction and turmoil.
Their inner mind will be pulled and agitated, making it difficult for *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* to manifest.

Therefore, one must dwell in mountain valleys or beneath trees; thus, external objects will not invade, one will be free from clamor and bustle, the mind will attain realization of tranquility, and *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* will easily be accomplished.

For this reason, Śāriputra also contemplated while dwelling amidst mountain valleys and forest trees. Whether sitting, walking, or practicing, regarding the cultivation [of these practices], it occurs throughout all four modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*).

There is nothing that is not permissible. As for what is now called "sitting," among the four modes of deportment, sitting alone is the most stable and secure, because it is through this posture that *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are easily accomplished.
Regarding the term "walking meditation" (*caṅkrama*), it is like the weaving of a worldly cloth: having gone forward, one returns again.
That which comes must likewise depart. Now, the practitioner desires to leave behind afflictions (*kleśa*) and come toward Bodhi;

for this reason, one must practice walking meditation (*caṅkrama*). The benefits of such walking meditation are manifold, as explained in the first part of the second volume of the *Fuxing* (Subcommentary).
One who contemplates this matter reflects: "The Bodhisattvas have received their predictions [of enlightenment], yet I am not included among them. Since—
Having reflected thus, he again sighed and reproached himself; hence the words "Alas," and so forth. From "We [are]" onwards, the text correctly clarifies his reflection.

The first three lines contrast him with the Bodhisattvas. By saying "we too are sons of the Buddha," it means that while Bodhisattvas are able to inherit the family business of the Tathāgata and are thus sons of the Buddha, we are also able to transcend the triple world and shatter [wrong] views.

If one reflects thus, one is likewise a son of the Buddha. Since we are also sons of the Buddha and have equally entered the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*), for what reason do the bodhisattvas receive the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) that they shall, in a future age, preach the unsurpassed path and be endowed with all the marks and manifold merits, while we cannot?
Therefore it is said that we have "equally entered," and so forth. Having attained Buddhahood, one will necessarily possess the thirty-two [major marks].
The [thirty-two] marks, the eighty minor characteristics, the ten powers, the liberations, the eighteen unique qualities, and so forth—for what reason do we alone lack these?
Therefore it is said, "golden-colored" (and so on). Such phrases as these summarize what the Bodhisattvas will attain in the future.
That is to say, the Bodhisattvas have attained such a vast multitude of qualities, whereas we have entirely lost them; therefore—
It says: "Thus (and so forth)... I alone have added one line and a half. Contemplating in response to the Tathāgata, the first line presents what the Buddha possesses;
the phrase "I contemplate" (*sva-vicintya*) refers to right reflection (*samyak-saṃkalpa*). The phrase "I [am]" (*aham*) is a self-reproach.
To contemplate that one has lost this benefit means that one cannot bring fame to the ten directions nor provide benefit to sentient beings.
Furthermore, I have constantly engaged in a single practice: contemplating the Buddha by way of pairing [his qualities].

As for whether this has been lost or not lost, it refers to all that the Tathāgata possesses—the deeds that fill the ten directions and benefit sentient beings—which we followers of the Two Vehicles...
Is it that we have ultimately lost it and can never recover it? Or is it that even later on, we will still be able to attain it and not lose it?
I have often observed the practice of pairing Bodhisattvas together for contemplation.
Since the Bodhisattvas are praised by the Buddha while we are censured by the Buddha, yet the Dharma-nature we enter is the same, why is there praise and censure?
It is suddenly and utterly different. For this reason, day and night, I have deliberated upon this matter.
△ Second, clarifying awakening within delusion:
Now I hear the Buddha’s voice, preaching the Dharma according to what is appropriate; it is untainted and inconceivable, leading all beings to the site of enlightenment.
I was originally steeped in false views and served as a teacher to the brahmins. The World-Honored One, knowing my mind, uprooted my errors and preached Nirvana.
I completely eliminated all false views and attained realization of the Dharma of emptiness. At that time, I thought to myself: "I have reached extinction."

Now I have realized for myself that this was not true parinirvāṇa. When I attain Buddhahood and am endowed with the thirty-two marks, and am revered by the hosts of devas, yakṣas, nāgas, and other spirits—only then can it be said that [suffering] is forever exhausted and extinguished without remainder.
The Buddha, amidst the great assembly, declared, "I shall become a Buddha. Upon hearing such a Dharma-sound, their doubts were entirely repented and eliminated.

The first line clarifies the present; that is to say, at the great assembly on Mount Ling, having heard the Buddha’s voice revealing the One by opening up the Three, they now know that the dharmas of precepts and goodness which the Tathāgata previously taught were in accordance with the capacities of humans and devas.

The teaching on the emptiness of the truths and conditions was given according to the suitability of the two vehicles. The teaching on the distinct Middle Way was given according to the suitability of the Bodhisattvas.
Reaching the present day, one should realize that this very essence is the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*): it is neither empty nor existent, and yet it is also not the middle.
It does not fall into the two extremes, nor does it fall into the middle way. Therefore, it is said: "Now I hear... (etc.).
"Causing the assembly to reach the site of enlightenment" means that the nine realms all return [to the One Vehicle] and the three vehicles all convene.
