It means to cause all sentient beings to attain the opening, showing, awakening to, and entering into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, thereby ascending to the field of Bodhi.
The next two lines describe the past, referring to the Tathāgata’s original intention: from the very beginning, he wished to preach the Great [Vehicle] for my sake; however, because of me—

In the past, he was attached to false views; moreover, it was not only that he himself was attached to the false, but he also sought to lead others with the false, acting as a teacher to the Brahmins.

"Brahmin" is a name for those outside the Way (non-Buddhists). He did not understand the laws of the world regarding arising and ceasing through causes and conditions, nor non-arising and non-ceasing; furthermore, he did not know [the nature] of the world or of sentient beings.
Regarding the causal origin: I merely reckoned that all dharmas arise from Brahmā, and thus I was called a Brahmacārin.

Having become attached to this heterodoxy, my faculties were such that I could not accord with the Great [Teaching] when I heard it; therefore, the Tathāgata preached the Lesser Nirvāṇa for me to uproot my false views.
Not realizing this was the Buddha’s skillful means, I relied upon it for cultivation and realization, and thereby attained [it].

To extinguish the afflictions (*kleśa*) and cross over birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). Therefore it is said: "I originally... (and so forth). Now, the following three lines specifically reveal awakening within delusion.

When it says "not a true extinction" (*parinirvāṇa*), it means that while the views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *vitarka-kleśa*) have been extinguished, ignorance (*avidyā*) has not yet been extinguished;

and while the limited分段 [birth-and-death] has been crossed, the transformative 變易 [birth-and-death] has not yet been crossed. This is because the Tathāgata previously stated: "I am for... [and so forth].
He established skillful means and showed them nirvana. Although I speak of nirvana, it is not true extinction.
Śāriputra attained realization through this, and thus it is said: "Only now have I awakened for myself; this is not a real parinirvāṇa.
As for the phrase "if one attains Buddhahood" and so forth, this is because the Tathāgata previously stated: "All dharmas, from the very beginning, are eternally quiescent."
The mark of cessation: "When the Son of the Buddha has practiced the Way, he shall become a Buddha in a future age. Śāriputra attained realization through this, hence it says:
"When one attains Buddhahood," up to "permanently extinguished without remainder. Regarding the passage "The Buddha, in the midst of the great assembly," etc.:
this is because the Tathāgata previously stated, "Whether śrāvakas or bodhisattvas, upon hearing the Dharma I preach, all shall attain [enlightenment]."
The Buddha has no doubts. Furthermore, it is said that the twelve hundred arhats shall all likewise become Buddhas. Upon hearing this, Śāriputra attained awakening;
thus he declared, "I too shall become a Buddha," for his doubts and regrets have been entirely eliminated. △ Third, [the section on] delusion within awakening.
Upon first hearing what the Buddha taught, my heart was filled with great alarm and doubt: "Could it be that a Māra has manifested as a Buddha to disturb and confuse my mind?

Regarding the phrase "upon first hearing what the Buddha taught," this refers to first hearing the teaching on the manifestation of the One by opening up the Three: "After a long time, the Buddhas' Dharma..."

"One must speak the truth. Because the Buddha, through the power of skillful means, had previously shown the teachings of the Three Vehicles—whereby it was formerly thought that the Three Vehicles were real—and now declares them to be skillful means, [the disciples] were greatly startled and suspicious, claiming this was the teaching of Māra.
△ Fourth, clarifying awakening within awakening.

The Buddha, through various causes and conditions, skillful parables, and eloquent speech, has taught this; my mind is as peaceful as the ocean, and having heard this, the net of my doubts is severed.
The Buddha has spoken of the Buddhas of the past, immeasurable in number and now extinguished, who likewise dwelt in skillful means and all preached this Dharma.
The Buddhas of the present and the future, their number being immeasurable, likewise employ various skillful means to expound this Dharma,
just as the World-Honored One of the present— from his birth and renunciation, to his attainment of the Way and turning of the wheel of Dharma— has also taught through skillful means.
"The World-Honored One teaches the true path; Māra does not possess such things. By this I know for certain that this is not Māra acting as a Buddha.
Because I had fallen into the net of doubt, I thought it was the work of Māra."
The first line generally clarifies all Buddhas above, opening the three to reveal the one. "The Buddha, by means of various [teachings]," etc., opens the provisional;
"various" refers to the provisional, and the real is thereby revealed as well. Hence it says, "The Buddha, by means of... (and so forth).
The two lines beginning with "His mind" are a transposed text; they should read: "I have heard that the net of doubt is severed, and his mind is as peaceful as the ocean. Next...
The Buddha spoke the following two lines to summarize the preceding distinct clarifications of the three periods of time, thereby opening the three to reveal the one.

Furthermore, the phrase "those who preach this Dharma" refers to what the Tathāgata previously stated: first, he established the provisional through the real; next, he opened the provisional to reveal the real;
and finally, he set aside the provisional to establish the real. Such teachings are not unique to me, Śākyamuni; they have also been taught by those of the past.

The same applies to all past Buddhas; therefore, it is said that they all likewise preached this Dharma. From the passage "As now" onwards, the text summarizes the preceding section to further clarify that Śākyamuni opened up the three vehicles to reveal the One Vehicle.
Regarding the phrase "As now," it means that the provisional comes first and the real follows last;

this is not limited to the Buddhas of the three periods alone, for I, Śākyamuni, am likewise so. Although I have taught expedient means, my intention has always been directed toward the ultimate reality. Therefore...
It is said that [the Buddha] also speaks by means of skillful expedients (*upāya*). The World-Honored One speaks the true path (*bhūtamārga*).

As for "Pāpīyān" and so forth: *Pāpīyān* here translates as "Evil-doer. Because he is able to perform various evil deeds with an evil mind, even if he were able to preach the Dharma, he could not speak of the true path;
therefore it is said, "Pāpīyān does not possess this [quality]. Since Pāpīyān lacks this quality, one knows that only [the Buddha]...
The Buddha was able to speak it. Previously, I had fallen into the net of doubt, saying such things as, "Could this not be Māra acting as a Buddha?
But now I know that it was truly the Buddha who acted as a Buddha and spoke it. Therefore it is said, "Pāpīyān" (and so forth).
△ Third, the verse summarizing the common conclusion.
Hearing the Buddha’s gentle voice, profound, far-reaching, and most subtle, as he expounds the pure Dharma, my heart is filled with great joy.
Doubts and regrets are forever exhausted; I abide securely within true wisdom. I shall certainly become a Buddha, revered by devas and humans.
"Turning the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma to teach and transform all bodhisattvas"—this verse refers to what has been heard from the Buddha now, which was previously unheard. Regarding "gentle voice":
if one were to say that the three vehicles are definitively three vehicles and the one vehicle is definitively one vehicle, that would be harsh and rigid, rather than gentle.
It is supple. Yet, what is taught as the three vehicles is itself the one vehicle. Outside of the one, there are no three;
the three and the one are perfectly interfused and do not contradict one another. Therefore, it is called the "Supple Sound.
The Dharma taught by this Supple Sound penetrates the three truths vertically and exhausts the dharma-realm horizontally; it cannot be conceived by the mind, nor can it...

Because it is spoken and deliberated upon, its words are profound and exceedingly subtle. When this Dharma is relied upon for cultivation, one can destroy ignorance and manifest the Middle Way; therefore, it is called the "Pure Dharma.

As for "my heart is filled with great joy," it means that through this realization, one immediately ascends to the first stage, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*); hence, it is called "Great Joy. [The text continues: "Doubt and regret..."
“Thus, the Tathāgata has forever exhausted doubt and regret; dwelling in true wisdom, he has become a Buddha.
I too have now forever exhausted doubt and regret, and shall therefore dwell as the Buddha dwells—dwelling likewise in true wisdom.
When the Tathāgata became a Buddha, he was revered by devas and humans, turned the great wheel of Dharma, and transformed bodhisattvas. If I become a Buddha, I shall likewise do so.”
Therefore it is said: "Doubt and regret" (and so forth). △ Third, the Tathāgata’s confirmation.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra: "I now declare before this great assembly of devas, humans, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others:
in the past, at the abodes of twenty thousand koṭis of Buddhas, for the sake of the unsurpassed path, I have constantly taught and transformed you."
"You, too, have followed and studied under me for a long night. It was because I used skillful means to guide you that you were born into my Dharma.
Śāriputra, in the past I taught you to set your will upon the Buddha-way, yet you have now forgotten it all and instead claim to have already attained parinirvāṇa.
I now wish to cause you to remember the path you originally vowed to practice, for the sake of all the śrāvakas."
"I have heard this Mahāyāna sūtra, titled the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, which teaches the Dharma for Bodhisattvas and is protected by the Buddhas.

Regarding this "narration and accomplishment": "narration" (*shu*) means to praise and recount; "accomplishment" (*cheng*) means to bring to fulfillment. It is certainly not a matter of praising others, as was understood in the preceding passage.
Nor is it a matter of praising others for future fulfillment, for such greatness is precisely what Śāriputra has realized through his own understanding.
It is only because of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* forty years ago that it is merely the Tathāgata’s single lifetime of transformative teaching;

therefore, the Tathāgata further confirms this by saying: "In the past, at the abodes of twenty thousand koṭis of Buddhas, I have constantly taught and transformed you for the sake of the unsurpassed path. Thus, it is not only today’s *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* that first teaches you.
Regarding "the Mahāyāna": those who have studied for a long night, although taught the Great [Vehicle], have not yet destroyed the views and afflictions within the realm of desire;
thus, they remain shrouded by defilements, which is why it is said they have "studied for a long night. As for the phrase "I, through skillful means," etc.:
Because they had not yet destroyed their delusions while studying the Mahāyāna, they subsequently regressed from the Great Vehicle and adopted the Small Vehicle.

Since they had taken up the Small Vehicle, the Tathāgata again received them through the Small Vehicle; thus it is said that he used skillful means to guide them so that they might be born within my Dharma.
This was not only the case for forty years prior; in the past as well, I once taught the Small Vehicle to you.
Śāriputra’s realization of the Lesser Vehicle occurred only forty years ago, whereas his realization of the Greater Vehicle occurs only today through the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

Therefore, the Tathāgata speaks this in order to advance his realization. Because he had regressed from the Great Vehicle, until this day he has completely forgotten his aspiration for the Buddha-way;
because he took up the Lesser Vehicle, when he first heard my teaching, he did not recognize it as a skillful means. Thus...
He contemplates and realizes [the truth], which means attaining *nirvāṇa*. Regarding the phrase "recalling the path practiced according to his original vows":

this refers to the past, when he was under twenty-two thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas. Having been taught the Great [Vehicle], he had already made the four great universal vows and had already practiced the Bodhisattva path.
However, because he had not yet entered the [definitive] stage, during the intervening period he took the small [vehicle] and forgot the great; hence it is said.

I wish further to cause you to remember this. As for the statement that "the teaching for Śrāvakas is the Dharma for Bodhisattvas," it is because once a Śrāvaka hears the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, it is revealed and manifested that they are, in fact, Bodhisattvas. △ Fourth, the superior faculties receive their prediction:
Having already attained understanding, one initiates practice based on that understanding; naturally, through such practice, one enters realization and accomplishes the Buddha-way. Furthermore—
One must clearly understand the bestowal of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*). Regarding the explanation of the bestowal of predictions herein, there are three intended meanings:

first, because in the forty years prior [to this teaching] no predictions had ever been bestowed upon the śrāvakas, the present bestowal of predictions upon the śrāvakas serves to manifest that the merit of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is supreme throughout the entire dispensation;
second, it is intended to spur those of middling and inferior faculties who possess dull roots, causing them to give rise to joy and aspiration; third, [the remaining meaning].
The prediction is bestowed in order to fulfill his former original vow. The text is divided into two parts: first, the prose; second, the verse.
The first part is divided into ten sections; the first is the section on time.
Śāriputra, in a future age, after immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable kalpas—
whereby the expression "after innumerable kalpas" is used because śrāvakas have been solely devoted to their own benefit and have never benefited others—

I shall bestow upon you the prediction of the eight stages, so that for the sake of sentient beings, you may undergo these innumerable kalpas and extensively perform the work of binding [the Dharma-knot].
Once the conditions for the Pure Land are fulfilled, one may then attain Buddhahood. II. Cultivating the Causes:
Making offerings to many, even thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas; upholding the True Dharma; and fully perfecting the path practiced by Bodhisattvas.
Making offerings to the Buddhas is the cultivation of merit; upholding the True Dharma is the cultivation of wisdom.
The path of the Bodhisattva consists solely of merit and wisdom. Since one now cultivates both simultaneously, one is thus able to fulfill the Bodhisattva path.
△ Third, the realization of the fruit.
He shall attain Buddhahood, known by the name Padmaprabha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna,
Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
Regarding the Buddha named Huaguang (Flower Light): "Flower" symbolizes the cause, and "Light" symbolizes the fruit; that is, wisdom.

Since Śāriputra was foremost among those of the Small Vehicle in wisdom, now that he hears this revelation and manifestation, his former Small Vehicle wisdom is entirely transformed into the wondrous wisdom of the Mahāyāna.
Because in the causal stage he was able to use wondrous wisdom to illumine the wondrous realm, the name of the fruit is thus given.
This is the Flower Radiance [Buddha]. △ Fourth, the land:
The name of the land is Free from Defilement (*Vimalā*). Its terrain is level and even; it is pure, adorned, peaceful, secure, and prosperous. Gods and humans abound there.
The ground is made of lapis lazuli. There are eight intersecting roads, demarcated on their sides by cords of gold.
Alongside them stand rows of trees made of the seven treasures, which are constantly laden with flowers and fruit.

The three delusions have not yet been destroyed; all such states are termed "defiled. Because one uses wondrous wisdom to contemplate and destroy ignorance, that land is named "Free from Defilement" (Vimalā).
△ Fifth, the preaching of the Dharma.

The Tathāgata Padmaprabha also taught and transformed sentient beings by means of the three vehicles. Śāriputra, although the time when that Buddha appeared was not an evil age, he preached the Dharma of the three vehicles due to his original vows.
Regarding the initial teaching of the Dharma, that Buddha explains away the doubt: "The present Buddha appears in an evil world of the five turbidities; therefore, he teaches the Three Vehicles.
Since the land of that Buddha is adorned and magnificent, it is not an evil world; why, then, does he also teach the Three Vehicles? To resolve this, he says:
"Although it is not an evil world, it is due to his original vows. There are two types of original vows: first,"
This refers to the past, when the Brahmin begged for his eyes and vowed that upon attaining Buddhahood, he would first preach the Small Vehicle.
Second, this refers to today, when one hears the five Buddhas reveal and clarify [the truth] and thereby attains understanding and awakening.

Since those five Buddhas all first employed provisional means, they also vow that upon attaining Buddhahood, they shall first preach the Three Vehicles; it is for this reason that those Buddhas likewise preach the three vehicles.
△ Sixth, the name of the eon:
that eon is named Mahāratnavyūha (Great Jewel Adornment). Why is it called Mahāratnavyūha? Because in that land, bodhisattvas are regarded as the great jewels.
Regarding the statement that bodhisattvas are "jewels," this refers to the meaning found in the *Chū* (Chu) scriptural tradition: "One does not treasure gold or jade;
only goodness is treasured. 7. The Number of the Assembly:
Those bodhisattvas are immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable; they cannot be reached by calculation or analogy.
It is not by the power of the Buddha’s wisdom that anyone could know [this]. When they wish to walk, jeweled flowers receive their feet. These bodhisattvas have not newly resolved their minds;
they have all long planted the roots of virtue. Under immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas, they have purely cultivated the Brahma-faring.
They are constantly praised by all Buddhas, always cultivate the Buddha-wisdom, possess great supernormal powers, and are well-versed in [knowledge].
The gateway to all dharmas is straightforward and without guile; their resolve and mindfulness are firm and steadfast. Such bodhisattvas fill that land.
First, this clarifies the number [of the assembly]. These subsequent lines praise their virtues: "those who purely cultivate the brahma-conduct" refers to the brahma-conduct of the six perfections.
It is as follows: if, while practicing giving, one perceives a donor, an object of giving, and a recipient, it is not called "pure cultivation.
Now, when practicing giving, one thoroughly realizes that the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*) are empty in essence; therefore, it is called pure cultivation.
Just as it is with giving, so it is for all other [perfections]. One who well understands the Dharma is said to destroy the dust-like delusions and thereby know all illnesses.
Knowing all medicines, one is able to provide the appropriate medicine according to the illness so that it may be taken;
subsequently, one naturally breaks through ignorance and flows into [enlightenment] spontaneously. Therefore, it is said that he is upright and without guile. △ Eighth, the lifespan.
Śāriputra, the lifespan of the Buddha Puṣpārāma will be twelve minor kalpas, excluding the time when he was a prince and had not yet attained buddhahood;
the lifespan of the people in that land will be eight minor kalpas.

Regarding the phrase "excluding the period as a prince": this is because the period as a prince constitutes his worldly lifespan. What is now referred to as twelve minor kalpas concerns only his life as a Buddha;
therefore, that period is excluded. △ Nine: The Stage of the Successor (Upapadya).
After twelve intermediate kalpas, the Tathāgata Padmaprabha bestowed upon the Bodhisattva Dṛḍhavati the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
He addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "This Bodhisattva Dṛḍhavati shall next become a Buddha, titled Puṣpadantapadavikrāmin, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. Such shall be his buddha-field."
It is likewise so.
Regarding the Bodhisattva named Kṣemadatta: "Kṣema" means that there is no delusion he has not shattered; "Datta" means that there is no virtue he has not perfected.
As for his addressing the bhikṣus, it was the Buddha Puṣparāja who conferred upon Kṣemadatta the prediction of enlightenment and issued this proclamation to those bhikṣus.

I, Qiu, am styled "Flower-Footed Peaceful Practice. Because that Bodhisattva was able to purely cultivate the Brahma-conduct during his causal stage, he was supported by precious flowers beneath his feet;
therefore, in the stage of fruition, he is styled "Flower-Footed Peaceful Practice. △ Ten: The True and Semblance [Dharma] Ages.
Śāriputra, after the parinirvāṇa of this Buddha Puṣpārāma, the True Dharma shall remain in the world for thirty-two intermediate kalpas,
and the Semblance Dharma shall likewise remain in the world for thirty-two intermediate kalpas.
△ Second, ten verses in verse form. First, the verse that anticipates the realization of the fruit.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"In a future age, Śāriputra shall become a Buddha, a Honored One of Universal Wisdom, named Flower Light (Puṣpārāma). He shall deliver immeasurable multitudes."

Regarding the Venerable Samantabhadra: he is able, by means of inconceivable and wondrous wisdom, to observe and illumine all things perfectly, thereby attaining the realization of the three wisdoms within a single moment of mind;
thus he is called "Universal Wisdom" (Samantabhadra). △ Second, the actual verse on the causal practice.
He made offerings to countless Buddhas, fulfilled the bodhisattva practices, and, through merits such as the ten powers, realized the unsurpassed path.
△ Third, the transposition of verses and the names of the kalpas.
After the passing of immeasurable kalpas, there was a kalpa named Mahāratnavyūha.
△ Fourth, the verse on the land:
The world was named Vimala; it was pure and free from defilement. Its ground was made of lapis lazuli, and its paths were demarcated by golden cords.
There are trees of various colors made of the seven treasures, always bearing flowers, fruits, and seeds.
△ Fifth, the verse that transcends numerical categories:
The bodhisattvas in that land are always firm in their resolve and mindfulness; they have all fully perfected the supernormal powers and the pāramitās.
Under countless Buddhas, he skillfully studied the Bodhisattva path.

One who has skillfully studied the Bodhisattva path is able to give rise to cultivation in accordance with the nature of reality; such that the entirety of cultivation returns to the nature, and cultivation and nature are non-dual.
Because principle and practice are identical as one, it is called "skillful study. △ Sixth, a retrospective verse on the preaching of the Dharma.
Such great beings as these were transformed by the Buddha Puṣpārāma.
By "such as these," it is evident that what is being taught is the Mahāyāna Dharma. Although the prose section explicitly explains the three vehicles (triyāna), [it is actually the Mahāyāna].
In this context, the Mahāyāna is clearly explained; they mutually elucidate one another. △ Seventh, the verse on the transcendence of the lifespan:
When the Buddha was a prince, he abandoned his kingdom and renounced worldly glory; in his very last body, he left the household life and attained the Way of Buddhahood.
The Buddha Flower-Light dwelt in the world for a lifespan of twelve minor kalpas; the people of that land had a lifespan of eight minor kalpas.
As for those who left home to attain the Way of the Buddha: since they were able to renounce their kingdoms and leave the household life, they had already eliminated the mind of stinginess.
Once the mind of stinginess was eliminated, the root of birth and death was severed; therefore, they were able to attain the Way of the Buddha in a subsequent existence. This is because—
Worldly glory is easily surpassed by the glory that transcends the world; yet worldly glory is not true glory, for only the glory that transcends the world is true glory.
△ Eight: A Verse on Surpassing the True and Semblance Dharma.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma shall abide in the world for thirty-two minor kalpas, extensively delivering all sentient beings.
When the True Dharma has been extinguished, the Semblance Dharma shall last thirty-two [years].
△ Nine: The Distribution of Relics.
The relics shall spread far and wide; devas and humans shall universally make offerings to them.
△ Tenth: A summary of joyful celebration.
All that was performed by the Buddha Padmaprabha was exactly like this. That Sage Honored One among bipeds is most supreme and without peer.
"That is indeed your own body; you should rejoice in this. △ 5. The Fourfold Assembly’s Joy.
Part Two. First, the introduction; second, the expression of realization. The first part has two sections. First, the description of the assembly's joy.
At that time, the fourfold assembly— monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—
as well as the great multitude of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and others,
seeing Śāriputra receive the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* before the Buddha, were filled with great joy in their hearts.

"Rejoicing with immeasurable exultation and great joy in their hearts" refers to these fourfold assemblies and the eight classes of beings. Having heard this revelation and elucidation, they have attained realization just as Śāriputra did;
they have been able to shatter ignorance and ascend to the first stage (bhūmi). Therefore, they likewise rejoice and leap for joy just as Śāriputra did.
[They] leaped up. △ Second, the description of the offerings:
Each one removed the upper garment they were wearing to offer it to the Buddha. Śakra-devānām-indra, Brahmā-devaputra, and the others [did likewise].
Together with countless sons of heaven, they also made offerings to the Buddha with celestial fine garments, celestial *māndārava* flowers, *mahāmāndārava* flowers, and so forth.
The celestial garments scattered there remained suspended in mid-air, revolving of their own accord.
Hundreds of thousands of millions of kinds of celestial music were performed simultaneously in the sky, as a rain of various celestial flowers fell.

Each act, such as shedding one's robes and scattering flowers, possesses symbolic significance. First, regarding the shedding of robes as an offering to the Buddha: robes carry the meaning of both bondage and liberation;

this symbolizes that liberation occurs precisely within bondage. Prior to hearing the revelation and manifestation [of the Truth], these fourfold assemblies and the eight classes of beings were some bound by the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), some bound by the dust-like and sand-like [afflictions] (*rajas-aṇu*), and some bound by the unconditioned...

Regarding those bound by ignorance, it is like clothing binding the body. Now that they have heard this revelation and clarification, they are able to understand that the vehicles of humans and devas are themselves the Buddha-vehicle, and that expedient methods are themselves the true Dharma.
Each is able to awaken to and enter [this truth], such that they are no longer bound by views and afflictions (*kleśa*), nor are they bound by the dust-like [afflictions] (*rajas*). Furthermore...
He is not bound by ignorance, just as the body sheds its clothing; therefore, he immediately removes his upper garment to offer it to the Buddha.
Since the Buddha is one who has attained great liberation, this symbolizes that what appears to be bondage is in fact liberation.
Next, the offering of celestial flowers symbolizes that cause and effect are simultaneous. For these flowers represent the cause, and furthermore, these celestial...
My son, before this was revealed, one only knew that a celestial cause could produce a celestial fruit.
Now, having heard this revelation, one knows that the very celestial cause can produce the fruit of the Tathāgata; therefore, one offers celestial flowers to the Buddha.
Since the Buddha is the personification of the ultimate fruit, this symbolizes that the cause is itself the fruit. Thus it is called "celestial."
The phrase "turning the garment in the void" symbolizes that complete cultivation resides within the fundamental nature.

For the sublime practices one cultivates originally arise from the emptiness of the primary meaning (paramārtha-śūnyatā), just as a garment exists within the void; now, through the arousal of cultivation, they return once more to that very nature.
Just as a garment moves within space, the celestial garments moving in the void symbolize that complete cultivation returns to the fundamental nature (*dharmatā*).
That musical instruments and performers act together in the void symbolizes that complete nature gives rise to cultivation.
This means that within the self-nature of the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), hundreds of thousands of kinds of subtle and wondrous practices arise, just like empty space itself.
Within this [assembly], they perform various kinds of music; thus, by means of this, it symbolizes that cultivation arises from the entirety of nature (*xing*).
Now, for what reason must one strip off clothes, scatter flowers, and perform music as an offering to the Buddha to serve as a symbolic manifestation?

There is no other reason than that, from the time of the introductory section (*pūrvāvadāna*), these fourfold assemblies and the eight classes of beings saw that which was illuminated within the light, or...
There was a bodhisattva named Yishangfu (Clothed in Superior Garments) who offered clothing to the Buddha and the Sangha in order to seek the path of the Buddha.
Furthermore, he heard it said in the *Past Revealed and Manifested* [Sutra]: "If a person offers even a single flower, or causes others to perform music, thereby making an offering to the Buddha..."
All have attained the Way of the Buddha; thus, having reached this moment, they have achieved understanding and realization.

Some shed their robes, some scatter flowers, and some play music as offerings to the Buddha. This precisely represents what they have received and understood: that the causes for humans and devas are, in fact, the Buddha-vehicle.
These fourfold assemblies and the eight classes of beings all share the same realization as Śāriputra; therefore, they are all filled with joy.
They leaped for joy and made offerings to the Buddha; thus one knows that after the first turning of the Dharma wheel, it was not only Śāriputra alone who attained awakening.
△ Second, the statement of realization, in two parts: first, the prose exposition.
And he spoke these words: "In the past, the Buddha first turned the wheel of Dharma at Vārāṇasī; now he again turns the unsurpassed, greatest wheel of Dharma.
That the Buddha's [teaching] is equal in the past and present is precisely because the initial *Āgama* represents a minor beginning, contrasted here with the present *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
The Treatise states: This is to reveal that the present [teaching] is unsurpassed, whereas that [previous teaching] is surpassed;
that the present is greatest and most subtle, whereas that is smallest and coarsest. △ Second, the verse summary.
At that time, the sons of the gods, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"In the past, at Vārāṇasī, you turned the wheel of the Dharma of the Four Truths, analyzing and explaining all phenomena—the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates."
Now, once again, you turn the most wondrous, unsurpassed Great Wheel of Dharma. This Dharma is exceedingly profound and subtle; few are those capable of believing it.
Since time immemorial, we have frequently heard the World-Honored One’s teachings, yet never before have we heard such a profoundly wondrous and supreme Dharma.
The World-Honored One has preached this Dharma, and we all rejoice in it. The one of great wisdom, Śāriputra, has now received the Honored One’s prediction;
we, too, shall likewise surely attain Buddhahood, becoming the most honored and unsurpassed among all worlds.

The Buddha-way is inconceivable; he teaches through skillful means according to what is appropriate. Whatever meritorious deeds I have, whether in this life or in past lives, together with the merit of seeing the Buddhas, I dedicate them all toward the Buddha-way.

The first line of verse provides the exposition. Regarding the phrase "discriminatively teaching all dharmas," it means that from the single true reality (*dharmatā*), one discriminates and teaches various dharmas such as the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), and the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*). [These are] the five groups.

This refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). This clarifies the opening of the provisional (*upāya-kauśalya*). Now, another line is added below to clarify the manifestation of the real (*bhūta-artha*).
Next, the line and a half beginning with "we" clarifies sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*). The two lines beginning with "the three great wisdoms" clarify the making of vows (*praṇidhāna*).
Regarding the phrase "The Buddha-way is inconceivable," it means that when Śāriputra becomes a Buddha, he will likewise first preach the three vehicles, yet his intention lies elsewhere.
Because it is the one reality, it is inconceivable. When we ourselves attain Buddhahood, it shall likewise be so.
(The fourth section, "That which I have done," consists of one line: Dedication. Hitherto, whatever I have performed, I have dedicated solely toward the realms of humans and devas.

Now that it has been understood that the vehicles of humans and devas are themselves the Buddha-vehicle, one therefore dedicates the merit of the human and celestial realms toward the path of the Buddha.
The first cycle of the Dharma exposition concludes here. II. The Parable Section consists of four parts: 1. The Parable of the Tathāgata; 2.
From the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding" onwards, the disciples express their realization; 3. From the "Chapter on the Simile of the Medicinal Herbs" onwards, the Tathāgata...

Explanatory Summary. From the "Chapter on Bestowing Prophecies" (*Vyākaraṇa-parivarta*) onwards, those of medium capacity receive their prophecies. The first section is divided into two parts: first, Śāriputra’s statement of his request;
second, from "At that time the Buddha said... onwards, the Tathāgata’s acceptance and response. The first of these two has two sub-sections: first, stating that he has no further doubts.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I now have no further doubt or regret;
in the presence of the Buddha, I have personally received the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

"Those who no longer have doubt or regret" refers to those who, upon first hearing the Tathāgata briefly reveal and clarify the teaching, gave rise to various doubts and regrets when it was said that the three vehicles are merely skillful means.
The Tathāgata then, for their sake, extensively explained the opening of the three and the revealing of the one, showing that the three and the one are mutually identical.
Doubt and regret have already been severed. Next, he presented his resolution before the Buddha, and the Tathāgata further confirmed it for him.
Thus, I now know that in the past I once made a great vow; the Buddha has granted me a prediction (vyākaraṇa) once more, which brings me unsurpassed fulfillment.

Therefore, I no longer harbor any doubt or regret. △ Second, the universal exhortation for the assembly: "This Śāriputra, having first received this supreme prediction, newly sets forth the Great [Vehicle]..."
Out of compassion, he practices the bodhisattva path; therefore, he makes this universal request for the sake of the multitude.

At the beginning of the Dharma-exposition, although he likewise requested it for the multitude, because he stated that even his own understanding was not yet complete, his practice remained largely self-centered and thus could not be called "universal.
Now, since he himself has no doubts and acts solely for the benefit of others, it is called "universal. The text is divided into two parts; the first is the request made on behalf of his peers.
These twelve hundred who have attained mastery of mind formerly dwelt on the stage of training (*śaikṣa*). The Buddha constantly taught and transformed them, saying:

"My Dharma can bring one away from birth, old age, sickness, and death, leading to ultimate *nirvāṇa*. These individuals, both those still in training and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), each thought for themselves that by being free from the view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*) as well as the views of existence and non-existence, they had attained *nirvāṇa*. Yet now, in the presence of the World-Honored One, they hear what they have never heard before.
Upon hearing this, all fell into doubt and confusion.

As for the statement "the mind attains mastery," it means that the bonds of the son have been severed. Regarding the phrase "my Dharma can bring about detachment," "Dharma" refers here to the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths.
Birth, old age, sickness, and death are the fruits of suffering to be abandoned; these constitute the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). A fruit must necessarily...

The cause (*hetu*) includes both the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*). That which is capable of abandoning [the defilements] is the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*). Nirvāṇa is the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
Furthermore, those who individually abandon the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), as well as the views of existence and non-existence (*bhavābhava-dṛṣṭi*), etc., are called "those in training" (*śaikṣa*).
Those who have attained nirvāṇa are called "those beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*). Regarding "hearing what was never heard before": whether it be briefly elucidated or extensively [explained].
These clarifications have never been heard before. Regarding the statement that "all fall into doubt and confusion":
upon hearing the brief clarification that the Three Vehicles are merely expedient means (*upāya*) while they themselves considered their own path to be ultimate, they fall into doubt.
Upon hearing the extensive clarification that even Arhats shall become Buddhas, while they themselves considered themselves incapable of such a responsibility, they fall into confusion. △
Second, it was at the request of the fourfold assembly:
"Excellent, World-Honored One! We pray that you will explain the causal conditions for the sake of the fourfold assembly, so that they may be freed from doubt and regret.
Regarding the request to explain the causal conditions for the fourfold assembly, some say that "causal conditions" refers specifically to the causal conditions of past lives. [End of] She [chapter].
"Ānanda, although you have already attained realization and received your prediction, you were still unable to discern the underlying capacity [of the assembly];

therefore, you did not request an explanation through parables, but instead requested an account of causes and conditions (*nidāna*). Now, when we speak of 'causes and conditions,' this does not refer to causes and conditions from past lives;

rather, it refers to the causes and conditions of the 'three before and the one after. This means that while in the past the three vehicles were taught, now only the One Vehicle is taught; ultimately, there is..."
"For what cause and condition do you wish for the Buddha to explain this, so that those four assemblies may know that the three vehicles are in fact the one vehicle?
Thus, when the Tathāgata provided his response through parables, he first clarified that those of the lineages of the three vehicles transmigrate through the five realms;
next, he clarified the use of the three carts as an inducement to lead them out of the burning house; and finally, he clarified the equal bestowal of the Great [Vehicle].
"The chariot reaches the four quarters. This clearly elucidates the causes and conditions for the three preceding [vehicles] and the one subsequent [vehicle].

Because it serves as a response to their request, after the formal application of the Dharma, it concludes by stating: "For this cause and condition, through the power of the skillful means of all Buddhas, they distinguish and teach the three within the single Buddha-vehicle.
This is the proof. Above, regarding the requests made by those of equal standing, it was stated that they all fall into doubt.

[The interlocutor] is confused. This statement requests that the causes and conditions be explained; the text merely clarifies them reciprocally. To speak for those who have fallen into doubt, their own confusion will naturally be dispelled.
II. The Tathāgata’s Acceptance and Response, in two parts: A. Prose Exposition. B. Verse Recitation. The first part [the prose exposition] has three sections.

First, the introduction of the intent; second, the formal exposition; third, the concluding response. Regarding the first two [sections], the initial part refutes the preceding [view], thereby suppressing the former position.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra: "Did I not previously state that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, by means of various causes and conditions..."
Parables, verbal expressions, and skillful means in teaching the Dharma are all for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
All that is spoken is for the purpose of transforming bodhisattvas.

The phrase "I previously," and so forth, refers to the chapter on the Five Buddhas within the *Dharmadeśanā* (Exposition of the Dharma); it conveys the intention of establishing provisional teachings for the sake of the ultimate reality.
△ Second, the subsequent permission is cited from the older version.
However, Śāriputra, I shall now further clarify this meaning by means of a simile, for those who possess wisdom attain understanding through similes.
The word "however" (*tathāpi*) is a term used to suppress a point and then raise it again; although it was previously rejected, it is now permitted once more. Therefore—
"It is thus, Śāriputra. As for the phrase 'now I shall speak equally,' it means that I have already extensively clarified the meaning of the three vehicles and the one vehicle.

You now request me to speak once more; I likewise have nothing else to say, but shall simply reiterate the meaning of the three vehicles and the one vehicle through the parable of the three carts and the single cart. [End of previous section] At the beginning...

To be able to comprehend and understand when the Dharma is preached is surely the mark of a wise person; that one can now attain understanding through a parable likewise does not detract from being a wise person.
△ Second, the actual exposition is divided into two parts: first, establishing the parable; second, applying it to the Dharma. The first part is further divided into two.
First is the general analogy; second is the specific analogy. The reason for these two sections—a general and a specific—is that analogies are used to illustrate the Dharma.

Since the preceding discourse on the Dharma contains both a brief and an extensive set of verses, the present general analogy illustrates the brief verses above, while the specific analogy illustrates the extensive verses above. Furthermore, the general analogy begins with twenty *koṭi* of Buddhas.
Finally, today’s *Lotus Sūtra* clarifies the Tathāgata’s transformative activities throughout his single career. Although the words are concise, the meaning is indeed comprehensive.

As for the distinct parables, they begin from the stage of the Dharma-body, where he illuminates capacities and contemplates phenomena, and conclude with the equal bestowal of the great white ox-cart;
this clarifies the Tathāgata’s pedagogical methods throughout his entire dispensation. Although the words are extensive, the meaning is...
It is not complete; therefore, the text is expanded or abbreviated, but the meaning is not expanded or abbreviated.

This is why only "general" and "specific" are mentioned, rather than "expanded" and "abbreviated"—the intention lies therein. Furthermore, this can be seen by examining how the four great disciples received and understood [the teaching].

There are two types of analogies, general and specific. The general analogy illustrates the period of transformative activity (*ekakāla-vaipākya-karma*) as clarified here, which likewise consists of five stages.

This refers to the stage prior to the Grounds (*bhūmi*), when one silently receives the Dharma-body and, without deliberation, knows in advance how to bestow transformation; it must necessarily be thus. The specific analogy reveals the reception of the Dharma-body and the illumination of capacities (*tīkṣṇendriya*).

This is why there are five stages within the single text, consisting of both general and specific [analyses]. First, the general analogy is divided: [The text continues with the specific divisions of the general analogy.]
The text consists of two parts. First, the introduction of the parable:
"Śāriputra, suppose there were a great elder in a kingdom, city, or village, who was advanced in years and possessed immeasurable wealth."
He possesses many fields and houses, as well as numerous servants; his home is vast and has but a single gate.
Many people—perhaps a hundred, two hundred, or even five hundred—dwell within it. The halls and pavilions are dilapidated and old;
the walls have crumbled and fallen, the bases of the pillars are rotten, and the beams and rafters are leaning precariously, all around at once.
The analogy can be seen in the text. To apply it to the dharmas: the borders and territories constitute a kingdom, which is a metaphor for the Unobstructed Land of True Reward (*sambhoga-kāya*).

The administrative centers constitute a city, which is a metaphor for the Land of Skillful Means with Remainder (*upapatti-bhūmi*). The neighboring villages constitute a settlement—that is, a hamlet—which is a metaphor for the Land of Common Abode for Ordinary Beings and Sages (*sahā-vāsa*).
Thus, the Tathāgata’s manifestation in these three lands is like a householder whose reputation extends throughout those three places.

Furthermore, the Tathāgata has exhausted the five stages of dwelling and forever eliminated the two types of death; he possesses the great virtue of severance (*prahāṇa-guṇa*), like an elder whose years have declined and who is decrepit and aged.
The Tathāgata is fully endowed with the immeasurable wealth of the Dharma and merit, like an elder whose riches are boundless.
The Tathāgata is able to draw near to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddhas and fully practice [their teachings].
The path and Dharma practiced by all Buddhas bring about the accomplishment of inconceivable, true wisdom and sublime insight.
Having accomplished this sublime insight, one no longer takes food as life nor a dwelling as a refuge; rather, one takes only wisdom as life.
Furthermore, wisdom serves as their dwelling place. It is like a householder who possesses many fields to sustain his livelihood and many houses to shelter his body.

The Tathāgata is fully endowed with the perfection of skillful means (upāya-pāramitā) and has accomplished inconceivable sovereign wisdom (prajñā), enabling him to guide and transform sentient beings according to their individual capacities, just as a householder employs many servants for service.
It is a service. As for the fact that his house is vast and expansive yet has only a single gate:

if this is used as a metaphor for the *sambhogakāya* (Real Reward) land, then the *dharmatā* (Dharma-nature) constitutes the house—namely, the non-obstruction between form and mind (*rūpa-citta*), which is the adornment of both the environment and its inhabitants.

This is precisely what takes wisdom as its gate. If it is used as a metaphor for the *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (Nirvana with remainder) land, then *nirvāṇa* constitutes the house—namely, the state of serene...
However, that which is "beyond things" and "cool and clear on the open ground" is precisely this. It takes partial emptiness as its gate.
If one uses the analogy of the Land of Common Residence (*sahā-loka-dhātu*), then the triple world is the house and birth-and-death is the gate.

Here, however, the Dharma-nature is taken as the house and wisdom as the gate; this is a comprehensive metaphor intended to clarify the stage of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body prior to the stages [of the ten bhūmis].
Regarding this matter: although there are currently three distinct lands, for now we take the Land of Real Reward as the place of residence.

The five hundred people represent the sentient beings of the five realms of existence. Dwelling in the hall below represents the Desire Realm; dwelling in the pavilion above represents the Form and Formless Realms.
Since all three realms are collectively impermanent, they are described as "decayed and worn out. The walls represent the four great elements.
The three realms are all inseparable from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), yet they collectively belong to the process of transformation; therefore, they are said to be "collapsing.

The four great elements constitute the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), which is like the foundation of a pillar; yet they collectively belong to the process of displacement and extinction, and are therefore said to be "decaying.

Within the life-faculty there is consciousness (*manovijñāna*), which is like the ridgepole and beams; yet it collectively belongs to the process of arising and ceasing, and is therefore said to be "tilting and perilous. From this...
Ignorance gives rise to craving, and in turn, craving nourishes ignorance.
Because ignorance and craving do not separate from one another, it is said that they "surround and coexist. To illustrate this principle through a verse, it is stated:
"In the same way as I am now, for the sake of bringing peace and security to sentient beings, I shall proclaim and reveal [the truth] through various gateways of the Dharma."
This is the analogy for the fundamental nature of the Buddha-way. "The great elder" corresponds to the aforementioned single character "I.
The two phrases "his house was vast and large" correspond to the aforementioned "various dharma-gates. "Five hundred people" corresponds to the aforementioned two characters "sentient beings.
△ Second, the explicit illumination of the burning house.
Suddenly a fire broke out, burning down the house. The elder’s sons—whether ten, twenty, or even thirty of them—were inside this dwelling.
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is originally non-existent; it exists only due to craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Therefore, it is said that "fire suddenly breaks out.

Because ignorance exists, the five turbidities and the eight sufferings arise; therefore, it is said that "the house and its contents are consumed by flames. The thirty children are a metaphor for sentient beings of the three vehicles' spiritual lineages.
Regarding the "five destinies above," this refers to humans, because they possess only the causal nature (*dharmatā-nimitta*).

There is no object-condition for this realization; it is what is called the primordial Dharmakāya. Because gods and dragons disregard it, the text refers only to "humans" as a way of disparaging them.

Now, however, he is addressed as "Son," because at the sites of twenty trillion Buddhas he once received the Great Transformation (Mahāyāna), yet he temporarily forgot it and grasped the Small [Vehicle], thereby returning to the cycle of transmigration.
Since he has already received the Buddha’s transformation, his nature is naturally and inherently connected to that of the Dharma.
In the Tathāgata, the way of a father exists; in those of the Three Vehicles, the way of sons exists. Therefore, they are called "sons.

To explain this by means of the analogy applied to the Dharma, it is clear: furthermore, if this burning house is contrasted with the aforementioned Dharma, it refers to the two characters "peace" (an) and "security" (yin) in the brief verse, as this [house] manifests a lack of such peace and security. As for the thirty sons...

The phrase "the superior one knows the dispositions and desires of sentient beings" refers to "sentient beings" within that single sentence; this is because they possess the natures of the three vehicles (*triyāna*).
△ Second, the four distinct analogies: First, the analogy of the elder going out to rescue [his children].

This is like the Tathāgata perceiving the capacities [of beings] from the state of the *dharmakāya* and manifesting through response out of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). Second, from "Furthermore, he reflects... onwards, [he] sets aside the small table and uses...
The analogy of the chariot; third, the passage beginning with "At that time the elder" and so forth, which is the analogy of bestowing the great chariots equally;

fourth, the passage beginning with "Śāriputra," which is the analogy of the elder not being false. These analogies illustrate how the Tathāgata has established his transformation through five periods throughout his entire life:

first, he concealed the real and provisionally employed the expedient; finally, he opened up the expedient to reveal the real. The first [section] is divided into two parts; the first is "seeing the fire."
When the elder saw this great fire rising from all four sides, he was immediately seized with great alarm and fear, and thought to himself:
"Although I am able to escape safely through this gate that is being consumed by flames, my children within this burning house take pleasure in their play;
they are neither aware nor conscious of it, neither alarmed nor terrified, even as the fire approaches their bodies and its agonizing pain cuts into them."
They feel no weariness or distress, nor do they have the intention to seek liberation.

This is a separate analogy, which elaborates upon the verses within the preceding "Explanation of the Dharma. The current statement, "The elder sees," is an analogy for my observation with the Buddha-eye;

it refers to observing the capacities of sentient beings from the stage of the Dharmakāya. As for the mention of the "great fire" and so forth, this is an analogy for the sentient beings of the six realms mentioned above.
Ignorance arises from the four inversions, just as a great fire breaks out from all four sides.
Because it was previously taught that [the fire] is "great" and yet one still remains within the triple world (*tridhātu*), it is called a "great alarm.

Since one is already within the triple world, one will inevitably be burned and harmed by the afflictions (*kleśa*) and the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) of that triple world; therefore, it is called a "great terror. As for the "gateways of burning," these are the aforementioned...
This is one gate. This single gate, when it resides in the Tathāgata, is the gate of wisdom;
when it resides in sentient beings, it is the gate of birth and death, and it is that which is burned. The Tathāgata is able to transcend birth and death and possesses great wisdom;
he is not afflicted by ignorance or craving, and therefore it is said that he has "attained exit. However, although it is so stated, as for the Tathāgata—

Although [the Tathāgata] is able to escape, sentient beings cannot escape. Since sentient beings cannot escape, the Tathāgata returns from his wisdom, mobilizing great compassion to enter into birth and death (*saṃsāra*) and guide sentient beings so that they may attain liberation; thus it is said, "although.
