Those who delight in and are attached to play and sport give rise to various cravings within the three realms and produce various forms of discrimination.
Regarding "lack of awakening" and so forth: they do not awaken to the principle of the true truth of *nirvāṇa*; they do not know the path of precept, concentration, and wisdom;
they are not startled by the bitter retribution of the twenty-five states of existence within the three realms; and regarding the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*)...
Because they do not fear the accumulation of causes consisting of the eighty-one categories [of afflictions], they are burned and harmed by the defilements;
thus it is said that "fire comes to oppress the body. Because they are not startled by the fruit of suffering, they continue to transmigrate through birth and death;
thus it is said that "suffering cuts into one's very self. Because they do not know that there is a Truth of the Path to be cultivated, therefore...

To say that the mind does not feel weary or distressed means that, because one has not realized that there is a Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) to be realized, one lacks the intention to seek liberation.
"Cutting to the core" (*qie ji*) refers to the character *ji* (self) in the phrase "one's own self" (*zi ji*); it should not be read as the character *xu* (empty/false). △ Second, providing rescue.
"Śāriputra, this elder thought to himself: 'My hands and body possess great strength;
I shall carry him out from the house using my lap, or perhaps using a small table.'"

Seeing the fire above and observing the six realms of existence, he now contemplates how to provide salvation; this is like the arising of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) within the discourse on the Dharma.
As for "body and hands": the body is a metaphor for wisdom, possessing the capacity for bearing burdens;

the hands are a metaphor for supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), possessing the function of lifting others up. The "lap" (*kuci*) is a metaphor for great loving-kindness (*maitrī*) that bestows happiness; the "table" (*mañca*).

This is a metaphor for using great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) to extract [beings] from suffering and lead them out from the "abandonment" (the *śaya*). The subsequent passage aligns this with the Dharma, stating that it causes them to "play" (enjoy).

In previous interpretations, this was categorized under the "abandonment" (*śaya*) section; however, in the present interpretation, it is included here. Therefore, this text arises in response to the preceding [section] as an expression of great compassion.

△ Second, the analogy of the "abandoned bedstead" and the "use of a carriage. This illustrates how [the Buddha], when the Great [Vehicle] is encroached upon, bestows the Small [Vehicle]. Thus, the Tathāgata... [is supreme].
First: This refers to the passage concerning the seven-day contemplation (*saptāha-cintana*) in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*. The text is divided into two parts: first, the discarding of the small table;
second, from "At that time, the elder... onwards, the use of the carriage. Regarding the first section on discarding the table, there is a slight difference from the older version.

In the older version, it begins with "This elder," whereas here it begins with "Furthermore. Each has its own intended meaning. This part is further divided into three: first, the actual act of contemplation; second... [text continues].
"Having formed this thought" and below, he fully informs his sons. "Although the father has compassion" and below, there is no capacity [in them], so he ceases his transformation.
This passage from "he abandons the small table" onwards—some say it originally does not belong above, nor should it be below; it is a textual interpolation.
Now I say: "He further reflects" refers to the reflection during the twenty-one days within the aforementioned Dharma-exposition.
Furthermore, this house has only a single door. This refers to what was stated above in the "Teaching of the Dharma": "The wisdom I have attained is subtle, wondrous, and supreme. And:

"Moreover, it is narrow and small," which refers to what was stated above in the "Teaching of the Dharma": "The faculties of sentient beings are dull; they are blinded by attachment to pleasure and ignorance. And:
"I shall preach for them," which refers to what was stated above in the "Teaching of the Dharma": "How can [it be explained]?"
This is the "crossing over. As for the passage beginning with "Though his father felt pity," this refers to the aforementioned explanation of the Dharma:

if one were to praise only the Buddha Vehicle, sentient beings submerged in suffering would be unable to believe in this teaching. As for the passage from the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding" (Śraddhāparivarta) stating, "At that time, the messenger ran swiftly to seize him...
until he fainted and fell prostrate on the ground," this is clearly evident from both the preceding and following contexts.
[The Master] said: "How can you say that this is a passage added later? The initial section is divided into two parts. First, he contemplates and describes it as being circular;
then, he further contemplates that this house has only a single door, which moreover is narrow and small, and that the children are all young and immature."
"Recognized objects. "Attached to places of play. "Or one shall fall and be burned by fire.
These passages refer to the period following the Tathāgata’s manifestation in response to the world, specifically the seven days of contemplation within the *Avataṃsaka*.
Regarding the phrase "furthermore, he contemplated again": in the preceding stage of the Dharmakāya, when he desired to act for the sake of saving beings, he did so through great compassion. First...
Having completed his prior reflections, as he is now about to manifest his response and sit at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), he intends to contemplate and proclaim the Perfect [Teaching].
Therefore, it says, "he further reflects again. That which is called "having but one gate" refers precisely to the One Vehicle’s Perfect and Sudden Teaching (*ekayāna-aupratyutpanna-śāsana*).
As in the previous three weeks, what is termed "subtle and wondrous, the most supreme" is that wisdom serves as the gate; this is identical to the aforementioned "having but one... [gate].

The gate is the same. The "house" refers to that which is explained: the Great Universal Characteristic Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Yet, it is described as "narrow and small" because the gate itself is not inherently small;
rather, it is called narrow and small because it does not accord with the limited capacities of sentient beings. This means that while the Dharma is great, the capacity of the being is small.
Regarding the phrase "the children are still young," although they were previously taught the Great [Dharma], they have now completely forgotten it; thus, the great capacity is entirely absent.
Therefore, they are called "infants. Since they lack the great capacity [for the Mahāyāna], they take pleasure only in the Lesser Dharma (*hīnayāna*). The Lesser is not ultimate;

yet, because they have accumulated the Lesser, they claim it to be ultimate. Thus, it is said that they "have no realization. Although the Lesser Dharma they delight in is not ultimate, if one practices in reliance upon it, one can still become free from craving and discrimination, and transcend the stage of birth and death (*bhavacakra*).
Birth and death. Yet they do not merely delight in the small; they still give rise to various cravings and views, becoming attached to birth and death.
Therefore, it is said they "cling to the place of play. "Play" refers to the causes of affliction and suffering, while "place" refers to the effects of birth and death.
Birth and death are simply the playful realms of affliction. Since they cling to birth and death, they will inevitably be afflicted by the five turbidities and the eight kinds of suffering.
It is burning; therefore it is said, "He may fall [into calamity]," and so forth. △ Second, reflecting on the specific instruction:
"I shall speak to him of matters that cause fear. This house is already burning; you should quickly depart at once, lest you be consumed by the fire."

"Being burned and harmed" refers to what is to be explained; it is also a term for contemplation. In the previous contemplation, he wished to speak of the Perfect [Teaching], yet there was no receptive capacity [in the audience].
However, fearing that the Dharma might be too great for their limited capacity and that listeners would not believe it, he contemplated once more, wishing to include [other teachings as well].
It is considered an auxiliary to the distinct [teaching]. Regarding "matters of fear": these are elucidated in the Distinct Teaching.

Suffering (*duḥkha*) has immeasurable aspects, as the retributions of the ten realms (*daśadhātu*) are not the same. Accumulation (*samudaya*) has immeasurable aspects, as the afflictions (*kleśa*) are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and are not the same.
Since both suffering and accumulation are thus immeasurable, they are truly terrifying and fearsome; hence, they are called "matters of fear."

Regarding the phrase "this house has already been burned": according to the distinct teaching (pṛthag-deśanā), one must destroy the afflictions (kleśa) to realize bodhi, and one must sever birth-and-death (saṃsāra) to attain nirvāṇa.
Within bodhi and nirvāṇa, there is exclusively purity, being devoid of afflictions and birth-and-death.

Since it is now said that [the house] has been "destroyed" and "severed," it is therefore said to be "already burned. The "house" is precisely the afflictions and birth-and-death. "It is fitting to exit quickly at once" means:
The Separate Teaching (biejiao) clarifies that there is bodhi to be attained and nirvana to be realized.

Since there is something to be realized and attained, one ought to swiftly emerge from afflictions and birth-and-death; therefore, it is said that "one should at this time swiftly emerge" for those who are being harmed by the fire.
Furthermore, as elucidated in the Separate Teaching (Pṛthagdharma): if one does not attain Bodhi, one will inevitably be burned by the fire of afflictions (kleśa);
if one does not realize Nirvāṇa, one will inevitably be harmed by the fire of birth and death (saṃsāra). One must therefore swiftly emerge from both afflictions and saṃsāra.
Regarding what is called "do not let [them perish]," and so forth: △ Second, he fully informs his sons.
Having formed this thought, he fully informs his sons according to what he had contemplated: "All of you, come out quickly!"
This is the initial correct exposition of the *Avataṃsaka*. Regarding "as one contemplates": first, one contemplates the desire to expound the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*);

second, one contemplates the desire to expound the Distinct Teaching (*bie*)—these are two successive phases. Regarding "fully informing the sons": for those with real capacity (*shiji*), the Perfect Teaching is expounded;
for those with provisional capacity (*quanji*), the Distinct Teaching is expounded. Since both teachings are expounded together, it is so stated.

He told them all: "You who are to depart swiftly—those who possess the true capacity (the *tathāgatagarbha*), I cause them to realize *bodhi* while remaining within afflictions (*kleśa*) and to attain *nirvāṇa* while remaining within birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*); this is 'swift departure.
Those who possess the provisional capacity, I cause them to shatter afflictions and attain *bodhi*, and to sever birth-and-death and realize *nirvāṇa*; this is 'swift departure. (4)

Regarding the teaching through debate: only the Separate and Perfect [Vehicles] are swift. Since the Tripitaka and Shared [Vehicles] do not even know that there is a realm outside the triple world, how could they be considered swift?
△ Third, the cessation of transformation due to lack of capacity, in three parts. First, a general indication of lack of capacity.
Although the father felt compassion for them and sought to entice and instruct them with kind words, the sons were attached to their play and refused to believe or accept his counsel.
"Although the father felt compassion" refers to the two preceding reflections.

"Enticing and instructing them with kind words" means that he did not speak directly of the Perfect [Teaching] alone, but combined it with the Distinct [Teaching] to assist in its manifestation; thus, it is called "kind. "Attached to their play" refers to—

Those who are greedily attached to birth and death, giving rise to various forms of craving and discrimination, and are unwilling to believe or accept [the teaching], do so because they are greedily attached to birth and death.
For their sake, the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) is expounded: that afflictions are themselves bodhi, and that birth and death are themselves nirvana.
If they still refuse to believe, for their sake the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao) is expounded: that one attains bodhi by severing afflictions, and severs birth... [and death].
Even though they have died and realized nirvana, they are still unwilling to believe and accept it. II. Specifically clarifying the lack of spiritual capacity:
They are neither startled nor afraid; they have no intention at all to escape, nor do they know what constitutes the fire or what constitutes the house.

What constitutes the deficiency? In the preceding section, the two teachings were not distinguished; therefore, it was called a "general heading. In this section, the two teachings are explained separately; therefore, it is termed a "specific clarification.

First, it clarifies the lack of capacity for the Separate Teaching; furthermore, below that, it clarifies the lack of capacity for the Perfect Teaching. Regarding the first point, it says: "not startled and not afraid."
Although the Tathāgata preaches the four truths in their infinite variety for such a person, they are not startled by the fact that afflictions differ as much as the sands of the Ganges;
nor are they terrified by the fact that the realms of birth and death differ in ten ways.
Since they are neither startled by the origin of suffering nor terrified by suffering itself, they [remain steadfast] before the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
The Dharma is the unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, it is not realized through deliberate contemplation; rather, it is the extinction of the path through non-mindfulness (*acitta*).
Thus, there is ultimately no mind that emerges [from it]. Next, to clarify the lack of capacity for the Perfect [Teaching], it says: "Not knowing what is fire, etc.
This refers to those for whom the Tathāgata preaches the Four Noble Truths of Non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*); they lack the capacity and thus do not understand.
Furthermore, not knowing what constitutes fire is precisely not knowing that there is no [independent] arising of the Truth of Accumulation (*samudaya-satya*).
This is because the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) clarifies that afflictions (*kleśa*) are themselves bodhi. If one knows the afflictions, one thereby knows bodhi.
Now, to say one does not know what constitutes fire is to not know that what is bodhi is itself the affliction. Not knowing what constitutes the house—

This is precisely not knowing the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) as being without action (*anabhisaṃskāra*). That which is abandoned—the "house" that is being burned—is itself birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
Generally, the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) clarifies that birth-and-death is itself nirvana. If one knows birth-and-death, one then knows nirvana.
Now, when it says "not knowing what constitutes the house," it means not knowing that what is nirvana is itself birth-and-death. Not knowing this—what could it mean?
This is a loss; it is precisely the failure to know the two truths of the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*) and cessation (*nirodha*).

In the Perfect Teaching (*yāna*), if one knows birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), one immediately attains the principle of cessation that is *nirvāṇa*; if one knows afflictions (*kleśa*), one immediately attains the path-dharma of *bodhi*.
Now, since they do not know suffering (*duḥkha*), they have already lost cessation; since they do not know the origin (*samudaya*), they have already lost the path. And yet, they...
To fully comprehend suffering and its origin is precisely to lose the Path and Cessation; therefore, it is said that not knowing them constitutes a loss.

Although the two preceding explanations—the Separate and the Perfect—may fail to inspire faith or understanding in those of dull faculties, they nonetheless fulfill the original intent of this teaching.
△ Third, the summary of the lack of capacity:
they merely run about to the east and west, looking only at their father.
Regarding the phrase "east and west" and so forth: since they are unwilling to believe in or accept the Separate and Complete Teachings, they lack the great capacity; as they lack it...

They possess great capacity, yet they take pleasure only in the Lesser Dharma. Although they delight in the Lesser Dharma, they still remain attached to birth and death—just as one might run eastward for play and end up in the west.
Being thus attached to birth and death while still delighting in the Lesser [Dharma] is like running westward for play and ending up in the east.
To merely look upon their father is to be like one who is deaf or mute; they neither see nor hear, but only...
They merely behold the body of one six feet tall clad in soiled robes; they merely look upon their father and yet do not recognize him as their father.
It is like a child of the world who, when playing, feels aversion upon recognizing his father has come—how could he simply look?
It is precisely because they do not recognize him as their father that they merely look upon him. Thus it is.

For example, when the Tathāgata manifests a body of a thousand *zhàng* in the form of Śākyamuni and preaches the teachings of the *Sūtra* of Perfect Fulfillment, those of the Two Vehicles do not recognize him as the Buddha;
they think he might be a king or someone like a king, and thus merely look upon him.
Yet, does one cease to be called a father simply because of such lack of recognition? Therefore, it is still said that "he looked upon his father. △ Second, the Use of the Chariots.
Third: First, employing skillful means.
At that time, the elder had this thought: "This house has already been consumed by a great fire; I and my sons [are within it]."
"If they do not emerge at the proper time, they will surely be consumed by fire. I must now employ skillful means to enable these sons to escape this calamity.
Having formed this thought, the Tathāgata first deliberated twice over [the teachings], and then spoke of the Distinct and Perfect [Vehicles]. Yet, regarding the Three Vehicles...

The sons of the lineage have no affinity for the Great [Vehicle] and take pleasure only in the Lesser Dharma; they are greedily attached to birth and death. How could the Tathāgata ever be willing to abandon them without transforming them?
Therefore, he wishes to receive them again through the Lesser [Vehicle]. He further engages in another round of reflection, which is what is meant by "he then forms this thought.
The phrase "this house" below refers precisely to the act of forming this thought; the preceding statement, "I am able regarding that which is... [refers to his capacity].
Having burned through it, they emerge safely from the gate. What, then, is meant by the statement, "If I and my children do not emerge in time," and so forth?
There is no other meaning here than this: the Tathāgata has long since attained the ultimate, unsurpassed *nirvāṇa* and emerged from birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
It is solely because the children of the three vehicles who were transformed by him in the past are still submerged in birth-and-death.
They die and are unable to emerge. It is because the Tathāgata is permeated by great compassion that he returns to manifest entry into birth and death, enabling them as well to attain nirvāṇa.
What was previously called "emerging" was spoken with reference to the Tathāgata’s own state;
what is here called "not emerging" is spoken from the perspective of those in the assembly of converts. Thus, the children of the three vehicles remain within birth and death.
It goes without saying that [ordinary beings] are burned by fire. Why, then, does the Tathāgata also say he is burned by fire?
It is because the sons of the Three Vehicles are burned by the fire of afflictions (*kleśa*), whereas if it concerns the Tathāgata, he is burned by the fire of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
As the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* says: "Because sentient beings are ill, the bodhisattva is also ill. Sentient beings...
The illness of ordinary beings arises from craving; the illness of Bodhisattvas arises from great compassion—this is precisely what is meant.
This is said with respect to transforming others, wherein they are said to be "equally burned" and "equally ill. Yet, the Great Sage ultimately is neither burned nor ill.
"To employ skillful means" refers to intending to attract them with something small. II. The Provisioning of the Three Chariots.
Part One: Knowing What They Previously Desired.
The father knew that each of his sons had previously desired various rare treasures and extraordinary objects, and that their hearts were set upon them. Their desires were certainly...
"Delighting in attachment.
Regarding the phrase "the father knows," it means that the Tathāgata knows through his inconceivable, skillful wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) for transforming others.
"Each has their own preferences" means that there are three distinct vehicles (*yāna*), hence the word "each. Although they differ, they are the same in being inferior.

They merely ride upon the *parinirvāṇa* of partial emptiness. As for what is called "the former mind," it refers to the period after they had received the Great [Vehicle] under twenty trillion Buddhas, whereupon they suddenly forgot it midway and took up the Small [Vehicle]. This inclination toward the Small has persisted for a long time;
it is not merely a matter of a single morning or evening. Therefore, it is said that this was what their former minds delighted in. It was like a rare and wondrous treasure.

"Things" refers to the two truths of the Path and Cessation in the Hinayana; by relying upon them, one may emerge from the cycle of birth and death within the triple world, and thus they are called "rare treasures and marvelous wonders.
As for the "Path," there are distinctions such as precept, concentration, and wisdom;

as for "Cessation," there are emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—hence the term "various. Those whose emotions inevitably delight in and cling to these will surely know that they are retreating from the Great [Vehicle].
They take pleasure in what is minor. △ Second, the actual presentation of the three carts, in three parts. First, the exhortation to practice:
He addressed them, saying, "The objects of your play and delight are rare and difficult to obtain. If you do not take them now, you will surely feel grief and regret later."
Regarding "playthings and delights" (*krīḍā-ramaṇīya*): the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) is a plaything to be cultivated, and Nirvāṇa is a plaything to be realized.
Because these do not exist within the three realms or the six destinies, they are rare; because they are lacking among the ninety-five types of heterodox paths, they are difficult to obtain.
"If you do not take them up now, you will surely grieve and regret later" means that if you do not cultivate the Path, then [you will suffer] affliction...
By what means are the afflictions (*kleśa*) destroyed? If one does not realize cessation (*nirodha*), by what means can birth and death (*saṃsāra*) be severed?
Therefore, if you do not now cultivate and realize [the Truths], you will inevitably be oppressed by afflictions and birth and death in the future, giving rise to various sorrows and regrets.
Using objects of pleasure and the like as metaphors, he exhorts [him] to turn toward the Four Noble Truths, saying: "This is suffering; you should know it."
"Up to this point, this is cessation; you should realize it for yourselves. △ Second, showing the signs:
"These various kinds of goat-carts, deer-carts, and ox-carts are now outside the gate; you may play with them."
Regarding the phrase "such as these," it was not previously specifically identified.

As for what constitutes "objects of play and enjoyment," the current mention of "various kinds" points directly to the differences between the three vehicles (*triyāna*), using them as a metaphor for "the various.

Furthermore, because the practitioners of the three vehicles each have different modes of cultivation and realization, they are also termed "various. Those currently outside the gate are the three [vehicles].
The vehicles are merely taught as skillful means; they exist outside of the single reality of true wisdom (*ekasatya-jñāna*).
As for those who can "play" [with them], although these means lie outside of true wisdom, they are nevertheless bestowed as skillful expedients.

If one can rely upon them, afflictions may be destroyed, birth and death may be severed, and the path of precepts, concentration, and wisdom may be cultivated—the gates of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
Cessation can be realized. Now, pointing to the three carts as a metaphor, it is shown that the Four Noble Truths are turned: "This is suffering;
its characteristic is to be known," and so on, up to "This is cessation; its characteristic is to be realized. △ Third, the realization.
"You all should quickly come out from this burning house. Whatever you desire, I shall give it all to you.
Regarding the phrase "whatever you desire" and so forth: if you desire the Śrāvaka-yāna, I shall immediately give you the Śrāvaka-yāna;
even if you desire the Bodhisattva-yāna, I shall immediately give you the Bodhisattva-yāna. That is to say, I now act as your guarantor.
"Entrust this matter; it shall never be in vain. This metaphor illustrates the turning of the Four Noble Truths, stating: "This is suffering. I have already known it;
I need not know it again. You, too, should know it. And so on, up to: "This is cessation. I have already realized it; I need not realize it again. You, too, should realize it.
When preaching, one must deeply grasp this essential meaning for it to truly accord with the intent of the text.
△ 3. The Sons Accept and Practice.
At that time, the sons, having heard what their father had said regarding the precious playthings that accorded with their wishes, each felt their hearts bristling with vigor.
Pushing and shoving one another, they vied with each other to run forth,
contending to escape the burning house. At that time, these were the sons of the lineage of the three vehicles who, having heard the Buddha preach the Nirvana of the Lesser Vehicle—

characterized by emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness— and the factors of enlightenment consisting of morality, concentration, and wisdom, were thus enticed and turned back by means of these minor teachings.
It captures the capacity for the great by means of the small; therefore, it is said to be "suited to what each desires.
As for "the minds being equal," this is because they are suited to their respective desires: thus, those of the three vehicles all rely upon it for their cultivation.

Those of the Śrāvaka vehicle resolve their minds by taking suffering as the initial gateway, while those of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle resolve their minds by taking origination as the initial gateway. [Those of] the Bodhisattva...
As for the vehicles, they take the Way as their initial gateway and give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment; each is courageous and sharp, which is why they are called "brave and keen.

Once the aspiration has been generated, one then cultivates contemplation. Although there are differences among the three vehicles, they are all exclusively the analytical negation of emptiness (*vibhajya-śūnyatā*).

Therefore, it is said that they "mutually push and displace. "Pushing" refers to investigating and seeking the principle of the truths; "displacing" refers to suppressing and subduing the afflictions of views and thought.
This refers to those of the Three Vehicles who, together employing the contemplation of analysis-emptiness, analyze and further analyze in order to clarify the principle.

It means "to sever delusions. *Tui* (推) is pronounced like *cuī* (摧), meaning "to crush" or "to push back. Those who "vie with one another in rushing forward" are the practitioners of the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*).

Among them, there are those who proceed toward the cause while already bearing the fruit; those who proceed toward the cause while awaiting the fruit; and those who proceed toward the cause while suppressing their delusions.
Therefore, it is said they "vie with one another in rushing forward. They vie because the causes pursued by the Three Vehicles differ, and furthermore, their practices...
"Commonly" means together. Regarding those who "vie to exit the burning house": the Śrāvakas sever the *samyaktva-nyāma* (the fundamental afflictions) and thus exit the burning house;

the Pratyekabuddhas penetrate the *vāsanā* (habitual tendencies) and thus exit the burning house; the Bodhisattvas, by means of the thirty-four moments of mind, suddenly sever the views, the thoughts, and the habitual tendencies, and thus exit the burning house.
They are said to "vie" because the latter surpasses the former. △ Third, the Equal Bestowal of Great [Blessings].
The chariots are like the four [vehicles]. First, the elder rejoices.
At that time, the elder sees that his sons have all emerged safely; they are sitting in the open air at the crossroads, free from all obstructions.
His mind is serene, and he leaps for joy with great exultation.

"Those who emerge in safety" refers to the followers of the Three Vehicles. Having emerged from the burning house of the triple world, they are no longer scorched or harmed by the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāva-kleśa*) or by birth-and-death with fixed limits (*paricchinna-jarāmaraṇa*), and thus attain peace and security.

"All [of them] within the [Four Truths]" means that the followers of the Three Vehicles likewise resolve their minds and initiate practice within the Four Noble Truths; having already shattered the afflictions of views and thoughts, they...
Enshrouded by afflictions (*kleśa*), they consequently settled into a one-sided emptiness and ceased to advance further.
Since the principle of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is now clearly visible, it is said that there are no longer any obstructions. As for their minds being serene:
the Tathāgata beholds his children within the triple world, delighting in play and sport while being consumed by fire; at this, his inner heart is filled with great [compassion].

[The Buddha was] struck with alarm; how could he have been at ease? Now, seeing the sons of the three vehicles safely emerge from the burning house of the triple world and not being scorched by the fire, the Tathāgata’s mind has consequently become at ease. As for his joy, it is not that he rejoices in their attainment of the Lesser Vehicle.
The Tathāgata’s intention is this: since they were able to believe, accept, practice, and realize even the Lesser Transformation, [he is joyful].
If one were to transform them through the Great [Vehicle], they would likewise certainly be able to believe, accept, practice, and realize it.

Since they have already attained the Small [Vehicle], one leads them from the Small back to the Great. Furthermore, that which was attained as the Small, once revealed and clarified, is entirely the Great;
therefore, they are filled with joy and exultation. △ Second, the sons request the vehicles.
At that time, the sons each said to their father, "Father, we pray that you grant us at once those playthings you previously promised:
the goat-carts, the deer-carts, and the ox-carts."
If we consider the literal wording—"I pray you grant me the goat-drawn carriage, the deer-drawn carriage, and the ox-drawn carriage"—this is a request for the small carriages of the Three Vehicles.
Because the children of the Three Vehicles heard what was promised by the Tathāgata and their wishes were thus satisfied, they vied with one another to exit the house.
Since the promise was made but the gifts were not yet delivered, they requested the very Three Vehicles that had been previously promised; this precisely corresponds to [the situation].

This was the period of the two types of ghee. When the Tathāgata bestowed the teachings of the Three Vehicles at the assembly of the Āgamas, as soon as he reached the Vaipulya [period], he immediately employed bodhisattvas from other directions to censure and refute [the adherents of the Lesser Vehicle]. Yet those of the Three Vehicles still remained in their original positions, dwelling merely in thatched huts;
this was the Vaipulya’s "seeking of the Small. At the assembly of the Prajñāpāramitā, when the Tathāgata commanded the turning of the teaching, [he did so].

"Still clinging to the Truth [of the Śrāvaka vehicle] and not yet having forgotten it, one has no intention of seeking or attaining [the Mahāyāna]. This refers to 'seeking the Small' within the Prajñāpāramitā period.

Tiantai says that 'seeking the Great' is a matter of adopting the meaning [of the teaching]. Within the Vaipulya (fangděng) period, upon hearing the disparagement of the Small and the praise of the Great, one feels shame for the Small and admires the Great.
If one speaks of admiring the Great, this is 'seeking the Great' during the Vaipulya period. During the Prajñā period, although there is no such intention..."

One should aspire to take up the great task of the Mahāyāna. Having already attained understanding, if one says they have attained understanding, this is precisely seeking the Great [Vehicle] at the time of Prajñā.
Question: The Tathāgata permitted the three carts as a metaphor for the Hīnayāna;

since one has already departed from the triple world and obtained the three carts, the small should not be sought again. One merely knows that the three carts are small, and having already obtained them, one still...

[The interlocutor] asks: "I do not understand what is meant by 'large. Why do you seek the large? [The Master] replies: "Although the three vehicles are metaphors for the Hīnayāna, they were originally intended as skillful means (*upāya*) for the Mahāyāna.
Thus, although one may transcend the triple world and realize *nirvāṇa*, these [teachings] have already been implicitly rebuked within the Āgamas."
Thus, one knows that what was previously obtained was small and not yet definitive; therefore, there is further the principle of "seeking the Great.
Just as the two types of milk-cream (sū) were already refuted and subsequently superseded by the turning of the teaching, they naturally ought to seek the Great.
△ Third, the Elder’s Equal Bestowal, in three parts. First, the actual equal bestowal.
Śāriputra, at that time the elder gave each of his sons an identical great carriage.
As for giving each a great carriage, it means that although the sons requested the three vehicles, when the Tathāgata bestowed them,
he granted the One Buddha Vehicle to those who had requested the vehicle of the śrāvaka, and likewise to those who had requested the vehicle of the bodhisattva.
He likewise grants them the single Buddha-vehicle; hence it is said that he bestows upon each of his sons an equal great carriage.
Indeed, prior to its revelation, the three vehicles were truly three vehicles and the one vehicle was truly the one vehicle, such that the two were not the same.
In this sublime assembly of the Lotus Sūtra, once the teaching is revealed and manifested, the three vehicles are shown to be but a single vehicle.
Apart from this single vehicle, no three vehicles can be found; how, then, could there be vehicles for śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas?
Thus, although the sons sought three [vehicles], the Tathāgata bestowed upon them equally the one. △ Second, showing the carts.

As for the essence (*tattva*): since there is already an essential nature (*dharmatā*), one must necessarily rely upon that principle to give rise to practice. Once practice is perfected, it can give rise to various functions.
The text is divided into three parts; first, the Dharmakāya is shown as the essence.
The carriage was high and wide, adorned with various jewels. It was surrounded by railings, with bells suspended on all four sides.
Furthermore, above it, canopies were spread and set up, likewise embellished with rare and diverse precious gems. Precious cords were interlaced as necklaces, from which hung many flower tassels.
Luxurious mats were layered upon one another, and crimson pillows were placed therein.
What is called the "chariot" is precisely the One Buddha Vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*). As for its being "high and broad," it is because the One Buddha Vehicle has no separate essence;
it takes the entirety of the ten dharma realms as its essence. Above, it reaches the limit of all Buddhas and is thus high.
Below, it encompasses the sentient beings of the nine realms and is thus vast; yet, height itself is vastness, and vastness itself is height.
That which is both height and vastness is precisely what all Buddhas realize—there is no realization apart from this.

It is the complete realization of the very equipment of the sentient beings within the nine realms; therefore, that which is the height of the Buddhas is simultaneously the vastness of sentient beings. Thus...
That which is vast and high is precisely what is possessed by sentient beings of the nine realms; there is nothing else that possesses it.
It is entirely the realization possessed by all Buddhas. Therefore, the vastness of sentient beings is itself the height of the Buddhas. Thus it is said:

the environment and inhabitants of Avīci hell are entirely situated within the self-mind of the Ultimate Sage, while the body and land of Vairocana do not exceed the state of the lowest ordinary being.
This single thought-moment is such that the ordinary and the sage are one and the same, and defilement and purity are of a single principle.
It takes the nine realms entirely as the Buddha-realm, and it takes the three vehicles as the One Vehicle. How lofty and vast is its essence!
Thus we know that the greatness of the Great Vehicle consists precisely in this loftiness and vastness. As for "various jewels" and so forth, these refer to the adornments of the vehicle's body.
This is a metaphor for the fact that within the body of the Dharma-body (dharmakāya), all merits are fully present. As for what is called the "Dharma-body":
"Dharma" refers to the three thousand realms; "body" (kāya) has the meaning of accumulation. Within a single moment of thought, the three thousand Buddhas are fully contained.
Yet the three thousand Buddhas are fully manifested within a single thought-moment; this is what is called the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

If one were to say that the essence of the pure Dharma-body does not possess all virtues, this would be merely one path of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekayāna*), referring to the Dharma-body of pure True Suchness (*tathatā*) as it is contemplated therein.
As for the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-yāna*), however, when it is pure, all is pure. How could there be [any lack]?

Because not even a single dharma is lacking, the Dharma-body is the essence of the One Buddha Vehicle. Its essence is fully endowed with all manner of merits, just as a great vehicle is adorned with various ornaments.

What is called "adorned with myriad jewels" refers precisely to the essence of the One Buddha Vehicle, which is replete with immeasurable treasures of meritorious dharmas; it is by means of these meritorious dharmas that [it is adorned].
It is adorned with the essence of the Single Buddha Vehicle (ekabuddhayāna), like a great chariot decorated with various jewels.
Within the essence of the Single Buddha Vehicle, it is fully endowed with immeasurable *dhāraṇī* gates; no evil is left unwarded off and no goodness is left unsustained, like a protective railing.
The essence of the Single Buddha Vehicle is fully endowed with the four kinds of unhindered eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*), like hanging bells.
The essence of the One Buddha Vehicle is fully endowed with unconditional great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*), which universally covers the entire Dharma-realm.
This great compassion is further adorned by immeasurable wholesome dharmas, just as a carriage has a canopy decorated with jewels.
Within this One Buddha Vehicle, the four great vows are fully present, like ropes woven into a network. It is also fully endowed with immeasurable... [unconditioned]... [dharmas].

Contemplating the causal practices is like a floral garland. Being fully endowed with hundreds of thousands of samādhis, as well as the meditations of contemplation, refinement, and cultivation, is like the layering of soft mats.
Being fully endowed with all practices of the dharma-realm is like placing a pillow.
△ Second, showing that Prajñā is the primary tenet.

He was drawn by white oxen, their coats pure and clean, their forms beautiful and well-proportioned, possessing great strength and vigor; their gait was level and steady, and they moved as swiftly as the wind.

The supreme *dharmakāya* is the essence of principle (*tattva*). If one relies upon this essence to give rise to practice, then it must be guided by the wondrous wisdom of *prajñā*, just as a great carriage is yoked to white oxen.
For white is the source of all colors, and the ox possesses the power of transport; likewise, *prajñā* is the source of all virtues and possesses the power of contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā*).
It is merit. Prajñāpāramitā can illuminate all things, yet there is no virtue it does not fulfill, like the skin of a white ox being full.
Prajñāpāramitā can shield against all things, yet there is no delusion it does not shatter, like the color of a white ox being pure.
Prajñāpāramitā can realize that which is difficult for all to realize, like the physical form of a white ox being beautiful. Thus, Prajñāpāramitā...
One practices all that is difficult to practice, like a white ox possessed of great strength and vigor.
In *prajñā*, both *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight) are equally clear and without deficiency; that is, one uses *śamatha* to arrest distraction and *vipaśyanā* to observe dullness.
Dullness and agitation are both completely exhausted; this is not comparable to that which possesses only a single wheel or a solitary wing.
It is just like the gait of a white ox, which is level and upright without any deviation, enabling one to flow in spontaneously and swiftly reach the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
Therefore, it is said that "its swiftness is like the wind. △ Third, showing liberation as its function.
Furthermore, it has many attendants who guard and serve it.
By practicing in accordance with its essence, one can give rise to the various functions of liberation. It is fully endowed with all the *pāramitās* of skillful means;
adapting to capacities and transforming beings, whether turning left or right, there is nothing it cannot do. It is like a great chariot.
...of many attendants to serve at his side. Yet, a single great vehicle manifests the three virtues perfectly;

it is inconceivable to such an extent. △ Third, the explanation of the reason why: that is to say, the sons each requested three [vehicles], yet for what reason did the Tathāgata give each of them only one?
Therefore, he explains and clarifies the reason for requesting three and being given one. The text is divided into two parts. First:
The formal explanation: Why is this so? This great elder possesses immeasurable wealth; his various treasuries are all overflowing.
He then thinks: "My wealth and goods are infinite; it would not be right to give inferior small carts to my children."
"These young children here are all my sons; my love for them is without partiality. I possess such great chariots made of the seven treasures, in number beyond measure.
I ought to treat them with an impartial mind and give each one of them; it is not fitting to make any distinction between them."
Why is this? This [passage] serves as the introductory heading; the section beginning with "This great elder" is the formal explanation.
First, it clarifies that the Tathāgata is fully endowed with the wealth of immeasurable merit and dharmas; therefore, what he bestows should not be inferior small carts.
Now, from the words "In this world," it clarifies that those of the three vehicles are all sons with whom [the Buddha] formed karmic connections in the past; thus, [he gives them...]

It is appropriate to distinguish them. Regarding the initial mention of "various treasuries" (*kośa*): the Tathāgata possesses the three aspects of wisdom, principle, and practice, all of which encompass the *dharmadhātu*;
hence they are called "treasuries. Since they all rely upon the true reality of the three thousand worlds (*trisahasra-lokadhātu*), they are called "various.
This refers to the wondrous principle of the inconceivable true reality of the three thousand worlds realized by the Tathāgata; its essence accords with the *dharmadhātu*, and it is without...

That which is not excluded is precisely the principle realized; this is the *garbha*. The Tathāgata’s wondrous wisdom of inconceivable three-thousandfold reality, which is able to accord with that principle, likewise has its essence coextensive with the *dharmadhātu* and contains nothing that is not included;
this is the wisdom that is able to accord, and it is the *garbha*. Furthermore, the Tathāgata’s inconceivable wondrous practice of three-thousandfold reality, which he brings forth...
Furthermore, it is the entire dharma-realm itself, containing nothing that is not included; thus, the practices that arise from it are the "treasuries.
Since these various treasuries are realized within oneself, they are said to be "full. By means of this self-realization, one transforms others, causing them also to realize what one has realized;
therefore, they are said to "overflow. Next, regarding the term "infant": although the teaching was great in the past, [it is now like an infant].
Now, having completely forgotten [the former], their great capacity is entirely subtle; hence they are called "children. As for saying they are all "sons":
although they currently take the small [vehicle], they previously received the great; thus, their natures are interconnected, and the role of father exists toward them from the Tathāgata.
Therefore, they are sons. Since they are all sons, how could his love be partial? Hence it is said that his love is without partiality. [The seventh...]
Regarding the "great chariot of the seven treasures": all vehicles of the seven stages of skillful means, once revealed by a single teaching, are in their entirety the One Buddha Vehicle;
therefore, it is called the great chariot of the seven treasures. As for the phrase "one should have an impartial mind":

if this child were my son while that one were not my son, there would be a distinction, and such a thing would be appropriate. But now that they are all equally my sons, how could [there be any partiality]?
There are two minds in between: does one give this person little while giving that person much?
Therefore it is said, "One should maintain an impartial mind" (and so forth). △ Second, the interpretive explanation.
Why is this? Because with these goods of mine, I could provide for an entire kingdom and yet still not run short; how much less so for my sons?
For what reason would I give them inferior vehicles, or have a mind that makes distinctions? Therefore, it is explained as "with these goods of mine" and so forth.
The elder refers to his own wealth and property, saying that he could provide for all the people of the kingdom.
Even so, it is not exhausted; this wealth is truly immense. How could it be given to those who are inferior?
Yet even the people of the entire nation are not impoverished, let alone a single family. Since they belong to the same family, they are all my children;
how could there be any distinction in what is given? To accord with this principle, the Tathāgata says: "I bestow the wealth of the Dharma of my merits universally upon all within the Dharma-realm."
"It is still not lacking," he said, meaning that this wealth of Dharma is exceedingly abundant. How could it be given to those of the Lesser Vehicle?
And how much more so when they are all sons with whom [the Buddha] previously formed karmic connections; how could there be any distinction among them?
Therefore, although the elder initially promised three carts, in the end he bestowed great carts equally upon all. Likewise, although the Tathāgata initially taught the Three [Vehicles],...
Vehicles. In the end, they all converge upon and return to the Single Buddha Vehicle. △ Fourth, the sons’ joy:
At that time, the sons each mounted a great vehicle; they attained what they had never experienced before, which was not what they had originally expected.

Regarding the statement "not what was originally hoped for": that which was originally hoped for in the past was merely to destroy the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāva-kleśa*), to emerge from the realm of birth and death with fixed limits (*paricchinna-bhava*), and to realize the partial truth (*ekadeśa-satya*).

Now, one is further able to destroy ignorance (*avidyā*), emerge from the realm of transformation (*nirmāṇa-bhava*), and realize the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*). Therefore, this is not what was originally hoped for. Thus, that which did not previously exist now exists.
That which was previously unattained has now been attained; therefore it is said, "I have attained what I never before had" (and so forth).

△ Third, the parable of the four elders being non-deceptive. First, the Tathāgata questions him:
"Śāriputra, what do you think? Would this elder be guilty of any falsehood in giving precious great chariots to his sons?"

Regarding the statement that there might be falsehood: it refers to the Tathāgata’s question, "Suppose a householder initially promised three carts, yet when he bestowed them, he gave only one great cart; would what was previously said regarding the three be false?"
For the Tathāgata knows for himself that there is no falsehood; once [the truth] is revealed through this single teaching, the three vehicles are immediately the one vehicle.
By now granting the one vehicle, he has effectively already granted the three vehicles.

However, as for his questioning Śāriputra, since the Tathāgata already knew that [Śāriputra] had attained realization and understanding, he also knew it was not false. Thus, he desired him to provide a response so as to enlighten the multitude.
...a class of beings. △ Second, Śāriputra’s response in acceptance, in two parts. First, the response that saving them from calamity was not in vain.
Śāriputra said: "No, World-Honored One. This elder merely enabled his sons to escape the disaster of fire and preserve their lives;
it was not a false or empty act. Why is this? If they have preserved their bodies and lives, they have already attained what is most essential—namely, their cherished playthings."
...the requisite provisions. How much more so, then, would he employ skillful means to rescue them from that burning house?

To say "no" means that although Śāriputra already understood that the three vehicles are identical to the one vehicle, and thus granted that both the three and the one are not false—since the three are likewise not in vain—he nevertheless replied, "No, World-Honored One. The following section, beginning with "This elder," provides the formal explanation.
It is not in vain. "To escape calamity" means to escape the calamities of the fruits of suffering arising from the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms.
"To preserve one's body and life" means to preserve the life of wisdom—the partial emptiness—of the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañca-dharmakāya*).

"Having already obtained articles of enjoyment" means that if one’s body and life are preserved, then the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) can be cultivated and *nirvāṇa* can be realized; therefore, it is said that one has obtained the implements of enjoyment.
Regarding "expedient means" (*upāya*) and so forth: this refers to the three vehicles (*triyāna*) permitted by the Tathāgata, which are originally established as provisional devices (*prajñapti*).
This is solely because he desires that the children of the three vehicles emerge from the triple world (*traidhātuka*) and escape the perils of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Therefore it is said:
"How much more so... (and so forth). △ Second, the answer that [the teaching] is not in vain when compared with the Great [Vehicle].
World-Honored One, even if that elder had not given so much as the smallest single chariot, he would still not have been guilty of falsehood. Why is this?
Because that elder had previously formed this intention: "By means of skillful expedients, I shall cause my sons to escape. For this reason...
It is not false; how much less so for the elder, who knows his own wealth to be immeasurable and wishes to benefit his sons by giving them all great chariots equally?
Among the three vehicles, the Śrāvaka vehicle is the smallest. To "form such an intention" refers to the aforementioned [passage].
In the *Upāyakauśalya-parivarta*, it says: "If I and my sons do not emerge at once, we shall surely be consumed by fire.
I must now employ an expedient means (*upāya*) to enable my sons to escape this calamity. Thus, the three vehicles were originally established as expedient means;
therefore, although they are not [ultimately] granted, they are not in vain. As for the phrase "how much more so," it means that...
Even bestowing [the gift] to the Lesser Vehicle is not in vain; how much more so when bestowing it upon the Great? If one attains the Great, the three vehicles are entirely the One Vehicle.
How could it then be in vain? Since both avoiding calamity and bestowing upon the Great are not in vain, the previous answer stated:
"No, World-Honored One" (and so forth). △ Third, the Tathāgata’s praise and exhortation.
The Buddha told Śāriputra: "Excellent, excellent! It is just as you have said. Śāriputra, the Tathāgata is also like this.

Regarding what is called 'the pair of excellences,' one is the non-false response that praises being delivered from calamity, and the other is the non-false response that praises being granted greatness."

"Furthermore, it is thus" (*fù rú shì zhě*) is a phrase used to introduce what follows based on what precedes. **2. Correlating with the Dharma.** Because the Dharma is difficult to understand, it is elucidated through parables.
By observing the Tathāgata’s words regarding the three carts and the single cart, one immediately understands the essential meaning of the three vehicles and the one vehicle.
The text is divided into two parts; first, the correlation of the general parable.
Thus, he is the father of all the world. Regarding all fears, decays, afflictions, anxieties, and the obscuration of ignorance, he has exhausted them forever without remainder;
he has fully accomplished immeasurable knowledge and vision, the powers, the fearlessnesses, and possesses great supernormal power.
Possessing the power of wisdom and fully endowed with skillful means, the perfection of wisdom, great kindness, and great compassion,
he is ever free from weariness and constantly seeks virtuous deeds to benefit all beings. He enters the decaying and dilapidated fire-houses of the triple world to deliver sentient beings from birth,
old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, and distress, and from the darkness of ignorance and the fires of the three poisons, teaching and transforming them.
One attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Regarding the phrase "all worlds," this includes the aforementioned realms of nations, cities, and villages; that is, the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*), the world of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha-loka*), and the world of lands (*bhājana-loka*).
If explained according to the literal text, these refer to the world of true retribution (*vipāka*) and the world with remainder (*sa-avaśeṣa-loka*).
"Interval" (*kṣaṇa*) means dwelling together within the world. "Father" refers to the Elder Upāli;

it signifies that within these three realms, the Tathāgata is the father of both those who are sons of the spiritual awakening of the true cause and those who are sons of the connection through the conditions of fulfillment—all of whom take the Tathāgata as their father.
"All fears," etc., refers back to the general analogy in the preceding text: "his years have declined and advanced," referring to the suffering of birth and death.
The fruit [of suffering] is most terrifying, most distressing, and most cause for anxiety. Because it consists of various divisions and transformations, it is called "all" (*sarva*).
Regarding "the obscuration of the darkness of ignorance": there are two kinds of ignorance, those pertaining to within the realms and those pertaining to beyond the realms;

these are the most profound obscurations, capable of veiling both the principle of the partial truth (*ekadeśa-satya*) and the true reality of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*). As for the Tathāgata, he is [free from these two].
Death is forever extinguished. The five abodes are completely exhausted; therefore, it is said that they are "forever exhausted without remainder. This clarifies the virtue of the Tathāgata.
Regarding "attainment," this corresponds to the aforementioned "immeasurable wealth" and "possessing many fields and houses.

"Immeasurable knowledge and vision" means knowing with the three types of wisdom within a single moment of mind, which constitutes immeasurable knowledge; seeing with the five eyes within a single eye, which constitutes [immeasurable vision].

It is immeasurable in its knowledge and vision. Furthermore, the Tathāgata, by means of the three types of wisdom and the five eyes, contemplates and illuminates all phenomena within the dharma-realm in their entirety;
since every phenomenon existing within the dharma-realm is fully encompassed within the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, it is called "immeasurable knowledge and vision.
This is real wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*). His powers and fearlessnesses are expedient wisdom (*upāyajñāna*). Thus, the Tathāgata possesses both the expedient and the real.

Because of these two kinds of wisdom, it is said that [all things] are fully accomplished. "Possessing great supernatural powers" and so forth corresponds to the aforementioned [phrase], "together with his attendants.
"Great kindness and great compassion" and so forth corresponds to the aforementioned, "his household is vast.

Regarding the statement "always without weariness," it means that the Tathāgata possesses unconditional great compassion (*nirālambana-mahāmaitrī*), and in every thought-moment, at every time, and in every place, desires to bestow [benefit] upon all.
Regarding the happiness of sentient beings, he possesses unconditional great compassion (*nirālambana-mahākaruṇā*).

Moment by moment, at all times and in all places, he desires to uproot the suffering of sentient beings; this mind of uprooting never ceases for even an instant. Therefore, it is said that he is always free from weariness.

Regarding those who constantly seek virtuous matters: since the Tathāgata is endowed with great compassion and desires to transform sentient beings, if they are to gain benefit through formal instruction, he emits various kinds of light and manifests various kinds of forms to cause them to gain that benefit.
If they are to gain benefit through vocal instruction, he speaks various kinds of words and proclaims various kinds of phrases to cause them to gain it.
Benefit. This refers to both form and sound; although they differ in various ways, all are termed "wholesome deeds.
They benefit all beings, encompassing the aforementioned multitude of people, up to five hundred.

As for the phrase "the burning house of the three realms," this employs both the dharma and the metaphor simultaneously. The "three realms" is the dharma, while the "burning house" is the metaphor. This corresponds to the aforementioned thirty [verses].

My son. Birth, old age, sickness, death, and so forth—when these suddenly ignite like fire, birth, old age, and the rest clarify the fire of the fruit of suffering (*duḥkha-phala*), while ignorance (*moha*) and the rest clarify the fire of the cause of origination (*samudaya-hetu*). As for the "three poisons," they are like worldly poisons;
if a person consumes them, they will inevitably ruin the body and cost one's life. Greed, anger, and ignorance are likewise. Sentient beings...
If one clings to them, one will lose the Dharma-body and forfeit the life of wisdom; therefore, they are called "poisons.

To teach and transform others so that they may attain Bodhi is, in essence, the same as the aforementioned single gate. It means that although the Tathāgata delivers sentient beings from old age and death, [the nature of the teaching remains unchanged].
The original intention was fundamentally to realize unsurpassed bodhi. △ Second, the synthesis of the individual parables, which has four parts:

first, the synthesis of the parable of the elder’s act of rescue; second, the synthesis of the parable of discarding the stools and employing the carts; third, the synthesis of the parable of bestowing the great carts equally.
The fourth section, "The Householder’s Non-False Simile," consists of two parts. The first part corresponds to seeing the fire.
[The Buddha] sees that all sentient beings are being scorched and boiled by birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress;

they undergo various sufferings for the sake of the five desires and material gain; and because of their greedy attachment and pursuit, they experience manifold sufferings in the present life and [will do so] hereafter.

They undergo the sufferings of the hells, animals, and hungry ghosts. Even if they are born in the heavens or among humans, they experience the suffering of poverty and hardship, the suffering of separation from what is loved, and the suffering of encountering what is hated.

Immersed in such various sufferings as these, sentient beings frolic with joy, neither perceiving nor understanding them; they feel no alarm, no fear, and do not give rise to weariness or seek liberation.
Liberation. Within this burning house of the triple world, they run hither and thither; though they encounter great suffering, they do not regard it as a calamity.
"First seeing the characters" corresponds to the elder's observation above. "All sentient beings" corresponds to the great fire arising from the four directions.
The phrase "briefly not corresponding" refers to [the elder] being greatly terrified and so forth. Furthermore, "and all the sons" corresponds to reaching the state of non-seeking.

This expresses the underlying intent. The text enumerates the eight sufferings; six of these sufferings correspond to the text as written. Furthermore, through attachment and craving, there is the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks.
With these seven sufferings, the "suffering of the mass of the five aggregates" (*pañca-upādāna-skandha-duḥkha*) is established.

Since the suffering of the mass of the five aggregates takes these seven sufferings as its basis, it may also be said that [the former] is identical to the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks. For by seeking, one cannot avoid [these sufferings].

Because one constructs and exerts effort, it is said that one undergoes various kinds of suffering. Furthermore, by the phrase "also," [it refers to] the suffering of the five aggregates being ablaze.
The five aggregates exist because of seeking and not obtaining. Again, the phrase "furthermore, below" refers to the past; "present" refers to the present.
The "future" refers to what follows. The first three [realms] are evil; the next three are good.
Because all six realms of existence possess the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), it is said that one undergoes suffering whether born in the heavens or among humans.

To "sink within them" means to be caught in the so-called river of afflictions (*kleśa*) and the ocean of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), from which one cannot emerge at all—just as when a person throws themselves into water, they see only water and nothing else.
When one sees people—sentient beings submerged in the eight kinds of suffering—one sees only suffering. Yet they do not regard this suffering as suffering;
on the contrary, they take it to be pleasure. Thus, they delight in the cycle of birth and death within the three realms and frolic therein with joy.

As for the description of them "running hither and thither," it refers to those who cultivate the causes of precepts and goodness, thereby eliciting the fruits of human or celestial rebirth, as if following [a path].
From the east to the west, among gods and humans, one again gives rise to craving and falls into the evil realms, just as if going from the west to the east.
△ Second, combined practice for salvation.
Śāriputra, having seen this, the Buddha thought to himself: "I am the father of all sentient beings;
I ought to uproot their suffering and distress, and grant them the immeasurable and boundless joy of the Buddha’s wisdom, so that they may sport therein."
This refers to the passage beginning with "The Buddha, having seen this, joined his palms and reflected thus," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "I [shall act] for them":
just as a worldly father will surely uproot the suffering of his child and surely bestow happiness upon them, how much more so for the Tathāgata, the Father who has appeared in the world?
Therefore it is said, "I should uproot [it]," and so on. "Causing them to sport" means uprooting the afflictions (*kleśa*) and [the cycle of] birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Suffering. [It is] the bliss of bodhi and nirvāṇa. △ Second, combining the analogy of discarding the stool and using the carriage, in two parts. First, combining the discarding of the stool:
"Śāriputra, the Tathāgata further had this thought: 'If I were to rely solely on the power of my supernatural faculties and the power of my wisdom, and were to discard..."
Regarding skillful means, when he praises the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, powers, and fearlessness for the sake of all sentient beings, these beings are unable to attain liberation thereby.
Why is this? Because these sentient beings have not yet escaped birth, illness, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction;
they are being burned by the burning house of the triple world. How could they possibly understand the Buddha’s wisdom?
Furthermore, he forms this thought—this refers back to the subsequent contemplation. In the preceding section, it was stated that he practices universal salvation;
here, it means that while within the stage of the Dharma-body, he perceives sentient beings amidst the five turbidities and gives rise to great compassion.
This statement further gives rise to this reflection: that he intended to preach the *Avataṃsaka*, the Great Teaching, and thus contemplated it for twenty-one days.
The phrase "but only," etc., corresponds to the aforementioned "there is only one gate. Above, wisdom was taken as the gate; here, spiritual power (*ṛddhi*) is mentioned.
Wisdom is the agent and spiritual power is the object; they are one and the same wisdom. Furthermore, as for the Tathāgata...
Knowledge and vision are the power of true wisdom (*prajñā*). Fearlessness is the power of skillful means (*upāya*) wisdom.
Sentient beings cannot be delivered by these [powers alone]; they are conjoined yet remain narrow and limited, such that they may even fall and be consumed by fire.
That they cannot attain deliverance is precisely because their spiritual capacity (*indriya*) is small. As for the Tathāgata above—
He knows and sees that while this Dharma is great, their faculties are currently small; therefore, they cannot be delivered by means of the Great Dharma.
[The text] briefly omits the passage beginning with "I shall now speak of fear," as it would not have accorded with them.
These sentient beings have not yet escaped birth, old age, sickness, and death, yet these sons delight in play and amusement, looking only toward their father. The words had not yet finished—

Regarding "not being spared from being burned by fire": this means that because the faculties (*indriya*) of sentient beings are small, if one were to preach for them the Great Dharma of the Tathāgata’s wisdom and the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, they would inevitably give rise to doubt upon hearing it and fail to believe. They would instead produce slander and fall into suffering;
therefore, it is said that they have not yet been spared from being burned by fire. II. The Combined Use of the Two Carts. A. Presenting the Simile.
Śāriputra, just as that elder, although he possessed strength in his body and arms, did not employ it,
but instead used earnest skillful means to diligently rescue his children from the perils of the burning house, and subsequently gave each of them a great vehicle of rare jewels.

Although his body and arms possessed great strength, the passage "each being given a large carriage" merely recounts that the elder, having first intended to provide rescue, ultimately bestowed gifts equally;
thus it refers to the text stating, "I shall now employ skillful means to enable my sons to escape this calamity.
Although it is but a single phrase, it retrospectively describes his previous actions. My own body...
"His hands have strength," and so forth. The subsequent single phrase, "He anticipates what is to follow," is a gift from [the Master].
△ Second, the actual application in three parts. First, the application of mindfulness through skillful means.
The Tathāgata is also like this. Although he possesses power and fearlessness, he does not employ them;

rather, by means of wisdom and skillful means, he rescues sentient beings from the burning house of the triple world and preaches the three vehicles: the Śrāvaka, the Pratyekabuddha, and [the Bodhisattva].
In the Buddha Vehicle, wisdom is the reality and skillful means is the provisional. Wisdom and skillful means are precisely the provisional that is identical to the real.
As for what is called the "Buddha Vehicle," it refers to the Bodhisattvas of the Tripitaka; within the Tripitaka, those of the Two Vehicles do not seek to become Buddhas.
Those who seek only extinction are [the Śrāvakas], whereas Bodhisattvas are resolute in their quest to become Buddhas.

Therefore, throughout three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, they subdue the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi- and bhāva-kleśa*), cultivate the practice of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), and further, during one hundred kalpas, cultivate the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).

Beneath the King of Trees, through thirty-four moments of mind, they suddenly sever the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of views and thoughts, thereby attaining Equal and Perfect Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). For this reason, this Bodhisattva is called the Buddha Vehicle (*buddha-yāna*).
In essence, the Bodhisattva is the cause and the Buddha-vehicle (buddhayāna) is the fruit. Because the fruit is mentioned within the context of the cause, it is called the "Buddha-vehicle.
This refers to the Buddha at the culmination of the fruit according to the Tripiṭaka. To claim that this is the single Buddha-vehicle of perfect, wondrous enlightenment would be a grave error.
II. The Combined Provisioning of the Three Chariots. Regarding the single passage on the "provisioning of the chariots," there are two parts above; first, knowing what preceded.

What is preferred. Second, the actual provision of the three vehicles. Now, we shall merely combine the actual provision with the preceding section on the actual provision. Within that [preceding] actual provision, there are three parts:

exhortation, demonstration, and realization; now we shall combine these. There is only a slight lack of sequential order. The text is divided into three sections. First, the transposed combination of the characteristics of demonstration.
And he spoke these words: "Do not take pleasure in dwelling within this burning house of the triple world. Do not crave coarse and wretched forms, sounds, scents, tastes, and textures.
If you become attached through craving, you will be consumed by fire. Depart quickly from the triple world, and you shall attain the three vehicles:
the vehicle of the śrāvaka, the pratyekabuddha, and the buddhayāna."
The statement "do not find pleasure in dwelling within the burning house of the triple world" indicates the characteristic of suffering (*duḥkha*).

"Do not covet the coarse and wretched five desires" indicates the characteristic of the origin of suffering (*samudaya*). The term "coarse and wretched" reveals that they are neither pure nor sublime.
If the five desires were pure and sublime, they would belong to the Tathāgata and would be what one ought to admire; however, these [desires] are coarse, evil, defiled, and wretched.
The five desires belong only to ordinary worldlings; therefore, do not be greedily attached to them. "You should quickly depart from the three realms" indicates the appearance of practicing the Way.
You shall attain the Three Vehicles—namely, the Vehicle of the Śrāvaka, the Pratyekabuddha, and the Buddha-vehicle.
This corresponds to the aforementioned various carts—the goat-carts, deer-carts, and ox-carts—which are currently outside the gate and can be used for play.
The carriage symbolizes the realization of the mark of cessation. Second, the leap-over practice serves as the verification:
"I now guarantee this matter for you; it shall never be in vain. You should simply cultivate with diligent perseverance."
The Tathāgata uses these skillful means to guide and encourage sentient beings, guaranteeing them a single phrase;
this corresponds to the principle that "whatever you desire shall be granted to you. This is the realization of the Truth of Cessation (Nirodha-satya).
"You should simply cultivate diligence with vigor; it is appropriate for you to come forth immediately. This is the realization of the Truth of the Path.
As for the term "enticing and encouraging," it was the Tathāgata’s original intention to speak directly of the Great Dharma of the Single Buddha Vehicle.

However, because the capacities of sentient beings were small and did not accord [with it], he temporarily used the Three Vehicles to entice them, causing them to emerge from the triple world (*tridhātu*). Thereafter—

From this, one advances toward the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Once the cessation of suffering (*nirodha*) is realized, its causes—the suffering and its accumulation (*duḥkha-samudaya*)—are thereby included therein.
△ Third, the retrospective synthesis and exhortation to practice:
He further spoke these words: "You all should know that these vehicles of the Threefold Dharma are all praised by the Sages as being sovereign."

They are unbound and have no further seeking or reliance. Riding upon these three vehicles, they enjoy themselves through the untainted faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, meditative concentrations, liberations, samādhis, and so forth, thereby attaining immeasurable peace, security, and happiness.
These two phrases regarding the Dharma of the Three Vehicles summarize the aforementioned points of being cherished, rare, and difficult to encounter.
That the Three Vehicles are praised by the sages is as stated in the *Dharmapada*: "The Buddhas of the ten directions all appear and console me with Brahma-sounds:
'Excellent, Śākyamuni! You, the foremost guide, have distinguished and taught the Three Vehicles for the sake of all classes of sentient beings.'"

Therefore, it is said that this is what the Sages praise. These three vehicles are able to sever the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāva-kleśa*) and are able to transcend the cycle of birth and death with its limited segments (*paricchinna-bhava*).
Thus, they are not bound by afflictions or the cycle of birth and death; they are sovereign and unattached, and do not undergo further existence.
Therefore, there is nothing upon which to rely; having accomplished what was to be done, there is nothing further to seek. By means of these three vehicles, one immediately attains happiness.
This corresponds to the previous statement: "If you do not take [this] now, you will surely feel regret later.

As for "delighting oneself," this refers to using the bliss found within the causes—such as the faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), and even the samādhis—as one's own enjoyment. It is immeasurable peace.

The "joy of seclusion" refers to the bliss of nirvāṇa, such as emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and signlessness (*animitta*). Thus, one should understand that the two phrases beginning with "sovereign" (*svatantra*) exhort one to know suffering (*duḥkha*) and abandon its origin (*samudaya*).

The section beginning with "by means of this" (*anena*) exhorts one to cultivate the path (*mārga*). The section beginning with "one immediately attains" (*pratilabhate*) exhorts one to realize cessation (*nirodha*).

Although the preceding [explanations] do not follow a strict sequential order, they collectively provide the exhortation, demonstration, and realization of the three turnings (*triparivarta*), none of which is lacking. However, this...
The three—exhortation, indication, and realization—are stated here according to their general categories. If one examines them closely, however, all three are present within each other.

For instance, in the initial "indication," the statement "Do not crave the five desires; do not dwell in the three realms" constitutes the exhortation (*kuan*). The statement "Quickly exit the three realms;
you shall attain the three vehicles" constitutes the realization (*zheng*). Within the second "realization," the phrase "maintain and entrust yourself to this matter" points to the three [vehicles].
That "mounting" for this purpose is the demonstration (*darśana*). That "one should simply cultivate diligence with vigor" is the exhortation (*anuśāsana*).

Within the three types of exhortation, the statement that "this Dharma of the Three Vehicles" is the demonstration; that "one shall thereby attain peace and happiness" is the realization (*sākṣātkriyā*).
△ Third, the unification of all sons in practice. The preceding parable explained the Three Vehicles in combination; here, they are opened up [individually].

It is said that there are three [types of people]. The three texts should all contain the phrase "possessing the nature of wisdom within. Wisdom (*jñāna*) refers to the wisdom that analyzes emptiness;
