"nature" (*prakṛti*) refers merely to the habitual tendencies from past lives. This refers to the past. From the passage "following the Buddha" downward, it concerns the arising of understanding in the present life through the teachings.
The teachings consist of the Four Noble Truths for *śrāvakas*, Dependent Origination for *pratyekabuddhas*, and the Six Perfections for *bodhisattvas*. From the passage "earnestly" downward...
This means that practice arises based on understanding. To analyze and further analyze, severing delusions to manifest the principle, is what constitutes diligence.
The section "seeking for oneself" and below concerns entering realization from practice. Since these three passages share a common theme, they are first set forth together;
the text is divided into three parts, the first of which corresponds to the Śrāvaka-yāna.
Śāriputra, if there are sentient beings who possess an internal nature of wisdom, who hear the Dharma from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and receive it with faith;
who apply themselves with earnest diligence, desiring to quickly escape the triple world and seek nirvāṇa for themselves—this is called the Śrāvaka Vehicle.
It is like those sons who, seeking the goat-cart, emerged from the burning house.
"Having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, the World-Honored One"—this corresponds to hearing what their father spoke regarding the objects of pleasure.

"They believed and accepted it"—this corresponds to having their wishes fulfilled, whereby their minds each became courageous and keen. "With earnest diligence"—this corresponds to pushing and shoving one another.
"Desiring to quickly escape the triple world"—this corresponds to racing together in competition. "Seeking for themselves nirvāṇa..."
"Pan. (The character for "pan") combines [the top radical] with the meaning of "leaving the house. The two characters below follow this pattern, as can be seen by analogy.

As for the "goat-drawn carriage": the goat does not look back at the herd; this is a metaphor for how the Śrāvaka only seeks self-benefit and does not benefit others. △ Second, combining [this with] the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle.
If there are sentient beings who, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, accept it with faith, apply themselves with diligent effort,
seek spontaneous wisdom, delight in solitary tranquility, and deeply understand the causes and conditions of all phenomena— this is called the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, like those sons of his.
To seek the deer-cart means to emerge from the burning house.
To speak of seeking "spontaneous wisdom" (svayambhū-jñāna) refers to the realm of dependent origination as contemplated by the Pratyekabuddhas;

it is not something based upon the Buddha, Arhats, devas, or humans. As for its being "primordially existent": since the object of contemplation is spontaneous, the contemplating wisdom is likewise spontaneous.
It is like the contemplation of a Pratyekabuddha: the flowers open in such a manner, and the leaves fall in such a manner.
This opening of flowers and falling of leaves is nothing other than dependent origination; it all arises spontaneously, with no artificial creation intervening.

Regarding the statement "profoundly knowing the causes and conditions of all phenomena": if one merely knows that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions, how can this be called profound knowledge?
It is because one is able to observe their arising in forward order and their cessation in reverse order.
By observing the past, one destroys the view of permanence; by observing the future, one destroys the view of annihilation. Therefore, it is called profound knowledge. [The Deer Cart]

In this case, the deer run side by side and look back at one another; this is analogous to the Pratyekabuddhas, for although they follow their own practice, they are also able to deliver their kinsmen.
△ Third, combining with the Bodhisattva Vehicle.

If there are sentient beings who, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, believe and accept it, and who diligently practice with vigor, seeking all-knowledge, the Buddha-knowledge,
self-arisen knowledge, teacherless knowledge, the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, the powers, and the fearlessnesses, out of compassion for their peace and happiness.
Benefiting immeasurable sentient beings, bringing profit to devas and humans, and delivering all, this is called the Mahāyāna.
Because Bodhisattvas seek this vehicle, they are called Mahāsattvas. They are like those children who, seeking ox-carts, emerged from the burning house.
Regarding the term "omniscience" (*sarvajñatā*): it refers to the illumination of all internal and external phenomena, such that there is nothing not clearly understood;
this is called omniscience. This is the wisdom cultivated during the causal stage. "Buddha-wisdom" is the wisdom realized at the stage of fruition;

it is the wisdom obtained by one who has reached the fruit of the Three Pitakas. "Self-arisen wisdom" (*svayambhū-jñāna*) is the wisdom that arises when performing transformations after the attainment of fruition.

He is able to establish teachings according to the capacities [of beings] and adapt those teachings to suit those capacities; when capacity and teaching coincide, there is nothing that does not fit perfectly.

Therefore, it is called "spontaneous wisdom" (svayambhū-jñāna) and "wisdom without a teacher. Regarding what is clarified in the Hīnayāna—that only one Buddha transforms the world and no two Buddhas transform it simultaneously—since only one Buddha appears in the world, there is consequently no other who could act as a Buddha for him.
A "teacher" (śāstṛ) is thus named for possessing "teacherless wisdom" (aśaikṣajñāna). Regarding the phrase "compassionately mindful of peace and happiness":

"compassionately mindful" refers to great compassion (mahākaruṇā), while "peace and happiness" refers to the attainment of bliss. By citing great compassion through "compassionate mindfulness," one knows that [the Buddha] will necessarily uproot [beings] from suffering.
To cite the attainment of bliss in the Land of Peace and Bliss, one knows that there must be Great Compassion; this is merely an ornamental phrasing.
As for those called "Mahāyāna," these Bodhisattvas are also termed "Great" when compared to the Two Vehicles within their own teaching. Regarding the "ox-cart":
the ox possesses the power of simultaneous transport, which serves as a metaphor for the Bodhisattva’s merit in transforming others.
△ Second, the analogy of bestowing great chariots equally upon the three [groups]. First, the presentation of the analogy:

"Śāriputra, just as that elder, seeing his sons safely emerge from the burning house and reach a place of fearlessness, reflected upon his own immeasurable wealth and bestowed great chariots equally upon all his sons."
△ Second, the formal application (*saṃyoga*). In the previous section on the parable, the "Joy of the Elder" was established; here, in the formal application, the "Escape from Peril" is established.
However, it is because the sons have escaped the peril that the elder is joyful; therefore, the initial "escape from peril" corresponds to the aforementioned "joy.
Second, from "The Tathāgata... onwards, this corresponds to the aforementioned "bestowing gifts. [Note: The second point regarding the "requesting of vehicles" is omitted in this application.

Fourth is "receiving and practicing. Since they have already escaped the danger, they will certainly seek out the chariots; once they have been granted them equally, they will certainly receive and practice [the teachings].
The two primary [chariots] and the two secondary ones—by citing the primary, the secondary are subsumed. Therefore, only the first and the third are combined, making two textual sections.
Just as the initial conjunction brings about deliverance from calamity, so too is the Tathāgata: he is the father of all sentient beings.

When he sees immeasurable billions of sentient beings emerging from the suffering of the triple world and the perilous paths of fear through the gateway of the Buddha’s teaching, and attaining the bliss of nirvāṇa, [he rejoices].
"Exiting from the suffering of the triple world" corresponds to the phrase "peacefully attaining exit. "By means of the Buddha’s teaching-gate" corresponds to the phrase "all at the crossroads.
"Attaining the bliss of nirvana" corresponds to the phrase "sitting in the open air without further obstruction.

Regarding the expression "by means of the Buddha’s teaching-gate," etc., this refers to the three vehicles being identical to the Buddha; first, the teaching of the Four Noble Truths for the śrāvakas.

Thus, for the Śrāvaka, suffering (*duḥkha*) is the initial gateway; for the Pratyekabuddha, origination (*samudaya*) is the initial gateway; and for the Bodhisattva, the path (*mārga*) is the initial gateway.

All alike emerge from the triple world (*tridhātu*). Furthermore, it may be said that the Śrāvaka emerges from the triple world through the Buddha’s teaching on the Four Noble Truths, the Pratyekabuddha through the Buddha’s teaching on Dependent Origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and the Bodhisattva through the Buddha’s teaching on the Six Perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). Each emerges from the triple world.
...and so forth. △ Second, the combined equal bestowal. There are three sections above; now they are combined. However, the order is not sequential, and they are further divided into three parts.
First, the explanation of the reason for the transposed combination.
At that time, the Tathāgata thought to himself: "I possess immeasurable and boundless wisdom, the powers, the fearlessnesses, and the treasury of all Buddha-dharmas.
All these sentient beings are my children; I shall bestow the Mahāyāna equally upon them, so that no one shall be left behind."
To attain extinction alone is to cause all to attain extinction through the extinction of the Tathāgata.
To say, "I possess an immeasurable treasury of Dharma," corresponds to the aforementioned "immeasurable wealth, all of which is overflowing.
That "all these sentient beings are my children" corresponds to the aforementioned "these young children here are all my sons. They are equal.
"Providing the great chariots" means not allowing anyone to receive anything else; that is, it is improper to give inferior small chariots to the sons.
Furthermore, one ought to treat them with an equal mind and give each of them [a great chariot], rather than making distinctions.

To say "attaining extinction alone" refers to the extinction of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). The Lesser Vehicle merely extinguishes the afflictions of views and thought (dṛṣṭi- and bhāva-kleśas), and merely delivers one from the cycle of birth and death (pariccheda-saṃsāra).
Therefore, it is said "alone. When the Tathāgata enters parinirvāṇa, he not only extinguishes *dṛṣṭi* (views) and *kleśa* (afflictions), but also extinguishes *avidyā* (ignorance);
he not only delivers [beings] from *paricchinna-bheda* (segmented death), but also delivers them from *pariṇāmi-vaipākika* (transformation-death).

Furthermore, the two characters for "alone" (*du*) and "attained" (*de*) should both be viewed as pairs. The preceding analogy contains two parts: "My wealth and property are infinite; they should not be given [to others]."

Those of inferior capacity are all my children; it is not fitting to treat them with distinction. Now, they are likewise two [groups], and I shall deliver them through the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata.
It is not right that those of superior status should not be granted to those of inferior status, nor should I allow them to attain parinirvāṇa alone.
It is not right that those of superior status should be treated with distinction. △ Second, the subsequent unification and the bestowing of equal gifts.

All these sentient beings who have been liberated from the three realms are fully provided with the means of enjoyment, such as the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), and so forth, of all Buddhas.
Regarding "the meditative concentrations and so forth of all Buddhas": *dhyāna* refers to the supreme, world-transcending meditative concentration; *samādhi* refers to the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.

Liberation is the inconceivable great liberation; it is not the same as the meditative concentration (dhyāna) mentioned above in the section on "Exhorting and Demonstrating Realization," which belongs to the teachings of the Tripitaka.
△ Third, a retrospective synthesis to demonstrate the substance of the vehicle.
All are of one characteristic and one kind, praised by the sages, and capable of producing the pure, wondrous, and supreme bliss.

This "one characteristic" takes the aforementioned Dharmakāya as its essence; that is to say, although all dharmas possess three thousand different natures and characteristics, yet when one dharma is raised, every dharma is true, and when one characteristic is raised, every characteristic is real.
It is the same *tathatā* (suchness) and true reality, the rational essence (*dharmakāya*) of the Dharma-body; therefore, it is said to be "one aspect" (*ekalakṣaṇa*).
This "one kind" corresponds to the Prajñā as its essence (*śarīra*), which is the wondrous wisdom of *prajñā*, the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

It is able to give rise to the pure, wondrous, and supreme bliss. Corresponding to this, Liberation (*vimukti*) is its function (*prayojana*); that is, by relying on the principle of the Dharmakāya, one gives rise to *prajñā*.
This wisdom employs the wisdom of *prajñā* to accord with the principle of the *dharmakāya*.
When the principle and wisdom are in profound accord, there naturally arises the bliss of liberation and mastery. Since there is no delusion that is not shattered, it is called "pure.
Since there is no virtue that is not complete, it is called "wondrous. Since it cannot be attained by those of the three vehicles or the nine realms, it is called "supreme. Furthermore,
As for "one characteristic," it refers to the principle-body (*dharmakāya*), whose essential nature is fundamentally devoid of differentiated characteristics.

Because the emotional attachments of sentient beings differ, within this single characteristic, ordinary people grasp at it as having characteristics, the followers of the Two Vehicles grasp at it as the characteristic of emptiness, and Bodhisattvas grasp at it as the characteristic of the Middle Way.
These are all differentiated characteristics and not the single characteristic. This is because its essence is originally profound stillness and tranquility.
It is not the mark of existence belonging to ordinary beings; it is not the mark of emptiness belonging to the Two Vehicles; it is not the mark of the middle way belonging to Bodhisattvas.
Rather, it is the single mark (*ekalakṣaṇa*). This single mark is precisely the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). The true mark is markless; it is only provisionally named the "single mark.
As for "one kind," the wondrous wisdom of *prajñā* is fundamentally without different kinds. Furthermore, this is due to the emotional attachments and clinging of sentient beings.

It is the same. Therefore, within a single category, for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), it becomes a contaminated seed; for those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), it becomes an uncontaminated seed;
and for bodhisattvas, it becomes both a contaminated and an uncontaminated seed. These are all distinct seeds and not a single kind.

For the essence of wisdom is fundamentally quiescent; thus, it is not the contaminated seeds of ordinary beings, nor the uncontaminated seeds of the two vehicles, nor the seeds that are both contaminated and uncontaminated of bodhisattvas—it is simply one kind of seed. Yet, Prajñā is originally without seeds.
It is merely a provisional designation for a single kind [of bliss]. Regarding what is called "the supreme bliss of purity and wondrousness":
the bliss possessed by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who are subject to outflows (*sāsrava*) is mundane; it is defiled rather than pure.

The bliss possessed by those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) who are free from outflows (*anāsrava*) is that of partial emptiness; it is coarse rather than wondrous. As for the bliss possessed by Bodhisattvas, which is both with and without outflows...
This refers to that which is sequential and possesses a superior [state], rather than being the foremost. The bliss of great liberation is not like this;
it does not resemble the defiled bliss of ordinary beings nor the coarse bliss of the two vehicles, and is therefore called "wondrous bliss.

It does not resemble the sequential and superior bliss of bodhisattvas, and is therefore called the "foremost bliss. Furthermore, its single characteristic is identical in essence, and its single type is identical in principle.

"Praised by the Sages, fit for use, pure and wondrous, foremost"—this collectively clarifies the three virtues (*triguṇa*). Because *prajñā* (wisdom) illuminates and realizes, it is called "pure" (*śuddha*).
Because *vimukti* (liberation) is functional and active, it is called "wondrous" (*praṇīta*). Because it is the ultimate within the *dharmakāya*, it is called "foremost" (*anuttara*).
△ Fourth, the analogy of the Elder’s non-falsity, in two parts. First, the presentation of the analogy.

Śāriputra, it is just as that elder first used the three carts to entice his children and later gave them only the great carts, adorned with precious things and foremost in security; yet that elder was not guilty of falsehood.
△ Second, the application of the analogy (in two parts). First, the formal application:
The Tathāgata is likewise thus; he is without falsehood. Initially, he teaches the three vehicles to guide sentient beings, and subsequently, he delivers them by means of the Great Vehicle alone.
Regarding the phrase "The Tathāgata and others," the meaning is as follows: Previously, the elder promised three carts and then gave one cart.

I, the Tathāgata, have already asked this, and you, Śāriputra, have already answered. Your first answer concerns escaping danger; your second answer concerns receiving the great [vehicle]. It is clear that there is no falsehood.
My initial bestowing of the three was followed by the single reality; this is just like the elder’s escape from danger and the giving of the great [cart], both of which were without deception.
It is false; therefore it is said, "Furthermore... (and so forth). △ Second, the explanation of the underlying intention:
Why is this? The Tathāgata possesses immeasurable wisdom, powers, and fearlessnesses, and is the treasury of all dharmas;
he is able to bestow the Dharma of the Mahāyāna upon all sentient beings, yet they are simply unable to receive it in its entirety.
△ Third, the conclusion.
Śāriputra, by these causes and conditions, you should know that it is through the power of skillful means that the Buddhas, within the single Buddha-vehicle,
distinguish and teach three.
The Tathāgata’s response consists of three parts. First is the introduction of the intent, which involves refuting the former [position] and accepting the latter.
Second is the formal exposition, which involves establishing analogies and applying them to the dharma. Now, this third part is the concluding answer to the question:

"Please explain the causes and conditions for the sake of the fourfold assembly. Regarding the phrase "by means of these," the intended meaning is that you previously asked: "I pray that you will explain..."
Regarding these causes and conditions, which serve to eliminate doubt and regret, I shall now provide an analogy, beginning from the parable and concluding with the application to the Dharma.
Using the shallow analogy of the elder’s three carts and one cart, I illustrate the profound Dharma of the Tathāgata’s three vehicles and one vehicle.
What is clarified herein is nothing other than the causes and conditions of the "three before and the one after. Therefore, you fourfold assembly should—

This is because it has been definitively resolved and rendered free of doubt. Therefore, it says, "By this... (and so forth). △ Second, the verse summary has two parts: first, the summary of the formal exposition;

second, from "You, Śāriputra," onwards, the summary of the exhortation to believe. Within the first part, the formal exposition, there is no summary of the preceding introduction or the subsequent conclusion;
rather, only the formal exposition itself is summarized. This is divided into two: first, the summary of the establishment of the analogy; second, the summary of... [the dharma].
This is correct. There are two parts to the first section. The first verse provides a general analogy, likening the aforementioned sudden outbreak of fire that consumes the house and its contents.
It does not briefly mention the single gate or the thirty children, because the "burning house" already encompasses the gate and the five hundred people.
This includes the thirty sons as well, because the gate does not depart from the house and the sons do not go outside the people [of the household].

Second, from "At that time, the master of the house" onwards, the verse provides a distinct analogy. The initial text is divided into five parts; the first is the direct verse on the basis of the analogy.
The Buddha, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Suppose there were an elder who had a large house; that house was long-standing and moreover dilapidated, with its halls and chambers high and perilous."

The bases of the pillars were crushed and rotten; the beams and rafters were leaning and slanting; the foundations and steps were collapsed and ruined; the walls were crumbling and split; the plaster was peeling away;

the thatched roof was falling down in disarray; the rafters and eaves were misaligned and detached; the surrounding enclosures were bent and crooked; and all was filled with various impurities. There were five hundred people there.
He dwells therein. The first line of verse corresponds to the passage above concerning "a great elder" and "a large house.

The [subsequent] lines correspond to the passage above concerning "the vastness of that household" and "the many hundreds of people," which refers to the multitude of persons. As for the correspondence to the Dharma: the elder is the Tathāgata.
"Come! This 'burning house' is precisely the triple world (*tridhātu*). Although this triple world is the transformed realm of the Tathāgata, it is also that which belongs to sentient beings.
Since the very first moment of non-awakening, sentient beings have congealed darkness into form and constructed lands through their perceptions;
this has been so for a long time. Therefore, it is said that the house is ancient. Although it has become a land in which they dwell,"

They must inevitably return to ruin and emptiness; thus, what was spoken of as flourishing suddenly falls into decay. "Decay" (dùn) means exhaustion and collapse; "ruin" (bì) means destruction and deterioration.
When situated above, it is a hall, like the two upper realms; when dwelling below, it is a house, like the desire realm.
Furthermore, these three realms are all collectively precarious; therefore, they are "highly dangerous. The three preceding phrases constitute a general explanation of the three realms. Next—

The three phrases concerning the base of the pillar specifically clarify the three realms. The base of the pillar is not far from the ground, just as the Form Realm (rūpadhātu) is not far from the Desire Realm (kāmadhātu).
The beams and rafters are constructed in the void, just as the Formless Realm (ārūpyadhātu) dwells at the very summit.

The foundation and steps rely entirely upon the earth, just as it is with the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*). Although the three realms differ in their upper and lower levels, they are all collectively subject to impermanence;
before long, they return to ruin and decay. Thus, it is said that they are "crumbling, rotting, leaning, and collapsing.
The four lines concerning the walls and partitions specifically clarify the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) present within the three realms. The walls...

The earth element is like the foundation; it is ultimately not solid, hence it is said to "crumble. The mud plaster is like the water element; it is ultimately not firm or congealed, hence it is said to "slump down.
The thatched roof is like the wind element; it ultimately ends in dispersion and ruin, hence it is said to "fall in disorder.
The rafters and eaves are like the fire element; they must ultimately be extinguished, hence it is said to "break away. The two lines following "the surrounding walls" summarize these points.
"Bound" means that the three realms are not separate from the four great elements, and the four great elements are not separate from the three realms;
they are equally impermanent and impure. Therefore, it is said that they are "completely obstructed, crooked, and filled everywhere with filth.

"Five hundred people" praises the aforementioned multitude of people, referring specifically to the five destinies (*pañca-gati*). Since the three realms consist solely of the abodes of these five destinies, it is said they "dwell therein."
Within this [passage]. △ Second, the analogy clarifies the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Now, in this text, some explain it by means of the three poisons, others clarify it by means of the six consciousnesses, some take the four inversions as the correspondence, and others cite the ten unwholesome actions to interpret the text;

none of these accord with the intent of the Sūtra. Only the interpretation based on the ten underlying tendencies (*daśānuśaya*) perfectly accords with the Buddha’s mind. How is this known? That is to say:
As the sutra says: "Because the Buddhas appear in the world of the five turbidities, they differentiate and teach the three vehicles within the single Buddha-vehicle.
Regarding the five turbidities, they are: the turbidity of views, the turbidity of afflictions, the turbidity of lifespan, the turbidity of sentient beings, and the turbidity of the kalpa.
Herein, it is clarified that the five sharp [afflictions] are the turbidity of views, and the five dull [afflictions] are the turbidity of afflictions. These two—

This is what burns; that which is burned consists of the impurity of lifespan (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*) and the impurity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*). When these four impurities are fully present, they constitute the impurity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*).

Because of these five impurities within the evil world of the triple realm, the Tathāgata perceives them from the stage of the *dharmakāya* and desires to give rise to great compassion to act as their savior. Yet, sentient beings are already being scorched by these five impurities.
Thus, they are unable to understand the Buddha’s wisdom. Therefore, the Tathāgata first provisionally establishes the three vehicles and subsequently teaches the one vehicle;
all these various expedient arrangements arise from this. For this reason, the ten afflictions (daśa-āsrava) accord with the Buddha’s intention.

If one were to interpret it otherwise, it would not accord with the sutra. The text is divided into three parts: first, the five dull [faculties]; second, the five sharp [faculties]; and third, the concluding clarification.

Regarding the first two [parts], there is first a specific indication and second a general explanation. Regarding the first [of these], there are five sections; the first is an analogy for the latent tendency of pride (*māna-anuśaya*).
Hawks, owls, eagles, vultures, crows, magpies, doves, and pigeons.

Regarding conceit (*māna*), there are eight types of conceit and seven types of conceit; briefly, there are three: namely, overweening conceit (*adhimāna*), self-conceit (*asmimāna*), and inferiority conceit (*ūnamāna*).

The owls and nightjars regard what is not their offspring as their offspring; this is analogous to the overweening pride (*adhimāna*) of one who has not attained [realization] yet claims to have attained it.
The eagles and vultures soar high and look down upon others, acting as leaders among the various birds; this is analogous to the pride of self (*asmimāna*).

The crows, magpies, and the like do not fly away from the ground and always remain close to humans; this is analogous to the pride of inferiority (*ūnamāna*). Regarding the pride of inferiority: even if there is but a single matter...
Originally one was unable to practice it. When others were practicing it, one would give rise to conceit, saying, "I too am able to practice this.

Although originally base and inferior, one still treats others with pride; therefore, it is called the pride of the base and inferior (*hīnādhimāna*). △ Second, an analogy for the latent tendency of hatred (*dveṣānuśaya*).
Vipers, snakes, vipers, and scorpions; centipedes and millipedes—anger also has three types:
anger that accords with reason, unreasonable anger, and anger arising from contention. Now, vipers and snakes are by nature venomous.
This is like unreasonably angry venomous snakes; though scorpions are poisonous, they only wound when touched by humans. This is like reasonably angry centipedes.
This is an analogy for anger arising from contentious debate. △ Third, an analogy for the latent tendency of delusion.
Lizards, centipedes, weasels, badgers, mice, and various other evil insects scurry about in all directions.
Feces and urine create a foul-smelling place where impurities overflow; dung beetles and other insects swarm upon it.
Ignorance (*moha*) is of two kinds: independent ignorance (*kevala-moha*) and associated ignorance (*saṃprayukta-moha*). Independent ignorance arises in dependence upon a tranquil mind;
because centipedes and millipedes always dwell in secluded and quiet places, they serve as a metaphor for independent ignorance. Associated ignorance is...
It is triggered by objective conditions. The weasel, the wildcat, and the mouse are restless and never still; thus they are used as metaphors for *saṃprayukta-moha* (associated delusion).
"Intermingling" means that when the mind is at rest, it gives rise to *svatantra* (independent) delusion, and when it encounters an object, it gives rise to *saṃprayukta* (associated) delusion;

because these arise intertwined and crisscrossing, they are called "intermingled. Because they arise with great speed, they are called "galloping. The place of foul-smelling excrement and urine is a metaphor for the body.
The mind and dharmas that are felt are precisely the objects of delusion: impurity, suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self.
Therefore, it is said that impurity overflows. From external objects, internal views arise, reckoning the impure as pure and so forth, like dung beetles gathering upon a place of stench.
△ Fourth, the analogy for the latent tendency of greed.
Foxes, wolves, and jackals chew, trample, and gnaw upon corpses; their bones and flesh lie scattered in disarray. Consequently, packs of dogs come vying with one another to seize and snatch them;
emaciated by hunger and filled with terror, they search for food everywhere.
There are two kinds of greed: powerful greed and powerless greed. Powerful greed refers to taking what belongs to others by means of one's own might;
this is called powerful greed. It is now illustrated by the analogy of the fierce fox and wolf.
Powerless greed refers to taking without any might, through piteous entreaty and begging for mercy; this is called powerless greed. Now...
The jackal’s weakness serves as a metaphor. To take [the prey] without satiety is like chewing for its flavor;
to take it without propriety is like treading upon it with contempt. This is the manifestation of greed. The corpse and its bones are the objects of that greed;
the insatiable pursuit is like gnawing until the remains are in disarray. The strong taking from the weak is like a dog.

They come to seize and snatch; their greedy seeking never ceases. Like those who are famished and emaciated, they employ all manner of means in their pursuit. Therefore, it is said they are "terrified and anxious.

Regarding the objects of the five sensory realms (*pañca-viṣaya*), there is nothing to which they do not become greedily attached; hence it is said they "seek food everywhere. △ Fifth, this is a metaphor for the latent tendency of doubt (*vicikitsā-anuśaya*).

To contend, grapple, snap at, and bark, with the inner mind failing to understand and unable to resolve what is right or wrong—this is called doubt. It is like a combatant who, while engaged in struggle, suspects his own actions to be wrong.
Furthermore, to claim something is correct is like reaching one's hand forward to seize; yet to claim it is incorrect is like drawing that same hand back.
When the mind is indecisive, the words are likewise unclear, much like the barking and howling of a dog.
△ Second, the general explanation:
"That house is terrifying; its manifestations are thus.

These two lines conclude the aforementioned five dull afflictions (*pañca-mṛdu-kleśa*). Regarding the phrase "its manifestations are thus," it means that [the afflictions] arise suddenly as pride (*māna*).
Even until a sudden doubt arises, there is no single certainty; therefore, it is said that they are "terrified," and so forth.
△ Second, explaining the five benefits, in two parts: first, a general explanation.
"They exist everywhere. This refers to the five *kleśas* of wrong views (*pañca-drṣṭi*), which pervade all four truths and the five aggregates; hence the phrase "everywhere" and so forth.
△ Second, specifically showing the five [wrong views]. First, an analogy for false views.
Yakṣas and evil spirits devour human flesh; poisonous insects and various malevolent birds and beasts conceive, give birth, and raise their young, each protecting them with care.
Yet the yakṣas compete to come and seize them for food. Once they have eaten their fill, their evil intentions grow even more fierce.
The sound of strife and contention is most terrifying.
Erroneous views are as swift as yakṣas. To deny the supramundane causes and effects of karma through erroneous views is like a ghost devouring human flesh;
to deny the mundane causes and effects of karma is like devouring the flesh of insects. Such is the world.
Such causes produce such effects; just as birds and beasts protect their own offspring, so too does one guard one's own [karmic] results.
To deny them through wrong views is like a ghost seizing food. When wrong views are established, it is like being satiated by eating;
when wrong views increase, they blaze ever more fiercely. To teach others with wrong views is like raising a clamor during a quarrel—it is truly terrifying.
Regarding "fear": to personally advance in wrong views is already terrifying, as one will inevitably fall into suffering.

To further teach others [in this way] causes others also to fall into suffering; therefore, it is most exceedingly terrifying and fearsome. △ Second, the analogy for the clinging to precepts and rituals.
The kumbhāṇḍa spirits crouch upon earthen mounds, or at times rise into the air by one or two feet to travel back and forth, sporting and playing wantonly.
They seize dogs by their two hind legs, throw them down until they cry out, and place their own feet upon the dogs' necks, finding pleasure in terrifying them.

To regard what is not a cause as a cause is called *śīlavrataparāmarśa* (clinging to precepts and observances). A person who clings to precepts can practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), yet they have not yet reached its fulfillment.

To sit crouching upon a mound of earth is like attaining the *kāmadhātu-samādhi* (concentration of the desire realm). To sit perched upon a mound of earth is like attaining the *rūpadhātu-samādhi* (concentration of the form realm).

To rise one foot above the ground is like attaining the *ārūpyadhātu-samādhi* (concentration of the formless realm). These types of tainted (*sāsrava*) meditative concentrations are subsumed [within this category].
When the mind is fixed in contemplation, it manifests before one, as if ascending upward; if the mind is not restrained, it is lost, as if descending back down.
At times it manifests, and at times it is lost; thus it is said that it "travels back and forth.
Because one reckons what is not a cause to be a cause and seeks pleasure for oneself, it is said that one "indulges in wanton play. It says:
Regarding the grasping of a dog by its two hind legs: that which is fundamentally not a cause is reckoned as a cause.

Just as grasping a dog by one leg—taking what is not a cause to be a cause—one thereby establishes a cause of suffering, which will inevitably bring about the fruit of suffering. Yet those people of false views claim it does not bring about the fruit of suffering;
this is like grasping a dog by only one leg. A cause of suffering must inevitably bring about the fruit of suffering, just as with the dog.
There is a sound. Now, one reckons that a cause of suffering does not bring about a fruit of suffering, like the sound lost when striking a dog.

"To place a foot upon the neck" means to take the foot of one's own reckoning—that a cause of suffering does not bring about a fruit of suffering—and place it upon the neck of another’s reckoning—that a cause of pleasure necessarily brings about a fruit of suffering.
When the former person hears what the latter has reckoned, they become terrified; this is a false view.
People consider themselves happy; thus it is said that they find pleasure in fearing dogs. △ Third, an analogy for the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi):
Furthermore, there are various ghosts whose bodies are tall and large, naked, black, and emaciated, who constantly dwell therein and emit great, evil sounds.
They cry out and beg for food.

Because the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) extends vertically through the three periods of time, it is called "long. Because it spreads horizontally across the five aggregates (pañcaskandha), it is called "great.
Since they cling to this view of a self, they lack the adornment of merit; therefore, they are said to be "naked. Because this is not a pure action (śuklakarman), it is said that...

"Black" means that he lacks the two adornments of merit and wisdom; hence, he is called "emaciated. That which constantly dwells within him refers to his clinging to the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi), whereby he cannot escape from birth and death.
Because he teaches others by means of this very [view], it is said that he "utters a great evil sound."
Because they seek the fruit of happiness by means of this, it is said that they "seek food. △ Fourth, an analogy for the grasping at views:
Furthermore, there are various hungry ghosts whose throats are like needles.

To regard what is not a fruit as a fruit is called the "view of attachment to views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*). To regard that which is not the fundamental state of *nirvāṇa* as the ultimate goal is like a ghost with a throat as narrow as a needle;
its life will not last long. △ Fifth, an analogy for the "extreme views" (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
Furthermore, there are various ghosts with heads like those of oxen; some eat human flesh, while others devour dogs.
Their hair is disheveled and matted, and they are cruel and treacherous. Driven by hunger and thirst, they cry out and run about in haste.
The calculation of the two views of annihilationism and eternalism is termed the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), like a cow's head having two horns.

To cling to these two views is to claim there is no cause for transcending the world, which is like eating human flesh; it is to claim there is no cause for the mundane world, which is like devouring a dog.
Having already calculated [the view of] annihilation, they further calculate [the view of] permanence, like disheveled hair.

Some cling to the existence of a remainder while denying it, or cling to the non-existence of a remainder while affirming it; hence it is called "harmful. To shatter this and cause it to be utterly exhausted, it is called "perilous.
Because there is no flavor of the Dharma to nourish the spirit, they suffer from hunger and thirst. They still use extreme views to instruct others, and thus they cry out and run about.
△ Third, the clarification of the causes and conditions has two parts. First, the clarification of the causal basis:
yakṣas, hungry ghosts, and various evil birds and beasts, driven by the urgency of hunger, look toward the four directions and peer through the windows and casements. Such are these various perils.
It is immeasurably terrifying. This dilapidated old house belongs to a single person who has recently gone out.

As for those who are driven by hunger and distress and wander in the four directions, this refers to body, sensation, mind, and phenomena (kāya, vedanā, citta, dharma) giving rise to the four perversions.

That is to say, one directs oneself toward the body and gives rise to the perversion of purity, and so on, up to directing oneself toward phenomena and giving rise to the perversion of self. With a distorted mind one grasps at objects; there is no correct contemplation.

"Like looking through a window or a lattice"—these two phrases serve as the conclusion. That the dilapidated house belongs to a single person is a metaphor for these three realms, which constitute the sphere of transformation for the Tathāgata.
The expression "having recently departed" is a metaphor for when the spiritual capacity (*mūla*) of those in this land is exhausted and conditions (*pratyaya*) arise elsewhere;
it signifies that the Tathāgata abandons this place to respond to beings there. Nevertheless, he does not depart forever.
Therefore, it is said that they were merely nearby. △ Second, the account of the house burning:
Not long after, a fire suddenly broke out in the house behind them; at once from all four sides, its flames blazed up together.
The ridgepoles, rafters, columns, and beams burst with a thunderous crack, snapping and falling; the walls collapse.
The various spirits and ghosts raise their voices in a great cry, while the eagles, vultures, and kumbhāṇḍas are struck with panic and terror, unable to escape.
Regarding "suddenly a fire breaks out": this refers to the arising of various afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth due to the Buddha’s response to sentient beings. Regarding "unable to escape":
because they give rise exclusively to either sharp or dull faculties, they are now being burned by the fire of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and afflictions;
none can attain freedom. How could one not fear this? Hence it is said: "They are utterly terrified and in a state of panic. △ Third, the analogy clarifies form (*rūpa*).
In this realm, fierce beasts and venomous insects hide within their burrows, and piśāca demons likewise dwell therein. Because their merit is meager, they are oppressed by fire;
driven together, they harm one another, drinking blood and devouring flesh. Those belonging to the species of jackals have already perished.
Various great and evil beasts vied with one another to devour them, while foul-smelling smoke and flames billowed, filling all four directions.

Those who hid in holes and burrows represent the dull underlying afflictions (*anuśaya*), such as sensual desire, which have turned toward the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) to practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*);
thus they are said to "hide in holes. The sharp underlying afflictions likewise turn toward the realm of form; thus it is said that the *piśāca* demons also dwell there.
Among them, all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) consist solely of phenomenal characteristics (*nimitta*); therefore, it is said that their merit is meager.

While the cultivation of dhyāna is the same for all, their attachments differ; therefore, it is said they mutually harm one another. Their attachment to meditative concentration is like drinking blood, and their craving for the merits of the *ārāma* (monastic grove) is like devouring flesh.
The jackal dies first, and is then devoured by the fierce beasts; thus, the craving for desire increases.

This refers to craving for form (*rūpa-rāga*). It is like a wild beast preying upon a jackal; whereas craving in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) pertains to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), it differs from that of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) which craves only distraction.
Therefore, it is likened to a great predatory beast. △ Fourth, the analogy for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Centipedes, millipedes, and various kinds of venomous snakes, scorched by the fire, scramble to flee their burrows; the *kumbhāṇḍa* spirits seize and devour them as they emerge.
Furthermore, various hungry ghosts have flames burning upon their heads; tormented by hunger, thirst, and heat, they run about in a state of frantic distress.

"Emerging from the hole" refers to proceeding from the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). "Taking food" refers to transforming craving for the realm of form into craving for the formless realm.
"Flames burning upon the head" is a metaphor for the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*);
although it stands at the very summit of the three realms and occupies the highest position, it likewise possesses afflictions (*kleśa*). △ Fifth, the summary of the three realms.
Such is that dwelling; it is truly terrifying, filled with poisonous harms and fires, and its various calamities are not just one.
This concludes the summary analogy by verse. II. The three verses on the specific analogies. First, the verse on the analogy of the elder’s act of rescue:

At that time, the owner of the house was standing outside the gate. He heard someone say, "Your sons, having previously come into this house while playing, are young and ignorant, and they remain there joyfully attached.
Having heard this, the elder was startled and entered the burning house.

Regarding the phrase "standing outside the gate": this means that provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) stands outside the gate of ultimate wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*). Because it now wishes to observe the capacities of sentient beings, it is said to be "standing.

Furthermore, it is like the Tathāgata having already emerged outside the gate of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). Regarding the hearing of someone say: this is a metaphor for unconditional great compassion (*apratihata-mahākaruṇā*).
As for first entering the house by way of playful sport: this is a metaphor for the twenty-two thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas.

When receiving the Great Teaching, he appeared as though he intended to leave the house; however, because he regressed from the Great Vehicle to adopt the Small Vehicle, he immediately fell into the triple world, and thus it is said he "entered the house.
Since his regression from the Great Vehicle has long been ongoing, it is said he was "already there.
Having regressed from the Great, his capacity for the Great is feeble, hence he is called "young. Having adopted the Small, he possesses only the capacity for the Small; therefore—
To speak of "lesser" means that by retreating from the Great [Vehicle], one lacks knowledge of the Great; by grasping at the lesser, one lacks knowledge of the lesser.

Although they grasp at the lesser Dharma, they still remain greedily attached to the five desires of birth and death; therefore, it is said they "delight in pleasure. The above verses describe seeing the fire.
The Tathāgata, through his unconditioned great compassion, takes these sentient beings as his object and, wishing to uproot their suffering, manifests [the following].
They are born into the three realms, like an elder who, having already stepped outside his gate, enters his house once more. Therefore it is said: "The elder... (and so forth).
△ Second, the verse on the analogy of discarding the small table and using the carriage, in two parts: first, the verse on discarding the small table; second, the verse on using the carriage.
The first three [verses]: The first verse concerns the actual practice of contemplation, which is appropriate for providing rescue and relief so that no burning or harm occurs.

Regarding the term "appropriate" (*fangyi*): "appropriate" (*fang*) refers to method (*upāya*), while "appropriate" (*yi*) carries the sense of being in accord (*anurūpa*). That is to say, by means of what kind of... contemplation?
This method is capable of saving [them]. It is precisely the skillful means (*upāya*) that clarifies both the inclusive and the distinct, and is intended for those of the three vehicles (*triyāna*).
△ Second, the verse on fully informing all the sons.

He exhorted his sons, describing their many afflictions and perils: the evil spirits and venomous insects, the spreading conflagration, and the succession of various sufferings that continue without interruption;
the poisonous snakes, vipers, and pythons, as well as the yakṣas, kumbhāṇḍa ghosts, jackals, foxes, and dogs.
Hawks, vultures, owls, and screech-owls, along with species such as centipedes—tormented by hunger and thirst, they are truly terrifying. Such is the difficulty of this place of suffering;
how much more so when there is a great fire!
"Addressing the sons" refers to the verses beginning with "Thus he reflects," as well as "I shall speak to you of fear," which constitute the full address.
This is the exposition of the two teachings: the Perfect (En) and the Distinct (Bie). The evil spirits depart below.
There are three instances of "sharp and dull," which serve as metaphors for the afflictions of the three realms outside the [Triple] World.

First, the single line on the "poison of evil spirits" metaphorizes the sharp and dull afflictions belonging to the Desire Realm outside the world. Second, the two lines on the "venomous snake" metaphorize the sharp and dull afflictions belonging to the Form Realm outside the world.
Third, the one and a half lines beginning with "the kumbhāṇḍa" metaphorize the [Formless Realm... outside the world.

Externally, there are no sharp or dull afflictions belonging to the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*). Regarding the phrase "this place of suffering and difficulty," it summarizes that the afflictions of the three realms beyond the aforementioned realms are the causes of suffering.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "even more like a great fire," this clarifies that within the three realms beyond [the Desire Realm], there is yet further the fruit of suffering consisting of the death and rebirth of transformation (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*). That is to say, in the three realms beyond, there exists this ignorance and affliction...
The causes of affliction and suffering are already fearsome and difficult to dwell in;

how much more so when one is further scorched by the fires of the fruit of birth-and-death characterized by changeability—when could one possibly remain? △ Third: A verse on the cessation of transformation due to a lack of receptive capacity.
The sons were ignorant; although they heard their father’s instruction, they remained attached to their pleasures and would not cease their play.
What is called "the father’s instruction" refers to the exhortations previously addressed to the sons.

Since the preceding verses elaborate upon the two modes of contemplation—the Perfect and the Distinct—as well as the full exposition of the two teachings—the Perfect and the Distinct—all of these are explained in reference to the realm beyond [this world]. △
The two verses employ the analogy of a chariot; the first verse concerns mindfulness and the application of skillful means.
At that time, the elder had this thought: "My sons are like this; they only increase my grief and distress. Now, regarding this house..."
There is not a single thing here that is worth enjoying, yet these sons of mine are so immersed in play and sport that they do not accept my instructions; they will surely be harmed by the fire.
Thereupon, he immediately reflected and devised various skillful means.

That which increases my affliction is this: when the Tathāgata, while in the state of the Dharma-body, beholds all sentient beings being scorched by the afflictions and the cycle of birth and death within the triple world, he is already filled with great alarm and distress. Now, he manifests entry into birth and death.
He informed [the people] most earnestly, yet they were unwilling to believe and accept it; therefore, his sorrow and distress increased all the more.

"There is not a single thing to be enjoyed" means that the coarse and scattered pleasures of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the meditative pleasures of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the tainted pleasures of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) are none of them truly eternal;
thus, it is said that there is not one thing to be enjoyed. △ Second, the verse on the three establishments (*prajñapti*):
He addressed his sons, saying: "I have various kinds of precious playthings—exquisite and beautiful chariots: goat-drawn carts, deer-drawn carts, and great ox-drawn carts.
They are now outside the gate. Come forth, and I shall provide these vehicles for you."
According to one's inclinations and desires, one may sport therein.

The first line and three phrases of the verse indicate its characteristics. "Exquisite jewel-adorned chariots" refers to the Three Baskets (Tripitaka) and the Three Vehicles (Triyāna), including all the factors of the path (mārga-dharma) and Nirvāṇa;
these are capable of transporting one beyond the ninety-five kinds of heterodox teachings as well as the three realms and the six destinies.
Birth and death reveal the partial truth; therefore, it is called a "wondrous jewel and fine carriage," yet this is not the wondrous jewel and fine carriage of the single Buddha-vehicle.
Next, the line "Come forth, you all" praises the exhortation to practice. The section beginning with "I, for your sake" praises the providing of testimony.
As for the statement "the one who fashioned these carriages," the three vehicles are fundamentally established as skillful means and possess no substantial reality.
Therefore, it is said that they "constructed" them. △ Third, the verse on the sons receiving and practicing [the teaching]:
Upon hearing this description of the various chariots, the sons immediately vied with one another, rushing out and reaching an open space.
They are free from all suffering and calamity.
Since they no longer possess the causes of affliction and outflows (*kleśa-saṃskāra*) as obstacles, it is said that they have "reached an open space.
Since they no longer possess the bitter torments of the fruits of segmented existence (*bhava*), it is said that they are "free from all suffering and calamity. △ Third, the verse on equal bestowal:
The great vehicle is likened to the four [lines]. The first verse describes the elder’s joy:
seeing his sons emerge from the burning house and stand at the crossroads, seated upon lion thrones, he exclaims in self-congratulation:

I am now joyful. These sons of mine were so difficult to conceive and raise; yet they were foolish and ignorant, entering this perilous house filled with many venomous insects and terrifying malevolent spirits, where fierce flames of a great fire burst forth from all four sides. And as for these sons—
Delighting in pleasure and play, I have already rescued them and enabled them to escape this calamity. Therefore, O people, I am now joyful.

As for "sitting upon the lion’s throne": because the children of the Three Vehicles have emerged from the triple world and reached the place of fearlessness, having attained peace and security, the Tathāgata likewise attains fearlessness; hence it is said that he sits upon the lion’s throne. He rejoices in his own well-being.

Regarding "joy" (*ruci*): it means that one is able to receive and practice even the small [teachings]. If the Great [Vehicle] is explained for them, they will likewise certainly receive and practice it.

Furthermore, once they have attained the small, one may lead them from the small back to the Great. Moreover, if that which has been attained as the small is revealed [as being the Great], [they will realize it].
The "entirety" is precisely the "Great. It possesses these many meanings, which the Tathāgata knows for himself, whereas the followers of the Three Vehicles do not know them;
therefore, he merely rejoices in himself. This refers to his happiness. In the prose section, sitting in the open air at the crossroads belongs to the son;

here, it belongs to the father. Since those of the Lesser Vehicle have already emerged from the three realms and attained realization equal to that of the Buddha, the two are mutually illustrated throughout the preceding and following sections.

[The Buddha] heard this. Yet, [the children] were all profoundly happy and at ease because of their father. This was because the father alone knew [their disposition], whereas the children did not. Regarding "nurturing" and so forth:

when they were taught the Great [Vehicle] by twenty thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas, it was like "giving birth. In the interim, they regressed from the Great and were again received through the Small [Vehicle], which is like "nurturing.
They were foolish; they regressed from the Great due to ignorance of it, and they took up the Small due to ignorance of it. Therefore...
Regarding the passage beginning with "I called them ignorant and small-minded; I have already saved them," etc.:

it is because the Tathāgata wished to cause them to sport in the wisdom of a Buddha that he first used the skillful means of the three vehicles and the minor teachings to entice them, so that they might escape the triple world, as they were merely clinging to the small [vehicle] and did not harmonize with the ultimate truth. △ Second, the verse on the sons requesting the carts.
At that time, the sons, knowing their father was sitting at ease, all went to where he was and said to him:
"We pray you grant us the three kinds of precious chariots as previously promised. Their father replied: "Come forth, my sons; I shall give you three chariots according to your desires."
"Now is precisely the time. Please deign to grant it.
This is explained according to the text. △ Third, the verse on the Elder’s bestowal upon the three [groups]. First, the verse that anticipates the explanation of the reason why.
The elder was immensely wealthy, possessing numerous storehouses filled with gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, and agate.
Regarding the phrase "immensely wealthy," this is a verse summarizing the aforementioned immeasurable riches and overflowing treasuries; it is merely an abbreviated prose passage.

The mention of gold, silver, and so forth is comparable to the Tathāgata’s teaching on the aspects of wisdom (*jñāna*), realization (*adhigama*), abandonment (*prahāṇa*), practice (*caryā*), stages (*bhūmi*), cause (*hetu*), and fruit (*phala*). There is nothing [in the treasure] that does not correspond.
It is not complete. △ Second, the actual verse exposition of the body of the chariot has three parts. First, the verse exposition of the Dharma-body as the essence:
"With various precious materials, they construct great chariots, adorned and embellished with ornaments, surrounded by railings, and with bells suspended on all four sides."
Golden cords crisscrossed as railings, and nets of pearls were spread above them.

Golden flower tassels hung down everywhere, and various colorful ornaments encircled the perimeter. Soft silks and cotton served as carpets and cushions, while exquisite, fine woolen rugs were spread upon them.
Worth hundreds of billions [in value], it is fresh, white, and pure, used to cover the top.
Regarding the phrase "those who construct the great chariots," the construction here is different from the previous construction of this chariot.
This refers to the fundamental *dharmakāya*, which is inherently possessed by every person. If it were not adorned with meritorious virtues, then even devas and nāgas...

Regarding that which is neglected: one must initiate cultivation from within the nature (*prakṛti*), further embellishing it with the conditions and causes (*pratyaya* and *hetu*). For this reason, it is said to be "constructed.

The exquisite, fine, and subtle [threads] are likened to meditations such as contemplation and refinement; all are the true aspect (*dharmatā*). △ Second, the verse indicates that Prajñā is the central tenet.
There is a great white ox, fat, strong, and powerful, with a beautiful form, yoked to a precious chariot.
△ Third, the verse shows liberation as its function:
it is attended by many retinues who serve and protect it.
△ 3. The Verse Summary of the Equal Bestowal:
By means of these wondrous chariots, he bestowed them equally upon all his sons.
This may be seen as a synthesis of the statement in the preceding prose section that he "bestowed one great chariot upon each of his sons. △ 4.
The verse says: "The sons were filled with joy.
At that time, the sons leaped for joy and, mounting these precious chariots, traveled through the four directions, sporting and delighting in happiness."
It is sovereign and unimpeded.

Regarding the statement "riding this precious chariot" and so forth, it means that one takes the Buddha-vehicle of the three virtues as the object of contemplation, and in turn, uses this very object to give rise to the wisdom of the contemplating subject.
Thus, wisdom is generated by the object, and the object is illuminated by wisdom; this is contemplation.
When the practice of merit is perfected, one is naturally able to proceed from the stage of semblance into the stage of partial realization.

From the first abode (*prathama-vihāra*) up to the tenth ground (*daśabhūmi*), at each successive level one is able to manifest the three virtues (*triguṇa*) and destroy ignorance (*avidyā*). Therefore, it is said that "one rides this precious chariot," and so forth.
This means that prior to ascending to the stages (*bhūmi*), one uses the wisdom of the three virtues to illuminate the objects of the three virtues; this is merely called "mounting the vehicle.
Once one has ascended to the stages and beyond, it is truly "having mounted [the vehicle] and traveling.

Upon reaching the tenth stage, one is able to flow into the ocean of the fruit of wondrous enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*) spontaneously; therefore, it is said to be "sovereign and unimpeded. "The four directions" refers to the forty stages. △
The second verse correlates the teaching with the analogy. First, the initial verse correlates the general analogy:
"Śāriputra, I am likewise so: the most honored among all sages, the father of the world, for all sentient beings."
All of you are my children. You are deeply attached to worldly pleasures and lack the mind of wisdom. There is no peace in the three realms;
they are like a burning house, filled with manifold sufferings and most terrifying. They are constantly beset by the calamities of birth, old age, sickness, and death, and such fires as these.
Blazing without ceasing.
Regarding the phrase "all sentient beings are his children": in the preceding general analogy, there are five hundred and thirty different types of children.
Five hundred are the children of the Tathāgata’s direct cause (*dharmatā-hetu*); thirty are the children of the Tathāgata’s conditions and secondary causes (*pratyaya* and *upaniṣad*). Now...

To summarize these points: it is therefore said that "all [beings] are thus. Because they have regressed from the Great Vehicle and adopted the Lesser Vehicle, it is said that they "lack the mind of wisdom.

Birth, old age, and so forth—these four—are the fires of the fruit of suffering (*duḥkha-phala*). The two characters for "sorrow" (*yōu*) and "affliction" (*huàn*) are the fires of the cause of accumulation (*samudaya-hetu*).
From the cause of accumulation one invites the fruit of suffering, and from the fruit of suffering one again gives rise to the cause of accumulation; hence, it is said to be "blazing."

Yet it does not cease; the rest may be understood accordingly. △ Second, the verse on the synthesis of the individual parables, in four parts. First, the verse synthesizing the parable of the elder’s rescue:
The Tathāgata has already departed from the burning house of the triple world, dwelling in tranquil seclusion and abiding peacefully in the forest wilds. Now, as for this triple world...
"All these are mine; all the sentient beings therein are my children. Yet now, this place is full of many calamities and hardships, and I alone am able to provide protection and rescue."

Regarding the phrase "the Tathāgata has already departed [from them]," it means that because the Tathāgata was able to draw near to immeasurable Buddhas and fully practiced the immeasurable path-dharmas of all those Buddhas, when one examines his afflictions (*kleśa*), both *dṛṣṭi-heya* (afflictions abandoned by insight) and *bhāvanā-heya* (afflictions abandoned by cultivation), as well as ignorance (*avidyā*), have all been exhausted.

When one examines his birth and death (*saṃsāra*), both the *paricchinna-bheda* (segmented) and the *pariṇāma-vikāra* (transformative) types have both vanished. Therefore, he is able to have already departed from the three realms (*tridhātu*). Since...
That which dwells apart from the triple world is the true realm of quiescent light (*śānta-prabhāsa*), free from all clamor and distraction; hence it is said to be "tranquil" and so forth.
Although this is realized through self-attainment, because one is permeated by great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), one must again manifest entry into the triple world to deliver sentient beings.
Thus, the triple world is the realm of those to be transformed, and sentient beings are the objects of that transformation.
"There is one who possesses this [seed]. Therefore, it is said that "the triple world is my own. The phrase "only I can save" reveals that no other Buddha is able to deliver them.
This is because the Tathāgata, at the abodes of twenty trillion Buddhas, planted the perfect seed of the One Vehicle;
thus, its beginning was already established. During the intervening period when they regressed from the Great [Vehicle], he again received them with the Small [Vehicle]. Thus...

The middle stage has already been accomplished. Today, by preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* in this royal city, I cause them to attain the opening, showing, awakening to, and entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
this is the completion of that final stage. Forming the karmic connection is I, Śākyamuni; as for their deliverance, it is also I, Śākyamuni.
From beginning to end, through the three stages of planting, ripening, and liberation, no other Buddha is involved. Therefore—
He says, "Only I can save you. △ Second, the verse on the combined analogy of discarding the bench and using the cart, in two parts. First, the verse on the combined analogy of discarding the bench:
Although he instructs and admonishes them, they do not believe or accept it, because their attachment to various sensual defilements is so deep.
Regarding the "spoken instructions": at the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka*, [the Buddha] exclaimed, "How marvelous! How marvelous!
All sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtue, and nature of the Tathāgata. Those of inferior capacity present in the assembly neither saw nor heard this.

Since they neither saw nor heard it, by what means could they have believed and accepted it? This refers to the verse in the prose section beginning with, "They merely run hither and thither," and so forth.
The passage beginning with "Regarding all those below" clarifies the reasons for their lack of faith. △ Second, the verse on the application of the vehicle:
By these skillful means, he teaches the three vehicles to enable all sentient beings to understand the suffering of the triple world, and he reveals and expounds upon it.
As for the supramundane path: these sons, if their minds are resolute, will be endowed with the three knowledges and the six supernormal powers;
some will attain the state of a pratyekabuddha, while others will become non-retrogressive bodhisattvas.

The prose section consists of three parts: first, the application of skillful means through mindfulness; second, the provision of the three vehicles; and third, the sons’ acceptance and practice thereof. Now, these are fully versified:
the first line versifies the application of skillful means through mindfulness; the second line and one phrase versify the provision of the three vehicles;
and the third line and two phrases versify the sons’ acceptance and practice. The first part is self-evident. The next [part] speaks of causing them to know.
"The fruits of suffering in the three realms" means causing them to know the causes and fruits of suffering within the world.
"Revealing the supramundane" means causing them to know the causes and fruits of the supramundane.

Regarding the phrase "these sons" among the three [vehicles], once they have heard the teachings on the three vehicles, they are able to believe and accept them as they are suited to those of lesser capacity.

And thus they initiate their practice. Therefore, they are called "these sons. "Certainty" means being resolute. That is to say, when a śrāvaka is resolute, he initiates his practice based on the Four Noble Truths;
up to and including when a bodhisattva is resolute, he initiates his practice based on the Six Perfections.

Through such practice, they enter into realization; thus, there are those who possess the three types of supernormal knowledge (*traividya*) and the six supernatural powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), and there are those who attain [the fruits].
Among those of the Śrāvaka vehicle, there are some who attain the Pratyekabuddha vehicle and some who attain the Bodhisattva vehicle.
Their non-retrogression refers to the thirty-four moments of mind; this is non-retrogression in terms of stage (*avasthā*). △ Third, the verse on the analogy of bestowing equal great chariots.
"Śāriputra, for the sake of sentient beings, I have used this parable to teach the Single Buddha Vehicle.
If you all can believe and accept these words, you shall all attain the path of Buddhahood. This vehicle is subtle and wondrous; it is pure and supreme."
Among all worlds, it is unsurpassed; it is what the Buddha delights in; it is that which all sentient beings should praise, make offerings to, and prostrate before.
It consists of immeasurable billions of powers, liberations, meditative concentrations, wisdoms, and the other dharmas of a Buddha.
Having obtained such a vehicle, they cause all their children to constantly sport day and night throughout kalpas, together with the bodhisattvas and the assembly of śrāvakas.
Riding upon this precious vehicle, they proceed directly to the site of enlightenment. For these reasons, one should seek it earnestly throughout the ten directions.
There is no other vehicle besides the Buddha’s skillful means.

In both prose and verse, as well as in dharma-explanations and parables, all four [elements] are present; now, however, only the bestowal by the elder and so forth is combined, while the preceding section also contains three.

This means "immediately and correctly bestowing" and "showing the body of the chariot," which explain the reason [for the bestowal]. Now, first, the reason is explained in combination with the two lines beginning with "O Śāriputra.
Next, the body of the chariot is shown in combination with the three lines beginning with "the vehicle."
The three combined accord with the three practices. That is to say, they correspond to the three types of conduct.

Regarding the initial explanation of the reasons, there are two parts above, which are also combined accordingly. The first practice has the meaning of "abundant wealth," which corresponds to "immeasurable wealth.
The second practice has the meaning of "many sons," which corresponds to "how much more so for the sons. In the first part, it says: "By means of this parable..."
The term “etcetera” refers exclusively to the white ox-cart, which serves as a metaphor for the Single Buddha Vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*).

As for what is called the Single Buddha Vehicle: it is that which can transport one back to the secret treasury of the three virtues. Regarding this Buddha Vehicle, if one examines the teaching that expresses it (*vyañjana*), there is only the teaching of the Single Vehicle;
there is neither a second nor a third. Thus, while the teaching is one, if one examines the principle expressed by it (*artha*), it is the Dharma... [text ends]... of the Dharma.
Abiding in the station of the Dharma, the characteristics of the world are eternally constant; thus, the principle is one. Discussing the practice that arises from it:
"Directly abandoning expedient means, he teaches only the unsurpassed Way"; thus, the practice is one. Discussing the person capable of cultivation:
If there are those who hear this Dharma, there are none who do not achieve the path of Buddhahood; yet since people are one [in nature], it is therefore called the Single Buddha Vehicle (Ekayāna).

Having thus taught the Single Buddha Vehicle for the sake of sentient beings, the convergence of many meanings is clearly established. Next, regarding the phrase "faithfully accepting these words" and so forth:
it means that the teachings, the principles, and the practitioners herein described are all without exception one; they are all without exception...
Excellent! Since you are able to believe and accept this, you know that if one hears the Dharma, there is no doubt they will attain Buddhahood.

The three vehicles are all the One Vehicle, and the nine realms all return to the Buddha-realm. How could there be anyone who would not attain Buddhahood? Therefore it is said, "All [sentient beings]" (and so forth).
Since all are capable of attaining Buddhahood, the many meanings of the term "seed" (*gotra*) are also clearly elucidated. Next...
This vehicle and so forth collectively demonstrate the body of the chariot. Above, there are three aspects, which are the essence, the principle, and the function of the three virtues (*triguṇa*).
Although the text here does not follow a sequential order, all [three] are nevertheless present. The first phrase provides a general synthesis; "pure" and following provide specific syntheses.

The first phrase synthesizes *prajñā* (wisdom); the passage beginning with "among all" synthesizes the *dharmakāya* (dharma-body); and the passage beginning with "immeasurable" synthesizes *vimukti* (liberation). The textual divisions are as follows.
Now, to explain this in summary: as for "this vehicle" (*yāna*) and so forth, it refers to the Buddha-vehicle of the three virtues.
Although these are what the Tathāgata has realized, there is not a single sentient being whose mind does not fully possess them; therefore, they are called "subtle" (*sūkṣma*).

Because that which is possessed by sentient beings is precisely what all Buddhas have realized, they are called "wondrous" (*miao*). Furthermore, there is nothing among the five abodes or two deaths that is not thoroughly exhausted.
Therefore, it is called "pure. Because it cannot be reached by the nine realms or the three vehicles, it is called "foremost.
This alone is the fundamental intention of all Buddhas and the great causal condition; thus, it is said to be "that which the Buddhas delight in.
Since this is the fundamental intention of all Buddhas and the great causal condition, it is that by which all sentient beings are revealed, shown, awakened to, and enter. Therefore, [it is] one...
All sentient beings should praise, make offerings to, and prostrate before [this].

"Immeasurable and so forth" clarifies that the One Buddha Vehicle is fully endowed with all dharmas, as well as the remaining dharmas of the Buddhas, which refers to the provisional teachings (*upāya-dharma*).
Thus, the body of the carriage, the white oxen, and the attendants are all in perfect accord. Next, having attained such departure, the three practices accord with the correct and equal bestowal.
The first line refers to the fact that [the gifts] were each bestowed upon the sons. The next two lines refer to the fact that they were all equal great chariots.

These two phrases alone within the preceding metaphor are not part of the formal outline (ko-wen). Regarding those who obtain such a vehicle, if one were to discuss this from the perspective of ordinary sentiment:
Thus, days and nights may be short and brief, while kalpas may be long and extended.
Yet, when one awakens to this Buddha-vehicle and practices it, the principle is fully manifested through practice, and practice accords with the principle;

cultivation arises from the nature, and cultivation returns entirely to the nature. Since principle, practice, cultivation, and nature are thus of one essence, then length and brevity, extension and brevity—[are no longer distinctions].
"Swift. This is likewise no different [from the previous case]. One does not perceive days and nights as being brief, nor does one perceive kalpas as being protracted.
Therefore it is said that "one has attained such a vehicle" (and so forth). △ Fourth, the verse on the analogy of the elder not being deceptive, in two parts:
first, the direct explanation.

I address Śāriputra: You all, my sons, and I, your father—throughout many kalpas you have been scorched by manifold sufferings, which I have rescued you from, causing you to emerge from the triple world. Although I previously spoke of your parinirvāṇa, [it was not yet final].
It merely brings an end to birth and death, yet in reality it is not extinguished. That which must now be accomplished is solely the wisdom of a Buddha.
When you say, "Through many kalpas," and so forth, it means that since you are my sons and I am your father, then whatever belongs to the father also belongs to the sons.
Why do you speak of the Lesser [Vehicle] instead of the Great? Therefore—

The commentary states: "You have been burned by suffering for many kalpas" (and so forth). This indicates that because their faculties were not yet in accord with [the Mahāyāna], he provisionally taught the Hīnayāna to enable them to escape the triple world.
As for the phrase "Although I... and so on, it means that since [the teaching] was intended solely for their rescue and deliverance...
It merely causes [beings] to emerge from the triple world; thus, what was previously taught is not ultimate. Therefore, it is said: "Although I have [said... (and so forth).
Since the three vehicles previously taught are not ultimate, what is it that constitutes the ultimate? It is for this reason [that the following is stated].

It is said that what must now be done is as follows (and so forth). If it is the wisdom of the Mahāyāna, then it not only exhausts the *paricchinna-bheda* (segmented) death, but also exhausts the *pariṇāmi-vaipākika* (transformative) death; therefore, it is ultimate. Thus one knows that where the three provisional [vehicles] are taught, they are fundamentally one reality;
and where this one reality is revealed, it is entirely identical with the three provisional [vehicles]. For this reason, both the one and the three are not false.
△ Second, the threefold turning and interpretation. First, clarifying that the provisional is identical to the real:
