"If there is a bodhisattva among this assembly who can listen with a single mind to the true Dharma of all Buddhas, the World-Honored Buddhas..."

Although those sentient beings who are transformed through skillful means are all bodhisattvas, those who are able to listen with a single mind hear the wisdom spoken by the Buddha through their own sublime intelligence;
it is like water merging with water, or space merging with space—therefore, it is called "single-mindedness. Regarding the phrase "although through skillful means," it is as the Tathāgata [taught].

The fundamental intent lies solely in the ultimate reality (*tattva*). Because the capacities [of sentient beings] do not accord [with that reality], one provisionally teaches expedient means (*upāya*).

One should know that these expedient means are entirely identical to the ultimate reality; therefore, bodhisattvas of sharp faculties who are able to listen with a single mind attain the ultimate reality even within the expedient means.
In this way, it is clear that the teachings of both the Small and Great Vehicles are entirely without falsehood. △ Second, clarifying the teaching of the provisional.

For this reason, if there are people of limited wisdom who are deeply attached to craving and desire, it is for their sake that the Truth of Suffering is taught; thus these sentient beings rejoice, attaining what they have never experienced before.
The Buddha’s teaching on the Truth of Suffering is true and without deviation. Yet, if there are sentient beings who do not know the root of suffering, [it must be taught].

They are deeply attached to the causes of suffering and cannot abandon them even for a moment. For their sake, I employ skillful means to speak the Way: "The cause of all sufferings has craving as its root.
If craving is extinguished, there will be no basis for them to depend upon; the total extinction of all sufferings is called the Third Truth."
For the sake of the Truth of Cessation, one practices the Path and becomes detached from all bonds of suffering; this is called attaining liberation.
From what, then, does such a person attain liberation? They merely become detached from falsehood and call this "liberation," yet in reality, they have not attained complete liberation.
The Buddha said: "Such a person has not yet truly attained parinirvāṇa. Because this person has not yet realized the unsurpassed Way, it is not my intention that they should reach final extinction."

This is the text concerning the Four Noble Truths. The reason for bestowing the Lesser Vehicle is that [the Buddha] considered that sentient beings possess limited wisdom and are furthermore deeply attached to the five desires;
therefore, having no other choice, he bestowed the Lesser Vehicle to accommodate those of lesser capacity.

However, the intention of the Tathāgata does not reside in the minor [teachings]. Some say that the character "dao" (path) in the phrase "the path of expedient means" (*upāya*) is not the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*);
"dao" is merely a word. If it were the Truth of the Path, then a single text would contain two Truths of the Path.
Nevertheless, there is no contradiction in the sense that it constitutes the Truth of the Path (mārga-satya). △ Third, the summary of the Great and Small Vehicles:
I am the Dharma King; possessing mastery over all dharmas, I appear in the world to bring peace and security to sentient beings.
This means that because the Tathāgata wishes to speak of the Great, he speaks of the Great; because he wishes to speak of the Small, he speaks of the Small;
and because he wishes to lead the Small back to the Great, he leads the Small back to the Great. Therefore, the conclusion states: "He is the Dharma King who has attained mastery.
This is possible because he has attained great mastery within the provisional and ultimate teachings of the Great and the Small. Although he himself has [attained this]...
The Dharma is sovereign. Desiring to use that which has been attained to transform and guide all beings, he appears in the world.

However, the purpose of his appearance in the world lies solely in bringing peace and security to sentient beings; therefore, he first bestows the Three [Vehicles] and only thereafter speaks of the One.
And all of these are not in vain. △ Second, the verse on exhorting faith. Regarding this section on exhorting faith:

the two cycles of the Tathāgata’s teaching—the Dharma-exposition and the parable—have now concluded. Those of superior capacity, such as Śāriputra, were already able to believe and understand during the Dharma-exposition.
Those of middling capacity, such as the four great disciples, will likewise certainly [believe] now upon hearing the parable-exposition.

They are able to believe and understand. However, as for those of inferior faculties, even after hearing the two cycles of teaching through both Dharma and parables, there may still be some who are unable to believe and instead give rise to doubt and slander. Therefore, the Tathāgata extensively exhorts them to have faith:
first, he clarifies that those who can believe this sutra are non-retrogressive; next, he clarifies that they are beyond the reach of the two vehicles; and next, regarding...
One exhorts based on the roots of transgression within the causes; that is to say, one who frowns with a face of resentment and harbors doubt will inevitably incur the retribution of sin.
One exhorts based on the retribution of sin in the effects; that is to say, when such a person’s life ends, they will inevitably fall into the three miserable realms.
This shall be explained extensively later as the manner of proclaiming [the teaching]; therefore, it is revealed again and again, for the purpose of...
Those who have already attained faith shall become firm; those who have not yet attained faith shall give rise to it; and those who wish to slander shall refrain from doing so.
Furthermore, this single passage does not exist without cause. If one investigates its source, it is because the preceding Dharma-exposition in verse is not false in its essence.

Regarding the two verses beginning with "In this world of the five turbidities... merely delighting in and attached to various desires," these should not be proclaimed erroneously within this extensive recitation.
Furthermore, regarding the single verse on "shame, remorse, and purity," this should indeed be proclaimed within this extensive recitation.
The text is divided into two parts; first, the brief introduction.
"Śāriputra, I have proclaimed this Dharma-seal for the sake of benefiting the world. In whatever region you may travel, do not propagate it recklessly."
Regarding the term "Dharma Seal" (dharmamudrā): this sutra is the fundamental intention for all Buddhas appearing in the world, from which it is fully expressed.

Through it, the Buddha's knowledge and vision regarding sentient beings are opened. That which is called "unchanging throughout the three periods of time and universally followed by the ten realms" refers to this.
Is this not a definitive standard that cannot be altered? Therefore it is said: "The Seals of the Dharma" (and so forth). △ Second, the explanation and establishment has three parts.
First, they are taught because they are beneficial.
If there are those who hear this and rejoice in it, receiving it upon their heads, you should know that such persons are *avaivartika*.
If there are those who believe in and accept the Dharma of this sutra, these persons have already seen past Buddhas, paid them respectful offerings, and also heard this Dharma.
If there are those capable of believing what you have said, they will see me, and they will also see you, as well as the community of bhikṣus and all the bodhisattvas.
Such a person is an *avaivartika*, which means one who is non-retrogressive.

Because they have heard [the teaching] and attained faith and understanding, they will certainly be able to give rise to practice based on that understanding and enter realization through that practice. Once they ascend to the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), they are immediately in the state of non-retrogression in thought.

Therefore, it is called *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive). To say that one has "already seen a Buddha" means that this sutra is the fundamental intention for the appearance in the world of all Buddhas;
thus, those who can believe in this sutra have already made offerings to the Buddhas of the past.
To say "believe what you have spoken" means that the Tathāgata is the Buddha who speaks, and this sutra is the Dharma that is spoken.
Therefore, by believing in the Dharma that has been taught, one sees the Buddha who taught it.

Having seen the Buddha who taught it, one also sees those who acted as his echoes and influences, those who initiated [the teaching], those for whom he was suited, and those with whom he formed a karmic connection. Thus it is said, "I see him" (and so forth).
Within this single passage, there are three meanings: first, the non-retrogressive bodhisattva; second, seeing the Three Jewels of the past.
Third, [the text] shows that the Three Jewels exist in the present. △ Second, concluding the preceding section and introducing the subsequent one:
This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is taught for those of profound wisdom; when those of shallow understanding hear it, they become confused and fail to comprehend it. All the śrāvakas—
Even Pratyekabuddhas are beyond the reach of their power regarding this sutra. Śāriputra, you yourself have entered this sutra through faith;
how much more so the other śrāvakas? Those other śrāvakas, because they trust the Buddha’s words, follow this sutra in accordance with it.
This is not within the scope of one's own wisdom.
The first two phrases conclude the preceding section; the subsequent passage beginning with "Those of shallow understanding" introduces what follows.
Regarding the phrase "entering by means of faith," Śāriputra, although he is foremost in wisdom, his wisdom belongs to the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna); therefore, he cannot enter the Buddha-wisdom.
As for those who are able to enter [the Dharma] through wisdom, it is entirely due to the power of faith and not the power of intellectual discernment.

Furthermore, although Śāriputra had already severed the afflictions of views and thought, if one were to clarify his stage according to the positions of the teachings, he corresponds to the seventh stage of faith (*śraddhā*) in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjia*), where he has attained a semblance of realization (*sādharmya*).

Entering the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*) from this state of semblance, he was then able to comprehend the Buddha’s wisdom; therefore, it is said that "one enters by means of faith. △ Three: Do Not...

Regarding "do not propagate recklessly": this does not merely mean that one must not propagate it at all; rather, it means that one should propagate what is worthy of propagation. If something is not worthy of propagation, do not propagate it recklessly.
This is divided into two parts: first, clarifying what is not worthy of propagation; second, from "If there are those of sharp faculties" onwards, clarifying what is worthy of propagation.
The first part is further divided into three sections. First, clarifying the person to whom it should not be spoken.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, do not preach this sutra to those who are arrogant, indolent, or possessed by the view of a self.
Do not preach it to ordinary people of shallow understanding who are deeply attached to the five desires; they will hear it and yet be unable to comprehend it.
Regarding the phrase "those who are arrogant and so forth," this refers to non-Buddhists who harbor views of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*) as well as ordinary worldlings who are attached to the five desires.

**II. Explaining the Sins of Not Believing and Accepting.** First, from the sixth line beginning with "If there are people here... for six lines, it explains that because they slander the sutra, they fall into hell.
Second, from the sixteenth and a half lines beginning with "From the earth... for sixteen and a half lines, it explains [the consequences] after emerging from hell.
They become animals. Third, if they obtain the lower seven stages, it clarifies that they emerge from the realm of animals and return to being human.
Fourth, as described in the following nine lines, it clarifies that even as humans they may still encounter the eight difficulties.
This is like the wheel of a chariot or the turning of a ring, never ceasing for a moment; this is due to their lack of faith in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
Therefore, the retribution for such actions at the time of fruition is as follows. The text is divided into four parts. First, falling into hell:
if a person does not believe and slanders this sutra, they sever all seeds of the Buddha in the world; or again, if they frown.
Yet you harbor doubts; listen now as I describe the retribution for this person's offense.

Whether the Buddha is in the world or has entered parinirvāṇa, should anyone slander such a sūtra as this, or upon seeing one who reads, recites, copies, or upholds it, treat them with contempt, disdain, or jealousy—[such a person shall suffer this fate].
Yet they harbor resentment; hear now further of this person’s retribution for their sin: when that person’s life ends, they enter the Avīci Hell and remain there for a full kalpa.
When the kalpa ends, they are reborn again; thus they continue in succession through incalculable kalpas.

Regarding the statement "cutting off the Buddha-seed in the world": even such acts as raising a hand, bowing the head, offering a single flower, or a single canopy all lead to the attainment of the Buddha-way.
This clarifies the Buddha-seed of the worldly *pratyaya-hetu* (conditioning cause). If one does not believe this, then one cuts off the worldly *pratyaya-hetu* Buddha-seed.
If there is anyone who hears the Dharma, there is none who will not become a Buddha. This clarifies the worldly *vibhāga-hetu* (discriminating cause).
The Buddha-seed. If one does not believe in it, then one cuts off the Buddha-seed that is the "revealing cause" (*vijñapti-hetu*) for the world.

However, the Buddha-seed that is the "direct cause" (*hetu-hetu*) seems impossible to cut off. If both the conditional and revealing causes are severed, by what means would the direct cause be manifested?
In that case, even the direct cause of the Buddha-seed within the world would be severed. Therefore, it is said: "Then one cuts off all... (and so forth). △ Second, becoming an animal.

Emerging from hell, they shall fall among the animals, such as dogs or jackals; their forms will be emaciated, dark-complexioned, and afflicted with scabies and leprosy, tormented by others and held in contempt and loathing by men, constantly distressed by hunger and thirst until their flesh and bones are withered away.
In life they suffer bitter torment; in death they are struck by tiles and stones. Because they have severed the seed of the Buddha, they undergo this retribution for their sins.
If they are reborn as a camel or among donkeys, their bodies must constantly carry heavy loads while being subjected to whips and beatings; they think only of water and grass, knowing nothing else.
Because they slander this sutra, they incur such transgressions as these. They may become jackals that enter villages with bodies covered in scabies and sores, and lacking one eye;
they will be beaten and pelted by children, undergoing various pains and sometimes meeting death.
Having died there, they further receive the body of a python; its form is vast and long, measuring five hundred yojanas.
It is deaf and mute, without feet, crawling along on its belly, being bitten and eaten by various small insects. Day and night it undergoes suffering without any respite.
Because they slander this sutra, they incur such offenses.

As for the statement that they fall among dogs and jackals: it is because those who ought to naturally respect and give rise to faith in this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* instead fail to believe it out of negligence and, conversely, give rise to slander; therefore, they fall among dogs, for the nature of a dog is characterized by negligence. This...

Regarding the Lotus Sutra, one ought naturally to give rise to courageous faith and uphold it as the fruition of one's own practice; yet, through negligence, one fails to believe and instead gives rise to slander.
Consequently, one falls into the state of a jackal, for the nature of a jackal is weak and pliant. One is then born among camels and donkeys.
This sutra is the most correct and great vehicle. If one gives rise to slander and lacks faith, it becomes a deviant vehicle;

therefore, one falls among camels and donkeys. Furthermore, those with only one eye—this sutra clarifies that all sentient beings can attain the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision—if one harbors doubt and gives rise to slander, what one perceives will be partial; thus, one becomes a jackal.
Furthermore, there is only one eye. Those who receive the body of a python do so because, being as ignorant and faithless as a python, they slandered this sutra.

As for the statement that "small insects bite and eat" them, it is because during their causal phase, when they slandered this sutra, the person before them was ignorant and there were others who believed their slander;
now, having fallen into the body of an insect, they undergo suffering, and thus [the retribution] returns to them.
They eat their flesh. △ Third, they are reborn as humans.
If they obtain a human birth, their faculties are dull and dark; they are short, deformed, crippled, blind, deaf, or hunchbacked. Whatever they say, [others do not believe].
People do not believe or accept [his words]. His breath is constantly foul-smelling. He is possessed by malevolent spirits. He is poor, lowly, and base, being made to serve others.

He suffers from many ailments and emaciation, having no one to rely upon. Even if he associates closely with people, they pay him no heed. Should he happen to acquire anything, [he loses it immediately].
Soon after, they are forgotten and lost. If one practices the way of medicine, treating illnesses according to prescriptions, it may instead increase the ailments of others or even cause death.
If one falls ill oneself, there is no one to provide relief or treatment; even if one takes excellent medicine, the condition worsens and intensifies. Or, if another person commits treason...
Those who have committed such offenses as plundering, robbing, and stealing shall suffer their calamities through no fault of their own.

As for those whose faculties are dull and obscured, if they can believe in this sutra, their faculties will become sharp and penetrating. Since they now do not believe and instead give rise to slander, their faculties remain dull and obscured;
yet if they could believe in this sutra, their bodies would grow tall, magnificent, and beautiful, with hands and feet that are supple and delicate.
[The Buddha] said, "Soft! Since you now do not believe, your body is thus stunted and ugly, and your hands and feet are withered and crippled.

Had you been able to believe this sutra, the eyes born of your parents would have seen through to the great trichiliocosm, and your ears would have heard through to the great trichiliocosm. Now that you do not believe, [the fruit of your merit is thus]."
Therefore, you are blind and deaf. Had you been able to believe this sutra, your mouth would have constantly emitted the fragrance of blue lotuses and other scents;
now that you do not believe it, your mouth is perpetually foul-smelling. Had you been able to believe this sutra, the various devas would have protected you day and night;
now that you do not believe it, you are possessed by ghosts. Had you been able to believe this sutra, you should have...
He was once honored with offerings from humans and devas; now that he does not believe, he is thus poor, destitute, and lowly.
Had he been able to believe this sutra, the youths of the various heavens would have served as his attendants; now that he does not believe, he is instead made to serve others.
The rest may be seen in the subsequent list. △ Fourth, encountering the eight difficulties.
Such a sinner shall never behold the Buddha, the King of all Sages, who preaches the Dharma to transform and instruct beings.

Such a sinner will always be born in difficult circumstances, mad, deaf, and mentally deranged, never hearing the Dharma for as many incalculable kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River.
Upon birth, they will invariably be deaf and mute; their faculties will be incomplete, and they will dwell constantly in the hells as if they were pleasure gardens.
They will regard other evil realms as their own homes, with camels, donkeys, pigs, and dogs as their places of activity. Because they slander this sutra, they incur such transgressions.
If they obtain a human birth, they will be adorned with blindness, deafness, muteness, and dumbness; with poverty and various forms of decay as their ornaments;
and with dropsy, consumption, scabies, leprosy, and abscesses as their clothing. Their bodies will constantly emit foul odors, being filthy and impure.

Deeply attached to the view of self, they increase their anger and lust grows so fierce that they do not distinguish between humans and beasts; because they slander this sutra, they incur such offenses as these.

Regarding those who are insane or deaf: had they been able to believe this sutra, their mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) would have been able to know that all necessities of life and worldly activities accord with the True Dharma.

Now, because they do not believe it, their minds are disordered. Had they been able to believe this sutra, all sounds would have pervaded the trichiliocosm, and they would have been able to hear the sounds of that trichiliocosm. Now, since they do not...
Because he lacked faith, he was born deaf and mute from birth. All of the above are the karmic results summoned by slandering the Dharma;
these are actual occurrences, not mere metaphors, nor are they symbolic representations of the Dharma. One should understand it thus. △ Third, the conclusion that unifies all common [teachings].
I tell you, Śāriputra: were one to speak of the offenses of those who slander this sutra, they would not be exhausted even at the end of an eon.
For this reason, I say to you: do not preach this sutra among people who lack wisdom.
The first line concludes the offense of lack of faith. The next line concludes those to whom [the teaching] must not be transmitted.
△ Second, clarifying those to whom it may be transmitted, in three parts: first, a general clarification of merit and wisdom.

If there are those of sharp faculties, whose wisdom is clear and lucid, who are widely learned and possess strong memory, and who seek the Buddha-way—for such persons as these, one may indeed preach it.

If there are people who have seen hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas in the past, who have planted various roots of goodness, and whose profound resolve is firm and steadfast; [for them, one may preach it].

Such a person may be taught this. The first one and a half lines clarify wisdom (*prajñā*): a person possessing wisdom does not share the shallow views of ordinary beings, but is able to believe and accept [the teaching];
therefore, it should be taught to them. The next one and a half lines clarify merit (*puṇya*): a person possessing merit does not [share the views of] outsiders...
Because they harbor the view of a self regarding the Way, one must likewise preach to them. △ Second, specifically citing the six perfections as six [sections].
First, clarifying diligence:
if a person is diligent, constantly cultivating a mind of compassion, and does not begrudge their own body or life, then one may preach to them.
△ Second, explaining meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
If a person is reverent, free from distracted thoughts, and has distanced themselves from all ordinary and foolish people to dwell alone in mountains and marshes—such a person as this...
Then one may explain it to them. Furthermore, Śāriputra, if one sees someone who has abandoned evil associates and draws near to virtuous friends, to such a person one may explain it.
That which is called a "good friend" refers to one who is able to discern the shallow and the deep—a person established in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Because such a person causes one to abandon evil associates (*pāpamitra*), it is said that those who are "nearby" are indeed good friends. △ Third, the explanation of upholding the precepts.
If you see a son of the Buddha who maintains pure precepts like a clean, bright pearl and seeks the Mahāyāna sūtras— to such a person as this,
you may then preach it.
△ Fourth, the elucidation of patience (*kṣānti*).
If a person is free from anger, upright and gentle, always compassionate toward all beings, and reveres the Buddhas—such a person as this...
Then one may explain it to them.
△ Fifth, explaining giving:
Furthermore, there are sons of the Buddha who, amidst the great assembly, with a pure mind, employ various causes and conditions, parables, and expressions.
He preaches the Dharma without impediment. It is only for such a person that one may preach.
"Preaching the Dharma equally among the assembly" means bestowing the wealth of the Dharma upon all. Since it says "various," it refers to the provisional;
since it says "without impediment," it refers to the real. Because he is able to bring the provisional and the real into mutual identity, he is so titled.
It is unimpeded. △ Sixth, clarifying wisdom:

If there is a bhikṣu who, for the sake of all-knowledge, seeks the Dharma in the four directions, receiving it with palms joined upon his head, and takes delight solely in its upholding and retention.
To such a person—one who would not accept even a single verse from any other sutra, let alone a Mahāyāna scripture—only then may one preach [this teaching].

Just as a person with a sincere heart seeks the relics of the Buddha, so too does such a person seek this sutra; having obtained it, they receive it upon the crown of their head, and that person shall no longer... [turn away].
Those who aspire to seek other sutras, yet have never even thought of the scriptures of non-Buddhists—such persons may be taught this.
Regarding the phrase "as if a person with a sincere mind," etc., it means that because one perceives their earnestness in seeking the Dharma, they may then be taught.
△ Third, the common conclusion and dedication.
I tell you, Śāriputra: those who seek the Buddha-way and for whom these characteristics are described would not reach the end of them even in the course of an entire kalpa.
Such persons as these are able to believe and understand; you should preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* to them.

Regarding the statement that "it cannot be exhausted even by the end of kalpas," one should know that the essence of the *dharmatā* (true reality) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* penetrates the three periods of time vertically and extends throughout the ten directions horizontally. It existed before heaven and earth yet its beginning is not seen;
it will exist after heaven and earth yet its end is not seen. Because it cannot be conceived through mind or speech, should anyone harbor doubts regarding it...
They give rise to slander; yet, for those who develop faith and accept and uphold [this teaching], the merits and demerits they thereby obtain could not be fully exhausted even in an entire kalpa.
The explanation of the "Parable Chapter" is concluded.

The Explication of the Lotus Sutra, Fascicle Two, Part Three.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty, by Imperial Decree.
Tiantai Teaching and Contemplation: Lecture Record of Master Yisong Compiled and Edited by the Eastern Ou Buddhist Xiaorou and Guanghe The Chapter on Faith and Understanding,
the Fourth of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* (The Lotus Sutra)
Regarding the sequential generation of this chapter, it is entirely because, within his discourse on the Dharma,
the Tathāgata extensively elucidated how all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time, as well as I, Śākyamuni, do not fail to open up the three to manifest the one.

He opened up his provisional teachings to reveal the ultimate reality. Thus, through this single round of discourse, those of superior faculties such as Śāriputra were immediately able to realize that the three vehicles are fundamentally the one vehicle. Although those of superior faculties attained realization, those of middling and inferior faculties remained deluded;
therefore, at the request of Śāriputra, the Tathāgata provided an illustrative explanation, first clarifying the general analogy by means of a parable.

Regarding the Dharma transformation throughout the five periods: it begins with the illumination of capacities upon the ground of the *dharmakāya*, and concludes with the bestowing of the white ox-cart and so forth.
Within this interval, the three carts are shown as an inducement, and the reasons for each bestowal are made manifest.

This precisely illustrates that the three vehicles taught through the Dharma-exposition (*dharmadeśanā*) are in fact the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Since the parables were established on the basis of the Dharma, they in turn serve to clarify the Dharma.
This is correct. Thus, both the dharma and the parable clarify the capacity and the object, marking both together.

Consequently, there were those of middling faculties, such as the four great disciples, who understood the profound dharma of the three vehicles and the one vehicle from the shallow parables of the three carts and the single cart.
Having attained realization, they then recounted what they had understood to the Buddha; therefore—

This single chapter on "Faith and Understanding" (*śraddhā-adhimukti*) is the text describing the realization and reception [of the Dharma] by those of middling faculties. Regarding the terms "faith and understanding":

that which is characterized by a profound mental inclination, a longing desire, and freedom from doubt is called "faith" (*śraddhā*). That which is as clear and distinct as an object illuminated by a lamp is called "understanding" (*adhimukti*).

Nevertheless, in what dharma does one ultimately have faith, and what does one understand? Generally speaking, "faith" means having faith that what was taught forty years ago was provisional (*upāya*), and having faith that what is being taught today in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the reality (*bhūta*).

Regarding these teachings of the provisional and the real, one has no lingering doubts or obstructions; hence, it is called "faith. As for "understanding," it means understanding that the provisional [teachings] of the past were not...

To depart from the real in order to possess the provisional is, in fact, to realize the provisional within the real. To understand the reality of today is likewise not to possess the real by departing from the provisional;
rather, it is to realize the real within the provisional. Thus, in this state, the provisional and the real are non-dual, and the provisional and the real are of one essence.

It is understood with perfect clarity; hence it is called "understanding" (*jie*). As Tiantai said: "When faith arises, understanding is born; when doubt departs, the principle becomes clear. This is precisely what is meant here.

Because one understands that the provisional is identical to the real, and that the three vehicles are identical to the One Vehicle, one knows that the Śrāvaka vehicle need not be shifted or transformed;
it is, directly beneath one's feet, the Buddha Vehicle. Therefore, it is said: "We..."
Now you are truly śrāvakas; by means of the sound of the Buddha-way, you cause all to hear. This is precisely the meaning of faith and understanding.

The text of this chapter is divided into two parts: first, the narrator’s account of their joy; second, from "We who dwell among the saṃgha" onwards, the disciples' presentation of their understanding.
The first part is further divided into three sections. First, the account of those who inspire joy.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti, Mahākātyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, and Mahāmaudgalyāyana—regarding the term "Venerable" (āyuṣmat):
Subhūti was foremost among those who understand emptiness; he had originally taken emptiness as his life-force (jīvita), and now...
Having heard the parables, he attained realization of the Buddha’s wisdom and took that wisdom as his very life; thus he was called Subhūti, meaning "Wisdom-Life.
As for why all three were titled "Mahā," Mahākāśyapa alone was consistently called Mahā to distinguish him from the other two Kāśyapas.
That the current two are also called Mahā must surely have a specific intention. [This refers to] Kātyāyana.
Among those of the Hīnayāna, Maudgalyāyana was foremost in doctrinal discussion; among those of the Hīnayāna, Maudgalyāyana was foremost in supernatural powers.
Now, having heard this parable, he is able to understand that the provisional is identical to the real.

Thus, his former Hīnayāna expertise in doctrinal discussion and supernatural powers is transformed into the inconceivable doctrinal discussion and supernatural powers of the Mahāyāna; for this reason, he is also called "Mahā."

Thus it is. Since both individuals have their own specific intentions, Kāśyapa is not a case of the general rule. Kāśyapa was foremost among those of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) in ascetic practices;

now that he is able to understand the provisional as being identical to the real, all his former Lesser Vehicle ascetic practices are fully transformed into the inconceivable and wondrous practices of the Mahāyāna.
Therefore, he is not a case of the general rule. △ Second, the description of the Dharma he delights in.
Having heard from the Buddha this unprecedented teaching— that the World-Honored One had bestowed upon Śāriputra the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—
he gave rise to a mind of rare wonder.

"Regarding what was heard from the Buddha," and so forth, this is a general summary of hearing the Dharma of the two cycles—the Parable and the Dharma-exposition—which were all unprecedented for the forty years prior.
When the World-Honored One bestowed the prediction upon Śāriputra, it specifically details what was heard during the Dharma-exposition:
whereas in the past he had only predicted the Bodhisattvas, now he bestows a prediction upon a Śrāvaka, giving rise to a sense of rare wonder.
A separate account of hearing the parables: the metaphors of the three carts and the one cart were previously unheard of;
having now finally heard them, he gives rise to a sense of rare wonder. △ Third, an account of his reverential demeanor.

Filled with joy and exultation, he immediately rose from his seat, adjusted his robes and bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with single-minded devotion joined his palms.
Bowing low in reverence and gazing up at the Honored One’s countenance, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Joyfully joining the palms and gazing upon the countenance," and so forth, have the same meaning as that explained previously regarding Śāriputra.
As for the mention of the "right knee" and "right shoulder," these signify compliance and obedience. Generally, the term "left" carries the sense of non-compliance;
therefore, those who practice external dharmas and do not accord with correct principle are called followers of the "left path" (vāmamārga). A reduction in official rank is called... [text ends]
This was a demotion. Now, the Tathāgata has provided this analogy and teaching.

That the four great disciples were able to believe, comply with, and receive it in such a manner is why he bared his right shoulder and rested on his right knee to manifest this. Single-mindedness is the mental karma (*manas-karman*).
To address the Buddha is an act of verbal karma; the rest are acts of bodily karma. Therefore, the three types of karma are presented together in this ritual of reverence.

II. The Responsive Audience’s Confession and Acceptance has two parts: first, the prose; second, the verse. The first [part] has two sections: first, a brief explanation based on the Dharma; second, from "World-Honored One, we...
onwards, an extensive elucidation by means of analogies. The first [of these two] also has two parts: first, recounting the past; second, clarifying the present. The first [of these]:
2. First, the introduction:
We occupy the foremost positions among the Saṃgha; our years are advanced and we are decrepit. We considered ourselves to have already attained nirvāṇa and were no longer capable of further service.

They no longer advance to seek *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, claiming that because they occupy the headship of the Saṅgha, their years are advanced in age, and they have attained the three meanings of *nirvāṇa*, they are incapable of the task (and so forth).

"Capable" (*kṣama*) means being able to bear and undertake the responsibility; thus, one should know that [the reasons] such as occupying the headship of the Saṅgha constitute two [grounds for refusal].

Under each phrase, there should be the phrases "incapable" (*akṣama*) and so forth. Furthermore, above the two phrases "knowing that [the Buddha] had grown old and attained *nirvāṇa*," the two characters "we" (*vayam*) should be added.
Only by thus connecting from the bottom up to the top will its meaning be fully revealed.
△ Second, the explanation and establishment has two parts. First, the direct explanation.

In the past, when the World-Honored One had been preaching the Dharma for a long time, I was seated among the assembly; my body grew weary and exhausted, and I thought only of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
As for the Bodhisattva teachings—sporting with supernatural powers, purifying Buddha-lands, and bringing sentient beings to maturity—I felt no joy or delight in them.
Regarding the phrase "those who have long been preachers of the Dharma" at the beginning: this establishes the meaning of dwelling at the head of the Saṃgha; thus it says "long.
This means that since the World-Honored One has long been preaching the Dharma, we too have long heard the Dharma. Because we have long heard the Dharma, we dwell at the head of the Saṃgha.
Now, being at the head of the Saṃgha and having long heard the Dharma, one would naturally find no joy in the teachings of the Bodhisattvas.
Therefore, it was said previously: "We occupy the foremost positions among the saṃgha, yet we are incapable [of fulfilling our duties]," and so forth.
That "the body is weary and lax" means that the years have grown old; because one remains long at the seat of assembly, the body becomes weary and lax, and thus the years grow old.
Since the years are advanced and the body is weary and lax, one no longer finds joy in the Bodhisattva-dharma. Therefore, it was said previously: "I..."
"Those of equal age are all decrepit... (and so forth). "But one contemplates emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
This explains the attainment of the meaning of *nirvāṇa*. Emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness are the three gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*) of the Hīnayāna;
they are the very samādhis that are cultivated. *Nirvāṇa* is liberation. By cultivating these three kinds of samādhi, one can reach *nirvāṇa*; therefore, it is so named.

These three are the gates to liberation. Regarding the samādhi of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*): if one calculates that there is a self (*ātman*) and what belongs to a self (*ātmīya*), then this is existence and not emptiness.
Now, by practicing this samādhi, one no longer calculates a self or what belongs to a self;
therefore, it is called the samādhi of emptiness. Regarding the samādhi of signlessness (*animitta-samādhi*): if one calculates that there is a...
To transcend the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism is to possess characteristics rather than being without characteristics.

Now, by practicing this samādhi, one no longer perceives oneness, difference, annihilation, or eternity; therefore, it is called the signless (animitta) samādhi. As for the wishless (apraṇihita) samādhi:
Although one does not conceive of "self" or "what belongs to self," one may still conceive of annihilationism or eternalism;
although one does not conceive of annihilationism or eternalism, one may still conceive of "self" or "what belongs to self. This is then "with effort" rather than "effortless.

Now, by practicing this samādhi, one no longer conceives of "self" or "what belongs to self," nor does one again conceive of annihilationism, eternalism, and so forth; therefore, it is called "effortless."
It is samādhi. Because of the three samādhis, one attains nirvāṇa. Having attained nirvāṇa, one contemplates only the three emptinesses and takes no delight even in the dharmas of a bodhisattva.
Therefore, it was said previously: "We have already attained nirvāṇa and shall not [further... (etc.).
From this, we know that within the current formal explanation as well, when the World-Honored One has finished preaching the Dharma...

"Even when one has long since descended [into the lower realms], there should still be the Dharma of a bodhisattva; even when one’s mind finds no joy [in the higher states], there should still be the Dharma of a bodhisattva.
At that time, while I was seated, my body became weary and I descended; therein too should there be the Dharma of a bodhisattva (and so forth).

Even when one contemplates emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) and descends, there should likewise be the Dharma of a bodhisattva (and so forth). What is called 'sporting with supernatural powers' (*abhijñā-vikrīḍana*) refers precisely to the bodhisattva."
This is the Dharma. Internally cultivating the methods of contemplation and externally transforming sentient beings constitutes the dual flow of the Way and contemplation.
Regarding "purifying Buddha-lands and bringing sentient beings to fulfillment": when a Bodhisattva practices giving, they gather in sentient beings through that gift;
by the time they attain Buddhahood, those sentient beings who are free from greed are born within their land. This is also the case when practicing up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Those who are born in this manner are all free from greed, and so on, up to being free from delusion; thus, the land is naturally purified.
This is what is meant by the saying: "When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure. △ Second, the further explanation.
Why is this? World-Honored One, you have caused us to emerge from the triple world and attain the realization of nirvana;
furthermore, you have caused us, who are already advanced in years, to [participate] in the Buddha’s teaching and transformation regarding the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of the bodhisattvas.
Not giving rise to even a single thought of fondness or delight—
this explains the aforementioned point regarding the Bodhisattva-dharma, up to the reason why the mind finds no joy or pleasure therein.
However, it does not follow the previous sequence. The first interpretation—that "emptiness" and so forth are merely being recollected—refers to the World-Honored One and others.
The second interpretation—that "I was seated at that time" and so forth—refers to the present [narrator] and others.

As for the two characters "we" (*vayam*) in the middle, they explain that since the preaching of the Dharma has already lasted a long time, this applies to both. Because the preaching of the Dharma has been long, the time I have been seated is likewise long; the intended meaning is "I."
It was previously stated: "The World-Honored One has long been preaching the Dharma, yet our minds find no joy in the teachings for bodhisattvas. Why is this?
It is explained further that there is no other reason; it is simply that the World-Honored One has caused us to rely upon the three trainings of precept, concentration, and wisdom.

Yet, having cultivated the samādhis of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), and having already emerged from the birth and death of the triple world to realize the true principle of nirvāṇa, they do not give rise to even a single thought of delight toward the Tathāgata’s teaching of bodhisattvas who advance in pursuit of bodhi.
Therefore, as I previously said: "One simply contemplates emptiness" (and so forth). Since this is the case for a single passage, it is likewise for all others.
The other two examples are likewise so. Thus, one should know that this passage also follows the pattern of the phrase "For what reason? which governs the subsequent text.
Regarding the Buddha’s teaching and transformation of bodhisattvas and others, it should be stated in full from the beginning:
"For what reason? The World-Honored One has caused us to emerge from the triple world and attain the realization of nirvana. Within the Buddha’s teaching and transformation of bodhisattvas...
[Sa... (as before). Next, the explanation should be stated as follows: "Why is this so? Furthermore, we are now all advanced in years.

Regarding the Buddha’s teaching and transformation of bodhisattvas... (as before). If one examines this closely, the first [version] is brief, while the latter [versions] contain the phrase "regarding the Buddha’s teaching and transformation of bodhisattvas" and so forth;
the second [version] omits the preceding phrase "Why is this so? Thus, in all three texts, the meaning is entirely obscure.

Regarding the structure: unless one contemplates it deeply, it cannot be understood. Thus, one knows that in the preceding "Correct Explanation," the three points beginning with "having long expounded the Dharma in the past" were used to explain the three points beginning with "dwelling at the head of the monastic community.

Now, in this [section], the meaning contained within "having long expounded the Dharma in the past" and the other two is applied to further interpret the three points beginning with "dwelling at the head of the monastic community. As for the phrase "not giving rise to a single thought":
Regarding those who delight in [the teachings]: if one were to discuss this from a general perspective, then the *Avataṃsaka* would be like the deaf and mute, and thus [the Dharma] would not arise;

the *Āgamas* would be like a guarantee, and thus it would not arise; the *Vaipulya* would be like parched and ruined grain, and thus it would not arise. However, speaking according to the ultimate reality, it is precisely the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Although one may comprehend and know it, there is no mind that seeks to grasp it. This is indeed the affair of a Bodhisattva; therefore, regarding the Bodhisattva—
The Dharma does not give rise to even a single thought of attachment or delight. △ Second, clarifying the present:
We now, before the Buddha, have heard the bestowal of the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* upon the śrāvakas.
His heart was filled with great joy; he had never experienced such a thing before. He thought, "I did not expect that today I would suddenly hear this rare Dharma.
I am deeply fortunate to have obtained such great and wholesome benefit—immeasurable treasures acquired without seeking."

First is the Dharma; next is the analogy of the "immeasurable" and below. Regarding the section from "In the beginning, middle, and now" up to "attaining what was never before attained," this clarifies hearing the teaching of the Dharma—namely, that those śrāvakas who were never previously given a prediction [of enlightenment] are now given a prediction as śrāvakas.
Now that I have received this prediction, my heart is filled with great joy; it is something unprecedented.
That I did not expect to attain such great and wholesome benefit even now clarifies the meaning of the parable.

This means that although the śrāvakas were predicted, had I not heard the parable, I would not have been able to understand and realize it, nor would the prediction necessarily have been granted. Therefore, this too was not yet [attained].
I am deeply grateful. Now, the Tathāgata, without waiting for my request, has spontaneously spoken this parable for our sake.
Having heard this rare analogy of the three carts and the single cart, I have come to understand the dharma that the characteristics of the three vehicles and the one vehicle are mutually identical.

Since one has already attained understanding and realization, one will necessarily receive a prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa) just like those of the highest faculties. Therefore, one should deeply rejoice, having obtained this great and wholesome benefit.

"Wholesome benefit" refers to the bestowing of a prediction. Thus, in the sūtra’s introductory section on the dharmas that cause joy, it is stated that when describing the discourse in terms of the Dharma (dharmadeśanā), Śāriputra was given the prediction;
and when describing the discourse in terms of parables (aupamya-deśanā), it is stated that he gave rise to rare... [and so forth].

There is a mind; indeed, the intention is rooted in this. Next, the analogy following "immeasurable" illustrates that [the teaching] was not delivered because of a request from those of middling capacity.
Therefore, it says "immeasurable" (and so forth). △ Second, the extensive clarification through analogy has two parts. First, the statement of the intent.
"Bhagavān, we now wish to speak by means of a parable to clarify this meaning.
Bhagavān, 'the equal' refers to the Tathāgata’s teaching of the parables of the three carts and the single cart.

Now that we have attained understanding of the dharmas of the three vehicles and the one vehicle—and since these dharmas were understood through parables—we shall likewise set them forth by means of parables."

[The commentary] explains: "Therefore it is said, 'World-Honored One' (and so forth). This meaning refers precisely to the principle explained above—that which is obtained spontaneously without seeking.
Thus, after establishing the analogy, it concludes: "I originally had no mind to hope for or seek anything;
now this treasure-trove has arrived of its own accord. After applying this to the Dharma, it concludes: "For this reason, we say that [it] was originally non-existent."
The mind harbors a longing; now the great treasure of the Dharma King has arrived spontaneously. △ Second, the actual exposition, which has two parts:
first, establishing the analogy; second, applying it to the teaching. The first part has two sections: first, the general analogy; second, the specific analogy beginning with "hired labor."
The reason there are these two versions is that within the Tathāgata’s previous parables, there were both general and specific ones;
now, as the four great disciples recount and acknowledge what the Tathāgata has taught, they likewise present two versions of parables, general and specific.
The general parable summarizes the Tathāgata’s guidance throughout his entire career, while the specific metaphors summarize the Tathāgata’s...

Regarding the establishment of the teachings in five periods, the general analogy begins with the period of being taught by two trillion buddhas when one was still young, which corresponds to the passage beginning with "his years were yet immature.

The middle section clarifies the regression from the Great [Vehicle] to the Small [Vehicle] and the wandering through birth and death, corresponding to the passage beginning with "he abandoned his father and fled.
The final section clarifies attaining deliverance in the royal city, corresponding to the passage: "If I obtain my son, I shall entrust him with my wealth."
These points clarify that [the parables] such as "finally at the royal city" and so forth concern matters of contemplation on the stage of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya-bhūmi*);

they are not matters of direct manifestation. As explained in detail below within the separate analogies: first, it clarifies the illumination of sentient beings by the Dharma-body stage, namely, "upon seeing the son, he immediately recognized him," and so forth;
next, it clarifies the preparation of the great [gift] according to their suitability, namely, "he immediately dispatched his attendants," and so forth.
Next, the harmonization through samādhi is clarified; this refers to the secret dispatching of two people, up to and including the overseeing and management of the various goods.

Finally, the revelation and clarification of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is clarified; this refers to the passage beginning with "This is truly my son. Thus, one should understand that these constitute the general parable.

This refers to the stage of the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) prior to [the realization of] the Grounds, where one presciently knows matters even before reaching the site of enlightenment under the Bodhi tree.
This serves as a distinct metaphor to clarify how the Dharma-body illuminates the capacities of beings up until the site of enlightenment, the Bodhi tree, and the five periods of teaching.

However, within this text, the phrasing is frequently intermingled and disordered; if not settled by means of its underlying meaning, it would seem difficult to understand. For instance, it says: "galloping... [and so forth].

He galloped through the four quarters until he encountered his own country; it is further said that he traveled through various villages and passed through cities and towns before finally arriving at the city where his father resided.
Furthermore, it is said that he traveled from place to place as a hired laborer until he happened upon his father’s house.
Such inconsistencies and variations arise because, in the past, the Tathāgata practiced as one of the two vehicles and subsequently established the One Vehicle.

Those with the "round" predisposition already possess the capacity for the Mahāyāna; among them, those who regress from the Great Vehicle and adopt the Small Vehicle are met by the Tathāgata through the Small Vehicle, as they already possess the capacity for the Hīnayāna. Thus, these two types of karma—Great and Small—are embraced within his heart.
Within this process, it is the natural law that either great capacities may move in secret or small capacities may emerge in concealment; these do not conform to a single standard.
Thus, if one speaks of the emergence of small capacities, it is said that he traveled through the four directions, wandering among various villages and going from country to country.

Regarding the passage beginning with "Hiring himself out from place to place... he went to a poor neighborhood," if it were only the great awakening (mahā-yāna) that had been triggered, one would say:
"He encountered [his father] while heading toward his own country; he arrived at his father's city; he encountered him at his father's house. This would not be a place where he obtained wealth.

Therefore, if there were only the small [vehicle] and no great [vehicle], one should not speak of "encountering [him] while heading toward his own country" and so forth. Conversely, if there were only the great and no small, then [the aforementioned account] should not exist.

Regarding the phrase "passing through kingdoms and cities" and so forth, because they possess both the great and the small [vehicles], they are presented here in an intermingled and alternating manner. Therefore, Jingxi said:

"The two karmas, great and small, through subtle permeation and manifest influence, form the conditions that elicit the Buddha's response. This is because one has already been taught the Great [Vehicle] in the past;
thus, the seeds of the great karma are contained within the breast. It is the natural law (*dharmatā*) that the great karma internally permeates, and the Tathāgata accordingly returns [to respond]."

It is through the great manifestation that [the response] is bestowed. If the great capacity is perfected, one then attains the response of the Buddha; this refers to the meaning of "encountering [him] and returning to one's original land," and so forth.

Having already been received by the small [vehicle], the seeds of the small capacity are contained within the breast; it is the natural law (*dharmatā*) that the karma of the small [vehicle] internally perfumes [the mind].
The Tathāgata then returns to manifest through the Small Vehicle. Once those of small capacity have been perfected, they are able to perceive the Buddha;
this refers to the passage concerning his journeying through kingdoms and cities, which is divided into four parts. First, the son departs from his father.
It is as if there were a man who, being still young, abandoned his father and fled. He lived in another country for a long time—perhaps ten, twenty, or even fifty years.
Having grown up and becoming further impoverished, he wandered in all directions in search of food and clothing.
Gradually traveling on, he encounters his own native land.

Regarding the phrase "there are people here," those of the Two Vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) understand this only according to their own respective capacities; thus, they take the Two Vehicles themselves to be "people.

As for the phrase "the years are still young," "years" refers to the spiritual capacity (indriya). At the very beginning, the Great Vehicle was taught, yet the capacity for the Great was still subtle; therefore—

Regarding the terms "infant" (*yòuzhì*) and "already" (*jì*): this means that since their great capacity (*mēi*) is already weak, they ought to remain constantly near the Tathāgata so that it may grow;
yet instead, they rebelliously abandon the Tathāgata. Their abandonment stems from the weakness of their capacity;
thus, being as young as infants, they abandon their father and flee. Just as when a child is young, he ought to remain constantly near his father.
Yet he instead abandoned his father and fled. Having abandoned the Tathāgata, he wanders through birth and death, sinking into the five destinies and unable to emerge from them.

Therefore, it is said that he lived abroad for fifty years; "abroad" refers to the three realms, and "fifty years" refers to the five destinies. That his age has grown great and he is further impoverished means:
Since the planting of seeds in the past, the great enterprise of the Dharma has served as an internal perfuming, whereby the great capacity has moved in secret.
Just as one grows with the passing of years, once the great capacity has been stirred, one should diligently seek the wealth of the Dharma.
They have been sent forth from birth-and-death, yet they instead greedily cling to birth-and-death; impoverished of the wealth of the Dharma, they are tormented by birth-and-death.
It is like a son who, having reached full maturity, ought to manage his own affairs, yet instead fails to do so.

Furthermore, they are impoverished and beset by suffering. Those who wander in all directions in search of food and clothing do so because, having long endured the sufferings of birth and death, a mind of weary detachment has arisen within them and they desire to seek liberation. Yet, although they wish to seek liberation, [they remain bound].

However, regarding the teachings of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles, they are ignorant of both; instead, they give rise to the four views, such as the view of permanence, with respect to phenomena such as the body, seeking thereby the auxiliary and the direct paths.
Thus it is said: "They gallop in the four directions in search of food and clothing."

The four directions represent the arising of the four inversions (*catur-viparyāsa*). Clothing is a metaphor for the auxiliary path (*sambhāra-mārga*), and food is a metaphor for the primary path (*mārga*).

Turning away from false views and returning to right view is like traveling by degrees. Although those of the two vehicles have already turned from the false toward the correct, what they seek is only the minor Dharma;
originally they had no intention for the Great [Vehicle], yet the great capacity has now arrived.
At this time, it is the natural law for [the father] to secretly initiate action.
It is like a destitute son who, though wandering about, seeks nothing more than a single garment and a single meal; he has no intention of reaching his native land, yet by chance, he arrives there.
△ Second, the father comes seeking his son.

His father had previously departed in search of his son but could not find him; he settled in a certain city where his family was immensely wealthy, possessing immeasurable riches and treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, crystal, pearls, and the like—such that all his granaries and treasuries were completely overflowing.
He has many servants, ministers, officials, and subjects; his elephants, horses, carriages, oxen, and sheep are beyond counting.
His income and interest extend throughout other countries, and his merchants and traders are also exceedingly numerous.

Regarding the phrase "having come first": after the Tathāgata had [taught] the two vehicles and [beings] subsequently regressed from the Great Vehicle, yet before their great capacity for it had been activated, he had already sought those with the potential to be transformed.

Therefore, it is said that they "first came seeking to be sons. Since they were previously taught the Great Vehicle, they are capable of inheriting the family legacy of the Mahāyāna through this [teaching];
thus, they are "sons. Having regressed from the Great Vehicle, they nevertheless still fled and avoided it.
Regarding birth and death, both the great and small capacities (*indriya*) are absent at this time; therefore, it is said that [the Buddha] cannot [act].
Since there is no capacity to be transformed, he must seek one out. When seeking, he must remain in a convenient location;

thus, he neither advances to dwell in the Land of True Reward nor retreats to abide in the Land of Common Residence, but stays between these two lands, dwelling in the Land of Expedient Means (*upāya*).
As for the remaining lands, they are therefore called "abiding in the middle. This refers to the *nirvāṇa* within the land of *sopadhiśeṣa* (with remainder), which constitutes a single city.

However, those who must dwell in the land of *sopadhiśeṣa* do so because, due to that remainder, they remain within the midst of the *sambhogakāya* (recompense) and *sahā* (co-resident) realms; thus, they abide therein.
If there is a being of great capacity for the *sambhogakāya*, [the Buddha] then manifests a *vaipākika-uttama-kāya* (supreme transformation body). And...
One should respond from above. If there are small-capacity beings dwelling together [below], one then manifests an inferior response-body and responds from below;
thus, remaining in the intermediate state with a remainder, one seeks out those of transformable capacity. It is convenient whether responding from above or below.
As for those whose families are exceedingly wealthy, this is the land of skillful means where the Tathāgata dwells; his self-enjoyment is entirely eternal.

The Land of Tranquil Light (*śāntaprabhāsa-kṣetra*) and the Land of Other-Enjoyment (*parasaṃbhoga-kṣetra*) are entirely lands free from obstruction; therefore, it is said that "his household is immensely wealthy.

This refers to the family of the True Aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). As for "wealth and so forth," the family of the True Aspect is fully endowed with the teaching, principle, wisdom, severance, practice, stages, cause, and fruit.
The "teaching" (*śāsana*) refers to the names that express [the truth], which collectively comprise seven categories, just as the seven types of precious treasures constitute wealth.

These are the general names for the treasures: gold is firm and precious like the *tathatā* (suchness); silver is white and pure like the *prahāṇa* (abandonment); lapis lazuli is transparent and clear like *jñāna* (wisdom);

coral is like *caryā* (conduct); amber is like the *avasthā* (stages); crystal is like the *hetu* (cause); and the essence of the pearl is like the *manasikāra* (mental application), which may be compared to the *phala* (fruit).
Being fully endowed with concentration and wisdom is like a storehouse; being fully endowed with skillful means (*upāya*) is like servants. Relying on reality...
They dwell together in the House [of the Tathāgata] and cultivate practice. The four teachings differ;

those who sever *dṛṣṭi* and *kleśa* through the four teachings are equally born into the *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, and thus they likewise reside in the House where the Tathāgata dwells while cultivating the *bhūtalakṣaṇa*.

Serving as ministers is like the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*); assisting as aides is like the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*); and serving as officials by drawing near is like the Common Teaching (*tongjiao*).

"Governance for the people is like the Tripiṭaka teachings. This clarifies the person capable of cultivation. The metaphors of the elephant, horse, and so forth refer to the contemplations being cultivated.
The elephant carriage is like the Perfect [Teaching]; the horse carriage is like the Distinct [Teaching];

the ox carriage is like the Shared [Teaching]; and the sheep carriage is like the Tripiṭaka. "Going out" refers to preaching the Dharma to transform others; "entering" refers to contemplating the mind.

Practicing for oneself brings rest to others, and practicing for oneself brings benefit to others. Regarding the phrase "extending throughout other lands": the Land of Peaceful Light (*śāntaprabhā*) is one's own land, while the three lands are other lands.
Because the Tathāgata can universally respond within these three lands, it is said that he "extends throughout other lands.
As for those who "trade and so forth," they are the bodhisattvas of this land who go there to hear the Dharma, and the bodhisattvas of that region who come [to this land].
This is the hearing of the sutra. △ Third, the son arrives at his father’s city.
At that time, the impoverished son wandered through various villages and passed through kingdoms and cities until he finally reached the city where his father resided.
Wandering through birth and death, they lack the wealth of meritorious dharmas; therefore, they are said to be "poor.
Although they currently possess no such wealth of dharma, because they once received the great transformation [of the teaching] in the past, they are called "sons.

Though they received the great [teaching] in the past, they have since completely forgotten it and have fled from birth and death, drifting through the triple world like traveling among various villages. Having remained in birth and death for so long, then—
Regarding all capacities, whether great or small, they naturally and spontaneously manifest in the interim. If a great capacity manifests, it is like traveling from one country to another;
if a small capacity manifests, it is like traveling from one village to another. Thus, it is said that he "traversed countries and villages.
Although both types of capacity possess the sense of manifestation, the small capacity must necessarily ripen first; therefore, it is said that he "finally arrived at" [that place].
The city where the father resides is that which the four great disciples have already divided among themselves;
it takes as its city the remaining lands of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), characterized by partial emptiness and *nirvāṇa*. △ Fourth, the father constantly thinks of his son.
The father constantly thinks of his son, with whom he has been separated for more than fifty years.

This father’s longing for his son is like the Tathāgata, who, from the presence of twenty trillion buddhas, planted great seeds so that [the son] might inherit and carry on the family business of the Mahāyāna.
Because he regressed from the Great Vehicle and temporarily forgot it while adopting the Small, the Tathāgata follows this teaching.
Greatly later, up until this day, I have constantly thought of the child who planted the seed.
Having departed from the Great [State] and entered the five paths of birth and death, I am separated from the Buddha like a son parted from his father for fifty years—
that is, for five lifetimes.
Yet he had never before spoken of such a matter to others; he merely contemplated it within himself, his heart filled with regret.
This is analogous to the five periods. "Never having spoken to others" means that he had never declared that there were children who had formed a karmic connection with this Mahāyāna.
At the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka*, the Tathāgata clarified that all sentient beings possess [the Buddha-nature].
The Tathāgata’s wisdom and virtuous nature—this is the Great. Yet he did not say it was the Great, nor did he explicitly explain the meaning of the Great;
even during the Avataṃsaka period, he never spoke of such matters to others.
When the Tathāgata was at the assembly of the Āgamas, he clarified the teachings of the Tripiṭaka; this is the Small. Yet he did not say it was the Small.
Furthermore, he did not explicitly state the meaning of "small. That is to say, during the period of the Āgamas, he never spoke of such matters to others.

He merely reflected within himself with a heart full of regret; since he had not told anyone that he had a son for whom he was karmically bound, he simply thought of this son to himself and harbored regret within. As for "regret": [it refers to this].

"Regretting that when I previously taught the Mahāyāna, I did not cause them to practice so as to enter its ranks"—this "regret" refers to the regret over having completely forgotten [the teachings] therein, thereby eventually retreating from the Great Vehicle and entering the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

This passage reflects how, within the Vaipulya sūtras of the Tathāgata, various rebukes and censures were skillfully employed through the medium of bodhisattvas from other directions; this is precisely what constitutes harboring regret and remorse in one's heart.
He thought to himself, "I am old and decrepit. I possess abundant wealth—gold, silver, and precious jewels—and my storehouses are overflowing. Yet I have no son;
once I pass away, this wealth will be lost and dispersed, with no one to whom it may be entrusted. For this reason, he earnestly and constantly remembered his son.
Again, he had this thought: "If I were to obtain a son, I could entrust my wealth and property to him; I would then be at ease and happy, free from further anxiety.
As for the reflection on old age and so forth, the Tathāgata contemplated that the time for his parinirvāṇa was drawing near, and considered all his teachings and principles.
Even the dharmas such as meditative concentration and wisdom would be severed if there were no sons of the Mahāyāna to inherit them.
For this reason, I am earnest and constantly mindful of those with whom I have formed karmic connections. This is the time when I receive the Prajñā of the Tathāgata.
By means of the Mahāyāna Dharma, he commands those of the two vehicles to turn their teachings toward the bodhisattvas; this is precisely his earnest remembrance of his son.
Furthermore, the phrase "he then forms this thought" and so forth refers to the time when he received the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

At the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the Tathāgata bestowed predictions upon those of the two vehicles, clarifying that their natures were fixed as father and son. When this moment arrived, [the karmic bonds] of former days...
The conditions have not been in vain; the original intention for appearing in the world has already been fulfilled, and the great causal conditions have already been clarified.
That which is called "the Dharma entrusted to the Dharma-minister" means that the Dharma-King has no further tasks; having only accomplished this matter, there is nothing else remaining.
Therefore, it is said that he is serene and joyful, with no further anxieties. The phrase "if I" refers to Prajñā (wisdom). This is indeed...
He implicitly understands that this is not actually the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* at this very seat, and therefore speaks of the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Nevertheless, within the general analogy, there are five periods; this implies that such matters existed prior to the stage of the Dharmakāya.
That is to say, from the time the Tathāgata first received instruction in the Great [Vehicle] under twenty billion Buddhas, and so forth through the intervening period—

At the time when they were regressing from the Great [Vehicle] to adopt the Small, he instead met them with the Small. Since they had long been wandering through birth and death, a mind weary of suffering arose;
their spiritual capacity was thus perfected and moved the Buddha. Yet, while the Buddha’s original intention was to bestow the Great [Vehicle], he subsequently reflected upon it.
First, one should propose the Great [Vehicle] as appropriate. If they do not find resonance with it, one must then explain the Small [Vehicle] for them.
If I speak of the Small, they will surely accept it with conviction. When they have accepted it, I shall then refute and refine them;
only after this can I deliver them through the Mahāyāna. This was indeed begun at the presence of twenty trillion Buddhas.

From that time until the present day at the Royal City (Rājagṛha), throughout the course of a single lifetime’s work of transformation, who could have foreseen such a thing before the Bodhi tree at the site of enlightenment?
Therefore, when he reached the time of sitting at the place of enlightenment, he first preached the Avataṃsaka Sūtra to accord with what was appropriate for the occasion.
Yet he truly neither saw nor heard anything, remaining as if deaf and mute. Thereupon, [the Buddha] spoke to him of the *Hīnayāna* (Small Vehicle), and he indeed provided confirmation of it.
Thereafter, [the Buddha] spoke of the *Vaipulya* (Extensive) teachings to rebuke him.

He preached the *Prajñāpāramitā* to refine them, and only thereafter did he preach this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* to cause them to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and receive the prediction of their future Buddhahood. The four great disciples previously did not understand this intention;

now, having heard the parables, they have attained awakening and immediately come to fully comprehend the intent behind the Tathāgata’s teachings throughout the five periods of his one-life career. Thus, the Tathāgata has long...
From the stage prior to the Dharmakāya, this has already been prepared and matured; thus, it is received intuitively.

Beginning from the source at the abodes of twenty trillion Buddhas and ending with the final entrustment of the treasure at the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, one employs the vision prior to the Dharmakāya stage to encompass the present occasion of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and by citing the birth prior to the Dharmakāya stage, one clarifies [the matter].
Today, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* has ripened; therefore, this general analogy encompasses a vast and far-reaching meaning, yet it also contains the five periods [of the teaching].
△ Second, the specific analogies. The general analogy, which covers the beginning and the end, has already been explained above.

Now, these specific analogies likewise begin from the Dharmakāya’s illumination of the capacities [of sentient beings] and conclude with today’s *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Thus, the general and the specific each form a complete whole.
This is because both [the general and specific] analogies possess a beginning and an end.

Therefore, following the general analogy, it was already stated that "if I obtain a son, I shall entrust him with my wealth and property," yet within the specific analogy, it is again stated that "the impoverished son works for hire" and so forth.

Furthermore, it is like "another day" and so forth. Moreover, there are two analogies, general and specific: at the beginning there is distance and proximity, but in the end they are identical in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

However, regarding the general analogy, from the time after being with twenty trillion Buddhas until the stage prior to the attainment of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), there is no premeditated foreknowledge;
yet there is transformation through five periods. Therefore, it is said that in the end they are identical in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Nevertheless, if one examines this closely:

In truth, they are not the same; they are divided into five parts. First, the reception of the *Avataṃsaka*; second, the reception of the *Āgama*; third, the reception of the *Vaipulya*; fourth, the reception of the *Prajñāpāramitā*;

and fifth, the reception of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. The first part is further divided into two: first, "the son seeing the father," which refers to the profound resonance of the great capacities of the two vehicles;
second, "at that time the wealthy father sees the sons," which refers to the Tathāgata’s great teaching being tailored to their suitability. The first [of these two] is...
4. The first [section]: The reason for seeing his father.
World-Honored One, at that time the impoverished son wandered about seeking employment.
"At that time" refers to the period after he had already regressed from the Great Vehicle. Having regressed from the Great Vehicle, he possessed no [Dharma].

Because he exhausted his wealth, he is called "poor" (qióng). Because he once received from the Great One, he is a son. To wander through various forms of hired labor and be employed by others is called being a "hireling" (yōng);
to exchange one's labor for wealth is called "hiring out" (zhèn). Because he has receded from the Great and entered into birth-and-death (saṃsāra), [he is thus described].

He grew weary of suffering and desired liberation; yet, not knowing the True Dharma, he clung to various views within the teachings of non-Buddhist paths in order to seek a single robe and a single meal—this is the meaning of "hired labor.
Later, he was able to turn away from the heterodox and return to the orthodox—this is the meaning of "successive progression. △ Second, seeing his father’s dwelling.
He encountered his father’s house and stood by the side of the gate.

Although he had turned from the heterodox to the orthodox, he still took pleasure in the Lesser Dharma. However, when the great seeds of his past nature reached this point, they naturally exerted a subtle influence, and thus his great capacity for enlightenment was stirred in secret;
hence it is said that he "encountered his father’s house. Although his great capacity was stirred, that which he took pleasure in...
The author [notes]: Because his every thought was fixed solely upon the partial emptiness of the Hīnayāna, it is said that he stood by the side of the gate.
△ Third, the vision of his father’s appearance:
From afar he saw his father seated upon the teacher’s throne, with a jeweled footstool supporting his feet, surrounded by various Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and householders.
All paid him respectful homage and surrounded him. Adorned his body with pearl necklaces worth ten million pieces of gold.
