His officials, citizens, and servants stood in attendance at his left and right, each holding white whisks. A precious canopy was spread over him, with various flowered banners hanging down.

Fragrant water was sprinkled upon the ground, and many varieties of famous flowers were scattered about. Precious objects were displayed in rows; as he brought them out, took them in, gave them away, or accepted them, there were all manner of such things.
Adorned with majesty and preeminent in spiritual power, he arrived at his father’s house when his great capacity had been moved in secret resonance; thus, he was able to see his father.

Because [the son] was attached to a biased emptiness and remained by the side of the gate, although he saw him, it was from afar. His sitting upon the lion throne and so forth were all seen from a distance.

Furthermore, because the Tathāgata has attained great fearlessness, he is said to "sit upon the lion throne. His two feet are a metaphor for meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
All the concentration and wisdom possessed by the Tathāgata rely upon the true reality (*dharmatā*), just as two feet rest upon a single jeweled footstool.

*Brāhmaṇa*—here translated as "Pure Conduct"—refers to the lineage of the Equal-Enlightened Kings (*samyaksambuddha*). *Kṣatriya* refers to the tenth stage (*bhūmi*). *Gṛhapati* refers to the third...

"The ten minds all reverently surround him" refers to the forty-one stages of the Great Beings (mahāsattva) of the Dharma-body surrounding [the Buddha] at once, like clouds enveloping the moon. "Pearls" refers to the sublime wisdom possessed by those in the forty-one stages.
"Necklaces" refers to the sublime practices arising from that sublime wisdom within the forty-one stages. This sublime...
This is the wondrous practice of wisdom. Because it is replete with ten thousand virtues, it is said to be worth ten million.
By means of this wise practice, complete with ten thousand virtues, one adorns the Dharma-body of the forty-one stages; thus it is said that "one adorns the body.
This refers to adorning the bodies of the forty-one stages beginning with the Brahmin, and does not refer to the body of the elder.
The officials, citizens, and servants are none other than the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings whose roots of merit have matured in previous lives.

Those standing in attendance at his left and right are the eight classes of beings who witness that the Tathāgata has already perfected the Middle Way, just as the elder occupies the central position. These eight classes...
Those who cultivate emptiness (*śūnyatā*) to sever the afflictions of views and thoughts are like those holding a fly-whisk to attend on the right;

those who cultivate the provisional (*prajñapti*) to sever the afflictions of "dust-sand" [in number] are like those holding a fly-whisk to attend on the left. This emptiness and the provisional are precisely the emptiness and the provisional of the Perfect and Distinctive [Vehicles].
This is to yield to the Tathāgata’s ultimate Middle Way; therefore, it speaks only of "left" and "right," yet in reality, one also cultivates the Middle Way and thereby severes ignorance.
Covering it with a jeweled canopy signifies that the Tathāgata, through his unconditioned great compassion (*nirālamba-mahāmaitrī*), universally covers all beings.
From within this unconditioned great compassion, he gives rise to the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) to gather and sustain all.
Like a canopy suspended with flowers, he manifests great supernatural powers (*mahā-ṛddhi*) to startle and move all beings.
Like a canopy suspended with banners, the Tathāgata is able to sprinkle the water of the principle of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) upon the mental ground of sentient beings' ignorance;
hence it is said that "fragrant water is sprinkled on the ground. To scatter various famous flowers is to cause all sentient beings to cultivate the forty-one stages.
This is the true cause. The arraying of precious objects is precisely that which causes all sentient beings to realize the partial fruits of the forty-one stages.
The taking out, bringing in, receiving, and giving are explained in the same manner as the previous explanation of income, expenditure, and interest. Such is the case.
This summarizes the various adornments mentioned above. Regarding the phrase "supremely venerable in majestic power" (*vibhūti-viśeṣa-guṇa*):
he possesses majesty (*vibhūti*) to subdue all beings, and virtue (*guṇa*) to gather in all beings. His radiance is boundless, and his physical marks (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) are boundless;

this is precisely the *vairocana-śarīra* (body of Vairocana) in its supreme manifestation. Therefore, it is said that he is "supremely venerable in majestic power. However, regarding the two vehicles (*dvaya-yāna*) within the *Avataṃsaka*...
In the midst [of his state], he neither saw nor heard; he was as if deaf or mute. How could he have been able to see such marks of the Tathāgata?
It is simply that, within the capacity of his faculties, this matter existed in a hidden, latent way. △ Fourth, seeing his father, he flees in avoidance.
When the impoverished son saw his father possessed of such great power and majesty, he was immediately seized with terror and regretted having come here. He thought to himself in secret:
"This man must be either a king or one equal to a king; this is not a place where I can obtain wealth through hired labor.

It would be better to go to the poor quarters, where there is room for me to exert my strength and where food and clothing are easily obtained. If I remain here long, I may be coerced and forced [to do what I do not wish]."
Having thought, "It was I who did this," he fled in haste.
His great power refers to the power of wisdom as well as the power of supernatural faculties (*ṛddhi*).

Because the Dharma is vast while his capacity is small, it is said that he immediately became filled with terror. The phrase "perhaps it is the King" means he suspected it was the Māra-king. Or perhaps...
The king and others immediately suspected that these were the sons of Māra or the subjects of Māra.

This was because they suspected that the Tathāgata was the king, and they suspected that the Bodhisattvas and the eight classes of beings were the king’s subjects and so forth; thus they said, "Perhaps it is the king and his subjects here.

"Hiring labor" refers to cultivating the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) of morality, concentration, and wisdom. "Obtaining goods" refers to realizing emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
To "create nirvana" in a "poor village" refers to the partial truth of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) of the Hīnayāna. Because it does not encompass all phenomena (*dharmas*), it is likened to a poor village.
Relying on this partial principle of emptiness, one gives rise to the contemplation of partial emptiness; this is like going to a poor village where there is ample room to exert effort.

By means of the contemplation of partial emptiness, one cultivates the primary and auxiliary practices, all of which can be easily accomplished—just as one might produce clothing by exerting effort [in that place].
"Food is easily obtained. To say "one dwells here for a long time" means that one abides in the Mahāyāna Dharma.
"To compel someone to act" means that one wishes to cause them to sport freely through wisdom and spiritual power. "Running swiftly" means to abandon the Great [Vehicle].
And departing, he immediately takes what is small. △ Second, the father sees his son, in two parts. First, seeing his son and perceiving his capacity:
At that time, the wealthy elder, while on the lion throne, saw his son and recognized him; his heart was filled with great joy, and he immediately had this thought:
"I have wealth and treasuries that must now be entrusted. I have constantly thought of this son, yet had no means to see him;
that he has suddenly come of his own accord is most gratifying to my wishes."
This was originally divided into four parts: first, seeing the son’s location; second, recognizing the son upon seeing him; third, the heart rejoicing at seeing the son;
and fourth, the wish being fulfilled upon seeing the son. Now, these are collectively explained as two:

when the Tathāgata sees the sons of the two vehicles and immediately recognizes them, it is because they were those with whom he had established a karmic connection in the past. Since they are sons with whom he has established such a connection, they are capable of [attaining enlightenment].

Because he has inherited the family legacy of the Mahāyāna, his heart is filled with great joy. Regarding the phrase "he thinks thus," it means that there is something to be entrusted to him as material wealth.
From the time after the Great Teaching until this very day, there has been no moment when he does not think of him; hence the words, "I constantly keep him in mind.
Because [the son] had regressed from the Mahāyāna and fled into the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), it is said that there was no way to see him. Now, the Great...
Seizing the opportunity, the Dharma naturally moves in secret, as if arriving suddenly of its own accord.

To say, "This is most suited to my wish," refers to the vow of the Tathāgata, which desires only to entrust the family legacy of the Mahāyāna to those children with whom he has formed a karmic connection (*karmayoga*).
Now that this great capacity (*mahā-organ*) strikes in secret resonance, the family legacy can from this point be entrusted; therefore, it is said, "This is most suited to my wish. The above.

The explanation of the stage of the Dharma-body, which illuminates the faculties and contemplates the dharmas, is complete. △ Second, the dismissal of the subsequent summary and the presentation of the provisional teaching.

This refers to the passage beginning with "Furthermore, he further contemplated... within the analogy of discarding the small table, which is intended for the Perfect [Teaching]. It also refers to the passage beginning with "I shall further explain... which serves as the presentation of the provisional teaching.

This is intended to distinguish [the provisional from the ultimate]. If one were to include this within the discourse on the Dharma, it would correspond to the verses beginning with "I first sat at the site of enlightenment.

The text is divided into two parts: first, the lack of capacity for the Great [Vehicle]; second, the cessation of the Great [Vehicle] and the suspension of its transformative activity. The first part has two sub-sections: first, the lack of capacity for the Perfect [Teaching].
Although I am old in years, I still cherish [this wealth]. He immediately dispatched an attendant to pursue him in haste and bring him back.
At that time, the messenger ran swiftly to seize him; the impoverished son was startled and terrified, crying out in grievance: "I have done you no wrong! Why do you seize me?"

"An old man who greedily clings" refers to the Tathāgata, who, although possessing immeasurable wealth of the Dharma, has no one to inherit it unless they were a son with whom he had established karmic ties in the past.
Now that his period of transformation is nearing its end and he will soon enter parinirvāṇa, he still greedily clings to this wealth of the Dharma.
"The bystander" refers to the Bodhisattvas; for the Tathāgata acts for the sake of each...
The Tathāgata is the primary subject of transformation, while the Bodhisattvas serve as his assistants. Thus, the Tathāgata is the principal transformer, and the Bodhisattvas are his attendants.

Regarding the term "dispatched" (quán): during the assembly at the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, when the four great Bodhisattvas expounded the forty stages, they each stated, "I speak this by receiving the Buddha's power";
therefore, it is called "dispatched. Regarding the term "immediately dispatched" (jíquán), as for example...
He has come from the presence of twenty trillion Buddhas to plant the perfect seed of the One Vehicle for those of the Two Vehicles.
Because they had regressed from the Great [Vehicle] and fled into the cycle of birth and death, the Tathāgata constantly thought of them, yet there was no way to meet them.

Although their great capacity has now been moved in secret, they have suddenly come of their own accord; however, because that which they delight in and cling to is only the minor Dharma, they immediately ran away.
And he departed. Thereupon, the Tathāgata immediately dispatched a bodhisattva to swiftly convert him by means of the Great Dharma of Sudden and Perfect Enlightenment;
hence it is said that he "immediately dispatched an attendant to pursue and bring him back. The phrase "to bring back" (jiāng huán) means "to lead back" (jiāng yǐn);
it signifies the desire to lead him back. The messenger ran swiftly to seize him, who was none other than the bodhisattva, acting in obedience to the Tathāgata’s command.

This refers to applying the Perfect and Sudden Teaching (yuan-dun fa) to those who are suited for it. Regarding the words "startled and alarmed" (*jing'e*): "startled" (*jing*) means startled with doubt; "alarmed" (*e*) means flustered and taken aback.
Because those of the Two Vehicles delight only in the Lesser Dharma, when they suddenly hear the Perfect and Sudden Teaching, it contradicts their mental dispositions.
Not knowing its source, they are thus startled with doubt and flustered. As for "crying out in resentment," this is because they take afflictions as...
"Enemy. For those who regard birth and death as suffering, hearing now that afflictions are identical to bodhi and birth and death are identical to nirvana is utterly inconceivable;
thus they cry out in protest. △ Second, the particular application lacks the capacity [to receive it].
The messengers seized him even more urgently and forcibly dragged him back. Thereupon, the impoverished son thought to himself, "I am innocent, yet I have been imprisoned;
this must mean certain death. He became increasingly terrified, fainted, and fell prostrate upon the ground.
Since the [Buddha] above found that the Perfect Teaching (yuan) lacked the capacity [of those beings], he again modeled it after the Distinct Teaching (bie).

Thus it is said: "The messenger grasps them ever more tightly. To say "ever more tightly" means that the Distinct Teaching clarifies that Suffering has immeasurable aspects and Origination has immeasurable aspects;

compared to the Perfect, this is even more difficult, hence the phrase "ever more tightly. "Forcibly dragging them back" refers to the desire that they must necessarily break [through their delusions].
One realizes awakening amidst immeasurable afflictions and attains nirvana by severing immeasurable birth and death.

To consider oneself blameless means: "I have always known only the birth, death, and afflictions within the realm of existence (*dhātu*), but I have never known the birth, death, and afflictions outside the realm of existence. Because I did not know them, I am as if blameless."
Furthermore, to desire to sever what one does not yet understand is like being imprisoned despite having committed no crime.
Since one has not yet understood [the truth] yet desires to sever immeasurable births and deaths and destroy immeasurable afflictions, regarding those births, deaths, and afflictions—
Yet they were unable to escape, just as one who is unjustly seized is certain to die. Previously they had only been startled, suspicious, and bewildered;
now they became even more terrified and panicked, fainting from distress and collapsing to the ground.
This is precisely because one is shrouded by ignorance and has stumbled upon the ground of ignorance. Regarding the three instances of the character "jiang" (將):

they all share the meaning of "guiding. Regarding the two instances of the character "qiang" (強): according to the sense of "seizing swiftly and grasping urgently," it should be read with the level tone (*píngshēng*) as the "qiang" in "forceful/haughty" (*qiángliáng*).
However, because it implies being "strained" (*biānqiǎng*), reading it with the rising tone (*shàngshēng*) is also acceptable. △ Second, "Sleeping" (*qǐn*).
The great sigh is transformed into three parts: first, the Tathāgata’s speech to the messenger; second, the messenger’s delivery of the message; and third, the joy of the impoverished son.
Regarding the first two, there is first the actual speech.
The father saw him from afar and said to his attendants, "There is no need for this man; do not force him to come here.
Sprinkle cold water on his face to bring him back to consciousness, and do not speak with him again."

"The father sees them from afar" refers to the Tathāgata seeing those of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha). Regarding the Perfect [Teaching], they are startled and cry out in resentment, yet lack the capacity;
regarding the Distinct [Teaching], they become even more terrified, yet still lack the capacity. They shall naturally set aside the Great [Vehicle].
Therefore, he says to his messenger: "This person is not required. This is the setting aside of the Perfect, meaning that the Dharma of the Perfect and Sudden need not be used for them.
"One should transform these followers of the Hīnayāna; do not force them [to come]. This refers to resting separately.
That is to say, do not forcefully transform these followers of the Hīnayāna by means of the methods for traversing the stages separately. As for what is to be rested upon, it is as follows:
one should use the water of the principle of the 'extinction through ashes' (kṣaya) from the Tripiṭaka to sprinkle upon those who are biased toward Nirvāṇa."
[This refers to] the face. Therefore, it is said that one should sprinkle cold water on the face; such is the minor teaching (hīnayāna), employed to accommodate those of inferior capacity.
Since they were on the verge of fainting, it is now said that they have been made to regain consciousness.

As for the Great Teachings of the Perfect and Distinct [Vehicles], they are not what those of inferior capacity can realize; do not speak of them further. Therefore, it is said: "Do not speak with him again. △ Second, the Turning.
The commentary says:
Why is this? The father knew that his son’s disposition was base and inferior, and he himself was aware of his own nobility and status, which the son found difficult to accept.
Having clearly recognized him as his son, he employed skillful means and did not tell others, "This is my son."
This means that when the Tathāgata previously spoke to the bodhisattvas, saying, "There is no need for this person;

do not speak with him again," it was because although the Tathāgata knew that these followers of the two vehicles had once received the great transformation and were indeed his sons, he also knew that they had regressed from the Great Vehicle to adopt the Small Vehicle, and that their aspirations were naturally base, low, narrow, and inferior. Therefore, he said, "The father knows... and so forth.

The Tathāgata, knowing for himself that his own majestic power and dignity are uniquely supreme, and that all his family affairs and noble status are likewise so, realized that it would not be easy even for one who were his son.

Therefore, he said, "knowing for himself" (and so forth). Because it was difficult for him to become a son, although he knew this person was a son through the connection of shared affinity (*karmapratyaya*), he employed skillful means and did not say to the Bodhisattva: "These two vehicles are the Tathāgata..."
Because he is a son who has come to form a karmic connection with me, it is said that [the King] "knows him thoroughly" (and so forth).
△ Second, the messenger transmits the words. The messenger says to him: "I now release you; go wherever you please."

This means that when a bodhisattva, having received the command of the Tathāgata, intended to transform those of the two vehicles by means of the Perfect and Distinctive teachings, the Tathāgata perceived their lack of capacity and said, "There is no need for this person; do not speak with them again.
Consequently, the bodhisattva also did not transform them with the Great Dharma. Therefore, it is said: "I now release you; go wherever you please."
This refers to your mind, which takes pleasure only in the Lesser Dharma.
Since I do not now transform you through the Great [Dharma], I shall instead follow the inclinations of your own mind. △ Third, the impoverished son rejoices.
The impoverished son was filled with joy at having attained what he had never experienced before. Rising from the ground, he went to the poor quarters to seek food and clothing.
Regarding his "joy," the followers of the Two Vehicles originally delighted in the Lesser [Vehicle]; when suddenly confronted with the Great Dharma, they were struck with alarm and terror.
Now, being told, "I release you; go as you please," they are not only free from fear and terror, but are moreover filled with joy.

This is joy. For those of the Two Vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas), minor dharmas are considered unprecedented; if they were taught the Great [Vehicle], they would lose that sense of the unprecedented.
Now, since they are not being transformed by the Great [Vehicle], it is said that they have "attained the unprecedented.
The Great Teaching is not something that accords with their limited capacities; therefore, they become bewildered and fall into the ground of ignorance. However, as for the Minor Transformation...

Because the capacities and characteristics interact, one accordingly arises from the stage of ignorance (*avidyā-bhūmi*). This arising occurs by relying on the principle of the truth of partial emptiness (*pradeśa-śūnyatā-satya*).

The contemplation of partial emptiness cultivates both the auxiliary path (*upāya-mārga*) and the direct path (*samyak-mārga*) in order to seek the *nirvāṇa* that is empty, signless, and wishless—just as one goes to a poor village to seek food and clothing. △ Second, receiving the *Āgamas*, part two. First:
First, he dispatched two attendants to act as transformations; second, the two Tathāgatas went themselves; and third, the first Tathāgata dispatched them secretly.
At that time, the elder, wishing to entice his son, devised a skillful means and secretly sent two men who were haggard in appearance and lacked majesty, saying:
"You may go to him and speak slowly to the impoverished son, saying: 'There is work here to be done; we shall pay you double wages.'"
"It is up to you. If the impoverished son agrees, bring him here and set him to work. If he asks what he is to do, you may simply tell him:
'I am hiring you to remove the refuse; the two of us shall also work together with you.'"

First, it is the same in dispatching those of their own kind; second, "you may descend" is the same in dispatching them for that specific task. Now, this is merely a general explanation of the method of guidance.

Regarding the phrase "the elder intends to guide and attract," although the followers of the Two Vehicles lack the capacity for the Great [Vehicle], how could the Tathāgata abandon them and fail to transform them?
If he wishes to transform them, he must use skillful means to guide and attract them.
It leads them forth; therefore, it is said that they are "to be enticed. The Mahāyāna is the ultimate reality and is not termed "enticement";

however, because the present skillful means are not the ultimate reality, they are called "enticement. Furthermore, one first uses skillful means to entice them, and subsequently leads them from those skillful means back to the ultimate reality;
thus, they are called "enticed. As for the "two persons," these refer to the two vehicles (the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles).
He is called "secret" because he conceals his status as a bodhisattva within; he is called "expedient" because he manifests as one of the two vehicles externally.

Because those of the two vehicles do not cultivate the primary and secondary marks, it is said that his physical form is haggard; because he lacks the adornment of merit, it is said that he has no majesty.
When it says, "You may go to him," it is because if he were adorned with the marks, they would feel fear and avoidance; now that he is haggard...
If one lacks majestic power (*tejas*), one is the same as those of the Two Vehicles.

By transforming those of a similar class through a similar class, and those who share the same purpose through shared purpose, they will inevitably believe and accept [the teaching]; therefore, it is said, "You may go to him.

Regarding the phrase "speaking slowly," as explained in the commentaries and sub-commentaries, this refers to taking the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) and the attainment of *nirvāṇa* as the place of practice. It is said, "Twice..."
Regarding that which is "straight" for you: if non-Buddhists practice the six modes of austerity, they merely attain the suppression of the afflictions of views and thought as their straightness.
If ordinary persons cultivate precepts and virtues, they merely attain the wholesome retribution of human and celestial realms as their straightness.

Now, if one can cultivate the factors of the path (*mārga-aṅga*), one will necessarily realize *nirvāṇa*. If one realizes *nirvāṇa*, not only are views and thoughts suppressed, but they are also severed.
Seeing and contemplating [the truths], one is given a price that is double. Not only does one attain the realms of humans and devas, but one also transcends the three realms;

thus, one is given a price that is double. Therefore, it is said: "I shall give you double the price. When bringing those who are to perform the work, one leads them to come and causes them to take up the task;
that is, one causes them to know suffering and sever its origin, to aspire toward cessation and cultivate the path, and so forth.

Regarding the causes and conditions: one contemplates their arising in forward order and their cessation in reverse order. The method for removing filth is also as explained in the commentaries and sub-commentaries.
When it says, "We two shall also work together with you," this means that we practice in common reliance upon the Four Noble Truths. As it is said:
"This is suffering; you should know it. This I and you know together. ... "Up to this is the path leading to cessation;
you should cultivate it. This I and you cultivate together. This is for the purpose of making [the messenger] act. △ Second, the messenger is found.
At that time, the two messengers immediately sought out the impoverished son; having found him, they fully related the aforementioned matter.
As for the two messengers, because they were of the same class and engaged in the same business, one was found as soon as he was sought.
"Fully related the aforementioned matter" means they reported exactly what they had been commanded above. △ Third, the impoverished son receives the instruction.
At that time, the impoverished son first took the wages and immediately received the manure. When the father saw his son, he felt pity for him and marveled at this:

that the son first took [the wages] was because he knew there was a Path to be cultivated and a Cessation to be realized, thereby obtaining the price of Nirvana and removing the manure of views and afflictions.
Furthermore, it can be understood that taking the fruit while still anticipating the fruit serves as the "price," by means of practicing the causes.
It is for the purpose of removal. To say that he "pities and marvels at" him means:
regarding the elder, he pities that what he has gained is small and marvels that what he has lost is great. Why is this? Because he removed dung, what he gained was small;
yet he was originally the elder’s son and ought to have obtained a treasure trove, thus what he lost is great. Regarding the Tathāgata, it is likewise to pity him...
As for that which was realized, they merely attained a partial emptiness and nirvana, yet they lamented what they had lost: unsurpassed bodhi.
△ Second, the Tathāgata’s own practice has two parts. First, discerning the capacities [of beings].

Furthermore, on another day, he saw from afar through a window the body of his son, emaciated and haggard, covered in filth, dust, and impurities. Regarding the phrase "furthermore" (*yǐ*) and so forth:
it means that the Tathāgata did not only secretly dispatch those of the Two Vehicles to perform transformations among their own kind; he also...

Furthermore, he himself performed the transformation [of beings]. However, it was not only after his attainment of the Way under the Bodhi tree that he began to transform them through the Lesser Vehicle;

rather, while in the Land of Constant Quiescent Light, within the stage of the Dharma-body, he had already perceived and known that there existed such capacities for the two vehicles of the Lesser Vehicle.

Therefore, it is said that "on another day" he acted; this means that he used the stage of the Dharma-body to discern their capacities, which constitutes "another day. This is the reception of the Dharma.

In the section on the teaching, there are verses such as "With my Buddha-eye I behold," and so forth. In the section on the parable, there is the passage beginning with "The elder saw this great fire.
Regarding the phrase "seen from afar through a window," it means that because those of the Two Vehicles delight only in inferior teachings, what they perceive is not correct;
therefore, when the Tathāgata examines their limited capacities, he does not employ the true wisdom of the Middle Way.
He observes them by means of the expedient wisdom used for transforming others, just as an elder does not see his son through the doorway but rather through a window.
Although the capacity [of the beings] exists because of prior karmic connections, it is fundamentally due to a natural affinity; thus, it is said that he "sees his son.
Because their great capacity has not yet matured, it is said that he sees him from afar. They possess no merit of their own.
Because he is adorned with the Dharma-wealth and the marks and signs of physical excellence, it is said that he is "emaciated and haggard.

Because he possesses the afflictions of conceptual discrimination and craving, it is said that he is "unclean, like excrement and soil. △ Second, the application of the teaching has three parts. First, concealing the superior and manifesting the inferior.
He immediately cast off his necklaces, fine soft garments, and ornaments of adornment;
he put on coarse, tattered, and soiled clothes, covered his body in dust, and took a refuse-basket in his right hand, appearing as though he were filled with dread.

The first three phrases conceal the superior; furthermore, by adding the following, they manifest the inferior. To say "immediately cast off" means that the teaching must necessarily accord with the capacity of the recipient.
Since that capacity is small, it is necessary to preach the Small Dharma; therefore, one first conceals the excellence of the Response Body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

The *ratna-ābharaṇa* (jeweled necklace) refers to the Tathāgata, who is fully endowed with the merits and sublime practices of the forty-two stages. The fine, soft, and superior garments refer to the Tathāgata... [text truncated]
The ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) to which he has come is the patience of quiescence (śānti-kṣānti).
His ornaments—namely, all the Tathāgata’s boundless marks and signs (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana) and boundless radiance—are now all concealed and do not manifest;

therefore, it is said that he has "removed his necklaces and so forth. Second, regarding the manifestation of inferior speech such as "I am further wearing [them]," this is intended to accommodate those of lesser capacity.

Having already concealed the *saṃbhogakāya* (the victorious response-body), he must again manifest the *nirmāṇakāya* (the inferior response-body) to preach the Dharma; therefore, it is said that he "puts on [clothing] again.
"Again" (*geng*) carries the sense of "changing" or "replacing. He manifests in the form of a six-foot-tall old bhikṣu; therefore, it is said to be "coarse and worn-out.

He demonstrates the two afflictions of birth and the Dharma; therefore, it is "soiled. As for "dust and dirt covering his body," this demonstrates the presence of the afflictions of views and thought.

"Annoyed," he took up a refuse basket; this indicates the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*). "With his right hand" indicates the vehicle of skillful means (*upāyayāna*).

"Appearing fearful" does not mean that the Tathāgata appeared fearful in the sight of the followers of the two vehicles, nor that the followers of the two vehicles perceived the Tathāgata as appearing fearful.
Rather, "appearing" (*zhuàng*) means "resembling. This refers to how other people, observing him, were attached to his worn-out [garments].
The appearance was such that it seemed as though the Tathāgata were possessed of fear. △ Second, the three turnings of the Four Noble Truths. Part Three: First, the exhortation to practice.
He spoke to the laborers: "You all must work diligently; do not be indolent. By means of this skillful expedient, you shall draw near to my son."
This is an analogy for using a carriage on a journey; therefore, it is said that there are also three turns of exposition. First, "exhortation to practice" (*pravartana*);

second, "subsequent indication of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-nirdeśa*); third, "immediate realization through testimony" (*sākṣātkriyā-sākṣya*). Within the first [turn], the single character "diligence" (*āyāsa*) exhorts that the Path (*mārga*) and Cessation (*nirodha*) should be cultivated and realized.
The single character "do not" (*mā*) exhorts that Suffering (*duḥkha*) and Origination (*samudaya*) should be known and abandoned.
He also exhorted him. To say that he answered with skillful means refers to how he obtained his son through the skillful means of exchanging fine garments for worn-out ones.
For once he was wearing the worn-out clothes and appearing inferior, all his conduct and attire became identical to those of his son.
Therefore, he was able to draw near. △ Second, showing the signs:
Later, he spoke again, saying, "Ho! Man, you shall always work here; do not go elsewhere again. I shall increase your wages."

First, the characteristics of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) are shown. Next, from the passage beginning with "In all existences" (*sarvabhava*), the characteristics of the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) are shown. Third, from the passage beginning with "For what reason?

(*tat kasya hetoḥ*), the characteristics of the two truths of Suffering (*duḥkha*) and Origination (*samudaya*) are shown. The initial word "Alas! (*aho*) is a term for startling and awakening; it refers to those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayānika*).

Originally, these were sons with whom [the Buddha] had formed a karmic connection; now, however, they have abandoned the Great Vehicle to take up the Small. Being deluded and ignorant, he rebukes them so as to cause them to awaken.

As for the term "men," it refers to those of the Two Vehicles who, having previously received the Great Vehicle, are soon capable of succeeding to the lineage and duties of the Tathāgata; therefore, they are called "men. It is through these three characters that the Tathāgata—
The two gates of subduing and gathering, as well as the two virtues of majesty and compassion, are both manifest here.

"You must always act in this way and not go elsewhere" means that you, followers of the Two Vehicles, must constantly cultivate the factors of enlightenment within the true teaching to realize *nirvāṇa*;
do not again be like the non-Buddhists of former times by giving rise to the four views, such as the view of annihilationism, nor like ordinary worldlings by giving rise to [afflictions].

The four views, such as purity and so forth, refer to the remaining [wrong] paths. If one can constantly cultivate the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma), then the nirvāṇa without remainder will naturally be attained;
therefore, it is said that "I shall constantly increase your price. To "increase the price" has the same meaning as the aforementioned "double the value.
Nirvāṇa is precisely the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya).
Whatever you may require—such as basins, vessels, rice, flour, salt, vinegar, or similar items—do not hesitate or feel any doubt.
We also have aged and infirm servants who will provide whatever you need. Set your mind at ease; I am like a father to you, so do not worry any further.

This demonstrates the characteristics of the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*). Briefly stated, the Truth of the Path consists of ethical discipline (*śīla*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*);

hence the reference to "basins and vessels. In detail, it comprises the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*); hence the reference to "belongings. A basin or vessel has the function of containing and storing;
likewise, ethical discipline serves as the foundation for all virtues and the foremost of all practices, just as a basin or vessel is able to contain.

A vessel contains all things; therefore, the bowl is used as a metaphor for the precepts. Furthermore, one who maintains the precepts does so without leakage, just as a vessel can hold objects without spilling them.

Just as rice and flour possess the power to sustain the body and the merit to nourish life—wherein the rice may be coarse and the flour fine, yet each has its own virtue—so too does meditative concentration (dhyāna) sustain the body and nourish life.
If it is mundane meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), it sustains the physical body composed of the four great elements and nourishes the retribution-life of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).

If it is supramundane meditative concentration, it sustains the Dharma-body of the five factors (*pañcadharmakāya*) and the wisdom-life of partial truth (*ekadeśa-satya-prajñā*). Therefore, rice and flour are used as metaphors for meditative concentration.
Salt has the taste of salinity; vinegar has the taste of acidity. Although salinity and acidity differ, both are able to harmonize flavors.
Likewise, although wisdom differs as mundane or supramundane, both are able to reconcile phenomena and principle.
Mundane wisdom can harmonize differentiated phenomena and the principles existing in the conventional world; supramundane wisdom can harmonize the phenomena of cultivation and practice.
This is the principle of true emptiness. Therefore, salt and vinegar are used as metaphors for wisdom.
Do not harbor doubts or difficulties within yourself, thinking that while you are practicing these brief or extensive categories of the path (*mārga-aṅga*), I am the Tathāgata.
I shall clearly point this out to you all. Therefore, you followers of the Two Vehicles should not give rise to anxiety or doubt, nor regard this as a hardship.
As for those who are "aged and decrepit," these are the messengers previously sent in secret, who temporarily practice the Two Vehicles.
It is not only I, the Tathāgata, who will distinguish the factors of the path (mārga-aṅga) for you and cause you to cultivate them.
There are also fellow practitioners of the two vehicles who can likewise analyze and point it out for you.
Because they manifest as those of the two vehicles, they are called "old and decrepit. Regarding the phrase "you should settle your mind well":
whether it be the Tathāgata or his fellow practitioners, all are able to analyze and point it out for you; you should therefore settle your mind well and practice accordingly. As for me...

"As for 'your father' and so forth: it means that because you are able to cultivate the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma), you will certainly be able to sever the afflictions of views and thought (dṛṣṭi-kleśa and bhāvanā-kleśa) in the future, escape the triple world (tridhātu), and realize nirvana.
You shall be a son of me, the Tathāgata, and I shall be your father. Now, while you are at the stage of cultivating the path, the Tathāgata is already like your father. Since he is like your father—"
"Then, whatever you require, I shall give it all to you. Do not worry further that you will not clearly understand the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).
Why is this? I am old and aged, while you are young and vigorous; when you work, you are never deceitful or lazy."
"Your anger, resentment, and complaints—I have never seen such evils in you before, as if you were some other hired laborer.
From this day forward, you are like my own son."

This demonstrates the characteristics of suffering and its origin. There are five obstacles to suffering; these constitute the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*). Since giving exists within origination, it inevitably invites suffering.
Now, by being able to eliminate these five obstacles, one can sever origination; this is precisely what is meant by "knowing suffering. Thus, this single passage [expresses both].
This indicates the characteristics of the two truths: the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) and the truth of the cessation of its origin (*samudaya-satya*).

"Deceit, indolence," and so forth refer to the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*); "all evils" specifically refers to these five hindrances. "The rest are people" refers to non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Regarding the phrase "Why is this so?": it asks how one can perceive me as being like your father; thus he says, "Why is this so? [He continues: "As for my age..."
"As for 'the eldest,' it means that because my time for transformation is nearing its end, I am considered old.
Because I am advanced in years, I am like your father. Since I am like a father, you are like a son. I am like a father because I am old;
you are like my son because you are young and strong, always working at your tasks and free from all evils. Thus he spoke.

Because those of lesser capacity increase [in virtue] as they reach maturity, those who constantly practice are those beginning from the stages of the five cessations (*pañca-vyupaśama*), the general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-smṛti*), the specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa-smṛti*), and up through the stages of *ūṣmagata*, *mūrdhan*, and the higher *kṣānti*.

Furthermore, there are entirely no non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) nor ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) with the various evils of the five hindrances; therefore it is said, "entirely not... and so forth. From here on...
Regarding "from now on": this refers to entering the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*) from the single moment of "Patience" (*kṣānti*).
Because the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharma is proximate to the Truth, it is said to be "like a son born [of the mother]. △ Third, the realization.
At that very moment, the elder gave him another name, calling him "Son.

"At that very moment" (*tatkṣaṇam*) refers to the time of entering the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), when one enters the sixteen moments of mind immediately following the World-First Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
Because it occurs in the span of a single moment, it is called "at that very moment. Once one has entered the Path of Seeing, one has already attained the first [fruit].
He is indeed a son of the Buddha. Therefore, while above it was simply said that he is "like" [a son], now it is said that he is further given a name and called a "child.
Here, "name" (名) carries the sense of "son" (子). The character for "name" is pronounced in the departing tone (*qùshēng*);

thus, when it says "he is named a child," it means he is designated as a child by way of name and form (*nāmarūpa*), but he is not yet actually a child. Only when the inheritance is entrusted to him does he truly become one.
Child, this is likely because you do not realize that both the great and the small possess the meaning of being "sons.

This refers precisely to the assembly of the Āgamas, where the Tathāgata instructs those of the Two Vehicles to cultivate the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma), from the stages of Heat (ūṣmagata) and Summits (mūrdhan) up to the Supreme Worldly Dharma (laukikāgra-dharma);

all these are considered "resembling sons. Therefore, it was previously stated only that they are "like sons. However, if one severs the afflictions of views and thoughts (dṛṣṭi-kleśa and bhāva-kleśa), exits the triple world, and realizes nirvāṇa, then...
These are true sons. If a bodhisattva were not to sever delusions, the meaning of being a "son" would not be established;
therefore, those now called "children" are actually the true sons of the Hīnayāna. If one speaks of entrusting the Mahāyāna sons, how could they be indiscriminately conflated with these?
△ Third, attachment to minor dharmas.
At that time, although the impoverished son rejoiced at this encounter, he still considered himself a lowly hired laborer;
for this reason, for twenty years, he was constantly made to remove dung.

The phrase "this encounter" refers to the act of inscribing characters upon the aforementioned [body] and naming it a child. Regarding the expression "still self-claiming," etc., this concerns the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

The disciple describes that the Buddha’s single transformation (*ekavyūha*) possesses two meanings: first, describing the fundamental intent behind the Buddha’s establishment of his transformative teaching;
second, describing the secret benefit that one may personally attain. For example, at the time of the *Avataṃsaka*, the Buddha’s intention was fundamentally to bestow the Great [Vehicle].
If they were among those of the Two Vehicles, [the Buddha’s teaching] was manifestly as if for the deaf or the mute, yet secretly it already possessed the benefit of being adapted to their capacity.

During the *Āgama* period, the Buddha’s original intention was to lead them from the provisional toward the ultimate; if they were among those of the Two Vehicles, it was manifestly a matter of providing reassurance, yet secretly it already possessed the benefit of leading them back to the ultimate.
During the *Vaipulya* period, the Buddha’s original intention was to cause them to feel shame regarding the Lesser Vehicle.
Regarding the "cultivation of the Great" (Mahāyāna): if one is among those of the Two Vehicles, it is manifest that they are merely staying overnight in a grass hut;

yet secretly, there is already the benefit of the Shared Teaching (Sādhāraṇa-yāna). At the time of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the Buddha’s original intention was that what they were to receive was already possessed [by them].

If one is among those of the Two Vehicles, it is manifest that they have no mind to hope for or seek [this]; yet secretly, there is already the benefit of the Distinct Teaching (Pratyekabuddha-yāna). Therefore, now...
The Āgamas are called "sons. Although they belong to the Hīnayāna, the Buddha’s intention was that these followers of the two vehicles were sons capable of inheriting the family estate;
yet the followers of the two vehicles did not realize this, but merely considered themselves Arhats. Thus, we know that [the term] "still considering oneself" (猶故自謂) refers to those four characters.
This is now, after awakening through the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, a recounting of former words; it is not as if they already knew [this] at that time.
Thus they come to know me. It is like a destitute son who, although the elder has bestowed a name upon him, still considers himself merely a lowly hired laborer.
Regarding the phrase "twenty years," the bestowing of the name refers to what is abandoned by the first fruit (*srotāpanna*);

it pertains only to the afflictions of view within the triple world, which collectively constitute one unimpeded [knowledge] and one liberation (*vimokṣa*). This proceeds from the contemplation of the heavy conditions.

True. Furthermore, by means of the nine unimpeded concentrations (*anantarya-samādhi*) and the nine liberations (*vimokṣa*), one cuts off the afflictions of the realm of thought (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*). Thus it is said that for twenty years one clears away dung;
this refers to proceeding from the second fruit toward the fourth fruit, the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) as an Arhat. △ Third, receiving the Vaipulya [sūtras].

After this period has passed, their minds will accord with one another and they will trust each other, such that there will be no difficulty in coming and going; yet, as for where they reside, they will still remain in their original places.

Regarding what is called "mutual trust": if the Tathāgata trusts the followers of the Two Vehicles while the followers of the Two Vehicles do not trust the Tathāgata, or if the followers of the Two Vehicles trust the Tathāgata while the Tathāgata does not trust the followers of the Two Vehicles, this would not be called mutual trust. Now...

The Tathāgata firmly trusts the followers of the two vehicles, and the followers of the two vehicles also trust the Tathāgata; therefore, it is called "mutual trust. Regarding the Tathāgata’s trust in the followers of the two vehicles:

this means that since they were able to believe in the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) in the past, they will certainly also believe and accept them if the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) is taught now.
Regarding the followers of the two vehicles’ trust in the Tathāgata: this means that when the Tathāgata previously taught the Lesser Vehicle, they practiced in reliance upon it.
"Therefore, there must be something to be realized. If you now explain the Great [Vehicle] to me, and I practice according to it, I too will surely attain realization.
As for "entering and exiting without difficulty," this is because, through his faith, he was able to enter and behold the Exalted One’s sublime and supreme form.
When hearing the teaching of the Great Dharma, they emerge to see the inferior response-body of sixteen feet; when hearing the teaching of the Small Dharma, they enter it.

Thus, whether entering or emerging from the Great or the Small, there is no doubt or difficulty. Since the Small is that which has been realized, it is naturally without difficulty; because one trusts that the Great is not erroneous, there is likewise no difficulty.
However, regarding their state of abiding and so forth, although they have no doubts or difficulties even concerning the Great Dharma, they remain attached.
Because [his capacity] was small, he remained in his original status as an Arhat and did not advance. △ Fourth, receiving the Prajñā [teaching], in three parts:
First, the Tathāgata commands him to know.
"World-Honored One, at that time the elder became ill; knowing for himself that he would soon die, he said to the impoverished son: 'I now..."
There is much gold, silver, and rare treasures; the storehouses are overflowing. You know exactly how much is there and what should be taken or given.
My mind is thus; you should embody this intent. Why is this? Now, I and you are no different.
You should apply yourself with diligence so that nothing is lost or leaked away.
Regarding the statement that he was "sick": conditions had arisen in other realms, and as he was about to respond to them, he spoke of being sick.

Although the karmic conditions in those other realms had indeed arisen, it was also because the karmic conditions in this land were exhausted; thus, the Buddha, wishing to respond to those others, manifested illness in accordance with their perception.
Furthermore, because sentient beings have illnesses, the Buddha also has illnesses; thus it is said that "the elder has an illness.

Regarding the phrase "he will not live much longer," this means that having completed his work of transformation in this land, he is about to enter parinirvāṇa. Once the great task of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is finished, he will then proclaim his entry into extinction.
Since the *Prajñāpāramitā* teachings now closely approach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, it is said that "not long" remains. As for the mention of gold, silver, and treasures...

"Treasures" (bao) refers to the Prajñāpāramitā, which encompasses both the general and the specific; it primarily explains the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao). Gold is the most precious, like the principle of the Perfect Teaching;
silver is next to gold, like the principle of the Separate Teaching (biejiao). The name "precious treasure" (zhenbao) is common to all, like the principle of the Shared Teaching (tongjiao).
A granary (cang) stores only rice, like the meditative concentration (ding) of the three teachings; a treasury (ku) contains various goods, like the wisdom (hui) of the three teachings.
Regarding the phrase "the more or less within it": "within it" refers to the encompassing perfect [teaching] (*yuan*);
"more or less" refers to the particular and general [teachings] (*tongbie*) that are encompassed, just as the quantity of objects resides within a container.

This is analogous to how the particular and general teachings encompassed reside within the encompassing perfect teaching. As for the particular practice, one studies all four gates extensively; therefore, it is called "much. As for the general practice...
The three persons share the same path of wordless discourse; hence, their words are few. Furthermore, if distinguished individually, there are fifty-two stages:
the severance of birth and death in two types, the destruction of afflictions in five abodes, and the manifestation of realization through three virtues.

Therefore, it is said that [the former] is "much. By contrast, the latter is "few," as its scope is limited: the stages of progress clarify only the ten bhūmis; birth and death involve only the *pariccheda* (segmented) realm;
afflictions consist only of the destruction of *dṛṣṭi-heya* and *bhāvanā-heya* [delusions]; and realization and entry pertain only to a single nirvāṇa. This is what should be accepted and rejected.
If there is the capacity for the Three Teachings, one should employ the methods of the Three Teachings to transform others and bestow them upon them;
if there is no such capacity, one should employ the methods of the Three Teachings for one's own practice and internalize them. Thus, it is called "taking and giving.
Since these are described as what is appropriate, within the context of self-cultivation and transforming others, one must further discern what is suitable for oneself. My mind...
"Thus, you should embody this intention," means that my Tathāgata-heart has already acted in this way;
you followers of the Two Vehicles should embody it and realize the intention of me, the Tathāgata. There is no other intention of the Tathāgata than this:
when I transmit the teaching to the Bodhisattvas, I have already commanded thus, "You should act according to my command," and it shall be so.
And as for this teaching: it is the intention of the Tathāgata to command you to receive and understand the Dharma.
Although he wishes to have you transmit this teaching to the Bodhisattvas, he also desires that you know it to be identical to that which belongs to the Two Vehicles;
you should understand this by embodying his intent. Thus, it is not different [from what they possess]. Since I have already commanded you to transmit the teaching, then that which you...
It is said: "As I have spoken, so it is; therefore, I say there is no difference. Furthermore, that which belongs to the Tathāgata is also that which belongs to the followers of the Two Vehicles;

therefore, I say, "Now, I and you are indeed not different. Regarding the phrase "you should apply your mind with greater care," this means that you followers of the Two Vehicles already applied your minds when you were previously clearing away the filth, and thus you were without negligence. However—

Judging by the present discourse: previously, one practiced only for oneself, which cannot yet be called "applying the mind. Previously, one merely destroyed one's own views and afflictions (dṛṣṭi-kleśa), which is still termed a "leakage" (āsrava).
Now, however, one teaches and transforms bodhisattvas; it is fitting that you act as I have said, causing all bodhisattvas to destroy ignorance (avidyā).
Compared to the previous practice for oneself, you ought to apply even greater effort. Therefore, it is said: "Do not allow any leakage."
Thus it was. △ Second, the disciple receives the instruction.
At that time, the impoverished son immediately accepted the command and took charge of all the goods: the gold, silver, rare treasures, and all the storehouses.
Yet he has no intention of seeking even a single meal.
That you have received this instruction is as clear as the text itself. △ Third, he still remains in his original place.
However, as for where he dwells, he is indeed in his original place; his inferior mind has likewise not yet been relinquished.

Regarding the phrase "has not yet abandoned": in the *Avataṃsaka*, one has not yet abandoned [the teachings] because one is like one who is deaf and mute; in the *Āgama*, one has not yet abandoned them because one provides guarantees;

in the *Vaipulya*, one has not yet abandoned them because one dwells in a grass hut. Now, in the *Prajñāpāramitā*, although one clings to the Truth without forgetting it, there is no seeking or grasping;
therefore, it is said that one has likewise not yet been able to abandon it. △ Five: Receiving the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Part Two: First, receiving the realization.
After a short time had passed, the father perceived his son’s disposition; it gradually became open and expansive, and he achieved his great ambition, coming to despise his former mindset.

"Open and expansive" means that in the *Avataṃsaka*, one attains openness and expansiveness through what is appropriate for the capacity [of the listener], while in the *Āgama*, one attains openness and expansiveness through what is used for guidance and attraction.
The Vaipulya sutras are harmonious and expansive through their censure and reproach; the Prajñāpāramitā sutras are harmonious and expansive through their refinement and elimination.

As for the present Lotus Sutra, it brings about harmony and expansiveness by means of the four kinds of flowers raining from the heavens, the earth shaking in six ways, and the emission of light, thereby startling and resolving all doubts.
For one who accomplishes the great aspiration, once the great capacity has been awakened, the great aspiration is spontaneously fulfilled.
The *prajñā* has already yielded specific benefits; now, one may attain the perfect benefit. Regarding "disdaining one's former mind":

this refers to the former mind that was greedily attached to minor teachings and delighted in clinging to *nirvāṇa*. Now that the great capacity [for enlightenment] has been awakened, one naturally develops a sense of disdain and rejection toward that former mind.
II. Receiving and Applying the Teaching (in four parts): 1. The Great Assembly Gathers Like Clouds.
As he was about to pass away, he summoned his son and gathered his kinsmen, as well as kings, ministers, kṣatriyas, and householders;
they had all assembled.

Regarding the term "kinsmen": when the Tathāgata was planting the seeds of his future enlightenment under twenty trillion Buddhas, there were various great Bodhisattvas who acted as his instigators or as his counterparts and echoes.

While they naturally occupied the position of fathers toward the Tathāgata, according to the natural law (*dharmatā*) of the Dharma, they stood to the great Bodhisattvas in the capacity of uncles and cousins; therefore, they are called "kinsmen. This refers to the kingdom.
The "King" refers to the Buddhas of the ten directions. The "Minister," who ranks below one person and above ten thousand, is a metaphor for the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

The "Kṣatriya"—meaning the royal caste—is a metaphor for the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*). The "Householder," one whose mind is pure and free from desire, is a metaphor for the thirty minds of the stages of Practice, Abiding, and Tending (*caryā-vihāra-pratipatti*).
Just as in the assemblies where twenty-two billion Buddhas of the past resided, there are none who do not gather here now.
Therefore, it is said that they have all gathered together. △ Second, the conclusion and correlation of the ancient and the modern:
He then declared himself, "Gentlemen, you should know: this is my son, born of me, in such-and-such a city."
"Abandoning me, he fled and wandered in hardship for over fifty years. His original name was so-and-so, while my name is such-and-such.
Long ago, while in our native city, I harbored deep anxiety and searched for him everywhere. Suddenly, here in this place, I have encountered and found him. He is truly my son."
"I am truly his father;
this is my son," and so forth. This means that the Tathāgata personally sowed the seeds of the One Vehicle for him under twenty thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas.
His entire Dharma-body and life of wisdom were born from the seeds sown by me, Śākyamuni, and have no connection to others.
The Buddha therefore says, "He is my son, born from me. As for what is called the "original city," it refers to that aforementioned city.

Since the seed sown by the Tathāgata is the perfect seed of the Mahāyāna, he employs the inconceivable, wondrous principle of *sambhogakāya* (the realm of tranquil light) entirely as his means of teaching.
Once they have received this instruction, they likewise take *sambhogakāya* as their...

Because they have practiced [the path], it is called the "original city. A certain city refers specifically to the City of Quiescent Light (Sukhāvatī). Having regressed from the Great [Vehicle], it is as if one has fled from the original city.
As for the phrase "this place," it refers to the co-residence within the triple world (*tridhātu*). Since one has already regressed from the Great, one enters into birth and death;
thus, one flees from the City of Quiescent Light and arrives at the realm of co-residence. This is like the aforementioned stopping over in a single city.

Between the *sahā* (Real Reward) and *sāmbhogika* (Shared Enjoyment) lands, the *śeṣa* (Remaining) land is taken as the intermediate space; thus, here it is the *śeṣa* land that serves as the interval.
Furthermore, it is simply for the sake of convenience that the *sahā* land is identified [as the destination]. Regarding the term "meeting" (*yu-hui*):

the followers of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayānika*) naturally and silently strike upon the Buddha with their great capacity (*mahā-viśaya*), while the Tathāgata, through his great compassion (*mahā-karuṇā*), spontaneously takes them as objects of his attention. Therefore, it is said they "meet."
He attained realization thereof (and so forth). △ Third, the formal entrustment of the family estate:
"Now, all the wealth and property that I possess are yours, my son. All that has previously been disbursed or received is known to you."

Regarding what was previously taught as being known by the sons—that is, the Mahāyāna dharmas they had already received and understood at the time of their initial instruction—the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* does not now repeat it for them.
Rather, it directly clarifies that these very dharmas are precisely those possessed by the followers of the two vehicles;
it merely reveals that they have now attained the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and are granted the prediction of attaining Buddhahood. △
Fourth, he attained joy regarding his karma.
World-Honored One, at that time, when the impoverished son heard these words from his father, he was immediately filled with great joy, having experienced something unprecedented.
He then thought to himself: "Originally, I had no intention of seeking anything; yet now, this treasure store has come to me spontaneously."
The two phrases regarding the "Treasure Store" refer precisely to what was previously mentioned: that immeasurable precious jewels are obtained spontaneously without being sought.
Thus, one knows that throughout the Dharma transformations of the five periods, from the perspective of the Buddha’s intent, he regarded the impoverished son as nothing other than a wealthy heir.

Yet, the followers of the Two Vehicles considered themselves merely lowly laborers. Therefore, from the *Avataṃsaka* until the present *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, over forty years have passed in which [the truth] has been gradually entrusted.
Regarding the entrustment of the family business: it was because the Tathāgata did not merely employ a single method, but rather used manifold means of guidance and subtle, skillful adjustments.

Yet the followers of the Two Vehicles claimed that [the fruit] was obtained spontaneously without seeking; they were utterly unaware that this was originally their own family treasure, which they failed to seek out.
The fruit has already been attained; why then do we only know it today? △ Second, the application of the analogy, in two parts. First, the application of the general analogy:
"World-Honored One, the great wealthy elder is the Tathāgata, and we are all like the sons of the Buddha."
The preceding section was a general analogy regarding a son seeing his father and a father seeing his son; now, it is summarized by saying, "We are all like sons of the Buddha.
Since we were previously taught the Great [Vehicle], we are fit to inherit the family estate of the Tathāgata and have already been named as sons.
Although we later regressed from the Great [Vehicle] and were subsequently received through the Small [Vehicle], we have now, at this royal city, heard the Dharma.

It is like understanding through two successive stages of revelation; one must know that such a person can inherit the Great Vehicle family estate of the Tathāgata, and is therefore called a "Son of the Buddha.

Although they are already known to be a son, because they have not yet received the Tathāgata’s formal confirmation and prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), they do not yet dare to assume the responsibility for themselves;
hence, he merely says "resembling" (*xi*). This single word "resembling" is sufficient to distinguish between those of superior and middling faculties.

Regarding these distinctions: when those of superior faculties attained understanding, they had not yet received a formal confirmation or prediction (vyākaraṇa), yet they immediately perceived for themselves, "We are now truly the sons of the Buddha.
Those of middling faculties, however, merely say that it is "as if" so. Part Two: Combining the General and Specific Similes, Five Sections.
First, combining the section on attaining the *Avataṃsaka*.
The Tathāgata has always said, "We are your children. World-Honored One, because of the three kinds of suffering, we have experienced various fevers and afflictions within saṃsāra;
deluded and ignorant, we took pleasure in and were attached to inferior dharmas.
Regarding the statement that "I always speak of you as my children," this refers to when the Tathāgata, during the assembly at the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, exclaimed, "How marvelous! How marvelous!
All sentient beings possess the wisdom and virtuous nature of the Tathāgata. Since all possess this virtuous nature, they are the children of the Tathāgata.
Since all are his children, then we of the two vehicles are likewise [the children of the Tathāgata].
"He has come as our son. Therefore, it is said that he constantly speaks of us as his sons.
"World-Honored One, regarding those whom we consider equal [to him]," although the Tathāgata says of us that we are his sons, at that time we neither saw nor heard [him].
This is because, due to the three types of suffering, we are burned by the fires of the various afflictions within saṃsāra and experience all manner of feverish distress;
furthermore, being deluded regarding the Mahāyāna, we do not understand it and instead take pleasure in and cling to the Lesser Dharma.
Thus we know that the Tathāgata has always said that we are collectively unfit vessels for the Great [Vehicle]. World-Honored One, we and the like—

"To collectively lead [the disciples] to sleep is the transformation of the Great Exhalation. △ Second, the collective summary of the Āgamas, in two parts. First, the collective summary of the prior dispatching of companions for transformation:
"Today, the World-Honored One has caused us to contemplate and eliminate the dung of conceptual proliferation regarding all dharmas. We, in regard to..."
Within this, he applied himself with diligent effort and attained nirvana. Having obtained the wage for a single day, his heart was filled with great joy;
he considered himself sufficient and said to himself: "Because I have applied myself with diligent effort within the Buddha-dharma, that which I have obtained is vast and abundant."

Regarding "contemplation": this means that upon hearing the Dharma, one gives rise to understanding; having eliminated [delusions], one gives rise to practice based on that understanding; and through practice, one attains realization.
Contemplation specifically refers to contemplating the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths: knowing suffering, severing the origin [of suffering], aspiring for cessation, and cultivating the path.
Regarding the phrase "the dung of conceptual proliferation concerning all dharmas": it refers to being attached to the notion that all dharmas are fundamentally the true mark (*dharmatā*). This is...

Regarding "for the sake of purification": because sentient beings are deluded and do not know [this], ordinary worldlings give rise to the four inversions—such as permanence and bliss—regarding all phenomena;
non-Buddhists give rise to the four views of annihilationism and eternalism regarding all phenomena.
Thus, they engage in conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) regarding all phenomena, which is as impure as excrement. Now, the two vehicles rely upon...
The Tathāgata’s Dharma of the Four Noble Truths removes the dung of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) from among all phenomena.
The "price of one day" for *nirvāṇa* is an instance where both the Dharma and its metaphor are presented together: *nirvāṇa* is the Dharma, and "the price of one day" is the metaphor.

By means of the *nirvāṇa* of the Hīnayāna, one merely transcends the *paricchinna-bheda* (segmented existence), merely severs the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*), and merely realizes partial truth (*ekadeśa-satya*).

This is like a destitute son who receives only a day’s wage. Furthermore, by clearing away the dung of frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*), one severs [the afflictions of] views and attains the first fruit (*srotāpanna*).
Within this state, by applying diligent effort, one reaches *nirvāṇa*; that is, through repeated contemplation, one takes true reality as an object and severs [the remaining afflictions].
Through reflection, one achieves the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). Having attained these, it is the guarantee. △ Second, the convergence with the Tathāgata’s own practice.
However, World-Honored One, you previously knew that our minds were attached to base desires and delighted in the Lesser Dharma; thus, you simply let us be.
"For the sake of making distinctions, you shall possess a share of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, which is like a treasure trove.
Regarding the phrase "The World-Honored One knew beforehand," it means that although we have taken a vow for the Lesser Vehicle,
the Tathāgata, while within the stage of the Dharma-body, has already known through his inconceivable, skillful wisdom for the sake of transforming others that we were attached to...
They delight in coarse and base five desires and in partial, inferior teachings, yet lack the capacity for the Great [Vehicle].
Therefore, although we originally possessed our share of the precious treasury, we were cast aside; nor did [the Buddha] make any distinction for us.

As for the statement that we were "cast aside," this is not the seeing of hearing-and-seeing (聞見); it is rather the seeing of abandonment and the seeing of compassion. Thus one should know that it was so in the world.
"O Honored Ones," etc., corresponds to the passage beginning with "Furthermore, on another day," which reflects the discernment of capacities within the stage of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

"The mind becomes attached," etc., corresponds to the passage beginning with "Immediately casting off," which is the teaching that employs the function of concealing the superior and manifesting the inferior.
△ Third, the combined summary of the Vaipulya [Sūtras].
"World-Honored One, by the power of skillful means, you have spoken of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
We have obtained from the Buddha the price of a single day’s wages—nirvāṇa—and considering this a great gain, we have had no aspiration or pursuit for this Mahāyāna."
Regarding the phrase "by the power of skillful means," etc.: the Tathāgata’s original intention was solely to speak directly of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.

However, because those of the Two Vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) cling to a partial truth and their great capacity has not yet been awakened, he spoke by means of partial skillful means when his original intent was to speak directly of the Perfect (the *yuan*);
he spoke by means of the Half (the *ban*) when his original intent was to speak directly of the Full (the *man*).
He then explained it thus: originally, he intended to speak directly of the ultimate reality, yet he spoke by means of provisional skillful means.
As for the statement that "one has gained much," the Nirvana attained merely involves severing the afflictions of views and thought; what was originally attained was small.
Yet we ourselves claimed to have already attained greatness. △ Fourth, the collective reception of the Prajñā:
"Furthermore, by means of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, we have revealed and expounded it for the sake of all bodhisattvas; yet as for ourselves, in this regard..."
We had no aspiration. Why was this? The Buddha knew our minds delighted in the Lesser Dharma; thus, by the power of skillful means, he taught us according to our capacities.
Yet we did not know that we were truly the sons of the Buddha.

The initial section is correctly aligned. Regarding the statement "due to the Tathāgata’s wisdom and so forth," this means that when those of the two vehicles are able to preach for the sake of bodhisattvas, it is entirely due to the empowerment of the Tathāgata’s wisdom; thus they are able to do so. It is not that the followers of the two vehicles can preach by their own power.
Although they preach for the sake of bodhisattvas, they themselves derive no small measure of joy from it; hence it is said, "and yet for themselves..."

(As stated above). Why is this so? It is because [the disciples] thought, "For what purpose was this spoken for the sake of the Bodhisattvas? Since they themselves lacked the aspiration [to understand], the commentary states:

"The Buddha knows us" (and so forth). This means that although the Tathāgata’s original intention was to enable us, those of the Two Vehicles, to realize and understand [the teaching], and thus to turn it toward others—that is, to apply it to what we ourselves possess—the Tathāgata further knew that we were clinging [to our own views].

The truth has not been forgotten. Because their minds delighted in the Lesser Dharma, the Tathāgata used the power of skillful means to say only, "By means of this Dharma, you shall instruct and transform the bodhisattvas," rather than saying that it was yours to possess from the beginning. According to the Tathāgata’s original intention, we are indeed his true sons;
yet we did not know that we were truly the Buddha’s sons. Therefore, although we acted as instructors for others, we ourselves [did not realize it].
This is the expression of their aspiration. △ Fifth, the combined summary of the *Lotus Sūtra* has two parts. First, the combined summary of the discernment of capacities:
"Now we, for the first time, know that the World-Honored One, regarding the Buddha-wisdom, has nothing he begrudges. Why is this?
Because although we have all along been true sons of the Buddha, we merely delighted in the Lesser Dharma. Had we possessed a mind that delighted in the Great [Dharma]..."
The Buddha then spoke the Mahāyāna Dharma for me.
This first section is the primary synthesis; the subsequent "therefore" and so forth provide a detailed explanation. Regarding the initial statement, "Now I have finally come to know," etc.:

the Tathāgata’s original intention was that from the moment he first sat at the site of enlightenment until this very day, there was never a time when he did not wish to impart the Buddha-wisdom to me.
"O Wisdom! Regarding the Buddha’s wisdom, he has no sense of stinginess or regret;

yet we were deaf and mute regarding the *Avataṃsaka*, unaware of it, and even regarding the *Prajñāpāramitā*, we were unaware because we lacked the aspiration to seek it. Now that we have attained clarity and ease, we finally understand.
Why is this so? It means: how could we have known that the World-Honored One, regarding the Buddha’s wisdom..."

Wisdom. Because there was nothing to be begrudged or withheld, it is further explained as follows: "The Buddha taught us the Mahāyāna dharma in the presence of twenty thousand Buddhas, and we are truly the sons of the Buddha.
It is because we have regressed from the Great [Vehicle] and delighted in the Small that the Tathāgata did not preach the Mahāyāna dharma for us.
Had we possessed the aspiration to delight in the Great, the Buddha would have [done so]."
I preach the Dharma of the Mahāyāna; for this reason, it is known that the Tathāgata has no begrudging or withholding regarding his Buddha-wisdom.
△ Second, the combined reception and application of the teaching. This section contains four parts: the gathering of the assembly, the formal assembly, the actual entrustment, and [the conclusion].
The attainment of the karma. Now, only the latter two [sections] are combined. The first combines the formal entrustment of the family estate.
Within this sutra, only the One Vehicle is taught; yet previously, before the bodhisattvas, the Buddha disparaged the śrāvakas who delight in inferior teachings.
However, the Buddha has in truth taught and transformed beings through the Mahāyāna.
Regarding the statement "among those in this sutra," it means that in the past we delighted in the Lesser Dharma and did not delight in the Great;
therefore, the Tathāgata did not preach the Great for us. Until today, however, we have accomplished the great aspiration.
"Out of self-reproach for our former thoughts, the Tathāgata has, within this sutra, taught us only the Great Dharma of the Single Vehicle (Ekayāna).
To say 'he teaches only the Single Vehicle' means that throughout the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the Dharma of the Single Vehicle;
there is neither a second nor a third. Even if there were three, they would all be distinguished from within the Single Buddha-Vehicle."
It is said that the three are also one; therefore, it is stated that "only the One Vehicle is taught.
