As for the phrase "in the past," since the three are identical to the one and there is only the one without three, when I previously delighted in the smallness of the Three Vehicles and the Tathāgata disparaged us before the bodhisattvas, the Tathāgata was already transforming us through the Mahāyāna.
However, we did not know that the three are identical to the one; therefore, we took pleasure only in the Lesser Vehicle.

The Tathāgata, wishing for us to know that the three are identical to the one, disparaged them. Is this not precisely the time of disparagement when he actually uses the Mahāyāna to teach and transform us?
It is not only today; as soon as he has taught the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* for our sake—
The Buddha Vehicle (*buddhayāna*)—that is, during the period of the Vaipulya (*vaipulya*) sūtras—he has already taught us the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the single Buddha Vehicle.
Inferring from this, it is clear that it is not only during the Vaipulya period that he taught the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* as the single Buddha Vehicle;

rather, within the Āgamas, the Avataṃsaka, and the Prajñāpāramitā, there is nothing that does not speak of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* as the single Buddha Vehicle. It is only that we were deaf to the Avataṃsaka.

"Ah! Having relied upon the *Āgamas* for confirmation, having made my dwelling in the *Vaipulya*, and having harbored no aspiration for the *Prajñāpāramitā*, I was therefore unable to fully awaken to the Buddha Vehicle.
Only now do I finally know this; hence it is said, 'As previously before the Bodhisattvas,' and so forth.
△ Second, the joy of attaining the karmic fruit.
Therefore, we say that originally there was no mind with any longing or seeking; now this great treasure of the Dharma King has arrived spontaneously.
All that a son of the Buddha ought to obtain has already been obtained.
The attainment of the karma can be seen according to the text. △ Second, the section on verses in two parts: first, verses on the preceding acknowledgment and understanding;
second, praising the profundity of the Buddha’s grace. The first part has two sub-sections: first, verses on acknowledging the teaching of the Dharma.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Today we have heard the Buddha’s teaching; with joy and exultation, we have attained what we never had before. Thus has the Buddha spoken of the śrāvakas."
One shall attain Buddhahood; this unsurpassed treasury of jewels will be obtained spontaneously without seeking.

△ Second, the verse on receiving the explanation by way of analogy, which has two parts: first, the verse establishing the analogy; second, the verse applying it to the dharma. The first [part] has two sections: first, the verse on the general analogy;
second, the verse on the specific analogies. The first [of these] has four sections: first, the direct verse on the son turning his back on his father.
It is like a young boy who, being immature and lacking discernment, abandons his father and flees, traveling far to another land and wandering through various countries for more than fifty years.
Regarding the initial statement about traveling far to another land: having first received the Great [Vehicle], one already resided in the native land of *Sukhāvatī* (the Land of Quiescent Light).

Yet, by abandoning the Great and adopting the Small, one flees from birth and death and instead arrives at this other land of shared residence (*sahā-loka*). This shared residence is extremely distant from the Land of Quiescent Light;

therefore, it is said to be "far. "Various lands" refers to the three realms (*tridhātu*); "fifty" refers to the five destinies (*pañca-gati*); and "remaining years" [refers to the remainder of one's life].
This refers to the path of the asuras, which branched out from among humans and devas. △ Second, the actual verse on the father coming to seek his son:
The father was filled with anxious concern and searched for him in all four directions. Having grown weary from his search, he settled down in a certain city and built a house there.
He amused himself with the five desires. His family was immensely wealthy, possessing much gold and silver, mother-of-pearl and agate, pearls and lapis lazuli;

he owned elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep, as well as palanquins, carriages, and vehicles. He held vast estates and many servants, and his dependents were numerous; his income and profits flowed in from every direction.
He traveled throughout other lands, and there was no place where merchants and traders did not find him.

Surrounded and venerated by multitudes numbering in the hundreds of thousands of millions, he was always cherished by kings and held in high esteem by all the ministers and noble clans for various reasons.
Those who come and go are numerous; such is their wealth and power.

Regarding the "four directions," the six destinies do not exceed the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*). The Tathāgata seeks among these four modes of birth for a sentient being who is a fit vessel for transformation;
thus, it is said that he "searches throughout the four directions. As for the phrase "exhausted from searching," the two characters for "searching" (*qiú*) refer to the capacity [for seeking].
Regarding the phrase "seeking the Tathāgata," the two characters "fatigued" (*pi*) are spoken in reference to the capacity of the seeker.
Because they have wandered through birth and death, their great capacity has not yet been awakened; therefore, they are said to be "fatigued.

Since they are fatigued due to a lack of such capacity, the Tathāgata whom they seek consequently halts at the state of *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana with remainder) while awaiting them. Therefore, it is said that he "suddenly stops at a single city. Thus it is stated.

Regarding "constructing and establishing": in the land of Tranquil Light (Sukhāvatī), one dwells in the heaven of the ultimate truth (paramārtha), which is spontaneously natural and requires no effortful creation.
Because [the Buddha] now resides in the nirvana of skillful means with remainder, it is said that he "constructs and establishes.
Regarding "delighting in the five desires for oneself": although the Buddha manifests in accordance with human laws, he nonetheless delights in himself by means of pure and wondrous five desires.
It is said that [the Buddha] is constantly cherished by the King; this means that the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) is what the *dharmakāya* (dharma body) keeps in mind.

The body in the land of skillful means is precisely the *nirmāṇakāya*. This response body must arise from the source and is never separated from the *dharmakāya*, just as an elder is constantly cherished by the King. As for the phrase "all conditions," it is as follows:
"Coming" refers to instances such as emitting light, shaking the earth, manifesting auspicious omens, or preaching the Dharma.
"Coming and going" refers to the multitude of bodhisattvas who come and go to hear the Dharma. △ Third, the verse that leaps ahead [describes] how the father constantly thinks of his son.
Now that I am advanced in years, my anxiety for my son increases all the more. Day and night I reflect on this, for the time of my death is approaching;
my foolish son has been away from me for over fifty years—what shall become of the treasures and goods in my storehouse?

The phrase "advanced in years" serves as a general metaphor that encompasses all five periods [of the Buddha's teaching]. Now, this verse specifically encompasses the period when the era of the *Prajñāpāramitā* transformation was nearing its end;
hence, it says "advanced in years. As for the term "foolish son," since he previously received the Great [Vehicle], he is indeed a son.
Because he has regressed from the Great [Vehicle] and is entirely shrouded by ignorance, he is said to be "deluded. △ Fourth, the verse following the son’s arrival at his father’s city:
At that time, the impoverished son sought food and clothing, traveling from town to town and from country to country, sometimes obtaining something.

Alternatively, they may find nothing at all; they become emaciated by hunger and their bodies break out with sores and scabs. As they gradually pass through these stages, they arrive at the city where their father resides.
Their minor capacity (*hīna-indriya*) is secretly activated, like traveling from village to village; their major capacity (*mahā-indriya*) moves in the dark, like traveling from kingdom to kingdom.
Although the capacities differ in magnitude, both possess the sense of being activated; yet, because the minor capacity must ripen first, it is said that one proceeds "from village to village."
There may be some attainment; yet, in the ultimate sense, there is originally nothing realized. Therefore, as one travels from country to country, there is likewise nothing attained.
Lacking the flavor of the Mahāyāna Dharma to provide nourishment and benefit, one is like one who is starving; lacking the marks and signs of physical excellence adorned by merit and virtue.
"Like one who is emaciated. It is not merely this; because further ignorance and craving arise, it is said that "sores and scabs form upon the body.
△ Second, the five separate similes in verse: first, the verse summarizing the *Avataṃsaka*; second, the verse summarizing the *Āgama*; third, the verse summarizing the *Vaipulya*;
fourth, the verse summarizing the *Prajñāpāramitā*; fifth, the verse summarizing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Of the first two, the first verse summarizes the child seeing [the treasure].

The father perceives that the great capacities of the two vehicles have silently struck a resonance; the two verses describe the father seeing his son, who has received the Great Teaching of the Tathāgata and is prepared for it.
This first section further consists of four parts; the first verse describes the cause by which he sees his father.
Passing from one place of labor to another, he eventually arrived at his father’s house. II. Verse on Seeing His Father:
At that time, the elder had spread a great jeweled canopy within his gate and was seated upon a lion throne.
△ Third, three verses describe the signs of seeing his father:
surrounded by his retinue and attended by various people; some were calculating gold, silver, and precious objects, while others were managing the expenditure and income of the estate.
Commentary on the Voucher:
Those who calculate wealth and treasures are the great bodhisattvas, who are able to understand the principles of the four kinds of dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) taught by the Tathāgata.
"Property" is a metaphor for the dharma-wealth of merit; the "voucher" is like the vows that have been made.
The *shu* (commentary) states: "This refers to the conduct that has arisen. △ Fourth, the verse on seeing the father and giving rise to avoidance:
When the impoverished son sees his father—noble, wealthy, and majestic—he thinks, "This must be a king," or [thinks he is] a king or the like; thus, he is struck with terror and wonders at himself.
"Why have I come here? he thought to himself. "If I remain for long, I may be coerced and forced into labor.
Having reflected thus, he fled away. He inquired after a poor neighborhood, intending to go there to seek work as a hired laborer.
△ Second, the verse on the father seeing his son. This section consists of two parts: first, the verse on seeing the son and perceiving his capacity.
At that time, the elder was seated upon the lion throne; from afar he beheld his son and silently recognized him.
In the preceding prose version there were four sections; here, however, only two are versified. The first two lines versify the scene of seeing the son.
The subsequent two lines, "seeing him from afar," versify the moment of recognizing the son. The former is self-evident;

as for the latter statement, "recognizing him silently," it means that he recognized this son with whom he had formed a karmic connection in the past, yet he did not speak of it to others—hence, "silent recognition. △ Second, the verse on dispatching [the servant].

The messenger was dispatched with instructions to pursue and bring him back. The impoverished son cried out in alarm; bewildered and distressed, he fell to the ground, saying, "This man is seizing me!"

"You will surely be killed; what use have you for food and clothing? It was I who brought you to this state. The elder knows his son to be foolish and base, yet he does not believe my words, nor does he believe that I am his father."

In the preceding prose section, the dispatching of messengers to summon [the disciples] and the instructions regarding their reception each have their own sub-sections; in the current text, these are omitted for brevity and are no longer divided.

The first line of verse praises the intended greatness for those who lack the capacity. The second and third lines, beginning with "These people," praise the setting aside of the Great Vehicle and the bestowing of the Small Vehicle.
Those who are ignorant and narrow-minded are called "ignorant" because they do not understand the Great Dharma, and "narrow-minded" because they lack the great capacity [for it].
Having ears, they do not hear the Perfect and Sudden Teaching; therefore, they do not believe my words. Having eyes, they do not see the body of Śākyamuni.
Therefore, he did not believe that this was his father. △ Second, the verse on receiving the Āgamas, in two parts. First, the verse on the previous dispatching of companions and transformation:
"By means of skillful expedients, he further dispatched other men—those with squinting eyes, of short stature, and of ugly appearance, lacking in majestic virtue. You should say to them:"
He said, "I shall hire you to remove all manner of filth and refuse; I will pay you double wages. Hearing this, the impoverished son rejoiced and followed him.
He removed the filth and cleaned the various rooms and dwellings.
The prose version contains three sections, but here only two are versified. The first two lines verse the Tathāgata’s secret dispatching [of the man].
The second line, beginning with "the impoverished son," exhaustively verses the son’s reception of the instruction; it is abbreviated such that the messenger’s seeking out [the son] is not versified.

Regarding the initial mention of "other people," these refer to those of the Two Vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas). They are called "others" in contrast to the bodhisattvas, as they perceive only the truth of partial emptiness.
Because they do not perceive the truth of the Middle Way, they are said to be "blind. Because they do not cultivate the marks and signs of excellence, they are said to be "dwarfish and ugly.
Because they lack the adornment of merit, they are said to be "without majesty. As for the phrase "purifying the rooms," the rooms are a metaphor for the five aggregates (*skandhas*).
Ordinary worldlings give rise to the four inversions regarding the five aggregates, while non-Buddhists cling to them.
The four views are all like impure rooms. Now, the followers of the Two Vehicles cultivate the Dharma of the Four Truths to eliminate these inverted views;
therefore, it is said that they "purify all the rooms. △ Second, the verse on the Tathāgata’s own practice has two parts. First, the verse on discerning the capacities [of beings].
From the window, the elder constantly saw his son; he thought to himself that his son was foolish and inferior, delighting in base activities.
II. Verse on the Application of the Teaching:
Thereupon, the elder put on tattered, soiled clothes, took up a dung-removal tool, went to where his son was, and approached him through skillful means.

He spoke to him, urging him to work diligently, saying: "I shall increase your wages, provide you with oil for anointing your feet, ensure your food and drink are sufficient, and furnish you with thick, warm bedding.
With such words of exhortation, you must work diligently. He further addressed him with gentle words: "If you were truly my own son..."
Above, there were three [points], but now only two are versified. The first line versifies the concealment of the superior and the manifestation of the inferior.

The subsequent two and a half lines, beginning with "expedient means" (upāya), versify the three turnings of the Four Noble Truths; the third point, the attachment to inferior dharmas, is omitted from the verse. The first [point] is evident.
The first two lines of the following verse praise the exhortation to practice. The subsequent line, "Since it increases your value," praises the indication of the characteristics [of the truth].

The statement "since it increases your value" refers to the *nirvāṇa* of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). The three lines beginning with "and the oil for anointing the feet" praise the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*). Here, the oil is a metaphor for ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Cultivating and upholding the precepts enables one to attain supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); it is like applying oil to the feet, which allows one to travel without hindrance.

Food and drink are a metaphor for meditative concentration (*samādhi*); concentration can nourish the Dharma-body and the life of wisdom, just as food and drink can sustain the physical body and the life of retribution.
Mattresses and bedding are a metaphor for wisdom (*prajñā*); wisdom can harmonize and adapt to both phenomena and principle, just as mattresses and bedding provide a place to lie down.
This regulates the body composed of the four great elements. Thus, this single phrase of painful words extols the two truths of suffering and its origin.
As for "suffering," it refers to the afflictions of birth and death, which are most terrifying; you must sever them. You must apply yourself with diligence.

He immediately instructed him to cultivate *sthānacitta* (the mind of abiding) until he reached the stage of *laukikāgra-dharma* (the highest mundane dharma). Third, the following two lines of the verse praise his realization:

by severing both *dṛṣṭi-heya* (afflictions abandoned through seeing) and *bhāvanā-heya* (afflictions abandoned through cultivation), he attained the first fruit [of the śrāvaka path]. Therefore, it says, "Just like my son.
△ Third, the verse praises his reception of the Vaipulya [sūtras].
The elder possessed wisdom; he gradually allowed [the son] to enter and exit.
△ Fourth, the verse on receiving the Prajñāpāramitā has three parts. First, the verse skipping ahead on the disciples receiving the teaching:
After twenty years, he took charge of the household affairs.
Because he occupied the rank of the two vehicles and was entrusted with the instruction of bodhisattvas, it is said that "twenty years have passed while he managed the household affairs.
△ Second, a retrospective verse on being commanded by the Tathāgata to take charge.
He showed him the gold, silver, pearls, crystal, and all the goods coming in and out, making him fully aware of them.
△ Third, the actual verse: "Still dwelling in his original place," meaning he remained outside the gate, lodging in a grass hut; he thought to himself regarding his poverty: "I have no such things."

Regarding the phrase "outside the gate": this refers to the provisional wisdom of the partial emptiness possessed by those of the Two Vehicles, which remains outside the gate of the Tathāgata’s true wisdom.

Regarding the phrase "dwelling in a thatched hut": just as worldly grasses arise and perish, those of the Two Vehicles cultivate the contemplation of analytical emptiness (*vibhava-śūnyatā*), observing that all phenomena arise through conditions and perish through conditions; hence it is said they "dwell in a thatched hut. Furthermore, they cultivate...
Because they [the Śrāvakas] are attached to the three Piṭakas and the arising and ceasing of the Four Noble Truths, it is said that they "dwell in a grass hut.

Because the followers of the Two Vehicles do not cultivate the primary and secondary marks (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana), it is said that they "think of their own poverty" (and so forth). △ Fifth, the verses summarizing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* have two parts. First, the verse on discerning the capacities of the disciples.
The father knew his son’s mind had gradually become vast and expansive.
△ Second, the verse on the application of the teaching has four parts.
First, the verse on the great assembly gathering together as he wished to bestow wealth and goods: he immediately assembled his kinsmen, the king, ministers, kṣatriyas, and householders.
△ Second, the verse concludes by correlating the past and the present:
"In this great assembly, he said, 'This is my son, who abandoned me to travel elsewhere for fifty years; now that I have seen him come of his own accord.'"
"It has already been twenty years. Long ago, in a certain city, I lost this son. Wandering everywhere in search of him, I have finally arrived here.

Regarding the phrase "having seen him myself" and so forth: when those with the capacity of the Two Vehicles approach to inspire the Buddha, he now regains his son; therefore it is said, "It has already been twenty years," and so on.
△ Third, the verse on the formal entrustment of the family estate.
"Whatever I possess—my house and my people—I entrust them all to him, allowing him to use them as he pleases.
Here, the house is a metaphor for the realm to be transformed, and the people are a metaphor for the multitudes to be transformed. △ Fourth, the verse on rejoicing in the attainment of karma.
The son thought to himself: "In the past, I was poor and my aspirations were base and inferior. Now, from my father, I have obtained great treasures, as well as a house and all manner of wealth.
I am filled with immense joy at having attained what I never had before."
△ Second, the application of the analogy in verse, in two parts. First, the application of the general analogy in one verse:
"The Buddha is also like this; he knows that I delight in the small.
"The Buddha is also equal [to the elder]" means that the elder first sought his son and subsequently stayed in a certain city. Every...
Every time he thought of this, he did not speak of it to others, but only regretted it within himself: "If I were to obtain a son, I would entrust him to his work.
Thus, with such earnest preparation and through various contrivances, the father came to know his son's intention; for the son was of inferior disposition.

If we speak from the perspective of the Tathāgata’s own domain, it is also like the arrangements made by the elder: first dwelling in the state of having something remaining (*sopadhiśeṣa*) in order to seek those with the capacity for conversion;
then, through intermediate and detailed adjustments; and finally, bringing about great liberation—this is because he knows that those of the two vehicles delight in the lesser [teachings].
II. Verses on the Synthesis of the Separate Similes (five parts). First, the verse synthesizing the *Avataṃsaka*.
It has never been said, "You shall become Buddhas.
Above, it was stated that the Tathāgata constantly says, "I am your father. This is a statement from the *Avataṃsaka*.
Now, to say that it has never been said, "You shall become Buddhas," is also a statement from the *Avataṃsaka*. This is likely because the former refers to the "direct cause" (*hetu*), whereas...
All possess [this nature]; how could it be that the two vehicles alone lack it? Therefore, it is said that [the Buddha] always speaks of them as his children.
Now, regarding their *pariniṣpanna* (perfected) and *paratantra* (dependent) natures, at this time the two vehicles have not yet initiated their practice; how then could they possess them?
Thus, it has never been said that they will become Buddhas. Furthermore, although the Tathāgata has indeed declared that all sentient beings possess the wisdom of the Tathāgata...
Regarding "virtuous nature" (*guṇatā*): if the followers of the Two Vehicles were at this time, they would neither see nor hear, being like the deaf or the mute.

The previous statement was made with reference to the Tathāgata, hence it says he "constantly speaks of [them] as sons. The present statement is made with reference to the followers of the Two Vehicles, hence it says they have "never been told that they shall become Buddhas.
Furthermore, the previous statement that "all possess wisdom and virtuous nature" implies that they indeed possess them.
Because one possesses Buddha-nature, one may be called a "son"; thus it is said that [the Buddha] constantly says, "I regard you all as my sons.
The statement that he has "never yet spoken" refers to the fact that he has never before declared that those of the Two Vehicles shall attain Buddhahood. △ Second, the verse summarizes the Āgamas.

As for our statement that we have attained the various outflows-free states (*anāsrava*), what is taught in the *Āgamas* refers to the fact that by practicing according to the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), one can attain the outflows-free state; if one realizes nirvāṇa, [this is so].
Thus, externally one does not leak into the stage of segmented birth-and-death; if one realizes the True Principle, internally one does not seep into the afflictions of views and thought.
Therefore, it is said that "one attains all that is without outflow" (*anāsrava*). △ Third, the verse on the *Vaipulya* (Extensive) [Sūtras].
Regarding the accomplishment of the Śrāvaka disciples of the Hīnayāna:
it is said that the Tathāgata skillfully relied upon Bodhisattvas from other directions to censure them in various ways and to praise them in various ways.
This was because he wished to bring to fruition our Śrāvaka disciples of the Hīnayāna, causing them to feel shame for their own inferiority and to aspire toward the Bodhisattva path.
...of great ears. △ Fourth, the verse on the synthesis of Prajñā, part five. First, the Tathāgata’s proclamation:
The Buddha commands us, "Proclaim the supreme path; those who practice this shall attain Buddhahood."
What is called the supreme path is the very essence of the wondrous wisdom of *prajñā*.

It not only empties the four marks of self and person, but also empties the mark of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) as well as the mark of non-phenomena (*adharmalakṣaṇa*). Since all marks are empty, then all phenomena—
There is nothing that can surpass it; therefore, it is called the Supreme Path (*anuttara-mārga*).
Regarding the phrase "cultivation and so forth," this means taking this very Supreme Path of universal emptiness as the object of contemplation (*ālambana*).
When wisdom is generated by means of this object, the wisdom that acts as the subject of contemplation is likewise entirely empty. This is the Supreme Prajñā.
This is wisdom. Herein, object and wisdom are merged, and subject and object become one as such, thereby accomplishing the supreme cause and attaining the supreme fruit.
Therefore, it is said that those who practice this shall attain Buddhahood. △ Second, the Buddha-sons receiving the teaching.
Receiving the Buddha’s teaching, I act as a great bodhisattva; by means of various causes and conditions, diverse parables, and manifold expressions, I preach the unsurpassed path.
△ Third, the Bodhisattvas obtain benefits.
All the sons of the Buddhas and others, having heard the Dharma from me, contemplate it day and night and practice it with diligent effort. At that time, all the Buddhas...
He immediately bestowed upon him the prediction: "In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood.
Regarding the phrase "those who hear the Dharma from me," this refers to those of the two vehicles who hear the Tathāgata’s Dharma.

Having heard it, they are able to understand it; therefore, they contemplate it day and night. Having understood it, they are able to practice it; therefore, they cultivate it with diligence. As for that which is observed...
The objects [of perception]—all their characteristics—are empty; the wisdom that contemplates them is likewise empty.
In this way, the emptiness of both the contemplator and the contemplated is itself empty; this is true diligence and true cultivation.
Because one is able to enter realization through such practice, the Buddhas bestow upon them the prediction that they shall become Buddhas. This is how the Buddhas attain their accomplishment.
There is nothing else to being a Buddha; it is simply because one is able to diligently cultivate the unsurpassed path.
Now, since these bodhisattvas likewise diligently cultivate the most supreme path, they are able to attain what the Buddhas have attained;
therefore, all Buddhas bestow upon them the prediction that they shall become Buddhas. △ Fourth, [the case of] having no aspiration oneself.
The secret treasury of the Dharma of all Buddhas is expounded for the sake of bodhisattvas alone, revealing its actual reality;
yet for my sake, this essential truth has not been taught.
Regarding "the equality of all Buddhas": this is the supreme path of the wondrous wisdom of *prajñā*.

It is called "secret" because its entire substance is fully present within the heart-mind of even a single moment of thought for all who abide therein. This is the essence of this supreme path of *prajñā*.
It contains all dharmas exhaustively, leaving nothing remaining; therefore, it is called a "treasury" (*garbha*).

Furthermore, this dharma of the secret treasury is not something that only I, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, am able to realize; rather, the Buddhas of the three periods of time are likewise able to realize it.
Thus, it is called "the dharma of the secret treasury of all Buddhas. The followers of the Two Vehicles claim that [this] secret treasury of the Buddhas—
This Dharma is the true reality of the essential truth. However, it was taught for the sake of Bodhisattvas, not for us followers of the Two Vehicles.
Therefore, having received the Buddha’s command, I have transmitted this teaching for the sake of Bodhisattvas; as for myself, I have no aspiration or resolve toward it.
△ Fifth, No Mind to Hope for Attainment, in two parts. First, the presentation of the analogy.
Just as that impoverished son, having come near his father, although he knew of all the goods, did not wish to take them in his heart.
△ Second, the application [of the analogy] to the two [aspects]. First, the direct application.
Although we have spoken of the precious treasury of the Buddha-dharma, our own lack of aspiration is likewise so.
△ Second, the explanation has two parts. First, the formal explanation.
"We have attained internal extinction and consider ourselves sufficient; we understand only this matter and nothing more.
Therefore, when we hear of purifying Buddha-lands and teaching sentient beings, we feel no joy or delight whatsoever."
Regarding the phrase "inner extinction" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and so forth: it refers to the extinction of the afflictions of views and thought within the inner mind.

That is to say, the reason we ourselves lack aspiration is that, having attained the inner extinction of the afflictions of views and thought and being able to escape the triple world externally, we consider ourselves sufficient; thus, we feel no joy or delight whatsoever in the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas. And yet...

This refers to the aspiration for seeking. △ Second, the further explanation. The intention is that since he has already stated that [his practice] is sufficient and he feels no longing or joy, this further explanation is provided for him. This also has two parts. First, the specific clarification.

Why is this? Because all phenomena are entirely empty and quiescent; they are without arising and without cessation, without greatness and without smallness, and are without outflows and unconditioned.
When one contemplates in this way, no joy or pleasure arises.
The first part clarifies that having already realized the three kinds of emptiness, there is no longer any longing or delight.
As for the phrase "all dharmas," this refers to all phenomena, whether mundane or supramundane, contaminated or uncontaminated.

Since these dharmas are all produced from conditions and all cease through conditions, they are empty and quiescent in their very essence. Because they arise from conditions, their arising is in truth non-arising.
If there were arising, then there would be ceasing. Now, since there is no arising, there is likewise no ceasing. This is what is meant by:
"That which was originally unarisen in the past is likewise unceasing now. This is precisely the liberation of emptiness. If there were arising and ceasing, [it would not be liberation].

Consequently, there would be characteristics such as large and small. Now, since there is neither arising nor ceasing, all dharmas possess not only the absence of the characteristic of largeness, but likewise the absence of the characteristic of smallness. This is precisely the liberation of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣa*).
If there were arising and ceasing, or if largeness and smallness could be apprehended, then there would be leakage and conditioned activity. Now, since all [dharmas]...

Regarding all phenomena (*dharmas*), since neither arising nor ceasing, nor greatness nor smallness, can be apprehended, one does not internally fall into the views and afflictions, nor externally fall into birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
Furthermore, within the triple world, there is no aspiration, seeking, or volitional construction.
This is precisely the liberation of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra-vimokṣa*). One who contemplates in this manner is contemplating the One.
All dharmas are entirely empty, signless, and without volitional activity; they do not themselves give rise to joy or delight.
Throughout the long night, we have been without craving or attachment toward the Buddha’s wisdom, and no longer harbor any aspirations for it, remaining thus with respect to the Dharma ourselves.
This refers to ultimateity;
it clarifies that one’s own words are ultimately realized, and thus there is no further longing or delight. Regarding the phrase "long night":

although the views and afflictions (dṛṣṭi-kleśa) have been destroyed, ignorance (avidyā) remains entirely intact; therefore, it is called the "long night. The remaining meanings may be understood accordingly.
For a long night we have practiced the dharma of emptiness and attained liberation from the afflictions of suffering within the triple world.
Abiding in our final bodies within the nirvana with remainder, we have not failed in the path through the Buddha’s teaching; thus, we have already repaid the Buddha’s kindness.
This clarifies that [the bodhisattvas] have already repaid the Buddha’s kindness; therefore, they feel no joy or attachment. △ Second, the summary:
Although we have expounded the Bodhisattva Dharma for the sake of the sons of the Buddhas to seek the Buddha-way, regarding this Dharma...
Forever devoid of aspiration or delight, the Guide has abandoned me; because he perceives my mind, he did not initially urge me forward by speaking of real benefits.
The first one and a half lines clarify that [the son] himself lacked the will or aspiration; the subsequent line beginning with "the Guide" clarifies that he did not urge him forward.

Because he himself has no aspiration and because the Buddha does not urge him, he has no intention to seek or take [the teaching]. △ Fifth, the verse that correlates with the *Lotus Sūtra* has two parts:

first, the verse correlating with the formal entrustment of the family estate; second, the verse correlating with the joy upon receiving the estate. The first of these two has two sections: first, the presentation of the analogy.
It is like a wealthy elder who, knowing his son’s inferior disposition, uses the power of skillful means to gently subdue his mind, and only then entrusts him with all his wealth and property.
△ Second, the actual verse:
The Buddha is likewise; manifesting rare and marvelous events, he knows those who delight in the Lesser Vehicle and, through the power of skillful means, disciplines their minds.
This is the teaching of great wisdom.
As for what is called a "rare occurrence," it refers to the harmonizing of the five flavors; this is indeed a rare thing. Regarding the taming of the mind:
beginning from concealing one's excellence and manifesting inferiority, up to the final command to turn and teach others—all these constitute the taming of the mind.
This is the matter. △ Second, the verse on the joy of attaining the karma, in three parts. First, citing the Dharma:
"Today we have attained what we have never before had; it was not what we previously hoped for, yet now we have obtained it ourselves."
△ Second, the citation of the analogy:
"Just as that impoverished son obtained immeasurable treasures.
△ Third, the detailed explanation in three parts. First, explaining "joy" by way of opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
World-Honored One, I have now attained the Way and its fruit; regarding the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*), I have attained the pure eye.
To say that one has "attained the Way and its fruit" means that one has attained the unsurpassed fruit of the Way of the Tathāgata.

The "untainted dharmas" refers to the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge. Once the Buddha’s knowledge is opened, the three types of wisdom are attained within a single moment of mind, such that they do not leak away.
It neither falls into emptiness nor into existence; it does not lapse into the middle way either. To obtain the pure eye is to open the Buddha’s vision.
Once the Buddha’s vision is opened, one observes with the five eyes as a single eye. Thus, we know that the wisdom-eye obtained is pure.
Since both the Buddha’s knowledge and the Buddha’s vision are attained, it is said that this explains "rejoicing" in terms of opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
...Furthermore, △ Second, explaining joy by way of attaining the fruit of the practice of precepts:
"For a long night, we have upheld the pure precepts of the Buddha; only today do we begin to receive their retribution within the Dharma of the Dharma King."
Having long cultivated the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), one now attains the untainted (*anāsrava*) and unsurpassed supreme fruit.

For those such as myself who formerly cultivated the pure precepts and pure conduct, they are now fully revealed and perfected as the wondrous precept of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*) and inconceivable practice.
Because the wondrous fruit is obtained through these causes, it is termed "the precept of attainment" (*pratilambha-śīla*).
This explains their joy by way of the fruit. △ Third, explaining their joy by way of the true nature of the two vehicles:
"We are now truly śrāvakas; with the sound of the Buddha-way, we cause all to hear. We are now..."
A true Arhat, among all the worlds—including devas, humans, Māras, and Brahmās—is universally worthy of receiving offerings therein. As for those like us:
in the past, we caused devas and humans to hear only the sound of the Śrāvaka; now, by means of the sound of the Buddha-way, we cause all to hear.
Therefore, we are truly Śrāvakas. In the past, we merely slew the thieves [of the afflictions] and were worthy of receiving offerings from others.
"He is worthy of offerings from the heavens. Since he does not now kill the thieves, he should receive the offerings of all the world;
therefore, he is truly an Arhat. This means that the Śrāvaka Arhats are all truly so; thus it is said, "truly [so] are the two vehicles," expressing their joy.
II. Praising the Profundity of the Buddha’s Kindness. Regarding this single passage praising his kindness, it follows the previous verse of the Tathāgata’s reiteration.
The parables having been concluded, he then addressed Śāriputra with a single discourse of exhortation to faith, ensuring that people would believe without any doubt.

Now that the four great disciples have finished their explanations, they have praised the profound depth of the Tathāgata’s kindness to the utmost, so that people may know how deep the Buddha’s grace is;
there is nothing else by which it can be repaid, save for believing what the Buddha has taught—this alone may serve as a repayment.
This will likewise cause people to give rise to faith and be free from doubt.

This is because these four great disciples not only understood the purport of the Tathāgata’s direct teaching through parables, but also believed and understood the purport of the Tathāgata’s exhortation to have faith.
The text is divided into two parts; the first is a general praise.
The World-Honored One’s great kindness is such that, through this rare occurrence, he has compassionately taught and transformed us for our benefit.
Throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas, who could ever repay it?
Regarding what is called a "rare and marvelous matter": if we discuss it from a distant perspective, it began with the great teachings at the abodes of twenty trillion Buddhas;
next, there were the minor connections during the intervening period; and finally, today, there is the harmonious adjustment of the five flavors. All of these are indeed rare and marvelous matters.
If we examine this closely, it was already extensively explained and revealed within the Discourse on the Dharma (dharmadeśanā), enabling those of superior faculties to enter into realization.
Now, by means of an illustrative discourse (aupamyadeśanā), even those of middling faculties are enabled to attain realization; this, too, is indeed a rare and marvelous occurrence.
That which is rare is simply this: that the provisional and the real are non-dual, and that the three and the one are mutually identical.

Since this is the fundamental intention of all Buddhas and the great causal condition (*mahā-pratyaya*), how could it not be rare? △ Second, the specific praise in two parts. First, explaining the inability to repay [the Buddha's kindness].
Providing for them with hands and feet, prostrating with one’s head in reverence, and offering every form of worship—none of these can repay their kindness.

Even if one were to carry them upon the crown of one's head or bear them on both shoulders with all one's heart and respect throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and furthermore offer exquisite delicacies and immeasurable precious garments; [it still could not repay them].
Furthermore, even if one were to offer various bedding and furniture, diverse medicinal decoctions, ox-head sandalwood, and all manner of rare jewels—

constructing stūpas and temples and spreading precious robes upon the ground— and were to perform such acts of worship for as many kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, one still could not repay [the Buddha's kindness].

The Buddha taught that the practice of the Dharma consists of three aspects: teaching, practice, and principle. These extend vertically through time and pervade horizontally across space; there is nothing that is not the Dharma-realm. This is truly because the retribution for such merit lies in its wide propagation.
Thus, the first [offering] is providing material support; the second is bearing it upon one’s head; the third is the four types of service; and the fourth is the construction of stupas and temples.
Fifth, the summary: "None can repay the Buddha’s kindness" is because these are all worldly things.
△ Second, explaining that one can only offer praise, in two parts: first, praising by way of knowing the Dharma.
The Buddhas possess rare, immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable great supernormal powers; they are the kings of all dharmas, untainted and unconditioned.
Yet, for the sake of those who are inferior, they endure such matters as these, and for the sake of ordinary people who grasp at signs, they preach according to what is appropriate.
The Buddhas have attained supreme mastery over all phenomena.
The phrase "great supernormal power" is a praise for the power of the Tathāgata’s supernatural faculties, which are untainted and unconditioned.
This praises the power of the wisdom possessed by the Tathāgata. By means of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, the three types of knowledge are attained within a single moment of mind;
thus, one does not fall into the extremes of emptiness, existence, or the middle. Therefore, it is called "untainted wisdom" (*anāsrava-jñāna*).

Since this wisdom is sublime, it is able to fully integrate nature (*xing*) to give rise to cultivation (*xiu*), fully integrate cultivation to return to nature, and rely upon principle (*li*) to initiate practice.
When practice accords with principle, then principle and practice are as one, and cultivation and nature are non-dual, such that there is no deliberate fabrication;

therefore, it is called "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*). The two phrases beginning with "immeasurable above" [in the verse] collectively govern the two phrases concerning supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), for the Buddhas possess the power of immeasurable and boundless supernormal powers and wisdom; thus, all phenomena—whether mundane or supramundane, such as hearing and so forth—[are manifested].
Having attained great mastery, he is called the "King of All Dharmas.
Because he is the King among dharmas, he is able to endure for us—people of inferior resolve—the act of concealing his excellence and manifesting inferiority;
thus it is said that he "is able to [act] for those who are inferior," and so forth. Because he is able to endure such matters, he accords with ordinary beings who grasp at signs.
It is appropriate to explain it for them; one who can act according to what is suitable does so because of mastery over the Dharma. Therefore, the Buddhas [say... (etc.).
△ Second, praising by way of knowing the capacities of beings.
He knows the various desires, inclinations, and capacities of all sentient beings, and according to what they are able to bear, he teaches the Dharma through immeasurable parables.
Furthermore, he knows which sentient beings have matured and which have not, based on their roots of goodness from past lives.
Having deliberated in various ways and distinguished [the capacities of beings] through knowledge, [the Buddha] taught the One Vehicle path as three according to what was appropriate.
In summary, the Tathāgata has nothing regarding the Dharma that he does not understand, and no capacity [of a being] that he does not know;

therefore, he is able to preach the Dharma according to their capacities and adapt the Dharma to suit those capacities. Since the capacities and the Dharma are thus mutually compatible, those who hear it will surely attain awakening. For this reason:
Those of superior faculties have already understood, and those of middling faculties also know this:

that it is the Tathāgata who, through rare deeds, out of compassion and for the sake of teaching and transforming us, has brought us benefit. Such profound kindness is as boundless as the Dharma-realm and as limitless as empty space;
we wish to repay it but are unable to do so, and can only offer praise in the hope that it may...
All realize the profound kindness of the Buddha and believe what the Buddha has taught without doubt. This concludes the Explanation of the Chapter on Faith and Understanding.

The fifth chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, "The Parable of the Medicinal Herbs," concerning what is called the "Sublime Dharma" (*saddharma*):

if one wishes to trace its origin, it is precisely as clarified in this present chapter—the Dharma of a single characteristic and a single flavor, which is an inconceivable Dharma. Indeed, all dharmas are fundamentally...
In its ultimate totality, it is of one and the same mark of reality and possesses the identical flavor of the finest clarified butter (*sarpis*).

However, because the emotional attachments and grasping of sentient beings differ from one another, they may grasp this single-marked Dharma as having marks, as having the mark of emptiness, or as having the mark of the Middle Way; therefore, the Tathāgata also teaches in accordance with what is appropriate for them.

Some speak of the flavor of milk that is both [fresh and processed]; some speak of the flavor of curd that is merely [processed]; some speak of the flavor of fresh butter that is opposed [to the previous];
and some speak of the flavor of refined butter that is accompanied [by further processing]. These characteristics are distinct characteristics rather than a single characteristic;
their flavors are distinct flavors rather than a single flavor. Therefore, these are coarse and cannot be called sublime. Upon reaching [this point]...
Now, with the opening and revelation of this single *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, all diverse characteristics become a single characteristic;

all diverse flavors are entirely of one flavor. Just as when "existence" is raised, everything exists—existence being the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*)—and when "emptiness" is raised, everything is empty—emptiness being the true mark—and when "the Middle" is raised, everything is the Middle—the Middle...
This is precisely the true reality (*dharmatā*). Therefore, all diverse characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) become a single characteristic.

Since all characteristics are identical within this one true reality, they all become the single flavor of unsurpassed *amṛta* (clarified butter) according to the four flavors—combined, simple, alternating, and continuous.
Thus, there is no longer any distinct characteristic or distinct flavor to be found; it is like jars, plates, hairpins, and bracelets being returned to the great furnace.
Yet they share the same essence of gold. Just as the Yangtze, Huai, Yellow, and Han rivers enter the great ocean and become one with its salty taste, it is called the "Sublime Dharma" (Saddharma).

To clarify this Sublime Dharma through a metaphor, it is exactly like a lotus flower. For the lotus remains ever pure even while situated in defilement, and its blossoming and fruition occur simultaneously.
Thus, the Sublime Dharma is such that within the coarse, there is the sublime, and they are one and the same.
The flavor of the single characteristic is such that, although the Dharma and its metaphor differ, they are equal by analogy;

thus, the essence of the wondrous Dharma is compared to the metaphor of the lotus. As for why this is called a "sūtra," it is because it was proclaimed from the golden mouth of our Buddha, the Tathāgata;
by relying upon it, one may reach the concentration of the single true characteristic, just as in the world...
This is the path.

As for the parable of the medicinal herbs, it is the manifestation of a single chapter; yet, if one discusses the sequential generation of these chapters, they all arise fundamentally from the four great disciples who, upon hearing the Dharma and its parables revealed in two successive stages, were likewise able to understand the Three Vehicles.
The whole is the One Vehicle. Thus, he set forth his understanding through a parable, saying:
"The Tathāgata is like a wealthy elder, while we of the Two Vehicles are like impoverished sons. This was when Shanggen expressed his realization.
Since the Tathāgata has already provided an exposition for them, he now provides an exposition for those of medium capacity as well.
Thus, the Tathāgata also provides this exposition: "You followers of the two vehicles say of yourselves that you are like destitute sons;
yet when I, the Tathāgata, observe you, you followers of the two vehicles are like medicinal herbs. Therefore, there is this Parable of the Medicinal Herbs.
This chapter is the text in which the Tathāgata confirms and completes the understanding attained by those of medium capacity.

Furthermore, regarding the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs," because the four great disciples attained awakening through the use of parables and likewise employed parables when expressing their realization, the Tathāgata now likewise confirms it by means of a parable; thus, it is named the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" Chapter. However...

In this chapter, although there are parables concerning mountains, rivers, clouds, and rain, the medicinal herbs alone are singled out for mention because the mountains and rivers are that which produce, while the medicinal herbs are that which is produced;
the clouds and rain are that which moisten, while the medicinal herbs are that which is moistened.
If one mentions the medicinal herbs that are produced and moistened, this includes both the clouds and rain that provide moisture and the mountains and rivers that produce them.
If one mentions the mountains and rivers that produce them, this likewise includes the medicinal herbs that are produced, yet it cannot include the clouds and rain that provide moisture.
However, if one mentions the clouds and rain that provide moisture, then they can likewise include [the mountains and rivers].
The medicinal herbs that are produced cannot encompass the mountains and rivers that produce them;
however, if one mentions the medicinal herbs, all such things are thereby included. Therefore, instead of mentioning the mountains, rivers, clouds, and rain, only the medicinal herbs are singled out.
The term "medicinal herbs" is used because they possess the meaning of "antidote," just as worldly medicinal herbs can counteract various diseases.
Furthermore, as clarified in the text of this chapter, there are three kinds of medicinal herbs: namely, small medicinal herbs, medium medicinal herbs, and superior medicinal herbs.
"Superior" refers to devas and humans; "medium" refers to those of the two vehicles (*dvayāyānika*); and "superior" refers to the bodhisattvas of the Tripitaka.

Devas and humans are able to counteract the three miserable realms through precepts and wholesome deeds; those of the two vehicles are able to counteract the three [miserable realms] through the truths and conditions (*satya-pratyaya*).
The realms. Bodhisattvas are thus able to use the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) as remedies for the six obscurations. Therefore, these five vehicles are all called "medicinal herbs.

However, in the Shared Teaching (*pāryāya-yāna*), one can use the realization of essence-emptiness (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) as a remedy for analytical contemplation (*vibhanga-vipaśyanā*). In the Distinct Teaching (*pratyeka-yāna*), one can use the gradual [approach] as a remedy for essence-contemplation.
In the Perfect Teaching (*ekayāna*), one can use the single mind (*ekacitta*) as a remedy for the gradual [approach]. This is how they are all...
They may be called medicinal herbs, yet they are not called medicinal herbs. This is because one wishes to distinguish the Bodhisattvas of the three teachings from the Bodhisattvas of the Tripitaka;
thus, both the Shared and Distinct Teachings take the names of the two trees because they are able to provide pervasive shade and shelter.
As for the Perfect Teaching, it is that which gives rise to the ground of the single reality, and it does not merely consist in remedial counteraction.

...and that is all. Nevertheless, although medicinal herbs differ in three types, if one points specifically to the intent behind the title of this chapter, it lies solely in the "medicinal herbs of medium capacity.
This is because this chapter is the Tathāgata’s exposition and confirmation of what has been realized by those of medium faculties.
△ Third, the Tathāgata’s Exposition and Confirmation, in two parts: first, the prose; second, the verses. First part: [Prose]

Three parts: first, a brief exposition establishing [the meaning]; second, an extensive exposition establishing it; third, a concluding summary and praise. The first [of these three] has two sections. First, the narration of what has already been received.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahākāśyapa and the great disciples: "Excellent, excellent, Kāśyapa!"
You have eloquently expounded the true merits of the Tathāgata; it is indeed as you have said.
As for the initial mention of "the great disciples," this refers specifically to the three beginning with Subhūti.
However, when inferred according to their meaning, it also encompasses others. This is because the first cycle of the parable was not intended for the understanding of only these four individuals.

Regarding the double expression of "Excellent": because the four great disciples, through both general and specific analogies, have grasped the two rounds of the Tathāgata’s teaching—both the Dharma and the parable—they have opened up the three to reveal the one and opened up the provisional to reveal the real.

Thus, they are not only able to understand the three provisional teachings spoken by the Tathāgata, but are also able to understand the one real teaching spoken by the Tathāgata; for this reason, he expresses it twice.
"Excellent! Furthermore, you are not only able to grasp the general analogy of the Tathāgata, but also able to grasp his specific analogies;
therefore, he twice uttered 'Excellent! In sum, within the context of the two vehicles, you have skillfully set forth your own understanding;
within the context of the Tathāgata’s own realm, you have skillfully conformed to the Buddha's mind. Thus he said, 'Excellent, excellent! Not so.
It not only captures the essence of the teachings of the five periods, but also encompasses the far-reaching intent of the single-period edification;
therefore, "Excellent, excellent! is stated twice. As for the phrase "well-spoken true merits of the Tathāgata," what are these true merits of the Tathāgata?
At the very beginning, at the abodes of twenty trillion Buddhas, for the sake of those of the two vehicles, [the Tathāgata]... [lowered...]
Regarding those with the perfect seed of the One Vehicle and those who temporarily regressed from the Great [Vehicle], they were subsequently received through the Small [Vehicle].
If, in this present life, the small tree ripens first, they are then led to realize *nirvāṇa*.

Upon reaching today’s *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, their three provisional means are opened and the one true reality is revealed, enabling them to attain the opening, showing, awakening to, and entering into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Thus it is.
From beginning to end, and including the intermediate stages, everything is none other than the Tathāgata’s true and real merit.

Although the teachings encountered and those used to guide others during the intermediate stages may be minor dharmas, their fundamental intention is truly to lead beings from these points back to the Great Vehicle.
Furthermore, once a single sūtra is revealed and made manifest, it is entirely the reality itself; therefore, from the beginning through the end, and including the middle, all is so.
All of these are genuine merits. You have spoken of such genuine merits; you have truly exhausted your words.
Therefore, it is said that they were "well-spoken. How is it known that this constitutes being well-spoken? It is because at the time of their presentation, [the meaning was fully grasped].
The general analogy summarizes the Tathāgata’s transformative guidance throughout his entire career, while the specific analogies summarize the teachings of the five periods.
Therefore, within the analogies, it says: "It was as if a wealthy elder had an only son, who had run away from home."
He then sought his son and halted at a certain city along the way. Later, seeing his son approaching, he immediately told his messenger to go and seize him.
The son, both startled and terrified, fell to the ground. Thereupon, the father secretly dispatched a messenger to lure him back;

he himself removed his precious garments and put on tattered rags, using skillful means to draw near and tell him to work diligently, calling him "son," and subsequently allowing him to enter and leave the house.
There is no difficulty. Next, he commands that the various goods be taken charge of; afterwards, he establishes the father-son relationship and entrusts the family estate to him.
Within the context of the Dharma, it is said: "In the past, for our sake, the Tathāgata descended into the great elements.

Because we regressed from the Great Vehicle and entered the cycle of birth and death, the Tathāgata then ceased his expedient means in the realm of conditioned existence (upapadya-parinirvāṇa) in order to seek [us]."
Regarding those with the capacity for transformation, when they later perceive our great capacity stirring in secret, we immediately employ the Great Vehicle as the appropriate means.
However, because we take pleasure in the Small Vehicle and do not yet accord with it, we ultimately cause the Two Vehicles to serve as an inducement.

Furthermore, while within the stage of the Dharmakāya, the Tathāgata foresaw that our small capacities would ripen first; he therefore concealed his excellence and manifested inferiority through skillful means.
The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* sūtra induces and certifies [the attainment of] nirvāṇa; next, the *Vaipulya* sūtras censure and refute; the *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras command and bring about awakening;

finally, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is preached to cause us to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Thus, both the dharma and its metaphors are clearly elucidated, and both the general and the specific are fully revealed.
Beginning from the presence of twenty trillion Buddhas and ending with the present day in this royal city, there is nothing that has not been recounted in detail.
This is precisely where his skillful exposition resides. "Truly as you have said" refers to all the true merits possessed by the Tathāgata;
they are indeed just as the four of you have stated. △ Second, recounting what has not yet been reached.

The Tathāgata further possesses immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) merits, which you would be unable to exhaustively describe even in immeasurable billions of kalpas. Furthermore,
regarding the phrase "the Tathāgata has equals," it means that although you may be able to skillfully describe the merits of the Tathāgata, yet as for the Tathāgata...
Furthermore, the Tathāgata possesses immeasurable, boundless, and incomparable merits.
If you followers of the Two Vehicles were to attempt to describe them, they would not be exhausted even at the end of an eon; they cannot be fully understood through a single analogy alone.
This is why it says, "Furthermore, the Tathāgata [possesses... and so forth. However, how can one ultimately perceive the Tathāgata?
Furthermore, there are immeasurable merits that cannot be fully described by those of the Two Vehicles.

If one examines what was previously understood in light of the present passage where the Tathāgata’s accomplishments are set forth, one will know that the Tathāgata possesses further immeasurable merits that the Two Vehicles cannot exhaustively describe. As it was stated in the previous summary: "The Tathāgata, for..."
For our sake, [the Tathāgata] has cast off his precious [robes] to don coarse ones, and concealed his excellence to manifest inferiority.
Thus, because there is this difference between concealment and manifestation, it appears as if excellence and inferiority were two distinct things.

However, in relation to the following passage—which states that the Tathāgata manifests his body like a cloud, pervading the trichiliocosm—since he manifests his body like a cloud, it is entirely a matter of the excellent arising as the inferior; it is entirely inferior.

This is precisely the supreme. The three bodies are one essence; since superiority and inferiority are not distinguished, how could there be any inequality regarding their concealment or manifestation?

This very triune body as a single body is the immeasurable merit of the Tathāgata, which the teachings of the two vehicles cannot exhaustively describe, for they fail to grasp what lies beyond their reach.
As stated above in the summary: "That which was taught forty years ago was provisional."
What is taught today in the Lotus Sūtra is the truth; thus, it appears as if there is a distinction between the provisional and the real.

However, in relation to the following passage—which states that the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma is like rain, falling equally upon all at once—since the Dharma is said to be like rain, this "at once" means that when the single, perfect voice is uttered, beings of different kinds all hear it; thus, what is real is itself the provisional.
Ultimate reality (*bhūtatathatā*) is indeed real. How could there be a distinction between what was provisional in the past and what is real now?

This very [reality] is the immeasurable merit of the Tathāgata, which cannot be fully exhausted by the teachings of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*). Furthermore, as stated above in the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra*:
"We who are here are truly śrāvakas; we are truly arhats. This appears to be the two vehicles, yet it is in fact the Buddha.
As for the "vehicle" (yāna): if one refers to the subsequent passage, it means that each receives nourishment according to its capacity and attains growth accordingly.
Thus, whether it be the nine realms, the three vehicles, or the seven kinds of expedient means, there are none that do not ultimately return to the Buddha-vehicle.
That is to say, the entire Dharma-realm is opened up such that all without exception shall become Buddhas; how could it be that only the two vehicles are [already] Buddhas? This is the Tathāgata’s...
His immeasurable merits cannot be fully described even by those of the Two Vehicles. Furthermore, as stated above in the Preface:
"We who have now attained the Way and realized the fruit"—this seems to imply that there is a Way to be realized and a fruit to be obtained.
However, when contrasted with the following passage, it says: "Yet these grasses and trees do not know this of themselves; only the Tathāgata knows it."
In the Dharma of a single characteristic and a single flavor, there is ultimate nirvana, the eternally quiescent mark that ultimately returns to emptiness;
therein, what path is there to be realized, and what fruit is there to be attained? This is the immeasurable and boundless [wisdom] of the Tathāgata.
The merit is incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*); even the teachings of the two vehicles cannot exhaustively describe it. △ Second, the detailed exposition of its fulfillment.

The reason for thus revealing this matter in such layered depth is that although the four great disciples had already understood the purport of the Tathāgata’s parables and the principles of their manifestation, there remained further points of realization beyond their grasp. Therefore, as...
I shall now provide a detailed exposition of each point, so that all may attain full understanding. The text is divided into three parts:
first, the direct indication through the Dharma; second, the skillful elucidation by means of analogies; and third, the application back to the Dharma.

This enables one to know the analogies by means of the Dharma and to understand the Dharma through the analogies, so that hundreds of thousands of humans and devas may all be able to comprehend that the Tathāgata further possesses the unconditioned.
This is because it measures his merit. First, he is the King of all Dharmas; for those of lower capacity, he manifests his body like a cloud, which serves as the basis for the subsequent metaphor.
This refers to the passage beginning with "pervading the three thousand great thousandfold worlds. Second, that which he has taught is not false.
1. "Preaching the Dharma for those below like rain" serves as the basis for the subsequent analogy of spreading [the rain]. This refers to the phrase: "At one time, it rains equally. 2.

"The three [vehicles] all reach the ground of wisdom" serves as the basis for the subsequent analogy of receiving moisture and growing. This refers to the passage beginning with: "Its moisture universally permeates...
reaching the blossoming of flowers and the ripening of fruit. 3. "Only the Buddha knows them all" serves as the basis for the subsequent [section on] each...

The phrase "not knowing for oneself" serves as the basis for the following analogy; this refers to the passage beginning with "even though on the same stage. First, regarding the division of the text according to the Dharma, there are four parts;
the first concerns the King of All Dharmas.
Kāśyapa, you should know that the Tathāgata is the King of all dharmas.

As for "all dharmas," this refers to the mundane and supramundane, the outflowing and non-outflowing, the wholesome and unwholesome, the false and correct, the partial and gradual, the complete and sudden, as well as the provisional and the ultimate dharmas. Within these various dharmas, the Tathāgata has attained great...
One who possesses mastery is called a king. Since one has attained mastery over all phenomena (*dharmas*), one does not merely attain great mastery over supramundane phenomena;
one is likewise able to attain great mastery over mundane phenomena. Furthermore, one does not merely attain great mastery over the phenomena of ultimate reality (*tattva*);
one is likewise [able to attain it] over the phenomena of skillful means (*upāya*).
One can attain great mastery. Yet, how is it known that the Tathāgata possesses mastery over all dharmas?

It is because when the Tathāgata wishes to speak of worldly dharmas, he speaks of worldly dharmas; and even when he wishes to speak of the dharmas of ultimate reality, he speaks of the dharmas of ultimate reality.
For this reason, he is said to have attained mastery over all dharmas. Furthermore, he wishes to reveal...

To manifest all dharmas means that, according to whatever worldly or world-transcending dharmas are taught, there is nothing that is not ultimately realized as being, in its entirety, identical with the single true reality (*dharmatā*). This is the attainment of supreme mastery.

It is just as stated in the previous passage, where the four great disciples, in praising the Buddha’s grace, said: "The Buddhas are rare; they possess immeasurable and boundless great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*)."
Power. It is untainted and unconditioned. The King of all dharmas. By means of what the four great disciples praised, one immediately knows that the Tathāgata is the King of all dharmas.
Therefore it is said, “Kāśyapa... [and so forth]. △ Second, the teaching spoken is not in vain.
Whatever is spoken is entirely without falsehood. Regarding this lack of falsehood:
since the Tathāgata is the sovereign of all dharmas, there is no principle he does not understand and no wisdom he does not manifest.
Therefore, it is only when there is nothing further to be said that he remains silent; if he does speak, it is necessarily in accordance with reality.
It is said that he speaks in accordance with wisdom; therefore, it is not false.
Since all that is spoken is non-false, it follows that not only are the supramundane dharmas spoken of non-false, but even the mundane dharmas spoken of are likewise non-false.
Not only is the true Dharma that has been taught not false, but even the expedient teachings that have been taught are likewise not false.

This is because the Tathāgata has already attained ultimate realization of the three thousand natures and characteristics—the principle of the true mark of all phenomena—and has thereby acquired the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). Thus, although the various phenomena he teaches possess differences...
They are not the same. If one [truth] is revealed and manifested, there is nothing that is not real; therefore, it is said that whatever is spoken is never false.
Because what he speaks is never false, he is the King of All Dharmas. Because he is the King of All Dharmas, he can manifest bodies like clouds.
Because what he speaks is never false, he can preach the Dharma like rain. △ Third, *Siddhi* (Universal Accomplishment).
Having reached the stage of wisdom,
one expounds all phenomena through the skillful means of wisdom; all that is taught reaches the stage of omniscience.
Regarding the phrase "equal toward all dharmas," this refers to the various dharmas explained above.
Within these dharmas, the Tathāgata is able to employ the skillful means (*upāya*) of his realized wisdom to expound them according to what is appropriate for sentient beings.
If it were the followers of the Two Vehicles, they would possess only wisdom but lack skillful means; whereas the Bodhisattvas possess only skillful means... [but] lack wisdom.
Because they lack such wisdom, they are all unable to expound upon all dharmas as appropriate.
The Tathāgata, however, is fully endowed with the perfection of skillful means and insight;

therefore, he is able to expound upon all dharmas according to what he has realized through his wisdom and skillful means, as is appropriate for each person or deva. That is to say, it is according to what is suitable for humans and devas.
By means of wisdom and skillful means, he expounds the precepts and virtues, according to what is appropriate for the two vehicles.
By means of wisdom and skillful means, he expounds the truths and conditions, according to what is appropriate for the Three Baskets (Tripitaka).

By means of wisdom and skillful means, he expounds the six perfections, according to what is appropriate for the Shared Teaching. By means of wisdom and skillful means, he expounds upon the non-... [emptiness].
"Arising according to what is appropriate for each distinct teaching, he employs the skillful means of wisdom (*jñānopāya*) to expound the immeasurable;
therefore, it is said that he expounds all dharmas through the skillful means of wisdom.

Regarding the statement, "The teachings he expounds all reach the stage of omniscience (*sarvajñatābhūmi*)," this means that although he teaches according to what is appropriate and thus each [teaching] differs, nevertheless...
Ultimately, all shall reach the ground of the true mark of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
This is because it was the original intention of the Tathāgata solely to expound all-knowledge for the sake of all sentient beings;

however, because the capacities of sentient beings were not yet in accord, he taught according to what was appropriate for the occasion. If this were not revealed and clarified, there would be only the distinction between the mundane and the supramundane.
Regarding the characteristics of the distinctions between the outflowing (*sāsrava*) and the outflow-free (*anāsrava*), once a single sutra has revealed them, they follow accordingly—
from the mundane precepts and virtues and the supramundane truths and conditions, up to the general realization of non-arising and the particularized immeasurables.
Though they differ in various ways, there is none that does not ultimately coincide with the ground of the true mark (*dharmatā*) and the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Therefore, it is said that the teachings he proclaims all reach the ground of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
Because they all reach the ground of wisdom, whatever he speaks is entirely without falsehood; thus, he is the King of all Dharmas. Because he has [reached] them all...

Having reached the stage of wisdom, it is like the various plants, thickets, forests, trees, and medicinal herbs that each receive nourishment according to their capacity and all attain growth accordingly. △ Fourth, only the Buddha knows them all.
The Tathāgata perceives and knows the ultimate destination of all phenomena; he also knows the profound mental activities and practices of all sentient beings with unimpeded penetration.
Furthermore, having thoroughly investigated and clearly understood all phenomena, he reveals to all sentient beings all-encompassing wisdom.
Regarding the phrase "The Tathāgata observes and knows," etc.: although all dharmas have reached the ground of wisdom, all sentient beings do not know this of themselves;
only the Tathāgata is able to know it. As for the reason why the Tathāgata knows it:
This is because the Tathāgata is able to observe and know the ultimate destination of all dharmas. "Observing and knowing" refers to the wisdom that performs the observation;
"all dharmas" refers to the objects of observation—namely, the various phenomena such as the biased and the heterodox, the Great and the Small Vehicles, and so forth, which were explained above.
Although these differ from one another in a thousand ways and ten thousand variations, for the Tathāgata, they are inconceivable...
Consider this through the wondrous wisdom of contemplation: there is nothing that does not ultimately converge upon the single Buddha-vehicle (ekayāna) of the perfect and sudden ultimate.
Since the Tathāgata is able to contemplate and know that all phenomena converge upon the One Vehicle, the teaching he expounds is the wondrous teaching.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "knowing the deep minds of all sentient beings" and so forth, it means that the Tathāgata does not merely contemplate...

He knows merely the ultimate destination of all phenomena. He also knows the nine realms, the three vehicles, and the seven kinds of expedient means, as well as the practices of the profound minds of all sentient beings.
It is not that he merely knows their practices; he also penetrates them with unimpeded mastery.
Furthermore, regarding the practices of their profound minds: if they are the sentient beings of the three miserable paths, then [he knows] their profound mental activities.
The conduct of those in the realms of evil is such; for humans and devas, that which is practiced with a deep mind is good;
for sentient beings of external paths, that which is practiced with a deep mind is heterodox; for sentient beings of the internal teachings, that which is practiced with a deep mind is correct;

for sentient beings of the six destinies, that which is practiced with a deep mind is with outflows (*sāsrava*); and for sentient beings of the two vehicles, that which is practiced with a deep mind is...
This is the untainted [state]. For those of the three vehicles, that which is practiced with the profound mind is partial;
for those of the Perfect Teaching, that which is practiced with the profound mind is perfect. Yet the Tathāgata illuminates them with the threefold wisdom of a single mind.
Although there are thousands of differences and myriad distinctions, they are all universally penetrating and unobstructed, as the Tathāgata has ultimately and fully realized through cultivation.
The entirety of evil is precisely inherent evil; the entirety of cultivated goodness is precisely inherent goodness. Good and evil are non-dual; the cultivated and the inherent are equal.
There is not a single evil that does not coincide with good, nor a single deviation that does not coincide with the correct.

This extends even to the point where there is not a single partiality that does not coincide with the perfect. Thus, the deviant and the correct are of one accord, and the partial and the perfect are one.

This essence is what is called "unimpeded penetration. Since the Tathāgata is able to fully understand that all his activities are unimpededly penetrating, then all his conduct constitutes sublime conduct (*sucarita*).

Furthermore, regarding one who has thoroughly investigated and clearly understood all phenomena, it means that the Tathāgata not only knows the unimpeded penetration of the conduct of sentient beings, but [understands all phenomena as well].
