...and so forth. Furthermore, regarding all phenomena of the three thousandfold nature and characteristics, he is able to exhaustively and clearly understand them as being identical to the single true reality (*bhūtatathatā*).
The Tathāgata is able to attain the three types of knowledge within a single moment of mind;

therefore, although he can exhaustively and clearly perceive them—despite their individual differences—they are identical to the single true reality. The Tathāgata is able to see with the five eyes within a single eye; therefore, he is able to...
Although all phenomena are individually distinct when investigated to their ultimate limit and fully understood, they are all the true nature (*dharmatā*).

Therefore, it is said that he has "thoroughly investigated and clearly understood all dharmas. Since the Tathāgata is thus able to thoroughly investigate and clearly understand that all dharmas are entirely the true nature, the principle he possesses is the sublime principle.
That he demonstrates wisdom to all sentient beings is truly due to the Tathāgata... [text continues]

Having personally been able to give rise to practice in accordance with the teachings and enter realization through that practice, one then desires to cause all sentient beings to likewise become non-dual with oneself;
therefore, one reveals to all sentient beings all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñā*). All-encompassing wisdom is precisely the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
By means of this knowledge of all modes, one is able to illuminate the sublime teachings and is able to give rise to the sublime [realization].

Practice is that which can accord with the subtle principle. Now, the Tathāgata wishes to cause sentient beings to give rise to practice based on the teaching, and through practice to realize the principle;

therefore, he reveals all-encompassing wisdom to all sentient beings. Because the Tathāgata is able to contemplate and know the ultimate destination of all phenomena, and even because he is able to reveal all-encompassing wisdom to all sentient beings, that which he...
The preaching of the Dharma reaches all the way to the stage of wisdom, and it is entirely without falsehood; such is the King of the Dharma.

As for the nine realms, the three vehicles, and the seven expedient means, they are like those various trees and medicinal herbs: although they share the same earth and the same rain, each is unaware of this for itself.
Part Two: Skillfully Clarifying through Similes (in four sections). First, clarifying the manifestation of the body through the analogy of clouds.

Kāśyapa, it is like this: suppose there were a great trichiliocosm, with its mountains, rivers, valleys, and lands, where various kinds of grasses, trees, thickets, forests, and medicinal herbs grow, each with different species and distinct names and forms. Then, dense clouds spread out, completely covering the entire great trichiliocosm.
This analogy above refers to these Kings of Dharma; that is, the Tathāgata manifesting his body as the master who performs transformations.

Since there is a master who performs transformations, there must necessarily be an object to be transformed. Therefore, the analogy of the three thousandfold world system and so forth is first explained to illustrate the objects to be transformed.
Next, the analogy of the dense clouds spreading everywhere is explained to illustrate the manifestation of the master who performs transformations.

The body and the objects manifested by it comprise the ten realms (*daśadhātu*). These ten realms necessarily arise from the inherent potentiality (*li-jù*) before they can be manifested as actual phenomena (*shi-zào*).
Therefore, first the metaphors of the mountains, rivers, lands, and so forth—which represent the productive capacity—are explained to illustrate the ten realms as inherent potentiality.
Next, the metaphors of the grasses, trees, thickets, and forests—which represent that which is produced—are explained to illustrate the ten realms as actual manifestation.
It is so. As for the mention of "three thousand," this refers to the small thousand, middle thousand, and great thousand [world systems]. This is a general enumeration.

By generally enumerating the three thousand worlds, it specifically illustrates the nature and characteristics of the three thousandfold world of provisional names and real dharmas—the dependent retribution.

The two characters "Great Thousand" (trichiliocosm) are mentioned separately; this separate mention of the great trichiliocosm serves as a general metaphor for the three thousandfold world-system’s nature and characteristics, all of which constitute a single, great, comprehensive dharma-gate.
The six characters "mountains, rivers, valleys, streams, land, and soil" [are likewise so designated].
This is the distinction. Collectively, it serves as a metaphor for the ten dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*).

Within a great trichiliocosm, mountains, rivers, valleys, and lands exist by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*); likewise, within the Great Universal Dharma-Gate, the ten realms exist by the very nature of things.
Furthermore, the mountains, rivers, valleys, and so forth are specifically metaphors for the four noble dharma-realms, while the two characters "land" (*tǔ dì*)—
This is a general metaphor for the Dharma-realm of the six classes of ordinary beings. To explain the characters: that which stands tall is a famous mountain;

that which flows is a stream. A mountain with its streams is a ravine; a valley through which a stream passes is called a gorge. That which can grow things is soil; that which can support and carry all is the earth.
The "produced" refers to the ten suchnesses as phenomenal creation (*samskrta*). The preceding section used analogies to clarify the inherent completeness of principle (*li-juzhi*);

since this inherent completeness exists, it must necessarily be manifested as phenomenal creation. Therefore, it speaks of the "produced" grasses, trees, and so forth, as well as mountains, rivers, and the land.

Thus, it is the nature of things (*dharmatā*) that [the three thousand realms] arise within such things as grasses and trees. In accordance with principle, they fully possess the three thousand; by the nature of things, they can constitute the phenomenal creation of the three thousand.
Grasses, trees, and so forth are metaphors for the ten suchnesses (*daśa-tathatā*). The preceding clarification of "principle-endowment" (*liju*) elucidates the ten realms;
since the ten realms necessarily possess the ten suchnesses, they are able to constitute the three thousand. This [present section], clarifying "phenomenal creation" (*shizao*), then...

This clarifies the ten suchnesses (*daśa-tathatā*). The ten suchnesses necessarily entail the ten realms (*daśa-dhātu*), which in turn constitute the three thousand worlds (*tri-sahasra*). This is merely a matter of mutual manifestation within the text.

The reason they are explained interchangeably is to conform to the structure of the text. Within the text, it is clarified that among the great trichiliocosm there are mountains and rivers, and within those mountains and rivers there are grasses and trees;
likewise, within the "Great Universal Dharma Gate" (*mahā-sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-dharmamukha*), the ten realms are fully contained. Thus, the ten realms...

Within this, there are ten aspects that follow the sequence of the text. "Mountains and rivers" take the sense of that which gives birth, serving as a metaphor for the inherent completeness of principle (*li*).

"Flowers and trees" take the sense of that which is born, and thus serve as a metaphor for the phenomenal creation of phenomena (*shi*). Although there is a difference between the inherent completeness and the phenomenal creation, [the underlying reality remains the same].
However, because the possession [of causes] gives rise to the activity, and the activity manifests the possession, they together constitute the realm of those to be converted.
Since there is a realm of those to be converted, the Tathāgata must necessarily manifest his body therein as the converter.
When he manifests his body, he can respond universally to all sentient beings across the ten realms; therefore, it is said that "dense clouds spread everywhere, covering all."
This refers to the trichiliocosm. Because the Tathāgata is able to manifest his body like clouds, he is the King of all Dharmas.
△ Second, the explanation of the analogy of the rain of Dharma.

"Pouring down equally at once" is a metaphor for the fact that what has been said above is not false. To say "pouring down equally at once" means that once the dense clouds have spread, rain will inevitably fall;
when it rains, it pours down equally at the same time, making no distinction between high and low ground. There is none.
Private Note: Since the Tathāgata manifests his body like clouds, he must necessarily preach the Dharma like rain.
At the time of preaching, [the teachings] are neither before nor after; they are a single wondrous sound, without interior or exterior, without high or low, and without large or small.
Thus, he proclaims them like rain without partiality; therefore, it is said that "at one time" [the rain] falls equally upon all. Because of this—
The Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma is like rain; therefore, whatever he says is never in vain.
△ Third, the analogy of receiving moisture and growth, in two parts. First, explaining the reception of moisture.
Its moisture pervades all: the flowers, trees, and forests, as well as the various medicinal herbs—those with small roots, small stems, small branches, and small leaves;
those with medium roots, medium stems, medium branches, and medium leaves; and those with large roots, large stems, large branches, and large leaves—all trees, both small and large.
According to the superior, middling, and inferior [capacities], each receives [the rain] accordingly.

This is illustrated by the statement that those at the highest level reach the ground of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*). The initial arrival [of the rain] illustrates how each receives its own portion and is moistened;

the subsequent equalization of the clouds illustrates growth. The initial statement regarding the universal soaking of grasses, trees, and so forth is clear from the text itself. If these points are synthesized:

As for "Dharma," it means that since the Tathāgata has preached the Dharma like rain, the moisture of the teachings he has proclaimed universally nourishes all sentient beings of the nine realms, the three vehicles, and the seven kinds of expedient means—just as the moisture of rain universally nourishes all herbs, trees, and medicinal plants.
This is the general summary; now, the small roots are specifically distinguished, namely, what is said:
Regarding all sentient beings: there are humans and devas who cultivate the goodness of ethical precepts, who are like minor medicinal herbs;

there are those of the two vehicles who cultivate the truths and conditions, who are like medium medicinal herbs; and there are bodhisattvas who cultivate the six perfections, who are like superior medicinal herbs.
There are bodhisattvas who cultivate the emptiness of essence, like small trees; there are bodhisattvas who cultivate the sequential and distinct [teachings], like large trees.
These seven kinds of skillful means differ according to their superior, middling, and inferior capacities, yet each receives the moistening nourishment of the Tathāgata’s teaching.
Human and celestial beings receive the moistening nourishment of the precepts and wholesome roots, and so on, up to the Distinct Teaching (biejiao).
They receive immeasurable moisture. Just as those grasses are of three kinds and trees are of two distinct types, each receives moisture according to its superior, middling, or inferior capacity.
However, these people of the seven stages of expedient means received different things before forty years had passed;
but now, upon reaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, they [receive] according to their [capacity].
There are differences of superior, middling, and inferior; yet there are none who do not each receive the moisture of the One Vehicle’s perfect and sudden teaching.
It is like those various plants: although each receives [the moisture] differently, they are all nourished by the same rain. △ Second, explaining growth.
The rain showered by a single cloud accords with their respective natures (*gotra*) so that they may grow, flower, and bear fruit;

this can be seen from the analogy itself. If we apply this to the Dharma: it means that the Tathāgata, having manifested his body like a cloud, speaks the rain of the single-flavored Dharma, which is able to perfectly accord with all the faculties, natures, and dispositions of the seven types of skillful means.

They attain growth. Just as the rain falling from a single cloud accords with the specific natures of the three types of grasses and two types of trees, causing them to grow and bringing forth flowers and fruit;

so too, before they are fully manifested, humans and devas attain growth in the precepts and wholesome dharmas, and even those of the Separate Teaching (Pratyekabuddha) attain growth in the immeasurable. If now...

When the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* reveals and clarifies [the truth], then according to the precepts and wholesome virtues of those among devas and humans, they grow only within the single Buddha-vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*).
Even according to their various and immeasurable distinctions, they likewise grow and flourish only within the single Buddha-vehicle.
Thus, all nine realms do not fail to return to the Buddha-realm; as for all three vehicles—

There is nothing that does not equally converge upon the One Vehicle. Since the nine realms all return [to the ultimate], and the three vehicles equally converge, then all the causes of the nine realms and the three vehicles—like the blossoming of flowers—without exception achieve the fruit of the Buddha-realm’s One Vehicle, like the ripening of fruit.
It is precisely because they receive nourishment and grow that they all return to the single Buddha-vehicle; therefore:
The Dharma that has been preached all reaches the stage of wisdom. △ Fourth, the analogy of each being unaware of itself:
although they are produced from the same ground and moistened by the same rain, the various grasses and trees each have their own distinctions.
This analogy is known fully only by the Buddha. As for the statement that they are "equal on one and the same ground," it refers to the three types of grass and two types of trees;

although they are all produced from the same ground and moistened by the same rain, these three grasses and two trees each perceive themselves as having thousands of differences and myriad distinctions, unaware that they were produced from the same ground and moistened by the same rain.
This refers to that which is moistened. For example, the five vehicles and the seven stages of expedient means (*upāya*) and so forth,

though all are produced from the same ground of wisdom and moistened by the same flavor of teaching, these individuals of the five vehicles and expedient means each consider themselves to possess distinctions,
not realizing that they are born from the same ground of wisdom and moistened by the same flavor of teaching.
Only the Tathāgata can know the three vehicles, the nine realms, the seven stages of expedient means, and so forth.
Although each has a thousand distinctions, they are all produced from the same ground of wisdom and moistened by the same flavor of the Dharma.
Because the Tathāgata can know them all, he is able to observe and know the ultimate destination of all phenomena regarding sentient beings.
That which is practiced by the profound mind can penetrate all things without obstruction. Regarding the three thousand dharmas, one can exhaustively understand them with clarity.
Because sentient beings each fail to know this for themselves, the Tathāgata subsequently reveals all-encompassing wisdom to all sentient beings, so that each may come to know it for themselves.
△ Third, returning to the analogy with the Dharma, there are four parts; first, the correspondence.
The manifestation of the body is like the metaphor of clouds.
Kāśyapa, you should know that the Tathāgata is also like this: appearing in the world is like the rising of a great cloud.
The Tathāgata manifests his body to respond throughout the ten realms, just as a great cloud rises and pervasively covers the trichiliocosm.
This is the realm (*dhātu*). It is precisely because his manifested body is like a cloud that he is the King of all dharmas.
△ Second, the combined teaching on the analogy of the rain of Dharma. Part one: presenting the Dharma.
With a great voice that pervades the world, [the Buddha addresses] devas, humans, and asuras.
Although only "humans, devas, and asuras" are mentioned, this cites the three wholesome realms to encompass the three unwholesome ones; these constitute the six ordinary states of existence.
As for the Four Sages, although their virtues and ranks differ, if one examines their manifestations, they do not collectively transcend the three kinds of goodness.
Thus, by citing these three kinds of goodness, the ten realms are fully encompassed. △ Second, the citation of analogies.
Just as that great cloud completely covers the trichiliocosm, I privately ask:
since it is appropriate to speak of the Dharma as being like rain, one should employ the analogy of pouring down rain; thus, one should say, "like that great rain."
"At one time, [the rain] falls equally throughout the trichiliocosm. Why, then, do you say it is 'like that great cloud covering everything'? Answer:

This is merely citing the manifestation of the body to illustrate the preaching of the Dharma. The preaching of the Dharma necessarily depends upon the manifestation of the body, just as there must be clouds for there to be rain;
therefore, the cloud is cited to illustrate the rain. △ Third: Exegesis of the Application. Regarding this—
In the midst of the great assembly, he uttered these words; this is what is meant by "preaching the Dharma like rain.

The phrase "the great assembly" explains "like rain," while the phrase "uttering these words" explains "preaching the Dharma. When interpreted according to this single principle, the meaning is perfectly clear.
Therefore, from here on, all [passages] explain that preaching the Dharma is like rain, such as when he utters the words, "I am the Tathāgata," which refers to that which is preached.
This is the Dharma. Within the great assembly, he proclaims again, saying: "You gods and humans, all should come here.
This is precisely like rain falling equally, without partial drops. The text is divided into two parts: first, explaining that the preaching of the Dharma is like rain;
second, clarifying the exhortation to listen and receive the teaching. The first part has five sections; the first explains the Ten Epithets.

In the midst of the great assembly, he proclaimed these words: "I am the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct, the Sugata, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One."
△ Second, the four great vows are proclaimed:

"May those who have not yet crossed over be enabled to cross over; may those who have not yet attained understanding be enabled to understand; may those who have not yet found peace be enabled to find peace; may those who have not yet attained nirvana be enabled to attain nirvana."
△ Third, he declares the three knowledges (*trividyā*):
knowing this world and the world beyond as they truly are.

Knowing this world as it truly is is the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*), by which one can know the present. Knowing the world beyond as it truly is [is the knowledge of the recollection of past lives].

This refers to the clarity of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), which can know the future. Taking these two as examples serves to include the clarity of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*), which can know the past.

To speak of "knowing as it truly is" (*yathābhūtaṃ prajānāti*): if one perceives that the characteristics of the past, future, or present can be apprehended, then it is not called knowing as it truly is.
Now, although the Tathāgata possesses the three clarities and knows the three periods of time, he does not perceive them as having [inherent existence].
The characteristics of the past, future, and present can be apprehended; therefore, it is said that one knows them as they truly are (*yathābhūtam*).

Since the ten ages of past and present do not depart from the present moment (*pratyutpanna-citta*), and even this present moment is ultimately unapprehendable, how could the three periods of time be apprehended?
△ Fourth, the explanation of knowledge and vision: I am the all-knower and the all-seer.
If one only knows existence, only knows emptiness, or only knows the middle way, then one cannot be called "all-knowing."

If one perceives only that which is obstructed and not that which is unobstructed, one observes only the conventional (saṃvṛti). If one understands only that which is unobstructed and not that which is obstructed, one merely realizes emptiness (śūnyatā).
In such cases, it cannot be called "seeing all. Now, the Tathāgata attains the three wisdoms within a single moment of mind and is thus able to perfectly know the three truths;
therefore, he declares, "I am the All-Knowing One. Furthermore, the Tathāgata contemplates with the five eyes within a single eye, and is thus able to...
He perceives all things completely; therefore, it is said that he is "one who sees all. △ Fifth, the exposition of the three karmas:
He is the knower of the Way, the opener of the Way, and the speaker of the Way.

"Knowing" refers to the mental karma (*manas-karman*) that discerns the capacities of beings. "Opening the Way" refers to the bodily karma (*kāya-karman*) that manifests supernatural powers—either by emitting light or shaking the earth—to reveal the unsurpassed path;
thus, bodily karma is said to "open the Way. "Explaining the Way" refers to the vocal karma (*vāk-karman*) of preaching the Dharma.
△ Second, clarifying the exhortation to listen and receive the teaching, in two parts. First, the formal exhortation.
"You, the assembly of devas, humans, and asuras, should all come here for the sake of hearing the Dharma;
that is to say, because the Tathāgata possesses the ten titles, as well as various merits such as the non-restraint of the three karmas."
Thus, he is able to preach the Dharma like rain. Therefore, you multitudes of devas, humans, and asuras should all come here to listen to the Dharma.
△ Second, the practice and observance.
At that time, countless thousands of myriads of koṭis of sentient beings came to where the Buddha was to hear the Dharma.
Because the Tathāgata exhorted them to listen for a single turn, countless sentient beings immediately received his instruction and came to where the Buddha was to hear the Dharma.
This is precisely the mutual resonance of the Way and its response; it is simply the meeting of the capacity [of the listener] and the teaching. △ Third, the collective reception.

The three analogies for the increase of moisture are as follows: first, the presentation of the Dharma; second, the citation of the analogy; third, the application and explanation. The first two [sections] are as follows: first, clarifying the preaching of the Dharma by observing the capacities of sentient beings.
At that time, the Tathāgata observed these sentient beings—their faculties being either sharp or dull, and their diligence being either vigorous or lax.

Regarding the phrase "at that time," it refers to the moment when the capacity of the recipient and the response of the teacher coincide. As for the sharpness or dullness of the faculties: "sharp" means quick and keen, while "dull" means slow and obtuse.
One should know that the faculties themselves possess neither sharpness nor dullness; rather, sharpness and dullness depend on the person. This is as in the case of first hearing the Dharma.
If one cannot understand immediately, this is called being dull-witted. However, upon hearing it once more, one can naturally understand; thus, one is able to transform dullness into sharpness.
Therefore, we know that sharpness and dullness depend on the person, rather than the faculties themselves being sharp or dull.
If one wishes to discuss the distinction between sharp and dull, then Bodhisattvas are sharp, while humans and devas are dull. As for those of the Two Vehicles, they are also sharp.
They are also dull. Since their faculties are unequal—some sharp and some dull—their respective karmic actions are likewise different in terms of progress or indolence.
Bodhisattvas are characterized by progress; humans and devas are characterized by indolence; and those of the Two Vehicles are both progressive and indolent.
The Tathāgata is able to perceive and know all such variations in the sharpness or dullness of faculties and the progress or indolence of karmic actions. Therefore, it is said: "He observes this."
(As stated above). According to their respective capacities, he preached the Dharma for them in various and immeasurable ways, causing them all to rejoice and swiftly obtain wholesome benefits.
"To preach the Dharma according to what they are capable of" means: for those capable among humans and devas, one preaches the Dharma of ethical discipline and goodness;

for those capable of the Two Vehicles, one preaches the Dharma of the Truths and Dependent Origination; and for those capable of the Bodhisattva path, [one preaches the Dharma of the Six Perfections].
He expounds the Dharma of the six perfections. Because there are many such diverse [teachings], it is said that they are "various and immeasurable.

Regarding the phrase "causing all to rejoice and swiftly obtain wholesome benefit": this means that he establishes teachings according to the capacities [of beings] and adapts those teachings to suit those capacities.
Since the capacity of the recipient and the teaching are mutually appropriate, one is able to obtain the benefits of the four *siddhāntas*.

Thus it is said that all are made to rejoice and swiftly obtain wholesome benefit. "Rejoicing" corresponds to the worldly benefit (*loka-siddhānta*). "Wholesome" corresponds to the benefit for others (*pudgala-siddhānta*).
As for "benefit," since one can obtain what is wholesome, evil is thereby eliminated; this simultaneously encompasses the remedial and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-siddhānta*) benefits. △
Second, explaining the benefits gained from hearing the Dharma:

When these sentient beings have heard this Dharma, they will enjoy peace and security in the present life, and in future lives they will be reborn in favorable realms, experiencing happiness through the Path.

They shall also hear the Dharma. Having heard the Dharma, they will be freed from all obstacles and, within the various teachings, gradually enter the Path according to their own capacity and ability.
Regarding the statement "those who hear this Dharma": if it refers to the period prior to forty years ago, then they heard various teachings such as the precepts and wholesome dharmas.
Hearing these dharmas also enables one to obtain peace and security in the present life, and to be reborn in a good realm in the future.

Furthermore, concerning those among humans and devas who hear the Dharma and clearly attain peace and security in the present life, this is because what they have heard consists of the precepts and wholesome dharmas.
Regarding the Dharma: the precepts refer to the five precepts, namely, not killing, not stealing, and so forth. When one maintains the precepts within, the mind naturally attains peace and security;
how could one then commit acts such as killing or stealing against external objects? Thus, the external environment also becomes peaceful and secure.
One should know that those who maintain the precepts are surely protected by deities who guard the precepts. To provide a brief illustration:
As for their number: one precept consists of five precepts; with five sets of five, there are twenty-five positions of precept-deities who provide protection for them.

Therefore it is said that one is at peace and secure in the present life. This is not true only for the present life; by taking the observance of the precepts as the cause, [one attains such results in future lives as well].
In the future, even if one is not born in the heavens, one will certainly be born among human beings; hence it is said, "one is reborn in a good destination.
Having been born in the heavens or among humans, one naturally becomes able to maintain the precepts; hence it is said, "one experiences happiness through the Way.

Furthermore, by adding the hearing of the Dharma, one advances the essence of the precepts; hence it is said, "one also obtains the hearing of the Dharma. Having obtained the hearing of the Dharma, how could one...
Furthermore, it invites obstacles such as the three miserable realms and the ten evil deeds; therefore, it is said that one "is free from all obstacles.
From this point on, one is able to gradually advance along the path of the Three Vehicles and Five Teachings; hence it is said, "among all dharmas...
(and so forth). If we discuss this according to the present sutra, it refers to hearing the Buddha’s knowledge and vision regarding the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all dharmas.
This is the Dharma. Through hearing, one attains understanding; through understanding, one practices; and through practice, one enters realization.

Thus, within this very life, one can enter the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, manifesting a portion of the three virtues (*triguṇa*), and destroying one grade of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Therefore, it is said that one is at peace in the present life. Having destroyed ignorance, although one currently dwells within the *sahā* world, if...
Having cast off this body, one is immediately able to give birth to the fruition of reality. That is to say, by means of causes that accord with reality, one realizes fruits that accord with reality;
with form and mind unimpeded, the environment and its inhabitants are adorned. This is precisely what it means to be reborn in a good realm.
Once born there, one can manifest bodies throughout the hundred worlds, sporting with supernatural powers and teaching and transforming all beings; this is receiving [the fruit] through the Way.
It is joy. Once one has ascended to the first abode (*prathamā bhūmi*), the Buddhas of the ten directions simultaneously preach the Dharma for them;

hence it is said that they "also hear the Dharma. Having heard the Buddhas preach the Dharma, they are able to advance through the second abode up to the tenth abode, the ten practices (*caryā*), the ten transferences (*pariṇāmanā*), and the various stages of the ten grounds (*bhūmi*). Within these various stages, at each and every stage...

Because it can destroy ignorance, it is said that "one is free from all obstacles. As for "gradually entering the Way according to one's capacity," this refers to being able to flow spontaneously into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge) starting from the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
It is precisely because they increase in unison that one is able to reach the ground of wisdom (*jñāna-bhūmi*) entirely. △ Second, the citation of an analogy.
Just as that great cloud rains upon all the grasses, trees, thickets, forests, and medicinal herbs,
each receiving its full measure of moisture according to its own nature and attaining growth accordingly.
△ Third Fascicle: Commentary.
When the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma, it is of a single characteristic and a single flavor.
"Of a single characteristic and a single flavor" means that although the Dharma preached by the Tathāgata contains both emptiness and various characteristics, it is like milk...
Although various flavors differ from one another, they ultimately share the same true reality (*dharmatā*); they are but a single *amṛta*.
For although the Tathāgata speaks of existence, he does so in contrast to emptiness; although he speaks of the characteristic of emptiness, he does so in contrast to existence;
and although he speaks of the characteristic of the Middle Way, he does so in contrast to both emptiness and existence. Since he speaks in contrast to emptiness...

Yet, when one speaks of existence, there is the characteristic of non-existence; and so on, up to when one speaks of the Middle Way in contrast to emptiness and existence, then the Middle Way lacks the characteristic of being "middle.
In this way, ultimately, it is neither empty nor existent, nor is it the Middle; it is solely the single true reality (*dharmatā*).
As for "one flavor": the Tathāgata originally intended to teach the single flavor, but because sentient beings' capacities were not in accord with it, he instead taught [the various vehicles].

Regarding the four flavors—milk, cream, curd, and ghee—which are categorized as both distinct and inclusive: although these four flavors differ, once they are revealed and manifested by a single sūtra, they become one and the same flavor of *amṛta* (the finest essence).

What are called the characteristic of liberation, the characteristic of detachment, and the characteristic of cessation, culminating in all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), are further explanations of the aforementioned single characteristic and single flavor. The characteristic of liberation is precisely the absence of the characteristic of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
The characteristic of detachment is precisely the absence of the characteristic of nirvana. The characteristic of cessation is precisely that even the characteristic of non-characteristic is absent.
When one ultimately reaches the state of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), there remains only the singular wisdom of true suchness (*tathatājñāna*).

Since this is the singular wisdom of true suchness, wisdom is identical to the suchness of the object, and the object is identical to the suchness of wisdom; thus, object and wisdom are a single suchness.
Object and wisdom are non-dual; according to their various characteristics and flavors, they collectively constitute a single characteristic and a single flavor.

Because they all constitute a single characteristic and a single flavor, the Dharma taught reaches the ground of wisdom, just as those three types of grass and two types of trees receive moisture and grow.
This section may also be understood from the phrase "at that time, innumerable... [and so forth].
"Below. Up to this point constitutes one section. The first part concerns the "receiving of nourishment"; the second part, from "Furthermore, all the sentient beings below," concerns "growth.
There are three parts: the teaching (*dharma*), the analogy (*upamā*), and their synthesis (*yoga*).

If one were to divide the text according to the first method, then within the context of gaining benefit from hearing the Dharma, the first part concerns the "receiving of nourishment," while the second part, from "Having already heard the Dharma," concerns "growth. This is fully contained within the presentation of the analogy.
"Fully receiving the moisture" is the analogy for receiving the moisture. "Each attaining growth" is the analogy for increasing.

△ Fourth, combining the analogies of each not knowing [it] themselves, in three parts: first, citing the Dharma; second, citing the analogy; third, resolving objections. The first part has two sections.
First, the formal exhortation:

There may be sentient beings who hear the Dharma of the Tathāgata, and if they uphold, read, recite, or practice it according to the teaching, the merit they thereby obtain will not be something they can perceive for themselves.
To hear the Dharma of the Tathāgata is to hear the Dharma of the Tathāgata’s single characteristic and single flavor. As for the statement that they do not realize it themselves:

because the Dharma they have heard is fundamentally of a single characteristic and a single flavor, yet sentient beings, though they uphold, read, and recite it, do not know it to be of a single characteristic and a single flavor; this is what is meant by not realizing the reality for oneself.
Thus it is. By the power of skillful means, the Tathāgata takes the Dharma of a single characteristic and a single flavor and explains it as having various characteristics and various flavors.
Sentient beings then recognize these as various characteristics and various flavors; this is their failure to realize the provisional nature [of the teaching].
△ Second, the turning explanation.
Why is this? Only the Tathāgata knows these sentient beings—their seeds, characteristics, and essential natures; what they mind, what they contemplate, and what they cultivate;
how they mind, how they contemplate, and how they cultivate; by means of which dharmas they mind, by means of which dharmas they contemplate, and by means of which dharmas they cultivate;
and by means of which dharmas they attain which dharmas. Sentient beings abide in various stages.
Only the Tathāgata perceives them as they truly are, with clear and unimpeded understanding;
that is to say, he knows why all sentient beings do not awaken to this themselves. Therefore, the interpretation is further explained:
only the Tathāgata knows these sentient beings. Because only the Tathāgata is able to know them, sentient beings do not know them. Such are their various characteristics.

Regarding the "essential nature" (*tattva*): "kind" (*gotra*) refers to the category; "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to the objective aspect; "substance" (*dravya*) refers to the material essence;
and "nature" (*prakṛti*) refers to habitual tendencies. "What is it that one recollects? and so forth—this is knowing the object of observation. "How does one recollect?

and so forth—this is knowing the observing contemplation. "By what dharma does one recollect? and so forth—this is knowing that the contemplation is aroused by the object, and that the object is illumined by the contemplation.
"What dharma attains what dharma" refers to knowing that the cultivation of causes brings about their respective fruits.
Regarding "sentient beings dwelling in various stages (*bhūmi*)," *bhūmi* here means "stages of attainment. This means that sentient beings may dwell in the stage of humans or devas, and so forth.

Even those who may abide in distinct stages of realization—this is the practice of the aforementioned profound resolve—the Tathāgata perceives them as they truly are, with clarity and without obstruction.

Although the stages in which sentient beings abide differ from one another, they are all, in their totality, the single stage of the true mark (*dharmatā*). Yet, among sentient beings, each remains unaware of this for themselves.
Within this single, ultimate ground, only the Tathāgata—viewing it with the inconceivable Buddha-eye—is able to know that they are one and the same ultimate ground.
That is to say, even the stages of humans and devas are themselves the stage of perfect reality;
even the successive, distinct stages are themselves the stage of perfect reality. Therefore, it is said that he perceives them as they truly are, with clarity and without confusion.
"Obstruction. This refers to the aforementioned unimpeded penetration. △ Second, the illustration:

Just as those herbs, trees, forests, and various medicinal plants do not themselves know their superior, middling, or inferior natures, the Tathāgata knows them to be a dharma of a single characteristic and a single flavor—namely, the characteristic of liberation, the characteristic of detachment, the characteristic of cessation, and ultimate nirvāṇa.
The *pāṇa* is characterized by constant quiescence and ultimately returns to emptiness;
that which is unaware of this refers to being unaware that the superior, middling, and inferior natures are all produced from the same ground.
It is moistened by a single rain. The Tathāgata explains this in the following section: "Ultimate nirvāṇa" means ultimate non-arising and non-ceasing.
*Nir* signifies non-arising; *vāṇa* signifies non-ceasing. This non-arising and non-ceasing is called Great Nirvāṇa.
Regarding the "characteristic of eternal quiescence," this refers to such non-arising and non-ceasing, and is not merely [the cessation] of the present.

The nature of the sun is neither arising nor ceasing; from the very beginning, it has been the mark of eternal quiescence. Because all phenomena (*dharmas*) are fundamentally quiescent, they do not become quiescent anew;
because all phenomena are fundamentally extinguished, they do not undergo further extinction. Therefore, it is the mark of eternal quiescence.
That which ultimately returns to emptiness is not an emptiness where even a speck of dust is purified away; rather, it is the foremost, inconceivable emptiness of the Mahāyāna.

The emptiness of meaning (*artha-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) are indeed the true emptiness (*bhūta-śūnyatā*). This true emptiness is not empty; it is fully endowed with all things.

Therefore, everything returns to it—namely, the three thousand natures and characteristics (*tri-sahasra-dharmasvabhāva-lakṣaṇa*) and the ten suchnesses of the hundred realms (*śata-dhātu-daśa-tathatā*). There is nothing that does not return to the ultimate emptiness.
For although the three thousand phenomena (*tri-sahasra-dharmas*) differ in a thousand ways and ten thousand distinctions, each being unique, they [all]... [do not exceed it].
The non-characteristics and characteristics are all real; phenomena and phenomena are both true. Yet, in their very essence, they are empty and quiescent;
therefore, ultimately, they all return to emptiness. Thus, this dharma of a single characteristic and a single flavor ultimately returns entirely to emptiness.

Only the Tathāgata knows this, whereas sentient beings do not know it themselves. Because the Tathāgata alone knows all things completely, he is able to observe and know the destination of all phenomena, as well as to investigate them thoroughly and with full clarity.
He is able to penetrate, without obstruction, the conduct of sentient beings according to their deep-seated inclinations. This is because sentient beings each lack such self-knowledge.

The Tathāgata demonstrates this through all-encompassing wisdom. Just as those three types of grass and two types of trees, though all sharing the same earth and receiving the same rain, attain growth accordingly. △ Third, resolving objections.

Having known this, the Buddha observes the inclinations of the minds of sentient beings and protects them. For this reason, he does not immediately teach them the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
He considers that while only a Buddha knows it completely, sentient beings each lack such self-knowledge; why then would he not immediately [teach] it to sentient beings?
Therefore, it is said in general: observing the desires of the minds of sentient beings, he protects them; thus, he does not speak immediately.
What has been explained above—whether by means of the Dharma, analogies, or applications—is intended to manifest, in its entirety, the immeasurable and boundless merits of the Tathāgata.
△ Third, the summary praise, which is twofold. First, the actual praise.

“O Kāśyapas, it is truly rare that you are able to understand the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma according to what is appropriate, and that you are able to believe and accept it—this is truly rare.
What you have previously understood may be called a skillful exposition of the Tathāgata’s true merits;
this is already rare enough. Now, for your sake, I shall describe that which you have not yet understood.”
When you hear this, you will surely be able to comprehend it and accept it with faith.

Furthermore, since you can also comprehend that the Tathāgata possesses immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) merits, this is not merely rare, but exceedingly rare. △ Second, the further explanation.
Why is this so? Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, teach the Dharma according to what is appropriate; it is difficult to understand and difficult to know. II. Verses in Praise.

These verses only praise and confirm [the preceding prose], but do not praise the concluding eulogy. Within the confirmation, they further do not praise the brief confirmation, but only praise the extensive confirmation.
This is divided into two parts: first, the actual verses praising the confirmation; second, the summary that reconciles the provisional [teachings].
True. Regarding the first three [verses], the first stanza directly indicates the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
The Dharma-King who destroys existence appears in the world; According to the desires of sentient beings, he preaches the Dharma in various ways. The Tathāgata is worthy of honor.

The wisdom [of this teaching] is profound and far-reaching. For a long time, I have kept this essential point silent, not being intent on expounding it hastily. Those with wisdom, upon hearing it, will be able to believe and understand;
those without wisdom will harbor doubt and regret, thereby suffering eternal loss. Therefore, Kāśyapa, I shall explain it according to their capacities, using various causes and conditions.
This causes one to attain right view.

Regarding the "King who destroys existence": that which is called "existence" (bhava) refers to the non-perishing of cause and effect. Within the realm of the triple world, views and afflictions serve as the cause, while the fragmented birth-and-death (pariccheda-śarīra) serves as the effect.
Beyond the realm of the triple world, ignorance serves as the cause, while the transformational birth-and-death (pariṇāma-śarīra) serves as the effect. All of these...
Because causes elicit effects and effects produce causes, neither is ever lost; therefore, it is called "existence" (*bhava*).
The Tathāgata has already thoroughly exhausted the five stages of dwelling and eternally eliminated the two types of death; thus, it is said that he has destroyed existence.
If existence were not destroyed, one would remain bound by numerous attachments among all phenomena and would not attain sovereignty. Since the Tathāgata has destroyed existence, then...
Because he has attained mastery over all dharmas, he is called the "Dharma King who has shattered existence.
Since the Tathāgata has already shattered existence and possesses mastery over the Dharma, he is able to transcend the triple world and dwell securely in the light of tranquility (*śāntaprabhā*).
Yet, although he himself has already been able to shatter existence, the sentient beings of the nine realms have not yet done so; it is for their sake that the Tathāgata now desires to...
Because they likewise shatter existence (*bhava*), they do not abide in nirvana, but instead reappear in the world.

Regarding the teaching of various dharmas according to the desires of sentient beings: since the Tathāgata has appeared in the world desiring that the nine realms likewise shatter existence, he must certainly preach the Dharma for them as a condition for shattering existence. If one is to preach the Dharma, it must necessarily...
To accommodate the capacities of beings, he preaches the Dharma in various ways according to whatever each sentient being desires.
Since the desires of sentient beings are manifold, the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma is likewise manifold;
that is to say, he teaches the dharmas of precepts and goodness according to the desires of beings among humans and devas, and according to the desires of beings of the two vehicles.
He teaches the Dharma of the Truths and their conditions; he teaches the Dharma of the Six Perfections according to the inclinations of Bodhisattvas and sentient beings.
This is the teaching of skillful means for transforming others, delivered in accordance with the intentions of sentient beings.
As for the actual Dharma of self-cultivation that accords with the Buddha’s own intent, the Tathāgata holds it in high esteem and protects it with mindful care. Therefore...
It is said that the Tathāgata holds this in high esteem. Yet, where can one see the locus of this esteem?
During the *Avataṃsaka* period, the Tathāgata did not speak of it; even during the *Prajñāpāramitā* period, he did not speak of it.
For more than forty years, he never spoke of it. Is this not proof that it is what the Tathāgata holds in the highest esteem? It is indeed held in high esteem.
What is this? It is precisely the wisdom of the Buddha; that which is called the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision.
This wisdom not only penetrates vertically to the very bottom of the profound source, but also extends horizontally to the furthest limits of the Dharma-realm;
therefore, it is said to be "profound and far-reaching. Because it is both profound and far-reaching, the Tathāgata honors and values it, and thus for a long time...
"To have remained silent" means not to be intent upon expounding quickly. This "essential point" refers to the wisdom of the Buddha; it is the very core of the teaching.
Because this had never been spoken before during the forty years [of his ministry], it is said that he "remained silent for a long time.

Indeed, the Tathāgata originally intended to speak of it, yet he did not hastily expound it immediately; therefore, it is said that he was "not intent upon expounding quickly. One who possesses wisdom...
This concludes the section. It reveals the intention behind not being intent on expounding [the teaching] too quickly.

That is to say, the reason the Tathāgata remained silent for so long and was not intent on expounding it hastily is that if those with wisdom were to hear it, they would be able to believe and accept it;
however, if those without wisdom were to hear it, they would inevitably give rise to various doubts and regrets. If such doubts and regrets arise, it constitutes a permanent loss.
Therefore, although the Tathāgata wishes to explain this, he does not strive to do so hastily.
For although the Buddha’s wisdom is profound and far-reaching, if those who possess wisdom hear it, they will accord with that wisdom through their own wisdom.
It is like water poured into water, or space merging with space; thus, one is naturally able to give rise to faith and develop understanding.
This is the underlying intent behind the fact that, at the very beginning of this sutra, the Buddha’s wisdom is praised solely in relation to Śāriputra.

Were a person lacking in wisdom to hear that sentient beings already possess the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, they would inevitably harbor doubt. To doubt is to lack faith; and to lack faith is to...
They give rise to slander. To slander is inevitably to fall into suffering. If one merely lacks faith, that is already a loss;
if one goes so far as to fall into suffering, is that not a permanent loss? Therefore, the concluding intent is stated: those with wisdom have faith, while those without wisdom harbor doubt.
For this reason, if one wishes to preach for them, one must act in accordance with the capacity and strength of the sentient beings.
This teaching must further be expounded for them through various causes and conditions, various parables, and various modes of expression.
Although it is taught according to their capacities by means of these various conditions,
one must ultimately ensure that they attain the Right View of the Tathāgata, rather than the false views of non-Buddhists or the views of existence held by ordinary worldlings.
The view of emptiness of the two vehicles and the view of the "middle" of the bodhisattvas are both not called right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*).
This refers precisely to what is meant by those from the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-vidyā*) downwards being called people of false views (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*).

Only the Tathāgata’s perfect realization of the three knowledges (*tri-jñāna*) and the perfect observation of the five eyes (*pañca-cakṣus*) differ from the views of non-Buddhists, ordinary beings, the two vehicles, and bodhisattvas; only this is called [right view].
This is right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*). Having taught according to their capacities, he causes them all to attain right view; thus, the provisional is itself the real.
This is what is meant by "all having attained the revelation, realization, entry, and penetration of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
I privately maintain that these four lines of verse serve as a summary of the preceding parable, and their meaning is sufficient. The first two lines praise these Kings of Dharma.
The analogy of manifesting bodies like clouds is the basis [of the following]. Next, the two lines concerning sentient beings illustrate that what was taught is not in vain;

this is the basis for the analogy of the rain of Dharma, both of which can be clearly seen. The two lines beginning with "The Tathāgata" praise the attainment of the ground of all-pervading wisdom (*sarvatraga-jñāna-bhūmi*).
This is the basis for the analogy of receiving nourishment and growth. For forty years prior, [the Buddha] had accorded with the capacities of sentient beings through his wisdom.
Through skillful means, he expounds such dharmas as the virtues of the precepts; yet when the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* reveals and clarifies [the truth], all shall reach the ground of omniscience.
That which was not spoken for forty years is only now being spoken because the Tathāgata holds it in profound esteem.
Thus, one should know that these two verses praise the aforementioned attainment of the ground of wisdom.

This is the prose commentary. The following line, "For these four reasons," is the verse that serves as the basis for the analogy that only the Buddha knows all things while each being does not know them themselves.
The various conditions—namely, teaching, practice, and principle—are used to open up the conditions for the Buddha’s correct view for the sake of sentient beings.
This means causing them to initiate practice in accordance with the teaching; through such practice, they realize the principle and thereby attain the Tathāgata’s right view.
Thus it is said that "by various conditions, they are made to attain right view. One should know that this single verse summarizes the preceding passage stating that "only the Buddha fully knows.
II. The second section, the verse on skillfully clarifying [the meaning] by way of analogy, has four parts. First, the verse on manifesting the body:
The Parable of the Cloud:
Kāśyapa, you should know that it is like a great cloud arising in the world, covering everything. The cloud of wisdom contains moisture;
its lightning flashes brilliantly and its thunder resounds afar, bringing joy to all beings. It eclipses the sunlight, making the earth cool and refreshing.
Massing and hanging down, it is as if one could grasp it.
Regarding the term "Wisdom Cloud" (*huiyun*): these two characters combine both the Dharma and its metaphor.

All the wisdom possessed by the Tathāgata can preach the Dharma to moisten and nourish sentient beings, just as clouds can bring down rain to moisten and nourish plants and trees; therefore, it is so called.
"Wisdom-cloud" refers to this. "Lightning" is a metaphor for the Tathāgata manifesting his body, which must emit radiance.

"Thunder" is a metaphor for the Tathāgata, after emitting light, must thunder the great Dharma-thunder to startle and awaken all beings. As for the phrase "causing the multitude to rejoice," it means:

If all sentient beings did not have the Dharma-rain of the Tathāgata to nourish their spirits, the radiance of his light to illumine their bodies, and the Dharma-thunder to startle them awake, then afflictions would have no means by which to be destroyed, and they would have no means by which to emerge from birth and death; how then could they attain joy and contentment?

Now, when the Tathāgata manifests his body like a cloud and appears in the world, there must necessarily be the rain of Dharma to nourish the spirit, the light of Dharma to illuminate the body, and the thunder of Dharma to awaken the mind.
From this, one can destroy ignorance and transcend birth and death; thus, he causes all beings to attain joy and contentment. When clouds arise, the sunlight is inevitably obscured.
It is like when a Tathāgata appears in the world, all ninety-five kinds of heterodox lights are necessarily eclipsed and do not manifest.
Just as the earth attains coolness when the sun is obscured, so too, when heterodox lights are eclipsed, the True Principle (saddharma) becomes manifest.
As for the description of clouds "hanging down in dense masses as if they could be grasped," it means that when the clouds are deeply concealed, the mountains [are revealed].
In the valleys, one cannot even see them; how could they be grasped? Now, as they arise in the world, they appear dense and vast, as if they could be grasped.
This is because if the Tathāgata dwells in the true realm of *sambhogakāya* (the Light of Peace), his entire body is the land, and the entire land is his body.
The environment and its inhabitants are of one suchness; form and mind are non-dual. Even all sentient beings [cannot perceive it].
One is able to see [the Buddha]. How could one not gaze up in reverence? Now that the Tathāgata has appeared in the world, all sentient beings are able to gaze upon him and look up to him;
it is like clouds arising in the world, which can be caught and grasped.
△ Second, the verse on the simile of the rain of Dharma.
That rain falls equally everywhere, descending simultaneously from all four directions. It flows in immeasurable torrents, saturating the entire land.

Whether in mountains, rivers, steep valleys, or remote recesses, it nourishes all that grows—herbs, trees, medicinal plants, large and small trees, the various crops of the hundred grains, sugarcane, and grapes.
That which is moistened by the rain is nowhere not made abundant; even parched ground is universally saturated, and medicinal herbs and trees alike flourish.

To say that "it falls everywhere in the four directions" means that at the time of preaching the Dharma, the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidah*) are proclaimed together, just as rain falls equally in all four directions.
"Throughout the land" clarifies the scope of those being transformed; "throughout the land" serves as a collective metaphor for the realm of those to be converted.
This encompasses both the principle-as-endowed (*li-jù*) and the phenomena-as-actualized (*shi-zào*). The distinctness of mountains and rivers serves as a metaphor for the ten realms (*daśadhātu*):

the mountain represents the Buddha-realm; the river represents the Bodhisattva-realm; the rugged valley represents the realm of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*); and the deep recesses represent the realm of the six classes of ordinary beings.
The various plants and trees that grow therein represent the ten suchnesses (*daśatathatā*) of the ten realms. The correct paths cultivated within these ten realms are like the hundred grains.
The "seedlings and crops" refer to the practices that assist the Path, such as sugarcane and grapes.
Whether primary or auxiliary, these are all moistened by the Dharma-rain of the Tathāgata; there is none that does not receive its nourishment, becoming abundant and fully satisfied.
The two lines concerning "dry soil" specifically single out the three lowest realms within the ten dharma-realms to speak of them.
Within the three miserable realms, being able to cultivate the wholesome precepts and contemplate the six pāramitās is like medicinal herbs flourishing on dry land.
Within the three miserable realms, being able to cultivate the sequential contemplation of the essence of emptiness is like trees flourishing on dry land.

Furthermore, the phrase "the entire land" serves as a metaphor for the Great Universal Dharma-gate; the mountains, rivers, and so forth serve as metaphors for that which is within the universal aspect.
It possesses the ten realms; this is the "inherent possession" (*li-jù*). The resulting grasses, trees, and so forth, serve as an analogy for the "constructed" (*shi-zào*) ten suchnesses.
△ Third, the verse on the analogy of receiving moisture and growing.
From those clouds issues water of a single flavor, which moistens the grasses, trees, and forests according to their respective capacities.

All the various trees—whether superior, middling, or inferior—each attain growth and development according to their size; their roots, trunks, branches, leaves, flowers, fruits, and radiant colors all flourish accordingly.
Wherever the single rain reaches, all things obtain freshness and luster.
As for those who receive its moisture according to their respective capacities: the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata is originally of a single flavor, yet it accords with the nine realms.
The three vehicles and seven stages of expedient means each receive their respective nourishment, just as various grasses and trees each receive the moisture from rain falling from a single cloud.
That is to say, according to the capacity of humans and devas, they receive the nourishment of precepts and goodness;
up to, according to the capacity of the distinct teaching (*biejiao*), they receive the nourishment of the immeasurable. This constitutes the fourth [section].

Ten years ago, the moisture received was such as this; yet if one were to reach the present *Lotus Sūtra*, then according to the distinctions of the nine realms, the three vehicles, and the seven expedient means, there is none who does not receive the moisture of the perfect and sudden One Vehicle.
"All inferior verses increase" means that they each attain growth according to their respective magnitude;
it does not mean that by being called "great," one attains the growth of the great, or by being called "small," one attains the growth of the small.
Rather, it means that although their magnitudes are unequal, they all grow in the same way. This is analogous to the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma, which accords with...
Although the nine realms, the three vehicles, and the seven stages of expedient means are unequal in their magnitude, they ultimately share the same growth within the single Buddha-vehicle.

Regarding the roots and stems: all sentient beings of the nine realms and so forth, upon hearing the Dharma of the Tathāgata, give rise to faith, which is like the roots of plants and trees; based on this faith, they develop understanding, just as one relies upon roots.
Yet there is the stem; based upon understanding, one cultivates the practice of the right path and the auxiliary paths, just as branches and leaves exist based upon the stem.
One cultivates the practices of the right path and the auxiliaries to establish the cause, just as flowers bloom from the branches and leaves.
Through the cause, one achieves the fruit, just as fruit is formed from the flowers. Having achieved it...
The fruit can give rise to wisdom; just as the fruit possesses radiance, so too does wisdom accord with principle, like radiance possessing color.
That "whatever is reached by the single rain all obtains freshness and luster" refers to the various inclinations and understandings of all sentient beings within the nine realms.
Although their respective causal and contributory factors, fruits, wisdoms, and principles do not...
...and so forth. That which is reached by the Tathāgata’s Dharma of a single flavor encompasses all the faith, understanding, and so on, within the entire Buddha-realm.
It is like the roots, stems, and other parts of plants and trees: although they each differ, when touched by the single rain, they all attain freshness and luster.
This is precisely what it means to receive the moisture of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. △ Fourth, the verse on each not [relying] on itself:
This is an analogy for understanding. Just as their physical forms and characteristics differ, and their natures and capacities vary in size,
yet that which moistens them is one and the same, and each flourishes accordingly— meaning that although plants and trees are unequal in size, the moisture they receive is identical.

This is a single rain. Although all are moistened by this same rain, those grasses and trees each think for themselves that they have been nourished and flourish, unaware that they are all equally moistened by one and the same rain. This is analogous to when the Tathāgata expounds the Dharma with a single voice;
according to the physical constitution, characteristics, and habitual tendencies of sentient beings within the nine realms, it is categorized into various [teachings] of great and small capacity.

They are not the same. Yet the teaching bestowed upon them is equally a single sound. Although it is a single sound, sentient beings of the nine realms do not realize that they are being addressed by the same teaching of a single sound; rather, each claims there is a distinction.
△ Third, the verse returns to the analogy of the Dharma in four parts. First, the verse correlates the manifestation of the body with the analogy of clouds.
The Buddha is likewise. His appearance in the world is like a great cloud that universally covers all things.
II. The second section, in verse, combines the teaching with the analogy of rain. First, the general summary in verse:
Having appeared in the world for the sake of all sentient beings, he analytically expounds the reality of all dharmas.

As for the statement that he analytically expounds the reality of all dharmas: it is the original intent of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world, which is solely to speak of the reality of the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all dharmas.
Because the capacities of beings do not accord with this, he analytically expounds [the truth] by means of differentiation from within that true mark.
Thus, there are various dharmas such as the sudden and the gradual, the śrāvaka, the pratyekabuddha, and the bodhisattva.
Since one can emerge from the one into the many, and likewise gather the many back into the one,
although they are explained through various distinctions and appear different in their manifold forms, ultimately they are all unified within the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
It is the reality. Therefore, it is said that he "analytically expounds the reality of all dharmas. △ Second, the specific verses are threefold.
First, the verse summarizing the ten titles:
The Great Sage, the World-Honored One, among all devas and humans, within the entire assembly, proclaimed these words: "I am the Tathāgata."
The Honored One among Two-Legged Beings appears in the world like a great cloud.
The two characters "Tathāgata" represent the beginning of his ten epithets, while the phrase "Honored One among Two-Legged Beings" represents the end of those ten epithets.
Because he alone is fully endowed with both merit and wisdom, he is the Honored One of both the mundane and supramundane worlds.
[End of section]. △ Second, the verse on the synthesis of the Four Great Vows:
To nourish and moisten all withered sentient beings, causing them all to leave suffering behind and attain the bliss of peace and security—the worldly happiness.
And the bliss of nirvāṇa.
Sentient beings have long lacked the rain of the Dharma to nourish them; they were like withered and parched plants and trees.
Now the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma, able to fully satisfy and moisten all sentient beings who are withered and parched. Sentient beings have long lacked the Dharma...

When it rains upon that which is withered and parched, it becomes the cause of the suffering of afflictions (*kleśa*) and is bound by the fruit of the suffering of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), such that one cannot escape it. Now, the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata moistens and nourishes them;
thus, it not only causes them to leave the cause of suffering but also enables them to leave the fruit of suffering. Therefore, it is said that "it causes all to leave suffering. Since—
One extracts them from suffering and shall, in turn, bestow happiness upon them; by being free from suffering, one is naturally able to attain happiness.
As for worldly happiness, it refers to the happiness of humans and devas. Regarding the happiness of Nirvana, there are differences between the Mahāyāna and the Hīnayāna. Within these two vehicles...

Furthermore, there is the distinction between the nirvana-with-remainder and the nirvana-without-remainder. Both cause one to leave suffering behind; these are the two vows: to deliver those not yet delivered and to liberate those not yet liberated.
To obtain peaceful and secure bliss; these are the two vows: to settle those not yet settled and to lead those not yet in nirvana to attain nirvana.
△ Third, the verse summarizing the exhortation to listen has two parts. First, the formal exhortation.
All you hosts of devas and humans, listen with single-minded attention; all should come here to behold the Unsurpassed Honored One.
△ Second, self-praise:
"I am the World-Honored One, whom none can equal. To bring peace and security to sentient beings, I have appeared in the world to preach for the great assembly."
The Dharma of the pure nectar is of a single flavor: liberation and nirvana. With a single wondrous voice, he expounds this meaning, constantly acting as the causal condition for the Mahāyāna.
As for the statement that "none can equal him": sentient beings within the cycle of birth and death are unable to sever it, nor are they able to shatter their afflictions (*kleśa*).
The Buddha, however, can sever what sentient beings find difficult to sever; the Buddha can shatter what sentient beings find difficult to shatter.
Therefore, there is none who can equal him. Since there is none who can equal him, he is the ultimate among men.
He is venerable. Since the person is venerable, the Dharma must necessarily be sublime; therefore, he teaches the pure Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.

To speak of the "pure Dharma of ambrosia" (*amṛta*) is to employ both a metaphor and its referent together. If one cultivates the pure Dharma, then the wisdom-life of the Dharma-body will not meet with premature death;
it is like consuming ambrosia, by which one can prolong one's years and avoid an untimely end.
It is longevity. Yet, the pure Dharma of ambrosia possesses no various flavors; it is but a single flavor. What is this single flavor?
It is what is called the characteristic of liberation, the characteristic of detachment, the characteristic of cessation, and the characteristic of ultimate nirvana, which is eternally quiescent.
For this reason, it is said that this Dharma is the single flavor of liberation and nirvana. With a single wondrous voice, he expounds and elucidates this meaning.
The pure Dharma is fundamentally of one essence, the wondrous flavor of *amṛta* (the finest clarified butter).

However, because the capacities and dispositions of sentient beings are not equal, the Tathāgata skillfully employs a single voice to expound the meaning of the pure Dharma, manifesting it as various flavors such as milk, curd, fresh butter, and refined butter.
Therefore, it is said that he expounds this meaning with a single wondrous voice. Although he thus expounds it...
For the sake of all flavors [of teaching], one should know that they always serve as the causal conditions for the Mahāyāna. Regarding what are called the causal conditions of the Mahāyāna:

the capacity of sentient beings is the cause, and the teaching of the Tathāgata is the condition. Thus, the teaching is established by virtue of that capacity, and the teaching is directed toward that capacity.
Although there are various differences among the teachings, they are collectively the One Mahāyāna; likewise, although there are differences in capacity, [they are all directed toward it].
Although there are various differences, they ultimately all constitute the One Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna).

Thus, whether it be the cause of the capacity [of the listener] or the condition of the teaching, both are the One Great Vehicle; therefore, it is called the "causes and conditions of the Great Vehicle.

Furthermore, the Tathāgata expounds the meaning of the pure Dharma with a single voice, constantly acting as the causes and conditions for the Great Vehicle. △ Third, the verse on receiving the moisture together.

The section on "Increasing" has two parts: the first verse combines [the image of] receiving moisture; the second verse combines [the image of] increasing. Regarding the first part, the first verse combines [the image of] observing the capacities of beings and preaching the Dharma:
"I observe that all things are universally equal, without distinction between self and other, and without feelings of love or hatred. I have no attachment."
Furthermore, he is without obstruction and constantly expounds the Dharma equally for all; as he does for one person, so it is for many.
He constantly proclaims the Dharma and never engages in other affairs. Whether walking, coming, sitting, or standing, he is never weary or fatigued, fully satisfying the world.
Like rain that universally moistens all, whether noble or base, high or low, those who observe the precepts or violate them, those whose dignified conduct is complete or incomplete,
those with right view or wrong view, and those of sharp or dull faculties— it rains the rain of Dharma equally upon them all, without weariness.

Regarding the statement, "I observe all things as equal": the Tathāgata observes and knows that the three vehicles are entirely the one vehicle, and that the nine realms all return to the Buddha-realm;
therefore, it is said that they are universally equal. Regarding the absence of a mind of attachment or aversion toward self or others:
because they are universally equal, he does not give rise to attachment toward those who are his own karmic connections.
Furthermore, he does not give rise to a mind of aversion toward those who lack the conditions for the teaching, nor does he harbor a mind of attachment.
He teaches the Lesser Vehicle only to them without any sense of limitation or obstruction, yet he does not teach the Greater Vehicle to them.
Therefore, he constantly preaches the Dharma with equanimity toward all. What is meant by "equanimity" is neither more nor less [than this].
If it were few, it would not be called "equality. If one were to preach the Truths and Conditions according to the capacities of the devas and humans, there would be much;
if one were to preach the precepts and virtues according to the capacities of the two vehicles, there would be little.
The Tathāgata is able to preach the Dharma neither too much nor too little; therefore, it is called "equality. This refers to the period of equal teaching prior to forty years ago.
Furthermore, the *Lotus Sūtra* of today causes all sentient beings to open, reveal, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

According to those of the nine realms, the three vehicles, and the seven expedient means, it teaches only the doctrine of the single Buddha-vehicle and the true reality of all phenomena; this is what is called the teaching of equality. Departing from this—
Regarding "coming," "sitting," and "standing": when conditions arise in other realms and one responds there, it is called "going," as in the phrase, "that person has recently departed.
When conditions arise in this realm and one returns to respond here, it is called "coming," as in the phrase, "startled, he enters the burning house.
To be inwardly in harmony with the principle is called "sitting," as in the phrase, "knowing his father, he sits at ease. Outward observation...
The term "standing" (立) is used here in the sense of a posture, as in the expression "standing outside the gate.

Since the Tathāgata’s sole activity is the preaching of the Dharma and he has never engaged in any other business, it is said that whether walking or coming, sitting or standing, he never experiences fatigue.
Yet there is weariness and indolence. Regarding the noble and the humble, the high and the low: gods and humans are noble; the three miserable realms are humble;

Bodhisattvas are superior; and the two vehicles are inferior. Although sentient beings possess various differences, from the perspective of the Tathāgata, they have never been anything other than equal.
He rains down the single-flavored rain of the Dharma equally upon all, whereby they obtain universal nourishment and growth.
