△ Second, the verse on the threefold benefit gained from hearing the Dharma. First, the general explanation:
All sentient beings who hear my Dharma abide in the various stages according to what they receive through their respective capacities.
The term "all" refers to those of the five vehicles. The term "various stages" (*bhūmi*) means the levels of attainment;

that is, whether one abides in the stage of humans and devas, or the stages of the two vehicles, and so forth—though each may abide in their respective stages, when they hear what is taught, it is the same single sound.
Part Two: Specifically showing the five [vehicles]. First, showing humans and devas.
Whether abiding among humans or devas as a Cakravartin King, Śakra, or one of the Brahmā kings—these are the minor medicinal herbs.

Regarding the Cakravartins, Śakra, and the Brahmā kings: these are mentioned by way of the superior to include the inferior. The Cakravartin is the lord of the human realm; Śakra is the lord of the Desire Realm (kāmadhātu);
and the Brahmā King is the lord of the Form Realm (rūpadhātu). The Cakravartin is able to preach the five precepts and the ten [virtuous actions].

Excellent. They teach and transform the people, serving as an antidote to the three miserable realms. Śakra and Brahmā also expound treatises on the transcendence of desire, serving as an antidote to the realm of desire.
Because they all possess the meaning of being an antidote, they are called medicinal herbs. △ Second, showing the two vehicles.
They know the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*), are able to attain *nirvāṇa*, give rise to the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*), and obtain the three insights (*trividyā*).
Dwelling alone in mountain forests, they constantly practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and realize the fruit of a pratyekabuddha. These are the medicinal herbs therein.

Those of the Two Vehicles, by means of their knowledge of suffering and their severance of its accumulation, merely avoid falling into the *viparyāsa* (perverted views) and the *kleśa* (afflictions) of the *paricchinna-bhava* (segmented existence).

As for those who constantly practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), they contemplate the process of arising in forward order and the process of cessation in reverse order; because they contemplate both the forward and reverse sequences, it is said that they "constantly practice meditative concentration.
Since the followers of the Two Vehicles are thus able to confront the birth-and-death and afflictions of the triple world, they likewise...
This refers to the medicinal herbs. △ Third, showing the bodhisattvas:
"Seeking the state of the World-Honored One, I shall become a Buddha; I shall practice the samādhi of diligence"—these are the superior medicinal herbs.
Nirvāṇa is the domain of the World-Honored One; because the World-Honored One abides in nirvāṇa, he has attained Buddhahood.

Since I seek the domain of the World-Honored One, I too shall become a Buddha. It is with the desire to become a Buddha that I seek the domain of the World-Honored One, and therefore I practice the six perfections.
As for what is called "concentration of diligence," it is among these six perfections—

In the middle [section], only two of these six perfections are mentioned. Not only can one personally employ the six perfections as remedies for the six hindrances, but one can also transform and guide all sentient beings, causing them all to employ the six perfections as remedies for the six hindrances;
therefore, they are called "superior medicinal herbs. △ Fourth, showing the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao).

Furthermore, O sons of the Buddha, those who single-mindedly devote themselves to the path of the Buddhas, constantly practice compassion, and know for themselves that they will become Buddhas with absolute certainty,
are called "small trees."

Regarding those who are said to "single-mindedly focus on the Buddha-way": these are those of sharp faculties within the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao). They not only perceive emptiness, but also perceive non-emptiness.
Having perceived non-emptiness, they employ the contemplation of the essence of emptiness to contemplate that which is non-empty, thereby seeking the Buddha-way.

Therefore, it is said that one should concentrate the mind on the Buddha-way. "Constantly practicing compassion" means emerging from emptiness into the provisional, where the contemplations of emptiness and the provisional flow together;
sporting in supernatural powers, purifying buddha-lands, and teaching and transforming sentient beings—this is what is called constantly practicing compassion.
"Having no doubt of becoming a buddha" means that by means of the wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment, one severs the remaining residual habits.
And thus they attain Buddhahood. △ Fifth, the demonstration of the Distinct Teaching (Bie-jiao):
Abiding securely in supernormal powers (abhijñā), they turn the wheel of non-retrogression and deliver immeasurable billions of hundreds of thousands of sentient beings. Such are these Bodhisattvas.
It is called the "Great Tree.
A Bodhisattva of the First Ground can shatter one grade of ignorance and manifest one portion of the three virtues;
by manifesting bodies throughout the hundred realms as Buddhas, they abide in supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). This constitutes their own attainment of non-retrogression in mindfulness. [End]
Because one desires to turn the non-retrogressive [wheel] realized by oneself in order to guide others, it is said that one "turns the non-retrogressive wheel" and so forth.
Within the stage of the Ten Practices (*daśapratipatti*), one horizontally studies the four teachings to transform and guide all beings;
therefore, it is called "turning the non-retrogressive wheel" (etc.). △ Third, the conclusion and clarification.

The Buddha teaches with impartiality, like a rain of a single flavor; yet according to the dispositions of sentient beings, what they receive differs, just as various plants and trees each absorb nourishment differently.
Using this analogy as a skillful means to reveal and instruct, the Buddha expounds the One Dharma through diverse words and phrases.
Regarding the Buddha’s wisdom, it is like a single drop in the ocean.

As for the differences in what is received according to the dispositions of sentient beings: although the Dharma taught by the Buddha is of a single flavor, that which is received by sentient beings varies.
Although the reception differs, it remains the same single-flavored Dharma. It is as follows:
Although that which is received by grasses and trees differs, it is nonetheless the same rain showered from a single cloud.
This metaphor uses the analogy of a single flavor of rain to represent the Dharma of the single-voice teaching. "Like a drop of the ocean" refers to this.
The Buddha’s wisdom is like a great ocean; the teachings spoken by his wisdom are like a single drop of that sea.
You should know that although it is but a small drop, its essence is identical to the entire tide.

For if one can hear even this single drop of the Buddha’s teaching and give rise to faith and understanding, and based on that understanding initiate practice, entering into realization through such practice, then one will be able to [attain the full ocean].
To reveal, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s wisdom—is this not like a single drop being identical to the entire tide?
△ Second, the verse on the convergence and growth in three parts. First, presenting the Dharma.
I rain down the rain of Dharma, filling the world. This Dharma of a single flavor is practiced according to one's capacity.
To practice according to one's capacity means that although one practices in accordance with what each sentient being’s strength can sustain, one nevertheless engages in cultivation.
One should know that these are all likewise the Tathāgata’s Dharma of a single flavor. △ Second, the illustration:
Just as in that grove, the medicinal herbs and various trees, according to their size, gradually increase in growth and flourish beautifully.
"Those such as these" refers to the fact that although grasses and trees differ in their degree of lushness and excellence according to their size, they are nonetheless all grown from the same earth.
Part Three: Explanation in Two Sections. First, a general clarification.
The Dharma of all Buddhas always employs a single flavor to cause all in the world to universally attain fulfillment; through gradual cultivation, they all realize the fruits of the Path.
Regarding "universally attaining fulfillment": when the ten realms are all opened, there is none that does not become a Buddha; thus, what world could there be that is not fully endowed?

As for the statement that those who practice gradually all attain the fruits of the Way, this does not mean that by practicing gradually through the causes of humans, devas, or the two vehicles, one returns to obtain the fruits of humans, devas, or the two vehicles. It means, from the beginning...
From the causes cultivated by humans and devas, one also attains the fruit of the unsurpassed Buddha-way.
Next, from the causes cultivated by those of the two vehicles, one also attains the fruit of the unsurpassed Buddha-way.

Following that, from the causes cultivated by Bodhisattvas, one also attains the fruit of the unsurpassed Buddha-way. Humans, devas, those of the two vehicles, and Bodhisattvas—these various [beings]...
There are differences in level. Those who attain results by practicing causes through gradual stages are all able to obtain the fruit of the unsurpassed Buddha Vehicle;
therefore, it is said that those who practice gradually all attain the fruits of the Way. △ Second, the specific demonstration has three parts.
First, the demonstration of the two vehicles.
The śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, dwelling in mountain forests in their final bodies, hear the Dharma and attain the fruits; these are called medicinal herbs, each attaining growth.

Those who dwell in their final body and attain the fruit upon hearing the Dharma do so by hearing the teaching on the reality-mark (*dharmatā*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* within the original station of the Two Vehicles,
thereby attaining the fruit of the unsurpassed Buddha-vehicle. △ Second, showing the Shared Teaching (*sāmānyayāna*).
If bodhisattvas possess firm wisdom, thoroughly understand the three realms, and seek the Supreme Vehicle,
they are called "small trees" that attain growth.
Regarding "those whose wisdom is firm": if the wisdom of a Bodhisattva of the *Zang* (Tripitaka) Teaching analyzes and further analyzes [phenomena] until emptiness is seen, it is not called "firm.
Now, because the *Tong* (Shared) Teaching is able to realize that [phenomena] are themselves emptiness, it is said to be "firm. Regarding "thoroughly penetrating the three realms":

this means destroying the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and thought (*saṃjñā*), and thereby transcending the *fen-duan* (segmented) birth-and-death. Regarding "seeking the Supreme Vehicle" (*yānottara*): this refers to...
These are precisely the bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (*pāryāya-śikṣā*) who sever delusions; they also seek the unsurpassed Single Buddha Vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*).
△ Third, the Distinct Teaching (*pratyeka-śikṣā*) is shown:
Furthermore, there are those who dwell in dhyāna, attain supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), hear that all phenomena are empty, and with great joy in their hearts, emit immeasurable rays of light.
To deliver all sentient beings is called the "great tree," which then attains growth.

Those who hear the Dharma with joy are those in the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) who hear of emptiness and are able to sever both views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), manifesting various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) themselves to transform and guide sentient beings. Now, it is clarified that the emptiness attained within this specific teaching is...

It was merely a partial emptiness. Now that the *Lotus Sūtra* has been revealed and manifested, this very partial emptiness is none other than the inconceivable true emptiness—what is called "when one is empty, all are empty. What dharma is not empty?

Therefore, it is said that hearing that all dharmas are empty is precisely the first stage of joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) in the Perfect Teaching; therein, the hundred realms manifest as Buddhas to transform and deliver sentient beings.
Because [the practitioner] is born [into this state], it is said that "the mind is filled with great joy. Emitting countless rays of light, they deliver all sentient beings;
this refers to practicing the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) by cultivating the provisional and shattering the "dust-sands" (of afflictions), thereby engaging in the guidance of others.

Having already shattered the "dust-sands" of view-delusions and thought-delusions, one will before long advance to shatter ignorance (*avidyā*), attaining the same perfect realization as the Buddha. This is precisely the growth of the Great Tree according to the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavahāra*). △ Four.
The verse provides the analogy that each is unaware of itself:
"In this way, Kāśyapa, the Dharma taught by the Buddha is like a great cloud; with rain of a single flavor, it moistens both humans and flowers."

"Each attains its own fruit, yet moistens the flowers of humanity"—this both employs a metaphor and expresses the underlying principle. It means that the great cloud rains down a rain of a single flavor which moistens the flowers of grasses and trees, causing each to attain its own fruit.
Although each attains its respective fruit, they are fundamentally all moistened by the same rain.
Yet the grasses and trees are each unaware of this; though they are all equally moistened by the same rain, it is as the Buddha taught:
that the Dharma of a single flavor moistens those on the seven stages of expedient means, and each attains the one reality. Although they share this same reality, [they differ in their realization].

Yet each of them is unaware of this; only the Tathāgata can know it all completely. △ Second, the conclusion that reconciles the provisional and the real. Part one: concluding the provisional. "Kāśyapa, you should know:
by means of various causes and conditions and diverse parables, I have revealed and shown the Buddha-way; this is my skillful means."
It is the same for all Buddhas.
Regarding the phrase "various causes and conditions": the capacity of sentient beings is the cause, and the teaching of the Tathāgata is the condition.

Since these capacities and teachings differ according to their respective levels of greatness or smallness, they are called "various causes and conditions. The parables likewise possess degrees of greatness and smallness.

It is the same. Therefore, it is called "various. Regarding "revealing the Buddha-way": although the causes, conditions, and parables all possess various differences, that which is revealed is ultimately nothing other than the Buddha-way alone.
To be able to reveal the Buddha-way through various causes, conditions, and parables is my skillful means (*upāya*). However, it is not only...
I am able to do this, and all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time are likewise able to do so.
△ Second, the realization of reality: "Now, for your sakes, I shall speak of the most ultimate truth: none of you śrāvakas have attained final extinction; that which you have practiced..."
This is the path of the bodhisattva; by gradually practicing and studying it, one shall all become Buddhas.

Regarding what is called the "most ultimate reality": if one were to say that what was spoken in the past was provisional and what is spoken today is real, then although this might be called "real," it would not be called the "most ultimate reality. However, as for what was spoken in the past—

Skillful means (upāya) does not exist separately from reality; reality itself is skillful means. The reality spoken of today does not exist separately from skillful means; skillful means itself is reality.
In this way, the present and the past are non-dual, and skillful means and reality are of one essence; this is what is called the "most real matter.
As for the statement that all śrāvakas have not attained parinirvāṇa: if one considers those of superior capacity such as Śāriputra, or those of middling capacity...
Regarding the four great disciples: they already knew that this was not true parinirvāṇa. Now, the Tathāgata wishes to spur those of inferior faculties;
therefore, he speaks of this to give rise to doubt and to shake their attachments. "You all" and so forth—this again refers to the four great disciples.
Although Bodhisattvas cultivate the path perfectly, coarse defilements must necessarily fall away first; now, the Śrāvakas have already...

By destroying the views and afflictions (*kleśa*), one becomes identical to the Bodhisattva for whom the "coarse impurities" have already fallen away; thus, what one practices is precisely the path of the Bodhisattva.
Now that the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena has been understood, one takes this as the object and gives rise to wisdom.

One then applies this to enter into the myriad practices (*sādhana*) to transform and guide sentient beings, cultivating merit and wisdom, and is thereby able to attain [the mastery over] kalpas and buddha-fields.

Adorned [with these virtues], they shall attain the Bodhi of Buddhahood; therefore, it is said that by practicing and studying gradually, all shall surely become Buddhas. The explanation of the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" chapter is complete.
*The Lotus Sutra of the Wonderful Law*, Chapter Six: "Bestowal of Prophecies."
Regarding the origin of this chapter: it generally stems from the Tathāgata’s first discourse on the Dharma, which was intended for the superior faculties of Śāriputra;
having attained understanding through it, Śāriputra set forth what he had realized to the Tathāgata, who then confirmed his realization and bestowed upon him a prophecy.
Following that, there was a second discourse by way of parables, intended for...
The four great disciples of middle capacity attained understanding and likewise presented to the Tathāgata what they had understood; the Tathāgata then confirmed their realization for them.
After confirming the realization of those of superior capacity, he immediately bestowed upon them the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
Now that the exposition for those of middle capacity has already been completed, it is natural that they too shall be granted a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*);
thus, this chapter exists as the passage in which the Tathāgata grants the prediction to those of middle capacity. Regarding the term "prediction" (*vyākaraṇa*):

if one explains the characters according to their primary meanings, "granting" (*shou*) means to bestow, and "recording" (*ji*) means to prophesy or predict. It is like the world's various things such as melons and eggplants, which may be...

Regarding the seeds for the coming year, one marks them with grass and bestows a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). Now, these four great disciples are able to understand the purport of the Tathāgata’s parables;
as they possess this Buddha-seed, they shall be able to attain Buddhahood in the future. Therefore, the Tathāgata grants them a prediction.
To speak according to the literal reality, "bestowing" (*śāsana*) refers to the giving of the holy word, while "granting" (*dāna*) refers to the fruit.
"Intentional naming and recording" refers to the Tathāgata’s speaking of matters such as the adornments of kalpas and lands from his golden mouth to the four great disciples;

therefore, it is called "bestowal. These four great disciples had first resolved their minds for enlightenment under twenty-two thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas, and their aspiration was directed toward attaining Buddhahood. Furthermore, when the four great disciples saw the Buddha bestow [the prophecy] upon Śāriputra...

Regarding the term "prediction" (vyākaraṇa): it refers to the statement that the twelve hundred arhats shall all likewise become buddhas. Furthermore, they possessed the aspiration for the fruit of buddhahood;
now, as the Tathāgata speaks of their attaining buddhahood regarding the kalpas and lands, this fulfills what was originally expected by their own minds.
Therefore, it is called a "prediction. Indeed, throughout the Tathāgata’s single lifetime of teaching and transformation, there are predictions bestowed everywhere.
If one compares the predictions (vyākaraṇa) found in this present sutra with those given during the preceding forty years, they do not correspond at all.
During those forty years, he merely predicted that bodhisattvas would become buddhas; he never predicted that śrāvakas would become buddhas.
He merely predicted that virtuous people would become buddhas; he never predicted that evil people would become buddhas. He merely predicted men [would become buddhas].
Regarding the attainment of Buddhahood: previously, he did not bestow predictions of Buddhahood upon women; he only bestowed predictions of Buddhahood upon those on the wholesome paths.

Previously, he did not bestow predictions of Buddhahood upon animals. Now, this sutra does not distinguish between the two vehicles, nor does it distinguish between evil persons, nor women, nor animals;
rather, it bestows the prediction of Buddhahood upon each and every one of them. This is what occurred forty years ago.
Since nothing [of this kind] has existed before, this sutra may be called the ultimate proclamation of the five periods, and its merit surpasses that of the entire dispensation.
It is because this sutra opens up all ten realms and brings together the three vehicles in equal assembly that it is able to be thus.
Furthermore, the "bestowal of predictions" mentioned herein refers precisely to the bestowing of predictions upon those of the śrāvaka vehicle. △ Four.
Regarding the two [sections] on the granting of predictions to those of middling capacity: first, the actual bestowing of the prediction; second, the promise to explain the causes and conditions.

Regarding the first of these two: first, the prediction given to Kāśyapa; second, the prediction given to the three individuals. Regarding the first of these two: first, the prose section; second, the verse section. Regarding the first of these two: first, the clarification of the causal practice.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, he addressed the great assembly, declaring:
"This disciple of mine, Mahākāśyapa, shall in a future age behold three million billion Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones."

"To make offerings, show reverence, respect, and praise, and widely proclaim the immeasurable Great Dharma of all Buddhas, saying that one shall attain equality"—this clarifies the timing of the cultivation of merit. "Offerings" and so forth clarify the sincerity of the three karmas.
"Widely proclaiming the Great Dharma" means to preach it and circulate it; this clarifies its cultivation.
This refers to wisdom (*prajñā*). The reason one must cultivate both merit and wisdom is that only when these two are perfected can one attain Buddhahood.
△ Second, explaining the attainment of the fruit, in four parts: first, explaining the becoming of a Buddha.
In his final body, he attained Buddhahood, named the Tathāgata Prabhāsa (Light), Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna,
Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
As for the Buddha named Prabhāsa (Light-Radiance), it was because in a former causal life, Kāśyapa once anointed the image of a Buddha with purple-gold (*cāmīkara*).
Consequently, he now experiences the perfection of his physical marks, such that his radiance eclipses all else, and he is named "The One Who Outshines Light" (*Kāśyapa*).
Now, at this great assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he has understood the Tathāgata’s parables and...
One attains the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and realizes the inconceivable light of wisdom possessed by the Tathāgata.
Therefore, that which was cultivated and realized during the causal stage is designated by the name "Light" from the perspective of the fruition.
This refers entirely to the inconceivable light of wisdom. △ Second, the clarification of the eon and the land.
The land is named Radiant Virtue (*Prabhāśrī*), and the eon is named Great Adornment (*Mahāvyūha*).
As for the land being named Radiant Virtue: it is because the light of wisdom attained within a single moment of mind illuminates the three inconceivable virtues;
therefore, the land is named Radiant Virtue. As for the eon being named Great Adornment: if...
In the world, one uses wealth and treasures as adornments, yet these cannot be called "great.
Now, that Buddha is able to fully realize the three types of knowledge and the three virtues; thus, he possesses the immeasurable dharma-wealth of supramundane merit as his adornment.
This is what is called "great. Because that Buddha possesses such great adornment, the eon is established [by that name].
This is the name; it is also called the "Great Adornment. △ Third, clarifying the Buddha’s lifespan:
the Buddha’s lifespan is twelve small kalpas.
△ Fourth, clarifying the True and Semblance Dharma periods.
The True Dharma shall remain in the world for twenty intermediate kalpas, and the Semblance Dharma shall likewise remain for twenty intermediate kalpas.

The realm shall be magnificently adorned, free from all impurities and evils; there shall be no shards, rubble, thorns, or the filth of excrement and urine. That land shall be level and even, without any elevations or depressions.
The ditches, pits, mounds, and hills have been transformed; the ground is made of lapis lazuli. Rows of jewel-trees stand in order, with golden cords delineating the sides of the roads.
Various precious flowers are strewn about, making the entire realm pure and serene. There are immeasurable thousands of billions of bodhisattvas in that land, as well as a multitude of śrāvakas.
They are likewise innumerable. There will be no demonic activities (*māra-karman*). Although there may be Māras and their followers, they shall all protect the Buddha-dharma.

As for the True Dharma (*saddharma*): during the initial several kalpas after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, the disciples of the Buddha will still be able to clarify the principles based on the teachings as they were spoken;
from these principles, they will be able to give rise to practice, and through that practice, they will be able to enter [the path].

Realization. When these four—teaching, principle, practice, and realization—are all fully present, then even though the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, he is as if still remaining in the world to teach and transform beings;
therefore, it is called the True Dharma (*saddharma*). As for the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpaka-dharma*): "semblance" means similar; it merely resembles the True Dharma.
This is because, although one likewise relies on the teachings to clarify the principles and initiates practice, one does not yet enter realization.
Those [who possess realization] are few. This state consists only of the three—teaching, principle, and practice—but lacks realization;

it is thus like the semblance of the True Dharma (*saddharma*). Therefore, it is called the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpaka-dharma*). If one speaks of the Final Dharma (*paścima-dharma*), then even practice is absent.
This is discussed in terms of the chronological sequence of the periods. However, if one investigates the reality of the matter, it depends solely upon the individual practitioner. It is not...

At this time, if one can, amidst the Dharma-ending age, rely upon the teaching of the One Vehicle of this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* to clarify the principle of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena,
and give rise to practice based on that principle, one will surely attain the opening, showing, awakening,
and entering into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, thereby entering into realization. Thus, although the time is that of the Dharma-ending age, it is as if it were the time of the Buddha.
In this world, there is no second [to me]. How could it be merely the period of the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma? Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"If, in the future final age, one believes in what you have spoken, then they shall see me, and they shall also see you, as well as the community of bhikṣus and all the bodhisattvas."

This is clear evidence. If, while the Buddha is in the world, one cannot clarify the principles according to the teachings and cannot enter realization through practice, then even though it is the Buddha’s era, it is no different from the Age of Decline (mofa); how could it be merely like the Ages of Orthodoxy and Semblance?

Thus we know that whether it is the Buddha’s own era or the final age, the True Dharma (*saddharma*) or the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpakadharma*), truly depends on the individual and has nothing to do with the time itself.

Some say that while the Buddha was in the world, it was called the True Dharma; after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, because only the physical images of the Buddha remain in the world, it is called the Semblance Dharma.
This view not only fails to clarify the meaning of the Semblance and True Dharmas, but...
Furthermore, it is not clear from this passage whether it refers to the Buddha’s lifespan being several kalpas long.
For while the Buddha was in the world, one would speak of the Buddha’s lifespan being several kalpas; why then would one speak of the True Dharma (Saddharma) lasting for several kalpas?

If the True Dharma were taken as the Buddha’s lifespan, would one then take the Buddha’s lifespan as his worldly age? As for the statement that "there are no demonic activities" and so forth, some people...

It is said: Since one has already attained Buddhahood, one thoroughly realizes that the suchness (*tathatā*) of the realm of Māras and the suchness of the realm of Buddhas are a single suchness, without duality.
Therefore, there are no demonic activities. If this were the case, then in every land where a Buddha attains enlightenment, there would be no demonic activities at all;
for when each Buddha attains enlightenment, they are all able to thoroughly realize both Māra and Buddha.

Because it is as it was before. Yet, why is it that there are still Buddha-lands where demonic activities occur? Thus we know that while this interpretation may seem plausible on the surface, it is truly without foundation.
Now, I say that the reason demons are able to afflict people is solely through the five desires (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*), which serve as the means of their disturbance.
In the present case, because Kāśyapa, during his causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*), was able to practice the ascetic virtues (*dhūta-guṇa*).
They are foremost in ascetic practice and possess few desires and contentment; therefore, when they reach the stage of fruition, no demonic obstacles arise for them.
This is precisely what is meant by the Bodhisattva’s ability to practice generosity during the causal stage, such that when he attains Buddhahood, beings free from greed come to be born in his land.
Those who protect the Buddha-dharma, even if there are Māras and their followers—
The people are all able to understand that the five desires are to be censured; therefore, they all protect the Buddha-dharma.
Thus, although there may be Māras present, there are no deeds of Māra. △ Second, the verse summary has two parts. First, the summary of the causal practice.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse, saying:
"I tell you, monks: with my Buddha-eye, I see that this Kāśyapa, in a future age, after the passing of incalculable kalpas..."
You shall attain Buddhahood. In a future age, you will make offerings to and attend upon three hundred trillion Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
For the sake of the Buddha’s wisdom, you will purely cultivate the brahma-conduct; having made the highest offerings to the Honored Ones among two-legged beings, you will practice all [virtues].
Unsurpassed wisdom.
△ Second, the four verses on attaining the fruit. First, the verse on becoming a Buddha:
In his final body, he attains the state of Buddhahood.
△ Second, the verse on the purity of the land:
That realm is pure; its ground is made of lapis lazuli. There are many jeweled trees arranged in rows along the roadsides, with golden cords demarcating the paths.
Those who behold it rejoice. It constantly emits exquisite fragrances and scatters various famous flowers of diverse wonders as adornments.
Its ground is level and even, without mounds or pits. The assembly of bodhisattvas is beyond calculation; their minds are harmonious and supple.
Having attained great supernormal powers, they uphold the Mahāyāna sūtras of all Buddhas.
The assembly of śrāvakas—those who have reached their final body of no-outflows and are sons of the Dharma King—is likewise incalculable; even with the divine eye, one could not count or know them.
As for those who cannot be known by the divine eye: Kāśyapa shall become a Buddha in the future; he is currently a son of the Buddha.
Therefore, the Tathāgata has come here and observed him with the Buddha-eye, for the Buddha is able to see him within the midst of future ages.
They shall surely attain Buddhahood. These present śrāvaka assemblies are, in fact, the sons of the Dharma King;
they must be observed with the Dharma-eye before they can be counted and known. Now, because you observe them with the divine eye, you are unable to count and know them.
△ Three verses on the Buddha’s lifespan:
That Buddha’s lifespan shall be twelve small kalpas.
△ Four verses on the True and Semblance Dharma periods.
The True Dharma shall remain in the world for twenty intermediate kalpas; the Semblance Dharma shall likewise remain for twenty intermediate kalpas.
Such were the circumstances of the World-Honored One Prabhāsa.

△ Second, the granting of predictions to two groups of three persons. First, the request of the disciples; second, the granting by the Tathāgata. The first section has two parts. First, the prose exposition.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Subhūti, Mahākātyāyana, and the others were all struck with awe and trembling. (1)
With palms joined, they gazed up at the Honored One’s countenance, their eyes never for a moment departing from it.

Herein, the account of the three great disciples all being struck with awe and trembling, yet experiencing this particular state of realization, is because they were people of middling capacity who attained understanding in the same manner as Kāśyapa; now we see that Kāśyapa was first...

Having already received the prediction, he knew for himself that he too would become a Buddha; yet, while the Tathāgata had not yet conferred the prediction upon him, he did not know what further intention the Tathāgata might have.
Thus, there arose this state of awe and trembling, and he spoke these words to request the prediction.
By this, one can discern that he was a person of middling capacity. II. Verse Summary.
Then, with one voice, they spoke this verse:
"O Great Hero, O World-Honored One, Dharma King of the Śākyas! Out of compassion for us, you have bestowed upon us the Buddha’s melodic voice."

One who is "greatly heroic and fierce" (mahāvīra) may indeed be called heroic and fierce when compared to ordinary people and non-Buddhists if they destroy the afflictions of views and thoughts (dṛṣṭi-kleśa) and sever the bonds of birth-and-death (pariccheda). However, such a person cannot be named "Greatly Heroic and Fierce.
Now, when the Tathāgata discusses the five stages of dwelling (pañca-vihāra), he has reached ultimate exhaustion; this not only destroys the afflictions of views and thoughts, but furthermore—
He has shattered ignorance. When one discusses the two types of death, he has brought them to ultimate extinction;
thus, he not only severs the death of the segmented realm (*pariccheda-maraṇa*) but also severs the death of the transformation realm (*pariṇāma-maraṇa*).

Therefore, he is the Great Hero and the Most Fierce One, the Honored One of both the mundane and supramundane worlds. Regarding the phrase "the Dharma King of the Śākyas": the Tathāgata was originally of the Śākya clan. If...
Had he not gone forth from the household life, he would have been a wheel-turning monarch among the Śākyas; now that he has become a Buddha, he is the Dharma King among the Śākyas.

When it says "granting the voice of a Buddha," it means the wish that the Tathāgata, from his golden mouth, grant the voice of the prophecy of attaining Buddhahood and the adornment of the kalpa and the land.
If you know my deep intention and grant me this prediction of enlightenment, it will be like sprinkling nectar that dispels heat and brings refreshing coolness.
It is like one who has come from a land of famine and suddenly encounters the meal of a great king; though the heart still harbors doubt and fear, one does not yet dare to eat immediately.
If we were further to receive the King’s command, only then would we dare to eat. We are just like this; we constantly contemplate the faults of the Hīnayāna and do not know what should be done.
Only upon attaining the Buddha’s unsurpassed wisdom shall we truly hear the Buddha’s voice saying, "You shall become Buddhas."
My mind still harbors anxiety and fear; thus, I have not yet dared to eat. Only if I receive a prediction from the Buddha shall I find true peace and joy.
This contains both a metaphor and its application to the principle. First, regarding the phrase "knowing my deep mind":
this is because the Tathāgata, in the section concerning those of superior faculties, stated, "I now wish to cause you to recollect your original practice of the Way," for the sake of all śrāvakas.
I have heard that people say this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* was preached [to us]. Furthermore, the four great disciples also all heard it in advance.
Therefore, my current thought is this: if those of superior faculties were already like this, then even though we are of middling faculties, we must also have heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
Thus, we too must surely have possessed profound resolve and original vows in the past; I have simply forgotten them. It is as if...

He must surely know this. Therefore, it is said that if the Tathāgata were to know our profound resolve and original vow—that we fundamentally desire to attain Buddhahood—then he would now appear before us and immediately bestow upon us the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). Were we to receive such a prediction, it would be like being sprinkled with nectar;
it would not only dispel our feverish distress but would also bring us refreshing coolness. To receive the prediction is like being sprinkled with sweet nectar.
“Those who are exposed” means that if they hear the bestowal of the prediction (vyākaraṇa), the fever of our trepidation will be removed and we shall attain coolness.

Regarding the phrase “as if coming from a land of famine,” it means that we and Kāśyapa are equally śrāvakas, equally attained to realization, and equally established by the Tathāgata; yet now Kāśyapa has already received the prediction.
Thus, we also know that we shall certainly receive the prediction of enlightenment; however, for a time, we did not dare immediately to accept this for ourselves.
To illustrate this by means of a parable: it is like [the story of] coming from a land of famine (and so forth). Coming from a land of famine is a metaphor for coming from among the śrāvakas.

The "royal feast" is a metaphor for hearing the prediction of attaining Buddhahood; "not daring to eat" is a metaphor for not yet daring to personally accept it. "Receiving the king's instruction" is a metaphor for the Buddha further personally bestowing the prediction upon him.
