That is to say, they constantly reflect to themselves: "That we have hitherto obtained only the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) is our own fault, not that of the World-Honored One.
He is one who dwells in supreme peace and bliss. If we receive the prediction of attaining Buddhahood, ignorance and its transformations will surely be shattered and severed;
the three wisdoms and three virtues will certainly be realized and manifested, and we shall never again be subject to the five stages of dwelling."
Bound by the fetters of the two deaths, we say, "May there be swift peace and happiness.
O Great Hero, O Fierce World-Honored One, you who constantly desire to bring peace to the world, we pray that you grant us a prediction; it is like one who must be taught what to eat when hungry.
The formal invitation is as in the text. △ Second, the Tathāgata bestows three predictions. First, the prediction for Subhūti; second, the prediction for Kātyāyana;
third, the prediction for Maudgalyāyana. Regarding the first two, there is first the prose section and second the verse section. Within the first [the prose], there are again two parts:
first, clarifying the causes of practice.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of his great disciples, addressed the bhikṣus:

“This Subhūti, in a future age, shall behold three hundred trillion nayutas of Buddhas; he shall make offerings to them, honor them, respect them, and praise them, constantly practicing the pure conduct and perfecting the path of a bodhisattva.”
△ Second, the explanation of attaining the fruit, in four parts. First, the explanation of becoming a Buddha:

In his final body, he attains Buddhahood, being named the Tathāgata Mingxiang (Name-Form), Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, and Bhagavat.
Regarding the name "Phenomenal Characteristics" (Nāmalakṣaṇa):

because Subhūti was foremost among those who attained understanding of the emptiness of the Hīnayāna during his causal stage, even now at this sublime assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he has fully realized that the emptiness of the Hīnayāna is itself the inconceivable, true emptiness of the Mahāyāna—a true emptiness that is not empty, yet is able to be fully endowed with all things; hence the name.
Because it encompasses all characteristics, one attains understanding through its causes and establishes names upon the effects; these are thus termed "characteristics of names.
△ Second, the clarification of kalpas and lands.
The eon was named Possessing Jewels (*Ratnasaṃbhava*). The land was named Jewel-Born (*Ratnajāta*). That realm was level and even; its ground was made of crystal and adorned with jeweled trees.
It was free from mounds, pits, sand, gravel, thorns, and the filth of excrement and urine. Jeweled flowers covered the ground, and it was pure throughout.
The people of that land all dwell in jeweled terraces and exquisite pavilions. His śrāvaka disciples are immeasurable and boundless, beyond what can be known through calculation or analogy.
The assembly of bodhisattvas numbers in the hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas.
As for the fact that both the eon and the land are named "Jewel" (Ratna): when Subhūti was first born, the treasure stores within his household were entirely emptied.
This served as a premonitory sign that he would be able to comprehend the emptiness of the Hīnayāna. Now that he has already comprehended the emptiness of the Hīnayāna, [the world is thus named].
The entirety is the Great Vehicle’s true emptiness; this true emptiness is not empty, for it is fully endowed with all things.
Therefore, the name of that eon is "Possessing Jewels," and the name of that land is "Jeweled Birth. △ Third, explaining the Buddha’s lifespan.
The Buddha’s lifespan was twelve minor kalpas.
△ Fourth, the clarification of the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma:
the True Dharma shall abide in the world for twenty minor kalpas, and the Semblance Dharma shall likewise abide for twenty minor kalpas. That Buddha constantly dwells...
He preaches the Dharma for the multitude in the midst of empty space, delivering and liberating immeasurable bodhisattvas as well as the assembly of śrāvakas.

That he dwells in emptiness to preach the Dharma is due to Subhūti; first, he understood the emptiness of the Hīnayāna, and subsequently, he understood that the very emptiness of the Hīnayāna is the true emptiness of the Mahāyāna. Upon attaining Buddhahood, he is then able to...

Abiding thus in the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) oneself, one further desires that all sentient beings may likewise understand and abide in that which one has understood and in which one dwells.
That is to say, for those who have not yet understood emptiness, one causes them first to understand the emptiness of the Hīnayāna;
and for those who have already understood the emptiness of the Hīnayāna, one causes them to understand [the Mahāyāna].
That which is the emptiness of the Hīnayāna is itself the true emptiness of the Mahāyāna.

For those who have already understood this true emptiness, he causes them to abide in the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*); therefore, when preaching the Dharma, he always dwells in empty space.
Regarding "delivering immeasurable śrāvakas," this refers to the śrāvakas who hear everything through the sound of the Buddha-way.
...and so forth. △ Second, the verse summary has two parts. First, the verse on the causes of practice.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"O assembly of bhikṣus, I now tell you all: you should all listen with a single mind to what I say. My great disciples..."

Subhūti shall attain Buddhahood; his name shall be Mingxiang (Renowned Appearance). He shall make offerings to countless tens of billions of Buddhas, following the conduct of those Buddhas and gradually perfecting the Great Way.
The first line is an exhortation to listen. The reason it is necessary to exhort one to listen is threefold: first, to clarify that what the Buddha has spoken is not false;
second, to demonstrate the certainty of attaining Buddhahood; and third, to serve as a warning and incentive for those of inferior capacity.
△ Second, the verse on attaining the fruit, in four parts. First, the verse on becoming a Buddha.
In his final existence, he attained the thirty-two marks of a great man; he was upright, exquisite, and beautiful, like a mountain of jewels.
△ Second, the verse on the purity of the land:
That Buddha’s land is foremost in its majestic purity; among sentient beings who see it, there are none who do not love and delight in it. Within that land, the Buddha—
He delivers immeasurable multitudes. Within his Buddha-dharma, there are many bodhisattvas, all of whom possess sharp faculties and turn the wheel of non-retrogression;
that land is constantly adorned by these bodhisattvas. The assembly of śrāvakas is beyond counting, and they have all attained the three types of supernormal knowledge.

He possessed the six supernormal powers and dwelt in the eight liberations. Endowed with great majesty and virtue, when that Buddha preached the Dharma, he manifested immeasurable and inconceivable supernatural transformations.
Gods and humans, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, all joined their palms together in reverence.
Listen to and receive the Buddha’s words.

As for those bodhisattvas within the land who are able to provide adornment: because these bodhisattvas have destroyed delusions and realized virtues, they are themselves capable of adorning [the land].
Therefore, if there are such adorned bodhisattvas within the land, then the land itself is likewise adorned.
...this adornment. Regarding the statement that they possess "great majesty and virtue": these śrāvakas possess majesty because they are able to sever the afflictions of views and thought;
they possess virtue because they are able to manifest the true principle. Compared to humans and devas, they are thus termed "great.
△ Third, the verse on the Buddha’s lifespan.
That Buddha’s lifespan shall be twelve small kalpas.
△ Fourth, the verse on the True Dharma and Semblance Dharma:
The True Dharma shall remain in the world for twenty small kalpas; the Semblance Dharma shall likewise remain for twenty small kalpas.

△ Second, the bestowal of a prediction upon Kātyāyana. This has two parts: first, the prose; second, the verse. The first part [the prose] also has two sections. First, clarifying the causes of his practice.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the assembly of bhikṣus: "I now tell you: this Mahākātyāyana..."
In future ages, they shall honor, serve, revere, and respect eight thousand billion Buddhas with all manner of offerings.
After each of these Buddhas has passed into parinirvāṇa, they shall erect stūpas for them, one thousand yojanas in height and five hundred yojanas in length and breadth,
made of the seven treasures— gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, pearl, and ruby— and adorned with various flowers and necklaces.
With powdered incense, incense for burning, and incense for smearing, as well as silk canopies, banners, and streamers, they shall make offerings to the stupas and temples.
After this, they shall likewise make offerings to twenty trillion Buddhas in the same manner. Having made offerings to these Buddhas, they shall fulfill the path of a bodhisattva.
△ Second, explaining the attainment of the fruit, in four parts. First, explaining the becoming of a Buddha:

He shall attain Buddhahood, with the name Yaṃbu-nadī-kāñcana-prabhāsa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyak-saṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣa-damya-sārathi, Śāstā deva-manuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat.
The Buddha’s name in that fruition-land is Jambunadaprabhāsa. "Jambunada" means Jambudvīpa;
it is the name of a tree. When its sap flows into the water, it turns into gold, the radiance of which is most brilliant and pure.
Now, among those of the Hīnayāna, Kātyāyana is foremost in debate.
Now, within this assembly of the Lotus Sūtra, even the discourses of the Hīnayāna are entirely transformed into Mahāyāna discourses;
thus, all such discourses are the inconceivable Prajñā of Words.
If one illuminates all things with this Prajñā, there is nothing that is not clearly understood, just like the radiance of Jambūnada gold. Therefore—
This is precisely what is meant by its name. △ Second, clarifying the purity of the land:
Its terrain is level and even; its ground is made of crystal; it is adorned with jeweled trees; and golden cords demarcate the sides of the roads.
Wondrous flowers cover the ground, which is everywhere pure; those who see it rejoice. There are no four evil realms—the paths of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, and asuras.
It is adorned by many devas and humans, as well as immeasurable tens of billions of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas.
Regarding "wondrous flowers covering the ground": the wondrous flowers symbolize the wondrous cause, while the ground symbolizes ignorance (*avidyā*).

Although the wondrous cause has been established, ignorance has not yet been exhausted; thus, it is like flowers covering the ground. Furthermore, the ground represents the ground of the principle of true reality (*bhūtatathatā*);
the true reality is manifested through the wondrous cause, just as the ground is covered by flowers. Knowing this wondrous cause, one will surely attain the wondrous fruit. Therefore...
Those who see him rejoice. △ Third, clarifying the Buddha’s lifespan:
the Buddha’s lifespan is twelve minor kalpas.
△ Fourth, clarifying the True and Semblance Dharma periods.
The True Dharma shall remain in the world for twenty minor kalpas; the Semblance Dharma shall likewise remain for twenty minor kalpas.
△ Second, the four verses in *śloka* meter: first, the verse admonishing the audience to listen.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"O assembly of bhikṣus, listen all with one mind; what I have spoken is true and without deviation."
△ Second, the verse on the causes for practice:
"Kātyāyana, you should, with various kinds of excellent offerings, make offerings to the Buddhas. After the Buddhas have passed into extinction..."
They erect stupas made of the seven precious jewels and likewise offer flowers and incense to the śarīra.
Regarding those who possess exquisite offerings, it is because they have realized that the three spheres are empty in essence:
internally, they do not perceive a person who offers; externally, they do not perceive a Buddha who is offered to; and in between, they likewise do not perceive anything that is offered.
It is complete; therefore, it is said to be "exquisite. △ Third, the verse on attaining the fruit:
In his final body, he attains the Buddha-wisdom and achieves equal and perfect enlightenment.
△ Fourth, the verse on the purity of the land.
The land is pure and serene; he delivers and liberates immeasurable billions of sentient beings, who are all honored by those of the ten directions.
The Buddha’s radiance is unsurpassed; that Buddha is named Jambūnada-prabhāsa (Jambu Golden Light). His bodhisattvas and śrāvakas—
He has severed all existence, which is immeasurable and innumerable, and thus adorns his land.

Regarding "bodhisattvas and śrāvakas who have severed all existence": the bodhisattvas sever existence as cause and effect outside the realms, while the śrāvakas sever existence as cause and effect within the realms. Since the term "realms" encompasses both the internal and external, it is said to be one.
...all of them. △ Third, the bestowal of the prediction upon Maudgalyāyana, in two parts: first, the prose; second, the verse. The first part [the prose] is further divided into two.
First, clarifying the causal practice:
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the great assembly: "I now tell you: this Mahā-Maudgalyāyana shall, by means of planting..."
With various kinds of offerings, they made offerings to hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, honoring and respecting them with reverence. After those Buddhas had passed into extinction,
they each erected stūpas and temples one thousand yojanas in height, five hundred yojanas in length and breadth, perfectly equal in all dimensions, composed of the seven treasures—
gold, silver, lapis lazuli, musaragalva, agate, pearl, and ruby— and adorned with various flowers, necklaces, ointments, powdered incense, and burning incense.
With silk canopies, banners, and streamers, they shall offer worship. After this, they shall likewise again offer worship to two hundred trillion buddhas, in the same manner.
△ Second, explaining the attainment of the fruit, in four parts. First, explaining the becoming of a Buddha:
He shall attain Buddhahood, and his name shall be Tāmālapatrānulepanagandha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
The One Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct; the Well-Gone One; the Knower of the World; the Unsurpassed One; the Tamer of Men; the Teacher of Gods and Humans; the Buddha; the World-Honored One.
As for the name of the Buddha, Tamālapatracaṃdanagandha: *Tamālapatra* means "natureless" (*amala*).
Regarding "perfume" (*gandha*): it carries the meaning of being pure, far-reaching, and subtly pervasive.

Since Maudgalyāyana was foremost in supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) among those of the Hīnayāna, his attainment of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* signifies that his former Hīnayāna powers have now become entirely the inconceivable powers of the Mahāyāna.
Before long, he will naturally be able to manifest emanations throughout the hundred worlds, just as the fragrance of perfume is pure and far-reaching.
Because he penetrates [the truth] in a hidden manner, he is thus named accordingly. △ Second, the explanation of the eon and the land:

The name of the eon is "Fulfillment of Joy" (Kṣema-pūrṇa), and the name of the land is "Delightful Intent" (Manoratha). That realm is level and even; its ground is made of crystal, and it is adorned with precious trees.

Scattered flowers of genuine pearls made it pure throughout; those who saw it were filled with joy. There were many devas and humans, as well as bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, their number being immeasurable.
The kalpa is named "Joy-Fulfillment" (Pramuditā) and the land is named "Delightful" (Abhirati).
Just as when people in this world possess a certain skill or art, anyone who sees them will inevitably feel joy;
so too, because that Buddha possesses immeasurable and inconceivable great supernormal powers (abhijñā), all who behold him will inevitably experience great joy. Therefore, that kalpa is so named.
Joyful and full; that land is thus named "Intentional Delight. △ Third, clarifying the Buddha’s lifespan:
the Buddha’s lifespan is twenty-four minor kalpas.
△ Fourth, clarifying the True and Semblance Dharma periods.
The True Dharma shall remain in the world for forty minor kalpas; the Semblance Dharma shall likewise remain for forty minor kalpas.
△ Second, the verses in praise consist of two parts. First, the verse on the causal practice:
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"This disciple of mine, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, after casting off this body, shall behold eight thousand two hundred trillion [Buddhas]."

For the sake of the Buddha-way, they made offerings and showed reverence to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; they constantly practiced the pure conduct (brahmacarya) in the presence of those Buddhas and upheld the Buddha-dharma for immeasurable kalpas.
After the parinirvāṇa of those Buddhas, they erected stupas made of the seven treasures, with tall poles and golden finials.
With flowers, incense, music, and song, they made offerings to the stūpas and shrines of all Buddhas.
△ Second, the verses on attaining the fruit, in four parts. First, the direct verses on becoming a Buddha:
Having gradually fulfilled the path of a bodhisattva, he attained Buddhahood in the land of Abhirati, named Tamāla.

Regarding the gradual fulfillment of the Bodhisattva path through the fragrance of sandalwood: this does not mean that there is a sequence where emptiness comes first, then the provisional, and finally the middle.

Rather, although the Bodhisattva practices all aspects of the path in a perfectly integrated manner, it is the natural law (*dharmatā*) that the falling away of delusions occurs in a temporal sequence; therefore, it is so described.
Gradually, he will fulfill the path of a bodhisattva. △ Second, the verse on the Buddha’s lifespan:
That Buddha’s life span shall be twenty-four kalpas.
△ Third, the verse on the purity of the land.
He constantly acts as a teacher for devas and humans, expounding the Buddha-way. His śrāvakas are immeasurable, like the sands of the Ganges;

they possess the three knowledges and six supernatural powers, and have great majestic virtue. His bodhisattvas are innumerable, firm in resolve and diligent in effort; regarding the wisdom of the Buddha, none of them ever regress.
To speak of "firm resolve" means that the resolve of the Four Great Vows is both steadfast and firm.
This is because one must certainly deliver all infinite sentient beings, and furthermore, one must certainly attain the unsurpassed Buddha-way.
Therefore, his resolve is indeed firm. △ Fourth, the verse on the True and Semblance Dharma:
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma shall remain for forty minor kalpas; the Semblance Dharma shall likewise endure for the same duration.
△ Second, the promise to explain the causes and conditions:
My disciples, endowed with majestic power, numbering five hundred, shall all receive predictions that in a future age they will attain [enlightenment].
"All shall attain Buddhahood. I shall now explain the causal conditions from past lives concerning myself and you all; listen well.
Regarding this Tathāgata’s prior promise to provide a general prediction followed by an explanation of the causal conditions:

for those of superior faculties, he speaks only after three requests, yet grants them the prediction without being asked. For those of middling faculties, he speaks immediately upon a single request."
The prediction will be granted later. Here, for those of inferior faculties, the Buddha does not wait for a request; he simply grants them the prediction and speaks for their sake.
He does this out of concern that those of inferior faculties might become terrified and develop a sense of discouragement;
thus, he comforts them in advance. By this, one sees the difference between the three types of faculties. The explanation of the "Chapter on the Prediction" is concluded.
The Seventh Chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, "The Parable of the Phantom City.

Regarding the origin of this chapter: it generally stems from the Tathāgata’s preaching of this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for the sake of the śrāvakas, with the intention that they all might attain the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; however, their faculties...
There are thus inequalities of superior, middling, and inferior capacities. Therefore, when the Dharma was preached once, only those of superior faculties were able to attain realization.
Once the superior faculties had realized it, the Tathāgata then completed the exposition for them and bestowed upon them the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*);
his task with them was finished. Yet, the middling faculties remained deluded; thus, he skillfully entrusted Śāriputra to request [the teaching] again, providing further analogies so that—
They attained realization. Once those of middle capacity had realized it, he likewise provided them with a descriptive prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), and his task for them was complete.
Although those of superior and middle capacity had awakened, those of inferior capacity remained deluded.

Now, wishing for even those of inferior capacity to attain realization, he did not wait for a request but spoke for their sake concerning the events of causes and conditions from past lives. Furthermore...

By means of the parable of the conjured city and the jewel-treasure, it illustrates the provisional establishment of the three vehicles to reveal the reality of the one vehicle, so that [the audience] may likewise attain realization as described in the "Middle" chapter. Therefore, this chapter exists;
it is the passage in which the Tathāgata explains the causes and conditions of past lives for those of inferior capacity. Now, regarding the beginning of this chapter:
It clarifies the causal conditions (*nidāna*) of past lives; if one discusses its conclusion, it culminates in the place of treasure (*ratnasthāna*).

It is only in the interim that it clarifies the parable of the conjured city (*nirmāṇapurī*). Furthermore, while this is called a single cycle of the *Nidāna-sūtra*, the chapter title does not indicate "causal conditions" nor does it indicate "the place of treasure," but merely speaks of the "Parable of the Conjured City. Why is this so?

Indeed, if one were to establish the name "causes and conditions" (hetu-pratyaya), one would only capture the distant causes and conditions of past lives while losing the immediate manifestation of reality in the present.

If one were to establish the name "Jewel-Store" (ratna-garbha), one would only capture the immediate manifestation of reality in the present while losing the distant causes and conditions of past lives. It is only because of this subsequent loss [in either case]...
It is near; it is far from the previous destination. Therefore, it is not named after the causal conditions of the former, nor is it named after the treasure-trove of the latter.
If one establishes the metaphor of the "transformed city" (*nirmita-pura*) as being situated between these two, then both the preceding and the succeeding stages can be encompassed;
thus, this alone is chosen as the name. For if one were to establish [the goal] merely as a transformed city, how could there be...?
Regarding this "transformed city," one should know that those of the Two Vehicles once formed great vows in the past;
because they wished to retreat midway, [the Buddha] provisionally manifested a single city as a place of rest. Thus, he secured the prior causes and conditions.
If one speaks of a single transformed city, one knows it is not the true, ultimate destination; one must proceed from the transformed city to reach the Treasure Mountain.
When this [present] stage is the true and ultimate destination, it subsumes the subsequent jewel-treasure destination.
Since both the preceding and the following can be subsumed, the name is specifically designated by means of the parable of the conjured city (nirmita-nagara) explained in the middle section.
Regarding the term "transformed city" (*nirmita-giri*): that which was non-existent and suddenly appears is called "transformed" (*nirmāṇa*);

that which wards off wrongdoing and resists enemies is called a "city" (*pura*). Just as something in the world that originally did not exist may suddenly come to be—this is "transformation"—and just as something in the world can prevent transgressions and resist invaders—this is a "city"—it serves as a direct metaphor for the two vehicles (*dviyāna*).

This Nirvana is fundamentally non-existent; it is established by the Tathāgata through the power of his inconceivable, skillful means for the sake of transforming others, and is therefore called "transformation.

Furthermore, because it can prevent the errors of the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhava-kleśa*), and repel the enemy of birth and death within the realms of segmented existence (*paricchinna-jāti-maraṇa*), it is called a "city.
△ Third, the explanation of the causes and conditions has two parts. First, the formal explanation.
The causal conditions. Second, the bestowal of predictions for those of inferior faculties. This has two parts: first, a brief indication that he clearly knows and perceives the distant past;

second, a detailed exposition of the causal conditions of his previous lives. The first [section] also has two parts: first, the prose; second, the verse. The first [of these] has four parts; the first clarifies the duration of time elapsed.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "In the distant past, immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago.
(2) This explains the Buddhas who existed [at that time].
At that time, there was a Buddha named Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna,
Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.

Regarding the name of the Buddha, Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū: because that Buddha is able to realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), and this wisdom extends horizontally across the entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) without anything it does not encompass, it is called "Great" (*mahā*).
Because it penetrates vertically through the three truths (*tisraḥ satya*) without anything it does not penetrate, it is called "Pervasive" (*abhijñā*).
Because it cannot be reached by any sentient beings of the three vehicles or nine realms, it is called "Victorious" (*abhibhū*).
This refers to "superiority. △ Third, it clarifies the kalpa and the land.
That land is named Good City (Kalyāṇī), and the kalpa is named Great Sign (Mahānimitta).

Regarding the name of that land, Good City: if one merely guards against the errors of *dṛṣṭi-āsrava* and *bhava-āsrava*, and merely wards off the enemies of the *paricchinna-bhava* (the realm of segmented existence).
Then it would not be called a "good city. Only when it can further prevent the transgressions of ignorance and repel the enemy of change is it called a good city.
Since that Buddha has realized the wisdom of great penetration, there is no transgression he does not prevent and no enemy he does not repel;
therefore, his land is named Good City. As for the eon being named Great Sign (Mahānimitta):
The Great Mark is the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). The wisdom of great penetration is the wisdom that is capable of contemplation; the true mark of all phenomena is the object of contemplation.
The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū was able to realize the object of contemplation by means of the wisdom capable of contemplation, thereby attaining Buddhahood;
thus, the Buddha is named Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, and the kalpa is likewise named accordingly.
This is a great sign. △ Fourth, clarifying that it has been a long time since his parinirvāṇa, in four parts. First, the Dharma:
"O bhikṣus, since that Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, a very long and vast period of time has passed."
△ Second, the two similes. First, clarifying the grinding of the earth of the lands.
For example, suppose there were someone who ground all the elements of earth within a trichiliocosm into ink.
Having passed through a thousand lands to the east, he places a single dot, as large as a mote of dust. Having again passed through another thousand lands, he places another dot.
This illustrates the kalpa of the "dot of a mote of dust."
In this manner, they would continue until the entire earth-element were exhausted by the ink. What do you think, monks?
Would a mathematician or a mathematician’s disciple be able to reach the limit of those lands and know their number? "No, World-Honored One. "Monks," [the Buddha said].
If one were to take all the lands this person has passed through—whether marked or unmarked—and grind them all into dust, with each particle of dust representing one kalpa;

[the time since] that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa would exceed even that number by immeasurable, boundless, hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeyas. △ Third, the combination. The time since that Buddha entered parinirvāṇa further exceeds this number, being immeasurable, boundless, and hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeyas.
Asankhyeya kalpas.
△ Fourth, the conclusion:
By means of the power of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, I observe that distant past as if it were today.
Now, this initial clarification of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision—that he is able to perceive the distant past—contains three intentions.
First, since the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision are thus, the accounts of past lives are certainly not false; this will cause those of inferior faculties to believe them upon hearing them.
Second, the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision are able to perceive the distant past, observing us two...
Vehicle. Long ago, even before such eons had passed, he already descended into the Great Element (mahābhūta), yet we still remain in the stage of the Lesser Vehicle (hīnayāna).
This causes those of inferior faculties to give rise to shame and remorse, thereby enabling them to exert themselves and advance.
Third, since the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision are thus, they are not within the reach of the two vehicles; this causes those of inferior faculties to give rise to a thirst [for the Dharma].

Looking up, they shall swiftly attain the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. △ Second, the verses in praise consist of four parts: first, the praise of the Dharma; second, the praise of the parable;
third, the praise of the application; fourth, the praise of the conclusion. The first part [the praise of the Dharma] further consists of two sections. First, the praise of the time elapsed.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"I recall past lives, through immeasurable and boundless kalpas.
(2) Verses on all the Buddhas.
There was a Buddha, the Honored One among Two-legged Beings, named Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū.
II. Verses on the Simile, in two parts. First, the verses on the place where the ground was rubbed and the country:
"Just as a person with great strength rubs the three-thousandfold world system, exhausting all the seeds of the earth therein until they are entirely turned into ink."
Having passed through a thousand lands, one places a single speck of dust. In this manner, proceeding successively, one places all these specks of dust and ink.
△ Second, the verse on the kalpas of wiping away the specks of dust.
In this manner, all these lands—whether marked or unmarked—are further ground entirely into dust. Let each particle of dust represent one kalpa.
[Verse 3, concluding:
The number of these minute particles exceeds even that; since the parinirvāṇa of that Buddha, such immeasurable kalpas have passed.
△ Fourth, the conclusion in four verses:
The Tathāgata’s unimpeded wisdom knows the parinirvāṇa of that Buddha, as well as his śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, as clearly as if seeing their parinirvāṇa occurring this very day.
O bhikṣus, you should know: the Buddha’s wisdom is pure and subtle, untainted and unimpeded, penetrating throughout immeasurable kalpas.

Regarding "the Buddha’s wisdom is pure, subtle, and wondrous": it is called "pure" because there is no delusion that remains unbroken; it is called "wondrous" because there is no virtue that is not manifested;
it is called "subtle" because all sentient beings can fully possess it within even a single fleeting thought-moment.

II. Extensive Explanation of Past Causes and Conditions. This has two parts: first, the prose (long-form); second, the verses (gāthā). The first part [of the prose] has two sections: first, the narrative of the causes and conditions; second, the clarification [of the result].
Establishing a Karmic Connection. Section Three. First, it clarifies the lifespan of that Buddha.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "The lifespan of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū was five hundred and forty million nayuta kalpas."
This means that while the lifespan of that Buddha was so exceedingly long, the present Buddha Śākyamuni has only eighty years.
Regarding the lifespan of a Buddha, there is fundamentally no such thing as long or short; it depends solely on whether there are sentient beings with the capacity [to receive the teaching].
If there is such capacity, the lifespan is extended to be long; if there is no such capacity, it is shortened to be brief. △ Second, clarifying that Buddha.
The fifth section concerns the attainment of enlightenment. First, it clarifies the period when he was about to attain but had not yet attained it.
That Buddha sat at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and, having already defeated the armies of Māra, was on the verge of attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Yet, the dharmas of the Buddhas did not manifest before him. This continued for one intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*), and even up to ten intermediate kalpas. [End of] the summary.
He sat in the full lotus posture, his body and mind unmoving; yet the teachings of all Buddhas still did not appear before him.

As for the phrase "originally sitting at the site of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*): "originally" (*ben*) refers to the past, as well as the primordial beginning. "About to attain" means he was on the verge of attaining it.
Regarding the statement that the Buddha-dharma did not manifest before him, this does not mean that there were delusions not yet destroyed, nor that there was any principle [not yet realized].
That which has not yet been manifested is simply because the capacity [of the beings] is not yet mature and the time has not yet arrived; therefore, it is said that it does not appear before them.

When the time for the Buddha-dharma to manifest arrives, one must inevitably preach the Dharma. Now, as the capacity is still immature and the time has not yet arrived, it is still not possible to preach the Dharma;
hence it is said that the Buddha-dharma has not yet appeared before them. △ Second, explaining the offerings of the various devas.
There were four acts of service. First, the Trāyastriṃśa gods prepared a seat.
At that time, the various devas of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven first prepared for that Buddha, beneath the Bodhi tree, a lion throne one yojana in height.
It was upon this that the Buddha sat when he was to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"When the Buddha shall attain Bodhi while seated here"—this is the mantra of aspiration uttered within the hearts of the devas when they spread the seat.
△ Second, the Brahma King rains down flowers.
Just as he sat upon this seat, the Brahma Kings rained down various celestial flowers over an area of one hundred yojanas.

Fragrant breezes blew from time to time, sweeping away the withered blossoms and raining down fresh ones in their place. In this manner, they offered worship to the Buddha without ceasing for ten minor kalpas, continuing to rain down these flowers until his parinirvāṇa.
Regarding "just as he sat": after the various devas had spread out the seat, the Buddha sat upon it neither too early nor too late; hence it is said "just as.

As for the statement that "he constantly rains down these flowers until his parinirvāṇa," this means that the Brahma King did not only rain down these flowers as an offering at the time when [the Buddha's] desire was being fulfilled or not yet fulfilled;
rather, from that unfulfilled state until the turning of the wheel of Dharma and the attainment of the Way, [he continued to do so].
From the turning of the Wheel of Dharma until his entry into nirvana, these flowers shall constantly rain down as an offering. △ Third and fourth:
The Four Heavenly Kings beat their drums;
the gods of the Four Heavenly Kings constantly strike celestial drums as an offering to the Buddha.

Regarding the striking of the drums: this signifies that at the time of that Buddha’s attainment of enlightenment, he acted as a friend who does not need to be requested, preaching spontaneously without being asked. △ Fourth, the various devas perform music.
The remaining devas performed celestial music for ten small kalpas until his parinirvāṇa; it was likewise so for all others.
△ Third, the true accomplishment of the Buddha-way.
"O bhikṣus, after ten intermediate kalpas had passed, the Dharma of all Buddhas appeared before the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū,
and he attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
△ Fourth, the offering of the retinue.
Before that Buddha had left the household life, he had sixteen sons. The eldest was named Zhijí (Jñānakūṭa).
Each of the sons possessed various kinds of rare and exquisite playthings. Hearing that their father had attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*...
The three who were to attain *sambodhi* all renounced their most cherished possessions and went to where the Buddha was. Their mothers wept as they followed and escorted them.

Their grandfather, the Wheel-Turning Sage King, together with one hundred ministers and the rest of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of people, all surrounded them and followed them to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), desiring to draw near to the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū and to offer him worship and respect.
He paid respect and offered praise. Having arrived, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and circumambulated him.
With single-minded devotion, he joined his palms. His father was named Jñānavijaya, and the son was named Jñānakūṭa;

although one was in the state of fruition and the other in the state of cause, such that cause and effect were distinct, the father and son were designated by names that corresponded to one another. Thus, the father—
His name was Jñānavijaya, and his son was named Jñānakoṣa. As for the weeping mothers, these were the wives of the Buddha Jñānavijaya.
When their husband went forth [into the religious life], they followed their son; now that the son has also gone forth, they have lost the one they could follow, and thus they weep.
Those who accompanied and saw him off did so for two reasons: first, because they were able to see him off...

My son, the first reason is that he has been able to behold his Buddha. His grandfather, the Wheel-Turning Sage King, was the father of the Buddha Jñānavijaya, yet he too prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet.
This is because a father can only give birth to a child’s physical body (janma-kāya).
Now that you have attained Buddhahood, you are able to preach the Dharma for your father.
A birth-body (janman-kāya) exists for but a single lifetime, whereas a dharma-body (dharma-kāya) extends through eternal kalpas.

When comparing the birth-body to the dharma-body, or a single lifetime to eternal kalpas, it would not be an error for the father to pay homage to the son. However, if one cannot be like the Buddha Jñānavijaya...
If one wishes to receive the father’s ritual honors, it is not yet known whether this may be done. △ Fifth, the fourfold verse summary on the retinue.
First, the general summary.
Gazing up at the World-Honored One, they spoke in verse, saying:
O World-Honored One of Great Majestic Virtue, for the sake of delivering sentient beings, you attained Buddhahood only after immeasurable billions of years.
All your vows are now fully perfected; how excellent, how auspicious, and unsurpassed!

The following three lines are for the purpose of delivering sentient beings; thus, one knows that the Buddha-dharma does not manifest for its own sake, but is fundamentally for the sake of sentient beings and has no concern with the Buddha himself.
"All vows fulfilled" refers to the four great vows, which have already been brought to completion.
△ Second, the specific verses.
The World-Honored One is most rare and marvelous: seated for ten minor kalpas, his body, hands, and feet remain tranquil, peaceful, and unmoving;
his mind is ever serene and calm, never once distracted.

This verse concerns whether [the practice] has been accomplished or not yet accomplished. Regarding the phrase "tranquil and unmoving," it means that by using the mind of the *dharmadhātu* to contemplate the principle of the *dharmadhātu*, once both the contemplator and the object of contemplation are realized as being the same *dharmadhātu*, the essence of the *dharmadhātu* is inherently quiescent.
How could there be any wavering or distraction? Thus, one knows that while sitting in a single posture—
For ten kalpas, and so forth, it is said that he was never distracted. △ Third, rejoicing in good fortune:
"Having attained ultimate and eternal nirvana and dwelling securely in the untainted Dharma, I now behold the World-Honored One, who has safely realized the Way of the Buddha."
We have attained a great benefit; we celebrate with immense joy. Sentient beings are constantly afflicted by suffering; blind and ignorant, they lack a guide.
They do not recognize the path that exhausts suffering, nor do they know how to seek liberation. Through the long night, the evil realms increase while the hosts of devas diminish.
"From darkness entering into darkness, one shall never hear the name of the Buddha.
This verse refers precisely to the realization of the Buddha-way. Regarding the phrase "ultimate and eternal quiescence": when no principle remains unmanifested, it is called "quiescence" (śānti);
when no obstruction remains unbroken, it is called "cessation" (nirodha). To be unmoved by the two extremes is called "peace" (kṣema); to not fall into the two extremes is [the state of] non-duality.
It is said: "Abiding. This means that regarding the principle of the Three Truths, there is not the slightest lapse; thus it is called the "outflow-free dharma" (*anāsrava-dharma*).
"Our inferior [state]" refers to the benefits following the attainment of the Way. "Obtaining good benefit" clearly elucidates the benefiting of sentient beings.
"Celebration" refers to rejoicing that the Buddha has attained the Way. "Joy" refers to having already beheld the Buddha. "Constant suffering and affliction" [refers to the state prior to this].
The phrase "and so forth" raises the fault of there being no Buddha in order to manifest the merit of there being one.
"Constantly suffering and distressed" refers to not knowing the Truth of Suffering; thus, there is only suffering, but no Truth. Suffering must have a source; if one encounters a Teacher...
Thus one knows the root of suffering and does not create its causes. To be blind and ignorant without a guide is to not know the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).

Not recognizing the path to the exhaustion of suffering is to not know the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*). Not knowing how to seek liberation is to not know the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
As the Great Sūtra says: "Because they do not know the Four Noble Truths, they have wandered for a long time. Now that this is no longer so...

Because they did not know the Four Noble Truths, they increased their rebirths in the evil realms throughout the long night, until they did not even hear the name of the Buddha. △ Fourth, the conclusion of the intent:
Now that the Buddha has attained the supreme, peaceful, and untainted path, we and the devas have obtained the greatest benefit.
Therefore, they all prostrate themselves and take refuge in the Unsurpassed Honored One.
△ Third, explaining that Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma, in two parts: first, requesting the teaching of various doctrines; second, requesting the preaching of the Lotus Sutra.
The first part has three sections; the first is the request by the prince.
At that time, after the sixteen princes had praised the Buddha with verses, they entreated the World-Honored One to turn the wheel of Dharma, all saying:
"May the World-Honored One preach the Dharma; it will bring great peace and security, out of compassion to benefit the devas and humans.
They spoke further in verse:
O Hero of the World, peerless and unequaled, adorned by a hundred merits, having attained supreme wisdom, we pray that you will expound it for the sake of the world.
Deliver us and all classes of sentient beings; explain and reveal it in detail so that they may attain this wisdom.
If we were to attain Buddhahood, so too would all sentient beings. The World-Honored One knows the thoughts within the deep minds of sentient beings;
he also knows the paths they travel, as well as their power of wisdom, their aspirations, and their cultivation of merit, along with the karmic deeds performed in their past lives.
The World-Honored One, having fully known all this, shall turn the unsurpassed wheel.

Regarding the phrase "the World-Honored One’s teaching of the Dharma": when the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma, he is able to cause sentient beings to shatter their afflictions and emerge from birth-and-death;

therefore, it is said that it brings great peace and security. "Compassion" (anukampā) has the meaning of loving-kindness and pity; pity uproots suffering, such that there is no suffering left unremoved.

To uproot [suffering] and bestow compassion and happiness—there is no happiness that is not bestowed. To cause sentient beings to attain inexhaustible abundance and benefit is what is meant by "compassionate and beneficial.
Regarding the phrase in the verse, "May [he] act for the sake of the world," etc.:

as for being adorned by a hundred blessings, the Tathāgata’s merit is already sufficient; as for attaining unsurpassed wisdom, the Tathāgata’s insight is already perfected. From [this point] onward...
Having already realized it oneself, one must still transform others; therefore, I pray that you will expound it for the sake of the world.
As for the phrase "to deliver us," it means that we and the Tathāgata share a common nature; thus, it is appropriate that he preach the Dharma to deliver us.
All other sentient beings should likewise be delivered. To distinguish and reveal this so that they may attain such wisdom—this is what is meant.

That is to say, first one employs the three vehicles to provide differentiation, and subsequently employs the single reality to provide revelation, ultimately enabling all sentient beings to attain the unsurpassed wisdom of the Tathāgata; it is not merely a matter of knowing what the mind thinks.
He also knows the conduct of the body. Furthermore, "knowing equally" refers to the merit and wisdom of the present life;
"the phrase of past lives" refers to the karmic actions of the past. There is nothing he does not know. Therefore, it is said above that the World-Honored One knows sentient beings.
The text below states, "The World-Honored One, having fully known [it]. This means he has already understood the capacities [of the beings].

Since he knows their capacities, it is appropriate that he should preach the teaching in accordance with those capacities, employing the teaching to meet those capacities; hence it says, "He shall turn the unsurpassed wheel.
Part Two: The Request of the Devas. Section One: The Tathāgata Manifests Auspicious Signs.

The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "When the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, five million koṭis of Buddha-worlds in each of the ten directions shook in six ways; and in the spaces between those lands,"
In those dark and hidden places where the majestic radiance of the sun and moon cannot reach, all became brilliantly illuminated.
The sentient beings therein were each able to see one another, and they all spoke these words: "How is it that sentient beings have suddenly appeared here? Furthermore, as for that realm:
The palaces of the various devas, up to the Brahma-palaces, shook in six ways; a great light shone everywhere, filling the world and surpassing the radiance of all the devas.

△ Second, the formal invitation by the various devas. This has two parts: first, clarifying the invitations from the nine directions; second, clarifying the invitation from the zenith. Regarding the first [of these], there are four sections:
first, the actual clarification of the eastern direction; second, the southeastern direction; third, again the southern direction; fourth, a brief illustration of the six directions.
Regarding the first of these seven [sections], there is the initial observation of signs.
At that time, within five hundred trillion lands in the eastern direction, the palaces of the Brahma heavens were illuminated by a radiance twice as bright as their usual light.
△ Second, the reflection of doubt.
The various Brahma kings each had this thought: "The radiance of our palaces today is such as has never been seen before.
By what causes and conditions does this sign appear?"
△ Third, the Council.
At that time, the Brahma Kings each went to one another and deliberated together on this matter.
Then, among that assembly, there was a Great Brahma King named Sarvaparitrāṇa (Savior of All), who spoke these verses for the sake of the Brahma host:
"In all our palaces, there is a radiance such as has never been seen before. What is the cause and condition for this? We should each seek it together:
Is a Great Virtuous Being born, or has a Buddha appeared in the world? For this great radiance shines everywhere throughout the ten directions."

The Brahma King is named "Savior of All. He does so by means of the discourse on transcending desire, thereby saving all sentient beings of the desire realm, causing them to leave behind the suffering of the five desires and attain the bliss of meditative concentration. △ Fourth, the investigation.
At that time, the Brahma Kings of five million billion lands, together with their palaces,

each took celestial flowers in the folds of their robes and traveled collectively toward the west to investigate the cause of these signs. There they beheld the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū at the site of enlightenment,
beneath the Bodhi tree, seated upon a lion throne, surrounded by devas, nāga kings, gandharvas, and kiṃnaras.
Gandharvas, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others respectfully surrounded him; they also saw the sixteen princes requesting the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma.
△ Fifth, the Offerings.
At that moment, the Brahma Kings prostrated themselves with their heads at the Buddha’s feet and circumambulated him a hundred thousand times. They then scattered celestial flowers over the Buddha;
the flowers thus scattered were as vast as Mount Sumeru. Furthermore, they used them to make offerings to the Bodhi tree. Its Bodhi...
The *tāla* trees were ten *yojanas* high. Having made offerings of flowers, each [Brahmā] presented his own palace to that Buddha and spoke these words:
"May you look upon us with compassion; for our benefit, we pray that you graciously accept and dwell in these offered palaces.
Then, before the Buddha, all the Brahmā kings, with single-minded devotion and in unison, spoke in verse:
The World-Honored One is most rare and difficult to encounter. Possessing immeasurable merit, he is able to rescue and protect all.
The Great Teacher of gods and humans takes pity upon the world; all sentient beings throughout the ten directions universally receive his benefit and grace.
We have come from five hundred million billion lands, having relinquished the bliss of profound meditative concentration for the sake of making offerings to the Buddha.
By virtue of our merit in previous lives, our palaces were most exquisitely adorned; we now offer them to the World-Honored One. We only pray that you will compassionately accept them.
"Scattering flowers as high as Mount Sumeru" does not mean that the flowers are as large as that mountain.
Rather, Mount Sumeru is formed by the accumulation of earth; here, it refers to the mass of scattered flowers piled up like a mountain. This also includes the offering trees.
The Buddha attained perfect enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree; thus, the Buddha is the subject of reliance (*āśrayin*) and the tree is the object of reliance (*āśraya*).
Because one honors the subject and, by extension, the object, both are offered together as an act of worship. As for the offering of palaces to the Buddha:
since all the palaces belonging to the various devas follow them wherever they go, they are able to be offered; these, however, are the fruits of contaminated merit (*sāsrava-puṇya*).
I am moved. Now, desiring to transform this into the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) of a Tathāgata, I offer it to the Buddha.

In the verse, the first two lines are a formal praise; "to rescue and protect all" means that great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) uproots suffering as "rescue," while great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) bestows happiness as "protection.
The subsequent line, beginning with "we," expresses the intent: having come from afar and abandoned [all else], [I now offer this].

The depth of this [practice] lies in its purpose of making offerings to the Buddha. To speak of "profound meditative concentration" (samādhi) is to contrast it with the desire for sensory dispersion as being profound.
The single line beginning with "Third, we... is an exhortation to accept and receive [the teaching]. △ Sixth, the request for exposition.
At that time, after the Brahma Kings had praised the Buddha with verses, each of them spoke these words:
"We pray only that the World-Honored One will turn the wheel of Dharma, deliver sentient beings, and open the path to Nirvana. Then the Brahma Kings, with one mind and in unison, spoke this verse:
"O Hero of the World, Honored One among the Two-legged, we only pray that you will expound the Dharma; by the power of your great compassion, deliver all suffering sentient beings.
△ Seventh, the silent assent:
At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū silently granted his permission.
Because the time had not yet arrived, I remained silent and merely granted permission to his request.
△ Second, clarifying the six [points] of the southeast direction; first, observing the signs.

Furthermore, monks, in five million billion lands to the southeast, the Great Brahma Kings each saw their own palaces illuminated by a radiance such as they had never experienced before; filled with joy and leaping for gladness, they conceived a sense of wonder.
△ Second, the deliberation.

They each went to one another’s abode to discuss this matter together. At that time, within that assembly, there was a Great Brahmā King named Mahākāruṇika (Great Compassion), who spoke these verses for the sake of the host of Brahmās:
What is the cause and condition for such a sign to appear? Within all our palaces, there is a radiance never seen before.
Is it because a Great Virtuous One has been born, or is it because a Buddha has appeared in the world? We have never witnessed such a sign; let us seek its cause with a single mind.

Passing through thousands of myriads of koṭis of lands, they followed the light together to investigate it. This was likely because a Buddha had appeared in the world to deliver sentient beings from suffering.

There was a Brahmā King named Mahākāruṇika (Great Compassion), who was able to preach discourses on transcending desire, thereby uprooting the suffering of all sentient beings within the realm of desire. △ Third, the investigation.
At that time, five million billion Brahma kings, together with their palaces,

each took celestial flowers in the folds of their robes and went collectively toward the northwest to investigate the cause of these signs. There they saw the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū at the site of enlightenment,
beneath the Bodhi tree, seated upon a lion throne, surrounded by devas, nāga kings, gandharvas, and kiṃnaras.
The mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others respectfully surrounded him; they also saw the sixteen princes requesting the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma.
△ Fourth, the offerings.
Then the Brahma kings prostrated themselves with their heads at the Buddha’s feet and circumambulated him a hundred thousand times.
They immediately scattered celestial flowers over the Buddha until the scattered blossoms were as high as Mount Sumeru; they also used them to make offerings to the Buddha’s Bodhi tree.
Having completed the floral offerings, each offered his own palace to the Buddha and spoke these words: "May you look upon us with compassion and bring us benefit."
"May you graciously accept these palaces we have offered. At that time, the Brahma Kings, before the Buddha, with single-minded devotion and in unison, spoke in verse:
We now pay homage to the Holy Lord, King of Devas, whose voice is like that of the kalaviṅka bird, who has compassion for all sentient beings.
The World-Honored One is most rare; he appears but once in a vast expanse of time. For one hundred and eighty kalpas, the ages passed empty, without a Buddha.
The three evil realms are filled, and the hosts of devas are diminishing. Now a Buddha has appeared in the world, acting as the eye for sentient beings;
he is the refuge for the world, the protector of all, the father of sentient beings, who brings compassion and benefit.
"It is due to the auspicious merit of our past lives that we have now encountered the World-Honored One.
△ 5. Requesting the Teaching:
At that time, after the Brahma Kings had praised the Buddha with verses, they each spoke these words: "We only pray that the World-Honored One will take pity on us..."
"Everyone! Turn the wheel of Dharma and deliver all sentient beings. At that time, the Brahma Kings, with one mind and in unison, spoke these verses:
"The Great Sage turns the wheel of Dharma, Revealing the characteristics of all phenomena; He delivers suffering and distressed sentient beings, Causing them to attain great joy."
When sentient beings hear this Dharma, they attain the Path or are reborn in the heavens; the various evil realms diminish, while those who practice patience and goodness increase.
That which reveals the characteristics of all phenomena is expounded from within the single characteristic—namely, that all phenomena are either empty, existent, or the Middle Way.
As for the statement "they attain the Path or are reborn in the heavens," it means that some may attain the path to Nirvana.
...or those who have merely attained birth in the heavenly realms. △ Sixth, the silent assent:
At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū silently granted his permission.

The Explication of the Lotus Sutra, Scroll Three, Part Three.
