△ Third, the actual clarification of the Southern [School], Part Six: First, beholding the signs.

Furthermore, monks, in five million billion lands to the south, the Great Brahma Kings each saw their own palaces illuminated by a radiance such as they had never experienced before; filled with joy and leaping for gladness, they conceived a sense of wonder.
△ Second, the deliberation:
they each went to one another’s place and discussed this matter together: "By what cause and condition do our palaces possess such radiance?"
Now, within that assembly, there was a Great Brahmā King named Subhadharma, who spoke these verses for the sake of the Brahmā hosts:
"The radiance of our various palaces is most majestic and brilliant; this cannot be without cause or condition—we should seek the reason for this sign."
For more than hundreds of thousands of kalpas, such a sign has never been seen before. Is it because a Great Virtuous Deva has been born, or because a Buddha has appeared in the world?
As for the Brahma King named *Sudharma*, he too merely points to the discourse on desire;

he is called "Sudharma" because he can expound upon the dharmas of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and so forth as the "Sublime Dharma" (*saddharma*), thereby transforming and dispersing sentient beings who are attached to desire. It is for this reason that he bears this name.
△ Third, the investigation.

At that time, five million *koṭis* of Brahma kings, together with their palaces, each took celestial flowers in the folds of their robes and went collectively toward the north to investigate this sign.
There they saw the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū dwelling at the site of enlightenment.
At that place, beneath the Bodhi tree, he sat upon the lion throne, surrounded by and revered by devas, nāga kings, gandharvas, kiṃnaras,
mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others; and they also saw the sixteen princes requesting the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma.
△ Fourth, the offering.

At that time, the Brahma Heavenly Kings prostrated themselves with their heads at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him a hundred thousand times, and immediately scattered celestial flowers over the Buddha.
The flowers thus scattered were like Mount Sumeru; they also used them to make offerings to the Buddha’s Bodhi tree. This was the offering of flowers.
Having done so, each offered their own palace to that Buddha and spoke these words: "May you look upon us with compassion and benefit us;
we pray that you graciously accept these palaces we have offered. Then, before the Buddha, all the Brahma kings, with one mind and in unison, spoke in verse:

The World-Honored One is exceedingly difficult to behold; he who has shattered all afflictions has not been seen for more than one hundred and thirty kalpas, until now we have finally obtained a single vision.
He fills all hungry and thirsty sentient beings with the rain of Dharma—this one of immeasurable wisdom has never before been witnessed.
Like the udumbara flower, which is encountered only today; our various palaces have been adorned by the grace of this light.
O World-Honored One, out of great compassion and pity, we pray that you will graciously accept them.
△ 5. Requesting the Teaching.
At that time, after the Brahma Kings had praised the Buddha with verses, each of them spoke these words:
"We pray only that the World-Honored One will turn the wheel of Dharma, so that all in the world—gods, Māras, Brahmas, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas—may all attain peace and security."
And thus they attain liberation. Then the Brahma kings, with one mind and in a single voice, spoke in verse:
"We pray that the Honored One among gods and humans will turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma; beat the great drum of the Dharma and blow the great conch of the Dharma."
May you universally rain down the great Dharma-rain and deliver immeasurable sentient beings. We all entreat you: please manifest your profound and far-reaching voice.
As for those gods, asuras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas who have attained peace and security—the gods are addicted to the five desires and thus lack peace;
Māra constantly seeks to afflict others and thus lacks peace; and although Brahmā has attained [his realm]...

Meditation is still subject to outflows (āsrava) and is therefore not peaceful. Although the śramaṇa practices according to the teachings, he remains at the stage of the cause and has not yet attained the realization of the fruit; thus, he too is not at peace. The brāhmaṇa, moreover, cultivates false dharmas.
When the mind wanders beyond the principles [of reality], it is not at peace. If the Wheel of Dharma is turned, then the gods of today will no longer be addicted to the five desires;
Māra will no longer afflict humanity; the Brahmās will turn away from outflows (āsrava) and achieve the state of being without outflows;
śramaṇas will attain realization of the fruits [of the path]; and brāhmaṇas will be transformed and enter into the correct [path]. Thus, all shall be at peace. And...
It means to deliver and liberate. In the subsequent verse, "turning the wheel of Dharma" means being able to crush and grind away all delusions;
"beating the drum of Dharma" means being able to cause all beings to be startled into awakening; and "blowing the conch of Dharma" means being able to cause all beings to... [attain realization].
To change the small and return to the great; to change the partial and return to the perfect.
To rain down the Dharma-rain is to enable all withered beings to attain moisture, and all who are hungry and thirsty to attain fullness. △ Six:
Silent Approval.
At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū silently granted his consent.
△ Fourth, a brief illustration for the six directions:
from the southwest down to the nadir, it was likewise so.
△ Second, the invitation from the zenith, in five parts. First, the observation of signs:

At that time, in five million billion lands above, all the Great Brahma Kings beheld their respective palaces, which were illuminated with a majestic radiance such as had never existed before. They leaped for joy and gave rise to a sense of rare wonder.
△ Second, the deliberation:
they each went to one another’s place and discussed this matter together: "By what cause and condition does our palaces possess such radiance?"
At that time, within that assembly, there was a Great Brahmā King named Śikhin, who spoke these verses for the sake of the Brahmā hosts:
"By what causes and conditions now do our various palaces possess such majestic virtue and radiant light, adorned in a manner never before seen?"
Such wondrous marks as these had never before been heard of or seen. "Is this for the birth of a Great Virtuous Heaven, or is it for a Buddha appearing in the world?
△ Third, the investigation:
At that time, five million billion Brahma Kings, together with their palaces, each took a lap-satchel and filled it with...
The celestial flowers, together with [the assembly], proceeded to the lower direction to investigate this sign.
There they saw the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū at the site of enlightenment, beneath the Bodhi tree, seated upon a lion throne.

He was surrounded by and venerated by devas, nāga kings, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, as well as the sixteen princes who were entreating the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma.
The Wheel of Dharma.
△ Fourth, the offerings:
At that time, the Brahma Kings prostrated themselves before the Buddha, circumambulated him a hundred thousand times, and immediately scattered celestial flowers over the Buddha.
The flowers they scattered were like Mount Sumeru, which they offered together to the Buddha’s Bodhi tree.
Having made this floral offering, each presented their own palace to that Buddha, saying: "We pray you will look upon us with compassion and benefit us;
we offer these palaces and entreat you to graciously accept them. Then, before the Buddha, all the Brahma Kings focused their minds with single-minded devotion.
In unison, they praised him with these verses:
"Excellent is the sight of all Buddhas, the Holy Honored Ones who save the world; you are able to urge all sentient beings out from the prison of the triple realm."
The Honored One of Universal Wisdom, Sovereign of Gods and Humans, out of compassion for all classes of sentient beings, is able to open the gate of ambrosia and extensively deliver all.
Throughout immeasurable kalpas in the past, time passed in vain without a Buddha; when the World-Honored One had not yet appeared, the ten directions were perpetually shrouded in darkness.
The three evil realms increase, and the asuras also flourish; the hosts of devas steadily diminish. Many die and fall into the evil realms;
they do not hear the Dharma from the Buddha and constantly perform unwholesome deeds. Their physical strength, vitality, and wisdom—all these decrease.
Due to the causes and conditions of sinful karma, they lose both happiness and the perception of happiness; abiding in the dharma of false views, they do not recognize virtuous conduct.
They fail to receive the Buddha’s transformation and constantly fall into the evil realms. The Buddha is the eye of the world, appearing only after a vast and long period of time.
Out of compassion for all sentient beings, you have appeared in the world; having transcended it, you have attained perfect enlightenment.
We are filled with great joy, as are all other beings, who marvel at this unprecedented event. Our various palaces have been magnificently adorned by the light of your presence.
I now offer this to the World-Honored One; I pray that you will compassionately accept it. By means of this merit, may it extend universally to all.
May we and all sentient beings together attain the Way of the Buddha.
The statement that those who die will mostly fall into the evil realms refers specifically to the various classes of devas. Because they do not hear the Dharma, their wisdom diminishes;
because they engage in unwholesome deeds, a hundred anxieties crowd their minds and ten thousand worldly affairs exhaust their bodies, and thus their physical strength and vitality decline.
"Losing happiness" means losing the happiness of the mundane world of humans and devas, as well as supramundane [happiness].
This refers to the forgetting of the bliss of nirvana. As for those who lose the perception of bliss:

because the causes and conditions of their karmic offenses are heavy, they not only lose the bliss itself, but even the very perception of bliss is lost. They are unable to contemplate the bliss of the human or celestial realms, nor the bliss of nirvana;
instead, they experience only the suffering of the three miserable destinies and the perception of suffering. "Emerging once after a vast period" means:

Regarding the various Brahmās who generally speak of having passed through many kalpas without seeing a Buddha and so forth, this refers to the number of kalpas that have already elapsed since their birth in heaven during which they have never seen a Buddha;
it does not necessarily require one to determine exactly which specific kalpa they were in or when they reached a particular kalpa devoid of a Buddha. △ Fifth: Requesting the Teaching.
At that time, five million billion Brahma kings, having praised the Buddha with verses, each addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We pray only that the World-Honored One will turn the wheel of Dharma, bringing peace and security to many, and delivering and liberating many.
Then the Brahma kings spoke these verses:
The World-Honored One turns the wheel of Dharma, beats the drum of the nectar-like Dharma, delivers suffering sentient beings, and reveals the path to nirvāṇa.
I pray only that you will accept my invitation and, with your great and subtle voice, compassionately expound the Dharma practiced throughout immeasurable kalpas.
Among these various devas and Brahmā kings who requested that he preach, those from the east would necessarily reach the west, and so on up to those from above who would necessarily reach below.
For when a Buddha appears in the world, he invariably descends from the central day of the central month into the central land and dwells therein upon the Middle Way;
therefore, when the Brahmās of the ten directions desire to see the Buddha, they all respectfully hasten toward the Middle Way. Thus...
This is truly seeing the Buddha. △ Third, the Tathāgata accepts the three [invitations]. First, accepting the invitation:
At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū accepted the invitation of the Brahma Kings of the ten directions and the sixteen princes.
△ Second, the actual turning [of the wheel]. This consists of two parts. First, the turning of the Four Noble Truths:
at that very moment, he turned the Wheel of Dharma with its three revolutions and twelve aspects—a wheel that no ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world could turn.
That is to say: "This is suffering; this is the origin of suffering; this is the cessation of suffering; this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering."

These Four Noble Truths are a concise explanation of the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), while the subsequent [section on] the twelve links of dependent origination is an extensive explanation of the Four Noble Truths.
The meaning is as detailed in the commentary (etc.). △ Second, the turning of dependent origination.

And he extensively expounded the Dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination: ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form;

name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions clinging; clinging conditions existence.

With birth as condition, there is aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair. With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases;
with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases;
with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, becoming ceases.
Cessation. With the cessation of existence, birth ceases. With the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction cease.
△ Third, the attainment of benefit:
When the Buddha preached this Dharma amidst the great assembly of devas and humans, six hundred trillion nayutas of people—
Because they did not grasp at any phenomena, their minds were liberated from all outflows (*āsrava*).
They all attained profound and wondrous meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the three knowledges (*vidyā*), the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*).

During the second, third, and fourth preachings of the Dharma, likewise, hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *nāyuta* of sentient beings, equal to the sands of the Ganges River, also—because they did not grasp at any phenomena—[were liberated] from...
Their minds were liberated from all outflows (*āsrava*). From that time forward, the assembly of *śrāvakas* became immeasurable, boundless, and beyond counting.
Those who speak of not receiving any phenomena are those who have already known suffering and have already abandoned its origin; they have attained liberation from all outflows.
Liberation means that one has already cultivated the Path and has already realized Cessation. △ Second, the request to preach the Lotus Sutra, in four parts.
First, the princes renounce the world:
At that time, the sixteen princes all renounced the world as youths and became śrāmaṇeras; their faculties were sharp and keen.
Possessing clear and penetrating wisdom, they have already made offerings to hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas, purely cultivated the Brahma-faring,
and sought anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Why did the sixteen princes renounce the world at that very moment? Because they had previously heard that their father had attained *bodhi*, they immediately abandoned all their treasures and went to the Buddha’s presence to request him to turn the wheel of Dharma.
Now, that Buddha has already taught them the Dharma of the Four Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, and they have thereby come to understand it. If it were not so...

To leave the household life means there is no other way to enter the Path; therefore, one leaves the household life. As for the phrase "the youth leaves the household life," it refers to entering the Path in the state of a *kumāra* (a youth).

To become a *śrāmaṇera*—the Sanskrit term *śrāmaṇera* is translated here as "ceasing [evil] and practicing kindness" (*xīcí*)—means to cease all evil and practice compassion; such a person is a disciple of the Buddha and is thus called a *śrāmaṇera*. However...
There are three distinct types. First is the "crow-chaser," referring to a śrāmaṇera of five or six years of age who does not understand what the Buddha has taught;

he may only be tasked with driving away crows. Second is the "nominal" [śrāmaṇera], referring to a śrāmaṇera of twelve, thirteen, or fourteen years of age who, although able to shave his head, is still unable to dye his robes and practice the teachings.
Dharma. However, he is merely a śrāmaṇera by name. Third is the "one who accords with the Dharma" (yogya-dharma).
This refers to a śrāmaṇera over twenty years of age who is already able to understand all the teachings of the Tathāgata and practices them accordingly.
By diligently upholding the ten precepts without contradicting the Dharma, he is in accord with the Dharma; therefore, he is called "one who accords with the Dharma. Of the aforementioned...
There are two kinds: the first is called "identity of form," and the latter is called "identity of dharma.

One should know that there are many types of śrāmaṇeras and they cannot be categorized as one. Now, these sixteen princes have already understood what the Buddha taught and have left the household life;
thus, although they are children, they are śrāmaṇeras who act in accordance with the Dharma. Their faculties are fully developed.

As for "sharpness": because one is able to see forms without being turned by forms, and so on up to perceiving mental phenomena (*dharma*) without being turned by phenomena, all six sense faculties are thus thoroughly penetrating and keen. Regarding "clarity of wisdom":
it should be known that having heard the Dharma spoken by that Buddha, one immediately gives rise to [realization] based on what was heard.
Wisdom is further able to illuminate objects through wisdom. Thus, the object is suchness and wisdom is suchness; wisdom is suchness and the object is suchness.
Object and wisdom are one as suchness; object and wisdom are non-dual. Therefore, all the wisdom he possesses is luminous and clear.
This clarifies the excellence of his present causes; what follows clarifies the excellence of his past seeds. Regarding the statement "purely cultivating the brahma-faring":
although the brahma-faring is manifold, it is not beyond the six perfections. He is able to realize that there is no gift to be practiced.

Yet this does not hinder one from practicing *dāna* all day long; even to the point of realizing that there is no *prajñā* to be practiced, one does not cease from practicing *prajñā* all day long—this is what is called "pure cultivation of the holy life" (*brahmacarya*).
For one who seeks *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, it is precisely because their present causes are superior and their past seeds are strong that what they seek within their minds...
They seek the three realms of existence; they do not seek the two vehicles, but seek only the path of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. △ Second, the formal request for the teaching of the Dharma:
They all addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, these immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of great virtuous śrāvakas have all already attained [their respective stages]."
It would be well, World-Honored One; you should also preach the Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi for us.

Having heard it, we shall all practice and study it together. World-Honored One, our aspirations, the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, and what is contemplated in our deep hearts—may the Buddha himself bear witness to this.

"Those śrāvakas who have all attained accomplishment" refers to those śrāvakas who, having heard the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination taught by the Tathāgata, were able to know suffering, abandon its origin, cultivate the path, and realize cessation.
Thus, their holy life was established, what was to be done had been accomplished, and they are therefore said to be "accomplished. "The World-Honored One should likewise act for me and others," etc.
That is to say, regarding the śrāvakas, once they have already attained accomplishment, it is appropriate to open up the three for them and reveal the one;
to open up the provisional and reveal the real. It is certainly proper that the Dharma of Bodhi be taught to them.
It is likewise appropriate for those of us who have not yet attained accomplishment. Therefore, it is said: "It should also be taught to us. Having heard this, we...

"Below" clarifies the meaning of what is "appropriate. This means that having heard [the teaching], one is able to practice it, and because it accords with the profound mind and original vows, it is what is appropriate.
The statement, "Having heard it, we all together shall practice and study," means that if the Tathāgata had not spoken, it would have been as it were;
but since he has spoken for our sake, we are not like other beings—such as devas and humans—who are struck by alarm and doubt. It is not so for us.
Those with overweening pride do not believe; yet they are able to practice according to what they have heard. Why is this?
It is because there is nothing distinct from what the Tathāgata has spoken that he speaks; rather, he speaks of that which we ourselves cultivate.
And if that which we cultivate is likewise nothing distinct from it, then one cultivates precisely what the Tathāgata has spoken. Therefore, if the Tathāgata were to deliver a single discourse...
At this time, we are all able to practice and study together. If what the Tathāgata speaks were something we could not practice and study, then the Tathāgata ought not to have spoken it for us.
Since we are now all able to practice and study, the World-Honored One should likewise speak it for us.
That the World-Honored One is "equal" means that it is not only I [who am so].
Because we shall practice and study together with him, this must now be explained. That is to say, our aspiration lies solely in the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision;
this is what we deeply contemplate in our hearts, and the Tathāgata will surely personally bear witness to and understand it.
Since the Tathāgata has witnessed and known that our aspiration lies solely in the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, then furthermore—
"You should also preach the Dharma of unsurpassed bodhi for us. Why? Even if one lacks the aspiration, it is still appropriate to practice and study;
likewise, even if one cannot practice and study, it is still appropriate to have the aspiration.
How much more so now, for we are both able to practice and study and also possess the aspiration."
"We pray that you would instead preach for us; therefore, we entreat the World-Honored One to likewise preach the Dharma of unsurpassed bodhi for us. △ Third, the preparation for renunciation.

At that time, among the multitude led by the Wheel-Turning Sage King, eighty trillion people, seeing that the sixteen princes had left the household life, also sought to leave the household life; the king immediately granted them permission.
The retinue led by the former Wheel-Turning King consisted of one hundred ministers and hundreds of thousands of millions of people;
even now among them, eighty trillion people have sought to go forth into homelessness.

When the king granted his permission, it was because that king also knew that a Buddha is difficult to encounter and the Dharma is difficult to hear, and that he had now both seen the Buddha and heard the Dharma.
If one follows the Dharma, one will obtain great benefit. However, if one does not leave the household life to practice it, then even though one sees, it is as if one does not see;
even though one hears, it is as if one does not hear; and even though one attains, it is as if one does not attain.

Even though he himself desired to leave the household life, his sons and grandsons have all already left the household life, yet none has succeeded to the position of a Wheel-Turning King. For this reason...

The state and its altars are of primary importance; therefore, he was simply unable to do so immediately. How could it be that the subjects and citizens requested his renunciation of the world and yet were instead refused?

Thus, he immediately granted permission for them to leave the household life. △ Fourth, the Buddha’s acceptance of the invitation, in four parts. First, the formal acceptance of the invitation and the teaching itself.

At that time, the Buddha accepted the śrāmaṇeras’ invitation. After twenty thousand kalpas had passed, he preached this Mahāyāna sūtra titled *The Lotus of the Wonderful Law* (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*), the teaching for bodhisattvas, which is protected by the Buddhas, amidst the fourfold assembly.
Having spoken this sūtra, the sixteen śrāmaṇeras, for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, all together received and upheld it.
Having mastered the recitation until it was fluent, he spoke [the sūtra] only after twenty thousand kalpas had passed.

Although the prince had requested the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the time for preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* had not yet arrived; therefore, during these twenty thousand kalpas, he preached the Vaipulya Prajñāpāramitā.
It is only when their capacity has matured that he then preaches the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. As the following verse states:
"To preach the six *pāramitās* and various matters of supernatural powers is to preach the Vaipulya; to distinguish the true Dharma and the path practiced by Bodhisattvas is to preach the *Prajñā*.
According to this, one should know that the three previous turnings of the Wheel of Dharma were preached [in those respective stages].

The Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination pertain to the Āgamas, the Small Vehicle, the initial [teaching], and those with combined capacities for both the Exoteric and Esoteric;
they must hear the *Avataṃsaka*, which is identical to the present [teaching] among the five periods of the Dharma. △ Second, whether the capacity has faith or not.
When this sutra was being preached, the sixteen bodhisattva śrāmaṇeras all believed and accepted it; among the assembly of śrāvakas, there were also those who believed and understood;
yet the rest of the sentient beings, numbering in the hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis, all gave rise to doubt and confusion.
The sixteen princes, having already formed their aspirations, were able to practice and study together; therefore, they all believed and accepted it.

Among the śrāvakas, there were also those with faith and understanding who believed that what was previously taught was small and coarse—this being the teaching of the two vehicles according to the intentions of others—and they now believe that what is being taught is great and subtle—this being the teaching of the Bodhisattva.

"Sā. Thus, one is protected and remembered by the Buddha. To understand that the "small" of the past is not distinct from the "large" of today, and to understand that the "large" of today is likewise not distinct from the "small" of the past—that is the "large.
This clarifies those who have faith; the remainder below clarifies those who lack faith. All other members of the assembly...

As for those who give rise to doubt, it is not because the power of the Tathāgata’s path has not been fully perfected, nor is it because the Dharma he has taught has not reached its ultimate excellence.
It is because these sentient beings, since the beginningless kalpas, have long been firmly shrouded by ignorance and afflictions;
therefore, although they hear this wondrous Dharma from the Tathāgata today, they remain as [one...]
At that time, they were unable to immediately understand that the nine realms are one and the same as the Buddha-realm, and that the three vehicles are fundamentally the one vehicle;
thus, doubt arose and delusion was produced. For although the Buddha-dharma is indeed inconceivable, the karmic power of sentient beings is likewise inconceivable;
therefore, even though they hear the wondrous Dharma, they still give rise to [doubt].

This is also a matter of doubt. Thus, one should know that the remaining twelve characters constitute the reason for the karmic connections formed in past lives and the cause for their revelation today;
all of these are contained herein. △ Third, the duration of the preaching of the sutra.
The Buddha preached this sutra for eight thousand kalpas without ever ceasing or resting.
Since that Buddha’s lifespan was immeasurable, he preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for eight thousand kalpas;
whereas the present Buddha’s lifespan does not exceed a hundred years, so he has preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for only eight years. △ Fourth, having finished preaching, he enters samādhi.
Having spoken this sutra, he immediately entered a quiet chamber and dwelt in meditative concentration for eighty-four thousand *kalpas*.
That the Buddha, after preaching the sutra, immediately entered into *samādhi*, was because he had already expounded various teachings for sentient beings and had preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*;
thus, the capacity of those to be transformed by that Buddha had been exhausted at this point. Although there remained others...
There were sentient beings who harbored doubts; however, their spiritual capacity was no longer directed toward that Buddha, but rather toward the Prince’s re-exposition of the teaching.

Therefore, [the Buddha] entered into meditative concentration to enable the Prince to provide the re-exposition so that they might establish a karmic connection. The account of the causal origins is concluded. II.
Clarifying the Establishment of the Karmic Connection (Four parts): 1. Clarifying the Dharma. 2. Presenting a Simile. 3. Applying the Simile to the Dharma. 4. Summarizing the Simile.

The first section also has three parts: first, clarifying the initial establishment of a karmic connection; second, clarifying their meeting in the interim; third, clarifying the current preaching of the Lotus Sutra.
Within the first two [parts], the first concerns the prince’s secret lecture.
At that time, the sixteen bodhisattva śrāmaṇeras, knowing that the Buddha had entered his room and was in silent meditative concentration, each ascended a Dharma seat.
For eighty-four thousand *kalpas*, they extensively expounded and analyzed the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for the fourfold assembly.
Each of them brought across six hundred trillion *nayuta* of sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them.
He caused them to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Knowing that the Buddha had entered the chamber, they understood the Buddha’s intention in entering it:

he wished for us princes to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* once more for the sake of those who were still in doubt. Therefore, each of us ascended the seat and extensively expounded [the teaching] among the fourfold assembly.
It is different; it is merely an extensive elaboration of what that Buddha had taught. When the Buddha preached this sutra, he did so for only eight thousand kalpas;
now the Prince has restated it over eighty-four thousand kalpas, extensively expounding and analyzing the meaning of what the Tathāgata spoke.
The Tathāgata entered his chamber knowing this, and the Prince knew this.
And thus he gave a re-exposition. This is truly what is meant by the mutual resonance of the Way between teacher and disciple, both of whom expounded it together.

Regarding each instance of "delivering" (du), there are two meanings: transformative deliverance (huadu) and transcendent deliverance (chaodu). His re-exposition was intended to eliminate doubts and delusions; this corresponds to the meaning of transformative deliverance.
His Dharma transcends the nine realms, the three vehicles, and the seven stages of expedient means; this corresponds to transcendent deliverance.
This is the meaning of "delivering" (tuo). Regarding "showing, teaching, benefiting, and gladdening": "showing" means providing guidance; "teaching" means providing instruction;
"benefiting" means causing them to obtain benefit; and "gladdening" means causing them to give rise to joy.
It may also be said that while the disciples receive benefit, the teacher experiences joy.
As for those who have resolved to attain *bodhicitta*, if they had previously heard [the teaching] and given rise to doubt, by what means could they have generated that mind?
Now, since the teaching has been reviewed for them, their doubts have been eliminated; thus, they are able to generate the aspiration for unsurpassed *bodhi*.
This is the Mind. △ Second, the praise by that Buddha, in two parts. First, the actual praise:
After eighty-four thousand kalpas had passed, the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū arose from his samādhi and proceeded to the Dharma-seat.
Sitting in a composed manner, he addressed the great assembly: "These sixteen bodhisattva śrāmaṇeras are truly rare;

their faculties are sharp and penetrating, and their wisdom is clear and bright. They have already made offerings to immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas, and in the presence of those Buddhas, they have constantly cultivated pure conduct (*brahmacarya*).
Having received and upheld the Buddha-wisdom, they reveal it to sentient beings, causing them to enter therein."

Regarding "sitting in composure": although the minds of the assembly who had previously harbored doubts were not yet directed toward that Buddha, their hearts seemed unsettled because they wished for the Prince to act as a *pūrvapakṣin* (an opponent in debate).

Now that the Prince has acted as the *pūrvapakṣin*, having removed their doubts and caused them to resolve their minds [upon the path], the Buddha’s mind has reached a state of composure; therefore, he immediately [arose].
He arises from meditative concentration and sits down again with composure. "Constantly practicing the pure life" praises his ability to cultivate merit.
"Receiving and upholding the Buddha’s wisdom" praises his ability to cultivate insight. Taken together, these praise his ability to practice for his own sake;
"revealing it to sentient beings and causing them to enter therein" praises his ability to transform others.
△ Second, the exhortation to draw near, in two parts. First, the formal exhortation:
"You all should repeatedly draw near to them and make offerings to them.
Since they possess neither merit nor cultivate it, and lack wisdom or its preparation, they are nonetheless able to transform others through their own conduct."
Therefore, toward others, one should not merely offer occasional service and offerings, but should rather approach them repeatedly and make offerings repeatedly.
△ Second, the explanation of the underlying intention.
Why is this? If any śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas can believe in the sūtra teachings spoken by these sixteen bodhisattvas,
and accept and uphold them without disparaging them, such persons shall all attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
This means that if one can believe what is taught, one will be able to attain bodhi and the wisdom of a Buddha;
therefore, one should repeatedly draw near to and make offerings to [the teacher]. For those śrāvakas who are able to believe and accept it, the Śrāvaka Vehicle is itself the Buddha Vehicle;
the same applies to pratyekabuddhas and bodhisattvas. Therefore, if one does not hear it, does not believe it, and does not uphold it, [one will not attain the goal].

That is all. If one is able to hear it, believe it, and receive and uphold it, then according to whether they are a śrāvaka, a pratyekabuddha, or a bodhisattva, they shall all attain the wisdom of the Tathāgata, which is unsurpassed bodhi.
As for the statement that they "shall all attain the wisdom of the Tathāgata," it is because this sutra can reveal the One Vehicle (ekayāna) by means of opening up the Three Vehicles (triyāna).
△ Second, clarifying their meeting in the interim.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "These sixteen bodhisattvas always delight in preaching this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
Each of these bodhisattvas has transformed six hundred trillion nayutas of sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, in birth after birth."
Those born together with the Bodhisattva heard the Dharma from him and all attained faith and understanding.
By these causes and conditions, they have encountered forty trillion Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, and even now, this number is not exhausted.
"The Buddha who spoke" refers to the present Śākyamuni, who issues this proclamation to the bhikṣus.
"One who always delights in preaching this sutra" refers to those who, throughout eighty-four thousand kalpas, have extensively analyzed and expounded it as their constant teaching.

Regarding the phrase "in every life they are born," this is because [the Buddha] previously established a karmic connection by reciting [this sutra] at the place of the Great Universal-Traveling Buddha (Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū), thereby acting as its foundation.
Within the perfect seed of the One Vehicle, there is a natural, inherent affinity between natures; thus, when a Bodhisattva is born, those sentient beings are born together with him.
Having been born together, they in turn hear the Dharma from the Bodhisattva and are able to believe and understand it.
By virtue of these causes and conditions—being born together, hearing the Dharma, and attaining faith and understanding—they encounter forty thousand [Buddhas].
Regarding these billions of Buddhas: it is a rule that wherever a Bodhisattva is born, they will inevitably encounter a Buddha.
Now, since sentient beings are born together with the Bodhisattvas, they likewise encounter the Buddhas. As for the statement that this does not apply to all at present:

this is not discussed in the case of those who attained realization immediately upon first forming a karmic connection; however, among them, there are those who subsequently regress from the Mahāyāna.

In the interim, they were received through the Small [Vehicle]; today, they are finally liberated through the Great [Vehicle]. There are also those who first formed a karmic connection with the most dull faculties;
these too will necessarily be liberated through the Great [Vehicle] later on. Therefore, even now, they are not yet fully exhausted.

△ Third, clarifying that the Dharma Flower is being preached now, in two parts: first, connecting the past and present; second, correctly preaching the Dharma Flower. The first part has two sections: first, connecting the assembly of the teachers.
Regarding the past and present of his disciples: there are two sections for this summary. First, the general explanation:
"O Bhikṣus, I now tell you: those sixteen śrāmaṇeras who were the disciples of that Buddha have all now attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
They currently reside in the lands of the ten directions, preaching the Dharma, and there are immeasurable hundreds..."
"Ten million billion bodhisattvas and śrāvakas as their retinue;

all have now attained equality" means that they were formerly disciples of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū while still on the path of causes, whereas now they have attained bodhi, being in the state of fruition. Formerly, under that Buddha, they preached the Dharma in secret; now...
This refers to preaching the Dharma throughout the ten directions. Formerly, during the time of the "repeated lecture" (fùjiǎng), there were immeasurable sentient beings who listened and received it;
now, there are immeasurable bodhisattvas and śrāvakas who serve as his retinue. △ Second, the specific demonstration.
Those two śrāmaṇeras will become Buddhas in the East. One is named Akṣobhya; he resides in the Land of Joy (*Abhirati*).
The second is named Sumerukūṭa. "Akṣobhya" is a Sanskrit term; in this [Chinese] language, it means "Immovable. Since the East is the source of all movement, and yet—
The Buddha is named "Immovable" because that Buddha is able to use the wisdom of suchness to illumine the realm of suchness.
Since the realm and wisdom are one as suchness, and the realm and wisdom are non-dual, there is constant illumination within stillness, and constant stillness within illumination.
Being constantly illuminated within stillness, he is immovable yet moving; being constantly still within illumination, he is moving yet immovable.
Therefore, that Buddha is named Akṣobhya (Immovable) and resides in the eastern direction.

Since quiescence and illumination are non-dual, and movement and stillness are mutually identical, he is able to bring benefit to all sentient beings through both speech and silence, such that there are none who do not rejoice;
thus his land is named "Joy. As for the summit of Mount Sumeru: Sumeru is composed of four precious substances. And...

It stands preeminent above the peaks of all mountains. Because that Buddha was able to ultimately realize the four virtues of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, he rose far above the summit of the mountain of nirvana; for this reason, it is so named.
In the southeast are two Buddhas: the first is named Siṃhaghoṣa (Lion-Sound), and the second is named Siṃhadarśana (Lion-Appearance).
As for Siṃhaghoṣa, he speaks with the fearless voice of a lion; when the hundred beasts hear it, their brains split asunder.
Because that Buddha is able to deliver definitive and fearless teachings, all sentient beings who hear them find their ignorance and afflictions [eradicated].
It is named as such because it causes afflictions to burst apart. As for the "lion-like appearance":

when a lion appears, all other beasts hide away; likewise, when that Buddha appears in the world, possessing great majesty and virtue, and great heroic prowess, all heterodox and external teachings are eclipsed and do not manifest, just like the lion.
When the cub emerges from its den, all other beasts hide away; therefore, it is called the Lion Mark (siṃhavijṛmbhita-lakṣaṇa).
To the south are two Buddhas: the first is named Ākāśastha, and the second is named Nityanirvṛta.

Regarding "abiding in empty space": empty space is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), while abiding is existence. Because that Buddha has realized and witnessed true emptiness (*tathatā-śūnyatā*), he dwells securely in the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
True emptiness is not empty; it is able to contain all things. Thus, it is existence that is itself emptiness;
therefore, it is called "abiding in empty space. Regarding "perpetual cessation": permanence is non-cessation, and cessation is non-permanence.

Birth is neither arising nor ceasing; this is called Great Nirvana. Because that Buddha is able to realize Great Nirvana, the name is established based on what he has realized; therefore, it is called "eternal cessation."
In the southwest are two Buddhas: the first is named Kṣemadatta (Imperial Mark), and the second is named Brahmakṣema (Brahma Mark).
As for Kṣemadatta, his marks are like those of a worldly emperor, whom all revere and look up to.

Because that Buddha has eternally eliminated the five abodes (*pañcavihāra*), he has severed what is difficult for others to sever; because the three virtues are perfectly manifested, he has realized what others have yet to realize.

That which is difficult to realize, he has realized; that which is difficult to sever, he has severed. Thus, he is universally revered by the sentient beings of the nine realms, and is therefore named "Imperial Aspect" (Dìxiàng).
As for the "Brahma Aspect" (Fànxiàng), it refers to the aspect of pure and white Brahma-conduct (*brahmacarya*).
This is because that Buddha was able to draw near to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, such that no delusion remained uneliminated. Furthermore...
One is able to fully practice all the path-dharmas of the Buddhas without doubt or interruption.
Since there is no delusion that is not eliminated, and with neither doubt nor interruption, one is singularly pure; thus, all things are pure. Therefore, it is called the "Brahma-characteristic."
There are two Buddhas in the western quarter: the first is named Amitābha, and the second is named Sarvalokadhātudurgatipariśodhana (Savior from All Suffering and Affliction of the World).
"Amitābha" means "Immeasurable Light" in this language, and it is also called "Immeasurable Life.
These names are given because that Buddha possesses immeasurable radiance and lifespan. [The second is] "Savior from All Suffering and Affliction of the World."

"Regarding 'all worlds,' this refers to the ninefold world. Affliction (*duḥkha*) consists of the afflictions of views and thought, as well as ignorance (*avidyā*), which serve as the cause of suffering.
The *pariccheda* (segmented) and *pariṇāma* (transformative) deaths constitute the fruit of suffering.

Since that Buddha has exhausted all five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vihāra*) without exception, he has already transcended all causes of suffering in the world; furthermore, the two types of death have ceased to exist for him without exception."
Thus, one has already transcended all the fruits of suffering in the world. Being able to transcend them oneself, one then enables others to transcend them as well;
therefore, it is called "transcending all the sufferings and afflictions of the world."
In the northwest are two Buddhas: the first is named Tamālapatracandanagandhābhijña, and the second is named Merudhvaja.
Regarding Tamālapatracandanagandhābhijña, "gandha" (fragrance) carries the meaning of being pure, far-reaching, and subtly pervasive. By means of this—
That Buddha, from within great wisdom, gives rise to great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
First employing supernormal powers and subsequently extracting [beings] through wisdom, he establishes transformation according to their capacities and adapts his teaching to those capacities.

When capacity and teaching merge in profound harmony, it is like the fragrance of incense—pure, far-reaching, and subtly pervasive; for this reason, he is so named. As for "Sumeru-appearance" (*Sumerukūṭa*), it refers to the appearance of Mount Sumeru.
It enters the water eighty-four thousand yojanas deep, and emerges from the water for eighty-four thousand yojanas as well.
Because that Buddha was able to cultivate eighty-four thousand Dharma-gates during his causal stage, he realized all eighty-four thousand Pāramitā-gates upon reaching fruition;
like the characteristics of Mount Sumeru, it both enters and emerges from the water.
It is eighty-four thousand yojanas [in height], and for this reason it is so named.
To the north are two Buddhas: the first is named Meghasvabhāva, and the second is named Meghasvarāja.
As for the Sovereign of Clouds (Meghasvabhāva): when clouds are spread throughout the world, they can be rolled up or unfurled with sovereign ease;
if one wishes them to be great, they become great, and if one wishes them to be small, they become small.

Likewise, when that Buddha appeared in the world, if he wished to be great, he could manifest a body of a thousand *zhang* as Śākyamuni, and if he wished to be small, he could manifest a body of sixteen *chi*.
As for my appearance, it manifests like clouds; therefore, this is how I am named. Regarding the King of Cloud-Sovereignty:
when clouds arise, they must surely rain; and at the time of raining, if one desires much, there is much.

If he wishes it to be small, it is small; if he wishes it to be great, it is great; if he wishes it to be minute, it is minute. When that Buddha manifests his body to preach the Dharma, if he wishes it to be sudden, it is sudden;
if he wishes it to be gradual, it is gradual. Whether partial or complete, great or small, provisional or real, half or full, there is nothing that is not thus.
Thus he is able to be the King of all Dharmas, raining down like a cloud’s rain, with absolute mastery over all things.
Therefore, it is by this that they are named. To the northeast is a Buddha named Destroyer of All Worldly Fears.
As for me, Śākyamuni Buddha, I have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in the Sahā world-system.
"Destroyer of All Worldly Fears": Birth-and-death and the afflictions are the greatest terrors of all the world, and they are the most difficult to destroy.
That Buddha, being able to destroy them himself and also enabling all sentient beings to destroy them, is therefore named "Destroyer of All Worldly Fears. Śākyamuni.
"Muni" is the Sanskrit term for Śākya, which here means "Able One" (Nengren). "Muni" is the Sanskrit term for "Silent One" (Jimo).
"Able One" is the clan name; "Silent One" is the personal name. As an Able One, he is fully endowed with great compassion; as a Silent One, he is fully endowed with great wisdom.
Because he is endowed with great wisdom, he is able to sever birth and death and realize nirvāṇa. Being endowed with great...
Because of his compassion, he does not abide in nirvāṇa, but returns to enter into saṃsāra.
Since he abides neither in nirvāṇa nor in saṃsāra, that which he abides in is solely the Middle Way. This is something difficult for all sentient beings to achieve;
our Buddha was able to do so, and is therefore named Śākyamuni (the Able One, the Silent One). Since this is difficult—
Those who are capable can achieve it; therefore, it is still within the land of endurance (*kṣānti*) that one attains enlightenment (*bodhi*).
△ Second, the conclusion and correlation of the disciples across past and present (in three parts). First, the narration of the causes and conditions.

"O bhikṣus, when we were śrāmaṇeras, each of us individually taught and transformed immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.
Having heard the Dharma from me, they set their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Among these sentient beings, there are some who now abide on the stage of the śrāvaka; I constantly teach and transform them toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
[They have not yet realized] anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. These people should enter the Buddha-way gradually by means of this Dharma. Why is this?
Because the wisdom of the Tathāgata is difficult to believe and difficult to understand.
Regarding these sentient beings who currently abide in the stage of the śrāvakas and so forth:
it means that originally they heard the Dharma from me with the aim of attaining bodhi. Had they achieved this, they would have already attained liberation.
However, there are those who regress from the Great Vehicle and adopt the Lesser Vehicle; therefore, I receive them through the Lesser Vehicle, and thus they now abide in the stage of the śrāvaka.
Although I cause them to abide in the stage of a śrāvaka, from the very beginning I have intended for them to attain bodhi through my teaching.
Because they have taken the lesser path, I have for the time being caused them to realize it by means of the śrāvaka-dharma.
Once they have realized the lesser, I shall then lead them back from that lesser stage and guide them toward the Great Vehicle; therefore, it is said: "should."

By means of these teachings, one gradually enters the Buddha-way. Regarding the term "gradual entry": initially, in the fundamental teaching concerning the Buddha-way, because [beings] regress from the Great Vehicle and adopt the Small Vehicle, the teaching temporarily employs the Small Vehicle as an intermediary.
This causes those with the capacities of the Small Vehicle to ripen first in this present life, where they remain as śrāvakas;
only thereafter are they led from the Small back to the Great. Therefore, it is called "gradual entry. Thus, one knows that at the beginning—
To say that they heard the Dharma from me for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* clarifies their initial entry into the Great Vehicle.

Next, to say that among these sentient beings there are those who currently abide in the stage of the *śrāvaka* clarifies their regression from the Great to the adoption of the Small, whereby they convert others through the Small and attain its realization. Finally, to say that I constantly teach and transform them toward *bodhi* [clarifies the ultimate goal].

This clarifies that although I have now brought about a minor transformation by causing them to abide as śrāvakas, my original teaching from the very beginning was directed toward the Great [Vehicle].
To say "these people" means that they should enter the Buddha-way gradually by means of this Dharma; thus, it is called "abiding in the minor" despite being so designated.
"However, one must necessarily proceed from this minor dharma to be led into the Great [Vehicle]. Why is this so? The following section explains the meaning of gradual entry.
Because the wisdom of the Tathāgata is difficult to believe and difficult to understand, it is necessary to enter it gradually.
△ Second, the formal conclusion and reconciliation.
Those immeasurable beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who were transformed at that time— these are you, O bhikṣus,
and the śrāvaka disciples who will exist in future ages after my parinirvāṇa.
"At that time," and so forth, refers to those who were re-examined and established in a karmic connection.
"You, all you bhikṣus," refers to those who currently abide on the stage of the śrāvaka. "Future disciples" refers to those who are not yet exhausted among the present assembly.
△ Third, resolving doubts and obstacles.
After my parinirvāṇa, there will be disciples who have not heard this sutra; they will neither know nor realize the conduct of a bodhisattva.

Regarding the merits they have attained for themselves, they will give rise to the thought that they have reached parinirvāṇa and will enter nirvana. At that time, I shall manifest as a Buddha in another land.

Furthermore, there is another name for this: although these people conceive the thought that they have attained extinction and enter into nirvana, they nevertheless seek the Buddha’s wisdom in that land.
There they hear this sutra and attain extinction solely by means of the Buddha-vehicle; there is no other vehicle.
Setting aside the skillful means by which the Tathāgatas preach the Dharma, some may harbor doubts, thinking:
"The present disciples have heard this sutra from the Buddha and thereby attained liberation;

therefore, we know they were those with whom the Buddha first established a karmic connection. However, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those who do not hear the Buddha preach this sutra [are not so]."
And thus they attain liberation. How is it known that these are also the Tathāgata’s original recipients of the karmic connection and his disciples who formed the beginning?
For this reason, the commentary states: "After my parinirvāṇa, although there may be disciples, if they do not hear this sutra..."
Those who claim to have attained ultimate *parinirvāṇa* merely harbor such a notion while remaining within the *sahā* world-system.
Once they have realized *nirvāṇa*, they will necessarily be born in the realm of *sopadhiśeṣa*; it is there that I shall manifest as a Buddha.

They shall instead hear it from me and thereby attain liberation, thus bringing their journey to its conclusion; for this reason, they too are my disciples with whom I have established a karmic connection.
That they shall attain equality solely through the Buddha-vehicle is precisely the teaching heard in that land.
Part Two: The Actual Exposition of the Lotus Sutra. This has two sections. First, clarifying the teaching of the ultimate truth.

"O bhikṣus, when the Tathāgata knows for himself that the time for his parinirvāṇa has arrived, and that the assembly is pure, their faith and understanding firm, their realization of the dharma of emptiness complete, and they have deeply entered meditative concentration, he then gathers the bodhisattvas and the assembly of śrāvakas and preaches this sūtra for them.
In the world, there are no two vehicles by which one attains extinction; there is only the single Buddha-vehicle by which one attains extinction."
Thus, the assembly is again purified; this signifies that their hindrances have been removed. Their faith, understanding, and so forth signify that their spiritual capacities have been awakened.

This is because the Tathāgata, regarding himself, knows that his period of guiding and transforming beings is about to end, while regarding others, he knows that their hindrances have been removed and their capacities have been awakened.
For this reason, he speaks of the "one reality. All bodhisattvas are those who arise as echoes and shadows [of his teaching].
The multitude [of bodhisattvas] and the śrāvakas are the assembly for whom this teaching is intended. The section beginning with "In the world" is precisely the exposition of the sutra.

There are none who attain extinction through the two vehicles, because they merely extinguish views and afflictions (dṛṣṭi-kleśa) and merely cross over the stage of limited birth (bhavāgra-pariccheda), rather than attaining true extinction.
Only those who attain extinction through the single Buddha-vehicle do so because they completely extinguish the five abodes (pañca-vāsa) and eternally cross over the two deaths (dvividha-maraṇa).
This is because it is true cessation. △ Second, explaining the preceding intent:

"Bhikṣus, you should know that the Tathāgata, through his skillful means, penetrates deeply into the nature of sentient beings and knows that their aspirations and inclinations lie in the Lesser Dharma."
They are deeply attached to the five desires. For their sake, he speaks of *nirvāṇa*. When such people hear this, they immediately believe and accept it, thinking:
"Since there is only the single Buddha-vehicle through which one attains extinction, for what reason did he previously bestow the three? To explain his intention for bestowing the three, it says:
"The Tathāgata, through the skillful means (*upāya*) of his transformative wisdom, has deeply entered into the transgressions of sentient beings."

Having eliminated the nature formed by past habits, one knows that all the present inclinations delight in the Lesser Dharma (*hīnayāna*) and are furthermore deeply attached to the five desires (*pañca-kāma*).
If one delights in the Lesser, the great capacity (*mahāyāna-kuśala-mūla*) has not yet been awakened; if one is attached to desire, the minor obstacles have not yet been removed.
Because they delight in the small and are attached to desires and the like, [the Buddha] speaks of nirvāṇa; thus, their own inclinations and pleasures are fulfilled.
Therefore, it is better that they do not hear it at all. If, however, they do hear it, they will then be able to believe, comply with, and uphold it.
Once they are able to believe and accept it, they will no longer be deeply attached to the five desires, and their obstacles will be removed. When those obstacles are removed, their...
The capacity [of the audience] spontaneously awakens; through this, when the teaching is presented as "Great," even those of great capacity can believe and accept it.

Thus, one knows the intent behind the three vehicles: first, because sentient beings delight in the small and are attached to desires; second, so as to provide the foundation for revealing the ultimate reality.
Therefore, although there are three provisional means, they ultimately and fundamentally return to the single reality. This is why it is called the "worldly" [truth].
There are no two vehicles by which one attains extinction; it is only through the single Buddha-vehicle that one attains deliverance. △ Second, the presentation of parables has three parts.
First, the analogy of the guide illustrates the initial formation of karmic conditions.
Suppose there were a perilous and evil road, five hundred *yojanas* in length, desolate and devoid of people, a place of great terror.

If there were a large multitude wishing to traverse this path to reach a place of precious jewels, there would be a guide— wise, discerning, and sagacious— who thoroughly knew the characteristics of the treacherous road,
both its obstacles and its passages, and who led the multitude, intending to cross over this difficulty.

The five hundred *yojanas* is a metaphor for the period before sentient beings have established the Great Vow (*mahā-praṇidhāna*); they are entirely bound by the afflictions of the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vihāra-kleśa*).
The delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) within the three realms constitute one hundred; the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*) in the desire realm constitute two hundred;

the delusions of thought in the two upper realms constitute three hundred; the "dust-like sands" of internal and external objects constitute four hundred; and the [delusions] outside the realms constitute... [five hundred].

"Five hundred" refers to the five hundred [stages]. Regarding "perilous and difficult evil paths": "perilous" (*hsien*) means obstructed and treacherous; "difficult" (*nan*) means calamitous and distressing.

Because the three hundred constitute the cause of birth and death within the realm of boundaries (*dhātu*), they invite the fruit of suffering characterized by *paricchinna-bheda* (segmented) existence.

Because the five hundred constitute the cause of birth and death beyond the realm of boundaries, they invite the fruit of suffering characterized by *pariṇāma* (transformative) existence. Such are the five stages of abiding (*pañca-vāsabhūmi*).
The cause of suffering is that which can summon the fruit of suffering—the two types of death—and is thus a perilous, obstructed, and calamitous evil path.
Regarding "vast and desolate, devoid of people": this affliction of birth and death has existed since the beginningless kalpas;
within it, there is neither bodhi nor nirvāṇa. Therefore, it is said to be vast and desolate, devoid of people. Fear.
As for the "place": it is such a place of birth-and-death and afflictions, where from kalpa to kalpa one emerges and submerges;
having been born, one dies, and having died, one is born again. Because of this cycle of birth and death, death and birth, there is no end to it.
This is indeed a place of dread, terror, and loathing. If there is a great multitude...

These are precisely the assembly of beings with whom he has formed karmic connections—six million billion nayutas of sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—who wish to pass beyond this path to reach the place of precious jewels; that is, those who wish to transcend this cycle of birth and death and its afflictions.
Regarding the path of perilous obstacles and hardships leading to the place of unsurpassed bodhi and nirvāṇa, there is a guide.
"Guide" has three meanings: the original guide, the guiding guide, and the instructing guide. This refers to the original guide.
The teacher with whom one first establishes a karmic connection is the Sixteen Princes.
The teacher who provides guidance is the teacher encountered in the interim; this is the Bodhisattva born simultaneously in every lifetime.

The teacher who provides instruction is the teacher who now preaches the Lotus Sūtra to reveal the ultimate truth by opening up the provisional; this is Śākyamuni Tathāgata. Although [these roles] appear in three places...
Although there are these differences, they refer to one and the same person. Taking the sense of the initial establishment of a karmic connection, he is called the "Teacher who First Guides.

Taking the sense of meeting him during the intermediate period, he is called the "Teacher who Guides. Taking the sense of delivering and liberating one today, he is called the "Teacher who Opens the Way.
When one investigates the beginning, the end, and that which lies between them, [it is all this one person].
Is this not the Buddha Śākyamuni’s skillful adaptation to circumstances for the sake of guiding and transforming beings?
This refers to the "one guide," who is the original teacher; that is, when he was still a prince. Regarding his being "wise and discerning":
at the time he was forming karmic connections with the multitude, he had already attained the purity of the six sense faculties, which is to say, his faculties were all penetrating and sharp.
Because their wisdom is clear and lucid, they are said to be "intelligent, wise, and far-sighted. Regarding those who well know the characteristics of the obstructions and openings of perilous paths:
"openings" refers to that which leads to the place of treasure; "obstructions" refers to that which prevents reaching the place of treasure.

All that arises from the causes and conditions of suffering and its accumulation (*duḥkha-samudaya*), as well as the six obscurations (*āvaraṇa*), are all obstructions and not openings. As for the path and cessation (*mārga-nirodha*)...
The dependent origination of cessation and the six perfections are all open and unobstructed.
This Prince, as the original guide and teacher, is able to know each one clearly: that which leads to the precious abode of Nirvana is open and unobstructed;
that which prevents reaching the precious abode of Nirvana is obstructed and not open.
Therefore, it is said that he well knows the characteristics of the dangers and the passages, both open and blocked, along the path.

"One who intends to lead the multitude" refers to those who, for the sake of all sentient beings, extensively explain and analyze the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* to establish karmic conditions with them.
"Desiring to pass through these difficulties" refers precisely to now generating the aspiration for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Having already generated this...

Regarding the "superior mind of the Way": from this point onward, one may rely upon it to emerge from the perilous path of birth-and-death and afflictions, reaching the precious abode of unsurpassed bodhi and nirvana; therefore, it is said that one wishes to pass beyond these difficulties.
△ Second, the parable of the conjured city illustrates encountering [the goal] midway.
The multitude he had led grew weary and despondent along the way, saying to the guide: "We are utterly exhausted and filled with fear;
we can proceed no further. The path ahead is still long, and we now wish to turn back."
"The middle way" does not refer to becoming weary or regressing halfway through a journey of two hundred and fifty *yojanas*.

Rather, it refers generally to the interval between the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*) and one's attainment of liberation today. It is within these two pillars that this occurs.

This is what is meant by "stalling midway. As for those who become weary and regress: this is generally because the assembly that has formed a karmic connection was originally, at the outset, ordinary worldlings of the broad ground (*pṛthagjana*).
Having been shrouded by ignorance from the very beginning, their obstructions were extremely deep and heavy;

therefore, although they have already resolved upon the Great Mind (*mahācitta*), they are unable to remain steadfast. If, in the interim, they encounter adverse conditions, they immediately regress from what they had attained.

Because they have resolved upon the Great Mind, it is said that they may become indolent and retreat. To say they are "exhausted" means that the power of their contemplation is weak while their hindrances are deep and heavy.
Furthermore, they are "fearful" because the afflictions of the five abodes have never been destroyed and the two kinds of birth-and-death have never been severed.
That they "cannot advance further" means they do not wish to give rise to practice based on their vows.

Furthermore, "the path ahead is still far" means that one has not yet traversed even a small portion of the five hundred *yojanas* of the afflictions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), the *saṃkhyeya-saṃkleśa*, and ignorance (*avidyā*).
"Now wishing to retreat" means wishing to withdraw from the great resolve (*mahā-citta*) that was initially generated and no longer proceeding forward in cultivation.
The above concludes the clarification of retreating from the Great Vehicle.
The Guide possesses many skillful means and thinks to himself: "These people are to be pitied; why do they wish to turn back, abandoning such great treasures?

Having formed this thought, by the power of his skillful means, he creates an illusory city within the perilous road, three hundred *yojanas* away, and addresses the multitude, saying: "Do not be afraid; do not turn back. Now, here is a great..."
There is a city where you may stay and do as you please. If you enter this city, you will find swift peace and security;
if you are able to proceed further, you may also reach the place of jewels.

Next, the reception by means of the small [vehicle] is explained. The term "guide" refers to the teacher who leads the way; this is none other than the co-emergent (*sahaja*) bodhisattva. As for the statement "you all must not fear," it means do not fear the long duration of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Since it was previously stated that one fears because "the road ahead is still far," he now tells them not to fear. "Do not retreat" means: * **Text:** 莫得退還者。 * **Translation:** Regarding "do not retreat": it means do not turn back. It is like a person traveling on a path who, having gone a short distance, suddenly sees a great mountain range and thinks, "I am unable to cross this mountain. Fearing that they will not reach their destination, they immediately turn back. This is called "retreating. Furthermore, it is like a person who, while crossing a river, suddenly sees a great whirlpool and thinks, "I cannot cross this river. Fearing that they will not reach the other shore, they immediately turn back. This is also called "retreating. Therefore, the Buddha tells them: "Do not fear the long duration of birth and death, and do not turn back. Why?
