This means that one must not allow the mind one has already generated to regress. Since it was said above that one now wishes to regress, it is stated here that one must not turn back.
"One may abide therein" means that one may rely upon it for cultivation and rely upon it for realization.
To act according to one's inclination is to cultivate the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*). How joyful!
One attains peace and security, which is the realization of the nirvana that is empty, signless, and wishless.
Because one has realized nirvana, one is no longer afflicted by the defilements within the realms; therefore, it is said that one has "swiftly attained peace and security.
"If one can reach the place of treasure, one may also go" means that you originally intended to reach the treasure of bodhi.
Because they were utterly exhausted, they stopped here. Once they have rested, if they wish to proceed further toward the place of treasure, they may also depart from this point.

Someone may doubt, saying: "Since this is merely a minor reception and does not explicitly reveal the provisional [teachings], why say that one may also proceed to the place of treasure? This arises from not understanding...
Within the three periods of the Āgamas, Vaipulya, and Prajñāpāramitā, although the provisional is not explicitly revealed, there is nonetheless the meaning of reaching the place of treasure.

This is because, while the manifest aspect of the Āgamas speaks only of arising and ceasing, the secret aspect contains countless humans and devas who attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Since they have been able to attain this patience of non-arising, [they have reached the goal].
Thus, the Āgamas themselves can lead one forward to the place of treasure; likewise, the Vaipulya sūtras aspire to the Great [Vehicle], and the Prajñāpāramitā brings about realization.
In terms of what they aspire to and what they realize, these are themselves the Vaipulya and the Prajñāpāramitā, yet they too can lead one forward to the place of treasure.
At that time, the exhausted multitude was filled with great joy and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence, exclaiming, "We have now escaped this evil path;

we have swiftly attained peace and security. Thereupon, the people entered the conjured city, conceiving the thought that they had already reached their destination and the thought that they were secure.
Next, I shall clarify the adaptation to the capacities of sentient beings and the provision of a provisional assurance.

Those who previously entered the city of transformation correspond to those who begin with the application of mindfulness and culminate in the attainment of the four fruits of arhatship; having accomplished what was to be done, they give rise to the thought that they have already crossed over.
Because there will be no further existence, one gives rise to the thought of peace and security. △ The Three Jewels serve as an analogy for the current preaching of the Lotus Sūtra.
At that time, the Guide, knowing that this multitude had already found rest and was no longer weary, immediately caused the conjured city to vanish.
He spoke to the multitude, saying: "Come, all of you! The place of treasure is near. That great city you saw earlier was merely a transformation created by me for the sake of providing rest."
This refers to the "Guide," which is the teacher who provides guidance; this is Śākyamuni Tathāgata.

"No longer experiencing fatigue" means that the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *saṃjñā-kleśa*) have already been destroyed, and birth-and-death in its delimited form (*paricchinna-jāti-maraṇa*) has already been severed.

Since the afflictions of views and thoughts have been destroyed and delimited birth-and-death has been severed, the minor obstacles have been removed and the great capacity [for enlightenment] is about to manifest. Once the great capacity...
When this is set forth, the great causal conditions [of the Buddha's appearance] can be clarified from this point on, and his original intention for appearing in the world can be fully expressed.
Thus, he immediately extinguishes the illusory city. As for the words "go and come," it means: do not go, and you should come.
"Do not go" means do not proceed toward the illusory city; "you should come" means you should come from the place of the treasure. The location of the treasure is near.

This term has two meanings. First, it means that they have already severed the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāva-kleśa*), and having emerged from the realm of birth and death (*pariccheda-utpāda*), they have already passed three hundred of the five hundred *yojana*s;

thus, it is said they are "near. Second, it means that although they have realized the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), once the teaching is revealed, the "resting city" (*nirvāṇa-pura*) is itself the "jewel-studded destination" (*ratnasthāna*);
thus, it is said they are "near. [The author] privately comments: Since they have attained rest, there is no further exhaustion.
For those who are weary, he immediately implements the provisional to enable them to realize the Lesser [Vehicle].
He then extinguishes the conjured city, [revealing that] the place where the treasure lies is near; this is the opening of the provisional to manifest the real.

That the conjured city is now close to the treasure-trove is precisely the opening of the provisional of the conjured city to manifest the reality of the treasure-trove. As for "going," do not go; as for "coming," you should come. Why?

"You should come here. Since the place of jewels is near, why would you not go? Because the great city you headed toward was a manifestation created by me, you must not proceed toward that manifested city and depart; rather, you should come from there to the place of jewels.

That great city you headed toward was a manifestation created by me"—this means that the provisional is discarded and the real is established. △ Third, the application to the Dharma, in three parts. First:
This is analogous to the parable of the guide.
Monks, the Tathāgata is likewise so. Now, for your sakes, I act as the great guide;
I know all of birth-and-death, the afflictions, and the evil paths—how perilous, difficult, and long they are—and what must be abandoned and what must be crossed over.
Regarding the phrase "birth-and-death afflictions": there are two kinds of birth-and-death and three kinds of afflictions;

therefore, the word "all" (*zhū*) is used. Regarding those who "should go and should be delivered": this refers to the fact that within these long and distant evil paths, there are both passages and obstructions. If it is a passage...
Then one should follow it and proceed to the place of treasure. If it is a blockage, then one should abandon it and cross over the perilous path.
△ Second, the combined analogy of the conjured city.
If sentient beings were to hear only of the Single Buddha Vehicle, they would not wish to see the Buddha nor wish to draw near him, but would instead think:
"The path of the Buddha is long and distant; only after enduring toil and suffering for a long time can it be accomplished.
Knowing such minds to be timid, weak, and inferior, the Buddha employs the power of skillful means to provide rest along the way, and thus teaches two forms of nirvāṇa.

Regarding the phrase "if sentient beings," etc.: it means that since they are obstructed by the three delusions and ought to be delivered, and since the jewel-precinct of Bodhi is where they ought to go, there can be only the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) by which they may be led and delivered.

Why, then, would one employ the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) as an intermediate stage? Therefore, it says, "if sentient beings," etc. "Timid" refers to being weak regarding the Great Dharma; "inferior" refers to...

This refers to delighting in inferior teachings. As for the "Middle Way," it is that which lies between the two pillars: after having generated the aspiration for enlightenment and before attaining liberation.
This is called the Middle Way. Regarding the "two types of nirvana," these refer to the nirvana of the śrāvakas.
The Pratyekabuddhas have both *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa with remainder) and *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa without remainder). △ Third, the analogy of the jewel-treasure:
If sentient beings abide in the two stages, the Tathāgata will then preach for them, saying: "What you have accomplished is not yet complete."
"Excellent! The stage upon which you dwell is close to the Buddha-wisdom. You should examine and deliberate that the nirvāṇa you have attained is not the ultimate reality;
it is merely the power of the Tathāgata’s skillful means to differentiate and teach three vehicles within the single Buddha-vehicle."
"The two stages" refers to the stage of the śrāvaka and the stage of the pratyekabuddha. [The author] privately comments:
If sentient beings abide in these two stages, it corresponds to the aforementioned "having already attained cessation, one establishes provisional means.
When the Tathāgata draws near to the Buddha-wisdom, it corresponds to "you all, go and come," which reveals the real by opening the provisional. This opens the two vehicles...
The phrase "the stage of abiding" clearly indicates being close to the wisdom of the Tathāgata.

The passage beginning with "one should observe" corresponds to the aforementioned Mahāyāna principle of discarding the provisional and establishing the real; for it is precisely these three meanings that constitute the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
△ Fourth, the citation of the parable.
Just as that guide, for the sake of providing rest, conjures a great city; and once they have rested, he tells them:
"The place of jewels is near; this city is not real, it was conjured by me."

The guide mentioned above is an analogy for the guide [of the Buddha]. The conjured city is an analogy for the conjured city [created by the Buddha] to bring about rest, corresponding to the initial formation of a karmic connection.

The passage beginning with "Once they knew they had rested" corresponds to today’s attainment of liberation; this is an analogy for the destination of jewels. Second, the detailed explanation of past lives.

The initial prose section on causes and conditions is concluded. △ Second, the verse summary has two parts: first, the verses summarizing the narrative of the causes; second, from "As for those śrāmaṇeras...

onwards, the verses summarizing the formal establishment of the connection. The first part has two sub-sections; the first summarizes the second major section above, the attainment of Buddhahood by that Buddha.

Second, requesting [the Buddha] to descend. This verse praises the third section above, "That Buddha’s Preaching of the Dharma," while briefly omitting the praise for the first section above, "The Lifespan.
Regarding the first four [verses], the first praises [the state of] being about to achieve [enlightenment] but not yet having achieved it.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū sat at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas. Yet the Buddha-dharma did not manifest before him, and he could not attain the Way of Buddhahood."
△ Second, verses on the offerings of the devas:
The various devas, nāga kings, and hosts of asuras constantly rain down celestial flowers to make offerings to that Buddha.
The various devas beat their celestial drums and performed manifold musical concerts. Fragrant winds blew away the withered flowers, while fresh and beautiful ones rained down in their stead.
Previously, this merely clarified the devas; now, it further clarifies the eight classes of beings, hence the mention of dragon kings (*nāgarāja*), asuras, and so forth.
The blowing away of the withered and the raining down of the fresh symbolizes that the appearance of that Buddha in the world is able to eliminate the ninety-five kinds of heterodoxies.
By means of this cause, he causes all beings to cultivate the perfect cause of the Mahāyāna. △ Third, the verse on attaining the Buddha-way:
After ten small kalpas have passed, he then attains the Buddha-way; all the devas and people of the world harbor hearts of exultation.
△ Verses 4: Offerings by the Retinue.
The sixteen sons of that Buddha, each surrounded by hundreds of thousands of millions of their own retinues, all proceeded together to the place where the Buddha was.
He prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet.

△ Second, the verses on that Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma, in two parts: first, the verses on requesting the teaching of various doctrines; second, from "At that time" (shí) to "sixteen" (shí-liù), the verses on requesting the preaching of the Lotus Sūtra.
The first part has three sections; the first is the verses on the prince’s request.
We entreat you to turn the wheel of Dharma; may the holy lion’s rain of Dharma satisfy us and all beings. A World-Honored One is extremely difficult to encounter;
he appears but once in a vast expanse of time.
"O Holy Lion," and so forth, are the words of the request for the turning of the Wheel of Dharma. Because he appears but once in a long period of time, he is difficult to encounter;
because he is so difficult to encounter, he ought to turn the Wheel of Dharma. △ Second, the verses on the requests of the devas, in two parts.
The first verse describes the manifestation of auspicious omens;
in order to awaken all sentient beings, he causes everything to tremble.
△ Second, the verse on the formal request has two parts. First, the extensive description of the eastern direction.
In the worlds of the eastern direction, across five hundred myriads of koṭis of lands, the palaces of the Brahmās were filled with a radiance such as had never before been seen.
When the Brahmās beheld this sign, they immediately came to where the Buddha was, scattering flowers as an offering and presenting their palaces to him.
He requested the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma, praising him with verses. Knowing that the time was not yet ripe, the Buddha accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
The first five lines of the verse describe the observation of signs; "but without doubt" and "and through deliberation" [refer to this].

Following this, one line describes the investigation. The two lines on scattering flowers describe the offering. The two lines on requesting the Buddha describe the invitation to teach. "The Buddha knew" [refers to the second part].
[This is] a verse. It is a silent assent. Regarding the phrase "the time has not yet arrived": phenomena fundamentally have no time; time exists only due to the capacity [of sentient beings].
Because the capacity has not yet matured, it is said that "the time has not yet arrived. △ Second, a brief verse on the nine directions.
In the three directions and the four intermediate points, as well as above and below, they likewise scattered flowers and offered palaces, entreating the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma.
"The World-Honored One is most difficult to encounter; we pray that by means of your original compassion, you will widely open the gate of ambrosia and turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma."
The first two lines are a general summary. The next line, "scattering flowers," specifically summarizes the offering.

The following five lines, beginning with "I entreat the Buddha," specifically summarize the request for the teaching; "World-Honored One" and so forth are the words of this request. As for the phrase "original compassion":

This is the compassion realized at the time of attaining enlightenment in the past. Because the realization of one brings about the realization of all, at the moment of attaining enlightenment, he also perfected Great Loving-kindness and Great Compassion.

Now, I only pray that you will universally bestow relief and extraction through the compassion originally realized, and widely open the gate of the nectar of immortality. △ Third, the verses on the Tathāgata.
The acceptance [of the invitation] consists of three parts. First, the verse on the formal acceptance:
The World-Honored One of Immeasurable Wisdom accepted the invitation of those people.
Second, the verse on the preaching of the Dharma.
I shall proclaim for you various teachings: the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, from ignorance through old age and death—all of which exist conditioned by birth.
You should understand these manifold faults and afflictions.

The various afflictions and sufferings refer to suffering and its origin within the Four Noble Truths, as well as, within the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, the delusions and karma of the past, the suffering of the future, and the suffering, delusions, and karma of the present. Regarding "that which should be known":

in the context of the Four Noble Truths, it means that one should know [the truth of suffering] and realize cessation through the cultivation of the path; regarding the links of dependent origination, it is as follows:
One should know that this is the contemplation of cessation. △ Third, the verse on the benefits gained:
When this Dharma was proclaimed, six hundred trillion nayutas attained the end of all suffering and all became Arhats.
During the second period of preaching the Dharma, ten million *koṭis* of beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges attained arhatship by not grasping at any phenomena.
From that time onward, those who attained the Way were beyond measure; even through calculations spanning ten trillion *kalpas*, one could not reach their limit.
Regarding "not receiving any dharmas": this means that the six sense organs do not receive the six sense objects, nor does one give rise to the six consciousnesses.
△ Second, the verse on requesting the preaching of the Lotus Sūtra has three parts; first, the verse on the prince’s renunciation of the world.
At that time, the sixteen princes left the household life to become śrāmaṇeras.
△ Second, the verse on the formal request for the preaching of the Dharma:
They all together requested that Buddha to expound the Mahāyāna Dharma, saying, "We, along with our retinues, shall all attain the path of Buddhahood."
"May we become like the World-Honored One, with the supreme purity of the eye of wisdom.
This is the request for him to preach the Dharma, made as they were about to depart on their journey together with their retinue, omitting for brevity the verses concerning their departure.

By saying "when one shall attain the Buddha-way," it is known that this is a request to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Regarding "the supreme purity of the eye of wisdom": *Note: The provided text contains a portion of a commentary on a Buddhist scripture, specifically a request for the Buddha to preach the Lotus Sūtra.*

If it were the World-Honored One [himself], one should speak of the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*). Yet, because it is called the wisdom-eye (*prajñācakṣus*), one should know that this wisdom-eye of supreme purity is in essence the Buddha-eye;
it is not the same as the wisdom-eye that merely discriminatively understands emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
If it were merely the wisdom-eye that knows emptiness, it would only destroy the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*); although it is indeed pure, it is not the supreme. Now, as for...
The wisdom-eye that has arrived not only knows emptiness, but also perceives non-emptiness. Since it perceives non-emptiness, this is precisely true emptiness.
Thus, when one is empty, all are empty; there is nothing provisional or middle that is not empty.

Since both the provisional and the middle are empty, it not only destroys the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), but also destroys the *rajas-aṇu* (dust-like) and ignorance (*avidyā*). All is pure.
Purifying all that is pure is called the foremost eye of wisdom. Such is the Tathāgata’s eye of wisdom, and we too wish to attain it.
△ Third, the verses on that Buddha accepting the invitation, in three parts: first, the verses on accepting the invitation to preach the Dharma.
The Buddha, knowing the mind of the youth and his practices in past lives, through immeasurable causes and conditions and various parables,
expounded the six *pāramitās* and the matters of the supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), analyzing the true Dharma and the path traversed by Bodhisattvas.
To speak of the six pāramitās and various matters of supernatural powers (abhijñā) is to speak of the Vaipulya [sūtras].
Next, the analysis of the following two phrases is the exposition of Prajñāpāramitā. What is called "the true dharma" refers to the Prajñā of the Real Mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa-prajñā).
From this single Prajñā of the Real Mark, it is differentiated into eighty-one categories of dharma. Furthermore, eight...
The eleven categories of all phenomena ultimately converge in the Mahāyāna; therefore, it is said that this is the "discrimination of the true Dharma.
△ Second, the verse on the correct exposition of the Lotus Sūtra.
He preached this Lotus Sūtra in verses as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
△ Third, the verse on having finished preaching and entering meditative concentration:
After that Buddha had finished preaching the sūtra, he entered dhyāna-concentration in a quiet chamber; sitting with a single mind in one place for eighty-four thousand kalpas.

Regarding "sitting with a single mind in a single place": the "single mind" is the wisdom that takes objects as its conditions (*ālambana*), and the "single place" is the objective realm (*viṣaya*) that is taken as its condition.
By means of the wisdom of suchness (*tathatā*), one illuminates the realm of suchness; by means of the realm of suchness, one gives rise to the wisdom of suchness.
Since realm and wisdom are non-dual, and subject and object are of one essence, the mind is one, and the place is likewise so.
This is the first point. Now, regarding the fact that after preaching the Lotus Sūtra, he sat in one mind and one place:

had this sūtra not been preached, his original intent for appearing in the world would still have remained unfulfilled, and the causal conditions for the Great Matter would still have remained unclarified.
Since this sūtra has now been preached, the causal conditions for the Great Matter are clarified and his original intent is fulfilled. Only...

Having realized this matter, there is nothing else remaining. Although there may be hundreds of thousands of sentient beings filled with doubt, their karmic capacity now lies with the Prince and no longer with that Buddha;
therefore, it is said that he immediately sat with single-minded focus in one place and entered meditative concentration.
△ Second, the verse on the formal establishment of the connection, in four parts: first, the verse clarifying the Dharma; second, the verse... [text truncated]

The analogy is presented in three verses, which correspond to the actual teaching; the fourth verse summarizes the analogy. The first section further contains three parts. The first verse concerns the initial establishment of karmic affinity:
these śrāmaṇeras, knowing that the Buddha had not yet emerged from meditation, preached the Buddha’s unsurpassed wisdom to immeasurable billions of beings.
Each sat upon a Dharma-seat and preached this Mahāyāna sūtra. After the Buddha had entered parinirvāṇa, they proclaimed and assisted in the transformation through the Dharma.
Each of these śrāmaṇeras saved six million billion sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
△ Second, the verses on meeting in the interim:
After that Buddha has passed into extinction, those who heard the Dharma will always be born together with their teacher in various Buddha-lands wherever they may be.

△ Third, three verses now explain the teaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. There are two parts: first, one verse on the summary of the connection; second, two verses on the actual exposition. The first part has two sections;
the first verse summarizes the connection between the ancient and modern identities of the Teacher.
These sixteen śrāmaṇeras have fully practiced the Buddha-way; they now currently exist throughout the ten directions, each having attained perfect enlightenment.
△ Second, the verse concludes by identifying the disciples of the past and present.
At that time, those who heard the Dharma were each in the presence of various Buddhas. Those among them who dwelt as śrāvakas were gradually taught the Buddha-way.
I was included among those sixteen, and I too once preached it for you. Therefore, by means of skillful expedients, I have led you toward the wisdom of the Buddha.
△ Second, the formal exposition in verse:
"For this fundamental cause and condition, I now preach the Lotus Sūtra to lead you into the Buddha-way; be careful not to harbor fear or alarm."
△ Second, three verses present analogies. First, the verse on the analogy of the guide:
"For example, there is a perilous and evil path, remote and desolate, abounding in venomous beasts; furthermore, it is devoid of water and grass—a place feared by all people."
There were countless thousands of myriads of people who wished to pass through this perilous road; the path was exceedingly vast and remote, extending for five hundred yojanas.
At that time, there was a guide who possessed powerful memory and wisdom, whose mind was clear and resolute, and who rescued the multitude from their hardships within the wilderness.
The mention of many venomous beasts is a metaphor for the afflictions (*kleśa*) and the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), which can wound the Dharma-body and the life-force of wisdom.
The absence of water and grass means that there is no Right Path, like the lack of water; there is no aid to the Path (*mārgasahāya*), like the lack of grass.

Furthermore, it signifies the absence of the Mahāyāna dharma of non-arising and non-ceasing, like the lack of water; and the absence of the Hīnayāna dharma of non-arising and non-ceasing, like the lack of grass. This is clearly understood.

"Certainty" means clearly discerning that "this is a passage" and "this is an obstruction," then decisively abandoning the obstructions to allow for passage, and never, under any circumstances, allowing a passage to become obstructed.
△ Second, the verse on the parable of the conjured city.
The multitude were all exhausted, and they said to the guide: "We are now utterly weary; we wish to turn back from here.
The guide thought to himself: "These people are truly pitiable. How can they wish to turn back and lose such great treasures?"

Immediately, he contemplated an expedient means: "I shall employ the power of supernatural transformations to manifest a great city, adorned with various dwellings, surrounded by gardens and groves, with canals, streams, and bathing pools, featuring double gates and lofty towers, all filled with men and women."
Having thus created this transformation, he comforted the multitude, saying, "Do not fear. Enter this city; each of you may follow what you please.
Once the people had entered the city, their hearts were filled with great joy, and they all conceived a sense of security, believing that they had already attained deliverance.

The first line of verse describes the regression from the Mahāyāna; the subsequent lines describe the Teacher’s reception [of beings] through the Hīnayāna. *Nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder) is like a city, while *Sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana with remainder) is like a walled town.
Within the factors of the path (*mārga-pakṣya-dharma*), in brief, they are precept, concentration, and wisdom, which are like the adornment of a dwelling.

In detail, they are the thirty-seven factors, which are like gardens and groves surrounding it. The channels and streams for bathing are a metaphor for the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*), and the double gates are likewise.

This illustrates those who have already attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) and beyond, whose repeated contemplation takes the Truth as its object until they reach the fourth fruit (*arhat*). It is like a lofty multi-storied pavilion.

Furthermore, it is illustrated that the emptiness-wisdom (*śūnyatā-prajñā*) attained is like a man, while meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is like a woman. The following verses provide a summary and confirmation of these points.
△ Third, the verse on the analogy of the treasure place.
The Guide, having rested, assembled the multitude and addressed them, saying: "You all should press forward; this was but a conjured city.
Seeing that you were utterly exhausted and wished to turn back midway, I employed the power of skillful means to temporarily manifest this city."
"You should now apply yourself with diligent vigor; together we shall always reach the place of treasure.
△ Third, the verses on the application to the Dharma, in three parts. First, the verse applying the analogy of the Guide:
"I am likewise thus, acting as the guide for all."
△ Second, the verse combines this with the parable of the conjured city:
Seeing those who seek the Way faltering and abandoning their efforts midway, unable to cross over birth and death or the perilous paths of the afflictions.
Therefore, by the power of skillful means, for the sake of providing rest, he speaks of nirvāṇa, saying: "Your suffering is extinguished; that which was to be done has all been accomplished.
△ Third, the verse on the analogy of reaching the place of treasure.
Having known that they had reached Nirvana, they all attained Arhatship. Thereupon, he assembled the great multitude and preached the True Dharma for them:

"The Buddhas, through the power of their skillful means, have distinguished and taught the three vehicles; yet there is only the One Buddha Vehicle. It is because it is a place of rest that two [vehicles] were spoken of."
I shall now speak the truth for you: that which you have attained is not extinction. To achieve the all-knowing wisdom of a Buddha, you must exert great diligence.
When you realize all-knowing wisdom, possessing the ten powers and other Buddha-qualities, as well as the thirty-two marks, that is true extinction.
"Having known [this]" means that once they know they have reached nirvana and attained arhatship, their minor obstacles have been eliminated.
Once the minor obstacles are eliminated, it is the natural law (*dharmatā*) that before long they will be able to arouse the great potential (*mahā-āśaya*).

Because their obstacles have been removed and their potential has been aroused, they then gather the assembly of bodhisattvas who act as echoes and shadows to initiate [the teaching], as well as those śrāvakas who are destined for it.
For the sake of the assembly of those with the karmic capacity, he preached the Dharma of ultimate reality (*bhūtatathatā*). As for this Dharma of ultimate reality:
first, he bestowed the three [vehicles] while concealing the one; next, he opened the three to reveal the one, opening the provisional (*upāya*) to reveal the real;
finally, he abolished the provisional to establish the real, harmonizing the three and returning them to the one.
Ultimately, it is neither provisional nor real; it is neither three nor one. This is what is called the True Dharma.
The skillful means of all Buddhas are of a single practice: since there is only this one reality, there is neither two nor three.
Since there are not three [vehicles], why did he initially bestow them as three? Since there are not two, why were there also two in the past?

Therefore, it is said that the existence of three is merely because the Buddha, through the power of skillful means and expediency, differentiated and taught them as three within the One Vehicle. As for the existence of two, it is due to...
Sentient beings give rise to various forms of indolence and regression regarding the single Buddha-vehicle; therefore, for the time being, I cause them to rest and speak of two vehicles.
Since the three are spoken of as skillful means and the two are spoken of as places of rest, there is fundamentally nothing that can be called "two" or "three.
There is only the single Buddha-vehicle, which is the ultimate and the reality. Even if...

The [teachings] of two or three vehicles are fundamentally not the ultimate reality. Now, for the sake of those who practice the two equalities—meaning that what was previously called "two" or "three" was all unreal—I shall now explain the reality for you.
The nirvāṇa that you have realized is not true extinction; only the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, the omniscience of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), is such.
It is true cessation. Since only the Buddha’s wisdom is true cessation, you should cultivate it and give rise to great diligence (*mahāvīrya*).

But what constitutes great diligence? If you can realize the "all-aspect omniscience" (*sarvākārajñatā*) realized by the Buddha, only then is it called great diligence; this is indeed true cessation. Thus, the Buddha has realized it.

That which is difficult for people to realize: one realizes all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), realizes the dharmas such as the ten powers (*daśabala*), and realizes the thirty-two marks (*dvātriṃśanmahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, one dwells in that which is difficult for people to dwell in:
dwelling in *prajñā*, dwelling in liberation (*vimukti*), and dwelling in the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). All-knowledge is precisely *prajñā*; the dharmas such as the ten powers are...
Liberation and the thirty-two marks are themselves the Dharma-body. Direct prajñā is not [itself] prajñā;
prajñā must necessarily possess liberation and the Dharma-body. Direct liberation is not [itself] liberation; liberation must necessarily possess the Dharma-body and prajñā.
This is directly the Dharma-body, yet not merely the Dharma-body. The Dharma-body necessarily possesses both prajñā and liberation.
Thus, these three virtues—raising one, all three are present; yet the three and the one are perfectly interfused. To speak of the three as the one, the one and the three are unimpeded;
they are neither vertical nor horizontal, like the character "卍" (svastika) of the West. They are neither conjoined nor separate, like the eyes of the Heavenly King. Therefore...
When one is purified, all are purified; when one attains mastery, all attain mastery;
when one reaches the ultimate, all reach the ultimate. This is that which the Tathāgata has realized and in which he dwells.
You should now exert great diligence to realize what the Buddha has realized and to dwell in what the Buddha dwells; this is true cessation.

I say that since the beginning, the two lines "knowing [the capacity]" constitute the bestowing of the provisional based on the real; next, the one and a half lines beginning with "thereupon" constitute the revealing of the real by opening the provisional;
and next, the lines beginning with "now for" constitute the abolishing of the provisional to establish the real. △ Fourth, the verse summarizes the parable.
The Guides of all Buddhas preach nirvāṇa for the sake of rest; once they know this rest has been attained, they lead them into the Buddha-wisdom.
This verse serves as an analogy for the method of "combining the stages" (*ti-he*). The first line combines the analogy of the Guide to manifest the initial formation of a karmic connection.
The second line combines the analogy of the conjured city to manifest the intermediate encounter. [Lines three and four...]
The phrase "the jewel-treasure" serves as a metaphor to manifest the deliverance of today. This concludes the explanation of the "Parable of the Phantom City" chapter.

In the title of the eighth chapter, "The Chapter on the Prophecy for the Five Hundred Disciples" of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, the term "wondrous Dharma" (*miaofa*) refers, upon examination, to three kinds of wondrous Dharma: first, the Buddha-dharma; second, the mind-dharma;
and third, the sentient-being dharma. If it is the Buddha-dharma, it is not identical to the mind-dharma or the sentient-being dharma. As for the mind...
Regarding the Dharma: the Buddha-dharma is not identical to the dharma of sentient beings, and the dharma of sentient beings is not identical to the mind-dharma or the Buddha-dharma;
if this were so, there would be differentiation rather than wondrousness. Now, when we speak of the Buddha-dharma, it is entirely identical to the mind-dharma and the dharma of sentient beings;

when we speak of the mind-dharma, it is entirely identical to the dharma of sentient beings and the Buddha-dharma; when we speak of the dharma of sentient beings, it is entirely identical to the Buddha-dharma and the mind-dharma. It is as follows:

This means that by raising one, all three are raised; by speaking of three, all three are one. Since the unity and threefoldness are perfectly interfused and inconceivable, it is called the "Wondrous Dharma" (*Saddharma*).

The reason why these three aspects can be mutually identical is that although the Buddha-dharma is sublime, the sentient-being dharma is vast, and the mind-dharma is immediate, when summarized in essence, they are of one and the same nature and characteristics of the three thousand worlds. Therefore...
They are identical in nature. For example, a single, infinitesimal moment of thought as it arises before us is called a mental dharma (*citta-dharma*).

Within this single moment, the entirety of the ten realms (*daśa-dhātu*) is fully present. Since each realm further contains all realms, there are one hundred realms. Each realm possesses ten suchnesses (*daśa-tathatā*); thus, across the hundred realms, there are one thousand suchnesses.
To this, we add another one thousand for the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), one thousand for sentient beings (*sattva*), and one thousand for lands (*bhājana-loka*).

Thus, the three thousand [realms] are established. Within these three thousand, the mental dharmas (*citta-dharma*) are fully present. Since this is so for the mental dharmas, it is likewise so for the Buddha-dharmas (*buddha-dharma*).
Since this is so for both the mental dharmas and the Buddha-dharmas, it is likewise so for the sentient-being dharmas (*sattva-dharma*).

These are thus mutually inclusive and mutually encompassing, like the jewels in Indra’s net, where each layer interpenetrates the others. Therefore, they are able to be mutually identical and perfectly interfused; this is the inconceivable mystery.
This is the Dharma. This is the wondrous teaching of the identity of these three aspects. To illustrate this through a metaphor, it is like a lotus flower in the world:
although it has many petals, it is a single flower; and although it is a single flower, it possesses many petals.
It is just like the wondrous Dharma, which is three yet one, and one yet three; therefore, the wondrous Dharma is compared to the lotus flower.
This is that which is universally followed by the ten realms and remains unchanging throughout the three periods of time;
hence it is titled the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.

If one clarifies the intent behind the introduction of this chapter: in general, following the completion of the first section on the Dharma-exposition (dharmadeśanā), the Tathāgata bestowed the prediction of enlightenment upon those of superior faculties;

next, following the completion of the first section on the parable-exposition (aupamyadeśanā), he bestowed the prediction upon those of middling faculties; now, with the causal-condition exposition (nidānadeśanā) having been completed—
This would naturally correspond to the prediction (vyākaraṇa) for those of inferior faculties.
Therefore, this single chapter is the text concerning how individuals of inferior faculties receive their prediction from the Tathāgata. Regarding the term "receiving the prediction":

before the Tathāgata has yet explained the causal conditions, he first grants them the promise of the prediction; thus, it is already bestowed. Consequently, the disciples here merely accept the Tathāgata’s...

This is the prediction [of their future enlightenment]. However, within this chapter, first Pūrṇa receives the prediction, next the twelve hundred receive it, and only at the end do the five hundred receive it.

Yet, when the title of the chapter is designated, it mentions only the "five hundred" and does not mention Pūrṇa or the twelve hundred; this is because the predictions for the five hundred share a common name.

Puming (Samantaprabha) and others simultaneously attained understanding; therefore, the text mentions only the five hundred and omits the rest. △ Second, the bestowal of predictions upon those of inferior faculties.
This section consists of two chapters. Now, for the first chapter, there are two parts: first, the prediction for Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra; second, the prediction for two thousand two hundred disciples.
The first part also has two sections: first, Pūrṇa’s silent reception of the prediction; second, the Tathāgata’s explicit bestowal of the prediction. First:
2. First, the account of what was heard:
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra heard from the Buddha this teaching on wisdom and skillful means, preaching the Dharma according to what is appropriate;
he further heard the bestowal of the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* upon the great disciples. Furthermore...
They hear of the events concerning causes and conditions from past lives; they further hear that all Buddhas possess the great sovereign power of supernatural penetrations (*ṛddhi*).
Hearing of this wisdom and skillful means (*upāya*), they realize that wisdom is the reality (*tattva*) while skillful means is the provisional (*upāya*).

This refers to the provisional and the real within the preaching of the Dharma. "Preaching the Dharma according to what is appropriate" means teaching the Three [Vehicles] in accordance with the suitability of those of middling faculties.

The single carriage is a metaphorical teaching; the three carriages are provisional, while the single carriage is the ultimate reality. This refers to the provisional and the real within the discourse on the parable.
Furthermore, hearing the bestowal of predictions upon the great disciples is the hearing of the predictions given during the two weeks of the discourse on the parable.
Moreover, hearing the accounts of past causes and conditions and so forth is the hearing of the discourse on causes and conditions.
It was thus. From the time he first received the transmission of the Dharma under the Buddha Jñānavijaya, he preached it extensively to establish karmic connections;
in the interim, he temporarily withdrew from the Mahāyāna and led others through the Hīnayāna; today, he has once again used the Mahāyāna to enable them to attain liberation.

In this way, the beginning, the end, and the intervening period are all matters of causes and conditions. Furthermore, I have heard that there is one who possesses great sovereign supernatural powers, as described above.

As for what is clarified: regarding the pulverization of atoms of lands and the metaphor of wiping away kalpas as dust—events as distant as these, when observed by the Tathāgata, are as if they were this very day.
Thus, that which is near today is not "near," and that which is distant over vast eons is not "distant. Distance and proximity are non-dual;
the present and the past are identical. This is the great sovereign supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) of the Tathāgata.

It is by the power of this. Furthermore, when the various guides first teach sentient beings to give rise to the Great Mind and reach the place of precious jewels, but they wish to turn back midway, he immediately manifests a city to allow them to halt there.
Once he knows they have rested, he then causes that manifested city to vanish, enabling them to reach the site of the treasures. All of these are the [powers] possessed by the Buddhas.
Such is the great supernormal power [of the Great Deity]. Furthermore, when first establishing a karmic connection, they were about to travel five hundred yojanas;
this was the initial guidance of the Great Master of Sovereign Power. Along the way, they encountered [the city] and rested at the illusory city.
This is the great sovereign spiritual power of the Guide who leads us; today he brings us across and delivers us, leading us directly to the place of treasure.
This is the great sovereign spiritual power of the Guide who opens the way. First, he plants the seeds for the conditions of the One Vehicle;
in the interim, he connects us to the nirvana of the Two Vehicles; and finally, he reveals the Buddha’s knowledge and vision—all of these are the Tathāgata’s great sovereignty.

Regarding the supernatural power, it says: "Furthermore, he heard... (and so forth). This is a general summary of his hearing the Dharma of "opening the provisional and revealing the real" (*kaiquan xianshi*) throughout the three stages of the teaching, which opens up the three vehicles and reveals the One Vehicle. II. Summary of what was understood, in three parts: 1. First, the summary of the exultation within his heart.
They attained what they had never before attained; their minds were purified and they leaped for joy.
"Attaining what they had never before attained" means that forty years ago, they did not know that the three vehicles were provisional.

Now, having heard the teachings of the three turnings from the Tathāgata, they have already been able to fully understand that the three vehicles, the three carts, and the illusory city are all expedient means.
This is entirely the reality of the single vehicle, the single chariot, and the true treasure-store.

This was something that did not exist forty years ago, yet it exists now; this was something that was not attained forty years ago, yet it is attained now. Therefore, it is said that "one has attained what was never before attained.
As for "the mind being pure and leaping with joy," this refers to Pūrṇa, who had previously shattered his [wrong] views.
[The practitioner] reflects: "Now that I have heard this teaching on causes and conditions, I have attained understanding and realization.

Relying upon it, I shall initiate practice, whereby I can shatter the sands of phenomena as well as ignorance, and enter the first stage, the Dwelling of Joy, manifesting my body throughout the hundred worlds."
Because he transforms and edifies all beings, it is said that his mind is pure and leaping with joy. △ Second, the description of his external demeanor of reverence:
He immediately rose from his seat, went before the Buddha, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and gazed up at the Honored One’s countenance.
Not for a moment did his eyes depart from this scene. That such a realm exists is entirely due to those of the three root-capacities;
though they are equally śrāvakas, there are distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior. For instance, Pūrṇa was one of inferior capacity; therefore, although—
Having heard the bestowal of predictions for those of superior and middling faculties, he further heard that permission was granted to bestow predictions upon those of inferior faculties;
yet, in his inner mind, he remained somewhat perplexed and undecided regarding the matter of the prediction. Therefore, he rose from his seat.
...until their eyes could not for a moment look away. △ Third, the description of their silent reflection and realization:
They then thought, "The World-Honored One is most extraordinary; his deeds are rare and marvelous.
He accords with the various dispositions of the world, employing skillful means and insight to preach the Dharma, thereby uprooting sentient beings from their attachments to all things. We..."
Regarding the Buddha’s merits, they cannot be fully proclaimed. Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, can know our profound mind and original vows;
thus, "to bring them to mind" means to contemplate them within the mind without speaking them aloud.

However, those of superior and middling capacities, after attaining understanding, all verbally express what they have realized. Now, Pūrṇa does not speak with his mouth, but only contemplates it within his own mind.

Regarding "recollection" (smṛti), there are four intentions. First, those of superior and middling capacity, having heard the teachings through both dharma and parable, are able to comprehend them clearly in their minds and subsequently express them clearly with their mouths;
thus, once they have attained understanding, each articulates what they have grasped. Now, Pūrṇa is of inferior capacity;
therefore, although he has already comprehended the teaching on causes and conditions (hetu-pratyaya) in his mind, he still...
Because they did not yet clearly understand it with their mouths, they merely thought of it in their minds and did not speak.

Second, when those of superior capacity present their understanding, it causes those of medium capacity to be moved; when those of medium capacity present their understanding, it causes those of inferior capacity to be moved.
Now that the three rounds of teaching have concluded, those of inferior capacity no longer have anything further to be moved by; therefore, they merely think of it in their minds and do not speak.

This is what is meant. Third, after those of superior capacity have expressed their understanding, the Tathāgata provides a formal endorsement for them, clarifying that they have grasped what they had not yet fully realized;
namely, that they previously understood only the provisional teachings of the forty years prior, whereas today they have attained the realization of the *Lotus Sūtra*’s ultimate truth.
Yet they still do not know that at the sites of twenty-two thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas, they had already been taught the Great [Vehicle].

Through the skillful use of general analogies, they comprehend the Tathāgata’s transformative activities throughout his entire career; through specific analogies, they comprehend the Tathāgata’s teachings across the five periods.
The Tathāgata, moreover, confirms their understanding and clarifies what they have yet to grasp, stating that the Tathāgata further possesses the *Anupama-sūtra*.
The measure of their boundless, asaṃkhyeya merits cannot be fully exhausted even if you were to speak for an entire kalpa.
Even those of superior capacity among men have not yet reached them; how much less could I possibly comprehend all the merits of the Tathāgata?
Therefore, I merely contemplate them in my mind and do not speak of them aloud. Fourth, although Pūrṇa and the others—though they are...
He conceals within while manifesting without; he was originally a bodhisattva. If he were to speak of this himself with his own mouth, it would be difficult for people to believe.
By having the Buddha reveal his traces to disclose his original nature, all people will believe without doubt. Therefore, he merely contemplates it in his mind and does not speak of it aloud.
"The World-Honored One is most extraordinary; that which he does is rare. Forty years ago, he also spoke of the provisional [expedient means].
He spoke of the truth, never stating that "this is provisional" or "this is real"; this is indeed the marvelous and rare quality of the Tathāgata.
Upon reaching today’s *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he not only explains that what was spoken forty years ago was provisional.
What is spoken today is the truth. Furthermore, the provisional teachings of forty years ago are the truth of today;
the truth of today is likewise the provisional teaching of forty years ago.
This is not merely extraordinary and rare, but is most extraordinary and most rare. Moreover, having completed one cycle of the Dharma teaching, he opened [the way].
By means of provisional skillful means (*upāya*), he reveals the ultimate reality (*bhūtatathatā*); he elucidates that skillful means is itself reality, and reality is itself skillful means.

This alone is already the marvelous and rare wonder of the World-Honored One. Furthermore, for those of middle capacity, he provides a complete cycle of parables to open up the provisional and reveal the real, demonstrating that the provisional and the real are of one essence and that the teachings of the past and present are non-dual. This is not merely marvelous; it is truly extraordinary.

How rare! And how truly extraordinary! How most rare indeed! Now, for the sake of those of us with inferior faculties, you have preached this one cycle of teachings based on causes and conditions, thereby revealing the provisional to manifest the ultimate, and clarifying that outside the provisional there is no ultimate.
In reality, there is no expedient means apart from the truth. This is not only extremely marvelous and rare, but is the most marvelous of marvels and the rarest of rarities.

To accord with the world, even for those who are greedily attached, the dispositions of sentient beings differ—there being distinctions such as the three vehicles, the five teachings, and the seven stages of expedient means. Therefore...

It is said that there are "various" [inclinations]. Some are attached to existence (*bhava*), some are attached to emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and some are attached to the middle way. Therefore, it is said that they are "everywhere.
Regarding the spiritual lineages (*gotra*) of sentient beings, there are those that are great or small, and those that are sudden or gradual.

Accordingly, the Tathāgata, in accordance with the gradual and small lineages of sentient beings, employs skillful means and provisional wisdom (*upāya-kuśala-jñāna*) to preach the gradual and small teachings for them, thereby uprooting their...
For those who possess the disposition for the sudden Mahāyāna yet cling to the duality of emptiness and existence,
one preaches the sudden Mahāyāna Dharma through the realization of true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*), thereby uprooting their attachment to the Middle Way. Furthermore,
for those who possess the worldly disposition within the realm of transmigration (*dhātu*), one preaches the Dharma through skillful means (*upāya*) to extract sentient beings [from suffering].

Regarding the attachment to the twenty-five states of existence within the three realms, and those who follow the dispositions of the mundane world beyond the realms, [the Buddha] preaches the Dharma by means of knowledge and vision.

He extracts sentient beings from their attachment to the three voids and causes them ultimately to return to the secret treasury of the three virtues. Nevertheless, the Tathāgata accords with all worldly beings...
Regarding the lineage of those born [in this state], there is no attachment whatsoever that is not uprooted, for they are fully endowed with the perfection of skillful means, knowledge, and vision.

It is precisely because it is thus that we, though wishing to speak of all the immeasurable and boundless merits of the Buddha, are unable to proclaim them; therefore, we merely contemplate them in our minds.
Yet they did not speak with their mouths, thinking: "Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, can know us.
As for the Buddha’s merits, we are unable to proclaim them; however, our own deep-seated resolve and original vow, only the Buddha can know.
Since only the Buddha can know them, the Buddha himself shall surely reveal our origins and manifest our fundamental nature, and bestow upon us the prediction of enlightenment. Therefore—

One merely contemplates it in the mind without speaking it aloud. "Deep mind" refers to one who inwardly conceals their status as a bodhisattva while outwardly appearing as a śrāvaka, thereby upholding and assisting in the propagation of the Buddha’s True Dharma, teaching and transforming sentient beings, and purifying buddha-lands.
"Original vow" refers to having formed the conditions for the One Vehicle in the presence of the Buddha Jñānavijaya, giving rise to the bodhicitta in pursuit of the Buddha-way.
For this reason, only a Buddha can know their profound mind; therefore, below, the Tathāgata reveals their origins and manifests their fundamental nature for them.
For this reason, only a Buddha can know their original vows; therefore, below, the Tathāgata bestows upon them the prediction of enlightenment (*bodhisattva-vyākaraṇa*).

Having silently received [the teaching], it is concluded. △ Second, the Tathāgata’s Manifestation of the Prediction, which has two parts: first, the prose; second, the verse. The first part has two sections:

first, revealing the fundamental by opening the provisional traces; second, formally bestowing the prediction. The first section has three parts: first, manifesting the traces by means of a single Buddha.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "Do you see this Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra?
I have always declared him to be the foremost among those who preach the Dharma. I have also constantly praised his various merits:
his diligent protection and upholding of my Dharma, his ability to instruct, benefit, and gladden the fourfold assembly, and his possession of complete understanding."

Commentary: The Buddha’s True Dharma brings great benefit to those who practice the same Brahma-faring life. Since the Tathāgata passed away, none have been able to exhaust the eloquence of his discourses.
When it is said, "Do you see this Pūrṇa? it refers to Pūrṇa. Although his outward form is that of a śrāvaka, he was originally a bodhisattva;

therefore, the question is asked, "Do you see him? When I have always praised him as being equal [to others], it means that he was not only foremost in preaching the Dharma forty years ago, but even today, at this sublime assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he is likewise foremost in preaching the Dharma.
First: He also constantly extols his various merits. What are these various merits of Pūrṇa?
In the *Avataṃsaka*, he manifests as one who is deaf and mute; in the *Āgamas*, he manifests as a guarantor of the precepts.
Within the Vaipulya sūtras, he manifested being subjected to rebuke; within the Prajñāpāramitā, he manifested having no desire for gain;
and today in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he manifests as one of inferior capacity—all of these are the various merits of Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra.

He who diligently protects, maintains, and assists in proclaiming my Dharma is one whom the Tathāgata can cause to propagate the transformation of the Dharma through the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*); yet Pūrṇa...
Pūrṇa, you are able to proclaim what the Tathāgata has proclaimed; therefore, it is said that you "assist in the proclamation.
As for the phrase "diligently protecting and upholding," the Tathāgata is able to adapt his teachings to suit the capacities of sentient beings and establish teachings according to those capacities.

When Pūrṇa assists in the proclamation, he is likewise able to do so; therefore, it is said that he "diligently protects and upholds while assisting in the proclamation. This refers to what is called the Āgama.

At that time, he diligently assisted in proclaiming the Dharma of the "half-letters. During the period of the Vaipulya sutras, he diligently assisted in proclaiming the Dharma that clarifies the "full" by contrasting it with the "half.
During the period of the Prajñāpāramitā, he diligently assisted in proclaiming the Dharma that brings forth the "perfect" while encompassing both the "common" and the "distinct."
Today, at this Dharma Flower [Sūtra], he diligently assists in proclaiming the purely perfect and uniquely wondrous Dharma.
Since he is able to assist in proclaiming various kinds of teachings, Pūrṇa is not merely one who is suited as the primary recipient (*pratipakṣa*) within the discourse on Dependent Origination;

he is also able to support the Dharma King, striking the gong to rouse and lead others, serving as a member of the assembly who acts as a catalyst through his influence and resonance. He is capable of—

Regarding "instructing, teaching, benefiting, and gladdening the fourfold assembly": while the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma was solely for the purpose of instructing, teaching, benefiting, and gladdening the fourfold assembly, now Pūrṇa, having thus acted as its protector and assistant in proclaiming it, is likewise able to instruct, teach, benefit, and gladden the fourfold assembly.
As for "fully explaining the Buddha’s true Dharma," it is as follows:
Throughout what has been taught during this single lifetime, there are teachings that are inclusive, those that are exclusive, those that are responsive, and those that are accommodative;
yet alongside these, there are those that are pure and perfect. In the Buddha’s original intent, it is not only the pure and perfect teachings that constitute the True Dharma;

rather, even the teachings that are inclusive, exclusive, responsive, and accommodative are all, without exception, the most great, central, and ultimate Dharma. Only Pūrṇa was able to fully embody this.

He fully explains this, meaning he is able to know the reason why the Tathāgata spoke of the "inclusive" (jian), and even able to know the reason why the Tathāgata spoke of the "pure and perfect" (chunyuan).
Therefore, it is said that he provides a complete explanation. He brings great benefit to his fellow practitioners of the Brahma-faring life;
that is to say, he transforms those of a similar kind through those of a similar kind, and leads them by means of expedient practices.

This is the actual practice. The preceding statement says that he is able to instruct, exhort, benefit, and gladden the fourfold assembly; this present statement says that he greatly benefits those who practice the same holy life (*sabrahmacārin*).

These are merely mutual clarifications of the text: the fourfold assembly is identical to those who practice the same holy life, and those who practice the same holy life are identical to the fourfold assembly.
Great benefit is identical to instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening, and instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening are identical to great benefit.

Indeed, because he is able to instruct, benefit, and gladden the fourfold assembly, and because he is able to bring great benefit to his fellow practitioners of the holy life, his eloquence in discourse is ultimate, supreme, and beyond further addition.
Therefore, apart from the Tathāgata, there is no one who can exhaust his eloquence in discourse. Yet, it is only the Tathāgata [who can do so].

Regarding those who are capable of reaching the ultimate: if we discuss this in terms of the fundamental ground, then the Tathāgata is the wondrous enlightenment of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao), while Pūrṇa is the equal enlightenment (děngjué) of the Perfect Teaching. Therefore, the eloquence of discourse possessed by Pūrṇa in his state of equal enlightenment—

Only the Tathāgata’s wondrous awakening can exhaustively master this. If we discuss it in terms of their manifested traces (*vṛtti*), the Tathāgata is able to proclaim the Dharma, while Pūrṇa is able to proclaim what the Tathāgata has proclaimed.
This precisely reveals that teacher and disciple sing in unison, and that the path of resonance and response intersects. Therefore, only the Tathāgata can fully encompass Pūrṇa’s [teaching].
This refers to eloquence. △ Second, revealing his fundamental nature by means of many Buddhas, in two parts. First, the actual revelation:
"You should not think that Pūrṇa was merely able to protect, uphold, and assist in proclaiming my Dharma;
he also, in the past, at the abodes of ninety billion Buddhas, protected, upheld, and assisted in proclaiming the True Dharma of those Buddhas. Among those who preached the Dharma, he was also..."

They are foremost and supreme. Furthermore, regarding the Dharma of emptiness taught by all Buddhas, they clearly understand and thoroughly penetrate it, attaining the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*).
They are always able to discern with precision and preach the Dharma with purity, free from doubt or confusion. They are fully endowed with the supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) of a bodhisattva.
Throughout his lifespan, he constantly practiced the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*). To those Buddhas and the people of that world, he was universally regarded as truly being a *śrāvaka*.
Yet Pūrṇa, by means of this skillful expedient, benefited immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings;
furthermore, he transformed immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* persons, causing them to establish themselves in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The first part clarifies that he was able to assist in proclaiming the teachings of the two periods: the *Āgama* and the *Vaipulya*.

The second part, following the phrase "furthermore, regarding the teaching of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) spoken by all Buddhas," clarifies that he was able to assist in proclaiming the *Prajñāpāramitā* teachings. As for "the teaching of emptiness":
That is to say, first, *prajñā* empties the four marks; next, it empties the mark of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*); and finally, it empties the mark of non-phenomena (*adharmalakṣaṇa*).

This emptiness, wherein all such marks are empty, is the emptiness of the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*); it is the ultimate, true emptiness. When this is clearly understood, there is no doubt or stagnation;
when one penetrates it, there is no obstruction. The four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*) constitute eloquence (*pratibhāna*); here, however, the term "wisdom" (*jñāna*) is used.

This is because wisdom is present in speech; therefore, it does not say that one attains the four unhindered eloquences (*pratisaṃvid*), but rather that one attains the four unhindered knowledges (*jñāna*).
"Always able to examine with precision" means being able to examine with precision and without doubt the principle of the *prajñā* of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
It is precisely because one can attain the four unhindered knowledges that one is able to examine the true mark with precision.
As for principle (*nyāya*), one is naturally able to accord with wisdom and speak in accordance with reality;
thus, one is able to preach the Dharma with purity. Since the person who speaks is pure, the Dharma spoken is likewise pure and free from doubt.

Regarding the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), if one follows the scriptural instructions, one can always examine them with precision; this constitutes the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*).
He preaches the Dharma with purity; his unimpeded eloquence is free from doubt, his unimpeded understanding of meaning is without confusion, and he possesses unimpeded readiness in exposition.
As for those who are fully endowed with the supernatural powers of a bodhisattva, it is because their wisdom is complete and their principles are clear.
Therefore, he possesses the power of great wisdom and the power of great supernormal faculties (*ṛddhi*), whereby he instructs and transforms bodhisattvas;
this is precisely his fulfillment of the power of bodhisattva supernormal faculties.
"In accordance with their lifespan" means that, following the lifespans of those ninety billion buddhas, he is able to constantly practice the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*). By these skillful means...
This refers to using the skillful means of "concealing within and manifesting without" to assist in proclaiming the Dharma of Prajñāpāramitā and to benefit all beings.

Furthermore, "benefiting all" and so forth are skillful means for opening up the provisional (*upāya*), while "transforming those below" is the skillful means for revealing the ultimate reality (*bhūta-artha*).
This clarifies that he is able to assist in proclaiming the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. That which is elucidated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is exclusively the knowledge of the Buddha.
This reveals the world-transcending original intent and the causal conditions for the One Great Matter.

Therefore, when assisting in its proclamation, one can cause sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Once the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are opened, unsurpassed Bodhi is established from this point onward.
Thus, it should be known that this is an auxiliary proclamation of the *Lotus Sūtra*. △ Second, the explanation of the underlying intention.
It is for the sake of purifying the Buddha-field that he constantly performs the work of a Buddha and transforms sentient beings.
Pūrṇa, whether regarding one Buddha or many Buddhas, in their traces or their essence, his ability to diligently assist in proclaiming the Way and the Dharma has no other purpose;
in short, it is for the sake of purifying the Buddha-field. One should know this. The Buddha—
The land is fundamentally neither pure nor defiled; purity and defilement arise from one’s own mind. Thus it is said:
"According as the mind is pure, so is the Buddha-land pure. This is precisely what that refers to. Regarding the phrase "purifying the Buddha-lands," as stated in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*:
when a bodhisattva practices the path, they are able to gather in sentient beings through giving; by the time they attain Buddhahood, sentient beings free from greed come [to that land].

Those who were born in that land and so forth are such examples. Now, Pūrṇa, because he assisted in proclaiming the Buddha-way and gathered in sentient beings, when he attains Buddhahood, those sentient beings whom he was able to teach will come to be born in his land.
As for those who constantly perform the work of a Buddha to transform sentient beings—the Tathāgata performs this work solely by means of preaching the Dharma—and now, Pūrṇa...
Ratnākara, you are also able to assist in proclaiming the Dharma and teaching and transforming sentient beings.
That is to say, regarding the Āgamas, you assist in proclaiming the teachings of the "half-syllables" (*ardha-akṣara*) and perform Buddha-work to teach and transform sentient beings;

even up to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, you assist in proclaiming the purely perfect teachings and perform Buddha-work to teach and transform sentient beings. △ Third, [the section] concerning the three periods of time.
To clarify the cause for this, there are two parts. First, the formal clarification:
"O Bhikṣus, Pūrṇa was also foremost among those who expounded the Dharma under the seven Buddhas; now, among those who expound the Dharma in my presence, he is likewise foremost.
In the Bhadrakalpa, he shall also be foremost among those who expound the Dharma under all future Buddhas."
Among human beings, they shall likewise be foremost; they shall all protect, uphold, and assist in proclaiming the Buddha-dharma.

Furthermore, in the future, they shall protect, uphold, and assist in proclaiming the immeasurable and boundless Dharma of all Buddhas, teaching and benefiting immeasurable sentient beings, causing them to be established in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The first seven Buddhas clarify their past existence. This mention of "seven Buddhas" must not be conflated with the ordinary reference to the seven Buddhas of the past.

In the common usage, these consist of the three Buddhas of the *Vibhūṣaṇakalpa* (Adorned Eon) beginning with Vipaśyin and ending with Śākyamuni, together with the four Buddhas of the present *Bhadrakalpa* (Auspicious Eon). Here, however, one must [refer] to the *Vibhūṣaṇakalpa*.
The four Buddhas and the three Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa—from Dezhin-shegpa (Guṇākara) at the beginning to Kāśyapa at the end—constitute the seven Buddhas.
The statement "now, in my presence" refers to Śākyamuni, thereby clarifying the present.
The statement "in the Bhadrakalpa, those yet to come," and so forth, clarifies the future; this refers to Maitreya, Siṃha, and the others.
"He has already departed. This clarifies that he assists in proclaiming the teachings of the previous four periods.
Furthermore, in the section "In the future," it clarifies that he assists in proclaiming the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. △ Second, the explanation of the underlying intent.
For the sake of purifying the Buddha-field, he constantly exerts himself with diligent vigor to transform and guide sentient beings.
△ Second, the actual bestowal of the prediction:
Gradually fulfilling the path of a bodhisattva, after the passage of immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he shall, in this very land, attain...
He attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and was named Dharmaprabhāsa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna,
Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
That Buddha took as many trichiliocosm world-systems as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River and made them a single buddha-field of seven treasures.

It serves as the ground. The earth is as level as the palm of a hand, without mountains, hills, streams, ravines, or gullies. Within it are towers and pavilions made of the seven treasures, filling the space.
The palaces of the various devas are situated near the void; humans and devas interact, being able to see one another. There are no evil realms, nor are there women.
All sentient beings are born by transformation and are free from sexual desire. They attain great...
They possess supernormal powers; light issues from their bodies; they fly with ease; their resolve and mindfulness are firm; they are endowed with diligence and wisdom;
they are all golden in color and adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man. The sentient beings of that land always partake of two kinds of food:
first, the food of the joy of the Dharma; second, the food of the bliss of dhyāna. There are immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya, thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas [of them].
The assembly of bodhisattvas has attained great supernormal powers and the four kinds of unimpeded wisdom, being well-able to teach and transform all classes of sentient beings;
such things are beyond the reach of calculation or reckoning by the assembly of śrāvakas, yet they have all fully attained the six supernatural faculties and the three types of clear knowledge.
It also possesses the eight liberations. That buddha-field is thus adorned and perfected with such immeasurable merits.
The kalpa is named Jewel Radiance; the land is named Good Purity. The lifespan of that Buddha is immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, and the Dharma remains for a very long time.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, stupas made of the seven treasures will arise and fill the entire land.
Regarding the term "gradually": this is neither the gradualness of partial progression nor the gradualness of sequential stages.
In sum, although the realization is perfect and complete, at the time of cultivation and advancement, one must proceed from cause to fruit; this is precisely what is meant by "gradually.
Therefore, it is said that according to principle, there is no duality between the beginning and the end, yet when discussing phenomena, cause and effect are clearly distinct.
Because it is non-dual, the understanding is perfect; because it is distinct and clear, the practice is gradual.
The Buddha is named Dharmaprabhāsa (Dharma-Light) because, while in the causal stage, he was able to assist in proclaiming the path and Dharma of all Buddhas;

thus, upon reaching the fruit, he was able to realize all the path and Dharma of all Buddhas, and could further use what he had realized himself to guide and benefit sentient beings, causing them to...
One attains clear understanding; it is called the "Light of the Dharma" because it reveals, awakens, and leads one into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Regarding the statement that humans and devas meet and both are able to see one another:

one should know that since that land is different from our present world, one must not harbor doubts or difficulties about it based on the fact that humans and devas in this world cannot see each other. If one follows the literal text...
Regarding this treatise: since it is stated that the palaces of the various devas are situated near space, then the honorable may be made humble, and the superior may be made subordinate.
If the honorable can be made humble and the superior can be made subordinate, then conversely, the humble may be made honorable and the subordinate may be made superior.
Thus, humans and devas are able to interact and see one another, attaining greatness.
Regarding supernormal powers (*abhijñā*): there are those attained through realization, those attained through cultivation, and those obtained as a result of retribution (*vipākaja*).

This refers specifically to those obtained as a result of retribution. As for the thirty-two marks (*dvātriṃśan mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa*), even the universal monarchs (*cakravartin*) of this land possess these thirty-two marks;
however, they differ from those of the Buddha in terms of clarity and excellence. Now, regarding the physical marks of the people of that country:

This may also be understood by analogy. Regarding those who feed on the joy of the Dharma (*dharmaprītyāhāra*): upon hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma, they nourish their spirits with the flavor of the Dharma;

thus, they take the joy of the Dharma as their food. Regarding those who feed on the delight of meditation (*dhyānaprītāhāra*): having heard the Dharma, they practice in accordance with it and are able to enter deeply into meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*).
They thereby nourish their spirits with meditative concentration; thus, they take the delight of meditation as their food. The name of the eon is...
"Jewel-bright" (Baoming) means taking the Dharma as a jewel. The country is named "Excellently Pure" (Shanjing):
it is "excellent" because that land is devoid of the evil realms; it is "pure" because it is free from women and sexual desire. △ Second, the verse summary has two parts.

The first verse reveals and clarifies; the second verse bestows a prediction. Regarding the first two [verses], the first verse reveals and clarifies the śrāvakas, while the second verse specifically praises Pūrṇa.
Regarding the former, there are five parts; the first is a general eulogy.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Listen attentively, O bhikṣus! The path traversed by the Son of the Buddha, Because he has skillfully studied expedient means, Is inconceivable."
Regarding the term "Son of the Buddha": although their outward manifestation is that of a śrāvaka, they were originally bodhisattvas;
thus, even as śrāvakas, they are capable of inheriting the Mahāyāna lineage of the Tathāgata. For this reason, they are called Sons of the Buddha.
As for those who skillfully learn the expedient means, only the Tathāgata is able to fully possess inconceivable expedient means;
yet those sons of the Buddha are likewise well able to learn the expedient means of the Tathāgata. Because they have learned them well, [they are so called].

Originally they are Bodhisattvas, yet they may manifest as being identical to those of the Two Vehicles, or manifest as being identical to non-Buddhists, or manifest as being identical to ordinary worldlings.
Such various matters as these are all inconceivable. △ Second, clarifying the causes and conditions.
Knowing that the multitude delights in minor dharmas and fears great wisdom, the Bodhisattvas manifest as Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
This is why the Sons of the Buddha study skillful means: it is because they know that sentient beings delight in the small and fear the great.
