High. To lose it would not make one low. Since they are equal and of one suchness, then according to the true cause (*tathāgata-garbha*), they should be granted the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
Therefore, the Ever-Venerable One said: "You shall all become Buddhas. This means that all sentient beings possess the true cause and shall indeed become Buddhas.
When the Dharma-sound reaches the ear, it immediately becomes the accomplishing cause (*pariniṣpanna-hetu*). As the sutra says:
The Buddha-seed arises from conditions; for this reason, the One Vehicle is taught. If there are those who hear the Dharma, there is not one who will not become a Buddha.

Since the Buddha-seed arises from conditions, and hearing the Dharma leads inevitably to Buddhahood, then with respect to the "perceiving cause" (*vidyā-hetu*), they too shall be granted the prediction of enlightenment.
Through hearing the Dharma, various practices are initiated, thereby constituting the "conditioning cause" (*pratyaya-hetu*). As the Sūtra says:
Even those who merely raise a single hand, or slightly lower their heads, or offer a single incense stick or a single flower, have all already attained the path to Buddhahood.

Since not even a single incense stick or a single flower fails to be a cause for attaining Buddhahood, then according to the principle of the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*), they too should be granted a prediction of enlightenment.

Therefore, regardless of whether it is during the Buddha's lifetime or after his parinirvāṇa, and irrespective of whether one’s understanding is profound or shallow, there is no one who does not receive this [prediction].
At that time, he shall receive the prediction of attaining Bodhi. △ Second, showing the five kinds of Dharma-preachers, in two parts: first, clarifying those in the present;
second, clarifying those after [the Buddha’s] extinction. The former has two parts: first, clarifying the inferior grade.
Furthermore, Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that if there are those who receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, or transcribe even a single verse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*,
and who regard this scripture with the same reverence as the Buddha, making various offerings of flowers, incense, necklaces, powdered incense, ointment incense,
burning incense, silk canopies, banners and flags, robes, and music, or even merely joining their palms in respectful salutation.

These people have already made offerings to ten trillion buddhas. Having fulfilled their great vows in the presence of those buddhas, they have been born in this human world out of compassion for sentient beings.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, if anyone asks, "What kind of sentient beings will attain buddhahood in future ages?
you should point to these people and say that they will certainly attain buddhahood in future ages.
Why is this? If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, regarding even a single verse of the Lotus Sūtra, receives, maintains, reads, recites, explains, or transcribes it;

and makes various offerings to the scripture with flowers, incense, necklaces, powdered incense, ointment incense, burning incense, silk canopies, banners, pennants, robes, and music; and joins their palms in reverent salutation—such a person, among all the worlds...
They should be revered and honored with the same offerings as those given to a Tathāgata.
You should know that such a person is a great Bodhisattva who has accomplished *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and, out of compassion for sentient beings,
has made a vow to be born in this world to extensively expound and analyze the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
The five types refer to receiving and upholding [the Dharma], and so forth, up to copying it.
Since these five all constitute being a Dharma Master (*dharmabhāṇaka*), one is only entitled to that name when one can use the sublime Dharma to regulate oneself and guide others.
If one merely receives and upholds it, or merely copies it, by what means does one regulate oneself, and by what means does one guide others?
Therefore, those who uphold [this teaching] must know the source from which it is upheld; likewise, even those who transcribe it must know the source from which it is transcribed.
Only then can they establish their own standard and guide others, thereby earning the title of "Dharma Master.

Indeed, that which this sutra elucidates is solely the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena; these phenomena are precisely the three thousand modes of existence and appearance (*sanqian xingxiang*).
Regarding the myriad phenomena of the hundred realms and thousand suchnesses—these three thousand phenomena are each and every one mutually true and each and every dharma is real.

They are the entirety of the true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Therefore, if a practitioner who upholds [this teaching] can understand that all which is expressed herein is none other than the true aspect, then at the very moment of upholding it, they will be in accord with all dharmas. How is this accord achieved?
This means that externally one does not perceive the sutra being held, and internally one does not perceive a person who can hold it.
Since internal and external are thus of one suchness (*ekalakṣaṇa*), the duality of subject and object is extinguished; this is what is called the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).

Although subject and object are extinguished, it does not preclude my being the holder and the sutra being that which is held, such that the distinction between subject and object remains clearly evident. This is... [the contemplation of existence].
This is called the contemplation of the conventional (parikalpita). At the point where the subject and object are clearly distinct, they are fundamentally extinguished;
at the point where the subject and object are extinguished, their clarity is not obstructed. This is what is meant by the contemplation of the middle way (madhyamaka).

If the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is perfected, the principle of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) naturally manifests. If the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti*) is perfected, the principle of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) naturally manifests.

If the contemplation of the middle (*madhyama*) is perfected, the principle of the middle truth (*madhyama-satya*) naturally manifests. Once the ultimate truth is manifested, the virtue of wisdom (*prajñā-guṇa*) is perfected;

once the conventional truth is manifested, the virtue of liberation (*vimukti-guṇa*) is perfected; and once the middle truth is manifested, the virtue of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya-guṇa*) is perfected.
When these three contemplations are cultivated perfectly, the three truths are perfectly revealed, and the three virtues are perfectly accomplished.
Thus, one may take this as a guide for oneself and also use it to guide others; therefore, those who receive and uphold [this teaching] are also called Dharma masters.
Since this is the case for receiving and upholding, the same applies to reading, reciting, explaining, and transcribing. Therefore, these five...
All such people may be called Dharma Masters. Regarding those who should regard [this scripture] with the same reverence as the Buddha:
when the Buddha was in the world, he alone was the most honored among all that is above and below heaven; he was revered by all within both the mundane and supramundane realms.

Although he has now entered parinirvāṇa, this sutra is precisely the manifestation of the Buddha’s original intent—the Dharma-body relic of the Great Matter. Therefore, one should regard it with the same reverence as [the Buddha].

The Buddha [says]: "In various ways" and below clarifies that those five kinds of Dharma-preachers are not merely able to receive, uphold, and even transcribe [the teachings], but because they are able to regard them with reverence as if they were the Buddha, they are also able to perform the ten kinds of offerings.

"O Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know" and below clarifies their past cultivation; it clarifies that out of compassion for sentient beings, they have been born into this human world. This is the clarification.

Regarding the manifestation of his merit, there are three ways of being born: those who are born through the power of supernatural faculties (*ṛddhi*), those who are born by virtue of their vows (*praṇidhāna*), and those who are born drawn by the force of karma (*karman*).

His current birth in this human realm is one born by virtue of his vows, for the purpose of circulating this sutra. The passage beginning with "If someone should ask" below clarifies his future retribution. Why? [Because...]

Therefore, the following passage clarifies the underlying intention. It asks: how is it known that this person’s past planting of seeds and present cultivation of merit result in such superior retribution?

Thus it says: "If a son of good family, etc., is able to take this sutra as their own standard in five ways and provide the ten kinds of offerings, then such a person is extremely rare. This refers to ordinary beings.
All the worlds should gaze upon and pay homage to him. "All the worlds" refers to the nine kinds of worlds;
for this sutra clarifies that all nine realms ultimately return to the Buddha-realm, which is the great causal condition for the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world.
He desires to cause all beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Such a person is able to take this sutra as their own guide.

By thus offering worship, one will before long be able to personally realize the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and furthermore, be able to guide others so that they too may realize the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Because of the power of their received vows, they take pity on sentient beings and come to this world to propagate the Dharma and transform living beings;
therefore, know that these are great Bodhisattvas whose past seeds were truly superior. This is indeed so.
This is understood. Since one is able to expound this sutra extensively, the excellence of the merit manifested thereby can also be known.
For this reason, one should honor such a person with the same offerings given to the Tathāgata.
That the excellence of the retribution received will lead them to attain Buddhahood can likewise be known. △ Second, explaining the superior grade.
How much more so for those who are able to fully receive and uphold it, and provide various offerings.

O Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that such persons, having voluntarily relinquished their own pure karmic retribution, will, out of compassion for sentient beings, be born in this degenerate age after my parinirvāṇa to widely expound this sutra.
This is even more so than those of the superior grade. "Receiving and upholding" refers to one of the five types of Dharma-preachers mentioned specifically here, which subsumes the other four.
"Various offerings" is a general description. To say "one who is able to do all" means being able to receive and uphold the entire sūtra, as well as being able to make all manner of offerings.
The former [grade] was only able to receive and uphold a single verse; therefore, this is the inferior grade.
Chapter. Herein, because one is able to receive, uphold, and make offerings to the entire work, it is called the "Superior Grade" (Uttama-pakṣa).
Next, from the section on Bhaiṣajyarāja downward, its meritorious practice is clarified. Regarding the phrase "pure karmic retribution":

if a person is able to receive and uphold [the teaching], they will necessarily be able to give rise to contemplative practice based on their understanding until they reach the stage of "semblance" (nirvedha-bhāgīya). If they reach the stage of semblance, then coarse defilements will first...
"Fallen. This refers to the retribution experienced when delusions of views and thoughts have already been eliminated and the six sense organs have attained purity.
This clarifies the seeds planted in the past. The passage beginning with "After my extinction" clarifies its present efficacy;

it means that because the retribution possessed by such a person is thus pure, the seeds planted in the past must be exceedingly superior. Having attained purity oneself, one further desires to cause others to do so as well.
Having attained purity, they relinquish the karmic retribution of their own pure state out of compassion for sentient beings.
By virtue of the power of their vows, they are born into this world of the five turbidities in order to extensively expound and analyze the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
Thus, the excellence of their future retribution—namely, that they shall become Buddhas—is self-evident and requires no further mention. △
Second, clarifying what occurs after my parinirvāṇa, in two parts. First, clarifying the inferior grade:

If there is a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, after my parinirvāṇa, is able to secretly preach even a single verse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* for the sake of a single person, you should know that such a person is an envoy of the Tathāgata, one dispatched by the Tathāgata, acting on behalf of the Tathāgata.
Regarding this matter, I humbly consider that for the sake of a single individual, if one were to explain even a single phrase,

there might be those of inferior capacity whose learning has not yet been broadened and whose insight has not yet been fully perfected, such that they would be unable to provide complete answers to various challenges and inquiries.
Therefore, they can only privately recite a single phrase for one person; they cannot extensively expound this sutra amidst a great assembly.
Regarding the term "messenger of the Tathāgata": one who is sent by a master is called a messenger.
Since the Tathāgata is the sovereign of a single transformation, and this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* teaches and transforms all beings, when he speaks this sutra—
Thus, he speaks in accordance with reality and discourses in conformity with wisdom; therefore, this sutra is the supreme, wondrous teaching.

Even if this Dharma-preacher were to privately explain a single phrase for a single person, it would be entirely that which has been spoken by the Tathāgata in accordance with reality and in conformity with wisdom.
Consequently, such a person is an emissary of the Tathāgata. Regarding the phrase "dispatched by the Tathāgata," the Tathāgata...
There is no other matter; his sole concern is to transform sentient beings through the preaching of the Dharma.

Yet, for this Dharma Master, even speaking a single difficult-to-articulate phrase constitutes preaching the Dharma, and even acting for the sake of a single person constitutes transforming a sentient being.
Therefore, he is one dispatched by the Tathāgata to carry out the work of the Tathāgata. △ Second, the explanation of the superior grade.
How much more so when one extensively preaches it for others amidst the great assembly?

Regarding the phrase "how much more so": even a Dharma teacher of inferior grade, possessing but a single verse, is still a messenger of the Tathāgata, dispatched by the Tathāgata to perform the work of the Tathāgata;
how much more so then a Dharma teacher of superior grade within the great assembly?
In the midst [of this], one does not merely steal it for oneself, but widely proclaims it to others; one does not merely recite a single phrase, but expounds it as an entire volume.
Is this not acting as an emissary of the Tathāgata, even to the point of performing the work of the Tathāgata?
△ Third, raising the offenses and blessings of those who believe and those who slander. First, clarifying that the slanderer incurs offense.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, if there were an evil person who, with an unwholesome mind, stood before a Buddha for an entire kalpa constantly reviling and abusing him,
his transgression would still be light. However, if a person were to utter a single evil word in disparagement of those, whether lay or ordained, who read and recite the Lotus Sūtra,
their transgression would be exceedingly grave.
Regarding the term "evil person": even within a single kalpa, the duration of time is exceedingly long; to constantly revile and abuse the Buddha is for one's speech to be extremely wicked.
By this, one naturally incurs immeasurable heavy retribution. Yet, even that is still light; therefore it is said, "If there is a person who... (and so forth).
As for a person who disparages [the Buddha] with a single evil word, such a person is not necessarily [one who has committed a fundamental offense].
This is an evil person; it is not necessarily the case that their inner mind harbors unwholesome intent, nor does the duration of time need to be long.
Yet, by disparaging them with a single word, the language used may not even be extremely coarse or malicious.
Nevertheless, the sin they incur is far more profound and heavy than the former case. This is the Tathāgata’s skillful means of making such comparisons.
This speaks to the extreme gravity of the sin of disparaging a Dharma Master, thereby clarifying that a Dharma Master must not be reviled;
it does not mean that there is actually such a thing as slandering the Buddha for an entire kalpa. Nevertheless, even the sin of ultimately slandering the Buddha is still relatively light.

Yet the sin of disparaging them is exceedingly grave. Why is this so? It is because, regarding the Tathāgata, there are no delusions or hindrances that are not destroyed, and no principles of truth that are not clearly realized.
Thus, even when reviled, he does not become angry; when praised, he does not rejoice; when opposed, he is not diminished;
and when favored, he does not increase. For such insults and abuse do nothing to diminish the Tathāgata.

Therefore, their offense is still relatively light. As for those who are householders or monastics, even if they are able to read and recite this sutra, yet have not yet broken through the obstacles of delusion and have not yet clarified the truth of the ultimate reality, they may give rise to anger at the mere mention of a single word of disparagement;
or there are those who, because of it, abandon what they have read and recited. This being so—
If one abandons recitation and study, by what means can understanding arise, leading to the arousal of practice and entry into realization?

Since one cannot achieve this oneself, how could one possibly teach and transform others? Therefore, the Way of the Dharma is severed from this point, and the lineage of the Buddhas is cut off from here.
Thus, the sin of disparaging it is exceedingly grave. II. Clarifying that the Faithful Obtain Blessings.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that whoever reads and recites the Lotus Sūtra is adorned with the adornments of the Buddha;

they are carried upon the shoulders of the Tathāgata. To whatever place such a person goes, one should face them in reverence, join one’s palms with single-minded devotion, and pay homage, making offerings with respect and praise, using flowers, incense, necklaces, powdered incense, unguents, and burning incense.
With canopies of fine silk, banners, streamers, robes, and delicacies, and by performing various musical performances—offering these supreme gifts among humans—one should worship them.
One should hold celestial jewels and scatter them; one should present heaps of heavenly treasures as offerings. Why is this so?
This person joyfully expounds the Dharma; upon hearing it for even a moment, they immediately attain the ultimate *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
As for the adornment of a Buddha, there is no other adornment than the adornment of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). Now this person reads...
When reciting, if one realizes that there is neither a person who recites nor a scripture being recited, then subject and object are extinguished;

this is precisely the adornment of oneself with the samādhi of the Tathāgata. Furthermore, within this state where subject and object are extinguished, it does not preclude me from being the reciter and the scripture from being the object of recitation; thus, subject and object are clearly distinguished. This is precisely...
They come to adorn themselves with wisdom. As for "bearing and carrying": that which rests on the back is called "borne" (he), and that which rests on the shoulder is called "carried" (dan).
That which the Tathāgata bears and carries is none other than unsurpassed bodhi. Now, this person reads and recites this sutra.
Thus, one is able to give rise to understanding, initiate practice, and enter into realization, thereby attaining unsurpassed bodhi. As for the destination reached:
those who can read and recite this wondrous Sūtra of the True Mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) are those who are borne by the Buddha.
For them, the person is entirely the Dharma, and the Dharma is entirely the person; every thought-moment is the True Mark, and likewise, every place is the True Mark.
Therefore, according to whichever direction one is facing, one should pay homage accordingly. Regarding "with a single mind" and so forth:
this means that one should not merely show reverence through the three karmas of body, speech, and mind, but should further add the ten kinds of offerings, such as flowers and incense.
Because he embodies the Dharma within himself and his person is entirely the Dharma, among humans he is the foremost among men, and among devas he is the foremost among devas.
He is the foremost among men; therefore, one should honor him with the supreme offerings of the human realm and present him with the gathered treasures of the heavens.
Why is this? [The following passage] explains this by way of a downward transition. The meaning is: why should one direct one's prostrations toward him, and even offer the treasures of the heavens?
Therefore, the explanation says: "This person joyfully preaches the Dharma; upon hearing it for even a moment, one immediately attains..."

This is because it leads to ultimate bodhi. As for the statement that "this person rejoices," it does not mean that they feel joy merely upon seeing someone perform prostrations, offerings, and so forth. Rather, it means they see that the person before them is capable of such [practice];

they recognize the person's earnestness regarding the Dharma and perceive their readiness as a vessel for transformation, and thus they give rise to joy. Furthermore, when preaching the Dharma, one need not...
"I have long heard [of this]. Upon hearing it even for a brief moment, one immediately attains ultimate Bodhi. Why is this?
If one hears other sutras and thereby gives rise to understanding and practice, then at the time of realization, one may only attain the Two Vehicles or only the partial, gradual path.

However, regarding this present sutra, if one does not hear it, that is one thing; but if one hears it and gives rise to understanding, practice, and realization, one then ascends to the stage of the first aspiration for enlightenment."
Abiding. A single arousal [of the mind] is the arousal of all; because the initial arousal of the mind and its ultimate consummation are not distinct, it is itself ultimate Bodhi.

△ Second, the verses in praise, in three parts: First, the exhortation to practice; second, the thirteen lines beginning with "If there be... which constitute the actual verses; third, the one line beginning with "Bhaiṣajyarāja...
which serves as a concluding eulogy. Regarding the first two [parts], the first is the exhortation to practice alone.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If one wishes to abide in the Buddha-way and achieve spontaneous wisdom, one should always diligently make offerings to those who receive and uphold the Lotus Sutra."

Regarding "spontaneous wisdom" (*svayambhū-jñāna*): this wisdom arises entirely from the principle of the true nature (*dharmatā*). Because it arises in accordance with the essence of reality, it does not depend on artificial effort;
hence it is called spontaneous wisdom. Regarding "those who make offerings and uphold [it]": those persons who uphold it have already been able to abide in the Buddha-way.
Therefore, those who wish to abide in the Buddha-way should make offerings, so that I too may attain it.
They abide in the Buddha-way. Those who uphold [this teaching] have already been able to accomplish spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*).
Therefore, those who wish to accomplish spontaneous wisdom should make offerings so that they too may attain the accomplishment of spontaneous wisdom.
△ Second, the exhortation to practice repeatedly.
If there are those who wish to quickly attain all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*), they should uphold this sutra and make offerings to those who uphold it.
Regarding "quickly attaining," this refers to ascending to the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) and opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision within this very lifetime.
This is even more urgent than the previous case; therefore, one should not only make offerings to and uphold [the teachings of] those who uphold it, but should also [practice them] oneself.

This is for the purpose of upholding [the teaching]. △ Second, the actual verses, which are twofold: first, verses on the five kinds of Dharma-preachers; second, verses on the offenses and blessings of faith and slander.
The first [section] is again twofold: first, verses on the present; second, verses on after extinction. The first [of these two] is again twofold: first, verses on the inferior grade.
If there are those who can receive and uphold the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, know that they are the messengers sent by the Buddha, out of compassion for all sentient beings.
△ Second, the verse on the superior grade.
Those who are able to receive and uphold this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* abandon the pure lands and are born here out of compassion for sentient beings.
You should know that such persons can be born wherever they wish; they are able to widely expound the unsurpassed Dharma in this degenerate world.
One should offer celestial flowers and incense, as well as celestial jewel-encrusted robes and heaps of exquisite heavenly treasures, to those who preach the Dharma.
△ Second, the verses on the two [periods] after his parinirvāṇa; first, the verse skipping ahead to the superior grade.
In the evil age after my parinirvāṇa, those who are able to uphold this sutra should join their palms in reverent salutation as if making offerings to the World-Honored One.
With the finest delicacies, various sweets, and diverse garments, they should make offerings to these sons of the Buddha, hoping to hear [this teaching] for even a brief moment.
△ Second, the verse summarizing the inferior grade:
If there are those who, in future ages, receive and uphold this sutra, I shall dispatch them among human beings to perform the work of the Tathāgata.
△ Second, two verses on the transgressions and blessings of faith and slander. First, a verse on the transgression incurred by the slanderer:
If, throughout an entire eon, one constantly harbors an unwholesome mind and, with a wrathful countenance, reviles the Buddha, one incurs immeasurable and heavy transgressions.
If there are those who read, recite, and uphold this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, yet for even a moment address them with evil words, their sin shall exceed that of the former.
△ Second, a verse on the merit obtained by those who have faith.
Suppose there were someone seeking the Buddha-way who, for the duration of an eon, stood before me with palms joined and praised me with countless verses.
Because of this praise of the Buddha, they would obtain immeasurable merit. Yet the merit of one who extols and praises the upholder of this sutra exceeds even that.
For eighty billion eons, one may offer the most exquisite forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, and tactile objects to those who uphold this sutra.
Having made such offerings, if one should hear it for even a moment, one ought to rejoice within oneself, thinking: "I have now attained a great benefit."
△ Third, the summary and praise. "O Bhaiṣajyarāja, I now tell you: among all the sūtras I have preached, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the foremost.
△ Second, clarifying the superiority of the Dharma upheld, in two parts: first, the prose; second, the verses. The first part has two sections; the first is the direct [explanation].
Praising the excellence of the Dharma. This section doubly demonstrates the three tracks (*triyāna*). The first four [sections] are as follows: first, praising by way of the teaching;

second, "One should know" and below, praising by way of the person; third, "Abiding below" and below, praising by way of the place; fourth, "There are many" and below, praising by way of practice. Within the first two [of these], the first is the actual praise.
At that time, the Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja: "Of the immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of sūtras that I have spoken—
those already spoken, those being spoken now, and those yet to be spoken— among them all, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is the most difficult to believe and the most difficult to understand."
Regarding the phrase "speaking again": previously, based on the person who is honored, this was already proclaimed as one instance of an edict.

However, the reason the person who can uphold [the teaching] is honored is entirely due to the excellence of the Dharma they uphold. Therefore, now, based once more on the excellence of the Dharma, it is proclaimed again as another instance of an edict.
*Mahāsattva* refers to a Great Bodhisattva; because they are able to give rise to the great mind (*mahācitta*) and cultivate...
Because they perform great practices, realize great fruits, and return to the Great Abode, they are called "Great Bodhisattvas. The passage beginning with "What I have [taught]" is a formal address;
it means that throughout my single lifetime, the sutras I have preached number in the tens of thousands, hundreds of thousands, and even millions.

Although they are exceedingly numerous, to speak of them in essence, they do not go beyond what has been taught, what is being taught now, and what will be taught hereafter. Regarding those of the past and the present...
Among all the teachings that have been spoken, only this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is the most difficult to believe and the most difficult to understand.
Yet, how is it known that those teachings already spoken are easy to believe and easy to understand?

Those "already spoken" refer to all the various sūtras from the *Prajñāpāramitā* downwards. These sūtras were taught either in combination with other doctrines, or as standalone teachings, or in contrast to others.

Or it may be taught by combining [the two]. Since there are both the "combined" (*jiantu*) and the "contrasted" (*duidai*) modes, then whatever is sudden therein is indeed sudden, and whatever is gradual is indeed gradual;

even down to the distinctions between the Great and Small Vehicles, the Half and Full Teachings, the Partial and Perfect, and the Provisional and Real—each being clearly differentiated, they will naturally become easy to believe in and understand.
In this present sutra, however, there is no longer any combination or contrast; it is solely and purely perfect.
Therefore, the gradual is itself the sudden; there is no gradual apart from the sudden. Even so, the provisional is itself the real; there is no provisional apart from the real.
Thus, this sutra alone is difficult to believe and difficult to understand. How can we see that what is being taught now is easy to believe and easy to understand?
What is being taught now is the *Anantarya-samudgata-nirdeśa-sūtra* (The Sutra of Immeasurable Meanings). Although they share the same seat and the same nectar of enlightenment (*amṛta*),...

In the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, that which is elucidated merely states that all phenomena arise from the single true reality (*ekasatyalakṣaṇa*), namely, emerging as the two teachings of sudden and gradual, as well as the three paths and four fruits;

it does not clarify the gathering of the many back into the one, and is therefore easy to believe and easy to understand. This sutra, however, clarifies the gathering of the many back into the one, according to what exists.

The two dharmas, the three paths, and the four fruits are all the single true reality; therefore, they are difficult to believe and difficult to understand. How can it be seen that when these are taught, they become easy to believe and easy to understand? "When these are taught" refers to the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*. Although it likewise possesses a single flavor, its subsequent exposition of the four teachings—supporting the precepts (*vinaya*) and discussing the eternal—is specifically intended for those of dull faculties in the final age. Furthermore, [the text continues: ...and... [text fragment] ...the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda Sūtra*, the *Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra*, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, and the *Amitāyus Sūtra*—these are all the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*. Why? Because they all expound the eternal, the blissful, the self, and the pure. Moreover, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* is the ultimate teaching among all the Buddha’s teachings. Why? Because it is the most profound and subtle. It is like the ocean among all waters, the sun among all fires, Mount Sumeru among all mountains, and space among all voids. It is also like the great physician among all physicians, the great king among all kings, and the great elephant among all elephants. It is also like the great jewel among all jewels, the great medicine among all medicines, and the great treasure among all treasures. It is also like the great Dharma-king among all Dharma-kings, the great Bodhisattva among all Bodhisattvas, and the great Arhat among all Arhats. It is also like the great teacher among all teachers, the great guide among all guides, and the great leader among all leaders. It is also like the great ship among all ships, the great bridge among all bridges, and the great ferryman among all ferrymen. It is also like the great non-consciousness among all non-consciousnesses, the great non-contact among all non-contacts, the great non-feeling among all non-feelings, the great non-thirst among all non-thirsts, the great non-grasping among all non-graspings, and the great non-becoming among all non-becomings. It is also like the great non-birth among all non-births, the great non-old-age among all non-old-ages, the great non-sickness among all non-sicknesses, and the great non-death among all non-deaths. It is also like the great non-suffering among all non-sufferings, the great non-emptiness among all non-emptinesses, the great non-falsity among all non-falsities, and the great non-delusion among all non-delusions. It is also like the great non-anger among all non-angers, the great non-hatred among all non-hatreds, and the great non-affliction among all afflictions. It is also like the great non-defilement among all non-defilements, the great non-purity among all non-purities, and the great non-impurity among all impurities. It is also like the great non-outflow among all non-outflows, the great non-leakage among all leakages, and the great non-turbidity among all turbidities. It is also like the great non-bondage among all non-bondages, the great non-fetter among all fetters, and the great non-obstruction among all obstructions. It is also like the great non-covering among all non-coverings, the great non-obscuration among all non-obscurations, and the great non-concealment among all concealments. It is also like the great non-hindrance among all non-hindrances, the great non-barrier among all barriers, and the great non-limit among all limits. It is also like the great non-boundary among all non-boundaries, the great non-extreme among all non-extremes, and the great non-center among all non-centers. It is also like the great non-beginning among all non-beginnings, the great non-middle among all non-middles, and the great non-end among all non-ends. It is also like the great non-past among all non-pasts, the great non-f

Because those who have not yet matured possess a mixture of provisional and small teachings, they find these easy to believe and easy to understand; this sutra, however, is purely one, perfect, and real.
It subsequently explains and reveals the *Zang*, *Tong*, and *Bie* [teachings], opening them up and manifesting them so as to form a single, pure, and perfect teaching.
Therefore, it is the most difficult to believe and the most difficult to understand. In short, there is only this.
This sutra is precisely that which fulfills the fundamental intention of all Buddhas appearing in the world;

it clarifies the causes and conditions of the one great matter, so that all sentient beings may attain the opening, showing, awakening to, and entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, whereby the nine realms all return to the same destination.

The three vehicles all converge herein; therefore, whether it has been, is being, or will be explained, this alone is the sutra. It is difficult to believe, and its understanding is likewise not easy.
△ Second, the statement of the underlying intent.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, this sutra is the secret and essential treasury of all Buddhas; it must not be distributed or recklessly bestowed upon others.
It is guarded by the World-Honored Buddhas and has never been openly proclaimed since the distant past.
Even while the Tathāgata is currently present, there are still many who harbor resentment and jealousy toward it, let alone after his parinirvāṇa.
Regarding the phrase "this sutra and others": it asks why this sutra alone is so difficult to believe and difficult to understand.

Therefore, its underlying intent is revealed: "This sutra is the secret and essential treasury of all Buddhas," and so forth. This essential point has been long kept in silence, not being hurriedly proclaimed;
because it is most profound and subtle, it is called "secret. All that is performed [by the Buddhas] is always for the sake of this single purpose. This is...

It is called "Essential" (*yao*) because it contains the essential principles. It is called a "Treasury" (*zang*) because it encompasses all three thousand natures and characteristics and the hundred realms and thousand suchnesses.
Indeed, it is the secret and essential treasury of all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time, including myself, Śākyamuni.
The Tathāgata has preached it for the sake of benefiting all worlds; thus, he firmly desires—
As for its distribution: although one certainly wishes to bestow it, one must not distribute it or bestow it recklessly.
Since this sutra is difficult to believe and difficult to understand, those who possess wisdom will naturally give rise to faith and understanding upon hearing it;
however, if those without wisdom hear it, they may not necessarily believe it, but instead may give rise to doubt and slander. Therefore—
There are those who would fall into suffering; for such individuals, this [teaching] would not only be of no benefit, but would actually cause harm.

Therefore, it must not be recklessly distributed or bestowed. Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, regard this sutra as the secret and essential treasury of all Buddhas, they guard, cherish, and protect it. It is thus maintained by the Buddhas.
Because it was protected [from those not yet ready], I have never explicitly taught it since more than forty years ago.
Since I have said that I have never explicitly taught it, it follows that I have indeed taught it secretly. Therefore, within the *Avataṃsaka*, it is not that it has not been taught;
rather, it was taught in conjunction with other [teachings] and was not explicitly revealed. This is even the case within the *Prajñāpāramitā*. It is not that... [it has not been taught].
It was never spoken [explicitly]. Rather, it was taught by way of "conjunction" (*dai*) while still maintaining the two [aspects], and thus was not revealed directly until this very day.

At the Great Assembly on Mount Ling, since the capacity [of the audience] has matured and the time has arrived, I have finally set aside the methods of "conjunction," "exclusive," and "partial conjunction," and am now teaching it directly and explicitly.
As for the phrase "and this sutra," it means that although today the capacity has matured and the time has arrived, [the teaching of this sutra is distinct].

To explain it clearly: however, because it is generally difficult to believe and difficult to understand, even when the Tathāgata himself is present and expounding it, if the mind, physical form, and actions of the speaker are preeminent, that which is spoken must be exceedingly sublime;
yet there are still many who harbor resentment and jealousy. To briefly illustrate this, when the fourfold assembly of humans and devas each gives rise to doubt and wavers in their attachments.
This is their resentment. When [the teaching] was explained in detail by Xu Guang, five thousand people left their seats and departed; this is their jealousy.

If, at the time after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, the person who can preach it does not necessarily possess superior karma of form and mind, then although what is preached is the Tathāgata’s wondrous Dharma, it may not necessarily be able to exhaust its full meaning.
If this were so, then those who harbor resentment and jealousy could be known even more clearly.
Because people have harbored resentment and jealousy toward this sutra—whether it was present in the world or after my passing—I have never revealed it openly from the past until now.
You must not recklessly distribute or bestow it upon others; in short, it is the secret and essential treasury of all Buddhas. And...
This is because it is most difficult to believe and difficult to understand. △ Second, the praise by way of persons:

"O Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that after the Tathāgata has passed into extinction, those who are able to write, uphold, read, recite, and make offerings [to this sutra], and who explain it for others—the Tathāgata shall clothe them with his robe, and they shall also be protected by the Buddhas currently residing in other directions."
Reflect: this person possesses the power of great faith, the power of aspiration, and the power of all roots of goodness.
You should know that such a person dwells together with the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata will then stroke their head with his own hand.
Because the Dharma is supreme, those who are able to write it down and uphold it, and even those who explain it, are likewise supreme.
The Tathāgata is one who is covered by robes; these robes are the Great Patience of Quiescent Extinction (*mahā-śānti-kṣānti*).
Since the Tathāgata dwells within this Patience of Quiescent Extinction while preaching this sutra, those who are able to receive, uphold, and [explain] it are likewise [supreme].
They cultivate the great patience of ultimate quiescence (*mahā-śānti-kṣānti*) and abide therein.
Since both their practice and their abiding are identical to the Tathāgata’s great patience of ultimate quiescence, the Tathāgata covers them with his robe.

Furthermore, they are those who are protected and remembered by all Buddhas; for this sutra is that which is protected and remembered by all Buddhas, and now they are able to receive, uphold, and maintain it.

Such a person is able to harmonize with the mindfulness of all Buddhas; therefore, the Buddhas employ their mindfulness that protects this sutra to, in turn, protect and sustain the person who upholds it.

As for those with great power of faith—whether it be the faith, precepts, and goodness of humans and devas, the faith in the truths and conditions of the two vehicles, or the faith in the six perfections of the bodhisattvas—all of these are likewise...
This is called faith, yet it cannot be called great faith, nor can it be called the power of faith.

Now, being able to receive, uphold, believe, and understand this sutra—since this sutra is the Perfect and Sudden Mahāyāna which elucidates the sole Great Matter of the causal conditions for enlightenment—the one who possesses such faith is said to have great faith. Because this faith is once held and forever maintained, it is called "great."

This is the power of faith. Regarding the power of aspiration: whether it be the aspiration for precepts and goodness by humans and devas, or even the aspiration for the six perfections by bodhisattvas, these are all called aspirations; yet they cannot be termed the "power of aspiration."
Now, being able to aspire to this sutra—aiming solely for the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena—is therefore called the power of aspiration.

As for the power of roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*): if humans or devas can cultivate the goodness of precepts, the two vehicles can cultivate the truths and conditions (*satya-pratītyasamutpāda*), and bodhisattvas can cultivate the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), these are also called roots of goodness; yet they do not [in themselves] receive the name "power of roots of goodness."

By the power of this, if one is now able to receive and uphold this wondrous sutra of the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, then one can give rise to the wisdom that contemplates the true mark within this wondrous realm of the true mark.

By using the contemplation to illumine the realm, and by using the realm to give rise to contemplation, when the realm and contemplation become as one, immeasurable roots of goodness will be born and grow from this; this is then called [the stage of] the various...
This is the power of the roots of goodness. To "dwell together with the Tathāgata" means that dwelling signifies a place of rest.
The Tathāgata has no other place of rest than the secret treasury of the three virtues (*triguṇa-guhya-kośa*), which serves as his abode.

Now, being able to receive and uphold this sutra, one is able to possess singular and perpetual faith; possessing such great power of faith, the virtue of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is accomplished. There is...
When the power of aspiration is firm and its source is profound, the virtue of liberation (*vimukti-guṇa*) is perfected.

When the power of roots of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*) enables perfect contemplation and perfect illumination, the virtue of wisdom (*prajñā-guṇa*) is perfected. Once these three virtues are perfectly accomplished, one is identical to the dwelling place of the Tathāgata;
that is, one is born into the family of the Tathāgata and dwells together with the Tathāgata. Thus, one becomes a... [Tathāgata].

As for those whose heads are stroked by the Tathāgata’s hand: having been born into the family of the Tathāgata and dwelling together with the Tathāgata, they are capable of inheriting the family estate of the Tathāgata and capable of succeeding to the position of the Dharma King;
therefore, the Tathāgata strokes their heads with his hand. Because they have had their heads stroked by the Tathāgata and have dwelt together with him, they also become [the Tathāgata’s...]
Because he is protected by mindfulness and covered by the [Dharma-]robe, the person is held in the highest esteem.
The reason the person is so esteemed is that the Dharma they uphold is supremely excellent. △ Third, praising him by way of his station.

Bhaiṣajyarāja, wherever this may be—whether it be where it is being preached, read, recited, written, or where the scroll of the sutra resides—one should erect a stupa made of the seven precious substances, making it exceedingly high, wide, and magnificently adorned. It is unnecessary to enshrine relics therein. Why is this?
Because within it already resides the entire body of the Tathāgata. This stupa should be honored with all manner of flowers, incense, and necklaces.
With silk canopies, banners, and streamers, and with music, song, and hymns, they shall offer worship, pay homage, show respect, and offer praise.
If there are those who see this stūpa, prostrate before it, and make offerings, you should know that all such persons draw near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Regarding the statement that "stūpas should be erected for all," if one discusses the erection of stūpas, there are four locations:
namely, where the Buddhas were born, where they attained the Way, where they turned the wheel of Dharma, and where they entered nirvāṇa.

Now, this wondrous sūtra is that from which the Dharma-body arises, that through which bodhi is realized, that by which the wheel of Dharma is turned, and that from which nirvāṇa is attained. Therefore, in accordance with these...
Wherever this sutra is preached, and wherever it remains, a stupa made of the seven precious jewels should be erected.
Within this [stupa] already resides the entire body of the Tathāgata; this is the entirety of the Dharma-body (dharmakāya).
Since the entirety of the Dharma-body is already present, there is no further need for the relics of the physical body (rūpakāya). All such [relics] are close to Bodhi.

This scripture elucidates that the sole object is unsurpassed bodhi; therefore, whether it be the site (*āśraya*) or the correct practice (*samyak-pratipatti*), by making offerings to this stūpa or even prostrating before it, one draws near to unsurpassed bodhi.
Because the Dharma itself is supreme, its location is likewise supreme, and thus one should erect stūpas everywhere. From this, it is known that one should perform prostrations and offerings.
This is because they all draw near to Bodhi. △ Fourth, praising the three [vehicles] by way of their practice. First, the Dharma; second, the simile; third, the application.
Regarding the first two, the first concerns the cause.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, there are many people, both lay and ordained, who practice the bodhisattva path;

yet if they are unable to see, hear, read, recite, copy, uphold, or make offerings to this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, you should know that such persons have not yet skillfully practiced the bodhisattva path.
If there are those who hear this sutra, they will be able to practice the path of the bodhisattva well.
Those who have not yet practiced the bodhisattva path well are the followers of the three vehicles, the five teachings, and the seven expedient means;
they initiate their practice based on the first three teachings. If one initiates practice based on the first three teachings, although it is indeed practicing the [bodhisattva] path...
Although one may practice the path of the bodhisattva, it cannot be called "virtuous conduct.
Because the teaching upon which it relies is both Hinayana and provisional, the conduct arising from it is likewise neither Great nor Real. Therefore, when the time comes to realize the fruit—

However, because they only attain the two vehicles of humans and devas, as well as the partial and gradual [teachings], although they are indeed practicing the Way, they cannot be said to be "skillfully practicing the Bodhisattva Way. Only upon hearing this sutra can one become a skillful practitioner;
for this sutra exclusively elucidates the Buddha’s knowledge and vision regarding the single great cause and condition, and thus that which expresses it is the One Vehicle.
The teaching of the Perfect Reality clarifies that all phenomena in the world are eternally abiding in their true nature (*dharmatā*);
thus, that which is expounded is the principle of the One Vehicle’s Perfect Reality. It clarifies that even raising a hand or bowing the head leads to the attainment of the Buddha-way;
thus, that which is initiated is the practice of the One Vehicle’s Perfect Reality. Therefore, by hearing the teaching of the Perfect Reality, one gives rise to...
When the practice of perfect reality manifests the principle of perfect reality, one is able to attain the perfect and unsurpassed Bodhi and open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
therefore, it is called "skillfully practicing the path of the Bodhisattva. △ Second, [the section] concerning the fruit.
If there are sentient beings seeking the Buddha-way who see or hear this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, and having heard it,
believe, understand, accept, and uphold it, you should know that such persons draw near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Regarding "having heard, one believes and understands," etc.: one believes that what was taught in the past was partial and provisional, while what is taught today is complete and real.

One understands that the partial and provisional of the past is precisely the complete and real of today, and the complete and real of today is precisely the partial and provisional of the past. Because practice arises from understanding, one upholds [the teaching]. Because...
Because one enters into realization through practice, one attains proximity to Bodhi. There are two kinds of proximity:
first, proximity in terms of immediate proximity, which refers to the fulfillment of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), being near the Bodhi of the First Abode (*prathamā-bhūmi*);

second, proximity in terms of relative proximity, which refers to the final mind of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi*), being near the Bodhi of Sublime Enlightenment (*suviśuddha-bodhi*). The present case concerns proximity in terms of immediate proximity. △ Second, the analogy: namely—
The preceding section clarifies that while one may initiate practice based on the three previous teachings, one does not yet skillfully practice the path of a bodhisattva.
Only by relying on the present sutra and initiating practice can one skillfully practice the path of a bodhisattva.
To illustrate this through a metaphor, it is like a person suffering from thirst (and so forth). The text is divided into two parts; the first is a parable concerning what is not yet skillful.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, it is like a person who, parched with thirst and needing water, digs for it on a high plateau;
yet seeing only dry earth, he knows that the water is still far off.

"Those who have people" refers to sentient beings who seek the Buddha-way. "Thirsty and exhausted" means that these beings have long dwelt in birth and death, being scorched by the fires of ignorance, afflictions, the five turbidities, and the eight sufferings; therefore, they are said to be thirsty and exhausted.
"Requiring water" means they require the water of the principle of unsurpassed bodhi to satisfy their thirst and exhaustion. Although they desire...
One seeks unexcelled bodhi, yet in seeking it, one does not find the proper method. To seek by relying on the three previous teachings is like that high plateau.
As for "seeking through excavation," this refers to relying on the Tripiṭaka (Śrāvaka) teaching to give rise to the contemplation of analytical emptiness;
relying on the Shared Teaching to give rise to the contemplation of essential emptiness; and relying on the Distinct Teaching to give rise to the contemplation of successive [emptiness].
Regarding the second contemplation: all such contemplations as these are practiced without being in accord with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*);

thus, they are like digging into high ground in search of water and seeing only dry soil, thereby knowing that the water is still far off. The contemplation of the emptiness of analysis (*vicāra-śūnyatā*) perceives only the partial truth (*ekadeśa-satya*);
the contemplation of the emptiness of essence (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) perceives only the truth that encompasses the middle; and the contemplation of the gradual stages perceives only...
Those who follow the distinct and gradual [teachings] do not perceive the water of the perfect and true principle; they are like those who see only dry earth and know that water is still far off.
△ Second, the analogy for wholesome conduct.
Exerting effort without ceasing, he eventually sees moist soil and gradually reaches mud; his mind becomes certain that water must be near.
"Without ceasing" means that by exerting effort without ceasing upon the high plateau, he eventually comes to see moist soil.

This is a metaphor for the three preceding teachings. Once the present sutra reveals and clarifies [the truth], the understanding of those three preceding teachings becomes perfect (round) understanding, just as when one applies effort without ceasing.

Since the understandings of the three teachings have all become perfect understanding, the contemplation that arises based on that understanding likewise transforms the contemplations of the three preceding teachings into perfect contemplation; thus, it immediately turns what preceded.
By means of the contemplation that analyzes the stages of the substance, one achieves the contemplation of the perfectly interfused Middle Way. This is like turning over moist soil.
By entering the stage of semblance through contemplative practice, one likewise transforms the views of the three previous teachings into the perfect view;
transforms the view of partial truth into the perfect truth; transforms the view that contains the middle into the immediate realization of the middle.
One turns away from the view of sequential progression and perceives perfect interfusion, like gradually reaching the mud at the bottom of a pond.

By entering through similarity, one attains partial realization (*praveśa*), breaking one grade of ignorance and manifesting one portion of the three virtues (*triguṇa*); this is like definitively knowing that water must be near.
△ Third, the synthesis, which further has three parts: first, the formal synthesis; second, the explanation of the intent; third, the exclusion of errors. Regarding the first two [parts]: first—
This analogy is not yet complete.

It is the same for the bodhisattva: if they have not heard, have not understood, and have not yet practiced this Lotus Sūtra, one should know that such a person is still far from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
If one has not heard, not understood, and is unable to practice this sutra, it corresponds to the aforementioned case where, upon reaching that high plateau, one still sees only dry earth;
such a person is still far from Bodhi, corresponding to the knowledge that the water is still far away.
△ Second, the analogy for good conduct.
If one hears and understands this, contemplates it, and practices it, one will certainly know that one is drawing near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
If one hears and understands this, applies effort accordingly without ceasing, contemplates it, and practices it, one will accordingly perceive the moistening [of the seeds].
Earth: one must know that awakening is near; when the mind is focused upon it, one knows for certain that water is near.
△ Second, the underlying meaning:
Why is this so? Because the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all bodhisattvas depends entirely upon this.
Sūtra: This sūtra opens the gate of skillful means and reveals the true reality. It is the treasury of the Lotus Sūtra, profound, firm, remote, and deep, such that no one can reach it.
Now, the Buddha teaches and transforms beings, bringing bodhisattvas to fulfillment, and thus reveals it for them.
"All Bodhisattvas" clarifies their cause; that is to say, the three classes of bodhisattvas are referred to as "all.

Regarding "Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi," the intent is that while in other sutras the three classes of bodhisattvas are unable to attain the fruit of bodhi, in this sutra alone, the three classes of bodhisattvas all attain the fruit of Buddhahood; therefore, it says "all bodhisattvas" (and so forth). This sutra...
The downward turning and emergence all belong to the meaning of "intention. To "open the gate of skillful means" (upāya-mukha) does not mean an opening in the sense of granting or bestowing;
rather, it is an opening in the sense of removing, reconciling, abolishing, and revealing.

Forty years ago, when it was not said that "skillful means is skillful means," the gate of skillful means was closed. Now, when it is said that "skillful means is skillful means," the gate of skillful means is opened.

If the provisional means (*upāya*) are not opened, then the ultimate reality (*bhūtārtha*) will not be revealed. When the gate of provisional means is opened, the characteristics of ultimate reality are revealed.
If one had not previously spoken of the three vehicles as provisional means, how could one know that the One Vehicle is the ultimate reality?

If one had not spoken of the three carts as provisional means, how could one know that the single cart is the ultimate reality? If one had not spoken of the conjured city as a provisional means, how could one know the [jeweled city]?

This is the ultimate reality. Now, by opening the expedient means of the three vehicles, the three carts, and the illusory city, the reality of the One Vehicle, the single cart, and the precious destination is revealed.

That which is "profound, firm, and remote" refers to the principle of true reality (*bhūtatathatā*). It is called "profound" because it penetrates vertically to the very source and bottom of the Three Truths;
it is called "remote" because it extends horizontally to the furthest limits of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). It is not [limited] by duality...
That which is invaded by the five abodes of death is called "solid" (*gu*). That which is profound, subtle, and wondrous, and thus inconceivable, is called "mysterious" (*you*).
As for "no one being able to reach it," this means that even those on the seven stages of expedient means cannot reach it; it does not mean that there is absolutely no one who can reach it.
Regarding "teaching and transforming" (*jiaohua*) and so forth: it refers to teaching and transforming the bodhisattvas of the three vehicles, all of whom attain the fulfillment of *bodhi*.
Since one can thus achieve bodhi, the bodhisattvas of the three preceding teachings have fully arrived at this profound, solid, and far-reaching treasury of sūtras.
Yet, for the sake of providing a single phrase of revelation, it comprehensively subsumes the aforementioned "opening of expedient means" and so forth.
The intent is that there is nothing other than the opening of expedient means and the revealing of the truth; this is because one desires to bring all three teachings to fulfillment.
One attains unsurpassed bodhi and reaches the profound, solid, and remote treasury of the sūtras.
Because it opens up skillful means to reveal the ultimate truth, all three teachings reach this treasury of the sūtras to achieve bodhi;
therefore, it is said that the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all bodhisattvas belongs to this sūtra. Furthermore, because they all belong to this sūtra, it is said that... [the text continues].
For those who have heard but not yet understood or practiced the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, bodhi remains far away.

However, for those who have heard, understood, contemplated, and practiced the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, they draw near to bodhi. Such successive reversals and resolutions constitute the meaning of "emerging from the mind."
And thus it is made clear. △ Third, the exclusion of those who are not [qualified].
"Bhaiṣajyarāja, if there are bodhisattvas who, upon hearing this Lotus Sūtra, are startled, doubtful, or terrified, you should know that they are bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds.
If śrāvakas, upon hearing this sūtra, are startled, doubtful, or terrified, you should know that they are [those who have increased their afflictions]."
Those with overweening pride and those who have newly resolved their intent have not yet opened the eye of the Way, nor have they destroyed ignorance;

therefore, upon hearing [this teaching], they are unable to believe or understand it, but instead give rise to alarm and doubt. Hearing it, they cannot rejoice, but instead give rise to fear. This is called overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
This refers to those who claim to have attained what they have not attained, and claim to have realized what they have not realized;
thus, taking little to be sufficient, they declare themselves to have reached ultimate nirvana and refuse to advance further—hence the name "arrogance" (*adhimāna*).

The reason one must undergo this round of discernment to exclude such individuals is that the original intention of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world was to cause all sentient beings to open, reveal, awaken to, and enter [the Dharma].

Regarding the Buddha’s knowledge and vision: if there are those who are startled, doubtful, or terrified, upon hearing this single instance of the exclusion of what is not [the truth], they will naturally cease to feel startled or doubtful, and cease to feel terrified;
instead, they will give rise to faith, understanding, and joy, thereby enabling the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Part Two: Repeatedly Demonstrating the Three Methods (in two sections). First, demonstrating the correct method. Second, "I, from... and so forth.
This clarifies the benefits. The first four [sections] begin with an inquiry:
"Bhaiṣajyarāja, if there be sons or daughters of good family who, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, wish to preach this Lotus Sūtra for the sake of the fourfold assembly, how should they preach it?"
△ Second, the summary:
These sons and daughters of good family, having entered the Tathāgata’s chamber, donned the Tathāgata’s robe, and sat upon the Tathāgata’s seat,
should then extensively expound this sutra for the fourfold assembly.
Regarding "entering the Tathāgata’s chamber" and so forth: a chamber has the sense of providing shelter.
If one enters the Tathāgata’s chamber, then all sentient beings are beneath that shelter. Clothing has the sense of providing protection.
If one dons the Tathāgata’s clothing, then all hindrances and afflictions are within that protection. A seat has the sense of providing stability...
Regarding the meaning of "stopping" (śamatha): if one sits upon the seat of the Tathāgata, then all dharmas are contained within that state of peaceful abiding.
Once the three tracks are fully perfected, one may use them to guide oneself and others.
Thus, one ought to extensively expound this wondrous *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for the fourfold assembly. △ Third, the explanation of its fulfillment.
The Tathāgata’s chamber is the mind of great compassion toward all sentient beings.
The Tathāgata’s robe is the mind of gentleness and patience. The Tathāgata’s seat is the emptiness of all phenomena.

"Great compassion is the chamber" means that there are three kinds of compassion: namely, compassion with a dharma-object (*dharmālambana*), compassion with a sentient-being-object (*sattvālambana*), and objectless compassion (*anālambana*).
Although the first two—compassion toward phenomena and sentient beings—are also called "compassion," they cannot be termed "great compassion.
What is here called "great compassion" is precisely objectless compassion. Regarding "objectless," it means there is nothing that is not its object.

Yet there is nothing that it does not take as its object. Great loving-kindness (*maitrī*) universally bestows happiness upon the entire realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), while great compassion (*karuṇā*) universally uproots suffering throughout the realm of phenomena.
Like a magnet attracting iron, it bestows and uproots spontaneously; this is "objectless" (*anālambana*) loving-kindness and compassion.
Since it bestows and uproots universally, there is not a single sentient being who is not covered by its protection. Therefore, it is called "Great Loving-Kindness."
Compassion is the dwelling place of the Tathāgata. Regarding "the mind of gentleness and patience is his robe":

gentleness is the capacity to endure, while humiliation is the object to be endured. When one perceives no external object to be endured and perceives no internal person who endures, this is called true patience. However, among the objects to be endured, there are internal objects.
Regarding external objects: internally, they consist of the delusions of views, afflictions, and the dust-like ignorance of the sands of the Ganges.

When these three internal delusions exist as obstacles and vexations, one should employ the great patience of quiescence to shield and protect against them. Externally, they consist of harsh speech, verbal abuse, and insults.

Furthermore, when external conditions such as blades and staves arise to cause obstruction and affliction, one is able to ward them off and protect oneself through the great patience of tranquil extinction (*śānti-mahākṣānti*).
Thus, there is not a single obstruction or affliction that does not fall within the scope of this protection.
Therefore, the mind of gentleness and forbearance is the robe of the Tathāgata. All phenomena are empty.
Regarding this seat: ordinary beings see all phenomena merely as existent; those of the Two Vehicles see all phenomena merely as empty;
and Bodhisattvas see all phenomena merely as the Middle Way. In these cases, they cannot yet be said to have realized the emptiness of all phenomena.
As for the emptiness of all phenomena, it means that when one is empty, all are empty—there is no provisional [existence].
That which is not empty within non-existence is ultimate emptiness, the emptiness of the primary truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), and the ultimate true emptiness.

Only then is it the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*). Since it is true emptiness, and true emptiness is not empty, there is not a single phenomenon that does not find its resting place therein.
Therefore, the emptiness of all phenomena is the seat of the Tathāgata. △ Four: Exhortation.
Having cultivated [this] and dwelt securely within it, he then, with a mind free from indolence, extensively expounded this Lotus Sūtra for the sake of the bodhisattvas and the fourfold assembly.
"To abide therein" means to abide within these three modes of practice (*trividha-yoga*). That is to say:

one must contemplate the emptiness of all phenomena while abiding in the mode of accomplishment (*sādhana-yoga*); externally, one endures offensive circumstances while abiding in the mode of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-yoga*);
and internally, one exercises great compassion while abiding in the mode of true nature (*tathatā-yoga*). Having thus [established] oneself in these three...
Being fully endowed with the three modes of conduct, one should in turn guide others, so that they too may become fully endowed with these three modes.
Furthermore, with an untiring mind, one should extensively expound this sutra for others. To speak of being "untiring" means to be untiring regarding these three modes of conduct.
Even when preaching the sutra, should there be those who do not believe and instead respond with abuse or physical assault, [one remains steadfast].

Regarding such matters, I shall not, on this account, abandon the propagation of the sutras. One should observe that externally there is no object to be sought, and internally there is no person capable of insulting.
Since both subject and object are absent, where could there still be matters such as verbal abuse, beating, or striking?
Internally, one should exercise great compassion; externally, one should contemplate the emptiness of all phenomena, remaining securely established in the three modes of conduct.
Within this [assembly], he has never for a moment ceased to propagate this sutra; this is what is called the "mind of non-laziness" with which he preaches this sutra.
Now, why must one enter the Tathāgata’s chamber and so forth in order to propagate the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*? There is no other reason:
the Tathāgata is the speaker, and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is that which is spoken. That the Tathāgata is indeed the Tathāgata is solely because of this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
That which constitutes the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is precisely the substance of these three modes.
If one wishes to propagate what is taught in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, one must enter the chamber of the Tathāgata’s capacity to teach, and so forth.

Furthermore, although these three modes reside within the Tathāgata’s capacity to teach and within what the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* teaches, they are fully possessed by sentient beings; therefore, it is said that they are "the minds of sentient beings."
This is precisely the great mind of compassion. It also reveals that in the *Lotus Sūtra*, there is not a single dharma that is not the equality of sentient beings and Buddhas.
△ Second, clarifying the benefits:
"O Bhaiṣajyarāja, in other lands I shall dispatch emanated persons to assemble for them a multitude to hear the Dharma; I shall also dispatch emanated bhikṣus."

Bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās shall listen to their preaching of the Dharma. These emanated persons, having heard the Dharma, will believe and accept it, following it in accordance and not opposing it.

If the preachers of the Dharma are in a secluded place, I will at that time dispatch many devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, and others to listen to their preaching of the Dharma. Although I may be in another land, I will from time to time cause them to do so.

As for those who preach the Dharma, they shall be able to see my body. If they should forget or lose any passages or readings of this sutra, I shall preach it again for them so that they may attain completeness.

The reason why I must dispatch emanated beings to the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of supernatural beings is that if the three modes and the fruit are complete, [the teaching will flourish].

Yet one is able to preach the Dharma. If there were no listeners for the Dharma, then the Way of resonance would not be established, the task of transformation and guidance would not be fulfilled, and by what means could the benefits of the Dharma be obtained?
Therefore, he extensively dispatches emanated beings, as well as the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings, to serve as the audience for the Dharma;
thus, the Way of resonance can be established, and the task of transformation and guidance is accomplished.
Consequently, one will be able to obtain the great benefit of the Dharma; its propagation shall not be in vain. As for "those who see my body":
the Buddha is the one capable of preaching this sutra. Since they are able to preach what the Buddha has spoken, they are thus seeing the one capable of preaching it.
The rest is self-evident. △ Second, the verse recitation in three parts: first, the direct recitation; second, the [subsequent] recitation... [text fragment].

The *mārga* (path). Three verses conclude with praise. Regarding the beginning, there is no verse that summarizes [the teaching] by way of doctrine, person, or location; rather, it only summarizes by way of practice, which is further divided into three parts.
The first verse summarizes the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Those who wish to abandon all indolence should listen to this sutra. This sutra is difficult to hear; those who believe and accept it are likewise rare."
Those who are indolent refer to those who practice based on the three preceding teachings and consider the partial and limited (the *hīnayāna*) to be sufficient; these are called the indolent.
If one hears this sutra, one will give rise to perfect understanding (*pariniṣpanna-adhimukti*) and initiate perfect practice (*pariniṣpanna-caryā*).
Therefore, one is able to abandon all forms of indolence. Furthermore, this single line may also be rendered as a verse to praise practice by way of its application, and thus it is cited:
This is the Dharma. Not yet skillfully practicing the path of a bodhisattva constitutes various forms of indolence;
skillfully practicing the path of a bodhisattva consists in hearing this sutra and abandoning all indolence. △ Second, the verse on the parable.
It is like a person who, thirsty and needing water, digs in a high plateau; seeing only dry earth, they know the water is still far off.
Gradually seeing moist soil and mud, they know with certainty that the water is near.
△ [The third verse concludes:
O Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that such persons as these, having not heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, remain very far from the Buddha’s wisdom.
If they hear this profound sūtra—the king of all sūtras—which definitively clarifies the Dharma of the śrāvakas, and having heard it, reflect upon it with earnest contemplation...
One should know that these people are close to the Buddha’s wisdom.

Regarding the phrase "decisively understanding" (*jue liao*): "decisive" (*jue*) means to open and resolve; "understanding" (*liao*) means to fully comprehend and sever [delusion]. The "Dharma of the Śrāvakas" refers to the Four Noble Truths.

If one merely knows the Four Noble Truths—the suffering to be known, the origin to be abandoned, the cessation to be realized, and the path to be cultivated—this is not yet called "complete eradication" (*parijñā*).
Because such a person has only abandoned delusion and is thus termed "liberated," they have in fact not attained all-encompassing liberation;
therefore, it cannot be called complete eradication. Now, this sutra provides for them a decisive resolution and complete eradication, specifically for the two types of Śrāvakas.
This is the Dharma of the Vehicle; it is the perfect and real Dharma of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), for the nine realms are equally opened and the three vehicles all converge therein.
Once this has been fully realized and severed, one is able to attain ultimate, true cessation (*nirvāṇa*) through the sound of the Buddha-way.
It causes all to hear; therefore, it is the Dharma of the Śrāvakas, yet it is the definitive realization. If one does not reach definitive realization, there is no mastery.
If one reaches definitive realization, then the provisional is the real, and the real does not depart from the provisional; the real is itself the provisional.

Skillful means (*upāya*) is not separate from reality (*bhūta*). Therefore, whether it be skillful means or reality, what was intended to be bestowed in the past was immediately bestowed, and what is intended to be revealed today is immediately revealed.
Thus, one attains great mastery and becomes the king of all sūtras. II. Verse on the Methodology (in two parts):
A. Verse showing the methodology. B. Verse clarifying the benefits. A. The first has three sections: 1. Verse indicating the heading.
If anyone shall preach this sutra, they should enter the chamber of the Tathāgata, don the robe of the Tathāgata, and sit upon the seat of the Tathāgata;
thus, amidst the assembly, they shall be fearless and extensively expound it in detail.
△ Second, the verse provides the explanation and establishment:
Great compassion is the chamber; gentleness and patience are the robe; the emptiness of all phenomena is the seat. Abiding therein, one preaches the Dharma.
△ Three verses exhorting practice:
When this sutra is being preached, if someone reviles one with foul language or strikes one with swords, staves, tiles, or stones, one should endure it by recollecting the Buddha.

Regarding "those who should endure": if we speak in terms of intention, it is the intention of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world—namely, the desire solely to cause all sentient beings to open, show, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, so that this sutra may be widely circulated.
