Therefore, those who propagate the sutra, even when faced with such matters as swords, staves, or harsh words, should simply contemplate and reflect upon this.
It is the intention of the Tathāgata that he endures such matters as these, single-mindedly propagating the sutra without giving rise to anger on account of them,
nor abandoning the propagation, so that people may, through hearing, give rise to understanding and practice, thereby entering into the realization of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
If one speaks according to the literal text, it means that the Tathāgata is showing me the method for propagating the sutra.
The *Kuangyi* (Commentary) says: "One should sit upon the Tathāgata’s seat, don the Tathāgata’s robe, and enter the Tathāgata’s chamber.
Since I am now one who propagates the sutra, even if there are those who cause me harm through harsh speech and the like, I shall keep in mind the Tathāgata’s admonitions;
with a gentle and supple mind, I shall endure these objects of endurance. Furthermore, it says:
Externally, one contemplates the emptiness of phenomena; internally, one cultivates compassion. Thus, one should practice patience for the sake of extensively expounding [the Dharma].
This is because one must be patient for the purpose of recollecting the Buddha. △ Second, the verse clarifies the benefits.
In thousands of millions of billions of lands, I manifest a pure and solid body, preaching the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas.
If, after my parinirvāṇa, there should be one who can preach this sutra, I shall dispatch four groups of transformed beings— bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and pure laymen and women—
to make offerings to that Dharma-preacher and to guide all sentient beings, gathering them together to listen to the Dharma.
If someone intends to inflict harm with swords, staves, tiles, or stones, I shall dispatch emanated beings to provide protection for them.
If a person who expounds the Dharma dwells alone in a secluded place, silent and free from the sound of human voices, and recites this sutra—
At that time, I shall manifest for them a body of pure radiance. If they forget any passages, I will explain them so that they may master them.
If a person possesses such virtues as these—whether preaching to the fourfold assembly or reciting the sutras in solitary places—they shall all behold my body.
If a person dwells in a secluded place, I shall dispatch devas, nāga kings, yakṣas, spirits, and the like to serve as an assembly to hear the Dharma.

Because this person delights in preaching the Dharma and distinguishes its meanings without hindrance, and because all Buddhas protect and keep them in mind, they are able to bring joy to the great assembly.
The first line is a general summary. Its meaning is that there is no land where I do not manifest my body, and no time when I do not preach the Dharma;
therefore, those who are able to receive and uphold [this teaching] can see my body and hear me preaching the Dharma, thereby attaining full mastery without any loss.
Observing this, it is evident that [the manifestation depends] on the presence or absence of the capacity [of the recipient]; it does not depend on the Buddha.
He manifests his body to preach the Dharma; hence it is said below that he "constantly dwells on Vulture Peak Mountain" and so forth, even unto preaching the Dharma.
Next, the section beginning with "If I... is a separate verse. Regarding the phrase "the pure radiant body":
the Tathāgata’s body is pure because it is not invaded by the two kinds of death, and it possesses radiance because it is not defiled by the five abodes. [End of] Analysis.
One who is without hindrance makes such distinctions as "this is provisional" and "this is real. Yet, the provisional is itself the real, and the real is itself the provisional;
therefore, there is no hindrance. △ Third, the verse concludes with praise.

If one draws near to a Dharma Master, one will swiftly attain the path of a Bodhisattva. By following and training under such a teacher, one shall behold Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
The first two phrases clarify that by drawing near to a Dharma Master who propagates the sutras, one personally achieves the causal conditions for the practice of Bodhi.
Because of this close association, one is able to realize the true nature of all phenomena (dharmas) and open up the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
thus, the fruit of Buddhahood is swiftly attained. The following two lines clarify that by complying with and learning from the teacher, one personally attains the vision of all Buddhas.

The Dharma Master then explains this according to the teaching: by initiating practice and entering into realization, if one now follows what has been learned, one will naturally attain that which all Buddhas have realized and will once again behold the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; hence it is said, "if one draws near," and so forth.
The preceding section has praised the person who upholds [the teaching] as being supremely venerable and the Dharma they uphold as being supremely excellent.
Thus, the veneration of the person serves to manifest the excellence of the Dharma; because the Dharma is excellent, it is titled "Dharma," and because the person is venerable, it is titled "Teacher.
Therefore, this is called the "Chapter on the Dharma-Master. This final verse specifically emphasizes the veneration of the person to manifest the excellence of the Dharma. As for the preceding...

Regarding the "Honored among Men," the final verse clarifies this honor by means of the excellence of the Dharma; it is essentially a comprehensive elucidation through the mutual illumination of the person and the Dharma.
This concludes the explanation of the "Chapter on the Teacher of the Dharma."
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Eleven: The Appearance of the Jeweled Stupa.

To clarify the general purport of this chapter: it is because the Tathāgata preached this single sutra with the desire that all sentient beings might attain the opening and understanding of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
His intention did not merely lie in benefiting those of a single time; rather, [it was for the sake of all].
If one wishes to extend [the benefits of this teaching] far and wide to the final age, it is essential to rely upon Dharma masters for its dissemination.

Therefore, within the text of the Superior Chapter, the person [who transmits the Dharma] is described as being most venerable and the Dharma as being most supreme; furthermore, the proper method for propagating the sutra is demonstrated.
Although these points have already been elucidated in this manner once, if there were no Buddha to serve as a witness and validation, then the Dharma...
The words regarding "supremacy" had not yet been verified, and people were still unable to believe and accept them; there were even those who gave rise to doubt.
Therefore, this chapter exists as a text to establish and prove the supremacy of the Dharma, so that people will certainly believe without doubt.
First, it is to encourage those in the assembly who have not yet attained faith; thus the following verse says:

"The Holy Lord, the World-Honored One, although he entered parinirvāṇa long ago, still comes for the sake of the Dharma while within the jeweled stūpa. Why, then, do you people not strive diligently for the sake of the Dharma?
Furthermore, this entire chapter is based upon the trace gate (*śeṣamukha*) which has been expounded, namely, the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena as realized by the Buddha.
Knowledge and vision are neither arising nor ceasing; arising and ceasing are one and the same. They are neither one nor many; one and many are unimpeded.
They are neither defiled nor pure; defilement and purity share the same source. Then, it was known that the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, who had entered parinirvāṇa long ago, emerged from the earth.
Abiding in mid-air within the jeweled stupa, he raised a great voice and praised, saying, "Excellent! This is cessation, yet not cessation.
The Tathāgata Śākyamuni was currently preaching the Dharma, having entered meditative absorption within the stupa of long-extinguished nirvana.
To proclaim that one shall enter *nirvāṇa* is for birth to be non-birth. Likewise, extinction is non-extinction.
Since birth is non-birth, one may realize and attain the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of knowledge and vision: that birth and extinction are of one suchness (*tathatā*).
Furthermore, it clarifies that the immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions are all emanations (*nirmāṇakāya*) of Śākyamuni. Since all Buddhas are likewise one with Śākyamuni—
The body is divided; thus, the many are not many. Since a single body of Śākyamuni can manifest as immeasurable Buddhas, the one is not one.

In this way, through the non-multiplicity of the many and the non-oneness of the one, one may realize the true characteristic of wisdom and vision, wherein the one and the many are without obstruction.
Furthermore, this clarifies the threefold transformation of the pure land, which, though ultimate—
That which is pure is originally formed from the impure land of Sahā; thus, this purity is not [inherently] pure.
Although the Sahā world is extremely defiled, it is able to transform into a pure land; thus, this defilement is not [inherently] defiled.
Through such non-purity of purity and non-defilement of defilement, one may realize the true mark (*dharmatā*). Defilement and purity—

They share the same source. Since each of these has been established through proof, it demonstrates that what the present Buddha teaches is not only true and unerring, but also shows that the present Buddha is as immediate as the ancient Buddhas who were distant in time.
This causes all beings to give rise to faith and be free from doubt. Furthermore, within this chapter, it first clarifies the manifestation of the jeweled stupa.

Next, the distant gathering of the emanated bodies is clarified; this is followed by the three transformations of the pure land, and finally, the Tathāgata’s universal proclamation and recruitment for the dissemination [of the teaching] are clarified.

Yet, why is it that within the title of the chapter, there is no mention of the distant gathering of the emanated bodies nor of Śākyamuni’s proclamation and recruitment, but only the mention of "beholding the jeweled stupa"?
This is because the cloud-like assembly of the emanated bodies was solely for the purpose of opening the jeweled stupa.
Having arrived, he then lifted up the jeweled stupa, thereby enabling the simultaneous assembly of the emanated bodies. Śākyamuni’s call for offerings was likewise not without cause.
Had the jeweled stupa not appeared, the teaching would never have been fully authenticated; thus, he had not yet called for its circulation.
Now, because the jeweled stupa has emerged, what was taught in the "Trace Gate" (Jikimon) has attained authentication, and therefore he calls for its circulation.
As for the term "penetration" (tōng), it refers to the raising of the jeweled stupa; it may also encompass the Tathāgata’s call for offerings.
Therefore, the title of the chapter merely indicates the "seeing" of the jeweled stupa. Regarding the character "see" (jiàn), some write it as "manifest" (xiàn).
If we speak from the perspective of the stupa itself, since this jeweled stupa emerges from the earth and dwells in mid-air, it might seem appropriate to use "manifest."

[This is] the title. However, the meaning clarified within the text is solely to provide proof and validation. What is taught in the *Jiemo* (Trace) section is intended to enable the fourfold assembly to all see and hear it;
therefore, the text says: "At that time, the fourfold assembly saw the great jeweled stupa dwelling in mid-air."
Furthermore, they heard the sounds emanating from within the stupa and all attained the joy of the Dharma.
Even those who longed to see him with joyful eloquence gathered from afar; as they all beheld the precious stupa, it is said that "the entire assembly all saw the Tathāgata."
Within the jeweled stupa, he sat upon a lion throne; it is further stated that he saw two Tathāgatas within the stupa made of the seven treasures.
Thus, one knows this was a vision and not a physical manifestation. The text of this chapter is divided into two parts: first, the prose exposition; second, the verse summary.
The first three [sections]: First, the precious stūpa emerges from the earth; second, from the passage beginning "At that time, Mahāpratibhāna," the emanated bodies gather from afar;

third, from the passage beginning "With a great voice," Śākyamuni issues his call for offerings. Within the first [of these three], there are five [sub-sections]: first, [the stūpa] abides in mid-air.
At that time, before the Buddha, there was a stupa made of the seven precious substances. It was five hundred yojanas in height and two hundred and fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
It emerged from the earth and remained suspended in mid-air, adorned with various kinds of precious objects.

It featured five thousand railings and ten million chambers, and was magnificently decorated with countless banners and streamers. Precious necklaces hung down, and ten thousand jeweled bells [resounded].
A hundred million [banners] were suspended above it, with the fragrance of *tamarapa* sandalwood emanating from all four sides and pervading the entire world.
Those various banners and canopies were composed of the seven treasures— gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, pearl, and ruby—
and reached as high as the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings.

The first passage, regarding the emergence of the jeweled stūpa, concerns the phenomenal aspect (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*). Since there exists a phenomenal aspect that serves as a signifier, there must necessarily be a fundamental reality (*tattva*) that is signified.
While the phenomenal aspect can be understood from the text itself, if one explains it in terms of the fundamental reality that it signifies:
Regarding the statement that there is a stupa made of the seven treasures before the Buddha:
the stupa represents the Dharmakāya, the fruit and virtue realized by the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna. This Dharmakāya is adorned with the noble wealth of the seven treasures.
Its being situated before the Buddha signifies that the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna has long since realized this fruit before me, Śākyamuni.
This is the Dharma-body of merit; therefore, it is said that before the Buddha there was a stupa made of the seven treasures.
As for its height of five hundred *yojanas*, this refers to when the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna realized this Dharma-body of meritorious fruit:

he necessarily proceeded from delusion to awakening, from cause to fruit, and from practice to realization. Since he proceeded from cause to fruit, he must have shattered the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vāsabhūmi*).
After [overcoming] the afflictions, one subsequently realizes this Dharma-body. If one breaks through the first dwelling of the delusions of view, it is as if rising one hundred *yojanas* high;
continuing in this manner until one breaks through the dwelling of ignorance, it is as if rising five hundred *yojanas* high.

Although the realized Dharma-body thus rises far above the surface of these five dwellings, it fundamentally does not depart from the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*), just like its length and breadth.
It is two hundred and fifty yojanas. It can destroy the twenty-five states of existence (bhava).
Its length is two hundred and fifty yojanas, by which one can attain the twenty-five royal samādhis; its breadth is likewise two hundred and fifty yojanas.
Regarding those who emerge from the earth and abide in mid-air: this fruition-virtue of the Dharma-body emerges without emerging, for it emerges from the ground of the principle of true reality;
it abides without abiding, for it abides in the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
Adorned with various precious objects, it takes concentration and wisdom as its ornamentation. The railings represent all the *dhāraṇīs*;
the niches represent all forms of compassion. Thus, the Dharma-body is neither biased nor can it be destroyed;
it is neither fixed in correctness nor does it fail to stand. Like countless banners, it can transform defilement into purity and transform the ordinary into the sacred.

It is like countless banners. As for "hanging jeweled necklaces," it means that from the principle of the Dharma-body, one gives rise to the causal practices of the eighty-four thousand Dharma-gates and accomplishes the eighty-four thousand pāramitās, descending to transform all beings, just as jeweled necklaces hang down.
When teaching and transforming, one must expound the Dharma, just as jeweled bells are suspended.
This is the supreme. Furthermore, the Dharma-body is fully endowed with the four virtues of permanence, bliss, self, and purity;

it enables all beings to cultivate and realize these, just as fragrant *tamālapatra* sandalwood scents emanate from all four sides. Regarding the statement that the banners and canopies are composed of the seven treasures:
this means that not only is the Dharma-body adorned by the seven noble riches (*saptadhanas*), but so too are all [the attributes] capable of...

The merit of its adornment is further accomplished by the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*). That it rises as high as the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings means that this Dharma-body is not without cause;

it extends vertically beyond the three periods of time and arises entirely from the nature of the unconditioned Four Noble Truths, just as a jeweled stupa rises as high as the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings. △ Second, the various devas.
They presented offerings.
The gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven rained down māndārava flowers as an offering to the jeweled stūpa.
All other devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth did likewise.
Tens of millions of billions of beings made offerings to the precious stupa with all kinds of flowers, incense, necklaces, banners, canopies, and music;
they honored, revered, and praised it.

As for the rain of flowers from the Heaven of the Thirty-three to make offerings to the stūpa, this symbolizes that all forty-two stages of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) achieve the perfect fruit through perfect causes.

The thirty minds constitute thirty [levels], the ten grounds constitute one, Equal Enlightenment constitutes one, and Wondrous Enlightenment constitutes one; together these form the Heaven of the Thirty-three, which is collectively a single heaven.
This refers to the forty-two stages, wherein one dwells together with the Heaven of the Ultimate Meaning (*paramārtha-deva*).
The raining of flowers signifies the fulfillment of the perfect cause (*pariniṣpanna-hetu*), while the offering at the stupa signifies the realization of the fruit-virtue of the *dharmakāya*.

As for the other devas and the eight classes of beings who likewise offer flowers and incense at the stupa, this symbolizes the causal practices of all those belonging to the seven stages of expedient means (*saptopāya*) within the three vehicles. It is also...
Furthermore, all are now able to realize the fruit of the Perfect [Teaching].

What was previously taught forty years ago—that the causes of the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*) could only realize the fruits of those expedient means—now, as all nine realms are opened and nothing remains outside this opening, the causes of the three vehicles, the five teachings, and the seven stages of expedient means can all realize the fruit of the Perfect and Subtle. Therefore, the remainder...
The devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings all made offerings to the precious stupa with flowers and incense. △ Third, the testimony of the ancient Buddhas:
At that time, from within the precious stupa, a great voice issued forth, praising: "Excellent, excellent! Śākyamuni, World-Honored One!"

World-Honored One, you have been able to preach for the great assembly the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*—the Dharma for instructing bodhisattvas, which is protected by the mindfulness of the Buddhas—by means of your impartial great wisdom.
It is so, it is so; World-Honored One Śākyamuni, all that you have spoken is truly real.
"Excellent!"—this double exclamation is indeed the fundamental intention of all Buddhas appearing in the world:

they desire only that all sentient beings may attain the opening, showing, awakening, and entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*), and that they may clarify and realize that all phenomena (*dharmas*) are entirely the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Now, within the "Trace Gate" (*tracimukha*), Śākyamuni Tathāgata has taught the three cycles of the Dharma through parables and causes and conditions; [therein] there is no...

Without revealing their provisional aspects to manifest their ultimate reality, and without revealing their threefold aspects to manifest their single aspect, [the Buddha] enables those of the three capacities to all understand the true mark of all phenomena and open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
This perfectly accords with the fundamental intention of all Buddhas; therefore, the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna praises this unremittingly, speaking in these two ways.
Excellent! That which is called "equal great wisdom" refers to subtle, vast, and inconceivable knowledge and vision.
It is not only Śākyamuni who possesses this; all Buddhas of the ten directions are likewise so. It is not only the Buddhas of the ten directions who possess this;
all Buddhas of the three periods of time are likewise so. Because this is what is common to all Buddhas, [it is called equal great wisdom].
It is called "equality. Furthermore, the vast wisdom realized by all Buddhas is not something separate from what is realized; it is entirely the realization of what sentient beings possess.
That which sentient beings possess is likewise not something separate from what is possessed; it is entirely the possession of what all Buddhas have realized.
Thus, ordinary beings and sages are of one suchness, and life and Buddha are equal. Therefore, it is called the "Great Equality."
This is wisdom. To speak of both as "thus" (*evam*) is precisely the terminology for establishing proof.
For "thus" in one sense establishes the principle that has been taught; "thus" in another sense establishes the capacity of the recipient.
To establish the principle means that what was taught above—namely, that the past was provisional—is indeed, in its true reality, provisional. Today...

This is the reality; it is truly real and truly real. Although there are provisional and ultimate [teachings], that which is spoken therein is none other than the truth of the Middle Way and the true mark (*dharmatā*).

Therefore, it is called "Thus" (*evam*). As for the "one who realizes the capacity," this refers to Śākyamuni Tathāgata, who is able to employ this wondrous principle of the non-duality of the provisional and the ultimate to accord with the perfect and ultimate reality of the One Vehicle.

He taught according to their capacities. Therefore, within the three cycles of the Trace Gate (Jikimon), he caused those of the three faculties to each understand the principle that the provisional and the real are non-dual.
This is precisely what is meant by "thus" (nyoze) in accordance with the capacity for the perfect One Vehicle (Ichijō).
Furthermore, the statement "all are truly real" refers to the fact that the principles of the provisional and the real as they were taught are entirely true and real. The passage [ends] here.
Those whose faculties are governed by the three roots are likewise all truly so. △ Fourth, the fourfold assembly’s astonishment and joy:
At that time, the fourfold assembly saw the great jeweled stupa abiding in mid-air and heard the sounds issuing from within the stupa.
All attained the joy of the Dharma, marveling at such an unprecedented occurrence. They rose from their seats, joined their palms in reverence, and withdrew to stand to one side.

Regarding "all attained the joy of the Dharma": the fourfold assembly, upon seeing the precious stupa emerge from the earth and abide in mid-air, had already gained benefit through this manifestation;
they were further moved by the sound that issued forth, which uttered the praise, "Excellent! Moreover, in...
Within the sound, there is a further benefit; whether it be the sound or the form, all derive benefit, and thus it is called "Dharma-joy.

As for "strange and unprecedented": the Tathāgata has preached the Dharma for over forty years, yet never before had such a jeweled stupa appeared before us, nor had a voice issued from within it to offer praise; now, for the first time, this has occurred. Therefore...

"How extraordinary and unprecedented! They withdrew to stand to one side because they did not know by what cause or condition this precious stūpa existed, nor did they know by what cause or condition it had emerged from the earth, nor by what cause or condition it spoke words of praise;
therefore, they withdrew to stand to one side. This was done in anticipation of the great joy described in the subsequent text.
This explains that which was asked. By interpreting this, the capacity to ask is revealed, and the meaning of not asking is fully elucidated. △ Five:
Question and Answer for Illumination, Part Two. First: The Bodhisattva’s Question.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Mahāpratibhāna.
Knowing the doubts in the minds of all the world’s devas, humans, asuras, and others, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, by what causes and conditions has this jeweled stūpa emerged from the earth, and why does it emit such sounds from within?"

Regarding "Mahāpratibhāna" (Great Eloquence): because this bodhisattva possesses great *pratibhāna* (eloquence), he is able to expound immeasurable dharmas within a single dharma, and immeasurable meanings within a single meaning.
His name, Mahāpratibhāna, is manifested based on these virtues. There are three points of inquiry:
first, the question as to what causes and conditions gave rise to this precious stūpa; second, the question as to what causes... [the text continues].
For what reason did it surge forth from the earth? He asked three times for what cause and for what reason he had spoken these words of praise.
△ Second, the Tathāgata’s response:
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāratnapratibhāna: "Within this precious stūpa lies the entire body of a Tathāgata from the distant past."
In the past, in the east, there were immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeya worlds. There was a land named Ratnaviśuddhā.
In it dwelt a Buddha named Prabhūtaratna. When that Buddha was practicing the bodhisattva path, he made this great vow:
"If I attain buddhahood, then after my parinirvāṇa, wherever in the lands of the ten directions the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is being preached, my stūpa-shrine shall appear."
In order to hear this sutra, they emerged before him to serve as witnesses and praised him, saying, "Excellent!
After that Buddha had attained enlightenment, at the time of his parinirvāṇa, he addressed the bhikṣus amidst the great assembly of devas and humans, saying: "After my parinirvāṇa..."
Those who wish to make offerings to my entire body should erect a great stūpa.

By the power of that Buddha’s supernatural faculties and vows, wherever in the worlds of the ten directions there may be one who preaches the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, that precious stūpa shall emerge before them.
With my entire body within the stūpa, I shall praise them, saying: "Excellent, excellent! Mahāpratibhāna, now many..."
The stūpa of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna emerged from the earth because he had heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* being preached; thus he praised it, saying, "Excellent, excellent!

This initial response to the second question regarding the emergence from the earth means that because that Buddha had made a great vow to bear witness to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he emerged from the earth.
His land was named Ratnaviśuddha, and his name as a Buddha was Prabhūtaratna; this was because of that Buddha—

Because during the causal stage he was able to exhaustively practice the immeasurable path-dharmas of all Buddhas, at the time of fruition he was able to realize the immeasurable dharma-treasures of merit of all Buddhas;
possessing only these manifold virtues without any defilement, his land is named "Jeweled Purity" (Ratnaviśuddha), and the Buddha's title is "Many Jewels" (Prabhūtaratna).
Regarding his acting as a witness: it is because the Buddha’s knowledge [perceives] the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
It is difficult to explain this vision, and for those who hear it, it is likewise not easy to believe.

Although the people of the three capacities have already achieved realization through what the Tathāgata taught during the three cycles of the Trace Gate (*jimen*), there are still those in future ages of dull faculties and small wisdom who cannot believe and instead give rise to doubt and confusion. Therefore, [the Buddha] provides proof to bring them to certainty.

They believe without giving rise to doubt. "Excellent! is a word of praise and confirmation. Second, from "That Buddha" onwards, this is the retrospective answer to the first question regarding the existence of this jeweled stupa;

it means that when that Buddha was about to pass into extinction, he issued a decree stating that if one wishes to make offerings to the *śarīra*, one should erect a great stupa—therefore, this stupa exists. Third, from "That Buddha" onwards, this is the direct answer to the [second] question.
He spoke three times in praise. This means that because those Buddhas wished to authenticate the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* which I was preaching, they spoke these words of commendation.

Regarding what is called "the power of supernatural faculties and vows": it is their supernatural power (*ṛddhibala*) that enables them to emerge before one in every single location throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
Wherever the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is being preached, they act as its protectors.
This is the proof; that is to say, it is the power of his vow. Because he alone possesses both supernatural powers and the power of his vow, he is able to manifest the sutra in every place.
△ Second, the distant gathering of the emanated bodies, in eight parts. First, the desire to see the jeweled stupa.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsukha-vyāhāra, through the supernatural power of the Tathāgata, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, we wish to behold this body of the Buddha."

Regarding the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) of the Tathāgata: Śākyamuni is the "causal person" (*hetu-pudgala*) of the present day, while Prabhūtaratna is the "fruition Buddha" (*phala-buddha*) of the past.
If the causal person of today wishes to see the fruition Buddha of today, there is no need for the supernatural power of the Tathāgata.
If the causal person of today wishes to see the fruition Buddha of the past, it would not be by means of the supernatural power of the Tathāgata. No.

This is indeed possible. Furthermore, if one wishes to see the Many Treasures Buddha, it is necessary for the manifested bodies to assemble. Once these manifested bodies have assembled, they will assist in the transformation of beings;
the Ancient Buddha will manifest his body to provide certification and completion. Thus, the tasks of the Trace Gate (Jikimon) are finished, and from this, the Origin Gate (Honmon) may arise.
The opening of the near city of Gayā proceeds from this, and the long and distant lifespan proceeds from this.
[This] manifestation—could it not be that the Tathāgata’s spiritual power has caused him to utter these words of aspiration and desire to be seen? 2.
The Gathering of the Emanated Bodies.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāpratibhāna: "That Buddha Prabhūtaratna possesses a profound and solemn vow: 'If I..."

When the jeweled stūpa emerges before the Buddhas for the sake of hearing the Lotus Sūtra, and there is anyone who wishes to show my body to the fourfold assembly, those emanations of that Buddha who are preaching the Dharma throughout the worlds of the ten directions will all gather together at one place;
only then shall my body appear. Mahāpratibhāna, as for my emanated Buddhas...
Those who preach the Dharma throughout the worlds of the ten directions should now assemble.

As for those who must gather as emanated bodies—desiring to bear witness to the realization of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, the true mark of all phenomena (*dharmatā*), the common source of defilement and purity, the non-obstruction between the one and the many, and the identity of arising and ceasing—it is necessary to manifest these through the transformation of lands by means of emanated bodies. However...
Later, when the stupa was opened, he invited [the Buddha] to sit; thus, it was necessary to assemble the emanated bodies. Furthermore, Muchilinda (Prabhūtaratna) emerged from the earth.
Although this serves as the realization of the Trace Gate, it actually functions to initiate the Origin Gate. Therefore, the vow states: "When that Buddha’s emanated bodies have assembled..."

Only then does my body manifest. If you insist on dividing my body and gathering it together before opening the stupa, it is precisely because you wish to reveal that all such Buddhas are bodies divided from within the traces of Śākyamuni;
for where there are traces, there must necessarily be an origin. As stated in the subsequent text: "To joyfully preach this Lotus Sūtra" is precisely [the point].

Please explain this regarding the Original Gate (Honmon). As for the gathering of the emanated bodies (bunshin), although it was for the purpose of opening the stupa, it was in truth intended to assist in manifesting the Original Gate.
Therefore, when the request to see the Many Treasures Buddha (Dharmakara) was made, the Buddha immediately declared, "My emanated Buddhas should now assemble.
Thus, one knows that by the time the provisional gate (Jikimon) had reached its conclusion, the emanated bodies were originally [intended to gather].

They should assemble to assist in the unfolding of the Original Gate. Even if the Many Treasures Buddha did not possess such a profound and solemn vow, his emanations would certainly have assembled as well.
Therefore, when the emanations were about to gather below, it was said:
"I shall now proceed to the Sahā world, to the place where Śākyamuni Buddha resides, and there I shall also make offerings to the jeweled stupa of the Tathāgata Many Treasures."
The intention [of the Buddha] was originally that the Trace Gate (jìmén) has already concluded and the Fundamental Gate (běnmén) should now begin; therefore, he ought to proceed there.

Since it is said that he shall "together with [the stupa of] Prabhūtaratna" [be present], the intention lies further in what follows. Thus, the verse below says: "Furthermore, my emanated bodies have come desiring to hear the Dharma.
This refers precisely to desiring to hear the Dharma of the Fundamental Gate. From this, we know that the long-cherished vow of Prabhūtaratna is in accord with that of the emanated bodies.

The assembly of those desiring [to hear the teaching] involves the profound convergence of many signs; this constitutes the essential pivot of the entire sutra, for it is precisely here that the central axis lies. III.
The Request for Assembly by Mahāpratibhāna.
Mahāpratibhāna addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, we also wish to see the World-Honored One and the various Buddhas who have manifested as emanations."
They prostrate and make offerings.
Those who wish to see [the Buddha] have already come forward with the desire to see Prabhūtaratna;
now, hearing that there are also the various manifested Buddhas, they likewise wish to see them. △ Fourth, the Tathāgata’s summons by light: Although that Buddha is indeed Śākyamuni...
The bodies emanated by Śākyamuni each have their own transformed realms; unless summoned by light, they would have no means of coming of their own accord.

Therefore, it is necessary to emit light to summon them. As for the necessity of emitting light from the *ūrṇā-kośa* (white tuft of hair), white is the source of all colors, signifying that wisdom is the foundation of all virtues. This inconceivable light of wisdom belongs to Śākyamuni and—

Regarding "the emanated bodies who have likewise attained what was realized": they are summoned by this because they have attained the same realization. Upon seeing them, they immediately arrive; the text has two parts.
First, the summoning of those in the eastern direction:
At that time, the Buddha emitted a single ray of light from his white tuft of hair, and immediately the eastern direction was seen, containing five hundred *koṭi-nayuta* [of worlds]. Constantly...
In as many buddha-lands as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, all those lands have crystal for their ground and are adorned with jewel trees and precious robes.
They are filled with countless thousands of myriads of koṭis of bodhisattvas, and precious canopies are spread everywhere throughout them.
Above the jeweled nets, the Buddhas of those lands speak all dharmas with great and wondrous voices;
and one sees immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of bodhisattvas filling all those lands, preaching the Dharma for the sake of the multitudes.
Furthermore, he saw immeasurable bodhisattvas preaching the Dharma for the assembly; leaders and their retinues proclaimed it together. △ Second, the summoning of the nine directions:
in the south, west, north, the four intermediate points, and above and below—wherever the light from the white tuft mark shone, it was likewise thus.
△ At that time, when the assembly of the five-part body was about to gather,
the Buddhas of the ten directions each addressed their respective bodhisattvas, saying: "Good sons,
we must now go to the Sahā world to the place of Śākyamuni Buddha, and also to pay homage to the precious stupa of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna."

Those who were to go have now departed; Śākyamuni’s threefold unfolding of his original intent has been fully expressed. The Great Matter has been clarified, and the purpose of the Trace Gate (Jikimon) is complete.
As for the arising of the Original Gate (Honmon), I shall go there to assist in its manifestation and to make offerings to Prabhūtaratna.
When Prabhūtaratna appears, he validates and confirms my Śākyamuni’s Trace Gate; in secret, he is the reality itself.
In order to initiate the fundamental teaching of our Śākyamuni, he has come specifically to provide certification.
Since we are all emanations of Śākyamuni, we must go there to receive his certification; therefore, we shall also make offerings together.
△ Sixth, the three transformations of the pure land, which further consists of three parts. First, the transformation of Sahā.
At that time, the Sahā world was instantly transformed into purity. Its ground became of lapis lazuli, adorned with jeweled trees.
Golden cords demarcated the eightfold paths. All villages, hamlets, towns, and cities, as well as great oceans, rivers, mountains, streams, forests, and marshes, vanished.
Great precious incense was burned, and *mandārava* flowers were strewn everywhere across the ground. Canopies of jeweled nets were spread over it.
Above, various precious bells were suspended. Only the assembly of this gathering was left behind; all other devas and humans were moved and placed in other lands.
At that time, each of the Buddhas took a great Bodhisattva as an attendant and arrived at the Sahā world. Each reached the foot of a precious tree;
every precious tree was five hundred yojanas high, its branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits adorned in successive layers of splendor. All...
Beneath each jeweled tree was a lion throne, five *yojanas* in height, likewise adorned with great jewels.
At that time, the Buddhas each sat upon these thrones in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*). In this manner, they gradually filled the entire trichiliocosm;
yet, as for the emanations of Śākyamuni Buddha in a single direction, they still remained as before.
"Not yet exhausted" refers to that which transforms into purity; this precisely means that within defilement itself there is purity.

"Each leading a great Bodhisattva" indicates that the Buddha is one who has attained the fruit, while the Bodhisattva is one who follows the path. The fruit is not separate from the cause, and the cause is not separate from the fruit; therefore, all...

Each Buddha is accompanied by one great Bodhisattva as an attendant. Furthermore, the Buddha represents the ultimate reality (the real), while the Bodhisattva represents skillful means (the provisional).
Since the provisional and the real are not separated from one another but constitute a single essence, each Buddha is accompanied by one Bodhisattva.

They were taken as attendants. Regarding these three transformations of the Pure Land, if one discusses them according to the literal text, they merely serve to accommodate the Buddhas who come to sit therein and to signify that defilement is itself purity.

However, if one discusses them according to the underlying intent, it is because the original purpose of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world was to cause all sentient beings to attain the opening, showing, awakening, and entry into the Buddha-dharma.
The knowledge and vision of ordinary beings who cling to existence; the knowledge and vision of the two vehicles who cling to emptiness;
and the knowledge and vision of bodhisattvas who cling to the middle—these are all vastly different from the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Within this, whether it be the past Prabhūtaratna, the present Śākyamuni, or the emanation bodies throughout the ten directions.

Although there are disparities between the ancient and the modern, the near and the distant, the one and the many, they are nonetheless identical in the knowledge and vision of the Buddha and identical in the realm of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

Since they are identical in the knowledge and vision of the Buddha, how could they ever admit the knowledge and vision of ordinary beings, those of the two vehicles, or even bodhisattvas? Therefore, the initial transformation of the pure land was precisely intended—

The first transformation of the pure land is intended to eliminate the knowledge and views of ordinary beings who cling to existence. The second transformation of the pure land is precisely intended to eliminate the knowledge and views of those of the two vehicles who cling to emptiness.
The third transformation of the pure land is precisely intended to eliminate the knowledge and views of Bodhisattvas who cling to the middle way.
Once the knowledge and views that cling to existence, cling to emptiness, and cling to the middle have all been eliminated, they are identical in being neither existent nor empty, and neither...

This is the knowledge and vision of the Tathāgata. Only when the nine realms all return to the Buddha-realm and the three vehicles fully converge into the One Vehicle does the original intent of the Tathāgata finally reach fulfillment. △ Second, the transformation of the eight directions.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha, wishing to provide space for all the buddhas he had manifested as emanations,
further transformed two million billion nayutas of lands in each of the eight directions, making them all pure and free from the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals.

As well as the asuras. Furthermore, he moved the various devas and humans and placed them in other lands. The lands thus transformed also had floors made of lapis lazuli and were adorned with precious trees.
These trees were five hundred yojanas high, their branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits arranged in successive layers of adornment.
Beneath each tree was a precious lion throne five yojanas high, adorned with all kinds of jewels.

Furthermore, there are no great oceans, rivers, nor any of the kings of mountains such as Mount Mucilinda, Mount Mahāmucilinda, the Cakravāḍa Mountains, the Mahācakravāḍa Mountains, or Mount Sumeru; all together constitute a single buddha-field.

The ground of jewels was level and even. Canopies of interlaced jewels covered it entirely. Banners and parasols were suspended above, great precious incense was burned, and celestial jewel flowers were strewn everywhere across the ground.
△ Third Transformation:
Śākyamuni Buddha, for the sake of the Buddhas who are to sit therein in the future, further transformed two hundred *nayuta* koṭis of lands in each of the eight directions,
making them all pure and free from the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals.
The asuras, moreover, moved the various devas and humans and placed them in other lands. The kingdoms thus transformed also had floors made of lapis lazuli and were adorned with precious trees.
These trees were five hundred yojanas high, their branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits all arranged in orderly adornment.
Beneath each tree there was a precious lion throne, five yojanas in height, likewise adorned with great jewels.

Furthermore, there were no great oceans, rivers, nor Mount Mucilinda, Mount Mahāmucilinda, the Cakravāḍa Mountains, the Mahācakravāḍa Mountains, Sumeru, or any other kings of mountains; it was entirely a single buddha-field of jewels.

The ground was level and even. Canopies of interlaced jewels covered it entirely. Banners and parasols were suspended above, great precious incense was burned, and celestial jewel-flowers were strewn across the earth.
△ Section Seven: The Assembling of the Emanated Bodies.

At that time, the emanated bodies of Śākyamuni from the east—numbering hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—each of whom was preaching the Dharma in their respective lands, all came together and assembled here. In this same manner, [the emanations from the other directions likewise gathered].
The Buddhas of the ten directions all came together and sat in the eight directions.
At that time, in each direction, there were four million billion nayutas of lands, filled everywhere with Buddha-Tathāgatas.
"Each preaching the Dharma as they have gathered": these Buddhas were each preaching the Dharma and transforming sentient beings in their own native lands;
now, by the light-summons of Śākyamuni, they have come into this Sahā world. △ Eighth: The Fivefold Intent to Open the Treasure Stūpa.
At first, the various Buddhas sent messengers to inquire after him. At that time, each of those Buddhas was seated upon a lion throne beneath a precious tree;
they all dispatched their attendants to offer greetings to Śākyamuni Buddha, each carrying a handful of precious flowers and addressing them thus: "Good son, you should go to [Śākyamuni Buddha]."
At Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, where Śākyamuni Buddha resides, speak on my behalf as follows: "Are you free from illness and affliction? Are you physically strong and at ease?
And as for the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, are they all secure and well? Then, scatter these precious flowers over the Buddha as an offering.
And he spoke these words: "That certain Buddha has granted his consent to open this jeweled stūpa. The dispatching of messengers by all the Buddhas was likewise;
they all sent their attendants. Those Buddhas are the bodies that were divided, and Śākyamuni is the body that performed the division.
Although there is the subject and the object, they are one and the same body and mind. How could there be a "self" body and mind?
Thus, when inquiring after one's own body and mind, one sends an attendant to inquire on one's behalf rather than inquiring of oneself directly. Regarding "few ailments":
the Tathāgata’s ailment arises from the ailments of sentient beings; if sentient beings have few ailments, then the Tathāgata also has few ailments.
Regarding "little affliction": if sentient beings are unable to apply themselves to great progress and are difficult to transform and deliver, the Tathāgata experiences affliction;
if sentient beings are easy to deliver, this constitutes the Tathāgata’s little affliction. Regarding "peaceful vigor":

if the great causal conditions have not been clarified and the original intent for appearing in the world has not been fully realized, then there is no peace; if [these are fulfilled], then there is peace.
The great causal conditions are clarified and the original intention is fulfilled; this is the tranquil power of the Tathāgata.

Regarding the fact that both bodhisattvas and śrāvakas are all at peace: if a śrāvaka has not yet severed the origin of suffering and realized its cessation, or if a bodhisattva is obstructed by the six hindrances, they have not yet escaped being scorched by the five turbidities and the eight sufferings, and thus have not attained peace. If a śrāvaka...
Hearing [the Dharma] enables one to accomplish the Four Truths; a Bodhisattva is able to accomplish the Six Perfections. Thus, both Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas attain complete peace and security.
Furthermore, if a Śrāvaka relies solely on the Four Truths and a Bodhisattva relies solely on the Six Perfections, they have not yet attained peace and security.
Only when the three vehicles converge in the One Vehicle is it called peace and security. This is for the purpose of opening [the minds of those who desire it].
This precious stupa refers to the Bodhisattva Mahāpratibhāna, who, desiring to behold the body of that Buddha, wishes to open this precious stupa.

We, the Buddhas of our various emanations, likewise desire to fulfill that same vow and wish to open this precious stupa to behold the body of that Buddha and together receive offerings. △ Second, the actual opening of the precious stupa.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha saw that all the emanated Buddhas had assembled and were each seated upon lion thrones.
Hearing that all the Buddhas had granted their consent to open the precious stupa together, he immediately rose from his seat and stood in mid-air.
All four assemblies rose and joined their palms, gazing at the Buddha with single-minded devotion. Thereupon, Śākyamuni...
The Buddha opened the door of the seven-jeweled stupa with his right finger, producing a great sound like the turning of a bolt and the opening of a great city gate.

As for its abiding in the midst of space: since the stupa was not originally there yet emerged, it emerged from the ground of *dharmatā* (the reality-limit); though it appears to abide, it does not truly abide.

He abides; he abides in the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*). Now, wishing to open this jeweled stūpa, he rises from his seat of the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*)—rising without rising—and dwells without dwelling, abiding within the emptiness of the ultimate truth.

"Opening the door of the jeweled stupa" signifies the opening of the provisional (*upāya*). Opening the stupa door with the right finger symbolizes that provisional wisdom opens the principle of the provisional.
Previously, the jeweled stupa was used to symbolize the fruit-virtue of the *dharmakāya*, which is the ultimate reality (*tattva*);

now, that which symbolizes the provisional is the provisional that is identical in essence to the real. This is illustrated by the two lines concerning "reversing the bolt and key," which clarify the opening [of the provisional].
This is the sound of the tower doors opening. "Guan" (關) refers to the horizontal beam used to close the gate; "yao" (鑰) refers to the lock. "Jie" (劫) means to remove.
To remove the gates and locks is like the opening of a city gate, from which a great sound issues forth. The sound of the current opening of the stupa is likewise so.
△ Third and Fourth: The Assembly’s Seeing and Hearing.
Immediately, the entire assembly beheld the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna within the jeweled stupa, seated upon a lion throne;
his entire body remained intact and undispersed, as if he had entered into meditative concentration. Furthermore, they heard him speak these words: "Excellent, excellent, Śākyamuni Buddha!
You have well expounded this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. It is for the sake of hearing this sutra that I have come here. At that time, the four...
The assembly saw the Buddhas who had entered parinirvāṇa countless thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas ago speak these words;
they marveled at this unprecedented occurrence and scattered clusters of celestial jewel-flowers upon the Buddha Prabhūtaratna and upon Śākyamuni Buddha.
That "the entire assembly all beheld the Tathāgata" signifies that at the time of the disclosure of the provisional (upāya), the true reality (bhūtatathatā) is immediately revealed.

Furthermore, hearing the words "Excellent! manifests the immediate realization and confirmation within the *Jikimon* (Trace Gate); the exclamation "How joyfully you have preached this Lotus Sutra" secretly initiates the *Honmon* (Original Gate).
The teachings expounded during the three cycles [of the *Hōben-bon*, *Shōhō-bon*, and *Hannya-haramitta-bon*] have now concluded; now, once again, he says "How joyfully."
As for "the speaker," it refers to what has been expounded above; this was merely the *jiamen* (trace gate). Now that the *jiamen* is concluded, the *benmen* (original gate) ought to arise;
therefore, he exhorts Śākyamuni to joyfully proclaim the long-distant original [teaching]. As for "marveling at what has never before occurred":
the fourfold assembly already considered what was taught in the preceding *jiamen* to be extremely rare; now that the discourse on the traces is finished, yet much...
The Tathāgata Ratna further requested Śākyamuni to quickly expound this sutra. How could he repeat what was already taught during the three weeks?
Or perhaps he would expound some other dharma; this would be even more rare than what was previously taught. Therefore, it is praised as "unprecedented.
As for scattering flowers upon the Buddha, it symbolizes that the perfect cause can realize the perfect fruit. Yet, [the flowers] were scattered upon two Buddhas.

Śākyamuni is the present Buddha, and Prabhūtaratna is the ancient Buddha. Since the fruit they have realized is identical, at the time of attaining that fruit, one does not merely attain the fruit of the present Buddha, but is also able to attain the fruit of the ancient Buddha.
Therefore, he scattered flowers as an offering to the two Buddhas to manifest this sign. △ He divided his seat and invited him to sit.
At that time, within the jeweled stupa, the Buddha Prabhūtaratna divided half of his seat with Śākyamuni Buddha and spoke these words:
“Śākyamuni Buddha, you may take this seat. Immediately, Śākyamuni Buddha entered it.
Within the stupa, he sat upon half of the seat, assuming the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).

First, he shared the seat; next, he immediately descended and sat upright. Although the ancient Buddha had entered parinirvāṇa long ago, by causing the present Buddha to sit upon his seat, it is clear that "extinction" is not truly extinction.
Thus, while the present Buddha currently dwells and teaches the Dharma, he enters into the state of the ancient Buddha who has long since passed away.
The stupa of the Buddha is such that its arising is non-arising, and its cessation is non-cessation.

That its arising is non-arising is because the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), which is the fruit and virtue realized therein, is fundamentally free from arising and ceasing. △ 5. The Fourfold Assembly Requests Blessings.
At that time, the great assembly saw the two Tathāgatas seated cross-legged upon lion thrones within the stupa made of the seven precious gems.
Each of them thought to themselves: "The Buddha is seated high and far away; we pray that the Tathāgata, by means of his supernormal powers, may cause us all to dwell together in the void.
Immediately, Śākyamuni Buddha, by means of his supernormal powers, caused the entire great assembly [to do so].
All are in empty space.

"All are in empty space" means they all abide in the emptiness of the primary truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*). One should know that Prabhūtaratna is the ancient Buddha and Śākyamuni is the present Buddha;
Prabhūtaratna and Śākyamuni are Buddhas, while the fourfold assembly and the devas and humans are sentient beings. The Buddha [is the one who]...
Thus, the sage is the fruit and the ordinary person is the cause; the sage is awakening and the ordinary person is delusion;
awakening is purity and delusion is defilement. Although such characteristics are various and distinct, they all equally abide within the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
This precisely reveals that the present and the past are as one, and that sentient beings and Buddhas are likewise identical.
Equality. For ordinary beings and sages share the same source; cause and effect are one and the same; delusion and awakening are of the same substance;
and defilement and purity are non-dual. △ Third, Śākyamuni’s call for offerings.
With a great voice, he proclaimed to the fourfold assembly: "Who among you is able to extensively expound the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* in this Sahā world-system?
Now is precisely the right time; before long, the Tathāgata shall enter parinirvāṇa. The Buddha wishes to entrust this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* to one who may uphold it."

"Chang" (唱) means to proclaim that one enters *nirvāṇa*. "Mu" (募) means to solicit and seek the circulation [of the teaching]. Regarding "proclaiming universally to the fourfold assembly with a great voice":

although the exposition of the Trace Gate (*jimon*) was nearly concluded, because the Buddhas of antiquity had not yet provided certification and the manifested bodies had not yet provided assistance, the Tathāgata did not immediately proclaim his extinction; rather, he solicited the circulation [of the teaching]. Now, the Buddhas of antiquity...

Since this has already been established as proof, and the manifestation of divided bodies has served to inspire it, it is evident that what was taught in the Trace Gate not only aligns upward with the ancient Buddhas but also reaches back to harmonize with those of the ten directions; there is no error whatsoever.
Therefore, so that people may surely believe, he raises a proclamation with a subtle, wondrous, and vast voice, universally summoning and addressing the fourfold assembly of devas and humans.
"Who can extensively preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*? I shall seek out those who will propagate it.
The Tathāgata will before long enter nirvāṇa"—this was his proclamation that he would enter nirvāṇa.

To say "before long" means that although the *Honmon* (the Fundamental Gate) has not yet been revealed, the task of the *Jakumon* (the Trace Gate) is already complete; this refers to the conclusion of the three cycles of teaching for the fourfold assembly.
The record of his parinirvāṇa is thus established. The Buddha’s knowledge and vision are opened; his original intent for appearing in the world is fully realized.

Having once again clarified the methods for propagating the correct path, and having further secured the conditions for the formal entrustment, the period of his transformative guidance is drawing to a close;
therefore, he shall soon enter nirvana. The Buddha wishes to entrust this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*—

There is a specific purpose for this entrustment. If the Buddha were still in the world, he would proclaim and expound it himself; since the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, it must necessarily rely on others for its propagation.
Therefore, he wishes to entrust this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* to those who are so situated. There are two such categories of persons.

The first is found in the "Dharma-preacher" chapter (*Dharmabhāṇaka-parivarta*), where, following the instructions of Bhaiṣajyarāja, it concerns the eighty thousand great beings (*mahāsattva*). And...

Regarding the eighty quadrillion nayutas of bodhisattvas seen in the "Chapter on Entrustment" (*Parīndanā-parivarta*), they are actually the bodhisattvas from the lower regions mentioned in the "Chapter on the Emergence from the Earth" (*Dharaṇī-prādurbhāva-parivarta*).
As for the statement that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* has a specific locus for its entrustment:

Thus, by briefly citing the title of the sutra, the entire work is fully encompassed; therefore, although it has not yet been explicitly stated in the main text, there is the phrase "there exists," which truly reaches back to the remote past and is not confined to its present traces.
△ Second, the verse summary has three parts. First, the verse on the emergence of the jeweled stupa.
The two verses describe the distant gathering of the emanated bodies; the three verses describe Śākyamuni’s call for volunteers. Of these, the first two concern the initial exhortation.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
The Holy Lord, the World-Honored One, though long since entered parinirvāṇa, still comes for the sake of the Dharma while remaining within the jeweled stūpa;
how can people not strive diligently for the sake of the Dharma?

Even those who have come for the sake of the Dharma—those Buddhas who have already cultivated and realized this sublime Dharma and have long since entered parinirvāṇa—still come to hear this sutra. As for the people present here now, although they have already heard this sutra...
However, since there are those who have not yet cultivated or realized this wondrous Dharma, how could one fail to cultivate, realize, and propagate it?
△ Second, the actual verse:
"Since the parinirvāṇa of this Buddha, throughout incalculable kalpas, I have heard the Dharma everywhere; because it is so difficult to encounter, this was the original vow of that Buddha."
"After my parinirvāṇa, wherever they may go, they shall always listen to the Dharma.
Regarding the phrase "listening to the Dharma everywhere," this refers to the emergence of witnesses wherever the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is being preached throughout the ten directions.
"Difficult to encounter" means that this sūtra is difficult to expound and difficult to hear, just like the udumbara flower.

The flower appears only when the time is right; if it is not the right time, the flower does not appear. Just as the flower does not appear if it is not the right time, this sutra is not preached if it is not the right time;
therefore, it is difficult to encounter. Although this sutra is difficult to encounter, that Buddha was able to allow listeners to hear it everywhere.
This is because that Buddha had previously made such a vow. △ Second, the verse on the distant gathering of the emanated bodies, in three parts.
First, the verse on the emanated bodies about to assemble:
"Furthermore, my emanated bodies—immeasurable Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—come desiring to hear the Dharma and to behold my parinirvāṇa."

The Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna has each relinquished their wondrous lands, as well as their assemblies of disciples, devas, humans, nāgas, and spirits, and all matters of worship, so that the Dharma may endure for a long time; therefore, they have come here.
Regarding "causing the Dharma to abide for a long time": the Buddhas of the ten directions are already beings who have attained the fruit;

yet they each relinquish their wondrous lands and other matters to come from afar to hear this sutra, so that all sentient beings who see them will immediately conceive the thought that it is difficult to encounter, and will themselves be able to believe, understand, practice, and propagate it. Thus we know that the emanation bodies come [for this purpose]. They are able to...
This is to cause [the Buddha] to dwell for a long time. △ Second, the verse on the threefold purification of the land:
in order to provide seats for all Buddhas, he uses his supernormal powers to move immeasurable multitudes and causes the land to be purified.
Regarding "moving the assembly to make it pure": one should know that the land is the *nirmāṇa-vipāka* (retributive environment), while the assembly is the *mūla-vipāka* (primary retribution).

The environment is neither inherently defiled nor pure; its defilement or purity depends on the primary retribution. Because sentient beings are impure, the land also becomes defiled; thus, [the Buddha] now moves the assembly.
This causes the land to be pure. △ Third, the verse on the gathering of the emanated bodies:
Each of the Buddhas proceeds beneath the jeweled trees, which are adorned with lotuses like a pure pond; beneath those jeweled trees...
Upon all these lion thrones sat the Buddhas, resplendent with light and adornment like great torches kindled in the midst of the night.
From their bodies issued a sublime fragrance that pervaded the lands of the ten directions; sentient beings, being perfumed by it, were overcome with joy, like those buffeted by a great wind.
It blows upon the small branches of the tree. By this expedient means, it causes the Dharma to abide for a long time.
Regarding "like a torch in the darkness": when a torch is lit in the midst of the night's gloom, it can dispel all obscurity;
likewise, the radiance of all Buddhas can dispel the darkness of ignorance. A great wind sucks up the small tree.
As for "branches," it means that small branches, when blown by a great wind, are entirely turned by the wind and cannot restrain themselves.
Now, sentient beings, being perfumed by the fragrance of the Buddhas' bodies, find their joy beyond self-mastery.
It is like a great wind blowing upon small branches. Regarding the long endurance of the Dharma:
if the Buddhas were to personally propagate it themselves, they would not clarify the skillful means for its endurance.

Now, having come to this Sahā world, he sits beneath a jewel tree, adorned like a lotus flower, emitting various radiances and causing all manner of fragrances to issue from his body, so as to cause all sentient beings—
All may see it, and by means of this, cause people to widely propagate this sutra so that it may endure for a long time.
This is the use of skillful means to ensure the Dharma remains for a long duration. Why is this? It is because the fragrance of the body is indeed a supreme and wondrous function.
The whole is liberation; light is the merit of contemplative insight (*vipaśyanā*). The whole is *prajñā*; the lotus is the essence of purity.
The whole is the *dharmakāya*. By means of this fragrance, one perfumes all sentient beings, causing them to perfect the virtue of liberation.
By means of this light, one illuminates all sentient beings, causing them to perfect [wisdom].
As for this virtue: when all sentient beings behold the Buddha’s adornments as being like a lotus flower, it causes them to accomplish the virtue of the Dharma-body.
Once these three virtues are accomplished, they enter together into the secret treasury, whereby they all attain the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Having realized the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, one is able to propagate and disseminate it in this manner oneself.

Therefore, by means of these skillful expedients (*upāya*), the Buddhas are able to cause the sublime Dharma to abide for a long time. △ Third, the verse on Śākyamuni’s call for recruitment, in four parts: first, the actual verse.
He addressed the great assembly: "After my parinirvāṇa, who will be able to protect, uphold, read, and recite this sutra? Now, before the Buddha, let each person speak their own vow."
Regarding the self-proclaimed vow: how can one protect this sutra? It is essential that one makes a personal vow.

This is because the principle of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena—the three thousandfold nature and characteristics—which is expounded in this sutra, is something inherently possessed by sentient beings themselves.
If one practices in accordance with this principle, whether raising one's hand or lowering one's head, every action becomes a cause for attaining Buddhahood. This...
That sublime practice is also that which sentient beings themselves inherently possess and already have, namely, the teaching that expresses this very sutra.
Within the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the Single Vehicle Dharma; there is neither a second nor a third.

This sublime teaching is likewise that which sentient beings themselves inherently possess and already have; for it is such that both the teaching and its underlying principle are fundamentally possessed by all sentient beings.
This is not the sutra of another person; therefore, whether one upholds it or reads and explains it, one must still take a personal vow.
Part Two: Exhortation to Uphold (in two sections). First, seven lines exhorting by way of the three Buddhas. Second, from "All good...
onwards, twenty lines exhorting by way of comparative evaluation. The first of these has two parts: first, the direct exhortation.
Although that Buddha Prabhūtaratna has long since entered parinirvāṇa, he utters this lion’s roar by virtue of his great vow.
You should understand this intention: that both I and the emanated Buddhas who have gathered here ask, "O sons of the Buddha, who among you is able to protect the Dharma?"
One should then make a great vow so that [this teaching] may endure for a long time.
The Lion’s Roar, from within the precious stupa, uttered a great sound and praised him, saying, "Excellent! Excellent!"

"It is so, it is so," and "Excellent! This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and other such teachings—these are all the lion’s roar of Prabhūtaratna, a discourse of definitive fearlessness. One should understand this meaning:
that although the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna has long since entered parinirvāṇa, he has now surged forth today to authenticate this sutra. What is his intention? It is to manifest his divided bodies."
The various Buddhas have each abandoned their wondrous lands to come here to hear this sutra; what is their intention?
Now I, Śākyamuni, proclaim this recruitment to circulate this sutra; what is my intention? Therefore, it is said: "One should know this intention.
However, when examined thoroughly, there is the testimony of confirmation by Prabhūtaratna, the arrival of the emanated bodies to listen, and the proclamation of the recruitment by Śākyamuni.
There is no other intention; it is solely to cause all sentient beings to open, show, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

As for "all you sons of the Buddha," if these sons of the Buddha can understand the intent of the three Buddhas and circulate it wherever they go and proclaim it everywhere, then this wondrous Dharma will naturally endure forever and ever.
It shall not be interrupted, and thus it will abide long in the world. △ Second, clarifying the benefits, in two parts. First, clarifying the benefit of protection and maintenance:
"Whoever is able to protect this Dharma of the sutra shall thereby be making offerings to me and to Prabhūtaratna. This Buddha Prabhūtaratna..."

Abiding within the jeweled stupa, they constantly travel throughout the ten directions. For the sake of this sutra, they also make offerings to all the emanated Buddhas who come, adorning and illuminating all the worlds.

Regarding the statement "to speak [of this] is itself an offering," it means that this sutra is the manifestation of the original intent for transcending the world by Śākyamuni and all Buddhas, clarifying the causal conditions of the Great Matter.
Furthermore, it is that which is collectively protected and remembered by both Śākyamuni and all Buddhas.
Therefore, if there are those who can protect and remember it, and receive and uphold this sutra, they will be identical to the mindfulness of all Buddhas.
Thus, one unites with the minds of all Buddhas. Is this not to make offerings to the Three Buddhas?
To offer in such a manner is the true offering of the Dharma. △ Second, clarifying the benefits of exposition and understanding.
If one speaks this sutra, one sees me; if one sees the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna and the various emanation Buddhas, one sees us. "I" refers to Śākyamuni, the person who is able to preach it;
therefore, if one can explain the sutras spoken by the Tathāgata, one sees the person who is able to preach them. Prabhūtaratna is the... [able one].

The realization is the witness, and the emanated bodies are those who hear. Therefore, if one can explain the sutras that constitute both the realized and the heard, one sees the Buddhas who are the realizers and the hearers.
To protect and uphold [the teaching] is to make offerings to the three Buddhas; to be able to explain it is to see the three Buddhas.
There is no greater benefit than this offering and vision of the Buddhas.
How could one not speak for the sake of protection? △ Second, the exhortation based on comparative evaluation, in two parts: First, the direct exhortation in eighteen lines;
second, the clarification of the benefits in the two lines beginning with "I have... The first part has two sections: first, the general exhortation.
"O sons of good family, each of you should contemplate this with earnest attention. This is a difficult task; you ought to give rise to great vows.
That this is a difficult task is why, at the beginning of the proclamation, it was said that one should personally utter a vow of truth; next, it was stated that one should give rise to great vows;
and later, when the circulation was again entreated, it was once more said that one should personally utter a vow of truth. This statement means that one ought to give rise to great vows."
Why is it that he exhorts and inspires them in this manner time and again? It is because the Dharma of this sutra is supremely excellent;
therefore, during his past causal stage, Śākyamuni Tathāgata made a vow to seek unexcelled bodhi, and upon hearing this sutra, he attained it.
Having now become a Buddha, he preaches this sutra, and his emanations gather from afar, coming desiring to hear the Dharma—this too is due to that vow.
Those who wish to hear this sutra [should know that] when the Bodhisattva Prabhūtaratna was practicing the bodhisattva path, he made a great vow, desiring to bear witness to this sutra.
Thus, there are no three Buddhas among them who did not make such a vow regarding this sutra;
therefore, those who propagate it should likewise make a great vow. △ Second, the specific comparison. This text of comparison consists of one section.
There are seventeen verses. If they are divided in detail: first, five verses concerning the speaker alone;
second, two verses concerning both the act of writing and receiving/retaining [the text], as well as having others write it; third, two verses concerning temporary reading alone;
fourth, two verses concerning both receiving/retaining and explaining; fifth, three verses concerning both expounding and listening, as well as receiving/retaining. And...
Regarding the inquiry into the meaning: there are six [sections] on the three practices, which primarily concern upholding them.

Now, I shall merely extract their essential points and provide a brief exposition concerning writing, reading, reciting, and receiving and upholding them. The text is divided into four parts; the first concerns the comparative evaluation through exposition.
Though one were to preach as many other sūtras as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, it would not yet be considered difficult;
nor would it be difficult to take Mount Sumeru and hurl it to countless Buddha-fields in other directions; nor would it be difficult to move the great trichiliocosm with a single toe.
To hurl it far away to another land would not yet be difficult; nor would it be difficult to stand at the Summit of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and expound for the multitude immeasurable other sutras.
However, if, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, one is able to preach this sutra amidst the evil age, that indeed would be difficult.
The first four lines concern that which can measure; the subsequent line concerns that which is measured. The text says:

"touching Mount Sumeru, shaking the great trichiliocosm, grasping empty space, entering the conflagration at the end of an eon," and so forth. These are not events that actually exist; rather, they are [the manifestations] of the Tathāgata.
To attempt to measure it and skillfully expound it—those who receive and uphold this sutra do so with great difficulty.

This is because such a matter is considered fundamentally the most difficult to accomplish. Yet, if one can uphold and expound this sutra, when measured against that standard, it is not actually difficult; it is only the upholding and expounding of this very sutra that is difficult. However, within this...
As for what was said: although all other sutras are exceedingly numerous, they are all merely provisional teachings and skillful means (*upāya*).
Since they are able to illuminate [the truth] through these very provisional and skillful wisdoms, even though they can explain such difficult matters, it is not yet to be considered difficult.
If this sutra were not based on the inconceivable, ultimate wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*) of the Mahāyāna, it could not [do so].

It is illuminated and understood; thus, it is difficult. To cast Mount Sumeru and shake the great trichiliocosm is certainly a difficult feat, yet it does not necessarily require one who possesses supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).
Even if one lacks supernatural power, if one possesses ordinary strength, one could still do it.
Furthermore, this is not yet difficult. If this sutra were not the power of the inconceivable wisdom of the Mahāyāna, it could not have moved;
therefore, this is indeed difficult. △ Second, the evaluation by way of transcription.
Suppose there were someone who could grasp empty space in their hand and travel about with it; this would not yet be difficult.
But after my parinirvāṇa, if one were to write it out oneself or cause others to write it out, that indeed would be difficult.
To grasp empty space with one's hands and travel about through it is indeed difficult;
yet, this is merely the emptiness of the mundane world, which those possessing ordinary powers might still be able to achieve, and thus it is not yet truly difficult.

To transcribe this sutra, however, is the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), which none but those endowed with the power of great wisdom can accomplish; therefore, it is exceedingly difficult.
...Furthermore, △ Third, regarding the comparative evaluation through recitation and chanting:

even if one were to place the great earth upon the tip of a toenail and ascend to the Brahma Heaven, it would not be considered difficult; yet, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, [to uphold this teaching] is far more so.
In this degenerate age, to read this sutra even for a moment is truly difficult.
