While it would certainly be a difficult feat to lift the great earth and ascend to the Brahma Heaven, even if someone with ordinary strength were able to do so by lifting the worldly earth to the worldly heavens, it would not yet be considered difficult. However, if...
To briefly read and recite this sutra is to ascend from the ground of the principle of true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) to the heaven of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
This cannot be accomplished by one who lacks the power of great wisdom; therefore, it is exceedingly difficult. △ Fourth, the comparative evaluation based on upholding and maintaining [the sutra].
Even if one were to carry a load of dry grass into the conflagration at the end of a kalpa and not be burned, that would not yet be difficult.

But after my parinirvāṇa, if one upholds this sutra and explains it for the sake of even a single person, that indeed is difficult. This is more difficult than if one were to uphold the eighty-four thousand treasuries of the Dharma.
To expound the twelve divisions of the sūtras for others and cause those who hear them to attain the six supernormal powers—though one may do so, it is not yet difficult.
But after my parinirvāṇa, to hear and receive this sūtra and inquire into its meaning and purpose—that indeed is difficult.

If a person were to preach the Dharma and cause thousands of myriads of koṭis—immeasurable, incalculable, and as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—sentient beings to attain arhatship and be endowed with the six supernormal powers, although such a benefit would exist, it would not yet be considered difficult. However, after my parinirvāṇa, if one can uphold [this sutra], that is truly difficult.
A scripture such as this is indeed difficult;
it is not burned by the kalpa-fire, nor is it consumed by the insentient fires of the world. Therefore, although it is difficult, it is not yet sufficient to be considered truly difficult.
If one upholds this sutra, one will not be burned by the fires of the afflictions of the five stages. Thus...

It is the most difficult of all. Although one may attain the eighty-four thousand treasuries of the Dharma, the twelve divisions of the sutras, and the six supernormal powers, these are all merely of the Hīnayāna; therefore, though they are difficult, they are not yet truly difficult.

If one can hear this sutra, it is the treasury of the Dharma of the perfect and real Mahāyāna, a section that is purely complete and uniquely wondrous. Because it involves the unconditioned and transformative supernatural powers, it is the most [difficult].
It is difficult [to attain]. To obtain the fruit of Arhatship is also to become a Śrāvaka Arhat of the Lesser Vehicle;
because one can only slay the thieves of views and afflictions, although it is difficult, it is not yet the ultimate difficulty.
If one upholds this sutra, one can slay the thief of ignorance and become a true Arhat, worthy of universal offerings from all the world; therefore, this is exceedingly difficult.
△ Second, the clarification of the benefits:
For the sake of the Buddha-way, throughout immeasurable lands from the beginning until now, I have extensively expounded various sutras; yet among them, [this one is supreme].
This sutra is the foremost. If there are those capable of upholding it, they uphold the body of the Buddha.
Regarding "from the beginning until now": the beginning refers to the initial commencement of the Buddha’s teaching, and the end refers to the conclusion of his teaching today.
As for "upholding the body of the Buddha," if we discuss this from a general perspective, the Buddha's body is that which is able to preach.
This sutra is that which is taught; therefore, to uphold this sutra that is taught is to have already upheld the Buddha-body that is the teacher.
To speak according to ultimate reality, this sutra takes the true mark of all phenomena (dharmas) as its essence.

If one can uphold this, one will thoroughly understand that all phenomena throughout the three thousandfold world system are true in their respective characteristics and real in each of their dharmas, thereby upholding the Buddha’s Dharma-body.
This sutra takes the cause and effect of the One Vehicle as its central theme; if one can uphold it, [one shall attain liberation].
Thus, one can by means of causes that accord with reality realize fruits that accord with reality, thereby upholding the Buddha’s reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*).
This sutra functions to sever doubt and give rise to faith; if one can uphold it, there will be no doubt that is not severed.
Faith is never without its arising; it naturally circulates wherever it may be, responding and transforming without fixed direction, thereby upholding the Buddha’s response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Since one who upholds this sutra upholds the Buddha’s three bodies (*trikāya*), how great is its benefit! The above constitutes the first exhortation based on the three Buddhas.
Second is the exhortation based on comparative measurement. Both begin with the formal exhortation and subsequently clarify the benefits. This concludes the general [section].
This third verse is Śākyamuni’s proclamation of the invitation. Within the four subsequent sections, the second—Exhortation to Uphold—is now concluded.
△ Third, the Explanation of the Intent: Why is it that, with reference to the three Buddhas and through a process of comparison, he exhorts one to uphold [the teaching] at every turn?
This is the intended meaning: those who are able to receive and uphold it will cause all Buddhas to rejoice on their behalf.
I rejoice and offer praise for this, so that one may swiftly attain the path of Buddhahood; thus, I repeatedly exhort you to uphold it.
The text is divided into three parts; the first is a renewed appeal for its circulation.
"Good sons, after my parinirvāṇa, who among you will be able to receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra? Now, before the Buddha, speak your own vow."
△ Second, explaining the Buddha’s joy:
This sutra is difficult to uphold. If one upholds it even for a moment, I shall rejoice, and so too shall all the Buddhas. Such a person—
Praised by all Buddhas,
those who even briefly uphold this [sūtra] shall immediately be the object of the Buddhas' joy and praise;

for this sūtra is that which all Buddhas have used to express their fundamental intent regarding the transcendence of the world and to clarify the causes and conditions of the Great Matter, and they together protect it.
Because one who possesses mindfulness can maintain it even for a brief moment, although it does not last long, they have already conformed to the mind of all Buddhas.
How could one not feel joy? How could one not offer praise? △ Third, the fruition is achieved through the cause.
This is indeed valor; this is indeed diligence; this is called upholding the precepts. One who practices the dhūtas will swiftly attain the unsurpassed, true path.
This clarifies that the cause is accomplished through this sutra, and the fruit is realized through this sutra. The first line concerns the accomplishment of the cause;
it states that one who is "valiant and diligent" is not so called if they merely uphold the sutras of the three preceding teachings. Such a person would not be termed valiant nor diligent.
Only now, by being able to uphold this profound, single-vehicle (ekayāna) teaching of perfect reality—which is so difficult to uphold—is one truly valiant and diligent.
This sutra is true valor and true diligence; it is what is called being one who upholds the precepts.
The meaning of the precepts is to prevent wrongdoing and cease evil. This sutra prevents every non-virtue of the five abodes and ceases every evil of the two deaths;
thus, one is able to uphold it. To do so is precisely what is called upholding the complete precepts. This sutra possesses [all these qualities].
Because one can uphold the inconceivable and wondrous practices of the *dharmadhātu*, this is precisely what is called practicing the ascetic austerities of *dhūta*.

Next, "half-practice" refers to the attainment of the fruit; once the cause has been perfected, the fruit is naturally achieved. Therefore, one is able to swiftly attain the unsurpassed path of Buddhahood.
To say "swiftly attained" means that in a single lifetime, one transcends and ascends to the ten stages (*bhūmi*). That is to say:
They shall travel through the four quarters until they reach the site of enlightenment. △ Fourth, the conclusion on the benefits:
Those who are able to read and uphold this sutra in future ages are true sons of the Buddha; they abide in the ground of pure goodness after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
One who can explain its meaning is the eye of all devas and humans in this world; in an age of fear, such a person can speak even for a moment, and all devas and humans should make offerings to them.
One who is a true son of the Buddha: this sutra is the family heritage of the Mahāyāna.
It is by means of this sutra that all Buddhas have attained great sovereignty and become kings of all dharmas.

Now, being able to read and uphold this sutra, one is capable of inheriting the Mahāyāna family heritage of the Tathāgata and can likewise succeed to the rank of the Dharma King; therefore, such a person is truly [a son of the Buddha].
He is a son of the Buddha. Being a true son, the ground upon which he dwells is the realm of the principle of the true mark (*dharmatā*), characterized by purity, harmony, goodness, and compliance.

Because he inwardly mobilizes compassion and outwardly perceives the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), he is able to shield himself from the various obstacles of affliction (*kleśa*) and abide in a state of pure goodness. Since the Eye of the World has clarified this meaning, [it is as follows].
He is able to teach and transform devas and humans, causing them to understand the meaning and attain clear realization;
therefore, he is the Eye of the World. Regarding the above, whether in prose or in verse, in all cases it first elucidates the emergence of Prabhūtaratna to authenticate this sutra;
next, it clarifies the gathering from afar of the emanated bodies to hear this sutra; and finally—
This section elucidates Śākyamuni’s exhortation to solicit offerings for the purpose of circulating this sutra.

The reason it is elucidated so extensively is precisely to verify and establish what was explained in the "Dharma Master" chapter: that the Dharma he upholds is supremely excellent, thereby causing all beings to develop faith and remain free from doubt.
This concludes the explanation of the Appearance of the Jeweled Stupa.

Tiantai Teaching and Contemplation Lecture Record by Master Yisong Compiled and Edited by the Eastern Ou Buddhist Xiaorou and Guanghe The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Twelve:
Devadatta (Note: The provided text contains a title and bibliographic information for a specific edition of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
As such, it does not contain the scriptural content of the chapter itself.)
If one wishes to investigate the origin of this chapter, it is because the Tathāgata, desiring to circulate this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*,
has— in the "Dharma-preacher" chapter— elucidated that the person who can uphold it is supremely venerable and the Dharma they uphold is supremely sublime.
Although this elucidation has been made in this manner, if it were not further authenticated, then...

People still did not believe this. Therefore, in the following "Jewel Stupa" chapter, it is clarified that Many Treasures (*Prabhūtaratna*) provides such testimony, the emanated bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) provide such assistance and inspiration, and Śākyamuni issues such a call for witnesses, thereby establishing the supremacy of the Dharma.
Since the Dharma has now been authenticated, how could the Honored One among Men be without proof?
Therefore, this chapter exists; it is the passage that serves as proof for the attainment of the status of a World-Honored One (Buddha).
Yet, how is it known that this chapter can serve as proof for attaining the status of a World-Honored One?

It is because herein, first, it clarifies that in the past, Devadatta propagated the sutra and attained the state of Tathāgata Devendra; next, it clarifies that today, the Dragon Girl heard the Dharma.

And yet he was able to realize the stainless realm. If even Devadatta—who committed the five heinous crimes and performed every kind of evil—could attain Buddhahood by virtue of propagating the sutras, then it goes without saying that those who possess goodness and can propagate the sutras will likewise achieve Buddhahood.
Even if the Dragon Girl were of the animal class and possessed a female body, she too [attained realization] through hearing the Dharma.
Having realized Bodhi, it goes without saying that such a person—a great man among gods and humans—is capable of hearing the Dharma and attaining Buddhahood.
Thus, according to the nine realms, the three vehicles, and the seven kinds of expedient means, one must know that for all sentient beings, if they do not propagate this sutra, let them not hear it.
However, if they can propagate and hear this sutra, then there is no [obstacle].
There are those who do not attain Buddhahood; yet since all have attained Buddhahood, how could humans not be most supreme?
Therefore, this chapter can serve as proof for the supremacy of humanity. Now, within this chapter, it first clarifies that although Devadatta propagated the sutras, he attained Buddhahood;
subsequently, it clarifies that the dragon girl heard the Dharma and—
He realized enlightenment. Why, then, does the title of this chapter mention only Devadatta and not the dragon girl?
There are several reasons for this. First, this chapter is intended to demonstrate that one can attain the status of a World-Honored One.
The intention lies in the widespread propagation of this sutra. Now, Devadatta is the one capable of propagating it, while the dragon girl is the one who hears the Dharma.

Since the intention is focused on propagation, only Devadatta—the one capable of propagating—is highlighted, while the dragon girl who hears the Dharma is omitted. Second, [it is because] he wishes to...
This reveals that Śākyamuni’s ability to expound this sutra today is entirely due to his past vows and diligent seeking;
thus he has attained the hearing, the cultivation, and the realization of it. Therefore, he is now able to preach this for the great assembly.
Once the great assembly has heard this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, they too shall cultivate and realize it just as the Buddha has, and they shall likewise bring forth a response to the Buddha.
Regarding the grace received today, one should further propagate it wherever possible by recollecting the vows of the past, ensuring that they are never interrupted;
for this reason, only Sudatta is mentioned, while the Dragon Girl is not. Third, Sudatta.

Since he is a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) of Śākyamuni, and the dragon girl is a disciple of Mañjuśrī, yet today Mañjuśrī addresses Śākyamuni as "Teacher," the dragon girl must be regarded by Datta as his great-great-grandmother.
It is only proper that a grandson yield precedence to his grandfather; therefore, only Datta is mentioned, while the dragon girl is not.

Furthermore, as for the fourth point regarding the two individuals: although both have attained Buddhahood, if it concerns the Dragon Girl, she will manifest her departure for the Immaculate World (*Vimalā-loka*) in the south to achieve equal and perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

As for the Bodhisattva Jñānākara and the Venerable Śāriputra, they were indeed those who did not believe; yet, having witnessed such a thing, they dared not fail to believe. Thus, the text says: "Jñānākara..."
The Bodhisattvas, Śāriputra, and the entire assembly accepted this in silence. Thus, they all believed that this dragon girl had already attained Buddhahood.

As for Devadatta, a man of many evils, although the Tathāgata prophesied that he would become a Buddha as a Heavenly King, it would still require more than immeasurable kalpas; since he has not yet reached that point in the present.
To achieve Buddhahood so swiftly makes it difficult for people to place their trust in it. Therefore, within the text, the Buddha himself encourages faith, saying:

"If one hears this 'Chapter on Devadatta' and, with a pure heart, believes and reveres it without giving rise to doubt, one shall not fall into the evil realms but will be born by transformation from a lotus flower.
Thus, while the Dragon Girl has now become credible, there are still those among the people who have not yet believed Devadatta.
Now, because one desires that people must have faith and not harbor doubts, only Pūrṇa is designated, while the dragon girl is not.
Fifth, although both attained Buddhahood and were realized as Honored Men, Pūrṇa was a male of the Śākya clan, whereas the dragon girl was a female of the animal realm;
thus, it is only natural that the female should yield to the male. Therefore...
In recording individuals, the humble are ranked below the noble; therefore, only Devadatta is mentioned, while the Dragon Girl is not.

Sixth, although both persons are explained together within this chapter, it first clarifies Devadatta, and subsequently—after Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta seeks to withdraw and the Buddha stops him and commands him to remain—it is only then that the Dragon Girl is explained. Thus, the initial instance is cited first.
Since he alone is worthy of being mentioned at the end of the subsequent section, only Devadatta is designated, while the Dragon Girl is not.
Seventh, given the six preceding points, it follows that the chapter title should naturally be "Devadatta."
Therefore, after the Tathāgata had fully explained the merits and rewards, he immediately proclaimed with his golden mouth:

"If there be good sons or good daughters who hear the 'Devadatta Chapter' of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*— and it should be noted that the title 'Nāga Girl Chapter' of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is not mentioned here—
one will know that the heading of this chapter was uttered from the Buddha's own golden mouth and was not added by a translator."
Furthermore, these additions were not inserted by the compilers of the sūtra;
therefore, they merely mention Devadatta while omitting the mention of the dragon girl. In the Sanskrit language, Devadatta means "Heavenly Heat.
Because he was a bodhisattva acting in reverse, committing every kind of evil and becoming an enemy of Śākyamuni, at the time of his birth, the hearts of humans and devas—

All were distressed by this, which is why it is called "Heavenly Distress" (*Tianre*). It is also called "Heavenly Bestowal" (*Tianshou*); because the parents prayed to Heaven for them and Heaven bestowed them upon them, it is also named "Heavenly Bestowal.

The text of this chapter is divided into two parts: first, citing the past to illustrate the universal application of the Sūtra; second, clarifying the present propagation of the teaching. The first part has two sections: first, the master and disciple universally applying the Sūtra;

second, correlating the ancient and the modern. The first of these [two] has two sections. 1. The Master and Disciple Universally Apply the Sūtra. 2. Correlating the Ancient and the Modern. The first of these [two] has two sections.
First, the prose; second, the verse. The first section has three parts. First, the king’s quest for the Dharma:
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas, as well as the fourfold assembly of devas and humans: "In the past, throughout immeasurable kalpas..."
In seeking the Lotus Sūtra, I was never weary or indolent.
When I say, "As for my past lives," this means that my ability to preach this sūtra for you today is not without cause;
it is because in former times I diligently sought this sūtra and practiced in accordance with it, whereby I finally attained Buddhahood.
Therefore, on this very day, I am now able to preach this sutra for you all. This is a general explanation of his past quest for the sutra:
throughout many kalpas, he constantly served as a king, making vows to seek unexcelled bodhi with a mind that never regressed.

This is a specific mention of the time period to clarify the seeking of this sutra. As for the statement "one who constantly acts as a king," one should know that this sutra is indeed the king among all sutras;
therefore, there are those capable of hearing, understanding, receiving, and upholding it, and practicing according to it.
If among humans, he will surely become a king among men; if in the heavens, he will surely become a king among gods.
Even if his karma is heavy such that he cannot escape the evil realms and falls among the class of animals, he will still surely become a king among birds and beasts.
Now, this king was able to diligently seek this sutra throughout immeasurable kalpas; for this reason, across many kalpas—

He was always a king of nations. Having become a king, the vows he made did not seek the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), nor did they seek the three realms of existence (*tribhava*), nor did they seek the state of a bodhisattva;
rather, he sought only the fruit of Buddhahood, unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
His mind never wavered; it was not turned back by the three realms of existence, nor was it turned back by the two vehicles, nor was it...
This is turned by the Bodhisattva; this clarifies his making of vows.
Desiring to fulfill the six pāramitās, he diligently practices giving with a heart free from stinginess, [offering] elephants, horses, and the seven treasures.
His kingdom, city, wife, children, slaves, servants, attendants, head, eyes, marrow, brain, body, flesh, hands, and feet—he did not begrudge his own life.
At that time, the people of the world had immeasurable lifespans; yet for the sake of the Dharma, he relinquished his royal throne and entrusted the administration to his crown prince.

He beat the drum and issued a proclamation, seeking the Dharma in all four directions: "Who among you can expound the Mahāyāna for me? I shall provide for them with all my life and serve as their attendant."
This clarifies the arising of practice. Regarding the statement "fulfilling the six pāramitās":

if one says that the six perfections are cultivated over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* and a hundred *kalpas*, such that there is a time of completion, this refers to the *Tripiṭaka* Bodhisattva fulfilling the six perfections as a matter of fact.
In this context, when that king desires to seek this sutra, he must fulfill the practice of the six perfections because—
The reality of all phenomena (dharmatā), which is the true nature (dharmatā) elucidated by this sutra, is fully complete within the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā).

Therefore, those who seek this sutra must practice the six perfections. To speak of "fulfilling the practice" means that, while realizing that within the dharmatā there is fundamentally no stinginess or greed, one does not obstruct the conformity with the dharmatā by practicing generosity throughout the day. Thus...
Upon reaching the thorough knowledge of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), there is fundamentally no delusion; yet, this does not obstruct one’s conformity with that nature.
To practice *prajñā* throughout the entire day is what is called fulfilling the six *pāramitās*. This section generally clarifies the desire to fulfill the six perfections.
From "diligently practicing giving" (*dāna*) onwards, it specifically clarifies the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*). At that time, the people of the world...
Below, this is a separate clarification of the *prajñāpāramitā*. By citing its beginning and its end, it encompasses the four [perfections] in between.

Within the separate clarification of *dāna* (generosity): elephants, horses, and so forth constitute the relinquishing of wealth; wives, children, and so forth constitute the relinquishing of the body.
Wives and children are the "external body," while heads, eyes, and so forth are the "internal body. Not begrudging one's physical life constitutes the relinquishing of life. This is why...

One must relinquish wealth, and furthermore, relinquish body and life. Since these three things are all fundamentally unstable, one relinquishes the unstable worldly wealth in exchange for the stable merit of the supramundane Dharma-wealth;
one relinquishes the unstable body composed of the four great elements in exchange for the stable Dharma-body of the Mahāyāna. One relinquishes...
One exchanges this life, which is not firm in body or mind, for the firm life of wisdom of the Mahāyāna.
△ Second, the Seer’s Exposition of the Sūtra:
At that time, there was a seer who came and addressed the king, saying: "I possess a Mahāyāna sūtra named the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. If you do not oppose it..."
I shall proclaim it for you.
"Not being in opposition to me" does not mean merely not being in opposition to my provisions;
rather, it means that I possess the sublime Dharma, and if you can practice according to what I have taught and cultivate it accordingly, I shall proclaim it for you. If you do not rely upon it...
If one does not practice, then even explaining it would be of no benefit; therefore, the verse says: "If there are those who can practice, I shall proclaim it for them.
△ Third, hearing the Dharma and receiving it with faith.
Upon hearing the words of the seer, the king was filled with joy and leaped for gladness. He immediately followed the seer, providing all that was required:
gathering fruit, drawing water, collecting firewood, and preparing food; even using his own body as a seat and bed, he served him with body and mind untiring throughout that time.
For a thousand years, for the sake of the Dharma, he served him with diligent devotion so that nothing was lacking.
Having first sought the sublime Dharma, he has now obtained it; thus his vow has been fulfilled and his quest has been realized.
Therefore, he rejoices and leaps for joy. △ Part Two: Verses in Praise, which has two sections. First, the direct praise; second, the explanation of the intent.
The first [section] has three parts. First, the praise of the king seeking the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“I recall a past kalpa, when for the sake of seeking the Great Dharma, though I was a king of the world, I did not crave the pleasures of the five desires.”
He struck the bell to announce to the four quarters: "Who possesses the Great Dharma? If you will explain it for me, I shall become your servant.
△ Second, the verse on the seer’s preaching of the sutra.
At that time, there was a rishi named Asita who came and addressed the Great King: "I possess a subtle and wondrous Dharma, rare in this world.
If you are able to practice it, I shall explain it for you."
△ Three verses on hearing the Dharma and receiving it with faith:
At that time, having heard the words of the seer, the king’s heart was filled with great joy; he immediately followed the seer and provided him with all that was required.
Gathering firewood and fruits and melons, he offers them with respect according to the season; because his heart is set upon the wondrous Dharma, his body and mind know no weariness or fatigue.
△ Second, the expression of his intention:
"For the sake of all sentient beings everywhere, he diligently seeks the Great Dharma; it is not for his own sake, nor for the pleasures of the five desires."
Therefore, having been a great king, he diligently sought and obtained this Dharma, ultimately attaining Buddhahood; for this reason, I now preach it for you.
△ Second, the conclusion connecting the ancient and the present, in three parts: first, the formal connection.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "The king at that time was none other than myself; the rishi of that time was the present Devadatta.
Part Two: Fully Explaining the Merit and Retribution. 1. First, explaining the merit and retribution of the disciples. 2. Second, explaining the merit and retribution of the teacher.
The first two [sections]. The first clarifies the accomplishment through causes:
"It is because of the spiritual friend Devadatta that I have fully perfected the six pāramitās, as well as loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity."
A "good spiritual friend" refers to this sutra as the teaching that expresses [the truth], the principle that is revealed, and the practice that is initiated;
Devadatta was able to understand each of these individually. He knew that this sutra is the teaching of the One Vehicle, the perfect and true, the unsurpassed *amṛta* (clarified butter).
He knew that this sutra is the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, wherein the provisional and the ultimate are unified.
The principle of non-duality: knowing that this sutra is the inconceivable practice of the *dharmadhātu*.
Thus, regarding its teaching, its principle, and its practice, one possesses thorough knowledge and skillful discernment; therefore, it is called a "good friend" (*kalyāṇamitra*).
As for the phrase "causing me to be fully endowed," it means that while initially one desires to fulfill the six *pāramitās*, now, by means of Deva...
Sudatta, you shall attain full perfection. Not only will you perfect the six pāramitās, but you shall also perfect the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*).
To bestow happiness is loving-kindness (*maitrī*); in bestowing happiness, there is no happiness that is not bestowed. To extract suffering is compassion (*karuṇā*);
in extracting suffering, there is no suffering that is not extracted. As for joy (*muditā*), it is to rejoice in all sentient beings, such that they may be freed from suffering and attain happiness.
Furthermore, those who practice renunciation are not only able to bestow happiness upon their kin, but can also uproot the suffering of their enemies.
△ Second, clarifying the attainment of the fruit.
The thirty-two marks, the eighty minor characteristics, the purple-golden hue, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four means of integration,
the eighteen unique qualities, and the supernatural powers of the path— all that led to the attainment of perfect enlightenment and the vast deliverance of sentient beings—
were all due to Devadatta as a virtuous friend.

When the cause is established, the fruit is naturally achieved; thus, one is able to be fully endowed with the thirty-two marks, and even fully endowed with the power of the divine path, thereby attaining equal and perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Having personally established the cause and achieved the fruit, one is further able to transform others, enabling them likewise to establish the cause and achieve the fruit; thus, one is able to extensively deliver sentient beings. All of this is due to the cause.

"Et cetera" (etc. means that being able to accomplish the cause, being able to realize the fruit, being able to practice for oneself, and being able to transform others—all these are made possible through Devadatta.
II. Explaining the Master’s Merit and Retribution (in four parts): First, explaining the timing of the attainment of the fruit.
He addressed the fourfold assembly: "Devadatta, after the passing of immeasurable kalpas, he shall attain Buddhahood;
his name shall be Tathāgata Devendra, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata. 2. Explaining the Name and Title of the Buddha’s Land.
Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One. The world is named Heavenly Path;
the Buddha’s title is Heavenly King. As for the land being named Heavenly Path, it is because during his causal stage he was a Bodhisattva who practiced contrary conduct. No...
Because he does not commit evil, at the time of his initial birth, the hearts of humans and devas are heated; thus he is named "Heated by Heaven" (Tianre).
When he reaches the stage of fruition, he is able to teach and transform all humans and devas through the unsurpassed Way, and among all dharmas...
Having attained great sovereign mastery, the Buddha is titled "Heavenly King" (Tianwang), and the world is accordingly named the "Heavenly Path" (Tiandao).
Third, regarding the lifespan and the preaching of the Dharma:

during the time when the Buddha Heavenly King dwelt in the world, he remained for twenty intermediate kalpas (*antarakalpa*), extensively expounding the wondrous Dharma for the sake of sentient beings along the Ganges.

Sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges attained the fruit of Arhatship; immeasurable sentient beings resolved their minds upon the path of Pratyekabuddhahood; and sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed path.
To speak of the "wondrous Dharma" refers precisely to the wondrous Dharma that is sublime within the coarse.
For that Buddha also first opened the provisional and subsequently revealed the ultimate; thus, the coarse dharmas he opened were themselves the wondrous Dharma.
Because he first opened the provisional, countless sentient beings attained the fruit of Arhatship and gave rise to the aspiration for Pratyekabuddhahood.

The mind reveals reality through its successive stages; thus, there are sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges who give rise to the aspiration for the Unsurpassed Way and reach the stage of non-retrogression.
Furthermore, there are three types of such aspiration: that of designation (*nāman*), that of resemblance (*pratirūpa*), and that of partial realization (*praveśa*).
If one initiates the *saṃnāha* (armor) at the very first thought and brings great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) to its conclusion when confronting hardships, this is the aspiration of designation.

If one says that when a bodhisattva of the ten wholesome paths arouses the great mind, they forever part from the ocean of suffering in the three realms, this is merely a semblance of arousing the mind.

If one says that at the very moment of first arousing the mind, one immediately attains perfect enlightenment, such that the entire body of wisdom is realized without depending on others, and that with one arousal all are aroused—such that when the direct cause (正因) is aroused, the conditional cause (緣因) and the completing cause (了因) are also aroused, and when the conditional cause is aroused... [the same applies]. This is likewise a semblance of arousing the mind.

At that time, the *liǎo-yīn* (the cause of realization) also arises; when the *liǎo-yīn* arises, the *zhèng-yuán* (the object-condition) also arises. This is precisely the awakening of the mind through partial realization (*fen-zhèng fā-xīn*).
One thereby attains the patience of non-arising (*wú-shēng rěn*).
To "attain the patience of non-arising" (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) means to mentally accept and affirm the principle of neither arising nor ceasing within one's heart.

There are, however, five types of patience: the patience of faith (śraddhā-kṣānti), the patience of subduing (dharmanidhyāna-kṣānti), the patience of compliance (anuloma-kṣānti), the patience of non-arising, and the patience of cessation (nirvāṇa-kṣānti).
To be able to believe in, understand, and mentally accept this principle of non-arising is called the patience of faith; this corresponds to the stage of names (nāma-caryā-bhūmi).

Furthermore, regarding this principle of non-arising (*anutpāda*), being able to contemplate it perfectly and illuminate it perfectly, and being able to accept it within the mind while subduing the afflictions (*kleśa*), is called "Patience of Subduing" (*kṣānti-avaivartika*);

this is the stage of contemplative practice (*ālocana-caryā*). Regarding this principle of non-arising, accepting it within the mind with gentleness, pliancy, and virtuous compliance, thereby attaining a state of correspondence and similarity, is called "Patience of Gentle Compliance" (*anulomikī-kṣānti*); this is the stage of [the semblance of] marks (*nimitta-sadṛśa*).

This is the stage of semblance (*sādṛśa-avasthā*). Regarding this principle of non-arising, one attains patient acceptance (*kṣānti*) within the mind and is able to clearly know that all phenomena are entirely without arising.

One destroys a portion of ignorance (*avidyā*) and manifests a portion of the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*). This continues until one destroys forty-one grades of ignorance and manifests forty-one portions of the three virtues;
this is called the "patience regarding non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), which is [the stage of] partial [realization].

This refers to the stage of realization. Regarding this principle of non-arising, one attains patient acceptance within the mind and is able to thoroughly understand that all phenomena are entirely neither born nor extinguished.
Both forms of death are exhausted, and the five stages of dwelling are forever eliminated.

Having ascended to the summit of the mountain of nirvāṇa, one reaches ultimate quiescence; this is called "patience of quiescence" (*kṣānti*), which is the ultimate stage. It should be understood as follows:

One should know the five kinds of patience (*kṣānti*). Although the fourth is specifically designated as "patience of non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), both the first and the last may also be termed "non-arising.
Furthermore, it is not only the patience of non-arising that is thus; the remaining four patiences may likewise be considered both initial and final.

For example, the initial "patience of faith" (*śraddhā-kṣānti*) may be called "faith-patience," while the subsequent four patiences may be termed "patience of extinction" (*nirvāṇa-kṣānti*); this applies to the higher [stages] as well.
The four kinds of patience (*kṣānti*) may all likewise be termed the patience of quiescent extinction (*śānti-kṣānti*).

Upon reaching the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*), there are three types of non-retrogression: namely, non-retrogression in terms of stage (*avasthā-avaivartika*), non-retrogression in terms of practice (*caryā-avaivartika*), and non-retrogression in terms of mindfulness (*smṛti-avaivartika*). These are capable of destroying [wrong] views.
Contemplation: When one ascends to the fruits of sagehood, one never again recedes from the station of a sage;

this is called "non-retrogression of position," which corresponds to the first through seventh stages of faith in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). When one is able to shatter the dust-like afflictions and engage in transformative guidance, one never again recedes from the practice of a bodhisattva;
this is called "non-retrogression of practice," which corresponds to the eighth through tenth stages of faith.
Being able to shatter ignorance and realize the three virtues, one then never regresses from the thought of the Middle Way; therefore, it is called "non-retrogression of mindfulness.

This refers to the stage from the first *bhūmi* (ground) onward. However, in the preceding text, it was first stated that one "gives rise to the mind for the Unsurpassed Way," next that one "attains the patience of non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and now it says one "reaches non-retrogression"; thus, these should be distinguished according to their sequential order.

This ensures that the words do not become redundant. Although the words follow a sequential order, the meaning is in fact perfectly integrated; thus, while it does not preclude non-sequentiality, the words are expressed in sequence.
Regarding the arousal of the mind for the Unsurpassed Way (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), among the three types of arousal, this is the arousal of the mind by name alone.

Among the five types, it corresponds to the two stages of "subduing" and "conformity" within the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Upon reaching the stage of non-retrogression, [it becomes the true patience].
Regarding these three types of non-retrogression, it refers specifically to the non-retrogression of mindfulness (*smṛty-avaivartika*).
This is the spontaneous entry into the ocean of the fruit of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), proceeding from the stage of *ā* to *cha*.

In this way, from the initial stage of "name" (*nāman*), through "contemplative practice" (*pratipatti*) and "semblance" (*pratirūpa*), up to "partial realization" (*praveśa*) and "ultimate fulfillment" (*niṣṭhā*), the complete sequence of the beginning and end of progressive cultivation is fully established within the fivefold stages of identity (*pañca-yoga*).
Yet the text does not constitute a redundancy. △ Fourth, clarifying the duration of the True and Semblance Dharma periods:
After the Tathāgata Devendra entered parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma remained in the world for twenty intermediate kalpas. His bodily relics [remained].
A stupa made of the seven treasures was erected, sixty yojanas in height and forty yojanas in length and breadth.

All the devas and human beings offered worship and service with various flowers, powdered incense, burning incense, ointment incense, robes, necklaces, banners, flags, precious canopies, musical performances, and hymns of praise.
Through this marvelous stupa of the seven treasures, immeasurable sentient beings attained the fruit of arhatship. Immeasurable...
Sentient beings awaken to the state of a pratyekabuddha; inconceivable sentient beings resolve their minds on bodhi and attain the stage of non-retrogression.
△ Third, exhorting faith and freedom from doubt.

The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "In a future age, if there are good men or good women who, upon hearing the 'Devadatta Chapter' of the Lotus Sutra of the Wondrous Dharma, believe and revere it with a pure heart and do not give rise to doubt or confusion, they shall not fall into hell."
Whether as hungry ghosts or animals, they shall be born before the Buddhas of the ten directions; in whatever place they are born, they will constantly hear this sutra.
If born among humans or devas, they will experience supreme and wondrous bliss; if before a Buddha, they will be born by transformation upon a lotus flower.
Regarding the phrase "pure mind, faith, and reverence": since it has already been stated that one must have faith and reverence, why is it further specified that the mind must be pure?
Generally, when a virtuous person attains Buddhahood, it is easily believed by others, and thus they are not exhorted to have a pure mind of faith and reverence.
However, in this case, Devadatta was an extremely wicked person, yet he too attained Buddhahood; therefore, regarding this, people— [would find it difficult to believe].
It is difficult to believe; therefore, I exhort all sentient beings that they must believe with a pure mind and pay respectful homage.

How does one believe with a pure mind? It means believing that the reason Śākyamuni attained Buddhahood was because he was able to fully realize that the cultivation of goodness is entirely identical to the inherent goodness of one's nature, and thus attained Buddhahood. As for Devadatta’s...

Regarding the attainment of Buddhahood: it is because one is able to thoroughly comprehend that the cultivated evil (*xi-è*) is entirely identical to the inherent evil (*xing-è*) that one attains Buddhahood.
Why is it that by thoroughly comprehending that the cultivated evil is entirely identical to the inherent evil, one is able to become a Buddha?

It is because all cultivated evil does not exist separately apart from the inherent nature; rather, it arises entirely from that nature. Since the cultivated evil is entirely derived from the nature...

When it arises, the entire body is itself inherent evil (*xing-è*). Yet, because this inherent evil is pervasive and interfused, it spontaneously encompasses the inherent good (*xing-shan*) of the Buddha-realm.
Thus, through such thorough realization, one is able to attain Buddhahood. However, ultimately, what constitutes cultivated good and inherent good, or cultivated evil and inherent evil?
There is no other distinction between inherent good and inherent evil than that which exists within a single moment of thought in sentient beings.

"What is contemplated within the mind" refers to the ten realms as they are inherently complete within the principle (*li*). The Buddha-realm inherent in the principle is "inherently good" (*xing-shan*);
the nine realms inherent in the principle are "inherently evil" (*xing-e*). As for cultivated good and cultivated evil, there is nothing else to them:

they are simply the ten realms as they are manifested through phenomena (*shi-zao*) when a sentient being gives rise to even a single thought-moment. The Buddha-realm manifested through phenomena is precisely cultivated good.

The phenomenal creation of the nine realms is precisely "cultivated evil. As for "cultivated good" being identical to "inherent good," the Buddha-realm as a phenomenal creation exists entirely through its inherent potential.
Thus, cultivation arises from nature; cultivation is originally nature. Through the totality of cultivation, one returns to nature; nature is originally cultivation.
Therefore, the *Fahua Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra) states: "One simply contemplates the inherent potential, and both [nature and cultivation] are present."
Both are negated and both are established. Both being the Dharma-realm means that when both are negated, one negation is the negation of all;

this is the inconceivable ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Both being established means that one establishment is the establishment of all; this is the inconceivable conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Both being the Dharma-realm means that the two extremes are mutually non-referential; one transcendence is the transcendence of all; this is the inconceivable Middle Way.
This is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Having observed that within the principle-endowment (*li-jù*), both negation and affirmation are simultaneous,

and both are the inconceivable three truths of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), how could this not mean that the inherent goodness of the principle-endowment gives rise to the cultivated goodness of phenomenal creation (*shi-zào*),
and that the cultivated goodness of phenomenal creation is fundamentally identical to the inherent goodness of the principle-endowment?

Therefore, one knows that cultivated goodness is entirely identical to inherent goodness. Once this is understood, then inherent nature and cultivation are non-dual, and cultivation and nature are of one suchness;
thus, one can attain Buddhahood. As for cultivated evil being entirely identical to inherent evil, it refers to the nine realms created through phenomenal activity.
Since it also exists by virtue of being inherently complete (*li-jù*), it likewise arises from nature (*xing*) through cultivation (*xiū*), such that cultivation is entirely identical to nature.
As for the statement that "the evil of nature is interfused" and spontaneously encompasses the goodness of the Buddha-realm within nature:
because the evil of nature and the goodness of nature are both fully present within the infinitesimal single thought-moment of a sentient being, how could they not be spontaneously encompassed?
It is so. As stated in the *Famen* (Gate of Non-duality): "Although the natures of clarity and turbidity differ, turbidity is inherently present from the beginning.
Although turbidity is inherently present, it is entirely clarity in its essence. Thus, one knows that the nature of evil spontaneously encompasses the nature of good.
How is this known? It is because the nature of the clear wave is itself the nature of good, while the nature of the turbid wave is itself the nature of evil.
The turbid waves are themselves the adventitious evil (*shū-aku*). That the turbidity is originally present means that the adventitious evil is entirely the original nature of evil (*hon-sei-aku*).
Although the turbidity is originally present, it is entirely pure; this means that the original nature of evil is entirely the original nature of good (*hon-sei-zen*).
Once one can realize this, all adventitious evil does not exist separately apart from the original nature; rather, it arises entirely from the original nature of evil. Since...

If one arises from the entirety of evil nature, then the entire body is itself the evil nature; yet, this nature is likewise non-dual, and the cultivated nature (śikṣā) and the inherent nature (prakṛti) are as one.
Thus, evil nature, by its spontaneous functioning, is itself good nature. How could it not be capable of achieving Buddhahood?
Thus, one should know that the reason Śākyamuni was able to attain Buddhahood was entirely because he was able to realize that cultivated goodness is itself inherent (nature) goodness;
and the reason Devadatta was able to attain Buddhahood was entirely because he was able to penetrate that cultivated evil is itself inherent evil.
To be able to believe in this way is what is called "pure-hearted faith and reverence. If one is born among humans or devas and receives superior [rebirth]...
"Experiencing bliss through the sublime" means receiving bliss by means of the Way. Since one is now able to believe in this sutra, the seed has already been established.
Once the seed is established, it will inevitably manifest as active practice;
therefore, in a future life, one will again be able to receive bliss through the Way. II. Clarifying the Propagation of the Teaching in the Present Life. Part One: Mañjuśrī’s Exposition of the Sutra.
Second, the two dragon girls attain Buddhahood. First, there are nine sections. First, regarding Zhiji’s request for his return:
At that time, in the region below, a bodhisattva named Zhiji, who had followed the World-Honored One Prabhūtaratna, addressed the Buddha Prabhūtaratna.
When returning to his own land,
the bodhisattva named Zhijī (Jñānakūṭa) is so called because this bodhisattva is able to cultivate all the wisdom of the Tathāgata;
having reached a state of true accumulation through long-term perseverance, he also attains the realization of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, and is therefore named Jñānakūṭa.
Furthermore, the land of Prabhūtaratna Buddha was originally located in the east; now that it has emerged from the earth, it is said to have "descended.

Zhi-ji’s intention was that Prabhūtaratna had come for the purpose of providing testimony for the *jimi* (trace) section; since that testimony has now been obtained, he requested that [the Buddha] return.
△ Second, Śākyamuni exhorts him to remain.
Śākyamuni Buddha said to Jñākūṭa: "Good son, wait a moment.
Here is a bodhisattva named Mañjuśrī with whom you may meet and discuss the sublime Dharma; you may then return to your own land."
"Wait for a brief moment" means that the Tathāgata exhorted them to wait and cease [their departure]. Within this, there are two intentions. First, regarding the proximate:

speaking according to the text, it is because he wishes for her to meet with Mañjuśrī and manifest the rapid attainment of Buddhahood by the dragon girl, thereby revealing the supreme dignity of humanity.
Second, regarding the remote: speaking from the perspective of the underlying meaning, it refers to the *jiamen* (trace-gate).
Although [the provisional teachings] have already been verified, the Root Chapter has not yet arisen;
one must still verify the Root Chapter before returning to one's native land. Therefore, the Tathāgata exhorted them to desist.
As for "being able to meet": Mañjuśrī is one of great wisdom, and thus Zhiji was able to meet him. This discusses the wondrous...
As for the Dharma: it is not that there is something separate by which one perceives the subtlety of the Dharma;
rather, it is through perfect cultivation and perfect realization that one swiftly attains Buddhahood—this alone is the subtlety of the Dharma. △ Thirdly, Mañjuśrī arrives.
At that time, Mañjuśrī sat upon a thousand-petaled lotus flower as large as a chariot wheel. The bodhisattvas who had come with him likewise sat upon precious lotus flowers.
They emerged spontaneously from the ocean, from the palace of the Dragon King Sāgara, and remained suspended in mid-air.

Proceeding to Vulture Peak Mountain, they descended from their lotuses and arrived at the place where the Buddha was. There, they prostrated themselves with their heads at the feet of the two World-Honored Ones.
Having completed his prostrations, he went to where Zhiji was, exchanged greetings with him, and sat to one side.
The thousand-petaled lotus, which is like a chariot wheel—the flower symbolizes the cause; the thousand petals symbolize the wondrous principle of the thousand suchnesses;
and the chariot wheel symbolizes perfection. This means that Mañjuśrī has realized this wondrous principle of the thousand suchnesses and acts accordingly.
Regarding the "wondrous cause," this cause is precisely the perfect cause of the Mahāyāna.
As for the bodhisattvas who have come together and likewise sit upon precious lotus flowers: since these bodhisattvas follow Mañjuśrī, they likewise practice the wondrous cause just as Mañjuśrī does;
therefore, it is said that they also sit upon lotus flowers. They emerge spontaneously from the great ocean.
"Abiding in the midst of empty space" means that this Great Vehicle’s perfect cause is not separate from its fruit;
therefore, it emerges from the ocean of the fruit of *sarvajñā* (omniscience) as if emerging from what is not [emerging], spontaneously surging forth. As for the term "spontaneously":

Since this perfect cause originally emerges from the ocean of fruition, it is established in accordance with the nature of reality; it does not depend on artificial construction, nor does it require effortful shifting.

Therefore, it is said to be "spontaneous" (*svayambhū*). Since it does not emerge from anywhere, it likewise does not abide, yet it abides—abiding in the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
The reason for abiding in emptiness is that, as previously mentioned, when the Many-Treasures Stupa was about to bear witness...
Because this sutra has arrived, the stupa emerged from the earth and remained suspended in mid-air.
Śākyamuni, wishing to open the stupa, likewise remained in mid-air. The fourfold assembly of humans and devas, empowered by the Buddha, also remained in mid-air.
Thus, Mañjuśrī, now emerging from the ocean, likewise remains in mid-air; this precisely symbolizes abiding while not abiding.
Each dwells in the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*). Here, someone may raise this objection:
"In the previous three transformations of the pure land, there were no great oceans or rivers. Why then does Mañjuśrī still emerge from the great ocean?

Now, it is said that the previous mention of the threefold transformation of the pure land refers only to the transformation of the sentient beings' perceptions (*citta-vikṛti*), not the transformation of the objective realm (*viṣaya*). It only transforms their...
The sentiment is as follows: previously it was said that there were no great oceans, yet the environment did not change; therefore, it is now said that [the assembly] emerged from the great ocean.
Since the environment did not change, the great ocean remains perfectly intact, for the Dragon Palace is sovereign.

"Proceeding to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa" means "proceeding and arriving. This signifies the subsuming of the derivative to return to the fundamental. From the lotus, they descend to the place where the Buddha is.
This signifies turning away from causes toward the fruit. Paying homage to the World-Honored One of Two Ages:
Prabhūtaratna represents non-extinction, and Śākyamuni represents non-arising; this is precisely returning once more to the wondrous principle of neither arising nor extinguishing.
△ Fourth, Jñatikauṇḍinya poses a question.
The Bodhisattva Zhijí asked Mañjuśrī, "Virtuous One, as you went to the dragon palace, how many sentient beings did you transform?
△ 5. Mañjuśrī’s response.
Mañjuśrī said, "Their number is immeasurable, beyond calculation, not to be proclaimed by mouth, nor fathomed by mind.
Wait but a moment, and you shall know it for yourself."
Regarding the phrase "their number is immeasurable": because it is incalculable, it cannot be proclaimed by speech;
because it is unfathomable, it cannot be measured by the mind. This clarifies that it cannot be known through inference (*anumāna*).

As for the phrase "wait but a moment and you shall know for yourself," this clarifies that it can only be known through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). △ Sixth, the testimony of the multitude's numbers.
Before he had finished speaking, countless bodhisattvas emerged from the sea, seated upon precious lotus flowers, and proceeded to Vulture Peak, dwelling in mid-air.
All these bodhisattvas had been converted and guided by Mañjuśrī; they were fully endowed with the practices of a bodhisattva and were collectively discussing the six pāramitās.
Meanwhile, those who were originally śrāvakas remained in mid-air, reciting the *śrāvaka* [sutras].
Regarding the practice of hearing [the Dharma]: they now all cultivate the meaning of emptiness within the Mahāyāna.
As for the six pāramitās, there are four types, namely: those with signs (sanimitta), those without signs (animitta), and those both with and without signs.

It is neither the mark of existence nor the mark of non-existence. What is now being spoken of is not the former three; rather, it is the six perfections of the mark that is neither existent nor non-existent.
When speaking of the practice of the śrāvakas, this does not refer to the śrāvaka practice of the Hīnayāna that knows suffering, abandons its origin, aspires for cessation, and cultivates the path;
rather, it refers to the four truths of non-action, which, by means of the sound of the Buddha-way, cause [beings to...]

That all have heard [the Dharma] is the practice of the Śrāvakas. That they now all practice the meaning of the Great Vehicle’s emptiness means that although they originally practiced the emptiness of the Hīnayāna, having now been transformed and delivered by Mañjuśrī, they all practice the meaning of the Great Vehicle’s emptiness.
△ Seventh, Mañjuśrī concludes with the benefits.
Mañjuśrī said to Zhijizhi: "The manner in which I taught and transformed beings in the ocean was such as this.
That the matter was such as this means that while the bodhisattvas all discussed together the six pāramitās, the śrāvakas spoke of the practices of the śrāvakas;
this is because they were now all practicing the meaning of the Mahāyāna emptiness. Furthermore, it may be said: 'As you previously asked me...'"
When you, O Benevolent One, went to the Dragon Palace, how many were you able to transform? I replied only that their number was immeasurable.
Those who have now all surged forth before us are precisely those transformed by me; therefore, it is said that "he taught and transformed them in the sea.
Such was the matter. 8. Stanza of Praise by Jñatikauṇḍinya.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Jñānakośa praised him in verse, saying:
"O one of great wisdom, virtue, and heroic vigor, who has transformed and delivered immeasurable multitudes! Now this entire great assembly, as well as I myself, have all witnessed it."
He eloquently expounds the meaning of the true mark (*tathatā*) and reveals the Dharma of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), widely guiding all sentient beings so that they may swiftly achieve *bodhi*.
Regarding "the one of great wisdom, virtue, and heroic vigor" and so forth:

this refers to Mañjuśrī, who is able to rely upon the inconceivable great wisdom of the Tathāgata to practice and realize it; thus, he is able to transform all bodhisattvas. If one were not endowed with such [wisdom]...
As for those with the merit of wisdom, they are unable [to do so]; therefore, he is called "One of Great Wisdom and Virtue.
While other bodhisattvas are also able to perform the work of transformation and deliverance, some do so only within this land, while others do so only in other directions.
Some exist only among humans, while others exist only in the heavens; yet Mañjuśrī is able to enter the dragon palaces within the great ocean to bring about their transformation and deliverance.
He is thus the most courageous and powerful of beings, and for this reason he is called "powerful and robust.
As for the phrase "and those whom I have already seen," it means that at first one does not know how many have been transformed, but now—
Not only do I know this, but the entire great assembly, including myself, all see that the multitude you have transformed is exceedingly vast and beyond counting;
for you are able to deliver and transform such a great number of beings.
Therefore, I praise you as one of great wisdom, virtue, and heroic vigor.
Furthermore, the multitude you transform is exceedingly vast, yet you do not allow them to become followers of the two vehicles or partial, inferior bodhisattvas;
rather, you cause them all to swiftly attain the realization of unsurpassed bodhi. That you are able to cause them all to achieve bodhi is entirely due to...
With great wisdom and heroic vigor, you have proclaimed and spread the meaning of the true nature (*dharmatā*), and have opened up and elucidated the Dharma of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
You have extensively guided all sentient beings, thereby causing them all to swiftly attain Bodhi.
As for the meaning of the true nature: in its primary sense, it is designated as being without marks (*animitta*) and yet not without marks (*na-animitta*).
The true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is the markless; it is the absence of the mark of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). The non-mark is the absence of the mark of nirvāṇa.
Since both extremes—birth-and-death and nirvāṇa—are not [existent], this is precisely the Middle Way, the true mark.
To speak of its ultimate reality, it is the true mark of the true mark of all phenomena (*dharmas*). That is to say, all phenomena have such marks, such natures, and so forth, up to...
This is the tenfold suchness (*daśatathatā*) of the ultimate equality of beginning and end. Within a single realm (*dhātu*), these ten suchnesses are fully present;

within the hundred realms, there are thus one thousand suchnesses. When categorized according to provisional names and substantial dharmas—including both primary and secondary retributions—there are three thousand suchnesses.
These three thousand natures and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are each and every one empty, provisional, and middle; yet every characteristic is real, and every dharma is true.
This is what is called the "true mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). This reveals its essence (*tattva*). The "Dharma of the One Vehicle" clarifies its central tenet (*mūla*).
As for the "cause of the Mahāyāna," it is the true mark of all phenomena; as for the "fruit of the Mahāyāna," it is likewise the true mark of all phenomena.
Therefore, the Dharma of the One Vehicle is precisely the clarification of the tenet of its cause and fruit. Since both the essence and the tenet are present, [the teaching is complete].
Thus, one is able to guide all beings, causing them to sever doubt and give rise to faith; this constitutes its function (*yòng*).
From this function, one returns to establish the fundamental principle (*zōng*) and manifest the essence (*tǐ*), whereby Bodhi can be swiftly attained.
It is precisely because it can expound the essence of the true nature (*shíxiàng*), can express the principle of the One Vehicle (*yīshèng*), and can initiate broad guidance.
Its function is to transform and deliver immeasurable sentient beings so that they may swiftly attain Bodhi; therefore, it is called "Great Wisdom-Virtue" and "Great Courageous Prowess.
△ Ninth, Mañjuśrī’s Summary and Confirmation.
Mañjuśrī said, "Within the great ocean, I have always preached only the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

II. The Dragon Girl Attains Buddhahood, in three parts: 1. Questions and answers that clarify the matter; 2. A renewed presentation of doubts and difficulties; 3. The benefits obtained by the assembly.
The first part [Questions and Answers] has two sub-sections: 1. Jñatikauṇḍinya poses the question.
Jñānākara asked Mañjuśrī, saying: "This sutra is profoundly deep and subtle, a treasure among all sutras, rare in the world.
As for why this sutra is called 'subtle' and so forth, it is because this sutra is the teaching of the perfect and ultimate One Vehicle (ekayāna), and not—"
It is called "profound" because it transcends the shallowness of the three vehicles, the five teachings, and the seven stages of expedient means.
It is called "subtle" because the essence of the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) expounded in this sutra is that which all Buddhas have realized and which all sentient beings inherently possess.

This sutra is the central doctrine of the cause and fruit of the One Vehicle; by being able to cultivate the perfect cause, one will surely attain the perfect fruit, yet the cause and fruit are not...
Second, it is called "wondrous" (miao). Furthermore, the essence of the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) of this sutra vertically penetrates the source of the three truths;
hence it is called "profound" (shen). The principle of cause and effect of this sutra is able to encompass immeasurable multitudes of wholesome qualities, as well as their realization and attainment.
Therefore, it is called "subtle. This Mahāyāna sūtra is such that nothing remains unsevered through its application, and nothing fails to arise through faith;
therefore, it is called "wondrous. Whether already taught or yet to be taught, this sūtra is the foremost, cherished and protected by all Buddhas;
therefore, it is called a "jewel among all sūtras. Whether this sūtra is expounded or heard, it is most difficult to encounter, as if—
The udumbara flower appears only once in a great while; therefore, it is said to be rare.
Are there any sentient beings who, by applying themselves with diligent vigor, practice this sutra and quickly attain Buddhahood?

"Are there any sentient beings who... and so forth means: although this sutra is extremely profound, subtle, and rare in the world, since you now constantly proclaim it within the ocean, are there any people capable of diligently practicing according to this sutra and swiftly attaining Buddhahood?
The intent of the question is to ask: since this sutra is so subtle and wondrous, if [one does not...]

If one practices in reliance upon this, that is sufficient; if one can practice in reliance upon it, one will certainly attain Buddhahood, and moreover, one will certainly do so swiftly. However, not knowing whether there are those capable of doing so, he asks:
"Is there perhaps any sentient being who, by practicing this sutra, will swiftly attain Buddhahood? Regarding the phrase "practicing this sutra," this sutra is precisely [the teaching of] all...
The sublime principle of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of phenomena: the practitioner means one who, relying upon this sublime principle, gives rise to sublime understanding;

from this sublime understanding, they initiate sublime practice. If sublime practice is perfected, then doubt will not fail to be severed and faith will inevitably arise, whereby one can spontaneously and swiftly achieve Buddhahood.
Furthermore, the passage "Moreover, this sutra is extremely profound," and so forth, corresponds to the preceding verse.

"Expounding extensively upon the profound... and so forth. The section "The ultimate reality" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) below refers to the essence of the meaning of the true mark. "Diligently applying oneself...
and so forth refers to the core tenet of the One Vehicle Dharma (*ekayāna*). "Quickly attaining Buddhahood" refers to the function of broadly guiding sentient beings to swiftly achieve *bodhi*.
△ Second, Mañjuśrī’s summary response.
Mañjuśrī said: "There is a daughter of the Dragon King Sāgara who is eight years of age. She possesses sharp faculties and wisdom;
she well understands the faculties, karmic actions, and practices of sentient beings; and she has attained the dhāraṇīs of the profound secret treasury spoken by all Buddhas."

They are able to receive and uphold [the teachings] in their entirety; they enter deeply into meditative concentration and thoroughly comprehend all dharmas; in a single kṣaṇa, they give rise to the bodhicitta and attain non-retrogression.
To know the faculties, karmic actions, and activities of sentient beings is to clarify that one knows their capacities (*mātr̥kā*).
"Faculties" refers to the seeds of the faculties possessed in the past; "karmic actions" refers to the karmic activities currently present. This is what it means to have attained *dhāraṇī*.
This clarifies that he knows the Dharma and is able to restrain and maintain all things; that he can receive and uphold the secret treasury of all Buddhas.
This clarifies that he is able to cultivate wisdom, entering deeply into meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and thoroughly penetrating all dharmas.
This clarifies that he is able to cultivate meditative concentration. As for "thoroughly penetrating all dharmas," it means clearly understanding and penetrating the fact that all dharmas are...
All things are indeed the true mark (*dharmatā*). However, it is only by entering the great samādhi of true dhyāna that one can subsequently attain thorough understanding.

This is because all dharmas are fundamentally the true mark; yet, due to the perceptions of sentient beings with distracted minds, they may see various dharmas as being existent, empty, or characterized by other such states. Since these individual perceptions are unequal, [then...]

It cannot be called the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). If one can enter deeply into the various dhyānas and great samādhis, then one sees that although all dharmas possess various distinctions, there is not a single dharma that is not true, nor a single characteristic that is not real; they are, in their very essence, empty and quiescent.
This is entirely the true mark (*dharmatā*). From the phrase "in a single instant" (*kṣaṇe*) onwards, it clarifies his ability to fulfill his own practice.

To "arouse the bodhicitta" is to arouse it without there being anything to arouse; this arousal occurs at the first stage, the Stage of Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpādabhūmi*), where one attains non-retrogression. This is to attain it without there being anything to attain;
it is the attainment of non-retrogression through mindfulness.

His eloquence is unimpeded. He regards all sentient beings with loving-kindness as if they were his own infants. Fully endowed with merit, he expresses through speech what his mind contemplates—subtle, wondrous, and vast.
Compassionate, benevolent, and yielding, his will is harmonious and refined; thus he is able to reach Bodhi.
This clarifies his ability to transform others. Because he has attained the first stage (*bhūmi*), he is able to manifest bodies throughout the hundred realms to teach and transform sentient beings.
He regards the three realms with universal benevolence and views the four modes of birth as his only child;
thus it is said that he cherishes sentient beings like his own infant children. The phrase "endowed with merit" and so forth clarifies the perfection of his causes, namely:

As explained above, he is fully endowed with all manner of merits: knowing the capacities [of beings] and knowing the Dharma, cultivating meditative concentration and wisdom, and practicing for his own benefit as well as transforming others.
Because these merits are complete, he is able to manifest through speech exactly what is conceived in his mind—subtle and inconceivable, vast and limitless—and thus he can bestow...
He delights in uprooting suffering through compassion; he is capable of universal love, humility, benevolence, and yielding.

Whatever his will is directed toward and whatever his mind pursues, it reaches the utmost harmony and refined gentleness. That he can attain Bodhi is the fulfillment of the fruition of these qualities.
△ Second, restating the doubts and difficulties in two parts: first, challenging the Perfect with the Partial; second, challenging [the Perfect] with the Provisional.
Indeed. Regarding the first two [sections], first is the objection raised by Jñānakuṭa.

The Bodhisattva Jñānakuṭa said: "I have seen that Śākyamuni Tathāgata, throughout immeasurable kalpas, performed difficult practices and asceticism, accumulating merit and virtue while seeking the path to bodhi without ever ceasing. He surveyed the trichiliocosm, and even..."
There is not even a space the size of a mustard seed where a bodhisattva has not sacrificed their body and life for the sake of sentient beings before finally attaining the path to enlightenment.
You do not believe that this woman could attain perfect awakening in a mere instant.
Regarding the phrase "the Bodhisattva Jñānākara and others," the meaning is that Mañjuśrī said:
"Although you have stated that the dragon girl can attain *bodhi* in an instant, even as I, Jñānākara, I cannot help but harbor some doubt.
I need not wait to compare this with the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time; rather, let us compare her directly to you, Śākyamuni, the Master of Transformation."
It can be seen. Thus it is said, "I have seen" (and so forth). Regarding "the time I have passed through": this refers to the period traversed by Śākyamuni, which is exceedingly vast and remote.
Regarding "the lands I have observed": the realms traversed are exceedingly extensive. Regarding "it was not merely":
the lives sacrificed were exceedingly numerous. Regarding "for the sake of sentient beings": this should correspond to the aforementioned point that the time [spent] was exceedingly long.
"Long. The earth is utterly vast; his lifespans are exceedingly numerous. Only after this may one attain Buddhahood.
It is clear, therefore, that Śākyamuni’s attainment of the Way was extremely difficult. You, Mañjuśrī, can also know and see this.
If a dragon girl attains Buddhahood in a mere moment, how can it be believed? Thus it is said: 'I do not believe,' and so forth. If one divides the text, [it reveals] my view.
The phrase "and so forth" generally clarifies that he practiced for many kalpas. The phrase "contemplating the three [equalities]" specifically cites the single practice of giving.
The phrase "lack of faith and so forth" formally concludes the refutation. △ Second, the Dragon Girl’s praise and explanation.
Before his speech had concluded, the Dragon King’s daughter suddenly appeared before him. She prostrated herself in reverence, withdrew to stand to one side, and praised him with these verses:
"Profoundly penetrating the characteristics of sin and merit, universally illuminating the ten directions.
First is the introduction by the sūtra compiler; next, from "profoundly penetrating" onwards, is the formal praise and explanation.

Some say that this verse spoken by the dragon girl is a praise of Mañjuśrī, yet they fail to realize it occurs before the Buddha. To praise Mañjuśrī at such a time seems illogical. Furthermore, it says:
"Only the Buddha shall bear witness to this. This clearly praises the Buddha rather than Mañjuśrī. The intention of the dragon girl was this:

"You, Bodhisattva Jñānakūṭa, say that you have seen Śākyamuni Tathāgata accomplish bodhi through difficult practices and asceticism over immeasurable kalpas; yet you do not believe that I can become a Buddha in a mere instant."
This is because you understand only the sequential and distinct, while failing to understand the perfect and sudden.
As for the Tathāgata, he profoundly penetrates the characteristics of both sin and merit and realizes them through his own self-attestation, saying: "I am able to attain Buddhahood in a mere instant.
The first two phrases praise the Tathāgata’s ability to know the principle of the true mark (*dharmatā*); as for the words "sin and merit":

As for this, if discussed from a general perspective, the three miserable realms are considered transgression, while the human and celestial realms are considered merit; the human and celestial realms are considered transgression, while the two vehicles are considered merit;
the two vehicles are considered transgression, while Bodhisattvas are considered merit; and Bodhisattvas are considered transgression, while the Tathāgata is considered merit.
However, if speaking in terms of ultimate reality, it is certain that the nine realms are transgression and the Buddha-realm alone is merit. Nevertheless, by means of...
When ordinary people observe this, they perceive the marks of transgression within the nine realms and perceive the marks of merit within the Buddha-realm.
Since these marks of transgression and merit appear to be obtainable, they cannot be said to have profoundly penetrated the truth.
However, when the Tathāgata observes it with his inconceivable, wondrous wisdom, he does not perceive any marks of transgression within the nine realms that can be obtained, nor does he perceive...

There exists the meritorious aspect of the Buddha-realm that can be attained. Why is this? Because the aspect of sin is entirely identical to the true aspect (*dharmatā*), and the aspect of merit is likewise entirely identical to the true aspect.
The Tathāgata, moreover, is able to fully comprehend that all aspects are but the single true aspect;
he perceives neither the aspect of sin nor the aspect of merit. Therefore, it is said that he profoundly penetrates the aspects of sin and merit. Furthermore, this sutra...
The nine realms are all opened, and the three vehicles meet in unison. It is like the sun at its zenith, where no shadow remains;
how could there still be the appearance of sin in the nine realms or the appearance of merit in the Buddha-realm? Yet, the Dragon Girl does not praise the Buddha by extolling these separately;
rather, she praises the Buddha because she has profoundly realized the nature of sin and merit. This is likely because Zhizhi did not believe her.
One can attain bodhi; yet, because one perceives her as the daughter of a nāga king, one clearly views her as a sentient being burdened by the suffering of sin.
Conversely, when viewing the Tathāgata, one sees him as one adorned with unsurpassed merit and virtue; therefore, one cannot believe [that she could attain it].
If one can profoundly penetrate the characteristics of sin and merit, then one will not perceive the nāga girl as a sentient being of sinful suffering.
Furthermore, one does not perceive the Tathāgata as being merely one adorned with merit; thus, one is naturally able to believe that even a dragon girl can attain Buddhahood.
Regarding "shining universally throughout the ten directions": the ten directions are the ten realms.
When one deeply penetrates the nature of both sin and merit, one perceives that there is no nine realms or Buddha realm to be grasped—yet the ten realms [are all such].
They are utterly extinguished. Although the ten realms are thus extinguished, yet the ten realms remain perfectly distinct.
Therefore, at the very point where one profoundly penetrates the characteristics of sin and merit, one is able to universally illumine the ten directions with inconceivable, wondrous wisdom.
Because the ten realms remain perfectly distinct, sin and merit are likewise not lost. These two phrases are a praise.
