The Tathāgata is able to know the wondrous principle of the true mark.
His subtle and wondrous pure Dharma-body is adorned with the thirty-two primary marks and the eighty secondary characteristics.
This praises the Tathāgata, who is able to accomplish a subtle and wondrous body. For when the principle known is profound, the body accomplished must necessarily be wondrous;

thus it is said, "the subtle and wondrous pure Dharma-body," and so forth. Although the Dharma-body is realized and attained by the Buddha, sentient beings—even within their most minute thoughts—are all likewise capable of possessing it; therefore, it is called "subtle. That is to say:
That which sentient beings possess, the Buddha realizes; therefore, it is called "wondrous. It is not defiled by the five abodes nor sullied by the two deaths;
therefore, it is called "pure. Taking all phenomena as its body, this body pervades the entire dharma-realm;
therefore, it is called the "Dharmakāya. Since it takes all phenomena as its body and pervades the dharma-realm, outside of these phenomena—
There is no further dharma; yet there is nothing that is not pervasive and nothing that is not complete. Thus, he possesses the thirty-two marks.
Since the body that can possess them already pervades the *dharmadhātu*, the marks possessed therein likewise pervade the *dharmadhātu*.
Therefore, each of the thirty-two marks is boundless in its manifestation. To cite any single mark is for it to be entirely identical with the *dharmadhātu*. The *dharmadhātu*...
Apart from this, there is no further dharma; these are precisely the thirty-two marks possessed by the Dharma-body.

Although the Dharma-body is capable of possessing these thirty-two marks, if they are not illuminated by wondrous wisdom, then the Dharma-body would merely possess the marks within itself, unable to employ those marks to adorn the Dharma-body. Yet, as for the Tathāgata—

Because one is able to contemplate and illuminate [reality] perfectly through sublime wisdom, one is thus able to use the marks and signs possessed [by the Buddha] to adorn the Dharma-body, even though they are not [inherently] ornaments.
However, the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs are all marks and signs belonging to the Response-body (nirmāṇakāya).
As for the Dharma-body, it is neither a mark nor a non-mark; how then can one speak of "thirty[-two]?"
There are two [types] and eighty kinds. For although the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) is neither with marks nor without marks, it is entirely identical to the Response-body (nirmāṇakāya).
Although the Response-body possesses the primary and secondary marks, it is entirely identical to the Dharma-body.
Since the Dharma-body is entirely identical to the Response-body, although it is neither with marks nor without marks, this does not preclude its being non-fully-endowed, and yet—
He is fully endowed with the thirty-two marks; the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is entirely identical to the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Therefore, although he possesses the marks and signs of excellence, this does not hinder his being non-adorned, yet it adorns the dharma-body.
That he is able to be thus is because the three bodies are entirely one and the same essence. Since the three bodies are entirely one and the same essence, how could the dharma-body...
It is not only entirely identical to the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body); it is also entirely identical to the *saṃbhogakāya* (recompense body) while being identical to the *nirmāṇakāya*.
Nor is it merely entirely identical to the *dharmakāya* (dharma body); it is also entirely identical to the *saṃbhogakāya*.
Thus, that which is adorned is the *dharmakāya*, and that which is able to adorn is the *nirmāṇakāya*. By means of that which is able to adorn, one employs adornment; this is...

This refers to the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body). Since the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) cannot adorn the *dharmakāya* (dharma body) by itself, it is entirely through the wondrous wisdom of the *saṃbhogakāya* that the *dharmakāya* can be adorned.
Therefore, the use of the character "yi" (by/with) and its reversal as "yī" (one) precisely reveals the power of the *saṃbhogakāya*.
Thus, the two lines beginning with "The subtle and wondrous pure dharma body" clarify that the *dharmakāya* is entirely identical [to the reward body].
This is the correspondence. By means of the two phrases concerning the eighty minor marks, it clarifies that the complete retribution of correspondence is itself the Dharma-body.
Because these three—[the Dharma-body, the retribution-body, and the correspondence]—are mutually identical, the body thus accomplished is truly subtle and wondrous.

The reason one is able to accomplish such a subtle and wondrous body is entirely due to profoundly penetrating the characteristics of sin and merit; the principle known therein reaches its ultimate depth.
Therefore, he is one whom devas and humans look up to with reverence, whom dragons and spirits all honor with respect, and among all classes of sentient beings, there are none who do not revere him.
This single verse in praise of the Tathāgata demonstrates that he is worthy of being honored by all; for the principle of what is to be known is, once realized, such that...

Profound. Since the body thus accomplished is so wondrous, it naturally becomes that which all sentient beings honor by bearing it upon their heads and gazing up at it, making offerings to it with reverence, and approaching it with profound respect and veneration.
Furthermore, it is heard that he shall attain Bodhi; only the Buddha shall personally witness and know this.
"I expound the Mahāyāna teaching to deliver sentient beings from suffering"—this single line summarizes the request for verification. Regarding the phrase "furthermore it is heard":

when he was practicing in the Dragon Palace and had already attained actual realization, Mañjuśrī must have certainly conferred the prediction of his future enlightenment upon him. Now, because of Zhijizhang...
Because of this inquiry, Mañjuśrī replied: "There is a daughter of the Dragon King who is only eight years old;
she is fully endowed with merit and is capable of attaining Bodhi. Thus it is said, "Furthermore, I have heard that one can achieve Bodhi.
As for the phrase "Only the Buddha shall bear witness," it means that although Mañjuśrī stated that the Dragon Girl could attain Bodhi in a single kṣaṇa, you, Jñānākara Bodhisattva...
Sakra said: "The Tathāgata Śākyamuni attained bodhi only after performing difficult practices and austerities for immeasurable kalpas;
I do not believe that a dragon girl can attain buddhahood in a mere instant. This is surely because she does not understand the characteristics of sin and merit.
Only the Buddha, who deeply understands the characteristics of sin and merit, should bear witness for me that she has attained bodhi."
Regarding the phrase "I, Kāśyapa, and others," it means that when the Tathāgata attained Buddhahood,
he became the object of veneration for all and proclaimed the teachings of the Mahāyāna to transform and deliver all suffering sentient beings.
If the Tathāgata can bear witness so that I may quickly attain Buddhahood, then I too shall be like the Buddha, proclaiming the Mahāyāna.
He teaches and delivers sentient beings from suffering. △ Second, using the provisional to challenge the real, in two parts: first, Śāriputra’s challenge; second, the Dragon Girl’s explanation.
The first [of these] has three sections; the first is the general statement challenging its being difficult to believe.
At that time, Śāriputra said to the dragon girl: "That you claim to attain the Unsurpassed Way before long—this is difficult to believe.
This was the doubt of the Elder Ajita; he had harbored it for immeasurable kalpas, yet now, in a mere moment, he has become doubtful.

Now, when Śāriputra says, "This matter is difficult to believe," the two characters "this matter" (是事) point simultaneously to both the female body attaining Buddhahood and [the attainment of the Way before long].
This is because one will attain Buddhahood before long. It is said that for a woman’s body to attain Buddhahood is indeed difficult to believe;
yet, that one will attain Buddhahood before long is likewise difficult to believe. △ Second, the specific explanation of what is difficult to believe.
Why is this? The female body is defiled and impure; it is not a vessel for the Dharma. How could one attain unsurpassed bodhi?

The path of the Buddha is vast and remote; only after passing through immeasurable kalpas, accumulating practices through diligent toil, and fully cultivating all the pāramitās, can one finally achieve it.
The passage beginning with "The female body is defiled and impure" is a specific explanation of the difficulty of believing that a female body can attain Buddhahood.
The passage beginning with "The path of the Buddha is remote and vast" is a specific explanation of the difficulty of believing that one will attain Buddhahood before long.

Here, Śāriputra’s statement that "the path of the Buddha is remote and vast" likely arises because, following the previous exposition of the Dharma and his own realization, he has heard the Tathāgata’s confirmation, saying: "I..."
In the past, at the abodes of twenty trillion Buddhas, I have constantly taught and transformed you.

Furthermore, according to the teachings on causes and conditions, a *kalpa* is as vast as the time it takes to grind down a vast land or the time it takes for dust particles to vanish; such was the duration of the remote past.

At the time of the Great Penetrating Wisdom Buddha (*Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū*), he planted for us the perfect seed of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Considering this, it is not that I have not [done so] at the abodes of those twenty trillion Buddhas.
They have made great vows and aspired to the Buddha-way; yet now they have completely forgotten them.

When they heard the re-explanation under the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, it was not that they did not resolve their minds upon the Unsurpassed Way; however, they subsequently regressed from that greatness.

From that time until today, they have first been established in the *Āgamas*, then subjected to censure and rebuke during the *Vaipulya* period, and finally refined through the *Prajñāpāramitā*. Furthermore...
For more than forty years, during the assembly at the Lotus Sūtra, I first heard the brief exposition; yet I still harbored attachments and gave rise to doubts.

Only after hearing the extensive revelation and clarification did I finally attain awakening through it. Following my confession and acceptance [of the teaching], I received the Tathāgata’s confirmation and bestowal of a prophecy;
nevertheless, I was still unable to immediately sit upon the site of enlightenment, and must once again pass through the...
It requires immeasurable *kalpas* to make offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, to cultivate immeasurable practices, and to deliver immeasurable multitudes before one can attain the Way of Buddhahood.
Is this not indeed remote and vast? Therefore it is said that the Way of Buddhahood is "remote and vast";

after passing through immeasurable *kalpas* and fully cultivating all the *pāramitās*, one finally achieves it. Although you are now able to resolve your mind [toward enlightenment], it is no more than this.
"It is merely as I originally resolved in my mind. How could I possibly attain Buddhahood so soon?
Therefore, your claim that I shall attain the Way before long is difficult for me to believe. △ Third, a further reaffirmation of his unworthiness as a vessel.
Furthermore, the female body still possesses five obstacles: first, one cannot become a Brahmā King; second, Śakra; third, a Māra King;
fourth, a Cakravartin Sage-King; and fifth, the body of a Buddha. How, then, can a female body swiftly attain Buddhahood?

The preceding passage merely stated that the female body is defiled and not a vessel for the Dharma; now, this is further clarified by explaining the characteristics of defilement and the lack of capacity as a vessel.
Thus it says, "Furthermore, the female body," and so forth. All five types [of obstacles] constitute hindrances, whereby one is unable to perform [the practice].
In short, it is because she is defiled and not a vessel for the Dharma. Next, the phrase "How can a female body quickly attain Buddhahood?

is a double conclusion regarding the difficulty of belief. This means that while the female body is defiled and subject to the five obstacles, even Brahmā—the lord of the form realm—can only attain his status after observing the five precepts and ten wholesome paths, as well as practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). As for women...
As for lustful desire, how could one possibly obtain it? Śakra, the lord of the desire realm, maintains the precepts and is virtuous;
furthermore, he possesses only slight desire and yet is able to obtain it. Women, however, have much desire; how could one possibly obtain them?

Māra, the king of the sixth heaven of the desire realm, the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*), although said to harass practitioners of the path, also maintains the precepts, is virtuous, and has little desire.

As for those who are able to attain it: women have many desires; how could they possibly attain it? Even a Wheel-Turning King clearly observes the five constant virtues, cultivates the ten wholesome actions, and possesses few desires, yet he is able to attain it. Women, however, cannot yet avoid the defilements of flattery, crookedness, and lust;

how then could they attain it? The Buddha-body is without delusion and cannot be destroyed; it is without obstruction and cannot be severed; only then is it fully realized. Women are characterized by lust.
Your desire is so intense; how could you possibly attain it? Such are the five obstacles. Setting aside the first four for now, as for the fifth:
one cannot become a Buddha. You are currently in a female body; how then could you become a Buddha? The path of Buddhahood is vast and remote;
only after passing through immeasurable kalpas can it be perfected. How could you possibly attain it quickly?
"Attains Buddhahood. Thus we know that the single phrase "How could it be? serves as a double conclusion. That a female body attaining Buddhahood is difficult to believe;

likewise, that one will attain Buddhahood before long is also difficult to believe. △ Second, the Dragon Girl’s explanation has two parts. First, an explanation by way of comparing the offering of the pearl.
At that time, the dragon girl had a precious jewel worth as much as the three thousandfold world-system. She took it and offered it to the Buddha, who immediately accepted it.
The dragon girl said to the Bodhisattva Zhijī (Jñānākūṭa) and the Venerable Śāriputra, "I offered this precious jewel and the World-Honored One accepted it;
was this matter not swift? They replied, "It was exceedingly swift. The girl said, "By means of your supernatural powers, observe..."
My attainment of Buddhahood was even swifter than this.
There is a precious jewel that symbolizes the perfection of the principle of the single true mark; its value equals that of the three thousandfold world system.
The offering symbolizes the fulfillment of the three thousand natures and forms (*trisāhasra-lakṣaṇa*).

Presenting it to the Buddha symbolizes the cultivation of the perfect cause (*pariniṣpanna-hetu*) and the attainment of the perfect fruit (*pariniṣpanna-phala*). The Buddha’s acceptance of it symbolizes his realization that [the practitioner] shall swiftly attain Buddhahood;
this is what the preceding verse means when it says, "Only a Buddha may verify this. "By your divine power" refers to the spiritual power possessed by the Bodhisattva.
...and the supernatural powers possessed by the śrāvakas. As for "attaining Buddhahood even more swiftly," this refers to the act of offering and receiving occurring simultaneously.
Although it is extremely swift, because the natural state of offering comes first and receiving follows, even such swiftness is still not ultimate swiftness.
As for attaining Buddhahood, there is nothing else to be attained; from the very beginning, the mind itself is [Buddhahood].
The Buddha. Since the mind itself is the Buddha, it is originally accomplished within one's own mind; there is no need for contrived arrangements, nor is there any need for shifting or transforming.
It is directly present right here, with no further distinction between before and after. Therefore, it is said that "returning" is swifter than this.
"Observing my attainment of Buddhahood" refers to the resolution of the doubt regarding a woman’s body attaining Buddhahood. "Returning is swifter than this" means...

This explains that the doubt regarding the difficulty of believing [the attainment] of Buddhahood before long is resolved. While the two individuals, Jñānākūṭa and Śāriputra, raised their objections, the Dragon Girl merely offered a single pearl;
thus, their doubts should have been cleared away. If she were not one who attained Buddhahood in that very moment, how could she possess such unimpeded eloquence?
△ Second, the explanation by means of her actual attainment of the Buddha-way.
At that time, the entire assembly saw the dragon girl suddenly transform into a man, fully endowed with the practices of a bodhisattva.
She immediately proceeded to the Stainless World in the southern quarter, where she sat upon a precious lotus flower and attained equal and perfect enlightenment.
Adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, she extensively expounded the sublime Dharma for all sentient beings throughout the ten directions.
It is said that citing empty words is not as good as verifying through actual facts.
In an instant, this one who was difficult to believe will before long transform into a man; this refers to the female body which was difficult to believe. Go forth, O Bodhisattva!
This merely clarifies the matter of attaining Buddhahood. As for those who go to the South, it is because the karmic conditions of that land have already matured.

The world is named "Stainless" (Amala) because while people generally perceive her body as the defilement of a female form, she is instead able to penetrate the Great Way of True Reality (dharmatā), seeing neither the distinction between male and female nor any difference between purity and defilement.
Therefore, that world is named "Stainless" (*vimala*). Furthermore, the dragon girl is one who has manifested a hundred worlds through her own body;

she is a Bodhisattva of the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) who has attained Buddhahood. Or rather, what Mañjuśrī propagated was merely the opening of the provisional to reveal the real within the Trace Gate (*jijimon*);
this is accomplished by those who have attained the patient acceptance (*kṣānti*) of being born as Bodhisattvas. From this point onward, if one speaks of one's own practice, it returns to...

Those who are able to hear this teaching of the Original Gate from here, or who hear of the revelation of the original and the manifestation of the traces from the presence of a Buddha in another direction, are truly Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-body;
they shall subsequently realize the state of the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha.

That he sits upon a precious lotus flower and attains Equal and Right Enlightenment symbolizes that cause is identical to effect and effect is identical to cause; cause and effect are simultaneous, a single essence without duality.
He universally expounds the sublime Dharma throughout the ten directions, as stated in the preceding verse:
"I propagate the Mahāyāna teachings to deliver suffering sentient beings. △ Third, the assembly gains benefit in two parts. First, humans and devas rejoice.
At that time, the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, the eight classes of devas, nāgas, and so forth, as well as humans and non-humans in the Sahā world,

all saw from afar that dragon girl had attained Buddhahood and was preaching the Dharma for the sake of the assembly of devas and humans. Their hearts were filled with great joy, and they all paid homage to her from afar.
Having seen that person attain Buddhahood and having heard them preach the Dharma, his heart was filled with great joy.
△ Second, the mutual benefit of both [spheres], in three parts: First, the benefit in that land.

Immeasurable sentient beings, upon hearing the Dharma, attained awakening and reached the stage of non-retrogression. Immeasurable sentient beings received the prediction of their future attainment of the Way.
The Stainless World shook in six ways.
"Upon hearing the Dharma and attaining realization," and so forth, refers to progressing from the stage of names and words to partial realization (*praveśa*).
The two lines concerning the "Stainless World" should follow "I pay respectful homage from afar to all" and precede "immeasurable sentient beings";
thus, their meaning becomes clearly manifest. △ Second, the benefits obtained in this land.
In this Sahā world, three thousand sentient beings dwelt on the stage of non-retrogression; three thousand sentient beings gave rise to the bodhicitta and received their predictions of enlightenment.
△ Third, the assembly remained silent.
The Bodhisattva Jñānakūṭa, Śāriputra, and the entire assembly accepted this in silence.
At this point, Jñānakūṭa believed in this perfect and sudden teaching and no longer raised difficulties regarding the gradual and distinct stages;

Śāriputra believed in this perfect and ultimate truth and no longer harbored doubts concerning the provisional and inferior vehicles. Having thus severed the [attachment to] the gradual, distinct, provisional, and inferior...
Through doubt, one gives rise to the sudden, great, perfect, and real faith; thus, it is also a benefit. However, as for Zhizhi and Śāriputra, how could they not know the perfect reality?
How could they not believe in the sudden greatness? Yet they still put forward doubts and difficulties. Within this, there are two intentions:

first, to ensure that those within the assembly who possess the dispositions of the gradual, distinct, or *hīnayāna* (śrāvaka) vehicles and have given rise to doubts will surely be able to sever them.
This gives rise to the faith of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching. Second, these two individuals repeatedly construct doubts so that the Dragon Girl repeatedly resolves their difficulties;

this is precisely to manifest that whoever practices this sutra—whether they be of the animal realm or possess a female body—can swiftly attain Buddhahood. This serves to prove that those who uphold it are most supremely venerable.
The Chapter on Śakra Devānām-indra concludes.

Regarding the intent behind the arrival of this thirteenth chapter, "The Chapter on Upholding" (*Dhāraṇī-parivarta*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*: it is primarily because the Tathāgata desires to cause this sublime sūtra to circulate that he [addresses] the Dharma...
In the "Chapter on the Teacher," it is revealed that the person [the Buddha] is most venerable and the Dharma is most supreme.
Yet, fearing that people might not yet believe this, the "Chapter on the Jeweled Stupa" further clarifies the emergence of Prabhūtaratna from the stupa and the gathering of his emanations from afar;
Śākyamuni then issues a call for witnesses to attest to the supremacy of the Dharma. Subsequently, in the "Chapter on Sadāprarudita," it is further clarified that Sadāprarudita in a former life...

They have mastered the sutras and are capable of becoming Buddhas as celestial kings. Today, having heard the Dharma, this dragon girl is likewise able to swiftly realize Bodhi and become a venerable person.
Through such repeated and layered proof, it is established that both persons and dharmas are equally supreme.
Therefore, herein, whether they be the assembly of bodhisattvas, the sangha of śrāvakas, or bhikṣuṇīs, each...
Each makes a vow, desiring to circulate [this teaching] because the Dharma is supreme and the person is honored.
Thus, one knows that this chapter is a text concerning the vows made by the holy multitudes of the three vehicles to propagate and uphold it.

Now, the beginning of this chapter clarifies how the assembly of bodhisattvas and others make vows to receive and uphold [the teaching], while the subsequent section clarifies Śākyamuni Tathāgata’s silent observation.

Regarding the exhortation to uphold [the teaching]: since the title of this chapter neither mentions "receiving and upholding" (*śrutam udgṛhṇāti*) nor "exhorting others to uphold," why is it simply titled "The Chapter on Upholding"?
It is because if one were to say "receiving and upholding," there would be a gain for what precedes but a loss for what follows;

if one were to say "exhorting to uphold," one would be citing what follows while omitting what precedes. Now, by simply saying "the chapter on upholding," both the preceding and the following are encompassed.

This is because [the capacity to] uphold has already been attained; therefore, the text does not mention "receiving and upholding" (*śrutodgraha*) or "exhorting others to uphold," but merely designates it as the "Chapter on Upholding" (*dhāraṇī-parivarta*).

To "uphold" means to receive [the teaching] within one's mind and to maintain it without loss. If one were to discuss "receiving and upholding" in its full sense, it would constitute one of the five types of Dharma-preachers (*dharma-bhāṇaka*);
since the text briefly cites this one type, it implicitly includes the other four, for those who merely receive and uphold do not exist in isolation.
This constitutes the propagation. Whether one reads it, recites it, explains it, or writes it down, all such acts are termed "propagation.
The text is divided into two parts: first, the bodhisattvas' upholding; second, the Tathāgata's exhortation to uphold. The first part has three sections.
First, the Bodhisattva makes a vow to transmit the sutras; second, the Śrāvakas resolve to propagate the teachings. Third, the nuns receive predictions to spread the Dharma.
Of these first two [sections], the first is an introductory narration by the compiler of the sutra.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāpratibhāna,
together with a retinue of twenty thousand bodhisattvas, all made this vow before the Buddha:

Regarding the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja and others: because the Tathāgata, in the "Chapter on the Dharma Master," addressed eighty thousand great beings and therein clarified that the Dharma is supreme and the person [who upholds it] is honored, he now makes a vow within this context, desiring to cause this sutra to circulate.
As for the Bodhisattva Mahāpratibhāna, because in the "Chapter on the Jeweled Stupa" he desired...
He beheld Prabhūtaratna and desired to assemble the manifested bodies [of Śākyamuni]. Subsequently, the jeweled stupa opened and the manifested bodies assembled.
Śākyamuni then proclaimed for them to circulate [the teaching], all of which originated from him; therefore, he now likewise makes a vow to circulate this sutra.
As for the "twenty thousand bodhisattvas," these are the eighty thousand mentioned in the *Dharmabhāṇaka-parivarta* who were informed by Bhaiṣajyarāja.
This is the numerical sequence within [the chapter]. Since the Tathāgata has issued this injunction, I shall likewise make a vow herein to circulate this sutra.
△ Second, the actual making of the vow, in two parts: First, a general exhortation that the Tathāgata need not be concerned.
"I only pray that the Tathāgata will not be concerned.
Regarding the phrase "I only pray," it refers to what the World-Honored One said above: "Who is able to extensively expound the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* in this Sahā world-system?
The Buddha wished to entrust this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* to someone, and thus he spoke again.
"O sons of good family, each of you should contemplate this with earnest attention; this is a difficult task, and you ought to conceive great vows.
Thus did the Tathāgata exhort them twice: once out of concern that there might be no one to propagate and disseminate [the teaching], and once out of concern for the difficulty of such propagation.
This may be called profound anxiety and urgent deliberation. Yet, as for us now, we only wish—
"World-Honored One, it is not that I am concerned there will be no one [to receive this teaching], nor is it that I am concerned it will be difficult to propagate. Therefore, I say:
'I only pray that the World-Honored One will not be concerned. II. A detailed explanation of the reasons why he is not concerned. This has two parts.
First, explaining that he is not concerned there will be no one [to receive the teaching].
"After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, we shall uphold, recite, and preach this sutra.
By "we," it is meant that the World-Honored One first had concern that there would be no one to propagate this sutra;
however, we vow that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, we shall uphold, read, and preach this sutra. Since we are able to uphold this sutra, then...
Since we have already become human beings, we therefore wish only that the World-Honored One does not harbor concerns regarding our lack of worthiness.
△ Second, the explanation of not harboring concerns regarding the difficulty of propagation.
"In the evil world of the future, sentient beings will have even fewer roots of goodness and will largely be characterized by overweening pride.
Regarding the phrase "in the evil world of the future" and so forth: it means that the World-Honored One further considered the difficulty of propagation;

yet we vowed that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, during the time of propagating this sutra within the turbid and evil world, although sentient beings would be difficult to transform, we would still preach it.

If they do not believe or accept it, and instead respond with insults and the like, we shall exert the power of great patience to propagate it, even at the cost of our own bodies and lives. Since we can act in this way, then even those who are difficult to transform—
They will certainly become more easily transformed. Therefore, we only wish that the World-Honored One would not concern himself with the difficulty of spreading [the Dharma].
As for the statement that roots of goodness will gradually diminish: at the time of the Tathāgata’s initial parinirvāṇa, there were still those who attained liberation;
compared to the era of the Buddha himself, they were already few. Next, there will still be those who practice dhyāna.
Regarding those established in meditative concentration (*samādhi*): if compared to those who have attained liberation, their roots of goodness are even fewer.
Next are those who still take pleasure in much learning (*bahuśruta*); if compared to those who practice meditation, their roots of goodness are even fewer still.
Finally, there are those who merely occupy themselves with building stūpas and monasteries; compared to the roots of goodness of much learning, theirs are even fewer.
Indeed, as we approach the final kalpa, there will be nothing but strife and contention.

Thus, in this present age, those who practice meditation disparage the teachings, while those who study the teachings revile meditation; furthermore, some revile the teachings with the teachings, and others revile meditation with meditation.
Therefore, their roots of goodness become even more diminished. That which is diminished is precisely the root of goodness, while that which increases is merely overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
Thus it is said that they abound in overweening pride. This overweening pride is not necessarily fixed;
having not yet attained the first fruit, they claim to have attained the first fruit; having not yet realized the four fruits, they claim to have realized the four.

As for the fruit: to categorically dismiss what others have said as wrong while asserting that only what one has said oneself is right, and thereby to treat all others with arrogance and contempt—this is precisely what is called "overweening pride" (adhimāna).
They crave gain and offerings, increase their unwholesome roots, and remain far removed from liberation;

though they are difficult to transform, we shall arouse the power of great patience to read and recite this sutra, uphold it, explain it, transcribe it, and perform various offerings, not begrudging our bodies or lives.
"Arising the power of great patience" refers back to the preceding text. It means that these sentient beings may be said to be the most difficult to transform and deliver;
yet although I know they are extremely difficult to transform, I resolutely desire to transform them.
If they are unable to give rise to faith and instead respond with insults and the like, we shall then give rise to patience;
not only shall we give rise to patience, but we shall give rise to great patience (*mahākṣānti*); not only shall we give rise to great patience, but we shall also cause that patience to be powerful.
Therefore, it is said that one "should give rise to the power of great patience. This means to follow along with the person before one.
Regarding all such obstacles and afflictions, I simply cultivate great compassion within and contemplate the emptiness of all phenomena without;
furthermore, being gentle, harmonious, and compliant, I do not allow myself to be disturbed by them.
This is what is called patience—patience toward everything, not merely enduring verbal abuse and insults, but also enduring blades, staves, and shards.
"Stone. It is not only that one endures blades, staves, tiles, and stones; one also endures the dust-like afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*).
It is not only that one endures the dust-like afflictions of views and thoughts; one also endures the heavy obstructions of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Therefore, to endure all through a single endurance is what is called "Great Endurance" (*mahākṣānti*). When one internally mobilizes compassion within this state, there is... [no further text].
There is no pleasure that is not shared, and there is no suffering that is not uprooted. Thus, there is not a single sentient being who does not fall beneath the sheltering canopy [of compassion].
When one contemplates the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā) from an external perspective, all dharmas must be understood as empty and quiescent in their very essence;
every characteristic is real, and every phenomenon is true. As it is said:
Thus, there is not a single dharma that does not abide within this state of peaceful rest.
At the very moment of arising in gentleness, one perceives no external object to be endured, nor does one perceive an internal person who endures.
Since both subject and object have been extinguished, how could there still be such objects as insults and the like?
In this way, there is not a single obstacle or affliction that does not fall within the scope of its protection.

Since there is not a single sentient being who is not covered by it, there is not a single dharma that is not brought to rest therein, and not a single obstacle or affliction that is not shielded by it. Thus...
This is what is called the power of great patience (*mahākṣānti*). Regarding those who do not begrudge their own bodies or lives:

they contemplate that the body currently possessed is nothing more than a body composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), and that the life currently possessed is merely a life sustained by the continuity of form and mind (*nāmarūpa*).
Therefore, he does not begrudge it, desiring only to obtain the wisdom-life of the Dharma-body. △ Second, the Śrāvakas’ aspiration to propagate the teaching, in two parts:
first, the five hundred [disciples] establish their vows.
At that time, five hundred arhats within the assembly who had received the prediction of enlightenment addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, we too vow that in other lands we shall extensively expound this sutra."
△ II. The Making of Vows by Eight Thousand (in two parts). First, the narration of their oaths:

Furthermore, eight thousand persons, both those still in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), who had received the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), rose from their seats, joined their palms toward the Buddha, and [spoke].
They made this vow: "World-Honored One, we too shall extensively expound this sutra in other lands.

The phrase "we too shall" refers back to the previous five hundred [disciples]. As for the "eight thousand who received predictions," this refers to those mentioned in the "Chapter on the Bestowal of Predictions upon the Five Hundred Disciples" as being absent from this assembly, regarding whom it was said, "You should proclaim it for them."
Since it is said that they were not present at the assembly, does this mean they were merely among those absent from the group of twelve hundred? △ Second, the explanation of the underlying intent:
Why is this so? It is because in this Sahā world, people are for the most part depraved and evil; they harbor overweening pride, and their merit and virtue are shallow.
It is because [their] minds are thin, turbid with anger, and crooked, lacking sincerity.
When we say, "We vow to propagate this sutra in other lands, but do not vow to do so in our own country," what is the intention behind this?
It is because the people of our own country possess the five turbidities in such great depth that they are difficult to transform; whereas we are but beginners.
Having resolved upon the Great Mind and newly begun to transform and guide others, those whose power of patience is not yet sufficient merely aspire to propagate the sutra in other lands.
That people are mostly coarse, depraved, defiled, and evil refers to the *sattva-kaṣāya* (the corruption of sentient beings). As for those with "overweening pride" (*adhimāna*):

they claim to have attained what they have not; they give rise to various conceptual discriminations and falsely establish a sovereign self, thereby insulting and humbling all others—this is called overweening pride.
This refers to the defilement of the view (*dṛṣṭi-kāṣāya*). Regarding those with shallow merit: if one’s merit were profound, it would be able to evoke superior and wondrous form and mind;
because merit is shallow, the form and mind thus evoked are merely subject to decay and diminution—this refers to the defilement of lifespan (*āyuḥ-kāṣāya*).

As for the defilement of anger and crookedness (*krodha-śāṭhya-kāṣāya*), this is merely a brief mention of one among the five dull afflictions (*pañca-mṛdu-kleśa*); that is, the defilement of affliction (*kleśa-kāṣāya*).

It is turbid; therefore, many people are corrupt and evil, even to the point of being full of anger, turbidity, and sycophancy, all gathered together in one place—this is precisely the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*).
Because of these five turbidities alone, they are difficult to transform; for this reason, he does not wish to remain in his native land.
△ Third, the section on the bhikṣuṇīs receiving predictions and propagating the Dharma, in three parts: first, receiving the prediction; second, the account of their realization;
third, the correspondence with the sūtras. The first two parts consist of: first, Pañcaśikha’s six thousand followers receiving the prediction; second, Yaśodharā alone receiving the prediction.
The first two [sections]. First, the bhikṣuṇīs made their request in silence.

At that time, the Buddha’s maternal aunt, the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī, together with six thousand bhikṣuṇīs—both those in training and those beyond training—rose from their seats, joined their palms with single-minded devotion, and gazed up at the Honored One’s countenance without blinking for a moment.
Śākyamuni’s aunt, whose name in Sanskrit is Prajāpatī and which here means "Great Path-Lover" (Mahāmāyā), so called because she delighted in the Great Way (Mahāyāna).
Below her is Gautamī, which means "Leader of the Nuns"; this is Prajāpatī herself, so called because of her great love.
The Way is capable of serving as the head of the assembly; thus, a single person may possess two names.

Regarding the phrase "gazing up," the intention is that the bhikṣus previously granted predictions had never yet reached this bhikṣuṇī. Although she is equally a śrāvaka, there is a distinction between male and female;
though she desired to obtain [the prediction], she did not dare speak of it, but merely fixed her gaze upon him. △
II. The Tathāgata’s Manifestation of the Prediction. Part One: Stating the Intent.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Gautamī: "For what reason do you look upon the Tathāgata with a face of sorrow?
Does it not occur to your mind that I have not mentioned your name to grant you the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? Gautamī—
Maitreya, I have previously given the prophecy for all śrāvakas in general.

As for those who looked upon the Tathāgata with a sorrowful countenance and so forth, I wished to know their minds; first one observes their physical expression, for if one observes external form, the internal mind can be known.
Therefore, when the Tathāgata observed their expressions, he immediately knew that he should grant them individual prophecies.

This is a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). When I previously spoke in general terms, it was because you looked at me with an expression of anxiety, as if thinking, "He has not mentioned my name in bestowing this prediction.
As for the other six thousand people, they likewise did not take their eyes off me for even a moment, as if thinking, "He has not bestowed a prediction upon us collectively. If you, Gautamī...
In that case, I should have separately stated your names for the sake of bestowing the prediction.
As for the remaining six thousand, they too certainly should have been predicted; however, I have already collectively predicted all the śrāvakas.

Since these six thousand people are also śrāvakas, they have already received their predictions, and thus I did not separately state their names. This was because I previously spoke of them in general.
It is just as in the previous "Chapter on the Five Hundred Disciples": the rest of the assembly of śrāvakas shall likewise be so.

For those who are not present in this assembly, you should proclaim it for them. Furthermore, in the "Chapter on the Dharma Master," all those seeking the vehicle of the śrāvakas who hear even a single phrase or a single verse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* before the Buddha, or even follow it for a single moment of thought—
"Regarding 'joy,' it refers to this: I bestow upon all of you the prediction that you shall attain Bodhi. II. The Actual Bestowal of Predictions. This has two parts.
First, clarifying the causal practices:
"Now, if you wish to know your predictions, in a future age, you shall [serve] under sixty-eight thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas."
In the midst [of the assembly], he served as a Great Dharma Master, together with six thousand bhikṣuṇīs, both those in training and those beyond training, all serving as Dharma Masters.
Regarding the term "Great Dharma Master": one takes the Mahāyāna as one's own standard and likewise uses the Mahāyāna to guide others.
Since the Dharma that serves as the standard is great, the person who applies that standard is also great; therefore, they are called a Great Dharma Master.
...Furthermore, △ Second, explaining the attainment of the fruit: "In this way,
gradually perfecting the Bodhisattva path, you shall attain Buddhahood, with the name Sarvasattvapriyadarśana Tathāgata,
Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi..."

"O noble husband, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One! Gautamī, this Buddha Whom All Sentient Beings Delight to Behold, along with six thousand bodhisattvas, shall each receive a sequential prediction of their attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

She was named Sarvasattvapriyadarśanā because, while practicing the causal path, she was able to give rise to the great resolve and delight in the unsurpassed Buddha-way, and she also caused all others to resolve their minds to seek the Buddha-way; furthermore, she served as the leader of the assembly of nuns.
Thus, all were delighted by her own practice as well as her transformation of others;

therefore, at the time of attaining the fruit, she became one whom all sentient beings of the nine realms joyfully beheld, and it was for this reason that her name was established. [The section on] Gotamī follows below.
The six thousand who have attained the fruit were originally śrāvakas; because they have now been transformed into bodhisattvas, they are called "six thousand bodhisattvas.

In the preceding request, first the leaders of the assembly requested, followed by the request of the six thousand. The Tathāgata’s exposition of his intent likewise first expounds upon the leaders of the assembly and subsequently upon the six thousand.
It clarifies that within the causal stage as well, he first clarifies the practice of the causes by the leaders of the assembly, and subsequently clarifies [the practice] of the six thousand.

Six thousand. Now, regarding the attainment of the fruit, he first clarifies the sentient beings and then the six thousand; these are distinguished as primary and attendant to establish their sequence.
△ Second, Yaśodharā alone receives a prediction. Part one: her thought and request.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Yaśodharā, mother of Rāhula, had this thought: "Among those who have received predictions from the World-Honored One, he alone has not mentioned my name."
△ Second, the bestowal of the prediction.

The Buddha addressed Yaśodharā: "In future ages, throughout the teachings of hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas, you shall practice the bodhisattva path and become a great Dharma teacher.
Gradually perfecting the Buddha-way, you shall attain Buddhahood in the land of Sukhāvatī, and your name shall be [Guangyan]."
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha,
Bhagavān named Sūryaprabhāsottama-raśmi-koṭi-saṃdarśana. The lifespan of this Buddha shall be immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
Regarding his becoming a Buddha in the Land of Excellence (Kṣemā): because during the causal stage he was the wife of a Bodhisattva who was gentle, kind, and compliant, his land is named "Excellence.
He is titled "Endowed with Ten Million Marks of Radiance" because during the causal stage he was able to fulfill true wisdom and served as the mother of Rāhula;
thus, upon reaching the state of fruition, he is naturally able [to manifest these qualities].
He was fully endowed with ten million rays of light and ten million marks; thus, these became his names. △ Second, the account of the reception, in two parts.
First, the narrator’s description of joy:
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī and the bhikṣuṇī Yaśodharā, together with...
His retinue was all filled with great joy, having attained what they had never experienced before.
As for their being "all filled with great joy": prior to receiving the prediction, some may have shown signs of sorrow, or some may have harbored anxious thoughts.
They desired to receive a prediction [of their future enlightenment], and now that they have received it, their wishes are fulfilled.
Consequently, they no longer harbor any anxious thoughts or expressions of sorrow; thus it is said that "they all rejoice greatly. Regarding the phrase "attaining what was never before attained":

previously, they had considered themselves to have already attained *nirvāṇa* through the vehicle of the *śrāvaka*, believing they could no longer attain the Buddha-vehicle. Now, they have attained it.
The prediction (vyākaraṇa) belongs to the Śrāvaka vehicle, yet it is the Buddha-vehicle. The extinction previously attained was not true extinction;
now, one attains true extinction—something that never existed before, which is now finally obtained. Therefore, it is said, "I have attained what I never had before.
△ Second, speaking in verse to express his realization.
Then, before the Buddha, he spoke in verse:
"O World-Honored One, Guide, who brings peace and security to devas and humans; having heard this, our minds are fully at ease."
Regarding the "Guide" (導師): "Guiding" (*dāu*) means to lead forth; it also means to open up and guide. Initially, the three vehicles (*triyāna*) are bestowed through provisional means (*upāya*);

subsequently, the one vehicle (*ekayāna*) is revealed through the ultimate truth (*bhūta*). That which leads by way of the provisional is because the capacities (*indriya*) of sentient beings have not yet harmonized with the truth;
therefore, the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) is first bestowed to bring peace and security to devas and humans. That which opens up the ultimate is because...
Since the faculties of sentient beings have now matured, the reality is subsequently revealed to bring peace and security to devas and humans.
Thus, whether through guidance or instruction, both are capable of providing peace and security to devas and humans.
In the past, we were guided by the Tathāgata, whereby we were able to shatter the afflictions of views and thought, emerge from the triple world, and realize nirvana. At that time—

"I thought my birth was already fulfilled; I would no longer undergo future existence. My mind attained mastery and peace, and I thought my holy life (*brahmacarya*) was established, what was to be done had been accomplished, and I was complete.
This was merely because I was deluded in the past and did not know. Now that I have heard the Tathāgata’s teaching given in three turnings, I have fully understood my former state.
That which has been attained is not true cessation. Previously one thought the mind was at peace, yet in reality it was not at peace;

previously one thought it was complete, yet in reality it was not complete. Only upon receiving the prediction of attaining Buddhahood does one finally attain peace of mind and finally attain completeness.
Now that she has already heard the prophecy, her mind is at peace and fully satisfied.
This single line of verse was explained by the bhikṣuṇī Cienling; therefore, it must be interpreted through the contrast of past and present, delusion and awakening.

In this way, it is identical to the explanations provided by the three [other] bhikṣuṇīs in their respective turn. Only then will it be revealed how a single verse contains immeasurable meaning. If one were to take it directly...
[Commentary on the Text]: This would already seem shallow. △ Third, connecting with the sutra:
After the bhikṣuṇīs had spoken these verses, they addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, we too shall be able to widely proclaim this sutra in other lands."
Regarding those who are also capable: it refers to the aforementioned bodhisattvas, who have made a vow to propagate the sutras in this land;

and the śrāvakas, who have made a vow to teach and transform others in other lands. As for us bhikṣuṇīs, although we certainly cannot propagate the sutras in this land like the bodhisattvas, we are nevertheless able to teach and transform others in other lands like the śrāvakas.
Therefore, it is said that one shall also widely proclaim this sutra in other lands. △ Second, the Tathāgata’s exhortation to uphold [the sutra] has two parts.
First, the Tathāgata’s silent exhortation:
At that time, the World-Honored One gazed upon eighty quadrillion nayutas of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
At that time, why did the Tathāgata, wishing to encourage them to uphold [the teaching], merely gaze with his eyes and not speak with his mouth? There are three reasons for this.
First, in the "Dharma Master" chapter (*Dharmabhāṇaka-parivarta*), he had already extensively revealed the supremacy of the person and clarified the excellence of the Dharma;
he now provides a detailed demonstration through the three guidelines. Second, within the two chapters on the "Jeweled Stupa" (*Ratnastūpa*) and "Devadatta" (*Devadatta*), he clarifies...
The emergence of Prabhūtaratna attests to this present sutra; the emanations gather from afar to hear this sutra.
Thus it is proven that the Dharma is supreme, demonstrating that even the evil man Devadatta can attain Buddhahood, and that a dragon girl, though of animal kind, can realize Bodhi.
This serves to establish the dignity of the person. Thus, through repeated clarifications and successive exhortations, the matter may be said to have been explained both thoroughly and exhaustively;
there is no need for further words. Therefore, he simply gazes with his eyes and remains silent.

Second: Although the great bodhisattvas mentioned above have been able to make vows to propagate this sutra, they have said only, "We pray that the World-Honored One does not worry about there being no one [to carry on the work], nor worry about the difficulty of its propagation; after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa, we..."
"You should propagate this sutra in this land; you must even give rise to the power of great forbearance and not begrudge your body or life.
If you can truly act in this way, it would certainly be praiseworthy. Yet, even so, it is not yet the ultimate excellence.
Therefore, when I previously asked, 'Who can widely proclaim this sutra in this Sahā world-system? I was merely speaking in terms of what is most accessible. But as for my—"
My intention has always been that [this teaching] should circulate everywhere throughout the worlds of the ten directions, not merely within this Sahā world.
Those bodhisattvas, upon hearing my words regarding this land, have made vows that are restricted solely to this land, never mentioning other regions.
Now, I desire that those bodhisattvas shall not limit themselves to this land alone.
To propagate this sutra, it is also necessary to spread its teachings in other regions. To speak plainly:
first, who could possibly act in a manner that seems to contradict the words used in this land? Second, it would seem difficult to fulfill the vows of the great bodhisattvas.
Desiring only to protect the prior words of those bodhisattvas, he merely looked with his eyes but did not speak with his mouth.
Third: The assembly of śrāvakas mentioned above has limited their vows exclusively to other lands, never extending them to this realm.
Yet, the Tathāgata’s intention is precisely that the Dharma should circulate everywhere throughout the ten directions.
When comparing other lands with our own country, those other lands are relatively easy to deliver, whereas this land is truly difficult.
However, regarding the Buddha’s intention, that which should take precedence lies solely in what is difficult.
Since those śrāvakas have made their vows only for other lands and do not mention their own country, they have not yet fully accorded with the Tathāgata’s intention.
Now, it is desired that the great bodhisattvas shall not only propagate the teachings in other lands, but shall also return to this very realm.
To propagate [the teachings]. To speak clearly: first, this seems to obstruct the vows of the śrāvakas; second, it accords with the vows of the bodhisattvas.
Because he wished to protect those śrāvakas and because the bodhisattvas had not yet been fully accepted, he merely looked upon them with his eyes but did not speak with his mouth.
How, then, can one discern that these three intentions were present? Let us examine the Bodhisattva’s propagation of the Dharma.
This can be understood from the text. As it says at the beginning: "Those bodhisattvas, out of reverence and compliance with the Buddha’s intention, then made a vow to propagate the sutra.
This explains the Tathāgata’s initial intent. Next, it says: "After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, we shall travel throughout the worlds of the ten directions," and so forth;
this indicates that they will propagate the sutra not only in this land, but also by going to other regions.
"To propagate and transform. This is the second meaning of the Tathāgata’s intent. Furthermore, it says:

"After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, we shall travel to the worlds of the ten directions; that is, not only will we propagate the sutra in other lands, but we shall also return to this land to propagate and transform."
This interpretation represents the third intention of the Tathāgata. Therefore, let us verify it through the following text;

thus we know that the Tathāgata merely observes and does not speak, possessing these three intentions. △ Second, the Bodhisattvas' propagation of the sutra has three parts. First, the narrator describes the scene.
These bodhisattvas were all *avaivartika*; they had turned the wheel of non-retrogression and attained the various *dhāraṇīs*.
They immediately rose from their seats, went before the Buddha, joined their palms with single-minded devotion, and formed this thought:
△ Second, the two bodhisattvas thought:
"If the World-Honored One commands us to uphold and proclaim this sutra, we shall, in accordance with the Buddha's teaching, widely disseminate this Dharma."
There are two stages of reflection here. Regarding the first stage, it says: "If the World-Honored One," and so forth.
When the great bodhisattvas see the Tathāgata looking at them, they immediately rise from their seats and approach the Buddha.
Thinking that since the Tathāgata has looked upon them, there must surely be some verbal instruction, they reflect: "Whatever the World-Honored One has to say... Great.
We all desire to uphold and preach this sutra. If you would indeed command us to uphold and preach this sutra, we shall widely proclaim this Dharma in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching.
Again, they thought: "The Buddha now remains silent; we see no instruction. What should we do?

Regarding the subsequent reflection, the phrase "again they thought" and so forth means that the great bodhisattvas had previously believed that the Tathāgata would certainly have something to say, which is why he looked toward them; yet now, having nothing else to say, he simply remains silent.
Although the Tathāgata has not personally issued a command for us to widely proclaim this sutra, it is certain that he did not do so without purpose;
thus we know that even though no explicit command was seen, in truth, he has already commanded us.
Yet, how should we propagate and circulate it so as to accord with the Tathāgata’s silent observation and encouragement to uphold it? Therefore, it is said: "I..."
What do you mean by this? It is not that the Tathāgata failed to issue an instruction, but rather that he merely gazed in silence, leaving us ignorant of where to turn.

This is how we know it: for once the Tathāgata had completed his threefold exposition and the fourfold assembly had attained full realization, the Great Matter was clarified and his original intent was fulfilled. What remained to be considered was...
I desire nothing more than that this sutra may circulate widely. Therefore, in the "Dharma Master" chapter, it is revealed that the person is most honored and the Dharma is most supreme;
furthermore, by providing detailed instruction on the three tracks, the intent behind its circulation can be said to be both thorough and ultimate.
Nevertheless, unless this is established through scriptural testimony, one has not yet seen how the Dharma is supreme and the person is honored. Thus...
Furthermore, by using the two accounts of Ratnadhvaja as corroboration, the supreme excellence of both person and Dharma can indeed be verified.

Thus, through these repeated and layered elucidations, there is no other intention than the desire that people throughout other lands and this world may widely propagate and disseminate [this teaching]. For this reason, Bodhisattvas such as Bhaiṣajyarāja and the five hundred [others...]
Among the śrāvakas, some have taken a vow to propagate [this teaching] in this land, while others have made a resolution to transform and guide beings in other directions;
they may be said to be well able to carry out the Tathāgata’s intent. Yet now the Tathāgata gazes silently upon us—could there be any further intention?
It is surely only because he desires us to widely propagate this sutra.

However, the Buddha did not explicitly state this in words. If we were to subtly examine the meaning behind the Tathāgata’s silent observation, would it not be that he had already fully exhorted [the practitioners] to uphold [the teachings] and detailed the methods and procedures, such that there was no further need for words here?
Or perhaps there remains something yet to be fulfilled regarding the vows previously made by the Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas?
Is it that we have not yet fully exhausted the excellence [of the teaching]? Nevertheless, the intention of the Tathāgata is certainly not something we can easily fathom;
yet when we reflect upon it repeatedly, it truly does not exceed this.
Therefore, how should we propagate [the teaching] so as to be able to fully exhaust the meaning of the Tathāgata’s silent observation? Thus he says, "How shall I [proceed]?"
△ III. The Bodhisattvas' Vows, in two parts. First, the introduction of the intent:

At that time, the bodhisattvas, out of reverence and compliance with the Buddha’s intention, and desiring to fulfill their own original vows, uttered a lion’s roar before the Buddha and made this solemn vow.
"Respectfully complying with the Buddha’s intention" has two meanings, one proximate and one remote. Proximately, it refers to respectfully complying with the Tathāgata’s silent observation.
Remotely, it refers to respectfully complying with the Tathāgata’s detailed exposition of the three tracks (*triyāna*), as well as his intent to proclaim and circulate [the teachings].
"Fulfilling one's own original vow" likewise has both remote and proximate meanings. First, the remote meaning: all... [text continues]
O Great Bodhisattva, when you first resolved to attain enlightenment, your original intention was to propagate the Buddha-way above and to transform sentient beings below;
this was your fundamental vow from days of old. Now, if you propagate and disseminate this sutra, then that ancient fundamental vow will be fulfilled.

Regarding the "two proximate [conditions]": when the great bodhisattvas perceived that the Tathāgata had revealed himself as the Honored One among men and his Dharma as supreme, and at the time he proclaimed the invitation for its circulation, they immediately made vows to propagate this sutra.
This is their fundamental vow from today. If they succeed in propagating and circulating this sutra, then their fundamental vow from today will also be fulfilled. Therefore, it says "and."
To fulfill one's own original vow and to utter the lion’s roar refers to that which the Tathāgata has taught as definitive fearlessness;
this is called the lion’s roar. It causes all bodhisattvas to make vows to widely propagate and proclaim this sutra;
because it then expounds what the Tathāgata has taught, it is also named the lion’s roar. Furthermore, the vow made by a bodhisattva is also called the lion’s roar.
The Lion’s Roar. Because the vows he has made must certainly be fulfilled in this way, and furthermore, because his vow to propagate the sutra in an evil age is itself fearless.
△ Second, the actual vow, in two parts: first, the long prose section.
“World-Honored One, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, we shall travel throughout the worlds of the ten directions,
enabling sentient beings to copy this sutra, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, explain its meaning, and practice according to the Dharma with right mindfulness.”
All of this is due to the Buddha’s majestic power. I pray that the World-Honored One, while remaining in another land, will behold us from afar and provide protection.
May those who travel to and fro throughout the worlds of the ten directions proceed to other lands and return to this realm to widely propagate this sutra.
This correctly captures the meaning of the Tathāgata’s silent observation; thus, he uttered these words.
This is the aspiration. One who practices according to the Dharma with right mindfulness is called "right" because they are neither partial nor biased.
If one practices according to the dharmas of virtuous precepts, then that mindfulness is biased solely toward existence and is not called "right.
If one practices according to the dharmas of the Truths and conditions, then that mindfulness is... [biased] solely toward... [nirvana].

To lean toward emptiness is likewise not called "correct. If one practices according to the methods of the Gate of Crossing (Dumen), then that mindfulness merely leans toward the middle and cannot be called "correct.

Now, if one can practice according to the dharma of the true mark (lakṣaṇa), then the practice arises entirely from principle, and cultivation is initiated entirely from nature; through this reality...
Taking marks as the object of contemplation, one returns from that object to give rise to the wisdom of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
By using wisdom to illuminate the object and the object to give rise to wisdom, object and wisdom become one and the same; subject and object are extinguished.
Thus, when there is existence, all things are simultaneously existent—not merely leaning toward existence alone—and when there is emptiness, all things are simultaneously empty.
It is not merely leaning toward emptiness; rather, in the Middle Way, all things are simultaneously centered. It is not merely leaning toward the Middle;
since it does not lean toward existence, existence itself is correct. Since it does not lean toward emptiness, emptiness itself is correct.
Since it does not lean toward the Middle, the Middle itself is correct. This is called practicing according to the Dharma with right mindfulness.

"Mindfulness. That "all this is through the Buddha's majestic power" means that he causes them to transcribe [the teachings], and even causes them to practice right mindfulness in accordance with the Dharma;

this certainly rests with us. However, as for causing them to achieve success in the transcription, and even achieving success in right mindfulness, these depend entirely upon the pervasive power of the Tathāgata’s majesty.
Furthermore, there is another interpretation: we are able to cause them to copy this sutra, and even to cause them to practice this sutra;
this is indeed the fulfillment of our own fundamental vows. Nevertheless, it is entirely due to the majestic power (*anubhāva*) of the Tathāgata that we are able to do so.
Moreover, because it is entirely the majestic power of the Tathāgata, we...
They will cause others to copy and practice [this teaching], so that they may act according to our instructions by copying and practicing it.
We pray, O World-Honored One, Guardian of Other Realms, that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, we [may do so].
When this sutra is being propagated, although the Tathāgata has manifested extinction within this Sahā world-realm,
he may yet appear under different names as a Buddha in other worlds or in the *sopadhiśeṣa* (with remainder) lands.
We pray only that the World-Honored One will behold us from afar and protect us— protecting both ourselves and those who are capable of propagating it.

This shall cause this scripture to be widely proclaimed. First, it is for the purpose of protecting the assembly of those to be converted, so that they may receive the teachings with joy and not fall into contradiction.
Regarding the statement here, "May the World-Honored One remain in other lands to provide protection," this is because the Tathāgata, in the "Chapter on the Dharma Master," said:
"If one can be fully endowed with the three modes of conduct, one shall propagate [the teaching]."

Regarding this sutra, in other lands, I shall immediately dispatch emanated beings from the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of supernatural beings to serve as the gathered audience and to provide protection;
they will act in accordance with the teaching without opposition, and so forth, until it says that they shall cause the speaker of the Dharma to behold my own body, and so on.
Therefore, within this context, the Bodhisattva, taking up the preceding meaning, says: "I only pray that you will behold us from afar and protect us," and so forth.
△ Second, the verse summary has three parts; first, the general vow for the circulation [of the teaching].
Then all those bodhisattvas raised their voices together and spoke in verse:
"We pray that you do not worry; after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, in the midst of the terrifying and evil age, we shall widely proclaim [the Dharma]."
△ Second, the detailed presentation of the three modes of practice has three parts. First, sixteen lines: donning the robe of patience. Second, one line beginning with "all aggregates":

entering the chamber of loving-kindness and compassion. Third, one line beginning with "I am...": sitting upon the seat of the emptiness of phenomena. The first part [of the first section] further has two sub-divisions.
First, clarifying patience toward worldly crowds:
"When there are ignorant people who revile us with harsh words and the like, or even inflict blows with knives and staves, we shall endure them all."

The first three phrases refer to the objects of endurance. Regarding the term "people without wisdom," this sutra clarifies that all sentient beings are capable of opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and that all dharmas attain the ultimate true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
When people with wisdom hear this, they are naturally able to believe and accept it; however, if people without wisdom hear it, they are unable to have confidence in themselves.
Even when they become Buddhas, they do not believe that all dharmas are the true nature (*dharmatā*). Since they cannot believe this, there are those who give rise to various slanders;
hence it is said, "with harsh words, insults, and the like. Furthermore, there are even those who inflict harm and injury upon them;
hence it is said, "and even employing knives and staves. The subsequent phrase, "we," refers to those who are able to endure these things.
Regarding the mind: "All such things should be endured" means that although others act in this way, I shall focus my thoughts solely on propagating the sutra.
Looking outward at all phenomena and directing compassion inward, I shall give rise to a heart of gentleness and virtuous endurance.
By enduring these matters, they will not become obstacles or afflictions, and I shall be able to propagate [the teaching] myself. △ Second, clarifying the method of endurance.
Section Two: First, clarifying the objects of endurance.
In this evil age, there are bhikṣus whose minds are crooked with false wisdom; claiming what they have not attained to be attained, they are filled with the pride of self-conceit.
There may be forest-dwellers in secluded places, wearing patched robes, who claim to practice the true path while despising those in the world.
Because they are greedily attached to gain and offerings, they preach the Dharma to laypeople and are venerated by the world as if they were arhats with the six supernormal powers.
This person harbors an evil mind and constantly dwells on worldly matters; while falsely claiming to be a forest-dweller (*āraṇyaka*), he delights in exposing our faults and speaks thus:
"These bhikṣus, for the sake of craving gain and offerings, preach the doctrines of external paths."
They have composed this sutra themselves to delude and mislead the people of the world. For the sake of seeking fame and reputation, they have made arbitrary distinctions regarding this scripture.
Constantly amidst the great assembly, they desire to disparage us, speaking thus to kings, ministers, brahmins, and householders.
And other members of the bhikṣu-saṃgha slandered me, speaking ill of me, saying: "He is a man of false views; he propounds the doctrines and arguments of non-Buddhists;
his mind is crooked with perverse wisdom. Because their vision was not upright, their wisdom was perverted; because their wisdom was perverted...
Therefore, the mind is also crooked. If one examines what is gathered by this deviant wisdom, there are two types: the broad and the narrow.
The broad refers to everything from the Separate Teaching (biejiao) downwards; all of these are deviant wisdom. Thus, it is as the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa said:
"We are all called people of wrong views. The narrow refers to monks who falsely assume the marks of dhyāna in order to seek the respect of others, or...
This refers to those who study geomancy, physiognomy, medicine, and the like. Regarding their disparagement of those in the human world:

while they themselves collect their three robes and dwell in seclusion, claiming to practice the true path, they instead look down upon those in the human world who propagate the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
This is because the propagation of this sutra must take place within the human world.
Regarding the term "human beings," it refers to the eight lines of verse situated within the two stages of patience (*kṣānti*).
The five and a half lines beginning with "claiming to have attained what one has not attained" should be understood as illustrating extensive false wisdom;

for they are able to preach the provisional and inferior teachings to laypeople (*avadātavasana*). Because they know only the inferior teachings and do not know the Great [Vehicle], they [preach] toward laypeople.

This refers to those who slander and obstruct the propagation of this sutra. Next, the two lines beginning with "Furthermore, they are always among the great masses" should clarify the narrow and heterodox wisdom.
Because such people possess only heterodox arts, kings and others believe in those heterodox arts and do not know the true path.
Since they are followed and trusted by kings and others, [the slanderers] direct their defamation toward those who propagate [the Dharma].
They are people of the Dharma. △ Second, explaining the mind capable of endurance:
"Out of our reverence for the Buddha, we endure all these evils. Because of this slighting remark, 'You are all Buddhas' [we endure it]."
Such words of contempt and derision, one should endure them all. In this defiled age of evil, there are many terrors;
malevolent spirits may enter their bodies and revile, abuse, and insult us. We, who revere and have faith in the Buddha, shall don the armor of patience.
For the sake of preaching this sutra, we endure these various hardships; we do not cherish our own bodies or lives, but only treasure the unsurpassed Way.
In future ages, we shall protect and uphold that which the Buddha has entrusted to us.

These four and a half lines concern the practice of patience through the propagation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. The subsequent two and a half lines concern the practice of patience through the universal application of skillful means (*upāya*).

Although the *Lotus Sūtra* itself is not a [mere] skillful means, since it is that which is propagated and made known, it may also be said to establish provisional teachings based on the ultimate truth.
As for the phrase "those who have many terrors," this refers to those with false wisdom and defiled, evil dispositions.
"When the Venerable Kāśyapa wished to disparage us, his mind became most perverse;
thus, evil spirits took advantage of this perversity to enter him, making him even more perverse so that he reviled and insulted us. This is what is meant by 'many terrors.'"
Regarding the phrase "the armor of patience," both the Dharma and a metaphor are presented together.
To practice patience is to remain unharmed by obstacles and afflictions, just as one who wears armor remains unharmed by swords and arrows.

World-Honored One, you yourself should know that in this defiled age there are wicked bhikṣus who do not understand the Buddha’s skillful means or the teachings spoken according to what is appropriate.
With foul mouths and frowning brows, they are repeatedly seen being expelled and kept far away from the stūpas and monasteries. Such are their manifold evils.
Because of the Buddha’s admonition, you should all endure these matters.

This refers to the patience practiced through the general expedient of walking meditation (*caṅkrama*). The Tathāgata, according to the capacities of beings—whether great or small—proclaimed teachings that were great or small.
Now, those who propagate [the Dharma] likewise possess capacities that are great or small, and thus they should preach accordingly to them. Thus it is said.

Although he followed the Small Vehicle, his intention was solely directed toward the Perfect [Vehicle]. Examining the meaning, at first he propagated the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (the Sūtra of the True Reality) and practiced patience;
this patience was for enduring the insults of those with broad but heterodox wisdom, because they did not know that there existed the Great [Vehicle].

Next, he propagated the *Upāya-kauśalya-sūtra* (the Sūtra of Expedient Means) and practiced patience; this patience was for enduring the insults of those with narrow wisdom, because they possessed only heterodox arts and small teachings.
They do not understand the Buddha’s skillful means. △ Second, entering the chamber of compassion:
In all villages and cities, wherever there are those who seek the Dharma, I shall go to their respective places and preach the teachings entrusted by the Buddha.

Since one can act as an uninvited friend and go to wherever they may be to preach the wondrous Dharma entrusted by the Buddha, what suffering is there that will not be uprooted, and what joy is there that will not be bestowed?
Therefore, know that this single line clarifies entering the chamber of compassion. △ Third, sitting upon the seat of the emptiness of phenomena.
"I am the messenger of the World-Honored One; dwelling among the assembly, I am fearless. I shall skillfully expound the Dharma; may the Buddha dwell in peace and security.
Since one is able to be gentle and patient, one will not be harmed by obstacles or afflictions; therefore, one dwells among the assembly without fear."
To teach according to the capacities of beings, without causing [the teaching] to be either too much or too little, is what is called "skillfully preaching the Dharma.
When one says, "I pray that the Buddha may dwell in peace," it does not mean wishing for the Buddha himself to dwell in peace;

rather, it means wishing that the Buddha, by the power of his majestic spiritual authority, will behold and protect from afar those of us who propagate the teaching, so that we may dwell in peace within the emptiness of dharmas.
This concludes the seating. △ Third, the conclusion and verification of realization:
"In the presence of the World-Honored One and all the Buddhas who have come from the ten directions, I have made this vow. The Buddha himself knows my heart."
The phrase "the World-Honored One" refers specifically to Śākyamuni; "all those who have come" refers to the emanated bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*), and also includes Prabhūtaratna.
When it says "the Buddha knows our minds," it means that all three Buddhas know our hearts.
Prabhūtaratna wishes to bear witness to this sutra, and the emanated bodies wish to assist this sutra; now we vow to propagate this sutra—how could we not know this?
