"Does the Buddha not know our minds? If we Śākyamuni Tathāgatas wished for us to propagate this sutra, he would simply observe us in silence;

yet even then, we would already have known the Tathāgata’s intention. Now, in accordance with the Buddha’s intention, we have spoken words of vow desiring to propagate this sutra—how could he not know our hearts? Therefore, it is said that the Buddha himself knows our minds."
Thus ends the commentary on the "Chapter on Entrusting.

The Fourteenth Chapter of the Lotus Sutra, "Peaceful Practices.

Regarding the origin of this chapter: it follows from the preceding "Chapter on the Entrustment," wherein those great bodhisattvas who have perfected the power of patience are able, by their own means, to propagate [the Dharma] within this defiled and evil world of Sahā.
While those who have attained mastery can penetrate this sutra, the śrāvakas are unable to do so;
they instead resolve to propagate and transform others in other lands because, being at the very beginning of their practice, their power of patience (*kṣānti*) is not yet sufficient.
Now, wishing to enable bodhisattvas who are likewise at the beginning of their practice to propagate this sutra within this land, Mañjuśrī makes a formal request on their behalf, and the Tathāgata...
He then revealed this to them through the four practices of peaceful dwelling;
thus, there is this chapter, which serves as the text for the method by which bodhisattvas at the stage of initial resolve propagate the sutra in this land.
Within this chapter, the beginning clarifies the peaceful dwelling of the body, the end clarifies the peaceful dwelling of vows, and the middle clarifies the peaceful dwellings of speech and mind.

Regarding the "practice of blissful conduct" (*sukha-caryā*): here, only the "blissful conduct of peace and bliss" (*anurakṣaṇā-sukha-caryā*) is indicated, while the initial "blissful conduct of the body" is not mentioned, nor is the subsequent "blissful conduct of the vow," nor the intermediate "blissful conduct of speech and mind."
If one speaks of the beginning, one loses the middle and the end; if one speaks of the end, one loses the beginning and the middle;

if one speaks of the middle, one loses the beginning and the end. Therefore, by merely designating "peaceful and happy conduct" (*sukha-vihāra*), it is able to encompass the beginning, the end, and the middle alike.
As for "peaceful and happy conduct," to explain it in its most general sense: it means that the body is free from peril.
That which is called "peace" (*āna*) is the state in which the mind is free from sorrow and affliction. That which is called "bliss" (*sukha*) is the practice of transforming oneself and others.
To speak according to ultimate reality: that which is unmoving is called peace; that which is not felt is called bliss. How is it unmoving?
This is precisely what is called "peace. If ordinary beings, in every thought-moment, cling to existence, they are moved by existence;
how could they be called peaceful? If those of the Two Vehicles, in every thought-moment, cling to emptiness, they are moved by emptiness;
how could they be called peaceful? If Bodhisattvas, in every thought-moment, cling to the Middle Way, they are moved by the Middle Way; how could they...
It is called "peaceful" (*an*). Now, if a bodhisattva at the initial stage of mind propagates this sutra, they will find peace in the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*).
Once they have found peace in the true reality, then according to all phenomena, there is nothing that is not entirely real; that is its very existence.
Existence is the true mark; this very existence is emptiness. Emptiness is the true mark; this very emptiness is the middle way. The middle way is the true mark.
Since whether it be existence, emptiness, or the middle, there is nothing that is not the true mark: when all things exist, they all exist together, yet one is not moved by existence;
when all things are empty, they all are empty together, yet one is not moved by emptiness; and so it is with the middle.
Thus, one is centered within all things; because one is not moved by that which is centered, one takes this immovability as peace.

How could it be that not experiencing [anything] is not called bliss? If one were to experience painful feelings, pleasant feelings, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings, then from the painful feeling would arise the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*);
from the pleasant feeling would arise the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*); and from the neither-painful-nor-pleasant...
Suffering is not a pleasant sensation; it arises from the suffering of conditioned existence (saṃskāra-duḥkha). How, then, could it be called pleasure?

Now, when a bodhisattva at the initial stage propagates this sutra, they settle their mind solely in the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) and right concentration (samyaksamādhi), and do not experience any sensations.
That is to say, they neither experience painful sensations, nor pleasant sensations, nor sensations that are neither painful nor pleasant.

Regarding sensation (*vedanā*): if one does not experience pleasant sensation, there is no suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*) for oneself; if one does not experience painful sensation, there is no suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkha*) for oneself;
and if one does not experience neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation, there is no suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*) for oneself.

One who is free from suffering does so because of non-appropriation (*aparigraha*); therefore, non-appropriation is taken as happiness. Since one is unmoving, one has already attained peace through non-appropriation.

Having already attained joy, one then cultivates one’s own practice (*sva-caryā*) from this point onward; once one’s own practice is perfected, one proceeds from here to transform others (*para-saṃgraha*);
thus, the transformation of others can also be accomplished. Therefore, it is called the "Chapter on Peaceful and Joyful Practice" (*Anurakṣita-śukla-dharma-paṭala*).

The text of this chapter is divided into two parts: first, Mañjuśrī’s praise and inquiry; second, the Tathāgata’s response and instruction. The former consists of two sections, the first of which is the praise.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, these bodhisattvas are truly rare;
out of reverent obedience to the Buddha, they have made great vows to protect [the Dharma] in the future evil age.”
To uphold, read, and expound this Lotus Sūtra:
when Mañjuśrī first posed his questions at the beginning, it was because the Tathāgata wished to preach this sūtra for the sake of all sentient beings.
To reveal, show, awaken to, and enter into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is impossible for anyone who does not possess great wisdom.
Since Mañjuśrī is the foremost of those possessing true wisdom, he was employed as the respondent prior to the "True Teaching" (Zhengzong) section;
now, following the "Circulation" (Liutong) section, he is again made the one who poses the questions. This is because it would be impossible to circulate [the teaching] without wisdom. △
Second, the question of the present:
"World-Honored One, how can a bodhisattva-mahāsattva in the future evil age be able to preach this sutra?
For the aforementioned bodhisattvas are those who have deeply practiced the power of patience and achieved its perfection; they are naturally capable of the three modes of conduct."

Having maintained the mind, one has thus mastered the sutras in this land. If a bodhisattva who is a beginner and has only recently set out on the path also wishes to propagate the sutras in this land in future generations, what other methods are there for them to rely upon for practice, apart from the three rules?
One may thus propagate and disseminate this sutra. △ Second, the Tathāgata’s response and instruction, in three parts. First, the general response:
The Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī: "If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, in the evil world of the future, wishes to preach this sutra..."
One should abide in four dharmas.
As for abiding in these four dharmas, it means that a bodhisattva at the initial stage who wishes to propagate this sutra in this land—what further dharmas are required?
Indeed, there are no other separate dharmas; by simply abiding in these four practices of peaceful dwelling, one will then be able [to fulfill this task] hereafter.
"In this evil age, one shall propagate this sutra in this land. As for the four dharmas, they are those of body, speech, mind, and vow.
Now, why must one abide in these four dharmas if one wishes to propagate this sutra? It is because if one can abide in the 'peaceful conduct of the body,' then that body will be upright;
it will act without being commanded. Therefore, if one wishes to propagate this sutra, one should abide in the [peaceful conduct] of the body."
This is the practice of peaceful conduct (*sukha-vihāra*). If one abides in the peaceful conduct of speech, then whatever is spoken will be accepted with faith by all people;
therefore, those who wish to propagate this sutra should abide in the practice of peaceful conduct of speech.

If one abides in the peaceful conduct of mind, then the mind will be free from jealousy and deceit, and naturally attract superior persons to assemble; therefore, those who wish to propagate this [sutra]...

Sūtra: One should abide in the practice of the Dharma of Peaceful Conduct through Mental Resolve. If one abides in the practice of Peaceful Conduct through Vow, one can uproot all suffering and bestow all happiness.
Therefore, those who wish to propagate this sūtra should abide in the practice of the Dharma of Peaceful Conduct through Vow.
△ Second, the detailed exposition has four parts. First, the exposition of Peaceful Conduct through the Body; second, the exposition of the Mouth... [text continues].
The Practice of Peaceful Conduct. Third, the peaceful conduct indicated by intention; fourth, the peaceful conduct indicated by vow. The first [section] consists of two parts:
first, the prose (long-form), and second, the verse (stotra). The first [of these two] consists of two parts: first, the heading.

First is "abiding securely. This refers to the bodhisattva’s sphere of practice (*caryā*) and sphere of intimacy (*upāsana*), by which one is able to expound this sutra for the sake of sentient beings.
Regarding these spheres of practice and intimacy, the two characters for "place" (*sthāna*) refer to the ground of the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*).
This ground of the reality-limit is that which a beginner bodhisattva who wishes to propagate this sutra ought to follow and practice.
One should draw near [to this]. Therefore, it is said that the "place of practice" (*caryā-sthāna*) is the "place of drawing near.
As for the "place of practice," it refers to taking the principle of the true reality (*satya-dharma*) as one's object with single-mindedness; this is called the place of practice.

That is to say, by means of the principle of the inconceivable truth of real marks (*lakṣaṇa*), one gives rise to the contemplative wisdom of the inconceivable observation of real marks, which in turn illuminates the objective realm of the truth of real marks. In this way, the objective realm gives rise to [wisdom].
Regarding "wisdom": with wisdom one illuminates the object; object and wisdom are as one, and subject and object are non-dual.

This is what is meant by the "place of practice. As for the "place of intimacy," while the aforementioned place of practice involves directly taking the principle of the truths as its object, the present place of intimacy involves extensively traversing all conditions through inconceivable, wondrous wisdom. These "conditions" are:
That is to say, the following text discusses the near in terms of the distant, the near in terms of the near, and the near in terms of that which is neither distant nor near.
By means of wondrous wisdom, one can employ these various conditions such that each and every one is the true reality (*dharmatā*).
They are mutually intimate and proximate, rather than being remote; this is what is meant by the "place of intimacy. This is why the word "place" (*chu*) is used twice.
The "ground of the reality-limit" (*bhūtakoṭi*) is the object of contemplation. The three characters "practice," "conduct," and "intimacy" are the wisdom that contemplates.
Furthermore, this subject and object of contemplation are twofold, yet they are not remote;
it is simply this infinitesimal thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*). When it is activated, it becomes the subject of contemplation, and it is also taken as the object of contemplation.
Although subject and object are distinct, they are entirely identical within a single thought-moment. This is precisely the sphere of practice and the sphere of intimacy for a bodhisattva;
whether as objective realm or as wisdom, both are utterly inconceivable. Being thus able to abide in the sphere of a bodhisattva’s practice, [one realizes this].
Rather, by directly taking the principle of the Truths as one's object, one is further able to abide in the bodhisattva’s state of proximity (*upaniṣad*) and extensively traverse various conditions;
thus, one’s own practice can be brought to fulfillment, and one is further able to transform others by widely expounding this sutra for the sake of all sentient beings.

△ Second, the explanation and establishment [of the two points]. First, the explanation and establishment of the "places of practice" (*caryā-sthāna*); second, the explanation and establishment of the "states of proximity" (*upaniṣad*).
Section Three: The First Refutation.
Mañjuśrī, what is called the "sphere of practice" (*caryā-viṣaya*) of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva?
Section Two: The Explanation.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwells on the ground of patience (*kṣānti-bhūmi*), these four characters—“dwelling on the ground of patience”—constitute the general explanation. "Patience" (*kṣānti*) refers to the mind that is able to endure; "insult" (*māna*) refers to the object toward which one endures;
and "ground" (*bhūmi*) refers to the ground of the principle of true reality (*dharmatā*). This means that although there is both the subject who endures and the object endured, [they are non-dual].

Although these differ [in their specific manifestations], they are all subsumed within the single ground of ultimate reality (*tattvabhūmi*). Therefore, it is called "patience" (*kṣānti*). As for "abiding":
if one is separated from the object that is endured, then there is no mind capable of enduring; if one is separated from the mind capable of enduring...
Furthermore, there would then be no object of patience whatsoever. In this way, the entirety of the subject is the object, and the entirety of the object is the subject;
thus, subject and object are non-dual. This is "dwelling without dwelling," which is to dwell on the ground of patience (*kṣānti*).
Now, as for the necessity of dwelling on the ground of patience in order to propagate this sutra: it is because when propagating this sutra, even if knives or staves [should be encountered]...

Regarding obstacles and afflictions such as verbal abuse and the like, if one does not abide in the ground of patience (*kṣānti*), one will inevitably be moved by them and will be unable to widely propagate [the Dharma].
Therefore, one must internally cultivate compassion and externally contemplate the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) while abiding in the ground of patience;
in that state, one does not even perceive a mind that "is patient," let alone [perceive an object of patience].
When one perceives an object toward which patience can be maintained, one will not be moved or disturbed by its hindrances and vexations;
thus, one is able to widely propagate [the teaching]. Therefore, those who wish to propagate this sutra must abide in the ground of patience.
Gentle, kind, and compliant, he is not impetuous or violent, and his mind is not startled.
Furthermore, while not engaging in any activity regarding phenomena, he contemplates all phenomena as they truly are; yet he neither acts nor discriminates.
This is the specific explanation: "Gentle, harmonious, and compliant" explains the single character *kṣānti* (patience), which refers to the mind capable of enduring.
"Without being impetuous, and the mind not being startled" explains the single character *māna* (insult), which refers to the object toward which one endures.
Furthermore, "not practicing anything regarding phenomena, yet contemplating all phenomena as they truly are" explains the single character *bhūmi* (ground).
This is the ground of the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*). Furthermore, there is neither practice nor discrimination; this explains the single character "abiding" (*sthiti*) as abiding without abiding.
First, the character "patience" (*kṣānti*) is explained: the phrase "gentle, harmonious, and compliant" refers to following whatever internal [afflictions], such as views and thoughts, may exist.
Regarding obstacles—such as external obstacles like verbal abuse—the Bodhisattva simply settles the mind upon the realm of the true mark (dharmatā) and gives rise to the wisdom that contemplates it.
This wisdom of contemplation then illuminates the realm of contemplation, remaining in no way discordant with the true mark;
therefore, it is called "gentle and flexible. Thus, the wisdom of contemplation and the realm of the true mark are in perfect correspondence.

Because they are similar, it is said that they are "well-conforming. Since they conform without contradicting the true nature (*dharmatā*), what internal or external obstacles could there be that one would not endure?

Second, regarding the explanation of the character for "insult" (*ruǒ*): "The words are not abrupt or violent, and the mind is not startled" refers to the subject that observes and the object that is observed.
Since they are neither in conflict nor merely compliant, the entire object is identical to the mind; thus, one is not disturbed by external objects.
Therefore, one does not act with impulsive violence toward objects. Since the entire mind is identical to the object, no internal mind can be apprehended;
therefore, the mind is likewise not agitated.
Third, the explanation of the character *di* (earth). It says: "Furthermore, while not engaging with phenomena (*dharma*), one contemplates all phenomena as they truly are.
Regarding the term "phenomena" (*dharma*): it refers to the phenomenon that is neither arising nor ceasing.

Nevertheless, although all phenomena possess arising and ceasing, one should know that arising arises from conditions, yet that arising is in reality no-arising; and ceasing ceases from conditions, yet that ceasing is likewise [no-ceasing].

It is not extinguished. Since all phenomena arise from conditions and cease with conditions, yet in their essential nature they are neither arising nor ceasing, one knows that because of the observing wisdom there is the observed object;
thus, while the observed object appears to arise from conditions, its arising is in truth no-arising. Because of the observed object there is the observing wisdom; thus...
The wisdom that is able to observe also appears to arise from conditions, yet this arising is truly no-arising.
If one is separated from the wisdom that observes, then there is no object to be observed; this observed object appears to perish due to conditions, yet this perishing is truly no-perishing.
If one is separated from the object to be observed, there is likewise no wisdom that observes; this [wisdom] that observes...
This wisdom also appears to cease in dependence on conditions; yet this cessation is not truly a cessation.
Since wisdom is neither born nor ceasing, it has no capacity to act upon phenomena. Since the object is neither born nor ceasing, there is nothing for it to act upon.
Thus, all phenomena are empty and quiescent in their very essence. Because when one is empty, all are empty, it is said that "with respect to phenomena, there is no [action]."
This is the practice. As for observing all phenomena according to their true mark (*yathābhūtalakṣaṇa*):
since "one is empty, all are empty," this is the true emptiness (*śūnyatā*). True emptiness is not empty; it does not obstruct any phenomenon.
Since "one exists, all exist," then all phenomena, as well as the observer and the observed, are entirely in accordance with the true mark. Therefore, it is said: ...and so forth.
It is to contemplate all phenomena as they truly are (*yathābhūta*). Since one does not engage with any phenomena, yet "one is empty and all are empty," this is true emptiness (*śūnyatā*);
it is the true reality of all phenomena. Since "one exists and all exist," this is wondrous existence (*prabhāsvara-bhāva*).
This true emptiness and wondrous existence is precisely the ground of the principle of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

Fourth, the explanation of the character for "abiding" (*sthiti*). Regarding the statement, "neither proceeding nor discriminating": the aforementioned "all is empty within one emptiness" does not obstruct "one exists and all exist.
Although "one exists and all exist," they are fundamentally and immediately "one is empty and all are empty.
In this way, the locus of emptiness is primordially existent, and the locus of existence is eternally empty; thus, it is entirely inconceivable.
This is the Middle Way of deliberation; hence it is said that "one neither practices nor discriminates.
"Not practicing" means there is no aforementioned capacity to practice or to observe. "Not discriminating" means there is no aforementioned object of practice or object of observation.

There is no capacity to practice or to observe because, apart from the object of observation, there can be no observer. There is no object of practice or object of observation because... [the text continues].
This is because there is neither a subject that observes nor an object that is observed. This is precisely the dwelling that dwells in non-dwelling.
△ Third, the conclusion of the name:
This is called the sphere of practice of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
△ Second, the explanation establishing the proximate bases (upaniṣad) has two parts.
First, the counter-interrogation: What is called the "proximate base" for a bodhisattva-mahāsattva?
△ Second, the explanation. Regarding this explanatory text, the ancient masters divided it into three sections; here it is divided into two. First, the clarification:
First is the place of initial intimacy. Second, "Furthermore, below," clarifies the second place of intimacy; this refers to "intimacy" by way of being neither distant nor near.
This first section has two parts: first, the formal explanation; second, from "Mañjuśrī" onwards, the conclusion of the name. The first of these two [parts] has two sub-sections.
First, discussing the near by way of the distant; second, from "always fond of" (*cháng hào*) downward, discussing the near by way of the near.

Thus one knows that the ancients categorized them according to their underlying intent, while the present [author] arranges them according to the text. The first section consists of ten items; the first is "keeping far from power and influence."
Regarding the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva not associating with kings, princes, ministers, or high officials:
since this section explains the objects of association, why does it state at the outset that one should "not associate"?
One should know that what are called "objects of association" are those places where the Bodhisattva intends to associate with the ground of the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Originally, it was not the intention for a bodhisattva to associate with those in positions of power and influence.
If one associates with those in positions of power and influence, then regarding the sphere of the true nature (*dharmatā*), one will inevitably fail to associate with it.

Conversely, if one does not associate with those in positions of power and influence, one will naturally be able to associate with the sphere of the true nature. Therefore, this is called "approximating by way of distancing."
This treatise addresses proximity. However, places of power and influence are inappropriate for one who is a bodhisattva.
When such persons wish to draw near to a bodhisattva, the bodhisattva should traverse them with sublime wisdom, causing each and every instance to accord with the true nature (*dharmatā*).
Only then is it a case of the bodhisattva extensively traversing the conditions of proximity. Thus, the text states:
It says: "When such persons as these come at times, he preaches the Dharma for them without any expectation.
This means that if they should approach the Bodhisattva, he would examine them with his wondrous wisdom and preach the Dharma for them;
yet, since the Bodhisattva fundamentally should not approach them, there is no expectation in his inner mind. This refers to not being intimate with the country.
Regarding kings and great ministers: when the Buddha was in the world, he likewise entrusted the Buddha-dharma to kings and ministers;
thus, kings and ministers were fundamentally the golden ramparts and moats for the Buddha-dharma. Why is it that now bodhisattvas should not associate with them?

For kings and ministers are those who possess power and influence. When a bodhisattva at the initial stage of resolve approaches them, it is impossible to avoid the arising of various attachments and longings; there are even instances such as the original story of King Yan.
Therefore, a bodhisattva who has newly begun their practice, if they wish to propagate this sutra, should keep them at a distance. △ Second, distancing oneself from heterodox outsiders.
One does not associate with various non-Buddhists, such as Brahmins and Nirgranthas, nor does one compose secular writings or verses in praise of external scriptures,
nor engage with the Lokāyatas or the Prati-lokāyatas.
This sutra is that which is most ultimate, most correct, and most great. It is fundamentally incompatible with those heterodox outsiders.
Even a bodhisattva at the initial stage of mind cannot avoid being turned by them if they draw near to such people;
therefore, when a beginner first practices and wishes to propagate this sutra, they must keep their distance from them. As for external books, they are indeed for the purpose of governing...
Regarding the worldly languages of those whose six sense faculties are purified, they are naturally able to remain in no contradiction with the true aspect (*dharmatā*).

However, since these are bodhisattvas at the initial stage of resolve, they must also keep them at a distance. As for the Lokāyatas and their like, they are characterized by master and disciple mutually refuting one another;
now, wishing to propagate this sutra, one must have the Way respond through mutual resonance, and master and disciple must be in harmony. Therefore, these too must be kept at a distance.
...Furthermore, one should not associate with those who engage in various forms of sport, such as wrestling, boxing, and the various acrobatic performances of the *naṭas* and others.
To propagate this sutra, one must employ a mind of meditative concentration. Idle play is the mark of one who is heedless and whose mind is distracted;
therefore, it should be avoided. △ Fourth, avoid butchers and those who keep livestock.
Furthermore, one should not associate with *caṇḍālas*, nor with those who raise pigs, sheep, chickens, or dogs, nor with hunters, fishermen, or those who follow any of the evil codes of conduct.
If one is to propagate this sutra, one must exercise unconditional compassion; for those who slaughter animals do so entirely out of a murderous intent.
Because they lack compassion, one must distance oneself from them.
Yet, if such persons should come, one should preach the Dharma to them without any expectation of reward.
This summarizes the four preceding types. Thus, for the speaker of the Dharma:
when a king comes, he preaches the Dharma for him so that he may transform his power and authority into virtuous protection.

When heterodox outsiders come, he preaches the Dharma for them so that they may turn from the heterodox to the orthodox, and turn from the external to become internal. When those who indulge in frivolous play come...
He preaches the Dharma for them to turn away their distraction and achieve a concentrated mind.
When butchers and livestock keepers come, he preaches the Dharma for them to turn away their murderous intent and cultivate the impulse for life.
Therefore, whenever these four types of people arrive, one should preach the Dharma for them. This is precisely because the Bodhisattva, through his wondrous wisdom, [is able to act thus].
One contemplates their power and influence, which immediately becomes a "good protection" (*sugupta*); even contemplating their murderous intent immediately becomes a "life-force" (*jīvita*).
Therefore, when preaching the Dharma for them, one is naturally able to transform their power and influence into good protection, and even to transform their murderous intent into a life-force.
This is how it should be when they come to approach you. As for a Bodhisattva...
A bodhisattva must always distance themselves from this; they should not, because of their association with it, become associated with it as well.
Therefore, although they preach the Dharma, they harbor no internal expectations, for they maintain this distance. △ Fifth, distancing oneself from the Hīnayāna.
Furthermore, he does not associate with those seeking the vehicle of the śrāvaka—whether bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās—nor does he inquire after them.
Whether in a cell, on a walking path, or within a lecture hall, he does not dwell together with them.
Should they occasionally come to him, he teaches the Dharma as appropriate, without harboring any expectations.
Although a bodhisattva has made the great vow to propagate this sutra, one who has only just begun to practice it has not yet attained firm resolve in the mind.
If such a person associates with those of the Hīnayāna, they may give rise to thoughts that the Buddha-way is long and distant; furthermore, this may even happen to those of small capacity.
Therefore, one should keep them at a distance. Since they are of the Lesser Vehicle, when they do come, one should [respond accordingly].
He teaches according to what is appropriate, leading those of the Lesser Vehicle toward the Great Vehicle. △ Sixth, regarding the thought of desire:

Mañjuśrī, furthermore, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should not take up the signs that give rise to thoughts of desire regarding the bodies of women while preaching the Dharma to them, nor should he delight in seeing them. If he enters another's home, he should not stay with young girls or virgins.
The young women converse together.
Herein, Mañjuśrī is mentioned repeatedly. It is further stated: "Moreover, as for the Bodhisattvas," referring to the five aforementioned types;

those who have just begun their resolve and practice find them easy to distance themselves from. These five types mentioned below are even more difficult to distance oneself from. Furthermore, regarding the five aforementioned types...
That which one must certainly distance oneself from consists of these five types mentioned below;
since they are still things that a beginner should avoid, the text emphasizes this point by repeatedly invoking Mañjuśrī and further referring to him as a "bodhisattva.

As for "that which can give rise to thoughts of desire," this refers to the appearance of a woman, for it is that which gives rise to a person's thoughts of desire; therefore, it is said to "give rise to" them.
Regarding the mark of lustful thoughts: if a bodhisattva preaches the Dharma to a woman, he should not preach by taking her physical appearance as the basis.

Furthermore, he should not take pleasure in seeing her; however, it does not constitute an offense if he sees her, provided he simply does not take pleasure in the sight. △ Seventh, the distant impotent.
Furthermore, one should not associate with or treat as close friends the five kinds of impotent persons.
△ Eight, avoiding harm:
one should not enter other people's homes alone. If there is a necessary reason to enter alone, one should simply maintain single-minded mindfulness of the Buddha.
To practice single-mindedly the recitation of the Buddha’s name is not the same as the ordinary recitation of Amitābha Buddha. It means one should think: "I am an envoy of the Tathāgata;
I have been dispatched by the Tathāgata to perform the work of the Tathāgata. Furthermore, one should contemplate the intent behind the Buddha’s appearance in the world:
it was solely his desire to cause all sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. One should embody this intent of the Buddha and propagate [the teaching].
This sutra enables all to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. △ Ninth, regarding distant censure and suspicion:
if one preaches the Dharma for a woman, one must not show one's teeth while smiling nor reveal one's chest. Even for the sake of the Dharma, one should not become intimate;
how much less so for other matters?
△ Tenth, regarding the avoidance of keeping [disciples]:
One should not take pleasure in keeping young disciples, *śrāmaṇeras*, or children; nor should one take pleasure in sharing a teacher with them.

This is because those who are young disciples have not yet established their character; though they may begin to master the scriptures at first, should they be kept [as permanent followers], [it would lead to complications].
I fear it would hinder the propagation of the Way. If one were to share the same teacher, there might be occasions for seeking further instruction, which is not the ultimate Way;
therefore, it is said that [the Buddha] did not delight in it. △ Second, discussing the near by means of the near.
One should always delight in sitting meditation in a secluded place to cultivate and collect the mind.
As for cultivating and collecting the mind: for a beginner, the mind is either dull or distracted.
Now, one should use contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) to observe dullness and thus cultivate the mind so that it attains clarity; one should use tranquility (*śamatha*) to arrest distraction and...
One gathers the mind so that it attains stillness; thus, it is precisely through *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight) that one is able to cultivate and gather the mind.
△ Second, the conclusion of the name:
"Mañjuśrī, this is called the first place of intimacy."
△ Second, explaining the second place of intimacy (*upaniṣad*). This refers to "intimacy" by way of being neither distant nor near. The text is divided into two parts:
first, the formal explanation; second, the summary of the name. The first part has four sections, the first of which is a general explanation.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates all phenomena as empty, according to their true nature (*yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa*).
Regarding the phrase "contemplating all phenomena as empty": "contemplation" refers to the wisdom that is capable of contemplating; "all phenomena" refers to the objects of contemplation.
Although all phenomena exist, they are by their very essence empty and quiescent; therefore, it is said that one contemplates all phenomena as empty. This...
This is precisely "one is empty, all are empty. As for "the true aspect" (yathābhūtalakṣaṇa), it refers to contemplating all phenomena as their true aspect.
Since "one is empty, all are empty" constitutes true emptiness (śūnyatā), it does not preclude "one exists, all exist."
Furthermore, all phenomena are entirely the wondrous existence of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

Not only is the object of contemplation entirely the empty and wondrous existence of ultimate reality, but the contemplating wisdom itself is likewise, in its very essence, both emptiness and wondrous existence.
Therefore, it is said that one contemplates all phenomena as empty, according to their true mark. In this context, "contemplating all phenomena as empty" means:
Regarding the "true aspect" (yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa): when the Tathāgata first arose from samādhi, he immediately extolled the two kinds of wisdom and the two objects of the Buddhas.
Wisdom is the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; the object is the true aspect of all phenomena.

His intention was that all sentient beings might likewise open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and awaken to the realization of the realm of the true aspect. Now, this is taught in the Trace Gate (jia-men).
The matter is concluded. Since it lies in the circulation [of the teaching], it is therefore stated explicitly.

To say that one contemplates all phenomena as empty and as their true reality (*yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa*) means that this contemplation is precisely the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*). "The true reality of all phenomena" refers to the objective realm of the true reality of all dharmas.
Part Two: Separate Explanations (divided into two). First, explaining the contemplation of the emptiness of all phenomena; second, explaining the contemplation of the one.
All phenomena are as their true mark (*yathābhūtalakṣaṇa*). [There are] three initial [points]. First, the phenomenon itself:
it is non-erroneous (*aviparyāsa*), immovable, non-retrogressive, and non-reversing.

Regarding "non-erroneous": ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) perceive impurity in the body and mind as pure; this refers to the four inversions (*viparyāsa*). The two vehicles (*śrāvakayāna* and *pratyekabuddhayāna*) [also perceive... *(Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment. The translation reflects the available portion while maintaining the technical terminology and structural flow of the original.)*

The four inversions, such as impermanence and so forth, are reversed. As for those Bodhisattvas who progress through partial stages, there are further four inversions, such as "both permanent and impermanent" and so forth.

Because ordinary beings and followers of the Two Vehicles who progress through partial stages do not realize that all phenomena are, in their very essence, empty and quiescent, they all give rise to these four inversions.
Now, the beginner Bodhisattva is able to see that all phenomena are empty; therefore, they do not fall into error.
"Immovable" means not being moved by the attachments of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), nor being moved by the emptiness of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
"Non-retrogressive" means being able to contemplate the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*) and ascending to the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*);

thus, one flows in spontaneously and naturally, and for this reason is non-retrogressive. "Non-turning" means that while ordinary beings wander through birth and death, they do so because they possess [something].

The turning away [from the truth] occurs because the followers of the Two Vehicles take the guarantee of nirvana as their goal; they are thus turned by emptiness itself, all due to their failure to contemplate [the ultimate nature].
Now, if one can contemplate the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmas*), one will naturally not be turned by the emptiness of ordinary beings or the Two Vehicles.
△ Second, the analogy:
Just as space has the nature of non-existence and all paths of linguistic expression are severed—
referring to this true emptiness of all phenomena— if one were to use a provisional metaphor to clarify it, it is like that which exists in the world.
The emptiness of this [world] and the emptiness of the world are but a single emptiness. Beyond emptiness, there is no further emptiness.
True emptiness (*zhēnkōng*) is likewise: when one is empty, all is empty; beyond emptiness, there are no further dharmas. As for the nature of non-existence:
the emptiness of the world is devoid of the four natures; true emptiness is likewise devoid of self and other.
This is the nature of both [existence] and [non-existence] being transcended. That all paths of language are cut off refers to the emptiness of the world;
it is inconceivable, yet the path of language is cut off. True emptiness is likewise inconceivable, yet the path of language is cut off.
The nature of non-existence is the emptiness of nature; that the path of language is cut off is the emptiness of characteristics. △
The three are merged;
there is no birth, no emergence, and no arising. It is nameless and signless, truly possessing nothing—this is called the true emptiness of all dharmas.
Because it is not like the ordinary person dwelling in birth and death, it is said to be "non-."
"Arising" does not mean emerging from birth and death as it does for the followers of the Two Vehicles; therefore, it is said that there is no "emerging.

It does not mean abandoning nature to speak of cultivation or abandoning cultivation to speak of nature, as is the case with the partial and gradual Bodhisattvas; therefore, it is said that there is no "arising.
"Nameless" means there is no name or designation by which it can be called. "Signless" means there is no appearance or characteristic by which it can be seen. In short, its very essence is emptiness.
It is quiescent, yet in reality nothing exists at all. △ Second, the explanation of contemplating all phenomena as they truly are:
they are immeasurable and boundless, unimpeded and unobstructed; they exist merely through causes and conditions and arise from inversion.
The aforementioned emptiness of all phenomena is true emptiness; where there is one emptiness, there is the emptiness of all.

The present suchness is wondrous existence; where there is one existence, there is the existence of all. Since it is wondrous existence, it is vast, penetrating, and perfectly interfused, being without limitation;
it pervades the entire dharma-realm without boundary or shore; it is layered upon layer, infinitely so.
Obstruction. It is inexhaustible and inexhaustible, yet there is no hindrance or barrier; therefore, it is said to be immeasurable, boundless, unimpeded, and unobstructed.
As for that which exists through causes and conditions and arises from inversion:

since all dharmas are identical to the true mark (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa*), being immeasurable, boundless, unimpeded, and unobstructed, they are fundamentally without arising and fundamentally without [cessation].
There is cessation. That is to say, if there is one who observes arising and ceasing, it exists merely through causes and conditions and arises from inversion.
Because sentient beings cannot contemplate all phenomena as they truly are, they pursue delusions through confusion.

Taking the false for the true—due to such inverted causes and conditions—one perceives only all phenomena as possessing characteristics such as arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing, and fails to see that all phenomena are in their true reality (*tathatā*).

However, since it is said that they exist by way of causes and conditions, their existence is not truly existent; yet this very existence is the true reality. Since it is said that [this perception] arises from inversion...
When there is arising, that arising is in truth non-arising, and yet arising is itself the true mark (*dharmatā*).
Since all are the true mark, one naturally does not perceive any characteristics of phenomena such as arising, abiding, changing, or ceasing;
rather, one contemplates all phenomena solely as they truly are. △ Third, the comprehensive inclusion.
Therefore it is said:
because they are non-perverted, up to being ultimately non-existent, it is said that one contemplates all phenomena as empty.
Because they are immeasurable and boundless, up to arising from perversion, it is therefore said:
To contemplate all dharmas as they truly are. △ Fourth, the exhortation to contemplate:
One should always joyfully contemplate such characteristics of dharmas.
This means that if a bodhisattva at the initial stage wishes to propagate and disseminate this sutra, they must always joyfully contemplate this "all."
The mark of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*). It is the suchness-mark (*yathābhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena.
△ Second, the summary of the name: This is called the second place of intimacy for a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
△ The second section, consisting of verses, is divided into three parts. First, a verse provides a general response.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"If there should be a bodhisattva who, in the evil world of the future, possesses a mind free from fear and desires to preach this sutra..."
Regarding the two phrases on "being without fear": if one cannot abide in the four modes of peaceful conduct (*caturvidha-sukha-vihāra*), the mind will be filled with many fears;

how then could one preach this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*? Now, a bodhisattva at the initial stage who is able to abide within these four modes of peaceful conduct exercises compassion externally while contemplating the true reality (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*) internally, thereby [overcoming] whatever obstacles may exist.
Regarding vexation: though one is not moved by it oneself, the mind remains free from fear, and one is naturally able to preach this sutra.
△ Second, the verse provides a detailed exposition, which is further divided into two parts. First, the practice and proximity are explained together.
One should enter places of practice and places of association, while always remaining far removed from kings, princes, ministers, and high officials;
from those who engage in dangerous games, from *caṇḍālas*, and from non-Buddhist brahmins.
The first two lines constitute the general heading. The line and a half beginning with "Always avoid kings" (*nityaṃ rājānam*) refers to distancing oneself from the laity.
The first three lines praise the avoidance of those with power and influence. The single line on "perilous places" (*viṣama*) praises the avoidance of public spectacles.
The single line on "caṇḍālas" praises the avoidance of butchers and those who deal in livestock. The single line on "heretics" (*tīrthika*) praises the avoidance of heterodox outsiders.
Furthermore, one should not associate with those who possess overweening pride, those who greedily cling to the Lesser Vehicle, scholars of the Tripitaka,
bhikṣus who have broken the precepts, arhats in name only, and bhikṣuṇīs who delight in frivolous laughter, who are deeply attached to the five desires, and who seek nirvāṇa in this present life.

He should not associate with any of these female lay devotees (upāsikā). If such persons should come to the Bodhisattva with a sincere heart for the purpose of hearing the Buddha-way, the Bodhisattva, with a mind free from fear and without harboring expectations, shall preach the Dharma for them.

"These are the distant Dharma assemblies. This is all a verse praising the distancing of the Hīnayāna. Regarding the "Three Piṭakas," they exist in both the Mahāyāna and the Hīnayāna, as detailed in the *Jizhu* (Collected Notes).
What is presented here is the Hīnayāna Tripiṭaka. The Tathāgata taught these Three Piṭakas originally as provisional and skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*);
yet, those [Hīnayānists] do not understand them as skillful means, and thus they greedily crave and cling to them. Now...
A bodhisattva of initial resolve who wishes to propagate this wondrous sutra should personally distance themselves from such persons. As for those bhikṣus who have broken the precepts:

the precepts serve to prevent wrongdoing and eliminate transgressions; thus, the initial ten precepts constitute the śrāmaṇera, the subsequent two hundred and fifty precepts constitute the bhikṣu, and finally, the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts constitute the bodhisattva. If a śrāmaṇera...
To uphold the practice by grasping its characteristics means to understand the origin of the ten precepts;
for a bhikṣu to uphold the practice by grasping its characteristics means to understand the origin of the two hundred and fifty precepts;

and for a bodhisattva to uphold the practice by grasping its characteristics means to understand the origin of the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts—only then is one a śrāmaṇera or even a bodhisattva. To speak now of "breaking the precepts" [refers to this].
Regarding the bhikṣu: that by which one is called a bhikṣu is solely because the precepts are the foundation of all virtues and the foremost of all practices.
If he should violate them, he does not even qualify as a bhikṣu; how much less could he hear the Mahāyāna Dharma of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, the Lotus Sūtra?
Therefore, one should not associate with such a person. As for an arhat, they are established as such by virtue of their realization.
[Their] title is merely a name now; even the followers of the Hīnayāna cannot attain it, so how could they hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the Dharma of the unsurpassed Buddha-way?
Therefore, one should not associate with them either. Those who are deeply attached to the five desires are *upāsikās* (laywomen).

Those who dwell at home and seek extinction in the present life are those who either seek the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), or seek it within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
"Transformation of the realm" (*dhātu-parāvṛtti*) refers either to seeking transformation within the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*).
"Such persons as these" is a concluding reference to the five types of people mentioned above. Regarding those who come with good intentions:
among the aforementioned five types of people, there are some who rely entirely on power and influence, some who are completely immersed in negligence, and some who exclusively engage in slaughter.
Among them, there are those who dwell exclusively in heterodox ways, and those who are solely attached to the Hīnayāna.
Now they have come to the presence of the Bodhisattvas who propagate this wondrous sūtra, having recognized what they must do, in order to hear the unsurpassed Buddha-way;
this is their sincere intention. As for the one who preaches the Dharma to them: since they have already come to hear it...

The Buddha comes from afar; upon his return, he shall preach the Unsurpassed Way for them, so that those who rely on their power and influence may turn toward becoming great protectors, and even those of the Hīnayāna may turn toward returning to the Mahāyāna.
Do not associate with widows, virgins, or those who are impotent; do not treat them as close friends.
Likewise, do not associate with butchers, executioners, hunters, fishermen, or those who kill for profit, who sell meat for their livelihood, or who traffic in female beauty.
One should not associate with such people at all. One must not associate with those who engage in dangerous wrestling, various forms of amusement, or with prostitutes.
Do not preach the Dharma to women in a secluded place. When preaching the Dharma, do not engage in joking or laughter.
Entering a village to beg for alms, he should take a fellow bhikṣu with him; if there is no bhikṣu, he should single-mindedly recollect the Buddha.
With the first line of verse, "Distant from lustful thoughts," he distances himself from lustful thoughts. With the line "Not a male," he distances himself from those who are not males.

With the four lines beginning with "Butchers," he further distances himself from butchers and those who keep livestock. With the line "Hawking and selling," he further distances himself from lustful thoughts. With the two lines beginning with "Perilous," [he distances himself from peril].
Furthermore, there is a verse on avoiding frivolous play: "The lewd woman, one line. Again, there is a verse on avoiding thoughts of desire:

"Do not go alone," one line. A verse on avoiding censure and suspicion: "Entering the village," one line. A verse on avoiding harm: "The Buddha ordained that when begging for food, one must always be with two others;
those who single-mindedly mindfully recollect the Buddha" refers to mindfully recollecting the Buddha’s ordinance regarding begging for food, and having no desire to cook over a fire.
The intent behind this is that a bhikṣu should inwardly relinquish the mind of arrogance and outwardly increase the merit of the *dānapati*.
He reflects: "How now shall I practice begging so that I may abandon my own pride and bring benefit to others, thereby acceding with the Buddha’s intention?"
This is what is called the "sphere of practice" and the "proximate sphere. By means of these two spheres, one is able to teach with ease. This practice encompasses all:
it consists of being able to directly take the principle of the Truths as its object internally, while externally traversing extensively through various conditions.
These are called the Bodhisattva’s sphere of practice and proximate sphere. By abiding within these two spheres, one’s own person— [Note: The source text appears to be incomplete at the end.]
One will be able to attain peace and happiness, and thus this sutra may be expounded extensively. Furthermore, this practice closely accords with and clarifies a single passage [from the prose]:

it is a verse concerning the "place of practice" (*caryā-sthāna*) within the prose section, which describes being gentle, compliant, and well-disposed, rather than impulsive or violent, and having a mind that is not startled.
Although "near place" (*upasthāna*) refers to the distant in terms of its scope, both the introduction and the conclusion employ the term "practice" (*caryā*) for both.
In the preceding verse, we see only texts concerning the distant; it is only the single category of "rearing" that is not versified.
As for the text concerning the "sphere of conduct," where exactly is it to be found? It is simply the single phrase "fearless" that constitutes the verse on the sphere of conduct.
This is because, being gentle, kind, and compliant, one does not act with sudden violence toward external objects.

Because one is not startled or terrified within the inner mind, one is thus able to have no fear in the heart, and can preach this sutra for the ten types of people, such as those with power and influence.
△ Second, the individual clarification of practice and proximity.
Furthermore, they do not practice; they do not differentiate between superior, middling, or inferior dharmas, conditioned or unconditioned dharmas, real or unreal dharmas, nor as male or female.
They do not apprehend any dharmas; they neither know nor see them.
Regarding the phrase "furthermore, one does not practice," this means that it is not merely a matter of distancing oneself from the ten types [of dharmas] as mentioned above;
rather, one must further refrain from practicing the various dharmas categorized as superior, middling, and inferior. Thus, it says "furthermore, one does not practice," and so forth.
"Superior" refers to the vehicle of the Bodhisattvas; "middling" refers to the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas; and "inferior" refers to the vehicle of the Śrāvakas. Furthermore, no...
They practice the conditioned dharmas of ordinary beings and the unconditioned dharmas of the two vehicles.
Among these, those who possess actual realization of the unconditioned dharmas are called "real dharmas," while those who lack such realization of the conditioned dharmas are called "unreal dharmas.
Furthermore, they do not discriminate between male and female; thus, they not only do not practice the real dharmas of the unconditioned, but [even] lack...
Within the Dharma, all that constitutes either wisdom or meditative concentration is likewise not differentiated.
"Not attaining equality" means that one does not merely refrain from practicing conditioned or unconditioned dharmas; furthermore, one does not apprehend these various dharmas themselves.
Therefore, it is said that there is neither knowing nor seeing.
This is what is called the "sphere of activity" (gocara) of a bodhisattva.
To summarize this term: it refers to being able to neither engage in nor differentiate among all phenomena, while simultaneously knowing and seeing all phenomena completely.
This is called the sphere of activity of a bodhisattva. Furthermore, by speaking of this "sphere of activity," it clarifies that—
The practitioner should know that by not practicing any other dharmas, one is practicing the dharma of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

This is to speak of practice by way of non-practice. By not practicing the superior, middling, or inferior dharmas, one must thoroughly comprehend that all dharmas are entirely empty and quiescent; when all is empty, everything is empty—this is the long practice.
Furthermore, within this [middle way], one does not engage with any phenomena (*dharma*). One does not apprehend any phenomena; one neither knows nor sees them.
Rather, one must thoroughly comprehend that all phenomena are entirely in accordance with their true nature (*tathatā*). Thus, while there is the "one," there is also the "all.

This is precisely what is meant by contemplating all phenomena as they truly are within the prose section. Furthermore, one does not engage in conceptual discrimination; rather, one must thoroughly comprehend [this].
All dharmas are utterly inconceivable; yet within one is all, and thus even within the prose section, there is neither practice nor discrimination.
In this way, directly taking the single mind as the object of the principle of the three truths is what is called the "place of practice."
All phenomena (*dharmas*) are empty and non-existent; they neither abide permanently, nor do they arise or cease.
This verse contemplates the emptiness of all phenomena. It is not that [emptiness] is distant or near—it discusses the "near.
To say that all phenomena are non-existent means that although all phenomena may undergo arising or cessation, they...
Arising is dependent arising; ceasing is dependent cessation. Since they are both dependently arisen and dependently ceased, they are fundamentally neither arising nor ceasing.
Their very substance is empty and quiescent, such that nothing exists. There is no permanence, nor is there any arising or ceasing.
This means that since all phenomena are empty and non-existent, their very substance is neither born nor extinguished, and thus they are eternally abiding.
Now, there is neither a permanent state that is free from arising and ceasing, nor is there any movement, transition, or occurrence of birth and extinction.
This is what is called the sphere of intimacy for the wise.
This is the name of the bond: namely, that it is empty and non-existent, neither arising nor ceasing;

yet there is no permanence of non-arising and non-ceasing, nor the arising and ceasing of movement and transformation. This is "one emptiness, all things empty," and it is the immediate sphere of the Bodhisattva.

Inverted conceptualization—regarding all phenomena as existent or non-existent, real or unreal, produced or unproduced—this verse contemplates the true mark (*yathābhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena. As for the phrase "inverted conceptualization" and so forth:
it means that while the aforementioned "one is empty, all are empty" constitutes true emptiness (*śūnyatā*), it does not preclude the fact that "one exists, all exist. And yet, these...
All phenomena are precisely their true marks (*yathābhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Since they are all precisely their true marks, there are no such things as existence and non-existence, reality and unreality, arising and non-arising, and so forth.

Yet, that there currently appear such marks as existence and non-existence, reality and unreality, arising and non-arising, and so on, is merely inverted conceptualization; therefore, one perceives all phenomena as having [such characteristics].
There are such characteristics as existence and non-existence. Since such characteristics arise from inverted conceptualization, one knows that all phenomena are fundamentally non-existent.
Although these various characteristics appear to exist, they are all entirely identical to the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
Dwelling in a secluded place, one cultivates the gathering of the mind, abiding immovably like Mount Sumeru.
This verse, as mentioned above, discusses the proximate in terms of the proximate and is thus visible.

Contemplate all phenomena as being entirely non-existent, like empty space, lacking solidity, neither arising nor emerging, neither moving nor receding, eternally abiding in a single mark. This is called "the proximate station."
Furthermore, this verse contemplates that all phenomena are empty, being neither distant nor near.
Regarding the statement "like space," the space of the world exists entirely due to ignorance; if ignorance were absent, the space of the ten directions would immediately vanish.
Therefore, space is not something solid or permanent. Now, when one contemplates all phenomena, they too are likewise [unsubstantial].
It is firm, yet it is universally one in emptiness and stillness. Regarding "not arising, not emerging, not moving, and not retreating":

since all things are empty and still, one does not remain in birth and death like an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), nor does one emerge from birth and death like those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
Furthermore, one is not moved by the two extremes (*antadvaya*), but is able to flow in spontaneously until reaching the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*). This is constant.

That which abides in the single characteristic likewise lacks characteristics such as arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing; it eternally and constantly abides as the single characteristic of universal true emptiness.
The second verse, which specifically demonstrates this, is concluded. △ Third, the conclusion on the accomplishment of practice.
If there should be a bhikṣu who, after my parinirvāṇa, enters this sphere of practice and its sphere of intimacy, he shall feel no timidity when preaching this sutra.
At times, a bodhisattva enters a quiet room and, with right mindfulness, contemplates the dharmas according to their meaning.

Regarding the statement "correctly recollecting and contemplating the Dharma according to its meaning": this means that if one wishes to expound the sutras, one must first internally contemplate the Dharma.

If one contemplates only existence, only emptiness, or only the Middle Way, there will be partiality in each case, and it cannot be called correctly recollecting and contemplating the Dharma. Now, when a bodhisattva at the initial stage propagates [the teaching]...
Now, this sutra has already enabled one to contemplate the true mark (*dharmatā*). By means of the true mark, wondrous wisdom is brought forth.

This is the arising of cultivation from within the entirety of nature, and the emergence of practice from within the entirety of principle. It is neither biased toward emptiness nor existence, nor does it rely upon the Middle Way;
rather, it is right mindfulness and right recollection. By means of this mindfulness and recollection, one follows its [the dharma's]...
Regarding the meaning of "explanation": it refers to observing the Dharma that has been taught; this clarifies his knowledge of the Dharma.
Emerging from meditative concentration, he reveals, transforms, and expounds [the teaching] for kings, princes, ministers, subjects, brahmins, and others.
When preaching this sutra, their minds are peaceful and secure, free from any timidity or weakness.
Mañjuśrī, this is called a bodhisattva who dwells securely in the first dharma and is able to preach the Lotus Sutra in future ages.
This demonstrates that he understands the opportune moment (*kṣaṇa*). His mind is peaceful and secure, free from any timidity or weakness.
If one does not understand the Dharma within and does not understand the opportune moment without, then the mind cannot avoid being uneasy and will be subject to much timidity and weakness.
Now, since he is able to know the Dharma and furthermore knows the opportune moment, he preaches the Dharma in accordance with that moment. By means of this...
The Dharma accords with the capacities of beings; there is nothing that does not fit them. How could there then be anything insecure, such as so-called cowardice or weakness?
This is called "abiding securely in the initial Dharma," meaning one is able to abide in the sphere of practice and the sphere of proximity, knowing the Dharma and knowing the capacities [of beings].
This is called a bodhisattva at the initial stage, abiding securely in the first body of peaceful conduct.
This is the Dharma. △ Second, showing the peaceful conduct of speech, which has two parts: first, the prose; second, the verse. The first part has two sections.
First, the heading:
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Final Dharma, those who wish to preach this sutra should abide in peace.
Pleasant Practice.
△ Second, the explanation has two parts. First, clarifying what should not be done:
Whether speaking aloud or reading the scriptures, one should not take pleasure in speaking of the faults of others or of the scriptures, nor should one treat them with contempt.
Other Dharma masters do not speak of the good or bad, the long or short of others;
nor do they mention by name the faults or evils of śrāvakas, nor do they mention by name their virtues to praise them. Furthermore, they do not give rise to thoughts of resentment or aversion.
Regarding "not speaking of the faults of persons or of the sūtras": "persons" refers to those capable of hearing the Hīnayāna; "sūtras" refers to the Hīnayāna teachings that are heard.

Although those who hear the Hīnayāna cannot rely upon the Great Dharma, if they practice what they hear of the Small Vehicle, they will likewise be able to sever the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*), emerge from the realm of birth and death by limited segments (*paricchinna-bhava*), and realize [the fruit].

Regarding *nirvāṇa*, if one were to speak of its faults, it would not necessarily cause one to enter the Great [Vehicle], but there are cases where, conversely, one might instead fall back and lose even the Small [Vehicle].
Therefore, one should not speak of such things. As for the scriptures of the Small Vehicle, they were spoken by the Tathāgata in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings;
fundamentally, they contain no fault. How could one speak of them as faulty? To say that one does not delight in speaking of them is precisely...
If one wishes to distinguish between the partial and the perfect, clarify the great and the small, and examine the provisional and the real, these are indeed matters that ought to be discussed.
However, if a bodhisattva who has newly resolved to propagate the sutras speaks with a sincere heart regarding the faults of others or of the scriptures, this is improper.
Furthermore, one must not disparage other Dharma masters; this clarifies that one should not be arrogant.
A Dharma master who is able to propagate the teachings of the *Upāya-kauśalya-sūtra*, although they may not be propagating the Mahāyāna, is nonetheless one capable of transforming sentient beings;

therefore, one should not treat them with contempt. Regarding "not speaking of the likes and dislikes or the strengths and weaknesses of others," this refers to not speaking of the faults of ordinary people. Below the section on the Śrāvakas, this is called "not speaking."
This concerns the likes and dislikes of those who practice the Hīnayāna. If one speaks of their faults, it causes them to regress from the Lesser Vehicle;
if one praises their virtues, it causes them to become attached to the Lesser Vehicle. Therefore, one should not speak of either.
Furthermore, one should not give rise to feelings of resentment or disdain, thinking: "They are followers of the Hīnayāna, and this obstructs my own [practice of] the Mahāyāna."
"To 'ride' [the vehicle] is to give rise to a mind of resentment. To say that they are followers of the Hīnayāna, and thus base, inferior, and narrow-minded, is to give rise to a mind of disdain.
Such thoughts as these should never be entertained. △ Second, clarifying what ought to be done."
Because they have well cultivated such a mind of peace and happiness, those who listen do not oppose their intentions;

when there are difficult questions or inquiries, they do not answer with the teachings of the Hīnayāna, but explain them solely through the Mahāyāna, enabling them to attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
"Not opposing their wishes" means that when a Bodhisattva propagates this sutra, if a person does not come to listen, that is that;
however, if they do come and their intention is to hear the sutra, then one should immediately preach this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* for them.

Therefore, it is said that one does not oppose their wishes; it does not mean that one preaches the Great [Vehicle] to those who desire the Great, or the Small [Vehicle] to those who desire the Small.

This is to avoid being contrary. Regarding those who raise difficult questions and the like: although that which the Bodhisattva propagates is exclusively Great, Perfect, and Real, there may be those who challenge the Great with the Small, the Perfect with the Partial, or the Real with the Provisional.
When the Bodhisattva addresses such challenges, he does not [respond] by means of the Small, the Partial, or the Provisional.
The first interlocutor raises an objection: "One should simply provide an explanation based on the perfect reality of the Mahāyāna.
Why? Because only the Tathāgata can clearly discern the capacities of beings; thus, whether he teaches the Great or the Small Vehicle, it always accords with their capacity and is without error.
Now, a bodhisattva at the initial stage of practice cannot necessarily discern capacities as clearly as the Buddha does. Should he [attempt to] expound..."
If one who possesses the capacity for the Great Vehicle is taught the Small Vehicle, it constitutes stinginess regarding the Dharma and a failure to accord with the recipient's capacity.
Now, to teach only the Great Vehicle so that they may understand it as the Mahāyāna is indeed appropriate; yet, if it is not the Mahāyāna, then it is not the Mahāyāna.
Nor does one lose the perfect seed. Therefore, one should teach only the Great [Vehicle] and not the Small.

To enable them to attain all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*), when those who have come to listen do not oppose one’s intent, and when those who pose difficult questions respond only with the Great [Vehicle], one will naturally cause them to attain all-encompassing wisdom. △ Second, the verse summary has three parts.
The first verse provides the heading.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The Bodhisattva always delights in preaching the Dharma with peace and security; upon a pure ground, he prepares a seat, having anointed his body with oil."
Having bathed away all impurities and donned fresh, clean robes, being pure both internally and externally, one speaks with constant joy of the teaching of peace and security;

that is to say, the propagator of the Dharma is able to exercise great kindness (*maitrī*), desiring to bestow happiness upon all sentient beings, and is able to exercise great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), desiring to uproot the suffering of all sentient beings. By bestowing happiness...
There is no happiness he does not bestow; he uproots suffering, and there is no suffering he does not uproot. This is what is called teaching the Dharma with peace and security.
It is not only for a single thought-moment that it is thus, but for every thought-moment it is so. It is not only at one time that it is thus, but at every time it is so.
It is not only in one place that it is thus, but in every place it is so. Therefore, it is said that he constantly teaches with joy, peace, and security.
This is the Dharma. This is precisely entering the chamber of compassion. Regarding "providing a seat upon a pure ground":
since one provides a bed and seat upon a pure ground, one is able to contemplate the emptiness of all phenomena; this is the seat of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*).
Regarding "anointing the body with oil and so forth": being gentle, harmonious, and compliant, one will not [be harmed] by oneself.
To be unmoved by all obstacles and afflictions means not being moved by the obstacles of views and afflictions (dṛṣṭi-kleśa); this is internal purity.
To be unmoved by obstacles such as verbal abuse means not being moved by external obstacles; this is external purity. This is the donning of the robe of patience (*kṣānti*).

Within this very practice of speech, one is able to fulfill the three guidelines (*tri-vidhi*); thus, one knows that within the practices of body, speech, and mind, there is likewise nothing that is not [perfected].
This possesses the three modes. △ Second, the verse explanation has two parts. First, the verse on what ought to be done:
"Taking one's place upon the Dharma-seat, one teaches according to the questions asked. If there be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, [and upāsikās...]"
To the upāsikās, kings, princes, ministers, officials, and commoners, he speaks with a gentle countenance on the subtle and profound meanings.
Should there be any questions or challenges, he answers according to the principles, elaborating and analyzing them through causes, conditions, and parables.
By these skillful means, he causes them all to resolve their minds toward enlightenment, gradually increasing their merit until they enter the path of the Buddha.
To sit upon the Dharma-seat means to sit upon the seat of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*). Monks and the like constitute the assembly of the Dharma;
kings and the like constitute the assembly of the laity. Whether toward those of the Dharma or the laity, one should always speak with a serene countenance.
For if I speak with a serene countenance, they will surely listen with joy; this is precisely not to oppose their inclinations. Accordingly...
"Answering according to the meaning" means answering in accordance with the subtle meanings expounded in the present sutra;

this is simply answering by means of the Mahāyāna teachings. Regarding "causes and conditions" and so forth, this also serves to reveal the skillful means (*upāya*) and does not merely repeat the prose section.
That is to say, if [the Buddha] perceives that the recipient is of a Hīnayāna disposition, he should first preach the Hīnayāna for them.
Thereafter, one causes them to give rise to the mind of the Mahāyāna and leads them into the Buddha-way. This is to lead them from the small toward the great;
hence it is said that they "gradually enter the Way. This is precisely what enables them to attain all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*). 2.
A subsequent verse on what should not be done:
He eliminates laziness and the thought of indolence, and being free from all sorrow and affliction, he preaches the Dharma with a heart of loving-kindness.
Day and night he constantly proclaims the unsurpassed path of the Buddha, using various causes and conditions and immeasurable parables to reveal it to sentient beings, causing them all to rejoice.
Regarding robes, bedding, food, drink, and medicine, one should have no expectations for them whatsoever.

Rather, with single-minded devotion, one should keep in mind the causes and conditions for preaching the Dharma, vowing to attain the Buddha-way and causing all beings to do likewise. This is the great benefit and the peaceful, blissful offering.
This means that regarding what should not be done, one should arouse diligence and swiftly abandon it; hence, it is said that "laziness and so forth are eliminated.

Following the section on preaching the Dharma with a compassionate mind, the following verse further describes what ought to be done. Regarding the phrase "by means of various causes and conditions," etc.:
This also clearly elucidates the skillful means (*upāya*). Regarding "causing all to rejoice": because he constantly teaches the unsurpassed Way, he is naturally able to cause people to rejoice.
This is precisely the time for opening up skillful means; it involves leading others from the small back toward the Great [Vehicle].
"Wishing to attain the Buddha-way" refers to self-benefit (*svārtha*), while "causing the multitude to do likewise" refers to benefiting others (*parārtha*).
This benefits both oneself and others; there is no benefit greater than this. Therefore, it is said: "This is the great benefit, the peaceful and blissful offering.

Herein, the peaceful conduct of speech is clarified. As for the frequent mention of the "mind" in both the prose and the verses, the mind is the source of speech, and speech is the sound of the mind; thus, while clarifying speech, the mind is also mentioned. △
The conclusion is formed by three verses:
"After my parinirvāṇa, if there should be a bhikṣu who is able to expound this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, with a mind free from envy and anger..."
There are no afflictions or obstacles, nor is there any sorrow or those who revile them; furthermore, there is no fear of being struck with swords, staves, and the like, nor is there any expulsion.
Because they dwell securely in patience, the wise person thus skillfully cultivates the mind and is able to abide in peace and happiness.
As I have explained above, the merit of that person cannot be fully exhausted even by calculation, enumeration, or parable throughout thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas.
△ Third, indicating the intention for the Practice of Peaceful Abiding, in two parts: first, the prose; second, the verse. The first part has three sections; first, the heading.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, in the future final age when the Dharma is about to perish,
receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra—
△ Second, the explanation has two parts. First, clarifying what should not be done.
"Do not harbor jealousy or a mind of flattery and deception.
The phrase "do not harbor" is a general clarification; "nor should you slight or revile," and so forth, is the specific clarification. This refers to those at the initial stage of the path.

One who propagates the Sūtra should externally exercise compassion and look down with pity upon sentient beings, while internally contemplating the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) and propagating the Buddha-way above.
Therefore, one should not harbor a mind of jealousy, nor should one harbor a mind of flattery or deception.
If one harbors jealousy, how can one exercise compassion and pity for sentient beings? Thus, jealousy—
One should not harbor a mind of envy. If one harbors flattery and deception, the inner mind will be false and illusory;
how then could one contemplate the true mark and propagate the Buddha-way? Therefore, a mind of flattery and deception should likewise not be harbored.
Furthermore, do not disparage or revile them. To seek out the shortcomings of those who study the Buddha-way is what is clarified here separately;
first, it clarifies that one should not despise the Separate Teaching (Pratyekabuddha-yāna). Those who study the Buddha-way refer to those at the initial stage of the Separate Teaching.
