One contemplates the principle of pure *tathatā* and seeks the path of the fruit-Buddha of wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue*).
However, those of the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*) can only contemplate "bare middle" (*danzhong*) and are further unable to exhaust ignorance (*avidyā*);
they are certainly deserving of rebuke. Yet, when a bodhisattva at the initial stage (*chuxin*) wishes to propagate this sutra, it is not yet appropriate to lightly rebuke them.
Furthermore, as for those who seek out their strengths and weaknesses: they too are able to seek the Buddha-way, which is indeed their strength;
however, that they sever only twelve grades of delusion and cannot exhaustively eliminate ignorance is their weakness.

If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās—whether they seek the path of a śrāvaka, the path of a pratyekabuddha, or the bodhisattva path—you must not disturb them or cause them to fall into doubt and regret by saying to them:
"You are very far from the Path; you will never be able to attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā). Why is this? Because you are negligent."
Such a person, due to indolence regarding the Path, is said to be "far removed from the Path.
This clarifies that one should not disparage those of the Shared Teaching (Prajñāpāramitā), for they are very far from the path of unsurpassed Bodhi.
This is because the Shared Teaching can only reach the "transformed city" (the provisional nirvāṇa) and cannot reach the "place of treasures" (the ultimate reality). Therefore...
They are far removed from the Way. Those who are heedless are individuals of dull faculties;

they perceive only emptiness and do not perceive non-emptiness, and thus are unable to advance toward subsequent teachings—this is called heedlessness. Those who are indolent are dull in the same manner as those of the Two Vehicles.
Although they are able to purify buddha-fields and perform such deeds as sporting with supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), their aspirations are directed solely toward partial emptiness;

therefore, they are said to be indolent. Although they are far removed from the Way and are thus negligent and indolent, those who have first resolved to propagate the sutras should not cause them distress.
Furthermore, one should not engage in frivolous speculation regarding all phenomena nor contend with others.
This clarifies that one ought not to disparage the teachings of the Tripiṭaka. What is elucidated in the Tripiṭaka consists of the four truths of arising and ceasing:
when suffering and its origin exist, then the path and its cessation do not; when the path and its cessation exist, then suffering and its origin do not. Awakening and affliction are likewise...

They lean toward one another; birth-and-death and nirvana are thus mutually characterized by arising and ceasing. This is precisely what gives rise to conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) regarding all phenomena.
One who propagates the sutras should not engage in dispute with those who proliferate such phenomena.
If one disparages what they have studied as being "small," then one is already disputing. If one says that what one propagates is... [the text here is incomplete].
"Great. This implies that there is something with which to compete. One should gradually lead [the mind] back toward the Great; this is precisely the absence of contention and competition.
△ Second, clarifying what ought to be practiced.
One should conceive the thought of great compassion toward all sentient beings; the thought of a loving father toward all Tathāgatas;
and the thought of a great teacher toward all Bodhisattvas. One should always, with a profound mind, pay respectful homage to the great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions.
One should preach the Dharma equally to all sentient beings, in accordance with the Dharma, neither too much nor too little, and so forth.
Even for those who deeply love the Dharma, one should not speak excessively.

Since all sentient beings are entirely adrift in the cycle of birth and death, one should conceive thoughts of great compassion toward them and desire to uproot their suffering. It is the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, who are able to bring this about.
My Dharma-body grows through them, and my life of wisdom is prolonged; therefore, one should regard them as a compassionate father and revere them deeply.

The great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, who practice the Bodhisattva path and are able to set an example for themselves and others, are the teachers of those at the initial stage of their first resolve and practice; thus, one should regard them as great masters and treat them with respect.
To respectfully receive and serve [the Dharma] means this. To preach the Dharma with equanimity refers to neither too much nor too little; this is what is called preaching with equanimity.
To say "neither too much nor too little" means that one is truly able to clearly discern the capacities of all sentient beings.
Then one should preach for them with impartiality, ensuring there is no error of excess or deficiency.
To preach the Great Dharma to those of small capacity is called "excess"; to preach the Small Dharma to those of great capacity is called "deficiency.
Those who deeply love the Dharma are individuals of small capacity who nonetheless have a profound affinity for the Great Dharma.
Although he deeply loved the Great Dharma, his capacity was in fact small;
because he had not yet attained accord with the Great Dharma, [the Buddha] likewise did not speak much for him. △ Third, the conclusion.
Mañjuśrī, when this Dharma is about to perish in the final age of the future,

those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who accomplish this third practice of peace and happiness will not be disturbed or troubled when they preach this Dharma, and they will find virtuous companions in the study of the Dharma.

Together they shall read and recite this sutra; furthermore, a great assembly will come to hear and receive it. Having heard it, they will be able to uphold it; having upheld it, they will be able to recite it;

having recited it, they will be able to explain it; having explained it, they will be able to write it down, or cause others to write it, and they shall make offerings to the scroll, honoring, respecting, and praising it.
Regarding "there is accomplishment": this clarifies that which should not be done and that which should be done; this is called accomplishment. Regarding "attaining good companions and the like":
this refers to being able to attract superior persons to assemble. △ Second, the verse summary has two parts.
The first verse provides the explanation; the second verse provides the conclusion. Regarding the first two [verses], the first verse concerns what should not be done.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
If you wish to preach this sutra, you should abandon jealousy, anger, and pride, as well as deceitful, delusive, and false intentions.

You should constantly cultivate straightforward conduct, not look down upon others, nor engage in frivolous speculation regarding the Dharma. Do not cause others to doubt or regret by saying, "You shall not attain Buddhahood."

One who constantly cultivates straightforward conduct is able to settle the mind in the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Through the realm of true reality, the wisdom that contemplates it is brought forth;
cultivation arises entirely from nature, and practice arises entirely from principle. To be thus in every thought-moment is called "constantly cultivating straightforward conduct.
Not to despise others means not to slight or revile those of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*) who study the Buddha-dharma.
He is a practitioner of the Way. Furthermore, he does not engage in frivolous discourse regarding the Dharma;

that is, he is one who does not dispute or contend with those who engage in frivolous discourse regarding the various dharmas within the Tripitaka. He does not cause others to doubt or regret, nor does he disparage those who have attained through the Shared Teaching.
△ Second, the verse on what should be practiced.
These sons of the Buddha preach the Dharma; they are always gentle and capable of endurance, compassionate toward all, and never give rise to a mind of indolence.
The great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions practice the Way out of pity for sentient beings; you should give rise to a heart of reverence, for they are my great teachers.

Regarding all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, one should conceive of them as one’s unsurpassed father; one should shatter the mind of pride and preach the Dharma without obstruction, never giving rise to a mind of indolence.
This means that at all times, out of compassion for all beings, one should arouse great vigor.

If one cannot give rise to loving-kindness (*maitrī*) yet wishes to bestow happiness upon all, or cannot give rise to compassion (*karuṇā*) yet wishes to extract suffering from all, this is called indolence (*kausīdya*).
Regarding the teaching of the Dharma without obstruction by destroying the mind of pride (*māna*):
if one teaches the Great [Vehicle] to those of inferior capacity, there is an obstruction toward them and pride within oneself. If...
To preach the Lesser Vehicle to those of great capacity constitutes pride toward oneself and an obstacle toward others;
whereas to preach with equanimity, neither more nor less than what is required, breaks through arrogance and is free from obstacles. △ Second, the concluding verse.
The third dharma is thus. The wise person should protect it and practice with single-minded ease and joy, being honored by immeasurable multitudes.
IV. Showing the Practice of Ease and Joy through Vows. This has two parts: first, the prose; second, the verse. The first part has two sections:
first, the explicit explanation of the practice of ease and joy through vows; second, a further praise of the excellence of this sutra’s Dharma. The first section has three parts: first, the heading.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, in the future final age when the Dharma is about to perish, there will be those who uphold this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
Regarding the phrase "in the latter age," etc.: Generally speaking, the teaching of the Tathāgata flourishes when there is a receptive capacity (*indriya*) and declines when such capacity is absent.
In the time of the latter age, sentient beings have heavy afflictions and obstacles, and thus that capacity is lacking.
Consequently, the Tathāgata’s teachings are either withdrawn to the celestial realms or taken into the dragon palaces; this is what is called the extinction of the Dharma. △ Second, the explanation.
Commentary:
Among householders and renunciants, one gives rise to a mind of great loving-kindness; among those who are not bodhisattvas, one gives rise to a mind of great compassion.
Regarding the terms "householder" and "renunciant": "house" refers to the house of the triple world (*tridhātu*).

Those who have already resolved upon the provisional mind of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) but have not yet cultivated or realized its skillful means, and thus have not escaped the triple world, are called householders.
One who has already been able to cultivate and realize skillful means and has transcended the three realms is called a renunciant (*pravrajita*).

One who propagates the sutra, if they wish to abide in the practice of the vow of peaceful conduct (*sukha-vihāra*), should give rise to a heart of great compassion toward those among the two classes of people—laypeople and renunciants—and desire to bestow happiness upon them. As for those who are laypeople, even though they have already...
Having resolved upon the mind of skillful means, they are as yet unable to realize even the Lesser Vehicle, let alone the Greater Vehicle;

yet now, I also wish to grant them the bliss of the Buddha-way. As for those who have left the household life, although they have already transcended the realm of conditioned existence (*bhavāgra*),...
Yet the process of transformation and change still persists; although the views and afflictions have already been destroyed, ignorance remains entirely intact.
Now, I also wish to bestow upon them the bliss of the awakening-dharma of unsurpassed Bodhi and the bliss of the quiescent extinction of unsurpassed Nirvana.
Therefore, one should give rise to great compassion toward both of these types of people.
Those who are not Bodhisattvas are the ordinary beings of the six realms. Among Bodhisattvas, there are those of the Mahāyāna and the Hīnayāna.
Now, as for the ordinary beings of the six realms, since they are unable to give rise to the mind of ultimate truth, nor can they give rise to the mind of skillful means, they are entirely...
Within the three realms and six paths of existence, beings transmigrate and revolve; there is no distinction between great and small. Therefore, it is said that they are not bodhisattvas.
Those who, at the initial stage of their resolve, propagate this sutra should give rise to a heart of great compassion toward these people who bear this single title.
Yet I wish to uproot their suffering. Although they possess none of it at all, whether great or small, I do not merely wish to uproot the causes and effects of suffering within their own realm;
I also wish to uproot the causes and effects of suffering beyond that realm.
Therefore, it is said that one should give rise to a mind of great compassion.
One should reflect as follows: "Such a person has suffered a great loss.
This means: how can one give rise to a mind of great loving-kindness toward those among householders and renunciants who are not bodhisattvas?
Among human beings, because they give rise to the mind of great compassion, it is said: "One should think thus: such a person has suffered a great loss.
By "such a person," one refers generally to those who have left the household life, those who remain in the household, and those who do not possess the three titles of a Bodhisattva.
Regarding the "great loss": if those of the two classes—those in the household and those who have left the household—[the former] first...
If one cannot give rise to the mind of true reality, one will be unable to attain realization of true reality; this is a failure.
To take the expedient mind that has been aroused and the expedient realization attained as being real is a great error.
If those who are not bodhisattvas are unable to arouse the mind of true reality, they must rely upon it [the expedient] to practice.

To claim realization under such circumstances is a failure; it further prevents one from giving rise to the mind of skillful means (*upāya-citta*) and practicing accordingly, which constitutes a great loss.

The Tathāgata’s skillful means consist in preaching the Dharma according to what is appropriate; yet [such a person] neither hears, nor knows, nor awakens to it, neither inquires, nor believes, nor understands it.
This passage clearly elucidates their great error. The intent is to ask: how can those who possess these three titles be so greatly mistaken?

Therefore, it says, "The Tathāgata’s skillful means," and so forth. This means that the three vehicles and five teachings spoken by the Tathāgata are indeed skillful means—the Dharma taught in accordance with what is appropriate for sentient beings—and yet those who are not Bodhisattvas do not [understand this].
They are able to give rise to the mind of skillful means; therefore, regarding these dharmas of skillful means, they neither hear them, nor know them, nor realize them.
This refers to those who, in relation to the Hīnayāna, do not hear, know, or realize [them].
If, in relation to the Mahāyāna, they are unable to give rise to the Great Mind, they likewise do not inquire. To speak for their sake when they have not inquired—this too [is a fault].

Because they cannot believe and accept it, they are unable to comprehend and understand it. This refers to those who, regarding the Great [Vehicle], neither inquire about it, nor believe in it, nor understand it.
Such individuals are not true Bodhisattvas; they possess nothing of either the Great or the Small [Vehicles]. Thus, they do not merely suffer loss, but suffer a great loss indeed.
As for those who bear the titles of both layperson and monastic, although they may have initiated expedient means and already realized expedient means—
Yet, not knowing that these skillful means are the Tathāgata’s teaching according to what is appropriate, they cling to them as being literal truth.
Consequently, regarding the Tathāgata’s teachings of skillful means according to what is appropriate, though they have heard them, they have not heard;

though they know them, they do not know; though they have awakened to them, they have not awakened. Even though one has already set forth and another has already attained realization, [they remain thus].
If one can give rise to the Great [Vehicle] and realize the Great, then regarding the Great Vehicle of the Tathāgata, one will neither question, disbelieve, nor fail to understand it.
These two classes of people—those known as householders and those who have left the home life—do not know the truth, yet they take skillful means to be the reality.
Thus, they do not merely suffer loss; they suffer a great loss indeed.
Although such persons may not inquire about it, nor believe or understand this sutra, when I attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
wherever they may be, I shall use my power of supernatural faculties and the power of wisdom to lead them so that they may abide within this Dharma.

This correctly clarifies the arising of his great heart of compassion. That is to say, although those three types of people neither inquire about, believe in, nor understand this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* of the Mahāyāna, when I attain bodhi, [I shall deliver them].

According to the specific stage in which they reside, I shall, by the power of my supernatural penetrations and wisdom, lead them to dwell securely within the Dharma of unsurpassed bodhi. "Stage" refers to the levels of spiritual attainment.
If they are householders who have already resolved upon skillful means, they reside within the stage of the *kalyāṇa-bhūmi* (the stage of virtue); and I, by means of my supernatural penetrations...
By the power of wisdom, I lead them from that stage of worthiness and establish them within the Dharma of Bodhi.
If there are those who have left the household life and have already realized skillful means, yet remain within the stages of the Lesser Sages, I shall,
by the power of my supernormal knowledges and wisdom, lead them from those stages of the Lesser Sages and establish them in Bodhi.
Within this Dharma, those who are not bodhisattvas lack it entirely, whether great or small; they remain within the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Yet, by the power of my supernatural penetrations and wisdom, I lead them from that very stage of ordinariness and establish them within the Dharma of Bodhi.
Once all have been led to abide within the Dharma of Bodhi, then there is...
What happiness would he not bestow? What suffering would he not eradicate? △ Third, the conclusion:

Mañjuśrī, if there are Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, accomplish this fourth dharma, they will be without fault when preaching this dharma, and they will always be [honored] by bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, [and upāsikās].
The laywoman Sē, kings, princes, ministers, and commoners, as well as brahmins and householders, made offerings to her, honoring, respecting, and praising her.
The devas dwelling in space also constantly attended upon her in order to hear the Dharma.
Whether she was in a village, a city, or a secluded forest, whenever anyone came wishing to challenge her with questions, the devas would constantly [protect her] day and night.
For the sake of the Dharma, they protect it, enabling those who hear it to all attain joy and remain free from fault.
Being able to abide in the peace and happiness of their vows, they give rise to great vows and generate compassion;
thus, they can enter the chamber of the Tathāgata and contemplate the emptiness of all phenomena according to whatever obstacles may exist.
"Affliction": because he cannot be moved by them himself, when he preaches the Dharma, there is no fault. This clarifies that he is without fault.
"Constantly for those below" clarifies that he is not only without fault, but moreover possesses attainment. "Bhikṣus and others" refers to the assembly of the Dharma;
"kings and others" refers to the worldly assembly. This clarifies that he is praised by people. "Space and below" clarifies his... [omitted].
They are protected by the various devas. As for "all attain joy," first, it is through the power of the devas' protection that they can cause the listeners to rejoice;
second, because the Bodhisattva answers their difficult questions solely from the perspective of the Mahāyāna, yet does not oppose their own inclinations, all thus attain joy.
Why is this? Because this sutra is protected by the spiritual power of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
That is to say, when this sutra is being preached, it is praised by people and guarded by devas. Therefore...
It is said: "This sutra is that which is protected by all Buddhas together.
Since the Buddhas collectively protect the sutra they propagate, those who propagate it are likewise protected by all Buddhas together.
If even the Buddhas protect it together, how could humans fail to praise it, or the heavens fail to guard it?
△ Second, a repeated praise for the superiority of this sutra’s Dharma, in two parts. First, the explanation by way of Dharma.
Mañjuśrī, in immeasurable lands, even the name of this Lotus Sūtra cannot be heard,
let alone being seen, received, upheld, read, or recited.
Regarding the phrase "in immeasurable lands," it means that forty years prior to the revelation and clarification of this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*,
not only could it not be seen or upheld in this Sahā world-system,
but even the name of it could not be heard in immeasurable lands— let alone being seen. How much less could it be attained?
Having received and upheld it, may I be able to read and recite it? Today, through this single revelation, I am finally able to know that this is the provisional and that this is the real;
I have heard the name of this principle of the non-duality of the provisional and the real, and having heard it, I have come to see it.
Having seen it, one is able to receive, uphold, read, and recite it. This explanation of the Dharma serves merely as the basis for the subsequent parable.
If, forty years ago, it had not been revealed and clarified, its name would not have been heard; thus, it served as the basis for the parable of not being given the jewel.
Today, having been revealed and clarified, one is finally able to see, receive, and uphold it; thus, it serves as the basis for the parable of being given the jewel.
△ Second, the explanation by means of two parables. First, the analogy of not giving the jewel; second, the analogy of actually giving the jewel. Regarding the first of these two: first, the parable.
"Mañjuśrī, it is as if a powerful Wheel-Turning Sage King, wishing to subdue various kingdoms through his majestic authority..."
Yet the various minor kings did not obey his commands. At that time, the Wheel-Turning King raised various armies and went forth to subdue them.
When the king saw the troops who had performed meritorious service in battle, he was immediately filled with great joy and bestowed rewards according to their merit, granting some land and houses.
Villages and cities; or he gives garments and ornaments for adorning the body;
or he gives various kinds of rare treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, coral, and amber; elephants, horses, carriages, and vehicles; slaves, servants, and subjects.
Yet, the bright pearl from within his topknot is the only thing he does not give. Why is this? Because this single pearl alone exists upon the crown of the king's head. If...
If he were to give it to him, the King and his retinue would surely be greatly astonished and amazed.

This is because, as mentioned above, if [the teaching] had not yet been revealed, its very name would not have been heard. Regarding the term "Powerful Wheel-turning King," this refers specifically to a Golden Wheel-turning King and not to the three preceding types;
therefore, he is called "Powerful. Only the passage below concerning the hair-tuft correctly clarifies that [the wheel] is not given.
"The jewel can be seen. Why is this? The following section explains the intention behind not giving it.
"Startled and amazed" means they were surprised that despite having only minor merit, he had no great achievements, yet he was immediately granted the jewel from within his topknot.
This was because [the Buddha] wished to protect his retinue from such astonishment; for this reason, he did not give it. Part Two: Synthesis.
Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata is also like this. By the power of meditative concentration and wisdom, he has attained the kingdom of Dharma and reigns over the three realms.
Yet, the various Māra kings refuse to submit. The Tathāgata’s noble and holy generals engage them in battle;
those who achieve merit therein also bring joy to his heart. Among the fourfold assembly, he preaches various sūtras for their sake, causing them—

Their hearts were filled with joy. He bestowed upon them the wealth of the dharmas: meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), liberation (*vimokṣa*), the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) and powers (*bala*).

Furthermore, he granted them the city of *nirvāṇa*, declaring that they had attained extinction (*parinirvāṇa*). He guided their minds, causing them all to rejoice; yet, he did not preach this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* for them.

He attains the land of Dharma and reigns as king over the three realms. This corresponds to the Universal Monarch (cakravartin) who, by means of his majestic power, seeks to subdue all other kingdoms.

Regarding the "land of Dharma" (*dharmarājya*): this is an instance where both the literal term and its metaphorical significance are presented together. The single character "Dharma" (*dharma*) refers to the teaching; the two characters "land" (*rājya*) are the metaphor.
Just as a Universal Monarch takes the four quarters as his kingdom, the Tathāgata takes all phenomena (*dharmas*) as his kingdom.
It is like the earth. Yet the various Māra kings refuse to submit and obey; this corresponds to the subordinate minor kings who do not follow their sovereign’s commands.
These "various Māras" are precisely the Four Māras. While the Tathāgata uses the Dharma to transform the Triple World, the Four Māras do not accept the Tathāgata’s transformation.
The noble sages and various generals fight together; this corresponds to mobilizing the army for a punitive expedition. "Noble" refers to the five [precepts].

The "stopping of the mind" refers to the seven types of noble persons, from the stage of the Worldly First Dharma up to the Sages, which includes the four types of noble ones from the Stream-enterer (Srotāpanna) up to the Arhat.
These noble persons begin by practicing the five methods of stopping the mind and ultimately sever the afflictions of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
all of this constitutes waging war against the four Māras. Those who achieve merit therein experience joy in their hearts, which corresponds to the aforementioned "victory in battle."
"Merit" refers to great joy. Regarding "those with merit," the noble ones (śaikṣas) possess the merit of subduing delusions, while the sages (aśaikṣas) possess the merit of severing delusions.
However, that these various generals—the noble ones and the sages—possess the merit of subduing and severing is all discussed merely in terms of their respective capacities.
In essence, the subsequent statement that he preached various sutras was spoken in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings.
Only after delivering these teachings did he achieve merit in the battle against Māra; and only after achieving such merit did he receive the field of the city of Nirvāṇa.

It is like a Wheel-Turning King who, seeing among his troops those capable of breaking through the enemy ranks and slaying their generals, first promises them a reward, saying: "Who can break [the array]?"
If an enemy is able to slay one of their generals, they should grant him a reward. When the troops hear this, they will courageously advance against the enemy and thereby achieve merit.
Once merit has been achieved, rewards shall be bestowed according to its degree, whether high or low.

Thus, when the worthy and sages exercise restraint and severance, they do so by relying solely on the specific circumstances; among the fourfold assembly, it is appropriate to bestow rewards upon them in accordance with their merit.
"Equal" refers to the various sūtras of the three vehicles. "Joy of mind" means causing one to attain the joy of Dharma-pleasure.
"Dhyāna" refers to the four dhyānas; "samādhi" refers to the eight samādhis; "liberation" refers to the eight liberations; "outflow-free" (anāsrava) refers to the three outflow-free states;
"faculties" (indriya) refers to the five faculties; "powers" (bala) refers to the five powers; and "all dharmas" refers to the remaining factors of the path. These constitute the Hīnayāna.

This is the cause. Furthermore, he teaches according to the capacities of beings; he expounds the factors of the path (mārga-aṅga) of the Hīnayāna, causing them to practice and engage in battle against Māra.
Moreover, that which he bestows as the city of Nirvāṇa is the fruit of the Hīnayāna.
This is precisely emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—nirvāṇa. It can prevent the errors of views and afflictions, and repel the enemy of the segmented realm;
therefore, it is called the City of Nirvāṇa. This is realized through cultivation; it is the reward for merit earned in the battle against Māra.
Furthermore, the worthy general receives his reward in the cause, while the holy general receives his reward in the fruit. Yet he does not...
While preaching this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, [the Buddha] combined all [his treasures] above, yet he alone did not give away the bright pearl from within his topknot.
In the preceding analogy, the reason for not giving it was explained; here, one should supplement this by explaining the reason why this sūtra was not preached.
It is said that these noble and holy generals possess only the capacity for the small vehicle (*hīnayāna*) and lack the capacity for the great vehicle (*mahāyāna*).

If one were to preach this sutra to them, even the great bodhisattvas would surely be astonished and wonder why, despite their possessing only the capacity for the small vehicle and lacking the capacity for the great vehicle, he should immediately preach this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* to them. This, then, constitutes the protection of the bodhisattvas.
Because of such astonishment and wonder, it is not explained. △ Second, the actual bestowal of the jewel analogy, in two parts. First, the parable:
"Mañjuśrī, it is like a wheel-turning king who, seeing among his troops those who have performed great service, feels profound joy in his heart."
This pearl, so difficult to believe in, has long resided within my topknot; I did not give it to others recklessly, yet now I give it to you.
This is a metaphor for how I have now revealed and clarified [the teaching] so that it may be received and upheld.

When it is said "now I give it," since there is already such great merit, the bestowal should likewise be grand; it cannot be merely a reward according to one's merit as before. Therefore, I give it from within my topknot.
It is a jewel. △ Second, the synthesis, which also has two parts. First, the synthesis of the great merit:
The Tathāgata is likewise thus; within the triple world, he is the Great Dharma King. He teaches and transforms all sentient beings through the Dharma.
When they behold the army of the noble ones battling against the demon of the five aggregates, the demon of afflictions, and the demon of death, he perceives their great merit.
Merit: extinguishing the three poisons, emerging from the three realms, and breaking the net of Māra. At that time, the Tathāgata likewise rejoiced greatly.

Regarding "teaching and transforming through the Dharma": while a Wheel-Turning King teaches and transforms the sentient beings of the desire realm solely by means of the ten wholesome dharmas, the Tathāgata teaches and transforms all sentient beings within the three realms by means of the Dharma of the Three Vehicles. He is able to...
To know suffering is to wage war against the Māra of the five aggregates (*skandhamāra*). To wish to sever the origin [of suffering] is to wage war against the Māra of afflictions (*kleśamāra*).
To wish to realize cessation is to wage war against the Māra of death (*mṛtyumāra*). To wish to cultivate the path is to wage war against the Māra of the devas (*devaputramāra*);
here, the Māra of the devas is simply not mentioned in brief. One who possesses great merit and achievement is one who has extinguished these three.
To emerge from the triple world and break the net of the four māras constitutes its great merit.
Having already severed suffering and its origin, and having already realized the path and its cessation, the capacity for the Lesser Vehicle (hīnayāna) is thus perfected.

Once the capacity for the Lesser Vehicle is perfected, it is a natural law that there subsequently arises a capacity for the Greater [Vehicle]. This capacity for the Greater [Vehicle] arises because it is triggered by the perfection of the Lesser.
Therefore, the very act of extinguishing the poison, exiting the realm, and breaking the net constitutes a great achievement.
Because of this merit of having a great capacity, the Tathāgata rejoices on their behalf. △ Second, the bestowing of the jewel.
This Lotus Sūtra can cause sentient beings to attain all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*). Throughout all worlds, it has been met with much enmity and is difficult to believe;
though previously unspoken, it is now being proclaimed.
This serves as proof of the excellence of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*. It possesses the three aspects of doctrine (*śāsana*), practice (*pratipatti*), and realization (*adhigama*);

all are one, and all are sublime. Although there are three textual divisions, there are also four meanings. From the beginning up to "all-knowledge" (*sarvajñatā*) constitutes the first [aspect], that of practice.

The two characters "sentient beings" (*sattva*) refer to those who practice; is this not the first [meaning], that of the person? Thus, the first section praises this sūtra by way of the unity of practice.
It is superior. When it speaks of "omniscience" (sarvajña), this does not refer to the omniscience of the Hīnayāna, but rather to the "all-aspect omniscience" (sarvākārajñatā) of the Mahāyāna.
Because all three types of knowledge are one essence within all-aspect omniscience, it mentions only "all" for the sake of brevity.
However, while all-aspect omniscience is the fruit, the cultivation of this sutra is the cause. Regarding the cultivation of this sutra—
Because one can thereby realize the fruit of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), this practice is both singular and sublime.
Regarding the phrase "all worlds" and so forth: although this sutra possesses such wondrous efficacy, the world at large is full of enmity and difficult to inspire with faith.
Because it is so difficult to inspire faith, I did not reveal its teaching for forty years prior.
It is only until this very day that it is finally being spoken. As for those with much resentment: when he was about to speak [the Lotus Sūtra], five thousand people withdrew;
these were precisely those who harbored resentment. Therefore, what was said above—that "this sūtra has many resentful and jealous ones even while the Tathāgata is present"—refers to this.
As for its being difficult to believe: when the Dharma was preached once, only those of the highest faculties were able to comprehend it.
Though [some] have awakened, those of middling and inferior capacities remain deluded; is this not indeed difficult to believe?
Mañjuśrī, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the foremost teaching of all Tathāgatas among all their teachings.
It is the most profound and is bestowed at the very end, just as that powerful king, having long guarded the bright jewel, now finally grants it to him.

First, regarding the "Exegesis of the Teachings" (Jiao-yi), there is one section praising the excellence of this sutra: first, the direct elucidation; second, the citation of the analogy beginning with "Just as that... and so forth.

The "various teachings" mentioned at the outset refer to what has already been taught, what is being taught now, and what will be taught hereafter. Regarding the statement that this is "most profound":
among the various teachings, there are distinctions such as the Great and Small Vehicles, the partial and the complete, the provisional and the real, and the coarse and the subtle;

therefore, some may be said to be shallow rather than profound. However, in the present sutra, there is nothing small that is not great, and nothing coarse that is not subtle; therefore, it is called profound. Furthermore,
That which is small is itself the great; outside of the great, there is no further smallness. This extends even to the point that what is coarse is itself the sublime;
outside of the sublime, there is no further coarseness. Therefore, it is not merely profound, but exceedingly profound. Furthermore, since the small is the great, the small is not [merely] small;
and so on, until since the coarse is the sublime, the coarse is not [merely] coarse. This is, then, the ultimate non-...
The small is not the great; it is neither partial nor perfect, neither provisional nor real, and neither coarse nor subtle.
Therefore, it is not merely profound, but exceedingly profound. Since it is the most exceedingly profound among all teachings, its doctrine is both singular and wondrous.
Mañjuśrī, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the secret treasury of all the Tathāgatas; it stands supreme among all sūtras.
Having been guarded throughout the long night and not recklessly proclaimed, only today do I now bestow it upon you and the others.
And he expounded it.
Third, unifying the principle as one, he praised the excellence of this sutra. Regarding the "Secret Treasury":
that which had never existed before for forty years is called "secret" (*mi*). That which cannot be fathomed by those of the three vehicles or the nine realms is called "mysterious" (*mi*). Third.
It contains all thousands of dharmas in their entirety; therefore, it is called a "treasury" (garbha).
This secret treasury stands above all the sūtras of the Three Vehicles, for its principle is singular and sublime. As for the phrase "guarded throughout the long night":
Forty years ago, because the obstacles of sentient beings had not yet been removed and their spiritual faculties had not yet been stirred, they remained entirely within the darkness of ignorance;
thus, the Tathāgata manifested himself in accordance with human laws and said that he would protect this sutra throughout the long night.
Today, as the faculties of sentient beings have been activated and their obstacles removed, I shall now propagate and expound it.
Because this sutra is supreme in its excellence and its practice is supreme in its excellence, it is met with much resentment and is difficult to believe; therefore, I did not speak of it previously.
Because the teaching of this sutra is supreme in its excellence and profound among all teachings, and its principle is supreme in its excellence, standing above all other sutras.
Therefore, throughout the long night, it has been guarded and not recklessly proclaimed. Yet, that which is manifested in the introductory section consists solely of these four ones;
that which is revealed in the main exposition consists solely of these four ones;
and that which is propagated and protected in the present day consists solely of these four ones. Thus, until the conclusion of the dissemination, it returns once more to these four ones.

This is to manifest the such-like excellence of this sutra. Had it not been revealed forty years ago, even its name would not have been heard, just as the wheel-turning king did not give away his jewel. Only from this day forth [is it revealed].

I shall now expound it for you all. This is precisely what is being revealed today, so that you may be able to see, receive, and uphold it—just as a wheel-turning monarch possesses his precious jewel.
△ Second, the verses in praise have two parts. First, the verses praising the explicit clarification of the vow.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Always practicing patience and compassion for all beings, one is then able to expound the sutras praised by the Buddha. In the future, during the final age..."
Those who uphold this sutra—whether householders or renunciants, and whether they are bodhisattvas or not—should give rise to compassion for them.

If such people do not hear or believe in this sutra, it will be a great loss for them. Once I have attained the Way of the Buddha, I shall employ various skillful means to preach this Dharma for their sake.
Causing them to abide therein means that those who constantly practice patience are gentle, kind, and compliant, remaining unmoved by obstacles or afflictions.
Having compassion for all means exercising great loving-kindness and compassion, desiring to bestow happiness upon all sentient beings and desiring to uproot all [suffering].
It is the suffering of sentient beings. Regarding the sūtra praised by the Buddha: this sūtra is that which is collectively extolled by all Buddhas.
How do they extol it? It is as stated above: this sūtra can cause sentient beings to attain all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
To practice this is sublime; among all that is taught in this sutra, this is the foremost teaching, and thus it is sublime.
This sutra is the secret treasury, and its principle is sublime. This is the praise.

Those with the initial resolve must necessarily be gentle, kind, and compliant, always practicing patience, exercising great compassion, and feeling pity for all beings, fully endowed with loving-kindness and compassion.
It is precisely because one is able to expound this sūtra praised by the Buddha in the future final age that this is established as a verse of summary;
the subsequent section beginning with "in the future final age" is a verse of detailed explanation. This means that having already felt compassion for all beings, one is thus able to expound it.
Therefore, in the future final age, those who wish to expound and uphold this sutra must give rise to vows of compassion.
But where should these be generated? Hence it is said: "within the household life, the monastic life," and so forth.
By means of various skillful means—that is, through the power of supernatural faculties (*ṛddhi*) and the power of wisdom—these are inconceivable skillful means—causing others to abide therein.
That is, wherever they may be, he leads them so that they may abide within this Dharma. △ Second, the verse on the repeated praise of the excellence of the Dharma has two parts.
First, the general verse on the analogies of not giving the jewel and giving the jewel.
It is, for example, like a powerful wheel-turning monarch who, when his soldiers have performed meritorious service in battle, bestows various rewards: elephants, horses, and chariots;
ornaments for adorning the body; as well as fields, houses, villages, towns, and cities; or he may grant them clothing and various kinds of rare jewels.

He joyfully bestows servants, wealth, and goods. If there is one who is brave and robust, capable of performing difficult tasks, the king unties the bright pearl from within his topknot and grants it to him.
△ Second, the summary verse combining the analogies of not giving the jewel and giving the jewel. First, the general explanation:
The Tathāgata is likewise; he is the King of all dharmas, possessing the great power of patience and the precious treasury of wisdom, and with great compassion...
Transforming the world in accordance with the Dharma—this "great power" is precisely the donning of the robe of patience (*kṣānti*).

Being able to abide in the ground of patience, one endures external obstacles from conditions and endures internal afflictions of the three delusions; this is what is called the great power of patience. Wisdom.

The "Treasury of Wisdom" refers to the seat of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*). The two characters for "wisdom" (*prajñā*) signify the Dharma, while the two characters for "treasury" (*kośa*) serve as a metaphor.
Thus, the Tathāgata is able to contemplate all phenomena with subtle and wondrous wisdom, seeing them all as entirely empty and quiescent.
This emptiness, however, is the true emptiness (śūnyatā), wherein the entire body is fully endowed with all phenomena (dharmas).
Furthermore, all these phenomena that are so endowed are themselves entirely the true emptiness. To illustrate this by means of a metaphor:
it is like a treasure trove that contains all manner of things, yet everything contained therein is exclusively treasure. Thus, the one of great compassion is precisely the entry into compassion.

This is the chamber. Because the Tathāgata is able, through unconditioned great kindness and great compassion, to universally bestow happiness upon all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm and universally uproot the suffering of all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm, it is called "Great Kindness and Compassion.
This is precisely what constitutes the Tathāgata as the Tathāgata; there is nothing else whatsoever. It is solely by means of these three tracks that one attains the state of being a [Tathāgata].

The Tathāgata. One who transforms the world according to the Dharma does so by using the threefold path of the Dharma realized by oneself to transform sentient beings, and also causes them to practice these same threefold paths of the Dharma.

Furthermore, the reason the Tathāgata is called "Tathāgata" is because he was able to cultivate the threefold path during the causal stage and was able to realize the threefold path at the stage of fruition.
The "tracks" (mārga). This is because, subsequent to the fruit, one is able to give rise to the three tracks. Herein, the three tracks are elucidated;
the statement that one "transforms the world according to the Dharma" refers precisely to the three tracks that arise subsequent to the fruit.

However, since these three tracks subsequent to the fruit arise entirely through cultivation and realization, practicing these three tracks is itself the accomplishment of the sublime essence of Prajñā.
To realize these three modes is to manifest the wondrous essence of the Dharmakāya;
to give rise to these three modes is to activate the wondrous function of liberation. Thus, when practicing these three modes, the entire true nature is perfected as contemplation;
when realizing these three modes, the entire contemplation is perfected as the true nature.
Regarding the nature: when these three tracks (trikāya) arise, they are entirely the manifestation and realization of true nature;
they are neither one, two, nor three, yet they appear as one, two, and three. They do not arise through cultivation or realization, yet they arise as cultivation and realization.
This is what is called the inconceivable three tracks of the Tathāgata. One who transforms the world according to the Dharma employs the function of these three tracks to bring about transformation.
Sentient beings may also be enabled to cultivate this, realize this, and further give rise to this. △ Second, the actual verse, which has two parts.
First, the verse on not giving the jewel.
Seeing all people undergoing various sufferings and afflictions, desiring liberation, and battling against the various māras, he preaches diverse dharmas for the sake of these sentient beings;
through great skillful means, he expounds these various sūtras.

Regarding the phrase "experiencing various sufferings and afflictions," once one has experienced these various sufferings and afflictions, one then recognizes suffering (*duḥkha*) and desires to sever its origin (*samudaya*).
Therefore, desiring to seek liberation through cessation (*nirodha*), one should engage in battle with Māra and cultivate the Path (*mārga*).

Furthermore, the phrase "seeing all things as equal" indicates that the Tathāgata is able to discern the capacities of sentient beings; this "seeing" refers to the skillful means (*upāya*) for transforming others.
"Wisdom" refers to illuminating and seeing. This constitutes the following line, which clarifies that the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma according to the capacities of sentient beings.
△ Second, the verse combines the original [mirror] with the pearl.
Having known the sentient beings and gained their capacity, I finally preach this Lotus Sūtra for them, like a king who unties his topknot to give away the bright jewel.
This sūtra is the most honored, the supreme among all sūtras; I have constantly guarded it and did not reveal it recklessly.
Now is precisely the time. I shall speak for your sake.
Those who attain their respective powers are the persons of the Three Vehicles, each attaining their own power. The Śrāvaka knows suffering and abandons its origin;

he cultivates the path and realizes cessation, thereby attaining the power of the Four Noble Truths. The Pratyekabuddha contemplates the process of arising in forward order and contemplates it in reverse order.
Through the power of the causes and conditions for cessation, the Bodhisattva is then able to eliminate the six obscurations and attain the power of the six perfections.

Regarding those for whom he preaches the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and other such sutras: having attained this power, those of small capacity have already achieved their goal, and before long, the capacity for the Great Vehicle will arise. Therefore, he preaches the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* for them, revealing their provisional [means] and...
This reveals the reality. To illustrate this by means of a metaphor: it is like a Wheel-Turning King who unties the great bright pearl from within his topknot and bestows it upon his generals.
The pearl was previously within the topknot and thus not seen; once the topknot is untied, the pearl is immediately visible.
Likewise, reality was previously concealed by skillful means and thus not manifest; now that those means are opened, reality is revealed.
It is just like untying a topknot to reveal the jewel. This passage below is a further exclamation. Regarding "not teaching falsely" and so forth:
forty years ago, I did not teach falsely because the capacity of the listeners was not yet mature and the time had not arrived;
therefore, I did not open the gate of skillful means nor reveal the true aspect. Now that their capacities are matured, it is precisely that time. Therefore, for this reason—
"You all should speak it," [the Buddha said], "in order to reveal its provisional means and to manifest its ultimate reality.

Furthermore, once they understood these two lines—which correspond to the second section of the verse—they were filled with great joy in their hearts. At the end, the subsequent lines correspond to the bestowal of the jewel;
this is also a direct praise of the excellence of the sutra. The first two lines correspond to the first section on practice, namely: "This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*... up to "...arrived here."

I shall now explain this. The two lines beginning with "As for the King" constitute the first [part], the verse on the unity of teaching (*śāsana-eka*), which refers to how this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* has finally been bestowed upon him until now.

The six lines following this [in the verse] constitute the second, the verse on the unity of principle (*tattva-eka*), which refers to how this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* has been expounded and spread until now.
Thus far, within the Tathāgata’s response and instruction, there are three parts; the first is the general response, namely—

If one wishes to preach this sutra, one should abide in four dharmas. Next, these four are specifically shown, each consisting of both prose and verse, thereby concluding the exposition of the four methods of peaceful conduct for body, speech, mind, and vows.

△ Third, the Conclusion on Benefits, Part Three: First, the Exhortation to Practice.
After my parinirvāṇa, those who seek the Buddha-way and desire to attain peace and security by expounding this sutra should draw near to these four dharmas.
△ Second, the demonstration of the benefits. This consists of fifteen and a half four-character verses and six five-character verses, divided into two parts:

first, clarifying the purity of the three types of retribution; second, clarifying the Buddha-activities within dreams. The first part has three sections; the first clarifies the purity of the present retribution.
Those who read this sutra will always be free from sorrow and affliction, and likewise free from illness and pain; their complexions will be bright and pure.

That they are able to read, recite, explain, and so forth is due to the power of the Lotus Sutra. They personally attain a mind free from sorrow and affliction because what it elucidates is the knowledge and vision of the Buddha alone.
Furthermore, the four great elements naturally become harmonious and they remain free from disease, because—

What has been realized is merely the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena. Since there is neither sorrow nor affliction, nor sickness or pain, one naturally attains a complexion that is fresh and bright.
△ Second, clarifying the purity of the retribution of birth.

They will not be born into poverty, nor into lowly or ugly circumstances; all sentient beings will delight in seeing them, as if yearning for sages and saints, and divine youths will serve as their attendants.
The Heavenly Boy serves as an attendant because this sutra is protected by all the devas.
Since one is now able to read and recite this sutra, among the fruits of retribution in this life, the devas—by means of the protection they extend to the sutra—will in turn protect the person.
Thus, they cause the boy to serve as an attendant. △ Third, the purity of the subsequent retribution.
Swords and staves cannot be brought against them; poisons cannot harm them. If someone reviles them with evil words, their mouth shall be closed.
They wander without fear, like the lion king; the radiance of their wisdom shines like the light of the sun.

Regarding "swords, staves, and so forth": since one is currently able to abide in the four practices of peaceful dwelling while reading this sutra, the inner mind naturally becomes gentle, compliant, and free from anger. Because there is no anger within, there is likewise no obstruction without;
therefore, even if obstacles such as swords and staves should arise during future retributions, they will be unable to inflict harm. Wisdom.

"Regarding 'the light of wisdom shines like the sun': all wisdom illuminates everything without exception, and is able to shatter ignorance and afflictions, just as the sun is able to illuminate all things and dispel every darkness. Part Two: Clarifying the Buddha-Activities in Dreams.
This has two sections: first, dreaming of the Dharma-transformation during the five periods; second, dreaming of the accomplishment of the Way through the eight phases.

The reason for having these dreams of the five periods and eight signs is that by contemplating the present, one is able to abide in the practice of peaceful conduct (*sukhavihāra*) and propagate this sutra;
thus, within a future retribution, one will certainly attain Buddhahood. Therefore, it was said previously:
"O Bhaiṣajyarāja, if someone asks, 'What kind of sentient beings shall attain Buddhahood in a future age? you should point them out."
These people will certainly attain Buddhahood in a future age. When they become Buddhas, they will inevitably preach in five periods and manifest the eight signs of enlightenment.
Therefore, although they have not yet actually attained such realization in the present, these omens first appeared within their dreams;
hence, there are these Buddha-activities within the dream. First, there are five [dreams]; first, he dreamed of flowers.
During the time of the ritual,
if within a dream one sees only auspicious things— seeing all the Tathāgatas seated upon lion thrones, surrounded by assemblies of bhikṣus who preach the Dharma;
and seeing nāgas, devas, asuras, and others, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, with palms joined in reverence.
He sees his own body there as it preaches the Dharma.

The first two phrases provide a general explanation. The subsequent statement, "seeing all Tathāgatas seated upon lion thrones," refers to the manifestation of the Tathāgata’s *sāmbhogakāya* (Śākyamuni) in a body one thousand *zhang* tall during the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, surrounded by the multitude of bhikṣus.
He preaches the Dharma. At that time, the Mahāsattvas of the Dharma-body, numbering forty-one stages, surround him like clouds enveloping the moon.

As for the preaching of the Dharma: it is the teaching of the Perfect Vehicle (Canyoujiao) for those with real capacity (shiji), and the teaching of the Distinct Vehicle (Biejiao) for those with provisional capacity (quanji).
Furthermore, seeing dragon spirits and others signifies that their roots from past lives have matured; these are the eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas.

As for seeing one's own body preaching the Dharma, this refers to those such as the four great bodhisattvas who, empowered by the Tathāgata, expound upon the merits of the forty stages. △ Second, dreaming of hearing the Āgamas.
Furthermore, he saw various Buddhas, their bodies golden in color, emitting immeasurable light that illuminated all things, and preaching all dharmas with the voice of Brahmā.
His physical appearance was golden; this refers to the thirty-two marks of the Elder Bhikṣu. He expounded all dharmas;

this refers to the exposition of the Four Āgamas, as well as the exposition of the Four Truths of Arising and Cessation, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, and the practice of the Six Pāramitās.
It also refers to the exposition of the Dharmas of the Tripitaka of the Hīnayāna—namely, morality, concentration, and wisdom. △ Third, the Dream.

When he saw the Vaipulya [sūtras], the Buddha was preaching the unsurpassed Dharma for the fourfold assembly; seeing himself situated therein, he joined his palms in praise of the Buddha and rejoiced upon hearing the Dharma.

He made offerings and attained dhāraṇīs, realizing the wisdom of non-retrogression. The Buddha, knowing his mind had deeply entered the path of the Buddhas, immediately bestowed upon him the prediction that he would attain supreme perfect enlightenment: "O son of good family, in a future age, you shall attain immeasurable wisdom."
The Great Way of the Buddha’s land is majestic, pure, and vast beyond compare. There are also the fourfold assemblies, who join their palms to listen to the Dharma.
Regarding the "bestowal of predictions," this refers to the bestowal of predictions upon the great bodhisattvas during the assembly of the Vaipulya sutras;
the phrase "you, sons of good family" and so forth is the very wording used for such predictions. △ Fourth, the dream of seeing the Prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, one sees oneself in mountain forests practicing wholesome dharmas.

To practice wholesome dharmas means that from the initial five aggregates up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), one cycles through the eighty-one categories of the Dharma, observing and illuminating each with the wondrous wisdom of *prajñā*. Therefore, it is said that one practices wholesome dharmas.
This is the Dharma. △ Fifth, regarding the time of dreaming of the Lotus Sutra:
one realizes the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena and enters deeply into meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), beholding the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Because of hearing the Lotus Sutra, one is thus able to realize the true reality of all dharmas and enter into profound meditative concentration and great samādhi.
In the middle [section], he beholds the Buddhas of the ten directions. △ Second, the dream of attaining enlightenment through the eight phases.

The previous five periods involved hearing the Buddha’s teachings within a dream and personally participating in those assemblies; now, regarding the eight phases, it involves dreaming that one’s own self attains enlightenment.
This is divided into two parts. First, a general explanation of the eight phases.
The bodies of all Buddhas are golden in color, adorned with the marks of a hundred blessings. To hear the Dharma and explain it for others, one constantly has such auspicious dreams.
This refers to the person who expounds the Dharma; they constantly possess this golden body, which is an auspicious dream of meritorious marks.
A golden body is precisely a body accomplished through the eight signs. Therefore, this is a general explanation. △ Second.
He further displays eight aspects:
moreover, he dreams that he becomes a king, yet abandons his palace, retinue, and the five exquisite sensual pleasures to proceed to the site of enlightenment;
there, beneath the Bodhi tree, he sits upon the lion throne and, having sought the Way for seven days, attains the wisdom of all Buddhas.
Having attained the Unsurpassed Way, he shall arise and turn the wheel of Dharma, preaching the Dharma for the fourfold assembly throughout thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas.
He will proclaim the wondrous Dharma free from outflows, delivering immeasurable sentient beings, before finally entering nirvāṇa, like a lamp extinguished when its oil is spent.
"Dreaming of becoming a king" refers specifically to dreaming of becoming a *cakravartin* (wheel-turning sage-king).

Having become a king, one must necessarily descend into the royal palace, dwell in the womb, and emerge from the womb before reigning as a king; therefore, know that this single phrase encompasses these three stages.
The three phrases following "leaving the palace" constitute the fourth stage, the mark of renunciation (*pravrajyā*). [The remainder concerns] dwelling at Bodhi...

The next line describes the sixth characteristic of attaining the Way of Buddhahood. Since one must necessarily subdue the Māras before attaining the Way, the mention of "attaining the Way" encompasses the fifth characteristic, which is the subduing of the Māras. Regarding the statement that he sought the Way for more than seven days:
Śākyamuni left home at the age of nineteen and attained the Way at thirty; thus, he sought the Way for over ten years.
The present mention of "seven days" is due to the varying speed with which the spiritual capacity (*indriya*) ripens.

The passage from "accomplishing the unsurpassed way" down to "one line and a half" represents the phase of turning the wheel of Dharma; the subsequent two lines represent the phase of entering *nirvāṇa*.
Smoke and the lamp are but a single entity; they cannot be analyzed as separate factors of stimulus and response. If one says, "when the fuel is exhausted, the lamp..."
It may be said that they "cease. Now, we must explain this by focusing solely on the aspect of the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

Furthermore, if one focuses solely on the aspect of the response-body, since it is said that "the smoke has ended" and also that "the lamp has been extinguished," this is because the Tathāgata’s body possesses two types of responses—the superior and the inferior.

Now, those with small capacities lack [the superior response], so the inferior response is withdrawn and returns to the fundamental Dharma-body, like the smoke ending. Those with great capacities lack...

The superior response is withdrawn and returns to the fundamental Dharma-body, like the extinguishing of a lamp. The above concludes the first section on exhorting practice and the second section on demonstrating the benefits.
△ Third, the general conclusion.
If, in a future evil age, one should preach this foremost Dharma, that person shall obtain great benefit, including all the aforementioned merits.
What is called "obtaining great benefit" refers precisely to the ability to attain the great benefits of the threefold purity of retribution, such as the Buddha-activities within dreams and so forth.
The Trace Gate is concluded. The commentary on the "Chapter on Peaceful Practices" ends here.
The Fifteenth Chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, "The Emergence from the Earth.
Regarding the origin of this chapter, it is entirely elucidated within this single scripture;

it does not go beyond the traces of the Tathāgata’s manifestation of transformation after attaining the fruit—specifically his recent appearance near the city—and the basis for his long-term realization of the duration of his lifespan. Such are these traces.
This consists of two sections. For forty years, this has not been clarified; it is the peerless proclamation that transcends all other sutras.
Only today, at the Great Assembly on Mount Ling, have the faculties of sentient beings matured and the time for its revelation arrived.
Therefore, within the preceding fourteen chapters, the Tathāgata has elucidated his fundamental intent for appearing in the world: the One Great Matter.
The causal conditions for this [teaching] involve opening up the three [vehicles] to reveal the one, and opening up the provisional to reveal the real;

this is called the "Trace Gate" (Jikimon). Once the Trace Gate is concluded, it naturally becomes necessary to open up the trace to reveal the fundamental, and to open up the near to reveal the distant;
thus there are the subsequent fourteen chapters, which are called the "Fundamental Gate" (Honmon). Within this Fundamental Gate—
In the middle [section], following the precedent of the Trace Gate (*jijimon*), there are likewise the three divisions of introduction, main body, and dissemination.

Now, first, as for the Bodhisattvas from the lower direction who emerge from the earth, manifesting various signs, those who were in doubt raised their doubts and those who had questions asked their questions;
this is the introductory section of the Origin Gate (*honmon*). Next, the Tathāgata briefly opens up the near [period] and briefly reveals the distant [period]. And...
Maitreya and the other Bodhisattvas each gave rise to doubts and were shaken in their attachments;
yet the Tathāgata extensively revealed the traces of his recent sojourn at the city of Gayā and fully manifested the basis of his vast and long-lasting lifespan,

so that they might all sever their doubts regarding the near and give birth to faith in the far-reaching, receive the prediction of the Dharma-body, and attain the benefit of increasing the Path— this is the original [text].
The first part constitutes the "Correct Division" (Zhengshengfen) of the Sutra. What follows is the "Elucidation":

there is the encouragement and entrustment regarding the four levels of faith during the present age, and the five grades of practice after the extinction [of the Buddha], which constitutes the "Circulation Division" (Liutongfen) of the "Root Chapter" (Benmen).
Thus, one should know that because the intention here is to initiate the discourse on the long-lasting lifespan, there is this passage concerning those who have emerged from the earth. It says:

As for those who emerged from the earth: these were bodhisattvas from the lower realms who, upon hearing the Tathāgata’s summons, emerged from the places where the earth had split open within this Sahā world-system.

The reason they emerged was precisely to initiate the long-standing foundation of the Tathāgata; for it was based upon that foundation established by the Tathāgata throughout kalpas of the distant past.

He had already realized unsurpassed bodhi long ago; yet, desiring to transform and guide sentient beings, he manifested traces from his original source, appearing to be born where he was not actually born.
He displayed his descent into a royal palace and his renunciation of the world. Not far from Gayā, beneath the Bodhi tree, he attained equal and perfect enlightenment.
This is merely the Buddha of the Tripiṭaka. Had this not been revealed and clarified for us, [the truth would remain hidden].
How could all sentient beings know that there are Buddhas for whom celestial robes serve as seats, Buddhas for whom precious flowers serve as seats, or Buddhas for whom empty space serves as a seat?

Yet, were it not for this emergence from the earth to act as the catalyst, how could their ancient, fundamental reality ever be made manifest? Why did they emerge? It was so that they might reveal the Tathāgata.
This is the fundamental source of all that has lasted long. For the Bodhisattvas who emerged from the earth are the disciples, while the Tathāgata is the Teacher;

the Bodhisattvas who emerged from the earth are those at the stage of cause, while the Tathāgata is the person of fruition. As it is said: "If you wish to know the teacher, you should observe the disciple.
Since the virtue of the disciple at the causal stage is already so profound and their rank so exalted, [how much more so is the case for the Teacher].
Since [the assembly] is so exalted, it goes without saying that their teacher is a realized person (*arhat*);
this is precisely because the cause reveals the fruit, and the disciples reveal the teacher.

Therefore, the Bodhisattvas emerging from the earth are presented as the introductory catalyst, which naturally manifests that the Tathāgata has long ago realized the primordial foundation of his vast and eternal lifespan.
Also. △ Second, the opening of the near to reveal the distant. This has three parts: First, the Introduction;
second, the Main Body, beginning from "At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva: 'Excellent, excellent... and below;

third, the section within the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merit" (Punyarāśi-parivarta), beginning from "At that time, the Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva... and continuing until the end of the sutra.

The section on the dissemination of the teaching (*pravartana-bhāga*) concludes with three parts. First is the sequence of manifesting signs, similar to the manifestation of auspicious omens in the "Trace Gate" (*jia-men*).
Second is the sequence of the inquiry by Maitreya Bodhisattva and the eight thousand others, similar to the doubts expressed in the "Trace Gate.
Third is the sequence of the dialogue beginning from "At that time, the emanations of Śākyamuni," similar to the dialogue in the "Trace Gate."

Since the Fundamental Gate (Benmen) lacks a beginning to the sutra, it has no general introduction (tongxu). Furthermore, regarding the specific introduction (biexu), there is no assembly of the multitude;

this is because the assembly of the specific introduction is identical to the "those who heard together" (tongwen) of the general introduction. As for the remaining three introductions, each is exactly like those in the Trace Gate (Jimen).
In the Trace Gate, there are the manifestation of auspicious signs, the arising of doubt, and the exchange of questions and answers to serve as the catalyst for the teaching. Thus, the Tathāgata...
He immediately opened up the three provisional means to reveal the one true reality.

Now, since this introductory section of the "Root Chapter" likewise possesses such an occasion for its commencement, he accordingly opens up the near traces to reveal the distant source. This initial section consists of eight parts; first is the request made by the bodhisattvas.
At that time, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who had come from other lands, numbering more than eight times the sands of the Ganges River,
rose within the great assembly, joined their palms in homage, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if you would permit us, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,
to remain in this Sahā world and apply ourselves with diligent vigor to protect, uphold, read, recite, copy, and make offerings [to the teachings]."
This sutra shall be extensively expounded in this land. Bodhisattvas from other directions shall request those who propagate the sutra.
Through hearing the section on the Trace Gate within the circulation [of the teaching], one realizes that the Tathāgata has revealed the supremacy of the person and the excellence of the Dharma;
by practicing the three modes and four conducts, if one propagates and circulates them, one will be able to attain the purity of the three rewards.
Furthermore, he was able to see within his dreams the Dharma-transformations of the five periods and the accomplishment of the eightfold path to enlightenment.
Through such various kinds of supreme and wondrous benefits, that bodhisattva rejoiced in these advantages;

therefore, he prostrated and addressed the Buddha, desiring to propagate this sutra in this Sahā world just as the twenty thousand bodhisattvas did in the "Chapter on Upholding. △ Second, the Tathāgata’s refusal.
2. Summoning from Another Realm.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas: "Stop, sons of good family! There is no need for you to protect and uphold this sutra."
The Tathāgata’s refusal has three intentions. First, these bodhisattvas originally came from other lands;
if he were to permit them to propagate the sutra in this land, who would then be there to teach and transform the sentient beings of those lands?
Therefore, he refuses them. Second, since they are bodhisattvas from other lands, they have a karmic affinity with the sentient beings of those lands. If...

These sentient beings have never established a karmic connection [with him]. Although he wishes to propagate this sutra and provide instruction in this land, he cannot avoid the fact that those who benefit will be few;
therefore, he restrains them. Thirdly, herein he intends to initiate the "Root Chapter" (Honmon).
If he did not first restrain the requests from other lands, by what means could he summon those from the lower regions so that they might emerge from the earth? Since...
If they do not emerge, how could they be distanced from their origin and yet give rise [to this teaching]?
This means that if one wishes to clarify the origin, it is necessary to summon those from the lower regions; since one now wishes to summon those from the lower regions, the [Buddha] stops them.
As for the statement "you do not need to come," it means that if there were no one in this land, you would be permitted [to come]; however, as there are already people here, you are not needed.
...and so forth. △ Second, summoning those from the lower direction.
Why is this? In my Sahā world, there are already bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the sands of sixty thousand Ganges Rivers.
Each of these bodhisattvas has a retinue as numerous as the sands of sixty thousand Ganges Rivers. These individuals are able to...
"After my parinirvāṇa, you shall protect, uphold, read, recite, and extensively expound this sutra.
This clearly indicates that it is not necessary for you [the present assembly] to do so; rather, it is a summons to those from the lower regions.
There are three meanings to this summons of the lower regions: first, the bodhisattvas of the lower regions are those transformed by me, and are thus my disciples.
First, as disciples who propagate their master’s scriptures, it is only fitting that they do so; therefore, they were summoned.
Second, since these bodhisattvas already dwell constantly in the Sahā world, they naturally share a karmic affinity with the sentient beings of this land;

thus, those who propagate the teachings will surely be able to gain benefit, and for this reason, they were summoned. Third, by summoning them to come, [the assembly] was made to be... the old [ones].

Regarding the term "those who dwell": because they harbor doubts concerning the causal dharmas, they pose questions; thus, by following from these [questions], one may reveal the near and manifest the far, which is why they are summoned.
The phrase "sixty thousand Ganges-sands" cites their leaders; that each of these has sixty thousand Ganges-sands refers to their respective jurisdictions.
These various individuals collectively refer to both the leaders and those under their jurisdiction.
△ Third: The Emergence of the Bodhisattvas, Part Six. First, the account of their emergence.
At the time when the Buddha spoke these words, the earth throughout the three thousandfold world system of the Sahā universe split open.
From within it, immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas simultaneously surged forth.
"At this time" refers to the moment when the summoning from the lower direction has been completed, thereby bringing the prohibition of other directions to an end.
"The earth all quakes and splits" signifies that, regarding the former, the teaching of the Trace Gate (Jikimon) has concluded and those who hear it are able to shatter their ignorance;

regarding the latter, it signifies that the proximate Trace is opened from this point onward, and the remote Origin (Hon) is revealed from this point onward. △ Second, the clarification of the physical marks.
These bodhisattvas all have bodies of golden hue, possess the thirty-two marks, and emit immeasurable light.
Regarding the phrase "their bodies are all golden-hued" and so forth:

since these bodhisattvas were originally transformed by the Tathāgata, their virtues must necessarily be profound and their stations necessarily high; therefore, they are identical to the Tathāgata. And...
Their bodies are all golden in color. Their bodies possess the thirty-two marks of a great man, and each mark emits immeasurable radiance.
△ Third, [the description of] their dwelling place: they originally all resided beneath this Sahā world, dwelling in the void of this realm.
Regarding the phrase "previously all," it means that they now emerge from the earth.
Prior to their emergence, in what place did these bodhisattvas reside? Therefore, it is said: "Previously, they were all beneath this realm."
It abides in the midst of space. If it were below this realm, it would not be here; if it were in the space of a lower realm, it would not be there.

Since it is neither here nor there, it precisely manifests as eternally abiding within the inconceivable Middle Way, the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*). △ Fourth, the account of its origin.
These bodhisattvas, hearing the sound of the voice spoken by Śākyamuni Buddha, came forth from below.
They thought: "Since these bodhisattvas already dwell below in this world-system, for what reason do they emerge from the earth?
Thus it is said that they heard the sound of the Buddha’s speech and came forth from below. The "sound of the speech" refers to the call [that summoned them].
