It is sound. However, if one examines the intent behind its emergence, there are four aspects. First, having heard the Buddha’s summons, it naturally emerges.
Second, for the sake of propagating this sutra, it likewise emerges. Third, all devas and humans cling to the proximate traces of the Tathāgata;
now, wishing to shatter that attachment to the proximate, it therefore emerges. Fourth, one...
All the devas and humans did not know that the Tathāgata had a distant origin; now, wishing to give rise to faith in that distant beginning, they have come forth.
△ Fifth, the enumeration of the assembly.
Each and every bodhisattva was a leader at the head of a great assembly, each bringing with them a retinue of sixty thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* [sands of the Ganges] followers;
how much more so those who brought retinues of fifty thousand, forty thousand, thirty thousand, twenty thousand, or ten thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* followers.
How much more so for even as many as one *gaṅgā-vāluka* [sands of the Ganges], half a *gaṅgā-vāluka*, a quarter, or even a ten-millionth part of a hundred-thousand-billion-*nayuta*.
How much more so for a retinue of ten-million-billion-*nayuta* followers; how much more so for a retinue of hundreds-of-millions;
how much more so for ten-thousands, millions, or even ten-thousand; how much more so for one thousand, one hundred, or even...

This applies even to those with ten disciples, let alone those who lead four, five, three, two, or one disciple; and how much more so for those who dwell alone, delighting in the practice of seclusion.
Instances such as these are immeasurable and boundless, beyond what can be known through calculation or analogy.
"Each and every Bodhisattva" refers to the leaders of the aforementioned sixty thousand *Ganges*-sands of Bodhisattvas.
"Chanting and guiding" means opening the way and leading forth. To open and chant is to be able to preach the wondrous Dharma;
to guide is to be able to transform sentient beings. This passage mentions those leaders, numbering sixty thousand *Ganges*-sands, each taking [their followers].
Regarding "sixty thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* followers, let alone those who lead them":
this means that the leaders of those with sixty thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* followers already number sixty thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka*.
How much more so for those who lead fifty thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* followers; their number exceeds even that of those who lead sixty thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* followers.
As for "belonging to" (shǔ zhě), their number is even greater than the aforementioned, not limited merely to sixty thousand Ganges-sands.
In sum, among the disciples, each subsequent group is fewer than the preceding one, whereas for the Teacher, each subsequent group is greater than the preceding one.
Observe that the words "moreover" (kuàng) and "about to" (jiāng) in the text all emphasize the perspective of the Teacher's side; therefore—
The latter refers to those who are single individuals; this refers exclusively to the masters.
Because sixty thousand *Ganges-sands* [of followers] is appropriate for the equality between master and disciple, this is established here as the standard.

As for retinues of fewer than sixty thousand *Ganges-sands*, they are reduced to fifty thousand, forty thousand, and so on, down to a single person. As for leaders, from sixty thousand *Ganges-sands*...
Once the sand has been piled up, it increases to seventy thousand or eighty thousand, reaching a point that cannot be known even by calculation or analogy.
Such comparisons as these are intended to provide a comprehensive summary. △ Sixth, the discussion on making offerings.
These bodhisattvas, having emerged from the earth, each proceeded through the air to where the many-jeweled, wondrous stupa containing the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna and Śākyamuni Buddha was located.
Upon arrival, they bowed their heads at the feet of these two World-Honored Ones.

They also went before the Buddhas seated upon lion thrones beneath the various jeweled trees, prostrating themselves in worship, circumambulating them three times to the right, and joining their palms in reverent salutation.
Having praised them with various kinds of eulogies appropriate for bodhisattvas, they stood to one side,
joyfully gazing up at the two World-Honored Ones.
Gazing up at the Honored One of Two Worlds: although Śākyamuni had already expounded the Trace Gate, he had not yet expounded the Origin Gate;

now, wishing for Śākyamuni to further expound the Origin Gate, they gaze upon him. Although Many Treasures had already testified to the Truth of the Trace Gate, he had not yet testified to the Truth of the Origin Gate;
now, wishing for Many Treasures to further testify to the Origin Gate, they gaze upon him.
To look up to him. △ Fourth, the Tathāgata manifests supernatural powers.

From the moment these Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas first surged forth, they praised the Buddha with various kinds of Bodhisattva dharmas of praise for a period of time lasting fifty minor kalpas. At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha remained silent.
They sat down, and the fourfold assembly likewise remained silent for fifty intermediate kalpas.
Through the Buddha’s spiritual power, he caused the great multitude to perceive this duration as being like half a day.
At that time, through the Buddha’s spiritual power, the fourfold assembly also saw the bodhisattvas filling the empty space of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of lands.
When he spoke of fifty minor kalpas, he caused the assembly to perceive them as half a day; this was taking the long as short.
The Tathāgata sat in silence, thereby accepting their praise; the fourfold assembly likewise remained silent, thereby honoring his praise.
Next, through the Buddha’s supernatural power, the fourfold assembly saw bodhisattvas filling the voids of immeasurable lands;

this was the seeing of the narrow as vast. Since these bodhisattvas had emerged solely from the Sahā world-system, the fourfold assembly now beheld them pervading immeasurable hundreds, immeasurable thousands, immeasurable tens of thousands, and immeasurable billions of lands.

The earth is empty space; thus, that which is narrow is seen as vast. Now, the reason the Tathāgata manifests this power of supernatural penetration (*ṛddhi*)—causing the multitude to see what is long as short and what is narrow as vast—is because this serves as the introduction to the immeasurable span of his life.
Yet, the life-span of the Tathāgata is fundamentally neither long nor short.
It is neither long nor short, neither broad nor narrow. Those who perceive distinctions of length, shortness, breadth, and narrowness do so only through the emotional perceptions of sentient beings.

Now, if one causes them to see fifty kalpas of length as being but half a day of shortness, then those fifty kalpas of length will not be long; thus, length is not long, and that half-day of shortness is not short.

Yet, shortness is not shortness. By causing that which is the narrowness of this Sahā world to be seen as the vastness of immeasurable billions of lands, the narrowness of the Sahā world does not remain narrow, for narrowness is not narrow;
and the vastness of immeasurable billions of lands does not remain vast, for vastness is not vast. Thus, it is neither long nor short, neither vast nor narrow—it is precisely thus.

In order to initiate a lifespan of great duration, he manifests this inconceivable supernatural power, causing that which is long to appear short and that which is narrow to appear wide. △ Five: The Bodhisattvas’ Salutation (in two parts). First:
Indicating their names.
Within this assembly of bodhisattvas, there were four leaders: first, Upariṣṭacārin; second, Anantacārin; third, Viśuddhacārin;
and fourth, Pratiṣṭhitacārin. These four bodhisattvas were the foremost among the multitude, serving as their guiding teachers.
Regarding "Superior Practice" (Urdhvaga-caryā): this Bodhisattva has already been able to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and has ascended to the stage of the Ten Abodes;
thus, all their practices transcend those of the Three Vehicles and the Five Teachings, as well as the seven kinds of expedient means, and are therefore called "Superior Practice.
Regarding "Boundless Practice" (Anantarya-caryā): this Bodhisattva has already been able to manifest the Buddha’s knowledge and vision...
Upon ascending to the stage of the Ten Practices (*daśa-pratipatti*), one is able to bring to completion the boundless practices of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
By means of perfect contemplation and perfect illumination as one's cultivation, it is called "boundless practice. Regarding the "pure practitioner":

this Bodhisattva has already been able to awaken to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddha-jñāna-darśana*) and has ascended to the stage of the Ten Transferences (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*). Prior to awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, however, [the practices] were...
In the state of having [phenomenal] activity, there still exists the distinction between principle and phenomenon, cause and effect, and self and other; this cannot yet be called "purity.

Now, having awakened to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and entered the ten stages of dedication (*daśapariṇāmanā*), there is no phenomenon that is not principle, no cause that is not an effect, and no self that is not other.
Thus, phenomena and principle are perfectly interfused, cause and effect are of one accord, and self and other are equal. Its...
Practice is that which is most pure; therefore, it is called "Pure Practice" (*śuddhacaryā*). Regarding the establishment of practice:
this bodhisattva has already been able to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and has ascended to the stage of the ten grounds (*daśabhūmi*).

Having already shattered the forty grades of ignorance, they have manifested the forty aspects of the three virtues (*triguṇa*). They are now able to flow spontaneously into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (omniscience).
The practice for unsurpassed bodhi is established from this point onward; therefore, it is called the "established practice" (*vyavasthāna-caryā*).

According to the fourfold classification, each of the four persons possesses the merits of all forty stages. However, when speaking of the actual reality, each of the four persons individually possesses the merits of all forty stages.
This is called the practice of superior conduct, up to and including the practice of establishing [others]. △ Second, the formal inquiry after well-being:
In the midst of the great assembly, they each joined their palms together, gazed upon Śākyamuni Buddha, and inquired after his welfare, saying: "World-Honored One," [they said].
"Are you free from illness and affliction? Are you dwelling in peace and happiness? Are those who are to be delivered easy to teach? Do you not cause the World-Honored One any fatigue?
At that time, the four great bodhisattvas spoke in verse: "The World-Honored One is at ease, with little illness and little affliction.
In teaching and transforming sentient beings, do you not experience weariness? Furthermore, are the various sentient beings easy to transform? Do they not..."
"World-Honored One, have you become weary?

Regarding the inquiry as to whether one has little illness and so forth, this is a question directed at the master who performs the transformation. "Little illness" means that the body is free from danger and is at ease;
"little affliction" means that the mind is free from anxiety and is joyful. Thus, one is naturally able to practice for oneself and transform others. Therefore—
"Having little illness and little affliction" refers to practicing in peace and happiness. "Those who should be delivered" below refers to the question regarding the assembly to be transformed;
that is, whether it is easy or not for those to be transformed and delivered to receive the Tathāgata’s teaching.
If it were easy to transform them, there would be no need for the Tathāgata to proclaim it repeatedly, and he would not himself fall into weariness or exhaustion.
It is sudden. For example, when the *Avataṃsaka* was first preached, sentient beings with great capacities immediately received the teaching;
next, when the *Āgama* was preached, sentient beings with small capacities immediately received the teaching;
next, when the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā were preached, sentient beings of both great and small capacities received the teaching; and today, when the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is preached...
If there were sentient beings with complete capacities who received the teaching, then the Tathāgata would not have become weary. If, from the initial preaching of the *Avataṃsaka*,
there had been no sentient beings with great capacity to receive the teaching, and up until today’s preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*,
there had likewise been no sentient beings with complete capacity to receive the teaching, then the Tathāgata would certainly have grown exhausted on their account.
Therefore, I now ask the World-Honored One whether you are weary or not. The subsequent verse states:

"Those who teach and transform sentient beings"—beginning with the *Avataṃsaka* and ending with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, there is nothing that does not consist of teaching and transforming sentient beings. VI.
The Tathāgata’s Response to the Question (in two parts): A. The Direct Answer.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these words amidst the great assembly of bodhisattvas: "So it is, so it is.
The phrase "so it is, so it is" is a term used for formal confirmation. It is exactly as you have asked:
"Does the Tathāgata have little illness and little affliction, and does he dwell in peace? As for me, the Tathāgata, I am indeed...
It is peaceful and blissful, just as you have asked. It is exactly so; thus the Tathāgata confirms the question regarding those to be transformed.
As for whether those who should be taught according to your inquiry are easy to instruct—those sentient beings to be transformed are indeed easy to deliver, just as you have asked.
Because the Bodhisattva has previously posed these two questions, the Tathāgata now confirms them both.
It is thus. II. Explaining and establishing [the meaning] has two parts. First, the direct explanation:
"O sons of good family, the Tathāgata is at ease, with little illness and little affliction; all sentient beings are easily transformed and delivered."
There is no fatigue.
These two phrases of the Tathāgata explain and establish the first point, "Thus," in order to answer that initial question. The meaning is:
when you previously asked the World-Honored One whether he was free from illness and at ease, I now truly say that I am at ease, with little illness and little affliction.
Therefore, I confirm you as being thus in this one respect. The three phrases concerning all sentient beings serve to explain and establish the subsequent "thus" in this one respect.
That is to say, you previously asked the World-Honored One: "Are those who should be delivered easy to transform?
Will it not cause the World-Honored One weariness? Now, they are indeed easy to transform and there is no weariness; therefore, I again confirm you.
It is the same for you as it is for this one. △ Second, the further explanation.
Why is this so? These sentient beings have, from lifetime to lifetime since the beginningless past, constantly received my transformation.
They have also, before the Buddhas of the past, paid respectful homage and planted various roots of goodness. When these sentient beings first see my body and hear my [teaching]...
They all believe and accept what is taught, entering the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
[The question arises: Why is it that sentient beings are so easily transformed and delivered, such that the Tathāgata never experiences weariness?
Therefore, he explains further, saying: "These sentient beings, from lifetime to lifetime until now... and so on, up to "...entering the Buddha-wisdom. This clarifies...

Those whose virtue is profound and whose faculties are sharp— referring to those from successive lifetimes onward— are the so-called forty-one ranks of Dharma-body Bodhisattvas at the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*,
as well as the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings whose roots have matured over past lives.
As for the phrase "first seeing my body," this refers to beholding the Tathāgata’s ten-thousand-fathom Vairocana body at the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
To "hear what I have spoken" means to hear the teaching of the *sūtra* in its entirety.
As for "all of them believe and accept it," this refers to when the Tathāgata, at the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka*, proclaimed: "How marvelous! How marvelous!
All sentient beings possess the wisdom and virtuous nature of the Tathāgata. When sentient beings of profound virtue and sharp faculties hear this, they immediately believe and accept it.
They are thus able to give rise to faith and understanding; through understanding, they are able to initiate practice; and through practice, they are able to enter into realization.
Therefore, it is said that "they all believe and accept, entering the wisdom of the Tathāgata."
Except for those who have previously practiced and studied the Hīnayāna—such persons I shall now also cause to hear this sutra and enter the Buddha’s wisdom.
This clarifies that they possess dull faculties;
as for the phrase "such persons," it means they were once recipients of the great transformation under the Great Penetrating Buddha.
This refers to those who later retreat from the Great [Vehicle] and take up the Small. I now also cause such people to hear this sutra and enter the Buddha-wisdom;
that is to say, although these individuals have meager virtue and dull faculties, they neither saw nor heard it during the *Avataṃsaka* period.
However, during the *Āgama* period, I caused them to realize the Small [Vehicle], and during the *Vaipulya* period, I rebuked them.

Prajñā serves as the means for their refinement. Now, having attained the removal of hindrances and the activation of the spiritual capacity, they are able to hear this sutra and likewise enter into the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
Thus, those of profound virtue, upon first seeing and hearing it, immediately enter the Buddha-wisdom;
they are certainly easy to deliver. As for those of meager virtue, I lead them by way of the small [vehicle].
They also enter the Buddha’s wisdom. They are likewise easy to deliver; because all sentient beings are easy to deliver, the Tathāgata experiences no weariness. △ Seven: Bodhisattvas Rejoice.
At that time, the great Bodhisattvas spoke in verse:
"Excellent, excellent! O Great Hero, World-Honored One! These sentient beings are easy to transform and deliver; they are able to question the Buddhas."
This profound wisdom—having heard it, we believe and practice it; we rejoice in it.
As above, the Tathāgata’s twin seals are thus; now the Bodhisattvas’ twin exclamations of "Excellent! [are likewise]. Regarding those who are able to inquire, etc.:
Because they are easily transformed and delivered, they are able to inquire about all the wisdom possessed by the Buddhas. Having inquired, they receive answers;

having received answers, they are able to hear them. Having heard them, they believe and understand. From this faith, they give rise to practice, whereby they immediately attain entry into realization.
Now, we rejoice in accordance with this, rejoicing in their ability to inquire and hear, and their ability to believe and practice.
Furthermore, the first line is a double expression of praise: one "Excellent! praises the Tathāgata’s blissful peace, and one "Excellent!
praises the ease with which sentient beings may be delivered. This can be understood by correlating it with the Tathāgata’s two-fold seal mentioned above.
Next, the six lines beginning with "Great Hero" (mahāvīra) are a specific verse response to the questions; this corresponds to the Tathāgata’s answer to them.
Regarding the Tathāgata’s question concerning peace and bliss, the great bodhisattvas received it in a single phrase from the Great Hero (Mahāvīra).
Regarding the Tathāgata’s answer concerning the ease with which sentient beings may be delivered, the bodhisattvas received it in five phrases concerning all sentient beings.
This is because the Tathāgata’s ability to bring peace and bliss derives from the Great Hero, while the ease with which sentient beings are delivered [derives from...]
Regarding those who are able to question, able to hear, able to believe, and able to practice: next, our single phrase of "rejoicing" (*anumodana*) is a general expression of rejoicing.
We likewise rejoice that the Tathāgata is at peace, and we likewise rejoice that sentient beings are easy to deliver.
△ The Tathāgata’s Commendation.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the foremost great bodhisattvas: "Excellent, excellent, sons of good family!
You are able to give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy toward the Tathāgata."

Regarding the phrase "those who are able [to act] toward the Tathāgata": previously it was said, "we rejoice," which refers to rejoicing in sentient beings' ability to inquire and their ability to practice.

Now, when it says "those who are able to give rise to a mind of rejoicing toward the Tathāgata," this is because that which sentient beings inquire about, hear, believe, and practice is, in fact, the wisdom of the Tathāgata; therefore, one rejoices in the sentient beings.

To give birth [to this mind] is precisely to rejoice in the Tathāgata. Furthermore, by twice exclaiming "Excellent! (sādhu), one has already twice described both the ability to rejoice in the Tathāgata and the ability to rejoice in sentient beings.
To be able to give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy toward the Tathāgata is to restate the ability to rejoice in the Tathāgata;
for while rejoicing in sentient beings is still considered an easy matter, [rejoicing in the Buddha is far more difficult].
To rejoice in the Tathāgata is indeed a difficult matter; therefore, the text reiterates his ability to rejoice in the Tathāgata.
The first section, the Sequence of Manifesting Signs, concludes. △ Second, the Section on Questions and Doubts, in two parts. First, the Arising of Doubt.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva and the assembly of bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of eight thousand Ganges Rivers,
all had this thought: "From the distant past until now, we have neither seen nor heard of such a multitude of great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas emerging from the earth,
standing before the World-Honored One, joining their palms in worship, and inquiring after the Tathāgata’s well-being."
Regarding the phrase "from of old," it means that from the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra until this very day, we have followed the Tathāgata;

it has not been for a mere morning or evening, but for a long time. Many Bodhisattvas from other directions have come to this assembly, and what we have seen and heard from them has not been little. Yet, we have never before seen or heard anything such as this.
The Bodhisattvas emerged from the earth and paid their respects to the Tathāgata. △ Second, the posing of questions, in two parts. First, the prose section:
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva Mahāsattva knew the thoughts of the bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of eight thousand Ganges Rivers...
As for what he contemplates: it is because he wishes to resolve his own doubts.
As for wishing to resolve his own doubts: Maitreya, the one who is next in line for Buddhahood—how could he truly not know, yet still have doubts?
Although I myself have no doubts, the assembly does; now, wishing to pose questions on their behalf for the sake of the assembly, I say that I too have doubts.
△ Second, the verse section has two parts: first, fourteen lines of the actual questions; second, five and a half lines requesting an answer.
The first part has three sections; the first asks from where he has come.
With palms joined toward the Buddha, he asked in verse:
"O Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings, please explain this to the immeasurable thousands of myriads of kotis of the great assembly of bodhisattvas, whom none have ever seen before."
From where have you come?
△ Second, asking by what causes and conditions you have gathered:
By what causes and conditions have you gathered this massive body and great supernormal powers, with wisdom inconceivable and a resolve as firm as adamant?
Possessing the power of great patience, they are a joy for all sentient beings to behold. From where have these individual bodhisattvas come?
The retinues they each lead are immeasurable in number, like the sands of the Ganges. Among them, there are some great bodhisattvas.

Sixty thousand Ganges-sands of such great assemblies, seeking the Buddha-way with a single mind—these great masters, sixty thousand as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, all came together to make offerings to the Buddha and to protect and uphold this sutra; fifty thousand Ganges-sands likewise came.

Their number exceeds even this: forty thousand, thirty thousand, down to twenty thousand and ten thousand; one thousand, one hundred, and so forth, even to a single *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (grains of sand in the Ganges);
half, or a third, or a fourth part; a ten-millionth part, a hundred-millionth, or a *nayuta* (ten million).
There are ten trillion disciples, down to five hundred million; their numbers exceed even those above.
From one million down to ten thousand, one thousand, and one hundred; fifty, ten, and even three, two, or one—those who are solitary and without retinue.
Those who delight in dwelling alone all came together to where the Buddha was, their number exceeding even that of the former assembly.
If one were to count these great multitudes by casting tally-sticks, one would not be able to know them all, even in more than *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
The first line consists of three phrases; this is the formal inquiry as to the cause. The subsequent nine lines, one by one, are verses enumerating the number of the assembly.
The initial phrase, "firm in resolve and mindfulness," refers to being able to seek the Buddha-way above and transform sentient beings below.
"Great power of patience" means being able to dwell permanently in this Sahā world. This is...
The power of patience is great. As for "from where does it come," this asks by what causes and conditions, and from what source, it has arrived.
By posing this question regarding the accumulation of causes and conditions, Maitreya already knows that the Tathāgata has arrived here;
he wishes to reveal the origin. Therefore, this single question may serve as the prologue to the Essential Gate (Honmon). Maitreya...
Did Aniruddha not see that the Tathāgata restrained the bodhisattvas from other directions? He immediately summoned those bodhisattvas, saying:
"I have sixty thousand bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; these individuals will, after my parinirvāṇa, be able to protect, uphold, recite, and extensively expound this sūtra.
Therefore, it is stated below that these great masters all came together to make offerings.
The Buddha, as well as those who protect and uphold this sutra—these are precisely the causes and conditions for those bodhisattvas to have come forth.
Therefore, one should know that regarding the question of "by what causes and conditions," how could it be that [the interlocutor] does not know that the Tathāgata intends to reveal their origin?
△ Third, he asks who their teacher is.
These assemblies of bodhisattvas of great majesty and vigor—who has preached the Dharma for them? By whom have they been taught and brought to fulfillment?

From whom did they first resolve their minds toward enlightenment? Whose praise of the Buddha-dharma do they extol? Which sutras do they uphold and practice? And which path of the Buddhas do they cultivate?
Regarding the term "great majestic power" (*mahātejas*): it refers to one's ability to sever afflictions (*kleśa*) and manifest virtuous qualities (*guṇa*).
When asking, "Whose Buddha-dharma and so forth do you praise? one is inquiring about the teacher; that is, praising and proclaiming the teachings of which Buddha.
Whose Buddha’s scriptures have they practiced and upheld? Whose Buddha’s path and Dharma have they cultivated and mastered?
△ Second, the request for an answer has three parts. First, the request for an account of their origins.
Thus these bodhisattvas, by means of their supernormal powers and great wisdom-force, cause the earth to split asunder in the four directions and emerge from within it.
World-Honored One, since my former days, I have never seen such a thing; I pray that you will tell us from where they come and the names of their lands.
△ Second, the causes and conditions for requesting an answer:
"I have constantly traveled through various lands, yet I have never seen such an assembly. Among this multitude, I do not recognize even a single person."
Suddenly emerging from the earth, I pray that you will explain the causes and conditions thereof.
△ Third, the request for the teacher’s response:
In this great assembly today, numbering immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions, all these bodhisattvas likewise desire to know this matter.
Regarding these assemblies of bodhisattvas, their causes and conditions from beginning to end—the World-Honored One of Immeasurable Virtue, we pray that you will resolve the doubts of the assembly.
As for these causes and conditions from beginning to end: "beginning" refers to the initial arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*), and "end" refers to its maturation.

That is to say, under which Buddha did they first arouse the mind, and through which Buddha were they finally matured? Regarding such causes and conditions of beginning and end, everyone in the assembly has doubts.
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will provide an enlightened response to resolve the doubts of the assembly.

Thus, it is said, "I only pray that you will resolve the doubts of the assembly," which refers specifically to resolving the doubts concerning from whom [the Bodhisattvas] first resolved their minds to attain enlightenment, as well as their subsequent praise, upholding, and cultivation [of the Dharma].
Furthermore, this is to resolve the doubts concerning from where [the teaching] comes, by what causes and conditions it is assembled, and from whom the Teacher [received it].
△ Third, the sequence of questions and answers, part two. First, the attendant’s inquiry; second, the divided bodies’ response. Regarding the first of these two:
first, identifying the Teacher who is questioned.
At that time, the various emanations of Śākyamuni Buddha, numbering immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis who had come from other lands in the ten directions,
sat cross-legged upon lion thrones beneath jeweled trees in the eight quarters.
△ Second, explaining the disciples who inquire.
The attendants of those Buddhas each saw these great assemblies of bodhisattvas emerging from the earth from the four directions throughout the trichiliocosm and abiding in the void.
Each addressed his own Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, these immeasurable [beings]..."
"Boundless, asaṃkhyeya multitudes of bodhisattvas—from where have they come?
This statement, "from where have they come," is a brief inquiry. Furthermore, by what causes and conditions have they gathered, and who is their teacher and leader?
Therefore, the answer below states: "This matter has already been asked," which refers to Maitreya’s three questions. Thus, it is known that this—
The intent of this single question encompasses two points. △ Second, the divided bodies receive the answer.
At that time, each of the Buddhas addressed their respective attendants: "Good sons, wait but a moment.
There is a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva named Maitreya, who has been predicted by Śākyamuni Buddha to become a Buddha immediately after him."
He asked about this matter, and the Buddha now answers it; you yourselves shall surely hear it through this.
Furthermore, there are three reasons for [the Buddha] waiting: first, Śākyamuni is the teacher of this world and naturally has disciples of this world;
we, as his emanations, are teachers from other worlds, and you bodhisattvas are the disciples of those other worlds.
Son, if one were a teacher of this world, one should answer the questions of the disciples of this world.
Now, since I am a teacher of another world, I should answer the questions of the disciples of that other world. This is the duty of a teacher of this world.
This is not my answer. First, these bodhisattvas have emerged from the earth; they are the ones who initiate the "Original Chapter" to reveal the distant by opening the near.
This matter should be elucidated by Śākyamuni himself; it is not a matter for elucidation by us, his emanations.
Second, since Maitreya has already asked the question first, Śākyamuni should provide the answer.

Nor is it necessary for us to provide an answer. Those who hear this shall hear the answer given by the Tathāgata regarding from what causes and conditions [this teaching] has arisen, and who its teacher and master is.
The introductory section of the Fundamental Chapter is hereby concluded. II. The Main Body of the Teaching (The Correct Doctrine) has two parts:
1. The Promise to Speak; 2. The Actual Exposition. The first part [the Promise to Speak] has two sections: 1. Prose; 2. Verse. The first [Prose]: [Note: The provided text fragment ends here.]
Third: The initial praise and narration.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva: "Excellent, excellent, Ajita!
You are indeed able to ask the Buddha about such a great matter as this."
Regarding the address to Maitreya: in the preceding Trace Gate (*śeṣa-mukha*), because the intent was to open up the three [vehicles] to reveal the one, he addressed the *śrāvakas*.
Now, in this Fundamental Gate (*mūla-mukha*), because the intent is to open up the near to reveal the far, he addresses the Bodhisattvas. As for the double exclamation of "Excellent" (*sādhu*):
one "Excellent" praises his skill in conceiving the doubt; the other "Excellent" praises his skill in posing the three questions. Thus he questioned the Buddha.
Regarding such great matters: when a Tathāgata appears in the world, there are two great matters.
The first is to reveal the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, causing all sentient beings to open, show, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
this is the great matter of the *jiamen* (trace-gate). The second is to reveal the Tathāgata’s long and distant lifespan, demonstrating that he has already realized *bodhi* since time immemorial.

This is the great matter of the Original Gate (*honmon*). Although the great matters of the Trace Gate (*jimon*) have already been elucidated above, the great matters of the Original Gate have not yet been revealed.
Furthermore, these great matters of the Original Gate are what people find difficult to inquire about;
that you are now able to ask the Buddha about them is truly excellent—thus he says "Excellent" (and so forth). △ Second, the Admonition.
"Agreed.
You all should be of one mind, don the armor of diligence, and resolve with firm intent.
△ Third, the formal granting of permission.
The Tathāgata now wishes to manifest and proclaim the wisdom of all Buddhas.
Having first promised to speak of his long-lasting lifespan, "to manifest" refers to his arising from samādhi at the beginning of the "Chapter on the Exalted Trace."
He then sighed over the wisdom of the Buddhas, which is profoundly deep and immeasurable; that gateway to wisdom is difficult to understand and difficult to enter.

It continues, stating that the *pāramitā* of skillful means, knowledge, and vision are all already fully perfected, whereby the wisdom of the Buddhas has already been proclaimed and already been revealed.
Now, within this context, it is further stated that he wishes to reveal the wisdom of the Buddhas.
O wise one, you should know that this long lifespan cannot be cultivated without wisdom, nor can it be realized without wisdom.
Therefore, the subsequent passage states: "Such is my power of wisdom; the light of my insight shines immeasurably;
my life-span lasts for countless eons, obtained through the long cultivation of practice. Thus, one knows that this longevity is entirely attained through the cultivation and realization of wisdom.
Regarding the lifespan: it is because he wishes to reveal the long duration of his original lifespan that he speaks thus;

furthermore, he intends to manifest and proclaim the wisdom of all Buddhas, the power of the sovereign spiritual transformations of all Buddhas, the power of the lion’s majestic stride of all Buddhas, and the fierce majesty of all Buddhas.
The power of great majesty (*mahāvaśitā*).
This refers to the permission to speak of how [the Buddhas] benefit sentient beings throughout the three periods of time.

The intent is that it does not merely manifest the wisdom of all Buddhas, but further seeks to reveal and proclaim their sovereign powers (*vaśitā*) and so forth. Thus, it speaks of the "power of sovereign supernormal knowledges" (*vaśitā-abhijñā-bala*).
This refers to how, in past lives, the Tathāgata manifested birth where there was no birth to teach and transform all beings,
being able to manifest spiritual wonders and clarity, penetrating and transforming all things, having attained the power of great mastery.
As for the power of the lion’s vigorous springing, this refers to how, in the present life, the Tathāgata manifests birth where there was no birth to teach and transform all beings.
To be able to renounce the world simultaneously throughout the worlds of the ten directions, and to attain enlightenment simultaneously in immeasurable lands—
this is the power of the Tathāgata’s majestic display (*vikrīḍita*). That which possesses fierce and great power is precisely the Tathāgata’s ability to benefit sentient beings in future ages,
severing what is difficult for people to sever and delivering those who are difficult to deliver.
To deliver those who are difficult for others to tame is the majestic power and great might of the Tathāgata.

The reason the Buddhas are able to benefit sentient beings throughout the three periods of time is that they are able to realize an immeasurable lifespan; therefore, throughout the three periods of time—
All are able to benefit sentient beings. △ Second, the verse summary has two parts. First, the verse summary of the admonition and permission.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
You should be diligent and single-minded; I wish to speak of this matter, so do not harbor any doubt or regret.
II. Verse on the Formal Granting:
The Buddha’s wisdom is inconceivable; you now exert the power of faith and abide within the goodness of patience. This Dharma has never been heard before.
Now you shall all hear it. I now comfort you: do not harbor doubt or fear. The Buddha’s speech is never untrue; his wisdom is immeasurable.
The supreme Dharma he has attained is profound and beyond conceptualization. Thus, I shall now speak.
All of you, listen with a single mind.

The first line of the verse separately permits the explanation of his long life span. From the words "Now you" [onward], the verse separately permits the explanation of how he benefits sentient beings throughout the three periods of time.
Regarding the phrase "the Dharma never heard before," this does not merely refer to what was not heard prior to the forty years; it refers to...
Even within the preceding Trace Gate of this present Dharma Flower Great Assembly, this has not yet been heard; it is only now, in the Fundamental Gate, that one shall finally hear it.
There is no speech of the Buddha that is not true; as it is said in the *Vajra*, he is "one who speaks the truth."
One who speaks the truth, one who speaks as it is, and one who does not speak deceptively; and as stated in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*:
"The unsurpassed Dharma is true speech; it is spoken according to reality, neither deceptive nor false.

If one investigates this according to its actual substance, as in the preceding section on the traces (*śeṣa-mukha*), if it speaks of the provisional (*upāya*), it is certainly provisional; if it speaks of the real (*bhūta*), it is certainly real. Now...

If it is said to be near, it is certainly near; if it is said to be far, it is certainly far. Such explanations regarding the provisional and the real, the near and the far, are all true and not false.
Part Two: The Actual Explanation, in two sections. First, a brief opening of the near to reveal the far.
Second, from the "Life Span" chapter onwards, an extensive opening of the near to reveal the far. The first section has two parts. First, the actual brief opening and revelation.
2. At that time, Maitreya descended and gave rise to doubts and attachments once more. This section has two parts: first, the prose; second, the verse.
The prose section has two parts: first, the direct answer.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, he addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva: "I now announce to you all within this great assembly, Ajita:

these great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, immeasurable, innumerable, and incalculable, who have surged forth from the earth—whom none of you have ever seen before—I have attained [this] in this Sahā world."
Having attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, he teaches, transforms, instructs, and guides these bodhisattvas,
subduing their minds and causing them to resolve upon the path.
"Ānanda," he called out again; this repeated address serves to introduce the formal response to his three questions from the point below.
First, he answers the question regarding who their teacher and leader is. As for the phrase "teaching, transforming, instructing, and guiding," it means that you have previously asked me:
"Who is it that preaches the Dharma to this assembly of bodhisattvas? and so forth.
They have been transformed and brought to fulfillment. I now tell you: these bodhisattvas were not taught by anyone else;
rather, after I, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, attained enlightenment here in this Sahā world, I taught these bodhisattvas.
You should know that it was I who taught them, revealed the path to them, guided them, and brought them to fulfillment. You asked again:
"From whom did they first resolve their minds? I shall now tell you: these bodhisattvas did not resolve their minds under anyone else;
rather, after I attained enlightenment, I disciplined their minds and caused them to give rise to the aspiration for the Way.
You should know that they resolved their minds because of me. As for "disciplining their minds," it means that these bodhisattvas had not yet [passed through] such...
Before they have been tamed, they have not yet avoided becoming attached to existence, dwelling in emptiness, or clinging to the Middle; thus,
the Tathāgata tames and subdues them so that they may return to that which is neither empty,
nor existent, nor middle, yet is simultaneously empty, existent, and middle.
All these bodhisattvas dwell in the space beneath this Sahā world.
As for your question regarding where these bodhisattvas have come from, I shall now tell you: these bodhisattvas [have come from here].
They all dwell in the void beneath this realm; thus one knows they have come from the void beneath this realm.
They read and recite the various sūtras with proficiency, contemplating and analyzing them, and maintaining right mindfulness.
Furthermore, you asked: "By whom are these practices upheld? I now tell you:
these bodhisattvas are able to read, recite, and master all the sūtras I have taught; thus, they are known to uphold the sūtras I have spoken.
You also asked: "In what Buddha-way do they practice? I now tell you: these bodhisattvas, regarding me...
Regarding the sūtras that have been taught, they are not merely recited and mastered through rote memorization;

rather, one is able to contemplate based on understanding, and to initiate practice based on contemplation. Therefore, it is said that "contemplating, discerning, and maintaining right mindfulness" constitutes knowing how to cultivate my path and Dharma.
As for "maintaining right mindfulness," these bodhisattvas are able, by means of such [wisdom]...
Taking the wondrous realm of the true nature (*dharmatā*) as explained here as the object, one gives rise to the wondrous wisdom that contemplates it;
then, with this wondrous wisdom of contemplation, one illuminates the wondrous realm of the true nature. In this way, wisdom is elicited by the realm, and the realm is illuminated by wisdom.
When realm and wisdom are thus of one suchness and non-dual, one naturally does not lean toward existence, nor does one lean toward... [non-existence].
It is not biased toward emptiness, nor is it biased toward the middle; therefore, this is right mindfulness. △ Second, the further explanation:
"Ajita, these sons of good family do not delight in being among the multitude or in speaking much.
They always delight in solitary places, practicing with diligence and vigor without ever resting, nor do they rely upon or dwell among humans or devas."

This commentary explains that he dwells in the empty space of this realm because he does not delight in being among the multitude, nor even in relying upon humans or devas to dwell; therefore, he abides in the empty space below this realm.
They always delight in profound wisdom that is free from all obstructions, and they also always delight in the teachings of all Buddhas.
To say that they "always delight in profound wisdom and the teachings of all Buddhas," etc., is an explanation of their thorough mastery through reading and reciting the various sūtras and so forth.
This is because they delight in the wisdom possessed by me, Śākyamuni, as well as that possessed by all Buddhas.
Thus, regarding all the sūtras, they are entirely recited, contemplated, and practiced. This profound wisdom is precisely the threefold wisdom within a single mind.
When one delights in the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of all modes manifests before one, enabling the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
When one delights in the knowledge of the paths of all types (*mārgajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths of all types manifests before one, enabling...
When one contemplates existence and delights in all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), then all-knowledge manifests before one, and one is able to contemplate the Middle Way.
When contemplating emptiness, then when one is empty, all are empty, and all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) is without obstruction.
When contemplating existence, then when one exists, all exist, and the knowledge of the modes of the path (*mārgajñatā*) is without [obstruction].
Regarding the absence of obstacles: when one contemplates the midst, then within that one midst there is all amidst;
thus, the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) is without obstruction. Therefore, it is said that one constantly delights in profound wisdom that is unobstructed.
This is the delight in the wisdom possessed by me, Śākyamuni. Yet, it is not only the delight in my own wisdom, but also the constant delight in [the wisdom of] the ten directions.
Because they possess all the dharmas of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, it is said that they also constantly delight in the dharmas of all Buddhas.
With single-minded diligence, they seek unsurpassed wisdom.
These two phrases explain how one attains accomplishment through being taught, transformed, and guided.
Because one is able to practice with single-minded diligence, at the time of my teaching, one immediately attains accomplishment. Thus, among the three questions:
He answered only the questions regarding from where he had come and who his teacher was, but did not answer the second question concerning the causes and conditions for his appearance.
This is because his emergence was not due to any other causes and conditions, but was solely for the purpose of initiating [the teaching on] the lifespan.
In this context, if the explanation were given directly here, it would not be necessary to elaborate upon it further below.
Since Maitreya likewise did not harbor doubts or give rise to attachments regarding this, he posed his questions;
how then could the Tathāgata have extensively revealed and clarified it? Therefore, I shall not now explain its causes and conditions.
Rather, following my answers to his two questions, I will briefly reveal it so that he may conceive doubt and make a formal request, after which I shall extensively clarify what is near at hand.
[The] trace [of the teaching]. To extensively reveal its distant origin, when one arrives at this point, one knows for oneself that its emergence has no other causes or conditions;
it is solely for the purpose of initiating the distant origin. Thus, the question regarding causes and conditions is answered of itself without being explicitly stated.
△ Second, the verse recitation, which has two parts. First, answering what was asked.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Ajita, you should know: these great bodhisattvas have, since incalculable kalpas past, cultivated the wisdom of the Buddha."
In this verse, the respondent answers the question. The first five and a half stanzas do not follow a sequential order;
they are simply divided into six parts without further sub-divisions. The first stanza explains "teaching and guiding," which refers to single-mindedly and diligently seeking unsurpassed wisdom.
"All have been transformed by me, causing them to resolve upon the Great Vehicle mind; these are my children.
These three lines of verse provide the direct answer. "Those whom I have taught and caused to resolve" refers precisely to those who have been taught, guided, and so forth.
Relying upon this world, they constantly practice the dhūta austerities; their aspiration is for quietude, and they abandon the clamor of the great assembly, taking no pleasure in much speaking.
This single line and phrase explains that [the Buddha] dwells in the empty space of this realm; that is, he does not delight in being among the multitudes.
In this way, these sons of mine study my Way and Dharma, constantly exerting themselves with diligence day and night, for the sake of seeking the Buddha-way.

This single verse explains that one who is proficient in reading and reciting the various sūtras will constantly delight in profound wisdom and will also constantly delight in the Dharma of all Buddhas.
What was previously termed "profound wisdom" refers to the wisdom of Śākyamuni; therefore, it is now said that one studies and practices my path and Dharma.
What was previously termed "the Dharma of all Buddhas" refers to the fact that one does so for the sake of seeking the Buddha-way.
This is precisely the seeking of the path of all Buddhas. This can be seen through the mutual elucidation of the prose and the verse.
Not only is this understood, but it is also verified that the aforementioned "profound wisdom" must indeed be the wisdom of Śākyamuni.
"Abiding in the space below the Sahā world"—
these two lines of verse answer the question of his place of origin, namely that he dwells in the empty space beneath this very realm.
"The power of one's resolve and mindfulness is firm; one constantly and diligently seeks wisdom; one preaches various sublime dharmas, and the mind is without fear.
This single verse further answers the master regarding the various sūtras and so forth.
Because one is able to contemplate, discern, and maintain correct mindfulness, one’s resolve and mindfulness become firm, and one diligently seeks wisdom. Thus, the resolve and mindfulness are firm.
"Gu" refers to the Four Great Vows: seeking enlightenment above and transforming beings below.

Because one has read, recited, and mastered various sutras, one is able to expound all manner of dharmas with a mind free from fear. "Sublime Dharma" (Miaofa) refers to the different aspects of the provisional and the real;

thus it is called "all manner of. Since the Real is itself sublime, the provisional is taught to lead those of lesser capacity; therefore, the provisional is also sublime. This answers the previous [question].
The questions have now been concluded. II. Opening the near to reveal the far:
"At the city of Gayā, sitting beneath the Bodhi tree, I attained supreme perfect enlightenment and turned the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma."
I have then taught and transformed them, causing them to first resolve their minds on the Way; now they all abide in non-retrogression and shall all attain Buddhahood.
I now speak these true words: you should believe them with one mind. From long ago, I have been teaching and transforming this assembly.
The first two lines briefly reveal the near [manifestation]. Next, the line beginning with "I now" briefly reveals the distant [manifestation].

Since it is said that he awakened the aspiration for enlightenment through his teaching at Gayā, and yet it is further said that he has taught these beings for a long time, the traces naturally reveal the manifestation, and the fundamental source naturally reveals the origin.
The first section, on the formal brief revelation and manifestation, is concluded. △ Second, the re-arising of doubt and attachment, in two parts. First:
Doubt arose within their minds.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva Mahāsattva and countless other bodhisattvas felt doubt and wonder at this unprecedented event, and they thought to themselves:
"How is it that the World-Honored One, in such a short interval of time, has brought so many to transformation?"
Regarding the phrase "causing immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) great bodhisattvas to abide in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,

while their minds were filled with doubt and so forth": this means that since it is stated that [the Buddha] attained enlightenment at Gayā and only thereafter taught and inspired them to resolve upon awakening, [it would seem there was no prior cause].
One should not say that [the Buddha] has been teaching these beings since time immemorial.
If he had been teaching them for such a long duration, then it would be inconsistent to say that they only now have resolved their minds. Between these two positions, doubt arises.
This is precisely a case of clinging to the near while doubting the distant; therefore, it is asked, "How could it be in so short a time? etc. △ Second, the expression of the statement.

The questions are twofold: first, the prose exposition; second, the verse summary. The first [section] has four parts: first, the Dharma; second, the parable; third, the application; fourth, the request for explanation. The first [of these four] has three parts:
first, clinging to what is near while doubting what is far.

He then addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, when the Tathāgata was a prince, he departed from the palace of the Śākyas and, not far from the city of Gayā, sat at the site of enlightenment and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
From that time until now, barely more than forty years have passed. World-Honored One, how is it that in such a short time you have performed such great deeds of a Buddha?"
By the power of the Buddha and by the merit of the Buddha, he teaches and transforms such an immeasurable assembly of great bodhisattvas,
so that they shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This refers to a person of twenty-five years of age; taking a hundred-year-old man as his son is the primary analogy.
That the Tathāgata was a crown prince is an adherence to what is proximate. The phrase "from this time onward" and so forth refers to what is distant.
As for the statement "more than forty years," prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he preached the *Āgama* for twelve years and the *Vaipulya* for eight years, totaling twenty [years].
The *Prajñāpāramitā* was taught for two years; when calculated together with the other periods, this totals forty-two years. Therefore, it is said to be "more than forty years.

"By the power of the Buddha" refers to the power of his supernatural faculties (*ṛddhi-bala*); "by the merit of the Buddha" refers to the power of his wisdom (*prajñā-bala*). △ Second, resolving doubts regarding the distance [of time].
World-Honored One, as for this assembly of great bodhisattvas, even if someone were to count them for thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas,
they could not exhaustively enumerate them nor reach their limit. For a long time past, these beings have planted various roots of goodness under immeasurable and boundless Buddhas,
accomplished the path of a bodhisattva, and have constantly cultivated pure conduct.
This refers to those who are at least one hundred years old; it also takes the young as an analogy for fathers.
The mention of "great bodhisattvas" and so forth clarifies the great number of such beings. The statement that they have existed "for a long time" clarifies the vastness of their duration.
They have planted various roots of goodness under all the Buddhas; this refers to the profundity of their practice.
They have accomplished the Bodhisattva path and constantly cultivated the pure conduct (brahmacarya); this refers to the loftiness of their stage.

Since such numerous Bodhisattvas of profound practice and high status have already existed for an extremely long time, how could the Tathāgata have taught and transformed them to attain [this realization] in such a short period?
"Or has he regressed? △ Third, a summary of the difficulty of belief:
"World-Honored One, such a matter as this is difficult for the world to believe.
This serves as the basis for the following parable regarding the difficulty of believing in this matter: namely, that while the teacher is extremely near, the disciple—
It is extremely remote; in all cases, it is difficult to believe. △ Second, the three parables. First, the parable of the young father:
Suppose there is a man with a handsome appearance and black hair, twenty-five years of age, who points to a hundred-year-old man and says, "This is my son."
This is like a teacher who is extremely close. △ Second, the parable of the old man:
that hundred-year-old man also points to the young man, saying, "He is my father; he begot and raised us."
This is like an elder disciple who is extremely distant [from his teacher]. △ Third, the general difficulty of belief:
This matter is difficult to believe;
it is, for example, as if there were a person in the world whose father was extremely young and whose son was extremely old—this would indeed be difficult to believe. △
The third section consists of three parts. First, the analogy of the father being young is combined [with the Buddha].
The Buddha is likewise: since he attained the Way, it has actually not been long.

This combines with the aforementioned analogy of the father being young; that is, to grasp what is near while doubting what is distant. △ Second, the analogy of the son being old is combined [with the Buddha].
Furthermore, this great assembly of bodhisattvas has, for the sake of the Buddha-way, diligently practiced with vigor throughout immeasurable thousands of millions of billions of kalpas;
they have skillfully entered, emerged from, and dwelt within immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of samādhis, and have attained great supernormal powers.

Having long cultivated the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), he was well able to practice all wholesome dharmas in their proper sequence; he was skillful in question and answer, a jewel among men, and most rare in all the worlds.

Yet today, the World-Honored One says that it was only when he first attained the Way of the Buddha that he first caused him to resolve his mind, teaching and guiding him toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The preceding analogy regarding the old man illustrates grasping at what is distant while doubting what is near. As for the statement "skillfully entering, exiting, and abiding":
if discussed in terms of stages (*avasthā*), then that which precedes the Path is "entering," that which follows the Path is "exiting," and that which is within the Path is "abiding.
If discussed in terms of practice (*caryā*), then the initial cultivation is "entering," and the manifestation of *samādhi* is "abiding. Regarding *samādhi*...

Arising from meditative concentration to transform sentient beings is "emergence. Although there are differences in the entry, abiding, and emergence of samādhi, it lacks the characteristics of entering, abiding, or emerging;

therefore, it is called "skillful. As for the gradual cultivation of wholesome dharmas, this is not a partial or sequential progression, but rather a sequence of non-sequential, perfectly integrated stages.
For while understanding may indeed be perfect, at the time of practice, one must necessarily proceed from the cause.

Up to the attainment of the fruit, when severing delusions, one must first address the coarse and subsequently the subtle. Depending on the sequence in which these delusions fall away, the contemplation becomes manifest from the minute;
thus, it is said to be "gradual. From the perspective of principle (*li*), beginning and end are non-dual; from the perspective of phenomena (*shi*), cause and effect are clearly distinct.
This is precisely what is meant. Those who are "jewels among humans" refer to those of the three vehicles, the five teachings, and the seven stages of expedient means.
"A treasure among men, rare in the world" refers to that which is rare within the nine worlds.
The above constitutes "clinging to the distant," while from "today" onwards constitutes "doubting the near. Clinging to the distant corresponds to the person who is a hundred years old;

doubting the near corresponds to pointing out that even the youth is the father. Furthermore, in the preceding section on the Dharma, the initial part first involves clinging to the near and doubting the distant; the text is complete in both cases.

[The section on] "Sufficiency. From the passage beginning with "The Tathāgata held [the Dharma] close for the sake of the crown prince and others" up to "from that time onwards," this refers to the doubt regarding what is distant.
Next, when one holds the distant as doubtful while taking the near as certain, there are only textual passages concerning holding the distant;

this refers specifically to the Great Bodhisattvas from the point of "constantly practicing pure conduct" (*brahmacarya*) onward. Yet, there is no mention of doubting the near. Nevertheless, the meaning of doubting the near must certainly exist; therefore, [this is] the topical outline (*kośa*).

This refers to the attachment to what is distant and the doubt regarding what is near. Next, combining the attachment to what is distant with the doubt regarding what is near, the text becomes complete.

The passage beginning with "This great assembly" below refers to the attachment to what is distant; the passage beginning with "Today, the World-Honored One" below refers to the doubt regarding what is near.

Thus, that which is absent in the *dharmas* (the doctrinal sections) is present in the *saṃghāta* (the combined sections), and that which is absent in the *saṃghāta* is present in the *dharmas*. In this way, the upper and lower parts mutually clarify one another.
This is because it is established as such. For example, although the text is brief, its meaning is fully complete.
First, the analogy of "there is a man twenty-five years old" represents clinging to what is near; pointing to a hundred-year-old man and saying, "He is my son," represents doubting what is distant.
Next, that hundred-year-old man represents clinging to what is distant; likewise, pointing to the young man and saying, "He is my father," represents doubting what is near. △
The third point is the general conclusion regarding the difficulty of belief.
That the World-Honored One, not long after attaining Buddhahood, was able to perform such a deed of great merit—this concludes the preceding section on the difficulty of belief.
First is the formal correspondence: "not long after attaining Buddhahood" corresponds to the analogy within the preceding section.
That it was difficult for the father to believe [his son] when he was young corresponds to the difficulty of believing in the Teacher when one is near to the Dharma;

yet, that he was able to perform such a deed of great merit corresponds to the elder son’s ability to believe in the Dharma when he is far from the Dharma—this is the disciple who is difficult to inspire with faith.
△ Fourth, the request to proceed.

Although we have faith in the Buddha and his teachings as they were spoken according to what was appropriate for each occasion, and though the words uttered by the Buddha have never been false—since he has fully realized and thoroughly mastered all that is known—we fear that new bodhisattvas who have only recently resolved to attain awakening might, upon hearing these words after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, fail to believe or accept them.
This could give rise to the karmic conditions of the sin of destroying the Dharma. Therefore, World-Honored One, we pray that you will explain this for us.
[The Buddha] spoke thus to remove our doubts and so that, upon hearing this matter, the good sons of future ages will likewise not give rise to doubt.
Although they may have faith in the Buddha and others, they would still not yet possess true faith. This is why it says below: "to remove our doubts. The Buddha—

Regarding "equal": it arises precisely from the inability to believe, yet one speaks of "belief" because the Buddha’s words are free from falsehood, as the Buddha’s wisdom fully penetrates all things.
To say they are "free from falsehood" refers to what was stated previously: that the Tathāgata is the King of all dharmas;
whatever he says is never false. To say he "fully penetrates all things" refers to what was stated previously regarding the Tathāgata.
He also knows the practices of their profound resolve and has attained unimpeded penetration. △ Second, the four verses in verse form: first, the verse on the Dharma; second, the verse on the simile;
third, the verse on the application; fourth, the verse on the request for explanation. The first [section] has three parts; first, the verse on clinging to what is near while doubting what is far.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"In the past, the Buddha departed from the Śākya clan and went near Gayā; he sat beneath the Bodhi tree, and not long has passed since then."

This single verse contains only words that address the attachment to the near, thereby encompassing the meaning of the doubt regarding the distant. △ Second, the verse on the attachment to the distant and the doubt regarding the near:
"These sons of the Buddha, their number is immeasurable; they have long practiced the path of the Buddhas and abide in the power of spiritual penetrations."
Having well studied the bodhisattva path and remaining unstained by worldly dharmas— like a lotus emerging from the water— they arose from the earth and,
with hearts full of reverence, stood before the World-Honored One.
These two and a half verses contain only expressions regarding the adherence to the distant, yet they encompass the meaning of doubting the near.
For one who adheres to the near will inevitably doubt the distant, and one who adheres to the distant will inevitably doubt the near;
since doubt arises from adherence, these two sections of verse all praise adherence while omitting doubt. △ Third, the concluding summary of the difficulty of belief in verse.
This matter is difficult to conceive; how can it be believed? The Buddha attained the Way so recently, yet that which he has accomplished is so vast.
We pray that you will dispel the doubts of the multitude by explaining this according to reality through detailed analysis.
The first two lines constitute the general summary. The next two lines provide the specific explanation. The line "The Buddha has attained" concludes that the teacher is difficult to believe;
the line "what has been accomplished" concludes that the disciples are distant from being believable.

While the prose version merely states that such matters are difficult for the world to believe, this [verse] now explains them in full detail. Next, the two lines beginning with "I pray" constitute the request.
Regarding "the doubts of the assembly": this refers to the doubts of present bodhisattvas such as Maitreya, as well as those of future bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds.
It also encompasses the various doubts of the assembly, such as clinging to the near while doubting the distant, or clinging to the distant while doubting the near.
This constitutes both the request and the response within the Dharma. △ Second, the verse on the analogy.
For example, suppose there were a man in the prime of his youth, twenty-five years of age, who showed people a hundred-year-old son with white hair and wrinkled face, saying, "This is my son.
And the son likewise said of him, "This is my father. That the father was young while the son was old would be something the whole world could not believe.
The first line and phrase eulogizes the analogy of the father’s youth. The subsequent phrase, “The son also says this is his father,” eulogizes the analogy of the son’s old age.

The third section, consisting of two phrases regarding the father’s youth, eulogizes the concluding summary of the analogy of the difficulty of belief. While the prose merely states that this matter is difficult to believe, here it is fully elucidated.
The two characters for “father’s youth” eulogize the conclusion of the father’s youth as being difficult to believe; [the following] “son’s old age” [eulogizes the son’s old age].
[The verse] concludes the section on the difficulty of belief; thus it says that the world does not believe [this]. △ Third, the verse on the analogy:
"The World-Honored One is also like this: though he has attained the Way but recently, these bodhisattvas are firm in resolve and without cowardice."
Having practiced the bodhisattva path for immeasurable eons, he is skillful in answering difficult questions;
his mind is fearless, his resolve in patience is firm, and he is upright and majestic. Praised by the Buddhas of the ten directions, he is well able to analyze and explain the teachings.
He does not delight in being among the crowds; he always prefers to dwell in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). For the sake of seeking the Buddha-way, he dwells in the lower void.
The first two lines of the verse combine the analogy of the father’s youth, which represents clinging to what is near while doubting what is far.

The second part, consisting of the three and a half lines beginning with "The second," combines the analogy of the son’s old age, which represents clinging to what is far while doubting what is near. Both passages likewise contain instances of attachment.
However, [the text] is brief regarding doubt. As for the statement that "the mind of patience is decisive":
patience clarifies its capacity to be gentle, harmonious, and compliant, such that it is not moved by internal or external obstacles and afflictions.

"Decisive" clarifies its capacity to settle the mind in the true reality (*dharmatā*), such that it is not moved by either emptiness or existence. Because it can flow in spontaneously, it is so described.
He is upright and handsome. Because he is able to sever delusions and manifest virtues, it is said that he possesses majestic power (*tejas*).
Furthermore, the two characters for "patience" (*kṣānti*) signify being able to don the robe of the Tathāgata; "resolute mind" signifies being able to sit upon the seat of the Tathāgata.
This means being able to contemplate all phenomena as being empty and quiescent in their very essence, such that one is not moved by any phenomena; thus, the mind is resolute.
It is concentration (*samādhi*). Being upright and possessing majestic virtue, one is able to enter the Tathāgata’s chamber;

that is to say, one can exercise great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) to uproot the suffering of the two extremes for all sentient beings. Therefore, it is said that being upright and possessing majesty, one is able to exercise great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*).
And they bestow the joy of the Middle Way upon all sentient beings; therefore, it is said that they are upright and virtuous.
This clarifies their ability to cultivate and realize the three tracks, as well as their capacity to give rise to the function of the three tracks. It is precisely because of this.
Therefore, he is praised by all Buddhas, for even the Buddhas attain their status as Buddhas solely by practicing and realizing the application of the three attachments.
△ Fourth, the verse requesting the teaching.
We have heard this from the Buddha; regarding this matter, we have no doubt. We pray that the Buddha, for the sake of future generations, will expound it so that they may attain understanding.
Should there be those who harbor doubts or lack faith in this sutra, they shall immediately fall into the evil realms. We pray that you will now provide an explanation.

These first two lines constitute the verse corresponding to our statement: "Although we have faith in the Buddha’s teachings as he has spoken them according to his suitability. The subsequent section beginning with "I pray that the Buddha...
constitutes the verse corresponding to "those who have newly resolved their minds," and so forth.
These immeasurable bodhisattvas—how could they have been taught and inspired to resolve for enlightenment, and established on the stage of non-retrogression, in such a short time?

This verse summarizes what is generally difficult to believe. The first two lines commemorate that not long has passed since they attained Buddhahood; the next two lines [commemorate their establishment].
The verse states that one is thus able to perform such deeds of great merit. This concludes the brief exposition.
The commentary on the "Chapter on the Emergence from the Earth" is finished. The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Sixteen: The Tathāgata’s Lifespan.
Regarding the origin of this chapter: although the provisional teachings of the three vehicles and five doctrines spoken by the Tathāgata have already been opened,
and the ultimate reality of the one vehicle has already been revealed,
there remain what are called the proximate traces of transformation enacted after the attainment of the fruit, and the remote foundation realized long ago, which have not yet been disclosed.
To reveal [the meaning], it is necessary to rely upon an introductory exhortation.
Therefore, although the Bodhisattvas from other directions had previously requested that the Sūtra be propagated, the Tathāgata restrained them.

By summoning those from the lower direction, immeasurable Bodhisattvas immediately surged forth from the earth, causing doubt to arise in the minds of Maitreya Bodhisattva and the rest of the assembly.
Regarding the "Question and Answer": there are instances where questions and answers arise in this manner; these are merely the preliminary lead-in (*youchi*) to the Main Gate (*benmen*).
Once the lead-in is manifest, the True Teaching (*zhengzong*) may then arise. Therefore, after the Tathāgata had answered Maitreya’s question, [the Main Gate begins].
Thus, he briefly opened up the near and briefly revealed the far. However, Maitreya Bodhisattva and the others again each moved from their attachments and gave rise to doubt;
they clung to the near while doubting the far, and clung to the far while doubting the near. To clarify this through analogy, it is said:

"It would be difficult for the whole world to believe that a father is young and his son is old," yet [Maitreya] says, "I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain this for me, so as to remove [my doubts]."
"We have doubts, and so too will the good sons of future ages upon hearing these words;
therefore, the Tathāgata now extensively elucidates what is near and reveals what is distant, thereby clarifying his long-lasting lifespan—this is the purpose of this chapter.
As for the term 'Tathāgata,' it means that the Tathāgata possesses three bodies (*trikāya*). If one speaks of the Vairocana..."
Vairocana pervades all places; every single form and every single fragrance is none other than the Middle Way—this is the Dharmakāya Tathāgata.

If one says that through the wisdom of suchness one accords with the principle of suchness, such that the principle is like suchness-wisdom and wisdom is like suchness-principle—this is the Sambhogakāya Tathāgata.
If one says that wisdom and principle merge in obscurity, yet are able to give rise to function, like the moon...
He is in the heavens; his reflection descends upon the myriad waters. This is the Nirmāṇakāya Tathāgata. If discussed in a general sense, here it refers solely to Śākyamuni Tathāgata;
however, if discussed in detail according to the text, since the subsequent passage mentions "all Buddhas and Tathāgatas," [it refers to them all].
All dharmas are thus. Therefore, the Tathāgata elucidated in this title also encompasses all Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
Regarding "lifespan" (*āyus-pramāṇa*): "life" (*āyus*) refers to the life-span; since there are the life-spans of the three bodies, there must necessarily be the measurement of the three lifespans.
As for the life-spans of the three bodies: the Tathāgata of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is, by virtue of its reality...
We offer this for your longevity. Whether a Buddha appears or does not appear, the nature and characteristics are eternally abiding. As stated in the subsequent text:
"Neither real nor unreal, neither suchness nor different"—this is the longevity of the Dharmakāya Tathāgata. As for the Saṃbhogakāya Tathāgata, wisdom constitutes his longevity.
The union of principle with wisdom is called "recompense" (saṃbhoga); the application of wisdom to accord with principle is his longevity. As stated in the subsequent text:

Such is the power of my wisdom; the light of my insight shines immeasurably. My lifespan spans incalculable kalpas, obtained through long-term cultivation of practice—this is the lifespan of the Sambhogakāya Tathāgata.
As for the Nirmāṇakāya Tathāgata, his lifespan is determined by the capacity and resonance of sentient beings.
Where there is form, life is long; where there is no form, life is short, as will be explained below.

It is neither born when it appears to be born, nor does it perish when it appears to perish; such is the lifespan of the Nirmāṇakāya Tathāgata. Regarding the measurement of the three types of lifespan:
the lifespan of the Dharmakāya is measured by being neither measurable nor immeasurable. As for the lifespan of the Saṃbhogakāya...
Prior to the Vajra Path, it is finite; subsequent to the Vajra Path, it is infinite. This serves as its measure.
Regarding the lifespan of the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body), it should correspond to the capacities of sentient beings. If the capacities of sentient beings are exhausted, it is finite;
