since that which arises from the essence is inexhaustible, it is also infinite. This serves as its measure. In sum, from—
The lifespan of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) up until the stage prior to the Vajra Path is finite.
From after the Vajra Path onward, the lifespan of the *saṃbhogakāya* (Enjoyment Body) is infinite. The lifespan of the *dharmakāya* (Dharma Body) is neither measurable nor infinite.
The lifespan of the *nirmāṇakāya* (Response Body) is both measurable and infinite. As it says in the passage below: "Since my attaining Buddhahood..."
"Greatly long-lasting; his lifespan is immeasurable for incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, eternally abiding and never perishing.
Thus, the "lifespan" mentioned here refers exclusively to the immeasurable lifespan of the *saṃbhogakāya* (Enjoyment Body). However, the *saṃbhogakāya* itself is not the *saṃbhogakāya*.
The Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya) necessarily possesses the Dharma Body (dharmakāya) and the Transformation Body (nirmāṇakāya); thus, the three bodies are perfectly complete.
Therefore, there are three bodies, three Tathāgatas, and likewise three spans of life.

If one were to discuss this specifically, the intent would be solely to reveal that Śākyamuni attained Buddhahood long ago and his lifespan is immeasurable, thereby manifesting his remote origin. Thus, although the Tathāgata is universal...
The three bodies of all Buddhas reside solely within the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body) of Śākyamuni.
Although longevity also extends to all three bodies, it is specifically the immeasurable lifespan of the *saṃbhogakāya* that constitutes what is called the "Chapter on the Lifespan of the Tathāgata.

Now, within this chapter, the first part clarifies his long and distant lifespan, while the subsequent part clarifies how he benefits sentient beings throughout the three periods of time; this is the title [of the current section].

In this section, only the span of his life is indicated, and the three periods of time are not mentioned. This is because his ability to benefit sentient beings throughout the three periods of time depends entirely upon the lifespan he has realized;
thus, the lifespan is the fundamental essence, while the three periods of time are the traces manifested from that essence.
Now, wishing to reveal the essence, he merely indicates the lifespan as the root, thereby encompassing the traces of the three periods of time. △ Second.

This consists of three parts: the broad opening, the manifestation of the near, and the revelation of the distant. First, the Tathāgata’s opening and manifestation; second, the attainment of the prediction by the Dharma-body;

third, Maitreya’s presentation and reception. Regarding the first two [of these], there are two sections: first, the admonition and exhortation; second, the formal exposition. Regarding the first of these four, there are three admonitions by the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas and the entire great assembly: "Sons of good family, you should have faith and understanding in the true and authentic words of the Tathāgata.
He further addressed the great assembly: "You should have faith and understanding in the true and authentic words of the Tathāgata.
And again he addressed the great assembly: "You should have faith and understanding in the true and authentic words of the Tathāgata."
The Tathāgata’s admonition consists of three sections. The first, beginning with "At that time," constitutes the first section.
The second, beginning with "Again he addressed," constitutes the second section. The third, beginning with "Furthermore he addressed," constitutes the third section.

Within the first section, the phrase "addressing all bodhisattvas" refers to the bodhisattvas who have come from other lands as transformation bodies, as well as the bodhisattvas of this land who have long resided here in Sahā. Below...
This refers to the fact that the various bodhisattvas have just now emerged; one should believe and understand the Tathāgata’s words of truth.

"Pointing to what preceded" refers to having already attained enlightenment at Gayā, whereupon he caused them to resolve their minds [on awakening]; this means that from time immemorial, he has been teaching and transforming these multitudes.
"Pointing to what followed" refers to the formal exposition below. Although there are differences between the extensive and the concise, or between the preceding and the following, they are the same.
Because it reveals both the fundamental and the manifested [aspects], these are indeed the Tathāgata’s words of true sincerity and ultimate reality.
They are spoken in accordance with principle and taught according to wisdom, for they are free from error or falsehood.
As they are words of sincere truth, you yourselves should naturally come to believe and understand them. "Belief" means believing that such a one is indeed the Tathāgata.
The "near traces" are, in this way, the "distant origin" of the Tathāgata. One who understands understands the traces of the Tathāgata;
there are no separate traces, for they are the traces manifested from the origin. One who understands understands the origin of the Tathāgata;
there is likewise no separate origin, for it is the origin revealed by the opening of the traces. This can be seen in both the second and third turns [of the wheel]. What...
Regarding the threefold admonition to believe: this lifespan of vast duration can only be known through direct realization;
it is fundamentally the most difficult thing to believe. Therefore, wishing to explain it, he first repeatedly issues these admonitions for the sake of inspiring faith.
△ Second, the Bodhisattva’s three requests.
At that time, the great assembly of bodhisattvas, with Maitreya at their head, joined their palms and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, we pray that you will speak of this;
we shall faithfully accept the words of the Buddha. Having thus petitioned three times, they remained silent.

Regarding "Maitreya as the leader": since Maitreya is destined to succeed Śākyamuni in the future, the lifespan that is to be revealed below is precisely what he is to realize and what he is to preach. Therefore, he was requested [to speak] as the leader.
"I only pray that you will speak. This expresses the wish to explain the causes and conditions of their near and distant origins. "Three times he said 'white'" refers to the three requests.
△ Third, the Bodhisattvas' repeated request:
they spoke again, saying, "I only pray that you will speak it. We shall faithfully accept the Buddha's words."
△ Fourth, the Tathāgata’s Repeated Admonition.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the bodhisattvas would not cease their threefold request, addressed them, saying: "Listen attentively."

It is said that those who possess these four admonitions and four requests perform the most supreme of deeds; therefore, they are treated with great solemnity. Part Two: The Actual Exposition, which has two sections.

First, the prose; second, the verses. The first [section] has three parts: first, the Dharma; second, the analogy; third, the application. The first [of these three] has two parts: first, clarifying the long-lasting lifespan;
second, clarifying the benefit of sentient beings throughout the three periods of time. The first [of these two] has three parts: first, directly relying on the Dharma...
He manifested the power of the Tathāgata’s secret supernatural penetrations. All the worlds—including devas, humans, and asuras—thought:
"Now Śākyamuni Buddha has departed from the palace of the Śākyas; not far from the city of Gayā, he sits at the site of enlightenment."

I have attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. However, son of good family, in reality, it has been immeasurable, boundless, hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas since I truly became a Buddha.

Regarding the phrase "First, the Tathāgata, etc.": "Spirit" (shen) refers to the innate principle possessed by the Tathāgata; "Penetration" (tong) refers to the enlightened wisdom possessed by the Tathāgata.
This principle and wisdom are, from the outset, equal in both the living and the Buddha, and identical for both the ordinary and the sage.
That which is common to all sentient beings can only be realized through wondrous wisdom by the Tathāgata alone.
This is the wondrous principle. When suchness and wisdom are thus unified as one, one spontaneously attains spiritual illumination and penetrates through transformation.
It encompasses the ten directions without exteriority and permeates the three periods of time without omission;

spanning from antiquity to the present, it is inexhaustible—this is indeed the power of the Tathāgata’s supernormal faculties (ṛddhi-bala). It is that which all sentient beings of the nine realms do not [attain].
It is called "secret" because it can be fathomed; it is termed "mysterious" because only a Buddha can exhaustively realize and know it. This first phrase provides a general explanation.
Next, from "all" onwards, the text specifically reveals the near to manifest the distant. Regarding the words "all" and so forth:

this means that once the Tathāgata has attained the power of secret supernatural faculties (*ṛddhi*), he possesses great sovereign mastery (*vaśitā*) and is thus able to manifest birth where there is no birth.
He preached the Dharma to transform and edify them; yet this was not a birth in the literal sense, but rather a manifestation of a proximate trace.
A proximate trace must necessarily derive from a remote origin. Thus, the Tathāgata possesses both the near and the far, both the trace and the origin.
While sentient beings know only the trace of the city of Gayā, they do not know the origin of his long-term realization. Therefore, he now reveals it for them.
The *Ji* (Trace) says: "All the world thinks that I have now attained bodhi. Since there is a near trace, there must be a distant origin;
therefore, its origin is revealed, saying: 'But, son of good family, it has actually been immeasurable kalpas since I truly attained buddhahood.
Indeed, the trace does not exist apart from the origin, nor does the origin exist apart from the trace; they are identical with the trace."
The fundamental is itself the trace; though the fundamental and the trace differ, they are one in their inconceivability.

Therefore, by revealing the proximate trace, the remote fundamental is immediately manifested. Such remote fundamentals and proximate traces all arise from the Tathāgata’s power of secret spiritual penetrations.
One should not cling to the proximate while doubting the remote, nor cling to the remote while doubting the proximate. △ Second, citing an analogy.
Section Two: Comparative Measurement. First, the Tathāgata asks:
Suppose there were five hundred thousand million billion *nayuta* *asaṃkhyeya* trichiliocosms, and someone were to grind them into fine dust.
Then, passing beyond five hundred thousand million billion *nayuta* *asaṃkhyeya* [worlds] to the east...
In the Saṃghāṭa world-system, one would drop a single mote of dust. Proceeding thus toward the east until all these motes of dust were exhausted—sons of good family, what do you think?
Is it possible to conceive of, calculate, or know the number of those world-systems?
△ Second, the Bodhisattvas’ response.
Maitreya Bodhisattva and the others together addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, these worlds are immeasurable and boundless;
they cannot be known by calculation, nor can they be reached by the power of the mind. All Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, by means of their outflow-free [wisdom]...”
Even with wisdom, one cannot contemplate or know their limit or number. We who dwell on the stage of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression) do not even reach an understanding of this matter.
World-Honored One, such worlds are immeasurable and boundless.

The phrase "not calculable by reckoning" clarifies that this is not known by ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). The phrase "all those below" clarifies that it is not known by those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
The phrase "we and others below" clarifies that it is not known by those who have attained non-retrogression (*avaivartika*). The phrase "World-Honored One" concludes the summary.
Thus, the reason why neither ordinary worldlings, nor those of the two vehicles, nor those who have attained non-retrogression can know its number is precisely the point of this analogy.

This is used as a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s long and far-reaching lifespan. As for the measure of this long and far-reaching lifespan, only the Buddhas are able to realize and know it exhaustively;
it cannot be known by the mundane wisdom of ordinary beings or the partial wisdom of those of the two vehicles.

Although Bodhisattvas are said to have attained partial realization, even if they reach the stage of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi), when compared to Wondrous Enlightenment (Suyabodhi), they are like looking at the moon through a fine silk screen;

thus, none of them can know [the Tathāgata’s lifespan]. Because they do not know the number of years of the Tathāgata’s long life, they likewise cannot know the number of the analogies used to measure it. △ Third, returning to the analogy with the Dharma.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the assembly of great bodhisattvas: "O sons of good family, I shall now clearly declare this to you:
take all these worlds—both those where atoms have been placed and those where they have not—and reduce them entirely to dust. Let each single atom represent one kalpa."
"Since I attained Buddhahood, more than these hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya kalpas have passed.
'Now I shall explain clearly' means that since you all do not know, I shall now distinguish and clarify it for you."

I have explained this for you. The first section, clarifying the long duration of his lifespan, is now complete. △ Second, clarifying how he benefits sentient beings throughout the three periods of time, which has three parts:

first, the actual clarification; second, the resolution of doubts; third, the demonstration that it is not in vain. The first part [the actual clarification] has three sections: first, clarifying how he benefited beings in the past; second, clarifying how he benefits beings in the present;

third, clarifying how he will benefit beings in the future. The first of these [benefiting beings in the past] has three subsections: first, clarifying how he descended from the fundamental to manifest traces.
Since that time, I have constantly remained in this Sahā world, preaching the Dharma and transforming sentient beings;
I have also guided and benefited living beings in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of asamkhyeya lands in other places.

The phrase "since that time" clarifies the manifestation from the fundamental source. The character "this" (is) specifically refers to the eons that have passed since attaining Buddhahood as mentioned above.
The section beginning with "I constantly" clarifies the descent of traces.
To say "constantly remaining here" means that at the time of descending traces, one does not depart from this Sahā world, nor is there any separate establishment elsewhere. That is to say:
This Sahā world of cohabitation is where I constantly reside. Therefore, the following verse says:
"Throughout incalculable kalpas, I have always been on Vulture Peak; while sentient beings see the end of the kalpa, my land remains peaceful and secure.
This means that I am constantly preaching the Dharma within the Sahā world. However, as for this land of cohabitation, if viewed from the perspective of the Tathāgata’s own realm...
It is entirely the Land of Peaceful Light (Sukhāvatī), yet sentient beings perceive it as the defiled land of Sahā.
Furthermore, "in other places" refers to responding to conditions wherever they arise in other directions; thus, the verse below says, "as well as in all other dwelling places.
One should know that being constantly present in Sahā and in other dwelling places are both manifestations of his proximity, yet this—
These traces all derive from what was manifested from the fundamental source. II. Explaining the Revelation of Traces to Manifest the Fundamental Source:
"O sons of good family, during this interval, I spoke of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara and others, and further stated that they entered into parinirvāṇa.
All such things were distinguished through skillful means."
Regarding "in the interim": this refers to the interval within this manifestation [of the Buddha's traces].
When I speak of "Dīpaṃkara and others," I am referring to the time when he offered seven stalks of flowers to the Buddha while practicing the causal stages;

at that time, Dīpaṃkara Buddha said, "You shall become a Buddha," and thus bestowed the prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*). As for the statement that he "entered into *nirvāṇa*," the word "his" (the pronoun *其*) is not... [omitted].
"Referring to Dīpaṃkara" means referring to the period during which Śākyamuni manifested his traces, wherein he taught and transformed sentient beings in the form of a bodhisattva;

when the karmic capacities of those beings were exhausted, he likewise entered extinction. To say that "all such [accounts] are distinguished by means of skillful means" means to clarify his causal practices, to clarify his receiving of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), and to clarify his entry into extinction—all of these are merely distinctions made through skillful means. Since this is so...
Expedient means are not the ultimate reality. That which is the ultimate reality has, in fact, realized the Way long ago.

To speak of these as "expedient means" and "distinctions" is to open up the provisional traces. Previously, had these not been called expedient means, the provisional traces would have remained closed;
now that they are called expedient means, the traces are opened and their fundamental basis is revealed. △ Third, clarifying the traces.
This is for the mutual benefit of beings. O sons of good family, if there are sentient beings who come to me, I observe their faith and other faculties—
whether sharp or dull— with my Buddha-eye, and according to what each should receive, [I teach them].

This means that since the Tathāgata has already realized the fundamental (ben), he must manifest traces (ji) from that very foundation. Therefore, this clarifies the benefits found within those traces.
"If there are sentient beings" refers to sentient beings who possess various capacities—whether complete or partial, sudden or gradual, provisional or real, Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna—and who come to me.
That is to say, they approach by striking and invoking [the Buddha's response] through these various capacities.
"Buddha. Regarding the phrase "I [behold] with the Buddha-eye," it means that since there is already a responsive capacity [in the sentient being], a response must necessarily be bestowed.
Therefore, I behold their capacity with the Buddha-eye. If this were merely observing the capacity, one would employ the Dharma-eye;
however, the term "Buddha-eye" is used here because all four eyes are subsumed within the Buddha-eye, and thus all are designated as the Buddha-eye. He observes their faith.
"Those with equal faculties" (*samendriya*): "faculties" refers to the five faculties; "faith" refers to the faculty of faith;
"equal" means equal to the four faculties of energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. "Sharp and dull": "sharp" means quick and keen; "dull" means slow and obtuse.

If distinguished according to the four teachings, the three [lesser] teachings are considered dull, while the Perfect Teaching (*vairocana-yāna*) is considered sharp. "According to those to be saved": according to their...

That which is appropriate for the capacities of sentient beings is how they are to be transformed and delivered. If their capacity is perfect (yuan), they should be delivered through the perfect and harmonious (yuanrong);

if their capacity is distinct (bie), they should be delivered through the sequential and distinct (lilie); if their capacity is universal (tong), they should be delivered through the realization of emptiness (tisong);
if their capacity is hidden (zang), they should be delivered through the analytical negation of emptiness (xisong). Therefore, it is said that [the Buddha] delivers according to what is appropriate.
Furthermore, in various places he speaks of his own name as being different, and his age as being greater or smaller; he also manifests by saying that he shall enter nirvana.
This means that once sentient beings have produced the conditions for response and the Tathāgata has manifested the response, then the Way of resonance and response will naturally act accordingly.

He preaches the Dharma. When preaching the Dharma, he may manifest birth where there is no birth; therefore, it is said that in various places he speaks of his own names being different, and his age being greater or smaller.
"Names" refers to the difference between the superior response-body (victorious response) and the inferior response-body;
the superior response-body has a great age, while the inferior response-body has a small age. Or, he may manifest extinction where there is no extinction, and thus likewise says:
When entering *nirvāṇa*, one should deliver them through extinction; thus, one brings about their extinction.
These are all benefits within the realm of form.
Furthermore, by means of various skillful expedients (*upāya*), one preaches the subtle and wondrous Dharma, enabling sentient beings to give rise to a heart of joy.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "by means of various [expedients]," it means that he does not merely manifest benefit through form, but is also able to manifest benefit through sound.
These "various expedients" refer to the three vehicles, the five teachings, and the seven types of expedients; these constitute the prior bestowal of provisional means (*upāya*).
The "subtle and wondrous Dharma" refers to the ultimate, subtle, and wondrous Dharma of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*); this constitutes the subsequent [bestowal of the ultimate truth].
This reveals the truth. By expounding the subtle and sublime true Dharma, one naturally causes the assembly to rejoice;
even when speaking of expedient means, one ultimately leads them back to the ultimate reality, and thus likewise enables sentient beings to rejoice.
Thus, throughout the past, the Tathāgata was able to manifest traces from his fundamental source, revealing the remote through the near and thereby bringing about various benefits.
Whether appearing in superior or inferior forms, or preaching provisional or ultimate teachings,
all of this is due to the fact that the Tathāgata has long since realized an immeasurable lifespan.

△ Second, clarifying the present benefit of sentient beings. Part one: The Tathāgata’s discernment of capacities.
"O sons of good family, when the Tathāgata sees sentient beings who delight in inferior teachings—those of meager virtue and heavy defilements—he says they 'delight in inferior teachings.
By 'delighting in inferior teachings,' he does not merely refer to those who are attached to a nirvana that is empty, signless, and wishless;
rather, it refers generally to those who cannot penetrate the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena and instead take pleasure in..."
There are those who take delight in the dharmas of precepts and goodness; some take delight in the dharma of emptiness regarding the conditions of the truths (*satya*);
others take delight in the dharma of distinct particulars. All such are said to delight in the Lesser Dharma (*hīnayāna*).

Furthermore, those who know only what is near and delight in its traces, without realizing that there is yet a further long and distant primordial source, are also called people who delight in the Lesser. Being of meager virtue, they are unable to practice.
Regarding the two causes—the conditional and the consummate—when defilements are heavy, there are many of the three delusions. △ Second, opening up the near to reveal the distant:
it was for such people that I said, "I left home at a young age and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

However, in truth, the time since I actually attained Buddhahood has been as long as this. It is only by means of skillful means (*upāya*) that I have taught and transformed sentient beings, leading them into the Buddha-way."
The Way is established in this manner.
"For such people" refers to those whose virtue is meager and whose defilements are heavy;
for their sake, the Tathāgata says, "I left home at nineteen and attained the Way at thirty," and thus speaks of having "left home young and attained Bodhi."
This was an explanation of the near; however, what follows from "But I" below is intended to reveal the distant.
The preceding discourse was merely for those of meager merit and heavy defilements.

In reality, since I attained the Way, it has been exceedingly long—far exceeding the immeasurable kalpas illustrated by the analogies previously cited. Yet, despite such a vast duration, [I have appeared] only because...
Regarding the word "etcetera": since it has been such a vast duration [of time], one could not have attained *bodhi* recently;
yet, to say that he left home at a young age and attained Buddhahood so soon is nothing more than a teaching given through skillful means (*upāya*) as appropriate to the occasion.

It was spoken solely with the desire to convert those sentient beings who delight in inferior teachings, whose virtue is meager, and whose defilements are heavy, so as to lead them into the Buddha-way. Thus, this was said. Now...
This was spoken as a skillful means; it is that I actually attained the Way long ago.
This passage reveals the recent traces of his initial renunciation and the near attainment of the Buddha-way, while manifesting the distant origin of his long-standing realization of Buddhahood.
△ Section Three: Benefiting Beings within the Traces (2). First, explaining the preaching of the Dharma:
"O sons of good family, all the sūtras expounded by the Tathāgata are for the purpose of liberating sentient beings; some speak of his own person."
Some speak of another’s body; some show their own body; some show another’s body; some show their own affairs; some show another’s affairs. The first two phrases constitute the general heading.
The subsequent "some speak of their own body" and so forth constitute the actual exposition. The heading is evident.
Within the actual exposition, speaking of one's own body refers to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); speaking of another’s body refers to the Response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
"Body. To show one's own body is to point to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). To show another's body is to point to the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
To show one's own affairs is to point by means of the primary retribution (*vipākaphala*). To show another's affairs is to point by means of the environmental retribution (*bhājanaloka*).
Whether it be the Dharma and the response, or the environment and the primary retribution—whether through exposition or pointing—these are all what is meant by [the teaching].

Regarding the phrase "the expounding of the sūtras": since the preceding text refers to "the sūtras being expounded" and the subsequent text speaks of "all that is spoken," it is understood that the passage concerning "one's own body and its affairs" and so forth all belong to what is being taught.
Furthermore, there is no necessity to distinguish between form and sound in order to explain this.
Therefore, this is simply referred to as "discourse. △ Second, clarifying that it is not false, in two parts.
First, the actual clarification: All that is spoken is real and not false.
The two phrases herein refer to the aforementioned statements, ranging from "speaking of one's own self" to "indicating matters concerning others.
Such teachings are all intended for the liberation of sentient beings; therefore, they are all thoroughly authentic and not false.

△ Second, the explanation of the two [aspects of non-falsity]. First, clarifying that it is not false because it accords with reality; second, clarifying that it is not false because it accords with the capacities [of beings].
The first section has three parts.
First, the formal statement: "Why is this so? Because the Tathāgata knows and perceives the characteristics of the triple world as they truly are."

Regarding the knowledge and vision of the characteristics of the three realms as they truly are: if one refers to the three realms within the world of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), there are the characteristics of the fruit of suffering—segmented birth and death (*pariccheda-jarāmaraṇa*)—within the twenty-five states of existence, as well as the characteristics of the accumulated causes of the ten underlying afflictions (*anuśaya*).

If one refers to the three realms outside the world of phenomena, there are the characteristics of the fruit of suffering—transformational birth and death (*pariṇāma-jarāmaraṇa*)—in forty-two stages, as well as [the characteristics of] the forty...
Regarding the characteristics of the two types of ignorance as the cause for the accumulation of afflictions: within the three realms of existence, ordinary beings know and perceive them as existent;
those of the Two Vehicles know and perceive them as empty; and Bodhisattvas know and perceive them as the Middle Way.
Since each of these has its own partiality, none can be said to possess "knowledge according to reality" (*yathābhūta-jñāna*) or "vision according to reality" (*yathābhūta-darśana*). Only...

The Tathāgata is thus able to know all three types of wisdom within a single moment of mind and see with all five eyes within a single eye; therefore, he knows and sees the characteristics of the triple world.
When there is existence, there is the existence of all things—this is not the same as the existence known and seen by ordinary beings.
When there is emptiness, there is the emptiness of all things—this is not the same as the emptiness known and seen by those of the Two Vehicles.
To be centered means that within one center, all are centered. This is not the same as the center known and seen by Bodhisattvas.
Such knowledge is called "knowledge according to reality" (*yathābhūta-jñāna*); such seeing is called "seeing according to reality" (*yathābhūta-darśana*).
This single phrase serves as the heading. △ Second, the detailed explanation.
There is no birth-and-death, neither retreating nor emerging; nor is there one abiding in the world, nor one who has entered parinirvāṇa.
It is neither real nor unreal, neither like this nor otherwise.
Regarding the phrase "there is no birth and death, etc.": ordinary beings perceive existence as having form;
therefore, within the three realms and six paths of rebirth, they are born and then die, and having died, they are born again, transmigrating in an endless cycle.
Now, the Tathāgata is able to know and see the characteristics of the three realms as they truly are, and thus differs from ordinary beings; for this reason, there is no birth or death.

Ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) create various kinds of evil karma; they may fall away from the human or celestial realms and descend into the three miserable paths (*trāya-patha*), and thus there is "receding.
Or, when their retribution for offenses in the three miserable paths is exhausted, they emerge as humans or celestials, and thus there is "emerging.
Since the Tathāgata is not like ordinary beings, he has neither such receding nor such emerging. As for those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*), they possess the mundane...
Regarding the causes and effects of the mundane world: because one can know suffering and sever its origin, it is said that there is "neither remaining in the world.
Regarding the causes and effects of the supramundane: because one can cultivate the path and realize cessation, it is said that there are "those who have attained extinction.

Now, the Tathāgata is able to know and see the characteristics of the three realms as they truly are, and thus differs from those of the two vehicles; therefore, he likewise "neither remains in the world."
There is neither a mundane world nor a supramundane state of extinction.

That which is neither real nor false, neither suchness nor different, is the view of the partial and gradual Bodhisattvas, who determinately perceive that there is a bodhi to be attained and a nirvana to be realized.
Therefore, this is real. It is certain that there are afflictions to be destroyed and birth-and-death to be severed; therefore, it is false.

Now, the Tathāgata differs from the Bodhisattva in that he thoroughly understands that *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa* are originally nothing other than birth-and-death and afflictions, and that there is nothing to be realized or attained;
therefore, it is not real. He thoroughly understands that afflictions and birth-and-death are originally nothing other than *bodhi*.
He teaches Nirvana. Since there is nothing therein that can be destroyed or severed, it is not false. The partial and gradual Bodhisattvas see emptiness by departing from existence;
therefore, this is "as-it-is" (tathatā). They see the Middle Way by departing from both emptiness and existence; therefore, this is "other.

Now, the Tathāgata differs from these Bodhisattvas in that he is able to simultaneously negate and simultaneously illuminate, such that both the biased and the deviant become the central and correct. Thus, since...
It is neither identical nor different. △ Third, the conclusion:
That which is not like the triple world yet is seen within the triple world—such a matter the Tathāgata perceives clearly, without any error.

Regarding the phrase "not like those within the three realms": this is because those within the three realms perceive the three realms in various ways—some perceive them as existent, some perceive them as empty, and some perceive them as being in between.
The Tathāgata, however, differs from those who perceive the three realms in such ways, for he is able to know and see them as they truly are. Such a matter is precisely...

This is the characteristic of the three realms. It is also the exit from birth and death for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), the extinction-in-this-life for those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), and the distinction between the real and the unreal for Bodhisattvas.

That the Tathāgata perceives these clearly without error means that the Tathāgata does not share the views of the three realms; therefore, he perceives the characteristics of the three realms as non-existent.

This is erroneous. It means that although the Tathāgata is without birth-and-death, and so forth up to "difference" and the like, regarding such matters he is able to see clearly without error. "Error" (*cò*) refers to deviation; "delusion" (*miù*) refers to falsehood.
This is because the Tathāgata is able to know through the three wisdoms within a single moment of mind, and see through the five eyes within a single eye, having ultimately realized...
The true reality of all phenomena is such that the ultimate of one is the ultimate of all; the purity of one is the purity of all;
and the mastery of one is the mastery of all. It is by knowing such matters and seeing such matters that this is understood.
All are entirely consistent with the true nature (dharmatā) and do not contradict it; they are all completely and identically the true nature, without any error.
Since the Tathāgata is thus able to know and see such characteristics within the triple world as they truly are, he is without error.
Thus, whatever is spoken is entirely in accordance with the principles of what is known; how could there be any falsehood? Therefore, it was stated above that all that is taught is not false.
△ Second, clarifying that [the teaching] is not false because it accords with the capacities [of beings].
Because sentient beings possess various natures, various inclinations, various conducts, and various conceptualizations and discriminations, [the Buddha],
wishing to cause them to give rise to roots of goodness, teaches the Dharma in various ways through numerous causes, conditions, parables, and expressions.
The Buddha-works he performs have never been suspended for even a moment.
Regarding the phrase "because all sentient beings are equal": it means that the Tathāgata does not speak merely according to the principle [of truth], and thus his words are not false;

furthermore, he is able to speak in accordance with their capacities, and thus his words are likewise not false. This is because sentient beings possess various dispositions, inclinations, conducts, and conceptions.
Because these are not the same, the Tathāgata also teaches various dharmas to accommodate them accordingly;
therefore, it was said above that all that is spoken is real and not false. What is now called "various natures" refers to the various habitual tendencies of the past.
"Various desires" refers to the various inclinations of the present.

"Various practices" refers to all external activities of the present body. "Recollection, thought, and discrimination" is a summary of the dispositions (*dhātu*) and the perceptions of practice (*saṃskāra-saṃjñā*).
All of this clarifies the capacities (*indriya*) of sentient beings. "Wishing to [teach] below" clarifies preaching the Dharma in accordance with those capacities.
The phrase "by means of various causes and conditions" refers to the dispositions, natures, practices, and perceptions of sentient beings.
Since these are manifold and not identical, when the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma, he accords with their respective capacities,
employing various causes and conditions, various parables, and various expressions.
As for this "manifold preaching of the Dharma," it means that when he perceives sentient beings who possess the capacity to attain joy, he then teaches them the *loka-nirukti* (worldly explanations).
Regarding the Dharma of *dāna*: even when seeing sentient beings who possess the capacity to enter into the principle, one preaches for them the Dharma of the *paramārtha-siddhānta*.

Although various teachings are thus expounded, they never concern the affairs of the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*), nor the affairs of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), nor the affairs of the partial or gradual [teachings]. They are intended solely for—
This is the work of a Buddha. Furthermore, the Buddha-work performed is not limited to a single thought-moment; rather, it is so in every thought-moment.
It is not limited to a single moment; rather, it is so at every moment. It is not limited to a single place; rather, it is so in every place.
Therefore, it is said that it has never been suspended for even an instant. Thus, the Tathāgata is able to discern within the present world.

The capacity [of the teaching] reveals the near while manifesting the far. Even those who receive benefit within the provisional traces do so because they are able to realize the long duration of the Buddha’s lifespan.
△ Third, clarifying the future benefit for sentient beings, in two parts: first, the longevity of the fruit.
In this way, since I attained Buddhahood, a very long time has passed; my lifespan is immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, eternally abiding and never perishing.
From the beginning until these *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, this clarifies that the lifespan realized in the state of fruition is long and far-reaching.
Regarding the statement that it is "eternally abiding and indestructible": by means of the life-span of the realized fruit, within future ages, it does not arise yet manifests as arising;

though it arises, in reality it does not arise. It does not perish yet manifests as perishing; though it perishes, in reality it does not perish. Thus, it benefits sentient beings eternally and without end.
For this reason, it is explained directly in terms of the life-span of the fruit. II. Illustrating by means of the cause.
"O sons of good family, the lifespan I achieved while originally practicing the bodhisattva path is still not yet exhausted; it is even twice as long as the number mentioned above.

This is an illustration of the cause by means of the effect, and the shallow by means of the profound. 'While I was originally [practicing],' etc., refers to when the Bodhisattva had already reached the first stage (bhūmi)."
This refers to the lifespan attained through partial realization. Because it is a result of partial realization, it is called a "cause.

Such a retributive lifespan naturally extends to the end of the future, surpassing the vast distance of eons as numerous as motes of dust mentioned above; therefore, it is said to be "twice the number above."
Since the lifespan of the cause is already thus, it goes without saying that the future lifespan of the fruit will be eternal. This is why the cause is cited as an illustration.
The preceding section has correctly elucidated the three periods of time. Part Two: Resolving Doubts, in two sections. First: Clarifying the proclamation of extinction within the traces.
However, at present there is no actual parinirvāṇa, yet he proclaims that he shall attain parinirvāṇa.

Regarding the phrase "at present" and so forth: some may ask, since the Tathāgata’s lifespan is immeasurable and he dwells eternally without ceasing, why does he manifest birth and manifestation of cessation within the three periods of time, as if there were actually birth and cessation? Therefore, it is explained as follows:
However, the present is not truly so. The Tathāgata is fundamentally neither born nor extinguished;

yet, for the sake of transforming sentient beings, he manifests birth, though his birth is in truth no birth. For the sake of transforming sentient beings, he manifests extinction, though his extinction is in truth no extinction.
However, his manifest birth can be understood as a transformation-birth (*nirmāṇa-upapatti*). His manifest extinction is likewise a transformation-birth;

that is to say, for those who are to be delivered through extinction, he manifests extinction. Since non-extinction would cause harm, while extinction brings benefit, he therefore manifests extinction.
This, too, is for the sake of transforming sentient beings. 2. Clarifying the Benefit of Proclaiming Extinction.
There are two further benefits. First, there is the prevention of decline.
The Tathāgata employs these skillful means to teach and transform sentient beings. Why is this? If the Buddha were to remain in the world for a long time...
Those of meager virtue do not plant roots of goodness; they are poor and lowly, greedily attached to the five desires, and have entered into the net of false views and discursive thoughts.
If they see the Tathāgata as always present and never perishing, they immediately give rise to arrogance and self-indulgence, harboring weariness and indolence.
They are unable to give rise to the thought that [the Dharma] is difficult to encounter, nor do they develop a heart of reverence.
By such means, one transforms sentient beings through the expedient of proclaiming extinction where there is no extinction.
Regarding the subsequent explanation of the downward turning, it first clarifies that those who do not hear the Dharma suffer loss; such people are those of meager merit.
They are unable to hear the Dharma and practice in accordance with the teachings; thus, they do not cultivate [the path]. They have not planted roots of goodness;

that is, they do not cultivate the two causes—the conditional (*pratyaya*) and the investigative (*nirvedha*). Since they do not cultivate these two causes, the true cause (*dharmatā-hetu*) has no means by which it can be manifested.
Furthermore, lacking the wealth of merit and Dharma as adornment, they are said to be "poor, lowly, and base. Since they lack...
Regarding "merit and the wealth of the Dharma," there is merely various conceptualization and craving; thus it is said that they "cling to the five desires and enter the net of false views.
Craving is the affliction of thought (*vitarka-kleśa*), which clings to the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*).

False views are the afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), which involve clinging to all phenomena and giving rise to discrimination. The section beginning with "If one sees" clarifies the person who hears the Dharma.
There is also harm for those who give rise to arrogance and self-indulgence. "Arrogance" (憍) refers to self-conceit; "self-indulgence" (恣) refers to unrestrained license.

To give rise to these is the arrogance and self-indulgence of overweening pride (*adhimāna*), whereby one claims to have attained what has not been attained and claims to have realized what has not been realized.

"Those who harbor weariness and indolence" refers to those who take pleasure only in the Lesser Dharma and are unwilling to advance. "Unable to gather them all under [the banner of] humility" means that if the Tathāgata were present...
In this world, those who have not heard the Dharma become greedily attached to the five desires and enter into false views;

those who have already heard the Dharma give rise to arrogance and indulgence, harboring weariness and indolence. In short, all of them are unable to conceive the thought that the Dharma is difficult to encounter, nor do they possess a heart of reverence.
If such is the case, then even while the Tathāgata is in the world, there will be harm. II. Manifestation.
This cessation is beneficial.
Therefore, the Tathāgata speaks by means of skillful means: "Bhikṣus, you should know that the appearance of Buddhas in the world is difficult to encounter.
Why is this? Because those of meager merit may, after passing through immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas, perhaps see a Buddha."
Or, regarding those who do not see [the Tathāgata]: for this reason, I say, "O monks, the Tathāgata is difficult to encounter.
When these sentient beings hear such words, they will surely conceive the thought that he is hard to meet;
with hearts full of longing and yearning for the Buddha, they will plant roots of goodness. For this purpose, although the Tathāgata does not truly pass into extinction, he speaks of extinction.
[The Buddha] said:

"The Buddha is difficult to encounter. If one says that the Buddha is as difficult to meet as the udumbara flower, or like a one-eyed turtle encountering the hole of a floating log, sentient beings who hear this will certainly conceive the thought that he is difficult to encounter and will develop a heart of reverence."

It is beneficial; therefore, it manifests cessation. As for those of inferior capacity who are explained below, they are those who cannot cultivate the six perfections and myriad practices and thus lack the causal conditions; they cannot cultivate the wondrous contemplation of the single mind.
Yet there are those who lack the cause of realization. Those with a modicum of wisdom whose hindrances are slight may sometimes see the Buddha;
those who entirely lack wisdom and whose hindrances are deep and heavy do not see him.

This [passage] concludes the preceding section by summarizing that, because he desires sentient beings to cherish and long for him, to give rise to thirsting admiration, and to plant roots of goodness, he manifests extinction even though he does not actually pass away.
In short, throughout the three periods of time, it is not that there is birth when there is no birth, nor extinction when there is no extinction;
all these are for the sake of transforming sentient beings, yet in reality, there is neither birth nor extinction. △ Third, Non-falsity.
Furthermore, son of good family, the Dharma of all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, is thus: for the sake of delivering sentient beings, it is entirely real and not false.

That the Dharma of all Buddhas is thus means that it is not only I, Śākyamuni, who possess such a long lifespan and am able to benefit beings throughout the three periods of time; rather, this applies to all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
Furthermore, there is such a lifespan as this, which is able to benefit beings throughout the three periods of time; all such cases are likewise so.

That it is for the sake of delivering sentient beings and is entirely real and not false means that although the Tathāgata manifests birth and extinction, it is solely for the sake of sentient beings and is in reality neither born nor extinguished.
Since there is no birth or extinction, there is only an eternally long lifespan, which is ultimately true.
It is real and not false. This concludes the first section on the Dharma. Second, the analogy:

It means that although the Tathāgata has fundamentally realized an eternally long life-span, his manifesting birth and manifesting extinction throughout the three periods of time are entirely for the sake of delivering sentient beings.
In reality, there is neither arising nor ceasing, yet it is not empty. To clarify this through a metaphor, it is like a skilled physician.
Although the skilled physician appears to come and go, he does so solely for the sake of treating his deluded children; in truth, there is no coming or going, yet it is not empty.

This passage consists of four parts: first, a metaphor for benefiting beings in the past; second, a metaphor for benefiting beings in the present; third, a metaphor for [benefiting beings in the] future...

They come to benefit sentient beings. The four clarifications establish that the metaphor is not empty. Regarding the first two [clarifications], the first metaphor—that what is not born appears as born—is like a skilled physician who is wise and discerning, well-versed in prescriptions and medicines, and adept at curing all manner of illnesses.
Regarding the "skilled physician": a skilled physician observes the complexion, listens to the voice, and examines the pulse, thereby being able to know the disease.

This is used as an analogy for the Tathāgata, who is able to expound the Dharma through the wheel of speech, manifest supernormal powers through the wheel of body, and discern the capacities of beings through the wheel of mind.
Regarding "possessing wisdom and intelligence": the skilled physician possesses wisdom, whereby he can understand the principles within medicinal substances; he possesses intelligence, whereby...
Being able to identify the root source within an illness is analogous to the Tathāgata possessing wisdom, which enables him to know the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
Possessing sagacity and penetration, he is able to discern whether the faculties (*indriya*) of beings are sharp or dull.

One who is skilled in compounding prescriptions is like a master physician who can skillfully compound medicinal formulas consisting of sovereign, minister, adjunct, and assistant ingredients, and who clearly understands the medicinal properties of cold, heat, sweet, and pungent flavors.
This is analogous to the Tathāgata, who is able to know the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates and can clearly elucidate the eighty-four thousand pāramitās.
Regarding the "skillful treatment of various ailments": these various ailments refer to the disharmony of the earth element, which results in diseases of stagnation;
the disharmony of the wind element, which results in diseases of trembling; and the disharmony of the water element, which results in diseases of congestion and swelling.
Regarding these illnesses: when the fire element is disturbed, there is the illness of feverish heat.
A skilled physician can treat that which is cold with heat, and that which is hot with cold, being fully capable of providing effective treatment.
By way of analogy, this refers to sentient beings who possess greed, those who possess anger, those who possess delusion, and those who possess an equal proportion of all three. And...
The Tathāgata possesses eighty-four thousand Dharma-gates to manifest eighty-four thousand pāramitās,
thereby treating the eighty-four thousand afflictions of sentient beings. The above all serves as a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s capacity for responsive manifestation.
That person has many children—perhaps ten, twenty, or even up to a hundred.

This is a metaphor for the responsive capacity of sentient beings. Having "many children" signifies that the Tathāgata, through his unconditioned compassion, universally covers all sentient beings of the nine realms and the three vehicles, regarding the four modes of birth as equal to an only child.
Since the three realms are treated with equal benevolence, there is not a single sentient being who is not a child of the Tathāgata; thus it is said that "there are many children.
Ten such beings are the children of the Śrāvakas; twenty are the children of the Pratyekabuddhas; and those numbering in the hundreds are the children of the Bodhisattvas.
Because they manifest through responsive transformation, they do not arise from birth, yet they cause sentient beings to obtain benefit.
...Furthermore, △ Second, the metaphor of non-extinction appearing as extinction:
because of certain circumstances, [the fire] travels far away to another country.
If the fuel of the mechanism were to suddenly cease, then the fire ought to perish; yet it does not perish, though it appears to do so. Therefore, it is said:

Because of certain circumstances, he travels far to another land; that is to say, the spiritual capacity (*mārga*) of this realm is exhausted, while conditions arise elsewhere, so he abandons this place to go to that one.
This metaphor illustrates that in the past, there was neither birth manifested as birth nor cessation manifested as cessation, yet he benefited sentient beings.
△ Second, the metaphor for benefiting beings in the present has two parts: first, the metaphor for non-birth manifested as birth; second, the metaphor for non-
The cessation of what is presently ceasing. The first five [verses] illustrate how, at the outset, those of the three vehicles were turned by the false;
subsequently, the sons drank another’s poisonous medicine, and when the medicine took effect, they became dazed and disoriented, wallowing upon the ground.
"The sons" refers to the sons of the three vehicles' spiritual capacities. "Thereafter" means after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa.
"Drinking another's poisoned medicine" is a metaphor for encountering a false teacher and receiving their false teachings.
If the Buddha were in the world, they would receive the true Dharma; because it is after the Buddha’s extinction, they receive the false teachings of a false teacher. And this falsity...
The Dharma [of such a kind] can destroy the Dharma-body and can extinguish the life of wisdom, just as worldly toxic drugs can destroy the body and life.
"The medicine causes dizziness and confusion" is a metaphor for how, once one has received false teachings, one gives rise to false views, perhaps adhering to the view of annihilationism.
Or they may calculate [existence] as permanent, like one who faints and becomes disoriented when medicine takes effect.
Once such false views have arisen, they will in turn invite bitter fruits and fall into the three miserable realms, wallowing upon the ground.

Thus, although their initial aspiration was fundamentally to seek escape from the triple world, because they have received false teachings and given rise to false views, not only do they fail to leave the triple world, but—
Instead, they fall into the three miserable realms. This is to seek ascent but instead descend; to seek emergence but instead enter [the cycle].
△ Second, an analogy for the Tathāgata’s manifestation of birth within the triple world.
At that time, his father returned home.

"Returning home" means that the Tathāgata, knowing that the children of the triple world were receiving false teachings and wishing to uproot those errors, returned to manifest birth within the household of the triple world.
△ Third, the parable of the Brahmā King requesting the turning of the wheel.
The Wheel of Dharma.
Among the sons who had drunk poison, some had lost their original minds while others had not;

upon seeing their father from afar, they all rejoiced greatly, prostrated themselves, and offered greetings, saying, "We have returned safely and in good health. We were foolish and mistakenly took poison; we pray that you will save and heal us."
Furthermore, they are granted an extension of life.

To lose one's original mind is to lose the seeds of the three vehicles (*triyāna*). If they are not lost, then even though one may receive false teachings, the seeds of the three vehicles have not yet been lost.
Because one is turned by what is false, it is called "remote. Originally, it is suchness (*tathatā*).
Those who were transformed in the past have a natural affinity with [the Buddha] by virtue of their innate nature; therefore, it is said that they "saw their father.

As for "all were greatly joyful," although there was a distinction between those whose minds were deranged and those whose minds were not, because they had all seen the Tathāgata, they were all filled with joy.
Regarding "having returned safely and in peace," this means that the Tathāgata is one who can bring us to a state of perfect safety and tranquility. Now...
They return to be born within the three realms and thus come back. As for "the foolish and deluded": "foolish" refers to ignorance, while "deluded" refers to perverse attachment.
The Three Vehicles are the correct path; yet because of their ignorance, they lose them. The false teachings are erroneous; this is due to their perverse attachment.
They have been turned by those [demons]. "We pray that you will save us and grant us further life.

Since we have mistakenly received false teachings, our Dharma-body and the life of wisdom shall surely perish. We pray that you will turn the Wheel of Dharma and once again preach the true Dharma of the Three Vehicles, so that our Dharma-body and the life of wisdom may grow anew. △ Fourth, the analogy is as follows:

Coming forth to establish the teaching according to the capacities of beings, the Father saw that his sons were suffering in such a manner; thus, relying on the prescriptions of various sutras, he sought excellent medicinal herbs of fine color, fragrance, and flavor.

All were fully prepared; they were pounded, sifted, and mixed together, then given to the sons to drink, saying: "This great and excellent medicine is complete in its color, fragrance, and fine flavor.
You should take it; it will swiftly eliminate your suffering and affliction, so that you shall no longer have any further ailments."

"Suffering" refers to the cause of suffering, which consists of afflictions and delusions (*kleśa-jñeya-āvaraṇa*), and its fruit, which is the suffering of birth and death within the realms of transmigration (*pariccheda-duḥkha*).

"The scriptures" refers to the Tripitaka and the twelve divisions of the canon. "Excellent medicinal herbs" is a metaphor for the subtle and wondrous Dharma-gates. "Color, fragrance, and flavor" are metaphors for precepts (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).

To give rise to understanding based on the teachings is like pounding [the herbs]; to give rise to practice based on understanding is like sifting [them]; and to enter realization based on practice is like [taking the medicine].
It is like a medicinal compound. "To cause them to take it" means to cause them to rely upon it for cultivation and realization.
"You all may take it," and so forth, means that you all may give rise to understanding based on the teaching, and give rise to practice based on that understanding;
once practice has arisen, one is able to enter into realization. Thus, not only will you not be turned aside by what is false, but you will also be able to realize nirvana.
Having destroyed the afflictions of views and thoughts and emerged from the triple world, it is said that "suffering and distress are swiftly eliminated.
△ Fifth, the parable of the sons hearing the Dharma and practicing it:
Among those sons, those who had not lost their minds saw this excellent medicine, whose color and fragrance were both excellent, and immediately took it.
The illness was completely eliminated and healed;

its effects were visible through their practice. This concludes the analogy for that which is not born appearing as born. △ Second, the analogy for that which is not extinguished appearing as extinguished:
Because those who possess the lineage of the Three Vehicles have been turned by false [views], that which is not born appears as born; yet one desires to uproot them.
[Objection: It is false. [Response: Those who have not lost their seeds, although they have already received transformation, may still lose their seeds and thus fail to practice accordingly;

therefore, they are not yet liberated from the present state of cessation, even though they have returned to it. The text is divided into two parts; the first is a metaphor for how there is impairment despite non-cessation.
As for the others whose minds were deranged, when they saw their father coming, they likewise greeted him with joy and asked for medicine to cure their illness;
yet, although he gave them the medicine, they refused to take it. Why was this? Because the toxic vapors had penetrated deeply and they had lost their original minds;
thus, they found no pleasure in these excellent colors, fragrances, and medicines. The father thought to himself: "This son is pitiable, having been struck by poison."
Their minds are entirely inverted. Although they see me and rejoice, seeking a remedy for their afflictions, they are unwilling to take such excellent medicine.
Their claim that it is "not delicious" arises because they have deeply entered into false teachings and thus regard the True Dharma as unpalatable.
That their minds are entirely inverted means that they cannot distinguish between the false and the true, taking the false for the true and the true for the false. △
"The two metaphors demonstrate that even when extinguished, there is benefit.
I shall now employ skillful means to cause you to take this medicine. He then spoke these words:
"You should know that I am now old and infirm, and the time of my death has arrived. This excellent and wholesome medicine remains here; you may take it and consume it. Do not grieve."
"It is not false. Having given this instruction, he went again to another country and sent a messenger back to announce: "Your father has already died.

At that time, the sons, hearing that their father had passed away, were deeply grieved and distressed, and they thought to themselves: "If our father were still alive, he would have compassion for us and been able to protect us;
now he has abandoned us and died far away in another country. We consider ourselves orphaned and destitute, with no one left..."
Relying on [the physician], he constantly harbored feelings of grief and sorrow; his mind was thereby awakened, and he realized that the medicine possessed color, fragrance, and exquisite flavor.
He immediately took it and ingested it, whereupon his toxic illness was entirely cured.
"Old age and decline signify that my transformation and guidance are nearing their end; the time of death has arrived, and I shall now enter parinirvāṇa.

As for the 'fine medicine' left behind here: while the Tathāgata remains in the world, he personally performs the work of teaching and transforming others. But if he intends to enter extinction, what he leaves behind is solely the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
You should take and consume them, and do not worry that you will not be cured. This means that you may..."

By relying on this, one gives rise to understanding and practices accordingly; one will certainly be able to shatter the afflictions of views and thought, transcend the triple world, and need not worry about failing to realize the fruit.
"Returning to another land" means that although one previously returned to birth within the triple world, one now departs once more for other regions to teach and transform beings.
"Sending a messenger back to report" means that although the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, yet...
His great compassionate heart, which is without conditions, has never for a moment been abandoned.
Therefore, although he himself travels to other lands to teach and transform others, he dispatches Bodhisattvas who rely on the four reliances to act as his guides.

These Bodhisattvas who rely on the four reliances are those sent by the Tathāgata, dispatched by the Tathāgata, and those who carry out the work of the Tathāgata; thus, they are called "messengers. This is the mind.
As for those who subsequently attain awakening: previously, because false teachings had deeply penetrated them, they had lost the original seeds of the Three Vehicles.
Although they heard the Dharma, they were unwilling to accept and practice it; this was because the Tathāgata remained ever-present and imperishable.
Now that they no longer see the Tathāgata, they conceive a sense of sorrowful longing and thereby plant roots of goodness. Consequently, the seeds of the Three Vehicles are able to sprout once again.

Therefore, it is said that the mind subsequently becomes awakened. As for "immediately taking and consuming [the medicine]": once one has awakened, one already knows what is deviant and what is correct;

thus, one immediately accepts and practices it. Regarding "the toxic illness being entirely cured": turning away from the deviant and returning to the correct, no longer being swayed by the deviant—this is the curing of the poison.
Furthermore, being able to shatter the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and emerge from the triple world (*tridhātu*) is the curing of the disease. (2)
The analogy for benefiting beings in the present is concluded. △ Third, the analogy for benefiting beings in the future:
Upon hearing that his sons had all recovered, the father immediately returned home so that they might all see him.

"Those who have all attained recovery" refers to those who have already achieved the destruction of views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), emerged from the triple world, realized *nirvāṇa*, and accomplished the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).
"Seeking out and returning to instruct those yet to see" means that once their capacities for the Lesser Vehicle have been fulfilled, their capacities for the Great Vehicle naturally arise;
therefore, they return—though not truly born—to manifest birth, coming to teach and transform others so that they may all attain opening, showing, awakening, and realization.
This is to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. △ Fourth, clarifying that the metaphor is not in vain:
"Good sons, what do you think? Is there anyone who could say that this skilled physician has committed the sin of falsehood?"
"No, World-Honored One.

Regarding the commentary's statement that "the metaphorical exposition is not in vain": the preceding metaphors for the three periods—past, present, and future—showing arising and ceasing in the present, all serve to transform sentient beings;
therefore, in reality, there is neither arising nor ceasing. Furthermore, this is because one is able to realize a long-lasting lifespan; thus, all [are so].

It is not false. Therefore, he further clarifies the analogy of non-falsity; that is, within the aforementioned dharmas, it is for the sake of delivering sentient beings that all is real and not false.
The initial question asks whether the skilled physician commits the offense of falsehood:

this means that although the skilled physician departs and returns, and having returned departs again—despite these comings and goings—it is entirely for the purpose of treating his son, and in reality, there is no [falsehood].
"Regarding his coming and going, would anyone say that this excellent physician commits the offense of falsehood by his coming and going?

"No," he replied, giving the lower answer. This means that although the excellent physician has coming and going, it is entirely for the sake of treating his son; yet in reality, there is no such coming and going.
Therefore, no one can say that his coming and going is false. △ Third, the synthesis.
The Buddha said: "I am also like this. Since I attained Buddhahood, it has been immeasurable, boundless, hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
For the sake of sentient beings, through the power of skillful means, I have said that I shall enter parinirvāṇa.
Yet, there is no one who can rightfully say that I have committed the fault of falsehood."

There is no one who can say that my statement is false. If it were truly the case that birth is birth and cessation is cessation, then it would be as if I were falsely claiming the existence of a self regarding phenomena that are subject to arising and ceasing. Now, I am born for the sake of transforming and delivering sentient beings;
yet this birth is not truly birth. I also cease for the sake of transforming and delivering sentient beings; yet this cessation is not truly cessation.
It is not extinguished; yet regarding the long lifespan that has been realized, there has never been any delusion.
Therefore, no one can say that my "self" is false in the manner of phenomena subject to arising and ceasing. △ Second, the three verses in verse form.

First, the verse on the Dharma; second, the verse on the analogy; third, the verse on the application. The first [section] further has two parts. First, the verse on the long duration of the lifespan.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
Since I attained Buddhahood, the number of kalpas that have passed is immeasurable—hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions, billions, and asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
II. Verses on Benefiting Beings in the Three Times (three sections): A. Verses explicitly clarifying [the benefit]. B. Verses resolving doubts. C. Verses showing it is not in vain.
A. Again, three parts: 1. Verses on the past. 2. Verses on the present. 3. Verses on the future. The first two [parts]: 1. First... [text breaks off]
The verse says: Though not born, he manifests birth;
constantly preaching the Dharma to transform and teach, he causes countless billions of sentient beings to enter the Buddha-way. Thus it has been for immeasurable kalpas.
It is said that he has preached the Dharma and transformed beings through birth by transformation, leading them into the Buddha-way for immeasurable kalpas. 2.
Verse on Manifesting Extinction While Not Being Extinguished:
For the sake of delivering sentient beings, he manifests nirvana through skillful means; yet in reality, he does not pass into extinction, but dwells eternally here preaching the Dharma.
I always abide here. By means of various supernormal powers, I cause sentient beings who are subject to delusion not to see me, even though I am near.
"Always abiding here" means that I constantly reside in this Sahā world as well as in other dwelling places.
Regarding "sentient beings with inverted views": ordinary worldlings possess the four inversions such as the notion of permanence;
sentient beings of the two vehicles possess the four inversions such as impermanence; and sentient beings who are bodhisattvas possess the four inversions such as both permanence and impermanence.
△ Second, two verses on the present. The first verse concerns non-arising appearing as arising:
"The multitudes see my parinirvāṇa; they extensively make offerings to my relics, all harboring longing and yearning, thereby giving rise to a heart of thirsty admiration."

Once the sentient beings had gained faith and submission, their natures became upright and their minds supple; with single-minded intent they desired to see the Buddha, not begrudging even their own bodies or lives.
Then I and the sentient beings together emerged from Vulture Peak Mountain.
First, it clarifies that sentient beings possess the capacity for spiritual resonance (*kigan*). Regarding the terms "upright" (*shitsujiku*) and "pliant" (*nanyō*):
prior to their conversion and submission, they were crooked and not upright, and rigid and not pliant.

Now that they have been converted and submitted, they are therefore upright without guile and pliant without rigidity or violence. Since this capacity for resonance exists, [the response] must necessarily...
In response to this, it is said: "Therefore, though not born, he manifests birth and emerges from Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa. 2. Verses on Manifesting Extinction While Not Being Extinct:
"At that time, I speak to sentient beings: 'I am always here and do not pass away. By the power of skillful means, I manifest both extinction and non-extinction."
In other lands there are sentient beings who revere, believe in, and delight [in the Dharma]. To them as well, I further preach the unsurpassed Dharma.
You do not hear this; you merely say that I have entered parinirvāṇa.
Regarding "that which currently exists neither perishes nor does not perish": this means that while it appears to perish as a current existence, in reality it does not perish.
One who does not hear this has not heard the unsurpassed Dharma that has been taught. △ Third, the two verses on the future: first, the verse on that which is not born appearing to be born.
I see all sentient beings submerged in suffering and affliction; therefore, I do not manifest my birth before them to cause them to give rise to longing and yearning.
Because their hearts are filled with such devotion and admiration, I then appear and preach the Dharma for them.

To thirst for, yearn for, and longingly admire [the Buddha] is itself the awakening of the capacity to respond. Once this capacity has been established, he manifests birth where there is no birth and responds by appearing in the world.
△ Second, the verse on manifesting extinction where there is no extinction.
Such is my supernatural power: throughout incalculable eons, I have always dwelt on Vulture Peak and in other various abodes.
When sentient beings see the end of a kalpa and it is consumed by a great conflagration, this land of mine remains peaceful and secure, ever filled with devas and humans.
The gardens and various halls and pavilions were adorned with all kinds of jewels; the jeweled trees bore many flowers and fruits, providing a place of pleasure for sentient beings.
The devas struck celestial drums and constantly performed manifold music, raining down *māndārava* flowers which they scattered over the Buddha and the great assembly.

"Such supernatural power" means that what appears to be extinction is not actually extinction; rather, it is through the power of the Tathāgata’s supernormal faculties (*ṛddhi*) that he is able to manifest in this way.
Vulture Peak Mountain is a land of common cohabitation within the Sahā world-system.

Yet, within the sphere of the Tathāgata, even this land of common cohabitation is fundamentally the Land of Tranquil Light (*śāntaprabhāsa*); therefore, it is said to be eternally abiding. Other dwelling places are merely provisional manifestations.
The "retribution" (fruit) is also, in fact, the land of other directions. It is the place where the Tathāgata dwells;
because the three calamities can never reach it, it is called "peaceful and secure. "Heaven" refers to the ten stages (*bhūmi*), and "humans" refers to the thirty minds.
Because these forty positions can partially realize the *jigō* (tranquil light), they also constantly fill the dwelling place of the Tathāgata. The "gardens and groves" symbolize...
The various types of meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) are fully present; the halls and pavilions represent the fullness of various forms of wisdom (*prajñā*).
The precious adornments represent the fullness of the wealth of meritorious dharmas, serving as their ornamentation. The jewel trees represent unsurpassed *bodhi*;
from this *bodhi*, the true causes for the forty-one stages arise like many flowers, culminating in wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
The unsurpassed fruit is like many fruits; yet this cause and fruit are also that in which the sentient beings of the nine realms constantly find delight.
The celestial drum symbolizes the unasked self-proclamation, while the musical instruments symbolize the proclamation through the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*).
The *māndārava* flowers symbolize the perfect cause; by cultivating this perfect cause, one will surely attain the perfect fruit. Therefore, they rain down [the flowers] to scatter over the Buddha.
It is also that which all sentient beings possess; hence, it is addressed to the great assembly. The first verse, which correctly elucidates [the meaning], is concluded.
△ Second, the verse explaining the resolution of doubts has two parts. First, the actual explanation.
"My pure land is not destroyed, yet the multitudes see it as utterly consumed by fire, filled entirely with grief, fear, and various afflictions.
These sentient beings of sinful karma, due to the conditions of their evil deeds, shall for incalculable kalpas not hear the names of the Triple Gem."
All those who have cultivated merit and are gentle, mild, and upright shall all see my body here preaching the Dharma.
At times, for this assembly, I speak of the Buddha’s immeasurable lifespan; to those who see the Buddha only after a long time, I speak of how difficult it is to encounter a Buddha.
As for the statement that since the Tathāgata has always resided on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, everyone should see him—why then is he not seen?
To explain this, it is said: "My pure land is not destroyed, yet sentient beings perceive it as being burned; such is the perception of sentient beings with evil karma."
In that case, even their names would not be heard, let alone being seen. Those who possess virtue will see my body and hear my teaching;
this is because the Tathāgata is fundamentally ever-present. It is only that sentient beings with evil karma do not see him themselves;
it does not concern the Tathāgata. △ Second, the explanation of the underlying intention.
Such is my power of wisdom; the light of my insight illumines the immeasurable. My lifespan lasts for countless kalpas, attained through long-cultivated practice.
This refers to how the Tathāgata, within the three periods of time, does not arise yet manifests arising, and does not cease yet manifests ceasing.
And thus he benefits sentient beings. Therefore, he expresses his intention, saying: "Such is the power of my wisdom.
Why is it that the power of his wisdom can be such? It is because the Tathāgata, by means of the light of wisdom, illuminates the immeasurable and realizes an eternally long lifespan;
therefore, he is able to act in this way. As for the phrase "the light of wisdom illuminates the immeasurable," it refers to the subtle...

Sublime wisdom illuminates the principle of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Since this principle of the true mark extends horizontally throughout the ten directions and vertically through the three periods of time, it is boundless and immeasurable; therefore, the light of the illuminating wisdom is likewise immeasurable.
△ Third, the verse on non-futility.
