"You who possess wisdom, do not harbor doubts regarding this; you should sever them so that they are forever exhausted. The Buddha’s words are true and not false.
As for those who do not harbor doubts, let there be no doubt concerning this long lifespan, which manifests birth and manifests extinction."
△ Second, the verse on the analogy:
Just as a physician, through skillful means, speaks of his death in order to cure his mad son; though he is actually alive, no one can say that he is speaking falsely.
△ Third, the verse on the application [to the meaning]:
I am likewise the Father of the World, rescuing all who suffer from affliction. For the sake of ordinary people who are deluded by inversion, though I truly exist, I speak of my extinction.
Because they constantly perceive me as being present, they give rise to hearts of arrogance and self-indulgence; becoming heedless and attached to the five desires, they fall into the evil realms.
I always know sentient beings—whether they practice the Path or do not practice it—and according to what is appropriate for their deliverance, I preach various dharmas for them.
Arrogance and indulgence are themselves delusion; negligence arises from delusion to produce karma; and falling into evil states is the retribution summoned by that karma.
Every time he formed this thought: "By what means can I cause sentient beings to enter the unsurpassed wisdom and swiftly achieve the Buddha-body?

This practice is the comprehensive summary; that is, every time he formed this intention, he did not know how he might be able to cause all sentient beings to open, show, awaken to, and enter the unsurpassed wisdom of the Buddha, so as to enable them to quickly attain it.
This is like the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body) of the Tathāgata’s long-lasting life span. The "Exposition on the Life Span of the Tathāgata" is hereby concluded.

Regarding the seventeenth chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, the "Distinction of Merit," as for the origin of this chapter, it generally derives from what the Tathāgata has previously elucidated concerning all that is long-lasting.
Regarding their life-span and their benefit to sentient beings throughout the three periods of time: they do not arise where there is no arising, nor do they perish where there is no perishing.
In every case, they extensively reveal the near to manifest the distant, and disclose the traces to manifest the fundamental source.
Thus, the bodhisattvas who had previously harbored doubts and wavered in their attachments are all able, through this, to sever their doubts concerning the near and give rise to faith in the distant.
When one increases the Way and diminishes the life [of worldly attachment], then various merits arise. Since there are already such merits, the Tathāgata ought to analyze them for the sake of others;

therefore, this chapter exists. Within this chapter, there is the Tathāgata’s bestowal of prophecy, Maitreya’s reception and exposition, the texts concerning the fourfold faith and the five stages, and the passage on the circulation [of the teaching]. What is discussed here is that very analysis.

Merit is itself the bestowal of prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). As explained in the "Chapter on the Former Deeds" (*Pūrvayoga-parivarta*), the various śrāvakas were able to sever their provisional doubts and give rise to true faith;

thus, the Tathāgata bestowed predictions upon each of them one by one. Now, as the Dharma is preached in this "Root Chapter," the great bodhisattvas are able to sever their proximate doubts and give rise to faith in the distant [truth], and he likewise bestows predictions upon them. Because...

Following the bestowal of the prophecy, the exposition is presented; because there is a "circulation" (prabhāvanā) based upon the "main body" (śarīra), only the "discrimination of merit" (guṇavibhāga) is indicated, thereby subsuming the other two.
"Discrimination" (vibhañjana) means to analyze and distinguish; "differentiation" (viśeṣaṇa) means to select and differentiate.

When the great bodhisattvas hear the Buddha speak of his lifespan, they are able to enter contemplation in accordance with what they have heard and practice it; this is termed [the discrimination of merit].
Merit refers to the cultivation of practice; when contemplation is perfected and one enters realization, there is attainment within the mind, which is termed "virtue.
Nevertheless, although all Bodhisattvas possess perfect hearing and perfect practice, at the time of realization and entry, they must proceed from cause to fruit.

Because the falling away of delusions has varying degrees of depth, some attain the stage of the Ten Abodes (*daśavihāra*), some attain the stage of the Ten Practices (*daśacaryā*), and some attain...

Regarding the "Ten Dedications" (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*): there are those who have attained the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), those who have attained the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), and furthermore, those who have merely attained a semblance thereof.
Because their levels of depth and shallowness differ, the Tathāgata has analyzed and distinguished each one individually;
therefore, it is called the "Chapter on the Analysis of Merit. The text is divided into two parts. First, the Dharma [teaching].
The body receives the prediction. Second, Maitreya’s presentation and summary. This section has three parts. First, the narrator’s introduction:

At that time, the great assembly heard the Buddha speak of his lifespan being so long and vast, such that immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings obtained great benefit.
"At that time" refers to the moment when the Tathāgata revealed his vast lifespan, benefiting sentient beings throughout the three periods of time;
it was the occasion when he extensively opened up the near to reveal the far, and opened the traces to reveal the fundamental, having just completed this task.

When one hears the Buddha say that his lifespan is so long and far-reaching, one hears him state that since his attainment of enlightenment, it has already surpassed the metaphor of a speck of dust within an aeon, being immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.

This is the teaching that throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and across the three periods of time, there is neither birth nor death, yet birth is manifested and death is manifested.
Those who attain great benefit, through the Trace Gate’s opening of the provisional to reveal the real, are disciples born of the physical body;

they are only able to sever doubts regarding the provisional and give rise to faith in the real, thereby receiving the prediction of attaining the Way through the eight phases of manifestation at the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*). Now, in the Root Gate, the Dharma...
Bodhisattvas in their final birth, upon hearing the teaching that reveals the near and manifests the far, are able to sever doubts regarding the near and give rise to faith in the far.
Thus, they not only attain the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), but there are even those who can attain unsurpassed *bodhi* within a single lifetime.
Consequently, the abundant benefits they possess are most vast and inconceivable; therefore, it is said that they "attain."
It is of great benefit. △ Second, the Tathāgata’s detailed exposition has two parts. First, the general introduction:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya: "Ajita, when I spoke of the long duration of this Tathāgata’s lifespan..."
△ Second, the correct analysis has two parts. First, the analysis of the merit of partial realization:
six hundred and eighty *koṭi-nayuta* of sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
They attain the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), which constitutes their differentiation into the attainment of the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*).
That is to say, when I speak of my lifespan, there are bodhisattvas who, upon hearing it, are able to form contemplations accordingly and thereby achieve realization and entry.
If one were to calculate their number, they would amount to six hundred and eighty million *nayuta* of Ganges Rivers.
The multitude of beings attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Thereupon, having heard what the Buddha had previously taught—
that things are neither real nor false, neither suchness nor different, and that there is no arising yet an appearance of arising, and no cessation yet an appearance of cessation—
the bodhisattvas immediately understood that although all phenomena appear to arise, their arising is born from conditions, and that arising is in reality non-existent.

Although there is arising, even within that which has cessation, cessation occurs through conditions; thus, cessation is in truth no cessation. By means of this principle of non-arising and non-cessation—the reality of non-birth—one brings it to patient acceptance within the mind.
In so doing, by attaining one, all are attained; therefore, one is able to attain the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena).
If one discusses the attainment of this patience, one has already entered the first stage (*prathama-vihāra*). Since this is the case for the first stage, [it follows for the others as well].
Then the subsequent nine stages may be understood. This refers to attaining the ten stages upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching on his long-lasting life.
Furthermore, there were a thousand times as many bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who attained the dhāraṇī-door of hearing and retaining.

This means that it is not merely six hundred *koṭi* nayutas, nor even those sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges who have attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and reached the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*).
Furthermore, there are thousands of times more bodhisattvas than that who have attained the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*) of the *dhāraṇī* of hearing and retaining.
Thus, it is said, "there are again a thousandfold more," and so forth. *Dhāraṇī* is translated here as "total retention" (*saṃgraha-vidhāraṇa*), meaning that one is able to...

They encompass all dharmas and uphold all meanings. When these bodhisattvas hear the Buddha’s teaching on his long lifespan, they are able to enter the ten practices; thus, one practice is all practices, and all practices are one practice.
They can encompass all dharmas without omission and uphold all meanings without loss; therefore, it is said that they have attained *dhāraṇī*.
Furthermore, there was another world where there were Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms of dust, who had attained the unimpeded eloquence of joyful speech (*pratibhāna*).

Those who have attained the unimpeded eloquence of joyful speech are those who have attained the stage of "clarity" (*vidyā*) within the ten stages of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). If they have not yet entered the ten stages of dedication, [they are still at this level].
Thus, there are distinctions between phenomena and principle, cause and effect, and self and other.
Now that one has heard the Buddha’s teaching on the lifespan and entered the Ten Dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*), all phenomena whatsoever will not fail to be subsumed within principle;
every cause that is performed will ultimately be fully realized as its fruit; and whatever practices one undertakes, one will be able to direct them all toward this goal.

Regarding others, his self-realization is thus: when transforming others, he is able to express immeasurable words within a single word, immeasurable dharmas within a single dharma, and immeasurable meanings within a single meaning;
therefore, it is said that he has attained the unimpeded eloquence of joyous speech (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).
Furthermore, there was another world-system where Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas as numerous as its atoms had attained hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of immeasurable *āvartana-dhāraṇīs*.
Moreover, there were Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in a triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system.

They are able to turn the irreversible wheel of Dharma. Furthermore, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in two thousand intermediate world-systems who are able to turn the pure wheel of Dharma.

Furthermore, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in a small thousand-world system who shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* after eight births. Furthermore, there are [those from] four sets of four world-systems.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in [a single] world-system shall, after four births, attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in three world-systems of four continents who shall, after three births, attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in two world-systems of four continents...
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, in two more births, shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Furthermore,
there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in one four-continent world-system who, in one more birth, shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
One attains the *amitabha-parivarta-dhāraṇī*. This is the attainment of the first stage (*bhūmi*). "Parivarta" means revolving:

it refers to revolving through the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) to enter the empty (*śūnya*), revolving through the empty to enter the conventional, and revolving through both the empty and the conventional to enter the middle (*madhyama*).

In the Separate Teaching (*pṛthag-deśanā*), one proceeds sequentially through the empty first, then the conventional, and finally the middle. Here, however, it is the Perfect Teaching (*paripūrṇa-deśanā*): revolving through the conventional to enter the empty—[and so forth].
At that time, when one emptiness is all emptiness; when revolving from emptiness into the provisional, one provisional is all provisional;

and when revolving from emptiness and the provisional into the middle, one middle is all middle—this *dhāraṇī* of revolving through emptiness, the provisional, and the middle can be attained by a Bodhisattva of the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*). Such a one is able to turn the Dharma of non-retrogression.

The "wheel" refers to attaining the second bhūmi. A bodhisattva of the second bhūmi personally realizes non-retrogression and, by means of that which he himself has realized, turns it into the minds of others, causing them also to realize non-retrogression;
therefore, it is said that he "is able to turn the wheel of the Dharma of non-retrogression. Being able to turn the wheel of the pure Dharma refers to attaining the third bhūmi.
The third stage, compared to the second, further advances by breaking through one grade of ignorance;
therefore, it is said that what was transformed in the second stage becomes pure. "To be attained after eight births" means attaining the fourth stage.
The fourth stage is separated from wondrous enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi) by only eight positions; thus, after eight births, one attains unsurpassed bodhi—this is the fourth stage. This...
The following stages—fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth—are omitted. One who is at the fifth stage shall attain *bodhi* after seven births;

one at the sixth stage shall attain *bodhi* after six births; one at the seventh stage shall attain *bodhi* after five births. One who shall attain it after four births corresponds to the eighth stage;
one who shall attain it after three births corresponds to the ninth stage; and one who shall attain it after two births corresponds to the tenth stage.
On this stage, one shall attain equal enlightenment in a single lifetime.
Regarding the merits attained throughout these forty-one stages, none but the wondrous wisdom of the Tathāgata can discern them;
therefore, the Tathāgata has distinguished each and every one of them. △ Second, the differentiation of similar merits.
Furthermore, there were sentient beings as numerous as the atoms in eight worlds who all resolved their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Regarding those who resolve their minds, there are three types; the present case is similar to that of the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Wholesome Paths who resolve upon the Great Mind.
The Arising of the Resolve. △ Third: The Assembly Presents Offerings.

When the Buddha had spoken these words regarding how the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas had attained great benefit from the Dharma, mandārava flowers and mahāmandārava flowers rained down from the void, scattering over the countless hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of jewel trees.
He scattered [flowers] upon all the Buddhas on the lion thrones, as well as within the stūpas made of the seven precious gems.
He also scattered them upon Śākyamuni Buddha on the lion throne, the long-extinguished Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, all the great bodhisattvas, and the fourfold assembly.
Furthermore, he rained down fine powders of sandalwood, aloeswood, and other incenses. In the midst of the void, celestial drums resounded spontaneously. Wondrous...

The sound was deep and far-reaching. Furthermore, a rain of a thousand kinds of celestial garments fell, with various necklaces—pearl necklaces, maṇi-jewel necklaces, and wish-fulfilling jewel necklaces—hanging down and pervading the nine directions.

Myriad precious incense burners burned priceless incense, which spontaneously reached everywhere to make offerings to the great assembly. Above each Buddha, there were bodhisattvas holding banners and canopies. Next...
Ascending further, they reached the Brahma Heaven. There, these bodhisattvas sang immeasurable verses with sublime voices, praising all the Buddhas and the great bodhisattvas.
Having heard the Tathāgata’s such detailed analysis, they attained the great benefit of the Dharma and were filled with joy.

This is the commencement of the offering. First, *māndārava* flowers rain down from the sky, signifying that from the heaven of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the perfect cause—the arousal of the bodhicitta—has been manifested; this signifies the attainment of corresponding merit.
Then, *mahāmāndārava* flowers rain down, signifying that from the heaven of the ultimate truth, the true cause—the [realization] of the forty-one stages—has been manifested.
This signifies the attainment and realization of meritorious qualities. The scattering of the *nirmāṇakāya* Buddhas signifies that this cause will inevitably result in the fruit.
Furthermore, regarding the scattering of Śākyamuni: while the aforementioned Buddhas are many, the present Śākyamuni is one.
This perfect cause is fundamentally one yet many, and many yet one; it is that which is unimpeded in its oneness and multiplicity.
Therefore, having manifested all the Buddhas, he further manifests Śākyamuni as a symbolic representation. As for Prabhūtaratna:
the aforementioned Śākyamuni is a Buddha of the present, whereas the present Prabhūtaratna is a Buddha who has entered parinirvāṇa. This perfect cause is fundamentally not...
Birth is not cessation; yet for those for whom birth and cessation are one and the same, he therefore scatters [flowers] over Śākyamuni and again scatters them over Prabhūtaratna as a sign.
Furthermore, as for scattering them over the Bodhisattvas: the three Buddhas above represent the fruit, while the present Bodhisattvas represent the cause.
This perfect cause is, from the beginning, both cause and effect; it is effect while being cause.
Because cause and effect share the same source, after manifesting the three Buddhas, he further manifests the Bodhisattvas as external representations. As for the fourfold assembly:
the aforementioned Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are sages, whereas the present fourfold assembly consists of ordinary beings. This perfect cause is, from the beginning, both ordinary and...

The "sages" are those who, while being sages, are yet ordinary beings; they are those for whom ordinary beings and sages are equal. Therefore, having already dispersed the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, he further disperses the fourfold assembly as a symbolic representation.
Next, he rains down fine powdered incense; this refers to the opening and revealing of the previous Trace Gate (Jikimon).
However, it is revealed that the provisional is itself the real; the three are the one. Provisional and real are non-dual; it is simply the perfect fusion of the three and the one.
Now, in this Revealing and Clarifying of the Essential Gate, it is revealed that the near is itself the far, and the trace is itself the source.
The distant and the near share a single boundary; the original and the manifested trace their source to the same origin.

Compared to the aforementioned "Trace Gate" (Jimon), this is even more profound, far-reaching, and subtle, capable of bestowing great benefit upon Bodhisattvas; therefore, it rains down fine powdered incense to manifest this truth.
As for the celestial drums sounding spontaneously in the void, they signify that the Tathāgata can, from the perspective of the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), respond without being asked.
And he speaks of himself. The phrase "wondrous voice, deep and far-reaching" signifies that which the Buddha has spoken;

it enables those who hear it to spontaneously enter the ocean of the fruit of wondrous enlightenment. As previously stated regarding his long and distant lifespan, he can further cause all bodhisattvas to...
Having realized the merits of the forty-one stages, one attains effortless entry [into the path]; thus, it is symbolized by a wondrous voice that is profound and far-reaching.
As for the rain of a thousand kinds of celestial garments: "garment" (cīvara) carries the sense of protection and concealment;
it symbolizes how the Tathāgata, through the unconditioned compassion of the dharma-realm, universally bestows both relief and extraction, hanging down various flower tassels.
These represent the sublime practices that have been manifested. The pearl necklace represents the sublime practice that is identical with the ultimate truth (*tathatā*).

The mani-jewel necklace represents the sublime practice that is identical with the conventional world (*saṃvṛti*). The wish-fulfilling jewel necklace represents the sublime practice that is identical with the middle way.
This is the wondrous practice that is simultaneously the True, the Conventional, and the Middle. Originally, it is possessed by all sentient beings of the nine realms;
therefore, it is symbolized by pervading the nine directions. As for the many precious incense burners burning priceless incense:
the burner symbolizes the causal mind of sentient beings, and the causal mind of sentient beings possesses the three virtues of the Tathāgata.
The Secret Treasury. The secret treasury of the Tathāgata’s three virtues fundamentally penetrates the causal mind of sentient beings.
It is like a furnace formed from various jewels; the furnace is composed of those very jewels. From this completeness, practice is initiated, like the act of smelting.
The priceless incense represents the object of contemplation, which is the supreme *sahā-lokadhātu* (the land of eternal quiescence).
As for the natural and universal offering to each and every Buddha in the great assembly:

since the fruit-virtue has already permeated the causal mind, the causal mind in turn penetrates the fruit-virtue, thereby manifesting it. Because the causal mind naturally penetrates the fruit-virtue, it is said:
It is spontaneously and universally present. Although it is the fruit of realized virtue (*phala-guṇa*), it is in fact the mind of the cause;
therefore, it is said that "one makes offerings to the great assembly. Although it is the mind of the cause, it is in fact the universal realization of the fruit;

therefore, it is said that "[the offerings] are upon each and every Buddha. Among those bodhisattvas who hold banners and canopies: a banner has the meaning of movement, while a canopy has the meaning of providing shade and protection. These truly represent all...
Great Bodhisattvas, having heard the Buddha’s teaching on the vast and long duration of his lifespan, are able to transform afflictions into bodhi and transform birth-and-death into nirvana;
they are further able to exercise great compassion to bestow happiness upon sentient beings.
Having exercised great compassion, he has already uprooted the suffering of sentient beings.

The fact that he ascends step by step as far as the Brahma Heaven precisely symbolizes that when a Bodhisattva hears the Buddha’s teaching on the lifespan, they are able to gradually destroy the three delusions and gradually manifest the three virtues, ultimately all returning to the Heaven of the Ultimate Truth (Paramārtha). As for the praise of the Buddha by Gadgadasvara, it precisely...

The Bodhisattva Maitreya, having already realized this for himself, is further able to proclaim the sublime Dharma through the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) and the eightfold voice (*aṣṭāṅga-svara*) in order to transform others.
Part Two: Maitreya’s Acceptance of the Teaching. This has two sections. First, the prose description of the ritual protocol.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these verses:
II. The Verses in Praise, Consisting of Three Parts. First, the verses on the benefits gained by the bodhisattvas.
The Buddha has preached a rare Dharma, such as has never been heard before. The World-Honored One possesses great power, and his lifespan is immeasurable.
When the countless sons of the Buddhas hear the World-Honored One’s detailed exposition, those who attain the benefit of the Dharma have joy suffuse their entire bodies.

The World-Honored One possesses great power; that is to say, the Tathāgata possesses the power of great sovereign supernormal faculties, the power of the lion’s springing leap, and the power of fierce majesty. Because he possesses such great power, his lifespan is long and immeasurable.
As for the expression "incalculable" and so forth, it means that the Tathāgata says this cannot be measured.
At the time of [their] lifespan, they cause the Bodhisattvas to attain various merits. The Tathāgata, in turn, distinguishes for each of them individually what has been attained;
thus, there are countless sons of the Buddha who, upon hearing this, experience joy that pervades their entire bodies.
△ Second, the verses on the Tathāgata’s distinctions have two parts: first, the verses distinguishing the merits of partial realization; second...
The verse distinguishes between similar merits; the first two lines clarify this individually:
"Either dwelling on the stage of non-retrogression, or attaining *dhāraṇī*, or possessing unimpeded eloquence, or the *koṭi-niyuta* *parivarta-dhāraṇī*."
There may be bodhisattvas, as numerous as the atoms in a great trichiliocosm, each of whom is able to turn the irreversible wheel of Dharma;
furthermore, there may be bodhisattvas, as numerous as the atoms in a medium chiliocosm, each of whom is able to turn the pure wheel of Dharma.
Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in a small chiliocosm who have each remaining eight births before they shall attain the path of Buddhahood.
Moreover, there are bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in four, three, or two such four-continent worlds who shall attain Buddhahood after a corresponding number of births.
Or there may be bodhisattvas, as numerous as the atoms in a single four-continent world-system, who have but one birth remaining before they shall attain all-knowledge.
△ Second, the summary:
Sentient beings such as these, upon hearing that the Buddha’s lifespan is long and far-reaching, obtain immeasurable, outflow-free, and pure karmic fruits.
Regarding "immeasurable and outflow-free" (*anāsrava*): if one discusses the outflow-free, even those of the Two Vehicles can attain it;

however, this is limited and cannot be called immeasurable. This is because they only destroy the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), while ignorance (*avidyā*) remains entirely intact;

and they only sever the *pariccheda-vidhvamsana* (segmented) existence, while the *pariṇāma-vidhvamsana* (transformative) existence remains fully preserved. Now, when the Bodhisattvas hear the Buddha speak of his lifespan, they do not merely...
It destroys the views and afflictions, and furthermore destroys ignorance; it not only severs the limited分段 (pariccheda) existence but also severs the transformative 變易 (pariṇāma) existence.
Thus, there is no further falling back into leakage, which is why it is called "immeasurable and outflow-free" (anāsrava). Having destroyed ignorance, one thereby severs transformative existence.
Thus, one is able to evoke the fruit of the pure retribution of true recompense. △ Second, the verse on the distinct similar merits.
Part two: first, the specific explanation.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings as numerous as the atoms in eight worlds who, upon hearing the Buddha speak of his lifespan, all resolve their minds upon the Unsurpassed Way.
△ II. Summary. The World-Honored One has preached immeasurable and inconceivable dharmas, which bring great benefit, as boundless as space. △ III.
Verses on the Assembly Offering Worship. Part 1: Individual Explanations.
It rained *māndārava* flowers and *mahāmāndārava* flowers. Śakras, Brahmās, and others, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, came from countless Buddha-lands.
They rained down sandalwood and aloeswood, falling in profusion and in disarray like birds swooping down from the sky, scattering as offerings before all the Buddhas.
In the midst of the void, celestial drums spontaneously produce wondrous sounds; ten million kinds of celestial robes swirl down from above.
Miraculous incense burners made of various jewels burn priceless incense, which naturally pervades everywhere as an offering to all the World-Honored Ones.
That great assembly of bodhisattvas held banners and canopies made of the seven treasures, of ten trillion exquisite varieties, reaching as high as the Brahma Heaven.
Before each and every Buddha, jeweled standards bore superior banners, and they likewise sang praises of all the Tathāgatas with ten million verses.
Regarding "the precious banner suspending the excellent pennant": the banner (*dhvaja*) is able to subdue the heterodox and manifest the orthodox;
the pennant (*patākā*), by its nature of movement, signifies turning away from the heterodox to return to the orthodox. △ Second, the general summary.
Such various matters as these had never occurred before; hearing that the Buddha’s lifespan is immeasurable, everyone rejoiced.
The Buddha’s fame resounds throughout the ten directions, widely benefiting all sentient beings. All have been endowed with roots of goodness, which assist their unsurpassed resolve.
That which has never before occurred—namely, the various kinds of offerings described above—fully represents the benefits obtained through the Original Gate (Honmon).
Therefore, from the Trace Gate (Jikimon) and prior, there have been no such offerings capable of representing [the Dharma] in this way.

"Those who possess roots of goodness" refers to those who possess the roots of goodness of both the two causes: the conditional cause (engi-in) and the direct cause (ryō-in). They are those who hear what the Buddha has preached.
Based upon the long-lasting life span, one gives rise to subtle and profound contemplation; this constitutes the fulfillment of the *nirvedhika-hetu* (the cause of penetration).
Based upon that same [life span], one gives rise to vast and sublime practice; this constitutes the fulfillment of the *pratyaya-hetu* (the causal condition).

Once both the causal condition and the penetrating cause are fulfilled, the *mūla-hetu* (the fundamental cause) manifests of itself. Therefore, it is said that these assist the unsurpassed mind. The above is the primary teaching of the *Honmon* (Original Gate).
The Section on the Main Body is concluded.
△ Third, the Section on the Propagation has two parts: First, from this point until the "Chapter on Never-Despising," which praises the propagation of the sutra to encourage its circulation.
Second, from the "Chapter on Supernatural Powers" until the end of the sutra, which is the entrustment of the propagation of the sutra to clarify its circulation.
Penetrating. The first two [periods]. First, the four types of faith in the present; second, the five grades after the extinction [of the Buddha]. Regarding the first four:
the first is the faith and understanding of a single thought-moment, which is the first faith. The second is understanding the purport of the words, which is the second faith.
The third is hearing this sutra extensively, which is the third faith. The fourth is profound mental faith and understanding, which is the fourth faith. Furthermore, the first...
II. First, the prose section; second, the verse section. Within the first [section], there are two parts. First, the presentation of causal practice:

At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya: "Ajita, if there are sentient beings who, hearing that the lifespan of the Buddha is thus long and far-reaching, are able to give rise to even a single thought of faith and understanding..."

Regarding those "sentient beings who are equal": this refers to those who, having previously heard my teaching on the life-span, have already attained the ten births and ten practices, up to and including those who have given rise to a corresponding mind.

If there are further sentient beings who hear what I have taught regarding the life-span—setting aside for now whether they practice in reliance upon it or realize it through it—even if they possess but a single moment of faith.
Explanation: If one considers the duration of time, it is extremely brief; if one considers the practice, it is most shallow. Nevertheless, the merit attained therein is likewise immeasurable.
To speak of "faithful understanding in a single thought-moment" (*ekacittotpāda-adhimukti*): "faith" (*śraddhā*) means to accept with conviction and to be free from doubt;
"understanding" (*adhimukti*) means to comprehend clearly and to be able to discern distinctly. This occurs within the present, infinitesimal single thought-moment of the mind.

To faithfully accept that the traces near the city of Gayā as spoken by the Tathāgata are the traces, while the long and distant life-span is the fundamental reality, and to be free from even slight doubt—this is called faith.
Furthermore, to be able to understand that these traces have no separate existence apart from the fundamental reality, for they are traces manifested from what was originally bestowed;
and that the fundamental reality likewise has no separate existence apart from the traces, for it is the fundamental reality revealed by opening up the traces.
The fundamental and the manifested are of one essence; the distant and the near are non-dual. To understand this with perfect clarity is what is called "liberation.
△ Second, elucidating the merits in three parts: first, the general indication.
The merit thus obtained is immeasurable.
△ Second, the comparative evaluation has two parts. First, the presentation of the comparison:

If there are good sons or good daughters who, for the sake of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, at [the time of... (Note: The provided source text is incomplete; the translation reflects the available portion.)
For eighty quadrillion nayuta kalpas, they practiced the five pāramitās— the pāramitā of giving (dāna), the pāramitā of ethical discipline (śīla),
the pāramitā of patience (kṣānti), the pāramitā of vigor (vīrya), and the pāramitā of meditative concentration (dhyāna)— excluding the pāramitā of wisdom (prajñā).
"Initially seeking Bodhi" clarifies the loftiness of his aspiration. "For eighty million *koṭi-nayuta* kalpas" describes the length of time.
"Practicing the five *pāramitās*" indicates the profundity of his conduct.
As for excluding *prajñā*, a single moment of faith and understanding is itself *prajñā*; since it is that which is being measured and evaluated here, it is temporarily set aside.
Thus it is. △ Second, the formal comparison:
Compared with the former merit by means of this merit, even a hundredth part, a thousandth part, a hundred-thousand-millionth part, does not equal one part of it;
indeed, it is beyond what can be known through calculation or analogy.
The reason they do not reach it is that, although their seeking is directed toward the heights, it does not exceed the path of the Buddha at the stage of fruition as taught in the Tripiṭaka;
although their duration is long, it does not exceed the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* and one hundred *kalpas* of the Tripiṭaka;
and although their practice is profound, it does not exceed the five *pāramitās* of the phenomenal realm in the Tripiṭaka. Now, having heard the teaching of the Tathāgata, they are able to...
With perfect faith and perfect understanding, although the time may be short and the practice shallow, the merit attained is inconceivable;
therefore, it is not something that can be reached by those [of the former stages]. △ Third, the conclusion and clarification.
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family possesses such merit as this, it is impossible that they would ever regress from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
One who possesses such merit has already perfected the perfect understanding (*pariniṣpanna-adhigama*). From this perfect understanding arises perfect practice;
from perfect practice, one will necessarily attain perfect realization. Therefore, regarding unsurpassed bodhi, there is no falling back.
Were there to be such a falling back, it would be impossible. Since there is no falling back from unsurpassed bodhi, then...
All the merits therein are such that they cannot be known through natural calculation or analogy, nor can they be reached by any means of comparison.
△ Second, the verses in praise consist of two parts: first, the praise of causal practice; second, the praise of merit.
The first two [verses]. The first verse presents the comparison; the second verse provides the actual comparison. These two [sections] consist of: first, the general summary.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
If a person seeks the Buddha’s wisdom, for a duration of eighty quadrillion nayutas of kalpas, they practice the five pāramitās.
The first line refers to the greatness of seeking it; the second line refers to the length of time; and the third and fourth lines refer to the depth of the practice.
△ Second, the individual verses on the five [pāramitās]; first, the verse on giving (dāna).

Throughout these kalpas, they made offerings of rare and exquisite food and drink, superior garments and bedding, and sandalwood monasteries adorned with gardens and groves, to the Buddhas, pratyekabuddhas and their disciples, as well as to the assemblies of bodhisattvas.
Such acts of giving as these are all of the most subtle excellence. Throughout the entirety of these kalpas, they dedicate them toward the Buddha-way.
That which is said to be "subtle and excellent" in every instance of giving refers, at its utmost limit, only to the precious things found within the human world. 2. Verses on Upholding the Precepts.
Furthermore, if one upholds the prohibitive precepts, pure and without flaw or leakage, seeking the unsurpassed path, they are praised by all Buddhas.
Because [the practitioner] is as bright as ice and frost, with no transgressions or violations, it is said to be "pure and without flaw or leakage.

Those who seek the Buddha-way should, in principle, seek the Buddha-wisdom within the general exposition (*saṃgraha-vibhāga*), as well as within the long prose section where it says "for the sake of bodhi."
△ Three verses on patience:
If a person practices patience and abides in the stage of pliancy, even if various evils should assail them, their mind remains unshaken.
Those who have attained some dharma harbor overweening pride; though they treat him with contempt and vexation, he is likewise able to endure it.
The first line clarifies endurance toward the worldly multitude, while the second line clarifies endurance toward the assembly of those who have attained dharma. △ Fourth, the verse on diligence:
If, moreover, one exerts diligent vigor, with resolve and mindfulness ever firm, throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas, remaining single-mindedly without slackening or rest.
△ Fifth, a verse on meditative concentration (dhyāna).
Furthermore, throughout countless kalpas, dwelling in secluded places, whether sitting or walking, he constantly restrained his mind by eliminating sleep.
By these causes and conditions, he was able to give rise to various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*). For eighty billion kalpas, he remained securely established with an undisturbed mind.
"Upholding this merit of single-mindedness, I vow to seek the unsurpassed path. May I attain all-knowledge and exhaust the limits of all meditative concentrations.

To speak of "removing sleep" is precisely to cultivate *vipaśyanā* (insight) by observing dullness; to "gather the mind" is precisely to cultivate *śamatha* (calm abiding) by settling it from distraction.
Thus one knows that meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) has not been accomplished; there is only dullness (*styāna*) and distraction (*auddhatya*).
Once dullness and distraction are eliminated, one is able to give rise to meditative concentration. The two lines concerning "all-knowledge" (*sarvajñatā*) constitute the making of a vow:
"Since there is no meditation without wisdom, may I attain all-knowledge," and so forth. △ Second, the verse on the formal analysis (*parīkṣā*).
If there are sons or daughters of good family who, throughout hundreds of thousands, tens of millions, and billions of kalpas, practice all these meritorious deeds as described above,
yet another son or daughter of good family hears me speak of this lifespan and believes it for even a single thought-moment, their merit shall exceed that of the former.
If a person is entirely free from all doubts and regrets and possesses deep-seated faith for even a brief moment, their merit shall be as such.
"All doubts and regrets" refers to proximate doubt; "faith for a brief moment" refers to remote faith.

As for "deep-seated faith," it means not only being able to believe in the remote origin through its proximate manifestations, but also being able to believe that the proximate is itself [the ultimate].
"Remote. This means that the trace is the very basis; therefore, it is said that they believe with a profound mind. △ Second, the verse on merit has three parts.
First, clarifying that the roots were deep in the past:
"There are bodhisattvas who have practiced the Way for immeasurable kalpas; upon hearing me speak of the lifespan, they are then able to believe and accept it."
"Practicing the Way for immeasurable kalpas" refers to practicing the Buddha-way throughout past lives.
In this way, their past seeds are profound and they have planted various roots of goodness; therefore, upon hearing what I say, they are able to believe and accept it.
△ Second, clarifying the gravity of their future vows.

May all such people as these receive this sutra upon the crowns of their heads. I vow that in the future I shall possess long life to deliver sentient beings, just as the World-Honored One, the King among the Śākyas, now roars the lion’s roar at the site of enlightenment and preaches the Dharma without fear.
"In future ages, we shall be honored by all; when seated at the site of enlightenment, our lifespan shall likewise be proclaimed as such.
Those "such persons" refers to those who are able to receive this sutra upon their heads;

having thus attained faith and understanding, they give rise to practice through that understanding, and through practice they enter into realization, thereby being able to realize a long-lasting lifespan and deliver sentient beings.
Therefore, he made a vow that in future ages he would live long to save sentient beings. "Just as the World-Honored One is today," means:
the World-Honored One today lives long to save sentient beings and is the King among the Śākyas;
if I were to live long to save sentient beings in the future, I too would be like the World-Honored One today, becoming the King among the Śākyas. Today... the World-Honored One.

"World-Honored One, you live long to deliver sentient beings and utter the lion’s roar. If, in the future, I am to live long to deliver sentient beings, I shall also be like the World-Honored One today, uttering the lion’s roar.
Today the World-Honored One lives long to deliver sentient beings and preaches the Dharma of fearlessness;
if, in the future, I am to deliver sentient beings, I shall also be like the World-Honored One today, preaching the Dharma of fearlessness."
Furthermore, today the World-Honored One, through his long life, delivers sentient beings and is thus honored and revered by all.
If, in the future, I were to deliver sentient beings through my long life, I too would be honored and revered by all, just as the World-Honored One is today.
"Today the World-Honored One, possessing long life, saves sentient beings; dwelling at the site of enlightenment, he proclaims his vast lifespan.
If, in the future, I am to save sentient beings with long life, I shall also be like the World-Honored One today, dwelling at the site of enlightenment and proclaiming my vast lifespan.
By interpreting it in this way, one can then see that his vow for the future is profound. △ Third, clarifying the present.
In this state of high merit,
those who possess a profound resolve, who are pure and upright, who have heard much and are able to maintain it in memory,
and who understand the Buddha’s words according to their meaning— such persons as these have no doubt regarding this.
Regarding the term "profound mind" (*gambhīra-citta*): it refers to one who is able to believe in the non-duality of the fundamental and the phenomenal.

Being able to both believe and understand, one is then able to give rise to practice from that understanding and enter into realization, thereby destroying ignorance and manifesting the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*) without any crookedness;
hence, it is said to be "pure and straightforward. The phrase "such persons as these" serves as a summary.
These are those whose roots are deep, whose vows are weighty, and whose merit is high. Naturally, regarding the long life-span spoken of by the Buddha, they are able to believe it without any doubt.
△ Second, explaining the purport of the words; this is the second faith. It is divided into two parts.
First, presenting the causal practice.
Furthermore, Ajita, if there are those who hear that the Buddha’s lifespan is long and far-reaching,
and understand the meaning of these words— provided they can at least believe and understand them with a single mind—

then those who understand the meaning of these words (where "words" refers to the verbal teachings that express and "meaning" refers to the intended significance expressed) will be able to briefly expound them for others.
Furthermore: △ Second, explaining the merit.
The merit attained by this person is without limit; it can give rise to the unsurpassed wisdom of the Tathāgata.
Those who are able to give rise to the wisdom of the Tathāgata, having themselves attained faith and understanding, further briefly explain it for others;
thus, both self and others will give rise to the unsurpassed wisdom of the Tathāgata. △ Third, extensively hearing this sutra constitutes the third stage of faith.
This is divided into two parts. First, presenting the causal practice.
How much more so for those who hear this sutra extensively; or teach others to hear it; or uphold it themselves; or teach others to uphold it; or write it down themselves;
or teach others to write it down; or make offerings to the scroll with flowers, incense, necklaces, banners, flags, silk canopies, fragrant oils, and ghee lamps.
The former merely provided a brief explanation for people; this, however, is able to expound it extensively for others. II. Explaining the Merit:
The merit of such a person is immeasurable and boundless, capable of giving rise to all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*).
The "Omniscient One" (sarvākārajñatā) is that which is expounded in this sutra; it is exclusively the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, the wisdom of all Buddhas.
Therefore, it is explained in detail for the sake of others so that both oneself and others may be able to give birth to omniscience.
△ Fourth, profound mental faith and understanding (*adhimukti*), which is the fourth faith. This is further divided into two parts. First, the introduction...
Regarding the practice of causes,
Ajita: if a son of good family or a daughter of good family, upon hearing me speak of the long duration of my lifespan, should believe and understand it with a profound mind.
Regarding those who possess deep faith and understanding: herein, they are able to take the long lifespan spoken of by the Tathāgata and enter it into their own infinitesimal single thought-moment;
and with their own infinitesimal single thought-moment, they contemplate the long lifespan spoken of by the Tathāgata.
In this way, they give rise to contemplation through the object, and illuminate the object through contemplation. Object...
Contemplate non-duality: the mind and the Buddha are one and the same. When the practice of contemplation is perfected, it is called "profound mind of faith and understanding.
△ Second, clarifying the merit:
this constitutes seeing the Buddha, who is always present on Vulture Peak, surrounded by a great assembly of Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas.
He preached the Dharma. Furthermore, he saw this Sahā world: its ground was of lapis lazuli, level and smooth;
it was demarcated by eight paths of Jāmbūnada gold; rows of jewel trees stood in order, and all the terraces and towers were made entirely of jewels.
The assembly of bodhisattvas all dwelt therein. If there is anyone who can contemplate in this manner, one should know that this is the mark of profound faith and understanding.
When the merit of their contemplative practice is perfected, the signs of success arise through visualization, and they thus obtain a vision of the Tathāgata.
Initially, they see the Buddha constantly residing on Vulture Peak (Gṛdhrakūṭa) preaching the Dharma; this is the expedient means of seeing him while remaining in the same realm.

For the Buddha is always present at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, preaching this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* to the bodhisattvas and śrāvakas; it is only because sentient beings are subject to delusion and inversion [of perception] that they do not see him.
They were unable to see him. As previously stated, although he was constantly near those sentient beings who were subject to inverted views, they did not see him.

Now, since they have attained profound faith and understanding and the merit of their contemplative practice is perfected, they have already subdued their inverted views and are able to see the Tathāgata, who is eternally present on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, preaching the Dharma together with the great Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas. Thus, while remaining in the same realm, they perceive the *upāya* (expedient means).
It is the "land. Furthermore, as seen below, this refers to seeing the *sahā* (together-abiding) realm as the *vipāka-rūpa* (recompense-realm). This can be understood by analogy.

Regarding the conclusion at the beginning of the section on the "five grades" after the extinction [of the Tathāgata]: these five grades after the Tathāgata’s extinction are the same as the aforementioned four levels of faith (*śraddhā*).
The reason why, having already clarified the four levels of faith, the five grades are further explained is out of fear that people might say...
While the Tathāgata was in the world, the Tathāgata himself was one whose mental, physical, and karmic activities were supreme;
therefore, even hearing [the Dharma] and gaining faith and understanding for a single thought-moment possesses such merit as this.

However, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, the mental, physical, and karmic activities of the person who can preach it may not necessarily be superior. As for the Dharma being preached, it is no more than white paper.

"Black" is merely a name; how could it possibly possess such merit? Therefore, having clarified the four kinds of faith during the present life, he further clarifies the five grades after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa, precisely to demonstrate that this applies regardless of whether the Tathāgata is in the world or has passed away.
If one does not propagate it, let it suffice that one has merely attained faith and understanding (*adhimukti*).

If one can indeed attain faith and understanding, and if one can propagate it, then one will certainly be able to obtain immeasurable and boundless merit. The text is divided into two parts: first, the prose section; second, the verse section.

The first part consists of five sections: first, the Chapter on Rejoicing (*Anumodanā-parivarta*); second, the Chapter on Reading and Reciting (*Paṭhanasvādhyāya-parivarta*); third, the Chapter on Expounding...

Chapter on the Dharma; Chapter Four, Clarifying the Concurrent Practice of the Six Perfections; Chapter Five, Clarifying the Proper Practice of the Six Perfections. Of the first two [chapters], the first presents the causal practice:
furthermore, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, if one hears this sutra and does not disparage it, but gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy.
Regarding the term "rejoicing" (*anumodana*): "following" (*anu*) means to accord with; "joy" (*moda*) means celebratory joy.
To accord means to have no opposition or rejection; to rejoice means to have no alarm or fear. This refers to the long life-span spoken of by the Tathāgata:
although it is that which all Buddhas have realized, it is entirely possessed by sentient beings. Previously one had not heard or known of it, but now one has heard it. Thus...
One then clearly realizes that the present, infinitesimal thought-moment is entirely endowed with the long-lasting lifespan realized by the Tathāgata;
thus, one gives rise to a heart of compliance and joy, free from any sense of resistance, alarm, or fear.
△ Second, the elucidation of merits.
It should be known that this constitutes the characteristic of profound faith and understanding;
herein the merits are briefly explained. Below, in the sixth fascicle, the Chapter on the Merits of Rejoicing (*Anumodanā-puṇya-parivarta*), these shall be explained in detail.

This is a merit. As for the statement, "it is already the mark of profound faith and understanding," if one were to discuss the marks of profound faith and understanding, they would correspond to the fourth stage of faith in the present;
however, this initial Chapter on Rejoicing corresponds only to the first stage of faith in the present.
Why, then, does it say it is "already the mark of profound faith and understanding"? There are two meanings to this. First, if it refers to the period after [the Buddha's] parinirvāṇa...
Consequently, this teaching becomes even more difficult to hear, and the capacity for it (*indriya*) becomes even more difficult to produce.

Thus, to be able to hear it and rejoice accordingly already constitutes the mark of profound faith and understanding. Second, one must rely on rejoicing and faith-understanding to be able to accomplish contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*).
Here, by citing the latter to clarify the former, it is said that this already constitutes the mark of profound faith and understanding. △ Second, Reading.
Chapter Two: On Recitation. First, the causal practice is presented:
"How much more so for those who read, recite, accept, and uphold it.
Second, the merits are explained.
Such a person shall be considered as one who bears the Tathāgata upon their crown.
Ajita, these sons and daughters of good family need not further erect stūpas and temples, nor construct monasteries, nor provide the four requisites for the Saṃgha.
Why is this? Because those sons and daughters of good family who receive, uphold, read, and recite this sūtra have already erected a stūpa.

To construct monasteries and provide offerings to the Sangha is equivalent to erecting a stupa of the seven precious substances for the Buddha’s relics, high and wide, gradually tapering upward until it reaches the Brahma Heaven, adorned with hanging banners, canopies, and various jeweled bells;

with flowers, incense, necklaces, powdered incense, ointments, and burning incense; with various drums and musical instruments, flutes, pipes, and lutes; and with all manner of dances and performances accompanied by exquisite sounds.
If one offers praise through song and hymns, it is equivalent to having made such offerings for immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas.
To "bear the Tathāgata upon one’s head" means that this sutra is the Dharma-body of all Buddhas;
therefore, to read and recite it is to bear the Dharma-body Tathāgata upon one’s head. There is no need to erect stupas or monasteries, nor to make offerings to the Saṃgha.
Generally, a practitioner at the stage of the initial resolve must cultivate contemplation of the principle (*li-guan*).
If one engages in various worldly activities, it will hinder the contemplation of the principle and prevent its accomplishment; therefore, such things are all unnecessary.

As for those who have already erected a stupa—since a stupa is intended to enshrine physical relics (*śarīra*), and this sutra is itself the relic of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*)—to read and recite it is equivalent to having done so.

Regarding the construction of stupas: for one who has already made offerings to the Saṃgha, by reading and reciting this sutra, they have thereby made offerings to the Saṃgha of Ultimate Truth (paramārtha-saṃgha).
Furthermore, if one is able to read and recite this sutra, it is called making an offering of the Dharma;
thus, throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas, one has already performed such offerings as hanging up banners, canopies, and the like. △
Chapter Two: The Exposition of the Threefold Knowledge. First, the citation of causal practice:
"Ajita, if after my parinirvāṇa there should be those who hear this sutra and are able to receive and uphold it—whether by writing it themselves or instructing others to write it."
△ Second, explaining the merits:
He established monastic dwellings and constructed thirty-two halls out of red sandalwood, each eight *tāla* trees in height, magnificent in their height, breadth, and adornment.
Within them resided hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus. There were also gardens, groves, and bathing ponds. [End of] Sūtra.
They shall practice meditation in caves, where robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal decoctions, and all manner of articles of comfort shall abound.

Such monasteries—halls and pavilions numbering in the hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions, and billions, beyond measure—shall manifest before them to provide offerings to me and the community of bhikṣus.
Therefore, I say that after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, if there are those who receive, uphold, and recite [this teaching]...
Recite it, explain it to others, write it yourself or instruct others to write it, and make offerings to the sutra scrolls;
there is no further need to erect stupas or temples, nor to construct monasteries or provide for the Sangha.

This chapter still pertains to the initial stage of the mind; one must diligently apply rational contemplation (*yoniśomanasikāra*). Therefore, it is likewise unnecessary to again construct stupas, temples, and the like.
△ Fourth, the Chapter on Concurrent Practice of the Six Perfections (2). First, citing the causal practices.
How much more so for one who can uphold this sutra while simultaneously practicing generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, single-minded concentration, and wisdom.

To be able to uphold this sutra means to uphold it through its phenomenal characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) and to uphold it through its noumenal characteristics (*tattvalakṣaṇa*). If one sees someone capable of upholding it...

"To uphold" means to uphold through the very fact [of their identity]. If the scripture that is upheld is entirely the mind that upholds it, and if the mind that upholds it is entirely the scripture that is upheld, then in this way, the grasper and the grasped are not distinct.
Although subject and object are not divided, this does not preclude their distinct manifestation as subject and object: I am the holder, and the sutra is that which is held;
this is the mutual support of principle and phenomenon. What is now called "the holder" refers to the accomplishment of the contemplation of principle.
Thus, they are able to maintain the integration of principle and phenomena. Regarding the simultaneous practice of giving and the other perfections:

once the contemplation of principle is established, one returns to employ wondrous contemplation to enter the gates of liberation. Consequently, when practicing giving, one perceives neither a giver nor that which is given;
likewise, when practicing wisdom (*prajñā*), one likewise perceives neither a contemplator nor that which is contemplated. Therefore...
Once the contemplation of principle is established, one may simultaneously practice the six pāramitās. △ Second, the elucidation of merit:
its virtue is most supreme, immeasurable and boundless, like empty space—east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, above, and below.
Immeasurable and boundless. The merit of this person is likewise immeasurable and boundless. They will swiftly reach all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
One who swiftly reaches all-knowledge is able to use practice to assist contemplation and use contemplation to manifest practice; thus, like...
A boat sailing with the wind, when further equipped with oars and paddles, can naturally reach the other shore with great speed.
It is like a bright lamp: when more oil is added, it becomes even brighter.

Thus, by flowing spontaneously, one may swiftly arrive at the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñajñāna*). △ Chapter Five: The Right Practice of the Six Perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*)
Second. First, the causal practice is set forth:

If a person reads, recites, receives, and upholds this sutra, explains it for others, writes it themselves or instructs others to write it, and further builds stupas and monasteries, making offerings and praises to the assembly of śrāvakas, and likewise with hundreds of thousands of millions...

They praise this Dharma with billions of verses, extolling the merits of the Bodhisattvas. Furthermore, for the sake of others, they explain this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* in various ways according to its meaning.

Moreover, they are able to maintain the precepts purely, dwell together with those who are gentle and mild, practice patience without anger, remain firm in their resolve and mindfulness, always value seated meditation, attain profound concentrations, and exert themselves with vigor.
Vigorous. It encompasses all wholesome dharmas, possesses sharp faculties and wisdom, and is adept at answering difficult questions.
From the initial stage of recitation and even teaching others to write it down, this is the accomplishment of wondrous contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

Once the practice of contemplation is perfected, every gate of liberation one encounters is none other than wondrous conduct. Thus, one is able to correctly practice the six perfections; the construction of stupas and so forth clarifies this correctness.

To practice giving—whether by erecting stupas for the Sangha or for individuals—is the gift of material wealth (*āmiṣadāna*). To praise the Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas is the gift of the Dharma (*dharmadāna*).
Since both these gifts of wealth and Dharma are none other than wondrous contemplation, although one practices giving, one does not perceive a giver, a recipient, or a gift;
this is what is called the correct practice of giving. Furthermore, one is able to maintain...

"Purity of precepts" clarifies the correct practice of maintaining the precepts. To speak of "purely maintaining the precepts" means that one is able to strictly guard them without defilement, making no distinction between those that are inherently grave and those involving censure or reproach. "With gentleness and humility" below clarifies the correct practice of patience (*kṣānti*).

Regarding "patience without anger," there are two kinds of patience: patience toward sentient beings (*sattva-kṣānti*) and patience toward phenomena (*dharma-kṣānti*). Patience toward sentient beings is...
To endure the afflictions of sentient beings is [the patience of endurance]; the patience of phenomena (*dharmakṣānti*) is to endure the afflictions of insentient things.

As these two types of affliction—arising from sentient beings and from phenomena—manifest before one, one is able to endure them through the patience of great quiescence (*mahāśāntikṣānti*); thus, there is no anger.

One whose resolve and mindfulness are firm has perfected the power of sublime contemplation (*pratyavekṣaṇā*), such that they perceive neither a subject who endures nor an object that is endured. They always value...

"Below. This clarifies right practice in meditative concentration (*samādhi*). When not a single thought arises and the boundaries of past and future are severed, this is the attainment of profound concentration.
"Diligence below. This clarifies right practice in diligence (*vīrya*). "Sharp faculties below. This clarifies right practice in wisdom (*prajñā*).
△ Second, the clarification of merit.
Ajita, if after my parinirvāṇa there are good sons and good daughters who receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra,
and who further possess such virtuous merits as these, you should know that these people have already set out for the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and are close to Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Seated beneath the site of enlightenment, Ajita, these good sons and good daughters—
O woman, wherever you sit, stand, or walk, a stūpa should be erected right there; all devas and humans should make offerings to it just as they do to the stūpas of the Buddha.

To uphold, receive, read, and recite this sutra refers to the accomplishment of the aforementioned sublime contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Furthermore, there are various other wholesome merits, which refer to the aforementioned correct practice of the six *pāramitās*.
Since one has already practiced both sublime contemplation and the correct practice of the six *pāramitās*, these practices are thereby perfected;

hence it is said, "one has already proceeded to the site of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*). There are two kinds of sites of enlightenment: the site for attaining the Way and the site for cultivating the Way. This is...
They have already proceeded to the site of the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga). Having cultivated the path, they will certainly be able to attain it;

therefore, it is said that they sit beneath the Bodhi tree, close to perfect enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi). Regarding the statement "one should erect a stūpa": at the place where a Tathāgata attained the Way, one should erect a stūpa.
Now, those of the fifth grade have already proceeded to the site of the path and are close to Bodhi; therefore, their [place]...
Wherever one sits, stands, or walks, one should immediately erect a stūpa there. △ Second, the verses in praise. First, the Chapter on Rejoicing (*Anumodanā-parivarta*):

as this is explained extensively in the lower fascicle, it is not versified here; instead, only the final four chapters are versified, divided into four parts. First, the verses for the second chapter, the Chapter on Reading and Reciting (*Vācanā-parivarta*).
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If, after my parinirvāṇa, one is able to receive and uphold this sutra, the merit of such a person shall be immeasurable, as has been described above."

This constitutes the fulfillment of all offerings: by erecting stupas for the śarīra, adorned with the seven treasures, their spires exceedingly high and broad, tapering gradually to reach the Brahma-heaven, with billions of precious bells that emit wondrous sounds when stirred by the wind.
Furthermore, throughout immeasurable eons, one shall make offerings to this stūpa with flowers, incense, various necklaces, celestial robes, and manifold music;
lighting lamps of fragrant oil and ghee, they shall constantly illuminate it on all sides. In the evil age of the final dharma, those who are able to uphold this sutra—
This concludes the preceding section on the full array of offerings.
△ Second, the verse summary of the third chapter, "The Exposition of the Dharma":
If one can uphold this sutra, it is as if the Buddha were present. One should construct monasteries out of ox-head sandalwood to make offerings.
There are thirty-two halls, eight *tāla* trees high. Exquisite food and fine garments, as well as beds and couches, are all fully provided.

It is the dwelling place for hundreds of thousands of beings; with its gardens, groves, various bathing pools, walking paths, and meditation caves, everything is adorned with every kind of excellence.
△ Third Verse: Chapter Four, On the Concurrent Practice of the Six Perfections.

If one possesses a mind of faith and understanding, and receives, upholds, reads, recites, or transcribes [this sutra], or further teaches others to transcribe it, and makes offerings to the scripture scrolls.
Scattering flowers, incense, and powdered incense, one should constantly burn *sumana*, *campaka*, and *atimuktaka* flowers with perfumed oil.
One who makes such offerings shall obtain immeasurable merit; as infinite as space is, so too is their merit.

How much more so for one who upholds this sutra, while simultaneously practicing giving, maintaining the precepts, enduring with patience, and delighting in meditative concentration—remaining free from anger and harsh speech.
The first three lines praise the perfection of the merit of wondrous contemplation; how much more so the final line, which praises the concurrent practice of the six perfections.
Delighting in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) simultaneously entails the attainment of diligence (*vīrya*).
Being free from anger and harsh speech is itself wisdom (*prajñā*), for anyone who harbors anger within and utters harsh words without is not a person of wisdom.
△ Fourth, the verse on the fifth chapter, "The Chapter on the Six Perfections of Right Practice," in two parts: first, the verse citing the causal practice.
They show reverence to stupas and shrines, remain humble toward all bhikṣus, distance themselves from prideful thoughts, and constantly contemplate wisdom.
When questioned or challenged, they do not become angry, but explain the teachings in accordance with the truth.
Revering stupas and temples is giving (*dāna*). Humbling oneself before bhikṣus is ethical discipline (*śīla*). Distancing oneself from an arrogant mind is diligence (*vīrya*).
Contemplating wisdom is meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Since there is no concentration without wisdom, one should constantly contemplate it.
Not becoming angry when questioned or challenged is patience; explaining the teaching in accordance with [the listener's capacity] is wisdom. 2. Verse on the Clarification of Merit:
If one can practice this conduct, the merit is immeasurable. If one sees such a Dharma-preacher, they have accomplished such virtues.
One should scatter celestial flowers and cover his body with celestial robes; bowing one's head to touch his feet, one should give rise to the thought of him as a Buddha.
Furthermore, one should reflect: "Before long he will go to the Tree of Enlightenment and attain the untainted and unconditioned state, bringing vast benefit to all humans and devas."

Wherever they dwell—whether walking, sitting, or lying down—even if it is merely to recite a single verse—a stūpa should be erected there, adorned with exquisite beauty and provided with all manner of offerings.
When a Son of the Buddha dwells in such a place, it becomes an object of enjoyment for the Buddhas.
One should always abide within this state, whether walking, sitting, or lying down.
One who gives rise to a mind that conceives of all beings as Buddhas will, once the merit of wondrous contemplation is perfected, be able to correctly practice the six perfections.
Thus, through the accomplishment of these practices, one will naturally enter realization from conduct; then, one will be no different from a Buddha. Therefore, one should give rise to such a mind.
It is like the perception of a Buddha. Regarding those who have attained the untainted (*anāsrava*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*): ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) fall into the three realms;
those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) fall into the three emptinesses; and Bodhisattvas fall into the gates of deliverance.
Because they are either biased toward existence, biased toward emptiness, or biased toward the Middle Way, they all possess outflows (*sāsrava*). Now, in this fifth chapter...
When a person hears the Tathāgata’s teaching on his immeasurably long lifespan and is able to cultivate contemplation based on principle (li-guan),
and further employs that contemplation as the gateway for correct practice, then all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are entirely the true mark of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu-tattva-lakṣaṇa).

The whole body is simultaneously empty, provisional, and the Middle; thus, it does not fall into the three realms of existence or the three types of emptiness, nor does it fall into the gates of liberation.
It is "unconditioned" because it gives rise to practice through the complete realization of principle, and gives rise to cultivation through the complete realization of nature.

Thus, one cultivates that which is not cultivated, realizes that which is not realized, and attains that which is not attained. Cultivating without cultivation, realizing without realization, and attaining without attainment—this is therefore called the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). As for "extensively benefiting humans and devas":
having attained the untainted (*anāsrava*) unconditioned, this is self-realization; being able to use this self-realization to transform others is what is meant by "extensively benefiting."
This concerns all humans and devas. Among these, one should erect a stūpa at the places where the Buddhas attained the Way and at the places where they turned the wheel of Dharma;
one should also erect a stūpa for those who are currently practicing the six perfections and are able to attain the untainted and unconditioned, for such persons are non-dual with the Buddha.
Therefore, wherever they dwell is itself the place where the Tathāgata attained the Way. This is what he taught.
The places where these verses are located are precisely the places where the Tathāgata turned the wheel of Dharma; therefore, stupas should be erected at all such sites.
To dwell in these places is to dwell in the ground of true reality (*bhūtatathatā*), for one thereby adorns oneself with the adornments of the Buddha.
Therefore, this is the enjoyment-body (saṃbhogakāya) of the Buddha. To constantly walk, stand, sit, and lie within it means that "within it" refers to the ground of the true nature (dharmatā).

Because one is able to contemplate the true nature of all phenomena (dharmas), one thoroughly realizes that every characteristic is nothing other than the true nature, and every phenomenon is nothing other than the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). Thus, in every thought-moment, at every time, and in every place, there is no...
It is not the true reality of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). Therefore, it is said that he constantly walks, stands, sits, and lies within it.
This concludes the commentary on the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merits" (*Vibhaṅga-guṇa-parivarta*). *The Lotus Sutra: A Detailed Exposition*, Fascicle Five, Part Three.

The Eighteenth Chapter: Merit of Rejoicing in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
Regarding the sequential development of this chapter: it arises generally because the Tathāgata has already extensively revealed the near [path].
By thus revealing its remoteness and extensively opening up its traces, it reveals its fundamental source;

thus, the great matter of the *Honmon* (Original Gate) is clarified, and the essential function of the *Shōshū* (True Doctrine) is completed. Since the True Doctrine is now concluded, that which is most important lies solely in its dissemination.
It is for this reason that this long and distant lifespan is exhorted and praised, and entrusted; everything is nothing other than this.
I desire that this Root Chapter be propagated everywhere so that it shall never be severed.

Within the section on exhortation and praise, I clarify that there are four levels of faith during the present age, and five grades of practice after my parinirvāṇa; in each case, I set forth their respective causal practices.
To clarify its merit, only the first chapter, "Rejoicing," briefly states its merits;
one should know that this has already served as a sign of deep faith and understanding, yet it has not yet been explained in detail.

Therefore, Maitreya, responding to the occasion, now poses a question, desiring to extensively reveal the causal practices and merits contained within the initial "Chapter on Rejoicing. Thus, there is this [section].

This is the text of the chapter. Regarding the phrase "merit of rejoicing" (*anumodana-puṇya*): "following" (*anu*) means to accord with; "rejoicing" (*modana*) refers to celebratory joy. With what does one accord?
It is by acceding to the principle of the Tathāgata’s long-lasting lifespan as taught, and the matters of his appearing and passing away;
one accords with this principle and does not oppose or reject it. What is the object of this celebratory joy? That is to say—

This is to rejoice in oneself and to rejoice for others; that is, to realize that the long life-span realized by the Tathāgata is precisely what is possessed within my own present, infinitesimal single thought-moment, and is likewise possessed by all sentient beings.
Since both myself and all sentient beings fully possess this in its entirety, it would suffice if we did not hear, practice, or understand it;

yet, if one can hear, understand, and cultivate it, one will be able to realize the Buddha’s long-lasting life-span and, throughout the three periods of time, manifest birth without being born and manifest extinction without being extinguished, thereby teaching and transforming all sentient beings. Therefore, I rejoice.
Subsequently, one further celebrates the person. When the practice of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) is accomplished, it is termed "merit" (*guṇa*).
