When realization arises from that practice, it is termed "virtue" (*guṇa*). △ The text is divided into two parts. First, Maitreya poses his question.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, if there are good sons or good daughters who, upon hearing this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, rejoice in it, how much merit will they obtain? And he spoke in verse:
After the Parinirvāṇa of the World-Honored One, if there are those who hear this sutra and are able to rejoice in it, how much merit will they obtain?
This section consists of both prose and verse. Regarding the phrase "good sons" and so forth: as previously stated, the Tathāgata distinguished four levels of faith for the present age;
after his passing, there are five grades [of practitioners], of which the latter four possess immeasurable merit. Indeed...
I already understand this. As for the initial "Chapter on Rejoicing," the Tathāgata spoke only briefly, which constitutes the mark of profound faith and understanding;
yet he has not yet extensively elucidated its merit. Therefore, I now ask the World-Honored One again:
if, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there should be one who hears this sutra and is able to act with such compliance and rejoicing, will they likewise attain [the fruit]?
Does one obtain the merit of humans and devas? Does one obtain the merit of the two vehicles? Does one obtain the merit of a bodhisattva?
Or does one obtain the merit of ultimate, unsurpassed bodhi? It is for this reason that it is said, "one obtains such a measure of merit."
△ Second, the Tathāgata’s response and instruction, in two parts: first, the prose; second, the verse. The first part has two sections:

first, clarifying internal sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*); second, from "Furthermore, Ajita... onwards, clarifying coming and going to hear the Dharma. The first of these has three sections: first, teaching one another in succession.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: "Ajita, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata,
if bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, or other wise persons— whether old or young—
having heard this sutra and rejoiced in it, depart from the assembly and go elsewhere, whether to a monastery or to a secluded place."

Whether in cities, towns, streets, villages, or rural hamlets, they shall expound [the teaching] according to their own understanding for the sake of parents, kinsmen, good friends, and spiritual mentors, to the best of their ability. Having heard it, these people shall rejoice and in turn teach others;
others, having heard it, shall likewise rejoice and teach others. In this manner, it shall be transmitted successively until it reaches the fiftieth person.
The phrase "monks and others" refers to the fourfold assembly as well as other wise ones;
those who manifest through great spiritual power among the eight classes of beings; those who appear in their traces born among humans and devas;

and furthermore, those who propagate the teaching by succession—all of these also expound [the Dharma] for their parents, kinsmen, good friends, and spiritual mentors, teaching one another in turn until it reaches the... [second generation].
Fifty. Thus, the first person at the beginning is solely the teacher, and the last person at the end is solely the disciple;
the forty-eight persons in between are those who form a succession of teachers and disciples. △ Second, the evaluation of merit has three parts.
First, having granted permission to speak, he said:
"Ajita, as for the merit of the rejoicing performed by those good sons and good daughters who are number fifty, I shall now describe it;
you should listen well."
△ Second, the presentation of that which is capable of measurement:
If there were sentient beings of the six destinies and four modes of birth—born from eggs or born from wombs—in four million billion *asaṃkhyeya* worlds.
Whether born from moisture or by transformation; whether with form or without form; with perception, without perception, or neither with nor without perception;
whether footless, two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed—whosoever among those counted as sentient beings seeks merit, whatever objects of enjoyment they desire, all shall be granted to them.
To each and every sentient being, [the merit] shall be given as much as would fill Jambudvīpa.
Gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, coral, amber, and various other exquisite treasures;
furthermore, elephants, horses, and carriages made of the seven precious gems, as well as palaces and towers—this great donor gave such gifts for a full eighty years.
Having done so, he then thought: "I have already bestowed upon sentient beings all manner of articles for their enjoyment, according to their every desire."
However, these sentient beings have all grown old; they are over eighty years of age, with white hair and wrinkled faces, and death will soon come for them.

I shall instruct and guide them with the Buddha-dharma. He immediately gathered these sentient beings together and proclaimed the transformative teachings of the Dharma, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them.
In that single moment, they all attained the stage of *srotāpanna*, the stage of *sakṛdāgāmin*, the stage of *anāgāmin*, and the stage of *arhat*.

The Way of Han [the Buddha] exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*). Within profound meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), he attained mastery over all things and was endowed with the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*).
As for the six destinies (*ṣadgati*): karma and conditions act as the "means of going," while birth and death act as the "place to which one goes. These means of going consist of both good and evil.
The destinations of rebirth involve the beautiful and the ugly. That which has form consists of the desire realm and the form realm; that which is formless consists of the formless realm.
That which possesses perception consists of the sphere of infinite space and the sphere of infinite consciousness; that which lacks perception consists of the sphere of nothingness.

That which is neither possessing nor lacking perception consists of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. It is not the possession of perception belonging to the spheres of infinite space or infinite consciousness, nor is it the lack thereof.
Regarding the state of non-conception in all places: the sentient beings of four hundred trillion *asaṃkhyeya* worlds represent the extreme limit of the multitude to whom gifts were given;
filling Jambudvīpa with the seven treasures represents the extreme limit of the breadth of the objects given;
and a full eighty years represents the extreme limit of the duration of the giving. This clarifies its...
"Being able to provide material gifts" and "forming this thought" [and so forth] clarify that one is able to provide the gift of the Dharma.
Phrases such as "I shall instruct and guide them with the Buddha-Dharma" are all internal reflections. One thinks:
"Although I have already bestowed upon them worldly pleasures, these sentient beings will soon die; they may then fall [into lower realms] and undergo suffering."

Regarding those who exist within the sufferings of the three miserable realms, I shall further grant them supramundane happiness and provide them with instruction and guidance through the Buddha-dharma.
"Thereupon he gathered [them]" refers to this correct instruction and guidance. "At one time... refers to hearing the Dharma and attaining benefit.
As for "exhausting all outflows" (*āsrava*): having attained the four fruits of the path, they no longer leak or fall into internal [defilements].
The ten afflictions (daśa-kleśa) do not leak out into the retributive fruits of the three realms of existence.

"Profound meditative concentration" refers to the meditative concentrations possessed by those of the Two Vehicles. △ Third, the formal comparison consists of three parts. First, the question of the Tathāgata:
"What do you think? Is the merit obtained by this great donor much or not?
He is called a "great donor" because he is able to practice both the gift of material wealth and the gift of the Dharma; for this reason, he is called "great."
△ Second, Maitreya’s reply.
Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, the merit of such a person is exceedingly great, immeasurable and boundless.
If this donor were merely to bestow all manner of articles of pleasure upon sentient beings, his merit would already be immeasurable; how much more so when he causes them to attain arhatship?”
The Result.
△ Third, the formal comparison.
The Buddha said to Maitreya: "I now speak to you clearly: if this person were to give all manner of articles of pleasure as alms to the four [assemblies],"

The merit obtained by causing the sentient beings of the six realms in hundreds of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* worlds to attain the fruit of arhatship does not equal the merit of rejoicing upon hearing even a single verse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* by the fiftieth person.
A hundredth part, a thousandth part, or even a hundred-thousand-millionth part does not equal one; it is beyond the reach of calculation or analogy.
When it is said that they do not compare to the fiftieth person, this refers to the great donor, who, despite the multitude to whom he gives, [is surpassed by the recipient].
It is exceedingly much; the objects bestowed are exceedingly vast; the time of bestowal is exceedingly long.
Yet it does not equal the merit of the fiftieth person who, upon hearing a single verse of this sutra, rejoices with even a single thought of sympathetic joy.
The reason it cannot reach that level is because the wealth bestowed consists of worldly riches, and the fruit obtained from it is likewise worldly.

This would merely be the fruit of the Hīnayāna. However, if one hears even a single verse of this sutra and is able to rejoice in it, then one can obtain the supramundane wealth of the Dharma, and may also attain the ultimate fruit of Buddhahood of the One Vehicle.

In this way, one not only destroys the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *saṃyojana*), but also destroys ignorance (*avidyā*); not only does one transcend the limited stages, but...
Even these [stages] emerge from transformation; all of this is attained through the initial single thought of sympathetic joy.
Thus, as for the merits therein, they are naturally inconceivable—how could they ever be compared to that?
△ Third, the illustration by comparison from the first chapter:

"Ajita, if such is the merit of rejoicing in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* even for the fiftieth person who hears it through successive transmission, it is immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*);
how much more so for those who hear it and rejoice at the very beginning of the assembly! Its...
The merit is even more supreme—immeasurable, boundless, incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*), and beyond comparison.
This refers to the fiftieth person, who is merely a disciple; his merit alone is already inconceivable.
How much more so for those in the intervening lineages of successive teachers and disciples, and how much more so for the very first person, who is merely the original teacher! Thus, his...

All such merits are even more inconceivable. Since it is thus in the first chapter on "Rejoicing," then as for the subsequent [stages] of reciting and expounding the Dharma, and further, practicing both [recitation and exposition] together with right practice—the inconceivability of their merit is beyond description.
How much more so when one advances to the stage of "semblance" and "partial realization"? II. Clarification.
"Coming and going to hear the Dharma" means not merely hearing it, but following it with joy; such are its merits.
Even if one merely listens, or shares a seat, or encourages others to listen, or practices fully, there are merits in each case.
Therefore, this is further clarified. The text consists of four parts; the first concerns listening for oneself.
Furthermore, Ajita, if a person, for the sake of this sutra, goes to a monastery and listens to or receives it for even a brief moment,
whether sitting or standing, by virtue of this merit, in their next rebirth they will obtain excellent and sublime elephants,
horses, chariots, precious litters, and celestial palaces.
To say that one should "listen and receive it for even a brief moment" refers to its causal practice. Based on this, the following clarifies its merit:
this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is indeed the Mahāyāna, the Single Buddha Vehicle, and the Supreme Vehicle. It possesses the power of great transport;
it not only carries one out from the three miserable realms, the triple world, and the three voids, but can also carry one back [to liberation].
If one is now able to listen to this secret treasury of the three virtues, one will obtain its power of transport.
Therefore, upon changing bodies, one will be able to obtain fine elephants, horses, and carriages; superior elephants, horses, and carriages; exquisite elephants, horses, and carriages;
and even ride in celestial palaces. △ Second, the sharing of seats.
Furthermore, if there is a person sitting at a place where the Dharma is being taught, and another person comes and encourages them to sit and listen,
or offers them half of their seat to sit upon, the merit of this person will cause them to obtain, upon rebirth, the seat of Śakra, the seat of Brahmā,
or the seat of a Wheel-Turning Sage King.
First, the causal practice is presented; next, from the words "this person" onwards, the merits are clarified. This sutra is able to definitively resolve the teachings for śrāvakas;

it is the king among all sutras. Having already been, currently being, and about to be explained as the foremost of all, one who now shares their seat and encourages others to listen will, upon rebirth, dwell among the heavens of the desire realm, become a king of the desire realm, and attain the status of Śakra.
As for the seat: in the heavens of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), he becomes a king of the Form Realm and attains the seat of a Brahmā King;
in the human world, he becomes a king among men and attains the seat of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*). △ Third, the exhortation to listen.
Ajita, if there is another person who says to someone else, "There is a sutra named the Lotus;

let us go together to hear it," and that person follows this instruction and hears it for even a brief moment, the merit of this person will be such that, upon changing bodies, they will be born in the same place as bodhisattvas who possess dhāraṇīs.
With sharp faculties and wisdom, for hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes, they shall never be mute or speech-impaired.
The breath is not foul. The tongue is always free from disease, as is the mouth. The teeth are neither stained nor black; they are not yellow, nor are they sparse.
They do not fall out, nor are they uneven or crooked. The lips do not hang down, nor are they retracted; they are neither coarse nor rough, nor are they cracked or chapped.
They are neither deficient nor deformed, neither slanted nor askew. They are neither thick nor large, nor are they dark or sallow. There is nothing unseemly about them.
He was not ugly. His nose was neither flat nor crooked; his facial complexion was not dark, nor was it overly long, nor was it sunken or distorted.
There was not a single unpleasing feature. His lips, tongue, and teeth were all perfectly beautiful. His nose was long, high, and straight;

his face was round and full; his eyebrows were high and long; his forehead was broad and level. He was endowed with all the marks of a superior person (*puruṣalakṣaṇa*). Throughout his successive lives...
[They] were born [in this world], saw the Buddha, heard the Dharma, and accepted his instructions with faith.
The former instance of being exhorted to sit and listen was one where they were already participants within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* assembly;

the present instance of being exhorted to go and listen is one where they had no intention of reaching the Dharma-gathering, yet they were exhorted so that the matter was accomplished. Thus, the initial passage first sets forth their causal practice.

Next, following those who are inferior, the text clarifies their merits. First, it generally clarifies their sharp faculties and wisdom; next, it specifically demonstrates the purity of the six sense organs.
Regarding the first point, concerning those born together with Bodhisattva Dhāraṇī: this sutra is the ultimate proclamation of the five periods and the source of all teachings.
Its principle surpasses all other scriptures, its merit exceeds that of the entire transformation [of the Buddha], and it is able to encompass them all.
Regarding those who [uphold] these various sutras, they are thus able to exhort others to hear this sutra;

by doing so, they will be born together with the Bodhisattvas of *dhāraṇī*. Once born together with the Bodhisattvas of *dhāraṇī*, their faculties (*indriya*) will naturally become sharp and clear, and they will abound in wisdom.
Following the passage on "a hundred thousand," the text specifically demonstrates the purity of the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi*). First, it clarifies...
The faculty of the tongue is pure; the nose is not flat or crooked. This clarifies that the person possesses the complete marks of a sage (*puruṣalakṣaṇa*) and that the faculty of the nose is pure.
Within these two passages, the purity of the faculty of the body is also clarified, referring specifically to the lips, face, eyebrows, forehead, and so forth.

Being born in every lifetime where one beholds a Buddha clarifies the purity of the faculty of the eye. Hearing the Dharma clarifies the purity of the faculty of the ear. To believe and accept the teaching [clarifies the purity of the faculty of the mind].

Instruction: This clarity of the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) and the purity of these six faculties all arise because the Bodhisattva has attained *dhāraṇī* and dwells together with them in one place. △ Fourth, the Practice.

Ajita, observe this: if merely encouraging a single person to go and listen to the Dharma produces such merit, how much more so for one who listens with a single-minded focus, recites it, explains it in detail for the sake of others in the great assembly, and practices according to what has been taught?

Regarding the practitioner who practices according to the teaching: the long lifespan that the Buddha has described above is, in its essence, possessed by every sentient being within a single fleeting thought-moment.

Since the Buddha and sentient beings are of one suchness, and ordinary beings and sages are equal, one takes this very [lifespan] as the object of contemplation. When the object and the contemplation are of one suchness, then—
They are able to enter and realize [the truth], and they also attain this long life span; their merit goes without saying. △ Second, the verse summary has two parts:
first, the verse on inward sympathetic joy; second, the verse on coming and going to hear the Dharma. The first part has three sections;
the first is the verse on teaching one another in succession.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If a person, at a Dharma assembly, hears this sutra—even but a single verse—and with sympathetic joy explains it to others,"
In this manner, the teaching was passed down in succession until it reached the fiftieth person.
II. Verses on the Measurement of Merit:
The merit obtained by the final person shall now be analyzed. Suppose there were a great donor who provided for an immeasurable multitude.
Having reached a full eighty years of age, according to his own desires, he beheld those signs of decay: hair white and face wrinkled, teeth sparse and form withered;
reflecting that death would not be long in coming, he thought, "I must now instruct him so that he may attain the fruits of the Path."
He then skillfully taught the true Dharma of Nirvana: "All things in the world are not solid; they are like foam, bubbles, and flames.
You all should swiftly give rise to a mind of weary detachment. When the people heard this Dharma, they all attained Arhatship.

One who possesses the six supernormal powers, the three knowledges, and the eight liberations, yet hears a single verse at the very end—the fiftieth time—and rejoices in it, that person’s merit surpasses the former; it cannot be compared by any analogy.
The first five lines and a half eulogize the capacity for evaluation. The next line eulogizes the actual evaluation. △ Third, the verses illustrate the initial chapter by way of comparison:
"If the merit from hearing [this] transmitted in such a succession is already immeasurable, how much more so for those who hear it for the first time at the Dharma assembly and rejoice accordingly."
△ Second, four verses on going and returning to hear the Dharma. First, a verse that skips ahead to exhort others to listen:
If one exhorts even a single person to lead them to hear the Lotus Sūtra, saying, "This sūtra is profound and subtle; it is difficult to encounter even in ten million kalpas."
He immediately accepted the instruction and went to listen. Having heard it for even a brief moment, he said: "The meritorious retribution of this person shall now be explained in detail:

in every lifetime he will have no afflictions of the mouth; his teeth will not be sparse, yellow, or black; his lips will not be thick, upturned, or cleft; nor will he possess any loathsome features."

His tongue was not dry, black, or short; his nose was high, long, and straight; his forehead was broad and level; and his face and features were entirely dignified and handsome, such that he was pleasing to behold by all people.
His breath was free from foul odors, and the fragrance of the *utpala* lotus constantly issued from his mouth.
△ Second, a verse summarizing what was just heard:
If one goes to a monastery with the desire to hear the Lotus Sutra, even hearing it for a brief moment brings joy; now I shall describe the merit thereof.
In future lives, one will be born among devas and humans, obtaining exquisite elephants, horses, and chariots, as well as precious palanquins and carriages, and riding within celestial palaces.
△ Third, the section on verses praising the sharing of seats.

If, at a place where the Dharma is being preached, one encourages others to sit and listen to the sutras, through this causal condition of merit, one shall obtain the seats of Śakra, Brahmā, and the Cakravartin.
△ Fourth, the verse on the correct practice.
How much more so for one who listens with a single-minded focus, explains its meaning and intent, and practices according to what has been taught; their merit will be beyond measure.
The five categories [of merit] following the parinirvāṇa have now concluded. This completes the *Anumodanā-puṇya-parivarta* (Chapter on the Merit of Rejoicing).
The Nineteenth Chapter of the Lotus Sutra, "The Merits of the Dharma-Preacher.
Regarding the origin of this chapter, it generally stems from the Tathāgata’s previous revelation of his long-lasting life span.
By opening up its proximate traces and revealing its remote origin, the great matter of the Root Chapter is thus clarified;
that is to say, there is only this matter to be understood, and no other. What is emphasized here is solely the desire to circulate this wondrous sutra among the heavens and the human world.
Therefore, the merits pertaining to the four levels of faith and the five grades of practice are explained.
Thus, [the Buddha] provides exhortations and praises for its circulation. However, while it has clarified the merit of its remote causes, the merit of its proximate fruits has not yet been revealed.
Now, this chapter is revealed to clarify the proximate fruits in order to encourage its circulation;
it does so by citing the results as they are to urge its dissemination. Therefore, there is this one chapter. It speaks of "The Merits of the Dharma Master."
This refers to the Dharma, which consists of the three thousand natures and characteristics and the ten realms with their thousand suchnesses.
If it pertains to the Trace Gate, it is called the "True Aspect of All Dharmas"; if it pertains to the present Essential Gate, it is called "neither suchness nor different.
Both are inconceivable, most profound, subtle, and wondrous Dharmas. One takes this Dharma as one's own standard, or upholds it.
Whether reading, reciting, copying, or explaining [the teachings], one uses these very practices as a standard for others;

or one teaches others to uphold them, even to the point of teaching others to explain them. Because one can thus use this sublime Dharma to regulate oneself and guide others, one is called a teacher (*śāstṛ*).
The accomplishment of the practice of regulating oneself and guiding others is termed "merit" (*guṇa*). Truly so.
That which is realized and attained is called "virtue" (*guṇa*). Virtue means that by practicing the Way, one attains realization within the mind.
Furthermore, this merit has no other source than the purity of the six sense faculties; this is precisely the merit of the Dharma Master. The text is divided into two parts:
first, a general explanation; second, a detailed exposition. The first part consists of two sections. The first section clarifies the five kinds of Dharma Masters.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Constantly Diligent:
"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives, maintains, reads, recites, explains, or transcribes this Lotus Sūtra..."
"At that time, the Buddha said" refers to the moment when the comparative assessment (*pramāṇa*) of the merit of rejoicing (*anumodanā*) from the first chapter was concluded.
Although there are differences between the four levels of faith and the five grades of practice due to the merits explained above, these are all causal merits.
Now, wishing to further clarify the resultant merits, the Buddha said (as follows). "Constantly diligent" means... diligence.

This means being unmixed; advancing without retreating. "Constant" means not limited to a single thought-moment, a single time, or a single place, but being able to remain unmixed and non-retrogressive in every thought-moment, at every time, and in every place.

Now, as for why he does not address others but addresses only those who are constantly diligent: it is to clarify that the merit of this fruit is intended solely to encourage and praise the stream [of practitioners].

It is pervasive. Yet, when one wishes to circulate it—whether in the present or in the future—one should, as is customary, apply diligent effort at every thought-moment, at all times, and in all places, circulating it without retreat or distraction; thus he informs them of this.
This is precisely what is meant by "employing the Dharma to conform to the person" and "using the person to manifest the Dharma. One should receive and uphold this...
Regarding "the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and others," this clarifies that he is able to take these as his own standard.
As for his guiding others, it refers to teaching people to receive and uphold [the teachings], up to and including teaching them to transcribe them; this clarifies the five types of Dharma-preachers.
△ Second, the clarification of the merits of the six sense faculties.
This person shall obtain eight hundred merits of the eye, twelve hundred merits of the ear, eight hundred merits of the nose,
twelve hundred merits of the tongue, eight hundred merits of the body, and twelve hundred merits of the mind. Adorned with these merits,
all six sense faculties shall be rendered pure.

Regarding the statement "one shall obtain eight hundred thousand, two hundred thousand, and so forth," some explain this by means of the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*) as elucidated in the *Śūraṃgama-samādhi Sūtra*.
They claim that for the eye, the front is entirely bright while the back is entirely dark; when looking to the left or right, one lacks a third part.
Therefore, they say the eye possesses only eight hundred merits and so on. However, they do not realize what that sūtra actually elucidates.

It is within the realm of outflows (*sāsrava*) and is subject to arising and ceasing. Yet, because one merely seeks to select the perfect penetration (*pariśuddha-avabhāsa*) of the ear-faculty as the essential method for entering the Path in this land, it is said: "In this land, the true substance of the teaching is purity found in hearing sounds.
If one wishes to attain *samādhi*, one must necessarily enter through hearing. Since this is entirely comprised of outflows and subject to arising and ceasing, it cannot [be the ultimate means].
To explain this: herein, it is only the Dharma Master who is thus, while others are not; for he is untainted (*anāsrava*) and not subject to arising and ceasing.
Now, regarding the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) clarified here, originally each one possesses twelve hundred merits.
How is this seen? It is because when a single faculty arises, it necessarily falls into a single realm. One...
Within the realms, there must be ten realms. Within one realm, there are ten suchnesses; within ten realms, there are one hundred suchnesses.
Since each single faculty already possesses one hundred suchnesses, and each faculty mutually possesses the other five faculties, there are six hundred suchnesses.
When these are all adorned with concentration and wisdom, there are one thousand two hundred suchnesses. Therefore, each and every faculty is fully endowed with one thousand two hundred suchnesses.

Regarding the "one hundred merits," as for the mention of "eight hundred," it is because once one has thoroughly realized the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, then defilement is itself purity, and that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) is itself without outflows (*anāsrava*). Regarding the principle thus perceived, there is originally neither increase nor decrease;
yet, within this state of no increase or decrease, there is increase and decrease. Therefore, the treatise speaks of eight hundred and twelve hundred [merits]. This is based on...
The principle perceived therein is discussed in terms of such expansion and contraction.

Furthermore, being able to contemplate the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena and attain correspondence and similarity therewith, one destroys the views, afflictions, and *rajas* (dust-like delusions). Thus, one attains sovereign efficacy:
if one wishes to expand, one expands; if one wishes to contract, one contracts. Therefore, it is said to be eight hundred or twelve hundred.
However, as for upholding [the Dharma], it relies solely on the faculty of mind; reciting it relies solely on the faculty of tongue;
and copying it relies solely on the faculty of body. How is it that by merely being able to uphold it, one attains the purification of the six faculties?

And how is it that by merely being able to copy it, one also attains the purification of the six faculties? One should know that while upholding is primarily centered in the faculty of mind, its influence extends to the others.
Consequently, they must also possess the remaining faculties to assist in its accomplishment; the same applies to reading, reciting, and copying.

Therefore, whether one is merely able to receive and uphold [the teachings], or even merely able to explain them, all shall attain the purification of the six sense-faculties. Yet, how is it that they are able to attain such purity?
It is because this Dharma Master, from the very beginning, was able to hear the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena in its entirety and thereby attained it.

Perfect understanding. Having now attained the perfect semblance of realization, one is able to see that every phenomenon is the Dharma-realm and that every characteristic is none other than the true mark (dharmatā).
Thus, that which is with outflows is itself without outflows; that which is defiled is itself pure.
Since the principle perceived by them is thus, all six sense faculties are likewise able to attain purity.
This is how purity is discussed in terms of the inherent nature of perceiving the principle. Furthermore, once a semblance [of realization] is attained, the coarse defilements fall away first;
having already shattered the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava* and *kleśa-āsrava*), one is naturally able to become pure. Indeed, the reason why people are unable to attain purity is as follows:
This is because [the nose] possesses discriminative craving; now that this has been destroyed, how could it not be pure?
Such is the discussion of purity in terms of destroying delusions. As the "Chapter on the Nose" states:

"To know good and evil, to distinguish noble and base, and to behold the adornments of celestial palaces—then the nose possesses the function of the eye. When one reads scriptures or hears the Dharma being preached...
If the nose can perceive [fragrance], then the nose possesses the function of the ear; for it can perceive the fragrances of the flowers, fruits, and seeds of various trees, as well as ghee and oil.
If the nose can perceive the entry into dhyāna—wherein there are eight tactile sensations—then the nose possesses the function of the body.

Furthermore, if it can discern minds of lust and anger, as well as those cultivating goodness, then the nose possesses the function of the mind. Since this is the case for one faculty, so it is for all others.
The same applies to the other five faculties. Having attained this mutual similarity, one is able to employ the six faculties interchangeably.
In ordinary people, each faculty is distinct and does not merge with the others; therefore, they are not pure. Now that the six faculties are used interchangeably, they are all pure.
Such is the discussion of purity in terms of mutual interchangeability. Part Two: A Detailed Demonstration of the Six [Faculties]. First, the demonstration of the eye faculty.
2. Showing the ear faculty; 3. showing the nose faculty; 4. showing the tongue faculty; 5. showing the body faculty; 6. showing the mind faculty.
Regarding the first two, the first consists of the prose section (*dīrghapada*).
These sons and daughters of good family, with the pure physical eyes born of their parents, see all the mountains, forests, rivers, and oceans within and without the trichiliocosm;
from below, as far as the Avīci Hell, to above, as far as the Peak of Existence (Bhavāgra), they also see all sentient beings therein,
as well as the places where they are born through the causes and conditions of their karma and their retributions— all they see completely.

"Know that the pure fleshly eye and so forth" means: if it were the fleshly eye born of one's parents, it could not see the five viscera through the skin, nor could it see external objects through walls; how then could it be pure? Now, being able to receive and uphold this...
The Sūtra states: "Having thoroughly realized the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, one naturally possesses the merit of the eye-faculty as an adornment;

thus, the eyes born of one's parents attain purity. Therefore, it is said that the 'pure physical eyes born of one's parents' perceive the trichiliocosm. This refers to the vastness of their horizontal vision.
From the Peak of Existence above to the Avīci Hell below—this describes the depth of his vertical vision.
This clarifies that he is able to see the lands and environmental supports (*āśraya-pratyaya*) of the ten realms, as well as all sentient beings therein.

He is able to see the conventionally designated (*prajñapti-sat*) sentient beings of the ten realms, as well as their karmic causes and conditions; he is able to see the substantial dharmas (*dravya-sat*) of the ten realms.

Regarding these five aggregates: if one discusses the causes and conditions of karma and its retributive fruits, there are those that are with outflows (*sāsrava*), those that are without outflows (*anāsrava*), those that are both with and without outflows, and those that are neither with nor without outflows. These are the various attachments and conceptual discriminations of ordinary beings.

These are the causes and conditions of outflowing karma (*sāsrava-karma*); they are the places of birth resulting from the retribution of outflowing karma, wherein one wanders through the three realms and revolves within the six paths.

The analytical contemplation of the essence (*tattva*) by the Two Vehicles constitutes the causes and conditions of non-outflowing karma (*anāsrava-karma*); the land of remaining skillful means (*upāya-śeṣa-bhūmi*) is the place of birth resulting from the retribution of non-outflowing karma.
That Bodhisattvas are able to shatter the dust-like and sand-like afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) is likewise [non-outflowing].
Regarding "outflows" (*āsrava*): as long as ignorance has not been destroyed, this is also "with outflows. The Tathāgata, by means of great wisdom, does not abide in birth-and-death;
thus, this is not "with outflows. By means of great compassion, he does not abide in nirvāṇa; thus, this is not "without outflows. As for "seeing all and knowing all":
he sees and knows the ten realms of the dependent retribution, the provisional names of the ten realms, and the real dharmas of the ten realms—all he sees and knows.

Because they are able to penetrate the reality of the three thousand natures and characteristics, the hundred realms and thousand suchnesses—the principle of the true mark of all dharmas—and because they have shattered the views and afflictions as numerous as motes of dust, attaining a semblance of correspondence with that reality, they are thus able to know and see them all.
This refers to the three thousand [realms] within the great trichiliocosm in this manner. As for the mention of "all mountains, forests, and so forth" both inside and outside, it is not...
Within a single world-system, they likewise see and even know as far as three thousand worlds beyond that boundary. II. Verse Summary:
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
If, within a great assembly, one preaches this Lotus Sūtra with a mind free from fear, listen now to their merit:
such a person shall obtain eight hundred supreme and distinguished eyes; because they are adorned with these, their vision is exceedingly pure.
With the eyes born of their parents, they see the entirety of the trichiliocosm:
the inner and outer Mount Merus, Sumerus, and Cakravāḍas, as well as all other mountains and forests, the great oceans, rivers, and streams; from the Avīci Hell below to the Peak of Existence above.
Within it, all sentient beings are seen by everyone; though they have not yet attained the divine eye, the power of their physical eyes is such as this.
Those with a mind free from fear are able to enter the Tathāgata’s chamber and exercise great compassion;
they are able to sit upon the Tathāgata’s seat and contemplate the emptiness of all phenomena; and they are able to don the Tathāgata’s robe, being gentle and patient. Furthermore...
Because he is able to practice the four kinds of peace and happiness through body, speech, and mind, his heart attains fearlessness.

As for the statement that "his eyes are exceedingly pure": if they were not adorned with meritorious qualities, they would merely be the physical eyes born of one's parents, which are inherently defiled. Now, however, they are adorned with such meritorious qualities.
Thus, nature itself makes it pure, and the eyes become exceedingly pure; this is why one can perceive principle, destroy delusion, and exercise mutual functions.

As for "seeing all things," this means being able to see the supporting environments and the provisional names of the ten realms, as well as the substantial dharmas of the ten realms—all of these can be seen.
This is so even though one has not yet attained the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) and the like.
If one wishes to perceive the dependent retributions (*niśraya-vipāka*) of the various devas, one must employ the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).

To perceive the dependent retributions of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), one must employ the wisdom eye (*prajñācakṣus*). To perceive the dependent retributions of the bodhisattvas, one must employ the dharma eye (*dharmacakṣus*).

To perceive the dependent retributions of the Tathāgata, one must employ the buddha eye (*buddhacakṣus*). Although at present one has not yet attained the divine eye, the dharma eye, or the wisdom eye...
The Buddha-eye is precisely the physical eye born of one's parents, yet it possesses the functional capacity of the five eyes;

therefore, it is able to see all ten realms. △ Second, the demonstration of the faculty of hearing, which has two parts: first, the prose section; second, the verse section. The first part [of the prose] has two sub-sections:
first, the introduction of the Dharma Master.
Furthermore, Nityodyukta, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives, maintains,
reads, recites, explains, or transcribes this sutra.

△ Second, the explanation of the merits has two parts: first, the actual explanation; second, the conclusion with essential points. The first part has two sections: first, the explanation of within the realm;
second, the explanation of outside the realm. The first of these two has two subsections: first, the general explanation.

He attains the merit of twelve hundred ears. With these purified ears, he hears all manner of languages and sounds within and without, throughout the trichiliocosm, from the Avīci Hell below up to the Peak of Existence above.
△ Second, the specific explanation: the sound of elephants;
the sound of horses; the sound of oxen; the sound of chariots; the sound of weeping; the sound of lamentation; the sound of conchs; the sound of drums; the sound of bells.

The sound of bells; the sound of laughter; the sound of speech; the voices of men; the voices of women; the voices of boys; the voices of girls; the sound of the Dharma; the sound of what is not the Dharma;
the sound of suffering; the sound of pleasure; the voices of ordinary beings; the voices of noble ones; the sound of joy; the sound of displeasure; the voices of devas; the voices of nāgas.
The voices of yakṣas; the voices of gandharvas; the voices of asuras; the voices of garuḍas; the voices of kiṃnaras; the voices of mahoragas;
the sounds of fire; the sounds of water; the sounds of wind; the sounds of hell-beings; the sounds of animals; the sounds of hungry ghosts;
the voices of bhikṣus; the voices of bhikṣuṇīs.
The sounds of domestic animals are those of sentient beings; the sound of a cart is that of a non-sentient being. The sounds of weeping, sorrow, and lamentation are those of sentient beings.
Sounds such as those from a conch shell are sounds produced by the combination of both sentient and non-sentient beings. Laughter and so forth [are likewise].
This also generally clarifies the sounds of the joy of sentient beings, such as the voices of the devas and others; it clarifies the voices of the eight classes of supernatural beings;
the sounds of the three calamities of water, fire, and wind; the sounds of the three miserable realms such as hell; and [the voices of] bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs.
This is a brief summary of two of the four assemblies. △ Second, clarifying those outside the realm:
the voice of the śrāvaka, the voice of the pratyekabuddha, the voice of the bodhisattva, and the voice of the Buddha.
This refers to the Four Noble Truths, Dependent Origination, the Six Perfections, and the myriad practices.

It is the sound possessed by all four types of noble beings when causes are exhausted and fruits are fulfilled. △ Second, the conclusion: To speak in brief, although all sounds—both internal and external—within the trichiliocosm...
Without having yet attained the divine ear, they hear and know all sounds with the pure, ordinary ears born of their parents;
thus they distinguish various types of voices without impairing the faculty of hearing.
The phrase "ordinary ears" refers to the ordinary fleshly ears born of one's parents. Regarding "not destroying the faculty of the ear":

if one were necessarily to hear celestial sounds with celestial ears, or even necessarily to hear the sounds of Buddhas with the ears of a Buddha, it would be necessary to destroy the faculty of the fleshly ears before one could hear them. Yet, here, with these very fleshly ears—
One is able to hear the voices of the heavens, and even with the physical ear of flesh, one can hear the voice of the Buddha;
therefore, there is no need to destroy the faculty of the physical ear. Since all ten realms can be heard, every dharma is discerned and every sound is listened to.
The reason one is able to do so is because of the capacity to realize the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
By principle, they attain similarity: that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) is itself without outflows (*anāsrava*), and that which is defiled is itself pure.
Therefore, one is able to hear the sounds of the ten realms with the ears of flesh born of one's parents.
△ Second, the verse commentary has two parts; first, the general explanation.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The ears born of one's parents are pure and free from turbidity or defilement; with these constant ears, one hears the sounds throughout the three thousandfold world-system."

△ Second, the specific verses are twofold: first, the verse that correctly explains; second, the verse that concludes. The former consists of two parts; the first verse concerns the interior of the boundary (*sīmā*):
the sounds of elephants, horses, chariots, and oxen; the sounds of bells, gongs, conchs, and drums; the sounds of lutes, harps, and *konghou*; and the sounds of flutes and pipes.
Pure and beautiful vocal melodies they hear without attachment; the voices of countless kinds of people they hear and can fully comprehend.
Furthermore, they hear the voices of the devas and their subtle, wondrous songs, as well as the voices of men and women, and the voices of boys and girls.
In the midst of mountains, rivers, and perilous valleys, the cries of the kalaviṅka and the jīvañjīvaka birds—all such sounds are heard.
There, the various cries of agony and manifold tortures of the hell-beings, and the sounds of hungry ghosts, oppressed by hunger and thirst, as they search for food and drink, are all heard.
When the various asuras dwelling on the shores of the great ocean converse among themselves, they produce great sounds;
yet the Dharma-preacher, dwelling here in this place, hears these various sounds from afar without his faculty of hearing being impaired.
Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, the cries and calls of birds and beasts—the person who preaches the Dharma hears them all.
Furthermore, the sounds of speech from the Brahma heavens, the Ābhāsvara, the Śubhakṛtsna, and up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven—all such voices are heard.

The Dharma Master dwells here and hears them all. Whether it be the entire assembly of bhikṣus or the bhikṣuṇīs who are reading or reciting the sūtras, or those who expound them for others, the Dharma Master dwelling here hears them all.
The first phrase refers to the category of animals. Bells, chimes, and so forth clarify the environment of retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*).
To hear these sounds without attachment means that if an ordinary person hears a sound contrary to their feelings, they become angry; if it accords with their feelings, they become attached;
and if it is a neutral sound, they are unable to discern it. All of these are termed "having attachment. Now, the Dharma Master’s faculty of hearing is pure.
Therefore, when hearing sounds that contradict one's desires, one does not feel anger; when hearing sounds that accord with one's desires, one does not feel attachment.
As for neutral sounds, one can clearly discern them; thus, it is called "non-attachment. The "voices of countless kinds of people" refers to the voices of those within the ten realms.

Furthermore, "hearing the voices of the various devas" refers to the voices of the heavens in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). "Mountains and rivers below" refers to the four miserable destinies (*caturgati*).

Regarding "Sound": the first line clarifies that animals, hungry ghosts, hell-beings, and asuras are all visible. The section beginning with "In the ten directions" further clarifies the realm of animals.
"Brahmā Heaven" refers to the heavens of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*). The section beginning with "All" clarifies the fourfold assembly.
△ Second, the verse on those outside the assembly:
Furthermore, there are various bodhisattvas who read and recite the sūtras and dharmas; if they explain them for others, or compile and interpret their meanings.

All such sounds and voices they shall hear. Those Great Holy Honored Ones, the Buddhas who transform sentient beings, preaching the subtle and wondrous Dharma within great assemblies—all these shall be heard by those who uphold this Lotus Sutra.
Regarding the "Compiler": "Compilation" means to compose according to one's own intention; "collection" means to adopt the writings of others. △ Second, the concluding verse:
Within the three thousandfold great thousandfold world-system, all sounds from within and without—from the Avīci Hell below up to the Peak of Existence above.
They all hear those sounds without their faculty of hearing being impaired; because their ears are keen and sharp, they are able to discern and know them all.
Even though those who uphold this Lotus Sutra have not yet attained the divine ear, using only the ears born of their physical birth, their merit is already such as this.
Regarding those with sharp and keen hearing: the ears of sentient beings are originally sharp and keen, originally all-pervasive, and originally pure.
However, due to various forms of craving and various forms of discrimination, that which was sharp and keen has become dull and obstructed;
that which was all-pervasive has become limited and narrow; and that which was pure has become defiled. Now, the Dharma Master...
By upholding this sutra, one is able to destroy the conceptualization of craving; thus, one attains sharp intelligence and purity.
Upon hearing all sounds, one is able to discern them: "This is the sound of the three miserable realms; this is the sound of humans and devas;
this is the sound of the Three Vehicles; this is the sound of the Buddhas. One distinguishes each one clearly, without [confusion].
There is an error here. △ Third, showing the faculty of the nose, in two parts: first, the prose; second, the verse. The first part has two sections. First, presenting the Dharma-preacher:
"Furthermore, Constantly Diligent, if good sons or good daughters receive and uphold this sutra, whether reading it or reciting it..."
Whether explaining it or writing it down.
△ Second, clarifying the merits, in three parts. First, the general clarification:
One accomplishes eight hundred merits of the nose. By means of this pure faculty of the nose, one hears throughout the trichiliocosm.
The realm. Various fragrances above, below, within, and without.
△ Second, specifically citing two [categories]. First, within the realm; second, outside the realm. The first of these has two parts. First, the desire realm.
The fragrance of sumanā flowers, the fragrance of jāti flowers, the fragrance of mallikā flowers, the fragrance of campaka flowers, the fragrance of pāṭala flowers,
the fragrance of red lotuses, the fragrance of blue lotuses, the fragrance of white lotuses, the fragrance of flowering trees, and the fragrance of fruit-bearing trees.
Sandalwood incense, aloeswood incense, tamālapatra incense, tagara incense, and ten million varieties of blended perfumes—
whether in powder form, pill form, or as ointment— those who uphold this sutra, while remaining here in this world, are able to distinguish them all.
Furthermore, he discerns individually the scents of sentient beings: the scent of elephants, the scent of horses, the scent of oxen and sheep, and so forth;
the scent of men, the scent of women, the scent of boys, and the scent of girls; as well as the scents of grasses, trees, thickets, and forests—whatever scents there may be, whether near or far.
They shall all hear [these scents] and distinguish them without error. Those who uphold this sutra, though dwelling here on earth, shall also smell the fragrances of the various devas in the heavens:
the fragrance of the pārijātaka and kovidāra trees, as well as the fragrance of māndārava flowers, mahāmāndārava flowers, mañjūṣaka flowers, and mahāmañjūṣaka flowers.

He perceives every scent produced from the blending of various powdered incenses such as sandalwood and aloeswood, as well as the fragrances of diverse flowers— indeed, there is no fragrance among these celestial scents that he does not perceive.
Furthermore, he smells the bodily perfumes of the devas, including the fragrance of Śakra-devānām-indra when he is upon his magnificent palace,
enjoying the pleasures of the five senses and engaging in play, as well as the fragrance when he is in the Sudharmā Hall for the sake of the Trāyastriṃśa devas.

They smell the fragrance when the Dharma is being preached; they smell the fragrance when [the gods] sport in the various gardens; and they smell the fragrances from the bodies of other devas, both male and female, all from afar.
In this manner, it continues successively.

First, the human realm is clarified. Fragrances such as *sumana* are the fragrances of the *niśraya-vipāka* (retributive environment). Furthermore, the section below clarifies the fragrances of the *sambhoga-vipāka* (retributive body).

Next, the section beginning with "Holding this" clarifies the celestial realms; the first part therein clarifies the fragrances of the *niśraya-vipāka*, while the section beginning with "Furthermore, one hears" clarifies the fragrances of the *sambhoga-vipāka*.
This "Sublime Dharma" (*Saddharma*) is so named because it consists of the ten wholesome paths of action (*daśakuśala-karma-patha*). As for the other devas... [text continues].
He transmutes [his state]: that very night he ascends to the Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmita-vaśavartin heavens, and descends to the gods of the Four Great Kings.
△ Second, the Form Realm (Rūpadhātu).
Even up to the Brahma-world and as far as the Peak of Existence, they likewise smell the fragrances of the bodies of all the devas,
as well as the incense burned by those devas.
The fragrance of the body is the fragrance of the primary retribution (*vipāka-phala*); that which is burned is the fragrance of the secondary retribution (*niṣyanda-phala*).

△ Second, regarding those outside the realms: the fragrances of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and the bodies of all Buddhas are likewise smelled from afar, and their locations are thereby known.
△ Third, the conclusion:
Although one smells this fragrance, the faculty of the nose is neither impaired nor deluded; if one wishes to discern it, one can explain it to others.
I recall this without error.
△ Second, the verse recitation has three parts. First, the verse that summarizes and clarifies the general meaning:
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
The nose of this person is pure; within this world, whether it be fragrant or foul substances, he perceives and knows all their various kinds.
△ Second, the verses separately cite two cases: first, the verse on the internal realm; second, the verse on the external realm. Regarding the first two, the first verse concerns the desire realm.
Sumanas, Jāti, Tamāla, and sandalwood; aloeswood and cinnamon fragrance;

the scents of various flowers and fruits, as well as the scents of all sentient beings—whether male or female—the teacher of the Dharma, though dwelling at a distance, perceives their location by smelling these fragrances.
The great universal monarch, the minor wheel-turning kings and their sons, the ministers, and all the palace ladies—their locations are known by the scent.
The precious jewels worn upon their bodies, as well as the treasures hidden within the earth, and the precious women of the universal monarch—all are known by the scent.
The various articles for adorning the body, such as garments and necklaces, and the many kinds of scented ointments—by smelling their fragrance, one knows those bodies.
Whether the devas are walking or sitting, whether they are sporting or manifesting supernatural transformations, those who uphold this Lotus Sūtra can know them all by smelling their fragrance.
The flowers, fruits, and seeds of all trees, as well as the fragrance of ghee and oil—those who uphold this sūtra, while dwelling here, shall know their locations entirely.
In deep and perilous mountain places where sandalwood trees are in full bloom, they shall be able to perceive by scent all sentient beings dwelling therein.
The Cakravāḍa mountains and the great oceans, and all sentient beings within the earth—the upholder of this sūtra, by smelling their fragrance, shall know the locations where they all dwell.
Asuras, male and female, along with all their retinues, when they are engaged in strife or in play—the upholder of this sūtra shall be able to know them all by smelling their fragrance.
In vast wildernesses and perilous defiles, lions, elephants, tigers, wolves, wild oxen, water buffaloes, and the like—he knows their locations by their scent.
If there are those who are pregnant, even before the sex of the child can be distinguished, as well as those without sense organs or non-humans, he is able to know them all by their scent.
By the power of smelling scents, he knows when one has first conceived, whether the pregnancy will be successful or unsuccessful, and whether it will result in an easy birth and a blessed child.
By the power of smelling scents, he knows the thoughts of men and women—whether their minds are stained by desire, delusion, or anger—and he also knows those who cultivate virtue.
The various hidden treasures within the earth—gold, silver, and all manner of precious gems contained in copper vessels—he can fully know by smelling their fragrance.
Regarding various kinds of necklaces and ornaments whose value cannot otherwise be discerned, he knows their worth, their origin, and their location simply by smelling their scent.
The various celestial flowers, such as the māndārava, mañjūṣaka, and pārijātaka trees—hearing their fragrance, he knows them all.
Regarding the celestial palaces, with their distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior, and adorned with various precious flowers—hearing their fragrance, he knows them all.

In the celestial gardens, the sublime palaces, and the various halls for contemplating the wondrous Dharma, he dwells in the midst of them and enjoys himself; by smelling their fragrance, he knows them all.
Whether the devas are listening to the Dharma or indulging in the five desires, whether they are coming or going, walking, sitting, or lying down—he smells their fragrance and knows them all.
The garments worn by the celestial maidens, adorned with exquisite flowers and fragrances—when they move about and sport, one can perceive all these scents;
thus it continues, ascending further and further.
The lines beginning with "Sumanas" and so forth describe the secondary retribution (upabhoga) of the human realm; the following two lines of verse describe the primary retribution (vipāka).

The next two lines of verse further describe the secondary retribution. Next, one line of verse concerning the various heavens describes the fragrance of the primary retribution of the desire-realm heavens (*kāmadhātu*).

The section on the various trees again describes the fragrance of the secondary retribution of the human realm. The section on sentient beings again describes the primary retribution within the earth.
"Sentient beings" refers to those in the hells and hungry ghosts. "Asuras" refers to the asuras below. "Wilderness-dwellers" refers to the various classes of animals.
"If there are... refers to human beings. "Attachment" is greed; "delusion" is ignorance; "anger" is hatred. These three poisons are unwholesome.
One who lacks these three poisonous minds is called a practitioner of virtue. Earth... [text ends]... Earth.

The middle and lower two lines further verse the *niśraya-vipāka* (the environment). Next, the first two lines of "Above the heavens" (*tianyǎng*) verse the *niśraya-vipāka* of the desire-realm heavens (*kāmadhātu-deva*).
Next, the three lines from "In the celestial gardens" (*tiānyuán*) below verse the *sambhoga-vipāka* (the primary retribution).

The phrase "recreating therein, listening to the Dharma, and sporting," etc., refers precisely to the *sambhoga-vipāka*. Thus, the subsequent single line verses the remaining heavens of the desire realm.
△ Second, the verses on the Form Realm:
"Up to the Brahma-world, those who enter and emerge from dhyāna—their scents he can all perceive. [He knows] the Ābhāsvara and Śubhakṛtsna heavens."
Even up to the Peak of Existence, he can perceive through the scent the initial birth and the subsequent passing away [of beings].
II. Verse on those outside the assembly:
"The multitude of bhikṣus are ever diligent in the Dharma; whether sitting or walking, they recite and chant the scriptures."
Or perhaps beneath forest trees, they sit in meditation with single-minded focus; those who uphold the sutras perceive their fragrance and know exactly where they are.
Whether the Bodhisattvas’ resolve is firm as they sit in meditation, recite and chant, or preach the Dharma to others, they are able to know it all by means of the fragrance.
Wherever the World-Honored One may be, revered by all, he teaches the Dharma out of compassion for sentient beings; by smelling their fragrance, he knows them all.
Sentient beings standing before the Buddha, hearing the sutras, are all filled with joy and practice according to the Dharma; by smelling their fragrance, he knows them all.
The first two lines of verse praise the śrāvakas who are exclusively dedicated to sitting meditation and are unmoved by dullness or distraction.
The next line praises the bodhisattvas, and the final two lines praise all Buddhas. △ Third, the concluding summary in verse.
Although they have not yet attained the bodhisattva’s untainted (anāsrava) dharma-arising nose, this upholder of the sūtra first attains this mark of the nose.
Regarding the phrase "although not yet attained," if it were the nose of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), it would be a fleshy nose born of one's parents and thus tainted (sāsrava).
However, that of a bodhisattva is capable of shattering ignorance; the nose they possess is—
This is the nose produced from untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas. △ Fourth, the demonstration of the tongue faculty has two parts: first, the prose; second, the verse.
The first part [the prose] has two sections. First, the introduction of the Dharma-preacher.
Furthermore, Nityodyukta, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives and upholds this sutra— whether reading it,
reciting it, explaining it, or copying it—
△ Second, the clarification of the merits, in two parts. First, the general clarification:
one attains twelve hundred merits of the tongue.
△ Second, the specific enumeration of six; first, clarifying that both the tongue and flavors are exquisite.
Whether good or foul, beautiful or unattractive, or even bitter and astringent things, whatever comes upon his tongue-root is transformed into a supreme flavor,
like celestial ambrosia, such that there is nothing that is not delicious.
That is to say, while delicious flavors are indeed pleasant, even those that are foul, unattractive, bitter, or astringent—
if they come upon the tongue of a Dharma Master— will all be transformed into supreme and exquisite flavors because his tongue is pure.
The reason they can be so transformed is that this sutra possesses but a single characteristic and a single flavor, being entirely uniform.
Because it possesses the sublime flavor of *amṛta* (the finest essence), one who is able to receive and maintain it attains purity of the tongue faculty;
thus, naturally, even bitter and astringent flavors are transformed into supreme and exquisite flavors.

For example, when a person in the world attains physical health and mental acuity, even coarse and unpalatable tastes are perceived as sweet; yet if they are afflicted by illness or distress, [they perceive things otherwise].
Thus, even the most exquisite flavors will be perceived as tasteless. △ Second, explaining that all his preaching is sublime:
If he uses his tongue-organ to deliver a discourse within the great assembly, he produces a profound and wondrous sound that is able to penetrate their hearts.
"Causing all to be joyful and happy;
among the great assembly. Since one is within a great assembly, the number of people is naturally vast and their capacities are not uniform.
Therefore, when preaching, he adapts to their capacities; he may speak of the Small Vehicle, or the Great Vehicle, or the partial, or the perfect, in various ways that differ from one another.
If he speaks of the Small for those with small capacities, then the Small can enter their hearts.
If he speaks of the Great for those with great capacities, then the Great can enter their hearts. Since both can thus enter their hearts, [the teaching is effective].
Thus, they are all caused to attain joy; even those who have ultimately attained the Small Vehicle are led back to the Great Vehicle, thereby attaining joy.
△ Third, the explanation of men and women practicing reverence.

Furthermore, the sons of gods, daughters of gods, Śakra, Brahmā, and all the other devas, hearing this profound and wondrous sound and the sequence of the discourse being expounded, all came to listen.
Likewise, the nāgas and nāga-daughters, yakṣas and yakṣa-daughters, gandharvas and gandharva-daughters, asuras and asura-daughters, garuḍas and garuḍa-daughters, kinnaras... [and so forth].
Naras and Kinnara women, as well as Mahoragas and Mahoraga women, all came to attend upon him out of a desire to hear the Dharma,
approaching him with reverence and making offerings.

Regarding the sequence of discourse: it refers to the speaker’s exposition of the teaching that expresses [the truth], the principle expressed therein, the practice initiated thereby, and the realization attained through it;
thus causing the listener to manifest the principle according to the teaching, initiate practice based on that principle, and enter into realization through practice.
This is why it is called a "sequence. 4. Explaining the Offerings Made by the Clergy and Laity.
As well as bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas and upāsikās, kings, princes, ministers, and their retinues,
minor wheel-turning kings, and great wheel-turning kings, with their seven treasures and thousand sons, and their internal and external attendants, all riding upon their palaces.

They all came together to listen to the Dharma. Because this bodhisattva was skilled in preaching the Dharma, the brahmins, householders, and the people of the country attended upon and made offerings to him for as long as they lived.
The fourfold assembly constitutes the community of the Dharma; kings and others constitute the secular community. Kings refers to minor kings (kṣudra-rāja).

Minor universal monarchs (cakravartin) refers to those with iron, copper, or silver wheels; great universal monarchs refers to those with gold wheels. Regarding the "seven treasures and a thousand sons":
a universal monarch must necessarily have a thousand sons, and all such thousand sons possess the seven treasures; therefore, it is so stated.
He possesses the seven treasures and a thousand sons. "King" (Rāja) means "one who is gone toward"; he is one toward whom the people of the entire nation turn.

As for being "skilled in preaching the Dharma," it is because this Bodhisattva is able to know the karmic actions, faculties, and capacities of sentient beings, and thus observes their capacities to preach the teaching.

He adapts the teaching to the capacity: if it should be small, he makes it small; if it should be great, he makes it great; if it should be partial, he makes it partial; if it should be... [complete].
If it is circular, it is perfectly circular; this is the ultimate destination. There is nothing too small for it, and nothing too large; there is nothing biased and nothing not circular.
This is what is called "skillfully expounding the Dharma. △ Fifth, explaining the four noble joys of seeing.
Furthermore, all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas always delight in seeing him.
If one considers the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas, these constitute the three vehicles; they are partial, provisional, and expedient.
What the Dharma Master now expounds, however, is the reality within the perfect One Vehicle. Thus, the three vehicles shall naturally converge and return to this One.
The partial should naturally converge into the perfect; the true should naturally converge into the Middle; the provisional should naturally converge into the real.
This is what those who delight in seeing the Principle ought to do. If this were the case for the Buddhas, why would they also delight in seeing it?
It is because the fruit-stage Buddhas realized through both the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings have only attained the partial truth; thus, although they are Buddhas, they [still]...

One must understand that [the Buddha] ultimately returns to the Perfect Middle; therefore, he is also joyfully seen. If it is the Buddha of the Separate Teaching, this refers to the distinct but partial Middle, which merely destroys twelve grades of ignorance;
therefore, he is also joyfully seen. As for the Buddha of the Perfect Teaching, although his wisdom is full, [he is joyfully seen].

The causes have been exhausted; the fruits have reached their ultimate limit. Nevertheless, regarding the Dharma that has been preached, it relies entirely upon this Dharma Master for its dissemination.
If it were not disseminated, the Dharma would naturally perish. Therefore, it is said that one delights in seeing him.
△ Sixth, clarifying that all Buddhas turn toward him.
In whichever direction this person may be, all Buddhas will turn toward that place and preach the Dharma;
they will be able to receive and uphold all the Buddha-dharmas, and furthermore, they will be able to produce the profound and wondrous sounds of the Dharma.
The reason why the Buddhas appear before such persons is as stated in the "Chapter on the Dharma Master" (Dharmabhāṇaka-parivarta) in the aforementioned Trace Gate (Ji-men):
"If there are those who receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, I shall manifest my body before that person.

If they should forget any phrases or clauses, I shall explain them for them once more, enabling them to attain mastery. Therefore, it is the same in this case as well; it is entirely due to [the power of] being able to...
Having realized the principle of the true reality (*dharmatā*), they preach the Dharma; this is non-dual and no different from what has been realized and taught by the Buddhas of the ten directions.
For this reason, all Buddhas proceed toward their location. Such individuals are fully capable of receiving and upholding the Buddha-Dharma.
It is not merely that he goes to those places; he further preaches the Dharma for them, enabling them to attain dhāraṇīs so that they may fully uphold all Buddha-dharmas.
Furthermore, as for his ability to produce sublime sounds, this is the work of this Dharma Master.

Some say that both [the sound and the dharma] are sublime. Having already been able to produce profound and wondrous sounds, he now, being empowered by the majestic spiritual authority of all Buddhas, is further able to produce the profound and wondrous Dharma, causing all who hear it to attain joy.
II. Verses in Praise (five parts). First, verses praising the excellence of both tongue and flavor.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The tongue-faculty of such a person is pure; they shall never experience foul flavors. Whatever they consume or eat shall all become nectar."
△ Second, the verse on the excellence of his teaching of the Dharma:
With a profound, pure, and wondrous voice, he teaches the Dharma to the great assembly; by means of various causes, conditions, and parables, he guides the minds of sentient beings.
All who heard it were filled with joy and prepared various supreme offerings.
Regarding the phrase "profound, pure, and wondrous voice": "profound" means deep and far-reaching; "pure" means stainless; "wondrous" means exquisite.
With such a profound, pure, and wondrous voice, amidst the great assembly of devas and humans, he further preached that which is profound...
Because it is a pure and subtle Dharma, it is said that he preaches the Dharma to the great assembly with a profound, pure, and subtle voice.
Regarding "by means of various causes and conditions" and so forth: when there are those of lesser capacity, he must accommodate them at their level;
therefore, he further employs various causes, conditions, and parables to expound for them, thereby inducing and guiding their minds so that they may achieve accomplishment.
It begins with the small and subsequently leads it back to the great. Those of small capacity, upon hearing the small Dharma, feel personal joy and provide various superior offerings;
those of great capacity, upon hearing the Great Dharma, likewise must feel joy and provide superior offerings.
However, for those of small capacity, it ultimately causes them to reach the Great [Vehicle], and thus they attain joy. △ Three.
The verse describes how men and women practice respectful homage,
and how the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and others all come together with reverent hearts to listen to the Dharma.
This person who expounds the Dharma, if they wish to fill the trichiliocosm with a wondrous voice, can achieve this at will.

That such a wondrous voice can pervade and reach [all places] is entirely due to this Dharma master’s ability to fully comprehend the subtle principle of the true mark (*dharmatā*), wherein the one and the many are unimpeded and the near and the far are identical. Thus, it is possible for them to act in this way. Indeed, this wondrous voice...
"One" is one; "three thousand" is many. "Wondrous Sound" is near; "the three thousand worlds" is far.

Yet, regarding the principle of true reality (*dharmatā*), the one and the many are without obstruction, and the near and the far are identical as one. Now, one is able to thoroughly comprehend this true reality.
Thus, the single wondrous voice is not one; the three thousandfold world-system is not many. The proximity of the wondrous voice is not near;
the distance of the three thousandfold world-system is not far. Therefore, it is able to pervade the three thousandfold world-system with its wondrous voice.
One can arrive at will whenever one desires. △ Fourth, a verse on the offerings made by the monastic and lay communities:
Great and small wheel-turning kings, together with their retinues of a thousand sons, constantly come with palms joined in a reverent heart to listen to and receive the Dharma.
The devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas, with hearts full of joy, will also constantly delight in coming to offer worship.
The Brahmā kings, Māras, Īśvaras, Maheśvaras, and all such hosts of devas will always come to his abode.

In this account of making offerings, only the assembly of laypeople is praised while the assembly of the Dharma is omitted; however, within the assembly of laypeople, there must necessarily be the assembly of the Dharma and others, as can be seen from the prose section.
"Mastery" (vaśavartin) refers to the heaven at the summit of the desire realm, namely, the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (paranirmita-vaśavartin).
Maheśvara is the deity at the summit of the Form Realm; he is Maheśvara. △ Fifth, the verse on seeing the four noble joys:
When the Buddhas and their disciples hear the sound of his preaching the Dharma, they constantly keep him in mind and protect him, and at times they manifest their bodies before him.
The two characters "Buddhas" (諸佛) in both the verse and the prose refer to the Buddhas themselves. The two characters "disciples" (弟子) refer to those of the Three Vehicles;
in both the verse and the prose, they signify those who "delight in seeing" (樂見). △ Fifth, the manifestation of the physical body has two parts:
first, the prose; second, the verse. The former has two sections; the first raises the topic of the Dharma Master.
Furthermore, Constantly Diligent: if good sons or good daughters receive and uphold this sutra—whether reading it, reciting it, explaining it, or transcribing it.
△ Second, clarifying the merits, in two parts; first, a brief clarification.
He attains eight hundred bodily merits and acquires a pure body like clear lapis lazuli, which all sentient beings joyfully behold.

Just as clear lapis lazuli can manifest all forms and images, so too the physical faculties of this Dharma Master are pure and can likewise manifest all forms and images, just like clear lapis lazuli. Because of this...
Because he is pure, there are no sentient beings who do not joyfully behold him. △ Second, the extensive explanation has two parts:

first, explaining the manifestation of the six classes of ordinary beings; second, explaining the manifestation of the four classes of noble ones. The first [of these two] has two parts: first, the general explanation.
Because his body is pure, the births and deaths of sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm— their high and low status, their beauty and ugliness,
and their rebirth in good or evil realms— all appear within it.
Regarding "at the time of birth and at the time of death," etc.: when causes and conditions harmonize, there is birth; when causes and conditions separate, there is death.

Due to light causes and conditions, one ascends to the upper realms; due to heavy causes and conditions, one falls to the lower realms. The upper realms consist of beautiful and excellent forms and minds;
the lower realms consist of ugly and foul forms and minds. Humans, devas, and asuras are the wholesome states; hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals are the unwholesome states.
This is the locus. △ Second, the specific explanation:
The Iron Ring Mountains, the Great Iron Ring Mountains, Mount Meru, Mount Mahāmeru, and all such mountains, as well as the sentient beings therein, all appear within it.
From below, reaching down to the Avīci Hell, to above, reaching up to the Peak of Existence (Bhavāgra), everything is present.
And all sentient beings appear therein. Initially, they appear horizontally:
the Iron Ring Mountains and so forth are the retributive environment (*āśraya-vipāka*), while the sentient beings within them are the primary retribution (*sattva-vipāka*).
Next, descending to clarify their vertical appearance: from the upper reaches of existence downward are the retributive environment, and the sentient beings therein are the primary retribution.
