△ Second, explaining the manifestation of the four types of noble beings:
whether it be śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, or buddhas preaching the Dharma, they all manifest their physical forms within [the practitioner's] body.
Regarding the statement that these six ordinary beings and four noble ones can all manifest [these realms]: it is because within the bodies of sentient beings, the ten realms are inherently present.
It is entirely due to sentient beings giving rise to various discriminations and craving that what is originally omnipresent and penetrating is thus obscured.
It was formed as something limited, obstructed, and unable to manifest. Now, this Dharma Master is able to receive and uphold this sutra, thereby attaining purity of the physical faculties.
Having shattered both views and afflictions, he has been able to completely eliminate all various forms of craving and discrimination.
By the very nature of reality (*dharmatā*), he is naturally able to achieve unimpeded penetration and universal pervasiveness; therefore, these very parents—
Within the body that is born, one can manifest according to the three realms of existence; one can manifest according to humans and devas;
one can manifest according to śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; and one can manifest according to bodhisattvas and buddhas.
This is due to nothing else but the fact that the ten realms are inherently present within the bodies of sentient beings. From this, it can be understood.
The nature is fully endowed [with all]. If the ten realms were not fully endowed within the nature, how could the forms and images of the ten realms be perfectly manifested within this body?
△ Second, the verse commentary has two parts: first, the actual versification; second, the concluding summary. The first part has two sections: first, the versification of the brief explanation.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"If one upholds the Lotus Sutra, their body will be exceedingly pure, like that clear lapis lazuli; all sentient beings will joyfully behold them."
Furthermore, just as a pure, bright mirror reflects all forms and images, so too does the Bodhisattva, within his purified body, perceive everything that exists in the world;
yet he alone perceives it with perfect clarity, while others do not see it.
The first two lines constitute the *dharma* (the subject). The next line is the analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*). The third pair of lines constitutes the application (*upanaya*).
The fourth pair of lines resolves the doubt. As for resolving the doubt: although the ten realms manifest perfectly, only the Dharma Master himself perceives them, while others cannot.
This is because his faculty of the body (*kāyendriya*) is pure, as he has realized the true aspect (*dharmatā*) in accordance with it. II. Verses Explaining in Detail.
Within his body appear all the various forms of the myriad beings in the three thousandfold world system— gods, humans, asuras, hell-dwellers,
hungry ghosts, and animals— as well as the palaces of the devas up to the very peak of existence.
The Iron Ring Mountains, Mount Meru, and Mahāmeru, as well as all the great oceans, all appear within his body.
Buddhas and śrāvakas, sons of the Buddha and bodhisattvas—whether alone or in a multitude—all appear preaching the Dharma.
The first three lines of verse describe the six classes of ordinary beings; the subsequent lines describe the four types of noble ones. Regarding the first section:

the first half-line refers to the primary retribution (*vipāka*), and the second half-line refers to the secondary environment (*niśraya*). The following line, beginning with "All Buddhas," describes the four types of noble ones.
"Whether alone or in an assembly, they all manifest when preaching the Dharma" refers to the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and those of the two vehicles, whether teaching a single individual or a multitude.
He preaches the Dharma. Or, while preaching the Dharma amidst the assembly, the four noble beings all manifest their physical forms within his own body. △ Second, the conclusion:
Although he has not yet attained the wondrous body of the dharma-nature that is free from outflows, because it is the pure and eternal essence, everything manifests therein.
△ Sixth, indicating the faculty of intention (manas-indriya), in two parts: first, the prose; second, the verse. The first part has two sections. First, the mention of the Dharma-preacher:
Furthermore, Sadāparibhūta, if any son or daughter of good family, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, receives and upholds this sutra...
Whether reading, reciting, explaining, or copying it.
△ Second, clarifying the merits in three parts. First, a brief clarification:
one attains twelve hundred merits of the mind.

△ Second, the extensive explanation of these two. First, the clear knowledge of the four noble dharmas; second, the clear knowledge of the dharmas of the six destinies. Regarding the first, there are three parts.
First, hearing one and understanding many:
by means of this pure faculty of mind, even upon hearing a single verse or a single phrase, one penetrates the immeasurable and boundless [teachings].
Regarding the meaning:
a single verse or a single line is "few," while the immeasurable and boundless is "many. Why is it that what is heard is one, yet it can explain the many?
It is because although a single verse or a single line is few, the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena (*dharma*) which they express is [immeasurable].
Although the measures are boundless and thus numerous, that which is expounded is solely the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.

Because their quantity, though differing, is one and the same true reality of all phenomena, one is able to hear one and understand many. △ Second, the ability to preach according to one's understanding.
Having understood this meaning, they are able to expound upon a single phrase or a single verse for one month, four months,
or even for a year;
that is, they expound the phrases and verses of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* exactly as they have heard them.
However, if there are those of lesser capacity, one must accordingly remain with them at that level of smallness; thus, it does not hinder further expounding the Bodhisattva vehicle.

For example, one might expound the Śrāvaka vehicle and the Dharma of the Four Truths for the duration of one month, expound the Pratyekabuddha vehicle and the Dharma of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination for four months, and [expound] for one year. △ Third, all that is taught is correct.
All the teachings he expounds accord with their underlying meaning and do not contradict the true nature of reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Even when he speaks of worldly scriptures, secular discourse, or the arts of livelihood, all such things conform to the True Dharma.
Regarding the phrase "according to their meaning and intent" and so forth: if one preaches the subtle and wondrous Dharma, it naturally does not contradict the true nature (*dharmatā*).
Even the teachings of the Three Vehicles that are spoken likewise do not contradict the true nature, because the understanding from which they arise is fundamentally perfect.

Those who teach the Three Vehicles do nothing more than accommodate the capacities and dispositions of sentient beings; yet when one investigates their original intent, it is fundamentally [the One Vehicle].
If one wishes to return to the ultimate reality, there is no contradiction between them. To re-examine this through the lens of ultimate truth:

the Dharma of the Four Truths of the Śrāvakas is, in its entirety, the Four Truths of Non-action; the Dharma of Dependent Origination of the Pratyekabuddhas is, in its entirety, the inconceivable Twelve Links of Dependent Origination;
and the practice of the Six Perfections of the Bodhisattvas is, in its entirety, the subtle... [truth].
Because the wondrous principle consists of the six perfections, the teachings of the three vehicles do not contradict the true mark (*dharmatā*).

If one speaks of worldly matters and so forth, it means that not only are the three vehicles taught without contradicting the true mark, but even the teachings on worldly phenomena likewise accord with the true dharma of the true mark and do not contradict it; for they are, in their very nature, conventional.
Yet within this, it is precisely because the mundane is itself the supreme supramundane Dharma.

This is because one has already attained purity of the faculty of mind, already attained corresponding conformity, already been able to penetrate the true reality (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*), and already been able to shatter the afflictions of views and thoughts;
therefore, such a state is attained. If one has not yet attained purity of the faculty of mind, I fear that [one has not yet attained it].
He is indeed capable of this. II. Knowledge of the Dharma of the Six Realms:
He thoroughly knows the mental activities, the mental movements, and the mental conceptual proliferations of all sentient beings within the six realms throughout the trichiliocosm.
Mental proliferation (*prapañca*) refers to clinging to existence rather than non-existence, or clinging to non-existence rather than existence;
it is also clinging to both, or to neither; and clinging to neither, or to both—this is what is called mental proliferation. △ Third, the conclusion.
Although they have not yet attained untainted wisdom (anāsrava-jñāna), their mental faculty (manas-indriya) is thus purified.
Whatever this person contemplates, deliberates, or speaks is entirely the Buddha-dharma; it is without exception true and is also that which was taught in the sūtras of previous Buddhas.
Regarding "untainted wisdom" (*anāsrava-jñāna*): the three wisdoms within a single mind are called untainted wisdom.
Since one attains these three wisdoms through a single mind, one naturally does not fall into the extremes of emptiness, existence, or the middle.

This untainted knowledge, from ascending to the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) up to the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), can be attained through partial realization and ultimate perfection; only then can one fully know the phenomena of the ten realms. Now...
One whose faculty of mind (*manas-indriya*) is pure, although not yet having attained partial realization of the ultimate, is nonetheless able to attain it in a manner that corresponds to it;
thus, with their faculty of mind purified, they are able to know the dharmas of the four noble truths and the six destinies.
As for such a person, although there may be differences in their reflections and speech, speech is but the [expression of] the mind.

Sound. Thought is the very basis of speech; therefore, it is not only that which is contemplated that constitutes the Buddha’s Dharma and is entirely true, but even that which is expressed through words is likewise the Buddha’s Dharma and is entirely true.

This is because they are able to penetrate the fact that every phenomenon is nothing other than the Dharma-realm, and every characteristic is nothing other than the true characteristic. This was also taught by the Buddhas of the past.
As for "the speaker," it means that these are not only my, Śākyamuni’s, teachings, but are also the teachings of all past Buddhas.
This is because the Way of every Buddha is the same. Since they are the teachings of Śākyamuni, they are also the teachings of the former Buddhas;
since they are the teachings of the former Buddhas, they are likewise the teachings of the present Buddha, the future Buddhas, and all Buddhas throughout the ten directions.
This is the Dharma of the Buddha; therefore, it is said that this was also spoken in the sutras of former Buddhas. △ Second, the verse summary has three parts.
First, the brief explanation summarized in verse:
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
The mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) of this person is pure, lucid, sharp, and free from turbidity or defilement.
II. The second section, in verse, provides a detailed explanation in three parts. First, the verse on knowing the four noble dharmas:
"By means of this wondrous mental faculty, one knows dharmas that are superior, middling, or inferior; even upon hearing a single verse, one penetrates immeasurable meanings."
He explained it in due order according to the Dharma, from months and four-month periods up to a year.
Regarding the phrase "the wondrous faculty of mind": this sutra is indeed profound and subtle;

since you are now able to receive, uphold, and circulate it, you shall attain the wondrous function of this sutra and be able to realize that outflows (*āsrava*) are themselves non-outflow (*anāsrava*).

The outflows (*āsrava*). To realize that arising and ceasing are themselves non-arising and non-ceasing, and that the essence of defilement is itself purity—therefore it is called the "wondrous faculty of mind.
Regarding the superior, middling, and inferior dharmas: if taken in a general sense, the Three Vehicles constitute the superior, middling, and inferior;

however, according to the specific discussion of the text, the three cycles [of teaching] constitute the superior, middling, and inferior. This extends even to two lines [of verse], which summarize the preceding line.
A single verse contains immeasurable and boundless meanings. Next, the second line correctly praises the teachings of the Three Vehicles and so forth.

"The moon" refers to the single moon; it praises the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas. From the four months to the year, the sequence can be understood. △ Second, praising the knowledge of the dharmas of the six realms of existence.
Within and without this world, all sentient beings— whether devas, nāgas, humans, yakṣas, ghosts, spirits, and so forth—
who dwell within the six realms of existence and harbor various kinds of thoughts, [the Buddha] knows them all at once through the retribution of upholding the Lotus Sūtra.
△ Third Watch Verse: Praising the Dharmas of All Buddhas.
The countless Buddhas of the ten directions, adorned with the marks of a hundred merits, preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings; he hears them all and is able to receive and uphold them.
They contemplate immeasurable meanings, and their preaching of the Dharma is likewise immeasurable. From beginning to end, they never forget or err, because they uphold the Lotus Sutra.

They fully know the characteristics of all phenomena; according to their meaning, they recognize their sequence. They penetrate names and language, and expound them exactly as they have understood them.
Whatever this person says is entirely the Dharma of the former Buddhas; because he expounds this Dharma, he possesses no fear among the assembly.
To contemplate immeasurable meanings is self-cultivation (*sva-pratipatti*); to preach the Dharma in immeasurable ways is transforming others (*para-vinaya*).
To recognize the sequence according to the meaning is that which is expressed (*vācya*); to master names and language is that which expresses (*vācaka*). As for the "sequence," it refers to...
This means that by knowing the teaching which expresses [the truth], one reveals the principle which is expressed; from the principle, practice arises;
and from practice, one enters realization. Therefore, it is called "knowing the sequence. △ Third, the verse concludes the section.
One who upholds the Lotus Sūtra has the faculty of mind purified in this way; though they have not yet attained the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*), such signs already appear beforehand.
This person, upholding this sūtra, dwells securely on a rare stage, and is joyfully loved and revered by all sentient beings.
Because they uphold the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, they are able to expound the Dharma through thousands of millions of skillful modes of speech and analytical distinctions;
thus, those who dwell in this rare stage—this sutra being most rare among all that has been, is being, or will be spoken—the stage in which they abide is likewise rare.
In this sutra, the nine realms are all brought together and returned to the Buddha-realm.
The three vehicles all converge in the One Vehicle; thus, one dwells securely in a state of rarity and is revered by all.
If sentient beings respond with joy, love, and respect, then there is the potential for transformation.
However, since this potential necessarily varies in degree—whether great or small—one accordingly teaches according to those capacities through thousands of millions of skillful means.

"Discriminating" refers to the teaching through discrimination. To discriminate means to distinguish that "this is small," "this is great," "this is gradual," "this is sudden," "this is partial," "this is perfect," "this is provisional," and "this is real. Having thus discriminated, one applies what is appropriate:

for those who should receive the Small [Vehicle], it is small; and so on, up to those who should receive the Real, it is real. Ultimately, all such [teachings] as the Small and the rest are led [toward the ultimate].
They return to the perfect reality. This is what is meant by being able to expound the Dharma through a thousand million kinds of skillful words.
One who is able to do so does so because they uphold the Lotus Sutra. The "Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma Master" is hereby concluded.
In the twentieth chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*,
"The Bodhisattva Never Disparaging," if one examines the sequential development of this section, it is entirely due to the fact that the Tathāgata’s long-lasting life span has already been clarified.
The prediction of the Dharma-body has already been bestowed, and thus the essential work of the Original Gate is complete. What is most important, however, lies solely in its propagation;

therefore, he proceeds to clarify the causal merits of the four levels of faith during the present age and the five grades of practice after his passing, as well as the resultant merits of the purification of the six sense organs, repeatedly exhorting [the practitioners] therein.
This is the praise for the propagation [of the sutra]. However, if it were not authenticated by this, people would still not believe it.

Now, wishing to authenticate that those who can receive, uphold, and propagate this sutra will naturally attain the merit and virtue of cause and effect, there is this chapter on the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging; it serves to certify the merits obtained through the propagation [of the sutra].
This is the literary style. Regarding the title designated as "The Bodhisattva Never Disparaging," that which is discussed throughout this sutra is as follows:

in the Trace Gate (Jikimon), it concerns only the opening, revealing, awakening to, and entering into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; in the Essence Gate (Honmon), it concerns only the eternal, unextinguished, and far-reaching span of life.
Although such Buddha-knowledge, Buddha-vision, and far-reaching span of life are—like... [as before]... though like... [Note: The source text appears to be truncated.]
It is that which one comes to realize through ultimate attainment; it is also that which is equally possessed by all sentient beings in the present.
From the very beginning, birth and Buddhahood are of one essence, and ordinary beings and sages are equal. This is what is called "Buddha-nature.
Although this Buddha-nature is equal, sentient beings are deluded and do not know it; only the Tathāgata is awakened to it.
Yet he was able to realize it. Now, because the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging wished to circulate this sutra, whenever he saw anyone, he would immediately proclaim:
"You shall all become Buddhas. Even when seeing the fourfold assembly from afar, he likewise proclaimed:
"You shall all become Buddhas. He even went so far as to strike them with sticks, wood, tiles, or stones, yet he continued to flee from them.
Dwelling afar, he raised his voice and proclaimed, "You shall all become Buddhas.
Because he was able to endure hardships and propagate the sutra, thereby attaining various merits, those who did not believe him at that time took this as his name.
When the Tathāgata preached the sutra, they served as witnesses; therefore, when the compilers of the scriptures assembled them, they established this as a single chapter.
As for its title, it is designated as the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging.

This is because he was able to personally practice the conduct of never disparaging, maintain the understanding of never disparaging in his mind, and proclaim the teaching of never disparaging with his mouth; therefore, he was named after that quality.
Because he is "Never-Disparaging," he is able to personally realize the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and furthermore, he can use this to teach others;
thus, benefiting both himself and others, he is called a Bodhisattva. The text of this chapter is divided into two parts: first, pointing back to the preceding discussion of offenses and merit.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta: "You should now know this:

if there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who uphold the Lotus Sūtra, and if someone should speak to them with harsh words, revile them, or slander them, they will receive a retribution for their great sin as previously described.
As for the merit they shall obtain, it is as previously described: [their] eyes and ears..."
The nose, tongue, body, and mind are purified.

He addressed Mahāsthāmaprāpta: "If, during the time of the Dharma's dissemination in the final age, the obstacles of sentient beings grow ever deeper while their wisdom diminishes day by day, then those who wish to propagate and spread it must be like Mahāsthāmaprāpta before they can do so."
Only by enduring hardships in propagating this sutra can one practice the three kinds of rules and the four modes of peaceful conduct, thereby ensuring that this sutra circulates wherever it may be.

Herein follows the formal instruction: as I have already explained above, if there are those who slander those who uphold this sutra, they shall incur immeasurable sin; whereas if there are those who are able to protect them...
Those who uphold this sutra shall attain all manner of merits; you should now know this.
As for the bhikṣus mentioned below, those who previously engaged in slander incur sin and receive the retribution of great offenses.
Even if one slanders and reviles without cause, baselessly defaming an ordinary person, one will likewise constantly receive the retribution of sin. Now, as for those who revile and slander...
Those who receive, uphold, and recite the Lotus Sūtra shall therefore incur the retribution of great sin, as previously stated.
This is precisely what is said in the "Dharma Master" chapter of the Trace Gate (Jikimon): "If there is an evil person who constantly reviles and insults the Buddha, their sin is still light;
however, if with a single word they disparage one who reads, recites, receives, or upholds the Lotus Sūtra, their sin is exceedingly heavy. This is the meaning. Indeed...
The Buddha has already attained the ultimate; though one praises him, he does not increase, and though one disparages him, he does not diminish.

Therefore, such an offense is still relatively light. However, if one disparages a person who upholds [the teachings], it causes that person’s great resolve to regress, and there are even those who fall away because of it.
Therefore, the offense is extremely grave. As for the phrase "that which is lowered," it refers to the fact that the one who upholds [the teachings] possesses merit.

...and so forth. △ Second, clarifying the present faith and slander. This has two parts: first, the prose; second, the verse. The first [part] has three sections: first, clarifying the causal conditions;
second, explaining the meaning; third, revealing the retribution. The first of these two [sections] clarifies the single Buddha.
Mahāsthāmaprāpta, in the distant past, beyond immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago,
there was a Buddha named King of Majestic Sound (*Bhīṣmagarjitasvara*), a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna,
Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
"Long ago," and so forth, refers to the time period. "There was a Buddha," and so forth, sets forth his name. As for the term "King of Majestic Sound" (Vaiśravaṇa):
because he destroys all delusions such that there is no delusion not destroyed, and because he manifests all wisdom such that there is no wisdom not manifested, he is called "Majestic" (Vai).
Because he expounds all dharmas such that there is no dharma not expounded, and because he covers all... [the text continues].
The capacity [of the teaching] reaches all who possess such capacity; thus, while the sounds of speech function to destroy delusion, there is nothing to be destroyed in that destruction.
While they manifest wisdom, there is nothing to be manifested in that manifestation. Furthermore, this does not preclude using wisdom to destroy delusion or using delusion to manifest wisdom.
Since delusion and wisdom mutually establish one another, by destroying delusion and manifesting wisdom, one attains mastery. Regarding the preaching of the Dharma, it is preached as non-preaching.

Regarding what has been said: although he is "clothed" by the capacities of sentient beings, there is nothing that clothes him; yet, he does not hinder the application of the Dharma to those capacities, nor does he preach the teachings based upon those capacities.
When capacity and Dharma merge into one another, his preaching of the Dharma clothes the capacities, and he attains mastery. Therefore, he is called a "King."
The kalpa is named Free from Decline (Vigata-vyaya); the land is named Great Achievement (Mahā-siddhi).
As for the kalpa being named Free from Decline: because there is no delusion that is not destroyed and no wisdom that is not manifested, all dharmas [are thus].
All calamities and misfortunes can be naturally distanced from it; therefore, that kalpa is named "Free from Calamity" (Li-shuai).

As for the land being named "Great Achievement" (Da-cheng), it is because there is no Dharma that is not taught and no capacity that is not reached; thus, among all sentient beings within the land, there are none who do not achieve fulfillment.
Therefore, the land is named "Great Achievement."
That Buddha, King of Majestic Sound, in that world, preached the Dharma for devas, humans, and asuras.
For those seeking to become śrāvakas, he taught the Dharma corresponding to the Four Noble Truths, so they might transcend birth, old age, sickness, and death, and ultimately attain nirvāṇa.
For those seeking to become pratyekabuddhas, he taught the Dharma corresponding to the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination. For all bodhisattvas, [he taught] by means of anuttara-samyak-...
Regarding the three types of enlightenment, he taught the Dharma corresponding to the six *pāramitās*. He perfected the Buddha-wisdom and attained great power.
The lifespan of that King of Dignified Sound Buddha was four hundred thousand *koṭis* of *nayutas* of *Ganges-sand* eons.

His True Dharma remained in the world for a number of eons equal to the dust motes of one Jambudvīpa. His Semblance Dharma remained in the world for a number of eons equal to the dust motes of the four continents. As for his...
After the Buddha has benefited sentient beings, he then enters parinirvāṇa.
Initially, he teaches the Dharma of the Three Vehicles; ultimately, he teaches the Dharma of the One Vehicle.
This is precisely to bring about the ultimate revelation, awakening, and entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and to bring about the ultimate realization of the long path.

This concerns the lifespan. For the Way of every Buddha is the same; thus, according to the nature of things, Śākyamuni first opened the teaching of the Three Vehicles and later revealed the One Vehicle, and King Vimalacandra did exactly the same.
These instances, such as that of King Vimalacandra, clarify the lifespans of the True and Semblance Dharma periods.
Regarding the statement that the True Dharma lasts for as many kalpas as there are atoms in a Jambudvīpa: this refers to the southern Jambudvīpa.

If one were to grind the continent of Jambudvīpa into fine dust, with each grain of dust representing one kalpa, the number of kalpas of the Semblance Dharma would be equal to the number of grains of dust from the four continents.
Having brought benefit to sentient beings, he will thereafter enter parinirvāṇa.
The intent of that Buddha’s appearance in the world was nothing other than to bring abundant benefit and profit to sentient beings.

Now, since he first sought to open the three [vehicles] and the three have already been opened, and subsequently sought to reveal the one [vehicle] and the one has already been revealed, he has already attained great benefit for sentient beings.
As for those who should attain liberation through parinirvāṇa, he returns to them.
Regarding his parinirvāṇa: △ Second, clarifying the appearance of many Buddhas.

After the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma have completely vanished, another Buddha will appear in this land, also named Vimalacandra-rāja (King of Majestic Sound) Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi... [and so forth].
The Honored One among Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One—thus, in succession, there were twenty trillion Buddhas, all bearing the same name.
That they all bore the same name means they were all titled King of Majestic Sound (Vaiśvānara-rāja). Since their names were identical, so too were their eons, lands, and teachings.
The Dharma, its lifespan, and the periods of the True and Semblance Teachings are all without exception the same. △ Second, the explanation of the names and meanings.

Since the underlying causes have been clarified, the names and meanings of those who believe and those who slander will naturally emerge. The text is divided into two parts; first, the naming of these individuals.

After the Tathāgata King of Majestic Sound had first entered parinirvāṇa and the True Dharma had ceased, during the period of the Semblance Dharma, monks of overweening pride possessed great power. At that time, there was a bodhisattva monk named Never-Disparaging.
"At the beginning" refers to that specific time. "Arrogant bhikṣus" identifies those who disparage [the teaching].
Because they have not attained the first fruit but claim to have attained it, and have not realized the four fruits but claim to have realized them, they are called "arrogant.
Regarding those "who possess great power": if the Buddha were still in the world, there would naturally be wise people capable of [discerning this].
Know that such a person merely claims to have attained and claims to have realized, yet in reality has neither attained nor realized.
Because people living in the Age of Semblance Dharma lack wisdom, they claim to have attained and realized, and others believe them to have already attained and realized.
Consequently, kings, ministers, and the common people all place their trust in and follow them; yet as for that person—
It is because of this that he came to possess great power. The phrase "at that time" and below serves to introduce the names of those who had faith.
Regarding the term "Bodhisattva Bhikṣu": it is because this bhikṣu was able to practice the path of a bodhisattva that he was called a "Bodhisattva Bhikṣu.
Regarding his name, "Never-Disparaging": it is because his body was able to practice the conduct of never disparaging others, and his mouth... [continued].
This is because he was able to proclaim the teaching of "Never-Disparaging" and maintained the understanding of "Never-Disparaging" in his mind.
△ Second, the explanation of the meaning, in three parts. First, the heading and inquiry:
"Mahāsthāmaprāpta, by what causes and conditions was he named 'Ever-Not-Light' (Constantly Never-Disparaging)?"

△ Second, the explanation and establishment [of the two]. First, the explanation of the meaning of the term "one who has faith. Second, the explanation of the meaning of the term "one who slanders. The first [section] has two parts.
First, clarifying that whatever is seen [is such].
Whatever bhikṣus this bhikṣu sees—whether bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās—he bows down to them all and praises them, saying:
"I deeply respect you all; I do not dare to treat you with contempt. Why is this?
You are all practicing the bodhisattva path and shall surely attain Buddhahood. Yet, this bhikṣu does not devote himself exclusively to recitation.
"Reciting the scriptures and performing prostrations alone—
'you all practice these equally' means that all practices currently performed by you are the path of the bodhisattva."
Then, in the future, he will certainly attain Buddhahood. For this bhikṣu already knows that what is expounded in this sutra is that all sentient beings possess the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
thus, by means of the conduct of a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī, [he shall realize it].
Although these are the three vehicles, in their essential nature they are entirely identical to the One Vehicle; this is precisely what is practiced by upāsakas and upāsikās.
Although these are the virtues of the precepts, in their essential nature they too are entirely identical to the One Vehicle.

Therefore, in order to circulate this wondrous sutra, it is manifested before the fourfold assembly, whereupon it is said: "You all practice the path of the bodhisattva and shall surely attain buddhahood."
This refers to a Buddha. It refers to such a bhikṣu who does not exclusively recite the scriptures but practices only prostrations;
one who does not exclusively recite this wondrous Dharma and other such sutras, but as soon as he sees the fourfold assembly, performs prostrations and says:
"You shall all become Buddhas. This is precisely what is called the "One [Practice]."
I rejoice in this mindfulness. This is precisely what is meant by the "Dharma Master of a Single Phrase. For that which is expounded by a single sutra is solely the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
now this bhikṣu has already attained perfect faith and perfect understanding regarding all sentient beings.
All possess the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Therefore, it may be that they do not see [it];
yet if they do see it, he immediately gives them seeds of potent poison and bestows upon them the prediction of the true cause (*samyak-hetu*).
Thus, although this is but a single phrase, it also serves to circulate the wondrous sutra. △ Second, going because of seeing from afar.
Even when he saw the fourfold assembly from afar, he would still go to them to pay homage and offer praise, saying:
"I do not dare to look down upon you; you shall all become Buddhas."
The reason there are these two sections is as follows: Generally, whatever was seen previously constitutes the dissemination of the Trace Gate (*jitemon*).
Next, because they saw [the Buddha] from afar and went toward him, and it was said, "You shall all become Buddhas," this clarifies that they shall all realize the long-lasting life span;
this is the dissemination of the Origin Gate (*honmon*). △ Second, explaining those who disparage [the teaching].
Regarding names and meanings:
among the fourfold assembly, there were those who gave rise to anger and whose minds were impure; they reviled him with harsh words, saying, "This is an ignorant bhikṣu.
From where has he come? He says of himself, 'I do not slight you,' yet he bestows predictions upon us that we shall attain [enlightenment]."

"You shall become a Buddha. We did not desire such false prophecies. Thus, for many years, we were constantly reviled, yet we harbored no anger. We always spoke these words: "You shall become a Buddha.
When he said this, the crowd sometimes struck and pelted us with sticks, wood, tiles, and stones; though we fled and stayed far away, we still cried out in a loud voice: "I..."
I do not dare to treat you lightly; you shall all become Buddhas.
Should there be those who harbor thoughts of anger or impurity, know that at such a time there will also be those capable of faith.
As for the statement "this is an ignorant bhikṣu," it refers to one who does not devote himself to recitation and whose inner mind lacks understanding. And yet...
It is due to a lack of wisdom. As for "from where have they come," it means that regarding their external bodies, they do not know from which direction they have come.
When they say, "I am not equal [to them]," this refers to speaking with ignorance from within their mouths.

This is precisely because they do not understand that their minds maintain the practice of *adhimātra* (not disparaging), their bodily conduct performs the practice of *adhimātra*, and their speech proclaims the teaching of *adhimātra*.

Regarding the statement that "prophetic declarations are not based on falsehood": this means that if one were to discuss prophetic declarations according to ultimate reality (*tattva*), then the one who bestows the prophecy must be a Tathāgata, and the one who is prophesied must be a Bodhisattva.
Now, you are not a Tathāgata, and we are not Bodhisattvas; therefore, it is known that the prophecy you have bestowed is empty rather than true, and false rather than real. As...
This false prediction is of no use to us; for we bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs practice the Dharma of the Three Vehicles and can personally realize the fruit of true nirvāṇa.
We upāsakas and upāsikās practice the Dharma of precepts and goodness, and can personally attain the state of a human or deva.
It is the fruit of reality; therefore, I do not accept your false prophecy.
It is simply that the fourfold assembly each regards what they themselves practice and have attained as being real, and thus [the Bodhisattva] says it is false and does not accept it.
As for never giving rise to anger when reviled, it is because he is able to practice the four kinds of peaceful conduct and abides in patience.
In this state, externally one does not perceive any object that is endured, and internally one does not perceive a mind that is capable of enduring.
Therefore, even when constantly subjected to verbal abuse and insults from others, the inner mind remains free of anger.

As for the phrase "or with sticks and wood," if one were to speak such words after having already been reviled, it would only further increase the resentment of the fourfold assembly; thus, [one should instead use] a stick.
They strike them with wood, or even hurl tiles and stones at them. Even when thus struck and pelted, they still keep their distance and cry out in a loud voice, "All shall surely become Buddhas.
This is because they know that although these people may destroy [the teachings] and lack faith, they will ultimately become Buddhas.
△ Third, the conclusion and manifestation.
Because he constantly spoke these words, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas,
and upāsikās who were conceited called him "Never-Disparaging."
It is said that he was called "Never-Disparaging" because he constantly spoke these words.
Due to this bhikṣu, whenever he saw anyone, he would immediately say: "I do not dare to disparage you; you shall all become Buddhas.
This was what he constantly said to those he saw nearby, and even when he saw the fourfold assembly from afar, he did likewise.
He went to praise them, saying: "You shall become Buddhas. Such were his constant words to those he saw from afar.
Though the people beat and threw sticks, clubs, tiles, and stones at him, he still retreated to a distance and stood there, crying out in a loud voice:
"I do not dare to slight you; you shall all become Buddhas. Thus did he see them being reviled.
This is what they constantly say. This applies not only to those they see nearby, but likewise to those they see from afar;
it applies not only to those who believe them, but likewise to those who disparage them.
Therefore, because those four classes of people perceive them both near and far, and among those who believe and those who disparage, they all say: "I dare not look down upon you."
"You all—each and every one of you—shall become Buddhas. For this reason, he named the man according to what he had said, calling him "Never-Disparaging.

△ Third, revealing the retributive fruits, which has two parts: first, revealing the fruit for those who believe; second, revealing the fruit for those who disparage. The first part [revealing the fruit for those who believe] has three sections:

first, the actual revelation; second, the identification; third, the exhortation to uphold. The first [the actual revelation] further has three parts: first, [The text continues with the specific details of the revelation.]

First, the manifestation of retribution; second, the manifestation of birth-retribution; third, the manifestation of subsequent retribution. Regarding the first two: the first clarifies his own practice.

When that bhikṣu was about to pass away, he heard in the midst of the void the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* previously preached by the Buddha King of Majestic Sound, consisting of twenty quadrillion verses.
He was able to receive and uphold them all, and immediately attained the aforementioned purity of the eye faculty.
His faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind became pure. Having attained this purity of the six faculties, his lifespan was further increased by two hundred trillion nayutas of years.
"Those who are about to die" refers to the period when death is imminent but has not yet occurred.

Regarding the phrase "hearing fully within the void," it is because by being able to circulate even a single phrase and being able to uphold even a single phrase, one has already attained mastery of the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) within that very phrase; therefore, one hears fully within the void.
The entirety of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* preached by the Buddha Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja while he was in the world has been received and upheld without loss.
Thus, one should know that what was previously stated—"All of you shall become Buddhas"—is but a single verse among twenty thousand million verses.
Since you have been able to receive and uphold it, the practice based upon it is already accomplished; therefore, you immediately attain the six [supernormal powers].

This is the proximate fruit of the purification of the faculties (*indriya-viśuddhi*). This purification of the six faculties is precisely the "purification of the six faculties by resemblance" (*pratibimba-ṣaḍindriya-viśuddhi*).
Regarding the further increase of lifespan: previously, one was on the verge of death but had not yet passed away;
now, having attained this superior reward as a proximate fruit, one's lifespan is further extended and life does not end. △ Second, clarifying the transformation of others.

He extensively expounded this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for others. At that time, the fourfold assembly of those with overweening pride—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—despised the man who had been given the name "Never-Disparaging.

However, when they saw him attain the power of great supernormal faculties, the power of eloquence in joyful exposition, and the power of great sublime tranquility, and when they heard what he preached, they all believed, submitted, and followed him.
This Bodhisattva further transforms and guides thousands of myriads of koṭis of beings, causing them to abide in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Regarding the extensive exposition of this sutra: previously, he was only able to receive and uphold a single phrase, and thus could only circulate a single phrase;
now that he has heard it in its entirety, he is able to receive and uphold it all, and thus extensively expounds it for others. This constitutes the complete circulation [of the teaching].
[This is] a section. Regarding those of the fourfold assembly who possessed overweening pride (*adhimāna*) at that time:

why did they previously revile and strike [the Buddha], yet now believe, submit, and follow him? It is because seeds had already been sown within the field of the eight consciousnesses (*aṣṭavijñāna*).
By the natural law (*dharmatā*), these gradually attained growth. Due to this growth, not only did their mouths cease from reviling, but their minds also came to believe.
I prostrate. Not only did he not strike or hurl [the object] with his hand, but he even followed along with his body.

As for the phrase "having attained great supernormal power" (*mahā-ṛddhi-bala*): "spiritual" (*shen*) refers to the celestial mind (*tianxin*), and "penetration" (*tong*) refers to the nature of wisdom (*hui-xing*).

If one has not yet attained this celestial mind and nature of wisdom, then naturally one will be obscured and lack spirituality, and obstructed and lack penetration. Now, this bhikṣu was able to receive, uphold, and propagate it.

Because of this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, one attains the celestial mind, wisdom, and nature, enabling one to manifest spiritual wonders and bestow names, to penetrate and transform, and to move freely to the left or right, such that there is nothing unsuitable.
Therefore, it is said that one attains great supernatural powers (*mahābhijñā*); this is precisely the purification of the faculty of the body (*kāyendriya-viśuddhi*).
As for "eloquence in joyful exposition" (*pratibhāna*), it is one of the four types of unimpeded eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*).

Furthermore, one who has not yet attained the unimpeded eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*) regards a single dharma as merely a single dharma, a single phrase as merely a single phrase, and a single meaning as merely a single meaning. Now, this bhikṣu is able to receive, uphold, and circulate this sutra;
he can expound upon a single dharma so that it becomes immeasurable dharmas, and he can expound upon a single phrase in such a way.
To express a single meaning through immeasurable phrases, and to express immeasurable meanings within a single phrase—this is called the eloquence of joyful speech (*pratibhāna*).
This is precisely the attainment of the purity of the faculty of the tongue. Regarding the power of great, sublime tranquility (*mahā-śānti*):

although the tranquility of the two vehicles, which sinks into emptiness and stagnates in stillness, is also called "tranquility," it cannot be called "great, sublime tranquility. Now, as for this bhikṣu...
To uphold and circulate this sutra enables one to be tranquil yet luminous, and luminous yet tranquil.

Because tranquility and luminosity are non-dual and because tranquility and luminosity are perfectly interfused, it is called the "great power of sublime tranquility. This is precisely the attainment of the purity of the sense-faculties.
Just as it is with the three faculties of body, tongue, and mind, so too it is with the three faculties of eye, ear, and nose. Therefore...
This is omitted and not further discussed. Because the fourfold assembly saw that he had attained the purity of the six sense faculties, they all believed, submitted, and followed him.
Due to the belief, submission, and following of the fourfold assembly, he further transformed tens of millions of billions of beings, causing them to dwell securely in Bodhi.
△ Second, revealing the retribution of birth.
After his life comes to an end, he shall encounter two thousand billion buddhas, all of whom will be identical to Candrasūryapradīpa;
within their teachings, they shall preach this Lotus Sutra.
The Buddha named Candrasūryapradīpa (Moon-Sun-Lamp Radiance) takes his name from the radiance of the three lights, which fully represents the three wisdoms (*trividya*).

That Buddha was able to perfectly contemplate the three wisdoms within the causal stage and perfectly manifest the three wisdoms upon the fruition stage, just as the three lights of the sun, moon, and lamp shine together;
thus he was so named. Within the teachings of those two thousand *koṭi* Buddhas, he preached this sutra.
This refers precisely to receiving, upholding, and circulating this sutra. △ Third, revealing the retributive result in a future life:
By these causes and conditions, he further encountered two thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas, all equally named Cloud Sovereign Lamp King (*Megheśvaradīparāja*).

Within the teachings of these Buddhas, he received, upheld, read, and recited [this sutra], and for the sake of the fourfold assembly, he preached this scripture; therefore, he obtained these eternal eyes.
His faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind were all purified. He preached the Dharma among the fourfold assembly with a heart free from fear, having attained great power.

This was the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sadāparibhūta. Having made offerings to such various Buddhas, honoring, respecting, and praising them, he planted various roots of goodness. Thereafter, he again encountered thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas, and likewise...
Among all the Buddha-dharmas, by accomplishing the merit of preaching this sutra, one shall attain Buddhahood.

The Buddha’s name will be Cloud Sovereign Lamp King (Meghasvaradīparāja), for that Buddha can manifest his body like clouds to respond to sentient beings of great capacity by appearing in the form of a ten-thousand-fathom Śākyamuni,
and to respond to sentient beings of small capacity by appearing in the form of a sixteen-foot [Buddha].
The body of this bhikṣu manifests both superiority and inferiority with complete mastery, like the rolling and unrolling of clouds;

his coming and going are unhindered, and for this reason he is named Cloud-Self-Mastery (Meghasvabhāva). Furthermore, he can destroy obstacles like a lamp; wishing to destroy the obstacle of phenomena (dharma-āvaraṇa), [he proceeds].

Thus, there is no obstacle of phenomena (*dharma-āvaraṇa*) that is not destroyed. To destroy the obstacle of principle (*tattva-āvaraṇa*), there is likewise no obstacle of principle that is not destroyed.
Because one is able to destroy both phenomena and principle with sovereign mastery, like a king, it is called the "Lamp King. Regarding the phrase "one who has attained this pure, eternal eye":
in the aforementioned present retribution, one has already attained a semblance of the purity of the six sense organs; now, this is precisely that which is capable of...
This refers to attaining the purification of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya-viśuddhi*). Regarding "the mind being without fear":

because one is able to attain the purification of the six sense faculties, one realizes that all phenomena are, in their very essence, empty and quiescent; furthermore, by exercising great compassion, one becomes gentle, harmonious, and compliant.
Thus, the mind is without fear. "Planting various roots of goodness" refers precisely to being able to cultivate the conditions and the understanding (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
This refers to the roots of goodness of the two causes. As for the "accomplishment of merit," it is the accomplishment of the merits of the six sense faculties.
Previously, one had already attained partial realization of the purity of the six faculties;

now, having further encountered ten trillion Buddhas, one proceeds from within that partial realization to further subdivide and further realize it. Thus, wisdom will approach fulfillment and [afflictions] will approach cessation.
It is complete. Because the cause is about to be exhausted and the fruit is about to reach its ultimate limit, it is said that he shall attain Buddhahood through the fulfillment of his merits.
△ Second, the summary and identification:
"Śrīmahādeva, what do you think? Was that Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging at that time anyone else? It was none other than myself."
This body is it.
You should know that Śākyamuni is none other than the One Who Is Not Disparaging; this was his cause in the past, and there is no other cause for it.
This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* served as that cause. His fruit today is likewise nothing other than this; there is no separate fruit for it.
Taking this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* as its fruit, since the cause is accomplished from this and the fruit is achieved from this, one may simply choose not to uphold and propagate it;

however, if one can uphold it and if one can propagate it, one will certainly be able to accomplish the cause and achieve the fruit, becoming a Buddha in the end without doubt. How could it be that one merely attains the proximate marks?
"It is not merely that it resembles [the fruit]; △ Third, the exhortation to uphold:
'If, in my past lives, I had not received, upheld, read, recited, and explained this sutra to others, I would not have been able to quickly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
It was because I, at the places of former Buddhas, received, upheld, read, and recited this..."
Because one explains this sutra for others, one will swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This means that had I, Śākyamuni, not received, upheld, and circulated this sutra during my causal stage, I would not have been able to swiftly attain bodhi today.
That I was able to swiftly attain unsurpassed bodhi was due to my receiving, upholding, and circulating it.
Because it is universally pervasive. Since I am thus, all sentient beings before me shall naturally uphold and circulate this sutra;
for by means of this sutra, one can swiftly attain Bodhi. Indeed, this sutra is uniquely pure, perfect, and wondrous;
therefore, if one can uphold it, one may, within a single lifetime, transcend and ascend to the tenth stage.
O Earth, will you not swiftly attain Bodhi? If one upholds the distinct sutras of the Tripitaka and the Shared Teaching, one will proceed by circuitous routes and be unable to attain it swiftly;
the present Perfect Sutra is that which leads to swift attainment. Thus, the preceding passage states:
"Those who wish to swiftly attain the wisdom of all modes should uphold this sutra. This refers precisely to this point. △ Second, the Manifestation.

There are three parts to the retribution for disparaging [the teaching]: first, the actual manifestation; second, the summary correlation; and third, the exhortation to uphold it. The first part has two sub-sections: first, the manifestation of the evil retribution;
and second, [the attainment of great power]. At that time, the fourfold assembly—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—were filled with anger.
Because of their malicious intent and because they held me in contempt, for two hundred billion kalpas they shall never encounter a Buddha, hear the Dharma, or see the Sangha;
for a thousand kalpas they shall undergo great suffering and affliction in the Avīci Hell.
"At that time" refers to the period when the Bhikṣu Never-Disparaging was practicing the conduct of never-disparaging.
Those who, out of anger, treated him with contempt did not merely fail to believe and accept his teaching; they instead responded with resentment.

To bestow upon him the name "Never-Disparaging" was itself an act of disparagement. As for the phrase "never encountering a Buddha," this refers to [the fact that] this entire *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*...
The Sūtra states: "The one who can preach is the person of ultimate realization; that which is preached is the subtle and wondrous Dharma;
and those who hear it together are the Saṃgha in whom principle and phenomena are in harmony—these constitute the Three Jewels of the One-Body Mahāyāna.
Now, even if the Bhikṣu Not-Light (Adhimātra-prasāda) were to preach but a single phrase for someone's sake, it would be equivalent to the entire canon. Yet they [the listeners] not only—"
Not only do they fail to give rise to faith and acceptance, but instead they give rise to anger;
not only do they fail to give rise to respect, but instead they give rise to contempt. Thus, they lack faith in the Triple Gem.

Because of this lack of faith in the Triple Gem, for two hundred billion kalpas, they constantly fail to encounter the Buddha, hear the Dharma, or see the Sangha. Since they have not encountered them...
The Triple Gem was his only refuge, yet his dwelling place was nothing but the retribution of suffering in hell. △ Second, revealing the reward of goodness:
Once these karmic offenses were exhausted, he again encountered the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging, who taught and transformed him toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The completion of this transgression refers precisely to the sin of slandering the sutras. Furthermore, one encounters those who do not slight others and who have resolved their minds on Bodhi.
Although at that time one may have lacked faith and produced slander, it should be known that the seeds of potent poison have already been sown within the field of the eight consciousnesses;
yet, because one has heard the words "all sentient beings shall become Buddhas," [the conditions for awakening are present].

It is the natural law that, over the course of incalculable eons, [the potential] naturally increases; because its seeds have grown, one encounters a bodhisattva and is able to resolve the mind for enlightenment.

Furthermore, by encountering one who is not disparaging (*adhimāna*), and since that non-disparaging person acts as a powerful, potent seed for one who was previously disregarded, the beginning has already been established.
Since the beginning was established by one who is not disparaging, the conclusion must likewise be achieved by one who is not disparaging.
Because it is light, one may encounter it again and give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment. Viewed from this perspective, it is evident that those with faith can certainly achieve bodhi;
yet even those who lack faith and engage in slander can also achieve it through the power of potent seeds.
If, upon hearing this, one can neither believe it nor reject it, such a person is what is called a commoner who is indifferent and self-satisfied;
how could they ever have a day of attaining Buddhahood? As for me, there is nothing I can do for them. △ Second, the conclusion and correlation.

"O Mahāsthāmaprāpta, what do you think? Were those four assemblies who constantly disparaged this bodhisattva at that time anyone other than these five hundred bodhisattvas in this assembly, such as Bhadrapāla and the others; these five hundred bhikṣus, such as Siṃhacandra and the others;
and these five hundred upāsakas, such as Buddhamati and the others? They have all [attained] Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Regarding "Threefold Bodhi," one who is non-retrogressive is called *Bhadra* in the Sanskrit language;
this is translated here as "Worthy Head" (*Xiánshǒu*), because such a person is able to serve as the foremost among the worthy.
He is also called "Well-Guarded" (Sugupta), because he is well able to protect the treasury of the Dharma.
Regarding the five hundred bhikṣus such as Siṃhacandra and others, this is an abbreviated expression; it should actually be stated as "five hundred bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs."
If it is claimed that "Nisi" is a name for an *upāsaka*, such a name never appears in any of the sūtras or teachings.
△ Third, the exhortation to uphold [the precepts].
"Mahāsthāmaprāpta, you should know that this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* brings great benefit to all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and enables them to reach anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Therefore, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should constantly receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, and transcribe this sūtra."
Regarding the term "great benefit": other sutras merely enable those with right view to obtain benefit, but cannot enable those with wrong views to do so;
they merely enable those who believe and accept them to obtain benefit, but cannot enable those who slander them to do so.
Thus, while these may indeed be beneficial, they are not called "greatly beneficial. This present sutra, however, is not limited to enabling only those with right view [to obtain benefit].
Those who believe and accept it shall gain benefit; furthermore, even those with wrong views who slander it will, by virtue of this potent and poisonous seed, achieve enlightenment.
Therefore, it is said that it brings great benefit. △ Second, the verse praise has three parts. First, the verse clarifies the causal basis.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"In the past there was a Buddha named King of Majestic Sound (Vaiśvānara-rāja). His spiritual wisdom was immeasurable, and he guided all—the devas, humans, nāgas, and spirits."
"Those who are collectively honored" refers to those whose divine wisdom (*jñāna*) is immeasurable; that is, their supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and wisdom are both limitless.
"Those who lead all beings" means that by means of the very same supernormal powers and wisdom they have realized for themselves, they lead and guide all sentient beings.
They shall also attain the realization of this infinite supernatural power and wisdom. △ Second, the verse explaining the meaning of the name:
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, at a time when the Dharma was about to perish, there was a bodhisattva named Constantly Not Disparaging (*Sadāparibhūta*). At that time, the fourfold assembly...
Attached to their views regarding the Dharma, they did not treat the Bodhisattva Sadāparibhūta with respect. He went to them and said to them, "I do not slight you;
all of you who practice the Way shall become Buddhas. When those people heard this, they treated the Bodhisattva Sadāparibhūta with contempt, reviling and abusing him.
They are able to endure it.
This refers to the period after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, specifically after the lifespan [of beings] and the True Dharma have been extinguished;

that is, at the time when the Dharma is about to perish, which is the time when the Semblance Dharma is about to end. As for those monks and nuns who are attached to the Dharma, they will, in every thought-moment...
They are attached to the dharmas that take the [four] truths as their object, and regard the Lesser Vehicle as the ultimate goal.
Upāsakas and upāsikās, moreover, are attached in every thought-moment to the dharmas of precepts and goodness, and regard the realms of humans and devas as the ultimate goal.
That I do not slight you is because this bhikṣu understands that all sentient beings possess the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Thus, by relying on this for cultivation and realization, one becomes non-dual with the Buddha; therefore, I do not dare to treat you with contempt or arrogance.

As for those who are able to endure it, they are able to maintain their minds through the three modes of practice (*trividha-yāna*): internally, they contemplate the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*);
externally, they exercise compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā*); and in between, regarding all instances of verbal abuse, physical assault, or striking, they simply—
Abiding in a state of gentleness and docility, one endures the difficulties of propagating the sutras. △ Third, the verses on the manifestation of the retributive fruits, in three parts.
First, the two verses on the dual retributions.

When their retributions for those sins have ended, at the moment of death, they shall hear this sutra. By the power of their supernormal faculties, their six sense organs will become pure and their lifespans will be extended.
Furthermore, they will extensively expound this sutra for all people, and all those attached to dharmas shall receive the grace of the Bodhisattva.
They were taught and brought to fulfillment, established in the Buddha-way. At the end of their lives, they were not disparaged; they encountered countless Buddhas.
Because they had preached this sutra, they obtained immeasurable merit, gradually perfected their virtues, and swiftly attained the Buddha-way.
The first phrase, "When their offenses have been completed," is a summary verse concerning the retribution for the offenses of those who reviled [the Buddha] in the prose section.

That is to say, because the fourfold assembly at that time treated me with anger and contempt, they shall for two hundred *koṭi* of kalpas never encounter a Buddha, never hear the Dharma, and never see the Saṃgha;
and for a thousand kalpas, they shall undergo great suffering and affliction in the Avīci Hell. Up to...
This section concludes; hence it says, "their offenses have been exhausted.

Some say that as clarified in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, if there are those who receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, yet are treated with contempt by others, then because of this contemporary contempt from others, their karmic offenses from previous lives—which would otherwise cause them to fall into the evil realms—are immediately extinguished.
[The afflictions] are extinguished. If one interprets it in this way, then one belongs to the category of the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging (Sadāparibhūta).
If [the text asks], "How could Sadāparibhūta have had fixed sinful karma in previous lives?"—it is simply that the fourfold assembly did not believe him and reviled him;

it is not that Sadāparibhūta had sinful karma in previous lives, but rather that he spoke of the completion of such karma. At the end of his life, he recited verses on the retribution for those who believe. This is the first verse of praise.

The line "In this life, not slighting [others] at the end of life" praises the retribution received in the present life (*drstadharma-vedanīya*). The two phrases "gradually becoming complete" praise the retribution received in the next life (*upapadya-vedanīya*). [The remaining part] praises the retribution received in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya*).
△ Second, the double verse that summarizes and correlates [the preceding].

At that time, the one who was not disparaged was none other than myself. As for the fourfold assembly who were attached to the Dharma at that time, having heard the words of the one who was not disparaged—"You shall become a Buddha"—they encountered countless Buddhas through these causal conditions; this includes the assembly of five hundred bodhisattvas present here today.
As well as the fourfold assembly—male and female lay devotees—it is these who are now before me listening to the Dharma.
△ Third, the double verse exhorting them to uphold [the teaching]:
"In previous lives, I exhorted all these people to listen to and receive this sutra, the foremost Dharma, which I have revealed and taught to others."

They cause them to abide in nirvāṇa. From lifetime to lifetime they uphold such a sūtra as this. Only after billions of billions of kalpas, reaching the inconceivable, do they finally hear this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
After billions of billions of kalpas, reaching the inconceivable, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones [appear].
When this sutra was thus spoken, practitioners who, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, hear such a sutra as this should not give rise to doubt or confusion.
They should, with a single mind, extensively expound this sutra; they shall encounter Buddhas in every lifetime and swiftly attain the path of Buddhahood.
That which is called the "Supreme Dharma" is not shared with others, but is exclusively, purely, perfectly, and uniquely sublime;
for it is beyond the reach of the three vehicles, the nine realms, and the seven stages of expedient means.

That which causes one to abide in nirvana is the Mahayana nirvana of non-arising and non-ceasing, not the partial emptiness of the Small Vehicle (Hinayana) nirvana. One should receive and uphold this in every lifetime.
This person, during the time of the Buddha King of Majestic Sound, first received and upheld a single phrase and later propagated the entire canon.

Subsequently, within the teachings of two thousand *koṭi* Buddhas named Candrasūryapradīpa, then within the teachings of Meghasvararāja, and finally within the teachings of ten million *koṭi* Buddhas, they likewise received, upheld, and propagated this sutra. Therefore...
This refers to receiving and upholding [the teaching] life after life. The passage beginning with "For billions of koṭis of kalpas" below concerns the difficulty of hearing this sutra;
it is intended to encourage its circulation. The first line concerns the difficulty of hearing it, while the next line concerns the difficulty of preaching it.

Therefore, the section beginning with "For this reason" is the formal exhortation. The meaning is that since one has now both heard and preached it, one should naturally act as such after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
"It shall circulate everywhere" is the second verse in this section, which exhorts one to uphold [the teaching].

"One should single-mindedly expound this sutra extensively" means that one should not preach the precepts and virtues of humans and devas, the truths and conditions of the Two Vehicles, or the gates of liberation for Bodhisattvas;
rather, one should single-mindedly receive, uphold, propagate, and disseminate this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. The above constitutes the exhortation.
The praise for the propagation [of this sutra] concludes here. The commentary on the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging" is finished.
*Exegesis of the Lotus Sutra*, Scroll Six, Part One;
*Exegesis of the Lotus Sutra*, Scroll Six, Part Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva under imperial decree during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Lectures and Records by Grand Master Yisong on the Tiantai Teachings and Contemplations.
Compiled and Edited by the Śramaṇa Xiaorou of Dong’ou and Guanghe.
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Twenty-one: The Supernatural Powers of the Tathāgata.

Regarding the sequential development of this chapter: it is entirely because the Tathāgata desires to circulate this Fundamental Gate so that it shall not be interrupted, that he has elucidated the causal merits of the four levels of faith and the five grades of practice. Furthermore...
Citing the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging of the past serves as the primary proof.
Having already exhorted and praised [the teaching] for its circulation, once that exhortation and praise are complete, it must then be entrusted back [to others] to encourage its further circulation.

To effect such an entrustment, one must first manifest supernatural power (*ṛddhibala*); therefore, there is this passage from the "Chapter on the Supernatural Power of the Tathāgata. As for the term "Tathāgata," it is because...
The Buddha possesses great wisdom and great compassion; therefore, he does not abide in saṃsāra, nor does he abide in nirvāṇa.
Being able to ride the path of reality as it is, he has come to achieve perfect enlightenment, and is thus called the Tathāgata.
Speaking according to the literal text, there is the Śākyamuni Tathāgata and there are the emanation (nirmāṇakāya) Tathāgatas; of these, Śākyamuni is the principal. The emanations...
The body is the companion; Śākyamuni is the one, while his manifested bodies are many.

This is precisely what is meant by the non-obstruction of the one and the many, and the perfect interfusion of the principal and the companions, whereby they together manifest spiritual power (*ṛddhi*). Regarding the term "spiritual method" (*shenfang*):

that which is wondrous and inscrutable is called "spiritual" (*shen*), and that which operates with sovereign freedom is called "power" (*li*). Now, as for why the Tathāgata is able to manifest such spiritual power, it is because...

Having ultimately realized the principle of the true reality of all phenomena—the three thousand nature-and-characteristics and the hundred realms and thousand suchnesses—he manifests function from essence and unfolds in accordance with his nature, displaying ten kinds of spiritual powers.
This causes all bodhisattvas, devas, and humans to behold these wondrous functions, so that they may naturally circulate everywhere, forever and without end. [End of] Chapter Text.

It is divided into two parts: first, the prose; second, the verses. The prose section has three sub-sections: first, the Bodhisattva receives his mandate; second, the Tathāgata manifests supernatural powers;
third, the summary of the essential points for circulation. The first of these two [sub-sections] consists of the narrative provided by the sūtra compiler.
At that time, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as numerous as the atoms in a thousand worlds, who had emerged from the earth, all stood before the Buddha with single-minded palms joined;
gazing up at the Honored One’s countenance, they addressed the Buddha, saying:

Regarding the bodhisattvas emerging from the earth all addressing the Buddha: it was because, within the introductory section of the "Original Gate," the Tathāgata had summoned those from the lower regions, declaring that in my Sahā world there are bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of sixty thousand Ganges Rivers who are able, after my parinirvāṇa, to widely expound this sutra.
Thus, when these bodhisattvas heard the Buddha’s summons, they immediately [emerged] from below.

They have arrived precisely for the purpose of circulating this sutra. Now that their lifespans have been discussed and the main body of the teaching has concluded, the Tathāgata further exhorts and praises them to circulate it; therefore, these bodhisattvas now all stand before the Buddha.
This is the formal statement for receiving the mandate to propagate the sutra. △ Second, the actual statement for receiving the mandate:
"World-Honored One, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, wherever the World-Honored One’s emanations reside, in whatever lands and places of parinirvāṇa they may be..."

This sutra should be expounded extensively. Why is this? For we ourselves also desire to attain this truly pure Great Dharma, to receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, transcribe, and make offerings to it.
"After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa" indicates the time; "the lands where his bodies are manifested" clarifies the locations.

The following section further explains the purpose of receiving this mandate: it means that the reason we wish to expound this sutra extensively is precisely because we are obeying the Tathāgata’s command, and it was indeed fitting to act in this way. Furthermore, we ourselves also desire to attain this...
The Great Dharma of True Purity; therefore, it should also be understood in this way. Regarding what is called the "Great Dharma of True Purity":

if one merely attains the wisdom of partial truth, destroys the delusions of views and thoughts, and manifests the principle of the partial truth, then that may be termed a "pure dharma," yet it cannot be called the "Great Dharma of True Purity. Now, as for what is called "True Purity" and "Great..."
The Dharma is that which can attain the three kinds of wisdom and is thus truly real; it can shatter the three delusions and is thus pure; it can manifest the three truths and is thus vast.
Through this attainment, the three wisdoms are attained simultaneously; through this shattering, the three delusions are all shattered;
through this manifestation, the three truths are all manifested. Thus, being truly real, pure, and vast, one attains mastery over all.
When one is pure, all are pure; when one reaches the ultimate, all reach the ultimate.
This is the inconceivable secret treasury of the three virtues, which resides within this sutra. Now we, too, desire to obtain it.
Therefore, it is explained at length. △ Second, the Tathāgata’s manifestation of supernatural powers has two parts. First, the general explanation:

At that time, the World-Honored One [addressed] Mañjuśrī and others—immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who had long resided in the Sahā world, as well as bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.
Before all the assemblies of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras,
mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others, he manifested great supernormal powers.

Mañjuśrī and others are those transformed within the realm of manifested traces (*traces*). The "original inhabitants" and others are those transformed within the realm of the fundamental source (*essence*).
Those who emerged from the earth, as well as the various bhikṣus and so forth, are the emanations gathered from the ten directions.
△ Second, a detailed explanation in ten parts. First, the protrusion of the tongue.
He extends his broad and long tongue, reaching as far as the Brahma Heaven.
Regarding the phrase "extending his broad and long tongue," this is a theme discussed throughout the sutras, whether concerning the provisional or the real, the trace or the fundamental.

This is spoken solely by means of the tongue-faculty (*jihvendriya*). Thus, the tongue-faculty is the speaker, while the provisional and the real, the fundamental and the manifested, are that which is spoken.
Now, wishing to manifest the excellence of what is spoken in order to encourage its circulation, it is necessary to employ the tongue-faculty as the means of manifestation.
That is to say, since the tongue-faculty that speaks is both broad and long, [it reaches] upward...
Reaching even the Brahma-world, the provisional means taught must be wondrous means; the reality taught must be wondrous reality;
the traces taught must be wondrous traces; and the fundamental source taught must be wondrous source.
Thus, whether provisional or real, whether trace or source, each and every one is wondrous; it is therefore naturally present wherever one goes.
It was thus circulated. Therefore, at the very beginning, he manifested signs to indicate that all that was taught is sublime, thereby causing it to be circulated.
△ Second, the emission of light:
from every pore, he emitted immeasurable and innumerable rays of light of various colors, which universally illuminated the worlds of the ten directions.
Under the various jewel trees, the Buddhas upon their lion thrones did likewise.
Śākyamuni Buddha and all the Buddhas beneath the jewel trees manifested this supernatural power for a full hundred thousand years,
after which they withdrew their tongues.
If, within the introductory section (*nidāna*) of the "Trace Gate" (*jiamen*), the Buddha was also able to emit light, yet it was emitted only from his eyebrows;
furthermore, it was only white in color and illuminated only the eastern direction—whereas here, it is said that light is emitted from all pores, not merely from between the eyebrows.
Moreover, it is said that he emits light of immeasurable colors, not just white, and that it universally illuminates the worlds of the ten directions, not just the east.
Why is it that these various aspects differ? It is because within the *Ji-men* (Trace Gate), the ultimate truth had not yet been revealed;
thus, it was known only by the Buddha himself. Therefore, he merely emitted light from the white tuft between his eyebrows, which illuminated the eastern direction.
Now, however, the provisional and the real, as well as the fundamental and the trace, have each been fully revealed, enabling all beings to sever their doubts regarding the provisional and the near.
Having given rise to the faith that distances them from reality, all sentient beings have already attained the opening, showing, awakening, and entry into the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision;
they have already clearly understood his long-lasting life-span. Therefore, within a single pore of his body...
