They emit countless rays of light of various colors that illuminate the worlds of the ten directions, precisely signifying that the nine realms all return to the Buddha-realm and that the three vehicles are entirely united within the One Vehicle, thereby manifesting the excellence of this sutra so that it may circulate forevermore.
The Buddhas seated upon lion thrones beneath the various jeweled trees are none other than the manifested bodies (nirmāṇakāya) of the Buddha. These manifested bodies...
As for the statement that "the various Buddhas likewise protrude their tongues and emit light," this refers to the Buddhas who have manifested as emanations (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Because they also wish to circulate this sutra everywhere within their own lands, they too are able to manifest these two kinds of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) just as Śākyamuni does.
The phrase "for a full hundred thousand years" indicates the duration of time during which these two kinds of supernatural powers are displayed; and therein he speaks this...

A portion of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states that [the Buddha] remained for only eight years, yet now manifests supernatural power such that it is said he has been present for hundreds of thousands of years.
This is because sentient beings, due to their emotional attachments, perceive distinctions of long and short durations.

As for the Tathāgata, however, there is fundamentally no limit of length or brevity; therefore, the eight years that seem short are not actually short, and the hundreds of thousands of years that seem long are not actually long.
"Long" is not "long. This, too, is a place of the Tathāgata’s inconceivability;
it is precisely intended to manifest that this sutra shall circulate in the final age, forever and without end. △ Third, the clearing of the throat.
"At one time they coughed.
Regarding "at one time they coughed": the emanated Buddhas of the ten directions and Śākyamuni Tathāgata did not precede or follow one another, but were perfectly simultaneous;
hence it is called "one time. "Coughing" refers to the sound of clearing the throat. "One" means to be unobstructed and flowing.
These are the characteristics [of the two aspects]: the first is the state of being about to speak. This refers to the two gates of the Manifest Trace and the Fundamental Source.

Since both have now been revealed and clarified, the original intention is fully realized and unobstructed; therefore, it is symbolized by "clearing the throat" (kǐngkài) to signify this thorough realization.

Having already explained the Trace and the Source, there is only the desire to entrust them so that they may circulate; therefore, it is symbolized by "clearing the throat" to signify the act of being about to speak. △
Four times he snapped his fingers;
they all snapped their fingers together. These two sounds reached throughout the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions.
As for "snapping one's fingers," it is like a person whose inner joy is extreme and who snaps their fingers externally; now, the traces and the origin of the Tathāgata are both like this.
The opening of the gate is now complete. All members of the great assembly have had their provisional and proximate doubts severed, and their ultimate and remote faith has been born.
With these doubts once and for all severed and this faith once and for all born, they have reached the pinnacle of dual joy;
thus, they express it by snapping their fingers. As for the equality of these two sounds, if this sutra were to be circulated—
At that time, it pervaded all of heaven and earth, extending widely to even the lands within a single mote of dust;
thus, by means of these two sounds, it reached throughout the ten directions to manifest its presence. △ Five: The Earth Trembles.
The earth shook in six ways;
when the preceding section on the "Trace" (迹门) was initiated, the earth shook in six ways.
That the earth now also shakes in six ways indicates that at the time of initiating [this teaching], it will certainly be able to overturn [delusion] at the time of expounding the sutra.
The destruction of the ignorance of the six stages now signifies the time of the circulation of this sutra, for it is also capable of overturning and destroying the ignorance of the six stages.
The five kinds of supernatural power mentioned above signify the benefits obtained in the present;
from the sixth [stage], the Joyful One (Pramuditā), onwards, the five kinds of supernatural power signify those of the future.
They obtained benefit. △ Sixth, the multitude rejoiced.
Among them were sentient beings: devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, and kiṃnaras.

The mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others, by the Buddha’s spiritual power, all saw this Sahā world with its immeasurable and boundless hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas beneath trees of various jewels upon lion thrones;
they also saw Śākyamuni Buddha together with the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, seated upon a lion throne within the jeweled stupa; furthermore, they saw...
Immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as well as the fourfold assembly, respectfully surrounded Śākyamuni Buddha.
Having seen this, they were all filled with great joy, having attained what they had never experienced before.

Regarding the sentient beings therein: they are those five thousand who withdrew from their seats, as well as the devas and humans who were moved [to other worlds] during the three transformations of the Pure Land, and furthermore, those who lost their resolve after regressing from the Mahāyāna following the parable of the skilled physician.
These sentient beings all see this Sahā world and so forth; they see the emanated Buddhas as many, while seeing Śākyamuni as one. This is the division.
Although his bodies are many, they are what Śākyamuni has divided; thus, many are not many. Although Śākyamuni is one, he is able to manifest divided bodies;

thus, one is not one. To see Prabhūtaratna is to see the past; to see Śākyamuni is to see the present. Although Prabhūtaratna is ancient, he shares his seat with Śākyamuni; thus, the ancient is not ancient.
Although Śākyamuni is of the present, he sits upon Prabhūtaratna’s seat; thus, the present is not present. To see the Bodhisattvas...

This is the noble; seeing the fourfold assembly as ordinary people. Although the bodhisattva is noble, he still associates with the fourfold assembly; thus the noble is not [separate from] the non-noble.

Although the fourfold assembly is ordinary, they are reached by the bodhisattva; thus the ordinary is not [separate from] the non-ordinary. Seeing the bodhisattva and the fourfold assembly together is the cause.
Seeing Śākyamuni Tathāgata is the fruit; yet Śākyamuni, surrounded by the fourfold assembly of bodhisattvas, is neither cause nor non-cause.
Śākyamuni Tathāgata, surrounded by the fourfold assembly of bodhisattvas, is neither fruit nor non-fruit. Thus, there is no obstruction between the one and the many;
past and present share a single limit; the holy and the ordinary are equal. This is the wondrous reality-mark (*dharmatā*) in which cause and effect are non-dual.

This principle is that which is elucidated by the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Because future sentient beings who enable the circulation of this scripture shall obtain such benefits, [the text] uses the characteristics of the non-obstruction between the one and the many to manifest it. △ Seventh, the Chanting of Sound.
Immediately, the devas in the midst of the void raised their voices and proclaimed:
"Beyond these immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeya worlds, there is a land named Sahā.
Therein dwells a Buddha named Śākyamuni, who is now preaching for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas a Mahāyāna sūtra titled the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, teaching the bodhisattvas..."
"Saddharma. It is that which the Buddha protects and keeps in mind. You all should rejoice with a profound heart, and you should also pay homage and make offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha.
These words were spoken immediately because [the Buddha] feared that although they might have seen his physical marks, they had not yet heard his teaching; therefore, the devas informed them.

All the devas are indeed great bodhisattvas; they represent those who, in future ages, shall propagate this sutra by expounding its wondrous teachings from the perspective of the emptiness of the primary meaning (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).

Those who rejoice with a profound mind (*adhyāśaya*) give rise to wondrous understanding based on the wondrous teachings, initiate wondrous practice based on that wondrous understanding, and enter into wondrous realization based on that wondrous practice; therefore, it is said, "rejoice with a profound mind."
Furthermore, those sentient beings of the future who wish to circulate [this teaching] shall hear this wondrous sutra;

they too must rely upon the instructions to give rise to understanding, initiate practice, and enter into realization. Therefore, having already heard the proclamation from within the void, he prostrates to Śākyamuni to manifest this intent. △ Eight: Taking Refuge.
When those sentient beings heard the voice from the midst of space, they joined their palms toward the Sahā world and spoke these words:
"Homage to Śākyamuni Buddha! Homage to Śākyamuni Buddha! Then, with various kinds of flowers and incense...

Necklaces, banners, canopies, and various ornaments for the body, as well as rare jewels and exquisite objects—those who twice invoke "Namo" do so with profound reverence. This arises from hearing the exhortations and rejoicings of the various devas.
The fact that those sentient beings take refuge signifies that they will be able to obtain benefits through both the provisional and the ultimate gates in the future.
△ Ninth, the distant scattering:
They all together scattered [offerings] from afar toward the Sahā world; the various objects thus scattered came from the ten directions, gathering like clouds.
It transforms into jeweled canopies that completely cover the space above all the Buddhas here.

As for those who scatter [flowers] from afar, they are said to be "scattering from afar" because they are facing the Sahā world from other directions. Although they scatter from afar, they are nevertheless able to reach this place;
thus it is said, "that which is scattered," and so forth. The jeweled canopies represent the causal mind of sentient beings. All that exists...
Concentration and wisdom are entirely subsumed within the compassionate merit of the Tathāgata’s fruition; thus they transform into a jeweled canopy to manifest this truth.
That it covers the Buddha everywhere signifies that the concentration and wisdom of the causal mind are the ultimate source of the fruition.
The compassion of the fruition-virtue is also that which is possessed by the causal mind;
therefore, it is manifested by transforming those offering implements into jeweled canopies that cover the Buddha.
Just as one is able to behold the Buddha, respond to his exhortations, take refuge, and present offerings, all of this is brought about by the inconceivable supernormal power of the Tathāgata.
This is intended to manifest that those sentient beings will also be able to derive benefit from this sublime sutra in the future; thus it is so.
This is a latent agreement with their capacities (*indriya*); such a matter exists [in the teaching], yet for those sentient beings, they are not yet immediately able to do so.
△ Ten: The Convergence of Lands.
Thereupon, the worlds of the ten directions were unimpededly accessible as if they were a single buddha-field.
Yet, within the worlds of the ten directions, there are various buddha-fields and various worlds, each distinct from the others.
How is it that they can be unified into a single field while remaining unimpededly accessible? This is because the lands of the Buddhas are, as if...
Within the Tathāgata, one spontaneously realizes that every land is none other than a Buddha-land, and every realm is none other than the Dharma-realm.
This is inherently all-pervasive, inherently penetrating, and inherently unobstructed; yet it is due to the emotional attachments of sentient beings [that this is not perceived].

Therefore, that which is seen as all-pervasive is perceived as limited; that which is seen as penetrating is perceived as obstructed; and that which is seen as unimpeded is perceived as having impediments.

Now, wishing to entrust this sutra for its circulation so that future sentient beings may all attain mastery of the wondrous principle of pervasive penetration, I manifest these supernatural powers to ensure that those who see them are not subject to limitation.
The minor obstructions are all seen as the worlds of the ten directions merged into a single land, thereby manifesting it.
One should know that the three transformations of the pure lands mentioned above have already merged them into a single Buddha-land;
now, this [transformation] is yet another merging performed outside of those transformed pure lands. △ Third, the summary and circulation of the essentials has three parts. First, the praise.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the great assembly of bodhisattvas, headed by Śikhin: "The supernatural power of all Buddhas is thus immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable.

Even if I were to use such supernatural power to describe the merits of this sutra for the sake of entrustment throughout immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeya kalpas, I would still not be able to exhaust them."

Regarding the phrase "Uttara-mati and the others": among the six million *nayuta* of bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who emerged from the earth at the Tathāgata’s summons, there were four leaders, Uttara-mati and the rest; here, their foremost representatives are mentioned.
Therefore it is said: "The superior practices of the Bodhisattvas," and so forth. Such are the supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) of the Buddhas.
This refers to the ten types beginning with the protrusion of the tongue and ending with the merging of the earth.

These ten types are immeasurable, boundless, and cannot be conceived by the mind or discussed in words; therefore it is said, "the supernatural powers of the Buddhas," and so on. If I were to [use] these...
Regarding "supernatural powers" and so forth: the ten kinds of supernatural powers of the Buddhas mentioned above may indeed be called inconceivable.
Yet, even with such supernatural powers, one seeks to describe the merit of this sutra and entrust it for its circulation.

Since even this cannot be fully exhausted, one knows that the merit of this sutra surpasses the inconceivable spiritual power of the Tathāgata, and is thus even more inconceivable. △ Second, the summary of the essentials.
To speak in brief. To speak in brief means that even if one wished to describe the merits of this sutra, one could not exhaust them.
If one were to take the particulars to form a whole, or proceed from the extensive to infer the concise, one would merely grasp its main framework and pull its collar. And yet...
In brief, all the teachings of the Tathāgata, even including all matters of profound depth,
are proclaimed and fully expounded within this sutra.
Regarding all the dharmas possessed by the Tathāgata:
what is called "all dharmas" refers to the teachings of the provisional and the real, and the teachings of the trace and the source.
Yet, that which is provisional is provisional while being real; that which is real is real while being provisional; and that which is the trace...
The fundamental is identical to the phenomenal; all that is fundamental is identical to the phenomenal.

Thus, although there are distinctions between the provisional and the real, the fundamental and the phenomenal, ultimately they are one in their inconceivability. The provisional is wondrous provisionality, and the real is wondrous reality.
The traces are wondrous traces; the source is a wondrous tree. These are indeed all the wondrous dharmas possessed by the Tathāgata, as well as all the Tathāgata’s sovereign spiritual powers.
Regarding sovereign spiritual power (*vibhutva-ṛddhi*): if one wishes to sever the provisional doubts of sentient beings, one severs them immediately;
if one wishes to sever the proximate doubts of sentient beings, one likewise severs them immediately. If one wishes to engender genuine faith in sentient beings, one engenders it immediately;
if one wishes to engender distant faith in sentient beings, one likewise engenders it immediately. In this way, one is able to cause all sentient beings to have no doubt.

It is uninterrupted; faith never fails to arise. This is the wondrous function of the Tathāgata’s all-encompassing sovereign spiritual power, the secret treasury of all the Tathāgata’s essential teachings.

That which is the treasury of secret essentials has never been revealed since ancient times; therefore, it is called "secret" (*bī*). Once this single sūtra is opened and revealed, there is nothing outside of it;
therefore, it is called "essential" (*yāo*). It fully possesses the three thousand natures and characteristics and encompasses the hundred realms and thousand suchnesses.
As for that which is expounded therein: every dharma is not other than the Dharma-realm, and every characteristic is not other than the true characteristic (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
This is indeed the treasury of all the Tathāgata’s secret essentials.
Regarding all the Tathāgata’s most profound matters:
what are called "matters" refers to all causes and effects. As for causes, they do not exist as distinct entities apart from being causes.
Taking the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena as its cause is the cause of the Mahāyāna.
Taking the true reality of all phenomena as its fruit is the fruit of the Mahāyāna. Although there are these two—cause and fruit—they are collectively one true reality.
That which is called "immeasurable manifold virtues" is subsumed under the term "cause," while immeasurable realizations [are subsumed under the term "fruit"].
It is attained. To speak of the fruit is to encompass it; this is indeed the entirety of the Tathāgata’s most profound matters.
All of these are proclaimed and clearly expounded within this sutra.
Regarding what is meant by "proclaimed and clearly expounded," if one considers the intention of the Tathāgata, from the very moment he first appeared in the world...

Regarding the intention to proclaim—that is, the desire to manifest and explain it—because the capacities of sentient beings have not yet been met, [the Buddha] may have taught by combining [Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna], or taught solely through the Small Vehicle, or taught in a dualistic (half-and-half) manner, or taught with partiality.
None of these are called "proclaiming," nor are they called "manifesting. In this present sutra, there is no longer any combining, sole [teaching], duality, or partiality.
It is solely because it is pure, perfect, and uniquely wondrous that both the provisional and the real, as well as the fundamental and the manifested, are all wondrous;
and because the teaching, the principle, the practitioner, and the practice are all one. Therefore, it is said that this sutra "proclaims and expounds" [the truth].

One should know that all existing phenomena take the "Wondrous Dharma" (Saddharma) as their name, and its sovereign spiritual power takes the severing of doubt and the engendering of faith as its function.
It serves as its function. Its secret and essential treasury takes the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena as its substance.

Its profound subject matter takes the cause and effect of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) as its core tenet. Its proclamation and explicit exposition takes the supreme flavor of *amṛta* (clarified butter) as its pedagogical characteristic.
△ Third, the exhortation and encouragement has two parts. First, the exhortation to receive and uphold [the teaching].
Therefore, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, you all should with one mind receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, copy,
and practice according to the teaching. In whatever land there may be those who receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, copy, and practice according to the teaching—

Regarding "one should receive and uphold it with a single mind": explained in a general sense, where there is no duality yet there is duality, and no triad yet there is a triad—this is called "a single mind.
However, if we discuss the ultimate reality, it means that one thoroughly realizes that all phenomena are entirely the true mark (*dharmatā*).
Thus, the entire sutra is the mind, and the entire mind is the sutra. Outside the sutra there is no mind; outside the mind there is no sutra. This...
Thus, externally one does not see any scripture being held, and internally one does not see a mind capable of holding it.
When subject and object have been extinguished and both environment and wisdom are tranquil, this is called "receiving and upholding with a single mind.
Since receiving and upholding is thus, so too are reading, reciting, explaining, and copying. As for practicing according to the teaching, it means practicing exactly as the Buddha has taught.

It is thus: relying upon the name of the "Sublime Dharma" (Saddharma), one explains the essence of the "True Aspect" (Tathatā); from the essence of the True Aspect, the principle of cause and effect arises;
and by means of the principle of cause and effect, the function of severing doubt is manifested. This is what is meant by "practicing according to the teaching.
Part Two: Exhortation to Make Offerings. This has two sections. First, the formal exhortation.
Wherever this scripture may reside— whether in a garden, in a grove, beneath a tree, in a monastic dwelling,
in a layperson’s house, in a palace hall, or in mountain valleys and wildernesses— in all such places one should erect a stūpa and make offerings.
△ Second, the explanatory interpretation.
Why is this so? One should know that this place is precisely the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
It is here that all Buddhas attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; it is here that all Buddhas turn the wheel of Dharma; and it is here that all Buddhas enter *parinirvāṇa*.
Nirvana. That is to say, wherever one receives and upholds this sutra, and even wherever the physical scroll of the sutra is located—
whether in a garden or even in the wilderness— one should erect a stupa there as an offering.
[The questioner asks: "Is it for the sake of veneration? Therefore, the present commentary explains: "One should know that this very place is a site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa)," and so on, up to:

"It is here that all Buddhas enter parinirvāṇa. As clarified in the Āgamas, there are four places—the place of birth, the place of attaining the Way, the place of turning the wheel of Dharma, and the place of entering nirvāṇa—where stupas should be erected. First, the place of birth.
This is the place where the birth-body (janma-kāya) was born; the present sutra states that it is the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).

This is the place where the dharma-body (dharma-kāya) was born. If one should erect a stupa even at the birthplace of the birth-body, how much more so should one erect a stupa at the birthplace of the dharma-body?
The place where the Way was attained belongs to the Buddha of the Tripiṭaka; now, by relying on this sutra, one can attain the [Buddha] beyond form.
To attain supreme enlightenment, wherever this sutra resides, a stupa must naturally be erected there.
Turning the wheel of Dharma refers to the wheel of birth and extinction; entering nirvana refers to the nirvana of partial truth.
This present sutra, however, is the wheel of unconditioned action and the perfectly complete, uniquely wondrous nirvana; therefore, a stupa must be erected. For this reason...
As stated previously: "The person who upholds [the teaching], the sutra that is upheld, and the place where the sutra resides—all of these should have stupas erected for them.

△ Second, the verse summary has two parts: first, the summary of the manifestation of supernatural powers; second, the summary of the essential points. The first part has two sections: first, the general summary.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The Buddhas, the saviors of the world, Abiding in great supernormal powers, For the sake of gladdening sentient beings, Manifest immeasurable spiritual transformations."

Regarding the phrase "the Buddhas who save the world" and so forth: this refers to myself, Śākyamuni, as well as the Buddhas of my emanations, all of whom possess great compassion and are thus able to rescue and deliver all beings from the sufferings of the world.

Because they have thoroughly exhausted the principle of the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, they spontaneously manifest through spiritual power, penetrate and transform things, and abide securely in supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*).
Originally abiding in the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), [the Buddha] now desires to cause sentient beings to attain great joy;
therefore, he manifests ten kinds of immeasurable spiritual power (*ṛddhi-bala*).

That is to say, arising function from essence, manifesting in accordance with the nature (*dharmatā*), and establishing them spontaneously without relying on artificial effort. △ Second, the individual verses.
The mark of his tongue reaches the Brahma-heaven; from his body he emits countless rays of light. For those who seek the Buddha-way, he manifests this rare and wondrous event.
The sound of the Buddhas’ clearing their throats and the sound of their snapping fingers are heard throughout the lands of the ten directions, and the earth shakes in six ways.
Because they are able to uphold this sutra after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, all Buddhas rejoice and manifest immeasurable supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*).
When it says "The Tathāgata manifests supernatural powers," this merely summarizes the first five types; thus, by implication, the meaning encompasses the latter five as well.

The phrase "Because the Buddha... and below serves as the conclusion. Since it states that he "manifests immeasurable supernormal powers," it naturally includes the final five types. Furthermore, regarding the first five types...
The first five [verses] represent those who have already attained benefit; the latter five represent those who will attain benefit in the future.
This is because the present subsumes the future. △ Second, the summary verse in three parts: first, the general summary.
Because of entrusting this sutra, even after praising those who receive and uphold it for immeasurable kalpas, one could still not exhaust the merit of such a person;
it is boundless and inexhaustible, like the empty space of the ten directions, such that its limits cannot be found.
The preceding long passage was spoken for the purpose of entrustment; even after speaking thus, the merits of this sutra could not yet be fully exhausted.
Now, in these verses, it is said that even praising those who receive and uphold it cannot yet be fully exhausted.

This is because since the merits of the sutra being upheld are inexhaustible, the merits of those who can uphold it are likewise so. This is the connection between the preceding and following sections.
This serves to clarify them mutually. △ Second, the four specific verses. First, the verse on the dharmas possessed [by the Buddha]:
"Whoever can uphold this sutra has already seen me, as well as the Buddha Prabhūtaratna and all his emanated bodies."
Furthermore, you see me today teaching and transforming the various bodhisattvas.

When it is said that those who uphold this sutra shall see us, Śākyamuni is the one who expounds the essential meaning of this sutra; Prabhūtaratna is the one who provides testimony to the essential meaning of this sutra;
and the emanated bodies are those who assist in bringing forth the essential meaning of this sutra. As for the various bodhisattvas...
Those who hear this and propagate the essential meaning of this sutra—from this day forward—will be able to receive and uphold this scripture.
They shall see Śākyamuni Tathāgata as before, preaching this sutra on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa;
they shall see the Stūpa of Prabhūtaratna Buddha as before, emerging from the midst of the air and praising them, saying, "Excellent! And they shall see the ten directions as before.
The Buddhas of the ten directions come together in this Sahā world to assist in the promulgation of this sutra.
As before, one sees the various bodhisattvas hearing this sutra together, each making vows to circulate it.
The reason one is able to see these Buddhas and bodhisattvas is that they uphold all the teachings possessed by the Tathāgata. △ Second, the verse on mastery:
By the power of this,
those who can uphold this sutra shall cause me, my emanations, and the Buddha Prabhūtaratna who has entered parinirvāṇa, all to rejoice.
They shall also see and make offerings to the Buddhas currently present in the ten directions, as well as those of the past and future, and likewise cause them all to attain joy.
Regarding those who can uphold this sutra and bring joy to all Buddhas: Śākyamuni is the one who issues the call; Prabhūtaratna manifests by dividing his body to provide assistance;
and [the third Buddha] provides testimony. Thus, the hearts of these three Buddhas equally desire the circulation of this sutra.
Now, if one can receive, uphold, and circulate it, one accords with the hearts of these three Buddhas. How could one not [attain this]?
This brings about joy; for the Way of each Buddha is the same. Thus, when the three Buddhas rejoice, all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time likewise rejoice.
When we see this, our doubts should be severed and faith will naturally arise.
This is because it is due to the power of sovereign spiritual efficacy. △ Third, the verse on the treasury of secret essentials.
The secret and essential Dharma attained by all Buddhas when seated at the site of enlightenment—those who can uphold this sutra shall likewise attain it before long.
Regarding these secret and essential Dharmas that one shall attain by upholding the sutra: they constitute the treasury of the Buddhas' secrets, which resides within this very sutra.
To proclaim, reveal, and expound them now, and to be able to receive and uphold this sutra, is already to have attained faith and understanding. By virtue of this understanding...
Arising from practice, one is able to personally enter and realize [the truth] through that practice;
thus, before long, one becomes non-dual with the Buddha and also attains this secret treasury of essentials. △ Fourth, verses on the profoundly deep matters.

Those who are able to uphold this sutra will possess inexhaustible eloquence in explaining the meanings, names, and phrases of all dharmas, just as the wind moves through space without any obstruction.
After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, they shall understand the sūtras spoken by the Buddha.
The causes, conditions, and sequence are explained according to their true meaning, just as the light of the sun and moon can dispel all darkness.
So too, this person walking through the world can extinguish the darkness of sentient beings, instructing immeasurable bodhisattvas so that they ultimately abide in the One Vehicle.
The meaning of all phenomena (*dharmārtha*) is that which is expressed; names and words are that which expresses.
This constitutes three of the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*). Eloquence (*pratibhāna*) is the fourth, the unimpeded analytical knowledge of eloquence.
When one speaks of the former three through eloquence, there is no exhaustion. To illustrate this by means of a metaphor: it is like the wind in the sky.

One who knows the sequence of causes and conditions as taught by the Buddha knows the Buddha’s causes and conditions; this is precisely knowing the single great cause and condition (*ekamahākaruṇā-hetu-pratyaya*).
One who knows the Buddha’s sequence knows that first there was the teaching through Dharma (*dharmadeśanā*), followed by the teaching through parables (*avadānadeśanā*).

The subsequent section is explained through causes and conditions. Following these three cycles—which open up the provisional to reveal the real—one must further open up the near to reveal the distant by teaching the Root Chapter;
this is precisely what constitutes knowing the sequence. As for the phrase "like the light of the sun and moon":
just as the sun and moon illuminate the world and there is no darkness they cannot dispel, so too the Bodhisattva is able to understand the sutra.
The sequence of the middle causal conditions is explained according to their meaning;
thus, it is already known that the Buddha’s two wisdoms—the provisional and the real—propagate this sutra and are naturally able to shatter the darkness of ignorance of all sentient beings.
Therefore, the concluding summary states: "This person... (and so forth). These two lines of the teaching precisely clarify the matter of profound depth. This is indeed...
The doctrine of the cause and fruit of the One Vehicle is entirely the true mark (dharmatā). △ Third, the concluding verse:
"Therefore, those with wisdom, having heard these merits and benefits, should receive and uphold this sutra after my parinirvāṇa."
Such a person will have no doubt whatsoever regarding the Buddha-way.
These two phrases mean that, by relying on the names that express [the truth], the essence of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is clarified;
and by means of the essence that is expressed, the thesis of cause and effect is revealed. From this thesis, the function arises. Once it has arisen...
By its application, one is able to establish the thesis and realize the essence; therefore, it is said that there is no doubt regarding the Buddha-way.
This concludes the commentary on the "Chapter on the Supernatural Powers of the Tathāgata."
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Chapter Twenty-two: Entrusting the Teaching.

If one wishes to discuss the sequential development of this chapter, it arises generally from the Tathāgata’s desire to circulate this scripture of the "Root Gate," thereby clarifying the causal merits of the four levels of faith and the five stages of practice, and further citing the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging.
With this as my witness, I shall provide the exhortation, praise, and circulation for what is called [this teaching]. It is only right that it be entrusted;
first, the supernatural powers must be manifested, and next, the essential points must be summarized, after which it may be done.

Once the ten kinds of supernatural powers have been manifested and the fivefold essential points have been summarized, it will naturally be appropriate to perform the entrustment with the Golden Mouth.

Because it would trouble the Bodhisattvas, this text was circulated wherever they were; therefore, following the "Chapter on Supernatural Powers," there is a chapter containing the passage on the entrustment (*parindanā*).
As for the term "entrustment" (*zhùlèi*): *zhù* means to entrust or commission, and *lèi* means to trouble or burden.
This refers to the Tathāgata’s golden mouth entrusting this sutra and burdening the great Bodhisattvas to propagate and expound it everywhere. And...

It circulates everywhere. This is because the Tathāgata himself realized the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, his long-lasting life-span, and what is called the rare *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Now, he desires that all sentient beings likewise realize what he has realized; therefore, regarding his traces—
The text establishes two gates, each presented in both brief and extensive versions, to reveal and clarify them for all sentient beings.
This is done so that they may sever doubts regarding the provisional and near, and give rise to faith in the real and far-reaching.

Thus, for some who have opened the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*), he bestows upon them the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of the eight phases [of a Buddha's life]. For others who increase their path and diminish their births, he bestows upon them the Dharma-prediction.
The prophecy concerning the body [of the Buddha] and the original intent for the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world are fully expressed herein.
Nevertheless, during his present lifetime, the Tathāgata himself acts as the guide; yet after his parinirvāṇa, it will be necessary for Bodhisattvas to propagate and transmit [the teachings].
For this reason, the Tathāgata again manifests great supernatural power, simultaneously stroking immeasurable Bodhisattvas with a single hand.

...upon the crown of his head. He then spoke words of consolation, saying: "For immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, I have cultivated this Dharma of Bodhi, which is so difficult to attain. I now entrust it to you all.
You should single-mindedly propagate and widely proclaim this Dharma, so that all sentient beings may universally hear and know it. The Tathāgata is the Great..."
"O donors, you too should follow and learn the Dharma of the Tathāgata; do not give rise to stinginess.

By such earnest entrustment, the great Bodhisattvas will be able to circulate it everywhere so that it may endure forever without interruption, thereby fulfilling the Tathāgata’s task of disseminating the teachings. Therefore, it is necessary to entrust this matter to them. △

The text of this chapter is divided into four sections: first, the Tathāgata’s entrustment; second, the bodhisattvas’ acceptance of the command; third, the conclusion of the task and the proclamation of dispersal;
and fourth, the joy of the assembly. The first section further consists of four parts, the first of which is the introductory narrative.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha rose from his Dharma seat, manifested great supernormal power,
and with his right hand stroked the crowns of the heads of immeasurable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, saying these words:
"To rise from the Dharma-seat" means to rise from the Dharma-seat consisting of half the throne shared by Prabhūtaratna within the jeweled stupa.
It should be understood that prior to the "Jeweled Stupa Chapter," this sutra was preached at Vulture Peak Mountain.
From the "Chapter on the Jeweled Stūpa" up to the "Chapter on Supernatural Powers," [the teaching] was spoken within the jeweled stūpa, and it was likewise spoken in mid-air.
Now, emerging from the stūpa, it is once again spoken upon Mount Ling. Regarding the touching of the Bodhisattva’s crown:
there are two meanings. First, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*—whether already taught, currently being taught, or yet to be taught—is the most supreme and honored.
Regarding this teaching: now, wishing to entrust this foremost Dharma, he touched the crown of his most honored head to manifest its significance.

Second, because this sutra is the most difficult to propagate—when the Tathāgata was still present in the world, there were already many who harbored resentment and jealousy, let alone after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa—he now desires that the great Bodhisattvas, in the future final age...
Because he was to propagate this sutra in the world, [the Buddha] comforted him by stroking his head, saying:

"If you can truly uphold the three kinds of rules and abide in the four practices for peaceful dwelling, you will naturally be able to propagate this sutra in the evil age to come without any difficulty.
II. The Entrustment has three sections. The text is divided into two parts. First, the instruction to propagate it alone.
The mind shall flow forth.
For immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, I have practiced this Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, which is so difficult to attain;
I now entrust it to you all. You should cause it to flow forth with a single-minded resolve.
I disseminate this Dharma so that it may be widely increased and expanded.
My cultivation of this Dharma throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas was solely for the sake of attaining this unsurpassed Bodhi.
Although one must achieve perfect understanding, perfect cultivation, and perfect realization, one must nevertheless proceed from cause to fruit, breaking through the forty-two [stages].
Regarding the ignorance within these categories, one must sever forty-two transformations and manifest the three virtues of forty-two divisions;
therefore, it must be attained through cultivation over such a vast number of kalpas.
That I now entrust this to you all means that such a Dharma, difficult to practice and difficult to attain, has now been cultivated, mastered, and realized by me.

I have attained it. I desire that all sentient beings shall likewise cultivate what I have cultivated, practice what I have practiced, and realize what I have realized. While I am in the world, I shall personally guide and transform them;
after my parinirvāṇa, I entrust this entirely to you, O Bodhisattvas, to propagate and disseminate it. Therefore, I now commit it to you as a final charge.

"You all! As for 'propagating with a single mind': if you were to direct yourselves toward the three realms of existence (*tribhava*) or toward the three vehicles (*triyāna*), you could not be said to be propagating with a single mind.

Now, you should not direct yourselves toward the three realms or the three vehicles, but solely toward unsurpassed bodhi while circulating this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. This is called propagating it with a single mind."

This is the Dharma. Regarding "extensively causing it to increase": if one is able to single-mindedly disseminate this Dharma, then in terms of one's own practice, one can further increase the Path and diminish birth;
if in terms of transforming others, then one person transmits it to two, and two persons transmit it to three.

Even if it is transmitted to hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, and billions of people, such that the lineage continues without interruption, its benefit will become vast and ever-increasing.
△ Second, the exhortation to ensure it is heard and known by all.
Thus it was said three times. The Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas bowed their heads in homage and spoke these words:
"For immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of asaṃkhyeya kalpas, we have cultivated this Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, which is so difficult to obtain.
We now entrust it to you. You should receive, uphold, read, and recite it, and widely proclaim this Dharma, so that..."

"All sentient beings shall universally hear and know" refers to merely upholding [the teaching] and so forth, as well as causing all to universally hear and know it. However, the meaning of these two passages mutually clarifies one another.
The former passage speaks only of the single-minded dissemination of this Dharma and its extensive increase, without mentioning its upholding or recitation.
Recite it. Proclaim this Dharma extensively so that all sentient beings may universally hear and know it.

Since this text merely mentions "upholding" (*dhāraṇā*) and so forth, as well as "causing all to hear and know," one should understand that what constitutes "upholding" and so forth is simply the single-minded dissemination [of the teaching].
Furthermore, because it causes [the Dharma] to increase extensively, it enables all sentient beings to universally attain it.
This is known through hearing. The meaning has never been deficient; it is merely that the phrasing is concise. △ Third, the threefold explanation. Why is this so?
Because the Tathāgata possesses great compassion, is free from all stinginess and parsimony, and is without fear;
he is able to bestow upon sentient beings the Buddha’s wisdom, the Tathāgata’s wisdom, and self-existent wisdom.

The meaning is: "For what reason? I, the Tathāgata, have thus placed my hand upon the crown of your head to cause you to disseminate [this teaching] with a single mind, and to proclaim it widely so that it may be heard everywhere.
He then further explains: "The Tathāgata possesses great compassion," and so forth, up to "spontaneous wisdom" (*svayambhū-jñāna*).
When it says he possesses "compassion," it refers specifically to the great compassion that is without conditions (*apratyaya-mahākaruṇā*). By means of this great compassion...
Therefore, because he can bestow all happiness upon others through his great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), he can extract all suffering from them.
In bestowing happiness, there is no happiness he does not give; in extracting suffering, there is no suffering he does not remove.

This is what is called "Great Compassion," and this is the dwelling place of the Tathāgata. Regarding "being free from all stinginess": when preaching the Dharma, even if there should be those who do not believe...

If one encounters those who subject them to verbal abuse, slander, or even weapons, tiles, and stones, yet does not preach the Dharma for them, this is called having stinginess and parsimony. The Tathāgata, however, is able to abide in the ground of patience;
regardless of the insults and other afflictions inflicted by others before him, he remains in the manifestation of quiescent extinction (*śamatha*), perceiving no agent [of harm].
When one endures what is to be endured, one further expounds the sublime Dharma for them without ever ceasing;

this is called being free from all stinginess and parsimony, and it is precisely the robe of the Tathāgata. Furthermore, as for "having no fear": if the mind has any attachment, there will be fear and dread.
The Tathāgata, however, is able to settle the mind in the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) and contemplate the emptiness of all phenomena, remaining unattached.
Emptiness and existence; not clinging even to the Middle Way, one is naturally free from all fears. This is precisely the seat of the Tathāgata.
As for being able to bestow upon sentient beings the wisdom of a Buddha:

it is because the Tathāgata is able to enter the chamber of compassion, don the robe of patience, and sit upon the seat of the emptiness of dharmas; therefore, he is able to [unify] the nine realms and the three vehicles into one.
For all sentient beings, there is the wisdom of the Buddha of All-Knowledge, the Knowledge of the Paths, the Wisdom of the Tathāgata, and the Spontaneous Wisdom of All-Aspect Knowledge.
It is said that our Buddha possesses these qualities for the benefit of sentient beings; therefore, he is called the Benevolent One (Śākyamuni).
The Tathāgata is the great donor to all sentient beings. You, too, should follow and study the Dharma of the Tathāgata;
do not give rise to stinginess or parsimony.
This must be understood in connection with the preceding text, which states that the Tathāgata is able to bestow the three subtle wisdoms; therefore, he is one [who is a great donor].

He is the great donor to all sentient beings. Why is this? For if one were to bestow the seven precious jewels and wondrous objects upon all sentient beings, this would merely be a gift of material wealth; it could not be called being a "great donor.

However, if one can cause all sentient beings to attain the stage of Srotāpanna up to Arhatship, thereby destroying their views and afflictions and emerging from the [limited] stages—[then one is a great donor].
This leads to the realization of nirvana; although this is also called the gift of Dharma, it is merely the fruit of the Lesser Vehicle and cannot yet be termed a "Great Donor.
Now, the Tathāgata is able to bestow upon all sentient beings the three perfect and wondrous types of knowledge.
Thus, it surpasses the worldly gift of material wealth and surpasses the supramundane gift of the Dharma; for this reason, he is called a Great Donor.
Having bestowed upon all sentient beings the three types of knowledge, all sentient beings are then able, by means of the Knowledge of All Modes (*sarvajñatā*), to contemplate emptiness;
by means of the Knowledge of the Path (*mārgajñatā*), to contemplate existence; and by means of the Knowledge of All...
The threefold wisdom contemplates the Middle Way. When contemplating emptiness, then one is empty and all are empty;
when contemplating existence, then one exists and all exist; when contemplating the Middle, then one is the Middle and all are the Middle.

Thus, as the three wisdoms are perfected, the three contemplations can be cultivated perfectly, whereby the three truths naturally manifest in their perfection and the three delusions are completely eradicated.
[This] refutes [the objection]. How could one not be called a Great Donor?

"You all should also be equal" means that while this has already been accomplished by the Tathāgata, if it were to apply to you Bodhisattvas—since you are the sons of the Tathāgata who shall succeed to the position of the Tathāgata—you ought, as a matter of course, to follow and learn the Dharma of the Tathāgata. Thus it is said.
What is it that one follows and learns? It is precisely the absence of stinginess that constitutes such following and learning.
Regarding "do not give rise to stinginess": according to the preceding text, it should have said, "Do not lack compassion; do not give rise to stinginess; do not give rise to fear.

That only "do not give rise to stinginess" is stated here is because its meaning encompasses [the others]. This is because the three modes of conduct, along with the sequence of rooms and seats, collectively constitute [this practice].
This is the robe of patience within. Now, do not give rise to stinginess; this itself is the robe of patience.
Therefore, you should internally contemplate the emptiness of all phenomena while externally exercising great compassion.

Regardless of the insults and afflictions directed at you by others before you, remain steadfast in the ground of patience, seeing neither one who endures nor that which is endured. This is simply to proclaim it for their sake.
To preach the sublime Dharma without the slightest weariness or retreat is what is meant by "not giving rise to stinginess. Thus, although only one [quality] is mentioned, it encompasses two.
Being able to act in this way, one is likewise able to bestow upon all sentient beings the three types of wisdom;
such a person is a great donor to all sentient beings and is truly capable of following and learning the Dharma of the Tathāgata.
...is so. △ Fourth, the exhortation and admonition, in two parts. First, the exhortation addressed to those with faith:

"In a future age, if there be good sons or good daughters who believe in the Tathāgata’s wisdom, you should expound this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for them, so that they may hear and know it, in order to enable those people to attain the Buddha-wisdom."

When this sutra is being preached, those who are able to have faith in the wisdom of the Tathāgata will find their obstacles naturally lightened, their faculties naturally sharpened, and their wisdom naturally deepened.
Since they are thus those whose obstacles are light, whose faculties are sharp, and whose wisdom is deep, [they shall attain it].

If they do not hear this, that is one thing; but if they hear it even once, they will be able to understand it according to what they have heard, act upon that understanding, and realize it through such practice.
Therefore, you should expound it for them. △ Second, the exhortation based on the lack of faith.
If there are sentient beings who do not believe or accept [this], you should instruct, benefit, and gladden them by means of other profound teachings of the Tathāgata.
If you can act in this way, you will have repaid the kindness of all the Buddhas.
Regarding the phrase "sentient beings who lack faith" and so forth: it means that for those who are capable of faith, one preaches this sutra to them.
If there are those who are unable to believe and accept the wisdom of the Tathāgata, then their obstructions are heavy, their faculties are dull, and their wisdom is shallow.
Since their obstructions are heavy, their faculties are dull, and their wisdom is shallow, they [are far from] the perfection of unsurpassed bodhi.
Regarding the Dharma of total fusion (*yōng*), he naturally did not accord with it.
Although this person did not accord with the Dharma of total fusion, if he were a bodhisattva, how could he be abandoned and left untransformed?

Therefore, one must further provide him with instruction and guidance within other profound and sequential dharmas, causing him to practice in reliance upon these sequential dharmas, and subsequently lead him [to the ultimate].
If one distinguishes [the provisional] and returns it to the perfect interfusion, one will likewise be able to obtain the benefit of the Buddha’s wisdom and give rise to great joy.
Regarding the phrase "other profound dharmas": the *Zang* (Āgama) and *Tong* (Vaipulya) teachings are "other" but not "profound"; the Buddha’s wisdom is "profound" but not "other.
As for the sequential and distinct teachings, they are "other" in relation to what follows, yet "profound" in relation to what precedes; therefore, they are called "other and profound. Thus...
Regarding those who have already repaid the Buddha’s kindness: this refers to you bodhisattvas.
Because you have attained partial realization through the Tathāgata, your sense of gratitude toward the Buddha’s kindness is indeed profound.
If you wish to repay the Buddha’s deep kindness, there is no other way to do so than to be able to believe in the wisdom of the Tathāgata and to preach this sublime sūtra for such people.

One should cause them to attain the wisdom of the Buddha. Toward those who are unable to believe and accept it, one should teach and instruct them with other profound dharmas, leading them from the provisional and distinct toward the perfect and harmonious, so that they may obtain great benefit and joy.

To be able to act in this way is to have repaid the deep kindness of the Buddha. This is because only by transmitting the Dharma and delivering sentient beings can one be called a true repayment of that kindness.
It is due to the grace of the Buddha. △ Second, the Bodhisattvas receive their mandate, in two parts. First, the description of their appearance:
At that time, when the various Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas had heard the Buddha speak these words, they were all filled with great joy that pervaded their entire bodies.
Increasing their reverence, they bowed their bodies and lowered their heads, joined their palms toward the Buddha, and together raised their voices, saying:
△ Second, receiving the command:
"As the World-Honored One has commanded, we shall fully carry it out. So be it, World-Honored One; may you have no further concern.
Thus did the assembly of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, three times in succession, speak with one voice: "As the World-Honored One has commanded, we shall fully carry it out. So be it."
Nevertheless, World-Honored One, please do not have such concerns.
As for the four phrases beginning with "As the World-Honored One has commanded," they are divided into four meanings: the first phrase is receiving the command to receive the True Dharma;

the second phrase is receiving the command to explain and interpret it; the third phrase is receiving the command to offer exhortations; and the fourth phrase is receiving the command to offer admonitions. Thus it is said: "As the World-Honored One..."
Regarding the Honored One’s command: it refers to when the World-Honored One above placed his hand upon my head and spoke these words:
"For immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, I have cultivated this Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, which is so difficult to attain.
I now entrust it to you all. You should single-mindedly propagate it and cause it to spread widely."
"Increase [this teaching]! You all should widely proclaim this Dharma so that all sentient beings may universally hear and know it.
This is the command of the Tathāgata. Thus, following the Buddha’s command, we shall single-mindedly disseminate it so that all may universally hear and know it;
therefore, it is said: 'In accordance with the World-Honored One’s command.'"
One should fully practice this. That is to say, as the World-Honored One has further stated: "The Tathāgata possesses great compassion;
he is free from all stinginess and possessiveness, and is without any fear. He is able to bestow upon sentient beings the Buddha’s wisdom and self-arisen wisdom."
"He is the great donor for all sentient beings. You should follow and study the Dharma of the Tathāgata;
do not give rise to stinginess or parsimony. This is what the Tathāgata intends for me to say.
We, therefore, shall practice in accordance with what the Buddha has taught; hence it is said, 'one should fully and respectfully practice.'"
"So be it, World-Honored One. This refers to what the World-Honored One has previously stated:
"In a future age, if there are those who have faith in the Tathāgata’s wisdom, you should expound this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for them, so that they may attain the Buddha-wisdom.
This was the Tathāgata’s exhortation to us in this manner, and regarding this we have no further doubt. If there should be anyone who...
Those who believe in it shall naturally explain this sutra for others, enabling them to attain the Buddha’s wisdom;
therefore, he says, "So be it, World-Honored One.
Regarding the wish that there be no further concern, this refers to what the World-Honored One previously stated: "If there are sentient beings who do not believe and accept..."
"In such cases, one should instruct, benefit, and gladden them within other profound dharmas. This is the Tathāgata’s admonition to me.

Thus, when we encounter those who lack faith, we shall first instruct them using the distinct, sequential teachings, and subsequently lead them back to the perfect, integrated [teachings], so that they may attain great benefit and joy. I only pray—"
The Tathāgata does not speak these words out of anxiety regarding sentient beings who lack faith in future ages; rather, he says, "I wish that you have no such concerns.
As for this repetition three times: above, the Tathāgata’s entrustment consisted of three stages; therefore, the Bodhisattva now receives the mandate.

There are also three rounds [of this ritual]. This is precisely the harmonious union of teacher and disciple, like the striking of a wooden block and a mallet, whereby they shall be able to widely propagate this sutra in future ages, continuing forever without end. △ Third, the conclusion of the proceedings and the announcement of dismissal.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha commanded all the emanated Buddhas who had come from the ten directions to each return to their own lands, saying:
"May the various Buddhas each abide as they please; let the stupa of Prabhūtaratna return to its former state."
Regarding "the various Buddhas each returning to their respective abodes": the emanated Buddhas came solely to open the Stūpa of Prabhūtaratna and to exhort the circulation [of the teaching].
Now that they have fulfilled the purpose of their coming by having exhorted [the assembly] and the stūpa has been opened, their intent is complete;
therefore, they may return to their own lands to transform sentient beings. The Stūpa of Prabhūtaratna Buddha may likewise [be closed as before].

Regarding the word "hence" (gu): there are two interpretations. First, it refers to the fact that the Many-Treasures Stūpa was opened because of the request of Mahāpratibhāna and the fourfold assembly to behold it.

Now that Mahāpratibhāna and the fourfold assembly have all seen it, the door of the stūpa may be closed again, just as when it first emerged; therefore, it is said, "it may be returned to [its original state]."
Therefore, secondly, it is said that the jeweled stupa emerged from the earth because he wished to provide testimony for this single sutra.
Although the present Root Section (Mūlaparivarta) has now received such testimony, there remains the Propagation Section (Prasāraparivarta), which has not yet been testified to.
Thus, while the emanated bodies depart, the Many Treasures Stupa remains as it was, awaiting the propagation [of the Dharma].
Only when the division of the emanations is complete may they return and vanish from the earth. While remaining here, they first cause the emanations to return to their respective lands;

the door of the Many Treasures Stūpa remains as it was before. Thus, one may verify that the emanations were manifested to open the stūpa, while secretly they were truly there to hear the "Root Chapter.
Manifestly, the Many Treasures Buddha serves to certify the excellence of the Dharma of the "Trace Chapter."

If the secret intention was still to certify the present teaching (the "Original Gate"), why did he not immediately command the emanated bodies to return to their own lands before the proclamation for the gathering?

If it were only for the sake of certifying the superiority of the Dharma, then at the beginning of the "Devadatta" chapter, he should have restored them to their original state. It is clear that the emanated bodies truly wished to hear the "Original Gate."
Because Prabhūtaratna truly desired to certify the realization of the Original Gate, he waited until this point before commanding his emanations to return to their respective lands;
the door of the Prabhūtaratna Stupa remained as it was. This is because by the time [the Buddha] arrived here, the near traces and distant origins had already been revealed and clarified.
The exhortation and entrustment have already been elucidated. Previously, light was emitted from afar to summon [the Buddhas], and their emanations arrived;
now, if it were not stated that each should return to their respective abodes, by what means would the emanations be able to return to their original lands?

Previously, the emanations gathered from afar and the doors of the stupas opened; now, if the emanations were not commanded to return to their countries, how could the doors of the stupas [be closed]?
Because it can be restored to its original state: previously, when the door of the stupa opened, [Śākyamuni] entered and sat upon his seat;
if it were not now restored to be as it was before, by what means could Śākyamuni have emerged from the stupa? Therefore, it is said herein:
"May each of the Buddhas return to their respective places, and the stupa of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna be restored to its former state. (4)
At that time, the assembly rejoiced.
As these words were being spoken, the immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions who had manifested as emanations and were seated upon lion thrones beneath jeweled trees,
as well as the Buddha Prabhūtaratna, along with the great multitude of bodhisattvas such as Urdhvaṅgama and others— immeasurable asaṃkhyeyas— and the śarīra [of the Buddha].
The fourfold assembly of śrāvakas headed by Pūrṇa, as well as all those in the world— gods, humans, and asuras—
hearing what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly delighted.
He manifested his body in order to open the stupa and to hear the *Honmon* (the Original Gate). Now that the stupa has been opened and the *Honmon* has been heard, he rejoices.
Many Treasures manifested himself to bear witness to this sutra; now both the *Jikimon* (the Trace Gate) and the *Honmon* have been fully witnessed and validated.
Therefore, they rejoice. Those such as Shangxing (Upāriṣṭa) were those transformed during the Original Teaching;

desiring to initiate the Original Gate and circulate this sutra, they have now achieved its initiation and have received the mandate to propagate it—hence their joy. Those such as Śāriputra were those transformed during the Trace Gate;
previously, in the Trace Gate, they heard that the provisional and the real are non-dual, and now they further hear the relationship between the Trace and the Original. Thus, they rejoice.
Because they are of one essence, they likewise rejoice. This concludes the explanation of the "Chapter on Entrustment.
Regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Chapter Twenty-Three, "The Past Deeds of Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja":
if one clarifies the sequential development of this chapter, it generally arises from the World-Honored One’s exhortation and praise for the propagation [of the teaching] mentioned above.
Thereafter, he immediately entrusted it to them for circulation, saying: "The Tathāgata possesses great compassion, is free from all stinginess and parsimony, and is without fear.
He is able to bestow upon sentient beings the Buddha’s wisdom, the Tathāgata’s wisdom, and spontaneous wisdom;
thus, he is the great benefactor of all sentient beings. You bodhisattvas should likewise [act as such]."
They follow and learn the Dharma of the Tathāgata; yet, they do not know what it is that constitutes the ultimate Dharma of the Tathāgata which they should follow and learn.

Therefore, within this context, the ascetic practices of Bhaiṣajyarāja, the offering of the bowl by Gadgadasvara, the Universal Gate of Avalokiteśvara, and even the exhortation of Samantabhadra are all elucidated as being precisely this.

It is those who are able to follow and study the Dharma of the Tathāgata. Now, wishing to set forth ascetic practices to clarify what should be followed and studied as a model for its dissemination, there is this passage from the "Chapter on the Original Deeds of Bhaiṣajyarāja.
As for the term "Bhaiṣajyarāja," it refers to his original name, *Prabhāketu*, during his past causal stage, because he heard [the Dharma].
The Tathāgata Sūryagarbha preached the sublime Dharma, whereupon [he] offered medicinal herbs from the Snowy Mountains to the Buddha and the Saṃgha.
Furthermore, he made a vow that in future ages he would heal the two types of illness—those of body and mind—for all sentient beings.
Consequently, all people rejoiced in his virtue and immediately named him Bhaiṣajyarāja (Medicine King); he still retains this original name, and is thus called by it.

Bhaiṣajyarāja, one is called a bodhisattva because they are able to realize the wisdom of the Buddha for their own benefit, and furthermore, because they are able to heal the dual illnesses of body and mind of sentient beings for the benefit of others; therefore, they are named a bodhisattva. As for the "original basis":

This was an event from a former time. That is to say, in the past, at the place of the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsaśrī, he heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and was able to practice according to its teaching, thereby attaining the *Sarvarūpasaṃdarśana-samādhi*.
Thereupon, he set fire to his body and burned his arms as an offering to that Buddha and the Lotus Sūtra.
This was because he valued the Dharma more than his life and preserved the Way while sacrificing his own person.
To practice such asceticism was precisely the conduct performed by Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja in the past; now, wishing to follow and learn the Dharma of the Tathāgata, [he acted thus].

To circulate this sutra, one should undergo ascetic practices such as those [described] therein; this would be sufficient. Therefore, it is titled "The Chapter on the Past Deeds of Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja.
The text is divided into four parts: first, the Bodhisattva’s inquiry; second, the Tathāgata’s response and instruction;
third, the benefits gained by the great assembly; and fourth, the praise of Prabhūtaratna. Regarding the first two parts: first, the formal inquiry.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how does the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja travel through this Sahā world?
World-Honored One, this Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja has performed hundreds, thousands, tens of millions, billions, nayutas of difficult and painful practices."
Regarding the Bodhisattva at the beginning of the assembly named *Śuddharaśmiprabha*: "Śuddha" (宿) refers to a previous life (*pūrvajanman*), not to a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*).

Because that Bodhisattva was able to cultivate the causes for the pure flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) during the causal stage of his past lives and thereby attained mastery, he was given this name.
The initial question, "How does he travel through the Sahā world? asks about the manner [of his arrival].

[The Buddha] traveled. This refers to how the World-Honored One had previously entrusted the matter to the great bodhisattvas, saying, "You all should also follow and study the Dharma of the Tathāgata.
According to my thought, O Puṣpākṣa, it is solely through ascetic practice that those who propagate this sutra ought to train.
I now first venture to ask the World-Honored One regarding this assembly.
Within this [assembly], how does the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja travel through the Sahā world to transform and deliver all sentient beings?
Thus it says, "World-Honored One," and so forth. Following "World-Honored One," the inquiry into his practices is as stated in the text.
△ Second, the request for an answer.

“Excellent, World-Honored One! We pray that you will briefly explain this. May the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others, as well as the bodhisattvas who have come from other lands and this assembly of śrāvakas, all hear it and rejoice.”
"May you briefly explain" means that although I have heard and know that the Medicine King has performed hundreds, thousands, ten thousands,
millions, billions, and nayutas of ascetic practices, I nevertheless do not dare to trouble the World-Honored One to demonstrate each one individually.
"I only pray that the World-Honored One, from among these many hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis, will briefly explain even one or two of them;

thus it is said, 'I pray for a brief explanation. As for 'hearing this, all rejoice,' it is because the eight classes of beings desire to protect and uphold the purport of this sutra, the bodhisattvas desire to circulate the purport of this sutra, and the śrāvakas desire to practice it."
The purport of this sutra is as follows: if one wishes to protect and uphold it, one may do so by means of these ascetic practices;
thus, there will be nothing that is not protected and upheld. If one wishes to circulate it, one may do so by means of these ascetic practices;
thus, it shall not be severed in the future. If one wishes to cultivate and practice it...
One may immediately take these ascetic practices as one’s cultivation; thus, one will skillfully practice the Bodhisattva path.
Therefore, whether they be the eight classes of beings, Bodhisattvas, or Śrāvakas—if they have not heard [this teaching], let it be so; but if they hear it even once, they will all rejoice. Part Two:

The Tathāgata’s Response and Instruction (in two sections). First, the response regarding ascetic practices; second, the demonstration of the superiority of this sutra. The first section has two parts.
First, the causal circumstances are set forth:

At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña: "In the distant past, immeasurable kalpas ago, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there was a Buddha named Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsaśrī Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata..."
The One Liberated in an Instant; the Unsurpassed One; the Tamer of Men; the Teacher of Gods and Humans; the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
That Buddha has eighty billion great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and a great assembly of śrāvakas as numerous as the sands of seventy-two Ganges Rivers.
The Buddha’s lifespan is forty-two thousand kalpas, and the lifespans of the bodhisattvas are equal to his. In that land there are no women, nor are there hells or hungry ghosts.

There are no animals, asuras, or other such calamities. The ground is as level as the palm of a hand, composed of lapis lazuli, adorned with jeweled trees, and covered by jeweled canopies from which hang jeweled flower banners. Throughout the entire realm, there are jeweled vases and incense burners;
pedestals made of the seven treasures stand beneath each tree, with every tree situated at a distance of one arrow-shot from its pedestal. All these jeweled trees possess—
Bodhisattvas and śrāvakas sat beneath them. Upon each of the jeweled terraces, there were ten billion devas who performed celestial music and sang praises of the Buddha as an offering.
First, the time period is indicated by the phrase "At that time. Next, the name of the Buddha is clarified by the words "Buddha Sun-Moon Pure Brightness" (*Sūryacandraprabhā-vimala-śrī*).
While the sun and moon of the mundane world possess the merit of illuminating and presiding over the realm, their clarity and transparency extend throughout both day and night;
this is because that Buddha was able, during the causal stage, to serve the Buddhas of the ten directions and draw near to them.
The ten billion Tathāgatas have all practiced the immeasurable path-dharmas of the Buddhas;

they are fully endowed with all skillful means, knowledge, vision, and the pāramitās. Their possessed ultimate wisdom (jñāna) is like the sun, and their possessed provisional wisdom (upāya-jñāna) is like the moon.
Having attained these two types of wisdom, there is no delusion that is not shattered and purified, and there is no wisdom that is not manifested.
It is luminous. Since delusions have been destroyed and wisdom revealed, his virtues in both self-cultivation and the transformation of others will necessarily be perfected;
therefore, he is named Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsaśrī. The passage "That Buddha" below clarifies those whom he transforms. The passage "The lifespan of that Buddha" below... [text continues].
This clarifies his lifespan. The passage "In that land, below" clarifies the purity and adornment of that buddha-field.

Regarding the phrase "Upon the jeweled terraces, the devas perform music and praise the Buddha in offering," one should know that the bodhisattvas and śrāvakas of that land sit beneath the jeweled trees, while the Buddha is upon the jeweled terraces; therefore, the devas desire to make offerings.
He also attended upon the Buddha atop the jeweled terrace where the Tathāgata was seated. △ Second, the explanation of his ascetic practices has four parts.
First, that Buddha’s preaching of the sutra:
At that time, that Buddha [taught] for the sake of the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana, as well as for the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.
The assembly: Regarding the preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for the sake of the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana, he is the one who is the primary recipient of the teaching;
therefore, it is said "for the sake of. He is named Sarvasattvapriyadarśana because that bodhisattva made a vow desiring to heal all sentient beings.
He gave rise to both physical and mental illnesses; therefore, all sentient beings took delight in seeing him and thus named him accordingly.
Furthermore, he was able to burn his body and arms, practicing asceticism to propagate this sutra and transform all beings.
Because sentient beings received its nourishment and benefit thereby, they all delighted in seeing him, and for this reason, he was so designated.
This is the name. △ Second, cultivation and realization according to the sutra:
This Bodhisattva All-Bhāvas-Visible-to-Delight delighted in practicing asceticism.

Within the Dharma of the Buddha Sun-Moon-Pure-Virtue-Luminosity, he practiced walking meditation with diligence and sought Buddhahood with a single mind. After twelve thousand years had passed, he attained the ability to manifest all...
The Samādhi of the Form Body (*rūpakāya*). Having attained this samādhi, the mind is filled with great joy.

To say that "one who seeks the Buddha with a single mind" is to understand it in its primary sense: such a person does not turn toward the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*), nor toward the two vehicles (*dviyāna*), but seeks only unsurpassed bodhi;
therefore, one says they "seek the Buddha with a single mind. However, to speak according to the actual reality, if one relies on the sūtras...
The true reality (*tathatā*) is taken as the object of contemplation, while the present, infinitesimal single thought-moment is taken as the contemplating mind.
By means of the mind illuminating the object, and the object giving rise to the mind, there is no object outside the mind and no mind outside the object. Mind and object are non-dual;
both subject and object vanish together. This is what is called "seeking the Buddha with the one mind. This clarifies the method of cultivation. One attains...
The Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Bodies (*Sarvarūpasaṃdarśana-samādhi*) clarifies its realization.
This Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Bodies is precisely the Samādhi of Universally Manifesting Physical Bodies.

The reason one attains this samādhi is that the *Lotus Sūtra* elucidates nothing other than the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena—the three thousand natures and forms and the ten suchnesses of the hundred realms. And...
This true reality of all phenomena (dharmas) is such that every phenomenon is truly real and every characteristic is authentically so;

therefore, one should practice based upon it and act according to what has been taught. By doing so, one can attain this Samādhi of the Universally Manifesting Form Body, through which, by the very nature of things, one can manifest forms in accordance with the ten realms of existence—namely, all forms as a single form, and a single form as all forms.
All bodies are one body; one body is all bodies. All manifestations are one manifestation; one manifestation is all manifestations.
The remainder is fully explained in the commentary (*yù jù shūshì*), etc. △ Third, repaying kindness by presenting offerings, in two parts. First, clarifying the present life.
Second, explaining the rebirth. This has two parts. First, forming the thought:
he immediately formed this thought, saying, "That I have attained the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Bodies is entirely due to the power of having heard the Lotus Sūtra.
I shall now make offerings to the Buddha Sun Moon Pure Bright Virtue and to the Lotus Sūtra."
"Regarding 'I have attained manifest enlightenment': this means that today I have attained this samādhi of the physical body. This is certainly not without cause.
When one investigates its origin, it is entirely due to having heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and thereby giving rise to understanding; based on that understanding, one initiates practice;
and through practice, one enters realization. It is for this reason that I am able to be thus. Part Two: Raising Offerings. This has two sections. First: Offerings of Supernatural Power.

Immediately he entered this samādhi. In the midst of the void, there rained down *māndārava* flowers and *mahāmāndārava* flowers, along with finely ground, solid black sandalwood, filling the void and descending like clouds. Furthermore, there rained down the fragrance of *gośīrṣa* sandalwood from the "This Shore" (*sītavana*);
six *zhu* of this incense was worth as much as the entire Sahā world, and it was used to make offerings to the Buddha.
