Regarding "entering this samādhi, etc.": By attaining the Samādhi of the Universal Manifestation of the Physical Body (Vairocanarūpakāya-samādhi), one has already perceived the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
Within this emptiness of the ultimate truth, one gives rise to a subtle, inconceivable, and perfect cause; therefore, flowers rain down.

Furthermore, because this perfect cause secretly penetrates the ocean of fruition, incense also rains down, and these are offered to the Buddha to symbolize it. As for the "six *zhu*": [this refers to the weight of the incense].
Twenty-four *zhū* constitute one *liǎng*. Six *zhū* are equivalent to two and a half *qián*.
△ Second, the offering by burning the body, which is further divided into three parts. First, the actual act of burning the body.

Having made these offerings, he arose from samādhi and thought to himself: "Although I have made offerings to the Buddha through my supernormal powers, it is not as good as making an offering with my own body.

He immediately consumed various incenses—sandalwood, *kunkuma*, *turuṣka*, *bhallātaka*, aloeswood, and resinous incense—and also drank the fragrant oils of the *campaka* flower for a full twelve hundred years.
Anointing his body with fragrant oil, he wrapped himself in celestial jewel robes before the Buddha Sun-Moon Pure Brightness (Sūryacandraprabhā-vimala).

Pouring over him various fragrant oils, through the power of his supernatural vows, his own body spontaneously emitted a radiance that shone throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of eighty billion Ganges Rivers.
Regarding the phrase "through supernormal powers, vows, and so forth": it was not with the fire of the world that he set his body ablaze, but rather with the fire of wisdom.
The reason he set his body on fire was that he wished to repay the Buddha’s kindness by practicing asceticism to propagate the sutras;
thus, he held the Dharma in high esteem while regarding his own body as insignificant, sacrificing his life to preserve the Way.
"Universal Radiance" (Guāngmíng biànzhào) correctly signifies that this ascetic practice is undertaken for the sake of propagating the sutra;
thus, it will naturally cause this sutra to circulate everywhere, forever and without end. △ Second, the simultaneous praise by all Buddhas, in three parts: first, the actual praise.
Therein, all the Buddhas simultaneously praised him, saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family! This is true diligence;
this is called the true Dharma; this is making offerings to the Tathāgatas."

Regarding the two instances where he said "Excellent": the first "Excellent" was in praise of his making offerings through supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), yet his mind remained unsatisfied and he further burned his own body as an offering.

The second "Excellent" was in praise of the fact that he did not merely burn his body, but could further, through the power of his supernormal faculties and vows, cause his body to manifest spontaneously while still remaining within samādhi.
This refers to those who perform true and wholesome offerings. This is the general praise. "Good son," [the Buddha] says, is the specific praise.
"This is true diligence; this is called true Dharma-offering. If one merely burns the body, it may be called diligence and it may be called an offering;
however, it is not called true diligence, nor is it called a true Dharma-offering.

Nurturing [this body], one now does not incinerate it with the fires of the mundane world, but rather uses the power of spiritual penetrations (*abhijñā*) and vows to spontaneously burn it with the fire of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Thus, one may give rise to penetrations through wisdom, manifest wisdom through penetrations, give rise to practice through vows, and fulfill vows through practice.
One then uses the fire of inherent virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*) to kindle the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
The body is naturally refined and unmixed; advancing without retreating—this is called true diligence. As for the offering of the true Dharma:
since one uses the fire of inherent virtue to kindle the body of ultimate reality as an offering, one perceives neither the body that is kindled nor the fire that kindles it;
furthermore, within, one does not perceive a body capable of kindling.
Externally, one does not perceive any Buddha who is being offered to. Why? Because their intrinsic virtue is fundamentally empty, for there is nothing that is not the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Since there is nothing that is not the Dharma-realm, it is the Dharma-realm that illumines the Dharma-realm, and it is the Dharma-realm that makes offerings to the Dharma-realm.
Naturally, this is free from subject and object, transcending all duality; thus, it is named "Self-attained."

This is the true offering of the Dharma. This is why, when the Great Master Zhiyi reached this passage, he was able to personally behold the assembly on Vulture Peak as if it were still present in all its solemnity.

It was because the Master had previously been able to contemplate according to the principle of "following the person," transcending subject and object, severing all dualistic dependencies, so that they naturally merged into one; thus he was able to do so. 2. Comparative Evaluation.
It cannot be equaled by offerings of flowers, incense, necklaces, burnt incense, powdered incense,
ointments, celestial silks, banners, canopies, or even the sandalwood from the shore of the ocean;
nor can it be matched by the giving away of kingdoms, cities, wives, or children.
All flowers, incense, and the like, as well as kingdoms and cities, are nothing but external objects.

Even if one were able to give away one’s wife and children, it would still not exceed the category of the external body. Now, to burn one’s own body is not merely to relinquish the internal body, but is to sacrifice one’s very life;
how could this be rivaled by external wealth or the external body? Indeed, even the mere act of burning the body cannot be equaled [by such things].
How much more so now, when by the power of supernatural faculties and vows, this natural body is not ignited by the fires of the world, but is instead ignited by the fire of wisdom;
it is the body of true reality (dharmatā), which is utterly beyond reach.
It requires no further elaboration. △ Third, the praise:
"Good sons, this is called the foremost gift; it is the most honored and supreme among all gifts, because it is the offering of Dharma to all Tathāgatas.
Having spoken these words, they each remained silent.
Regarding the statement that "the foremost gift is the most honored and supreme," one contemplates this through principle and enters into it. Fire is the fire of inherent virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*);
the body is merely the body of true reality (*dharmatā-kāya*). Therefore, the subsequent explanation states: "Because one makes offerings to all Tathāgatas with the Dharma.
Furthermore, taking what is elucidated by the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and manifesting it as sublime practice (*caryā*) is likewise the foremost, as is the case in the Sutra. Most...
He is the most honored and supreme. Thus he accepts offerings from those below. △ Third, the period when his body burns with fire:
His body burns for twelve hundred years; after this time has passed, his body is finally exhausted.
△ Second, explaining his rebirth in five parts: First, his miraculous birth into a royal family.

After the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana had performed such a Dharma-offering, at the end of his life, he was reborn in the land of the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsaśrī within the household of King Vimalacandra. There, sitting cross-legged, he suddenly—

They are born by transformation (*upapāduka*). As for those born by transformation into the royal family, it is because they wish to draw near to that Buddha, hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and circulate this sutra.
In their previous lives, they attained patience (*kṣānti*) as physical bodies; here, they possess the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), and thus they are born by transformation.
Thus, one should know that this transformation-born [being] is also one aspect of the *rūpakāya-samādhi*.
△ Second, the narration of the original event: acting as his father, he spoke these verses:
"Great King, you should now know: while I was walking there, I immediately attained the samādhi that manifests all bodies.
Exerting great diligence, I relinquished my beloved body."
Having spoken these verses, he addressed his father, saying: "The Buddha Sun-Moon Pure Brightness Virtue is still present in the world today.

Having first made offerings to that Buddha, I attained the *dhāraṇī* for understanding the languages of all sentient beings, and I further heard this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, including its eight hundred thousand million billion *nayutas*, *khangara*, *vimbara*, and *akṣobhya* verses."
"Great King, I shall now return to make offerings to this Buddha.

Obtaining the *dhāraṇī* for understanding all languages is wisdom; previously obtaining the *samādhi* of the Universal Manifestation of the Physical Body was concentration (*samādhi*). Yet, wisdom does not exist apart from concentration; rather—"
It is concentration itself as wisdom; concentration does not exist apart from wisdom, but is concentration precisely as wisdom.
Thus, although there are two names, their essence is one. Because he has attained the samādhi of the Universal Manifestation of the Physical Body, there is no body that he does not manifest.
Because he has attained the dhāraṇī of the Understanding of Languages, there is no...
He possesses the Dharma but does not preach it; that is to say, he manifests forms according to the capacities of beings and proclaims the teachings through various sounds and voices.

As for the phrase "I and others before me," it refers to the fact that in previous lives, having already heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, they practiced in accordance with it and attained the *rūpakāya-samādhi*;

at that time, they also attained the *dhāraṇī* of speech. It has never happened that one attains meditative concentration (*samādhi*) but not wisdom (*prajñā*), or that one manifests a body but does not preach the Dharma.
However, after performing the offering of self-immolation by means of supernatural power twice, the wisdom attained becomes even deeper;
thus, the concentration (*samādhi*) one possesses also becomes increasingly profound. Speaking specifically in terms of wisdom, it is therefore said: "I first [attained... (and so forth).
Furthermore, he knows that the sutras heard in previous lives were all but partial; from this point onward, he hears the complete sutras, which is why it says, "hearing them again" (and so forth).
As for *kiṃkara* and the others, these are names for four types of numbers in the western [tradition] consisting of ten billion (*koṭi*).
A *nayuta* is one hundred thousand billion; a *kiṃkara* is one million billion.
*Vibhara* means ten million billion (*koṭi-niyuta*). *Akṣobhya* means ten trillion (*nayuta-koṭi*).
△ Third, seeing the Buddha’s praise and exhortation, in two parts: first, the praise.
Having finished speaking, he immediately sat upon a platform made of the seven precious gems and ascended into the void to a height of seven *tāla* trees.
He proceeded to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, joined his ten fingers and toes in reverence, and praised the Buddha with a verse.
His countenance is most wondrous and sublime; his radiance illuminates the ten directions. I have previously made offerings to him, and now I come once more to behold him in person.
Regarding the phrase "his countenance is most wondrous and sublime": *rong* (countenance) refers to deportment; *yan* (face) refers to facial features;
*qi* (wondrous) means extraordinary; and *miao* (sublime) means exquisite. The countenances of all sentient beings within the nine realms are not termed "wondrous and sublime," for ordinary persons—
All [such appearances] are of a coarse and harsh countenance. The followers of the Two Vehicles do not cultivate the primary and secondary marks (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana);
theirs are therefore haggard and withered countenances. Although Bodhisattvas can partially realize them, they may still be called "marvelous";

yet because their ignorance is not yet exhausted, they cannot yet be called "extremely marvelous. Only the Tathāgata is ultimately perfected and complete; therefore, he is called "extremely marvelous."
"Exquisite! As for 'the radiance illuminating the ten directions': the ten directions were originally shrouded in delusion and fundamentally enshrouded in darkness.
Now, as the Tathāgata illuminates them with radiance, all delusion is utterly removed and all darkness is entirely dispelled.
As for 'I have just made offerings': 'just' does not mean merely 'just now'; it means neither before nor after, occurring simultaneously."

"To encounter" means "to happen upon. The meaning is that as soon as they had seen the Buddha or heard the Dharma, they immediately attained samādhi and made offerings through their supernormal powers;
furthermore, they even offered their own bodies as fuel for the flames.
These acts occurred neither before nor after one another, but rather two by two, meeting one another. Therefore, it is said, "I happened to have made offerings previously. △ Second, the exhortation.
At that time, after the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana had spoken these verses, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, World-Honored One, you still remain in the world."
"Still remaining in the world" does not mean that I have already made offerings to his physical body;
rather, it means that although twelve hundred years have passed, the World-Honored One still remains in the world and has not entered parinirvāṇa.

This refers to entreating the World-Honored One to continue teaching the Dharma in the world to deliver sentient beings—precisely requesting him to turn the Wheel of Dharma and exhorting him to remain in the world.
...in the interim. △ Fourth, the Tathāgata’s entrustment has three parts. First, the proclamation of his passing:
At that time, the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsa addressed the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana: "Good son..."
"The time for my parinirvāṇa has arrived; the moment of final extinction has come. You may prepare a seat; tonight, I shall enter parinirvāṇa.
△ Second, the entrustment.

Furthermore, he commanded the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana: "Good son, I entrust to you the Buddha-dharma, as well as the various bodhisattvas, the great disciples, and the Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
I also entrust to you the three-thousandfold great thousand-world system made of the seven treasures, its various jeweled trees and jeweled terraces, and all the attendant devas."

I entrust them to you. After my parinirvāṇa, all my relics are likewise entrusted to you; you should cause them to be widely disseminated, establish extensive offerings for them, and construct many thousands of stūpas.
This means causing the Buddha-dharma entrusted to them to circulate widely;
this means making extensive offerings to the śarīra entrusted to them. △ Third, entering parinirvāṇa.
Thus, after the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsa had instructed the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana,
he entered parinirvāṇa during the final watch of the night.
Although the Bodhisattva above has had two births, when discussing that Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma, it was solely this single assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
Therefore, his proclamation of extinction was a proclamation of extinction made within this assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, just as the present Buddha now proclaims his extinction, saying:
"The Tathāgata shall soon enter parinirvāṇa; the Buddha wishes to entrust this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* to those who are worthy."
This is so. As for "entering extinction," it means that after preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he no longer preached the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and thus entered extinction.
This indicates that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* constitutes the conclusion of the five periods [of the Buddha's teaching].

Therefore, it was stated above that the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana, having heard this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* being preached, sought the Way with a single mind and attained universal manifestation.
The Samādhi of the Form Body. Having attained this samādhi, he immediately entered it; from the midst of space, flowers and incense rained down as an offering to the Buddha.
Having made this offering, he arose from the samādhi and thought to himself, "It would be better to offer my own body.
He then consumed various perfumes and even set his body ablaze, continuing for twelve hundred years. All [of these acts]...

This was also the case during the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Therefore, in his subsequent birth, he recounted his past life, stating that the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsa is still currently present;
this indicates that that very Buddha is still preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and thus [the Bodhisattva] was born by transformation into the royal family.
His intention was to hear this sutra again, to circulate this sutra further, and to make offerings once more to that Buddha.

Thus, upon seeing him, he immediately exclaimed, "World-Honored One, World-Honored One," as if the Buddha were still present in the world. One invocation of "World-Honored One" was an exhortation for the Buddha to preach the *Lotus Sutra* for a long time;
the other invocation of "World-Honored One" was an exhortation for the Buddha to remain in the world for a long time. From this, one may know...

That Buddha’s proclamation of his parinirvāṇa occurred while he was still at the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; his entry into extinction coincided with the conclusion of the *Lotus Sūtra*.
For this reason, the aforementioned self-immolation lasted only one thousand two hundred years; because it took place during the preaching of the *Lotus Sūtra*, the duration could not but be brief.
Had it been extended beyond the time of burning the arm, that Buddha would already have entered parinirvāṇa. Once again...
"How could I have heard this again? By whom was that Buddha entrusted with it? Thus, he sought the Buddha with single-minded devotion for twelve thousand years.

Furthermore, he consumed the fragrant oils of various flowers for one thousand two hundred years, and his body remained ablaze for another twelve hundred years—all during the time when that Buddha was preaching the Lotus Sūtra. The lifespans of that Buddha and his bodhisattvas were all forty-two thousand years.
"Ten thousand kalpas" refers to the fact that one must necessarily pass through several kalpas before preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. This also represents one's own practice (*sva-caryā*).
Thus, "ten thousand two hundred" and "one thousand two hundred" both represent hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and giving rise to wondrous conduct from wondrous understanding.
Indeed, when a single faculty encounters a single object, even a fleeting moment of thought arising possesses the ten realms (*daśa-dhātu*). Within these ten realms...

It possesses one hundred realms. Each of these one hundred realms possesses one thousand suchnesses; thus, the six sense organs possess six thousand. When these are confronted with the six sense objects, they become twelve thousand.
If we consider the six sense organs alone, when each is cultivated through the application of both *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight), they likewise constitute twelve thousand.
Therefore, the full twelve thousand years are used as a symbolic representation. As for the "one thousand two hundred years":

Generally, each of the six sense organs contains one hundred realms; thus, across the six organs, there are six hundred. When these are confronted with the six sense objects, they become twelve hundred.

If, moreover, they are considered individually within the six organs—taking for example the wearing of incense and the drinking of oil, where the incense represents *śamatha* (calm abiding) and the oil represents *vipaśyanā* (insight)—then through this *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, the six organs become pure, and thus they likewise amount to twelve hundred. However, as for the body and time...

Since the fire of the inherent virtue (xingde) burns the body of true reality (shixiang), the six sense organs that are burned and the six sense objects that are burned are all inherent virtue and all true reality;
they likewise number one thousand two hundred. Therefore, each is represented by the figure of one thousand two hundred years.
If one were to burn an arm for seventy-two thousand years, this would correspond to the period after that Buddha had preached the sutras and entered parinirvāṇa;
therefore, it can be extended to such a great length. This also symbolizes that the transformation of others is inexhaustible.
Furthermore, within a single faculty there are a thousand suchnesses; since one faculty possesses all five faculties, within a single faculty, they are all complete.
There are six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*), which constitute six thousand. Since each of the six organs possesses six thousand, they total thirty-six thousand.
These are further correlated with the six objects (*ṣad-viṣaya*), thus resulting in seventy-two thousand to represent them.
Alternatively, if one considers the six organs alone, the two arms symbolize the provisional and ultimate wisdoms used in preaching the Dharma, thereby also constituting seventy-two thousand.

If one considers the two arms as representing meditative concentration (samādhi) and wisdom (prajñā), they likewise constitute seventy-two thousand [units]. Thus, when the body is set ablaze, it is not short;

yet when the arms are burned, it is not long. Furthermore, the time of burning the entire body refers to the birth-body (janma-kāya), while the time of burning the arms refers to the dharma-body (dharma-kāya); this is why there is no distinction between extension and brevity. △
The Five Bodhisattvas Receiving Their Mandates, Part Five. First: Erecting a Stupa for Offerings.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana, seeing the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, was filled with grief and distress, longing for the Buddha.
He immediately used *candana* sandalwood from this side of the ocean to construct a pyre and cremated the Buddha’s body. The fire—
After his parinirvāṇa, his relics were collected and placed into eighty-four thousand precious jars, with which eighty-four thousand stūpas were erected.
These were three world-systems in height, adorned with pinnacle poles, draped with various banners and canopies, and hung with many jeweled bells.
△ Second, the offering by burning one’s own arm.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana thought to himself again: "Although I have made this offering,"
His heart was still not yet satisfied. "I shall now further make offerings to the śarīra," he said, addressing the assembly of bodhisattvas, great disciples, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and all others.
"You all should maintain single-minded mindfulness as I now make offerings to the śarīra of the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsa.
Having spoken these words, he immediately stood before the eighty-four thousand stūpas.
Nevertheless, with arms adorned by a hundred merits, he made offerings for seventy-two thousand years.
His previous instance of erecting a stupa was receiving life to offer to the *śarīra*; his burning of an arm here was receiving life to propagate the Buddha-dharma.
Since burning an arm is itself a Dharma-offering, he performed ascetic practices to spread the sutras, thereby...
The assembly obtained benefit for their ears. △ Third, the benefits obtained by the great assembly:

it caused countless seekers of the śrāvaka vehicle and immeasurable asaṃkhyeya persons to resolve upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and enabled them all to dwell in the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Bodies.
△ 4. The Bodhisattvas’ Manifestation of Retribution.
At that time, the bodhisattvas, devas, humans, asuras, and others, seeing that he was without arms, were distressed and filled with grief, saying:
"This Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana is our teacher; he is the one who has taught and transformed us."
Now, having burned his arms, his body was no longer complete. At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana made this vow before the great assembly:
"I have sacrificed both my arms; I shall certainly attain Buddhahood with a golden-hued body.
If this is true and not false, may my two arms be restored as they were before. Having made this vow, they were naturally restored once more. Because of this—
This is brought about by the bodhisattva’s merit and wisdom being pure and profound.
When I severed my two arms, someone manifested them through the two obstacles of principle and phenomena (*li* and *shi*). If this were so, my two arms would be restored;
how could the two obstacles then arise again? You should know that these arms, adorned with the hundred blessings, are the complete manifestation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Wisdom. Therefore, it is said next: "This is brought about by the merit and wisdom of the Bodhisattva. Merit is concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom is insight (*prajñā*).
Because concentration and insight originally arise from the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*), and now, through their dissolution, they return to that nature, it is said that "he gave up both arms.
As for "attaining the golden body of a Buddha," this refers to the previously mentioned "body of universal manifestation" (*sarvarūpakāya*).
Samādhi is already a partial realization; what is now said is that he shall certainly attain the ultimate Buddha-body.
That his two arms are as they were before means that he returns from nature to cultivate practice, and through concentration and wisdom, transforms and teaches all sentient beings.
△ Fifth, the five great chiliocosms manifest auspicious omens.
At that time, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and the heavens rained down precious flowers;
all humans and devas attained what they had never experienced before.
△ Second, the conclusion and correlation of the ancient and the present, in two parts. First, the correlation:
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña: "What do you think? As for the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana..."

Could this have been anyone else? It was none other than the present Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja. The number of times he has sacrificed his body as an act of giving is thus immeasurable, numbering hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas.
△ Second, the exhortation to uphold [the teaching].
"Sukhāvatīkūṭarāja, if there should be one who resolves to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and is able to burn their fingers,
or even a single toe, as an offering to a Buddha stūpa, this is superior to offering kingdoms, cities, wives, children, and the three..."

If one were to offer all the great trichiliocosm lands, their mountains, forests, rivers, and ponds, along with all manner of rare treasures, as an offering, it would not equal the merit of one who offers even a single finger—not the foot of a hand or foot, but the "complete" foot [of the body]. Such a person is capable of burning their own fingers.
One might burn a single joint, or two joints, or three joints; three joints constitute a complete finger.
Thus it is said, "even to the extent of a single toe. If this refers to the feet as in "hand and foot," how could one possibly burn a toe of the foot to offer to the Buddha?
A kingdom and city are external wealth, while a wife and children are the external body; therefore, these are all inferior [to internal offerings].
This is the giving of one's own body. △ Second, showing the superiority of the sutra, in four parts.

First, the comparative evaluation: "If, moreover, there were a person who filled the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system with the seven treasures and offered them as alms to the Buddhas, the great Bodhisattvas, the Pratyekabuddhas, and the Arhats, the merit obtained by that person would not equal that of receiving and upholding this Dharma."
In the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, it is stated that even a single four-line verse brings the greatest merit.
"The seven treasures filling the great trichiliocosm" refers to the fact that the objects offered are both precious and numerous.

"Offering to the Buddha and the Three Vehicles" clarifies that the recipients of the offering are both venerable and supreme. Yet, this does not equal the merit of receiving and upholding [the teaching].
Regarding this sutra, even a single four-line verse: although the items offered above may be precious and numerous, they are merely worldly wealth.
If one can receive and uphold this sutra, one will obtain the unsurpassed Dharma-wealth of supramundane merit;
therefore, it is supreme and cannot be equaled by those offerings. Furthermore, as for the person to whom the offerings were made above—though...
It is honored and supreme. Yet, by means of this sutra, the Buddha attained the fruition of his goal; by relying on this sutra, the Bodhisattvas attain the cause of their path;
and by means of this sutra, those of the Two Vehicles find their ultimate convergence. Therefore, whether it be for realization or for practice, [this sutra is essential].

If all [teachings] ultimately converge through this sutra, then receiving even a single four-line verse from it brings forth merit greater than that of making offerings to Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and those of the Two Vehicles.
△ Second, the actual praise has two parts: first, praising the essence of the sutra; second, praising the function of the sutra.
The first part has five sections; the first concerns the analogy of mountains and seas.
Sukhāvatī-vyūha-rāja, it is like this: among all the streams, rivers, and great waters, the ocean is the foremost.
This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is likewise so; among all the sūtras spoken by the Tathāgatas, it is the most profound and vast.
Furthermore, it is like the earth-mountain, the Black Mountain, the Lesser Iron Ring Mountains, the Greater Iron Ring Mountains, and the Ten Jewel Mountains—among all mountains...
Among [all mountains], Mount Sumeru is the foremost. This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is likewise so; among all sūtras, it is the most supreme. Regarding the first pair of verses:

the first refers to the ocean, and the second refers to the mountain. In both cases, the metaphor comes first, followed by the application to the teaching (*yōjā*). Now, I shall provide a combined explanation of these. It should be understood as follows:

It is said: The preceding section relied on comparative measurement to clarify the excellence of that which can hold [the teaching], while the subsequent section relies on analogies to manifest the excellence of that which is held.
Thus, there are five pairs, all of which are established by means of metaphors.

To say that this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the most profound and vast is like saying that even the great currents of cultivated streams, the Long River, or the Great River are neither profound nor vast [in comparison].
There is only the great ocean, which is both deep and vast. It is like the sūtras spoken by the Buddha forty years ago:
the initial flavor of milk is like a stream; the next, the flavor of curd, is like a brook; fresh butter is like a river; and clarified butter is like a great river.
These four flavors of sutras are all not profound or great; only this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the supreme flavor of clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
It is from here that the causal conditions of the Great Matter are elucidated, and it is by means of this that the long and distant lifespan is revealed.
It is profound because its depths cannot be fathomed, and it is great because its boundaries cannot be investigated. That which is called "vertical" penetrates through the three...
The source of the Truths extends horizontally to the very limits of the Dharma-realm, just as the great ocean is the deepest and most vast among all bodies of water.

Second, it is like comparing mountains: this sutra is said to be the highest of all, for in the forty years prior to this, the Tathāgata had sometimes taught the vehicle of humans, which is like an earthen mountain, or the vehicle of devas...
The Vehicle of Humans and Gods is like the Black Mountains; it can only lead one out of the three miserable realms, but cannot lead one out of the triple world (*tridhātu*).
The Vehicle of the Śrāvakas is said to be like the Lesser Iron Ring Mountains; the Vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas is said to be like the Great Iron Ring Mountains;
and the Vehicle of the Bodhisattvas is said to be like the Ten Treasure Mountains. As for the Vehicles of the Two [Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha], they can only lead one out of...

The three realms cannot transcend the three emptinesses. Although those of the Bodhisattva Vehicle can transcend the three emptinesses, they achieve only a partial and gradual realization, unable yet to attain perfect integration.
Only this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the single Buddha-vehicle, capable of ultimately transporting all beings back to the secret treasury of the three virtues.
Regarding all its teachings, practices, persons, and principles, there is nothing that is not entirely one; all provisional [expedients] are [ultimately] so.
In truth, both the fundamental and the manifested aspects are entirely wondrous.
They are like Mount Sumeru, composed of the four treasures, which rises eighty-four thousand *yojanas* above the water; among all mountains, it stands at the very summit as the foremost.
△ Second, regarding the moon and the sun.
Furthermore, just as among all the stars the Moon Deity is the foremost, so too is this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*;
among the hundreds of thousands of millions of kinds of sūtras and dharmas, it is the most illuminating.
Moreover, just as the Sun Deity is able to dispel all darkness, so too is this sūtra; it is able to shatter the darkness of all that is unwholesome.
The second pair consists of one [verse] concerning the month and one concerning the day; the analogy is as previously explained.
This sutra is the most illuminating among all the teachings of the Tathāgata throughout his entire life—whether already taught, currently being taught, or yet to be taught.
Among these three periods of teaching, the other sutras he has spoken are like the various stars; though they may be said to shine brightly, they illuminate objects only dimly.

[This point] is unclear. Only the inconceivable provisional wisdom (*upāya-prajñā*) taught in this sutra can manifest all principles, realize all virtues, and destroy all delusions, just as the Moon Deity is preeminent in its illumination. Second, it is further like the sun:
when the solar disk is at its zenith at midday, there is no darkness that it does not dispel; it is exactly so with the true reality (*tattva*) taught in this sutra.

Wisdom is able to shatter the various darknesses of ignorance and unwholesomeness. Other sutras may only be able to destroy the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), or only be able to destroy the *rajas-reṇu* (dust-like) afflictions; or they may be able to destroy ignorance without exhausting it completely.
However, the inconceivable true wisdom contained within this sutra destroys all at once and severs all at once.
It cuts them off completely. It not only destroys the delusions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), but can also destroy the delusions as numerous as motes of dust (*rajas*).

Not only does it destroy the delusions as numerous as motes of dust, but it can also exhaustively eradicate ignorance (*avidyā*). For there is no delusion that it cannot destroy, just as the Sun Deity is able to dispel all darkness.
△ Third, [the section] concerning humans and devas.
Furthermore, just as among all minor kings, the Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin) is the most supreme, so too is this sutra;
it is the most honored among all sutras. Again, just as Śakra is the king among the Thirty-three Heavens, so too is this sutra; it is the king among all sutras.
The "Three and One Pair" consists of two parts: the first concerns humans, and the second concerns devas; the metaphorical interpretation is consistent with the previous explanation.
A Wheel-Turning King is able to transform the world through the ten wholesome paths of action and stands as the foremost among the minor kings scattered like grains of millet.
This sutra clarifies that all phenomena are entirely the true mark (*dharmatā*), and it is able to give birth to the unsurpassed goodness of all sentient beings—namely, to cause them to...
The three vehicles are merged into the One Vehicle, causing the nine realms to return to the Buddha-realm.
Since all are thus merged into the One Vehicle and equally return to the Buddha-realm, this is the ultimate consummation of generating goodness.

Therefore, among all sutras, it is the most honored, just as a Wheel-Turning King is the foremost among minor kings. Second, as for the comparison with the heavens below, while various sutras may only clarify partial emptiness, [this one does not].
If it were merely to explain illusory existence, or solely to reveal the "Middle Only," it could not serve as the crown of all sutras;

it would be no more than a scripture concerning the Heaven of the Thirty-three Gods alone. This present sutra, however, clarifies the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, the measure of their long-lasting lifespan, and the principle that if they are empty, all are empty; if they exist, all exist; and if they are the Middle, all are the Middle.
Yet it is able to serve as the crown of all scriptures; it is the king among all sūtras, just as Śakra is the king of the thirty-three heavens.
△ Fourth, [the classification] according to ordinary beings and sages.
Furthermore, just as the Great Brahmā King is the father of all sentient beings, so too is this sutra the father of all noble ones—
both those in training and those beyond training— as well as those who have resolved to attain the bodhisattva mind.
Moreover, just as among all ordinary persons, the *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, *arhat*, and *pratyekabuddha* are considered foremost, so it is with this [sutra].

The sutra is likewise so. Among all the discourses spoken by the Tathāgatas, those spoken by Bodhisattvas, or those spoken by Śrāvakas, it is the most supreme. One who is able to receive and uphold this sutra is likewise so;
among all sentient beings, they too shall be the most supreme.

The four [sections] consist of one pair: the first concerns ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), and the second concerns noble ones (*ārya*). The metaphorical interpretation is consistent with the previous explanation.
The Great Brahmā King is the sovereign of the trichiliocosm; since all sentient beings are born and grow from him, he is the father of sentient beings.

In this sutra, however, it refers to all those of the seven sages and four saints, those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and the bodhisattvas who have resolved their minds through the three teachings. All [of these]...
According to their habitual tendencies, they attain manifestation; just as that Brahmā King is able to give birth to all things and serves as their father.

Second, furthermore, regarding the distinction between the noble and the ordinary: while ordinary persons are unable to destroy afflictions and transcend birth and death, the four fruits of the noble ones and the pratyekabuddhas are all able to destroy afflictions and all able to transcend birth and death.

Therefore, among all ordinary persons, it is the foremost. It is like the various sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata, which cannot ultimately destroy ignorance nor ultimately transcend the transformation-death (*pariṇāmi-maraṇa*);
they are not the foremost, just as ordinary persons cannot destroy afflictions and emerge from birth-and-death. This sūtra, however, can exhaustively eliminate ignorance.
Afflictions are completely exhausted and the death-rebirth of transformation is ended.
Just as those who have attained the four fruits or the Pratyekabuddhas can destroy afflictions and emerge from birth-and-death, they are the foremost among ordinary persons.

Furthermore, it clarifies that because the essence of the sutra one upholds is supreme, the person who upholds it is naturally able to destroy ignorance and emerge from the death-rebirth of transformation; and likewise...
First: Just as among ordinary beings, the four fruits and the pratyekabuddhas are considered foremost; fifth, regarding cause and effect:
among all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, the bodhisattva is foremost, and this sutra is likewise so. Regarding...
Among all the teachings of the various sūtras, it is the most supreme. Just as the Buddha is the King of All Dharmas, so too is this sūtra the king among all sūtras.
The five pairs [of verses]: the first concerns the cause; the second concerns the fruit. The analogy is consistent with the previous explanation.

Although those of the Three Vehicles are alike in being at the stage of the cause, the followers of the Two Vehicles can only benefit themselves and cannot benefit others; therefore, they are not the foremost.
The Bodhisattva is thus able to benefit both themselves and others; therefore, among the two vehicles, they are the foremost.
While various sutras—including this present sutra—all clarify causes, those causes elucidated in other sutras may be the causes for humans and devas, or the causes for the three vehicles.
Just as those two vehicles are not the foremost, so it is with what is clarified in this present sutra.
Its cause is not something distinct that serves as its cause; rather, it takes the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena as its cause.

It is entirely the subtle, inconceivable, and perfect cause of the Mahāyāna, and is therefore the most supreme among all the teachings of the various sūtras, just as that Bodhisattva is the foremost among the two vehicles. Second, as for "like the Buddha," [it is] below...
In terms of the fruit: the Tathāgata is able to attain great mastery among all dharmas; therefore, he is the King of all dharmas.
As for this sutra being the king of all sutras: the fruits elucidated by other sutras do not exceed the fruits of humans and devas or the fruits of the three vehicles;
thus, they lack mastery and are not called "kings. Now, as for the fruit elucidated by this sutra...
The fruit of this illumination has no other distinct nature as its fruit; it takes the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena entirely as its fruit.
This is the inconceivable fruit of the Mahāyāna, which is most sovereign;
therefore, among all sutras, it is the king, just as the Buddha is the king among all dharmas. Through the five pairs of analogies presented above, one may know this.
The excellence of the essence of this upheld sūtra is unsurpassed and beyond compare. △ Second, praising the function of the sūtra, in two parts.
First, praising its function of uprooting suffering:
"O宿王華 (Sudhānapuṣpa), this sūtra can save all sentient beings; this sūtra can cause all sentient beings..."
"Free from all suffering and affliction;
this sutra can save all sentient beings" refers to the three vehicles and the nine realms.

"Free from all suffering and affliction" means that the two kinds of birth-and-death constitute the fruit of suffering and affliction, while the afflictions of the five abodes constitute the cause of suffering and affliction.
The cause—namely, the fruit of the two deaths and the cause of the five abodes—is that which can oppress all sentient beings and afflict all sentient beings.

Only the power and function of this sutra can cause all sentient beings of the three vehicles and nine realms to escape from such suffering and affliction. This is truly because what is elucidated in this sutra is exclusively...
This true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena means that the entirety of the causes of suffering—the afflictions—is itself bodhi;
and the entirety of the effects of suffering—birth and death—is itself nirvāṇa. What suffering is there to be abandoned?
And what suffering is there that is not abandoned? △ Second, the praise of the function of bestowing bliss, in three parts.
First, regarding the Dharma:
this sutra is able to bring great benefit to all sentient beings and fulfill their aspirations.
As for "fulfilling their aspirations," it means that it can bestow the unsurpassed bliss of the Three Vehicles and the nine realms. And [it is] great...
It is the benefit of abundance. △ Second, the analogy:
It is like a cool pond that can satisfy all who are parched; like one who is cold finding fire; like a naked person finding clothing;
like a merchant finding his master; like a child finding its mother; like one crossing water finding a boat; like a sick person finding a physician; like...

It is like obtaining a lamp in the darkness, like a poor person finding treasure, like subjects gaining a king, like merchants reaching the sea, and like a torch dispelling the gloom—these are the twelve metaphors used to illustrate the function of bestowing bliss. First, the "cool pond" is a metaphor for this sutra;
it is the supreme, cooling flavor of *amṛta* (clarified butter), which can provide sentient beings with the flavor of the Dharma to nourish their spirits. Therefore...
It is said that [this sutra] can satisfy all thirst and deprivation. It is like one who encounters fire when cold;
the fire of the inherent virtues contained within this sutra can eliminate the cold of sentient beings' afflictions. It is like a naked person obtaining clothing;
this sutra possesses the great robe of merit, which can shield sentient beings from the nakedness of birth and death. It is like a merchant finding his master... this [sutra].
This sutra enables all sentient beings to open, reveal, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision,
acting as a guide for all beings, like merchants who have found their leader, or like children who have found their mother.
This sutra enables sentient beings of the nine realms to attain subtle and wondrous true wisdom, just as a child relies upon its mother for support.

It is like finding a boat when one wishes to cross over; this sutra is the profound boat of Prajñāpāramitā, capable of enabling sentient beings of the nine realms to cross the river of the two deaths and reach the other shore of Nirvāṇa. It is like finding a physician when one is ill;
this sutra is the unsurpassed medicinal medicine of great compassion, capable of healing the dual illnesses of body and mind of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, it is like one who finds a lamp in the dark; this lamp of wisdom contained within this sutra can destroy the darkness of ignorance in sentient beings.

It is like a poor person finding treasure; this sutra can bestow upon all sentient beings the supreme wealth of the Dharma and merit, just as a poor person acquires treasure. It is like a subject obtaining a king; this sutra... [text continues]
It clarifies the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena and possesses an eternal life-span.
It is that toward which all sentient beings turn for refuge and guidance, like subjects who have found a king, or like merchants who have found the sea.
The profound wisdom of all Buddhas elucidated in this sutra is like a great ocean; all sentient beings, by relying upon this wisdom, are able to attain [liberation].
Regarding the supramundane wealth of the Dharma, it is like a merchant obtaining the ocean; it is like a torch dispelling darkness.
The light of wisdom elucidated in this sutra is able to shatter the darkness of the three delusions.

Among these twelve metaphors, only the first and the last concern the subject (the agent) in relation to the object (the goal); the ten intermediate metaphors all concern the object in relation to the subject. Thus they alternate.
This clarifies that, in the Perfect Vehicle, the essence of birth-and-death, afflictions, bodhi, and nirvāṇa is non-dual.
△ Third, the Convergence: This Lotus Sūtra is likewise; it can cause sentient beings to leave behind all suffering and all ailments.
To be able to untie all the bonds of birth and death means to be able to leave behind all suffering— namely, the three types of suffering and the eight types of suffering within the realms,
as well as the suffering of transformation and ignorance beyond the realms. To be able to leave behind all illness and pain refers to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) of all sentient beings.
When they are not harmonized, illness arises. This sutra clarifies that all phenomena are entirely the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

If one can thoroughly comprehend that everything is entirely the true mark, then one will understand that all earth, water, fire, and wind are such that earth is the nature of earth, fire is the nature of fire, water is the nature of water, and wind is the nature of wind. Thus, although the four great elements exist, [they are but their own nature].
Though these differ, they are all subsumed within the single reality of the nature-virtue (*dharmatā*). What illness or what pain could there be that is not transcended?

That which can untie the bonds of birth and death consists of the five abodes (*pañca-vihāra*), which are the causal bonds of birth and death, and the two deaths (*dvi-maraṇa*), which are the resultant bonds of birth and death.
This sutra can cause the two deaths to perish forever and the five abodes to be completely exhausted; thus, it is that which can [liberate].
This means that the two bonds of birth and death are untied. Since there is no suffering from which one is not separated and no bond that is not untied, one is then able to attain happiness.
The above concludes the formal eulogy. △ Third, the clarification of merit, in two parts. First, clarifying the merit of hearing the entire sutra.
Second, explaining the merit of hearing a single verse. This section has two parts. First, explaining the merit of copying the text:

If a person hears this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, whether they write it themselves or cause others to write it, the amount of merit obtained—even when measured by the Buddha’s wisdom—cannot be fathomed.
Regarding "measuring the amount": this means that one cannot even conceive of its magnitude, much less measure its smallness;
in short, its limits cannot be reached. △ Second, explaining the merit of making offerings.
If one were to write out this sutra scroll, and offer flowers, incense, necklaces, burning incense, powdered incense, and ointment incense; banners, parasols, and robes;
and various kinds of lamps—butter lamps, oil lamps, lamps of various fragrant oils, lamps of *campaka* oil, and lamps of *sumanā* oil.
The merit obtained from making offerings of *pārala* oil lamps, *bharuṣka* oil lamps,
and *nāvamālī* oil lamps is likewise immeasurable.

△ Second, explaining the two aspects of hearing about the virtues of a single person. First, explaining the reception, upholding, and practice; second, explaining sympathetic joy and praising what is good.
The first [section] has three parts; the first is the general heading.
Ratnakusumaguṇasāgaravikrīḍitābhijña, if there are those who hear this "Chapter on the Past Deeds of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja," they shall likewise attain immeasurable and boundless merit.
To say they attain boundless merit means that it is not only those who hear the entire sutra as described above who possess such immeasurable and boundless [merit].
The Merit of Boundlessness: Even by hearing this single chapter on the Medicine King, one shall likewise possess immeasurable merit.
△ Second, the specific demonstration has five parts. First, the merit of not receiving a female body.
If there are women who, upon hearing this "Chapter on the Past Deeds of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja," are able to receive and uphold it,
they shall exhaust their female bodies and never again undergo them hereafter.
As for women, they are indeed those whose obstructive karma is profound and heavy, being different from men.
If even a woman with such profound and heavy obstructive karma possesses such merit upon hearing [this teaching], then how much more so for others!
As for men, if they were to hear this sutra, their merits would be self-evident without needing to be described; therefore, the text mentions only women.

Regarding those who will never again receive a female body after exhausting this present one, as clarified above, if they hear this sutra, they can attain the *sarvarūpasaṃdarśana-samādhi* (the samādhi of universally manifesting physical forms) and thereby know the Buddha-nature. As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "If..."
Those who do not know the Buddha-nature are all called women. If there is a woman who can know that she certainly possesses the Buddha-nature within herself, she is then a man;
how could she ever again receive a female body? △ Second, the virtue of being able to give birth in the Pure Land.
If, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, during the final five hundred years, there should be a woman who hears this sutra and practices according to its teachings,
at the end of her life here she will immediately go to the World of Peace and Bliss, to Amitābha Buddha and the assembly of great bodhisattvas.
They dwell surrounding their abodes, born within lotuses upon jeweled thrones.
"The final five hundred years" refers to the period when strife is firmly established.

"Practicing according to the teaching" means being able to give rise to inconceivable and wondrous conduct based on the principle of the true reality (*tattva*) that is expressed; it is to give rise to practice through that principle.
To practice in accordance with the principle is what is meant by "practicing according to the teaching.

Being able to practice according to the teaching, one can then thoroughly realize the true mark (*dharmatā*) and manifest the Pure Land. Yet, there is no separate Pure Land; the Pure Land is entirely identical to the mind-only (*cittamātra*).
Likewise, there is no separate Amitābha; Amitābha is entirely identical to one's own nature (*svabhāva*). Therefore, regarding one's life...
At the time of death, one goes where one has not previously gone—to the world of peace and bliss. One sees what was not seen before—one beholds the Tathāgata Amitābha.
One is born where there is no birth—arising upon a lotus jewel-throne.
Now, while there are pure lands in the ten directions and Tathāgatas in the ten directions, according to the teachings of the sutras...
Question: Why is it that one speaks only of the Land of Peace and Bliss and mentions only Amitābha Tathāgata? Answer:

It is because the minds of sentient beings in this land are largely distracted. Now, wishing to harmonize their scattering and restrain their disorder, one must cause them to focus single-mindedly on a single point.
Therefore, one speaks only of the Western Pure Land as the object for focusing the mind with single-minded concentration.

Yet it does not mention the pure lands of other directions. As for Amitābha, because he made forty-eight great vows during his causal stage to extensively embrace all sentient beings, the beings of this Sahā world share the deepest affinity with that Buddha;
therefore, it speaks only of Amitābha Tathāgata. △ Third, Attaining the Patience of Non-arising.
Virtuous one,
you will no longer be afflicted by greed and desire, nor will you be afflicted by anger and delusion, nor will you be afflicted by the defilements of pride and envy.
You shall attain the bodhisattva’s supernormal powers and the forbearance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
They are not afflicted by greed and the like; that is, they are not afflicted by the obstacles of the three poisons.
Thus, they naturally attain the bodhisattva’s dharma-patience of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).

Because they are able to practice according to the teaching and thoroughly comprehend the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, they do not perceive even the slightest phenomenon arising, nor do they perceive even the slightest phenomenon ceasing. By means of this—
This principle of neither arising nor ceasing is accepted within the mind; one can naturally spiritualize and clarify it, and penetrate and transform it.
Thus, one immediately attains the bodhisattva’s supernormal powers and the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
△ Fourth, the ability to see the virtues of all Buddhas.
Having attained this patience, their faculty of the eye becomes pure. With this purified faculty of the eye, they see seven million twenty billion nayutas of Ganges-sand-like Buddhas, Tathāgatas.
Regarding the "purity of the eye-faculty": since this occurs after the attainment of *kṣānti* (receptivity), it constitutes partial realization (*pradeśa-prativedha*) of purity.
Because one possesses the eye-faculty that realizes this partial purity, one sees all by seeing one, thereby perfectly beholding all Buddhas.
Indeed, upon entering the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), a person at the level of partial realization is able to manifest bodies throughout the hundred realms to perform transformations.
He guides all sentient beings. Since he himself is already able to manifest as a Buddha within the hundred realms, how could he not perceive all Buddhas?
△ Fifth, the virtue of being praised by all Buddhas.
At that time, all the Buddhas, from afar, praised him together, saying: "Excellent, excellent!

Son of good family, because you are able to receive, uphold, read, recite, contemplate, and explain this sutra within the Dharma of Śākyamuni Buddha, the merit you obtain is immeasurable and boundless.
Fire cannot burn it; water cannot sweep it away. Your merit is shared by a thousand Buddhas."

Even if one were to speak for an aeon, one could not exhaustively describe it. You have now been able to defeat all the mara-enemies, destroy the army of birth and death, and utterly annihilate all other adversaries.
Son of good family, hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, by means of their supernormal powers, protect you together.
Within all the worlds, among gods and humans, there is no one like you, except for the Tathāgata.
Among all the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and even bodhisattvas, none possess wisdom and meditative concentration equal to yours.
The statement that "fire cannot burn [it]" and so forth is not a false claim, nor is it a mere metaphor; rather, it is a factual reality.

Indeed, the reason sentient beings are burned by fire and swept away by water is that they fail to comprehend the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, giving rise to various conceptual discriminations and even committing unwholesome deeds, thereby inviting rebirth.
Upon death, one is then burned by the fire and drifted away by the water of the fruits of suffering— the afflictions, fetters, and karmic deeds—
and thus is likewise drifted by the water and burned by the fire of the world. Now, if one is truly able to uphold this sutra,
truly able to transcribe this sutra, truly able to read and recite this sutra, and truly able to practice this sutra, then one will be able to realize [the truth].
Having realized the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*), one personally does not give rise to various conceptual discriminations or craving;

one does not create various evil karmas, nor does one summon the cycle of birth and death. Thus, one is not burned by the fire of afflictions, fetters, karma, and the fruits of suffering, nor swept away by water.
If even the fires of the three obstacles cannot burn one, how much less could the fires of the mundane world possibly burn? III.
Even water that obstructs [the world] cannot wash it away; how much less, then, could the waters of the mundane world? Therefore, it is said that fire cannot burn it and water cannot wash it away.

As for those protected by hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, because they are able to receive, uphold, recite, and contemplate this sutra, they act in accordance with the hearts of all Buddhas; thus, by means of their supernormal powers...

...of their power. They shall protect [him] together. "With the sole exception of the Tathāgata" means that while those of the Three Vehicles are able to practice, they still abide in the stage of cause;
the Tathāgata, however, has already attained the ultimate and abides in the stage of fruition. Because cause and fruition are not the same, he is excluded.
Among all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas, there is none whose wisdom and meditative concentration are equal [to his].
The wisdom and meditative concentration possessed by those of the two vehicles are merely that of the Lesser Vehicle;
the wisdom and meditative concentration possessed by Bodhisattvas are merely partial and gradual. Now, if one is able to receive, uphold, and practice this sutra, then all such wisdom—
All forms of meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi) belong to the Mahāyāna; they are perfectly integrated (yuanrong). The small and the great cannot be compared to one another;
how could the partial and the perfect coexist? Therefore, there is nothing equal to them.
The second section, the specific demonstration, is hereby concluded. △ Third, the comprehensive inclusion.
Ratnakusuma, this bodhisattva has accomplished such merit and the power of wisdom.
II. Explaining the Rejoicing in and Praising of Excellence:
If there is anyone who, upon hearing this "Chapter on the Past Deeds of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja," is able to rejoice in it and praise its excellence, that person...
In this present life, his mouth constantly emits the fragrance of blue lotuses, and from the pores of his body, the fragrance of ox-head sandalwood constantly issues forth.
The merits he attains are as described above.
Regarding the statement that "the mouth constantly emits the fragrance of a lotus": it is because of the wondrous Dharma of this sutra.

Just as a lotus grows from a place of mud yet remains pure, first as a flower and then as a fruit, so too, by being able to rejoice in and praise what is good, the entire sutra is one's mind, and the entire mind is the sutra.
Therefore, one is able to constantly emit the fragrance of the blue lotus from the mouth. This is the merit.
As for those mentioned above, they too shall likewise attain these five kinds of merit. △ Fourth, the entrustment has three parts.
First, the entrustment to cause circulation:
"Therefore, Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña, I entrust this 'Chapter on the Past Deeds of Bhaiṣajyarāja Bodhisattva' to you. After my parinirvāṇa..."
After my passing, during the final five hundred years, you must widely proclaim and disseminate [this teaching] throughout Jambudvīpa so that it shall not be severed.
Let not evil Māras, the minions of Māra, nor the various devas, nāgas, yakṣas, kumbhāṇḍas, and others, find any opportunity to cause harm.
"Regarding Jambudvīpa, this is said for the time being with respect to those who find it difficult [to understand].

'Do not allow it to be severed' means that if this sutra were not circulated, then the Buddha’s knowledge and vision would have no way to be opened to all sentient beings, and the seed of the Buddha-nature would be cut off. You must circulate this sutra so that..."

May all sentient beings universally attain the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, so that the seeds of their buddha-nature are never severed, and no evil Māras may find an opportunity to exploit them.
This refers to the fact that evil Māras constantly seek to obstruct and harm those who propagate this sutra;
if those who propagate it become even slightly attached to the five worldly desires, they will immediately fall prey to them.
They will seek opportunities to prevent it from circulating. When you propagate this sutra, do not allow them to find such an opportunity.
△ Second, the entrustment to guard and protect [the teaching].
Ratnakusuma, you should, by means of your supernormal powers, protect this sutra. Why is this?

This sutra serves as the excellent medicine for the illnesses of the people of Jambudvīpa. If anyone who is ill hears this sutra, their illness will be immediately extinguished, and they shall neither grow old nor die.
Regarding the phrase "illness is immediately extinguished" and so forth, there are two interpretations: one based on phenomena (*dharma*) and one based on principle (*tattva*).

One should understand that while illness belongs to the sick person, the one who is ill with illness has never been ill; while old age belongs to the aged, the one who is old with old age has never been old;
while death belongs to the dead, the one who is dead with death has never been dead. Therefore, it is said that "illness is immediately extinguished," and there is neither aging nor dying.
As for "matters," all sentient beings have only two kinds of illness: those of body and mind. When the four great elements are out of harmony, there is bodily illness;
if one hears this sutra, then by the power of the sutra, one is able to harmonize what was disharmonious, and thus bodily illness is immediately extinguished.
When various discriminations and craving arise, there is mental illness; if one hears this...
By being able to receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, one does not give rise to the conceptualization of craving;
thus, the illnesses of the mind are extinguished, and it is said that "illnesses are immediately extinguished. As for "not aging": if one hears this sutra, one's complexion becomes bright and pure.
Therefore, it is said that they do not age and do not die. This sutra clarifies the measure of a long and distant lifespan;
if one hears it and is able to practice accordingly, one will personally realize this long and distant lifespan and thereby attain immortality.

Furthermore, as in the case of the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging, who, when his life was about to end, heard this sutra and had his lifespan further extended—this is precisely what is meant by "not dying."
...and so forth. △ Third, the entrustment to provide offerings:
"Sudhana-śrī, if you see anyone who upholds this sutra, you should take blue lotuses filled with powdered incense and scatter them upon that person.
Having scattered them, you should form this thought: 'This person will before long surely gather grass and sit [upon it to attain enlightenment].'"
At the site of enlightenment, having shattered the armies of Māra, one shall blow the Dharma conch and beat the great Dharma drum to deliver all sentient beings from the ocean of old age,
sickness, and death. Therefore, those who seek the Buddha-way, upon seeing anyone who receives and upholds this sutra,
should give rise to a heart of reverence toward them in this manner.

Regarding "taking grass and sitting at the site of enlightenment": if discussed according to the teachings, this refers to the Buddha of the *Tripiṭaka* (Śrāvaka) stage, who sat upon a seat of grass beneath the Bodhi tree to attain perfect enlightenment. Now, since one has received and upheld this sutra...

Thus, one is naturally able to attain perfect realization (*pariniṣpatti*). Yet, although one has personally attained perfect realization, because the capacities of sentient beings include those suited for the Tripitaka, one must manifest as a Buddha of the Tripitaka;
therefore, one likewise takes grass and sits at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
This refers to a Bodhisattva of the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) who, by dividing his body into hundreds of worlds, manifests as a Buddha of the Tripitaka to guide all beings.
Birth. This refers to returning from the Three Piṭakas to the Perfect Harmony (yuanrong). One who is to blow the Dharma conch shell, having already defeated Māra, will naturally achieve the Way.
After achieving the Way, one must preach the Dharma, causing beings to abandon the Small Vehicle and return to the Great, and to abandon the Gradual and return to the Sudden;
therefore, it is said that one "should blow the Dharma conch shell. If there are sentient beings who are indolent or regressive, and do not...
Those capable of advancing to shatter ignorance are startled into awakening and urged forward, so that they may break through ignorance;
thus it is said that he "beats the Dharma drum. △ Third, the benefits gained by the great assembly.
When this "Chapter on the Past Deeds of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja" was being spoken, eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas attained the dhāraṇī for understanding the languages of all sentient beings.
△ Fourth, the praise by Prabhūtaratna.
From within the jeweled stupa, the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna praised the Bodhisattva Rājāgraputra, saying: "Excellent, excellent, Rājāgraputra!
You have accomplished inconceivable merit, being able to question Śākyamuni Buddha in this manner."
This matter benefits all immeasurable sentient beings.
Regarding the double exclamation of "Excellent, excellent": one "excellent" praises his ability to inquire about the ascetic practices of Bhaiṣajyarāja;
the other "excellent" praises his ability to act as the Tathāgata’s entrusted representative. This concludes the explanation of the past life of Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja.
Chapter Concluded.

The twenty-fourth chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, "The Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara.
Regarding the origin of this chapter: it stems entirely from the World-Honored One.
Having previously, because the bodhisattvas had received their mandate to propagate the sutra, manifested ten kinds of supernormal powers and established five essential points as an entrustment.
He entrusted them with the circulation of this sutra. Simultaneously, with one hand, he placed it upon the crowns of the heads of immeasurable bodhisattvas and spoke these words:
"For immeasurable hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeya kalpas, I have cultivated this dharma of enlightenment so difficult to attain.
Now I entrust it to you. You should single-mindedly propagate this dharma, so that..."
May all sentient beings universally hear and know this: the Tathāgata is the great benefactor of all sentient beings.
You, too, should follow and learn the Dharma of the Tathāgata; that is to say, you should train in ascetic practices and train in supernormal powers.

As for ascetic practices, they have already been explained above. Now, wishing to elucidate supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), there is this chapter titled "The Supernormal Power of Gadgadasvara Propagating the Sūtra. Regarding the term "Gadgadasvara" (Wonderful Sound):
in terms of the principle realized, the practice cultivated, and the teaching mastered, all may be called "Wonderful Sound. As for the principle realized...
This is because, by being able to penetrate the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, every phenomenon is simultaneously true and every characteristic is entirely real.
Thus, even the sounds they produce are fully realized as being the entire Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Therefore, according to the principle they perceive, they are named "Wondrous Sound" (*Ghoṣa*). As for their practiced conduct, it is due to their past causes that...
Having offered one hundred thousand kinds of musical instruments and eighty-four thousand precious bowls to the Tathāgata Cloud-Thunder-Sound King, he has now been moved to circulate this sutra;
thus, he is surrounded by a great multitude of followers and attended by those who possess the vessels of the Path.
Consequently, according to the practice he has cultivated, he is also named "Wonderful Sound."

Furthermore, as for the teachings he disseminates: by virtue of his power of supernatural faculties (*ṛddhi*), he manifests bodies within the ten realms throughout this world and other lands to propagate this wondrous sutra.

He causes all sentient beings to hear what he preaches, so that each may understand and realize the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision and his far-reaching lifespan. Therefore, with respect to the teachings he disseminates, and furthermore—

He is thus named "Wonderful Sound. As for a bodhisattva, he is one who, being personally able to give rise to practice in accordance with principle and master the teachings, also causes all sentient beings to give rise to practice in accordance with principle and master the teachings; this constitutes both self-benefit and the benefit of others.
Therefore, he is called a Bodhisattva. △ The text of this chapter is divided into six sections: first, Śākyamuni’s radiance; second, Gadgadasvara’s arrival from afar;
third, the miraculous power that facilitates the sutra; fourth, the mutual benefits obtained; fifth, the return to one's own land; sixth, the increase in the Way through hearing this chapter.
The first two [sections] consist of: first, the emission of light.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha emitted the radiance from the *uṣṇīṣa* of the marks of a Great Man, as well as the light from the white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā-kośa*) between his eyebrows.
Regarding the emission of the radiance from the *uṣṇīṣa* of the marks of a Great Man: it was because, during my causal stage as a Tathāgata, I was able to respectfully follow and serve my teachers.
Because it is long, it now produces upon the fruit [of Buddhahood] the ability to manifest a great radiance within the *uṣṇīṣa*.
This is the mark of a Greatly Awakened Sage; therefore, it is said that he emits the light from the *uṣṇīṣa*, one of the marks of a Great Man.
Now, in emitting this light, he desires that those Bodhisattvas shall obey the commands of me, the Tathāgata, and cause [this teaching] to circulate everywhere.
This is because of this sutra. Furthermore, regarding the emission of light from the white tuft between the eyebrows:
in the preceding Trace Gate, [the Buddha] emitted this light because he wished to initiate this sutra on the Middle Way and the True Mark (dharmatā).

Now, because he wishes for those bodhisattvas to circulate this sutra on the Middle Way and the True Mark, he again emits this light. △ Second, the actual illumination, in two parts. First, the illumination.
Second, illuminating the body. Regarding the first two [aspects], the first is the general illumination of all lands:
it universally illuminates one hundred and eight myriads of koṭis of nayutas of Buddha-worlds, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, in the eastern direction.
Regarding "shining universally upon the eastern direction": the east is the foremost of all moving things; therefore, by mentioning it, the remaining nine directions are included.
This constitutes his universal illumination of the ten directions. △ Second, the specific illumination of one land.

Beyond this number, there is a world named Pure Light Adornment. In that land dwells a Buddha named Pure Flower Constellation King Wisdom Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Being.
The Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One, was surrounded by a respectful assembly of immeasurable and boundless bodhisattvas as he preached the Dharma for them.
The radiance from the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows of Śākyamuni Buddha shone everywhere throughout that land.
The world is named Pure Light Adornment (*Vimalaprabhā-alaṃkāra*). Because of the Buddha of that world, there is no affliction that is not destroyed, and thus he possesses the virtue of abandonment;
there is no wisdom that is not manifested, and thus he possesses the virtue of realization. It is by means of these two virtues that the world is adorned.
Therefore, that world is named Pure Light Adornment (*Vimalaprabhā-vyūha*). The Buddha’s title is Pure Flower Constellation King Wisdom (*Vimalapuṣpa-nakṣatra-rāja-jñāna*).

Because during his causal practices in past lives he was able to cultivate the causes of the seven factors of enlightenment—the pure flowers—when he attained the fruit, he was able to realize the threefold wisdom within a single mind.
Thus, when his self-nature illuminates emptiness, all things are simultaneously empty; yet when it illuminates existence, [all things are simultaneously present].
Thus, all things are simultaneously within [the state of] existence; when illuminating the center, all things are simultaneously within the center.

One thereby attains great mastery. This fruit is obtained through the cultivation of its cause. One should know that the cause is not separate from the fruit, and the fruit is not separate from the cause.

Although cause and fruit differ, they are one and the same wondrous wisdom; therefore, he is named "Pure Flower Constellation King Wisdom" (Viśuddhapuṣpanakṣatrarājajñāna). △ Second, illuminating the body, in three parts. First:
He became renowned.
At that time, in the land of Universal Pure Light Adornment, there was a bodhisattva named Gadgadasvara.
△ Second, praising his virtues.
For a long time he has planted the roots of all virtues, and having made offerings to and drawn near to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas,
he has fully accomplished profound wisdom.
To speak of "planting the roots of all virtues" refers precisely to the cultivation of wisdom (*prajñā*), for wisdom is the root of all virtues and the foundation of the myriad practices (*sādhana*).
To speak of "making offerings to the Buddhas" refers precisely to the cultivation of merit (*puṇya*). Thus, one plants the roots of all virtues;
yet, without wisdom, there is nothing that can be cultivated. Therefore, one is able to accomplish profound wisdom. With a single mind, [one realizes] the three...
"Wisdom" means that it illuminates all emptiness as empty, all existence as existent, and all the middle way as the middle way;

thus one knows that profound wisdom establishes and perfects the planting of the roots of all virtues. Next, "attaining the wondrous departure" explains the perfection of making offerings, up to the point of "hundreds of thousands" and so forth;
because one makes offerings to the Buddhas, there is no merit that is not cultivated, and thus one is able to attain [the goal].
Regarding the great samādhis: one attains the Samādhi of the Wondrous Banner Mark (*Sudarśana-lakṣaṇa-samādhi*).
"Samādhi" here is translated as "right reception" (*samyag-āpatti*); because it does not receive any [defiled] sensations, it is called "right reception. "Samādhi" refers to the "Wondrous Banner."

Regarding the "mark" (lakṣaṇa): the banner signifies the crushing of the heterodox and the manifestation of the orthodox; thus, there is no heterodoxy that is not crushed, and no orthodoxy that is not manifested.

To say it is "wondrous" means that the orthodox is precisely the heterodox, and the orthodox does not depart from the heterodox; it is not that there is a separate orthodoxy existing apart from the heterodox.
Therefore, it is called the Samādhi of the Wondrous Banner Mark.
The Lotus Samādhi.
As for "Lotus," it means that one is able to personally comprehend that all dharmas are entirely the true mark (*dharmatā*). This is because every dharma is true and every characteristic is real.
The Samādhi of Pure Virtue (*viśuddhaguṇa*).
