Regarding "pure virtue": it is called "pure" because there is no delusion that is not destroyed; it is called "virtue" because there is no wisdom that is not manifested.
Thus, both this purity and this virtue are obtained through this samādhi.
The Samādhi of the King of Constellations’ Play (*Rājarṣi-vikrīḍita*). Regarding "King of Constellations": "Constellation King" (*rājarṣi*) is an alternative name for the moon.

Just as the moon can wane and wax, the Bodhisattva can manifest a superior body to respond to those of great capacity, and can manifest an inferior body to respond to those of small capacity, just like the moon.
It can diminish excess; because it is like a playful sport, it is called the *Śakraparipṛcchā-samādhi* (Samādhi of the Play of the Lord of Constellations).

As for the *Animitto-nimitta-samādhi* (Samādhi of the Non-conditioned), "non-conditioned" means that it can spontaneously bestow happiness upon all sentient beings and uproot [the suffering] of all sentient beings.
"Suffering. It is so named because it is like a magnet that spontaneously attracts iron.
Regarding the Samādhi of the Wisdom Seal (*jñānamudrā*):
"Wisdom Seal" means that one spontaneously attains the three wisdoms within a single mind, and thereby seals emptiness with the wisdom of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
Sealing existence with the knowledge of the modes of the path, and sealing the middle with the knowledge of all modes, it is therefore called the Seal of Wisdom (*jñāna-mudrā*).
This is the Samādhi of Understanding the Languages of All Sentient Beings.

One who understands the languages of all sentient beings is so named because they are able to fully comprehend all the diverse and different dialects of all sentient beings. Should they have anything to say,
this single voice can cause all sentient beings to each attain understanding according to their own kind.
The Samādhi that Accumulates All Merits (*Sarvaguṇasaṃcaya*). Regarding "accumulating all merits":
one is able to take what one has personally realized and teach it to others; this is called "merit" (*guṇa*). To transform that merit so that it returns to oneself is called "virtue" (*guṇa*);
when this is attained within the mind, it is termed virtue. As for "all," it does not exceed the Dharmakāya, Prajñā, and Vimukti.
Because one is able to personally accumulate the secret treasury of the three virtues, it is named accordingly.
Regarding "Pure Samādhi":
"pure" means being able to perfectly destroy the three delusions.
The Samādhi of the Play of Supernatural Powers (*ṛddhivikrīḍita*).
As for "the play of supernatural powers": one naturally possesses great wisdom and great compassion, and is thus able to spontaneously grant [benefit] and extract [suffering].
One manifests through spiritual power and clarifies through insight; one penetrates and transforms like a player. For this reason, it is so named.
The Samādhi of the Torch of Wisdom.
As for "Torch of Wisdom," it is like a worldly torch that can dispel all darkness; possessing great wisdom, it can shatter the gloom of ignorance, and thus it is so named.
The Samādhi of the King of Adornments.
As for the King of Adornments: he is able to personally fulfill both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) as his adornment.
Thus, concentration is itself wisdom, and wisdom is entirely concentration. Having attained great mastery over concentration and wisdom, he is therefore named the King of Adornments.
The Samādhi of Pure Radiance (*viśuddha-prabhā-samādhi*).
Regarding "pure radiance": it is called "pure" because it can completely sever the three delusions; it is called "radiant" because it can completely manifest the three wisdoms;
and it is called "luminous" because it can completely realize the three virtues.
The Samādhi of the Pure Treasury.

Regarding "Pure Treasury": "Treasury" (zàng) takes the sense of containing or storing within. Within the present, infinitesimal thought-moment of the mind, it contains and stores the three thousand natures and characteristics and the ten realms, each with their thousand suchnesses; because it can manifest all of these, it is so named.
The Unshared Samādhi.
"Unshared" means that it belongs to those of the Great Vehicle’s Perfect and Sudden teaching; it is not shared with the partial and gradual teachings of the Two Vehicles.
It is the Sun-Turning Samādhi.
Regarding "the revolving sun": it refers to being able to revolve from the provisional into the empty, yet not dwelling in the empty;
revolving from the empty into the provisional, yet not dwelling in the provisional; and revolving from both the empty and the provisional into the middle, yet not dwelling in the middle.
It is named such because it is like the solar disc revolving through the sky, yet not dwelling in the sky.
He attains hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, billions, and even as many as the sands of the Ganges of such great samādhis.
The phrase "attaining such as these" serves to conclude by summarizing what has been described above. △ Third, the actual illumination.
Śākyamuni Buddha radiated light upon his body.
The reason he illuminated his body was that he wished him to comply with the Buddha’s command and propagate this wondrous sūtra of the Middle Way and True Reality.
△ Second, the distant arrival of Gadgadasvara, in two parts: first, clarifying the causes and conditions; second, the actual departure.
[The first four chapters: First, the request by Gadgadasvara to go [to this world].
He addressed the Buddha Pure Flower Constellation King Wisdom (*Śuddhāṣaṇapadmavuṣitacandrarāja*), saying:
"World-Honored One, I shall go to the Sahā world to pay homage, draw near to, and make offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha, and to see the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta."
[Sa]. Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, Bodhisattva Śūradatta, Bodhisattva Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña, Bodhisattva Viśiṣṭacāritra, Bodhisattva Vyūharāja, and Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyasamudgata.
As for those who wish to pay homage to Śākyamuni and others, it is because in their past causal stages, they were once transformed, guided, and educated by Śākyamuni.

Mañjuśrī possesses great wisdom; he is able to initiate this sutra, he is able to proclaim this sutra within the ocean, and he is able to inquire about the methods for circulating this sutra for beginners. [Medicine King...]
King [Bhadrapāla], he is one who can burn his own body and arms to propagate this sutra through ascetic practices;
Śūradatta, he is one who can preach mantras to protect and spread this sutra; Puṣpadanta, he is one who can inquire about the ascetic practices for propagating this sutra;
and Uttaramati, he was originally transformed by Śākyamuni and is able to act as [a protector].
He who has emerged as the supreme head and received the mandate to propagate this sutra is King Śrīsaṃbhava;
he is one capable of turning others away from error toward the right path and practicing this sutra. Bhaiṣajyasamudgata is like Bhaiṣajyarāja;
by means of his supernormal powers, he turned King Śrīsaṃbhava away from error so that he might practice this sutra. Therefore, all wish to behold them.
...and so forth. △ Second, the admonition of that Buddha:
At that time, the Buddha Pure Flower Constellation King Wisdom addressed the Bodhisattva Wonderful Sound, saying: "Do not disparage that land, nor give rise to thoughts of it being inferior.
Good son, that Sahā world is uneven with high and low ground; it is filled with mountains of earth and stone, and is foul and impure."
It is filled. The Buddha’s body is short and small, and the bodies of the assembly of bodhisattvas are likewise small;
yet your body is forty-two thousand *yojanas* in height, while my body is six million eight hundred thousand *yojanas*.

Your body is preeminent in its beauty, possessing hundreds of thousands of millions of merits, and its radiance is exceptionally sublime. Therefore, go, and do not disparage that land, whether it be the Buddha, the bodhisattvas, or the country itself.
Regarding the earth, they give rise to inferior conceptions.

This is why it is necessary to provide them with admonitions: while the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara, abiding in the stage of Equal Enlightenment, would naturally not give rise to inferior conceptions, those in his retinue may be beginners who do give rise to such inferior conceptions.

Such things exist. Therefore, that Buddha issued this series of proclamations, admonitions, and injunctions to Gadgadasvara, so that the assembly following him would not give rise to such thoughts. Nevertheless, regarding what all Buddhas cultivate and realize—
All are indeed the same; yet lands differ as pure or defiled, and the bodies of Buddhas differ as superior or inferior.

This is simply because they accord with the differing capacities of sentient beings. If the capacity of sentient beings is inferior or small, then one should respond to them with a defiled land and an inferior body.
If the capacity of sentient beings is great or superior, then one should respond with a pure land.

He waited for them by manifesting a superior body; thus we know that lands have no inherent purity or defilement—purity and defilement arise from the beings themselves—and that Buddhas have no inherent superiority or inferiority—superiority and inferiority depend on the capacity of the recipient. △ Third, Miaoyin receives the mandate.

The Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara addressed his Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, that I am now going to the Sahā world is entirely through the power of the Tathāgata, the playful mastery of the Tathāgata’s supernormal powers, and the adornment of the Tathāgata’s merit and wisdom."
"All this is due to the power of the Tathāgata" means that the Tathāgata is able to penetrate all dharmas as being empty and quiescent in their very essence,
all of which are the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), and thus he perceives no distinction between purity and defilement, or superiority and inferiority. Therefore, as I now proceed to that land,
I too shall follow and learn from the Tathāgata, likewise perceiving no distinction between purity and defilement, or superiority and inferiority.
Yet one does not give rise to thoughts of inferiority oneself. Regarding what is called "the Tathāgata’s playful exercise of supernatural powers" (*ṛddhi-vikrīḍita*):
the Tathāgata possesses compassion, capable of bestowing happiness and extracting suffering; he manifests through spiritual power and clarifies through penetration, transforming things as if in play.
I too should now follow and learn the Dharma of the Tathāgata, and thus act accordingly. Furthermore—
One should not give rise to thoughts of inferiority. Regarding the statement that the Tathāgata is adorned with merit and wisdom:
the Tathāgata possesses great adornment, and thus is not afflicted by any obstacles. Now, I am going to that land.
One should likewise study the Dharma of the Tathāgata accordingly, so as not to be troubled by various obstacles and to further clarify the absence of inferior thoughts.
△ Fourth, the preliminary manifestation of auspicious signs has six parts. First, the transformation of lotus flowers.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara, without rising from his seat and without moving his body, entered into samādhi. By the power of this samādhi,
not far from the Dharma-seat on Vulture Peak Mountain, he manifested eighty-four thousand lotus flowers made of various jewels,
with stems of Jāmbūnada gold, petals of white silver, filaments of diamond, and [seats] of kiṃśuka gems.
He used it as his terrace.
△ Second, Mañjuśrī’s inquiry:
At that time, the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, seeing this lotus flower, addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, this..."

For what cause and condition has this omen appeared first? There are many tens of millions of lotuses, with stems of Jāmbūnada gold, petals of white silver, filaments of diamond, and pedestals made of karketana jewels.
△ Third, the Tathāgata’s response:

At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī, saying, "This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gadgadasvara wishes to come from the land of the Buddha Śubhavyūharāja, surrounded by eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas."
Having arrived here in this Sahā world, they have made offerings to, drawn near to, and prostrated before me; they also wish to make offerings and listen to the Lotus Sūtra.
△ Fourth, further inquiry.

Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, what roots of goodness has this bodhisattva planted, and what merits has he cultivated, that he is able to possess such great supernormal powers? What samādhi does he practice? We pray that you will tell us the name of this samādhi;
we also wish to diligently cultivate its practice. Only by practicing this samādhi can one see this bodhisattva."
Regarding his physical appearance, stature, and his dignified deportment in coming and going, I only pray that the World-Honored One, by means of your supernatural powers,
will cause that Bodhisattva to come so that I may behold him.
Regarding the phrase "causing me to obtain a vision": previously, when Gadgadasvara requested to go, he spoke of seeing Mañjuśrī as well; now, Mañjuśrī speaks of causing me to obtain a vision.
This is because both individuals dwell together at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyaksambodhi), yet they merely hear of one another without seeing each other.
Now, they wish to practice this sutra together and to circulate this sutra together.
Because they wished to together establish the causes and conditions for the transformation of beings, Miaoyin (Ghoṣadatta) desired to see Wenshu (Mañjuśrī), and Wenshu desired to see Miaoyin.
△ Fifth, the recommendation of Prabhūtaratna.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī: "This Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, who has been extinguished for a long time, shall now manifest his form for your sakes."
I shall now manifest that sign for you all; thus, the merit lies with Prabhūtaratna and not with me, Śākyamuni.
For since the Tathāgata previously emitted light from afar to illuminate him, he has already been summoned and caused to come.
Now, because Mañjuśrī asks again, I command Prabhūtaratna to return, summoning him once more by means of my voice. △ Sixth, announcing his arrival.
At that time, the Buddha Prabhūtaratna addressed those bodhisattvas: "Come, sons of good family! The Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī wishes to see you.
This concludes the preceding account of the causes and conditions. II. The Actual Departure (in four parts): 1. The Journey with the Retinue.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara vanished from that land and set out together with eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas.
As they passed through various countries, the earth shook in six ways, and everywhere there fell rains of seven-jeweled lotuses;
hundreds of thousands of celestial musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck.

Regarding the statement "the six kinds of earth tremors," etc.: when the Sublime Sound (Ghoṣadatta) traveled through various lands and came to this realm, it was none other than his desire to circulate this sutra.

Because he is able to cause all sentient beings to overturn and shatter the ignorance of the six stages, the six kinds of earth tremors manifest this. Because he is able to achieve the unsurpassed, perfect cause, flowers rain down.
This is manifested. Should there be one of great capacity who does not wait for a question, [the Buddha] shall preach for them;
thus, hundreds of thousands of celestial instruments sound spontaneously without being struck to manifest this. △ Second, the description of ascending the platform.

The eyes of this bodhisattva are as vast as the petals of a great blue lotus; even if a hundred thousand million moons were joined together, his countenance would be more upright and beautiful than that.
His body is of a true golden color, adorned with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of meritorious qualities.
With majestic power blazing forth and radiance shining brightly, his various marks were perfectly complete, like the solid body of Nārāyaṇa.
He entered a pavilion of the seven treasures and ascended into the void, remaining at a height of seven *tāla* trees above the ground.
Surrounded by a multitude of bodhisattvas who paid him reverent homage, he came to this Sahā world, to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
△ Second, the inquiry regarding the transmission of the essential meaning has two parts. First, the presentation of offerings:
Having arrived, he descended from the seven-jeweled terrace and, taking a necklace worth hundreds of thousands, went to the place where Śākyamuni Buddha was;
he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and presented the necklace.

Regarding the offering of the necklace: first, because he was once a disciple in the past and has today come from afar, it is entirely appropriate according to the ritual decorum between teacher and student and the constant laws of human relations.

Second, it serves to manifest his own causal practices, which shall surely result in the meritorious virtues of the Tathāgata’s fruition. △ Second, the formal inquiry, in three parts. First, the inquiry.
The emanated Buddha addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the Buddha Pure Flower Constellation King Wisdom inquires after the World-Honored One: Are you free from illness and affliction?
Are your daily activities light and easy? Do you dwell in peace and happiness? Are your four elements in harmony? Can you endure the affairs of the world?"
△ Second, he asks about the assembly to be converted:
"Are the sentient beings easy to deliver? Do they not have much greed, anger, delusion, jealousy, stinginess, or pride?

Are they not lacking in filial piety toward their parents, respect for śramaṇas, or right view? Do they possess a virtuous mind? Do they restrain the five sensory faculties? Thus he asked the World-Honored One regarding the assembly.
"Born. Can one subdue all demons and enemies?
In this passage, the character "wu" (無) in "wuxiao" (無孝) is not present; it runs directly into the following text. The character "bu" (不) in "bushi wuqing" (不攝五情) is likewise absent.
"Directly penetrating upward. This is an abbreviated expression; in full, it should state: "Is there no failure to be filial toward one's parents?
Is there no lack of respect for śramaṇas? Are there no wrong views? Is there no unwholesome mind? Is there no failure to restrain the five sensory faculties?
△ Third, questioning the Buddha Prabhūtaratna.

"Has the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, who entered parinirvāṇa long ago, come from within his stupa made of the seven precious gems to listen to the Dharma? Furthermore, inquire after the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna’s well-being:
Is he at ease, free from affliction, and able to endure remaining for a long time?"
These three preceding questions were all asked by transmitting the intent of that Tathāgata. △ Fourth, the aspiration to see Prabhūtaratna has three parts.
First, Gadgadasvara’s aspiration to see him.
“World-Honored One, I now wish to see the body of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna. I pray only that the World-Honored One will show it to me, let me see it.
To say “show it to me, let me see it” means, as Mahāpratibhāna [the Bodhisattva] wished to see that Buddha, one must first assemble the emanated bodies;
only then can the stupa be opened and he be seen. Now, since the door of the stupa remains closed and is not to be opened again, unless the power of the Buddha intervenes...
[End of section]. There is no way for me to see him. △ Second, Śākyamuni transmits his words:
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha said to Prabhūtaratna Buddha, "This Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara wishes to see you."
△ Third, the praise by Prabhūtaratna.
At that time, the Buddha Prabhūtaratna addressed Gadgadasvara, saying: "Excellent, excellent!
It is because you wish to make offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha, to hear the Lotus Sutra, and to see Mañjuśrī and the others that you have come here."
As for those who are able to make offerings to Śākyamuni, Gadgadasvara was originally one possessed of merit;
now that he is able to make offerings to Śākyamuni, his merit becomes even more profound. As for those who listen to the Lotus Sutra, Gadgadasvara was originally one possessed of wisdom.
Now that he is able to hear the Lotus Sutra, his wisdom has become even deeper.
Because both his merit and wisdom are profound, [the Buddha] praises him by exclaiming once more, "Excellent! Mañjuśrī is foremost among those of great wisdom;
that he is now able to proclaim and circulate this sutra, and that we can witness it all together, is why [the Buddha] can yet again praise him by exclaiming, "Excellent! once more.

...Thus it is. △ Third, the supernatural powers (ṛddhi) and the penetration of the sutra, in two parts: first, an inquiry into the supernatural powers; second, an inquiry into the samādhi. The first part has two sections:
first, Puṣpadatta poses the question.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Flower Virtue addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, what roots of goodness has this Bodhisattva Wonderful Sound planted, and what merits has he cultivated, such that he possesses these supernormal powers?"
The Bodhisattva is named Flower Virtue (Guṇakusuma). He is so named because this Bodhisattva is able to adorn the fruit of his merit with the causes of ten thousand virtues.
As for this supernatural power, it certainly does not exist without a cause. I now ask the World-Honored One:
ultimately, what roots of goodness and merit from past lives enabled him to be thus? △ Second, the Tathāgata’s response.

The demonstration has three parts: first, the answer to the initial question; second, the answer to the second question; and third, the answer regarding the supernormal power. The first two [parts] have an initial section for the direct response.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Flower Virtue: "In the past, there was a Buddha named Cloud Thunder Sound King (Meghadundubhisvararāja), a Tathāgata."
Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. His land was named Manifesting All Worlds, and his eon was named Joyful Vision.

The Bodhisattva Wondrous Sound, for twelve thousand years, made offerings to the Buddha Cloud-Thunder-Voice King with one hundred thousand varieties of music and presented him with eighty-four thousand bowls of the seven precious gems.
By virtue of these causes and conditions and their karmic retribution, he has now been born in the Pure [Land].
In the land of the Buddha Padmashri-raja (Flower Constellation King Wisdom), there is such supernatural power.

That Buddha is named Meghadundubhisvararaja (Cloud Thunder Sound King). Because that Buddha manifests his body like a cloud and preaches the Dharma like thunder, expounding all dharmas with a subtle and wondrous voice, he has attained great mastery; therefore, he is named Cloud Thunder Sound King.
Furthermore, the name of the land is "Manifesting All Worlds. "All worlds" refers to the thirty kinds of worlds.
Because that Buddha can manifest forms according to the various types of beings to teach and guide each one, the land is named accordingly.
As for the eon being named "Joyful Vision," since that Buddha is able to teach and transform all worlds, [the eon is so named].
All sentient beings who see him are without exception filled with joy; therefore, the kalpa is named "Joyful Vision.
As for those who offer worship with music and dance, because they are able to realize that sound is itself the Dharma-realm, they should give rise to practice within the Dharma-realm;
thus, they raise an offering of the Dharma-realm while returning to use music and dance as their offering. As for those who offer worship with an almsbowl, because...
Because he was able to realize that form is itself the Dharma-realm, he used his almsbowl to present an offering to the Dharma-realm.

As for your question regarding what roots of goodness he possessed to have such supernormal power: it was precisely through the roots of goodness from making this offering to the Dharma-realm that he came to possess such supernormal power. II. Conclusion and Correlation.
"Śubhavyūha, what do you think? At that time, in the presence of the Buddha Ghoṣadatta, was the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara—
who offered musical instruments as an act of worship and presented precious vessels— anyone other than this very Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gadgadasvara?"
△ Second, answering two questions:
"Śrīgarbha, this Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara has already made offerings to and drawn near countless Buddhas, having long planted the roots of virtue.
Furthermore, he has encountered hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
Making offerings to all Buddhas is the cultivation of merit; planting the roots of virtue over a long period is the cultivation of wisdom. As for your question regarding what merits there are:
there is this supernatural power (*ṛddhi*). Because one is able to cultivate the merits of both merit and wisdom, such supernatural power exists.
△ Third, the answer concerning supernatural power has three parts. First, a general explanation.
"Śubhavyūha, you see only that the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara’s body is here; yet this bodhisattva manifests various bodies everywhere to preach this sutra for the sake of all sentient beings."
"Manifesting various bodies" refers to manifesting the bodies of the ten realms. "In every place" refers to lands such as the Land of Common Dwelling and the Land of Residual Existence.
"Expounding this sutra" means that although the manifested bodies differ, what is taught is exclusively this wondrous sutra;
it reveals the power of the wondrous voice to circulate [the teaching], so that those who hear it may, according to their respective capacities, immediately [attain realization].

This is the Buddha Vehicle. △ Second, the specific demonstration has two parts: first, clarifying that what is not born manifests as birth; second, clarifying that what is not extinguished manifests as extinction.
The first part has two sub-sections; the first is the manifestation of the bodies of the six classes of ordinary beings.
Sometimes he manifests in the form of Brahmā; sometimes in the form of Śakra; sometimes in the form of Īśvara;
sometimes in the form of Maheśvara; sometimes in the form of a celestial general; sometimes in the form of Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King;
sometimes in the form of a universal monarch (cakravartin); sometimes in the form of various minor kings; sometimes in the form of an elder; or sometimes in the form of a householder.
They may manifest in the body of a minister, or the body of a brahmin, or the bodies of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās;
or they may manifest in the bodies of elders, lay devotees, or women;
or they may manifest in the bodies of ministers’ wives, or brahmin women, or boys and girls; or they may manifest as devas.
With bodies such as those of nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, they preach this sutra.
Furthermore, for all those in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, animals, and various places of hardship, [they act as their protectors].
They are all able to provide rescue and relief, even reaching into the king’s inner palace, where they manifest in female form to preach this sutra.
The Brahma King is the lord of the Form Realm; Śakra is the lord of the Desire Realm; and Īśvara is the lord of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations.
This is the summit of the desire realm; Mahādeva is Maheśvara. This is the summit of the form realm. By mentioning the sovereign deities at the summit of these realms, all other deities are included.
As for the wheel-turning kings (*cakravartin*), they comprise all four types; as for minor kings, they are the "scattered grains" (*kṣudraka*). From "All those with...
onwards clarifies the manifestation of bodies in various difficult circumstances; in the eight places of difficulty, there is everywhere the supramundane, sudden, and complete [teaching].
At such opportune moments, he likewise manifests his body to preach this sutra, enabling beings to attain liberation.
Flower Virtue, this Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara is able to rescue and protect all sentient beings in the Sahā world.
This Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara thus manifests various transformations and appears here in this Sahā land for the sake of all beings.
When this sutra is preached, there shall be no diminution whatsoever in his supernormal powers, transformations, or wisdom.
By means of such manifold wisdom, this bodhisattva illuminates the Sahā world, causing all sentient beings to each attain what they need to know.
It is likewise so throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions.
This means that those who manifest various bodies as described above do so all because they have attained supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*). Regarding the term "rescue and protection":

"rescue" (*jū*) refers to rescuing and uprooting [suffering], while "protection" (*go*) refers to guarding and sustaining. Rescuing and uprooting is great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) that extracts one from suffering;
guarding and sustaining is great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) that bestows happiness. As for "having no diminution in supernormal powers or wisdom," this means that even though one may manifest...

Whether manifesting as the body of a human or a deva, or even appearing in the forms of queens of various difficult-to-conquer realms, the Bodhisattva’s supernormal powers and wisdom remain forever unshaken and never diminished. They are like a worldly bright lamp:
one may take from it without end, and it illuminates infinitely, yet it never suffers any loss or diminution. Thus, they cause all sentient beings to each obtain what they require.
Regarding "those who know": speaking in general terms, this refers to the teaching of a single sound, whereby beings understand according to their own kind and each attains what they know.

However, speaking in terms of the ultimate reality, it specifically refers to this Bodhisattva manifesting in various bodies for the sake of all sentient beings, preaching this wondrous sutra so that all sentient beings may each attain the opening, revealing, awakening to, and entering into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Each...
They attain clear understanding of the extent of their lifespan, even throughout the worlds of the ten directions, each attaining such knowledge.
△ Second, manifesting the bodies of the four noble beings.
If there are those who are to be liberated by appearing in the form of a śrāvaka, he manifests in the form of a śrāvaka and preaches the Dharma for them.
If there are those who are to be liberated by appearing in the form of a pratyekabuddha, he manifests in the form of a pratyekabuddha and preaches the Dharma for them.

If there are those who are to be liberated by appearing in the form of a bodhisattva, he manifests in the form of a bodhisattva and preaches the Dharma for them. If there are those who are to be liberated by appearing in the form of a Buddha, he immediately manifests...
He manifests in the form of a Buddha and preaches the Dharma for them. In this manner, he manifests various forms according to what is appropriate for those to be saved:
for those who should be saved by means of the Śrāvaka vehicle, he preaches the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths;

for those who should be saved by means of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, he preaches the Dharma of Dependent Origination; and for those who should be saved by means of the Bodhisattva vehicle, he preaches the Six Perfections.
This Dharma is such that for those who are to be delivered by means of the forms of the three vehicles,

he immediately manifests the forms of the three vehicles and preaches the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* for them, causing all those of the three vehicles to ultimately converge in the single Buddha-vehicle.
And thus they attain deliverance. Regarding those who should be reached through the form of a Buddha, this must be distinguished:
there is the Buddha at the culmination of the three vehicles (*triyāna*), the Buddha of partial realization in the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-yāna*), and the Buddha of ultimate perfection.

What is manifested here is the Buddha at the culmination of the three vehicles and the Buddha of partial realization in the Perfect Teaching, which causes them to attain the ultimate state of wondrous enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*) of the Perfect Teaching.
This is the Buddha. △ Second, clarifying that although there is no extinction, he manifests extinction:
even for those who are to be saved by means of extinction, he manifests extinction.
△ Third, the comprehensive summary.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Flower-Virtue Sublime-Sound has accomplished the power of great supernatural penetrations and wisdom;
such are his deeds.
△ Second, the inquiry regarding samādhi, in two parts. First, the Bodhisattva’s question.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Flower Virtue addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, this Bodhisattva Wonderful Sound has deeply planted roots of goodness.
World-Honored One, in what samādhi does this bodhisattva abide, such that he is able to manifest transformations everywhere in this manner to deliver and liberate sentient beings?"

Regarding those who have deeply planted roots of goodness: as the World-Honored One has just now clarified for me, I already know that the Bodhisattva Wonderful Sound was able to offer music and precious bowls to the Buddha Cloud-Thunder-Voice King;
furthermore, he has long planted the foundations of virtue, making offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, such that there is no wisdom he does not possess and no merit he has not cultivated. Thus, his...
In former times, during the causal stage, it may be said that he deeply planted roots of goodness and profoundly cultivated merit;

thus, it is clear why he possesses such supernormal powers. Yet, we do not know what samādhi he currently dwells in, by which he is able to manifest bodies within the ten realms throughout this land and other directions, preaching the subtle and wondrous Dharma, and appearing in whatever form is necessary to deliver those who are to be saved.
"What body did he see? △ Second, the Tathāgata’s response:
The Buddha told Flower Virtue Bodhisattva, "Good son, that samādhi is named ‘Manifesting All Physical Bodies.
It is because the Bodhisattva Wonderful Sound dwells within this samādhi that he is able to thus benefit immeasurable sentient beings."

As for your question regarding which samādhi he dwells in: that which he dwells in is not some other samādhi, but is precisely the *Sarvarūpasaṃdarśana-samādhi* (the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Bodies).
Because he dwells in this samādhi, he is able to manifest forms according to the various types [of beings] to deliver and liberate sentient beings.
One who is able to attain this samādhi does so by virtue of having thoroughly understood the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and all that it elucidates.
This is because it is the wondrous principle of the true mark (*dharmatā*) of phenomena.
Since all phenomena are the true mark, every phenomenon is authentic and every characteristic is real. Taking up any single form (*rūpa*), all forms are that one form;
taking up any single body, all bodies are that one body. One who can penetrate this principle attains these three [realizations].
In this state of profound stillness, one is able to manifest all within a single manifestation, and manifest a single manifestation within all manifestations.

Thus, when it is appropriate to manifest the bodies of the three miserable realms, one immediately manifests the bodies of the three miserable realms; when it is appropriate to manifest the bodies of the eight difficulties, one immediately manifests the bodies of the eight difficulties;

when it is appropriate to manifest the bodies of the six classes of ordinary beings, one immediately manifests the bodies of the six classes of ordinary beings; when it is appropriate to manifest the bodies of the four types of noble ones, one immediately manifests the bodies of the four types of noble ones—and so on, even unto infinity.
When they should be born, they do not actually arise but manifest arising; when they should perish, they do not actually cease but manifest cessation.
Through such various transformations, they deliver sentient beings—all of this is due to abiding in this samādhi. △ Fourth, the mutual benefit [of both lands], in two parts.
First, the benefit obtained in that land.

When this "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara" was being preached, the eighty-four thousand people who had come together with the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara all attained the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Forms.

Regarding the bodhisattvas who have all attained samādhi: Miaoyin (Wonderful Sound) has long practiced with a profound resolve and has already achieved this Samādhi of the Universal Manifestation of Physical Forms.
As for those who have come together here, they are practitioners who have only recently begun their initial resolve.
Now, having heard Śākyamuni Tathāgata elucidate what Miaoyin has attained, they too shall be able to attain that of Miaoyin.
This is what has been attained. △ Second, the benefits obtained in this land:
In this Sahā world, immeasurable bodhisattvas have likewise attained this samādhi as well as dhāraṇīs.
Regarding "samādhi and dhāraṇī": Miaoyin attained this samādhi and also attained total retention (dhāraṇī).
Therefore, he was able to be wisdom within concentration and concentration within wisdom; abiding in samādhi, he preached the Dharma according to the capacities of beings.
Now, the immeasurable bodhisattvas in this land, having heard the Buddha’s elucidation, have likewise attained what he attained. △ Five: Returning Home.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gadgadasvara, having made offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha and the stūpa of Prabhūtaratna Buddha,
returned to his own land. As he passed through the various countries, the earth shook in six ways and precious lotus flowers rained down, producing a hundred [kinds of]...

With hundreds of thousands of millions of various kinds of musical instruments, having arrived in his own land, surrounded by eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas, he went to the place where the Buddha Pure Flower Constellation King Wisdom was and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I have gone to the Sahā world to benefit sentient beings;
I have seen Śākyamuni Buddha and the stupa of the Buddha Many Jewels, and I have paid them homage and made offerings. Furthermore—
He beheld the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, as well as the Bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja, Vīryadatta,
and Śūradatta; he also caused these eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas to attain the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Forms.
It is said that the arrival of Gadgadasvara in this land was for only two purposes: first, to make offerings to Śākyamuni and to behold the stupa of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna.
Now that he has already made offerings to Śākyamuni and beheld Prabhūtaratna, it is logical that he should return home.
When he previously set out on his journey, all the lands he passed through shook in six ways, precious lotus flowers rained down, and celestial music played spontaneously.
Ming! Now, returning to my native land, I am likewise so. Both my coming and my going are for the sole purpose of circulating this sutra.
Upon my arrival, I was indeed able to cause sentient beings to shatter the ignorance of the six stages and achieve the unsurpassed perfect cause.
If I encountered those of great capacity, I would preach spontaneously without being asked.
This was manifested by the shaking of the earth, the raining of flowers, and the playing of music. Now, as they depart, it is likewise so;
therefore, it is again manifested by the shaking of the earth and other such signs. Regarding "addressing the Buddha" and so forth:

previously, when they set out, they addressed the Buddha, requesting to go to the Sahā world to make offerings to Śākyamuni and Prabhūtaratna, and to see Mañjuśrī and others. Now that the matter has been accomplished...
Having returned to his own land, he again addressed his Buddha. △ Sixth, the increase of the Path upon hearing this chapter:

While this "Chapter on the Coming and Going of Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara" was being preached, forty-two thousand devaputras attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and the Bodhisattva Flower-Virtue (*Puṣpadatta*) attained the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*.
As for the Son of Heaven attaining the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*):

when he hears this chapter, he is able to penetrate the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all dharmas, such that he perceives not even the slightest dharma arising, nor does he perceive even the slightest dharma ceasing.

Because he accepts this principle of non-arising within his mind, he is able to attain the patience of non-arising. This attainment occurs at the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*).

Furthermore, as for the Bodhisattva Huade attaining the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*, it was because at the time he heard this chapter, he was able to thoroughly comprehend the principle of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), knowing that all phenomena are truly such and that every characteristic is entirely real; beyond the true mark, there is nothing else.
There are no further marks; beyond the Dharma-realm, there are no further phenomena.

Therefore, one is able to attain the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*, which is the oneness of purity and the total purity of all things, the oneness of mastery and the total mastery of all things, and the oneness of ultimate realization and the total ultimate realization of all things.
This concludes the explanation of the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara."
The Universal Gate Chapter, the Twenty-fifth, of the Lotus Sutra of the Wonderful Dharma. To clarify the sequence of this chapter:

following the preceding section where the Tathāgata entrusted the great bodhisattvas with the task of learning the Tathāgata’s Dharma—specifically, that they should learn the practice of asceticism as exemplified by the King of Medicine—it states:
*...* (Note: The provided source text appears to be truncated; the translation reflects the available portion.)

One should follow and learn from his spiritual powers, as exemplified by Gadgadasvara. Furthermore, there is what is called the "Universal Gateway Manifestation," which one should likewise follow and learn from, as exemplified by Avalokiteśvara.
Thus, we know that immediately following the "Gadgadasvara Chapter" is the text of this single chapter on the "Universal Gateway of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
The five characters for "Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva" refer to the person, while the two characters for "Universal Gateway" [refer to the method].
The title consists of both the Dharma and the person. Thus, it is called the "Universal Gate Chapter of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
Regarding the person, "Avalokita" (Contemplation) refers to the Bodhisattva’s capacity for contemplation;
"World-Sound" (Loka-svara) refers to the object of the Bodhisattva’s contemplation. This is because worldly people perceive sounds through the faculty of hearing; this Bodhisattva...
Thus, one does not hear sounds with the ears, but rather uses wondrous contemplation to contemplate all sounds existing within the world;

therefore, he is named Avalokiteśvara (Contemplator of the Sounds of the World). However, the "Contemplator of the Sounds of the World" mentioned here differs from that explained in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
That text explains the self-cultivation practiced during the causal stage, and thus says: "First, within the midst of hearing..."
Entering the stream, the objects of perception vanish. Once that which is entered has been exhausted, the two characteristics of motion and stillness clearly do not arise.
It continues until it says, "When birth and death have ceased, quiescent extinction manifests. This precisely clarifies the initial cultivation of the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty;
it receives its name based on the self-practice cultivated during the causal stage. Herein, one fully realizes that self-practice and...

"Accomplishing the transformation of others" means being able to observe all the sounds of sentient beings within the ten realms, manifesting various forms and preaching the subtle and wondrous Dharma to enable them to escape suffering and affliction; thus it receives this name.
This refers entirely to the transformation of others, which is why it differs from his own practice (*svayam-caryā*). However, how does he observe the world?
Regarding these sounds: there are all sentient beings in the world who dwell within the seven perils and cannot escape them;
those who abide in the three poisons and cannot achieve liberation; and those who harbor the two types of seeking and cannot fulfill their aspirations.
If such sentient beings do not invoke the name of the Bodhisattva, [they shall not attain deliverance].
Thus it is said. If one recites his name even once, the Bodhisattva will attend to that person's voice and cause those who are beset by the seven calamities to ultimately attain deliverance;
those who are mired in the three poisons to ultimately attain liberation; and those who harbor the two types of seeking to ultimately fulfill their vows.
This is what is meant by the principle that the capacity of the practitioner and the response of the environment are in perfect accord, such that there is nothing that does not harmonize in mystery.

Therefore, he is named Avalokiteśvara. As for the term "Bodhisattva," it is because when one uses wondrous contemplation to contemplate the sounds of the world, one is able to cause immeasurable sentient beings to all attain liberation from various sufferings and afflictions;
thus, by fulfilling all that pertains to one's own practice, one accomplishes the benefit of others. Therefore, he is named a Bodhisattva. Next, regarding the Dharma:
Regarding the term "Universal Gate" (*samantamukha*): "universal" (*samanta*) has the meaning of being all-pervasive, while "gate" (*mukha*) is designated by way of entering and exiting.
If a gate were not pervasive, it could not extensively transform all beings; thus, such a gate would be partial rather than complete, and restricted rather than universal.
Now, this Bodhisattva, relying on the principle of true reality (*bhūtatathatā*), opens the universal gate and is able to practice perfect contemplation.

The ten dharma realms: [the Buddha] responds perfectly to sentient beings of the nine realms, causing them all to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and to be delivered from all suffering and affliction.
That is to say, by means of thirty-two bodies, he universally responds to the capacities of all beings, manifesting in every land.
There is no one who is not delivered by non-arising; thus, the gateway that he possesses is all-pervasive, perfectly interfused, and inconceivable.

This is why it is called the "Universal Gateway Chapter" of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara. The explanation of the chapter title is hereby completed. The text of this chapter is divided into two parts:
first, the inquiry and response that illuminate the meaning; second, the benefits gained upon hearing the chapter. First:

II. First, the prose section; second, the verse section. The first [section] has two parts: first, the question regarding the person of Avalokiteśvara; second, the question regarding the Dharma of the Universal Gate.

The first [of these two] has two parts: first, the question posed by the Bodhisattva; second, the answer given by the Tathāgata. The first [of these two] has two parts: first, the introduction provided by the narrator of the sutra.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these words:
"When a bodhisattva puts forward a question, there are two intentions. The first is that Avalokiteśvara is able to contemplate with wondrous contemplation..."

Regarding all sounds and the various capacities of those in the world, there are those with latent capacities that receive a latent response, and those with latent capacities that receive a manifest response; though such cases differ in these many ways, it is the Bodhisattva who [responds].
All those who are to be delivered, he delivers and liberates them; thus, this process is infinitely layered and inexhaustible.

For this reason, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati poses this question. Second, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara is able to manifest through the Universal Gate to circulate this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, whether among humans or devas, or within any buddha-field.
As for these subtle particles of earth, they shall naturally circulate everywhere, forever and without end.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati poses this question. △ Second, the Bodhisattva’s formal inquiry.
“World-Honored One, for what causes and conditions is the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara named ‘Avalokiteśvara’?
II. The Tathāgata’s Response (in three parts): 1. The General Response.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati: “Good son, if there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of sentient beings...”

They undergo various sufferings and afflictions. Upon hearing of this Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, if they single-mindedly invoke his name, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva will immediately behold their voices, and they shall all attain liberation.

Regarding the phrase "if there are immeasurable [beings] and so forth": this means that when you ask by what causes and conditions one is named Avalokiteśvara, you should know that there is no separate cause or condition;
rather, it is precisely the cause and condition of the profound union between the responsive capacity (*ki*) and the object of response (*ō*), which is termed "Avalokiteśvara.
The initial passage beginning with "If there are... clarifies that undergoing suffering constitutes the responsive capacity, numbering in the hundreds of thousands of immeasurables.
"Ten trillion sentient beings"—this refers to all within the nine realms; speaking of even a single realm, there are as many such sentient beings.
This is stated to show that those who undergo suffering are exceedingly numerous. Regarding those who experience various afflictions:
in the three miserable paths (durgati), there are the sufferings of the three paths; in the human and celestial realms, there are the sufferings of humans and devas; and among the three vehicles...
Thus, there are the sufferings of the three vehicles. In brief, view-delusion, thought-delusion, and ignorance constitute the causes of suffering and affliction for all sentient beings;
the *pariccheda* (segmented) and *pariṇāma* (transformative) deaths constitute the effects of suffering and affliction for all sentient beings.

This clarifies that the sufferings they undergo are likewise exceedingly numerous. Next, from "hearing this" onwards, it clarifies their capacity to form the resonance of the responsive stimulus. Hearing...
This Avalokiteśvara may be heard of from a Dharma master, or from a spiritual friend, or from within the sūtra scrolls.

One invokes his name with single-mindedness. There are differences between the provisional (phenomenal) and the ultimate (principle). As for single-mindedness in the phenomenal sense, it means not being divided by duality, nor divided by triality;
focusing the mind exclusively on one object is called single-mindedness in the phenomenal sense. Single-mindedness in the ultimate sense...
This is the state where subject and object are extinguished, yet subject and object remain perfectly distinct; this is what is called "single-mindedness in principle" (*li-yi-xin*).
Regarding "at that very moment" (*ji-shi*) below: it clarifies the capacity for response. "At that very moment" means that the invocation does not precede, and the response does not follow;
invocation and response are simultaneous, neither before nor after. Therefore, it is said "at that very moment. Observe its sound.
Regarding "sound": the contemplation is that which contemplates, while the vocal sounds are that which is contemplated. Regarding "all attain liberation":
although those who suffer experience an extreme abundance of suffering, they are nonetheless able to attain liberation.
The reason they are able to attain liberation is because this Bodhisattva possesses the power of great wisdom and great [compassion].
Possessing supernatural powers and great wisdom, one is able to bestow happiness upon all sentient beings;
possessing great supernatural powers, one is able to extract the suffering of all sentient beings. Therefore, one is able to cause all sentient beings—
All shall attain liberation from all suffering and affliction. △ Second, the specific answers are threefold: first, clarifying the seven calamities;

second, clarifying the three poisons; third, clarifying the two pursuits. Regarding the first [of these three], there are two parts: first, the actual clarification; second, the concluding praise. Regarding the first [of these two], there are seven [calamities]. First, the calamity of the great fire.
If there are those who hold the name of this Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, even if they enter a great fire, the fire shall not burn them;
this is due to the majestic spiritual power of this Bodhisattva.
Regarding "entering fire without being burned": this means that if one can hold the Name, one will not enter the great fire oneself;

even if one should enter the midst of a great fire, one will not be burned by it. Generally, when people of the world enter fire and are burned by it, it is entirely because they cannot hold the Name;
thus, they give rise to various conceptualizations and craving, and consequently [are consumed].
When one is scorched by the fire of afflictions (*kleśa*), one creates various unwholesome karmas; thus, one is then scorched by the fire of the bonds of karma.
When one revolves through birth and death (*saṃsāra*), one is then scorched by the fire of retributive results (*vipāka*).
Since one is already scorched by the fires of these three obstacles, one is likewise scorched by the fires of the world. Now, if one can hold the Name, then one will not [be so scorched].
Arising from craving and attachment, one does not commit evil karma and does not invite the cycle of birth and death;
thus, one is not personally burned by the fire of the fruits of karmic bondage and afflictions, and consequently is not burned by the fires of the world.
Not only is one not burned by the fires of the world, but one is moreover able to accomplish the three virtues. Because...
By virtue of upholding the Name, one is able to thoroughly comprehend that all afflictions (*kleśa*) are in their very essence entirely identical to *prajñā*;
that the karma of karmic bonds is in its very essence entirely identical to liberation (*vimukti*); and that the retribution of fruits is in its very essence entirely identical to the *dharmakāya*.

By means of these [realizations], it is said that one is no longer burned by the fires of the three obstacles; rather, the three obstacles themselves are, in their entirety, the three virtues (*triguṇa*).
It is because Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva possesses the power of great majesty and virtue that such a thing can be attained.
△ Second, the peril of great waters:
If one is being swept away by a great flood, by invoking his name, one will immediately reach shallow ground.
Regarding "immediately attaining a shallow place": although one may not yet reach the further shore, one nevertheless finds a shallow place.
If we speak in terms of the great waters, there are likewise the waters of afflictions (*kleśa*), karmic bonds, and the retribution of fruits.

Whether it be humans and devas who distance themselves from the three miserable realms, the two vehicles who escape the triple world, or even Bodhisattvas who ascend to the first stage (*prathama-vihāra*) of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-yāna*), all [attain such shallow places].
This is called a "shallow place. △ Third, the peril of the black wind:

Suppose there are hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of sentient beings who, seeking treasures such as gold, silver, lapis lazuli, tridacna shell, agate, coral, amber, and pearls, enter the great ocean. Even if a black wind should blow their ship and cast it adrift, falling...

In the realm of the rākṣasa demons, if there should be even a single person among them who invokes the name of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, all such people shall attain liberation from the perils of the rākṣasas. For this reason, he is named Avalokiteśvara.
Regarding the statement that "if one person calls out the name, all people are liberated," there are two interpretations.
First, it correctly demonstrates that the Bodhisattva possesses great majestic spiritual power; thus, although only one person calls the name, all people are liberated from their distress.
Second, it is because those people have already entered the sea together and were collectively driven by the black wind.
Being adrift together in the land of the rākṣasa demons, their sorrows and anxieties are interconnected; likewise, their hearts seeking liberation must also be identical.
Because their hearts seeking liberation are identical, even if only one person holds the Name, all may escape the calamity.
By this causal connection—referring collectively to the three aforementioned perils—one is able to invoke it.
This is called the causal condition for attaining liberation; therefore, he is named Avalokiteśvara. △ Fourth, the peril of swords and staves:

If there should be another person who is about to be harmed, and they invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, the swords and staves held by their assailants will immediately break into pieces, and they shall attain liberation.
"Facing the threat of being harmed" refers to the threat of slaughter and the threat of being beaten or thrown.
△ Fifth, the peril of evil spirits:
if the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system were filled with yakṣas and rākṣasas wishing to come and harass people, upon hearing them recite [the name],...
As for those who bear the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, even these various evil spirits cannot even look upon them with malevolent eyes,
let alone inflict harm;
they cannot even cast an evil eye upon them because they have heard the invocation of the name of Avalokiteśvara, whereby their evil [intentions]...
The mind transforms into a compassionate mind, and the malevolent gaze likewise transforms into a compassionate gaze; therefore, one is unable to look upon others with a malevolent eye.
△ Sixth, the hardship of shackles and fetters.
Furthermore, if there are people— whether guilty or innocent— who have their bodies bound by cangues, shackles, stocks, or fetters,
should they invoke the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, all such restraints shall be broken and destroyed, and they will immediately attain liberation.
"Sealed and bound in his body": "Sealed" (jian) refers to being sealed with a seal; "bound" (xi) refers to being fettered.

One who is fettered is not necessarily sealed, but one who is sealed is necessarily fettered. Therefore, it is said that he is "sealed and bound in his body. △ Seventh, the difficulty of hostile bandits.
Suppose that throughout a trichiliocosm there were enemies and bandits filling every place.
There was a merchant leader who, taking many merchants and carrying heavy treasures, was traveling along a perilous road. Among them, one person raised this cry:
"O virtuous sons, do not be afraid! You should with one mind invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara. This Bodhisattva..."
He is able to bestow fearlessness upon sentient beings. If you all invoke his name, you shall attain liberation from these enemies and bandits.
When the merchants heard this, they all raised their voices together, saying: "Namo Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva!
Because they invoked his name, they immediately attained liberation.

Regarding the "trichiliocosm": this clearly demonstrates that even those who possess so much can attain liberation; thus, it is evident that those with less can do so as well. As for the term "enemies and bandits":
an enemy necessarily seeks to take one's life, whereas a bandit seeks only to plunder one's wealth. Regarding the plundering of wealth:
It does not necessarily involve taking life; however, those who take life will inevitably plunder wealth. Therefore, they are called "vengeful thieves. △ Second, the concluding praise:
"O Akṣayamati, such is the majestic and sublime power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara."
"Sublime in this way" refers to the appearance of sublime vastness; it describes his supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*). Transversally, they pervade the ten directions;
vertically, they penetrate the three lands (*tri-bhūmi*). If one were to discuss the seven calamities, they exist only within the Land of Common Dwelling (*saha-loka-dhātu*);

yet the supernormal power of a Bodhisattva not only penetrates the Land of Common Dwelling, but also reaches as far as the Land of Residual Karmic Retribution (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*) and the Land of Replete Retribution (*vipāka-pūrṇa*).
It is vast, pervading the ten directions. △ Second, explaining the three poisons. Now, as for the three poisons:
if one loves oneself, it is called desire (*kāma*); if one loves others, it is called lust (*rāga*). To resent oneself is anger (*pratigha*); to resent others is hatred (*dveṣa*).

To be ignorant of oneself is folly (*moha*); to be ignorant of others is delusion (*avidyā*). If these are spoken of individually, they are simply termed greed, hatred, and delusion (*lobha*, *dveṣa*, *moha*). This—

These three types are all called "poisons. Just as worldly toxic drugs are certain to harm the body and cause the loss of life, these three types can all harm the *dharmakāya* and cause one to lose the life-force of wisdom; therefore, they are called poisons.

The repeated use of the word "many" precisely demonstrates that if even a great amount can be abandoned, then it goes without saying that a small amount will be as well. The text is divided into two parts.
First, the explicit explanation; second, the concluding praise. The first section has three parts. First, regarding lustful desire:
if there are sentient beings who have much lustful desire, yet constantly keep Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva in mind with reverence, they shall immediately be freed from it.
Regarding desire:
those who have much lustful desire are such because all sentient beings establish their very nature and life through lustful desire.
Without lust they are not born; without lust they do not die. Therefore, lustful desire is the root of birth and death.
Therefore, know that you must sever [these afflictions] yourself. If you wish to eliminate them, you must necessarily rely upon Avalokiteśvara;

thus, you should constantly recollect the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara. As for "constant recollection," speaking in terms of practice, it means not being dualistic regarding duality, nor triadic regarding triad;
with single-minded concentration, without the slightest interval—this is called constant recollection.
Speaking in terms of principle: one takes one’s own mind as the subject that recollects and Avalokiteśvara as the object recollected.

One’s entire subjective mind of recollection is itself the object recollected, Avalokiteśvara; and the entirety of that object recollected, Avalokiteśvara, is itself my subjective mind of recollection.
Thus, subject and object are merged and unified, yet this does not preclude my mind from functioning as the subject that recollects.
Avalokiteśvara is that which is contemplated; yet, while subject and object remain distinct, this is indeed constant mindfulness.
One thus attains freedom from desire because, through the capacity for such constant mindfulness, the Bodhisattva necessarily responds with his majestic spiritual power.
Thus, one can personally become free from lustful desire. △ Second, regarding anger:
if one has much anger, by constantly mindfuly recollecting and reverently honoring Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, one will immediately become free from anger.
Regarding what is called "anger and resentment": it is said that when a single thought of anger arises, a million gates of obstruction open.
Thus one knows that anger and resentment are the root of all evils. Therefore, by constantly recollecting Avalokiteśvara, one will be able to leave anger behind.
[This refers to] hatred. △ Third, delusion.
If one has much delusion, by constantly recollecting and paying homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, one will immediately be able to leave delusion behind.

As for "having much delusion," it is not merely being ignorant of a single thing that constitutes delusion; rather, it refers to those who cling to the views of annihilationism or eternalism, or who propound the doctrine of causelessness.
Those who slander the Mahāyāna are all what is called "deluded. This delusion can indeed be abandoned if one constantly recollects Avalokiteśvara.
Thus, whether it be lust, anger, or delusion, one is able to [overcome them].

Regarding the statement that "by mindful recollection of Avalokiteśvara, they all immediately attain liberation": this is because the minds of sentient beings can only maintain a single focus at a time and lack dual functioning;
it is entirely due to their inability to constantly recollect Avalokiteśvara that they frequently indulge in lust, anger, and ignorance.
If one can constantly keep Avalokiteśvara in mind, then the mind will always abide in Avalokiteśvara.
Furthermore, by being encompassed by the majestic spiritual power of Avalokiteśvara, one is able to attain liberation. △ Second, the concluding praise.
Akṣayamati, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara possesses such great majestic spiritual power that he brings benefit to many.
Therefore, sentient beings should constantly keep him in mind with devotion.
Regarding the two characters "Great Majestic Spiritual Power" (Mahā-vīrya-prabhāva): these refer to the aforementioned majestic spiritual power capable of transcending the three poisons.
Because he possesses great majesty, virtue, and wisdom, he is able to contemplate all things with perfect clarity; because he possesses greatness...
Through supernatural powers and vows, one is then able to deliver all beings. "To bring great benefit" means to enable sentient beings to depart from the three poisons.

"One should constantly keep this in mind" means that because the minds of sentient beings, in every thought-moment, are never without the three poisons—when they do not think of greed, they think of hatred; when they do not think of hatred, they think of [delusion].

Regarding ignorance: if one can constantly keep Avalokiteśvara in mind, one will naturally not harbor the three poisons. △ Third, the explanation of the two; fourth, the request for the three [blessings].
First, the formal explanation; second, the concluding praise; third, the resolution of doubts. Regarding the first [the formal explanation], there are two parts: first, the request for a son.

If there is a woman who wishes to give birth to a son, by paying homage to and making offerings to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, she will immediately give birth to a son endowed with merit, virtue, and wisdom.

Regarding those who are men of both merit and wisdom: if one possesses only merit but lacks wisdom, then although they may have many riches and treasures, their fame cannot reach far. If one possesses only wisdom but lacks merit, [the same result follows].
Thus, although one may achieve great renown that reaches far and wide, one cannot possess abundant wealth and treasures.
Now, when we speak of merit, virtue, wisdom, and insight, it refers not only to having abundant wealth and treasures, but also to achieving renown that reaches far and wide. △ Second, seeking a wife.

If one desires to obtain a daughter, there shall be born a daughter who is upright and possesses auspicious marks (*lakṣaṇa*), one who has planted the roots of merit (*kuśalamūla*) in past lives and is loved and respected by all people.
Regarding a daughter who is upright and possesses auspicious marks: if she were merely upright but lacked auspicious marks, she would be a mere human being.
Though one may possess the marks [of a noble person], if one lacks physical excellence (*abhirūpa*), then even if one possesses wealth and honor, one cannot be loved and cherished by others.
Now, it is said that one who possesses both physical excellence and the marks not only is loved and cherished by others, but furthermore receives wealth and honor. △ Second, the concluding praise.
Akṣayamati, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara possesses such power.
To possess such power is precisely to possess the power capable of fulfilling the two kinds of seeking. △ Third, resolving doubts.
If there are sentient beings who reverently pay homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, their merit shall not be in vain.
As for what it means for merit not to be in vain: suppose there are those currently seeking sons or daughters, yet they do not obtain them—how is this so?
The commentary then explains: It is not necessarily the case that one must worship with a sincere heart;

even if one worships with a sincere heart yet fails to obtain a son or daughter, the resulting merit and virtue will never be in vain. △ Third, the exhortation to uphold [the practice] has three parts. First, the direct exhortation.
Therefore, all sentient beings should receive and uphold the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
"Therefore" means that [the Bodhisattva] is able to deliver one from the seven calamities, able to cause one to leave the three poisons behind, and able to fulfill the two kinds of seeking.
Because such is the case, all sentient beings ought to hold his name. △ Two.
The third section on comparative evaluation begins with the Tathāgata’s question:

"Ajita, if there were someone who were to receive and uphold the names of sixty-two billion *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* bodhisattvas, and furthermore provide them with offerings of food, drink, clothing, bedding, and medicine for as long as they lived—what do you think of this, Ajita? Would this virtuous man..."
"Good son, good woman, are not your merits great?
You have received and upheld the names of Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of sixty-two billion Ganges Rivers; this refers to the vast number of their names."
"Throughout one's entire life" refers to the longevity of upholding the name. "Offering the four requisites" discusses the excellence of such offerings.
△ Second, the Bodhisattva’s response:
Wujinyi (Akṣayamati) said, "Very much, World-Honored One."
△ Third, the formal comparison. The Buddha said:

"If there is another person who receives and upholds the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, even for a single moment, and pays him homage and makes offerings, the merit of these two persons shall be exactly equal and no different; it cannot be exhausted even in hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas."
"Exhaustively":
this refers to the smallness of the names of Avalokiteśvara that are upheld. "At one time": this clarifies the brevity of the duration.
"Merely prostrating": this clarifies the inferiority of the offering. As for the phrase "perfectly equal and without difference," although one may uphold [the name]...
Their names may be many or few; the duration of time may be long or brief; and the offerings provided may be superior or inferior.
Yet the merit of these two persons is entirely immeasurable, equal, and without distinction. The reason they are without distinction is as follows:
Indeed, sixty-two billion bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, have likewise not gone beyond realizing this true mark (*dharmatā*).
Avalokiteśvara, too, has realized this true mark. Because that which they have realized is the same single true mark, within this true mark—

Fundamentally, there is nothing to be obtained in terms of quantity or magnitude, duration or brevity, superiority or inferiority. Therefore, the merit of these two individuals is exactly equal and without difference.
Furthermore, this lack of difference arises because the one and the many are non-obstructive, and duration and brevity are not two.
△ Third, the summary.
"Akṣayamati, by upholding the name of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, one obtains such immeasurable and boundless benefits of merit.

Having thus finished the question regarding the person of Avalokiteśvara, [the second part] consists of two sections concerning the Dharma of the Universal Gate (*Samantamukha*): first, the question posed by the Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how does the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara traverse this Sahā world?
How does he preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings? What are the matters concerning the power of his skillful means?"
This refers to one who contemplates Avalokiteśvara, being able to abide in the Dharma of the Universal Gate (Samantamukha) to deliver all sentient beings.

When delivering beings, one must necessarily employ the mental faculty (manas-karma) to discern their capacities, the verbal faculty (vāk-karma) to preach the Dharma, and the physical faculty (kāya-karma) to manifest supernatural powers.
Therefore, the present inquiry concerns the Dharma of the Universal Gate by way of these three faculties. It says:
"What is it like to roam this Sahā world? asks concerning his body-wheel (*kāya-cakra*).

"How does he preach the Dharma for sentient beings? asks concerning his speech-wheel (*vāk-cakra*). "What is the nature of the power of his skillful means (*upāya*)? asks concerning his mind-wheel (*manas-cakra*).
II. The Tathāgata’s Response. This is further divided into four parts: first, the individual responses; second, the general response; third... [text continues].

Exhortation to Offerings; Fourth, the Conclusion. Regarding the text herein, if it appears contrary to the preceding discussion, one should understand that the seven difficulties mentioned above, along with the three poisons and two pursuits, represent the manifest capacity (*mārga*) and the hidden response (*yìng*).
Herein, as for which body should be used to deliver beings, the manifestation of whatever body is necessary to preach the Dharma represents the hidden capacity and the manifest response.
Thus, the preceding and following contexts illuminate one another. There is absolutely no occasion without a response, nor is there ever a response without an occasion.

Furthermore, above, there is first a general answer followed by a specific answer; below, there is first a specific answer followed by a general answer. Above, there is an exhortation to uphold the Name.
The subsequent exhortation to offer worship is also clearly elucidated in the text; a detailed examination will make this evident. The initial specific response is divided into two parts.

First, the clarification of the Buddha’s body: the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati, saying, "Good son, if there are sentient beings in a certain land who should be [reached] by means of the Buddha-body..."
For those who are to be delivered by means of the Buddha-body, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva immediately manifests in the form of a Buddha and preaches the Dharma for them.
For those who are to be delivered by means of the Pratyekabuddha-body, he immediately manifests in the form of a Pratyekabuddha and preaches the Dharma for them.
For those who are to be delivered by means of the Śrāvaka-body, he immediately manifests in the form of a Śrāvaka and preaches the Dharma for them.

"For those who should be saved by a Buddha-body" refers to the discernment of their capacities through mental action (*manas-karman*). "Immediately manifesting a Buddha-body" refers to the manifestation of supernormal powers through physical action (*kāya-karman*).
"And preaching the Dharma for them" refers to the preaching of the Dharma through verbal action (*vāk-karman*).

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "should be [saved] by a Buddha-body," this answers the question concerning the power of his skillful means; what is the nature of that matter? This is the inquiry concerning mental action. Immediately—
"Manifesting the Buddha-body" answers the question regarding the physical activity (*kāyakarman*) of how one wanders through this Sahā world.
"Expounding the Dharma for them" answers the question regarding the verbal activity (*vākkarman*) of how one expounds the Dharma for sentient beings.

There are three kinds of Buddha-bodies: namely, manifesting a superior body for those who are to be liberated by the manifestation of a superior body; [manifesting] an inferior [body] for those who are to be [liberated by it];...

For those who are to be delivered through a "lesser body," he manifests a lesser body. For those who are to be delivered through a "combined body"—that is, by means of both the lesser and the superior—he manifests a combined body.
This preacher of the Dharma differs from [the teaching in] the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, where one teaches whatever dharma is appropriate for a given occasion;
here, he teaches exclusively the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* so that all sentient beings throughout the dharma-realm may ultimately converge upon the Single Buddha Vehicle. Furthermore...
Regarding the fact that this does not explicitly mention the "Bodhisattva body," some say it should be understood as being included within the Buddha body.
One should know that while the thirty-two manifestations are the bodies that appear, the Bodhisattva is the body that manifests them.
Although there are differences among these thirty-two bodies, they are all equally manifestations of the single body of the Bodhisattva; thus, every individual body is [the Bodhisattva].
This is a Bodhisattva. Therefore, although he does not manifest in the form of a Bodhisattva, in meaning he is indeed complete [in those qualities].
If one follows the example of what was manifested by the Sublime Sound (Ghoṣadatta) above, it has never been absent; it is merely omitted here for brevity.
This is likewise true for all those from the Pratyekabuddhas downward. Each and every one possesses the three answers, and the Dharma they preach is entirely the Sublime Dharma (Saddharma).
...and so forth. △ Second, clarifying the ordinary body, in four parts. First, manifesting the bodies of various devas:
To those who are to be delivered by the body of a Brahmā King, he immediately manifests the body of a Brahmā King and preaches the Dharma for them.
To those who are to be delivered by the body of Śakra, he immediately manifests the body of Śakra and preaches the Dharma for them. To those who are to be delivered by the body of Maheśvara...
For those who are to be delivered by appearing in the form of Īśvara, he manifests the body of Īśvara and preaches the Dharma for them.
For those who are to be delivered by appearing in the form of Maheśvara, he manifests the body of Maheśvara and preaches the Dharma for them.
