For those who are to be delivered by appearing in the form of a celestial general, he manifests the body of a celestial general and preaches the Dharma for them. For those who are to be delivered by appearing in the form of Vaiśravaṇa...
For those who are to be delivered through the form of a body, he manifests as the body of Vaiśravaṇa and preaches the Dharma for them.
As for the body of a Great General of the Heavens, this refers to the Great General Sanzhi. As for the body of Maheśvara, this refers to the Māra-king of the Desire Realm.
For their sake, he preaches the wondrous Dharma, causing them to thoroughly comprehend that the nature of the realm of Māra is identical to the Buddha-nature.
The realm is suchness; it is the one suchness, which is non-dual suchness. Vaiśravaṇa means "Much-Hearing" (Duowen);
he is the Heavenly King of the North. △ Second, manifesting in the form of a human being.
To those who are to be saved by the body of a minor king, he manifests the body of a minor king and preaches the Dharma for them.
To those who are to be saved by the body of an elder, he manifests the body of an elder and preaches the Dharma for them.

To those who are to be saved by the body of a householder, he manifests the body of a householder and preaches the Dharma for them. To those who are to be saved by the body of a high official, he manifests...

He manifests in the body of a minister and preaches the Dharma for them. To those who are to be liberated by appearing in the body of a brahmin, he immediately manifests in the body of a brahmin and preaches the Dharma.

To those who are to be liberated by appearing in the bodies of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās, he immediately manifests in the bodies of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās and preaches the Dharma for them.

He preaches the Dharma. To those who are to be liberated by appearing in the form of a householder, a lay devotee, a government official, a brahmin, or a woman, he manifests in the body of a woman and preaches the Dharma for them.
To those who are to be liberated by appearing in the form of a boy or a girl, he manifests in the body of a boy or a girl and preaches the Dharma for them.

Regarding the manifestation as a minor king (*kṣudrarāja*): this must include both universal monarchs (*cakravartin*) and minor kings of the *śūdraka* type. Among universal monarchs, those with the golden wheel are "great," while the other three are "minor.
Among the *śūdraka* kings, those of the primary lineage are "great," while the vassal states are "minor. Since even these minor ones manifest, [the others do so as well].
The greater [manifestations] can be understood by this principle; therefore, he merely manifests the bodies of minor kings. A "longer" (zhǎngzhě) possesses the virtue of leading others.
A "lay practitioner" (jūshì) is one who purifies the mind and diminishes desire, dwelling in the Way for oneself. An "official" (zǎiguān):
"minister" (zǎi) takes governance as its meaning, while "office" (guān) takes functional capacity as its meaning. △ Third, manifesting the bodies of the eight classes of beings.
For those who are to be delivered by means of the bodies of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras,
mahoragas, humans, or non-humans, he manifests all such forms and preaches the Dharma for them.
△ Fourth, manifesting as the Dharma-body Protector:
For those who are to be delivered by means of the Vajrapāṇi deity, he immediately manifests as the Vajrapāṇi deity and preaches the Dharma for them.
As for the Vajrapāṇi deity, he is so named because he constantly holds a vajra-treasure mallet in his hand.
If we discuss its causes and conditions: In the distant past, there was a king who had two wives.
One wife gave birth to a thousand sons, all of whom became Buddhas—beginning with Vipaśyin and ending with Ruci Buddha.
The other wife gave birth to two sons; one vowed to exhort his thousand elder brothers to turn the wheel of Dharma, and the other vowed to protect and uphold them.
Regarding the Dharma-teaching of his elder brother: the deity who now wields the vajra-treasure mace is the second son born of the second consort;
he is the one who vows to protect the Dharma-teaching of the thousand brothers. Because he desires to protect the Buddha-Dharma, he constantly wields the vajra-mace.
The above entirely clarifies that Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva is able to rely upon the principle of true reality (*dharmatā*).
He opens the universal gate. With thirty-two bodies and nineteen modes of preaching the Dharma, he has completed his specific answers.
△ Second, the general answer:
"Ajita, this Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara has accomplished such meritorious virtues; by means of various forms, he wanders..."

The various lands where sentient beings are delivered and liberated in their manifold forms refer to the forms of the ten dharma realms. Since it specifies "manifold," this does not stop at the thirty-two bodies.
As for "wandering through various lands," these are the lands of the ten directions; since it specifies "various lands," then...

It does not stop at the *sahā* world of common dwelling. Thus, although the previous section spoke of "distinction," its phrasing was extensive while its meaning was actually brief, as it explained only the thirty-two bodies within this land of common dwelling.

Furthermore, although this current section speaks of "generality," its phrasing is brief while its meaning is actually extensive; herein, it also fully incorporates the three answers mentioned above, through various...
"Form. This single character signifies that the mental karma (*manas-karman*) mirrors the capacities of sentient beings. Question: What are the manifestations of the power of skillful means? Answer:
"Various forms" refers to the physical karma (*kāya-karman*) manifesting supernatural powers. Question: How does one roam throughout the Sahā world? Answer:
To deliver and liberate sentient beings refers to the verbal karma (*vāk-karman*) preaching the Dharma. Question: How does one preach for the sake of sentient beings? △
The third section, "Exhortation to Offerings," consists of six parts.
First, the Tathāgata’s direct exhortation: "Therefore, you all should with one mind make offerings to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is able to bestow fearlessness amidst terrors and urgent perils; for this reason, in this Sahā world..."
Throughout all worlds, he is universally known as the Bestower of Fearlessness.
II. The Bodhisattvas Offer Worship:
The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, I shall now offer worship to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara."
He immediately untied from his neck a necklace of various precious jewels worth hundreds of thousands of taels of gold and gave it to him, saying:
"Virtuous one, accept this gift of Dharma, this precious jewel necklace."
Prompted by the encouragement of the Tathāgata, Akṣayamati immediately untied the necklace from his neck as an offering.
The neck represents the true mark (*dharmatā*), while the necklace represents practice. Its value of hundreds of thousands signifies the eighty-four thousand *pāramitās*.
Thus, when a bodhisattva gives rise to practice based on the principle of the true mark, they bring forth cultivation entirely from within the nature (*xing*). Entirely...

The practice of the Dharma according to principle is established in accordance with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) and involves no creator; therefore, it is symbolized by the removal of the necklace.
As for the statement "receiving this gift of Dharma," if it were a necklace, it would be a material gift (*āmiṣadāna*); why then is it called a gift of Dharma?
For one who can thoroughly comprehend the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), there is nothing that is not sublime contemplation; thus, wealth is itself the Dharma. As it is said:
"That which is equal regarding wealth is also equal regarding the Dharma; that which is equal regarding the Dharma is also equal regarding wealth.
Just as the Medicine King (*Bhaiṣajyarāja*) made a true offering of the Dharma, this very giving of material wealth is, in fact, the giving of the Dharma. △ Third, Avalokiteśvara does not accept it.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara was unwilling to accept it.
There were two reasons for his refusal to accept: first, although Akṣayamati had received the Tathāgata’s command to make offerings, he had thus raised the offering;
however, Avalokiteśvara had not received the Tathāgata’s command to accept the offering, so how could he accept it?
Therefore, as for his refusal to accept them, it can be seen from the following text. Second, those *mālā* (necklaces) offered by him fully represent the practice of the causal stage (*hetu-caryā*).

Now, Avalokiteśvara is likewise situated within the causal stage; both are at the level of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*). If one is in the causal stage, one is destined to realize the fruit (*phala*).
There is no case where the cause returns to realize the cause, nor where cultivation returns to realize cultivation. Therefore, he was unwilling to accept them.
Thus it was said. △ Fourth, the Bodhisattvas’ Repeated Request:
Ajita, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati, again addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying: "O Benevolent One, out of compassion for us, please accept this necklace."
Regarding the phrase "pitying us": although Akṣayamati and Avalokiteśvara are both at the stage of a cause, there is nonetheless a distinction between their initial mind and their subsequent mind.
Thus, the one with the subsequent mind should pity the one with the initial mind; for this reason, it is said that he "pities us."

The term "etc. (等) means that this applies equally to all the fourfold assemblies of devas and humans. This shows that the Bodhisattva’s offering and service are performed not only for his own sake, but also on behalf of others.
△ Fifth, the Tathāgata commands him to accept [the offerings].

At that time, the Buddha addressed Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva: "You should take pity upon this Akṣayamati Bodhisattva, as well as the fourfold assembly, and the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas."
Because they are humans and non-humans alike, they accept these ornaments.
This means that since they have already made offerings out of compassion for the multitude, you too should accept them out of compassion for the multitude.
△ Sixth, Avalokiteśvara accepts the offerings.

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, out of compassion for the fourfold assembly, as well as for the devas, nāgas, humans, non-humans, and others, accepted the necklace and divided it into two parts.
One part he offered to Śākyamuni Buddha; the other part he offered to the stupa of Prabhūtaratna Buddha.
Because Avalokiteśvara accepted [the teaching] upon the encouragement of the Tathāgata, he immediately received it; thus, it can be understood that the former [Śāriputra] did not accept it.
As for dividing it into two parts, this symbolizes all his practices, which entirely rely upon the true mark (*dharmatā*).
Thus, one does not perceive even the slightest dharma arising, nor does one perceive even the slightest dharma ceasing; the entire body is neither born nor extinguished—this is the true mark.

This practice honors the two Buddhas, symbolizing the attainment of the fruit that is neither born nor extinguished. Because Śākyamuni is currently present yet proclaims his desire to enter parinirvāṇa, he represents non-arising;
because Prabhūtaratna has entered parinirvāṇa and once praised [this teaching] as "Excellent" from within his stupa, he represents non-extinction.
Therefore, this signifies that [the teaching] is not extinguished. Furthermore, the manifestation of the cause through practice naturally accords with the fruit;
although it was received by virtue of the Buddha’s command, it is thus returned to the two World-Honored Ones. △ Fourth, the summary.
Akṣayamati, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara possesses such sovereign spiritual powers as these while wandering through the Sahā world.
△ Second, the verse summary. These verses do not exist in the Qin edition; they were translated by Jñānagupta. Hereafter...
Supplemented from the Qin edition. The Great Master Ciyun provided an exegesis based on the underlying meaning; that which is compiled in the *Kezhu* (Sectional Commentary) is precisely his exegesis.
It is now divided into two parts. First: The Bodhisattva’s Question.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati asked in verse:
“World-Honored One, endowed with wondrous marks, I now ask you again: For what cause and condition, O Son of the Buddha, is he named Avalokiteśvara?”

Regarding the phrase "asking them again": although the above questions have already been posed and the Tathāgata has provided answers for each one, we now wish to examine their meaning in further detail;
therefore, he speaks these verses once more. The line beginning with "For what cause and by what condition" asks why the three types of karma are as they are;
this is the summary verse of the inquiry. The two lines beginning with "O Son of the Buddha" [serve as the response].
This is a separate verse of inquiry. △ Second, the Tathāgata’s response, in two parts. First, the general response:
"The Honored One, endowed with wondrous marks, answers the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati in verse: 'Listen to the practice of Avalokiteśvara; he skillfully responds to all places.'"
His great vows are as deep as the ocean; throughout inconceivable kalpas, he has served many billions of Buddhas and made vast, pure aspirations.
"Listen well, you all"—the meaning of this is that you have asked by what causes and conditions he is named Avalokiteśvara, and I shall now further explain this for you.
Listen with truth and sincerity. As for the practitioner of Avalokiteśvara, [Avalokiteśvara] is...
Great compassion and wisdom are able to give rise to inconceivable and wondrous practices because they skillfully respond to all directions and locations.
As for "all directions": horizontally, they pervade the ten directions; vertically, they penetrate the three lands.
Because there is no land within the ten directions or the three lands where [the Buddha] does not appear, he is able to seek out sounds to rescue those in suffering and deliver sentient beings.

This is called the "Responsive Excellence. Because one has thoroughly realized the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena—wherein every phenomenon is true and every characteristic is real—the lands of the ten directions are entirely the mind-only, and all sentient beings are likewise the self-nature.
Thus, it is the Mind-Only Avalokiteśvara who manifests in the land of mind-only, and the Self-Nature Avalokiteśvara who delivers sentient beings of self-nature.
It is established in accordance with the true nature (*dharmatā*) and does not rely on artificial fabrication; therefore, it is "skillfully appropriate.
This clarifies his wondrous conduct. Below the phrase "vast vows" (*mahāpraṇidhāna*), the text clarifies his aspiration.

Regarding the statement that "the vast vows are as deep as the ocean," it means that the vows he has generated seek, above, to propagate the Way of all Buddhas, and below, to transform the beings of the nine realms. As it is said:
Reaching to the heights above and penetrating to the depths below, it is thus said to be like the ocean.
"Inconceivable eons" refers to the duration of time experienced, which is exceedingly vast; this is what is meant by "inconceivable.

Within these inconceivable eons, he attended upon many thousands of billions of Buddhas, and in the presence of those many thousands of billions of Buddhas, he was further able to give rise to a vast and pure resolve.
This is the vow. As for the previous mention of "vast vows" (mahāpraṇidhāna) and this subsequent mention of "vow" (praṇidhāna): the former was a general resolve, while this is a specific vow.
Because he possesses the practice of great wisdom, he is able to contemplate all things with perfect clarity;
because he possesses the vow of great purity, he is able to deliver all beings extensively. △ Second, the detailed response, which has two parts. First, the response in verse.

[The Buddha] shows [the benefits]. The two verses exhort [the audience] to uphold [the teaching]. The first two [verses] concern Avalokiteśvara himself; the second two concern the Dharma of the Universal Gate. Regarding the first two, the initial verse is a general summary: "I have briefly explained for you:
hearing his name, seeing his body, or calling him to mind—none of these pass in vain; they can extinguish all suffering within the realms of existence."
Regarding what I have briefly explained for you: the causes and conditions thereof are exceedingly numerous and immeasurable;
I am likewise unable to explain them to you in detail one by one, but shall instead speak of them to you in brief. As for the phrase "hearing the name" and so forth:
there are those who hear the name and uphold it, and there are those who see the physical form and pay homage and make offerings.
If there are those who constantly maintain mindfulness and reverence so that their minds do not pass in vain, then their spiritual capacity has already become sincere;

they will surely evoke a response. Thus, whether suffering within the twenty-five realms of existence, encountering the seven calamities, meeting with the three poisons, or being caught in the two types of seeking, those who hear the name, behold the physical form, or bring it to mind shall experience the mutual resonance of cause and effect, whereby all [sufferings] are eliminated.
This follows the vows. △ Second, the specific verses are divided into two parts: first, the verses on the seven calamities along with the addition of other calamities;
second, the verses on the three poisons as well as the two types of seeking. The first part is further divided into twelve sections; the first is the direct verse on the calamity of the great fire.
Even if someone should give rise to a malicious intent and push one into a great pit of fire, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, that fiery pit will transform into a pond.
Regarding the phrase "recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara": the mind that is capable of recollecting is itself the Avalokiteśvara being recollected;

the entirety of the Avalokiteśvara being recollected is itself the mind capable of recollecting. Originally, there is neither "this" nor "that. One should know that although there is no subject or object, [the transformation occurs].
It does not hinder the fact that the subject and object remain distinct: my own mind is the one who recollects, while Avalokiteśvara is the one recollected.

The recollecting subject is the invocation; the recollected object is the response. Thus, although there is no distinction between self and other within the ultimate reality, we nevertheless differentiate between them.
The first two lines describe encountering difficulty; the third line describes holding the name; the fourth line describes receiving the response. The following eleven lines are all...
There are three meanings; the division of the text follows the same pattern. △ Second, the verse on the peril of the great waters:
"Whether drifting upon the vast ocean, facing the perils of dragons, fish, and various spirits, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, the waves cannot submerge one."
△ Third, the difficulty of falling from Mount Sumeru:
Should one be on a peak of Mount Sumeru and be pushed over by someone, by the power of recollecting Avalokiteśvara, one will abide in the sky like the sun.
△ Fourth, there is the difficulty of falling upon a diamond mountain.
Even if one is pursued by evil people and falls down a diamond mountain, by recollecting the power of that Avalokiteśvara, not even a single hair can be harmed.
△ Fifth, the verse on transcending the calamity of vengeful bandits:

If one encounters vengeful bandits surrounding them, each wielding a blade to inflict harm, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, they will all immediately give rise to a mind of loving-kindness.
△ Sixth, the verse following the previous one on the perils of swords and staves:

Should one encounter the suffering of royal punishment, On the verge of execution as life draws to its end, By recollecting the power of that Avalokiteśvara, The blade shall instantly shatter into pieces.
△ Seventh, the verse summarizing the difficulty of shackles and fetters:
Whether imprisoned or bound by shackles and fetters, with hands and feet constrained by cangues and manacles, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, one is released and attains liberation.
△ Eighth, the verse on the difficulty of poisons:
"Regarding various poisons used in curses and incantations intended to harm one's body—if one recollects the power of that Avalokiteśvara, they shall return to the person who sent them."
Someone may raise this doubt: "If the retribution falls upon the perpetrator himself, it seems as though the Great Compassion of the Bodhisattva is deficient.
However, since the victim invoked Avalokiteśvara and was thus delivered from the peril, we know that had the perpetrator himself invoked Avalokiteśvara, he too would certainly have been delivered.
How, then, could there be any deficiency in Great Compassion? △ Ninth: A Recapitulative Verse on the Peril of Malevolent Ghosts.
Or if one encounters evil rākṣasas, venomous dragons, various ghosts, and the like, by recollecting the power of that Avalokiteśvara, they will all at once dare not cause harm.
△ Tenth: An added verse on the peril of ferocious beasts.
If one is surrounded by fierce beasts with fearsome, sharp teeth and claws, by recollecting the power of that Avalokiteśvara, they will flee swiftly to boundless directions.
△ Eleven: An added verse on the peril of venomous snakes.
The venomous vipers, snakes, and scorpions, whose poisonous breath is like smoke and fire—upon recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, they turn back immediately upon hearing his voice.
△ Twelfth: An added verse on the calamity of hail and rain.
When clouds and thunder roll, lightning flashes, and hail falls with torrential rain, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, they shall be dispersed and vanish in a timely manner.
Unseasonable thunder and rain are likewise among the calamities; these are all brought about by the evil karma of sentient beings.
How much more so when one can recollect Avalokiteśvara—then karma itself will be transformed and the calamity itself will be resolved. Therefore, they are dispersed and vanish in a timely manner.
△ Second, two verses on the three poisons and the two types of seeking:
"Sentient beings are beset by calamities; immeasurable suffering oppresses their bodies. By the wondrous power of wisdom, Avalokiteśvara can rescue the world from its suffering."
"Entrapped in distress": this refers to being entrapped by the three poisons and the two types of seeking.
The three poisons take that which exists as suffering; the two seekings take that which does not exist as suffering. Although existence and non-existence differ, the entrapment is one and the same.

[The Bodhisattva] can only rescue one from the suffering of the three poisons and the two seekings. The above constitutes the verse-response regarding the person who contemplates Avalokiteśvara. △ Second, the verses [of praise].
The Universal Gate Dharma has two parts. First, the general verse:

Possessing the power of supernatural penetrations, And extensively cultivating the skillful means of wisdom, Throughout the lands of the ten directions, There is no realm where he does not manifest his body.
△ Second, the three individual verses. First, the verse answers regarding bodily action:
The various evil destinies— Hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals, And the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death— He causes them all to be gradually extinguished.
The phrase "various kinds" and so forth refers collectively to the nine realms as the evil destinies (*durgati*), with only the Buddha-realm being considered wholesome.

The single phrase "hell" specifically singles out the three miserable paths (*tiryag-yoni*). Regarding "gradually causing them to be extinguished": it means causing humans and devas to extinguish the three miserable paths;

causing those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) to extinguish the triple world (*tridhātu*); and causing Bodhisattvas to extinguish the three emptinesses (*trīṇi śūnyatāni*). Thus, it is gradual.
Extinguished. Ultimately, it causes one to enter the secret treasury of the three virtues. △ Second, the verse answering regarding the mental karma:

"The contemplation of reality, the pure contemplation, the contemplation of vast wisdom, the contemplation of compassion, and the contemplation of loving-kindness—may I always aspire to and constantly gaze upon them."
Stainless and pure light; the sun of wisdom destroys all darkness. It can subdue the winds and fires of calamity, universally illuminating the world.
Because contemplation can manifest principle, it is called "True"; because it can destroy delusion, it is called "Pure. In manifesting principle, there is no principle that is not manifested;
in destroying delusion, there is no delusion that is not destroyed. Therefore, it is called "Vast Wisdom. This refers to one's own practice.
Furthermore, when transforming others, if one wishes to employ great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) to uproot suffering, one does not depart from this contemplation;

hence it is called "compassion. If one wishes to employ great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) to bestow happiness, one likewise does not depart from this contemplation; hence it is called "loving-kindness."
In this way, for the sentient beings of the nine realms—at every thought-moment, at all times, and in every place—may he grant his responsive manifestation so that they may gaze upon him;
hence it is said, "constantly wishing and constantly gazing. The two lines concerning "stainless" eulogize wisdom (*prajñā*).

While the preceding spoke of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), this speaks of wisdom; for there is nothing to be contemplated in contemplation—it is wisdom itself that constitutes contemplation. This is why it is called "wisdom-contemplation."
By comparing the present with what precedes it, one knows that these five contemplations are all wisdom. △ Third, the conclusion answering the bestowal and extraction:
The thunderous roar of the precepts, whose essence is compassion; the wondrous great cloud of a benevolent mind; raining down the nectar of the Dharma rain, extinguishes the flames of affliction.

In places where one is involved in litigation before the authorities, or amidst the terrors of a military array, by recollecting the power of that Avalokiteśvara, all enemies shall retreat and disperse.
This clarifies how compassion extracts suffering and loving-kindness bestows happiness, with each dharma mutually interpenetrating the other.
Just as Heaven must first thunder and spread clouds before it desires to rain, so too does the Bodhisattva manifest his form and preach the Dharma, desiring to rescue sentient beings.

Suffering. To bestow happiness upon sentient beings, one must likewise spread clouds and thunder, manifesting supernatural powers with the body while pouring down the rain of ambrosia through the mouth by preaching the Dharma.
△ Second, the verse on exhortation to uphold [the teaching].
The Sublime Sound, the Avalokiteśvara, the Brahma-sound, the Tide-sound—surpassing all sounds of the world. Therefore, one should constantly keep him in mind;
at every thought, do not give rise to doubt. The Pure and Holy Avalokiteśvara can act as a refuge in the face of suffering, affliction, and the peril of death.
Possessing all merits, gazing upon sentient beings with eyes of compassion, an ocean of immeasurable accumulations of merit—therefore, one should pay homage to him.
Regarding "Wonderful Sound" (Ghoṣadatta): some point to the Bodhisattva Ghoṣadatta of the preceding chapter as being this "Wonderful Sound," but this is most incorrect.

Because when the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara contemplates the sounds of the world through his wondrous contemplation, he is able to see that all phenomena are truly such and all appearances are truly real;
since every sound is the entirety of the true mark (*dharmatā*), he is called "Wondrous Sound Contemplating the Sounds of the World.
Furthermore, regarding the object of contemplation—the wondrous sound—and the contemplating wisdom—Avalokiteśvara—whether it be the object or the wisdom, [they are both one].
Since both share the same essence of the bodhisattva’s single thought-moment, the objective realm is "Wondrous Sound" (Ghoṣa) and wisdom is "Avalokiteśvara.
"Sanskrit Sound" (Brahmaghoṣa) refers to thoroughly realizing that the observed realm is entirely empty and quiescent; it is thus free from desire and pure.
"Ocean Tide Sound" (Sāgaraghoṣa) means that upon hearing its sound once, he immediately manifests his body to preach the Dharma, just like the sound of the ocean.

He does not miss the proper time. As for the Pure and Holy One, Avalokiteśvara, since he was originally the Tathāgata Dharmaprabhāsa of the past and has already attained ultimate realization, he now turns his compassionate vessel backward to deliver all sentient beings.
Flowing against the current, he manifests a trace of ignorance characterized by the appearance of birth, yet in reality he has already been able to exhaust it;
therefore, he is called a "Pure Sage. △ Second, the benefits gained from hearing this chapter.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Earth-Holder rose from his seat, came forward, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, if there are sentient beings who hear this chapter on Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva—concerning his sovereign karma and the supernatural powers manifested through the Universal Gate—"

It should be known that the merit of such a person is not small. When the Buddha preached this "Universal Gate" chapter, eighty-four thousand sentient beings among the assembly all resolved their minds upon unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, which is peerless.

First is the praise by the Earth-Holding Deity; next is the benefit received by the great assembly. Within the first section, the "Chapter on Avalokiteśvara" describes the sovereign activity [of the Bodhisattva], which refers to the person who is Avalokiteśvara;
the "Universal Gate Manifestation of Supernatural Powers" refers to the Dharma of the Universal Gate.
Following the passage beginning with "Next, the Buddha said," it should be understood that this correctly clarifies the attainment of benefits. This concludes the commentary on Avalokiteśvara.
The "Universal Gate" Chapter of the Bodhisattva concludes.

The Dharani Chapter, the Twenty-sixth of the Lotus Sutra.
If one clarifies the sequence of the successive development of this chapter, it generally proceeds as follows:

since the Tathāgata has already once entrusted [the teaching] for its circulation, he causes all bodhisattvas to study the Tathāgata’s Dharma accordingly, so that they may disseminate it wherever they go.

In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it is said that one should follow and learn from their ascetic practices, one should follow and learn from their supernormal powers, and one should follow and learn from their Universal Gate [samādhi], just as those such as Bhaiṣajyarāja, Gadgadasvara, and Avalokiteśvara did.
However, in the evil world of the future, there will be many afflictions and obstacles; if one does not rely upon dhāraṇīs as an external protection, then how...
It is through being unimpeded wherever one may be that [the teaching] is circulated. Therefore, following the "Chapter on Avalokiteśvara," there is this "Dhāraṇī Chapter";
it is the text concerning external protection for circulation. As for the term *dhāraṇī*, it is a Sanskrit word;
here it is translated as "Total Retention" (*zongchi*). This is because it summarizes all that is wholesome and maintains all meanings. Furthermore, it is said:

Restraint and maintenance: that is to say, restraining all evil and maintaining all good. For humans and devas, this means restraining the evils of the three miserable realms and maintaining the goodness of the precepts.
For those of the Two Vehicles, it means restraining the evils of the triple world and maintaining the goodness of the truths and conditions.
The Bodhisattva obstructs the evils of the three emptinesses and maintains the virtues of the six perfections.
If we speak according to this present sutra, there are no evils of the nine realms, the three vehicles, or the seven kinds of expedient means that are not obstructed;
and there are no virtues of the true reality of all dharmas realized by the Buddhas and their long-lasting life-span that are not maintained. However, as for the dhāraṇīs, some...
It is employed for the purpose of treating illness; some employ it for the purpose of extinguishing transgressions; others employ it for the purpose of protecting the Dharma.
Now, this is neither for treating illness nor for extinguishing transgressions; it is precisely employed for the purpose of protecting the Dharma.
That it is able to protect the Dharma is truly because the Buddhas have realized the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
The essence of the far-reaching lifespan now gives rise to inconceivable function from its inconceivable essence;
thus, it is able to protect and uphold the Buddha-dharma, eliminate all obstacles, and ensure that it circulates everywhere without interruption.
△ The text of this chapter is divided into three parts: first, the measurement of merit; second, the recitation of mantras for protection; third, the benefits obtained by hearing this chapter.
[The Chapter on] Increasing Benefit. Part One. Two Sections. First, the Bodhisattva poses the question:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, if there are good sons or good daughters who are able to receive, uphold, and recite the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, if..."
If one recites and masters [the sutra], or transcribes it into a scroll, how much merit will one obtain?
△ Second, the Tathāgata’s response and instruction has three parts. First, the Tathāgata’s question:
The Buddha addressed Bhaisajyarāja: "If there are good sons or good daughters who make offerings to eight hundred million nayutas..."
"Furthermore, suppose there were as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River. What do you think? Would the merit obtained thereby not be great?
△ Second, the Bodhisattva’s reply.
"Very much so, World-Honored One.
△ Third, the formal comparison.
The Buddha said: "If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were able, regarding this sutra, to even receive and uphold a single four-line verse..."
Verse: To read, recite, and understand the meaning, and to practice according to the teaching, brings forth immense merit.
△ Second, the protection through the recitation of mantras has three parts: first, the Bodhisattvas; second, the Heavenly Kings; third, the Rākṣasas.
While it is common for Bodhisattvas and Heavenly Kings to protect the Buddha-dharma across all sutras, the Rākṣasas were originally ghosts that feed upon human flesh and cause affliction.
Regarding those who cause disorder: there are now those who possess a mind of protection and maintenance; this is due to the power of the wondrous sutra.

Thus, their evil minds are transformed into virtuous minds, and their afflictive disturbances are transformed into great protection. Therefore, within this sutra, vows are also made for the sake of such great protection.
This is divided into two parts: first, Bhaiṣajyarāja; second, Śūradatta. The first part is further divided into four sections; the first is as follows:
"Please speak.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, I shall now provide the dhāraṇī-mantra for those who preach the Dharma, in order to protect them."
Regarding the term "dhāraṇī-mantra": "mantra" is a word of the Flower Language (Chinese); it is not a Sanskrit term. A mantra is a prayer for blessings.

By virtue of the power of the mantra, one prays for blessings and immediately obtains them according to one's wishes; therefore, it is called a "prayer for blessings. It is like the *mínglíng* (a type of caterpillar) in the world.
Any mantra for subduing insects, such as "Lüwo, Lüwo," immediately brings about their submission.
It is also like a secret command within an army, where those who violate it are not pardoned. Furthermore, these are the "five reasons for not translating" among the esoteric words of the Buddhas.
△ Second, the actual recitation.
That is, the mantra is spoken as follows: *Anile | Manile | Māṇe | Mamāṇe | Jvale | Cāledhe | Śame | Śalivarte*.
Śānte. Mukte. Mukta-ri. Sva-ri. Avaśa-ri. Yau-ri. Sva-ri. Kṣaye. Akṣaye. Agini. Śānte. Śa-ri. Dhāraṇi.
Alukha-vasa-pa-ca-vikṣaṇi. Niviti. Abhantara-niviti. Adanta-pariśuddhi. O.
Kauṣṭhila. Maukauṣṭhila. Araḷe. Parāḷe. Śukradhe. Asamasame. Buddhapraticchede. Dharmapraticchede.
Saṃghanirghoṣaṇi. Vāśa vāśa śuddhe. Mandra. Mandrākṣaya-te. Yaulūṭa. Yaulūṭa-kau.
Śalaya. Akṣara. Akṣayyadāya. Aparu. Amaraṇadāya. (Forty-three phrases) △ Third, the concluding praise.
World-Honored One, this dhāraṇī mantra has been spoken by as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in sixty-two billion Ganges Rivers.
If anyone should violate or harm this Dharma-preacher, they would thereby have violated and harmed all those Buddhas.

As for the statement that "to injure or destroy a Dharma teacher is to injure or destroy all Buddhas," this *dhāraṇī* mantra is precisely what has been spoken by all Buddhas; thus, the entire mantra is the Buddha himself.
Now, since one protects the Dharma teacher by means of this mantra, the person is entirely identical with the mantra. Therefore, to injure or destroy the Dharma teacher protected by this mantra is...
This is because they have slandered and destroyed these sixty-two billion Buddhas.
If the sin of slandering even a single Buddha is already boundless, how much more so for slandering such a multitude of Buddhas? The gravity of that sin is profound and beyond description.
△ Fourth, the praise and narration.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha praised the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, saying: "Excellent, excellent!
Bhaiṣajyarāja, because you have compassionately protected this Dharma-preacher, you have spoken this dhāraṇī, which will bring great benefit to all sentient beings."
First, "Excellent!"—this praises his ability to protect the Dharma Master through mantras. Second, "Excellent!"—this praises his ability to bind and extol the mantras he has spoken.
[It is said that] if one harms the Dharma Master, it is as if one harms the Buddha; thus, it causes all beings to not dare to harm or destroy the Dharma Master.
Regarding the statement that this brings great benefit to all sentient beings: if the Dharma Master obtains this protection...
If one can uphold and propagate this wondrous sutra everywhere, then all sentient beings who hear it will be enabled to open,
reveal, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, thereby fully understanding the long-lasting life span realized by the Tathāgata.
Therefore, this mantra is spoken to protect the Dharma Master and enable sentient beings to obtain abundant benefit and profit.
△ Second, the section on "Courageous Bestowal" has three parts. First, the request for its exposition.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Vīradatta addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, I too shall proclaim a dhāraṇī for the protection of those who read, recite, receive, and uphold the Lotus Sūtra. If this Dharma-master obtains this dhāraṇī, then as for yakṣas..."
Whether they be rākṣasas, pūtanas, kiṃkaras, kumbhāṇḍas, or pretas, those who watch for and seek out their vulnerabilities will be unable to find an opportunity.
△ Second, the actual recitation.
Then, before the Buddha, he spoke the mantra, saying:
*Cule*, *mahācule*, *ucche*, *mucche*, *ale*, *arapace*, *nirhate*, *nirha*.
Lita bate, icini, vecini, jicini, neli cini, neli civate.
(Thirteen phrases) △ Third: Concluding Praise.
World-Honored One, this dhāraṇī mantra has been spoken by Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, all of whom likewise rejoice in it.
If anyone should injure or defame this Dharma-preacher, they would thereby have already injured and defamed these Buddhas.
"Also all rejoice" means that this mantra was spoken by all the Buddhas;
if this mantra protects the Dharma Master, then all those Buddhas who spoke it likewise rejoice. II. The Two Heavenly Kings.
Part One: Vaiśravaṇa. Part Two: Dhṛtarāṣṭra. Section One: The Initial Request to Preach.
At that time, Vaiśravaṇa, the World-Protecting Heavenly King, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, out of compassion for sentient beings and in order to protect this Dharma-preacher, I too shall recite this dhāraṇī.”
△ Second, the actual exposition.
That is to say, he spoke the mantra:
*A-li, na-li, śu-na-li, a-na-lu, na-li, ku-na-li* (six phrases).
△ Third, the praise of the merits.

By means of this divine mantra, the World-Honored One protects the Dharma-preacher; I, too, shall personally protect those who uphold this sutra, so that within a range of one hundred yojanas, there shall be no calamities or afflictions.
△ Second, Dhṛtarāṣṭra (The King Who Upholds the Nation). Part Three. First, the request for the teaching.
At that time, the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra was present in this assembly, surrounded with reverence by thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas of gandharvas.
He approached the place where the Buddha was, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I too, by means of the dhāraṇī..."
This is the *dhāraṇī* spell that protects those who uphold the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
△ Second, the actual recitation of the spell;
he then spoke the spell, saying:
Agane, game, kauri, gandhāri, cāṇḍāli, mātaṅgi, sarakṣi, vīraseni, atti. (Nine phrases.
△ Third: Concluding Praise.
World-Honored One, this is a dhāraṇī divine mantra spoken by forty-two billion Buddhas.
If anyone should harm or defame this Dharma-preacher, they would thereby harm and defame these Buddhas.
△ Three rākṣasīs, five [sections]. First, the listing of their names:
At that time, there were rākṣasī women and others; first was named Lambā, second was named Vilambā, and third was named Jambhī.
The fourth is named Flower Teeth; the fifth, Black Teeth; the sixth, Many Hairs; the seventh, Insatiable;
the eighth, Wearing Necklaces; the ninth, Gaurī; and the tenth, Seizer of the Vital Essence of All Sentient Beings. These are the ten rākṣasīs.
Together with the Mother of Ghosts (Hārītī), her son, and their retinue, they all went to where the Buddha was.
II. Requesting the Teaching:
In unison, they addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, we also wish to protect those who read, recite, accept, and uphold the Lotus Sutra."
...shall eliminate their misfortunes and afflictions. If there should be anyone who seeks out the faults of this Dharma Master, they shall find no opportunity to do so.
△ Third, the actual recitation of the mantra: Then, before the Buddha, he spoke the mantra, saying:
Itiri. Itimin. Itiri. Atiri. Itiri. Nirī. Nirī. Nirī. Nirī. Nirī. Lohi. Lohi. Lohi. Lohi. Tahi. Tahi. Tahi. Dohi. Tohi (nineteen phrases).
△ Fourth, the taking of the vow:
"May it fall upon my head rather than afflict the Dharma Master.
Whether they be yakṣas, rākṣasas, pretas, pūtanas, kumbhāṇḍas, piśācas, vetālas, kaṭapūtanas, umarukas, or..."
Bhramara, whether it be yakṣas or kumbhāṇḍas, or humans or kumbhāṇḍas;
whether it be fevers lasting one day, two days, three days, four days, or up to seven days; or chronic fevers;
whether in male form, female form, boy form, or girl form—even in dreams—do not cause them any distress. [This applies] even before the Buddha.
Then he spoke this verse:
"If anyone does not comply with my mantra and disturbs the one who preaches the Dharma, their head shall split into seven pieces, like the branches of an *ari* tree."
As is the crime of killing one's father or mother, as is the calamity of pressing oil with fraudulent measures, as is the sin of Devadatta for splitting the Saṃgha—
those who offend this Dharma Master shall incur such calamities as these.
When the rākṣasīs had spoken this verse, they addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, we too shall personally protect those who receive,
uphold, read, recite, and practice this sutra, causing them to attain peace and security, to be free from all decline and affliction, and to neutralize all poisons."
"Yakṣas and so forth" refers to those spirits capable of causing disturbance and chaos. Regarding the phrase "the sin is like that of killing one's parents":
worldly parents merely give birth to the physical body; thus, the sin of one who kills their parents is indeed grave.
However, if any sentient being should cause disturbance to a Dharma teacher, the sin is not merely like that [of killing parents].
It is merely the offense against one's biological parents. Now, when it is said "like" (如), this is merely citing the most serious cases in the world as examples. △ Five: Praising and Describing.
The Buddha addressed the rākṣasīs: "Excellent, excellent! Even if you were merely able to protect those who receive and uphold the name of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, their merit would be immeasurable;

how much more so if you protect them while they fully receive and uphold it, and make offerings to the scripture with flowers, incense, necklaces, powdered incense, ointment incense, burning incense, banners, canopies, music, and various lamps—such as lamps of ghee and lamps of oil."

O Gautama, you and your retinue should protect such Dharma-preachers who offer hundreds of thousands of kinds of offerings, such as oil lamps of various fragrant oils, oil lamps of sumana flowers, oil lamps of campaka flowers, oil lamps of vārṣika flowers, and oil lamps of utpala flowers.
"Excellent! Excellent! This praises his ability to recite mantras to protect the Dharma Master. "Excellent! Excellent!
This praises him not only for using mantras as protection, but also for being able to make vows as protection. "You all should provide such guardianship."
He further exhorted them with earnestness, thereby encouraging their progress because they were capable of protecting [the Dharma]. △ Third, the benefits gained upon hearing this chapter:
When this "Chapter on the Dhāraṇī" was being preached, sixty-eight thousand people attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The benefits gained from hearing this chapter are as can be seen in the text. The explanation of the "Chapter on Dhāraṇīs" is complete.
Regarding the "Chapter on the Past Deeds of King Suprabha" (Chapter Twenty-Seven) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*:
if one traces the origin of this chapter, it generally stems from the fact that [the king] had previously attained dhāraṇīs, which served as an external [condition].
If you protect [this teaching], you may then follow and study the Dharma of the Tathāgata and cause it to circulate wherever you go.
Once you can follow and study the Tathāgata’s Dharma and cause it to circulate everywhere, you should then possess a spiritual power like that of the deity Gadgadasvara.
By means of the Samādhi of Universally Manifesting Physical Forms, he propagated this sutra according to the capacities of various beings;
even within the inner palace of a king, he manifested in the form of a queen and preached this sutra, causing sentient beings with wrong views to turn toward right view.
Thus, the evidence for its universal circulation is clearly revealed; hence there is this "Chapter on the Past Deeds of King Wonderful Adornment. The name of the king was...

As for "Wondrous Adornment" (Miaozhuangyan): because even during his causal stage he had heard this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and practiced it accordingly, he was able to adorn himself with the adornments of the Tathāgata; thus, during his causal stage, he may be called "Wondrous Adornment.
If one discusses his state of fruition, he was able to become the Buddha Śālarāja; this is precisely based upon his causal practices.
In practicing, one prefigures the fruit of enlightenment; this may also be called "wondrous adornment. This adornment has no other source than concentration (samādhi) and wisdom (prajñā).
Entire concentration is wisdom, and entire wisdom is concentration. Although the names "concentration" and "wisdom" differ, their essence is one.
Therefore, it is named "Exquisite Adornment. The original account is as explained in the commentary (*yǔshū*) [and so forth]. △ The text of this chapter is divided into four sections.
First, the causal circumstances are set forth:
At that time, the Buddha addressed the great assembly: "In the distant past, beyond immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable eons..."
Incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Meghadundubhisvararājasaṃkusumitābhijña, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
His land was named Prabhasavyūha, and his eon was named Priyadarśana.
The Buddha’s name is Cloud-Thunder-Sound Constellation-King-Flower-Wisdom (Meghadundubhisvararāja-puṣpadhvaja-jñāna).

Because that Buddha was able to cultivate the causes for the pure flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment during his past causal stage and thereby attained mastery, upon reaching the stage of fruition, he was able to realize the subtle and wondrous threefold wisdom of the single mind.
Thus, he can manifest bodies like clouds and preach the Dharma like thunder; his perfect voice brings equal understanding to all.

He is sovereign; because he is able to manifest and preach according to what he has cultivated and realized, he is named Cloud-Thunder-Sound-Constellation-King-Flower-Wisdom (Meghadundubhisvararāja-puṣpadhvaja-jñāna).

As for the name of his land being "Radiance" (Prabhāsa), it is because that Buddha himself is already able to illuminate everything perfectly with the three wisdoms, and is further able to cause all sentient beings to likewise illuminate everything perfectly with the three wisdoms, thereby eliminating ignorance.
It can completely eliminate all darkness and ignorance; therefore, that land is named "Radiance.

As for the kalpa being named "Joyful Vision," it is because it enables all sentient beings to achieve the perfect illumination of the three types of wisdom and the perfect destruction of the three delusions, such that there are no sentient beings who do not rejoice; thus, the kalpa is named "Joyful Vision. △ Second, the actual explanation.
The fourth *pūrvayoga*. First, the account of his emergence:
Within that Buddha’s Dharma, there was a king named Wonderful Adornment (*Suśobhana*). The king’s consort was named Pure Virtue (*Viśuddhaguṇā*).
They had two sons: the first was named Pure Treasury (*Viśuddhagarbha*), and the second was named Pure Eye (*Viśuddhanetra*).
"Exquisite Adornment" (Miaozhuangyan) has a meaning as explained by its title. As for the lady named Jingde (Pure Virtue): "Fu" (夫) means to support;
it refers to one who is able to assist in proclaiming the transformation [of others] and rectifying the state.

Although she manifests in a female body, she is in fact able to shatter ignorance and realize the three virtues (*triguṇa*). She is not defiled by the five obstacles; being defiled yet pure, she is therefore named Pure Virtue.
As for these two sons: the first was named Jingzang (Pure Treasury) because he could destroy ignorance and give rise to all supreme dharmas of merit and wealth;

thus he was named Pure Treasury. The second was named Jingyan (Pure Eye) because he could destroy ignorance such that his physical eyes, born of his parents, possessed the functional power of the five eyes; thus he was named Pure Eye.
Thus we know that the Lady and her two sons are all called "Pure" (*viśuddha*) because, taken collectively, they are capable of destroying ignorance.

Individually, however, they are respectively named "Virtue," "Treasury," and "Eye" because they are capable of realizing the three virtues, generating the wealth of the Dharma, and possessing the function of the five eyes.
Nevertheless, the three virtues, the wealth of the Dharma, and the five eyes are fully possessed by all three persons.

Sufficient. However, each [name] cites only one [attribute] to manifest their virtuous names. △ Second, praising their virtues, in two parts. First, praising their cultivation of the bodhisattva path:
"These two sons possess great supernormal powers, merit, and wisdom; they have long cultivated the path practiced by bodhisattvas. So it is said.

That is to say, they clearly understand and thoroughly penetrate the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*),

the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*), the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*), the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*), as well as loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity,
up to and including the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*).
First, the two adornments are clarified. Because he possesses great supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), there is no merit or wisdom that he has not cultivated.
Second, from "Dānapāramitā" onwards, his six perfections are clarified. Regarding what is called the "Upāyapāramitā," this is not the upāya among the ten perfections;
whereas Prajñā above is ultimate wisdom (*jñāna*), the present upāya is provisional wisdom (*upāya*). Provisional and ultimate...
The two types of wisdom constitute the perfection of prajñā in general. From "the two, compassion and so forth" below, its four immeasurables are clarified;

from "even unto" below, its factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) are clarified. Regarding the phrase "clearly understood and thoroughly penetrated," it refers to these factors that assist the path.
To know each and every thing with complete clarity, without any doubt or obstruction, is called "clear understanding" (*prabhāsvara*).
To be thoroughly pervasive in each instance, without any hindrance, is called "penetrating mastery" (*prativedha*). △ Second, praising his attainment of various *samādhis*.
Furthermore, one attains the Bodhisattva’s Pure Samādhi.

Regarding the "purity" of the Bodhisattva: upon attaining this samādhi, one is able to completely shatter the three delusions within oneself, and can also cause others to completely shatter the three delusions.
Thus, in both self-cultivation and the transformation of others, one is able to destroy delusion; therefore, it is called the "Bodhisattva’s Purity."
The Sun and Constellations Samādhi.

Regarding "sun and constellations": the sun is able to illuminate the day, and the constellations are able to illuminate the night. Upon attaining this samādhi, one is naturally able to personally realize and witness both provisional and ultimate wisdom.
If one illuminates principle with ultimate wisdom, it is like the sun illuminating the day. If [one illuminates phenomena with provisional wisdom], it is like...

When expedient means and wisdom reflect upon the capacities of beings, it is like the constellations illuminating the night. Thus, when the profound principle reflects upon capacities, there is nothing that is not appropriately addressed;
all of this arises from this samādhi, and for this reason it is so named.
The Samādhi of Pure Light (*Vimalaprabhā*).
As for "Pure Light," it is so named because it can destroy all delusions and manifest all-encompassing wisdom.
The Samādhi of Pure Color (*Vimalavarṇa*).
Regarding "pure form" (*śuddharūpa*): it is able to shatter ignorance and realize that form is itself the *dharmadhātu*.
It can universally manifest form-bodies to respond to the capacities of beings throughout the ten *dharmadhātus*; therefore, it is called pure form.
The Samādhi of Pure Illumination (*vimalāloka*).
As for "pure illumination," it is able to spontaneously destroy ignorance and manifest the wondrous wisdom of the Middle Way.

By means of this wondrous wisdom, one perfectly illuminates all things and perfectly contemplates all things, such that there is nothing not clearly understood; therefore, it is named "Pure Illumination."
The Samādhi of Constant Adornment (*nitya-vyūha*).
Regarding "constant adornment": one is able to use concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) as adornments. Concentration is entirely wisdom, and wisdom is entirely concentration;
one constantly abides in both concentration and wisdom without dullness or distraction. Therefore, it is named the Samādhi of Constant Adornment.
The Samādhi of the Treasury of Great Majestic Virtue. Within this samādhi, one thoroughly penetrates all things.
As for "Great Majestic Virtue," there are no among the three delusions that are not completely eliminated, and there are no among the three virtues that are not fully realized;

therefore, it is named "Great Majestic Virtue. Furthermore, regarding all the natures and characteristics of the three thousand worlds, and the wondrous principles of the ten realms and the thousand suchnesses—there is none [that is not mastered].
Because it is not fully revealed, it is named the "Treasury of Great Majestic Virtue. △ Third, the ten sections on transforming through practice. First, that Buddha’s preaching of the sutra:
At that time, that Buddha, wishing to guide King Subhavyūha and out of compassion for sentient beings, preached this Dharma.
Regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the phrase "desiring to guide them" and so forth:
because in their past causal stage they had also heard and practiced this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, yet were turned by the five worldly desires, they fell into false views. That Buddha...
Because they wished to cause him to turn away from error and return to the right path, they said, "We wish to guide him. 2. Requesting Their Mother to Go and Listen.
At that time, the two sons, Viśuddhagarbha and Viśuddhanetra, went to their mother’s place. Joining their ten fingers and palms together, they said:
"We pray that you, Mother, will go to the presence of the Buddha Ghoṣeśvararājasumerugarbha. We, too, shall attend upon, draw near to, and make offerings to him."
He urged his parents to pay homage. Why was this? Because this Buddha was preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* amidst the assembly of all devas and humans;
it was fitting that they should listen to and receive it.
3. The Mother Urges the Father.
The mother said to her sons, "Your father believes in and accepts the teachings of non-Buddhists and is deeply attached to the Brahmanical dharma.
You should go and inform your father so that we may all go together."
△ The four sons gave rise to wrong views.
Viśuddhagarbha and Viśuddhanetra joined their ten fingers and palms together and said to their mother: "We are sons of the Dharma King, yet we have been born into this family of wrong views."
△ The five mothers caused [him] to manifest transformations.
The mothers said to their sons: "You should all take concern for your father and manifest spiritual transformations for him. If he should see them, his mind will surely become pure;
or else, listen to us as we go to the place where the Buddha is."
"One whose mind must be pure" refers to those who are intent upon the Brahmanical dharma; their minds are already impure.
Now, if one manifests supernatural transformations (ṛddhi-prātihārya) so that they may behold them, they will naturally give rise to a sense of wonder.
Thus, they can turn from the heterodox to the orthodox, and their minds will attain purity. 6. The son immediately manifested his supernormal powers.
Thereupon, out of filial devotion for their father, the two sons rose into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees.

They manifested various supernatural transformations, walking, standing, sitting, and lying down in mid-air; water issued from the upper part of their bodies while fire issued from the lower, and fire issued from the upper part of their bodies while water issued from the lower.
At times they manifested massive bodies that filled the void, and then again appeared small; from small, they again...
He manifested great powers: he vanished from mid-air and suddenly appeared upon the ground; he entered the earth as if it were water and walked upon water as if it were solid ground.
He displayed such various supernatural transformations that his father, the king, attained pure faith and understanding.
Regarding the phrase "various supernatural transformations," this refers to such acts as walking, standing, and sitting within empty space.

These various manifestations, in their entirety, do not exceed the eighteen transformations. The reason they can manifest in this way is that the natures of empty space, earth, water, fire, and wind are fundamentally all-pervasive;
therefore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* uniformly designates them as "Great. Due to the various [perceptions] of sentient beings...
Due to the discrimination of craving and attachment, they become obstructed and fail to achieve harmonious integration.
Now, Pure Treasury and Pure Eye have been able to shatter ignorance and realize that emptiness is the emptiness of nature; that earth is the earth of nature, and even wind is the wind of nature.
Among these five great elements, they are naturally able to divine and clarify them, penetrating and transforming them, such that all attain autonomy.
He is present without any obstruction; therefore, he can walk, stand, sit, and lie down within empty space, as well as emit water from his body and so forth.
△ Seventh, the father gives rise to faith and understanding, in three parts. First, he joins his palms toward his son.
At that time, the father saw that his sons possessed such supernatural powers; his heart was filled with great joy at this unprecedented occurrence.
Joining his palms toward his sons, he said: "Who is your teacher? Whose disciples are you?"
"Attaining what has never been attained before": Previously, he was devoted to the Brahmanical dharma;
those Brahmans, even if they possessed supernatural powers, could not exceed one or two kinds and were unable to manifest these eighteen kinds of transformations.
Now, having witnessed these eighteen kinds of inconceivable supernatural transformations, it is said that he has "attained what has never been attained before. 2. The Son’s Reply to His Father.
The two sons asked, "Great King, that Buddha Cloud-Resounding Voice, King of the Constellations and Flower-Wisdom,
is currently seated upon the Dharma throne beneath a bodhi tree made of the seven precious gems, extensively preaching the Lotus Sūtra amidst the assembly of devas and humans from all worlds."
"The Sūtra is our teacher; we are its disciples.
Regarding "The Sūtra is our teacher," this was the answer to the father's question, "Who is your teacher?

It means that the teacher is the Buddha Cloud-Thunder-Sound-Constellation-King-Flower-Wisdom (*Meghadundubhisvararāja-puṣpadhvaja-jñāna*). Regarding "We are its disciples," this was the answer to the question, "Whose disciples are you?"
Your question shows that you are a disciple of the Buddha Cloud-Thunder-Sound-Abiding-King-Flower-Wisdom.
△ Third, the father wishes to go together.
The father says to his son: "I now also wish to see your teacher; we may go together."
△ Eight Daughters Request Ordination. Part Two. First, the request to their mother; second, the mother’s permission for ordination. The first section has two parts. First, the direct request:
At that time, the two daughters descended from the sky and arrived at their mother’s side. Joining their palms, they said to their mother: "Our father, the King, has now [passed away]."
With faith and understanding, we are capable of generating the mind set on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. We have already performed our filial duty for our father;
we pray that our mother will grant us permission to leave the household life and practice the Way under that Buddha.

When it is said, "We have already performed the work of a Buddha for our father," this means that the reason we were born into the royal family was solely to perform the work of a Buddha for our father.
Now that our father has attained faith and understanding, and has turned from the heterodox toward the orthodox, we have indeed performed the work of a Buddha for him.
Since the work of a Buddha has been accomplished, there remains nothing further to be done. Therefore...
"We pray that you will grant us permission to leave the household life. △ Second, the recitation of verses:
At that time, the two sons, wishing to restate their intent, addressed their mother in verse.
"May our mother release us so that we may leave the household life and become śramaṇas. Buddhas are extremely difficult to encounter; we shall follow the Buddha in our training.
As rare as the udumbara flower, it is even more difficult to encounter a Buddha, and it is likewise difficult to escape from all perils. We pray that you will grant us permission to go forth."

Regarding the phrase "like the udumbara flower" and so forth: the udumbara flower is said to appear only once every three thousand years, serving merely as an auspicious omen for a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*).
Even when a Buddha appears in the world, there may still be one hundred and eighty kalpas that pass by empty, without a Buddha appearing.

Therefore, encountering a Buddha is even more difficult than the appearance of the udumbara flower. To be liberated from all calamities is likewise difficult; for these "calamities" refer to the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*).
Among these eight difficulties, there is the state of being before or after a Buddha’s appearance. Now that I have encountered a Buddha, I am thus freed from those difficulties.
Yet, if I do not follow the Buddha’s teachings, though freed, I am not yet truly free. For this reason, I pray that you will grant me your ear.
"Grant us permission to leave the household life so that we may follow and study under the Buddha. 2. The Mother’s Permission for Their Ordination:
The mother then said, "I grant you permission to leave the household life. Why is this? Because a Buddha is difficult to encounter."
△ Ninth, he vowed to go at that time to listen to the Dharma.

Thereupon, the two sons said to their parents: "Excellent, parents! We pray that you will go at this time to the place of the Buddha Cloud-Thunder-Sound King-of-Flowers-Wisdom, to attend upon him and make offerings. Why is this? Because a Buddha is difficult to encounter, like the udumbara flower."
"Like a one-eyed turtle encountering the hole in a floating log, we have, through the profound depth of our past merit, been born at a time when the Buddha-dharma exists.
Therefore, parents, you should grant us permission to leave the household life. Why is this so?"
"Buddhas are difficult to encounter, and such times are likewise rare to meet.

Since our noble mother has already granted permission for us two sons to leave the household life, we now pray that our parents will also go together at this same time to the presence of the Buddha Cloud-Thunder-Sound to attend upon him.
To say 'Excellent, O Parents'—the father was previously deeply attached [to worldly things]."
"According to the Dharma of the Brahmins, having now witnessed this miraculous manifestation, we are able to turn away from evil and return to the right path. We also wish to see our teacher;

he may truly be called a 'wonderful father. Our mother was able to enable us to manifest supernatural powers to convert our father and further permitted us to leave the household life to cultivate the Way;
she may truly be called a 'wonderful mother. This is the reason for our initial words."
The phrase "How rare it is for a Buddha to be encountered" clarifies the parents' intention when they went to the Buddha's dwelling.
Next, the question "For what reason? serves to further clarify the intention of seeking ordination, and also explains the mother's consent for his ordination.
△ Tenth, the accomplishment of the merit of transformation.
At that time, the eighty-four thousand women of King Susīma’s harem were all capable of receiving and upholding this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
The Bodhisattva Viśuddhanetra had long since attained mastery in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Samādhi*.

The Bodhisattva Viśuddhagarbha had, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, attained mastery in the *Samādhi of Departing from All Evil Destinies*. [He] desired to cause one...
Because all sentient beings were freed from the various evil realms, the king’s consort attained the Samādhi of the Gathering of All Buddhas and was able to know the secret treasury of all Buddhas.
In this manner, the two sons, through the power of skillful means, skillfully transformed their father, causing his mind to attain faith and understanding and to take delight in the Buddha-dharma.
Regarding the statement that the Bodhisattva Pure Eye has long since attained mastery in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*:

it is because he is able to see all phenomena (*dharmas*) perfectly as being entirely the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) and the entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Thus, whatever single phenomenon is raised, there is none that is not the dharma-realm;
whatever single mark is raised, there is none that is not the true mark. In this way, every phenomenon is true, and every mark is the true mark.
All are real, for they are able to thoroughly comprehend all phenomena without any obstruction.
Regarding the Bodhisattva Pure Treasury’s mastery of the Samādhi of Transcending All Evil Destinies (*durgati*): this term "evil destinies" does not refer exclusively to the three evil realms.

Rather, according to the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavahāra*), all stages prior to ascending to the [first] Ground (*bhūmi*) are termed evil destinies. Thus, Tiantai said: "In the Separate Teaching, prior to..."
Those who have regressed from the stages [of bodhisattvahood] are all called people of false views;

yet the Bodhisattva Viśuddhagarbha is able to realize that the biased and the deviant are all fundamentally the center and the right, because although he traverses the various evil destinies, they are in fact the perfectly integrated path of goodness.
As for the King’s consort, she has attained the Samādhi of the Gathering of All Buddhas, and thus possesses the secret treasury of the three virtues of all Buddhas.
Because one can personally accumulate and achieve this, it is called the "Samādhi of the Collection of All Buddhas. Now, Lady Jingde has attained this samādhi;
therefore, she is able to know the secret treasury of all Buddhas. This secret treasury is nothing other than the secret treasury of the three virtues (*triguṇa*).
It is called "secret" because only a Buddha can realize it; it is called [the treasury] because it is inherently possessed by sentient beings.
"Esoteric" (*mi*) means "treasury" (*garbha*), for it contains the three thousand worlds within itself. Regarding the phrase "skillfully transforming his father":

had he simply exhorted him to go to the Buddha’s presence to hear and receive the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the father-king might not have conceived faith and understanding, nor would he have listened to his words.
Now, by first manifesting supernatural transformations to inspire faith and understanding, the king desires to see [the Buddha] without even waiting for verbal exhortation.
Because you are their teacher, they are said to have been "well-transformed" by him. Those who take delight in the Buddha-dharma also wish to see the teacher of the two sons;
this refers precisely to the thought of taking delight in the Buddha-dharma. △ Fourth, receiving transformation, in six parts. First, seeing the Buddha and making offerings.
1. That Buddha’s bestowal of the prophecy; 2. Leaving home to practice the Way; 3. Praising the two sons; 4. That Buddha’s expression of praise; 5.
Praising the Buddha and establishing vows. Regarding the first five [sections], the first concerns approaching [the Buddha] and paying homage.
Thereupon, King Wonderful Adornment, together with his ministers and retinue; Lady Pure Virtue, together with her ladies-in-waiting and retinue;
and the king’s two sons, together with forty-two thousand people, all went at once to the place where the Buddha was.
Having arrived, they prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and withdrew to stand to one side.
△ Second, the Buddha preaches the Dharma for him.
At that time, the Buddha preached the Dharma for the king, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him. The king was filled with great joy.
△ Third, the actual presentation of offerings.
At that time, King Subhavyūha and his consort untied from their necks pearl necklaces worth hundreds of thousands and scattered them over the Buddha.
The scattering of these necklaces over the Buddha symbolizes that all causal practices shall result in the attainment of the merit of fruition; thus they untied their necks and so forth.
This signifies that the causal practice issues forth from the true mark (*dharmatā*) as the wondrous contemplation of the hundred realms and thousand suchnesses.
△ Fourth, the preliminary manifestation of the retribution:
within the void, there appeared a four-pillared jeweled terrace; upon this terrace was a great jeweled couch, spread with hundreds of thousands of myriads [of precious coverings].
Celestial garments. Upon them is a Buddha, seated in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka-bandha*), emitting great radiance.

Regarding the phrase "in the midst of the void," this symbolizes that through causal practice, one achieves the four virtues of permanence, bliss, self, and purity from the perspective of ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
As for the great precious throne within the platform, it symbolizes that the four virtues are unified as one.
This represents the subtle and wondrous Great Nirvana. All of these signify the essence of the Nirvana that the King shall realize in the future.
The spreading of hundreds of thousands of millions of celestial garments signifies the arising of function from the essence. The garments carry the meaning of covering;
they represent unconditional compassion that universally covers all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm. Upon them is the Buddha’s seated posture.
The one who sits emitting light signifies that he shall attain the fruit of Buddhahood; at the time of sitting at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), he illuminates all sentient beings.
△ Fifth, the reflection on rarity.

At that time, King Wonderful Adornment had this thought: "The Buddha’s body is rare and extraordinary; it is upright, majestic, and uniquely sublime, having perfected the foremost and most subtle of forms."
Regarding the statement that "the Buddha’s body is rare": this refers to the emanated Buddhas who emit light while seated upon celestial robes.
As for the praise of the Buddha in the subsequent text, that specifically praises the Buddha Cloud-Thunder-Sound-Constellation-King-Flower-Wisdom.
Regarding the phrase "the foremost, most subtle form," it is not something that can be attained by any sentient beings within the three vehicles or nine realms; therefore, it is so described.
First, as for its characteristics, they are boundless, uniquely distinguished, and most exalted; therefore, it is subtle and wondrous. Second, regarding the Buddha’s bestowal of the prediction:
at that time, the Buddha Cloud-Thunder-Sound-Constellation-King-Flower-Wisdom addressed the fourfold assembly, saying: "Do you see this Sublime Adornment?"

"O King, do you stand before me with palms joined? This king shall become a bhikṣu within my Dharma; through diligent cultivation and assistance in the dharmas that aid the path of the Buddha, he shall attain Buddhahood.
His name shall be Śālavṛkṣarāja (King of the Śāla Trees), his land shall be named Mahāprabha (Great Light), and the kalpa shall be named Mahocchrayarāja (Great High King).
That Buddha Śālavṛkṣarāja shall have an immeasurable assembly of bodhisattvas and an immeasurable number of śrāvakas."
That land is level and upright; such are its merits.
As for the phrase "dharmas that assist the Buddha-way," "assist" means to protect and support, as well as to aid in proclaiming [the Dharma].
Regarding the Buddha’s title "King of the Śāla Trees": in Sanskrit, *śāla* means "firm" or "solid. This is because at the time of his attaining Buddhahood, he was able to—
His unconditional great compassion universally covers all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm, just as the shade of the king of sturdy trees covers everything;
therefore, the Buddha is titled the King of Śāla Trees. This is because at the time of his attaining Buddhahood, he perfectly realized the three wisdoms.
The three truths are perfectly manifested, and the wisdom of those truths is fully revealed; since every detail is complete down to the finest hair, his land is named "Great Radiance" (Mahāprabha).

Because the wondrous principle he has realized is vast, expansive, lofty, and remote—transversely exhausting the entire Dharma-realm and vertically penetrating its very source—the eon is named "Great High King" (Mahocchrayarāja). △ Third, leaving home to practice the Way.
The king immediately entrusted the kingdom to his younger brother and, together with his consort, two sons, and all his retinue, went forth from home to practice the Way within the Buddha-dharma.
Having gone forth, for eighty-four thousand years he constantly applied himself with diligent vigor to practicing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
After this period had passed, he attained the Samādhi Adorned with All Pure Merits.
One who attains the Samādhi Adorned with All Pure Merits is able to use the concentration and wisdom of a Tathāgata as adornment;
this is called "merit" (gong). Furthermore, they cause all sentient beings to likewise use the concentration and wisdom of a Tathāgata as adornment, returning the transformative merit to themselves;
this is called "virtue" (de). Since one possesses both such adornments and virtues, then...
There is no delusion that is not destroyed; thus, the one is pure and all are pure, and all are pure and the one is pure.
Therefore, it is said that he has attained the Samādhi Adorned with All Pure Merits. △ Fourth, praising the two sons.
He immediately ascended into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, these two sons of mine have already performed the work of a Buddha.
Through their supernatural transformations, they have turned away my perverse mind and caused me to dwell securely within the Buddha-dharma.
Having been able to see the World-Honored One, these two sons are my true spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), for they desired to awaken my roots of goodness from past lives."
