"Because he has brought me great benefit, he has come to be born in my family.
First, he praised his ability to turn my current perverse mind through supernatural transformations;
next, he praised his ability to act as a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) by awakening my roots of goodness from past lives. This spiritual friend is, indeed, a 'teacher' spiritual friend. △
5. That Buddha’s Commendation.
At that time, the Buddha Cloud-Thunder-Sound-Constellation-King-Flower-Wisdom addressed King Subhavyūha, saying: "So it is, so it is;
it is just as you have said. If good sons or good daughters, by virtue of having planted roots of goodness, obtain excellent knowledge in every lifetime."

"Know this, Great King: a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) is able to perform the work of a Buddha, instructing, teaching, benefiting, and gladdening others, leading them to enter into Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Great King, you should know that a spiritual friend is a great causal condition;
it is they who transform and guide one so that one may see the Buddha and give rise to the mind set on Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Great King, do you see this?"

"Are these two sons not so? These two sons have already made offerings to, approached, and reverently served sixty-five hundred thousand million billion nayutas of buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.
In the presence of those buddhas, they upheld the Lotus Sutra and, out of compassion for sentient beings with wrong views, caused them to abide in right view."
The first [section] is thus; it describes how he was able to praise the two sons for their supernatural transformations that converted the heterodox. The second is thus;
it describes how he was able to praise the two sons as being spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). Next, from "Great King, you see" onwards, it describes what he did not yet know;
for he only knew that his two sons had today become spiritual friends, but he did not yet know [the full extent].
The two sons were already able to cultivate merit and wisdom; they were able to take pity on those with wrong views and cause them to attain right view.
That they had already made offerings to various Buddhas clarifies that they had already cultivated merit.

That they had received and upheld the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* from the various Buddhas clarifies that they had already cultivated wisdom. That they took pity on sentient beings with wrong views clarifies that they had already...

He is able to take pity upon all sentient beings of the three vehicles, the five teachings, and the seven kinds of expedient means who hold erroneous views, causing them to turn back toward the correct view of the ultimate, perfect, and true One Vehicle. △ Sixth, praising the Buddha and establishing vows.
King Subhavyūha immediately descended from the midst of the void and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the Tathāgata is most rare and marvelous.
By virtue of his merit and wisdom, the fleshly protuberance upon his crown radiates brilliant light; his eyes are long and wide, of a deep azure-blue;
the tuft of hair between his eyebrows is as white as a conch shell or the moon; his teeth are white, even, and closely set, constantly emitting radiance; and his lips..."

The color was a beautiful red, like that of the *bimba* fruit. At that time, King Subhavyūha, having praised the Buddha for such immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of merits, joined his palms with single-minded devotion before the Tathāgata and addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“World-Honored One, it is unprecedented! The Dharma of the Tathāgata is fully accomplished and inconceivable, subtle and wondrous.”
"Regarding merit, the practice of the teachings and precepts, and peaceful, blissful goodness:

from this day forward, I shall no longer act according to my own whims, nor shall I give rise to wrong views, arrogance, anger, or any other evil thoughts. Having spoken these words, he prostrated before the Buddha and departed.

"Regarding the statement 'no longer acting in accordance with one's own mind': this means that whereas in the past one has consistently acted according to one's own mind, becoming greedily attached to the five worldly desires (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*), from this day forward one no longer greedily clings to the objects of the five worldly desires;
therefore, it is said that one no longer acts in accordance with one's own mind. Regarding 'not giving rise to wrong views' (*mithyādṛṣṭi*): this means that..."
Regarding various wrong views, one previously discriminated between characteristics such as annihilationism and eternalism; now, one no longer clings to such views as annihilationism or eternalism.

Therefore, it is said that "wrong views do not arise. It is not only that one does not act according to one's own mind or give rise to wrong views, but one also does not give rise to various evil states of mind such as arrogance.
This concludes the second section, which clarifies the fundamental matter. △ Third, the conclusion.

Bringing together the ancient and the present, the Buddha addressed the great assembly: "What do you think? Was the King Subhavyūha anyone else? He is none other than the Bodhisattva Puṣpadatta here now.
And as for the Lady Viśuddhaguṇā, she is none other than the Bodhisattva Prabhāsa-vyūha-lakṣaṇa before me now. Out of compassion...

It was because of King Wonderful Adornment and his retinue that they were born there. Those two sons are none other than the present-day Bodhisattva Medicine King and the Bodhisattva Superior Medicine.
These Bodhisattvas, Medicine King and Superior Medicine, have accomplished such great merits as these;
having planted the roots of all virtues under immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas, they have brought them to fulfillment.
Regarding these inconceivable and virtuous merits: if there are those who know the names of these two bodhisattvas, all the worlds—including gods and humans—should likewise pay them homage.
The Bodhisattva Radiant Adornment (Prabhāsa-vyūha-lakṣaṇa) is none other than the Bodhisattva Wonderful Sound (Ghoṣadatta); there is no separate bodhisattva by that name.

Because he possesses the appearance of Wonderful Sound and is foremost among those who are upright and adorned, Śākyamuni Tathāgata previously shone his light upon his body as he came from the east; therefore, he is called "Radiant Adornment before the Buddha."
Regarding the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Simha": this refers to what occurred prior to the preceding section.

That chapter states, "Even within the royal harem, he transformed into a female body," which precisely clarifies this point. Next, from the section on Bhaiṣajyarāja onwards, there is a separate eulogy of the two sons.
△ Fourth, the benefits gained upon hearing the chapter.
When the Buddha spoke this chapter on "The Past Deeds of King Wonderful Adornment," eighty-four thousand people were distanced from dust and freed from defilement,
attaining the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena.
"Free from dust and defilement" does not merely refer to being distanced from the dust and defilements of conceptual discrimination, craving, and afflictions;

it extends even to being distanced from the dust and defilements of the darkness of ignorance. Regarding the "purity of the Dharma-eye," although this term is found within the Tripitaka of the Lesser Vehicle, here it refers to the first stage (*bhūmi*) of the Perfect Teaching, where one attains the purity of the Dharma-eye by partially shattering ignorance.
This is because the *Vaipulya* (Extensive) is employed to clarify the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* (Pure). The explanation of the "Chapter on the Past Deeds of King Subhavyūha" is complete.

Regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, Chapter Twenty-eight, "The Encouragement of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva," if one discusses the sequence of mutual generation for this single chapter, it all originates from the Tathāgata’s preaching of this entire *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

In the *Lotus Sūtra*, regarding the Trace Gate (*jimen*), there is the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, the fundamental intention for appearing in the world, and the causal conditions for the Great Matter.

Regarding the Source Gate (*benmen*), there is the long-lasting lifespan, that which was realized long ago, the wisdom of all Buddhas, and the benefit of sentient beings throughout the three periods of time. Such discourse as this is not [merely] existent.
One who is not a person of great wisdom cannot fully comprehend it; one who does not possess great practice cannot cultivate it.
Therefore, it begins with Mañjuśrī as the initiator and concludes with Samantabhadra as the inspirer.

This means that the beginning is accomplished through *jñāna* (knowledge) and the end is accomplished through *prajñā* (wisdom), whereby the purpose of this entire sutra may be fulfilled. Thus, there is...
This is the chapter titled "The Exhortation of Samantabhadra. Regarding the term "Samantabhadra": his conduct pervades the entire dharma-realm, hence it is called "Universal" (samanta);
he occupies the station of the ultimate sage, hence he is called "Worthy" (bhadra). As for his conduct pervading the dharma-realm:

it is because he is able to give rise to dharma-realm conduct, sever the delusions of the dharma-realm, and realize the virtues of the dharma-realm by following its principle. As for that which he follows...

That which arises, that which is abandoned, and that which is realized—not a single one of these is not the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). Therefore, it is said that their practice pervades the dharma-realm universally.
One who stands at the pinnacle of the sages is called a "Worthy One" (ārya); because they can manifest the principle part by part, their manifestation is now nearing its consummation.

It proceeds stage by stage; having proceeded, it is about to reach its ultimate limit. It severs afflictions stage by stage; having severed them, they are about to be perfected. It realizes virtues stage by stage;

having realized them, they are about to be fulfilled. In terms of its principle, it is about to be exhausted; in terms of its practice, it is about to reach its limit; in terms of its severance, it is about to be perfected.
Realization is about to be perfected; thus it is said that one whose stage approaches the ultimate sage is called "Worthy" (xian). As for a Bodhisattva:

being able to personally accord with the principle of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), initiate practices of the Dharma-realm, sever delusions of the Dharma-realm, and realize the virtues of the Dharma-realm constitutes self-benefit.

Furthermore, being able to cause all sentient beings likewise to accord with the principle of the Dharma-realm, initiate practices of the Dharma-realm, and sever delusions of the Dharma-realm constitutes the benefit of others.

The virtue of realizing the dharma-realm is that which benefits others. Because one is thus able to benefit oneself and further benefit the stages [of the bodhisattva path], one is called a *bodhisattva*.
Regarding the term "exhortation and arousal" (*kuan-fa*), there are two meanings: first, "exhortation" (*kuan*) refers to entreaty, while "arousal" (*fa*) refers to illumination.
It means entreating the Tathāgata to once again illuminate the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, as the text says: "I only pray that the World-Honored One will, for our sake..."
"Explain this, son of good family! How can sons and daughters of good family, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, obtain this sutra?
It is for their sake that the World-Honored One has taught these four dharmas. This is the exhortation to inspire and clarify.
Second, "exhortation" (quan) means to guide; "inspiration" (fa) means to stimulate. It refers to guiding sentient beings and providing them with profound encouragement.
"Arise! Practice this sutra as clarified within its text. I shall ward off external obstacles and instruct you in the internal Dharma;

I pray that you be protected by this mantra. This extends even to future causes and proximate fruits, all of which serve to exhort sentient beings and deeply stimulate them to practice this sutra. This is precisely the exhortation to inspire and advance them.

In summary, the four characters "Samantabhadra" (Puxian) and so forth refer to the person; the two characters "exhortation" (quanfa) refer to the Dharma. By presenting both the person and the Dharma together, the title of this chapter is established;
hence it is called the "Chapter on the Exhortation of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva. The text of this chapter is divided into four sections:
first, the narrative by the scribe regarding the ritual proceedings; second, the exhortation of Samantabhadra; third, the praise and description by the Tathāgata; and fourth, the assembly.

The benefits received are twofold: first, arriving together with the assembly; second, extending reverence upon arrival. These two points are further divided into two: first, [the arrival] with the Bodhisattvas.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, by means of his sovereign supernormal powers, majestic virtue, and renown, was accompanied by great Bodhisattvas.

Immeasurable and boundless, beyond calculation, they came from the eastern direction. All the lands they passed through trembled universally, as precious lotus flowers rained down and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of various kinds of musical instruments were played.
Regarding the terms "spiritual power," "majestic virtue," and "renown": "spirit" (*shen*) refers to the celestial mind, and "penetration" (*tong*) refers to the nature of wisdom.
This celestial mind and nature of wisdom are, from the beginning, identical for both ordinary beings and sages; they are equal in both sentient beings and Buddhas.
However, because sentient beings are obscured by the darkness of ignorance, they are unable to manifest this nature and do not attain mastery. Now, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva...
Being able to accord with the substance of the dharma-realm, one gives rise to the practice of the dharma-realm; thus, one spontaneously accomplishes the function of the dharma-realm.

Therefore, by spiritualizing and clarifying it, and by penetrating and transforming it, one attains the power of great supernatural penetrations (*abhijñā*). Yet, as for these supernatural penetrations:
It arises as the entire body, established in accordance with the nature (*dharmatā*), without depending on artificial construction and without requiring effortful alteration.
It is that which is spontaneously effortless and, in its very essence, unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); therefore, it is called "sovereign.

Having attained this sovereign power of great supernormal faculties (*abhijñā*), delusions are naturally not left unbroken and possess majesty; principles are not left unverified and possess [realization].
"Virtue" means that while there is inner majesty and power, there is also external renown.

Regarding the phrase "all the lands through which he passes are universally shaken," this is because when Samantabhadra comes from the east, desiring to circulate this sutra, he is naturally able to cause all sentient beings to shatter their ignorance;
thus, it is symbolized by the shaking of the earth. This brings about the realization of the True.
For this reason, the raining of flowers is used to symbolize it. When there is a great capacity [in sentient beings], he expounds the teaching for them without waiting for a question;
thus, the playing of music is used to symbolize it. The previous arrival of Gadgadasvara from the east was likewise intended for the circulation of this sutra.
Since the circulation of this sutra is the same [in both cases], the benefits it brings are also the same.
The same applies here; thus, the manifestation [of his form] is likewise identical. △ Second, as for the eight classes of beings:

He was further surrounded by a great assembly of countless devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others, each manifesting their majestic power and supernormal faculties.

As for "each manifesting the power of majestic virtue and supernormal abilities": since these eight classes of beings follow Samantabhadra together, they are each able to cultivate the conduct of Samantabhadra;
they will certainly attain the virtues of Samantabhadra together, and thus they are also each able to...
He manifested the power of his sovereign majesty and supernatural penetrations. △ Second, having arrived, he proffered his respects:
Having reached the Sahā world, at Vulture Peak Mountain, he bowed his head and face to Śākyamuni Buddha and circumambulated him seven times to the right.
△ Second, Samantabhadra’s Exhortation to Resolve, which has two parts: first, the exhortation to clarify the truth; second, the exhortation to spur one toward practice.
The first part has two sub-sections:
first, the Bodhisattva’s exhortation to resolve. He addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, in the land of the Buddha Ratnatejobhyudgatarāja, I have heard from afar of this Sahā world..."
World-Honored One, you have preached the Lotus Sūtra together with immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of bodhisattvas who have come to hear and receive it.
We pray that the World-Honored One will explain this for us: how can sons and daughters of good family, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, obtain this Lotus Sūtra?

As for the Buddha named Ratnatejobhyudgatarāja: because that Buddha is fully endowed with all the merit and the wealth of the Dharma pertaining to the supramundane, there is no delusion he has not shattered and no virtue he has not realized;
he transcends the three vehicles, the five teachings, the seven kinds of expedient means, and the sentient beings of the nine realms, and has attained great mastery among all dharmas. Therefore...
He was named King Supreme Jewel Power. Hearing from afar that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* was being preached was precisely his "hearing with the mind penetrating the ten directions.
Indeed, the ear-faculty and all sounds possessed by sentient beings are fundamentally pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm;
it is only because they are firmly shrouded by ignorance that their ear-faculties become obstructed, such that they hear only what is near.
That which is distant cannot be heard; all sounds are likewise obstructed. Here [the ear] is pervasive, but there it is not pervasive.
Now, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva is able to give rise to dharmadhātu-practice according to the principle of the dharmadhātu and can accomplish the function of the dharmadhātu;
thus, his faculty of hearing naturally and universally hears the entire dharmadhātu. As for the Tathāgata, however—
Having already attained the ultimate state, with wisdom perfected and severance complete, all his sounds—without even waiting for speech—are naturally able to pervade the entire Dharma-realm.
Therefore, although the Tathāgata speaks this sutra here, the bodhisattvas in that land are naturally able to hear what is being said from afar.
As for the words, "We pray only that the World-Honored One will explain it for us," since...

The previous statement that he "heard from afar" the preaching of the Lotus Sūtra refers to the fact that both the Tathāgata’s gates of the original and the manifested have already been fully expounded, and that Samantabhadra has likewise heard each and every part of them. That he now further says, "I only pray that you will preach it," is as follows:
What has been explained previously— whether provisional or ultimate, fundamental or derivative, teaching or practice, or whether concerning persons or principles—
was derived from the general to manifest the particular. Now, desiring that the Tathāgata gather these particulars to form a whole,
so that sentient beings of the final age may easily uphold and cultivate it, [the author] again exhorts the Tathāgata to...
In order to elucidate what has been explained above, the four dharmas that follow constitute the general synthesis formed by gathering the particulars of this entire treatise;
these four dharmas encompass the whole work. How can one obtain this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*?
This means that, though it may seem impossible, one is able to generate understanding based on the sūtra, and from that understanding, [realization] arises.
Practice. Because one attains realization through practice, it is asked: "How can one obtain this sutra?
△ Second, the Tathāgata’s response and instruction has three parts. First, the brief introduction.
The Buddha told Samantabhadra Bodhisattva: "If good sons or good daughters accomplish four dharmas, they shall obtain this Lotus Sutra after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata."
Regarding the statement that one shall obtain this sutra by accomplishing four dharmas: you asked how it is possible to obtain this sutra, and I now tell you this.
To obtain this sutra, there is no other method apart from these; if one can accomplish four dharmas, then one will be able to obtain this sutra.
For when these four dharmas are accomplished, the entire sutra is already present, and one may rely upon them.
Thus, one gives rise to understanding, initiates practice, and enters into realization. Therefore, one can accomplish the four dharmas only by necessarily obtaining this sutra.
△ Second, the explanation of its fulfillment:
first, being protected and remembered by all Buddhas.

Those who are protected and remembered by all Buddhas do so because of the principle and realm of the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) as they have clarified it, and the attainment of their long-lasting life-span—things which had never been spoken of for forty years prior.

This is that which is protected, sustained, and cherished by all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time throughout the worlds. Since they are thus protected and remembered by all Buddhas, then their...
The principle that explains this is subtle and wondrous, beyond the reach of thought; yet this principle is one.

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family can, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, accomplish even this first dharma and be protected and remembered by all Buddhas, then the person will be entirely identical with the principle. Therefore, they shall be able to obtain this sutra.
Second is "planting the roots of all virtues.

Regarding the planting of the roots of all virtues: that which is elucidated in this sutra—the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, the wisdom of all Buddhas—is the foundation of the myriad virtues and the root of all goodness.
Since it is the root of all virtues, it is precisely what is elucidated in the present sutra.

The practice of this is inconceivable, yet the practice itself is one. If a son or daughter of good family is able, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, to accomplish this second dharma and plant the roots of all virtues, then they will embody the person who practices;
thus, they shall be able to obtain this sutra.
Third is entering the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
As for "entering the stage of right determination," this refers to the stage of determination elucidated in this sutra;

it is the concentration of the true reality (*tathatā*) of the Mahayana, rather than the false concentration of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), nor the indeterminate state of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). Therefore, one is able to enter this...

Right Concentration. Yet, as for the person, they are one. If a son or daughter of good family is indeed able, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, to accomplish this third dharma and enter the stage of those fixed in right determination (*samyaktvaniyāma*), then the entire sutra is realized in that person.
Thus, they are able to attain this sutra.
Fourth is the arousal of the mind to rescue all sentient beings.

Regarding the arousal of the mind to rescue sentient beings: this sutra clarifies only the single great cause and condition (ekamahā-kṛtya-hetu-pratyaya), desiring to cause all sentient beings to fully attain the opening, revealing, awakening to, and entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. This is what is meant by "directly abandoning expedient means."
It is only that I speak of the unsurpassed path, yet the teaching is one and the same.
If good sons or good daughters, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, are able to accomplish this fourth dharma and give rise to the mind to save all sentient beings.
Thus, the complete person is itself the teaching; therefore, one is able to obtain this sutra. △ Third, the conclusion and exhortation:
"Good sons and good daughters, if you thus accomplish these four dharmas, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, you will certainly obtain this sutra."
These four dharmas encompass the entire sutra. If one can achieve them, then the principles for the practitioner will be perfectly complete without exception;

the provisional and the real, as well as the original and the manifested, will all be wondrous without exception. Therefore, one will certainly obtain this sutra. △ Second, exhortation and inspiration, in two parts:
first, specific clarification; second, general exhortation. The first [section] has four parts. First, warding off external difficulties.

At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, in the final five hundred years, during the age of turbidity and evil, I shall protect those who receive and uphold this sutra;
I shall eliminate their misfortunes and afflictions, causing them to attain peace and security."
May no one who seeks an opportunity to find an opening— whether it be Māra, or the sons of Māra,
or the daughters of Māra, or the subjects of Māra, or those possessed by Māra; or yakṣas, or rākṣasas, or kumbhāṇḍas, or piśācas,
or kaṭapūtanas, or pūtanas, or vetālas, or any other such beings who afflict people— be able to gain any advantage.

The phrase "in the final five hundred years," and so forth, refers to making vows and establishing aspirations to protect and propagate those who uphold this sutra, ensuring they attain peace and security.
Next, the mention of "Māras and others" identifies the devils and spirits capable of causing disturbance and confusion;
the former refers to the Māras who inflict such harm. The phrase "if one is possessed by a Māra" refers specifically to a practitioner of the path.
This is because one has been possessed by Māra. When, during the time of practice, one gives rise to a single thought of attachment to desire, Māra seizes the opportunity and possesses them.
Once possessed by Māra, they also seek to disturb and disrupt those who propagate the Dharma.
Yakṣas and the like are precisely the ghosts capable of causing such affliction. △ Second, the internal methods of the Teaching, in three parts: First, practicing while standing and reciting.
Whether this person is walking or standing, if they read and recite this sutra, at that time I shall mount the white elephant king with six tusks and,
together with a great assembly of bodhisattvas, go to their location, manifest my own form, provide offerings and protection, and comfort their mind.

Furthermore, for the sake of making offerings to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, there is the King of the Six-Tusked White Elephant. The elephant possesses the power of transport, symbolizing the practice of the Dharma-realm cultivated by Samantabhadra;
it is able to transport sentient beings forward toward the ocean of fruition. White is the source of all colors, and thus—
There is the practice of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), which is entirely guided by wondrous wisdom; thus it is symbolized by white.
The six tusks symbolize the practice of the Dharma-realm, which does not transcend the Six Perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).

In summary, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra is able, within the dharma-gates of the Six Perfections, to employ the single mind and the threefold wisdom to observe and illumine them perfectly, thereby integrating himself into their midst.

Thus, one accomplishes the inconceivable practices of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). One is able to spontaneously flow into the ocean of the fruit of wondrous enlightenment (*samyagbodhi*), bearing the burden of all sentient beings and attaining great mastery among all phenomena.
Therefore, one rides upon the white six-tusked elephant king as a symbolic manifestation. △ Second, if one sits in contemplation:
If this person sits and contemplates this sutra, at that time I shall again mount the king of white elephants and appear before that person.

If there is even a single word or a single verse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* that they have forgotten, I shall instruct them and recite it with them, causing them to once again master it thoroughly.
At that time, those who receive, uphold, read, and recite the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* will obtain a vision of me.
Their bodies were filled with great joy, and they became even more diligent in their practice.

Because they had seen me, they immediately attained samādhi and dhāraṇīs, namely the *Sūtra-dhāraṇī*, hundreds of thousands of millions of *Sūtra-dhāraṇīs*, and the *Dhāraṇī of Skillful Means in the Sound of the Dharma*. They attained such dhāraṇīs as these.
Previously, he merely engaged in recitation; now, he is able to practice according to the sutras through contemplation.
Regarding "with great joy and increased diligence": because he now beholds the body of the Bodhisattva, he experiences immense joy and consequently redoubles his diligence.
"He immediately attains samādhi and dhāraṇī": *samādhi* is meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and *dhāraṇī* is...
Dhāraṇī is wisdom. This is precisely wisdom within concentration and concentration within wisdom.
Although the names "concentration" and "wisdom" differ, their essence is one; therefore, at the very moment one attains samādhi, one also attains dhāraṇī.
The *vartanī-dhāraṇī* is the turning from the provisional into emptiness. The hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *vartanī-dhāraṇīs* are the turning from emptiness into the provisional.
The *dharmasvara-upāya-dhāraṇī* is the turning from both emptiness and the provisional into the Middle.
Regarding these three *dhāraṇīs*: if they were according to the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), then emptiness would come first, the provisional second, and the middle third;
they would proceed sequentially and remain distinct rather than being integrated. Now, however, this is the inconceivable perfect fusion (*yuanrong*), attained within a single mind.

Therefore, when revolving through emptiness, one emptiness is all things empty—there is nothing provisional or middle that is not empty. This continues even when revolving through the middle, where one [middle] is all... [all things].
Among all that is central, there is nothing that is not central—neither the provisional nor the empty. Therefore, it is said that he has attained samādhi and so forth.
△ Third, the three weeks of diligent practice, in two parts: first, manifesting the body and preaching the Dharma.
World-Honored One, if in a future age, during the final five hundred years, amidst a world of turbidity and evil, there should be bhikṣus,
bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who seek, uphold, read, recite, or transcribe this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, and desire to practice it,
they should for twenty-one days apply themselves with single-minded diligence. Once those twenty-one days are complete, I shall—
Riding upon a six-tusked white elephant and surrounded by immeasurable bodhisattvas,
he manifests before those beings with a body that all sentient beings delight to behold, preaching the Dharma for them, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them.
Regarding the phrase "thirty-seven days," this refers to fixing a specific period to attain realization.
That is, one determines that within thirty-seven days, realization shall be attained; hence the expression "thirty-seven days.

If, during these thirty-seven days, one is indeed able to give rise to practice based on understanding and thereby enter realization through that practice, then one achieves what was expected. If, however, one cannot enter realization, this is called...
This would result in missing the appointed time. △ Second, the recitation of the mantra for protection, in three parts. First, the request for its recitation:

"I shall also bestow this *dhāraṇī* mantra upon them. Because they obtain this *dhāraṇī*, no non-human beings (*amanuṣya*) will be able to cause them harm, nor will they be deluded or disturbed by women. I myself shall also constantly protect these people. Only...
"I pray that the World-Honored One will grant me leave to speak this dhāraṇī mantra.
△ Second, the actual recitation:
thereupon, before the Buddha, he spoke the mantra, saying:
Atandi. Dandapādi. Dandapati. Dandakośali. Dandasudali. Sudali. Sudaravati. Buddhavarsane. Sarvadhāraṇyāvartani. Sarvavaśāvartani. Susāvartani. Saṃghaparivartani.
Kṣaṇi. Saṃghanirghātani. Asaṃkhyeya. Saṃghavagati. Tiri asmi saṃghatulyā arade parāde. Sarvasaṃghati-samādhi-garandi. Sarvadharmasuparikṣite. Sarvasattvarūpa-kauśalya-ā...
Śāgadi. Sināpikiliditi. (Twenty phrases. △ Third, the concluding praise:
"World-Honored One, if there should be a bodhisattva who hears this dhāraṇī, one should know that it is the supernatural power of Samantabhadra."
Power. If this Lotus Sūtra circulates throughout Jambudvīpa and there are those who receive and uphold it, one should form this thought:
"All of this is due to the majestic spiritual power of Samantabhadra."
△ Third, showing the superior causes:

If there are those who uphold, read, recite, correctly contemplate, understand the meaning and intent, and practice according to the teaching, one should know that such persons are practicing the conduct of Samantabhadra;
they have deeply planted roots of goodness in the presence of immeasurable and boundless Buddhas, and for all Tathāgatas...
He came and stroked his head with his hand, saying:
"As for 'right mindfulness,' if one is biased toward emptiness, biased toward the provisional, or biased toward the Middle, then what is being recollected cannot be called right.
Now, taking the true reality (dharmatā) as the object of mindfulness, within a single thought-moment, it is both empty and provisional."
It is precisely central and free from partiality; therefore, it is called "right mindfulness. Regarding "practicing according to what has been taught":

one generates understanding based on what is taught in the sūtras, acts in accordance with that understanding, and realizes [the goal] through such practice; this is what is meant by "practicing according to what has been taught.
As for "being touched on the head by the hands of all Tathāgatas," it is because one is able to maintain right mindfulness as taught.
Through practice, one can spontaneously accomplish the supreme cause. If the supreme cause is accomplished, one shall surely attain the rank of Tathāgata;
therefore, all Buddhas stroke one’s head with their hands. △ Fourth, showing the proximate fruit, in two parts: first, showing the merit and retribution of copying [the sūtra];
second, showing the merit and retribution of upholding and reciting it. The first part has two sub-sections: first, the actual demonstration of copying.
If one merely copies it down, at the end of that person's life, they shall be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

At that time, eighty-four thousand celestial maidens will perform various musical performances and come to welcome them. That person will then wear a crown of the seven treasures and enjoy themselves with delight among the court ladies.
△ Second, a comparative illustration regarding upholding and reciting:
how much more so for those who receive, uphold, recite, and correctly contemplate it, who understand its meaning and intent, and who practice according to what is taught.
△ Second, showing the merit and retribution of upholding and reciting.

If there is anyone who upholds, recites, and understands the meaning and intent of this [sūtra], at the end of their life, a thousand Buddhas will extend their hands to them, ensuring they have no fear and do not fall into the evil realms.
They shall immediately go to the Tuṣita Heaven to the abode of Maitreya Bodhisattva.
Maitreya Bodhisattva possesses the thirty-two marks of a great being and is surrounded by a multitude of great bodhisattvas numbering in the hundreds of thousands of myriads.
Therein, one is born into the retinue of billions of celestial maidens. Such are the merits and benefits [of this sutra].

Regarding "the thousand Buddhas extending their hands": because this sutra is the fundamental intention for the appearance of all Buddhas in the world and the causal condition for the One Great Matter, it is taught identically by every Buddha. It is that which every Buddha extends his hand toward; therefore, if...
One who is able to receive and uphold [this teaching] will be taken by the hand by a thousand Buddhas.

Having been taken by the hand by a thousand Buddhas, one will naturally be free from the five fears, will not be born in the evil destinies, and will instead be born in the good realms. "Tuṣita" is a term in Sanskrit;
it means "Contentment" (Zīzhú) in this language, because one knows contentment regarding the objects of the five desires. Maitreya currently resides there.
Regarding the "Heaven": generally speaking, whenever a Tathāgata appears in the world, he invariably manifests the eight phases of attaining enlightenment (*aṣṭa-prakāra-abhisambodhi*).
The very first of these phases is his descent from Tuṣita Heaven into the royal palace.
Now, as Maitreya succeeds Śākyamuni, when he attains Buddhahood in the future, he too will surely again manifest these eight phases; therefore, he dwells in this heaven, within this celestial realm.
They transform and guide all beings. When the Bodhisattva descends to be born [in the human realm], they descend simultaneously;
some act as the Bodhisattva’s influence, some as his inspiration, and some as his primary audience (the *pratipakṣa*).
Therefore, they reside in advance in this heaven to transform and guide all. As for Maitreya possessing the thirty-two marks, it is because of his station...

Dwelling in Equal Enlightenment, they are not far from the Buddha; therefore, they also possess the thirty-two marks, though there is simply a distinction between clarity and obscurity, or superiority and inferiority.
The above concludes the specific indications. △ Second, the general exhortation has two parts. First, the actual summary exhortation.
Therefore, the wise person should with single-minded devotion either write it themselves or cause others to write it, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, maintain right mindfulness of it,
and practice according to its teaching.
△ Second, establishing a vow to protect the sutra:

"World-Honored One, by means of my supernormal powers, I shall now protect this sutra. After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, within Jambudvīpa, I shall cause it to be widely circulated so that it shall not be interrupted."
△ III. The Tathāgata’s Praise and Narration, in three parts: first, the general praise; second, the specific praise; third, the concluding summary. The first two [parts]: first, the praise.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha praised him, saying: "Excellent, excellent! Samantabhadra, you are able to protect and assist this..."
"Excellent!"—the first instance praises his ability to exhort and request the Tathāgata to reveal and re-expound this sutra. The subsequent "Excellent!
praises his ability to provide guidance and encouragement, leading sentient beings to advance in the cultivation of this sutra. △
Second, the description:
You have brought peace, happiness, and benefit to many sentient beings. You have already accomplished inconceivable merit and profound, great compassion.
Since long ago, you have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and are thus able to...
I make this vow of supernatural power to protect this sutra. By my supernatural power, I shall protect those who are able to receive and uphold the name of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.

To bring about the great peace, happiness, and benefit of sentient beings means to exhort the Tathāgata to re-expound the sublime Dharma so that the particular may be integrated into the whole, making it easy for sentient beings to practice, uphold, and master.

Furthermore, it means to guide and inspire sentient beings to apply themselves with profound diligence in the cultivation of this sutra; all of these are what is meant by bringing peace, happiness, and benefit to many sentient beings.

Regarding the phrase "profound and great compassion": it is called "profound compassion" because, vertically (*ūrdhvam*), it can bestow and extract the suffering and happiness of sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions;
it is called "great compassion" because, horizontally (*tiryak*), it can bestow and extract the suffering and happiness of sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
"I shall [employ] supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and so forth" refers to the aforementioned Samantabhadra...
It merely speaks of protecting and upholding those who receive and maintain this sutra; for since the person is the Dharma they uphold, and the Dharma is entirely the person.
Now, the Buddha says that protecting and upholding the name of Samantabhadra is called "the person upholding [it]," because the person is entirely the name.
△ Second, the specific praise has four parts: first, describing the internal Dharma; second, describing the manifestation of the superior cause.

Third, the description of the proximate fruits; fourth, the description of warding off external calamities. The first [section] also has three parts. First, the description of establishing the practice of recitation:
"Samantabhadra, if there are those who receive, uphold, read, recite, correctly contemplate, cultivate, and transcribe this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*..."
It should be known that such a person sees Śākyamuni Buddha.
As for seeing the Buddha Muni, it was stated above that he manifests himself to provide offerings and protection; such a person is indeed a bodhisattva.
Presently, because you possess a human body, when it is said that you "see Śākyamuni Buddha," this refers to seeing the body of a person who has attained the fruit;
it is not merely seeing your own causal human body. This is because the sutra is that which is taught, and Śākyamuni is the one who teaches it.
Therefore, if one can receive and uphold the sutra that was taught, one sees Śākyamuni, the Buddha who is the teacher. △
Second, the description of sitting in contemplation:
One who hears this sutra from the Buddha’s own mouth should be known as one who has made offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha;
one should be known as one whom the Buddha praises, saying, "Excellent!"
Regarding what was said above concerning those who have forgotten verses and gāthās, I shall instruct them;
now it is said that they hear this sutra directly from the Buddha’s own mouth, which means it is not merely being taught by you, O Bodhisattvas.

Regarding what was said above about seeing my body and feeling great joy, now it is said that they make offerings to Śākyamuni; this means they feel joy upon seeing the person who has realized the fruit, rather than [merely seeing me].
It is merely that you see me rejoicing because of others. Previously, it was said that one immediately attains samādhi and dhāraṇī;
now it is said that the Buddha praises one as "Excellent. This means that one is able to adorn oneself with the adornments of the Buddha;
therefore, the Buddha praises one as "Excellent," which implies that one has attained not only the concentration and wisdom derived from others, but more than that. △ Three.
Regarding the description of three weeks of diligent practice:
one should know that such a person will have their head stroked by the hand of Śākyamuni Buddha;
one should know that such a person will be covered by the robe of Śākyamuni Buddha.
Previously it was said that I shall mount a six-tusked white elephant and surround myself with bodhisattvas;

previously it was also said that my body, which is joyfully beheld, would appear before such a person and preach the Dharma for them. Now, however, it is said that Śākyamuni will personally stroke their head.
Because they are able to receive and uphold this sutra and cultivate this sutra, they shall before long enter [nirvāṇa].
Regarding the station of consecration: for this reason, the Tathāgata strokes their heads with his hand. Previously, they requested protection through mantras;

now, Śākyamuni is able to cover them with his robe. Because they are able to receive, uphold, and practice this sutra, they are able to attain the Tathāgata’s Great Samādhi of Tranquil Extinction (mahā-śānti-kṣānti); therefore, they are covered by the Tathāgata’s robe. △ Second.
To describe the superior causes:

such a person no longer craves worldly pleasures; they do not take pleasure in the scriptures or writings of non-Buddhists, nor do they delight in associating with such people or with those who are evil—whether they be butchers, or those who raise pigs, sheep, chickens, or dogs. Or...
Hunter, if one sells their own beauty, that person’s mind is upright and honest; they possess right mindfulness and the power of merit.
Such a person is not afflicted by the three poisons, nor are they troubled by jealousy, self-conceit, false pride, or overweening pride.
This person has few desires and is content, and is able to cultivate the conduct of Samantabhadra.
It is stated above that because one has deeply planted roots of goodness in the presence of the Buddhas, it is now described as follows:

"This person no longer craves worldly pleasures," and so on, up to "possessing the power of merit. That is to say, since one has been able to deeply plant roots of goodness, one naturally does not crave worldly pleasures and possesses the power of merit;
and since one does not crave worldly pleasures, one is able to deeply plant [roots of goodness].
This refers to the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*). Since it was stated above that the Buddhas stroke their heads with their hands, it is now described as follows:

such a person is not afflicted by the three poisons or various forms of pride (*māna*). Because they are not afflicted by the three poisons or various forms of pride, the Buddhas stroke their heads with their hands;
because the Buddhas stroke their heads with their hands, they are not afflicted by the three poisons or various forms of pride.
This is also a cause for vexation. Since it was stated above that one should know such a person practices the conduct of Samantabhadra, it is now described here:
such a person has few desires and is content, and is thus able to cultivate the conduct of Samantabhadra. △ Third, describing and showing the proximate fruit.
Samantabhadra, if after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, during the final five hundred years, there should be anyone who sees another receiving,
upholding, reading, or reciting the Lotus Sūtra, you should form this thought: "This person will, before long, proceed to the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa),
destroy the hosts of Māras, attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, turn the wheel of Dharma, beat the drum of Dharma, blow the conch of Dharma, and rain down the Dharma."
[It will rain. When seated amidst the great assembly of devas and humans upon the lion Dharma-seat, one should proceed to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and so forth;
all these matters should be understood as referring to the Perfect Buddha (*saṃbuddha*). As for what was stated above regarding "if one merely transcribes [the text],"...
Those who [merely] give rise to [faith] shall be born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; those who uphold [the sūtra] shall be born in Tuṣita.
Now, it is said that by upholding, reading, and reciting it, before long they shall all attain Buddhahood through the eight phases. Therefore, it says:

"If one sees someone who upholds, reads, and recites the Lotus Sūtra, one should form this thought," and so forth. To "destroy the hosts of Māras" is precisely to subdue Māra. Having subdued Māra, [one proceeds].
One immediately attains the Buddha-way; hence it is said that one "attains *sambodhi*.
Having attained *bodhi*, one must necessarily preach the Dharma, transferring what one has realized into the minds of others; hence it is said that one "turns the wheel of Dharma.

Having turned the wheel of Dharma, one is necessarily able to urge sentient beings forward and shatter their ignorance; hence it is said that one "beats the drum of Dharma. Having shattered ignorance, oneself...
One is able to transform the small into the great and transform the partial into the perfect; hence it is said that one "blows the Dharma conch.

Since one has transformed the partial and the small to return to the Perfect and Sudden, one can thereby nourish the Dharma-body and foster the life of wisdom; hence it is said that one "sheds the Dharma rain."
The celestial beings and others seated there were just like the present Buddha; he was preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* universally to eighty thousand humans and devas.
Therefore, from the time he arrived at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), all [events] should be interpreted according to the Perfect Buddha.
△ Four: Describing the Warding Off of External Difficulties. Part One: Explaining the retribution for upholding [the sutra] and for slighting or slandering it. Part Two: Explaining the praise.

This includes [the retribution for] even slight laughter. If one clarifies the retribution for upholding, reciting, and praising [this sutra], it will enable people to admire its merits and take joy in them, thereby upholding and disseminating this scripture.
If one clearly understands the retribution for disparaging and deriding others, one will naturally be terrified of the transgressions incurred thereby and refrain from such acts;
thus, all external difficulties will be warded off. This section consists of two parts.
First, the merit and reward of receiving and upholding [this scripture] are clarified:
If Samantabhadra, in a future age, receives, upholds, reads, and recites this sutra, that person shall no longer be greedily attached to clothing, bedding, food, drink, or articles of livelihood;
their vows shall not be in vain, and they shall also obtain these benefits in the present life.
Regarding "merit-retribution":
as for obtaining merit-retribution in the present life, the previous statement that one is born in the Trāyastriṃśa or Tuṣita heavens refers precisely to retribution obtained in the present life;
therefore, it is now stated that one also obtains merit-retribution in the present life—that is, within this very lifetime.
Within this, one is able to shatter ignorance and transcend to the ten stages; this is precisely because of upholding, receiving, reading, and reciting this sutra.
△ Second, clarifying the retribution for the sin of disparaging [the sutra].

If someone should speak words of contempt and disparagement, saying, "You are merely a madman; practicing such deeds in vain, you shall ultimately gain nothing," then as a karmic retribution for such a sin, that person shall be blind from lifetime to lifetime.
Regarding the phrase "slight and disparage," if one practices and upholds this sutra, one will naturally be able to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Because they cannot give rise to such faith, they disparage those who receive and uphold it, calling them mad and saying things such as, "You are merely a madman.

As for the phrase "they shall be blind life after life," if one receives and upholds this sutra, one will then be able to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; [therefore, those who disparage it] shall be blind in every generation.
He acts as the eyes for sentient beings of the nine realms. Those who disparage and revile one who upholds [this teaching] shall, consequently, be without eyes life after life.

△ Second, explaining the rewards for praising [the teaching] and so forth, as well as the retribution for turning it into ridicule; this has three parts. First, explaining the meritorious reward for praising [it].
If there are those who make offerings to and praise [this person], they shall obtain manifest retribution in this very life.
△ Second, explaining the retribution for exposing faults:
If one sees someone who upholds this sutra and exposes their faults and evils—whether real or unreal—this person, in the present...
In this world, one may contract leprosy, whether the accusation be true or false; yet this is not the fault or transgression of the upholder of the sutra.
Whether true or false, the upholder of the sutra is fundamentally without fault. It is that person who, through falsehood and fabrication, claims such a thing exists. Therefore, if...
Indeed, although what was said there was a fabrication, a person of wisdom who hears it will not believe that account.

Therefore, even if people do not believe it because it is not true, the one who fabricated the falsehood is nonetheless not without karmic retribution. Thus it is said: "In this present life... and so forth.
Regarding those who contract white leprosy: those who are able to receive and uphold this sutra shall instead be adorned with the adornments of the Tathāgata.
As for those who now manifest such faults, they will naturally incur the disease of white leprosy as their own adornment.
△ Third, the retribution for the sin of derisive laughter.
If one mocks them with derision, they shall, in every lifetime, have teeth that are sparse and missing; have ugly lips and a flat nose; have hands and feet that are twisted and contorted;
have eyes that roll to the corners; have a body that is foul-smelling and filthy; and suffer from malignant sores and pus, dropsy, shortness of breath, and various other grave and evil illnesses.
△ Third, the conclusion and summary.
Therefore, Samantabhadra, if you see one who receives and upholds this sutra, you should rise to welcome them from afar, treating them with the same reverence as you would the Buddha.
△ Section Four: The Benefits Accrued to the Fourfold Assembly, in two parts. First, the summary of the benefits accrued from hearing this chapter.

When this "Chapter on the Exhortation of Samantabhadra" was being preached, bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, immeasurable and boundless, attained hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *varta-dhāraṇīs*.
Bodhisattvas equal in number to the atoms within a trichiliocosm became fully endowed with [these qualities].

The Samantabhadra Path consists of hundreds of thousands of myriads of kotis of *svādhiṣṭhāna-dhāraṇī*. "Svādhiṣṭhāna" (revolving) means revolving from the provisional into the empty, revolving from the empty into the provisional, and revolving from both the empty and the provisional into the middle;
it is the *dhāraṇī* that encompasses the perfect fusion of the three truths. Of these *dhāraṇīs*, there are one hundred thousand myriads of kotis.
...up to as many as hundreds of billions. △ Second, the conclusion on the benefits of hearing the entire sutra:

When the Buddha spoke this sutra, the great assembly—including Samantabhadra and all the other bodhisattvas, Śāriputra and all the other śrāvakas, as well as devas, nāgas, humans, non-humans, and others—were all filled with great joy; they received and upheld the Buddha’s words and paid homage.
And they departed.

As for "all were filled with great joy": having heard the Trace Gate (Jikimon), the Buddha’s knowledge and vision opened of themselves, and the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena became clear of itself.
Furthermore, having heard the Origin Gate (Honmon), his long and distant lifespan became accessible, and the benefiting of sentient beings throughout the three periods of time became possible.

Therefore, he rejoices. Regarding those who receive and uphold the Buddha’s words: they should receive and uphold the correct teachings of both the provisional and fundamental gates as objects for cultivation and realization;
furthermore, they should receive and uphold the dissemination of both the provisional and fundamental gates as objects for exposition and proclamation.
As for "bowing and departing": having attained joy and having attained the capacity to receive and uphold [the teaching], one should further feel gratitude for the Buddha’s benevolence.
And they paid homage.
*The Explication of the Lotus Sutra*, Fascicle Seven, Part Two (End).
